then, in the evening, he went to see the buddha and said: "venerable sir, when i went to jantu village for alms today, i saw such a place, and it occurred to me that this is indeed sufficient for a clansman to arouse energy for nibbana. it is a good, delightful place. if the blessed one permits me, i would like to go there to meditate." then the buddha replied: "meghiya, i am currently alone. wait a little until another monk arrives." but venerable meghiya did not comply. once more he said to the blessed one: "venerable sir, for the blessed one there is nothing further to be done; everything is completed. there is nothing more to add to the state you have achieved. but for me, there is still much work ahead. to attain nibbana, i must add more to what i have done; there is much to be done by way of meditation. therefore, if the blessed one allows me, i shall go." for the second time, the blessed one said: "meghiya, i am alone at this moment. wait until another monk arrives." even then, he did not obey. a third time he pleaded, saying that there was nothing further for the blessed one to do, but that he himself had work to do. therefore, if the blessed one would allow him—and here the word *padhana* is used, *padhana* meaning intense striving—"if you allow me to apply *padhana*-exertion for meditation, i shall go there." at that moment, the buddha neutrally remarked: "well, meghiya, when you speak of applying *padhana*-exertion, what can we say? go, then, and do as you wish." thus, the buddha gave permission with a neutral attitude (*majjhatta*).
so, venerable meghiya, with great expectations and determination, set out for that mango grove. having arrived, he prepared a seat in a good spot under a fine mango tree and sat down to meditate. but no sooner had he sat down for meditation than streams of thought (*vitakka*) began flowing into his mind. unwholesome thoughts—thoughts of sensual desire (*kama-vitakka*), thoughts of ill-will (*byapada-vitakka*), and thoughts of cruelty (*vihimsa-vitakka*). you all know that these are the opposites of right intention (*samma-sankappa*) in the noble eightfold path—namely, wrong intentions (*miccha-sankappa*): thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of cruelty. these came flooding into his mind. he tried to meditate the entire evening, but he could not concentrate or unify his mind. thereupon, a great sense of spiritual urgency (*samvega*) arose in him: "alas! i ordained out of genuine faith. is it not truly astonishing that thoughts like these should flood my mind in this manner?" then, in the evening, he went back to the buddha and declared: "venerable sir, i went and sat down for meditation. but from the moment i sat down, grand thoughts, thoughts of ill-will, thoughts of cruelty, and thoughts of sensual desire have been flooding my mind." at that moment, the buddha delivered a profound and valuable discourse: "meghiya, if one's concentration (*samadhi*) is not strong, not mature, there are five qualities, five factors, that help to bring that concentration to maturity. what are these five factors?"
what is the first factor? it is when a monk has a good noble friend, when he possesses the blessing of a noble friend. that is the first factor: the presence of a noble friend. what is the second factor? it is when a monk is fully accomplished in the moral virtue (*sila*) appropriate to him. that is, he guards the disciplinary rules (*vinaya*), seeing danger in the slightest faults, strictly observing the precepts, training himself in accordance with them, and fulfilling moral virtue. this refers to being virtuous. what is the third factor? it is when a monk has the opportunity to hear dhamma discussions concerning the "ten talk-topics" (*dasa-kathavatthu*) which aid in, and inspire thoughts directed toward, nibbana. what are the ten talk-topics mentioned in the dhamma? here, too, the buddha lists them one by one: talk on wanting-little (*appiccha-katha*), talk on contentment (*santutthi-katha*), talk on seclusion (*paviveka-katha*), talk on aloofness from society (*asamsagga-katha*), talk on arousing energy (*viriyarambha-katha*), talk on moral virtue (*sila-katha*), talk on concentration (*samadhi-katha*), talk on wisdom (*panna-katha*), talk on liberation (*vimutti-katha*), and talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimutti-nanadassana-katha*). these are the ten talk-topics. if we understand them briefly: talk on wanting-little (*appiccha-katha*) means talks concerning the reduction of desires. pious devotees, "talks" here refer to matters heard during a dhamma sermon or perhaps a dhamma discussion. the monk gets the opportunity to hear a dhamma discussion or sermon where his noble friends explain the benefits of having few desires—talk on wanting-little. next, talk on contentment (*santutthi-katha*) means talks about being satisfied with what one receives. talk on seclusion (*paviveka-katha*) refers to talks regarding living in deep physical and mental solitude and its value—its benefits. then, talk on aloofness (*asamsagga-katha*) means separating oneself from groups, from the herd. you know that whether we look at wild buffaloes or other animals, they have a habit of moving in herds. generally, human beings also have a habit of living in herds. living without the herd, without a crowd, is a great torment for many. that is why we have talk on aloofness—the value of living while guarding one's mind from the herd and the currents that come with it. that is, the benefits of living without entanglement with crowds: talk on aloofness. then, talk on arousing energy (*viriyarambha-katha*) is about initiating effort—the talk on the benefits of exerting and initiating energy to burn away defilements, to draw near wholesome states, and to remove unwholesome states. the subsequent terms are self-explanatory. talk on moral virtue (*sila-katha*) means talks on morality. talk on concentration (*samadhi-katha*) means talks on concentration. talk on wisdom (*panna-katha*) is on wisdom. talk on liberation (*vimutti-katha*) is about nibbana. talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimutti-nanadassana-katha*) is about the insights pertaining to nibbana. thus, having the opportunity to hear matters regarding these ten talk-topics is a highly valuable gain for a monk—to prepare his mind. then he says: utilizing these, what is the fourth factor? it is when a monk, with intense, unrelenting, and active energy, applies himself to the task of abandoning unwholesome thoughts and acquiring wholesome qualities. this is called aroused energy (*arabdha-viriya*). that is the fourth factor. what is the fifth factor? it is when a monk is endowed with a penetrating wisdom that constantly sees rise and fall—which is called *udayabbaya*—giving him a deep understanding of the impermanent (*anicca*) nature of the world. he becomes one who possesses a penetrating wisdom that constantly perceives arising and passing away.
thus, these five factors are extremely helpful for a person to prepare their mind before embarking on meditation. what are these five factors? briefly stated, a monk—and though we say "monk," you may understand this to apply to any meditating practitioner (*yogavacara*)—has a noble friend. you should know that "friend" here is not used in the common social sense. in the dispensation (*sasana*), a noble friend (*kalyana-mitta*) is not someone who merely puts an arm around your shoulder. a social friend or companion is someone with whom one associates in good or bad times. that is not what "noble friend" refers to here. that is not why the word was used. when the buddha speaks of a noble friend (*kalyana-mitta*), we can understand how profound a term this "friend" actually is. he is a teacher whom one must revere, worship, and from whom one must seek advice. therefore, the first factor mentioned here is association with a teacher. the second factor is being virtuous in the moral virtue (*sila*) appropriate to oneself. the third factor is the ten talk-topics in the manner described. just as this was said regarding the monks, you too should have the opportunity to listen to dhamma discussions, talks, and sermons concerning nibbana, and relevant to nibbana, to assist in your meditation. then, the fourth factor is to apply effort—intense and unrelenting effort—in accordance with that. the fifth factor is one's power of wisdom—applying well-established mindfulness and wisdom to engage in that work. these five factors are foundational and primary for anyone embarking on the quest for nibbana with a deep purpose.
having explained this, the buddha then declared: "meghiya, one who has brought his concentration to maturity by relying on these five qualities, these five factors, must next develop four meditations." what are they? he lists them as follows: one must develop the meditation on foulness (*asubha*) to abandon lust (*raga*). you know that the meditation on foulness is practiced to free the mind from lust—which is a grave defilement carried throughout this long samsaric journey. similarly, one must develop loving-kindness (*metta*) to eliminate ill-will (*byapada*), which is hatred or anger. you see, then, that through these two, the buddha prescribed the medicine for both attachment and aversion. thirdly, he lists—as the third meditation—mindfulness of breathing (*anapanasati*). one must develop mindfulness of breathing, which is establishing mindfulness on the in-breaths and out-breaths. what is its function, its primary purpose? it is the cutting off of thoughts (*vitakkupaccheda*)—the severing of conceptual thoughts. directing the mind to one's breathing helps to cut off thoughts. generally, when thoughts are flooding in, one does not even remember that one is breathing. yet, when one, with effort, focuses the mind on this subtle process, no room is left for thoughts. that is why it was stated that mindfulness of breathing is especially helpful in cutting off thoughts. and what is the fourth meditation? the buddha instructed to develop the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*). frequently maintain the perception of impermanence. this helps to eradicate the conceit "i am" (*asmimana*). underlying what the ordinary world calls pride, conceit, or arrogance, lies a very subtle aspect of conceit called the conceit of "existence" or "i am"—the conceit *asmi*. the perception of impermanence helps to eradicate this very conceit.
in this manner, the buddha taught four meditations. having declared this, he then showed venerable meghiya their profound connection and the reason for presenting them in this way. although the perception of impermanence was given as the final meditation, he showed that one can proceed directly to nibbana through this very perception of impermanence: "meghiya, in one who perceives impermanence, the perception of not-self (*anatta-sanna*) becomes established. one who perceives not-self eradicates the conceit 'i am'—the subtle conceit of 'existence'—and, in this very life, here and now, attains that nibbana which puts an end to samsaric suffering, reaching the noble state of nibbana." thus he declared. having declared this, he also uttered two verses of solemn utterance (*udana*), expressions of joy, on that occasion. these are not the verses we took as our theme earlier, but are in addition to them. there, the buddha spoke two verses demonstrating the pressure one experiences from thoughts, and his own freedom from them:
*khudda vitakka sukhuma vitakka*
*anuggata manaso uppilava,*
*ete avidva manaso vitakke*
*hurahuram dhavati bhantacitto.*
this means: trifling thoughts, subtle thoughts—*khudda vitakka, sukhuma vitakka, anuggata manaso uppilava*—thoughts that cause the mind to float or drift, arising from within the mind itself. an ignorant person (*aviddu*), not understanding these thoughts of the mind, becomes bewildered, confused, and dazed—just as it happened to venerable meghiya—and lets these thoughts run hither and thither within the mind. it is as if one is running here and there. you know that even if the physical body does not run around, when these thoughts arise in the mind, it is as though one is running hither and thither. a person with a distracted mind is like an ordinary animal that runs about in response to every passing thought. describing how a person who cannot control their thoughts falls into such a state of restlessness, he then states in the next verse:
*ete ca vidva manaso vitakke*
*atapiyo samvarati satima*
*anugate manaso uppilave*
*asesamete pajahasi buddho*
thereupon, he spoke concerning himself. understanding this class or collection of thoughts—*ete ca vidva manaso vitakke, atapiyo samvarati satima*—what does the buddha, or a wise person, do? being *atapi*, which means possessing defilement-burning energy, and being mindful (*satima*), he restrains these thoughts. he tames them. the solemn utterance expressed here is that an awakened one is entirely free from all such thoughts that arise in the mind.
what was the mistake made by venerable meghiya? we can understand that he went for a good purpose—for intense striving (*padhana-viriya*). that is why the buddha finally said, "well, if you say so, what can we say? go then." but he went before the right time had arrived. he was too hasty. this is what we must understand. meditation is a noble aspiration, but venerable meghiya was overly hasty. furthermore, he committed a serious error: disobeying the words of the buddha. he made that request a third time. this is a serious action, akin to the offense of disparaging the noble ones (*ariyupavada*). the consequence of this action alone is sufficient to agitate the mind. it is that serious. having come as an attendant, he forgot his duties, ignored his duties toward the buddha, disregarded his advice, and went off to meditate in that manner. it was a grand idea, but he was not prepared for the task. his mind was not yet ready. even when it comes to driving a vehicle, if one gets a new car but does not know how to drive, one must display the letter "l" and drive for some time with an experienced person seated beside them. similarly, this venerable monk was someone who should have taken instructions from the buddha and proceeded only when the time was right. yet he was hasty, driven by pride and conceit. that is why he went so far as to say, "for the buddha, the work is done, but for me it is not yet so." in response to that, the buddha delivered those verses we took as our theme, which reveal the nature of the mind:
*phandanam capalam cittam*
*durakkham dunnivarayam*
*ujum karoti medhavi*
*usukaro’va tejanam.*
this is taught with an excellent simile. you know that in these dhammapada verses—this being a verse from the citta vagga—the buddha employs extraordinary similes. here he describes the nature of the mind: *phandanam capalam cittam durakkham dunnivarayam*. this mind—*phandanam* means flickering or trembling. this is explained as the trembling nature of the mind in the ordinary samsaric being when confronted with objects such as forms and sounds. the mind trembles—*phandanam*—and *capalam*, it is fickle. now, venerable meghiya went with the intention of realizing nibbana. yet, the mind is fickle; in the end, he was overcome even by thoughts of sensual desire. such is the nature of the mind. there is nothing strange about it; this is a state to be expected. because a mind that has run on the circular track of samsara for so long cannot be pulled out of it all at once. the samsaric momentum is still active. to counter this, a substantial inner momentum must arise. it is for this purpose that the five factors mentioned earlier, such as association with a teacher, are helpful. so—*phandanam capalam*—this mind is fickle. you all know what "fickle" means; it needs no further explanation. but here, "fickle" does not merely mean being untrustworthy in speech. we often apply "fickle" to words, but here "fickle" means that instead of doing what it set out to do, the mind does something else entirely. that is why it is said: *phandanam capalam cittam*. *durakkham* means difficult to guard. the simile given for this is like the difficulty of guarding a ripe paddy field from cattle. similarly, it is difficult to guard the object of meditation, to maintain the mind on the object of meditation—*durakkham*. simply put, this mind is difficult to guard. likewise, *dunnivarayam* means it is difficult to restrain the mind from wandering toward unwholesome objects. it is difficult to protect the mind. when it attempts to break free and crash through (one's restraint), preventing it is no easy task. such is the condition of the mind. declaring the truth as it really is is the characteristic feature of a dhamma sermon by the buddha. so, these weaknesses of the mind are to be expected. *ujum karoti medhavi*—yet, what does the wise one (*medhavi*) do? he straightens his crooked, warped, and fickle mind. how? here the simile is given: *usukaro'va tejanam*—just as a fletcher (arrow-maker) straightens his arrow. straightening an arrow: let us say one brings from the forest a piece of wood with a good core, heats it over a fire, and if it is bent, straightens it using wedges or similar methods. then, by applying oil, tempering it, and sharpening it well, an arrow is made. once the arrow is fashioned, it is so strong and performs such a great task that a skilled archer can split a horsehair by the flash of lightning. devotees, you have heard this simile: "to shoot a horsehair from afar in the dark, if the flash of lightning is missed, the shot fails." thus it is said. realizing nibbana is a similar feat. what is referred to here is developing the power of wisdom to realize nibbana. all of this is done through the mind, is it not? just as a fletcher, through systematic effort, tempers, straightens, and sharpens an arrow, the wise person straightens his mind—even a mind with such weaknesses. thus it was declared. similarly, he next presents another simile:
*varijo’va thale khitto*
*okamokata ubbhato*
*pariphandatidam cittam*
*maradheyyam pahatave.*
here too, a simile is given. the home of the fish is water. just as a fish pulled out from its watery home and cast upon dry land struggles this way and that, when one attempts to escape from the familiar kingdom of mara, this mind thrashes about like "a fish pulled from the water." through these two verses, the buddha revealed the true state of the mind.
thus, this is a highly valuable discourse (*sutta-desana*) for us in several ways. we can supplement our understanding by reflecting on the background story. here we have presented the general meaning of the verses. even when we reflect on the story, as mentioned before, a meditator's—a practitioner's—intention to realize nibbana is good. that desire is noble. however, the mind must be prepared in a suitable manner. for this, desire (*chanda*) is required—an intense desire is needed. first and foremost, the primary requirement is guidance from a teacher. that is why association with a noble friend is essential. next is the intense desire, the strong yearning called *chanda*. a person must truly possess a powerful yearning. now, venerable meghiya thought that simply because he ordained with the intention of realizing nibbana, or with great faith, these defilements would not flood his mind. thinking thus, he was thrown into dismay (*samvega*). but this is a natural law (*dhammata*). let us reflect on this using the analogy of a vehicle. when a vehicle is parked in a garage, it does not meet with accidents. a vehicle in a garage never experiences anything called a road accident. it is only when it is taken onto the road that it must face hazards. similarly, as long as a practitioner is merely thinking, "i must meditate," there is no danger. it is on the day he actually plunges into it and enters seclusion that the pressures of mara arrive. that is the reality. it is something to be expected. the buddha advises us to go prepared for this. as described, there must be association with a teacher. one must respectfully follow those instructions. then, there must be intense desire. next, one must be accomplished in moral virtue. if one is not virtuous, remorse arises. when one sits down to meditate, thoughts of remorse flood in: "alas, i have done such and such things!"
you all know that anyone who meditates, who attempts to concentrate the mind, must be aware of the five hindrances (*nivarana*) that obstruct concentration—whether conceptually or practically. these are *kamacchanda*, *byapada*, *thina-middha*, *uddhacca-kukkucca*, and *vicikiccha*. in english, these correspond to sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and worry—restlessness being agitated thoughts about the future, and worry being remorse over past actions and words (these two are grouped together)—and finally, doubt or indecision: "will this work or not?" it is by freeing the mind from these factors that one makes the mind tranquil. concentration (*samadhi*) means tranquility.
the aforementioned factors help to eliminate these hindrances. especially, if one's moral virtue is impure, worry and remorse (*kukkucca*) will arise in the manner described. thoughts regarding one's past will come flooding in: "i have done such and such things." therefore, one must be endowed with moral virtue. furthermore, by hearing the ten talk-topics, one gains some understanding of nibbana and the path, and one must also train oneself accordingly, gaining an understanding of the virtues to be practiced, such as wanting-little and contentment. next, aroused energy (*arabdha-viriya*) means one must proceed with a firm, unwavering determination. furthermore, one must be a person of wisdom—an intelligent, wise individual. such are the requirements. ignoring these matters, and especially disregarding one's duties to the buddha as he did, one cannot succeed in meditation. when one turns one's back on the teacher's advice, no progress can be expected.
thus, we can draw many valuable lessons from that story. let us now consider the other matters—specifically, the four meditations mentioned. if we reflect on them, we can see that the sequence in which the buddha presents these four meditations is systematic. often—in fact, always—the best way to verify whether a discourse is indeed the buddha's is to see how logically these factors fit together. they align in an extraordinary manner: the first leading to the second, the second to the third, the third to the fourth, and the fourth to the fifth, and so on.
here, even when prescribing the meditations, he introduces the first one to counter the strongest samsaric habit within a being—as you all know, this strongest habit is lust (*raga*), attachment. whether subtle, gross, or intense, attachment is the very nature of samsara; in another sense, craving (*tanha*) is nothing but this. therefore, the remedy for it is the meditation on foulness (*asubha*). particularly, this attachment arises due to the attachment one has toward one's own body. developing the meditation on foulness lies in realizing the foul nature of the body. whichever meditation object (*kammatthana*) is used—whether one of the thirty-two impure parts of the body such as hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, and teeth, or a corpse in a state of bloatedness (*uddhumathaka*)—frequently contemplating the foulness of this body is called the perception of foulness (*asubha-sanna*). this perception of foulness must be developed to abandon lust.
then, just as there is attachment on one side, there is aversion (*patigha*) or friction on the other—often arising when attachment is not satisfied. aversion is also a serious weakness of the mind. the remedy for it is the meditation on loving-kindness (*metta-bhavana*). you can understand this very easily.
now, this discourse is about preparing the mind, straightening the mind. the mind becomes crooked, warped, and fickle primarily between these two poles (of attachment and aversion). but that is not all. generally, we speak of the five cords of sensual pleasure (*panca-kamaguna*)—the objects that enter through the five external senses: eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. the ordinary world believes that it is because of these that our minds are disturbed. therefore, some think: "if i close my eyes, block my ears, shut down these senses as much as possible, and go to a secluded place, i will be able to realize nibbana." this is a misconception. because all the sensory objects gathered through these five senses accumulate in the mind. you see various recording devices appearing in this day and age; our consciousness (*vinnana*) is much like them. the vast array of samsaric habits acquired throughout the past round of rebirths are all stored in this consciousness (*vinnana*)—our attachments and aversions. similarly, the objects experienced through the five senses are deposited in the mind in some manner. these five senses sit around and, like messengers, bring everything and deposit it in the mind. these accumulated deposits in the mind surface precisely when one goes into solitude and sits down alone. no form comes to the eye; no sound comes to the ear. one is protected from all of them. yet, from within the mind, there arise various defiled thoughts (*vitakka*) from consciousness (*vinnana*), emerging according to one's samsaric character and kamma. it was to these that venerable meghiya succumbed. such is the situation. it is as a remedy for this that the buddha next prescribes mindfulness of breathing (*anapanasati*).
mindfulness of breathing is a highly subtle meditation. to use an analogy: though there are many subjects of meditation (*kammatthana*), mindfulness of breathing is the royal highway. we can call it the royal highway because every buddha attained buddhahood through mindfulness of breathing. if you reflect, you will realize that once the mind has been calmed by auxiliary meditations such as foulness or loving-kindness, one's mindfulness (*sati*) naturally establishes itself on the in-breath and out-breath. mindfulness of breathing means mindfulness directed toward the inhalation and exhalation. normally, people do not direct mindfulness to this. most do not even remember that they are breathing; they think of this as a machine that runs perpetually. the ordinary world forgets that everything depends on this thread of life. but when those two heavy defilements, lust and ill-will, are subdued through the meditations on foulness and loving-kindness, mindfulness of breathing becomes very easy.
however, mindfulness of breathing is prescribed here to cut off thoughts. some practitioners remark: "even though the buddha said this is to cut off thoughts, it is precisely when we sit down for mindfulness of breathing that thoughts come flooding in!" that is not surprising. sometimes, an illness surfaces only when one begins to treat it. the illness is inside. therefore, one must be prepared to face it; the appropriate medicine must be available. that is the situation with mindfulness of breathing. it is not that the illness was absent; rather, the existing illness surfaced. some physicians do exactly this: before curing an illness, they administer a strong purgative to bring the illness to the surface, and only then do they give the curative medicine. similarly, it purges the mind in that manner. yet, underneath, the mass of thoughts emerges. how powerful this is can be seen from the experience of this venerable monk. he must have strived the entire evening, seated comfortably cross-legged under that beautiful, delightful mango tree—yet he could not concentrate his mind. only when it became completely impossible did he leave. such is the power of the momentum of thoughts. that is the astonishing thing. it is this mass of thoughts that overwhelms the world. they arise from within the mind according to one's kamma and temperament. mindfulness of breathing helps to cut them off. through mindfulness of breathing, one understands them at various levels. only when the illness surfaces at its respective levels can the remedy be applied. thus, when the mind scatters through these inner thoughts, one eventually gains an understanding.
now, let us consider the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*). let us understand why the buddha taught the perception of impermanence as the fourth step. this is a profound concept. if you understand this—having applied the remedies for lust and ill-will, and having brought the illness (thoughts) to the surface through mindfulness of breathing—one realizes: "my battle now is with these thoughts." what are thoughts? sensory objects gathered through the five senses throughout samsara, and in this life—whether recently or in the distant past—remain stored in the mind. they surface and trouble the meditator. when they arise, the practitioner must battle them. that is why it was said: *atapiyo samvarati satima* (the ardent, mindful one restrains them).
what the buddha described in those earlier verses as "trifling thoughts, subtle thoughts, which followed, agitate the mind" (*khudda vitakka, sukhuma vitakka, anuggata manaso uppilava*) are very small things—not grand matters. sometimes, it is a word spoken by someone years ago, giving rise to ill-will. or a form barely seen somewhere years ago, on which thoughts arise. they break in with such force that they seem impossible to remove. a practitioner experiences such states. at those times, one sees what a grave obstacle thoughts are to meditation. one must be strong to cut them off. thus, those minor, trifling thoughts arise from within the mind and cause it to drift. how does one restrain them? by being *atapi*—possessing the defilement-burning energy that allows no entry to them. the object of meditation (*kammatthana*) is what assists in this.
you know that when the paddy is ripening, one tethers an ox to prevent it from wandering into the crop. the ox tries its best to reach the crop, but failing to do so, it eventually returns and lies down by the post. such is the value of binding the mind to a meditation object (*kammatthana*). it is only in relation to a meditation object—when one has grasped a meditation object—that one can recognize when the mind has strayed. some people think that by merely watching the mind wander, they can make it tranquil. that does not work. you can never tame a wild bull by running along with it. instead, you must give it an anchor; you must tie it to a post. once tethered, every time it pulls away, using defilement-burning energy and mindfulness—where mindfulness (*sati*) assists—and applying the qualities of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajanna*), which are mindfulness and wisdom, one swiftly brings it back to the post, back to the meditation object, not letting the mind wander far. if you let the mind wander far, before you know it, you will lose all awareness of where you are. such is the nature of thoughts.
this is why, as those who have a basic understanding of the mind know, when something makes contact (*phassa*), an impression is made. based on that, a feeling (*vedana*) arises. that feeling may be pleasant or painful. neutral feeling is barely noticed, and regarding it, there is generally a state of ordinary, often ignorant, equanimity; mostly, it is pleasant or painful feeling. based on these two, a perception is formed. one grasps a perception as good or bad. upon that perception, thoughts (*vitakka*) are built. once one is overcome by those thoughts, something else occurs, which can be called conceptual proliferation (*papanca*). conceptual proliferation means that due to these thoughts branching out, one eventually falls into an extraordinary, grave delusion. one wanders hither and thither within these thoughts, running to the past and the future, to the point of not knowing where one is. these stages are described in the dhamma: "what one feels (*vedeti*), that one perceives (*sanjanati*); what one perceives, that one thinks about (*vitakketi*); what one thinks about, that one conceptually proliferates (*papanceti*)." subject to conceptual proliferation (*papanca*), one is overwhelmed by a tangled web of thoughts whose beginning or end cannot be found, eventually becoming enslaved by the very thoughts of one's own making, forgetting the very purpose of one's endeavor. in this way, the mind becomes utterly distracted.
why does all this happen? it is due to improper attention (*ayoniso manasikara*). here, the meaning of the word wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*) taught by the buddha becomes important. everyone knows what attention or reflection (*manasikara*) is. our minds have the capacity to attend to things. we reflect on something, bringing it to mind. the ordinary world performs this attention improperly (*ayoniso*). in some old translations, this is rendered as "unwisely" or ignorantly. for our times, we can understand it as "inappropriate attention" or ignorant attention—a wrong way of reflecting that gives room to defilements. wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*) means reflecting with wisdom. if we consider it more deeply, *yoniso* means directing the mind to the very source where a thought arises—focusing the mind on the very cause of the illness. that is the kind of reflection a meditator must practice: wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*). this is the case here as well: preventing the mind from wandering far. once contact (*phassa*) occurs, if one immediately gives way to feeling (*vedana*), perceptions (*sanna*) follow. as soon as perceptions arise, one follows those signposts to construct thoughts (*vitakka*) in the mind. becoming enslaved by those thoughts is what is called conceptual proliferation (*papanca*).
such is the state of affairs in this world. the entirety of samsara exists within this. it is within these thoughts, by the mind itself, that samsara is created, and it is by the mind itself that one is liberated from samsara. from this, we can understand the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*) taught by the buddha. indeed, anyone in the ordinary world can conceptualize the perception of impermanence. we all observe impermanence in daily life: something that existed decays. that is the gross, coarse aspect of it. the deepest aspect of the perception of impermanence arises from seeing the impermanent nature of thoughts themselves. one gains an understanding—through that very discipline—of how these thoughts, which we grasp as "my thoughts," scatter, and how the mind scatters due to the influence of past defilements. that discipline is practiced to make the mind tranquil through concentration (*samadhi*). yet, what a tranquil mind realizes—realizes in accordance with reality (*yathabhuta*)—is the very nature of the mind: there is no single mind here, nothing to be claimed as "i." different thoughts arise at different moments; they are thoughts that exist for a mere moment. one realizes that it is because we grasp them tightly through grasping (*upadana*) that this entire samsaric process is created and becoming (*bhava*) is maintained.
that is what the buddha declared: in one who has the perception of impermanence, the perception of not-self (*anatta-sanna*) becomes established. one who has the perception of not-self, having eradicated the conceit "i am" (*asmimana*)—the subtle conceit of "existence"—is comforted by the noble, deathless nibbana in this very life (*dittha-dhamma*). because, due to the distracted and scattering nature of the mind, one realizes that there is nothing here to be grasped as "i," no such thing as a self (*atta*). these thoughts arise, and even as they vanish on the spot, one understands that there is nothing to grasp as "i" or "mine." a thought grasped as "i" ends and vanishes in the next moment. this is realized only when mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajanna*)—the combination of mindfulness and wisdom—are fully applied.
this, too, is indeed a form of concentration (*samadhi*). on one occasion, when describing four developments of concentration (*samadhi-bhavana*)—let us mention only the relevant one—the buddha asked: "monks, what is the development of concentration that leads to mindfulness and clear comprehension?" he explained: "here, a monk knows feelings (*vedana*) as they arise, knows them as they persist, and knows them as they pass away. he knows perceptions (*sanna*) as they arise, knows them as they persist, and knows them as they pass away. he knows thoughts (*vitakka*) as they arise, knows them as they persist, and knows them as they pass away." what is the principle (*dhammata*) within this? it comes down to those three words: arising, persisting, and passing away; they arise, persist, and pass away. briefly, there is only arising and passing away. but what we call "persisting" is actually that grasping (*upadana*)—the act of holding on. in that moment of holding on, it "persists." within that persistence, a "person" appears. thus, that is all there is in the world: arising, persisting, and passing away.
this is realized most profoundly—for in the material world, the difference between arising and passing away is difficult for most to perceive. their decay is not recognized by the ordinary world. it is only on the day an object is thrown away, discarded on a garbage heap as useless and finished, that its decay is acknowledged. yet, the arising and passing away—the impermanence—of the material world is of a very gross, coarse level. this impermanence is perceived in its subtlest form precisely by observing these thoughts: seeing how they arise, persist, and pass away. a mind made tranquil through mindfulness of breathing begins to realize this.
in that meditation, the effort is to keep mindfulness anchored at the point of contact of the breath. yet, in the meantime, those thoughts arise. thoughts of the past or various other things come up, and one must subdue them. through the understanding that this is the actual state of the mind, one eventually realizes that there is no self (*atta*) to be found even in consciousness (*vinnana*). we can generally comprehend the lack of a self in form (*rupa*) easily when it decays. feeling (*vedana*)—as one feeling arises and another follows—can also be understood with some effort. perception (*sanna*) is slightly more difficult, and the impermanence of preparations (*sankhara*), which are volitions, is also somewhat difficult. but consciousness (*vinnana*) is the great illusion, the grandest illusion of beings in this world. the buddha himself compared consciousness (*vinnana*) to an illusion. this is something one must experience for oneself. the path to this is what the buddha has shown here by presenting these meditation objects in a systematic sequence.
therefore, reflecting on this, you too should understand that one who aspires to the life of a practitioner, who hopes to embark on this path, must not think of it as an easy task. if one assumes it is easy, one will soon become disillusioned. knowing that it is a difficult task, preparing the mind, and arousing great energy, one must embark on this work. otherwise, what happens? one either blames the teacher or blames the meditation. does someone stop driving simply because road accidents occur? no. there can be many reasons for a road accident; sometimes it is the driver's own ignorance. in the same way, because some people experience mental tension and various difficulties through meditation, some in this era think that meditation is an easy path to distract the mind. this is a mistaken view. it is those who are hasty, like venerable meghiya, who act and think in this manner, and who fall into such states.
the wise person remembers those instructions given by the buddha. we must embark on this work having prepared the mind. what assists in this, foremostly, is association with a teacher. the buddha, as we stated earlier, is the world's incomparable noble friend (*kalyana-mitta*). after the buddha passed away, and indeed even while he was alive, the chief disciples like venerable sariputta and other great arahants were like parents to the community, helping disciples to reach the state of arahantship. next were the eighty great disciples, followed by other members of the sangha according to their capacity. after they passed away, as long as this dispensation (*sasana*) exists, whether lay or ordained, any person who has walked this path of meditation, achieved some progress, and possesses understanding of it, is indeed the noble friend, the teacher. one must be ready to take steps in accordance with the situation, obedient to their words. for this, humility is required.
the other factors are strengthening the mind through moral virtue, hearing the dhamma, and so forth; generating an intense desire (*chanda*), a strong yearning; then exerting energy; and intelligently, wisely applying the mind—wisdom (*panna*). these factors are supportive. the same applies to the prescribed path of meditation. without mixing them up or entangling them, one must enter that path of meditation. what should be done first must not be done later, and what should be done later must not be done first. some leap into mindfulness of breathing because it is a highly valued meditation, but they are not prepared for it. consequently, they complain: "although the buddha said to practice mindfulness of breathing to cut off thoughts, for me, only thoughts arise when i try." some even go so far as to blame the buddha's teaching.
what is the reason for this? it is the coarse level mentioned earlier. you know how a carpenter uses a plane. consider it: first, he uses the coarse plane to smooth out the rough parts. having done that, by adjusting the blade or using another plane, he shaves the next layer, and then uses a finer plane. a similar process applies to the mind. the mind has coarse levels and subtle levels; coarse levels are eliminated only by a coarse remedy. that is helpful. some people hesitate, claiming that the meditation on foulness is not suitable for laypeople. whether lay or ordained, if one seeks nibbana, this is helpful. even if we reflect on this society and look at laypeople, how many crimes occur because of ignorance regarding these defilements of lust and so forth? if there were some restraint and discipline regarding them, even society would become far more peaceful. even within a household, there would be discipline and restraint. the same applies to the other defilement, ill-will (*byapada*). humans mostly live within these two—attachment and aversion. but once they are subdued, one must proceed further. that is where the simile of the fine plane applies. that is what must be taken up there. it is what the buddha described as "trifling thoughts, subtle thoughts."
venerable meghiya went thinking: "just because i have seen a delightful mango grove, if i go there and meditate, i can immediately realize nibbana; i can achieve in a single afternoon what the buddha strived so hard to accomplish." everything else was perfect: the mango grove was delightful, the shade was good, and the seat was fine. all was well, yet he could not tame his mind. why? because underneath arose those thoughts—all the debris, just like the debris swept away when a stream swells after a heavy rain. a practitioner striving for nibbana must face such situations.
at such times, one must not be discouraged. it is something to be expected. that debris must flow out somehow. you know what happens after taking a purgative—there is no need to describe that in detail. after taking a purgative, one thinks: "alas! is this the reality? is this the nature of the body i claimed as mine? is this the nature of food?" in such moments, this is clearly realized. similarly, when one sits down for mindfulness of breathing after fulfilling the preliminary requirements, the stream of debris emerges from within the mind. yet, through that, discipline is achieved, and through discipline, understanding arises. one realizes that this mind is difficult to tame. but why do we tame it? to sharpen this understanding. this is the middle path (*majjhima patipada*). a highly profound matter is present here. if taken to extremes, there is no progress. the solution to the problem of escaping samsaric existence—which no other teacher could resolve—was presented by the buddha through the middle path. initially, calming the mind is necessary; unifying the mind is necessary. though we say "unifying" the mind, this mind is not a single entity. when it is unified, one perceives its scattering nature. it scatters moment by moment. due to accumulated kamma, character, tendencies, and temperament, various thoughts (*vitakka*) arise. one is not discouraged by them. instead, what does one ultimately do through them? one sees that there is nothing here to grasp. where there is grasping (*upadana*), there is mara. where there is grasping, there "i" exist. one then sees: "grasping is the source of all trouble." one beholds the truth in accordance with reality (*yathabhuta*). all this is impermanent (*anicca*). what is impermanent is suffering (*dukkha*); because one grasps what is impermanent, one falls into suffering. furthermore, one realizes: "nothing can be claimed as 'i' or 'mine' or kept under my control."
when that realization arrives, when it arrives in its depth, it is then that one peels away the final scab called the conceit "i am" (*asmimana*), as the buddha declared. it is through this scab of "existence"—"i am"—that the entire world is measured. "i" is generally a gross, coarse notion; that is what is called the view of an existing group (*sakkaya-ditthi*). merely eliminating the view of "i" and "mine" does not complete the task. the subtlest level is "am-ness"—not even "i am," but simply "am"—which remains deposited in the mind at an extremely subtle level. this is seen clearly only when the scattering nature of the mind is thoroughly realized and grasping is abandoned. where there is grasping—at the moment of contact (*phassa*), feeling (*vedana*) arises through grasping. grasping there turns it into perception (*sanna*). perception turns into thought (*vitakka*). grasping that thought leads to conceptual proliferation (*papanca*), beyond which the mind eventually turns into a virtual madhouse. to prevent this, one must abandon the wrong path of improper attention (*ayoniso manasikara*). the battle does not begin from the far end. it begins as the buddha declared in the very first verse of the dhammapada:
*manopubbangama dhamma*
*manosettha manomaya*
the realization that everything arises from the mind itself emerges clearly at that deep stage of meditation.
therefore, you must reflect on this. on this valuable poya day, we must not arouse faith merely by thinking about the buddha's physical life. one who truly recognizes the buddha is one who has actually realized nibbana. until then, we see only a physical form, or a buddha conjured up by our thoughts. thus, if we hope to see the buddha, if we hope to recognize him, we must walk the path to nibbana. we must realize this very truth. only then will we truly see the buddha. only then will our faith in the buddha be perfected.
therefore, through this dhamma listening on this valuable day, some matters pertaining to the ten talk-topics may have been conveyed to you. it is still possible to benefit from this dispensation in this very life. some consider this to be outdated. but the very same fires that burned during the buddha's time are burning today—the fires of lust, hatred, and delusion. nibbana, then, is the extinguishing of these fires. it is nothing else; it is not some exotic world, nor is it some celestial realm as some believe. it is simply nibbana. in samsara, there is burning. in its place, the buddha presents nibbana. in samsara, there is existence. realizing that this existence is suffering (*dukkha*), bringing about its cessation is what we called escaping from the circular track of samsara. revolving on the circular track of samsara is wandering (*samsarana*). escaping from it is deliverance (*nissarana*). viewed from the perspective of defilements, nibbana is liberation from the kingdom of mara!
taking this state as the ultimate goal of your life, during this rare human existence, during this rare period of a buddha's appearance, and in the closing stages of this dispensation—for in a few generations, it will become impossible to benefit from this dhamma because association with teachers will be lost. those who can advise on this path to nibbana, those who are engaged in these practices, will become impossible to find. one might find the rare "black cumin" (*kalu-nika*) more easily than them. therefore, keeping in mind the buddha's advice on diligence (*appamada*), you must make a firm determination to walk this path to nibbana without delay.
you should know that by listening to this dhamma sermon, several highly important wholesome qualities have arisen within your minds even at this moment. particularly, faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*) are listed among the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*). functioning as both faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*)—faith is both a faculty and a power, a capability as well as a source of strength. similarly, energy follows faith; through the energy applied to burn defilements and draw near wholesome states, mindfulness arises. maintaining mindfulness for a long period is what becomes concentration. eventually, mindfulness overflows and turns into concentration. to a concentrated mind, wisdom arises—seeing things as they really are (*yathabhuta*). these five—faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—fully operate as faculties and powers precisely when one correctly embarks on meditation for nibbana. i hope this dhamma sermon has helped you to arouse them, at least to some degree, in accordance with your capacity for meditation.
may the power of generating these qualities of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom through listening to such a sermon enable you, through your utmost efforts in this very life, to realize the stages of stream-entry (*sotapatti*), once-returning (*sakadagamita*), non-returning (*anagamita*), and arahantship, escaping from this entire mass of samsaric suffering and attaining the noble, deathless nibbana. furthermore, may the store of merit gathered through this preaching and hearing of the dhamma be shared with the guardian deities of the dispensation, and all beings from avici to akanittha who await these merits—including your departed relatives. may they all rejoice in these merits, obtain the association of noble friends, and swiftly escape all samsaric suffering to find peace in the noble, deathless nibbana. with this aspiration, let us transfer merits by reciting these verses:
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 009
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #9
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No. )
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Attanāva kataṃ pāpaṃ, attajaṃ attasambhavaṃ; Abhimatthati dummedhaṃ, vajiraṃ vasmamayaṃ maṇiṃ.
From:
Verse 161 from the Attavagga (Chapter on the Self) of the Dhammapada
Dear Listeners,
When some people see a person who has lived a good life in society meet with death due to a sudden accident or an enemy's hostility, they might think, "Look at what happened to him despite living so well," and begin to doubt the value of a principled life. They weaken their faith in the fruits and results of wholesome and unwholesome actions (kamma). This kind of doubt arises because they do not have a proper understanding of the subtle workings of the wheel of kamma.
The Buddha declared that beings must themselves be held responsible for the wholesome and unwholesome kamma they perform out of ignorance and craving—shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving—actions performed selfishly with the conceit of "self". He declared that they must experience the fruits and results of these actions, and that sooner or later, they will have to face their consequences. Although the subtle workings of kamma were not visible to other religious teachers, they were clearly perceived by the Buddha. Therefore, on certain occasions when such erroneous views arose in society, he would recount the past story related to the present incident as an illustration—as empirical evidence—thereby presenting such direct proof to the world. In doing so, he seized the opportunity to rescue people from the path of woeful states and guide them toward happy realms and Nibbāna.
The background story of the verse we have chosen as our theme today is of a similar nature. During the time when the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana monastery, there lived in the city of Sāvatthī a faithful stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) lay disciple named Mahākāla. He was accustomed to regularly observing the eight precepts. Eight days a month, he would come to the monastery, observe the precepts, and spend the entire night listening to Dhamma sermons. He was deeply devoted to this practice. One night, while this lay disciple was at the Jetavana monastery, a band of thieves broke into a nearby house. Hearing the noise as they were preparing to take the goods, the homeowners woke up and began chasing the thieves. The thieves started running, dropping the stolen goods here and there. One of the thieves fled along the path leading to the Jetavana monastery with the goods he had taken. By that time, in the early morning, the lay disciple Mahākāla had come to the pond to wash his face. What did this thief do? Seeing the lay disciple, he dropped the bundle of stolen goods right where the lay disciple was standing—likely in an attempt to deceive the pursuing crowd—and ran away. When the homeowners arrived, they saw the bundle of goods and found the lay disciple there. They grabbed him, shouting, "You broke into our house, and now you are standing here pretending to listen to Dhamma, posing as a pious lay disciple! You are a thief in disguise!" They beat him mercilessly, killed him, and left his body there.
In the morning, some novice monks came to the pond to fetch water. Seeing the lay disciple lying dead in this manner, they went and reported it to the Buddha: "Venerable Sir, that innocent lay disciple, the one who listened so well to the Dhamma sermons, has been beaten to death and cast aside."
The Buddha said, "Monks, although looking at his conduct in this life, it may seem that this lay disciple met with an undeserved death, yet, in terms of the evil kamma he performed in the past, this death is entirely fitting." Then, he related the story of the past.
In the past, at the entrance to a forest in a border village of the Kingdom of Benares, the king had stationed a royal guard, as travelers were frequently harassed by thieves lurking in that forest. What was the guard's duty? It was to provide security to those who traveled to and fro along that forest path. One day, a certain man arrived there in a carriage, accompanied by his beautiful wife. As soon as the guard saw her, he felt a lustful attachment and devised a scheme to detain them. Although there was plenty of time left to travel safely, he said, "It is too late in the evening now. Therefore, stay here today. I will provide lodging in my house, and you may leave tomorrow morning." But the man replied, "No, no, there is plenty of time. Please let us proceed." What did the royal guard do? He used his men to forcibly stop the carriage and provided lodging and food for both the man and his wife there. During the night, he employed a trick. He had his men hide a gem belonging to the household inside their carriage. Furthermore, he created a noise as if thieves had entered the house. The next morning, after the couple had departed, he ordered his men, "Go and search those who are leaving this village. A gem in our house has gone missing; thieves have taken it." So, the guard's men went, stopped and searched the carriage, retrieved the gem they themselves had hidden, and brought the man before the village headman with a false accusation: "He has stolen the gem of the royal guard who gave him shelter." The village headman, unaware of the actual facts, ordered that the man be beaten and executed. The Buddha explained the consequences of that unwholesome act of taking life. As a result of that unwholesome kamma, the royal guard suffered for a long time in the Avīci hell, and as a residual effect, in the final portion of those consequences, he was beaten to death in a similar manner for a hundred lifetimes. The Buddha pointed out that what happened to Mahākāla on this occasion was indeed the very same consequence, and that this story was about him. Having explained this, the Buddha said, "Monks, if a person, being thus deluded, performs an evil kamma, it will bring results in this manner," and he uttered the aforementioned verse of Dhamma together with a simile.
*Attanāva kataṁ pāpaṁ*
*attajaṁ attasambhavaṁ*
*abhimatthati dummedhaṁ*
*vajiraṁ vasamayaṁ maṇiṁ*
"By oneself is evil done, born of oneself, produced by oneself. It crushes the foolish person, just as a diamond crushes a gem born of rock."
The meaning of this verse is that evil kamma, which is born of oneself and produced from within oneself, destroys the foolish person, just as a diamond-jewel (vajra) born of stone cuts and destroys the very stone from which it arose.
Here, in this verse too, a gem is mentioned. There seems to be some subtle connection to the background story. However, there is a much deeper meaning here. When it is said "done by oneself," we see the sense of personal responsibility. In the past, that lay disciple, driven by selfishness and harboring the conceit of "self", committed that evil deed. The inevitable consequence of that false accusation—for indeed, it was a false accusation—is what he had to experience in this lifetime. Thus, although in the world we often see seemingly innocent people being killed, the Buddha-eye perceives their past connections. We can understand this through this story. Here we clearly see that when the lay disciple Mahākāla was a royal guard in the past, he violated the third precept and also the first precept by causing the taking of life of an innocent man. What he experienced now was the verdict of that false accusation. It was because of this that the thieves dropped the bundle of stolen goods right there. It was kamma that inclined the thieves' minds to drop it there. There is a wondrous karmic connection in these events. We can see that this reality underlies everything we hear about. Today, too, many such incidents occur. Events similar to those described in this present and past story are still seen in the world today. We can understand from this that the law of kamma and its result is subtly hidden within all these occurrences.
Next, we must contemplate the deeper aspect of this matter. Now, this verse repeats several times phrases like "done by oneself", "born of oneself", "produced of oneself". Thus, "self" is emphasized. Indeed, this verse comes from the section called the *Atta Vagga* (Chapter on Self). Many translate this easily as "soul" or "self". But in this section of the Dhammapada, there is a discussion about oneself. Many interpret this as a permanent soul, but what is referred to here is not a permanent soul. Some debaters argue: "If this Dhamma is a teaching of Not-self (*Anattā*), how can one be held responsible for one's actions? How is responsibility demonstrated? After all, the one who experiences the result is not the same 'self'!" They try to escape through such arguments. But what is the meaning here? Shrouded by the veil of ignorance and bound by the fetters of craving (*taṇhā*), the world of living beings generates intentions. You have heard the phrase: "*Cetanāhaṁ bhikkhave kammaṁ vadāmi*"—"Intention, O monks, is what I call kamma." You must have heard this many times. The Buddha has shown that intention itself is kamma. Thus, through the ignorance that supports that intention—the feeling of "I" and "mine"—the concept of "self" arises. Having generated that conceit of "self" and acting with thoughts of one's own pleasure, protection, progress, and gain, the consequences of those actions must be experienced by oneself sooner or later. Why is this? Feeling (*vedanā*) is something that occurs with extreme rapidity. The activity of the mind is exceptionally swift. If it is directed in the wrong way, we can understand that it leads to great destruction. If a driver of a fast-moving vehicle, due to negligence or drowsiness regarding the controls operated by his hands and feet, lets the steering wheel slip even slightly, where will it end? The mind is just like that; it operates with extreme rapidity. It is something that changes so swiftly that nothing in the world can compare to it—hence it is described as *lahuparivattaṁ* (swiftly changing). Therefore, if such a mind, in accordance with the law explained by the Buddha, leans toward unrighteousness, unwholesomeness, and evil, then one has to suffer grave consequences for a very long time. Not just in one lifetime—depending on the strength of that intention—the Buddha has shown that the results of certain kammas are experienced in this very life as *diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*. The results of other kammas are experienced in future lifetimes as *aparāpariyavedanīya*. In this manner, the results of kamma are generally explained in various ways. Yet, when we contemplate deeply, the Buddha declares that the domain of kamma is unthinkable (*acinteyya*). The entanglement of kamma is that dangerous. The vast accumulation of kamma performed across various lifetimes gathers and deposits in consciousness (*viññāṇa*), only to resurface some day as fruit and result. This is the perilous nature of existence in this world that we can understand through this.
Furthermore, we must constantly reflect on the relationship between kamma and its result. For, as mentioned earlier, some might think, "Is it not someone else who experiences the result of the kamma I perform?" In the next life, one might not know that they committed this deed. But to use a simple analogy: if one pours poison into a flowing stream at one point, and someone takes water further downstream, they can be harmed by that poison. The mind-stream (*citta-santāna*) is just like that. If an unwholesome quality—a defilement—is added to the mind-stream, it will resurface over a long period of time as ripening results to bring retribution to oneself.
Among our Buddhists, there is a saying regarding this ripening of kamma, known as *kamma-sarikkhatā* (the correspondence of action and result). As illustrated by these two stories, the connection between kamma and its result often shows a close similarity—a kind of parallelism. Moreover, even Western scholars who are waking up to this reality use a new analogy to describe the working of kamma—how actions return to the doer. The kamma performed by oneself returning to oneself is sometimes compared to a weapon used by certain indigenous tribes called a "boomerang." When the boomerang is thrown at an animal, it hits the target and returns right back to the hand of the thrower. Kamma has a similar returning nature. If kamma originates from a particular mind-stream, it returns to that very same mind-stream. Therefore, one cannot escape by saying there is no "self." For we know that *saṁsāra* is the uninterrupted continuity of the stream of aggregates—even though there is no permanent soul—comprising form, feeling (*vedanā*), perception, Preparations (*saṅkhāra*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*). Within that stream of aggregates, sooner or later, in accordance with the law of kamma, the results will inevitably surface.
Since such a state of affairs exists in the world, we must be exceptionally mindful of it. In this era of terror and violence, many people's understanding, belief, and faith (*saddhā*) in kamma tend to disappear. It is often forgotten. Such is the perilous condition of the world.
Therefore, to constantly remind us of this law of kamma, there is a valuable discourse taught by the Buddha called the *Ṭhāna Sutta*. In that discourse, the Buddha points out five facts. We shall focus here particularly on the last point mentioned. To help one reflect on kamma, turn one's mind away from bad conduct, and direct it toward good conduct, the Buddha presents a certain formula to be constantly reflected upon (*abhiṇhaṁ paccavekkhitabbaṁ*). Whether lay or ordained, male or female, this is a matter that should be regularly reflected upon by everyone:
"*Kammassakomhi kammadāyādo kammayoni kammabandhu kammapaṭisaraṇo.*
*Yaṁ kammaṁ karissāmi kalyāṇaṁ vā pāpakaṁ vā tassa dāyādo bhavissāmīti*
*abhiṇhaṁ paccavekkhitabbaṁ.*"
This is how one should think. "*Kammassakomhi*" means—here too, if there is anything that can be taken as "self" or "mine", it is kamma alone. "*Kamma-sako*"—"*sako*" means "one's own". Thus, the general meaning is: "I am the owner of my kamma." "*Kammadāyādo*": "I am the heir to my kamma." "*Kammayoni*": "Kamma is the womb from which I am born." My origin, my beginning, is from this kamma. What is called "I" is indeed intention itself, which is taken as "I". That is why it says "*kammayoni*"—kamma also arises from the conceit of "I" and "self". "*Kammabandhu*": "Kamma is my kinsman." The only relative one has as a support is kamma itself. "*Kammapaṭisaraṇo*": "Kamma is my refuge; kamma is my support." "*Yaṁ kammaṁ karissāmi kalyāṇaṁ vā pāpakaṁ vā tassa dāyādo bhavissāmi*": "Whatever kamma I shall do, whether good or evil, of that I shall be the heir." It is stated that this is what should be constantly reflected upon by everyone—lay or ordained, male or female.
The result or benefit of doing so is declared thus: in a person who reflects in this manner, bad bodily conduct, bad verbal conduct, and bad mental conduct—misdeeds done through body, speech, and mind—are either entirely eradicated or at least attenuated. This means that the best method to avoid bad conduct is to regularly apply this law of kamma to one's own mind. "Kamma is what is truly mine." When one thinks in this way, one realizes that the things one desperately grasps onto as "I" in moments of impulsiveness or haste in society are not what the Buddha pointed out. What remains with one in the end is the momentum of kamma generated within one's own mind. That is indeed what brings happiness or pain to oneself.
Accordingly, we should contemplate the terrifying nature of this entanglement of kamma, which the Buddha has illustrated on many occasions in this manner. That is to say, when experiencing the result of kamma, we generally do not realize that it is a karmic retribution, even though it is clearly seen by the Buddha-eye. Instead, we think it is something done to us by others. Perhaps even the lay disciple Mahākāla—though details are not given, and being a devout lay disciple he might have tried to compose his mind—nevertheless, when those homeowners came and beat him to death, he might have felt anger, thinking, "Alas, they are killing me, an innocent man." He too must have considered himself innocent. There was even room for such an unwholesome thought to arise. But if one contemplates deeply according to that formula, no matter what misfortune or enemy hostility befalls one, one should think: "This is something of my own making." Now, who was the executioner of the lay disciple Mahākāla? It was himself! If we contemplate in accordance with the Dhamma, according to the principles of the Dhamma, the ultimate cause of anyone's death is an unwholesome act of taking life committed by themselves in the past. That is how we must contemplate. The proximate cause of death, the reason for death—we are not referring here to the mind at the moment of death—the cause of death is an unwholesome act of taking life committed by oneself in the past. This is clearly illustrated here. The death of the lay disciple Mahākāla was brought about by a taking of life he himself committed. He himself was his own executioner. It was not anyone else; he was his own executioner.
If we accustom ourselves to contemplating in this manner, we can easily bring the mind to equanimity (*upekkhā*) in such situations, in accordance with the Buddha's word. It may not be directly perceived by us. Since we do not possess higher spiritual powers (*abhiññā*), we cannot see that "this particular kamma has caused this particular event to happen to me." However, if we practice reflecting on this as a universal law of nature—knowing that the Buddha’s word is true—we realize the Buddha has declared: "Kamma alone is my inheritance; kamma alone is my kinsman." It can be a relative or an enemy. In this regard, we should understand that wholesome kamma is one's true kinsman, while unwholesome kamma is one's enemy. The Buddha has pointed this out too, when speaking of kamma.
*Caranti bālā dummedhā*
*amitteneva attanā*
*karontā pāpakaṁ kammaṁ*
*yaṁ hoti kaṭukapphalaṁ*
Thus the Buddha has declared: "Foolish and ignorant people go about acting as enemies to themselves, performing evil kamma which yields bitter fruit." "*Amitteneva attanā*"—they behave as if they are enemies to themselves. Why? Because by "*karontā pāpakaṁ kammaṁ yaṁ hoti kaṭukapphalaṁ*"—by performing evil deeds that bring bitter consequences, these foolish individuals live as enemies to themselves. Thus, while it is said that kamma is one's kinsman (*kammabandhu*), if we consider unwholesome actions, they can turn out to be one's enemies.
Therefore, reflecting that this law of kamma—this natural law of kamma—is embedded in every single event that happens to us, often helps us, in accordance with the Buddha's words, to subdue impulsiveness, haste, and anger. This is something that must be constantly contemplated in a practical manner.
Furthermore, this story reveals to us another important matter: the significance of the five precepts (*pañcasīla*). The five precepts taught by the Buddha are no trivial matter. Within this virtue (*sīla*), all the situations in which a being's mind leans toward unwholesomeness in this long *saṁsāra* are briefly and simply contained. In general, any unwholesome kamma we perform falls under either the first precept—the unwholesome act of taking life—or under taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, or taking intoxicants, as the primary categories. One could describe various branches and sub-branches of these, but these are the main ones. Thus, the consequences of the evil kamma related to the five sins we committed in that past *saṁsāra* are what we experience day by day in various ways. It is not only death, as mentioned before, but also illness, various disasters, loss of wealth and crops, and all such daily adversities—the cause of every single one of these is the terrible unwholesome kamma committed by oneself in the past. But that is not the only danger of kamma. As mentioned earlier, due to not knowing the true nature of kamma, one gets entangled in the ball of karmic thread. Indeed, the Buddha compares *saṁsāra* to a tangled ball of thread. How does it become a tangled ball of thread? We receive a certain result according to the kamma we have performed. When that result comes, we do not know how it happened. We tangle it further by generating more kamma in response to it. By harboring ill-will (*dosa*) toward those who instrumented that result—and not only that, but by succumbing to various defilements (*kilesa*) because of it—we entangle our kamma further and accumulate still more kamma. Such is the perilous state of this entanglement of kamma. And it is not only oneself who gets caught in this entanglement. When a kamma is performed, and when its result is experienced, there are others who join in. There are others who rejoice in it. We know that after giving a gift (*dāna*) or performing some other valuable meritorious deed, we share those merits with others. On such occasions, there is an opportunity for others to rejoice in that merit, and instead of falling into woeful states, to generate wholesome qualities that lead to happy realms. That is the good side. The word "rejoicing" (*anumodanā*) is generally used in connection with wholesome deeds. But, meritorious devotees, we also see in society many instances where people rejoice in unwholesome deeds.
You know very well, especially in this era, that when one's friends or relatives gain some profit, even in an indirect or improper way, one rejoices over it. If that action was unwholesome, if that person accomplished it in a wrong way, then by rejoicing, we too are sharing in that unwholesome deed. Or, particularly if a friend has committed some serious wrong—such as wrong view, theft, or other corrupt activities—one either assists them through body and speech, or rejoices mentally, thinking, "Oh, how wonderful!" Nay, even when an enemy dies, there is a habit among beings to exclaim "Sādhu! Sādhu!" and thus rejoice in it. Such is their delusion. What does one do by this? One takes upon oneself something unrelated—something that does not belong to oneself—and binds oneself to that unwholesome kamma. Thus, although the word "*anumodanā*" is used in connection with wholesome deeds, we unwittingly participate in unwholesome deeds as well. This happens due to that very ignorance. That rejoicing too is kamma. Even if another person did the deed, when one rejoices in it mentally, one's own feeling (*vedanā*) becomes soiled by it. Through that, one accumulates unwholesome kamma for oneself. We must guard against such situations.
In the world, there are various political parties and factions. However, the Dhamma mentions two parties that exist eternally in the universe: the *devas* (gods) and the *asuras* (demons). There is a perpetual struggle between these two factions. The Buddha states that when Tathāgatas appear in the world, the party of the *devas*—that is, the deities—grows stronger, while the faction of the *asuras*—the demons and hungry ghosts—declines, grows weak, and decreases in number. What does this mean? When beings incline toward wholesomeness, more gods are born in the world. Conversely, as they incline more and more toward unwholesomeness, those born in the lower realms like demons (*yakkhas*) and hungry ghosts (*petas*) increase. This is the kind of competition that exists in the world. This can be designated as black and white. When considered in terms of the Dhamma, the conflict between the wholesome and the unwholesome can be seen as white and black—the white side being wholesome and the black side being unwholesome. These are the two parties that eternally exist in the world, not the political parties we think of. Therefore, we must consider which party we belong to, and which party we vote for—the black party or the white party? Voting for the white party is called *kusala-chanda* (desire for wholesomeness) in the Dhamma. It is voting for the wholesome. There is also a bad side to desire (*chanda*), known as *chanda-rāga* (lustful desire). That goes toward the unwholesome. If one develops an attachment that leans toward that passion called *chanda-rāga*, it leads to ruin. *Kusala-chanda*, however, is a good thing because it is a valuable urgency or a desire for the Dhamma that culminates in Nibbāna. We must understand that these two forces exist in the world. If we do not shape our lives properly according to this Dhamma of the Buddha, we cannot tell into what abyss our journey will eventually end. Such is the situation.
Therefore, we must contemplate especially on the observance of virtue (*sīla*). Even on this occasion, you have observed virtue—whether it is the eight precepts with right livelihood (*ājīva-aṭṭhamaka-sīla*), the eight Uposatha precepts, or in some cases, the ten precepts. We must reflect on its value. How precious is this virtue (*sīla*) declared by the Buddha! In this path of Dhamma, virtue is only the first step. Yet, how valuable is that which is contained within it! The training of body and speech is also something that must be carried out systematically.
Sīla means "tame-ness" or "gentleness." If we translate it into Sinhala, sīla is *hīlākama* (tameness). We see the value of this tameness when we observe the behavior of a trained elephant. The mahout rides on the back of such a massive beast and makes it perform various tasks. Similarly, one rides a fast-running horse, taming it to do one's bidding. When even a wild beast, once systematically tamed, can perform such remarkable tasks and be of great use, how much more so with ourselves?
If we thus discipline our body and speech in accordance with this virtue (*sīla*) declared by the Buddha—then, what is contained within is not just body and speech. Our bodies are not machines. The mind is the forerunner that enables these bodily and verbal actions to operate, in accordance with the verse: *manopubbaṅgamā dhammā* (mind is the forerunner of all states). The primary cause is the mind. In truth, what is contained within this virtue is not a meaningless repetition of training rules—as the Sangha often points out, like the story of "how the village rustic observed the precepts" without understanding. It must be taken to heart. Even if we recite them in Pali for the sake of tradition and respect, we must understand their meaning. The precept regarding abstaining from killing living beings—*veramaṇī* means abstaining, and *virati* means abstinence—is what is difficult. Doing is easy; abstaining is difficult. When one says, "I undertake the precept of abstaining, the rule of self-discipline," it means one is voluntarily—not because someone else forced it, but out of one's own free will—observing it and depositing that determination in the mind. It is like issuing a command to one's own wisdom. In our activities, there are things done impulsively according to our whims, and things done through thoughtful reflection. There is a vast difference between the two. Within each of us, there is a certain capacity called "wisdom"—what is known as mindful understanding—the ability to do things thoughtfully. But this must be brought out with effort. Why? Because the nature of *saṁsāra* is to flow downward toward the unwholesome, like a stream. Therefore, this wisdom remains buried. We usually act according to our whims and our superficial minds, which are often inclined toward the unwholesome. Yet, there is a capacity of wisdom, a power of understanding (*paññā*) within us. That very idea is what is called reflection (*paccavekkhaṇā*).
If we consider the word reflection (*paccavekkhaṇā*) deeply—it is like a person going before a mirror to look at themselves. It is to contemplate something calmly. When preparing to go on a journey or attend a wedding, one dresses up and goes before a mirror to see if there are any flaws or if one's ornaments are placed correctly. Similarly, within our minds, there is a capacity to reconsider, a capacity to reflect back (*āvajjanā*). Specifically, we have the ability to pause and ponder, "Is this indeed so?" That is what is called reflection. Even the Buddha used the simile of the mirror to advise us to contemplate and examine how things are.
The Buddha briefly explained the nature of the wholesome and unwholesome to Ven.
