thus, in this way, perhaps because this child lived a very miserable life, by the time he was about sixteen years old, he contracted jaundice—a severe case of jaundice. his mother, the brahmin woman, told the brahmin to go and bring a physician. this brahmin said, "can't you see how my wealth will be destroyed if i bring a physician?" having said that, instead of bringing one, he went to physicians and, in a roundabout, casual manner, tried to find out their remedies. he asked what medicines are given for such and such illnesses. physicians, too, often give casual answers to such roundabout questions. and so, the physicians casually said that the bark of such and such trees is good for such illnesses. this brahmin returned home, searched for these barks, and treated his son with this home-made, quack medicine. this quack medicine did not work. the child's illness became critical and aggravated, reaching an incurable state. at last, when there was no other choice, the brahmin went and brought a physician. the physician, upon seeing him, immediately realized: "if i undertake to treat this patient, my reputation will be ruined." therefore, he quietly slipped away, saying, "i have some other business, please call another physician."
then the brahmin realized that the child was now on the verge of death. next, he thought, "when my son dies, those who come to the funeral house will see the wealth inside my home." thinking so, he laid the dying child on the porch, out on the veranda. on this very day, the buddha, as was his custom, emerged from the attainment of great compassion in the early dawn and surveyed the world, whereupon mattakundali appeared in his buddha-eye. that knowledge of the attainment of great compassion is a wondrous knowledge unique only to a buddha. it is a wondrous kind of attainment that arises in a buddha, backed by the wisdom and great compassion developed throughout the entirety of samsara. when the buddha emerges from this attainment and surveys the world, he mostly sees those who have performed various merits under past buddhas, which have now matured. at any rate, mattakundali, who was preparing to end his life in this miserable manner, appeared in the buddha-eye of the buddha.
thus, out of great compassion, the buddha, surrounded by the community of bhikkhus, walked for alms along the street where the brahmin's house was located. when he reached the house, the buddha saw that the child was lying down facing the inside of the house—that is, facing the wall. seeing this, the buddha, in order to draw his attention, projected a buddha-ray, a single ray of buddha-light, in that direction. when the light fell upon the wall, the child turned and looked. upon seeing the physical form of the buddha, a great clarity and faith arose in him, and he thought, "alas, because of my foolish father, i did not get the opportunity to see such a buddha, to attend on him, to listen to the dhamma, or to offer alms." then he tried to raise his two hands to place them on his forehead in worship. however, due to his weak state, he could only join his fingers. then he thought, "all i can do now is to clarify my mind," and with his whole heart, without any doubt, dedicating his entire mind, he clarified his mind toward the buddha. as he was looking at the buddha, the buddha thought, "this merit is enough for him," and he departed from there. just as the buddha walked out of sight—beyond the range of vision—the child mattakundali passed away, dying with that very clarified mind, and was reborn in the tavatimsa heaven as a young deva adorned with golden ornaments in a golden mansion of thirty leagues.
having been reborn there, he then looked to see how he obtained this celestial fortune. all such devas reflect in this manner: "how did i come to this state?" then he saw the condition of his father, the brahmin. after burning the corpse, the brahmin went to the cemetery every day and wept, crying, "where is my only son? where is my only son?" the young deva saw this behavior of the brahmin. seeing this, mattakundali deva thought he should teach him a lesson. in the likeness of mattakundali, but as a youth adorned with golden ornaments, he came near the cemetery and began to weep. the brahmin, seeing this young deva—perhaps because he resembled his own child—felt a special affection and asked, "why are you weeping?" then the deva said, "i have obtained a golden carriage frame. because i cannot find good wheels for it, i am planning to die of grief," implying he would commit suicide. then the brahmin said, "if you want, i will make wheels for you out of gold, silver, or brass, however you want." when he said this, the young deva replied, "i have no use for other wheels; i want the sun and the moon." then the brahmin said, "why is this foolish child wishing for something he cannot obtain?" then the young deva said, "i am wishing for the sun and the moon, which are visible. you are wishing for a deceased son, wishing for someone who cannot be seen. who of us two is the greater fool?" hearing this, wisdom dawned on the brahmin. he also extinguished his grief. having extinguished it, he thanked mattakundali deva and declared, "i have extinguished my grief." he then asked, "who are you?" the deva replied, "i am your son. having clarified my mind in my final moment, as the result of that wholesome thought, i obtained this rebirth." then the brahmin said, "i never saw you giving alms, observing virtue, or listening to the dhamma. how did you obtain this state?" then mattakundali deva declared, "when the buddha came here, i clarified my mind. as a result of that bright, clarified mind, i obtained this state." then he advised the brahmin, "you too, go to the triple gem for refuge and undertake the five precepts. see the buddha, give alms, listen to the dhamma, and gather merit in that way." having said this, mattakundali deva disappeared.
the brahmin too went to see the buddha, invited him for alms, and prepared alms at his home. the buddha and the community of bhikkhus arrived for the alms. even a crowd of wrong-viewed people gathered at the brahmin’s house. on this occasion, after offering the alms and after the meal was finished, the brahmin questioned the buddha: "without giving alms, observing virtue, or listening to the dhamma, is it possible to obtain celestial fortunes merely by clarifying one's mind toward you?" then the buddha declared: "why, brahmin, did not your own son tell you this?" when the buddha declared this, some in the crowd developed doubts. "how can one obtain such great fortune merely by clarifying the mind?" the buddha then resolved that mattakundali deva should arrive there along with his celestial mansion. accordingly, the young deva arrived at that spot with his mansion, descended from it, paid homage to the buddha, and stood to one side. the buddha, by questioning the young deva himself about the action he had performed, cleared the doubts of the crowd through a question-and-answer dialogue. the crowd then developed great confidence. "how wondrous is the quality of the buddha! merely by clarifying one's mind toward a buddha, one can obtain such fortune!" they developed great joy and faith. to clarify this matter further, the buddha, based on this event, gave a highly valuable dhamma message to the world through the verse we mentioned earlier:
mano pubbangama dhamma – mano settha manomaya
manasa ce pasannena – bhasati va karoti va
tato nam sukhamanveti – chaya’va anapayini
that is to say, "mind precedes all mental states; mind is their chief, they are mind-made." here, "dhamma" is generally explained as the mental states that arise in the mind, such as feeling (*vedana*), perception, and volition. mind precedes all of them; mind is supreme to them. they are formed and created by the mind. because this is so, "if with a pleasant mind one speaks or acts, happiness follows him, like a shadow that never departs." the buddha declared that the pleasant results of that action follow the person who performed it, just like one's own shadow. the meaning of this verse is so deep that, upon hearing it, not only mattakundali deva but also the brahmin adinnapubbaka attained the fruit of stream-entry. that is to say, perhaps their past matured merits surfaced upon hearing this verse. not only that, it is said that eighty-four thousand beings attained dhamma-realization. here, "thousands" includes devas as well. when we preach the dhamma, it is not only the visible humans who listen, but various non-humans, devas, and spirits who wish to escape from the suffering of samsara and have faith in the triple gem also listen. especially when the buddha preaches the dhamma, everyone listens. that is why those who reaped the benefits are mentioned in thousands.
therefore, we must reflect on this verse. we must also bring the lesson from the background story of this verse close to our lives. from every dhamma sermon and every verse, we must gather some lesson, some dhamma message for our life. listening to the dhamma is not something where merit is gathered merely by the act of hearing. therefore, we can understand that this story is an excellent illustration of how the mind is primary to everything. when we look at the life led by adinnapubbaka, this fact becomes clear to us. no matter how much wealth this brahmin had, he was poor in mind. from this, we can see that being rich or poor is not something that happens through wealth alone. even if one has great wealth, if that person is miserly, he is always poor in mind. due to his miserliness, he thinks, "this is not enough," or "i am still poor. i am not truly rich yet." thus, despite having so much wealth, the brahmin adinnapubbaka was poor in mind—a very destitute person. moreover, the darkness and narrowness of a miserly mind were visible in what the brahmin said and did. from this, we can see that this mind is primary to everything. furthermore, there is the darkening of the mind and its illumination. this is something that must be contemplated very deeply. the buddha has declared that there is a class of dark qualities, and likewise, a class of bright, illuminating qualities.
"abandoning dark qualities, let the wise person develop bright qualities," the buddha declared. dark qualities—meaning greed, hatred, and delusion—these are black/dark qualities. non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are bright qualities. these are illuminating qualities. they are called *sukka-dhamma*. in this way, we see that the brahmin had darkened his mind due to dark qualities. on the other hand, when we reflect on it, the young child mattakundali was not as rich as the brahmin. at the moment of death, he was extremely poor and helpless, having only the two pieces of gold hanging from his ears. yet, how did he obtain such a celestial state of existence? he became rich in mind. he enriched his mind. how did he enrich his mind? we must reflect on this well. he enriched his mind by taking the most sublime, supreme gem in the world as the object of his mind. among all the gems in the world, the buddha-gem is supreme and foremost, as the buddha himself declared. this is also mentioned in the ratana sutta:
'yam kinci vittam idhava huramva
sagge su va yam ratanam panitam
na no samam atthi tathagatena'……
it is mentioned in this manner. if there is any wealth or gem in the world—in this world, or in another world, or in the celestial worlds—none of those gems is as valuable as the buddha-gem, the tathagata. moreover,
'yam kinci ratanam loke
vijjati vividha puthu
ratanam buddhasamam natthi
tasma sotthi bhavantu te'
there are verses of blessing like this. whatever diverse gems exist in the world, there is no gem equal to the buddha-gem. not only that, the buddha himself had to declare—since the world did not recognize the tathagata—that a fully enlightened buddha is the supreme person in the world. in the aggappasada sutta, the buddha declared:
"bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, multi-footed, with form or formless, percipient or non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—the tathagata, the worthy one, the fully enlightened one, is declared supreme among them. those who have confidence in the buddha have confidence in the supreme. and for those who have confidence in the supreme, the result is supreme."
"bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are beings... (gloss of the sinhala text) among all these beings, the tathagata, the worthy, fully enlightened one is supreme and foremost. bhikkhus, those who clarify their minds toward the supreme buddha, clarify their minds toward the foremost person in the world. the result of clarifying the mind toward the foremost person—toward the foremost object—is also supreme," the buddha declared in the aggappasada sutta. from this, we see how immensely fruitful it is to clarify the mind toward the buddha. sometimes we might think, "how can one obtain such fortune merely by clarifying the mind for a single moment?" especially in this era, it is a time when the mind goes toward external things rather than the mind itself. the world talks a lot about their size, magnitude, and wondrous nature. they doubt the power of this unseen mind, the power that can be generated in a single moment. "how can one obtain such a great fortune by doing just this?" but we must reflect: the functioning of the mind is extremely rapid and swift. within this swiftly functioning mind, a power that brings immense fruits can be generated in a single moment. here, mattakundali clarified his mind toward the buddha for only a brief moment, a short time. even that is not necessary. if, for a very brief moment, like the snapping of fingers, some clarity or opening occurs in the mind, through that, one can reap highly valuable and immense benefits. you know—let us think of a dark night. like the rain-stormy nights we have these days, let us think of a night where the darkness is so thick it cannot be pierced. if lightning strikes for a single moment in such a night, in that very brief instant, everything around becomes clearly visible. in the same way, an opening is created in the mind according to the clear object one takes, according to the object toward which one clarifies the mind. in such a dark night, one can get a lot of work done from the light of lightning that appears for a brief moment. there are those in the past who worked in this way. there are stories of the past; just like the marksmen of today, the archers of those days demonstrated their skills (it is mentioned in this way): to show his skill and win prizes, or to set records, an archer stands ready with his arrow in the dark night. he waits for the lightning to strike. far away, a very fine hair taken from a horse's tail is hung. now, what is the feat to be performed? he must split this horsehair with his arrow. he stands ready for this. the moment the lightning strikes, he shoots. if he does this correctly, he is a skilled archer. this is given as a simile—he performed such a great feat within a split second. you have heard our buddhist poets express this:
"if the flash of lightning is missed
when shooting a horsehair from afar in the dark, one misses.
if one does not achieve the path and fruit of nibbana now
when this lightning-like body is obtained, it will be missed in the future."
lovəda sangarava - 25
if one manages to shoot the horsehair in the dark at that precise moment, then one can reap the benefits. many people talk about this "instant" (moment) nowadays. "we must work swiftly in this life." we are talking about the moments within this life. but the buddha declares that our entire human existence is just a single moment, a brief instant. he declares this with reasons. to us, this seems like a long time. but when compared and contrasted with the life spans of the brahma realms which last for aeons, this human life of less than a hundred years is like a single moment. this life, which we think of as so grand and in which we spend a few years in this long samsara, is actually a single moment. therefore, the buddha refers to this entire human life as a single moment. the buddha particularly demonstrates that the human existence obtained during the time of a buddha's arising is not just a moment, but a consummation of the moment (*khana-sampatti*). it is described as an extremely rare opportunity, a rare moment—a consummation of the moment. if one is born in a region where one can listen to the dhamma, with the capacity for understanding and wisdom to practice the dhamma during the time of a buddha's arising, that is called *khana-sampatti* (the consummation of the moment). it is an extremely valuable moment. that is the moment the poet illustrated. "when this lightning-like body is obtained" refers to this human existence. this human body exists for such a brief moment, just like a flash of lightning. therefore, we must understand this moment, as buddhists, looking at this entire human life as a single moment.
if we reflect in this way, generating wholesome thoughts and performing meritorious deeds is not something we should wait to do until our final moment, like mattakundali did. we should not entertain the wrong view that we can go to heaven by doing this only at the moment of death. sometimes, some people think this way nowadays. they gather wealth unlawfully and commit various crimes. at the final moment, they expect to summon a bhikkhu, listen to a little dhamma, and go to heaven. mattakundali was able to do that because he was someone who had fulfilled perfections and developed himself under past buddhas; but things do not succeed for everyone just because of that. in truth, mattakundali deva obtained such a state due to a certain natural law (*dhammata*), a deep principle concerning kamma. for, beings are born in various places according to their kamma. however, what is called *asanna-kamma*—the kamma generated in accordance with the sign (*nimitta*) that appears at the moment of death—is extremely powerful. that is why the buddha walked there to give mattakundali an opportunity to purify his near-death mind and perform merit. but not everyone can perform that feat. sometimes, due to the unwholesome deeds done during one's lifetime, another sign appears, and one is forced to take birth in a bad destination. the archer shot the horsehair in that manner only after putting in effort and training for a long time. it is not something that can be done all at once. what we have to understand here is that we must not wait until the near-death moment or old age. thinking of our entire life as a single moment, we must always strive to generate this mind—this pleasant, clarified, pure, and bright mind—within ourselves. for, if those dark qualities present themselves, we will fall into darkness. if we bring forward bright qualities, we will be born in a good place. not only that, we can gradually draw closer to nibbana. nibbana means liberating the mind from these dark qualities of greed, hatred, and delusion.
from this, we can understand the value of this moment, and also that this is something that must be practiced and trained constantly. just as the archer strives in this regard, a buddhist must always keep watch over the mind. "are the states arising in this mind things that lead to the mind's clarity, or are they things that agitate it?" now, the word for clarity—here, "pasanna" means clarity. in the case of mattakundali deva, what is mentioned is the fruit of that clarified mind. we can understand the value of clarity: after a rain, when water flows with mud, looking very unpleasant, what is the state of our mind? next, when we look at clear, pure water, our mind becomes clear. in the same way, when we collect a noble object, a supreme object like the buddha into our mind, when we bring it close to our mind, our mind becomes clear. therefore, the word that goes hand in hand with faith (*saddha*) is *pasada* (clarity/confidence). it is said, "saddha-pasannena" (clarified with faith). clarity goes together with faith. from this, we see that faith in the triple gem is an extremely important thing. a mind lacking faith in the triple gem is darkened by doubt, hesitation, and skepticism—just like troubled, muddy water. but if someone develops faith in the buddha, a great clarity arises in the mind along with it. this is something that you can realize even in your day-to-day life.
that mattakundali deva clarified his mind by seeing the physical form, the body, of the buddha. although we do not get to see that physical body of the buddha now, we can see his dhamma-body. we can see the quality-body of the buddha. therefore, what we specifically have to understand here is the value of the 'recollection of the buddha' (*buddhanussati*). contemplating the qualities of the buddha. through the qualities of the buddha, we can see the buddha. if we contemplate the ninefold qualities of the buddha, direct our mind toward those qualities like *arahant*, bring forward some quality that suits our mind, and train ourselves to bring up some word like "arahant, arahant, arahant" or "buddho", "samma-sambuddho" constantly in our mind like a meditation, we can obtain great clarity and a light for our day-to-day activities. as stated in the verse, if someone speaks or acts with a pleasant mind, a clarified mind, the happy results follow him like his shadow. it is our mind that provides light to the words we use and the actions we perform. when this mind is clarified, a great light is created in the mind, like a flash of lightning on a pitch-black night.
therefore, to constantly bring up clarity toward the triple gem in the mind, one must practice contemplating the qualities of the buddha as the recollection of the buddha (*buddhanussati*). while traveling in a vehicle, while in a city—now there is no specific time. we must think that every moment is the near-death moment now. especially when thinking about these times, some people think of the near-death moment as being eighty or ninety years old, surrounded by children and grandchildren. now we must step out onto the road thinking we are in our near-death moment. such is the state of affairs. therefore, we must be much more mindful of the mind. if we pass away—if we die suddenly—at a bad time, when the mind is corrupted, darkened, or muddied, where will we go and be born? in a dark place. either in hell, the ghost realm, or the demon realm. we said that there are two groups: dark qualities and bright qualities. there are two factions in this mind. whatever factions there may be in the world, we must be concerned about the factions in this mind, because we carry our mind wherever we go. therefore, the dark faction in this mind consists of greed, hatred, and delusion. these three are the prominent figures of that dark faction: greed, hatred, and delusion. there are many other subsidiary qualities associated with them. next, the bright qualities that support nibbana are non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred, and non-delusion. at first glance, there seems to be nothing there when we say "non-greed" (*alobha*). what is this non-greed? it is sometimes difficult to understand. this non-greed means turning away from greed. turning away from greed may sometimes be thought of as a small thing. this is not a small thing. this is called a mental factor of abstinence (*virati-cetasika*)—the thought of abstaining.
this thought of turning away (abstaining) is a very powerful thing. now, something that mainly supports this is virtue (*sila*), the undertaking of virtue. undertaking the precepts. on this occasion, for you to abstain from killing living beings—indeed, when undertaking the precepts, one must pronounce the word "veramani" (abstinence) well. "panatipata veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami"—i undertake the precept of abstaining from destroying life, from killing living beings. this is a promise one makes to oneself, that "i accept this and put it into practice." though one declares this in front of the sangha, it is actually a promise to oneself. or, one places it in one's mind: "i will spend this day in this manner, based on this practice." then, for the person who has resolved thus, let us say an occasion arises—either for food, for pleasure, or to settle a grudge—where he feels like killing someone or an animal. the moment that thought arises, he can push it aside through non-hatred. he brings forward loving-kindness (*metta*), compassion (*karuna*), sympathy, and non-harming (*avihimsa*), recalls the virtue he has undertaken, and abstains from it. taking this as an illustration, that moment is an extremely valuable moment—the power of the mind to turn away. that is what is called the mental factor of abstinence (*virati-cetasika*). it is called *sampatta-virati* (abstinence when confronted with an opportunity). that is, the opportunity to commit a sin arose, but one does not do it. one withdraws one's hand. say, to commit a theft—he knows it is a valuable thing belonging to someone else. it is right in front of him, and no one is around. all he has to do is look around and quietly extend his hand. but at that moment, the mind says, "do not do that." why does it feel that way? it is because of undertaking that virtue: "adinnadana veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami." accordingly, we see that this undertaking of virtue is no small matter. it is not merely a custom—nowadays, at every meeting or festival, to show that one is a buddhist, they repeat the undertaking of virtue. but when we reflect on its depth, how powerful and important a thing is it? it is the first step in our life. thus, in this way—it is called "by way of substitution of opposites" (*tadanga-vasena*)—the mind distances itself from the defilements. for each such moment, by applying a wholesome thought, one distances the unwholesome thought. one must also accumulate wholesome thoughts within oneself for this. one must develop loving-kindness to overcome hatred. to overcome greed, one must develop giving, generosity, and the quality of sacrifice. to overcome delusion, one must utilize understanding, wisdom, reflection, wise reflection, and contemplating things as they really are. therefore, the moment we say "non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion," it seems as if there is nothing there. but if we analyze and reflect on it, we are talking about a power here—called *virati* (abstinence)—that can subdue and drive away those unwholesome qualities that come from outside as visitors and enemies.
this is not a feat that can be done all at once. therefore, we must constantly develop the mind by way of meditation. the buddha mentions three words when declaring meditation: "asevati, bhaveti, bahulikaroti." one constantly associates with a wholesome object. if it is the recollection of the buddha, one constantly associates with a word like "arahant, arahant, arahant" or "buddho," like one's companion at home, constantly bringing it up and living with it—*asevati*. *bhaveti* means one develops it. when one says it a second time, a greater power comes to the mind than the first time. saying that word "buddha" ten times, a thousand times, a million or a billion times, one's faith in the triple gem develops more and more. this is not merely reciting it as a mantra. the heart must function along with it. a clarity must arise in the heart. in the same way, if one develops loving-kindness, using the words "may they be well and happy," one must constantly associate with that meditation object according to what one has chosen. one must strive to develop the mind through that—this is meditation (*bhavana*).
next, there is a word, *bahuli-kamma*—*bahulikaroti*, making much of it. that means not just for a day or two, or for an hour or half-hour, but abundantly. one must strive oneself. no matter how many activities one has in day-to-day life, if one has understood the value of one's mind—we take so much trouble for this body. to nourish this body, to bathe it, wash it, adorn it, all of this. this "foul body that is left behind." how much do we attend to it? yet, we do not think about the value of the mind even for a very brief moment of the day. it is this mind that helps us to escape from samsara, and also to bring about a good destination (*sugati*). if one reflects in this way, one becomes keen about meditation. in the manner described by *asevati, bhaveti, bahulikaroti*, one must constantly bring up a wholesome object to the mind and live with it. even if it seems difficult or troublesome at first, once it is practiced, one can do it effortlessly, as if naturally—almost automatically. when one puts on a pair of spectacles for the first time, it is a great nuisance. but after a few days, one can work very easily with those spectacles. after some time, one even looks for them while they are on one's face, asking, "where are my spectacles?" why is this? to that extent, the spectacles have become a part of one's body.
the meditation object is also like that. then, to the person who has developed the recollection of the buddha, when danger comes—nowadays, people sometimes scream, "budu amme!" (oh buddha, mother!). according to past customs, the word "budu" (buddha) has been integrated into our society. but that is not a mechanical utterance when pain arises. it is from the whole heart—mattakundali obtained that state by clarifying his mind with his whole heart, not by saying it merely as a custom or a mantra. one must reflect in that manner. one must reflect on the maximum benefit one can gain from every story and strive to reap it. one must reflect on the maximum benefit and strive to reap it. according to the matters stated in this verse, we see that our mind is primary to the words we use and the actions we perform. that is the uniqueness of the buddha's dhamma. nowadays, there are various scientific methods of thinking. they are often formulated according to wrong views. because they give priority to physical and external things. because they are clearly visible and possess colorful qualities, we are deceived by them. but the buddha has pointed out the truth. in this long samsaric journey of ours, what is primary, what goes ahead—what helps our actions (*kamma*) to become good or bad—is this mind that arises in us.
"mano pubbangama dhamma – mano settha manomaya"
not only that, they are created by the mind itself. according to this story, it is very clearly shown. that celestial body of mattakundali was created by the mind itself. it was visible to humans. beings present at that time saw: "alas, by merely clarifying his mind toward the buddha at the final moment, the brahmin’s son obtained such a celestial state of existence with golden ornaments, didn't he?" that is why, through that very faith, the other necessary qualities gathered in his mind and he attained the realization of the paths and fruits. therefore, very valuable and deep dhamma is contained within this story which we might think of as simple.
thus, creating an opening in the mind at each such moment is what is done through practicing virtue and other qualities. this is the purification or clarification of the mind by way of substitution of opposites (*tadanga-vasena*). there are three stages in this effort of development. they are mentioned in the dhamma as *tadanga* (substitution of opposites), *vikkhambhana* (suppression), and *samuccheda* (eradication). what is done through virtue (*sila*)—in observing the precepts—is that at each moment, one presents a wholesome thought and drives away the unwholesome. next, a slightly more established and developed stage than that is concentration (*samadhi*). that too is like this: if one develops meditation through the recollection of the buddha and the like, and controls the running mind—the mind that runs after various things and objects—through some good meditation subject, through the words "may they be well and happy" or through some meditation object like "buddho" or "arahant," after some time, the mind becomes calm. this calming is called concentration (*samadhi*). the qualities that darken the mind are referred to in the dhamma as hindrances (*nivarana*). sensory desires, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and worry, and doubt—all of these are suppressed, and just as the mud settles and the water in a pond becomes clear, an occasion comes when the mind is clarified. that is called concentration (*samadhi*). that is also a stage one can experience through a meditation subject—a very special state where the mind's clarity is greater than before.
next, finally, the stage that goes even deeper is called eradication (*samuccheda*). there are those heavy defilements, the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), which we have carried along throughout samsara. they lie suppressed. to dry them up, to eliminate them, one must develop wisdom (*panna*). by reflecting on this entire body, on this life, as impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*), and developing insight (*vipassana*), at some point, the mind becomes illuminated. it becomes illuminated by wisdom. the qualities that support this are, as stated in the satipatthana sutta, mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajanna*), developing mindfulness, and wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*). if one reflects in that manner and develops meditation so that wisdom grows, and if one develops the three characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and not-self, then at the moment of realizing the paths and fruits, through insight-wisdom, one can generate the power within the mind to destroy the lower layers of those unwholesome deeds, or defilements, that we carry throughout samsara.
thus, virtue (*sila*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*)—this is the dispensation (*sasana*); this is what belongs to us. many people explain the buddha's dispensation in various ways. but the buddha's dispensation is actually the cultivation of virtue, concentration, and wisdom within one's own mind-stream (*citta-santana*). what helps in this, the first necessary thing, is our understanding of the value of this mind of ours—that the mind precedes everything, that the mind is chief, and that these are made by the mind. regarding those celestial states of existence, it is very well known how they are made by the mind itself. leaving that aside, though we do not think about it day-to-day, let us say the potter who makes a vessel like a pot makes it with some mental picture or plan of that pot, and according to that, he takes a lump of clay and creates a pot. likewise, if someone manufactured everything that is in front of us, the first perception (*sanna*) of that manufacturing occurred in the mind. a plan arose. even when building a building, it is the same. so, where did this plan arise? in the mind. later, using the four great elements—earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and air (*vayo*)—when it appeared as a form (*rupa*), then next, we are deceived by it. humans think this is the great thing. but many people do not think about the plan that lies beneath this. what the buddha did was to remind the world of this. it is through that alone that one can escape from samsara. therefore, one must reflect with wisdom. this is what is called right view (*samma-ditthi*). wrong view (*miccha-ditthi*) means giving priority to unsuitable, improper, or wrong things. right view, correct vision, means bringing forward those qualities that help one escape from the suffering of samsara, in the manner declared by the buddha.
therefore, according to this verse, we must reflect. we must reflect on our own lives—regardless of age limits. "how am i leading my life? is it in the way the world says, in the way society goes, or in the way pointed out by the buddha?" reflecting thus, one must prepare a plan necessary for one's day-to-day life. in this plan, there must be a place for virtue (*sila*). there must be a place for concentration (*samadhi*). there must be a place for wisdom (*panna*). "a place" means understanding their values and leading one's day-to-day life in a way that brings them forward. on this occasion, you undertook virtue—the eight precepts with right livelihood as the eighth (*ajiva-atthamaka-sila*). through this, you can liberate the mind by way of substitution of opposites (*tadanga-vasena*). just like the archer shooting the horsehair by the light of lightning, in those minor moments when unwholesome thoughts present themselves—when a thought to do wrong arises—you present your virtue and drive it away. next, if someone has developed the power of concentration, he can experience the mind's clarity, pleasantness, and light for a longer period. next, through the realization of the paths and fruits—stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship—if someone has developed wisdom, developed insight-knowledges, and obtained that liberation from samsara, then he can experience the most valuable state in the world—the purest state of one's mind.
therefore, you must reflect on utilizing this dispensation of the buddha, on utilizing the human existence we have obtained. this is an extremely rare thing. even devas sometimes say that this human existence, this human world, is the best place to realize nibbana. though it is a short, brief period, if utilized properly during this time, this human mind can be elevated to the highest state. that is why buddhas are born only in the human world. that is why a buddha arises and appears only in the world. reflecting in that way, you must take advantage of the opportunity you have received. from every dhamma sermon, you must gain some lesson for your life, reflect on the defilements that arise in the mind as dark, and to drive them away, you must develop those wholesome qualities called *sukka-dhamma* in your mind: generosity, loving-kindness, wisdom, and dhamma-realization. on this occasion, even by listening to the dhamma, you can clarify your mind. for, through the dhamma, we see the buddha. when listening to the dhamma, the doubts, worries, and hesitations in one's mind are removed, and a clarity arises in the mind. clarity of mind is extremely necessary. it is through that that the true nature of the world is seen. when the mind is darkened, darkened by delusion (*moha*), the true nature is not seen. therefore, one's words go wrong, and both words and actions incline toward the unwholesome and sinful side. therefore, this samsara is generally a journey that inclines toward defilements, inclines toward darkness. to escape from this, one must generate a great power.
in truth, when we consider the meanings of the two words *kusala* and *akusala*, *kusala* means being skilled. *akusala* means being unskilled. in this samsaric journey, inclining toward the plane of misery is being unskilled; inclining toward good destinations is being skilled. next, having to continue in samsara is being unskilled; bringing the suffering of samsara to a swift end is being skilled. reflecting in this way, what we call mundane and supramundane *kusala*—this *kusala* means being skilled, being skilled. this being skilled, like the archer, is not something that can be done all at once. this must be developed over a long time. therefore, from today itself, you must strive at every moment—without thinking there is no time. in day-to-day life, people say there is no time. but everyone has time that is wasted. this can be well recognized; although you may not hear it in dhamma sermons, there is a word often heard in society: "loitering" (wasting time/loitering). this wasting of time is a time when rust accumulates in the mind, a time when the mind is darkened. this wasting of time is often heard of in day-to-day life, especially in cities: "i went to such and such an office and wasted time there." wasting time on the road. this occasion is an extremely good opportunity to bring forward your practiced meditation subject—let us think of the buddha-gem; like taking a gem from one's pocket, looking at it, and rejoicing, on such occasions, if you bring forward the buddha-gem—the supreme gem in the world mentioned here—in a way invisible to others, not because others would snatch it, as they might have no use for it anyway—but by bringing forward the buddha-gem: "buddho, buddho, buddho" or "arahant, arahant, arahant," then he has made use of that wasted time. or, "may they be well and happy," some meditation subject he has taken. or, the in-breaths and out-breaths of one's body, which is called mindfulness of breathing (*anapanasati*). if one utilizes those wasted, spent times, then without even knowing it, he becomes a meditator. in the end, almost without knowing it—we say "without knowing it" because the behavior of the mind is so wondrous—if the mind has matured, at unexpected moments, one even obtains the realization of the paths and fruits almost without knowing it.
in the past, when the buddha preached the dhamma, the saying that someone became an arahant or a stream-enterer even while listening to a sermon is sometimes misunderstood by modern intellectual scholars. "we too can do it that way," they think. it was only to those minds that had practiced and trained in those qualities over a long period under past buddhas or in past dispensations, and developed them to a high level, requiring only a tiny bit more, that the realization of the paths and fruits could be obtained so swiftly. one should not think that everyone is like that. but the lesson we have to take from it is: if someone wants to obtain such a state in such a short time, it must be practiced over a long period. it must be trained. one must strive to create opportunities for that within one's own life.
thus, on this valuable uposatha day, you undertook a valuable virtue—the eight precepts with right livelihood as the eighth (*ajiva-atthamaka-sila*). if this is not merely a custom, reflecting on each one—what is present here is a set of principles concerning the control of body and speech—this is virtue (*sila*). to protect it, the mind must support it. the mind supports it through what was called the mental factor of abstinence (*virati-cetasika*)—that mind of turning away. one must bring forward the mind of turning away from these stated matters. saying "do not do these things" is easier. that is why the buddha has applied the word *veramani* (abstinence) in these qualities of virtue. scholars sometimes think there is nothing in this. it is in this that something exists. therefore, this eight precepts with right livelihood as the eighth—if one directs the mind well even when undertaking this virtue, that moment is also an occasion when a great opening is created in the mind. "i did these things before. from now on, i will not do them," one places a resolution in the mind. that is a great thing. if that resolution was taken in the morning, and if one was able to protect it throughout the day, a clarity, confidence, and happiness arise in one's mind in the evening. such is virtue. next, likewise, if one has practiced some meditation subject in day-to-day life—on those wasted times mentioned earlier—without saying it is difficult or there is no time, during whatever leisure moments or times one can be happy and rejoice, if one brings forward that meditation subject and develops the mind, then without even knowing it, one grows in concentration (*samadhi*). at some point, the mind can even fall into absorption (*jhana*). having worked hard and contemplated that meditation subject, when one lies down on the bed, one may obtain absorption even while on the bed.
it was by doing so that lay devotees of the past, like nakulamata, nakulapita, citta the householder, and anathapindika, obtained such high states. those were not lives spent being immersed in matters of money; such was not the way of buddhist lay devotees, upasakas and upasikas, during the buddha's time. inclining toward the dhamma, somehow finding time for the dhamma, they were able to develop concentration in that way. next, what is more valuable is finally utilizing that concentration to understand the true nature of the world—its impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*) nature—through the very events that happen in day-to-day life. in truth, every event that happens in the world can be placed within these three characteristics: impermanent, suffering, and not-self. this is a three-character sign. this sign can be seen everywhere. wherever one looks. but for that, proper reflection must be present. there must be correct vision, which is called wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*). for the person with correct vision, insight can be developed through the streams, brooks, and rivers flowing in this world, the fruits and flowers falling from these trees, and through everything. the three characteristics of impermanent, suffering, and not-self can be seen. in that way, one must reflect well on how one can guide one's mind in day-to-day life. without putting this off saying "i cannot," and thinking "i must clarify my mind only in old age or at the near-death moment to go to a heaven like mattakundali," if one thinks so, then this dhamma sermon has been understood in a wrong way. it has been understood in a perverted way. that is not how one should think. there is a saying in this world: "if it is this much for that, how much would it be for this?" in that way, if one can do such a great thing with the mind in a brief moment, what can one not do when it is well developed? one must reflect in that manner.
reflecting thus, today, through the undertaking of virtue, and through listening to the dhamma and clarifying the mind toward the triple gem, you made a beginning in traveling on the path of dhamma declared in this verse. we must aspire: "may this store of merit generated through that, by cultivating and developing within our mind-stream the spiritual faculties and powers (*indriya* and *bala* qualities) that support nibbana—such as faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—enable us, if possible in this very life, through the realization of the paths and fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship, to realize this noble dhamma of nibbana, and escaping from all samsaric suffering (*dukkha*) such as birth (*jati*), aging (*jara*), sickness, and death (*marana*), to attain the peace of supreme nibbana."
likewise, to whatever extent there is a host of right-viewed devas and brahmas protecting the dispensation, and likewise, whatever devas and deities residing in this sacred place who wish for merit and wish for nibbana, may they all rejoice in this merit of our preaching and hearing of the dhamma. having rejoiced, may they all realize supreme nibbana through their aspired enlightenment (*bodhi*). whatever relatives have passed away and departed to the world beyond, and not only that, whatever beings from avici hell up to the akanitha heaven who wish for merit and wish for nibbana, may they all rejoice in our merit of preaching and hearing the dhamma. having escaped from their miserable destinations and walking on the path of dhamma, may they all attain the peace of supreme nibbana as quickly as possible. now, let us share merit by reciting verses in this manner.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 014
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #14
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No. )
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Susukhaṃ vata jīvāma, verinesu averino; Verinesu manussesu, viharāma averino. Susukhaṃ vata jīvāma, āturesu anāturā; Āturesu manussesu, viharāma anāturā. Susukhaṃ vata jīvāma, ussukesu anussukā; Ussukesu manussesu, viharāma anussukā.
From:
Verses 197-199 from the Sukhavagga (Chapter on Happiness) of the Dhammapada
Dear Listeners,
The desire for happiness is a common phenomenon shared by all living beings in the entire human world. The whole world is engaged in a journey of seeking happiness. However, this journey in search of happiness often ends in suffering (*dukkha*). The reason for this is that the ordinary worldling, whose eyes are covered by ignorance and bound by craving (*taṇhā*), seeks happiness through the wrong path. They have fallen into this state because they do not correctly know either true happiness or the path to it. Aspiring to fulfill the perfections (*pāramīs*) for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand cosmic cycles, our Teacher of the Three Worlds, the Buddha, attained Supreme Enlightenment on a Vesak full-moon day like today, in order to introduce the true happiness and the path to true happiness to the beings of the world who are running around in search of it. The Buddha, utilizing His great wisdom and great compassion, intervened on many occasions and delivered Dhamma discourses to steer the beings of the world away from seeking happiness through the wrong path and to introduce them to true happiness. Now, these three verses we have taken as our theme, along with their related story, demonstrate to us how the Buddha, relying on His quality of supreme guide of persons to be tamed (*anuttaro purisadamma sārathī*), employing skillful means out of great compassion, and clarifying the true nature of the Dhamma with great wisdom, brought peace and solace to the world.
A river named Rohini flows between the city of Kapilavastu, belonging to the Sakya clan, and the city of Koliya, belonging to the Koliya clan. Having built a dam across this river and utilizing its water, the farmers of both these cities—of both these kingdoms—cultivate their fields. During a certain drought, both groups realized that the water was depleting, saying, "Both of our groups cannot carry out this cultivation; this water is sufficient only for one group." Then, these two factions gathered and began to dispute and argue to claim the water for themselves. Having fallen into bickering, quarreling, and trading insults about their lineages, this commotion eventually reached the ears of the royal clans and the royal palaces of both factions. Ultimately, circumstances developed to the point of a major war. The kings of both sides, chanting battle slogans, set out for war. Precisely at dawn on that day, when the Buddha was surveying the world with His great compassion, He saw that if He did not visit the place, his own two relative royal clans would destroy each other, resulting in a great bloodbath. Seeing this, the Buddha traveled alone through the air and sat cross-legged in mid-air over the middle of the Rohini River.
As soon as the Buddha arrived there and they saw Him, the kings of both the Sakya and Koliya clans cast down their weapons and paid homage to Him. The Buddha asked, "Great kings, what is the cause of this dispute?" Those kings were unable to declare in one voice what the primary cause of this war was. Why? Because after they had insulted each other's lineages, it was actually the hatred (*dosa*) arising from those insults that had dragged them into war in this manner. Even the kings themselves did not know the underlying cause. Then they stated to the Buddha: "We do not know. Perhaps the commander-in-chief knows." When the commander-in-chief was summoned and questioned, he too said he did not know. He said, "Perhaps the viceroy (*yuvarāja*) knows." Questioning in this manner, it was finally revealed that the dispute initiated by the farmers was the cause that had set the stage for this war. Then the Buddha asked both factions, "Great kings, how much is this water worth?" "Water, Venerable Sir, is worth very little. Water is a thing of negligible value." "How much are these warrior-kings (*kṣatriya*) worth?" "That, indeed, is of priceless, inestimable value." "Then, great kings, why do you destroy precious human lives for the sake of something so worthless?" When the Buddha questioned thus, the kings had no answer to give. Thereafter, the Buddha preached the Dhamma through the verses we have themed. He uttered those verses declaring, "You are all keeping your minds in an extremely restless state through hatred, defilements, and the pursuit of fivefold sensual pleasures; but among such a world, I live experiencing true happiness in this manner."
"Ah, happily do we live, free from hatred among the hateful;
Among hateful men, we dwell free from hatred."
"Ah, happily do we live, free from hatred among the hateful"—among hateful human beings, among the hateful living beings of the world, we—"we" refers to the Buddha and those noble ones who have calmed their defilements—dwell free from hatred. "Ah, happily do we live" means very happily; *sukhaṃ* means happiness, and *susukhaṃ* means extreme happiness. Experiencing happiness of the very highest level, we dwell free from hatred among a hateful world. "Among hateful men, we dwell free from hatred." We dwell free from hatred among hateful beings. Similarly, "Ah, happily do we live, free from affliction among the afflicted"—among beings afflicted and diseased with defilements, we live very happily, free from affliction—without that affliction of defilements. "Among afflicted men, we dwell free from affliction"—among such beings afflicted by defilements, we dwell free from affliction. In the same way, "Ah, happily do we live, free from anxiety among the anxious"—among restless beings who are anxious and straining themselves in the pursuit of the fivefold sensual pleasures, we live happily, free from such searching. In that manner, the Buddha uttered these three verses based on the happiness of Nibbāna (Nibbāna-sukha*) He had attained. Upon hearing this, many attained the fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). Furthermore, the war ended right there.
Now, let us direct our thoughts toward this peaceful message of solace given by the Buddha. Particularly, with reference to this incident, we can understand the manner in which anger, rage, and hatred arise in the world. Whatever wars occur in the world, the beginning of every single one is the human mind. The hatred that arises as a seed in a human mind gradually matures. Once this becomes resentment, and ultimately deep-seated hatred, that defilement burns oneself while burning others, directing beings toward destruction for a long time. Furthermore, you have heard the past stories regarding the elder Devadatta. How many aeons (*kalpas*) into the future did that hatred Devadatta conceived against the Bodhisatta in the past extend? It is the impermanent (*anicca*) nature of such things in the world that we must contemplate first of all. Especially, this era is one in which the fire of hatred, the fire of anger, is spreading everywhere, both in this country and in the entire world. In such a context, what the worldling considers as happiness is fighting and gaining victory. There is a concept called "drinking the cup of victory"; many people, without recognizing the restlessness within themselves, expect peace and solace by subduing or putting to death their opponent and then celebrating victory. But the Buddha has declared:
"Victory breeds hatred; the defeated lies down in suffering (*dukkha*).
The peaceful one lies down happily, abandoning both victory and defeat."
If someone achieves victory, what arises from it is further hatred. The peaceful person, having abandoned both victory and defeat, dwells happily. Moreover, it is the word of the Buddha that hatred is never appeased by hatred. Thus, we understand how much destruction this thought of hatred causes throughout the world. If this is not properly treated at its very inception, it is just like a pathogen. Now, in a place where pathogens spread, some form of vaccination or immunization is required. Where there is no immunization, pathogens multiply dangerously and make a person sick. It is the same with this hatred. In some people, when proper practices like loving-kindness meditation (*mettā-bhāvanā*) are absent, these tendencies become character traits. There is a constant state of irritability, hatred, and overflowing anger. Such a person is described in the Dhamma as *arukūpamo puggala*, "a person comparable to an open sore." *Aruka* means a wound or sore. When a person with an open sore goes into a crowd, whenever the crowd jostles even slightly here and there, this person gets angry because his wound gets irritated. In that way, a person with intense hatred is compared to a wounded patient. Due to that hatred, a nature of constant collision arises. He collides everywhere—with people, and often with things. With every such collision, what is the transformation that occurs within this person’s mind? Not only does that dangerous defilement of hatred manifest at that particular moment, but it also leads him to states like demons, hungry ghosts (*petas*), or hell (*niraya*) according to karma over a long period in *saṃsāra*, bringing him long-lasting suffering (*dukkha*). Moreover, once that thought grows, it expresses itself through the tongue as harsh speech. It does not end there. After bickering and quarreling, it manifests in action, leading one to dangerous unwholesome deeds such as the destruction of life. In this way, one must contemplate the disadvantageous side (*ādīnava*) of hatred beforehand.
Next, the Buddha has declared five methods to appease deep-seated hatred—which is called *āghāta*, harboring resentment or a grudge. First—there is no need to explain this anew—is loving-kindness (*mettā*) itself; practicing loving-kindness meditation. Second is compassion (*karuṇā*). In certain situations, compassion also helps to understand the weaknesses of one's opponent. Considering it as a saṃsāric weakness, as an illness, one should look at the person who has harbored resentment or hatred as a sick person, as a wounded patient. Then, by making compassion the path and the medium, one can appease the deep-seated hatred or intense resentment that has arisen within oneself. In other instances, equanimity (*upekkhā*) is used. Equanimity means impartial looking. Contemplating: "This person's body and my body are both made of these great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind (*pathavī, āpo, tejo, vāyo*). Toward which part of this person am I directing hatred?" In this way, one endeavors to arouse equanimity. The Buddha has declared that equanimity is also something that aids in appeasing hatred. Also, there is "forgetting and non-attention" (*asati amanasikāra*—not remembering, not paying attention). Hatred grows because it is repeatedly brought to mind. To remove this tendency of its arising, one must try not to pay attention to it. One must direct the mind to ignore it. It is because of the intention of revenge for the wrong done to oneself that it keeps arising repeatedly. Instead, one must try to forget it. Also, another method is shown: contemplating in accordance with the Dhamma that all beings are owners of their karma (*kamma-dāyāda*). That is, thinking of the natural law (*dharmatā*) that according to karma, whoever does wrong will experience its fruits and results. Now, for many people, hatred arises—what they call "righteous anger"—in order to "teach others a lesson." Thinking in that way: "I must teach them a lesson." But one does not see the hatred within oneself. It remains hidden as a deceptive state (*vañcaka dhamma*). Therefore, one must think: "This is the natural law of the world. If someone commits a wrong, they will have to suffer the consequences according to karma. We should not become the instruments for that. If we become the instruments to punish them, we too will have to experience the retributive results." In this manner, the Buddha has shown five ways to appease deep-seated hatred.
This is something one can experience and utilize for oneself in daily life. Furthermore, a monk highly renowned in this dispensation for virtues such as loving-kindness and compassion is the Chief Disciple, the Great Sariputta. On one occasion, he expounded five ways to the community of monks to appease this deep-seated hatred called *āghāta*. He presents incredibly wondrous similes. He demonstrates: suppose someone has conceived hatred or resentment toward another person. That person's physical conduct is impure—that is, his bodily behavior is very bad—but his verbal conduct is very pleasant and good. Or, there is no fault in his verbal behavior. Venerable Sariputta demonstrates with a simile how one should act when hatred arises toward such a person. Just as a monk who uses rag-robes (*paṃsukūla-cīvara*), while walking along a path or street, upon finding a piece of cloth, steps on one end with his left foot, tears off the clean portion with his right hand, takes it and goes his way; likewise, at that moment, one should not contemplate that person's bad physical conduct. Without thinking about his physical behavior, one contemplates only the good side. Bringing to the fore the fact that his verbal behavior is good, one appeases one's own hatred. This is the simile he gives. This is not to be taken as something unique only to those monks, but each individual must understand it through the help of this simile. This refers to a person who has both a good side and a bad side. Or let us say, the bad side is the physical conduct, and the good side is the verbal conduct. If we want to cultivate our hatred and resentment, we are inclined to think only of the bad side. Sometimes, the virtue of a person, which is as vast as a mountain, can be erased by a fault as small as a shred. One enjoys a certain misplaced pleasure, a misplaced delight, through that thought of hatred. But one does not benefit; one burns. That happens because of contemplating what should not be contemplated. Therefore, Venerable Sariputta declares, taking that simile to heart—monks who wear rag-robes do not just abandon a dirty piece of cloth when they find it. They take only the usable portion of it. In the same way, recollecting the good side of that person, one inclines one's mind toward loving-kindness. One inclines it toward compassion. Thus, one appeases that deep-seated hatred which yields dangerous results.
Similarly, in the next simile, there is a person whose physical conduct is pure, but verbal conduct is impure. That is, the actions done by body are good, but the things done by speech are bad. What is the simile Venerable Sariputta gives to appease the deep-seated hatred that arises toward such a person? Suppose someone, in a time of great drought, during the hot season, comes searching for water with a severe thirst. There is a pond, but its water is covered with algae. Since he needs to drink water, he somehow pushes aside the algae with both hands, drinks as much water as he needs, and goes his way. In that simile, the algae represents the shortcomings in that person's speech. What is shown is that without contemplating those, one should take only the good part. In that manner, according to the diversity of each individual, Venerable Sariputta has shown a way to discipline one’s feelings, a method of proper reflection.
Next, thirdly, it is shown: indeed, there can be a person whose physical conduct is very bad, and verbal conduct is also very bad, but occasionally, from time to time, a pure and clear state of mind arises, though very rarely. The simile Venerable Sariputta gives to appease hatred toward such a person is truly wonderful. Suppose in a time of drought, a person is searching for water, extremely thirsty. On his way, there is no water anywhere else. There is only a little water in a puddle formed by a cow's footprint. Seeing this, this person does not think, "Now I must bring a bucket and drink this water" or "I must put both hands in and drink it." Why? Because then the water will get muddied. That is something that cannot be done. Therefore, depending on the situation, what does that person do? He falls on all fours like a cow and laps up the water with his tongue. Why? Because of his thirst in the drought. What does Venerable Sariputta show through this simile? No matter how bad a side that person has—there is nothing of worth in his physical conduct, nothing of worth in his verbal conduct—yet occasionally, just like a brief flash of lightning in a pitch-black night, a tiny opening appears in his mind. That is enough for one to cultivate loving-kindness and arouse compassion. That is the lesson Venerable Sariputta teaches. Forgetting the unsuitable side and contemplating, "Oh, although he is so bad, is there not at least this little bit of good to be taken from this person?" one appeases one's hatred. All this is done for one's own sake. If that fire of hatred grows in one's mind, one will have to suffer grave consequences in *saṃsāra* as well. Not only that, but even in this life, because it grows and ultimately leads to brawls, murders, and so on. That is the third simile.
Next, Venerable Sariputta demonstrates: indeed, there can be a person whose physical conduct is very bad—nothing of worth. Verbal conduct—also nothing of worth. Furthermore, it is said that not even occasionally, like a flash of lightning, does any goodness arise in his mind, nor does any pleasant state arise. To put it briefly, he is a person of whom there is "absolutely nothing of worth." Yet, the attitude one must adopt even toward such a person is shown next. Suppose someone sees an extremely poor, sick, and helpless person traveling on a desert road. He has no food to carry, no water to drink, no guide to show the way, no food, and no medicine. In that manner, in an extremely miserable and helpless state, he travels along the path. How does a wise person who sees this contemplate? "Oh, if only someone would help this helpless person and show him the way! If only someone would give him some food, some medicine, so that he would not perish but somehow survive!" In this way, a thought of compassion is aroused. Generally, such thoughts arise in those who feel compassion when seeing such a person. Through this simile, we are to think that even if there is absolutely nothing of worth to be taken from the person who has done wrong to us, we must still show compassion to that person. What we show through all these similes is the application of one's mind to the simile, and thereby taking what is useful for one's own life. This concerns the fourth person.
Next, fifthly, it is shown: now, sometimes such things also happen in society. A person’s physical conduct is very good, and verbal conduct is very good. There seems to be absolutely no fault, yet for some reason, hatred arises, perhaps due to a personal matter. When such hatred arises, it is very easy to appease it. For this too, Venerable Sariputta gives a simile. Suppose in a drought, a thirsty person searching for water finds a full lake or pond, with good shade, clean water, and shaded trees all around. Just as that person, without any trouble, drinks water, bathes to his heart's content, and remains peacefully and happily under a tree; likewise, contemplating the good side of that person, and thinking, "Even though hatred arose in me toward him, he is a person of such good virtues," and bathing in those virtues—bathing in that river of virtues—one must appease the fire of one's hatred. This is what Venerable Sariputta demonstrates.
In this manner, we must now contemplate. What do we see through this? Underlying the path of our life and every action we perform is the attitude we adopt toward something. "Attitude" means the way we look at something. We can change that; it is not a permanent thing. We are capable of changing it. The Buddha declares that this change must be done in accordance with the Dhamma. Now, in the Dhamma, there are two types of reflection: wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) and unwise attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*). All defilements (*kilesa*) arise from that improper way of reflecting on things related to them. Therefore, to be freed from them, one must train oneself in proper reflection, which is wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*). Here, Venerable Sariputta has demonstrated exactly this wise attention through these similes. The Buddha has explicitly permitted that if, in any manner, unwholesome states are subdued and wholesome states (*kusala*) arise, one must reflect in that manner. Utilizing any simile as an aid, or employing any method, one must contemplate in such a way that unwholesome states—namely, greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dosa*), and delusion (*moha*)—are suppressed. One must reflect in a way that eliminates them, not in a way that increases them. For that, one has the right to guide one's mind by prioritizing any simile, mental image, or wholesome thought. It is by systematic cultivation in this manner that what we call an "attitude" is formed. Now, if we consider a person who does not even know what loving-kindness meditation or loving-kindness is, his perspective on the world—the way he looks at the world—is such that he collides everywhere. He makes his entire life a mess. He destroys himself and destroys others as well.
On the contrary, if someone starts at least gradually, and instills in their mind the statement we made at the beginning of this sermon—that is, the desire for happiness is a natural law in the entire world of living beings. Then, loving-kindness (*mettā*) means digesting this concept of the desire for happiness in the world into one's own mind. The reason why this mind is constantly scattered and does not rest on a single object is the arising of these defilements of greed, hatred, and delusion. Therefore, if we feed our mind a certain natural law common to the world—that everyone desires happiness—we can settle our mind within that. Thus, by condensing it into a single phrase like "may they be happy" and repeatedly bringing it to mind, bringing it to mind again and again, one’s attitude is transformed. Moreover, many other virtues, such as concentration (*samādhi*), are developed because of it.
The Buddha has shown countless benefits of these. You may have heard of the daily experienced benefits of loving-kindness meditation mentioned in the *Mettānisaṃsa Sutta*. If a person's mind is liberated through that loving-kindness meditation—what does it mean for the mind to be "liberated"? When we say "deep-seated hatred," right there is a bond, a bondage; the mind is bound. Due to some repulsive sign, or due to the intention of revenge for a wrong done to oneself, the mind is in a state of friction both day and night. It is like a bondage. It is a grave bondage—the bondage of hatred. It is because of this that some people continue to take revenge on each other throughout *saṃsāra*. Therefore, instead of that, one brings forward the liberation of the mind. This is called the "mind-deliverance of loving-kindness" (*mettā-cetovimutti*). When loving-kindness meditation is well-digested into the mind, the state of having a pure mind of loving-kindness spread toward the entire world is shown as mind-deliverance—*mettā-cetovimutti*. The Buddha has shown eleven benefits, experienced even in daily life, of a mind that has reached such a state of mind-deliverance—the mind-deliverance of loving-kindness. One can obtain very peaceful sleep—peaceful sleep in daily life. Next, one can wake up refreshed. One does not see bad dreams. Next, one is dear to human beings. One is dear to non-human beings. Even the protection of devas is secured. Furthermore, from various dangers that may come to oneself—dangers from poison, weapons, etc.—one is often protected by the very power of that mind of loving-kindness. Also, the mind quickly becomes settled; it becomes concentrated. The color or radiance of the face increases. Moreover, at the time of death, one can pass away with clear mindfulness. If one has not attained any paths and fruits, if one has not realized Nibbāna, at the very least, one is reborn in the Brahma worlds. In this manner, the Buddha has declared numerous benefits for the person who develops loving-kindness meditation to the level of mind-deliverance.
Therefore, on such a noble Vesak full-moon day, we must make a resolution—not much is needed to steer our lives in the right direction. Only a very small change needs to be made. Now, we know that even to operate a massive machine, perhaps a machine that has stopped, only a small bolt is needed, or just correcting a small defect. In the same way, it is not a huge thing that helps to change one's attitude here. Sometimes, it is just a single word. One instills the concept, the word "may they be happy," into one's mind as meditation. Meditation (*bhāvanā*) is not something strange. It is a special power developed by repeatedly bringing a wholesome mind, a wholesome object, to one's mind. This power is called "repetition" (*āsevana*). That is, through repeated association, one can generate great power in one's mind. That is why when speaking of meditation, it is said: *āsevitā, bhāvitā, bahulīkatā*—associated with, developed, cultivated. Constantly associating with the thought of loving-kindness means repeatedly bringing it to mind.
In that way, there is a nature in that thought that liberates the mind. Why? Because the mind is narrow and enclosed. Within the fence of selfishness, the minds of the world's beings are narrow and enclosed. It is by freeing oneself from that selfishness that one is able to maintain the thought, "may others be happy." That making happy often begins with those around oneself, with one's relatives, parents, children, and so on. But one must not stop there. Next, neighbors, then neutral people, and finally even enemies—everyone. Conquering enemies in the true sense is not done through wars and such, as mentioned before. Conquering the enemy is done by appeasing that thought of hatred. The enemy is inside the mind, not the enemy outside. It is that same person; but once anger arises, he becomes the enemy. The difference between enemy and friend is nothing other than the attitude one has toward that person. Therefore, the moment that attitude changes, that enemy becomes a friend. That is why Buddhist scholars have stated—as a simile—if we want to walk on this earth, and if we think of walking only after removing all the thorns on the earth, that will never be accomplished. Instead, when one wears shoes, one is not harmed by those thorns. In the same way, if one thinks, "I will sleep peacefully only after killing all the enemies in the world," that can never be completed. Killing enemies in the world and leaving only those whom one likes is never something that can succeed. Instead, what is to be done, as shown in the simile of wearing shoes, is to guard one's mind. When the enemy within one's mind is slain—for this enemy is born in one's mind—if that enemy is slain, it is as if all enemies have been slain. In this manner, Buddhist philosophers have presented various principles and hypotheses. It is through developing one's own mind in terms of meditation based on these that those benefits can be seen.
Thus, it is so regarding hatred. Regarding other defilements too, we must constantly contemplate according to the phenomena of wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) and unwise attention. It is these three defilements of greed, hatred, and delusion that carry us through *saṃsāra* for a long time. Now, greed is what the Buddha has shown there as "affliction." The world is constantly sick. Afflicted by defilements—to be freed from this affliction of defilements, one has to appease the defilements of craving (*taṇhā*), desire, and greed. Similarly, the world is in a state of anxiety, always restless. Because of that endless search, because of the intense greed for fivefold sensual pleasures, we see how much destruction or how much suffering (*dukkha*) the world accumulates due to its running in search of various fashions, trends, or useless things. Sometimes falling into debt, they accumulate a mass of suffering because they lack an understanding of true peace, the happiness of peace. Therefore, according to the Buddha's word, we must always contemplate, especially with loving-kindness. This era is one in which the entire world is being destroyed by hatred. Because of this, in daily life, one must consider some meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) as one's "workplace." To carry on daily life, one does various industries and jobs. But all of these help only to maintain one's body—to maintain the body which one thinks experiences happiness. It is this mind that carries us throughout the entirety of *saṃsāra*. We leave the physical carcass here. But it is in the form of paying debts to the defilements developed in the mind, and to the karma performed, that beings travel in *saṃsāra* for a long time.
Therefore, much more special care must be given to this mind of ours than to this body. This mind can be soiled very easily. Various objects in the world flow in, and the mind is prone to be agitated either by hatred, by lust (*rāga*), or by delusion. To prevent this, some method must be applied to concentrate the mind. If a person instills the thought "may they be happy" into the mind at the very moment of waking up in the morning, and then, resolving for a few minutes, practices maintaining the mind within that thought, he gradually becomes able, as the Buddha declared, to bring up that thought from time to time in all four postures, even while performing other activities. Furthermore, he gains the power to emit that thought of loving-kindness—that stream of loving-kindness—to everyone who comes before him. The person who has developed such mind-deliverance of loving-kindness is the one who experiences numerous benefits of loving-kindness, just as the Buddha declared.
Next, another thing that is helpful is compassion (*karuṇā*). Loving-kindness is generally toward beings who are similar to oneself. Compassion is mostly toward those who are in suffering (*dukkha*). "Being in suffering" means sometimes those who are not seen before us, or seeing someone who has got injured, we sometimes feel compassion. But like the Buddha's great compassion, we must think that all beings in this *saṃsāra* must be the objects of compassion. Every being fallen into the suffering of *saṃsāra* can be made the object of compassion. Thinking thus, we use compassion to help remove that thought of hatred.
Likewise, to dwell happily in daily life as the Buddha declared—to dwell happily in the manner of "Ah, happily"—the virtue called appreciative joy (*muditā*) is helpful. These are shown as the sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*). Often, there is envy in society. If someone appears higher than oneself, or uses more luxurious things, there is envy toward that person. There too, there is a state of irritability, of intolerance. Instead, the entire world of beings desires happiness—every single one. One must think of their being happy as one's own being happy. This is what appreciative joy is. Even for oneself. Now, parents are happy when their children grow and develop. But those same parents, when their neighbors achieve some progress, conceive jealousy about it. There we see, then, that this happens due to a certain defect, a flaw, in the mind. Instead, one must think: just as one thinks of one's own children, especially the entire world of beings desires happiness. Thinking, "Every single person being happy is just like my being happy," one cultivates the virtue of appreciative joy. The virtue of appreciative joy is an extremely rare virtue in society. It is because of its lack that envy and the like spread excessively.
