"queen mallika learns very well, but vasabhakhattiya, the blessed one's kinswoman, does not learn properly," he said. it was on that occasion that the buddha preached the two stanzas we took as our theme. he uttered those two stanzas giving the idea that this dhamma becomes truly meaningful only to the one who learns it properly, retains it, and puts it into practice. let us look at their meaning.
*yathapi ruciram puppham, vannavantam agandhakam,*
*evam subhasita vaca, aphala hoti akubbato.*
"just as a beautiful flower, colorful but scentless, so is a well-spoken word fruitless for one who does not act upon it."
then the other stanza:
*yathapi ruciram puppham, vannavantam sagandhakam,*
*evam subhasita vaca, saphala hoti pakkubbato.*
"just as a beautiful flower, colorful and full of scent, so is a well-spoken word fruitful for one who acts upon it." in this manner, those two stanzas were delivered.
that is the background story of those stanzas. now, before we delve into the meaning of the stanzas themselves, there are certain lessons we can take as examples from the background story we have related so far. indeed, this lay disciple chattapani is a worthy character of that nature. through the incident described, we can understand that he was someone who lived according to the values and virtues developed in accordance with the buddha's teachings, like a fragrant flower—a person possessing the power of the dhamma. his way of acting with a certain strength of dhamma, giving precedence to respect for the teacher over royal respect without being subservient to titles and positions, is evident in his remaining seated when he saw the king in the presence of the buddha. that is indeed a great example for the people of today as well. for it is to the dhamma that the primary place must be given. cowering and being subservient before such worldly state power is an insult to the dhamma.
likewise is the other point. when the king, pleased with him, invited him to preach the dhamma to the queens, an ordinary person would have seen it as a great opportunity to gain royal favor, wealth, and honor, thinking, "this is excellent, your majesty, i shall come tomorrow, or even today," and would have highly welcomed and accepted the task of preaching to the queens. but this lay disciple thought far-sightedly about the danger involved. understanding that various complications could arise from this, his ability even at that moment to decline the king's request was a highly valuable quality. we must understand through this that, like a colorful and fragrant flower, a profound spiritual integrity lies behind the character of chattapani upasaka.
now, the news about the queens is not so important there. the main point the buddha showed us by using that incident as a basis is that this dhamma is not something to be confined only to learning. only when it is put into practice can the true power and benefit of this dhamma be obtained. no matter how beautiful a flower is, if it has no scent, it is just like a paper flower. there is no real benefit in a paper flower. that is the point shown here. therefore, in connection with this, let us now reflect on this true dhamma.
when we speak of this true dhamma, you can bring to mind the six qualities of the dhamma. everyone knows these six qualities: *svakkhata* (well-expounded), *sanditthika* (directly visible), *akalika* (immediate/timeless), *ehipassika* (inviting one to come and see), *opanayika* (leading inwards/progressive), and *paccattam veditabbo vinnuhi* (to be personally realized by the wise). from the way these six qualities are explained, we can understand that this true dhamma is indeed like a challenge for practice. in short, the buddha explained the word *svakkhata* in this manner: "monks, in a poorly-expounded (*durakkhata*) dhamma and vinaya... now, *svakkhata* means well-expounded, beautifully taught; whereas *durakkhata* means badly expounded, wrongly expounded." if you understand those two words in that way, then you can understand the passage declared by the buddha: "monks, in a poorly-expounded dhamma and vinaya, the lazy person (*kusita*) dwells in comfort." that is to say, in a dhamma that is taught wrongly or not properly, in that dhamma-vinaya—meaning in that dispensation—the lazy, indolent man lives comfortably and happily. "but in a well-expounded dhamma and vinaya, it is the energetic person (*viriyavanta*) who dwells in comfort." in a dispensation of well-expounded dhamma, it is the energetic one who lives happily. a very profound matter is expressed here. why was it said that the lazy person lives in comfort in that dhamma-vinaya? through that, we can also grasp the meaning of that word. we said that the term implies a wrongly or badly expounded dhamma. what is the idea there? if a dhamma sets forth a certain goal, but that goal cannot be achieved by practicing that dhamma, then it is a poorly-expounded dhamma-vinaya (*durakkhata*). a well-expounded dhamma-vinaya (*svakkhata*) is one where whatever it promises to deliver is properly accomplished. therefore, if one exerts effort in a poorly-expounded dhamma-vinaya, it is useless; it is a wasted effort. it is of no use. that is why it was said that the lazy person dwells in comfort. since the well-expounded dhamma-vinaya is fruitful and fulfills the desired goal, in that dispensation, it is indeed the energetic one who achieves those results, rejoices, and dwells in comfort. that is the idea behind the term *svakkhata*.
let us understand the other terms based on that as well. you all may have heard about them to some extent. next, the specialty of this dhamma lies there. a very profound idea is expressed there. this dhamma is not something where you do it now and get the results only hereafter. it is *sanditthika*—its results can be seen right here and now, before one's very eyes; that is its specialty. *sanditthika* means, just like saying "sanditthiko dhammo", it can be experienced in this very world, in this very life. next, *akalika* (immediate/timeless) means without delay, meaning there is no gap of time between the effort made and the result. in short, there is no gap between the path and its fruit. if one is engaged in the path of practice, that path culminates immediately in the fruit. since there is no interval in between, it is *akalika*—there is no time gap there. *sanditthika, akalika*. *ehipassika* means that within this dhamma itself, there is a challenging power that says, "come and see!" that is to say, it is as if the dhamma itself is crying out, saying: "put this dhamma into practice and see!" next, *opanayika* means: if it said "come and see," the next step is leading, drawing close; *upanayati* means bringing close. where does it lead? not to any external place, but within, into the heart. that is *opanayika*. since the results of this practice must be experienced from within, this dhamma must be brought right inside. next, that is exactly why it is finally said: *paccattam veditabbo vinnuhi*—it is a dhamma to be personally realized by the wise. it cannot be shown to another. it is a dhamma that each individual must realize for themselves by walking along this path of practice.
now, based on that, we can see that on one hand, this dhamma is for the energetic—inviting them to put this dhamma into practice and obtain its fruits. thus, a very valuable idea is expressed there. next, let us see: we mentioned at the very beginning that the buddha commenced his dhamma sermons with the *dhammacakkappavattana sutta*. in short, the *dhammacakkappavattana sutta* is presented as the very first sermon in our dispensation. indeed, its core and essence is the question of the path of practice (*patipada*). in that sermon, the buddha showed the world a certain middle path, going between two extremes. what are the two extremes? one extreme is indulgence in sensual pleasures (*kamasukhallikanuyoga*). the other extreme is self-mortification (*attakilamathanuyoga*), which was shown by various teachers of that time like the niganthas and other sectarians—the attempt to achieve liberation by severely tormenting the body. rejecting both, the buddha revealed an entirely new path of practice called the middle way. it is known in brief as the noble eightfold path. you all have understood this to some extent. the path that is capable of bringing about a complete transformation of a person's life, consisting of eight steps or eight factors, is called the noble eightfold path: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. thus, this noble eightfold path is introduced as the middle path. that brings us next to the subject of this middle path.
what is present within this middle path (*majjhima patipada*) is the very same energy (*viriya*) we mentioned earlier. there is a way of applying this energy in a moderate measure; in other words, it is a path of practice that shows a certain balance of energy. so, in this regard, we should reflect as follows: the buddha has pointed out "right effort" (*samma vayama*) within this noble eightfold path itself. *samma vayama* means right effort. correct exertion means the way energy must be applied in the proper manner. this is also called the great efforts (*sammappadhana*). this word *padhana* also means supreme effort or exertion. the words *vayama*, *viriya*, and *padhana* are largely synonymous. thus, this energy, known as the four great efforts (*sammappadhana*) or right effort (*samma vayama*), has been shown by the buddha in four ways. they are briefly known by these words: *samvara* (restraint), *pahana* (abandoning), *bhavana* (developing), and *anurakkhana* (protecting/maintaining). *samvara* means closing or preventing, if we take its simple meaning. *pahana* means removing or discarding. *bhavana* means developing or cultivating, and *anurakkhana* means guarding or maintaining. next, let us consider why this energy was shown in four ways. the buddha has explained that this stream of consciousness (*citta-santana*) is like a flowing river. thus, the buddha analyzed this mind as having the characteristic of movement—meaning in the sense of moving and flowing—or as something possessing a dynamic nature like a flowing river. therefore, this energy is something that must be applied with great care, systematically. indeed, it becomes fourfold.
as an analogy, you all know that if a dam is to be built across a swiftly flowing river, a fourfold effort is required. before building the dam, the incoming unwanted water must be blocked; it must be closed off (*samvara*). next, the unwanted water already remaining there must be removed (*pahana*). meanwhile, in the sense of *bhavana* (development), one must begin the preliminary work of building the dam, gathering the necessary materials, and starting to construct the dam. then, in keeping with the word *anurakkhana* (maintenance), one must engage in guarding it; it must be protected and reinforced so that it is not swept away again. indeed, those four points are expressed in the buddha's analysis of the four great efforts (*sammappadhana*). why do we explain this in such detail? because nowadays, various people have opinions regarding the work of the mind, saying: "this is not something where energy, exertion, effort, or striving should be applied. one should just watch the mind as it goes of its own accord." in truth, because they do not understand the fundamental principles of the middle path which the buddha presented as so supreme, many people these days have turned this practice into mere "doing nothing" (idleness). following the views put forward by certain philosophers who have no correct understanding of this dhamma, and lacking proper comprehension of the path of practice in this dispensation, they interpret it as just sitting idle. but if you just let the mind wander as it likes and simply watch it, the task will not be accomplished. one has to keep in mind the analogy of building the dam.
if we are to condense this noble eightfold path, it consists of *sila* (morality), *samadhi* (concentration), and *panna* (wisdom). it is the threefold training of morality, concentration, and wisdom that is contained within this noble eightfold path. morality (*sila*) means the restraint and discipline of body and speech. concentration (*samadhi*) means the one-pointedness of mind. wisdom (*panna*) means seeing in terms of *anicca* (impermanent), *dukkha* (suffering), and *anatta* (not-self) through insight (*vipassana*). there is a very ancient stanza that encapsulates this, which you all often use even as a protective chant (*paritta*):
*sabba papassa akaranam, kusalassa upasampada;*
*sacitta pariyodapanam, etam buddhana sasanam.*
we have translated it into sinhala, and you may have heard it: "refraining from all evil, the attainment of the wholesome, purifying one's own mind—this is the message of all buddhas." this is an eternal truth. it is not just the advice of one buddha, but *buddhanam sasanam*—the message of all buddhas. within it are morality, concentration, and wisdom. "refraining from evil" is morality (*sila*). "the attainment of the wholesome" (*kusalassa upasampada*) refers to concentration (*samadhi*). it means entering and dwelling in the jhanas. when considered as one-pointedness of the wholesome mind, the concentrated mind is expressed within this attainment of the wholesome. next, there is a dhamma passage, a word of the buddha: "one is purified through wisdom" (*pannaya parisujjhati*). based on that, we can understand that ultimate purification is attained through wisdom (*panna*). the purification of the mind at the highest level is accomplished by wisdom. therefore, to fulfill this threefold training, energy is required; exertion is required. it does not happen just like that. it does not happen automatically. it does not happen by merely watching the mind. that energy must be applied carefully, systematically, and progressively. that is why the buddha points out: "just as the great ocean slopes gradually, deepens gradually, even so in my dispensation there is a gradual training." *anupubbakiriya, anupubbapatipada*—a gradual training, a gradual performance, and a gradual path of practice. it is through such a wonderful process, bound by an amazing relationship of causes and conditions, that this liberation can be attained.
and that becomes further clear to us through what is known as the four great efforts (*sammappadhana*). it is an extremely profound matter, and at the same time, highly practical. for those rationalists—indeed, those who give primary place only to intellect—the true taste of this dhamma cannot be enjoyed; its true fragrance cannot be obtained. but through this gradual path, it can be attained. thus, the four great efforts are described in this way. although we state the pali passages, we will apply the sinhala explanation. keep them in mind so that if any issues arise regarding these, they can be resolved; we shall state the pali passage first. it is as follows: *anuppannanam papakanam akusalanam dhammanam anuppadaya chandam janeti vayamati viriyam arabhati cittam pagganhati padahati.* once the meaning of this passage is explained, the others will be easy to understand. for the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states: *chandam janeti* means one generates desire, an earnest wish. *vayamati* means one makes an effort or exertion. *viriyam arabhati* means one arouses or initiates energy. *cittam pagganhati* means one upholds the mind, makes a firm determination. next, *padahati* means applying the supreme effort—an outstanding exertion made even at the risk of one's life. thus, this series of terms is applied to the four great efforts.
the first one, as we said, is for the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states. that is exactly what is meant by restraint (*samvara*). next, for the discarding of arisen unwholesome states: *uppannanam papakanam akusalanam dhammanam pahanaya*. for the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states, one must apply the same desire (*chanda*), etc., in the same manner. next, what we mentioned as belonging to the aspect of development (*bhavana*) is: *anuppannanam kusalanam dhammanam uppadaya*—for the arising of unarisen wholesome states, one must make a similar effort. next, finally it says: *uppannanam kusalanam dhammanam thitiya asammosaya bhiyyobhavaya vepullaya bhavanaya paripuriya chandam janeti, vayamati viriyam arabhati cittam pagganhati padahati.* strengthening that dam is no easy task either. that must be why so many words are used there. for the maintenance (*thitiya*) of arisen wholesome states, for their non-confusion (*asammosaya*), for their further growth (*bhiyyobhavaya*), for their plenitude (*vepullaya*), and for their fulfillment by development (*bhavanaya paripuriya*), one must similarly generate desire, make an effort, arouse energy, uphold the mind, and apply supreme exertion.
look then, in what a wonderful manner the buddha has shown these four great efforts in accordance with the nature of this mind. a mind that flows like a river as mentioned before—constructing this dam is something that must be done with extreme care. similarly, the person who aspires for liberation must apply those four types of energy according to the occasion. next, this goes even further. if we reflect further, why did the buddha use so many words regarding energy? there, too, lies a wonderful ascending sequence. the buddha has described in a few words the mental sequence through which our mind directs itself towards something and proceeds up to supreme energy. *chandam janeti* means generating an interest or intent. first, there must be an interest, a desire. that is the beginning, that is the direction. next, one makes an effort (*vayamati*). within the word "effort" is a certain testing of "can i do this?"—a preliminary attempt, an exertion. next, *viriyam*—here, one truly gets down to the work, initiates the task. while proceeding in this way, obstacles arise. it is at that moment that one must firmly uphold the mind, as expressed by *cittam pagganhati*; one must bring forth the power of determination. having established that power of determination, understanding that this task—which seemed impossible—is something that must absolutely be done, and putting one's life at stake, one accomplishes the task through supreme exertion. that is represented by the word *padahati*. in this series of terms applied to energy, the highest word is *padhana*. this does not mean "chief" or "main" (*pradhana*) as in our ordinary sinhala language. in the pali language, *padhana* is used in the sense of supreme, ultimate energy. thus, the matter regarding *chanda*, etc., has been briefly mentioned to you.
next, among the *bodhipakkhiya dhammas* (factors of enlightenment) shown by the buddha, some of you might have heard that, regarding energy, there is another matter just as important as the four great efforts. for those who are keen on the path of practice, there is mention of the four bases of success (*iddhipada*). *iddhipada*—when we say *iddhi* (psychic power/success), we immediately think of someone flying through the air. but, devotees, *iddhi* is a word that means accomplishment, fulfillment, or making something successful. even in daily life, the things required to achieve success and accomplishment in any endeavor are called *iddhipada*. the word *pada* (base/foot) is used there to mean the factors that help in achieving success. the buddha highlights four such factors in this manner: *chanda* (desire/intention), *viriya* (energy), *citta* (mind/determination), and *vimamsa* (investigation/wisdom). indeed, these have been mentioned here in some way or another. the very essence of that energy which was expressed through words like *chandam janeti*, *vayamati*, etc., is what is presented here as the *iddhipada*. in fact, as shown by the buddha, the practitioner, the yogi who engages in the four great efforts in the manner described, reaches a point where they can understand the secret of success regarding their own endeavor, in accordance with their temperament. the secret of the success of one's energy can vary according to each individual's temperament. some people achieve their aspirations by putting forward *chanda* (intention/desire). *chanda* means interest or desire. those are the temperaments of whom we hear in the world: "if i set my mind to something, or if i develop an interest in it, i will do it and will not look back." next are the energetic (*viriya*) temperaments. it is through that very effort of *chandam janeti*, *vayamati*, etc., that they understand the secret of success within themselves. the second is energy (*viriya*). there are some who say: "if i put energy into something, i will see it through to the end. i will not back down." next, there are others for whom *citta* (mind/determination) is the base of success: "if i make a determination regarding something, i will abide by that determination. i will accomplish it somehow." for such a person, *citta* is the base of success. *vimamsa* means investigative wisdom. that was not directly mentioned earlier, but through it, we can understand wisdom (*panna*). the one who relies on this base of success, *vimamsa*, is of a wise temperament. that is, investigative wisdom: "i must do this and see how it works. i am curious to see if what is said is true." there are those who engage in this effort by bringing forward such an attitude.
to help an ordinary person, who may not have much interest in such doctrinal matters, understand this point, we can give a helpful analogy. let us assume there is a boulder that is a nuisance to our work. we feel like pushing it aside. first, the interest, the desire, arises for it (*chanda*). since the boulder does not budge merely because one has the desire, what does one do next? one makes a certain effort (*vayama*). one makes a small exertion to see: "can i lift this or push it aside?" that exertion is, in fact, a testing of one's strength. inserting something underneath it, like a crowbar, one tries to see if it can be moved—that is *vayamati*. thus, *chandam janeti, vayamati*. next, *viriyam arabhati*. once it is understood that it is possible, one arouses energy. slowly, one begins to lift it. as one gets close to lifting it and pushing it over, one realizes that this is no easy task. perhaps it might fall back on oneself. the mind might also start to waver. at that very moment, one makes a firm determination: "even if i die, i will not abandon this task i have started," and pushes it all the way over. that is what is represented by the word *padahati*—the supreme energy (*padhana viriya*). next, through engaging in this very exertion, the power of wisdom arises naturally within oneself. from those experiences, investigative wisdom arises. today, we say of such a person: "he is an experienced person." that is the wisdom, the investigative insight, gained from the wealth of experience acquired through such work. thus, through this, we can understand the value of those *iddhipadas*.
these days, these matters seem as if they are hidden within the dhamma. but if we bring them to light, they are extremely important, especially for those devotees who wish to experience this dhamma practically. sometimes, the rationalists may not like these things very much. now, there is a certain trend going on. you all must understand this. according to this intellectual and rationalist attitude, they expect instantaneous realization of the truth. there are indeed certain discourses where, as the buddha preached to people of immense paramis like bahiya daruciriya, they attained arahanthood almost instantly. certain scholars who have studied those discourses twenty or thirty times imagine themselves to be wise, belonging to that special category, even though no internal transformation has taken place within them. they underestimate the fundamental virtues such as faith (*saddha*) and morality (*sila*). showing no interest in them, they expect instantaneous liberation merely by listening to the dhamma. that is entirely a delusion. for the buddha has pointed out five "liberating occasions" (*vimuttayatana*) that help in attaining nibbana—not just one. a person can attain realization of the path and fruits: while listening to the dhamma, while teaching the dhamma, while reciting the dhamma, while reflecting on the dhamma, and finally, it is shown, while systematically developing a certain theme of concentration (*samadhi-nimitta*). yet, out of those five, some people think that everything can be accomplished merely by listening. that is possible only for those highly exceptional individuals. it happens very rarely. especially in this era, we can assume that it is extremely rare. it was in an era when beings of great merit lived, and when those possessing higher knowledges (*abhinna*) like the buddha—who could read the mental capacity of others—were present to guide them, that someone could realize arahanthood instantly through a brief sermon. therefore, one should not think that just because one holds a long list of academic degrees, one also belongs to that rare category.
indeed, there is another similar analysis shown in the dhamma. the buddha points out a certain fourfold classification based on the capacity of individuals for realization: *dukkha patipada dandhabhinna* (painful progress with slow realization), *dukkha patipada khippabhinna* (painful progress with swift realization), *sukha patipada dandhabhinna* (pleasant progress with slow realization), and *sukha patipada khippabhinna* (pleasant progress with swift realization). if we put it in sinhala, here *patipada* refers to the course of action including the effort, etc., mentioned earlier. thus, the first category is: progress is painful and realization is slow. next, the second category: progress is painful but realization is swift. then the third category: progress is pleasant but realization is slow. and the fourth is: progress is pleasant and realization is swift. it is to this fourth category that individuals like bahiya daruciriya, who possessed a highly supreme power of paramis, belong. so, that capacity is not present in everyone. one must understand this for oneself. the dhamma mentions those suttas upon hearing which people attained arahanthood instantly, or which caused arahanthood. certain scholars study them with great enthusiasm and keen interest. but they do not put them into practice. the attitude mostly prevalent today is that these stages of realization can be attained merely by studying the dhamma. that is entirely wrong. if those virtues such as faith and morality are lacking—in short, if faith (*saddha*) is absent... faith is shown as the seed of all virtues in this dispensation. a heart without faith is a dry heart. no virtues can grow there. therefore, if one studies the dhamma with a rationalistic attitude, without faith, doubting, and subjecting it to constant criticism and speculation, even if one studies it, no path or fruit will be attained. except, perhaps, for imagining that one has attained them. thus, we must realize that no matter what we expect, this task is not that easy. if it were so easy, there would be no need for a buddha for this task. a buddha appears in the world to present a certain unique matter which no other teacher could discover, even by practicing those extremely difficult disciplines. the fundamental principle of that is the middle path, the middle way (*majjhima patipada*). within that middle way lies that very effort which must be applied with great care, as shown by the buddha in his explanation of the fourfold energy. one cannot be in a hurry for this either. just letting the mind wander as it likes and watching it is an extreme akin to indulgence in sensual pleasures (*kamasukhallikanuyoga*). that is, letting it drift as it pleases. that way will not work either. nor can one do it by struggling and agitating.
in this connection, the buddha has preached a valuable discourse that brings us closer to this point. it is known as the *oghatarana sutta*. that analogy will be highly useful to you in understanding this fundamental principle. on one occasion, a deva came and asked the buddha: "o sorrowless one, how did you cross over the flood?" here, what was called the "flood" refers, in the doctrinal sense, to the four floods: sensual desire (*kama*), becoming / existence (*bhava*), views (*ditthi*), and ignorance (*avijja*). you have heard of the flood of sensuality (*kamogha*). the flood of sensuality means the torrent of sensual desire, which flows all over the world. the flood of sensual desire is flowing. this life is a matter of these four floods: sensual desire (*kama*), becoming / existence (*bhava*), views (*ditthi*), and ignorance (*avijja*). all of these are like torrential floods. thus, within this existence, existence is a dynamic, moving thing in that very manner. what the buddha is showing here is a massive, flowing flood. how does one cross over this flood then? this is no easy task. there are four floods: the flood of sensuality (*kamogha*), the flood of becoming / existence (*bhavogha*), the flood of views (*ditthogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avijjogha*). the deva is asking how he crossed over these. the buddha's reply is: *appatittham anayuham*—"without halting, without straining/struggling." "without standing still, and without struggling, did i cross over the flood." here, standing still (*appatittham*) refers to indulgence in sensual pleasures (*kamasukhallikanuyoga*). next, struggling (*anayuham*) refers to self-mortification (*attakilamathanuyoga*). you can understand this with reference to the *dhammacakkappavattana sutta*. then the deva asks further details: "how did you do that?" to that, the buddha replies: "friend—*avuso* means friend—friend, when i stood still, i sank; when i struggled, i was swept away by the flood." those are the two extremes. it is by avoiding those two extremes that one must travel on this path of dhamma. it is there that the middle way lies; it is there that the middle path is found.
therefore, this is not something that happens of its own accord or merely by wishing, by completely abandoning energy and just watching the mind wander. why are people inclined towards such an attitude? you all know the social environment of today. due to the advancement of science and technology, in your daily lives at home as well as in your office work, you do things almost instantaneously. everything is instant. science and technology provide facilities to get everything done instantly. now, many people expect to find that same instantaneous nature in this dhamma and in the realization of the dhamma as well. that is a mirage. that is a wrong idea. because the environment in the past was one that truly supported spiritual development. but you can imagine how the environment of today is, judging by the way daily life is spent. how complex it has become due to this material progress! on one hand, it seems like a great advancement, but humans are deteriorating terribly, falling into animalistic states. these minds have fallen to the levels of demons, hell-beings, and hungry ghosts (*peta*). in such an era, it is difficult to find a proper, quiet environment—not only in noisy cities or villages but even in a forest, it is extremely difficult to find a secluded place. in such an age, you must think for yourselves: is this something that can be achieved by doing nothing, when it actually requires one to exert much greater effort, increasing one's energy hundreds and thousands of times? according to that, we should realize the value of the middle path shown by the buddha.
to explain it a bit more deeply, we can speak about the extreme we mentioned. the difference between the practice followed by the niganthas and the practice prescribed by the buddha for the sangha helps us understand this. let us bring this out briefly to suit the occasion. now, you may have heard that what belongs to the monks is the four requisites (*cattaro paccaya*): robes (*civara*), almsfood (*pindapata*), lodging (*senasana*), and medicinal requisites (*gilanapaccayabhajja*)—the things necessary to sustain life. the buddha has pointed out the course of practice to be adopted when using them, which is to reflect upon them (*paccavekkhana*). this reflection is briefly introduced as restraint by knowledge (*nana-samvara*), a restraint accomplished through wisdom and knowledge. first, let us take the practice of the niganthas. what was it? the niganthas saw that things like food and clothing are what draw worldly people towards sensuality. that is obvious even when one goes to a city. due to fashions regarding these, worldly people are drawn to sensuality. therefore, what was the extreme practice adopted by the niganthas? discarding clothing entirely (practicing nudity), and regarding food, you might have heard that there were even those who ate excrement in those times. in that way, they turned that effort into an extreme distortion; they struggled.
but the buddha showed a different path instead. these four requisites are things we can neither do with completely (in an attached way) nor do without. what is this becoming / existence (*bhava*)? it is a flowing stream. now, you know that in a place where a strong current is flowing, if one wants to go from here to the opposite bank, one cannot go in a straight line as if drawing a straight line. after entering the water, one has to go to the opposite bank while yielding somewhat to the flowing current. suppose you are caught in a current while swimming. what happens? you cannot just fight it head-on. nor can you do nothing. one must escape and save oneself carefully, wisely, and gradually. that is the kind of path of practice the buddha points out. therefore, what is to be done is not the discarding of robes, nor resorting to distorted foods like excrement. rather, the buddha prescribed the manner of using them with restraint of knowledge (*nana-samvara*), with wisdom, turning it into a meditation, by way of reflection (*paccavekkhana*).
if we mention briefly, taking just one or two examples—regarding almsfood, it is said: let the monks reflect in this manner before consuming almsfood. that is indeed like a meditation: "i do not take this food for amusement, for intoxication, for physical beauty, or for brawn, as laymen do. but solely for the maintenance of this holy life (*brahmacariya*), for the realization of nibbana." first, that purpose is considered. next, secondly, also related to it is the meditative attitude regarding food and this body. it is developed as meditation, and also as the repulsiveness of food. there is a meditation called the analysis of elements (*dhatu-manasikara*): this food is made up of earth (*pathavi*), fire (*tejo*), wind (*vayo*), and water (*apo*) elements. likewise is this body. next, one reflects that this food, made of earth, water, fire, and wind elements, which was clean, becomes dirty, impure, unappealing, and repulsive once it enters this dirty, impure body of mine. see then how the buddha solved the problem of food—which the niganthas feared and discarded—through the middle path. he made that very food an aid to nibbana. the purpose of this is: this body is maintained for nibbana, merely for sustenance. this is not like the fashion with which the ordinary people of today, who strive to remain in becoming / existence (*bhava*), treat food. it is not that running after food that is mentioned here. merely, a certain control is exercised over it. looking at them from a balanced perspective, it is then turned into a meditation. that shows the middle way pointed out by the buddha. giving one example is sufficient. thus, there are such passages of reflection regarding all four requisites.
through these, we must understand that nowadays, large crowds are drawn to the idea that the task is easy. it appears easy, but through that, a serious wrong view (*miccha-ditthi*) is spreading, which is contrary to this middle path. doing nothing is indeed something pleasing to many. if all of this can be achieved by doing nothing, why exert oneself? why keep precepts? why meditate? some even say that meditation is unnecessary. "there is no need to control the mind in the name of meditation. let it go where it wants and just watch." if those people were to enter the water, and if they were to just watch while crossing a torrential flood, they would be seen acting contrary to their own words. to satisfy their material needs in daily life, they are compelled to act in a way that is close to those very *sammappadhana* and *iddhipada* mentioned earlier. this shows us that the buddha has brought to light a wonderful natural law (*dhammata*) regarding our stream of consciousness (*citta-santana*). he saw this properly; he saw its true reality. having seen that, he said that the human mind functions in these four ways. likewise, the buddha pointed out a balanced path of practice to be followed with great care. therefore, we must highlight these points. especially since this is an era when various wrong views are spreading, some people—especially those we call rationalists (not that we say this as an insult, but such an attitude is prevalent nowadays)—study the dhamma and possess some understanding of it. through that scholarship, from the knowledge they have gained, some believe they have complete comprehension of this dispensation. no, devotees, this dispensation is threefold: *pariyatti* (learning), *patipatti* (practice), and *pativedha* (realization). if only learning (*pariyatti*) existed, then the view held by those scholars would be correct. but here, it is not limited to learning alone. it must be put into practice—*patipatti*. next, the culmination of practice is realization (*pativedha*)—one must penetrate it with insight wisdom (*vipassana-panna*), in its supreme form through meditation. that is why the motto of the buddhists in the past—which is rarely heard nowadays—was: *sunatha, dharetha, caratha dhamme*—"listen, retain, and practice the dhamma." "listen, retain, and walk in the dhamma."
"listen, retain, and practice the dhamma; listen, retain, and walk in the dhamma." this point is further clarified by the passages shown by the buddha regarding the listening to the dhamma, showing that this was preached for a practical purpose. regarding the proper listening to the dhamma, it is mentioned as follows: or, regarding a person who has a correct understanding of the dhamma, these words are mentioned. such a person—let us say, in modern terms, such a scholar or such a disciple—has the dhamma... and many words are used for this: *suta, dhata, vacasa paricita, ditthiya suppatividdha*. that person has heard the dhamma (*suta*), and retains it (*dhata*)—not having heard it through one ear and let it out through the other. next, they have not stored it in computers and set it aside. in those devotees who have stored the tipitaka in computers, the dhamma may not be present within. that is just an action. they did not take it within. that is why in the past, they spoke of the lineage of reciters (*bhanaka*); in those times, there were individuals of single-minded listening (*ekasuta*). they retained what they heard upon merely hearing it once. next, *suta, dhata*—they retained the dhamma. "there is a great book at home, but its name is not remembered"—our ancestors began to say this only after the custom of memorizing the dhamma was lost. nowadays, this is considered unnecessary, and sometimes even laughable. but the one who wishes to make use of it retains that dhamma in the mind, like storing lion's fat in a golden casket. having retained it through *suta, dhata*, they do not stop there. *vacasa paricita*—they must master it verbally. they must recall and memorize it from time to time. next, it is not reciting it like a parrot. those words—the things spoken of—must be turned over in the mind, investigated, and examined. investigating in this manner, *ditthiya suppatividdha*—when examining it thus, one obtains the ability to penetrate it through right view. through those words, then, it is shown that the dhamma is a practical thing. dhamma-listening must be done in that manner, with a practical purpose and attitude.
the same is shown in another way. the manner in which a noble disciple (*ariyasavaka*) listens to the dhamma is described as follows: it is shown how a noble disciple listens to the dhamma, in short, in a way that leads to the realization of the path and fruits. a noble disciple listens in this manner: *atthikatva manasikatva sabbacetaso samannaharitva ohitasoto dhammam sunati*. at some point, a noble disciple, having paid attention (*atthikatva*), listens with the primary thought: "this dhamma is of benefit to me." not with the purpose of analyzing this, writing a book about it, or obtaining a degree. he listens to the dhamma with the thought: "this is of use to me. there is a benefit in this for me." next, *manasikatva*—reflecting upon what is heard, contemplating word by word at the very moment of listening. without going into thoughts and speculations like: "i already know what is being said. what is there to explain about that?"—he contemplates it word by word. *sabbacetaso*—not with half the mind here and the other half at home. *sabbacetaso, samannaharitva*—directing the entire mind to it, focusing attention, applying complete attention. *ohitasoto dhammam sunati*—he listens with inclined ears. this is an ancient expression: listening with inclined ears. we see certain animals inclining their ears. we cannot tell from the outside whether humans are inclining their ears or not. but listening with inclined ears means full attention. it means directing one's attention completely to it. nowadays, since we have various scientific ears (recorders and devices) instead of our own ears, we leave them to listen, and when the dhamma is preached, we step aside. this is just like saying, "there is a great book at home, but its name is not remembered." those words can be applied today to modern machines like computers and cassette recorders. "there are many cassette tapes of the most talented monks in our house. but we have no time to listen." it is just like that.
such is the attitude prevalent today. nevertheless, there is that intellectual attitude: "if we can produce light whenever we want by pressing a button, why can't we produce the light of wisdom merely by listening to a short sermon?" some people raise such arguments nowadays. "this is an extremely advanced era. in such an era, if they could achieve these in the past, in an era of bullock carts, why can't we do so now?" people who ask such questions have indeed come and questioned us. we have to remind them of the difference between the environment of those times and that of today. the spiritual environment in those days was truly wonderful. everyone was a seeker of truth. among the brahmins as well as others, there was indeed a massive effort made for liberation. even if they sometimes went astray. today, in which direction are people running? towards material progress. everyone is running after that, caught up in that current, chasing a mirage. among those who are running, even if you do turn towards the dhamma, you have to operate amidst a massive array of obstacles. devotees living in household life come and tell us: "we would like to meditate. but the children do such things all night... we don't need to describe it—they are in front of this or that machine. or our lives are spent in the midst of a massive din." there is a great sense of frustration in them.
through that, we can understand that in this day and age, that state can be achieved only by putting in double, triple, or even a hundredfold energy. holding degrees and being learned alone will not bring about the paths and fruits. you do not belong to the category of swift realization (*khippabhinna*) just because you think you do. that is a point we must retain well in our minds. reflecting in this way, today this group of devotees, practicing a simple life, a large number of you have observed the eight precepts for this uposatha day, and others have established themselves in higher virtues. that is the importance of morality (*sila*). without taking the first step properly, the final result alone cannot be achieved. these factors of morality, concentration, and wisdom are interconnected. this is something bound by causal relationships. just as we often remind you regarding *samma ditthi*, *samma sankappa*, etc., there is a wonderful relationship of cause and effect between each and every step in the dhamma. that is why it was said that there is a gradual sequence. that sequence cannot be broken. therefore, one must start from the very alphabet. one must go down to zero. one must start with morality (*sila*). one must start with faith (*saddha*). fundamentally, faith. faith is the seed in this dispensation. no virtues accumulate in a heart devoid of faith. it is with faith aroused that one next approaches a teacher. *saddhajato upasankamati*—"one with faith approaches," as pointed out by the buddha. having approached, one listens to the dhamma, retains it, and reflects on it in that manner. in that way, systematically embarking on the practice, generating great desire and energy, and getting down to the practice, one can accomplish this ultimate goal.
thus, although the buddha set the wheel of dhamma in motion on a day like today, the power of that wheel of dhamma seems to be fast fading away from this society due to the spread of such wrong views. therefore, wise devotees must reflect. what must be done first cannot be put off for later. nor can what must be done first be completely discarded. therefore, those virtues of faith (*saddha*) and morality (*sila*) must be completed first. it is upon those virtues that the mind can next be composed in concentration (*samadhi*). it is to a concentrated mind that impermanence (*anicca*) and unsubstantiality (*anatta*) are understood by way of wisdom (*panna*) and insight (*vipassana*). the supreme, peaceful, and sublime deathless nibbana, which is free from all samsaric suffering such as aging (*jara*), illness, and death (*marana*) shown by the buddha, can be attained through the realization of the paths and fruits of sotapanna, sakadagami, anagami, and arahant. thus, you must understand that within this brief period of time, we have briefly touched upon many facts. this is for you to reflect upon further. these points were mentioned not merely for you to stop at reflecting, but to adjust your lives in accordance with their practical value.
thus, in connection with this, you have established yourselves in morality, disciplined your body and speech, and listened to the dhamma with focused attention for about an hour. listening to the dhamma is said to be a meritorious deed, a wholesome act (*kusala*), because it is something that aids your nibbana. that listening to the dhamma is highly beneficial. it even provides the strong supportive condition (*upanisraya-sampatti*). by the blessings of that listening—if we look at these blessings in this very world, in a directly visible (*sanditthika*) and immediate (*akalika*) manner—let us resolve that we have used this brief time to develop within ourselves the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) of faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*). through that dhamma power, may you find the rare association of admirable friends (*kalyana-mitta*), even with difficulty or by making your way through thick forests, and before this lamp of the dispensation is extinguished, may this serve as a strong supportive condition (*upanisraya-sampatti*) for you to escape this perilous samsara and attain sublime nibbana through the realization of the paths and fruits of sakadagami, anagami, and arahant. likewise, make a wish that if there be any beings in this universe, from the lowest avici hell to the highest akanittha heaven, who wish to rejoice in this wholesome deed of dhamma preaching and dhamma listening, may they all rejoice in this merit and find peace in sublime, deathless nibbana through the bodhi of their aspiration. with that aspiration in mind, recite these verses:
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 023
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #23
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No. )
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Anikkasāvo kāsāvaṃ, yo vatthaṃ paridahissati; Apeto damasaccena, na so kāsāvamarahati. Yo ca vantakasāvassa, sīlesu susamāhito; Upeto damasaccena, sa ve kāsāvamarahati.
From:
Verses 9-10 from the Yamakavagga (Chapter of Pairs) of the Dhammapada
Dear Listeners,
The supreme inheritance that the world receives from a Fully Enlightened Buddha is the Dispensation of the Buddha (*Sambuddha Sāsana*). We consider that safeguarding this *Sambuddha Sāsana* for a long time for the welfare and happiness of gods and humans is the duty of every Buddhist. If we are to fulfill that duty properly, we must possess a correct understanding of its spiritual and dispensational values. That is why on this Vesak Full Moon Day, we chose these two verses as our theme.
The Buddha preached these two verses at the Jetavana monastery, focusing on a certain incident concerning Ven. Devadatta. On one occasion, the two chief disciples, Ven. Sāriputta and Ven. Moggallāna, having obtained permission from the Buddha, journeyed from Sāvatthī to Rājagaha with their respective entourages of five hundred monks each. The residents of Rājagaha, coming together collectively—in groups of two or three, or fifteen—began to offer alms and engage in works of charity for the chief disciples and their retinues. One day, when Ven. Sāriputta was organizing a meritorious deed, he declared:
"O lay devotees, if someone gives alms himself but does not encourage others to establish themselves in the practice of giving—meaning, he does not inspire others to give alms—such a person will obtain wealth and material resources in whatever future births (*jāti*) they are born, but will not obtain the wealth of having a retinue of followers. Another person does not give alms himself but encourages others to do so. In the future, that person will not receive wealth and material resources, but will only receive the wealth of a retinue of followers. Yet another person neither gives alms himself nor encourages others to do so. Such a person will obtain neither wealth nor a retinue in their future births (*jāti*). Fourthly, it is shown that another person gives alms himself and also encourages others to establish themselves in that practice of giving. (What we now call collecting donations is 'establishing others in practice'.) Such a person, in future births (*jāti*), will receive both wealth and a retinue," so he declared.
A certain wise man who was listening to this thought: "I must act in a way that I obtain both of these blessings." After the crowd departed, he approached Ven. Sāriputta and said, "Venerable Sir, I invite you and the Sangha to alms tomorrow." Ven. Sāriputta asked how many monks were in his retinue, and when he was told there were about a thousand, the man declared, "I hope to offer alms to all those thousand monks tomorrow." Ven. Sāriputta consented by silence.
Now, even though this man said this, he made the invitation without any prior preparation. Walking through the streets of the city, he rallied the people, crying out: "Mothers and fathers, I have invited a thousand monks for tomorrow. Bring whatever alms-materials you can, according to your means. Let us gather in one place and prepare the alms!" Thus he encouraged the people. Accordingly, a large number of people took responsibility for ten, twenty, or even a hundred monks, and brought alms-materials to the venue. A certain wealthy devotee brought a saffron robe worth a hundred thousand coins and gave it to the organizer of the alms—the lay devotee—saying, "If there is any shortage of alms-materials, sell this robe and settle the expenses. If there is no such shortage, offer this robe to any monk of your choice."
So, the alms-giving went very well the next day. There was no shortage of anything. This robe, this saffron robe, remained. The alms-organizer said to the gathering, "A certain person offered me this highly valuable robe. All the alms-giving activities are now finished. To whom shall we offer this robe?" Then someone said, "Let us offer it to Ven. Sāriputta, the Chief Disciple, the Arahant." Another group said, "This Ven. Sāriputta only comes and goes during the harvest season. But Ven. Devadatta is not like that. He is like the water kept in our homes. He is there for all our auspicious and inauspicious occasions. Therefore, let us give it to Ven. Devadatta." Since there were two factions, the alms-organizer held a small vote at the alms-hall. Here is the result of the vote: Ven. Devadatta won by a majority of four votes as the person worthy of receiving that robe worth a hundred thousand. The faction of the Chief Disciple Ven. Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, lost.
Somehow or other, they gave that robe to Ven. Devadatta. When Ven. Devadatta cut it, dyed it, and wore it, walking about in the city, the people felt a certain displeasure at his behavior. Perhaps he walked about in an arrogant manner, wandering here and there. People began to say, "This robe is suitable for Ven. Sāriputta, but certainly not for Devadatta." Sometime after this incident, a certain monk came from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī to see the Buddha. When the Buddha was inquiring about the health and welfare of the two chief disciples from that monk, that monk related this incident. Then the Buddha said, "Monk, not only in this life, but in the past too, Devadatta wore a robe unsuitable for him and was reviled by others," and he related a certain Jātaka story.
In the past, there was an elephant hunter in Benares who killed elephants. He lived by going into the forests, killing elephants, and selling their tusks, claws, meat, and so on. In some forests, there were large herds of elephants. In one forest, the elephants had a custom: whenever they saw the Paccekabuddhas living in the forest, before going to find food, they would bow down at the knees of the Paccekabuddhas and then depart. One day, this elephant hunter saw this incident. He fell into reflection: "Why do these elephants bow down to these Paccekabuddhas? It must be because of the robe. If I too can get a robe, I can carry out this elephant hunting very well." Having thought thus, what did he do next? When a Paccekabuddha had entered a pond to bathe, the hunter stole the robe left on the bank. Wearing it, what was his next trick? Wrapping the robe from his head downwards, he hid his elephant-killing weapon, his tool.
Thinking it was a Paccekabuddha, the elephant herd would bow as they went past. After the herd had passed, the elephant hunter would strike and kill the very last elephant with his weapon, sell its tusks and so on, and throw the remaining flesh in the forest.
While this was going on for some time, the Bodhisatta became the leader of that elephant herd. The Bodhisatta realized that his herd was diminishing. Reflecting on the cause, he suspected, "This danger must be coming from that particular person." Letting the other elephants go ahead, he walked last, at the very end, one day. When the Bodhisatta, the elephant king, approached after the other elephants had gone, the elephant hunter cast aside the robe and struck with his weapon. Since the Bodhisatta elephant king was alert, he jumped back, avoided the weapon, and then leapt forward to catch the man, saying, "Was it not you who destroyed my herd?" What did the hunter do then? Shielding himself behind a tree, he held the robe out in front of him. When he held the robe in front, the Bodhisatta elephant king thought: "If I destroy this man who is now holding this robe, it would be an insult to hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants. It would mean erasing that respectful fear from my mind." Therefore, without killing him, he spared him, but admonished and condemned him: "You are wearing a garment suitable only for those who are free from passions!" and disgraced that man.
Having related that past event, the Buddha said to that monk: "That elephant hunter was indeed Devadatta. In the past, too, he did such a thing." And then he uttered those two verses we took as our theme:
"Whoever, not having cast out the stains of defilements, devoid of self-control and truthfulness, wears the saffron robe, is not worthy of the saffron robe."
"But whoever has cast out the stains of defilements, is well-established in moral virtue, endowed with self-control and truthfulness, is indeed worthy of the saffron robe." This is the meaning contained in those verses.
Now let us consider what lessons we can learn both from this primary incident and from the Jātaka story. When we think of the lighter side of this story, even the exemplary action of that alms-organizer can be taken as a lesson for us. Even in these times, regarding meritorious deeds such as alms-givings, there is a practice called *sammādam kirīma* (collecting donations). Indeed, this word *sammādam* is mentioned in the Dhamma as *samādāna* (encouraging or taking upon oneself). Now, you are very familiar with the term *sīla-samādāna* (undertaking moral virtue). You are not so familiar with the term *dāna-samādāna* (undertaking giving), but instead, there is the term *sammādam* for alms. That too expresses the same idea: making others accept the practice of giving. It was because they accepted it that those people contributed according to their ability. This is indeed in accordance with the Dhamma declared by the Buddha, which Ven. Sāriputta pointed out here. It is something that leads to obtaining the wealth of a retinue of followers. Why? When one encourages others in giving, acting as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇa-mitta*), that too is a wholesome act—inclining others toward the wholesome. So, to cultivate both these types of wealth, we see that the wise man organized that alms-giving with great honesty and fairness. He started without any prior preparation for a thousand monks. Not only did he complete everything in a single night and finish the alms-giving, but he also did not use the extra robe in an inappropriate way. According to the intention of the person who offered it, he held a vote and gave it to the one chosen by the vote, regardless of whether that person was truly suitable.
Next, we must also reflect a little on what was expressed there regarding Ven. Devadatta. Popularity is not a yardstick for virtue. In terms of popularity, the Chief Disciple Ven. Sāriputta lost to Ven. Devadatta. Yet, Devadatta did not practice in a manner suitable for that robe. It was because of this that he became the target of public blame. Moreover, Ven. Devadatta did not stop there. Having obtained a robe that even the Chief Disciples did not receive, he was driven further by the pride that arose within him. The Buddha has declared: "*Dāruṇo lābhasakkāro*"—"Gain, honor, and renown are dreadful, bitter, and harsh." Why? Because through them, some people use their popularity in a dangerous manner, attempting to live their lives in an unrighteous way. This is exactly what happened to Ven. Devadatta. What did Ven. Devadatta do next? He thought, "If I am to obtain gain, honor, fame, and praise, I must secure the royal patronage of some king." Thus, Prince Ajātasattu, who had a claim to the kingdom of Magadha, came to his mind. He used a certain tactic to win over Prince Ajātasattu. Ven. Devadatta possessed supernormal knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the power to perform psychic wonders (*iddhi*). So, by psychic power, he manifested a body wrapped in terrifying snakes to frighten Prince Ajātasattu, appearing on his lap. After the prince was frightened, he transformed back to his normal form and won him over. Prince Ajātasattu was won over by those psychic powers. From then on, Prince Ajātasattu went to see Ven. Devadatta twice a day, morning and evening, with five hundred chariots. He also sent five hundred dishes of highly delicious food to Ven. Devadatta. When the monks reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha declared: "Monks, do not be envious of the gain, honor, fame, and praise of Ven. Devadatta. The acquisition of these gains and honors will lead only to the decline and ruin of Ven. Devadatta. Just as when a fierce dog gets a sniff of bile on its nose, it becomes even more fierce and violent, so does Ven. Devadatta behave." Thus he made a prediction about the future.
Likewise, Ven. Devadatta then persuaded Prince Ajātasattu, telling him to kill his father, King Bimbisāra, and quickly become king, saying, "I will kill the Buddha and take over the empire of the Dhamma." Actually, the root cause for this was an earlier incident when Ven. Devadatta stood up while the Buddha was preaching the Dhamma to a gathering and requested, "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is now old and advanced in years. Hand over the congregation of monks to me. Let the Blessed One retire and dwell in quiet ease." The Buddha censured him. "I would not hand over the leadership of the Sangha even to the Chief Disciples; how then should I hand it over to one like you?" he rebuked. Angered by this, Ven. Devadatta, with the assistance of Prince Ajātasattu, plotted to assassinate the Buddha. Prince Ajātasattu tortured his father to death in a horrific manner, committing a grave karma of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*). After securing the kingdom of Magadha, Devadatta came and said, "Now you have accomplished your task; now help me with mine." Then he devised schemes to assassinate the Buddha.
The first scheme he employed was sending archers when the Buddha was dwelling quietly in the forest. He assigned one archer to shoot the Buddha. To ensure this archer was killed on his return, he stationed two other archers on that path. To kill those two on their way back, he stationed four others on another path. To kill those four, eight others. To kill those eight, sixteen others. Ven. Devadatta planned this assassination of the Buddha through such an extraordinary, cunning, and conspiratorial plot to keep it an absolute secret. However, when the man who went to shoot the Buddha approached, his body became stiff due to the Buddha's spiritual majesty, and unable to do it, he confessed his mission. The Buddha preached the Dhamma to him and sent him back by another path. Likewise, through the power of the Dhamma, all those other men stationed on the path—in groups of two, four, eight, and sixteen—came to see the Buddha, listened to the Dhamma, became faithful, and did not carry out the intended task.
When Ven. Devadatta came to know of this, he thought, "Now I must kill the Buddha myself." He climbed the Gijjhakūṭa (Vulture Peak) mountain and, while the Buddha was walking up and down below, hurled down a massive boulder. While the boulder was falling, two other rocks emerged through the Buddha's spiritual majesty and stopped the boulder. However, a splinter of stone struck the sole of the Buddha's foot, causing a severe and painful wound. The physician Jīvaka had to treat it. By this act, Devadatta fell into the grave *ānantariya-kamma* of shedding the blood of a Buddha with malicious intent.
Since he still could not assassinate the Buddha, what did Ven. Devadatta do next? He bribed the elephant keepers and arranged to release the elephant Nālāgiri, having fed it alcohol, onto the path where the Buddha and the Sangha were walking. As the elephant Nālāgiri came charging in a terrifying manner, kicking up dust, the Buddha directed a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and subdued the elephant, making it kneel down. When all three attempts failed, a huge public protest arose among the citizens and residents of the city, saying that King Ajātasattu was helping such a sinful person. King Ajātasattu was forced to withdraw all the support he had been giving to Devadatta. At this point, Ven. Devadatta thought: "How can I regain gain and honor?" Then a sinful thought occurred to him: to create a schism in the Sangha (*saṅgha-bheda*)—to split the monks and take a group of the harmonious Sangha with him to start a separate dispensation. Along with the arising of this sinful thought, his previously held psychic powers vanished. Later, Ven. Ānanda informed the Buddha of this news. The Buddha declared: "Behold, then, Devadatta is going to bind himself to another extremely grave *ānantariya-kamma*." Paying no heed to any advice or admonition, Ven. Devadatta presented five special demands—the five precepts (*pañca-vara*)—to the Buddha, things that ordinary people would easily find appealing. When the Buddha rejected these five demands, he won over five hundred newly ordained monks to his faction and went to Gayāsīsa—the noble place we now call Bodh Gaya—and started a separate dispensation. Placing two disciples, Kokālika and Kaṭamorakatissa, on either side as his chief disciples, he started a dispensation with the demeanor of a Buddha. This continued for a short time. Meanwhile, on one occasion, the Buddha sent the two chief disciples, Ven. Sāriputta and Ven. Moggallāna, to bring this group back. When they arrived, Ven. Devadatta was preaching the Dhamma in the manner of a Buddha. He was deceived into thinking that the two chief disciples had also joined his side. Having preached the Dhamma to some extent, he delegated the preaching of the Dhamma to them in his place and went to sleep. In the meantime, the two chief disciples presented the Dhamma correctly, turned the minds of all of Devadatta's followers back, and returned through the air with that group to see the Buddha.
Kokālika, Ven. Devadatta's chief disciple, woke Devadatta up—it is said he kicked him in the chest to wake him—and told him what had happened. Due to the intense shock and grief, Ven. Devadatta began to vomit blood. It is said he vomited warm blood. Because of that mental shock and vomiting of blood, Ven. Devadatta suffered terrible physical pain for nine months. In his final moments, hoping to see the Buddha, he told his followers, "Take me to Jetavana." When this news arrived, the monks told the Buddha, "Ven. Devadatta is coming." But the Buddha declared, "In this life, Devadatta will not get to see me again. In whatever manner he comes to Jetavana, he will not see me." Initially, his followers were reluctant to carry him, saying, "When you were healthy, you harbored such hatred toward the Buddha, and now you ask us to carry you?" Then Devadatta said, "Even so, the Blessed One has no hatred toward me." Somehow he persuaded them. So, the followers placed Ven. Devadatta on a litter and carried him near Jetavana. Placing the litter by the side of the pond near Jetavana, those who brought him went down to the pond to bathe. Meanwhile, Devadatta, sitting on the litter, put his feet on the ground. As his feet touched the ground, the earth split open, flames emerged from the Avīci hell, and it is recorded that he went down to the Avīci hell. It is said that at that final moment, Ven. Devadatta uttered a certain verse taking refuge in the Buddha.
So, that was the fate of Ven. Devadatta. In the beginning, the Buddha pointed out that the cause for this was gain and honor. Gain and honor are extremely dreadful things. It was because of the pride of obtaining the robe that should have rightfully gone to the Chief Disciple Ven. Sāriputta, as mentioned at the beginning of this story, that he went on to seek further popularity, gain, and honor, and got entangled in such a multitude of sinful deeds. Accordingly, we can understand that, as the Buddha also declared, gain and honor are extremely dangerous. The Buddha explained the misfortune that befell Ven. Devadatta to the monks through four similes: "Monks, a banana tree bears fruit only for its own destruction. So too does a bamboo tree; if it flowers, the bamboo tree is destroyed. If a reed flowers, the reed is destroyed. If a she-mule becomes pregnant, she dies because of that pregnancy. In the very same way, gain, honor, and renown have arisen only for the destruction of Devadatta." Thus he declared. Accordingly, we can understand that popularity, gain, and honor often lead human beings toward dangerous, unwholesome actions.
Furthermore, when we reflect on this Jātaka story, we can extract certain advices of contemporary relevance. In this Jātaka story, it was mentioned first of all: what did the elephant hunter use for his elephant hunting? A robe stolen from the Paccekabuddhas. Devout lay devotees, in our Dhamma books, this robe is described as the "banner of the Arahants" (*arahaddhaja*). What is meant by the "banner of Arahants"? Now, let us imagine a pageant (*perahera*) coming. We understand who is in the pageant by the flag carried at the front. Similarly, when one sees the robe, what is the thought that arises? It is the thought: "This is either an Arahant or a group of people practicing the path to Arahantship, striving for Arahantship." That is the thought that arises when a group of people wearing this robe approaches. That is why it is called the banner of Arahants. But if this banner of Arahants is put forward for other purposes, for other fronts, it is just like the elephant hunter using the robe stolen from the Buddha for elephant hunting.
Therefore, the most valuable thing is to protect the banner of Arahants as a banner that represents that journey toward Nibbāna, that aim, that objective, the journey toward Arahantship. We mentioned earlier about protecting a dispensation. We can draw that idea from this Jātaka story. Furthermore, in some other places, this robe is also referred to as a suit of armor. Now, King Dhammāsoka had a brother named Prince Tissa, who had obtained the position of sub-king. However, Prince Tissa, having developed a strong aspiration for Nibbāna, was ordained in the dispensation. He was so fond of solitude that in the Dhamma texts, he is referred to as Ven. Ekavihāriya. This royal prince became a monk who loved to live alone. After ordination, so strong was his aspiration for Nibbāna that he uttered a certain verse to reveal his hope for Nibbāna. The idea expressed in that verse is this: "I am entering the forest wearing this armor. I will not come out of the forest without ending the battle against defilements and becoming an Arahant." Thus, it is clear that armor—devout lay devotees, armor is a garment used in war, in battle, to protect against arrows. So, using the robe as armor for the battle against defilements, as a protection for the battle against defilements, is appropriate. But presenting the robe to escape the consequences of committing other wrongs and bad actions is not in accordance with the dispensation. It is not something aligned with the dispensation. It would be just like the elephant hunter who, when punishment drew near for the crime of killing elephants, took off the robe and held it out in front of him. Thus, we can understand various matters and advices through the medium of this Jātaka story.
So, from all this, we see that dispensational values can be overshadowed by gain, honor, fame, and praise. That is why the Buddha constantly highlighted their danger. On certain occasions, the Buddha compared this to a dung beetle. When a dung beetle gets a pile of dung, a ball of dung, it rolls it along, full of pride. The Buddha gave this simile, saying that when a monk says very proudly, "I have invitations from such and such places; I have no shortage of the four requisites," if he speaks like this, he is just like that dung beetle. The Buddha has shown this in a way that conveys censure. Moreover, we now know that once caught in the wave of gain and honor, the valuable virtues that are considered the eternal values of the Sangha are lost. What are those virtues? Fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*), contentment (*santuṭṭhitā*), and ease of maintenance (*subharatā*). Fewness of wishes means having few desires, being satisfied with little. If one gets caught in the wave of luxury and extreme luxury coming from lay society, one is swept away. Just like a sandcastle on the beach being washed away and destroyed by wave after wave during the monsoon season, that virtue of fewness of wishes is destroyed by luxurious and extremely luxurious invitations. Everyone can understand something from this. Likewise, contentment—the virtue of being content with what one receives. That too belongs to the monks. Contentment with the four requisites. Contentment with the eight requisites (*aṭṭha-parikkhāra*). The monks who were content with the eight requisites. Eight requisites. Now, I do not know if we can even count how many they are. The things considered essential as requisites are increasing day by day. Similarly, ease of maintenance—meaning being easy to support. As monks gradually lean toward a luxurious life, the responsibility falling on the lay followers to support them becomes heavier and heavier.
Likewise, an important point is that the Buddha has shown that a true monk should not maintain improper relationships with laypeople. Now, at the alms-hall, the Devadatta faction praised Devadatta by saying, "Ven. Sāriputta only comes during the harvest season. But Ven. Devadatta helps us in all matters, weddings and funerals, just like a water vessel kept at home." Like a vessel of water: anything, anytime, you can take it, drink it, use it. If a monk falls to that level, there is a risk of him going down the path of Devadatta's objectives. Such a dangerous thing is popularity. As soon as popularity arises, next comes the expectation of office—gaining positions. Through that, without even realizing it, one is directed toward an undisciplined path contrary to the dispensation. Instead, what the Buddha points out is that monks should remove improper lay associations and lead their lives in a manner that accords with their ultimate goal, the path to Nibbāna. Leave alone other things, even treating laypeople in an improper way is called "corrupting families" (*kula-dūsana*). Why is the word *kula-dūsana*—corrupting families—used? Because it corrupts their faith. It is with great faith, deep faith, immense faith, that lay devotees offer the four requisites to the Sangha. Maintaining relationships with laypeople in an irregular, improper manner causes that faith to be corrupted. We see this from the actions of Ven. Devadatta.
Yet, in society generally, it is those with such attitudes who are respected, who become popular, and to whom most people give their votes. We must bear in mind that if the dispensation is to last for a long time, we must give our vote to the wholesome desire—to the wholesome side. To that side. Thus, we were able to extract a large number of such matters from this story.
The Buddhas introduce a Sambuddha Sāsana to this world having truly understood the nature of this saṃsāra (round of rebirths). The Buddha has declared in various sutta discourses that whatever one receives, whether it is kingship, the status of a treasurer, or the status of a wheel-turning monarch, all of it is impermanent (anicca). Sometimes, in these times, some people read with great desire the parts in those sutta discourses concerning the wealth of wheel-turning monarchs. But they ignore the ending of the suttas: "Monks, all this is impermanent (anicca). Those wheel-turning monarchs are no more, those queens are no more, those princes are no more. All that wealth is now destroyed. Therefore, be disillusioned with Preparations / preparations / volitional activity (saṅkhāras). All these Preparations / preparations / volitional activity (saṅkhāras) are impermanent (anicca)." It is in this manner that the Buddha brings forward past stories, stories of wheel-turning monarchs, and so on. Accordingly, what is shown is the nature of suffering / unsatisfactoriness / stress (dukkha) in this saṃsāric life. It is true that by putting patches on these, lay life is maintained to a certain extent. But it is from among the lay devotees that a monk is born into the world at some point. In situations like this, whatever lifestyles you may have, whatever clothes and ornaments you may have at home, putting them aside, removing them, and turning to a simple life for this one day, you get an opportunity to reflect deeply on your life and the world, away from your homes. Through such a beginning, if someone reflects deeply on their life, on their saṃsāric becoming / existence (bhava), and at some point develops disillusionment—disillusionment with saṃsāra—it is at that moment that they enter the monastic life.
What, then, is the purpose of ordination? *Pabbajjā* means crossing over from this suffering (dukkha) of saṃsāra. A person enters ordination with the primary objective: *sabbadukkhaniassaraṇa nibbāna sacchikaraṇatthāya*—for the sake of release from all suffering (dukkha) and the realization of Nibbāna. Even today, when the monastic robe is tied around the neck, that phrase is recited. This ordination is for the sake of realizing Nibbāna, which is the departure from all suffering (dukkha). Then, what is meant by the preservation of the dispensation? When we think of the Sangha in the dispensation, you have heard the term "the Great Sangha of the Eight Noble Individuals" (*aṭṭha-purisa-puggala*). Why is this Great Sangha of the Eight Noble Individuals a special concept for the lay devotee? Because, when viewed from the perspective of lay life, Nibbāna is a very distant thing, a very remote path. But these Eight Noble Individuals are those who give us the understanding that people like us have also traveled this path on various occasions and have put an end to the suffering (dukkha) of saṃsāra. Those eight individuals who are walking on that path and who have reached the fruits of that path—namely, Sotāpanna, Sakadāgāmi, Anāgāmi, and Arahant—are like a lamp-post, a row of lamps on the path to Nibbāna. Through them, we receive a certain light, knowing: "We too can walk on this path." That is the value within the Sangha Sāsana, the dispensation. As long as these monks practice on that path to Nibbāna, so long—as the Buddha also declared on his deathbed—as long as they fulfill those thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*), this world will not be empty of Arahants. Because, if one understands the practical aspect of the Dhamma shown by the Buddha and acts accordingly, practices accordingly, one can attain these even today. If we do not properly understand the values of such a salvific Sambuddha Sāsana, and instead use the robe merely as a flag or a suit of armor, the dispensation will decline rather than endure for a long time for the welfare and happiness of gods and humans.
This is indeed the lesson we can draw from this story. We must reflect: how do we enter this path? Through virtues such as moral virtue (*sīla*). The Buddha has shown that concentration (*samādhi*) is built on the foundation of moral virtue (*sīla*).
