That is to understand the suffering (*dukkha*) contained in it, even for a short while. Yet, we always like to change postures and conceal that suffering (*dukkha*). That is where ignorance (*avijjā*) lies. It is the same with other things. However, the Buddha brings this out to open our eyes: "We solved this same equation over a long period, but the correct answer did not come."
Therefore, in this era of a Buddha's appearance, we must contemplate by regarding what is valuable as valuable, without narrow objectives such as meditating merely to cure minor illnesses and small ailments. We must engage in Dhamma practice and meditation with the determination: "This entire saṁsāra is like a hospital, and I must obtain complete cure and leave it." If we do so, only then can we utilize this Buddha's Dispensation properly. Only then can we help others to utilize it as well.
The essence of the Buddha's Dhamma lies within the Four Noble Truths. What is called the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*)—form, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), Preparations (*saṅkhāra*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*)—every single one of these that is held onto is pointed out by the Buddha as suffering (*dukkha*). *"Saṅkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā"* — in brief, the Buddha declares that the five aggregates of grasping are themselves suffering (*dukkha*). That is the essence of the Truth of Suffering. Next, the Buddha declares: "Why does this state of suffering (*dukkha*) exist? It is due to craving (*taṇhā*)." Due to the unquenchable thirst of craving (*taṇhā*), living beings run in this saṁsāra for a long time. They draw their last breath with the hope of obtaining in the next life at least the wishes they could not obtain in this life. They do not understand their substancelessness.
Therefore, according to the accumulated kamma, one is born in those various places. It is not as one wishes. According to the kamma performed by oneself over a long period, the wheel of kamma turns on one side in this manner. Subjugated to that, living beings swim in an ocean of tears and an ocean of blood over a long period of time. So, indeed, when we think in that manner, we must contemplate: if we are to protect the Buddha's Sasana, if we are to protect the Dhamma, we must enter upon this deep aspect. We must go from danger (*ādīnava*) to escape (*nissaraṇa*), without remaining in danger (*ādīnava*) forever. For that, one must think with wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) about one's own life. Now, some people say various things about the meditation on foulness (*asubha-bhāvanā*), and so forth. However, if someone wishes to be liberated from saṁsāra, this impermanent (*anicca*) nature—the aforementioned beauty of form fades away, the strength of the body fades away, and the state of old age arrives. Instead of one's two legs, one has to depend on the four legs of the bed. Thinking about those lives, and next, thinking about other things—even the possessions one considers one's own—every single thing is subject to impermanence (*aniccatā*). These are things the Buddha reminds us of. Why does He remind us of every single one of these? Because the weariness (*nibbidā*) towards saṁsāra is essential for escaping from saṁsāra. Sometimes, a special event can bring that out from within such sorrowful situations. That can be brought out only if a noble friend (*kalyāṇa-mitta*) or the necessary Dhamma instruction falls into place at the right time. Otherwise, one falls back to sleep. One falls back to sleep again and again. That is the situation in this long saṁsāra. Ignorance (*avijjā*) means neglecting, forgetting; it is very easy. That is why this is called a dream of life. Therefore, to escape, one must remain awake, both regarding one's own life and the nature of the world. One must practice seeing in accordance with what was pointed out by the Buddha. Instead of the perception of permanence (*nicca-saññā*), one must generate the perception of impermanence (*anicca-saññā*). That is why the mind must be brought to a level where one can look at the world without those perversions (*vipallāsa*)—without distorted views and distorted states. The distorted views are: regarding what is impermanent (*anicca*) as permanent, regarding what is foul as beautiful, regarding what is subject to suffering (*dukkha*) as happiness, and regarding what is not-self (*anattā*) as self. That is the view of perversion (*vipallāsa*) existing within worldly beings. To conquer that, if one constantly trains the mind to see impermanence (*aniccatā*), from then on, one sees this gradually breaking down. Seeing it break down, fear arises: "Oh, is it not a breaking thing? Is it not a rotting fence that I am holding onto?" Many people think their lives are highly secure. They have bank deposits, they have children who have obtained high positions. In the end, when looking at the final period, the banks also collapse, and the children do not look after them. In the end, all those rotting fences that were held onto fall down. What remains for oneself is only the four legs of the bed. At that moment, what helps is indeed the Dhamma. If one has obtained some (Dhamma) in the past, that is the consolation at that moment. One must contemplate in that manner.
We brought out various Dhamma points through this short story. We do not always say these things merely for the aesthetic interest of the story. Through each of these, certain Dhamma principles can be brought out to help our lives. In the Buddha’s time, those who lived with that Dhamma—sometimes a Brahmin comes and asks the Buddha, "How long is this aeon?" Due to the faith (*saddhā*) generated through that, in the end, he becomes a Buddhist. But nowadays, there is a way of thinking that treats this as something not belonging to oneself, discussing this world and space. That does not help one's life. They use them as means of obtaining various degrees. However, those must be brought close to one's life. The Buddha has already declared the essence of all these things. Whether we spend millions of money to go to strange worlds or not, when we die, we travel according to kamma. No vehicle is needed for that; no strange satellite is needed. Instead, at the moment of death, automatically along with that mind, in some instances, one goes to the Brahma realms. It is through that aforementioned strength of wholesome actions, not through other artificial strengths. Therefore, because of the nature of this existence (*bhava*), we must bring out these Dhamma values. We must bring them out because they are now fading away rapidly. There is a tendency to bring out other things through that aforementioned practice of worldly development and cemetery development. If this Dispensation is to survive for a long period, we must bring out the path to Nibbāna pointed out by the Buddha to the world, Nibbāna, and we must direct our minds to the things that help towards it. We must teach them to others.
Thinking in that manner, now, on this valuable day, these devotees, having established themselves in a virtue (*sīla*) that helps in traveling the path of Dhamma according to their respective measures—at this moment, they have observed the livelihood-as-eighth virtue (*ājīva-aṭṭhamaka-sīla*), and the eight virtue-rules of the precept day (*upoṣatha-aṭṭha-sīla*). In that manner, there are also those who have observed the ten virtue-rules (*dasa-sīla*) that help in meditation. Having established oneself in virtue of that kind, and having directed the mind to meditation, and having brought this mind—which was scattered by globalization and other things—to this place at this moment and directed it to the Dhamma, you have brought out the power of a concentrated mind through a certain meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Next, you must utilize a Dhamma sermon of this kind: if the three characteristics of impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anattā*), which help in overcoming the fear of saṁsāra, are developed more and more to some extent in daily life, they will become perfections (*pāramī*). Even if they are not obtained in this life, they can be obtained at some point. However, we must be energetic and, without delaying heedlessly, resolve to realize it in this very life. Before the Buddha's Sasana ends, through this path of meditation and with the association of noble friends (*kalyāṇa-mitta*), by practicing this Dhamma and meditation, we must obtain—at the minimum, if nothing greater—the path-knowledge of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa*), which is the greatest and most valuable power of escaping from the four planes of misery. If possible, may we be completely liberated from the entire saṁsāra and cross over from this ocean of tears and ocean of blood to obtain the supreme, deathless, great Nibbāna of Arahantship, through this strength of virtue, concentration, and wisdom (*sīla-samādhi-paññā*) fulfilled today! You must wish: "May this be obtained through listening to this Dhamma sermon!" Now, may all those who wish for the merit of Nibbāna—from Avīci to Akaniṭṭha, including our relatives—rejoice in this mass of merit we have accumulated so far through this Dhamma sermon! Having rejoiced, with the aspiration to escape from all saṁsāric suffering (*dukkha*) such as birth (*jāti*), decay and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), and sickness, and to find peace in the supreme, deathless, great Nibbāna, recite these stanzas and share the merit:
“*Ettāvatā ca amhehi.........*”

(pahankanuwa sinhala audio dhamma sermon no.80)
namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa
(homage to the blessed one, the worthy one, the fully self-enlightened one)
pali stanza:
alankato cepi samam careyya, santo danto niyato brahmacari; sabbesu bhutesu nidhaya dandam, so brahmano so samano sa bhikkhu.
from:
verse 142 from the dandavagga (chapter on punishment) of the dhammapada
dear listeners,
the blessed one declared that due to various kinds of intoxication, worldly beings fall into heedlessness in this samsara. in addition to natural intoxications such as the intoxication of youth (*yobbana-mada*), the intoxication of health (*arogya-mada*), the intoxication of life (*jivita-mada*), and the intoxication of wealth (*bhoga-mada*), the dhamma indicates that the most well-known intoxication in society—the intoxication of liquor—is also a cause for heedlessness. what helps one to escape from all these intoxications is *samvega* (spiritual urgency). the background story for the stanza we have chosen as our theme today reveals how *samvega*, arising out of the sorrowful situations in life, can help a person conquer all these intoxications and draw closer to nibbana.
the lord buddha preached this stanza concerning king pasenadi kosala’s minister named santati. when this prime minister, santati, returned after suppressing a rebellion on the borders of king kosala's kingdom, the king, as a special privilege, granted him royal luxury for seven days. this does not mean he gave him the kingdom itself; it was more like an honorary title. he arranged for him to enjoy pleasures equal to royal luxury—the fivefold sensual pleasures (*panca-kama*). so much so, that a female dancer skilled in dancing and singing was handed over to him for his entertainment. thus, this minister santati spent seven days enjoying liquor, watching those dances, and listening to songs. on the seventh day, he set out to go to the bathing ford, riding on an elephant with his retinue. on the way, seeing the buddha walking for alms, he bowed his head in respect to the buddha and went on. at that moment, the buddha showed a gentle smile. since there is a special significance to such a smile, venerable ananda usually asks, "exalted one, what is the reason for showing that smile?" when asked thus, the buddha declared, "even though this minister goes on like this now, today itself, adorned in all his garments and jewelry, he will come to me, listen to a stanza, and attain final extinguishment (*parinibbana today." among the crowd who heard this, those with wrong views thought, "this recluse gotama says whatever comes to his mouth; today we must be prepared to expose his falsehood and disgrace him." that group prepared themselves in that manner. those with right views and faith were eager, thinking, "we must witness this miraculous event."
meanwhile, during the daytime, minister santati engaged in water sports and then went to the drinking hall in the park. there, the dancer went onto the stage and began to perform her dance. in order to display her dancing grace to the best of her ability, this woman had not eaten properly for all seven days. at this moment, due to hunger and exhaustion, a severe ailment suddenly arose, and she fell down dead right there, with her eyes and mouth wide open. when the minister asked to have her examined, the people said, "now her life has ceased." as soon as he heard this, a great *samvega* (spiritual urgency) and grief arose in this minister. so much so, that due to the *samvega* that arose, his seven days of intoxication subsided right there. he thought, "to whom should i go to subside this grief of mine? i must go to the buddha." in the evening, he came to the buddha, along with his retinue, adorned in his garments and jewelry in that very manner. when he related this story to the buddha, the buddha said, "santati, not only in this life, but in this long samsara, the tears you have shed due to this woman dying in this very manner are greater than the waters of the four great oceans." thus instilling the fear of samsara, he preached a short stanza of deep meaning:
*yam pubbe tam visosehi,*
*paccha te mahu kincanam;*
*majjhe ce no gahessasi,*
*upasanto carissasi.*
when looked at in terms of meaning, in terms of literal meaning, it has to be translated like this: '*yam pubbe tam visosehi*' — whatever there was before, dry it up; '*paccha te mahu kincanam*' — let there be nothing for you afterwards; '*majjhe ce no gahessasi*' — if you do not grasp anything in the middle either; '*upasanto carissasi*' — you will wander completely at peace.
it is said that by deeply considering this brief advice, the sorrow-stricken minister santati attained arahantship at that very moment. along with this, some texts mention that if a person has cultivated meditative absorptions (*jhana*) in the past, they surface. now, here, it is said that he obtained not only the state of *jhana*, but even direct knowledges (*abhinna*). for next, it is said that the arahat santati, after attaining arahantship, examined his life-preparations (*sankhara*) to see how long his life would last. knowing that he would have to pass away (attain *parinibbana, he asked permission from the buddha, saying, "please give me permission to attain *parinibbana*." the buddha said, "very well, but before that, declare to this assembly the past kamma that helped you to become an arahat. and do this not sitting on the ground, but rising into the air." at that moment, it is mentioned here that the arahat santati declared his past history in this manner:
"ninety-one aeons (*kalpas*) ago, during the time of vipassi buddha, i was born in the kingdom of bandhumati and wondered what would be a good livelihood to pursue. when i thought about what occupation would not cause harm or injury to others, i felt that the activity of a dhamma announcer (*dhamma-ghosaka*) was the best occupation. the activity of a dhamma announcer means wandering about proclaiming to people, encouraging them to perform meritorious deeds like giving alms, to observe the precept days, to listen to the dhamma, and to be devoted to the triple gem. so, i started to behave in this way in society as a profession. king bandhumati, who was the buddha's father, came to know about this, summoned me, and asked, 'what are you doing and how are you doing it?' when i told him, 'i am practicing the profession of a dhamma announcer,' he said, 'very good. but you are doing this by walking on foot, aren't you? for this work, you should travel on horseback,' and he gave me a horse. he told me to perform this duty riding on a horse while wearing a garland of flowers. after i had done this for some time, the king summoned me again and said, 'a horse is not sufficient; do this work traveling in a chariot drawn by four horses.' then, for the third time, he summoned me again and assigned me to perform this work of a dhamma announcer adorned in garments and jewelry, riding on an elephant, having also given me various forms of wealth, possessions, and resources. in those days, the lifespan of human beings was extremely long. during the time of vipassi buddha, i performed this task of a dhamma announcer for eighty thousand years." declaring, "it is as a result of this that i obtained this state," minister santati entered into the fire-element attainment (*tejo-dhatu-samapatti*) right there in the air and kindled fire in his own body. the blood and flesh of his body were consumed. at that time, the buddha had a cloth spread out to collect the burnt bone relics and had a stupa built there at the four-way junction, wishing, "may people worship this stupa and accumulate merit."
after this event, after this miraculous event, a discussion arose among the monks: "this minister santati attained arahantship while adorned in his garments and jewelry. do we call this person an ascetic (*samana*), a monk (*bhikkhu*), or a brahmin (*brahmana*)?" a discussion of this nature arose. having heard this, the buddha uttered the stanza on that occasion, which is presented as follows:
*alankato cepi samam careyya*
*santo danto niyato brahmacari*
*sabbesu bhutesu nidhaya dandam*
*so brahmano so samano sa bhikkhu*
the meaning of it is: "even if someone is adorned in garments and jewelry, if they are peaceful, tamed, established in celibacy, having laid aside cudgels and weapons towards all beings, having a practice of non-violence, discarding uneven conduct and practicing even conduct—to such a person, whichever word is used, whether ascetic, brahmin, or monk, there is no wrong. this is the idea conveyed by that stanza."
that is the story. what we have to extract from this story and event is—indeed, one might wonder how a layperson, having been intoxicated for seven days in that manner, could attain arahantship. one should not misunderstand this. however, it is connected to past kamma. only to someone who has the power of past perfections (*parami*) does the buddha preach the dhamma, looking at the right moment. this dhamma is of such a timeless nature (*akalika*) that, though short, if it is deeply understood, that person can escape from samsara at that very moment. there are many such highly miraculous things in dhamma stories. in this day and age, someone might even question them.
now, if we analyze this, what we have to say is that even if we think about this story, at first glance there is only one drama. but there is no wrong in thinking that there are two dramas. because within this entire samsara existence, there are three stages: gratification (*assada*), danger (*adinava*), and escape (*nissarana*). gratification means enjoyment. worldly beings are tempted to enjoy sensations based on the fivefold sensual pleasures (*panca-kama*). especially animal beings. even human beings—ordinary persons—live in the fivefold sensual pleasures. that is where they are. what we call "stages" is also one such stage. next, when experiencing this, at a certain point, danger arises from within it itself—gratification and danger. at that moment, worldly beings are tempted to think. they wonder, "why does this happen to us? why do we get such sorrowful results?" and fall into contemplation. next, they begin to search. a way to get out of this, to be free. that is what is called "escape" (*nissarana*). escape means leaping out of this circular wheel of samsara—the stage of escape. for that, if one meets a noble friend (*kalyana-mitta*), a buddha, at the right time, one can attain the escape called nibbana. those are the three stages. all of these are contained within the short seven-day experience of minister santati. that royal luxury of seven days was a false royal luxury. it was perhaps the liquor that helped him forget its falsity and impermanence (*aniccata*). he was intoxicated for all seven days. from this sleep—instead of sleepiness, it was intoxication—he awoke from this sleep, this dream of life, when he saw the tragic drama of that actress’s dance. it became a drama. when we think a little about that, it is rare to see that final scene of an actor's or actress's life on a stage. that is the final scene of the dance of all of our lives. but we can contemplate that in a deeply moving way (*samvegi*). that woman must have danced because she could not avoid dancing. because it was her profession. but at that moment, the dancing was done in madness. a certain passage in the buddha’s dhamma is clarified to us by this. the buddha described this drama—now, in these times, artists who enjoy aesthetic pleasure might feel some displeasure toward the buddha about such things—but the buddha compared drama to madness: *"ummattakamidam, bhikkhave, ariyassa vinaye naccam"* — "monks, in the discipline of the noble ones, dancing is madness." so, this fits perfectly here. indeed, she danced unable to bear the pain of hunger. that is exactly what we say on some occasions: if someone is made to stand on a heated iron stage, the effort they make to shift their feet will appear to those looking as a dance. to a foreigner, it might even be a dance worth filming. thus, according to the buddha's word, it is clear that this dancing is like madness. now, this fits perfectly. in the end, it was a struggling due to the pain of hunger. she struggled and fell, with both her eyes and mouth open. that is the final dance. we do not say this in mockery of dancing; these are natural occurrences. but the world forgets this, due to various intoxications such as the aforementioned intoxication of liquor. this reality (*yathabhuta*) became manifest to minister santati. through that, a deep weariness (*nibbida*) arose. indeed, to cross over from samsara, weariness—which is called *nibbida*—is essential. it arises in each individual at their own level. in daily life, we experience the suffering (*dukkha*) of separation from loved ones. but it does not go that deep. here, it was immediate. through that *samvega*, his intoxication subsided right there. that is why the buddha declared it in that stanza. "peaceful, tamed..." — indeed, during that short time, through the weariness (*nibbida*) that arose from it, a certain restraint must have developed in that person. time is not the issue here. a great transformation had occurred in him by the time he came to see the buddha, due to that *samvega*. he was no longer the same minister as before.
so, somehow, through the drama we see that the minister saw gratification, and then danger (*adinava*) due to the sudden death of the actress. next, he came to the buddha seeking escape (*nissarana*). to help with that escape, although the buddha’s sermon was a short stanza, we know it was wonderful. it is something beyond our imagination. the buddha sees the dispositions and latencies (*anusaya*) of characters, and the strengths they have brought from the past. if they have practiced meditation subjects (*kammatthana*), he sees that too. it is according to those that the buddha utters a stanza.
now, this stanza is a deep stanza. in the past, through the merit of being a dhamma announcer (*dhamma-ghosaka*)—encouraging others towards the dhamma is a great merit. the greatest thing one can do in the world is to establish others in the dhamma. if he did this for his entire life, there must have been a vast mass of merit, a strength of perfections (*parami*), within that person. it surfaced, ripened, and matured through that short stanza uttered by the buddha. that stanza is like a riddle to an ordinary person. what does it say? "*yam pubbe tam visosehi*" — if there was something before, dry it up. what is this thing that was there before? past preparations (*sankhara*). the buddha told minister santati, "the tears you have shed in this long samsara due to this very woman dying in this very manner are greater than the four great oceans." thus, such life stories are mentioned in the dhamma—some people come together as husbands and wives five hundred times, or even more. they come together as parents and children, and in various other ways in this long samsara due to the power of attraction they have for one another. what we have to understand here is that minister santati must have had some samsaric connection with that actress. be that as it may, with that samsaric background, minister santati understood the side of danger (*adinava*)—that he had shed an ocean of tears over a long period in samsara for this very woman. now, here, it is as if the buddha declared, "dry up that ocean!" and what is contained within that are past preparations (*sankhara*). let us analyze this term *sankhara* a little.
the term *sankhara* is used in many contexts. but to truly understand this deeply, it must be understood through meditation. briefly, it can be explained in relation to drama. in ancient india, the word *sankhara* was often used in connection with drama. before an actress comes onto the stage, how much makeup and dressing up does she do? even today you know, don't you? there are various kinds—we don't need to specify—indeed, nowadays we see actresses even on the high road. why? because they are not in their natural state. they come onto the stage having made a change by applying various colors. these are called makeup preparations (*anga-sankhara*). they make many artificial, deceptive modifications to suit the scene presented in the drama. that is basically the meaning of the word *sankhara*. therefore, it is in accordance with this deep meaning that the buddha designates everything we do in our entire life as preparations (*sankhara*). in the very effort we make to live, within the good or bad kamma, when considered deeply, what exists is our making a personality, grasping it as "i" and "mine".
it is deeply shown in the dhamma that in one place, an untaught worldling regards form as self. *"rupam attato samanupassati"* — he regards form as self. *"ya kho pana samanupassana — sankharo so"* — that very regarding as self is a formation (*sankhara*). because the buddha has shown that what is called the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*)—whereby an ordinary worldling thinks that there is a self, grasping it as "i" and "mine"—is a falsely assumed thing. or rather, it is something made up. how is it projected? one has a body. one either thinks, "this is my self," or that "the self possesses a body," or thinks "my self is within form," or "form is within the self." in this manner, looking at each of the aggregates in four ways has been shown by the buddha as a formation (*sankhara*). one regards form as self; one regards self as possessing form; one thinks that form is within self; one thinks that self is within form. what this indicates is the inability to let go of form. it is like seeing one’s photograph and saying, "ah, this is me! this is my childhood; this is my youth." thus, one has taken form as "i". in the same manner is feeling (*vedana*). in the same manner is perception (*sanna*)—recognition. in the same manner are preparations (*sankhara*). making preparations is taken in that way. now, when that actress comes onto the stage, she is not the same person who was behind the stage. at that moment she thinks, "i must perform this character." it is not like being at home. thus, there too, we see the deceptive nature of these preparations (*sankhara*). that is why preparations are compared to a banana trunk. a banana trunk has no essence, no heartwood; it is substanceless. consciousness (*vinnana*) is this thinking of "i" and "mine", it is to that mind. in this way, when considering each of these, right there are preparations (*sankhara*). this is a small clue given to understand preparations (*sankhara*). the buddha shows this as something occurring due to ignorance (*avijja*). what is ignorance? it is not knowing that this entire samsaric existence is suffering (*dukkha*). because of not knowing it as suffering (*dukkha*), we perform a great deal of preparations (*sankhara*) in this life. the buddha says that, in the end, suffering (*dukkha*) is received within that. since we do not understand this, we go on and on in samsara accumulating preparations (*sankhara*). that is what is contained in this brief story—the dhamma of dependent arising (*paticca-samuppada*), in short. thus, somehow, those preparations are past preparations (*sankhara*). in the past, minister santati understood that all preparations (*sankhara*) associated with that woman were impermanent (*anicca*). "*yam pubbe tam visosehi*" — he dried up those preparations (*sankhara*). he dried up that grief.
next, "*paccha te mahu kincanam*". those devotees who practice insight meditation (*vipassana*) know that what is called investigation of preparations (*sankhara-sammasana*) means contemplating preparations (*sankhara*). now, in the dhamma, in insight meditation, it is said that what we take as kamma in the world are these very things. these are all our preparations (*sankhara*). indeed, when it is said "all preparations are impermanent" (*"sabbe sankhara anicca"*), it refers to these thoughts of ours, the thoughts (*vitakka*) that arise in the mind within this existence. indeed, the past is something grasped by the mind, isn't it? there, too, are preparations (*sankhara*). the buddha declares that every single one of those past preparations (*sankhara*) is impermanent (*anicca*). likewise, they are substanceless; there is no essence to be grasped as "i" or "mine". next, because those past preparations (*sankhara*) are no longer there, it becomes easy for us. we can contemplate it like waking up from a dream and realizing that the dream was false. therefore, it is easy for an insight meditator (*vipassana-yogi*) to understand the impermanence (*aniccata*) of past preparations (*sankhara*). it is the same regarding future preparations (*sankhara*). according to that same principle, one can understand that if one generates preparations (*sankhara*) in the future, they will likewise perish.
but the most difficult thing is the present. the present is the middle: "*majjhe ce no*". the ordinary person grasps the preparations (*sankhara*) of this present—called *paccuppanna* (the present)—tightly. otherwise, there is no existence either, is there? what is past, one can easily understand, "what is gone is gone." what comes in the future has not arrived yet; even if it comes, one can think, "it is just that much." but the form, feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), preparations (*sankhara*), and consciousness (*vinnana*) of this very moment are held onto tightly. now, here, the feat performed by minister santati was seeing this with wisdom through that *samvega* that arose, through the weariness (*nibbida*) towards samsara. that is how the realization of the paths and fruits (*magga-phala*) occurs. the insight knowledges (*vipassana-nana*) arising out of impermanence (*aniccata*) mature, and through the breaking of that, weariness (*nibbida*) towards samsara arises. through weariness (*nibbida*), the desire to be liberated from samsara arises. through that, by deeply seeing the three characteristics, as a result of a highly rapid and subtle transformation occurring in the mind, one obtains the realization of the paths and fruits. thus, what is fundamental to this is the weariness (*nibbida*) towards samsara, against the background of this event. that is why the buddha, like 'hitting the nail right on the head,' waited exactly until the time of that person's arrival. that is why the buddha showed a gentle smile. the buddha sees the moment when this person can be helped. otherwise, when minister santati bowed his head and was leaving, he could have said, "wait a moment, listen to this sermon and then go," couldn't he? no, he waited until he had gone through all of that and returned humbled. only after his intoxication had subsided, and when the time had arrived, did he deliver that short sermon. santati understood it most deeply. "*majjhe ce no gahessasi*" — if you do not grasp the middle, the present preparations (*sankhara*) either, "*upasanto carissasi*" — you will wander completely at peace, which refers to arahantship.
that is what we have to extract from this story. many such events are mentioned in the dhamma. in this day and age, someone might question this. likewise, on the other hand, we must say that taking this as a general rule, some people might think that just by hearing a short stanza, anyone can obtain this state. we should not think in that way generally. this is an extraordinary occurrence. it is not an ordinary thing; highly extraordinary events are recorded in this dhamma. one must understand their background properly.
then, next, what we need to bring out here is what causes weariness towards samsara. we also started with this life—now, here, it was not only the intoxication of liquor; within this, what must have helped minister santati perform such a heroic deed were also the intoxication of youth (*yobbana-mada*), the intoxication of health (*arogya-mada*), and so forth. it was with their support. next, the intoxication of life (*jivita-mada*)—he conquered others and returned. next, the intoxication of wealth (*bhoga-mada*)—royal luxury was given. it was on that very intoxication born of wealth that he began to enjoy royal luxury for the entire seven days. if we think about it, this "middle" is indeed those seven days. he understood the emptiness of the royal luxury enjoyed during those seven days. then, it is easy to let go of it. if it was understood in that way, the grief caused by this event subsided right there. one was able to conquer that grief. next, the danger of this samsara is understood even more deeply: "have we not spent such a long time in samsara in this manner, is it not an ocean of tears?" so, this aspect—this aspect of the dhamma—is not brought out by most people in this day and age. we have mentioned on many occasions that now the trend is, both for protecting our dispensation (*sasana*) and for carrying this dhamma forward, what is mostly brought out is the side of worldly development. developing the world. the buddha has said: *"na siya lokavaddhano"* — "do not be a developer of the world," or "do not be a developer of cemeteries." developing this samsara is a practice of worldly development and cemetery development—the weariness towards samsara does not fit with that. therefore, much attention is not paid to such things in this day and age. however, during the buddha’s time, on many occasions, to the monks and laypeople who listened to the buddha's dhamma, and to those who came to ask questions, he constantly reminded them of sermons that created a wonderful, powerful sense of urgency (*samvega*) and weariness towards samsara.
these are called the *anamatagga* (suttas). in the *anamatagga samyutta*, several such dhamma sections are mentioned. why are they called the *anamatagga* suttas? the buddha repeatedly reminds us that this samsara is something whose beginning and end are not visible. the beginning of this cannot be found; to illustrate this, there are similes—it is said that upon hearing those discourses, monks attained arahantship right then and there. now, here, we started by speaking about the ocean of tears. that discourse is mentioned in more detail in the dhamma. the buddha asks, "monks, what do you think, which is greater? the tears you have shed over this long samsara—while wandering for a long time covered by ignorance and bound by craving—due to associating with the disagreeable and separating from the agreeable, or the water in the four great oceans?" when that question is asked, the monks humbly declare, "exalted one, if we have properly understood the dhamma preached by you, the tears we have shed in this long samsara due to associating with the disagreeable and separating from the agreeable in such situations are indeed greater, and the water in the four great oceans is less." "sadhu! sadhu! so it is, monks," the buddha declares. because this samsara is something whose beginning and end are not visible. a starting point cannot be declared. for those running in samsara for a long time, it cannot be said, "here is the beginning." preaching in this manner that the first beginning is not visible, he then says in that discourse to become weary (*nibbida*) towards all those preparations (*sankhara*).
thus, next he says, "monks, if you collect the tears you have shed in this long samsara solely for your mothers, those tears are greater than the four great oceans." just as a teacher in a school repeatedly brings up a certain point to make the children understand it deeply, the buddha also asks, "what do you think, monks? are the tears shed for your mothers greater, or is the water in the four great oceans greater?" next, he asks the same about fathers, daughters, and so on—due to the loss of relatives, the loss of wealth, and the calamity of disease—asking, "are the tears shed due to these greater, or is the water in the four great oceans greater?" the answer given to that is that the water in the four great oceans is less, and the tears are greater. in this way, there are many discourses in various places regarding the ocean of tears.
similarly, next there are other discourses about an "ocean of mother's milk." there, too, the same is asked: "monks, what do you think? is the mother’s milk you drank while running in this samsara—covered by ignorance and bound by craving—greater, or is the water in the four great oceans greater?" there, too, the monks reply, "if we have properly understood the exalted one's dhamma, that mother's milk is indeed greater, and the water in the four great oceans is less." thus, by that too, the length of this samsara and the fact that we have traveled in this samsara for such a long time is shown.
likewise, there is another discourse that is even more stirringly urgent (*samvegajanaka*): about the "ocean of blood." it is a highly famous discourse. this was preached to thirty monks who came from the city of pava, who were earnest practitioners of ascetic practices (*dhutanga*). when those thirty monks came to the buddha, they had not obtained any of the paths and fruits. but the buddha began the discourse: "monks, what do you think, which is greater? the blood that has flowed when you had your heads cut off in this long samsara, or the water in the four great oceans?" the monks replied, "if we have properly understood the buddha's dhamma, that blood is indeed greater." he does not stop there. next, the buddha asks, "is the blood shed by you solely while being cows, solely while being buffaloes, while being sheep, while being goats, while being pigs, while being chickens, greater, or is the water in the four great oceans greater?" these devotees know that even when thinking about the present times, this is not an exaggeration. when we think about the quantity of animals being killed, some of them might even be one's relatives. the buddha never utters an exaggeration. an exaggeration is a falsehood. therefore, this is not a falsehood. it is said that there is not even a simile for this.
in this manner, there are other highly wonderful discourses. from various perspectives, the buddha points out the danger of this samsara. indeed, we spoke of the objects of urgency (*samvega-vatthu*), didn't we? decay, illness, death, and so forth are well-known. there is another: the suffering (*dukkha*) experienced in the past samsara, and the suffering (*dukkha*) to be experienced in the future—if one does not become an arahat. these, too, are objects of urgency (*samvega-vatthu*). in this day and age, not much consideration is given to them. however, to a faithful person, these suttas are highly meaningful if they sink in deeply. to put it briefly, it is mentioned that upon hearing this discourse, the thirty monks who came from pava destroyed all defilements (*asava*) and obtained supreme arahantship.
from this, we see that without generating *samvega* regarding this samsara, without generating weariness towards samsara, one cannot attain these high states. without being weary of the world, one cannot attain supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*). one must become weary at various levels. some people might be afraid, thinking, "if we do that, we cannot carry on our lay life." there are different levels. if, at that moment, the mind is directed to that supramundane state, what the buddha preaches is nothing strange. it is the necessity of understanding the four noble truths. this is what the truth of suffering (*dukkha-sacca*) in the four noble truths is. nowadays, the truth of suffering is explained as applying only to those who are sick in hospitals, to the poor who have nothing to eat and drink, or to those who expect various positions in the world—not getting what one wants is suffering (*dukkha*). if those things are provided, it is happiness. ideas about the buddha's sasana are moving within such a narrow vision. but indeed, if someone hopes for nibbana, and if a great *samvega* arises in them, thinking, "have we not traveled in samsara for such a long time in this manner?"—it is through that that one becomes weary of existence (*bhava*). without being weary of existence—what the buddha has pointed out as the lust for existence (*bhava-raga*) is the subtlest attachment within worldly beings, the attachment to existence, to continuity. to break that, one must constantly contemplate the terrifying nature of samsara, and the length of samsara.
there are other discourses of that very kind. in one discourse, the buddha declares one's maternal lineage. that too is a good simile. the buddha presents that too like a story: "monks, if you cut all the trees, leaves, branches, and twigs in this entire land of jambudipa into four-inch pieces, and taking each piece, say: 'this is my mother,' and taking the next piece, say: 'this is my mother's mother,' and taking the next piece, say: 'this is my mother's mother's mother'—if you go on counting the past maternal lineage in this way, the wooden pieces will run out, but the maternal lineage will not be exhausted." he presents even that simile, which shows that we have traveled in samsara for such a long time in this manner. next, he points out the same regarding fathers.
the buddha declares that if you make the entire earth into a heap of clay and make small clay balls, and discard one clay ball saying, "this is my father," "this is my father's father," "this is my father's father's father"—even by counting in this manner, the number of past fathers cannot be exhausted.
there are discourses of that kind. in another place, there is a discourse about the length of an aeon (*kalpa*). there too, a monk comes and asks the buddha, "exalted one, how long is this aeon?" "monk, this aeon cannot be measured and completed in terms of years, hundreds of years, thousands of years, or hundreds of thousands of years." "in that case, exalted one, can you give a simile?" "what is the simile? suppose there is a great mountain, one league (*yojana*) high, one league wide, and one league long. it is a solid mountain with no crevices in the middle. once every hundred years, a man comes with a cloth of kasi silk and wipes that mountain, then goes away. by such wiping with the kasi cloth, wiping once every hundred years, that mountain of one league in height, width, and length would wear away, but the aeon would not wear away. so long is an aeon."
another simile is presented: suppose there is a city with iron walls, one league in length, width, and height, filled with mustard seeds. once every hundred years, a person comes and removes one mustard seed. those mustard seeds would run out, but the aeon would not wear away.
in another place, it is mentioned: a brahmin comes and asks, "exalted one, how many aeons have there been in the past? how many past aeons?" then, when the buddha said that a number cannot be given and a simile was requested, he said, "brahmin, if there is a quantity of sand from where the river ganges begins to where it flows into the sea, and if each grain of sand could be counted, the number of aeons one has spent in the past is even greater than those grains of sand." it is pointed out in this manner.
another person asks—though it was not in response to a question—on an occasion when the buddha delivered a special sermon about the size of that aeon. when the buddha came near the vepulla mountain, the vepulla mountain in india: "monk, if the skeletons discarded by a single living being within a single aeon were collected together, and if those collected skeletons did not perish, they would be larger than this vepulla mountain," the buddha declared. what this shows is how long a person goes on being born and dying, discarding skeletons in this manner, within a single aeon. there are many such discourses in the dhamma.
through each of these, we can understand that what the buddha brought out based on those *anamatagga* suttas was the terrifying nature of this samsara. because, we know the uniqueness of the buddha's dhamma. the buddha is not outstanding because he gave some novel social philosophy to the world. true, those things are also there. however, the most important thing—which also helps in the long-term survival of the buddha's sasana—is declaring the path to the problem faced by worldly beings when searching for a way to cross over from this samsara over a long period of time. then, only the person who understands the terrifying nature of samsara feels like crossing over from it. therefore, indeed, one must constantly direct the mind to these things: the suffering (*dukkha*) experienced in past samsara. it was to help with that that the buddha explained the length of samsara in various ways. when thinking about these similes, one is filled with great wonder. they might seem like exaggerations. however, through each of them, we must contemplate that for such a long time, living beings have traveled covered by ignorance and bound by craving (*tanha*). one must contemplate: "we have swum in such an ocean (of tears), we have swum in an ocean of mother's milk, we have swum in an ocean of blood."
even if we think about the lineages of parents, we are highly proud of various relationships. next, the buddha declares, "monks, we have traveled for such a long time in this samsara that it is almost impossible to find anyone in this world who has not been one's mother. it is difficult to find someone who has not been one's mother, who has not been one's father, who has not been one's son, who has not been one's daughter." then, one might think about this distinction of male and female. one must understand that even that does not belong to oneself. due to various demeritorious deeds (*kamma*), there can be changes in the distinction of male and female. looking at it from that perspective, according to the buddha's word, we can understand: "those who are near us are our mothers, our fathers, our children." it is precisely because of not knowing this that it is called a drama. that is why the entire existence is a drama. the ordinary world does not understand this deep reality. the ordinary world sees only the lifespan starting from the mother's womb and ending at the cemetery. to scientists and everyone else, only that much is visible to the physical eye. only that much is visible to the physical eye. to those with direct knowledges (*abhinna*), a greater extent is visible. to us, only the animal world is visible. the ghost realm (*peta-loka*) can also be known by some to a certain extent by inference. but those divine realms (*deva-loka*) and brahma realms (*brahma-loka*) are deeply visible only to those with direct knowledges (*abhinna*). other than that, ordinary persons, like blind people saying there is no sun or moon, say, "where are they? there is only this world. so, as long as we are in this world, we should eat and drink well. it is enough if we find the necessary economy etc. and live well." such is their view. but that is not it. we pay homage to the buddha because he discovered liberation from this samsara, which no other teacher could discover. the buddha has shown a highly wonderful dhamma—a path of escape (*nissarana-magga*). indeed, to enter upon this, one must understand gratification and danger (*adinava*). if someone is prompted to think about this, using the very danger (*adinava*) that arises within gratification as a footing, and if they are assisted by a noble friend (*kalyana-mitta*)—if the dhamma falls into place at the right time—even if that person cannot perform it as rapidly as minister santati did that escape (*nissarana*), they can obtain those aforementioned states even today by engaging in meditation.
we must then contemplate: this is the real essence, the heartwood of this dhamma. this is the practice leading to nibbana. we must do what is relevant to that. indeed, what is called the three characteristics—impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*)—that is the essence of the buddha's dhamma. the impermanent nature, the suffering nature, and the not-self nature of this entire existence. when we say suffering (*dukkha*), it is generally not just painful feeling (*vedana*). now let us look at that separation from the loved ones. in lay life, coming together with loved ones is inevitably regarded as a grand festive occasion. that is called auspicious (*mangala*). then, when a situation arises like the one experienced by minister santati, the word *'ava'* (un-) is prefixed to it. next, it ends in an inauspicious event (*avamangala*). that is the life story. therefore, according to that, let us contemplate that every union ends in separation. it is said, *"samyoga viyoganta"* — "all unions end in separation."
that is why the buddha points out that holding onto this entire fivefold aggregate is itself suffering (*dukkha*). whether one holds onto form, feelings (*vedana*), perceptions (*sanna*), preparations (*sankhara*), or consciousness (*vinnana*)—within all of them, the drama created through grasping (*upadana*), the drama of thinking "it is i," breaks down. now, a photograph taken during youth, or when one was good-looking, is completely distorted after several years. so, one cannot say it is oneself. indeed, why? because this form is not self. the nature of form is to change constantly. yet, we take only the good part as form. it is the same with other things. every single one of them changes. it is due to that impermanence (*aniccata*). due to that very impermanence (*aniccata*), one has to constantly repair it. within repair, too, there is what is called formation (*sankhara*). it is like a breaking-down vehicle—the number plate is there in the same way—but after fitting parts together, we do not regard it as a new vehicle, do we? it runs with parts falling off. now, indeed, our life is also like that. think about it.
through medical discoveries, although we say "this is i, this is mine," when we return from a hospital, other people's blood, other people's organs have been grafted into us. even the few teeth in our mouth do not belong to us. even the spectacles on our eyes. although we say, "i can see," we see thanks to the spectacles. wearing such artificial things, this entire life of ours is a drama. that is why all these things are called preparations (*sankhara*). that is why when someone dies, they put up notices saying *"sabbe sankhara anicca"* (all preparations are impermanent). if only one could understand even by that little bit that this entire samsara existence is a heap of preparations (*sankhara*). the buddha understood this most deeply. the background to that is that long samsara existence. now, sometimes, this has been revealed through various empirical facts; it has been revealed through discoveries made using various modern methods regarding rebirth. sometimes, the person who was one's mother in this life goes and is born as one's own child. there is a dramatic nature of this kind in this samsaric existence. that is why the buddha declared that in this long (samsara), there is no one who has not been one's mother, one's son, or one's daughter. so, if this entire samsara existence is a performance of this kind, escaping from this is indeed happiness.
what is called the truth of suffering (*dukkha-sacca*) is the fact that when we look deeply into everything from birth to the end, there is the nature of suffering (*dukkha*). due to impermanence (*aniccata*), we have to go on repairing and preparing these things. that preparing itself is suffering (*dukkha*). it is something with no essence or heartwood to be called "i" or "mine". it is only by properly understanding this that one can be liberated from samsara. therefore, the person traveling on the path of insight (*vipassana*) must start by observing arising and passing away (*udayabbaya*) to the extent they understand it in daily life, and make an effort to understand it deeply: how the parts of the body wear out, about painful feelings, and so forth. it is because we cannot remain in one posture that we turn to the other side. that is why it is deeply pointed out that we conceal the nature of suffering (*dukkha*) in this body by changing postures. sometimes, the teacher advises the practitioner (*yogavacara*) to remain in the same posture, experiencing the pain, and to contemplate in order to understand the painful feeling (*vedana*). that is to understand the suffering (*dukkha*) contained in it, even for a short while. yet, we always like to change postures and conceal that suffering (*dukkha*). that is where ignorance (*avijja*) lies. it is the same with other things. however, the buddha brings this out to open our eyes: "we solved this same equation over a long period, but the correct answer did not come."
therefore, in this era of a buddha's appearance, we must contemplate by regarding what is valuable as valuable, without narrow objectives such as meditating merely to cure minor illnesses and small ailments. we must engage in dhamma practice and meditation with the determination: "this entire samsara is like a hospital, and i must obtain complete cure and leave it." if we do so, only then can we utilize this buddha's dispensation properly. only then can we help others to utilize it as well.
the essence of the buddha's dhamma lies within the four noble truths. what is called the five aggregates of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*)—form, feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), preparations (*sankhara*), and consciousness (*vinnana*)—every single one of these that is held onto is pointed out by the buddha as suffering (*dukkha*). *"sankhittena pancupadanakkhandha dukkha"* — in brief, the buddha declares that the five aggregates of grasping are themselves suffering (*dukkha*). that is the essence of the truth of suffering. next, the buddha declares: "why does this state of suffering (*dukkha*) exist? it is due to craving (*tanha*)." due to the unquenchable thirst of craving (*tanha*), living beings run in this samsara for a long time. they draw their last breath with the hope of obtaining in the next life at least the wishes they could not obtain in this life. they do not understand their substancelessness.
therefore, according to the accumulated kamma, one is born in those various places. it is not as one wishes. according to the kamma performed by oneself over a long period, the wheel of kamma turns on one side in this manner. subjugated to that, living beings swim in an ocean of tears and an ocean of blood over a long period of time. so, indeed, when we think in that manner, we must contemplate: if we are to protect the buddha's sasana, if we are to protect the dhamma, we must enter upon this deep aspect. we must go from danger (*adinava*) to escape (*nissarana*), without remaining in danger (*adinava*) forever. for that, one must think with wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*) about one's own life. now, some people say various things about the meditation on foulness (*asubha-bhavana*), and so forth. however, if someone wishes to be liberated from samsara, this impermanent (*anicca*) nature—the aforementioned beauty of form fades away, the strength of the body fades away, and the state of old age arrives. instead of one's two legs, one has to depend on the four legs of the bed. thinking about those lives, and next, thinking about other things—even the possessions one considers one's own—every single thing is subject to impermanence (*aniccata*). these are things the buddha reminds us of. why does he remind us of every single one of these? because the weariness (*nibbida*) towards samsara is essential for escaping from samsara. sometimes, a special event can bring that out from within such sorrowful situations. that can be brought out only if a noble friend (*kalyana-mitta*) or the necessary dhamma instruction falls into place at the right time. otherwise, one falls back to sleep. one falls back to sleep again and again. that is the situation in this long samsara. ignorance (*avijja*) means neglecting, forgetting; it is very easy. that is why this is called a dream of life. therefore, to escape, one must remain awake, both regarding one's own life and the nature of the world. one must practice seeing in accordance with what was pointed out by the buddha. instead of the perception of permanence (*nicca-sanna*), one must generate the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*). that is why the mind must be brought to a level where one can look at the world without those perversions (*vipallasa*)—without distorted views and distorted states. the distorted views are: regarding what is impermanent (*anicca*) as permanent, regarding what is foul as beautiful, regarding what is subject to suffering (*dukkha*) as happiness, and regarding what is not-self (*anatta*) as self. that is the view of perversion (*vipallasa*) existing within worldly beings. to conquer that, if one constantly trains the mind to see impermanence (*aniccata*), from then on, one sees this gradually breaking down. seeing it break down, fear arises: "oh, is it not a breaking thing? is it not a rotting fence that i am holding onto?" many people think their lives are highly secure. they have bank deposits, they have children who have obtained high positions. in the end, when looking at the final period, the banks also collapse, and the children do not look after them. in the end, all those rotting fences that were held onto fall down. what remains for oneself is only the four legs of the bed. at that moment, what helps is indeed the dhamma. if one has obtained some (dhamma) in the past, that is the consolation at that moment. one must contemplate in that manner.
we brought out various dhamma points through this short story. we do not always say these things merely for the aesthetic interest of the story. through each of these, certain dhamma principles can be brought out to help our lives. in the buddha’s time, those who lived with that dhamma—sometimes a brahmin comes and asks the buddha, "how long is this aeon?" due to the faith (*saddha*) generated through that, in the end, he becomes a buddhist. but nowadays, there is a way of thinking that treats this as something not belonging to oneself, discussing this world and space. that does not help one's life. they use them as means of obtaining various degrees. however, those must be brought close to one's life. the buddha has already declared the essence of all these things. whether we spend millions of money to go to strange worlds or not, when we die, we travel according to kamma. no vehicle is needed for that; no strange satellite is needed. instead, at the moment of death, automatically along with that mind, in some instances, one goes to the brahma realms. it is through that aforementioned strength of wholesome actions, not through other artificial strengths. therefore, because of the nature of this existence (*bhava*), we must bring out these dhamma values. we must bring them out because they are now fading away rapidly. there is a tendency to bring out other things through that aforementioned practice of worldly development and cemetery development. if this dispensation is to survive for a long period, we must bring out the path to nibbana pointed out by the buddha to the world, nibbana, and we must direct our minds to the things that help towards it. we must teach them to others.
thinking in that manner, now, on this valuable day, these devotees, having established themselves in a virtue (*sila*) that helps in traveling the path of dhamma according to their respective measures—at this moment, they have observed the livelihood-as-eighth virtue (*ajiva-atthamaka-sila*), and the eight virtue-rules of the precept day (*uposatha-attha-sila*). in that manner, there are also those who have observed the ten virtue-rules (*dasa-sila*) that help in meditation. having established oneself in virtue of that kind, and having directed the mind to meditation, and having brought this mind—which was scattered by globalization and other things—to this place at this moment and directed it to the dhamma, you have brought out the power of a concentrated mind through a certain meditation subject (*kammatthana*). next, you must utilize a dhamma sermon of this kind: if the three characteristics of impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*), which help in overcoming the fear of samsara, are developed more and more to some extent in daily life, they will become perfections (*parami*). even if they are not obtained in this life, they can be obtained at some point. however, we must be energetic and, without delaying heedlessly, resolve to realize it in this very life. before the buddha's sasana ends, through this path of meditation and with the association of noble friends (*kalyana-mitta*), by practicing this dhamma and meditation, we must obtain—at the minimum, if nothing greater—the path-knowledge of stream-entry (*sotapatti-magga-nana*), which is the greatest and most valuable power of escaping from the four planes of misery. if possible, may we be completely liberated from the entire samsara and cross over from this ocean of tears and ocean of blood to obtain the supreme, deathless, great nibbana of arahantship, through this strength of virtue, concentration, and wisdom (*sila-samadhi-panna*) fulfilled today! you must wish: "may this be obtained through listening to this dhamma sermon!" now, may all those who wish for the merit of nibbana—from avici to akanittha, including our relatives—rejoice in this mass of merit we have accumulated so far through this dhamma sermon! having rejoiced, with the aspiration to escape from all samsaric suffering (*dukkha*) such as birth (*jati*), decay and death (*jaramarana*), and sickness, and to find peace in the supreme, deathless, great nibbana, recite these stanzas and share the merit:
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 040
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #40
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.176)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Atītaṃ nānvāgameyya, nappaṭikaṅkhe anāgataṃ; Yadatītaṃ pahīnaṃ taṃ, appattañca anāgataṃ. Paccuppannañca yo dhammaṃ, tattha tattha vipassati; Asaṃhīraṃ asaṅkuppaṃ, taṃ vidvā manubrūhaye. Ajjeva kiccamātappaṃ, ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suve; Na hi no saṅgaraṃ tena, mahāsenena maccunā. Evaṃ vihārimātāpiṃ, ahorattamatanditaṃ; Taṃ ve bhaddekarattoti, santo ācikkhate muni.
From:
Bhaddekaratta Sutta (MN 131) from the Majjhima Nikāya
Dear Listeners,
The sole Teacher of the world, the Supreme Fully Self-Enlightened Buddha, clearly explained to the world the significance of this present moment. The world mostly lives in a dead past. Or else, in an unborn future. Without one's knowledge, the present moment slips away. It is these four verses expressing the importance of the present moment that we have chosen as our topic today. These four verses are found in the *Bhaddekaratta Sutta* of the *Majjhima Nikāya*. Indeed, four consecutive suttas under the name *Bhaddekaratta* can be found in the *Majjhima Nikāya*: the *Bhaddekaratta Sutta*, the *Ānanda Sutta*, the *Mahākaccāna Sutta*, and the *Lomasakaṅgiya Bhaddekaratta Sutta*. In all four of these suttas, these same four verses are found as the theme or the main topic. From this, one can appreciate how important and meaningful these verses are. Furthermore, detailed expositions of these verses are found in all four suttas. In truth, every single one of these expositions is directly relevant to insight meditation (*vipassanā*). That is why we have specifically brought up this sutta discourse.
Now, the introductory story (*nidāna*) of this *Bhaddekaratta Sutta* is briefly given as follows: While the Buddha was residing at the Jeta Grove monastery in Sāvatthī, he directly addressed the Saṅgha and declared, "Monks, I shall expound to you the summary (*uddesa*) and the exposition (*vibhaṅga*) of 'one who has an auspicious day' (*bhaddekaratta*). Listen and pay close attention."
You may not be familiar with these two words, *uddesa* (summary) and *vibhaṅga* (exposition). They represent a distinctive feature of the Buddha's teaching style. On certain occasions, before presenting a lengthy explanation, the Buddha would first present a summary of what he intended to declare as a thematic passage. This is called the *uddesa*. Then, the *uddesa* is subsequently analyzed and explained in detail as the *vibhaṅga*. This is characteristic of the Buddha's method of teaching. In this sutta as well, the Buddha said, "Monks, I shall declare this summary and exposition to you," and the four verses he first presented as the summary (*uddesa*) are what we have taken as our topic today.
Now let us try to understand the general meaning of these four verses.
"Do not run after the past" (*atītaṃ nāvagameyya*); "do not long for the future" (*nappaṭikaṅkhe anāgataṃ*). "What is past is left behind" (*yad atītaṃ pahīnaṃ taṃ*); "and the future is yet unreached" (*appattañca anāgataṃ*)—the future has not yet arrived. "And whoever with insight sees each present state as it arises, right there, right there" (*paccuppannañca yo dhammaṃ tattha tattha vipassati*); "unconquerable, immovable, knowing that, the wise one should cultivate it" (*asaṃhīraṃ asaṅkuppaṃ taṃ vidvā manubrūhaye*). Unentangled by and unprovoked by that present state, indeed, that is what the wise person should cultivate.
Next: "Today itself the effort should be made, who knows if death will come tomorrow?" (*ajjeva kiccaṃ ātappaṃ, ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suve*). The duty to be done must be striven for today itself. "Who knows if death will come tomorrow?" "For there is no bargaining with Death and his great army" (*na hi no saṅgaraṃ tena mahāsenena maccunā*). There is indeed no agreement or contract for us with the King of Death who has such a mighty army, is there? "One who dwells thus ardently" (*evaṃ vihārīmātāpiṃ*)—one who acts and dwells in this manner, with such understanding and realization, cultivating ardent energy, "tireless day and night" (*ahorattamatanditaṃ*), cultivating energy day and night without laziness, "him indeed, the peaceful sage calls one who has an auspicious day" (*taṃ ve bhaddekarattoti santo ācikkhate munī*). The peaceful sage—meaning the Buddha Himself—declares him to be a *Bhaddekaratta*.
Thus, I have given the general meaning. To make this resonate more deeply in the heart, we have rendered it into Sinhala verse in this way:
*Do not run after what has gone,*
*Do not stand yearning for what is to come.*
*Take what is past exactly as past,*
*See the future as yet unreached.*
*Subjecting the presently arisen things as they come,*
*To the wisdom of insight,*
*The wise one cultivates in this manner,*
*The unattached, unprovoked insight.*
*Do today itself what must be done,*
*For death may indeed come tomorrow.*
*There is surely no bargaining possible,*
*With Death who has such a great army.*
*Dwelling thus day and night without laziness,*
*Living in a way that burns up the defilements,*
*The Sage declares that such a monk*
*Is delighted in the supreme solitude.*
Even though we translated it in that manner, the word *bhaddekaratta* has been a puzzle for scholars since ancient times. Both the commentators and Western scholars have offered various interpretations, particularly concerning what is meant by the word *eka* (one/sole) in *bhaddekaratta*.
Now, in an exposition written by us about forty years ago on this very sutta discourse, we presented an interpretation for this word *bhaddekaratta*. In short, it is based on that interpretation that we referred to "supreme solitude" here. We understood it in this way: we took the word *eka*—and demonstrated with supporting evidence—that the word *eka* signifies solitude or seclusion. Thus, *bhadra* means auspicious or good, and *ratta* means attached or delighted. Therefore, the meaning we presented was: one who is delighted in the auspicious, or rather, the most noble seclusion or solitude.
We drew support for that meaning from a certain short sutta discourse found in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*. It reads as follows: When the Buddha was residing at the Bamboo Grove (*Veḷuvana*) in Rājagaha, there was a certain monk who lived completely alone amidst the community of monks. The other monks referred to this bhikkhu as "Thera"—by the name "Thera"—though we do not know for what reason. Thus, the sutta featuring that monk named Thera is called the *Theranāmako Sutta*. The unique characteristic of this bhikkhu named Thera was that he was an *ekavihārī*—meaning he behaved in accordance with solitary dwelling, was a solitary dweller, engaged in solitary living, and also spoke in praise of the virtues of solitary dwelling. Let us highlight here a few words that describe his conduct, as they will assist in this explanation. His daily routine is recorded in this way: *So eko gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisati, eko paṭikkamati, eko raho nisīdati, eko caṅkamaṃ adhiṭṭhāti*. The word *eko* (alone) was repeated several times. What does it mean regarding his daily routine? He enters the village for alms alone, departs from the village alone, sits in meditation in private (*raho*) alone, and walks on the ambulatory (*caṅkama*) alone.
Then, some other monks went and reported the uniqueness of his behavior to the Buddha, saying: "There is this bhikkhu named Thera who lives as an *ekavihārī* (solitary dweller) and keeps speaking in praise of the virtues of being an *ekavihārī*." The Buddha sent word, saying: "The Teacher is calling you, tell him to come here." When that bhikkhu arrived, the Buddha asked him: "How is it, Thera, that you dwell as an *ekavihārī* and speak in praise of the virtues of being an *ekavihārī*?" Thereupon, he declared his aforementioned daily routine: "Venerable Sir, Blessed One, I enter the village for alms alone, depart from it alone, sit in meditation alone, and walk on the ambulatory alone. That is how my dwelling as an *ekavihārī* is."
Then the Buddha said: "Thera, there is indeed that kind of solitary dwelling (*ekavihāra*). I do not say it is not so. However, I shall tell you at this moment how this solitary dwelling—this solitude—becomes perfected in every sense, and how it is detailed and made truly meaningful. Listen well." Thereupon, the Buddha declared the following words, which we have taken as our supporting evidence, as they are very closely related terms: "Thera"—this is said regarding a certain bhikkhu—"what is past is abandoned" (*yaṃ atītaṃ taṃ pahīnaṃ*); he has abandoned past things, treating them as gone. "What is future is relinquished" (*yaṃ anāgataṃ taṃ paṭinissaṭṭhaṃ*); he has let go of future things. "And desire and lust (*chandarāgo*) for currently acquired forms of existence (*paccuppannesu ca attabhāvapaṭilābhesu*)—meaning whatever presents itself in the present—is thoroughly subdued" (*suppaṭivinīto*). "It is in this way, Thera, that this solitary dwelling (*ekavihārī*) is fully completed and perfected in every sense," so the Buddha declared.
Thus, from this discourse we can see, firstly, that the meaning of the word *eka* is the state of being an *ekavihārī*—solitude. We have demonstrated this by citing other passages showing that the word *eka* was used in ancient times as a specific term denoting solitude. Secondly, as shown by the Buddha, this state of being an *ekavihārī* is not merely remaining physically apart from the conventionally accepted crowd. Now, those of you who have studied this Dhamma would know that three types of seclusion (*viveka*) are presented in this Dhamma. Seclusion is shown in three senses: physical seclusion (*kāya-viveka*), mental seclusion (*citta-viveka*), and seclusion from assets/defilements (*upadhi-viveka*). Physical seclusion (*kāya-viveka*) is what everyone knows. One thinks, "I will leave all this behind and go to the forest. By going to the forest and staying alone, everything will be solved." That, too, is helpful for meditation, of course. Yet, it is the lowest level of being an *ekavihārī*.
The second level is mental seclusion (*citta-viveka*). Aided by that seclusion, if one suppresses the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and attains concentration—attaining states of meditative absorption (*jhāna*) in the manner of "secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states" (*vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi*)—that is mental seclusion. The sages of the past who attained *jhānas* reached that point.
Behold, seclusion from assets (*upadhi-viveka*) is the deepest seclusion shown in this Dhamma. Seclusion from assets is Nibbāna. To help you understand this term "seclusion from assets" (*upadhi-viveka*), one must first understand the meaning of the word *upadhi* (assets/acquisitions/fuel). This word *upadhi* is mentioned in the Dhamma in two senses. In the mundane sense, *upadhi* means gold, silver, pearls, gems, houses, land, wife, and children—things regarded as one's possessions, wherein the sense of "mine-ness" dwells. In the mundane sense, these are *upadhi*. In the deeper sense, *upadhi* refers to our samsaric assets. What is that? It is a term you have heard of: the five groups of grasping (*pañca-upādānakkhandha*). The five groups of grasping (*upādāna*) are the five heaps we hold on to and cling to. Anyone would have heard these five words: the heap of form, the heap of feeling (*vedanā*), the heap of perception (*saññā*), the heap of preparations (*saṅkhāra*), and the heap of consciousness (*viññāṇa*). Thus, in the sense of holding on and clinging to them, they are grasping (*upādāna*). However, if one stands established upon them as though they were assets—at the moment one regards them as things upon which one's self-identity rests—those very graspings (*upādāna*) are regarded as assets (*upadhi*). So, depending on the perspective from which we look, if we take these five heaps as things clung to at a given moment, they are five heaps of grasping (*upādāna*). If we consider them in the sense of relying upon them, or as things gathered and piled up, behold, they are assets (*upadhi*).
Next, along with that, let us say that the word "heap" (or group) might be a problem for many. Why is this called the "heap of form", "heap of feeling"? The word is *khandha*. Indeed, the word *khandha* is the word used when saying "five aggregates" (*pañcakkhandha*). *Khandha* means heap, aggregate, or mass. What is this heap? The Buddha has explained this as well. This heap is eleven-fold. It is shown elsewhere as: *atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ, ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā, oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā, hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā, yaṃ dūre santike vā*—making eleven aspects. The three periods of time mentioned here are shown first: past heap of form, future heap of form, present heap of form; then internal (*ajjhatta*) or external (*bahiddhā*), which is two-fold; then gross (*oḷārika*) or subtle (*sukhuma*); then inferior (*hīna*) or superior (*paṇīta*); then far (*dūre*) or near (*santike*). Behold, each aggregate is divided in this eleven-fold manner. So, these are indeed what we are holding on to as assets. The moment when every single such asset (*upadhi*) is relinquished is what is called Nibbāna. That is why a term used to describe Nibbāna is *sabbūpadhipatinissaggo*—the relinquishment of all assets. That state of relinquishing all assets is indeed the aforementioned seclusion from assets (*upadhi-viveka*). That means Arahantship. That is the highest seclusion.
Now, the advice given by the Buddha to that bhikkhu named Thera is actually concluded with a certain verse—a verse that depicts an Arahant:
*Sabbābhibhuṃ sabbaviduṃ sumedhaṃ,*
*Sabbesu dhammesu anūpalittaṃ.*
*Sabbañjahaṃ taṇhakkhaye vimuttaṃ,*
*Tamahaṃ naraṃ ekavihārīti brūmi.*
Behold, that solitary dwelling (*ekavihārī*) is in truth found only within an Arahant; this is declared to that bhikkhu through this verse. "*Sabbābhibhuṃ*"—conquering all; "*sabbaviduṃ*"—knowing all; that wise person; "*sabbesu dhammesu anūpalittaṃ*"—having an unstained nature toward any thing, or rather toward all things; "*sabbañjahaṃ*"—having abandoned everything; "*taṇhakkhaye vimuttaṃ*"—liberated through the destruction of craving (*taṇhā*); "*tamahaṃ naraṃ*"—to that person, to that human being, to that Arahant, I say "solitary dweller" (*ekavihārī*). Thus did the Buddha conclude his advice to the Thera. From this, we can contemplate and understand: behold, seclusion from assets (*upadhi-viveka*) is indeed the highest, consummate seclusion. To make it resonate more deeply, we called it "supreme solitude"—the ultimate seclusion. Thus, *bhaddekaratta* refers to that monk who is delighted in that supreme solitude. It was to demonstrate this that we presented that supportive sutta.
Next, let us say that what we discussed so far were just the verses. The Buddha presented those verses as the summary (*uddesa*), as the synopsis. Along with that, the Buddha presented the exposition (*vibhaṅga*) to the Saṅgha in this manner: "And how, monks, does one run after the past?" Having previously said "do not run after the past," he now questions and explains how one chases after the past. Herein, a certain bhikkhu thinks thus: *Evaṃrūpo*—"I was of such a form in the past." He brings up that thought, thinks about the past, and generates a delight called *nandi*—*nandi* being another name for craving (*taṇhā*)—toward that past form. It is through generating that delight that one goes into the past. Therefore, it is not by the mere remembering of the past. Rather, one generates attachment, craving (*taṇhā*), for the past form. The same applies to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), preparations (*saṅkhāra*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*). That is how one runs after the past.
Next, he shows: "And how, monks, does one not run after the past?" Here, it is shown that if one does not generate that delight called *nandi* toward the past form, feeling, etc., behold, one is freed from that. One is freed from running after the past. The same is said regarding the future.
