in line with that simile, the buddha next presents another factual event: "monks, such an event also occurred. a skilled, wise cowherd of magadha, in the very same way, in the last month of the rainy season during autumn, properly examined this bank of the river, properly examined the further bank, and crossed his herd of cattle at the proper ford." the buddha beautifully describes the manner in which they were crossed. first, that cowherd took the bulls who were the leaders of the herd (*gopitaro goparinayaka*), the chief cattle, and they cut across the river's current, went forward, and crossed over safely. secondly, the strong cattle and cows of the herd similarly cut across the river's currents, went forward, and crossed over. thirdly, the grown heifers and young bulls likewise cut across the river's current, went forward, and crossed over safely. fourthly, the weak calves of the herd were also taken across, cutting through the current, going forward, and crossing over safely. then the buddha declares something further, something very special: "monks, such a thing also occurred on that occasion. there was a newborn calf in that herd, born that very day, who, being urged on by its mother's lowing"—there is a unique phrase mentioned there, which scholars interpret in various ways: *matugoravena vuyhamano*. as you merit-seeking devotees know, after a cow gives birth to a calf, she makes a special protective sound, like "hum, hum." urging the calf forward with that sound, or searching for it when lost; encouraged by that lowing sound of the mother, the newborn calf also went forward safely through the water parted by its mother’s chest and crossed over.
then the buddha explains according to that simile: "what was the reason? that cowherd was wise. he properly examined this bank, he properly examined the further bank, and he crossed the cattle at the proper ford. that is why it was successful. in the same way, monks, if any ascetics and brahmins are skilled regarding this world, skilled regarding the next world, skilled regarding the realm of mara, skilled regarding what is not the realm of mara, skilled regarding the region subject to death, and skilled regarding the region free from death; if anyone thinks it fit to listen to such ascetics and brahmins and thinks it fit to place faith in them, that will lead to their benefit and happiness for a long time." having declared this, using the actions of the skilled cowherd as a simile, the buddha next explains the corresponding reality regarding the individuals in this dispensation (*sasana*): "just as, monks, that cowherd first crossed the bulls, the leaders of the herd, so too, monks, the arahants in this dispensation, having severed the ten fetters (*samyojana*) that bind one to samsara, and having destroyed the taints (*asava*)"—many other terms describing arahants are mentioned there—"the arahants in this dispensation cross over safely to the further shore of nibbana, having cut all ten fetters." thus, that is the simile for them. the arahants, having destroyed all defilements and become pure, cross over safely.
secondly, showing the second point, just as the strong cattle and cows of the herd crossed over safely next, in this dispensation, what is spoken of next—as you merit-seeking devotees know—is about the non-returner (*anagami*) noble individuals. now let us define the ten fetters (*samyojana*) for those who do not know. fetters are described as the bonds that tie one to samsara. they are: dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*), skeptical doubt (*vicikiccha*), adherence to rules and rituals (*silabbata-paramasa*), sensual lust (*kamaraga*), ill-will (*patigha*), craving for fine-material existence (*ruparaga*), craving for immaterial existence (*aruparaga*), conceit (*mana*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), and ignorance (*avijja*). these ten are known in the dhamma as the ten fetters (*samyojana*). the ten fetters are divided in the dhamma, dear devotees, into the lower fetters (*oramabhagiya*) and the higher fetters (*uddhambhagiya*). the lower fetters belong to this side—when we look from this side, the five fetters on this side. the higher fetters belong to the upper side. so, regarding the non-returner (*anagami*), it is mentioned that they have severed those five lower fetters, and as you may have heard, they are reborn spontaneously (*opapatika*), without parents, in the pure abodes (*suddhavasa*). they take birth in the pure abodes of the brahma world: aviha, atappa, sudassa, sudassi, and akanittha. moreover, the meaning of the word *anagami* is "one who does not return here." the non-returner does not come back to this world. another phrase is used in the dhamma for this: *anavattidhammo tasma loka*—not returning from that world. they do not turn back from the brahma world. the non-returner who has attained that state is compared to the second category of cattle. thus, regarding those individuals, the buddha declares that while the arahants have crossed over, these individuals "will cross over." it is stated in the future tense; they will definitely cross over, with certainty. the buddha affirms this decisively regarding non-returners. now you can understand that second point.
thirdly, just as the grown heifers and young bulls were crossed over, in this dispensation, we next have the once-returner (*sakadagami*). you have probably heard the meaning of the word *sakadagami*: one who comes to this world only once more. regarding once-returners (*sakadagami*), this is how it is described in the dhamma, and in this sutta too, it is said that they have severed the first three fetters—the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*), skeptical doubt (*vicikiccha*), and adherence to rules and rituals (*silabbata-paramasa*)—and in addition, they have thinned out the defilements of lust, hatred, and delusion. so, they have severed three fetters and thinned out lust, hatred, and delusion. to cut through the river's current, the buddha here compares it to cutting through mara’s stream: *marassa sotam chetva*—having cut mara’s stream. mara’s stream is craving (*tanha*). cutting through the stream of craving (*tanha*), this third group will also cross over. they will definitely go. it is something that happens in the future. they return only once, but they will definitely realize nibbana. that is the third category.
in the fourth category are the weak calves. that simile is shown regarding the stream-enterer (*sotapanna*). regarding those who have severed only the first three fetters—dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*), skeptical doubt (*vicikiccha*), and adherence to rules and rituals (*silabbata-paramasa*)—the buddha often mentions *sambodhiparayano* (bound for awakening) and *avinipatadhammo* (not subject to ruin/rebirth in lower worlds). they do not go to the hells anymore; they do not go to states of misery. special things are mentioned about the stream-enterer too. just as arahants are spoken of from that end, if we look from this end at the level of ordinary people, the stream-enterer is indeed a noble being. yet, here they are compared to the weak calves. why is that? "calves" because they have severed only three out of the ten fetters. this is not said to disparage them, but this much is certain. it is mentioned in other places regarding them—even if not in this sutta, you merit-seeking devotees have heard it—the stream-enterer is described as *sattakkhattuparama*, meaning they take birth at most seven more times. within seven lifetimes, they will somehow bring an end to samsaric suffering (dukkha). there are the words *niyato sambodhiparayano*—destined with certainty for awakening. "awakening" (*sambodhi*) means nibbana, or arhatship. they will attain arhatship. that reassurance exists for the stream-enterer too. moreover, *avinipatadhammo* means they are free from rebirth in the hells and states of misery. thus, they are compared to the weak calves.
now comes a deeper part. for the next, fifth category, the buddha shows words that most of you have probably not heard: "just as, monks, that newborn calf, born that very day, crossed over urged by its mother's lowing and with her assistance, so too in this dispensation there are two groups of individuals: those called *dhammanusari* (dhamma-followers) and *saddhanusari* (faith-followers)." these two groups are even below the level of stream-entry (*sotapanna*). yet the buddha declares even of these two groups that, like the newborn calf, these two tender ones will also definitely cross over. this is a source of great consolation in this dispensation. it shows that it does not end only with the stream-enterer; there is still room for others. this means that the buddha has revealed a middle path by which even those newborn calves can cut through mara's stream and cross over. so, those two categories of individuals, the *dhammanusari* and *saddhanusari*, cross over in that manner. we shall speak of them to you devotees in due course. let us first finish this story. in brief, this is all that is said here. compared to that calf are the noble individuals in this dispensation named *dhammanusari* and *saddhanusari*. those two groups, who are mentioned in places describing virtuous people (*sappurisa*), will also, just like the others, definitely cross over someday.
having said this, the buddha explains the reason for it by making a declaration akin to a lion's roar: "monks, why is this so? because, monks, i am skilled regarding this world"—the word used is *kusalo* (skilled)—"i am skilled regarding the next world, skilled regarding the realm of mara, skilled regarding the region subject to death, and skilled regarding the region free from death. therefore, monks, if any deem it fit to listen to me, and deem it fit to arouse faith in me, that will lead to their benefit and happiness for a long time." having declared this, he uttered the three verses we have taken as our topic, which culminate that discourse.
*ayam loko paro loko janata suppakasito...* the meaning of this verse is: this world and the world beyond have been well declared by the one with deep understanding—it is understood here that it refers to the buddha, the fully self-awakened one. next, it says: *yanca marena sampattam*—that which can be reached by mara; *appattam yanca maccuna*—and that which cannot be reached by death. both of these have been declared by the fully self-awakened one.
*sabbam lokam abhinnaya sambuddhena pajanata, vivatam amatadvaram khemam nibbanapattiya.* having known the entire world through direct knowledge (*abhinna*), with supreme wisdom, the fully self-awakened one who understands, has opened the door to the deathless (*amatadvaram*), the secure door to the deathless, for the attainment of nibbana.
the next verse says: *chinnam papimato sotam viddhastam vinalikatam, pamojjabahula hotha, khemam... bhikkhavo.* that victory is then declared by the buddha in the next verse: *chinnam papimato sotam*—the stream of the evil one, that stream which was mentioned, has been severed. *viddhastam*—it has been destroyed; *vinalikatam*—the pride of mara has been rendered useless. therefore, *pamojjabahula hotha*—be full of joy and happiness, o monks. "seek the secure..." here, it means to aspire for nibbana. so, we have discussed almost the entirety of that sutta.
now, what remains is for us to say something by way of commentary. especially from the points mentioned in the sutta, through the comparison of the simile and the reality, you merit-seeking devotees can understand this. even though more details are not given, everyone has heard at this point the descriptions of the stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, and arahant. something unique mentioned here, however, is the *dhammanusari* and *saddhanusari*. it is on this that we will make a special commentary. these two groups are only briefly mentioned in this sutta. however, in certain places in several suttas, the buddha describes these two generally unrevealed/uncommon individuals in this manner. specifically, in the *alagaddupama sutta*, it is mentioned that the *dhammanusari* and *saddhanusari* are indeed destined with certainty for awakening (*sambodhiparayano*), bound for nibbana or arhatship in this dispensation.
their qualifications are mentioned next in the *kitagiri sutta* of the *majjhima nikaya*, where they are presented more clearly at the end of a list of seven types of individuals. regarding the *dhammanusari* individual, it is mentioned in the *kitagiri sutta* as follows: that *dhammanusari* individual has, to a certain extent, reflected upon and scrutinized with wisdom the teachings declared by the tathagata, and has gained a conviction in them. the pali phrase used for this is also deep: *mattaso nijjhanam khamanti*. to a certain degree or measure, *nijjhanam khamanti* means we can say they have become convinced. having thought and reflected, they have reached a certain conclusion: "ah, this is indeed so." that is on their part. next, the special thing is that within this *dhammanusari* individual, there are established—as you merit-seeking devotees have also heard among the thirty-seven aids to awakening—the five spiritual faculties (*indriya*): faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*). thus, the five spiritual faculties—the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*), energy (*viriyindriya*), mindfulness (*satindriya*), concentration (*samahindriya*), and wisdom (*pannindriya*)—are established within this *dhammanusari* individual. that is why an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*) does not possess them. even if they think they do, in no way whatsoever—*sabbena sabbam sabbatha sabbam*—are these five faculties established in an ordinary worldling. faith may be present, and the other qualities may be present, but they have not reached the status of a spiritual faculty (*indriya*). thus, at the very least, that status has been attained by this *dhammanusari* individual. so, why is the word *dhammanusari* used? there is a deep meaning for the reason here. among those five faculties, some have developed a particular one strongly in samsara. for some, the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is strong. now, in this *dhammanusari* individual, the faculty of wisdom (*pannindriya*) is strong. while all five are established, the faculty of wisdom is particularly strong, enabling them to proceed with their practice. further details are mentioned about this. if we speak systematically, that is what is described in the *kitagiri sutta*.
similarly, next, regarding the *saddhanusari* individual, they differ from the *dhammanusari* in that while the former walks this path in accordance with the dhamma, the *saddhanusari* individual crosses over in accordance with faith, utilizing faith as their support. therefore, regarding that person, the buddha does not speak of a conviction in the dhamma, but something special is said there: *yassa saddhamattam hoti pemamattam*—"who has a mere degree of faith, a mere degree of love" toward the tathagata. they have faith and love toward the tathagata. now we can think of cases like ven. vakkali, whom you have heard of. due to a highly developed faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*), perhaps from associating with buddhas in past samsaric lives, they have without any doubt a deep faith and love toward the tathagata. that is why they are called *saddhanusari*. thus, the *dhammanusari* individual has the dhamma convinced to some extent. the *saddhanusari* individual does not even have that, but they have faith and love toward the tathagata. in addition to that, just like the former individual, they also have the five faculties established: faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*). they possess that qualification as well. now you merit-seeking devotees have some understanding of these two.
next, if anyone wishes to find a good sutta to learn more about these two, there is a section of teachings in the *samyutta nikaya* called the *okkantika samyutta*—a word of the buddha, a buddha-discourse. *okkantika* is a word that carries the meaning of "entering into" or "descending into." indeed, it is in that *okkantika samyutta* that these two are specifically spoken of. in that *okkantika samyutta*, the buddha declares as follows: "monks, the eye is impermanent (inconstant), subject to change, subject to becoming otherwise." the words used are *aniccam*, *viparinami*, and *annathabhavi*. just like the eye, all six—including the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind (*mano*)—are impermanent (inconstant), subject to change, subject to becoming otherwise. regarding these declared facts, a person has, to a certain extent, gained a conviction. that is, the *dhammanusari* individual has not yet realized them through direct knowledge and vision (*nanadassana*). yet, by directing the mind to them, they have become convinced to a certain degree: "this is indeed so." *pannaya mattaso nijjhanam khamanti*—they have accepted it through wisdom to a certain measure. thus, something is declared there regarding that *dhammanusari* individual. along with that, several other details are mentioned to identify that individual. regarding that person, the words *okkanto sammatta-niyamam* are used. then the buddha declares that, in addition to the aforementioned qualification, this person:
the meaning of *okkanto sammatta-niyamam*, dear devotees, is: *sammatta* means correctness or rightness. you devotees know the word *samma*. *sammatta* means the state of being correct or right. therefore, they have entered the path of certainty, which is correctness. when the mind has entered this certainty of correctness, it does not turn back to the wrong side again. there are two states: *micchatta* and *sammatta*. *micchatta* is the state of wrongness, while *sammatta* is the state of rightness. thus, this *dhammanusari* individual has entered into the certainty called *sammatta*, having arrived at the correct path, the right way. alongside that, it is said: *sappurisabhumim okkanto*—the *dhammanusari* individual has entered the plane of the virtuous (*sappurisa*). devotees, the terms *sappurisa* (virtuous) and *asappurisa* (non-virtuous) are not used in the dhamma merely in their worldly social meanings. the word *sappurisa* is applied to individuals. in the *sappurisa sutta* of the *majjhima nikaya* and other texts, it is applied to the noble (*ariya*) individual. the true *sappurisa* is that person—the noble individual. therefore, *sappurisabhumim okkanto* means that this *dhammanusari* individual has also entered the plane of the noble ones. next, another qualification is mentioned: *vitivatto puthujjanabhumim*—they have transcended the plane of the ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*), going beyond the worldling's plane. next, another thing is said: *abhabbo tam kammam katum yam kammam karitva nirayam va tiracchanayonim va pettivisayam va...* that means this *dhammanusari* individual is incapable of performing any unwholesome karma (*kamma*) that would cause rebirth in hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. they cannot do it. that is what *abhabba* (incapable) means. this too is a massive qualification. now, we cannot say this about any one of you devotees—that you are incapable of doing so. this is the buddha's word. the word *abhabba* is a special word. it means they can never do it again. and finally, the most special point is shown: that *dhammanusari* individual will not pass away without realizing the fruit of stream-entry (*sotapattiphala*). they will not die without realizing the fruit of stream-entry. therefore, if by any chance the *dhammanusari* individual fails to become a stream-enterer beforehand, at the very last moment, before death, they will definitely become a stream-enterer. this is the word of the buddha. that is why you merit-seeking devotees have now understood something about the *dhammanusari* individual.
explaining the *saddhanusari* individual is easy now, because in addition to the other points, it is also mentioned here. the *saddhanusari* individual does not have those insights regarding impermanence (inconstancy) to that extent; they have not even gained a slight conviction in that way. but they possess faith and love. now, whatever we mentioned as the special qualifications of the *dhammanusari* individual, all of those are possessed by the *saddhanusari* individual as well. what are they? having entered the certainty of correctness, having entered the plane of the virtuous, having transcended the plane of the ordinary worldling, they are incapable of performing any karma that would lead to rebirth in states of misery such as hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. next, they will definitely attain the fruit of stream-entry before death. thus, for you devotees who previously knew only of the four types of noble disciples, there is this kind of refuge in the dispensation. therefore, it is not just those four. indeed, if one walks the path of the dhamma correctly as introduced by the buddha with genuine faith, then at the very least, like that newborn calf crossing over under its mother's protection, they too can cross over. the special thing is that before death, according to the buddha's word, even when facing the death-sensation (morana vedanava / pain of death), they will practice insight (*vipassana*) and become stream-enterers. that is what is declared there.
from there, let us proceed. you devotees have heard that on a day like today, in the *dhammacakkappavattana sutta*, the buddha introduced this noble eightfold path as the middle path. i believe you all know this. if we briefly consider at this moment what the middle path is: you devotees have heard of the two extremes that existed in the world, namely *kamasukhallikanuyoga* (devotion to sensual pleasure) and *attakilamathanuyoga* (devotion to self-mortification). devotion to sensual pleasure can be understood as living a loose life, eating and drinking and enjoying the fivefold sensual pleasures without any belief in a next world, and without a correct understanding of this world. devotion to self-mortification means needlessly torturing the body in order to save the soul, believing that nibbana can be realized through that alone—thus having no understanding of the further shore. both of those groups continue endlessly in samsara. that is why the middle path discovered by the buddha—which he identified as the middle path—is indeed the noble eightfold path itself, which is secure. such is the declaration.
even if we do not discuss that sutta at length: to convey the meaning, among whatever beings there are—footless, two-footed, four-footed, many-footed, with form, formless, percipient, non-percipient, neither percipient nor non-percipient—the tathagata is declared supreme. if anyone places faith in the tathagata, they have placed faith in the supreme being in the world. next, it says finally: *ye buddhe pasanna, agge te pasanna; agge kho pana pasannanam, aggo vipako hoti*—"those who have confidence in the buddha have confidence in the supreme; and for those with confidence in the supreme, supreme is the result." if someone has aroused faith in the tathagata fully self-awakened one, they have aroused it toward the supreme being in the world. therefore, that speaks of its benefits. they do not go to those extremes mentioned.
so, to speak further, first we must now discuss some deeper matters regarding the noble eightfold path. you devotees might have heard of a sutta called the *aggappasada sutta*. the buddha has preached the *aggappasada sutta* in a way that deeply touches a faithful person, speaking about himself. since we are speaking of faith here, we have mentioned this on certain occasions. this discourse is such a powerful declaration: *yavata satta apada va dvipada va catuppada va, bahuppada va, rupino va, arupino va, sannino va, asannino va, nevasanninasannino va, tathagato tesam aggamakkhayati, araham sammasambuddho...* "to whatever extent there are beings—footless, two-footed, four-footed, many-footed, with form, formless, percipient, non-percipient, neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—the tathagata is declared supreme among them, the worthy one, the fully self-awakened one." the benefits of gaining faith in the supreme person are likewise supreme. in the same way, the sutta speaks of the dhamma. let us bring out the portion regarding the dhamma here, as a deep point is mentioned: *yavata, bhikkhave, dhamma sankhata...* "monks, to whatever extent there are preparations (sankhara)..." dear devotees, *sankhata* (prepared/conditioned) means things that are constructed out of causes and conditions. everything in the world is like that—something constructed out of causes and conditions. *asankhata* (the unprepared/unconditioned (asankhata)) refers to nibbana, in the sense of not being constructed out of causes and conditions. there are these two: *sankhata* and *asankhata*. among all conditioned things (*sankhata*): *yavata, bhikkhave, dhamma sankhata, ariyo atthangiko maggo tesam aggamakkhayati*—of all conditioned things, the noble eightfold path is declared supreme. having said that, it continues in the same way: *ye kho pana ariye magge pasanna, agge te pasanna; agge kho pana pasannanam, aggo vipako hoti...* therefore, if one establishes confidence in the noble eightfold path, that confidence yields the supreme result and benefit.
why do we highlight this here? because the noble eightfold path is conditioned (*sankhata*). this is a great wonder: through something conditioned (*sankhata*), one proceeds toward the unconditioned (asankhata). a logician of today might argue: "how can one go from the conditioned to the unconditioned?" that is precisely where the genius of the buddha lies! utilizing the conditioned, the middle path—just as that cowherd understood this bank and the further bank, and crossed over one group first with wisdom at the proper ford, and then through the faith generated by that, crossed the second group with a specific examination, finally crossing the entire herd down to the newborn calf born that very day. in the same way, we must understand that the buddha crossed beings over through this noble eightfold path.
next, let us turn to another aspect. you devotees have heard so much about the noble eightfold path and its eight factors. but many have not even reflected on why it is called a single unit, the "noble path" (*ariyo maggo*). all these eight factors form a single unit. *maggo*—the path is actually the right concentration (*samma-samadhi*) that comes at the end. right concentration is the actual path. to explain this, we must point out that the eightfold path has both a mundane (*lokiya*) and a supramundane (*lokuttara*) aspect. there is a profound sutta discourse in the *majjhima nikaya* that reveals this, named the *mahacattarisaka sutta*. drawing from that *mahacattarisaka sutta*, let us proceed forward from there. in this *mahacattarisaka sutta*, the buddha declares: "monks, i shall expound to you noble right concentration (*ariya samma-samadhi*) with its vital conditions (*saupanisam*) and its requisites (*sapariharam*)." you devotees know what *parikkhara* (requisites) means—requisites offered to the sangha are things that support life, things relevant to it. in the same way, the buddha delivered this discourse saying, "i shall expound to you noble right concentration with its supporting conditions (*saupanisam*) and its requisites (*sapariharam*)." through this, the buddha directly shows that the first seven factors stand as requisites for right concentration. the seven factors—right view (*samma-ditthi*), right intention (*samma-sankappa*), right speech (*samma-vaca*), right action (*samma-kammanta*), right livelihood (*samma-ajiva*), right effort (*samma-vayama*), and right mindfulness (*samma-sati*)—are required for establishing right concentration. this is a very deep matter. given the time we have, let us mention this at least to generate interest, as it is highly relevant and important, especially since this aspect is barely considered in this day and age.
thus, in speaking of noble right concentration, the buddha repeatedly utters a highly astonishing sentence that highlights the importance of right view (*samma-ditthi*): "monks, therein right view comes first (*tatra, bhikkhave, samma-ditthi pubbangama*)." he constantly reminds us: right view comes first, right view comes first. many people raise the question of why it is placed at the front. right view comes first. what is the reason for this? now, consider this: even to acquire right view, a form of right view is required! sometimes we have to state things that seem like riddles: even to develop right view, one needs right view. what is the reason? the buddha explains it in this way: right view is the forerunner because, before acquiring right view, one must recognize wrong view (*miccha-ditthi*) as wrong view. for that too, right view is required! thus, in defining right view, that is how the buddha shows why right view is the forerunner: one understands wrong view as wrong view, and one understands right view as right view.
then, he shows something further—from here onward, the path becomes extraordinary. at this point, the buddha declares right view in a manner not found in other places: "monks, i say right view is twofold (*samma-ditthim paham, bhikkhave, dvayam vadami*)." what is this twofold nature? he shows the two types next: "monks, there is a right view that is accompanied by taints (*sasava*), siding with merit (*punnabhagiya*), ripening in the acquisitions (*upadhivepakka*)." "acquisitions" (*upadhi*) refers to worldly resources and possessions that support one in samsara. there is a right view that yields these; that is mundane right view. "and there is, monks, a right view that is noble (*ariya*), taintless (*anasava*), supramundane (*lokuttara*), which has become a factor of the supramundane path." those are the two.
out of these two, many people only know or have heard of the ten-point right view. perhaps you devotees have heard the opposite—the ten claims made by those with wrong view about the world. in brief, they say: "there is no giving, no sacrifice, no offering; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no next world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously born beings; there are no ascetics and brahmins who have correctly understood this world." this ten-point doctrine of "there is not" is called wrong view. to all ten, the buddha says "there is." that is mundane right view: there are benefits and results of giving; there are results of wholesome and unwholesome actions; there are results of supporting parents; there are spontaneously born beings in this world; and there are ascetics and brahmins who explain this world and the next. this "is" perception replaces the "is-not" perception—asserting "there is" for what the others denied. that is the middle path. those who make the "is-not" claims go to hell. if they say "there are no such things, let us eat, drink, and perish," they go to hell. at that level, the buddha expounded this mundane right view, which helps one avoid misery and attain happy states. yet, one does not cross over from samsara through this alone. that crossing over is achieved through the second type of right view.
the buddha accepts the former as *sasava*—that right view is accompanied by taints, yet it is *punnabhagiya* (siding with merit). it leans toward merit. unlike the other group that leans toward demerit with wrong view, this leans toward merit, toward the side of goodness. it also yields acquisitions as results (*upadhivepakka*) in samsara, bringing good rebirths. that much is there, and it is good for that purpose. but one must also be liberated from samsara, must one not?
now, that is achieved through supramundane right view. what is described there is an extraordinary thing. that noble, taintless (*ariya anasava*) right view arises in that supramundane path-moment. within an extremely brief moment, an incredibly wondrous thing occurs: at a certain point, all eight factors align and arise simultaneously in a single mind-moment to cross over. it is a highly wondrous event, about which various controversies exist. in that moment, right view is described not through the ten mundane items, but as wisdom (*panna*), investigation of states (*dhamma-vicaya*), and so forth, relevant to that state. in that moment, right view manifests in the form of investigation of states (*dhamma-vicaya*), wisdom (*panna*), and the faculty of wisdom (*pannindriya*). that is supramundane right view.
similarly, we may not be able to describe each factor in detail due to time constraints. but keep this in mind: the buddha shows that while you devotees may have heard to some extent about right view, right intention, and so on—and can read about them in books—here, in the supramundane path, each of these is defined in a unique way. in that path-moment, they manifest in an extraordinary form. right intention does not manifest merely as ordinary thoughts (*vitakka*). it is not like how people think in the world. even in terms of wrong intention (*miccha-sankappa*), right view is required to recognize wrong intention as wrong, and right intention as right. first, right view must lead. next, while in the ordinary world, the three intentions—intention of renunciation (*nekkhamma*), non-ill will (*avyapada*), and non-cruelty (*avihimsa*)—are called right intention, in the supramundane state, it is the application and directing of the mind (*takko vitakko*) toward concentration; that mental power of directing is what is called right intention (*samma-sankappa*).
furthermore, what must be specifically noted is that right speech (*samma-vaca*), right action (*samma-kammanta*), and right livelihood (*samma-ajiva*) do not manifest in the supramundane path-moment as they do in ordinary situations. one has already abstained from those wrong behaviors beforehand. when that moment arises, the abstinence is already complete. therefore, they manifest as abstinences (*virati*). there is no special effort to abstain in that moment; the abstinence is already established. thus, one is detached from those three.
in this manner, next, he reveals something highly wondrous. in the supramundane state, protection is provided to that mind in three ways by the three factors: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness. in that supramundane state—that is, when path-knowledge (*magga-nana*) arises—they perform a special function, a special task. the words the buddha uses for their action toward that mind are *anuparidhavanti* and *anuparivattanti*. *anuparidhavanti* means they run along in association with it; *anuparivattanti* means they revolve in association with it. thus, this supramundane path-moment—the journey of using the conditioned (*sankhata*) to reach the unconditioned (asankhata)—is a highly wondrous and miraculous event. in it, protection is provided to that mind. right view leads, right effort supports from behind by giving a push and providing security, and right mindfulness remains close at hand to assist.
even if it is not an orthodox simile from the texts, we have on some occasion expressed this in a way that touches your hearts. today, when prominent politicians or vips travel, there is no need to explain—one group of security personnel moves ahead, another group follows behind to protect them from danger, and another group stays right next to them. it is exactly like that. just as the great figures of the world travel with such security, the two beautiful words *anuparidhavanti* and *anuparivattanti* appear there to describe the retinue that accompanies noble right concentration as it performs its immense, powerful task. these three factors—right view, right effort, and right mindfulness—provide security during the supramundane path-moment. similarly, with the other three factors we mentioned earlier, in daily life one constantly makes an effort to abandon wrong speech and practice right speech. in that way, it is merely a training (*sikkha*). that training is practiced over a long time. when that training is perfected, in that moment it is described as *arati* (avoiding), *virati* (abstinence), and *pativirati* (refraining)—that person has distanced themselves far from it. this abstinence (*virati*) itself becomes a protection for noble right concentration.
the internal, inner nature of these eight factors is truly wondrous and miraculous. we simply go on repeating "eight," but through these eight, on one hand, a being is prevented from falling into states of misery and is directed toward happy realms by that mundane right view accompanied by taints (*sasava*). supramundane right view performs an even more powerful task: transcending this worldliness in the state of path and fruit. to put it briefly, let us consider it this way: while practicing a concentration such as mindfulness of breathing (*anapanasati*) as shown by the buddha, if one also develops insight (*vipassana*) into the three characteristics (anicca, dukkha, anatta), then by the time the factors of awakening—specifically, the thirty-seven aids to awakening (of which those five we mentioned are the spiritual faculties)—are perfected, it happens almost effortlessly. it occurs naturally, and at that point, there is a powerful disenchantment (*nibbida*) toward the five aggregates (*pancakkhandha*). through that disenchantment, one attains the supramundane state. one lets go of this bank and leaps to the other bank. in that moment, protection is provided to that right concentration. devotees, it is about that right concentration that you have all heard in the *ratana sutta*:
> *yam buddhasettho parivannayi sucim, samadhimanantarikannamahu,*
> *samadhina tena samo na vijjati...*
"the pure concentration which the supreme buddha praised, and which they call the 'immediate concentration' (concentration with immediate result)—no equal to that concentration is found." it is that immediate concentration (*anantarika-samadhi*) that is spoken of there. the *anantarika-samadhi* highly praised by the buddha is indeed path-concentration (*magga-samadhi*). immediately following that path-concentration, one realizes the fruit (*phala*). that is why it is called "immediate" (*anantarika*).
it is mentioned in the commentaries that scholars of the past had various controversies regarding this. but to be brief due to time constraints: you devotees have heard of the eight noble individuals. if asked, you might immediately answer, "the one on the path of stream-entry, the one in its fruit," and so on. that is how people answer: the four paths and the four fruits. but, devotees, this is how it is mentioned in the dhamma. the eight noble individuals are mentioned in several places, not just one, as follows: *sotapanno*, *sotapattiphala-sacchikiriyaya patipanno* (one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry), *sakadagami*, *sakadagamiphala-sacchikiriyaya patipanno*, *anagami*, *anagamiphala-sacchikiriyaya patipanno*, and so on. that is how the eight are spoken of. thus, what must be specially noted here is that although we use the words *magga* (path) and *patipada* (practice/way) as synonyms, there is a certain difference between them. one enters the path by fulfilling a course of practice (*patipada*); it is within that course of practice. now this aligns. we began this sermon, or rather highlighted as a special point, the two individuals: *dhammanusari* and *saddhanusari*. it is often said of these two that they are "on the path of stream-entry" (*sotapatti-magga*). what we must say is that they are those who are in the course of practice (*patipada*) leading to that supramundane path. it was mentioned, was it not: *sotapanno, sotapattiphala-sacchikiriyaya patipanno*. if it could be said briefly, the buddha would have said directly "those on the path of stream-entry." since the path of stream-entry is momentary, how can it apply to all eight? if the mind-moment is just one flash, how can gifts be given to all eight? now here, we showed that those two individuals, the *dhammanusari* and *saddhanusari*, are in the category of *sotapattiphala-sacchikiriyaya patipanno* (practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry). it is clearly visible, is it not? the buddha declared that before death, these two will somehow reach the fruit of stream-entry. therefore, they too are noble (*ariya*) individuals. they have entered the plane of the virtuous, having transcended the state of the ordinary worldling. the problem lies right there. therefore, in accordance with the dhamma and the suttas, we must apply this to the course of practice (*patipada*). those who have entered the practice that leads to entering the path of stream-entry are called *patipanna* (practitioners). those who have entered that practice are the *saddhanusari* and *dhammanusari*. it is not the path of stream-entry itself—if the path of stream-entry arises, the fruit follows directly, immediately. that is what "immediate" (*anantarika*) means. thus, the supramundane path is different. what is spoken of here is the course of practice (*patipada*). hence, there is a verse in the *anguttara nikaya* that makes this very clear:
> *patipanna cattaro ca, phale thita...*
> *esa sangho ujubhuto, panna-sila-samahito*
"four practicing and four established in the fruit, this is the upright sangha, composed of wisdom, virtue, and concentration." *patipanna*—it could have said *maggattha* (established in the path) there. but it does not. you devotees have heard the word *maggastha* (on the path). there is no mention of *maggastha* here; it is *patipanna*. "four practicing (*patipanna*) and four established in the fruit (*phale thita*)"—there are the eight. the four who have entered the practice (*patipada*) and the four established in the fruit. "this is the upright sangha" (*esa sangho ujubhuto*). these are described as the eight upright noble individuals, "endowed with wisdom, virtue, and concentration" (*panna-sila-samahito*). the eight shown in this verse are what we specifically mentioned. although we generally treat "path" (*magga*) and "practice" (*patipada*) as synonymous, there is a distinction here. therefore, in identifying and introducing noble individuals, we must be careful: it is not "established in the path" (*maggattha*) that is meant, but rather having entered the practice (*patipada*) for realizing the fruit of stream-entry. this would need to be explained in more detail; it is not simple.
who are the eight? the stream-enterer; the individual who has entered the practice for realizing the fruit of stream-entry; the once-returner; the individual who has entered the practice for realizing the fruit of once-return. we spoke specifically of the one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry. you devotees can deduce the rest. suppose someone has attained the fruit of stream-entry. if they do not fall into negligence as a negligent disciple (*sekha*), but continue to work further, walking that path of knowledge, then from that point on, the practice they undertake from being a stream-enterer until they become a once-returner is called *sakadagamiphala-sacchikiriyaya patipanno*—striving to reach the fruit of once-return. one can understand it in that way, up to the last one: the arahant, and *arahattaya patipanno*—the arahant, and the individual practicing for the realization of arhatship.
thus, what we have expounded to you devotees is deep. if deep dhamma is unnecessarily simplified and presented as shallow, it would lead to the destruction of the dhamma. without simplifying it in that manner, but presenting the dhamma as dhamma, we have explained this middle path as set forth by the buddha to some extent within one hour to you devotees on this valuable day. this aspect of the dispensation is now largely forgotten. therefore, you devotees have kept virtue (*sila*) today on this valuable day to the best of your ability. many lay devotees who come to us now say: "i do not want to be born in samsara anymore. i must go somewhere and attain the paths and fruits as quickly as possible. i want to go somewhere and ordain." everyone speaks in this way. thus, we presented this to help those people, so that they may reflect. even if one cannot attain the fruit of stream-entry, this is a great consolation. let us at least strive to be like that calf urged on by its mother's protective lowing. that is what we have to say to you devotees.
thus, through the virtue kept today, the meditation practiced, and this insight-oriented dhamma sermon heard, may you devotees be able to bring your learning and meditation to fruition as quickly as possible, realize those noble states mentioned, and cross over the entire wilderness of samsara, facilitating this crossing from this shore to the other shore. in the past, "going from this shore to the other shore" did not mean traveling abroad; it meant crossing over this ocean of samsara. may you devotees receive the necessary strength, power, and massive energy for that purpose. may your learning and meditation quickly bear fruit, and may you gain the ability to reach that peace of nibbana. from the avici hell to the akanittha heaven, if there be any who wish to rejoice in the merits of this dhamma preaching and dhamma hearing, may they, through that rejoicing, realize the supreme, great, deathless nibbana by means of their aspired-for enlightenment (*bodhi*). may you devotees also receive the strength and power to realize that supreme, great, deathless nibbana very soon. with that aspiration, let us recite these verses.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 043
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #43
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.206)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Cattāro ca paṭipannā, cattāro ca phale ṭhitā; Esa saṅgho ujubhūto, paññāsīlasamāhito. Yajamānānaṃ manussānaṃ, puññapekhāna pāṇinaṃ; Karotaṃ opadhikaṃ puññaṃ, saṅghe dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ.
From:
Aṭṭhapuggala Sutta (AN 8 tradition)
Dear Listeners,
It was on an Esala full-moon poya day like today that the Tathāgata, the Blessed One, the Fully Enlightened Samma Sambuddha, after attaining supreme enlightenment, delivered his first Dhamma sermon, the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*, to the group of five monks—Kondañña, Bhaddiya, Vappa, Mahānāma, and Assaji—at the Deer Park in Isipatana, Benares. Upon hearing that sermon, Ven. Koṇḍañña realized the noble fruit of Stream-entry (*Sotāpatti-phala*), marking the very first appearance of the Noble (*Ariya*) Saṅgha in the world. It is indeed this Noble Saṅgha that is referred to in the virtues of the Saṅgha (*Saṅghaguṇa*) which you, meritorious friends, frequently recite. In that recitation of the Saṅgha’s virtues, mention is made of eight individuals belonging to the Blessed One's disciple-community (*Sāvaka Saṅgha*). Today, we have chosen as our theme two verses from the *Aṭṭhapuggala Sutta* in the Book of Eights (*Aṭṭhaka Nipāta*) of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, which speak about these eight individuals.
*"Cattāro ca paṭipannā cattāro ca phale thitā"* — The four who have entered the path of practice and the four established in the fruit.
*"Esa saṅgho ujubhūto paññā-sīla-samāhito"* — This is the upright Saṅgha, endowed with the virtues of wisdom, ethical conduct, and concentration.
*"Yajamānānaṃ manussānaṃ puññapekhāna pāṇinaṃ"* — For those humans who make offerings, for living beings seeking merit,
*"Karotaṃ opadhikaṃ puññaṃ saṅghe dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ"* — for those performing merit that leads to rebirth-assets, what is given to the Saṅgha yields great fruit.
This same quality of yielding great fruit is what is found in the passage on the virtues of the Saṅgha that you often chant:
*Supaṭipanno bhagavato sāvaka-saṅgho, ujupaṭipanno bhagavato sāvaka-saṅgho, ñāyapaṭipanno bhagavato sāvaka-saṅgho, sāmīcipaṭipanno bhagavato sāvaka-saṅgho, yadidaṃ cattāri purisayugāni aṭṭha purisapuggalā, esa bhagavato sāvaka-saṅgho, āhuṇeyyo pāhuṇeyyo dakkhiṇeyyo añjalikaraṇīyo anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassa.*
Since you recite this passage frequently, many of you likely know its meaning as well.
*"Supaṭipanno bhagavato sāvaka-saṅgho"*: The community of the Blessed One's disciples has entered the path of good practice.
*"Ujupaṭipanno"*: They have entered the path of upright practice.
*"Ñāyapaṭipanno"*: They have entered the path of practice in accordance with the law/method (*ñāya*).
*"Sāmīcipaṭipanno"*: They have entered the path of proper practice.
*"Yadidaṃ cattāri purisayugāni aṭṭha purisapuggalā"*: That is, the four pairs of persons, the eight individual persons.
*"Esa bhagavato sāvaka-saṅgho"*: This is the Blessed One's community of disciples. After declaring their virtues, their qualifications to receive offerings are then shown:
*Āhuṇeyyo*: They are worthy of gifts brought from afar.
*Pāhuṇeyyo*: They are worthy of hospitality.
*Dakkhiṇeyyo*: They are worthy of offerings given with the next world in view.
*Añjalikaraṇīyo*: They are worthy of reverential salutation with hands joined above the head.
*Anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassa*: They are the incomparable field of merit for the world.
Now, let us first present the analysis and exposition of this passage found in the Commentaries. In the *Visuddhimagga*, in the section on recollections (*Anussati Niddesa*), Ven. Buddhaghosa explains these main terms. Someone might ask, "What is this 'pair' (*yugala*)? Who are the eight individual persons?" To this, the commentators present the meaning as follows. The four pairs of persons are shown as: *"Cattāri purisayugānīti paṭhama-maggatho phalaṭṭho"*—one who is on the first path and one who is established in its fruit. That is, one on the path of Stream-entry (*Sotāpatti-magga*) and one established in the fruit of Stream-entry (*Sotāpatti-phala*). In the same manner, one on the path of Once-returning and one established in the fruit of Once-returning, and so on, up to one on the path of Arahantship and one established in the fruit of Arahantship. The Commentary applies the exposition of "one on the path" (*maggaṭṭha*) and "one established in the fruit" (*phalaṭṭha*). It is according to this that the popular usage of "the four paths and the four fruits" (*satara-maṅga satara-phala*) has come about today.
However, a certain problem arises from this. What is it? It is mentioned in the Dhamma, when speaking of the unmediated concentration (*ānantarika-samādhi*), that the realization of the fruit occurs immediately after the supramundane path. Let alone other places, this is mentioned even in the *Ratana Sutta*, which you know so well:
*Yaṃ buddhaseṭṭho parivaṇṇayī suciṃ, samādhimānantarikaññamāhu, samādhinā tena samo na vijjati...*
It is stated that the pure concentration praised continuously by the Buddha is called "unmediated" (*ānantarika*), and there is no concentration equal to that concentration. The meaning of this word *ānantarika* is that immediately after the path-concentration, one falls into the fruit. Therefore, if one enters the fruit immediately after the path-concentration, how can we distinguish the four on the path from the four established in the fruit? This very question has been discussed among the Saṅgha since ancient times. Many people have presented this question to us too, in person. Although I have given various answers, I thought at this moment that if I deliver a sermon on this, it will be easier in the future to just tell people to listen to this discourse in order to express my view on the matter. That is why I am specially delivering this sermon.
When speaking of this discussion on *maggaṭṭha* and *phalaṭṭha*, it is found in the *Ratana Sutta* itself, which you know very well, at the point of declaring the virtues of the Saṅgha:
*Ye puggalā aṭṭha sataṃ pasatthā, cattāri etāni yugāni honti, te sugatassa sāvakā dakkhiṇeyyā, etesu dinnāni mahapphalāni, idampi ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ, etena saccena suvatthi hotu.*
There too, it is told to us: *"Ye puggalā aṭṭha sataṃ pasatthā"*—which means, meritorious friends, "the eight individuals praised by the virtuous (*sato/sataṃ*)." *"Cattāri etāni yugāni honti"*—there are four pairs here. *"Te sugatassa sāvakā"*—those disciples of the Sugata are worthy of offerings; that is how it is mentioned here.
However, when trying to explain this, our Commentator Ven. Buddhaghosa begins with the first line of the verse we quoted: *"Cattāro ca paṭipannā cattāro ca phale thitā"*. But when explaining it, he only uses the two words *maggaṭṭha* and *phalaṭṭha*. Not only that; it is a very surprising thing. We can clearly point out an instance of distortion of meaning even during the Commentarial period. Because, in analyzing this verse, those who know the Pali language understand that *"ye puggalā aṭṭha sataṃ pasatthā"* refers to eight individuals praised by the virtuous. But someone who is incompetent and does not know Pali might mispronounce this verse and say *"Ye puggalā aṭṭhasatā"* (pronouncing it as *aṭṭhasataṃ*, meaning one hundred and eight). Even the pronunciation there is wrong; it distorts the meaning. Yet, even to this, the Commentator says as follows: after first stating the correct meaning, "praised by the virtuous," he then says, "or else..." (*athavā*) and makes it one hundred and eight by adding and multiplying. That is why even today, preachers often talk about "one hundred and eight persons," having with great effort constructed a list of one hundred and eight. This does not fit at all. It does not fit at all. Here, it is not talking about one hundred and eight. If we look at the word of the Buddha, *"ye puggalā aṭṭha sataṃ"*, this word *sataṃ* can be understood even by those who do not know Pali if we give an example. In the *Dhammapada* it is said: *"Sataṃ hiso priyo hoti, asataṃ hoti appriyo"* ("He is dear to the virtuous, and disliked by the unvirtuous"). Therefore, *sataṃ* refers to virtuous people, not the number one hundred. Thus, it appears that even the Commentator has left room for that incompetent exposition. Well, let us take that as an incidental matter.
But the main point is that, in explaining this, although the verse says *"cattāro ca paṭipannā cattāro ca phale thitā"*, they have not seen—or they have not accepted—as important that there is a difference in meaning between "path" (*magga*) and "practice" (*paṭipadā/paṭipanna*). We said that the supramundane path is instantaneous. Immediate to it, the fruit is received. Yet, the Buddha uses the word *paṭipanna*—one who has entered the practice. So, understand the difference between the path (*magga*) and the practice (*paṭipadā*) in this way: the path may exist, but the training in accordance with the path, or the practicing of that way, is what is indicated by the word *paṭipanna*. If the Buddha wanted to, he could have stated this verse as: *"cattāro ca maggaṭṭhā cattāro ca phale thitā"*, couldn't he? Think about it. He could have said *maggaṭṭha* and *phalaṭṭha*, just as the commentators say. But how was it used here? *"Cattāro ca paṭipannā cattāro ca"*. Not only that. Now we will introduce to you the context, as we have quoted the first two verses of this discourse. Prior to these two verses, the Buddha begins that discourse in the Book of Eights of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* as follows: *"Aṭṭhime bhikkhave puggalā āhuṇeyyā pāhuṇeyyā dakkhiṇeyyā añjalikaraṇīyā anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassa."* "Monks, there are these eight persons..." endowed with those virtues of being worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, etc. Even if I do not recite it in full, try to understand it. Next, those eight are identified in this way: the Buddha lists them as *sotāpanno, sotāpattiphala-sacchikiriyāya paṭipanno; sakadāgāmī, sakadāgāmiphala-sacchikiriyāya paṭipanno; anāgāmī, anāgāmiphala-sacchikiriyāya paṭipanno; arahā, arahattāya paṭipanno* (one who is practicing for the realization of Arahantship). Why did the Buddha use this long phrase? For ease, he could have just said *maggaṭṭha*, couldn't he? See indeed, the word *magga* is not even used there! Instead, remember that in *supaṭipanno, ujupaṭipanno*, and in every other place in the passage on the Saṅgha's virtues, it does not speak of *magga* (path); it speaks of *paṭipanna* (practice). This is an extremely important point. For all this time, people have not paid attention to this. *Supaṭipanno, ujupaṭipanno*—the practice is something that goes on over a certain duration of time. However, with the supramundane path, one immediately falls into the fruit. Therefore, you cannot divide them and give alms separately to eight distinct individuals.
Yet, the commentators present another almost humorous reason for this. Our Ven. Buddhaghosa himself raises the question: "How can we not give to these eight?" and presents this as an illustration: Supposedly, a monk who has begun insight meditation—an *āraddha-vipassaka* monk—goes near a house, stands in front of it (while still meditating), and hands his bowl to the household. While they are offering alms into the bowl, this monk enters the path. This is how they explain it! That is a highly unnatural explanation. There is no such trouble once we bring the word *paṭipadā* (practice) forward. That is what is in the word of the Buddha. Why was it stated in this long form: "practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry"? There is no mention of "path" (*magga*) at all. "Practicing for the realization of the fruit of Once-returning..." Therein lies a deep matter. Keep in mind that this is the Buddha’s own word. We give priority to the word of the Buddha over the commentators, and over the words of Buddhaghosa. That is why I say this. I am reminding you of this because for a long time, a wrong idea and to some extent a distortion of this Dhamma has existed. Because of that, a problem has arisen. But if we take the word *paṭipadā*, there is no problem; we can perfectly give alms to eight distinct individuals.
Next, one may ask: "Who are those included in this category of 'practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry' (*sotāpattiphala-sacchikiriyāya paṭipanno*)? Who are the ones practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry?" It is there that we must bring to light several discourses on this matter. In relation to this point, we have previously delivered a sermon based on the *Cūḷagopālaka Sutta*. But to put it briefly here, there are two types of special individuals who belong to this category: the "Dhamma-follower" (*dhammānusārī*) and the "Faith-follower" (*saddhānusārī*). They have not yet become stream-enterers, but they are two highly special individuals. Why? As we go further into the sutta, you will see. So much so that it is said in the Buddha's own words that those individuals belonging to the category of Faith-follower and Dhamma-follower will not pass away without realizing Stream-entry. Therefore, those two are certainly training in the path of Stream-entry—they are training in that practice.
Indeed, let us quote from those discourses themselves. The *Alagaddūpama Sutta* of the *Majjhima Nikāya* is a discourse that wonderfully emphasizes the well-expounded (*svākkhāta*) nature of the Buddha's teaching. That discourse concludes as follows: "In this well-expounded Dhamma, whoever is a Dhamma-follower or a Faith-follower is bound for enlightenment (*sambodhiparāyaṇā*)." Generally, the term "bound for enlightenment" (*sambodhiparāyaṇā*) is used for those established in Stream-entry. Yet, the Buddha uses the term "bound for enlightenment" even for these two who are on this side of Stream-entry. See, that is how it was said there.
Let us go further. Next, there is a better explanation in the *Cūḷagopālaka Sutta*, along with a very beautiful simile. The Buddha preached the *Gopālaka Sutta* in the city of Ukkācelā on the banks of the Ganges in the Vajjian country, addressing the monks with a profound simile. "Monks, in the last month of the rainy season, a foolish herdsman of Magadha, of very little wisdom, tried to cross his herd of cattle in this way: Without properly examining this shore, and without properly examining the opposite shore, he tried to cross his cattle at a non-crossing place (not the correct ford), and the herd was swept away by the current and met with destruction. But a certain wise herdsman of Magadha, having well examined this shore and well examined the opposite shore, crossed his herd of cattle at the correct ford." The Buddha beautifully presents the manner of crossing: "First, the bull-leaders and the guides of the herd crossed over first. Next, behind them, went the strong bulls and the steer to be tamed (*balavagāvo dammagāvo*). Then, behind them, went the heifers and the young bulls. After them, went the weak calves." And then, a wonderful thing is said: so great was the skill of this herdsman that finally, even the calf born that very day crossed over, drawn by the lowing of its mother (*mātugāviyā rāvena*—the mother cow lowing to urge the calf). Encouraged by the sound of its mother, even the newborn calf crossed over. This is not just an ordinary simile. To put it briefly, that unskilled herdsman represents the ascetics and brahmins of other sects. That herdsman knows neither this shore nor the other shore. Trying to cross at the wrong ford, they lead to destruction. But the Tathāgata, the Fully Enlightened One, (referring to himself), like the wise herdsman, crosses them over at the correct ford, systematically and after careful examination. It is this last category that should receive our attention. Who is this calf born that very day? In that context, the Buddha identifies them as the "Dhamma-follower" (*dhammānusārī*) and the "Faith-follower" (*saddhānusārī*). Thus, the Dhamma-follower and Faith-follower represent the entry-level or minimum stage. Yet, even those two ultimately cross over. That is why they are called "bound for enlightenment." That is the *Cūḷagopālaka Sutta*. There is much to say, but that is why I am explaining it briefly.
Next, there is another discourse where we find more details about these two, in the *Okkantika Saṃyutta* of the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*. More details are mentioned there. There, addressing the monks, the Buddha says: "Monks, the eye is impermanent (*anicca*), subject to change, subject to becoming otherwise." In the same way, he speaks of the six senses: ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. "If anyone accepts this fact with faith and applies themselves to the practice, that person is a Faith-follower (*saddhānusārī*)." "Next, if anyone accepts this fact to a certain extent with wisdom and trains accordingly, that person is a Dhamma-follower (*dhammānusārī*)." This means that among our faculties (*indriya*), the person in whom the faith-faculty (*saddhindriya*) is dominant goes toward the side of the Faith-follower, while the person in whom the wisdom-faculty (*paññindriya*) is dominant becomes a Dhamma-follower. These two are indeed special individuals. Next, the Buddha says something very unusual about them here, showing that they are not ordinary or insignificant persons.
In the *Okkantika Saṃyutta*, the Buddha declares concerning those two that they have "entered the path of rightness" (*sammatta-niyāmaṃ okkanto*)—there is an unusual term there. Meritorious friends, we can describe *sammatta-niyāma* as: both of them have fallen into the natural law of correctness. To put it even more clearly, they have entered the plane of the virtuous (*sappurisa-bhūmi*). The word *sappurisa* is often applied to the Nobles (*Ariya*). Next, it is said that those two have entered the plane of the virtuous, having transcended the state of a worldling (*puthujjana*). Then a special thing is said: these two individuals, the Faith-follower and the Dhamma-follower, do not commit any evil deed that would lead them to hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. Next, it is said that these two will not pass away without realizing Stream-entry. The word *abhavya* (incapable / impossible) is used there. *"Abhabbo"*—there is the Buddha's word that they are incapable of passing away without realizing Stream-entry. Now, we get further details about these two who possess such distinguished qualities from the *Kīṭāgiri Sutta*. In the *Kīṭāgiri Sutta*, the Buddha states that both of them possess the five spiritual faculties—faith (*saddhā*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*)—which are unique to the Nobles and not possessed by ordinary worldlings. Anyone might say, "We have them too." But the faculties are not established in them. Yet, in these two, they are indeed established. So, there is some deficiency, and it is that deficiency which must be filled. But we have to understand that this deficiency will somehow be filled within this very life.
However, unfortunately—though we should perhaps not say this, and some might criticize us—yet, in the *Puggalapaññatti* treatise, when attempting to explain the "incapability" (*abhavyatā*) declared by the Buddha regarding these two, the Faith-follower and the Dhamma-follower, they provide a somewhat unfitting explanation. There, these two are referred to as *ṭhitakappī*. *Ṭhitakappī* supposedly means that these two can arrest or halt the eon (*kappa*). They say that these two can stop the running and destroying of the eon. How do they stop it? In this manner: Now, imagine for a moment that the eon has life. Now is the time the eon is running/ending. While running, the eon looks around and sees that there are a Faith-follower and a Dhamma-follower who have not yet attained Stream-entry. So, the eon supposedly stops—without running further—until those two attain Stream-entry! To us, this seems like putting the cart before the horse. If we reflect deeply on the Buddha's word, we must understand that a person's most precious moment is the moment of death. We have heard that some have attained Arahantship at the moment of death. Although it is a disputed story, we have told you about three monks who attained Arahantship even as their throats were being cut. That is to say, the moment of death is the occasion to decide between death and deathlessness. If there was a slight deficiency in this life, there is no need for any external talk about the eon. In that very context, the Buddha's word "incapable" (*abhabba*) meant that if the Faith-follower and the Dhamma-follower do not realize the fruit of that path during this lifetime, they will realize it at least at the moment of death. It is enough to state just that. But preachers still use that kind of story and the term *ṭhitakappī* today. They say *ṭhitakappī* means these two can stop the running of the eon. We have to say that this is somewhat unfitting.
Well, that is the story of the eight persons; keep it in mind. The Buddha does not just say *maggaṭṭha* and *phalaṭṭha*. He uses a long phrase: "practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry," and so on. He had to speak in that way because of that reason: the supramundane path is instantaneous. It is instantaneous. You cannot isolate it to give alms to it. But you can do so for someone training in the practice. See in our recitation of the Saṅgha's virtues: *supaṭipanno, ujupaṭipanno*—it is the word *paṭipanna*. There is no talk of *magga* (path) in it. It is *paṭipanna*, *paṭipanna*. Merely by training in the practice, they are worthy of receiving alms and offerings. I mentioned this specifically because someone might ask about the path and fruit of Stream-entry. You can infer the rest, meritorious friends. Let us assume someone has become a Once-returner. They do not just remain inactive from that point. There, the word *sekha* (learner/trainee) is used. *Sekha* means a training person. They train all the way up to Arahantship. Their work is not yet finished. Some, due to various reasons, fall into negligence. They are called *pamāda-sekha* (negligent trainees). Visākhā, Anāthapiṇḍika, and others could not go beyond that level due to various worldly reasons. That is a different matter. But the general rule is that after becoming a Stream-enterer, one enters the next path of insight (*vipassanā-vīthi*).
Now we have finished talking about the eight persons. Next, we bring forward the story of nine persons. What is that? In the Book of Nines (*Navaka Nipāta*) of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, there is a discourse like this: *"Nava ime bhikkhave puggalā āhuṇeyyā pāhuṇeyyā... añjalikaraṇīyā anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassa."* "Monks, there are these nine persons in the world who are worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality... an incomparable field of merit for the world." How did the "eight persons" we mentioned become "nine persons" here? I am mentioning this because it is also a disputed point. Now, everyone knows the eight persons. In addition to those eight, there is the word *gotrabhū* (one of the lineage / change-of-lineage). This word *gotrabhū* is indeed a word that is also used when describing the cognitive series of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa-vīthi*). It is the brief, instantaneous moment that exists between being a worldling (*puthujjana*) and receiving the path-fruit. If I illustrate this with a simile from the *Visuddhimagga*, it will be easy for you, meritorious friends, to understand this. This entire activity of insight, this practice, exists by depending on some aid. What is used as an aid for insight? The investigation of Preparations (*saṅkhāra-sammasana*). Having investigated Preparations, at the end, one lets go of Preparations (*saṅkhāra*) as well. This is illustrated with a good simile, which is an acceptable simile: During the rainy season, when trying to cross a stream, if there is no bridge, what do you do? A strong man, thinking wisely, grabs a hanging creeper from a tree and swings. Having swung and swung, as soon as he gets close to the opposite bank, he lets go of the creeper. If he keeps holding on, he will swing back to this side, won't he? So, in that brief moment, he lets go of the creeper and lands on the opposite side. That momentary, suspended time of letting go of the creeper is called *gotrabhū*. Understand it in that way. It is an extremely subtle moment, an extremely subtle stage in the cognitive series of insight, until one falls into the fruit. So, how can one catch that moment to give alms? That is why they said that when standing in front of a house, while alms are being served into the bowl, the monk practices insight! That is the kind of artificial explanation they give. None of that is necessary. As we said, these people also explain the word solely on the basis of insight meditation. That is wrong. Why? The *gotrabhū* stage is already included in "practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry." Keep in mind that "persons practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry" is a broad stage. You cannot isolate *gotrabhū* as a separate category in that way.
Then, how do we explain this word *gotrabhū*? That is the question. To find the answer to this, we must go to the *Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta*. The *Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta* in the *Majjhima Nikāya* is highly popular among Dhamma preachers. You, meritorious friends, must have heard it frequently at almsgivings during the sharing of merits (*bhattānumodanā*). The introductory story of that discourse is extremely special when we discuss the virtues of the Saṅgha. It is shown as follows: When the Buddha was residing at the Nigrodhārāma in Kapilavatthu, the city of the Sakyans, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī (the Buddha's foster-mother), brought a pair of new cloths she had spun and woven with her own hands, and offered them to the Buddha. "May the Blessed One, out of compassion for me, accept this." What did the Buddha say? A very surprising thing was said on that occasion: *"Saṅghe, gotami, dehi; saṅghe dinne ahañceva pūjito bhavissāmi..."*—"Gotamī, give it to the Saṅgha. When it is offered to the Saṅgha, I too will be honored." A second time and a third time, Pajāpatī Gotamī made her request. In addition, Ven. Ānanda joined in and said, "O Blessed One, please accept this. When the Blessed One lost his mother, it was this foster-mother who nursed him. She is the one who raised you." When that was said, the Buddha addressed Ven. Ānanda and delivered a sermon. That sermon presents a wonderful analysis regarding almsgiving. To put it briefly, it begins like this: "individual offerings" (*pāṭipuggalikā dakkhiṇā*). Fourteen such individual offerings are shown. Let us consider them briefly. First is an offering given to the Tathāgata, the Samma Sambuddha, personally. This is the kind of offering Pajāpatī’s was, because it was a personal thing. It was his foster-mother, offering it to her child; a personal gift. See, what a wonderful quality of the Buddha: he redirected even a personally offered gift to the Saṅgha. Right there, the world has a great lesson to learn. He offered it to the Saṅgha because he himself is included in the Saṅgha. Next, he mentions a personal offering given to a Paccekabuddha. Next are the eight persons mentioned earlier: to an Arahant, then to one practicing for the realization of Arahantship, then to a Non-returner (*Anāgāmī*), to one practicing for the realization of the fruit of Non-returning, and so on—the eight persons mentioned. Thus, if we take those eight and the first two, understand them as ten. Now, about the eleventh: the eleventh is "one who is free from lust regarding sensual pleasures among outsiders" (*bāhiresu kāmesu vītarāgo*)—there could be outside ascetics or rishis. They come at the next level, the eleventh. This is in terms of the order of respect. Next is shown the virtuous worldling (*sīlavanto puthujjano*). As the thirteenth, the unvirtuous worldling (*dussīlo puthujjano*). As the fourteenth, an animal. In that instance, the Buddha described these fourteen in descending order.
But when explaining the benefits of giving (*dānāniśaṃsa*), the Buddha explains it in ascending order. In these times, someone might call it exaggeration, or say these were added later. However, this is how the Buddha explains it: Giving an offering to an animal—one can expect a hundredfold benefit. Giving to an unvirtuous worldling, a thousandfold. Giving to a virtuous worldling, a hundred thousandfold. Giving to an outsider ascetic free from sensual lust, a hundred thousand times ten million fold. Next, giving to one practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry—such as the Faith-follower or Dhamma-follower—the Buddha says it is incalculable (*asaṅkheyyaṃ*), immeasurable (*appameyyaṃ*); it cannot be counted, it cannot be measured. From that point upward, he says something wonderful. If it is already incalculable and immeasurable, you cannot increase it further, can you? Therefore, from that point upward, the Buddha uses the exact same phrase. *"Ko pana vādo"*—which means, meritorious friends, "What then to speak of...?" In old books, they translate this as "what need is there to speak of...?" Thus, by offering alms to that person practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry, the benefit is incalculable and immeasurable; and for those higher than that, he continues to say: *"ko pana vādo"*—what need to speak of it? What need to speak of it? This demonstrates the power of the benefit. You can understand this, meritorious friends. It is shown in ascending order, starting from the animal and going upward. Next, he says that these are the individual offerings (*pāṭipuggalikā dakkhiṇā*).
Next, the Buddha shows seven kinds of offerings made to the Saṅgha (*saṅghagatā dakkhiṇā*). He shows them as follows: In the terms we use today: an offering to the dual Saṅgha (both communities) headed by the Buddha. During the Buddha's lifetime, lay disciples like Anāthapiṇḍika offered such alms to both the bhikkhu and bhikkhunī communities with the Buddha at the head. This is of the greatest fruit and benefit. After the dual Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, next is an offering to the dual Saṅgha of bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs after the parinibbāna of the Tathāgata. That is the second. The third is an offering to the bhikkhu Saṅgha after the parinibbāna of the Tathāgata. The fourth is an offering to the bhikkhunī Saṅgha. The fifth is shown in a different way: A donor requests from the Saṅgha: "Please give us a certain number of bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs on behalf of the Saṅgha." That is the fifth offering. The sixth is shown as requesting only bhikkhus: "Please give us only bhikkhus." The seventh is requesting only bhikkhunīs and giving to them. Those are the seven offerings to the Saṅgha.
After that, the Buddha mentions an unusual thing. "Monks, in the future there will be unvirtuous, evil-natured monks, with yellow robes around their necks, who are regarded as *gotrabhū*." Those unvirtuous, evil-natured ones who wear the robe hanging around their neck are called *gotrabhū*. The word *gotrabhū* in this context should be understood not in the sense of insight (*vipassanā*). According to the donor's understanding and the person's appearance, this individual represents the Saṅgha—by the mere fragment of the robe hanging around their neck. That is to say, it is merely an indication of the Noble lineage (*ariya-gotra*). It is in that sense that we explain this word. Next, the Buddha says that even if one makes an offering to such individuals on behalf of the Saṅgha, that offering too is incalculable and immeasurable. This has been a subject of controversy. Western critics, in particular, reject this discourse because of this. Those people say that this is a discourse fabricated by monks during the decline of the dispensation in order to secure alms. This is a very profound discourse. Not a single word can be removed. But the way it is understood is wrong. So, this point is indeed highly controversial—this matter of unvirtuous monks with robes around their necks. Yet, the donor offers alms to them by keeping in mind the Saṅgha.
To beautifully answer any question that might arise regarding this, the Buddha states a certain point. He shows four kinds of purification of an offering (*dakkhiṇā-visuddhi*). Meritorious friends, "purification of an offering" refers to the ways in which an offering made to the Saṅgha is purified. The first purification is shown as: *dāyakato visujjhati no paṭiggāhakato*—purified on the part of the giver, but not on the part of the recipient. The next one is purified on the part of the recipient, but not on the part of the giver. Then, purified neither on the part of the giver nor on the part of the recipient. The last one is purified both on the part of the giver and on the part of the recipient. Consider this division of pure and impure briefly: The giver being pure means they are virtuous and of good character (*sīlavā kalyāṇadhammo*). The recipients being impure means they are unvirtuous and of evil character (*dussīla pāpadhamma*). So, here too, the Buddha has shown a certain hint. This *kāsāvakaṇṭha gotrabhū* individual reminds that faithful giver of the Noble Saṅgha-treasure (*Ariya Saṅgha-ratana*). This is something you know very well: one can go to a heavenly world by giving alms. But think about it, can one go to a heavenly world merely by consuming alms?
