Although we preach this much about meditation, some minds are drawn to that scientific physical philosophy, taking it as the latest and most modern philosophy. Those who have got lost within it as a philosophy are not ordinary people; the purpose of saying these words was to show that nuclear physicists are among them. According to these most modern concepts and discoveries, we ultimately return once again to that very Dhammapada passage declared by the Buddha: *"Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, manoseṭṭhā manomayā"*.
Therefore, today, I hope you devotees have gathered at least some small fragment regarding that powerful perception of the impermanent (*anicca-saññā*) which, as mentioned earlier, is capable of destroying the entire mass of defilements, and which supports insight (*vipassanā*). May the virtue practiced, the meditation cultivated, and this Dhamma sermon heard by you devotees today support you to escape from this world situated within this fathom-long body—from this entire existence (*bhava*) which brings the suffering of birth (*jāti*), decay and death/aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), and so forth—and may this Dhamma sermon support you to realize that noble state of Nibbāna through the penetration of the paths and fruits of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti*), Once-returning (*sakadāgāmitā*), Non-returning (*anāgāmitā*), and Arahantship. Let us aspire that whatever beings from Avīci to Akaniṭṭha wish to rejoice in the merit of this Dhamma preaching and Dhamma hearing, may they realize those highest goals expected through that rejoicing. May everyone, through the power of this merit, attain the supreme, deathless, great Nibbāna. Let us share the merit by reciting these verses.

author: ven. katukurunde nanananda thero
(pahankanuwa sinhala audio dhamma sermon no.155)
namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa
(homage to the blessed one, the worthy one, the fully self-enlightened one)
pali stanza:
duppabbajjam me duradhivasa geha; dhammo duradhigamo, bhoga kiccha vutti; no itaritareneva yuttam, cintetum satatamaniccan'ti.
from:
heragatha (khuddaka nikaya) of the pali canon, specifically from the verses of elder jenta (jentattheragatha, thag 1.111).
dear listeners,
the buddha has praised the perception of the impermanent (*anicca-sanna*) as a meditation capable of uprooting all defilements. developing the perception of the impermanent paves the way to understanding the three characteristics of existence: the impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self/non-self (*anatta*). today, we have chosen as our theme a joyful utterance (*udana*) of a certain arahant who attained arahantship by constantly developing the perception of the impermanent. during the time of the buddha, jenta, the son of a regional king in the magadha country, was inclined toward the going-forth even in his youth due to the power of his past merit; however, a doubt (*vicikiccha*) arose in his mind. the going-forth is extremely difficult. dwelling in the household life is equally arduous. realizing this nibbana is also a very deep matter; the dhamma is profound. on the other hand, earning wealth while living in the household life is also difficult. spending some time in hesitation, wondering what he should do, he eventually came to meet the buddha, listened to the dhamma, developed a certain degree of faith (*saddha*), and went forth. although he went forth, it appears that for a certain period of time, such hesitant thoughts (*vitakka*) continued to dominate his mind. nevertheless, putting forth great effort, he developed the perception of the impermanent as his meditation, and through that meditation subject (*kammatthana*), he attained arahantship. after becoming an arahant, remembering the hesitation that had been in his mind, he joyfully made this utterance of joy with great delight. that verse is the one we have presented as our theme.
*“duppabbajjam me duradhivasa geha”* — going-forth is extremely difficult for me, and dwelling in the household life is equally arduous. *“dhammo (gambhiro) duradhigamo”* — the dhamma is profound and difficult to penetrate. acquiring wealth and material resources is also difficult. *“kiccha vutti no itaritareneva”* — after going forth, one has to utilize the four requisites in the spirit of contentment with whatever is received (*yathalabhasantosa*). when going on almsround (*pindapata*), on some days one receives little, and on other days one receives much. on some days it is coarse; on other days it is delicious. it is one of the two. this is how the going-forth is. therefore, *“kiccha vutti no itaritareneva”* — our livelihood in this going-forth is also very difficult. but conquering all those thoughts, in the end, that venerable one states: *“yuttam cintetum satatam-aniccatam”* — "it is indeed proper to constantly contemplate this impermanence (*aniccata*)." because he saw its benefits, this is briefly what is narrated in this story.
with this as our starting point, let us try to bring out some dhamma points that the buddha declared concerning the dhamma of impermanence (*aniccata*). indeed, there is a certain passage wherein the buddha addressed the sangha on one occasion, declaring the powerful strength of this perception of the impermanent. if we express it in sinhala: "monks, the perception of the impermanent, when developed and cultivated frequently, brings to an end all sensual lust (*kamaraga*). it brings to an end all lust for form (*ruparaga*). it brings to an end all lust for existence (*bhavaraga*). it brings to an end all ignorance (*avijja*). it brings to an end and uproots all conceit of 'i am' (*asmi-mana*)." having declared the strength and benefits of the perception of the impermanent in this manner on that occasion, he addressed the sangha and further explained how the perception of the impermanent is to be developed to yield such great benefits. generally, where the meditation on the perception of the impermanent is shown, you devotees might have seen, especially in discourses like the *girimananda sutta*, where ten perceptions are mentioned. when listing those ten meditation subjects in the *girimananda sutta*, the perception of the impermanent is placed right at the beginning. so here too, the buddha declared that the sangha could attain these benefits by developing the contemplation of the impermanent regarding the five aggregates of grasping/holding (*pancupadanakkhandha*).
these five heaps—form (*rupa*), feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), preparations/volitional activity (*sankhara*), and consciousness (*vinnana*)—are what you devotees have heard of as the five aggregates of grasping/holding (*pancupadanakkhandha*). *upadana* means grasping or holding on. what the buddha has shown is the constant contemplation of the impermanence of these five heaps that are held onto. the manner of this contemplation is also shown in some places in this way. here too, he declares to the monks: *"iti rupam, iti rupassa samudayo, iti rupassa atthangamo"*—"such is form, such the arising of form, such the passing away of form." in the same way, "such is feeling (*vedana*), such the arising of feeling, such the passing away of feeling," and likewise for perception (*sanna*), preparations (*sankhara*), and consciousness (*vinnana*). the buddha declared that a practitioner (*yogavacara*) must constantly contemplate impermanence in whatever way these arise in the mind. these five heaps are indeed the five heaps that we embrace, which we declare as 'i' and 'mine'.
why these are called "heaps" (or aggregates) is also analyzed. it is declared in the buddha's own words. they are analyzed in eleven ways. each of these heaps can be past, future, or present—there are three right there. it could be a past form that comes to mind, a future form, or a present form. likewise, internal (*ajjhatta*) or external (*bahiddha*)—it could be a form regarding oneself, or a form regarding another. sometimes, a form regarding oneself is compared with a form regarding another: "i am more beautiful than them," or "uglier," and so on. these too are things grasped. thus: past, future, present; internal, external; further, gross or subtle; inferior or superior; and finally, far or near. this completes the eleven-fold classification. past, future, present, internal, external, gross, subtle, inferior, superior, far, and near—this is the eleven-fold way the buddha's word analyzes them. thus, regarding form, feeling, and so on, these are the heaps. we live with these heaps, we carry them on our shoulders, they constantly flow into our minds—either as past things, past forms, future forms, and so on. now, all these five heaps are described in the dhamma as the prepared/conditioned (*sankhata*)—as things that have been prepared or constructed.
what is the nature of these prepared/constructed things? they appear to us as permanent (*nicca*); through that very preparation, we try to establish ourselves in them as something stable. this is why they are called *sankhata*. though they are preparations (*sankhara*), they are prepared (*sankhata*). *sankhata* means prepared or constructed things. now, the buddha points out three characteristics of the prepared. "monks, there are three characteristics of the prepared. what are the three characteristics? in every prepared thing, an arising is discerned: *'uppado pannayati'*. likewise, a passing away is discerned: *'vayo pannayati'*. an arising is discerned, a passing away is discerned. thirdly, it is said: *'thitassa annathattam pannayati'*. even regarding that which we assumed to be stable or static (*thiti*), an alteration—a change into something other—is discerned." so the buddha is pointing out the actual state of arising and passing away.
but within the prepared (*sankhata*), we construct a state called "existence" or "stability" (*thiti*). we construct a "present moment". what is now being shown is that this present moment is constantly changing. thus, in true insight (*vipassana*), rather than past or future preparations (*sankhara*), it is the present preparations that are taken as the object in intense insight. the buddha declared on one occasion: "monks, past forms and future forms are impermanent (*anicca*). what need is there to speak of present forms?" he reminds us that even this "present" which we think of as so significant is likewise impermanent. it also changes, being subject to alteration (*annathabhavi*). yet, it is this very nature of alteration that the world grasps onto as existence (*bhava*) and grasping/holding (*upadana*), trying to establish an existence there. it is within that mental state that various kinds of sorrow (*soka*), lamentation (*parideva*), suffering (*dukkha*), and despair (*domanassa*) arise due to these five aggregates. why? because when that foundation we constructed decays, cracks, and collapses—forgetting that it collapses without our knowledge—when we stand upon it, we fall down with its collapse. those are the characteristics of the prepared (*sankhata*). some people present *uppada*, *thiti*, and *bhanga* (arising, static phase, dissolution) as equivalent. but the important point the buddha brings out here is that even that which we assumed to be static (*thiti*) is constantly changing. because of this,
in discourses like the *bhaddekaratta sutta*, it is shown that generally, worldly beings have a longing for the past. "ah, if only that past thing were still there, how good it would be!" they also look forward to the future. thus, the buddha declared: *"yad-atitam pahinam"*—the past is abandoned, what is gone is gone; *"appattan-ca anagatam"*—the future has not yet arrived. therefore, longing for the past is futile. since future things have not yet arrived, taking delight in them is also futile. next, *"paccuppannan-ca yo dhammam tattha tattha vipassati"*—one should see the present phenomenon right there, in each place. one should see it right there through insight (*vipassana*). to see it right there through insight means to see those preparations (*sankhara*) that construct the prepared (*sankhata*). the things that help to construct a prepared thing (*sankhata*) are called preparations (*sankhara*). no matter how often we hear these words, their meaning is sometimes not clear. these *sankhara* mean preparations or constructions. it is through these preparations that a prepared/constructed thing is made.
but what lies at the root of these preparations/constructions? ignorance (*avijja*). you devotees have heard the phrase *"avijja-paccaya sankhara"* (dependent on ignorance, preparations arise) in discourses on dependent arising (*paticca-samuppada*). the most fundamental preparation pointed out by the buddha is this body we grasp onto, which is prepared/constructed through in-breathing and out-breathing (*assasa-passasa*). it was because they could not understand even its impermanence (*aniccata*) that ancient hindu yogis took this breath as a "life-force" (*prana*) or soul (*atman*). what a foolish thing to do! this life-force, which is in-breathing and out-breathing, is constantly changing; even within a single breath, the insight-practitioner perceives it in waves, realizing that there is a vast amount within a single inhalation. yet, the ordinary world grasps tightly onto those preparations (*sankhara*). thus, the body is prepared/constructed by this in-breathing and out-breathing. this is the primary preparation. of course, food, drink, and so forth also play a part. similarly, speech—the words we speak—we take very seriously, as we must in ordinary life. but its true nature is shown to be prepared/constructed by thought-conception and discursive thinking (*vitakka-vicara*), which is a stream of thoughts within the mind. that too is constantly changing. it is from those preparations (*sankhara*) that speech is prepared. next is this mind which we think of as so colorful and complex, which we take so seriously. it is prepared/constructed by perception (*sanna*) and feeling (*vedana*). because of this, perception and feeling are called mental preparations (*citta-sankhara*). thus, what do these preparations—bodily preparation (*kaya-sankhara*), verbal preparation (*vaci-sankhara*), and mental preparation (*citta-sankhara*)—do through these constructive processes? what they do is what comes next in dependent arising (*paticca-samuppada*): consciousness (*vinnana*) and name-and-form (*namarupa*).
the buddha has pointed out this consciousness (*vinnana*) as an illusion (*maya*). this consciousness always co-exists with name-and-form (*namarupa*). consciousness grasps an object, and the buddha presents that grasped object as name-and-form. regarding this name-and-form, no matter how much we think about it, we cannot understand form on its own in that way. name (*nama*) also assists in it. the mind cannot grasp a form in isolation; name and form always go together. therefore, the object that comes to the mind is designated as 'name-and-form'; otherwise, the buddha could have called it 'mind-form' (*citta-rupa*). now, the ordinary world thinks that 'mind' and 'form' exist as two separate things. physical scientists also think that form exists separately on its own. if so, the buddha could have called it 'mind-form' (*citta-rupa*) or 'mental-form' (*mano-rupa*). why did he call it 'name-and-form' instead? it is because form can only be recognized through the naming (*nama*) that is given to it. and it is through the resistance or impingement (*patigha*) presented by form that the concept of impingement comes to the name (*nama*). this relationship is shown by a well-known simile accepted in buddhist thought since ancient times, which you devotees may have heard—the journey of a blind man who can walk and a lame man who can see. the lame man climbs onto the back of the blind man and shows the way. similarly, name can see but cannot walk, while form can walk but is blind. everyone knows these two as name-and-form. insight-practitioners identify the object that comes to the mind as name-and-form. thus, contemplating these preparations (*sankhara*) of name-and-form is what belongs to the insight-practitioner. through this, the capacity to quickly see that widely assumed impermanence (*aniccata*) right there, is present within those very phenomena (*dhamma*) of name-and-form.
what is analyzed as name-and-form phenomena—specifically name-phenomena (*nama-dhamma*)—are the five phenomena: feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), intention/volition (*cetana*), contact (*phassa*), and attention (*manasikara*). you can think of them like the five fingers of a hand: feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention. many people, not only in modern times but since the distant past, have tried to alter this classification of name-phenomena. some suggest putting contact (*phassa*) at the beginning. but the buddha's word says: feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention. feeling is the first. next are perception, volition, contact, and attention in that order. however, logically speaking, it is true that contact (*phassa*) occurs before feeling. but one should not move contact to the front. that is what we have to say. contact must remain in its place. feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention. what is the reason? think about it for a moment. our hand touches a hot object. after touching it, we do not think about the contact (*phassa*) first. we think first of the feeling (*vedana*). activity arises through feeling, and it is through feeling that those physical phenomena are identified. primarily, although we describe it, this does not take a long time. in a split second, as soon as the hand touches the hot object, it is instantly withdrawn. within that, there is the entire group of name-phenomena just mentioned. through feeling (*vedana*), there arises the perception (*sanna*) that the hand is burning. through perception, there arises the volition (*cetana*) that the hand must be withdrawn. next, attention (*manasikara*) is directed to the burnt spot. thus, it is through the name-phenomena of feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), volition (*cetana*), contact (*phassa*), and attention (*manasikara*) that form is identified.
next, as for things belonging to form—what is called form (*rupa*)—you devotees have heard of the great primary elements (*mahabhuta-dhamma*), namely earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and wind (*vayo*). they are called "great primaries" because they cannot be identified individually; they always exist in a mixed state. but we identify them according to their characteristics. those characteristics are what are called name-phenomena (*nama-dhamma*). that is why we said form is recognized through those name-phenomena. what gives name-phenomena the concept of resistance, the concept of contact, are the physical phenomena. this point is shown very deeply in this dhamma. the buddha divides the word contact (*phassa*) into two parts: designation-contact (*adhivacana-samphassa*) and resistance-contact (*patigha-samphassa*). "designation" (*adhivacana*) refers to name (*nama*). thus, within this contact, there is both a naming and an impingement/resistance, and they are mutually supportive. from that simile, you devotees can understand why all these points are shown in the dhamma: it is on the day we understand the true nature of this illusion of consciousness (*vinnana*) that weariness (*nibbida*) toward preparations (*sankhara*) arises. as long as weariness toward preparations does not arise, and as long as there is attachment to preparations, the prepared (*sankhata*) continues to be constructed.
the buddha shows this next: where is this prepared/constructed (*sankhata*) manufactured? this prepared is manufactured within the six sense-bases (*salayatana*). in modern times, one may understand "bases" as spheres of experience, and that is fine if it helps. it is within these six sense-bases that the five aggregates of grasping/holding (*pancupadanakkhandha*) are prepared, created, and produced. what are the six? eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. they are called the base of eye-contact (*cakkhu-samphassayatana*), the base of ear-contact (*sota-samphassayatana*), and finally, the base of mind-contact (*mano-samphassayatana*). why are they called bases (*ayatana*)? they belong to two sides; to be a base, there must be two. the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, and so on, going down to the mind and thoughts/ideas (*manodhamma*) that come to the mind. although we do not list them all, you devotees can infer all six. the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, and so on. now, the deepest point is the sixth: the mind. the objects that come to the mind are called *dhamma* (phenomena/ideas). we are frequently reminded of the dhammapada verse: *"manopubbangama dhamma, manosettha manomaya"*. according to this verse spoken by the buddha, regarding these *dhamma* or "things"—we in the world think that things exist separately on their own. but what is the actual state of affairs? the mind precedes these "things". furthermore, between the two, the mind is supreme. finally, it says *manomaya*—these things are made of the mind. that is what is difficult for the world to accept. it is a very difficult state to accept: that these things in front of us are prepared/constructed by the mind. it is a very profound matter.
so to clarify this point and the impermanence (*aniccata*) in it, the buddha impresses this perception of the impermanent (*anicca-sanna*) upon the minds of the sangha in a very powerful discourse, the *dvaya sutta*. he presents it in a wonderful way. the theme of that discourse is *dvayam*—meaning 'dyad' or 'pair', concerning 'two'. "monks, consciousness (*vinnana*) arises dependent on a dyad." we think that consciousness exists independently on its own. but consciousness arises dependent on a dyad. what is the dyad? the eye and form; thus, eye-consciousness arises dependent on the eye and form. ear-consciousness arises dependent on the ear and sound. infer in this way. finally, mind-consciousness arises dependent on the mind and mind-objects (*dhamma*). apart from this, there is no such thing as consciousness (*vinnana*) on its own. thus, in accordance with the dhamma, there are six types of consciousness. as we mentioned earlier, there is a rapid, reciprocal conditioning (*annamanna-paccayata*) or mutual causal relationship between consciousness (*vinnana*) and name-and-form (*namarupa*). thus, what is called consciousness (*vinnana*) is those six. eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. how does the buddha demonstrate the impermanence (*aniccata*) of each of those types of consciousness? consciousness arises dependent on a dyad, such as the eye and form. then he tells the sangha: "monks, the eye is impermanent (*anicca*), subject to change, subject to alteration. form is also like that; impermanent, subject to change, subject to alteration." in all of these, the word *cala* (unstable/moving) is used. even in modern times, we speak of movement/oscillation (*calanaya*). the eye, form, and everything are in constant motion. they are constantly moving. they are constantly wearing away. *"cala ca eva vaya ca, anicca viparinamino"*—they undergo change/transformation, and they undergo alteration (*annathabhavi*). this is said to impress it upon the mind. thus, the eye is impermanent (*anicca*), constantly trembling and changing. forms are also like that. next, he says that the consciousness (*vinnana*) that arises from the coming together of the eye and form is also impermanent and subject to change.
then the buddha asks the sangha a question: "monks, how could consciousness (*vinnana*), which arises from the coming together of two impermanent things, be permanent?" he asks this. thus, that eye-consciousness (*cakkhu-vinnana*) is also impermanent. but he does not stop there. next, the buddha declares that the coming together of the eye, form, and eye-consciousness is contact (*phassa*). the meeting of these three—the eye, form, and the eye-consciousness arising from them—is the moment of contact. that eye-contact (*cakkhu-samphassa*) is also impermanent. it also changes. it also undergoes alteration. there too, the buddha asks: if eye-contact arose dependent on certain causes and conditions (*hetu-paccaya*), those causes and conditions are also impermanent and subject to change. then he asks, how can that which depends on changing causes and conditions be permanent? in this manner, the buddha attempts to impress upon minds the impermanence of every single aspect of these six sense-bases (*salayatana*). thus, the insight-practitioner realizes this truth of impermanence through constant perception of the impermanent (*anicca-sanna*) and by applying attention (*manasikara*) to those name-phenomena. when contemplation is applied more and more subtly, that "foundation"—that state of stability (*thiti*) we assumed—becomes narrower and narrower. indeed, the "present" is not something that can be measured. it is a squeezed state between the past and the future. if someone is asked, "what is 'now'?", can they answer? what is 'now'? one has to answer according to the context. 'now' could sometimes refer to a long period. sometimes, depending on the situation, it could be very narrow. thus, for the insight-practitioner, 'now' becomes narrower and narrower as attention becomes subtler, as attention becomes stronger. through this insight-attention—this radical attention/wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*) which sees things right there—that perception of permanence (*nicca-sanna*) wears away. when the perception of permanence wears away, a prepared/constructed thing (*sankhata*) is not built up there. within these few words, you devotees can understand many points relevant to insight (*vipassana*).
next, the buddha points to the common term applied to these words about impermanence: "knowledge of things as they are" (*yathabhuta-nana*). on one occasion, the buddha declares how nibbana emerges through these six sense-bases. or rather, how instead of the five aggregates growing, they wear away. first, he shows how they are built up. if someone does not know the eye as it really is (*yathabhuta*), and does not know forms as they really are. by "as they really are," one must understand: they do not know their impermanence (*aniccata*). not knowing their impermanence, disregarding their impermanence, disregarding the impermanence of the consciousness (*vinnana*) that arises dependent on the eye and form, disregarding the impermanence of the contact (*phassa*) that arises therefrom, disregarding the impermanence of the felt experience, feeling (*vedana*), and so forth arising from that contact—if one does not know them as they really are, that person develops attachment toward them, develops craving (*tanha*), and through that arising of craving, they are built up. that anchors itself. let us think of the form components present in that moment—say, a moment one is pleased with. those relevant aspects of form come together and build up one's aggregate of grasping/holding for form (*rupa-upadanakkhandha*). the feelings relevant to that compile together, and "i experienced such feeling on such a day, in such a situation"—thus feelings are built up. "i was one who had such a form," "i was one who had such feeling," and so on, and regarding the other aggregates too, in this way, the five aggregates of grasping/holding (*pancupadanakkhandha*) are separated and constructed, flowing out from those six sense-bases (*salayatana*). this happens by taking the six sense-bases as permanent, taking each part of the six sense-bases as permanent, due to the lack of knowledge of things as they are (*yathabhuta-nana*). next, the buddha shows the other side of this: going toward nibbana. so that is how the prepared (*sankhata*) is made, that is how it is built up.
he also shows how they wear away. how is that? if an insight-practitioner sees right at each point: "the eye is impermanent (*anicca*), it changes, it undergoes alteration, it undergoes *annathabhava*," and lives constantly with this understanding, then in that moment, those experiences wear away right then and there; they do not go and pile up. they do not pile up as grasping/holding (*upadana*) or as the prepared (*sankhata*). when this becomes powerful, it is then that one can realize even that noble nibbana called the cessation of the six sense-bases (*salayatana-nirodha*). the cessation of the six sense-bases is the state of the cessation of existence (*bhava-nirodha*). this is what is called nibbana. that is why the buddha declared: "within this very fathom-long body, i declare the world, the arising of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world." the buddha points this out based on these very six sense-bases (*salayatana*). the culmination of impermanence (*aniccata*) is the signless (*animitta*). three things are shown as aids to nibbana: the signless (*animitta*), the desireless/uncommitted (*appanihita*), and the void/empty (*sunnata*). the signless (*animitta*) refers to the culmination of the perception of the impermanent. when the perception of the impermanent is developed to its utmost, no sign (*nimitta*) comes to the mind. a state arises where the mind cannot take up any sign. it is then signless (*animitta*). this is itself a name for nibbana. for that very reason, if something is impermanent,
...it is of the nature of suffering (*dukkha*). where there is the nature of suffering, there is no desire. *panidhi* means desire or aspiration. thus, it is called the desireless/uncommitted (*appanihita*). why did we say that by developing the perception of the impermanent (*anicca-sanna*), all three characteristics are developed? it is because it is stated in the dhamma: *"yad-aniccam tam dukkham, yam dukkham tad-anatta"*—a passage frequently mentioned in the dhamma. whatever is impermanent (*anicca*) is suffering (*dukkha*). if it is suffering, it cannot be a self (*atta*); it cannot be maintained as 'i' and 'mine'. thus, when these three characteristics are developed to the highest level, when impermanence is developed to the highest, the mind goes to the signless (*animitta*). it is like the gateway to nibbana. next, the desire called aspiration (*panidhi*) disappears because of that nature of suffering. that is called the desireless/uncommitted (*appanihita*). next, if there is no state of self (*atta*), it is void/empty (*sunnata*). where there is a self, one grasps a "thing". where there is no state of self, it is void. this indeed approaches the subject of voidness (*sunnata*).
in the past, when the buddha preached this dhamma, he brought up and compared various teachings and views (*ditthi*) of the teachers of that time, polishing and highlighting this dhamma. today, we are compelled to speak in the same way in this dhamma. why is that? in this era, physical science is something that many people talk about, and to which many minds are drawn. even nuclear physicists themselves have now realized the shortcomings in some of the fundamental hypotheses of physical science. what was the mistake they made? instead of what we mentioned earlier from the dhammapada verse, *"manopubbangama dhamma, manosettha manomaya"*, those people thought that there was some separate thing, distinct from the mind and undetected by the mind, existing on its own. this is not just their delusion; it is an idea coming down from the past. the view that there is some truly existing substance, a reality existing permanently, has existed since ancient times. next, that there is an "atom" as something real, some truth independent of the mind. but now, they have come to understand the buddha's word to such an extent that those nuclear physicists themselves—even the leading ones of this recent era—say that as long as something is not measured, one cannot attribute qualities or characteristics to it as "such-and-such a thing".
furthermore, let alone anything else, one cannot even say that something exists as long as it is not measured. what this demonstrates is—as you devotees may have heard in our previous sermons—that nibbana is described as "the crushing of the conceit 'i am'" (*asmi-mana-samugghata*). it is according to this viewpoint of 'i am' (*asmi*) that these five aggregates operate. when one assumes 'i am', one measures accordingly. there is a valuable discourse in the buddha's own words that declares this measuring. on one occasion, ven. ananda explains to the sangha something declared by the buddha: a definition of the word "world" (*loka*). what is the "world"? "that by which one gains a perception of the world, that by which one does a measuring of the world, that is called the 'world' in this noble discipline." that by which one identifies the world, that by which one does a measuring of the world, is what is called the "world" in this dispensation, according to this noble discipline (*ariya-vinaya*). with what does one measure? here are the things with which one measures: with the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and finally, with the mind—with these six sense-bases. it is stated that without these measurings, there is no world. so this is the very story that these people have had to accept. without a measurement, where there is no measuring, one cannot attribute anything to a thing; one cannot even say that it exists. likewise, one cannot speak of any characteristic of that existing thing.
to what extent—those devotees who do science may have heard—this is called quantum physics. this is the latest branch of physical science considered the most advanced in recent times. even the philosophers presenting quantum theory have now had to accept that where there is no observation, one cannot say that something exists. as long as there is no observation, one cannot say that something exists; that is to say, without observation, one cannot say that something exists separately on its own. one cannot say that there is a separate world independent of the mind. to what extent—some of those leading nuclear physicists say that when their observations become contradictory, when with every observation their premise that 'there is a separate thing on its own' is disproved, having nothing else to do, in the end they say: "if i had known earlier that one could not escape this quantum leap after seeing the results of these observations, i would not have laid my hands on this." those scientists say this. having nothing they can do, they have become perplexed. they started from the wrong end: assuming that things exist independent of the mind. they still continue to look with that idea, assuming that such a thing exists. but in the end they realize, and they are forced to say, especially regarding whether electrons exist: "if by the mere act of our looking, that electron is disturbed, how can we know its true state?" thus, if it changes even by the mere extent of our directing the mind to it, how can we say what it is? they have had to face such a dilemma. what is the reason for this? now, let us state the corresponding part in our buddha-dhamma. the buddha has preached a discourse—since we have declared this discourse on previous occasions, it is nothing new to those devotees who have heard our sermons.
on one occasion, the buddha said to the sangha: "monks, if other sectarians (*annatitthiya*) come and ask you such questions, what answers would you give them?" this shows that the buddha had prepared the minds of the sangha to answer when such questions arose. the buddha says: "other sectarians might come and ask you questions like this: 'what is the root of all things? what is the arising of all things? where do all things originate? toward what are all things directed?'" there are many such questions. we will shorten them according to the situation in a way relevant to this topic. then the monks say: "we do not have the ability to answer these. may the blessed one himself explain." thereupon, the buddha delivers that discourse: "if they ask so, monks, say this:
*"chandamulaka, avuso, sabbe dhamma"*—'friends, all things are rooted in desire/interest (*chanda*).' *chanda* means desire or interest. our mind is directed toward something first of all because of the desire for it. let us take *chanda* as a lighter shade of craving (*tanha*). thus, it is within a sense of purpose or need that even those scientists engage in research—it is because of *chanda*. they expect to analyze the atom or its components; they have a great interest in it. that *chanda*—all things are rooted in desire (*chanda*). next, it says: *"manasikarasambhava sabbe dhamma"*—all things originate in attention (*manasikara*). to express *sambhava* in sinhala, it means the arising of all things; everything is met by us when our attention, our contemplation, is directed to it. that is the very point about "observation" mentioned earlier. if by our very act of observing, the thing we subject to observation changes, how can we know its true state? that is the question they ask. this demonstrates that there is nothing apart from the mind. this is *manomaya*! if those scientists had correctly understood these three phrases—*"manopubbangama dhamma, manosettha manomaya"*—they would not have fallen into this. they started from the wrong side, saying that "things" exist.
next, there is another aspect: *"phassasamudaya sabbe dhamma"*—all things arise from contact (*phassa*). what is called contact? just now we spoke of the six sense-bases (*salayatana*). each of these bases is called the base of eye-contact (*cakkhu-samphassa*), the base of ear-contact (*sota-samphassa*), the base of nose-contact (*ghana-samphassa*), and so forth. both words *phassa* and *samphassa* are used. thus, it is through these bases that contact arises, and it is from contact that a thing originates. it is by mental contacting that those things are constructed. regarding *"manopubbangama dhamma"*, it is when there is mind-contact (*mano-samphassa*) that the thing taken as its object emerges: contact (*phassa*). furthermore, the buddha used this word contact (*phassa*) in the *brahmajala sutta* to dismantle all speculative views (*ditthi*). how did the buddha reject even those views established by the ancient sages who, far exceeding the achievements of modern scientists, developed the mind, developed all five supernormal knowledges (*panca-abhinna*) to the extent of seeing past births, and stood upon that direct experience? "that too is dependent on contact." "that too is dependent on contact." he dismantles them by that very fact. what does it mean to say that it arises dependent on contact? it is connected to the mind. it is not something correct, not the ultimate reality. that is the point. now, to clarify these points further, later two illustrations are given, which have been frequently shown to you devotees. but before that, let us mention another thing stated by those nuclear physicists, which was referred to earlier: "if by the mere directing of our mind to something—by the mere directing of our mind toward what we intend to observe—it is disturbed, how can we know its true state?"
the best answer to that question is found in two points we previously presented as similes when explaining the phenomena of name-and-form (*namarupa*). one is the dog walking across a footbridge, who is deceived by his own reflection. thinking it is another dog, if he is angry, he growls, or if he is pleased, he wags his tail. otherwise, he keeps looking to see who is there. but that problem is resolved in this way: as we briefly mentioned, the dog thinks: "i look because it is visible." but "it is visible because i look." what happened to this dog is what happens to most people. that dog on the footbridge, going to the middle of the bridge, looks at the reflection cast in the water and thinks: "i look because it is visible." but it is visible because he looks. that "looking" is what is called observation. now, connect those words. through this, one can understand that regarding this name-and-form (*namarupa*), even scientists are already caught up in the name-phenomena (*nama-dhamma*) within that act of looking. a separate reality cannot be seen on its own. *"manopubbangama dhamma, manosettha manomaya."*
another simile for this was presented recently when explaining name-and-form (*namarupa*) phenomena, and it seems this simile has become popular with many for various reasons. what is it? we illustrated it using an ancient greek myth. briefly, there is an ancient myth about narcissus, a beautiful greek youth who had never seen his own face. while walking in the forest, as he bent down over a pond to wash his face, he mistook his own reflection for a water nymph dwelling in the water and tried to embrace her. he tried all day, and for many days, and in the end, he sacrificed his life. when narcissus reached his hands into the water to embrace the nymph, each time he did so, the water was disturbed and rippled. now, consider that it is through our very attention (*manasikara*), through our very attempt to know what it is, that it is disturbed—this is the kind of disturbance meant. what, then, is being looked at here? it is name-and-form (*namarupa*). although it is taken as a separate thing, what is constantly the object of our mind and consciousness (*vinnana*) is name-and-form. this is a form merely in name. it is not real form. it is not the reality (*yatha*). as we said, form is recognized through name because of that naming. and the concept of impingement/resistance is given to name through form. why is it said that one cannot attribute qualities or characteristics to either of them? this too has been shown very well by the buddha in a very profound discourse named the *mahanidana sutta*.
a discourse showing a very profound aspect of dependent arising (*paticca-samuppada*), a very profound aspect concerning the word contact (*phassa*), was preached step by step by the buddha to ven. ananda. we have also shown this on various occasions. briefly, he demonstrates contact through the relationship between name and form, stating that without those modes, signs, and characteristics by which the group belonging to name is designated, no concept of designation regarding physical form would be manifest. that is to say, without those name-phenomena of feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), volition (*cetana*), contact (*phassa*), and attention (*manasikara*), no identification of physical form can be made. next, without those physical impingements/resistances arising from earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and wind (*vayo*) which belong to form, no talk of sensory contact, impingement, or experiencing regarding name-phenomena would be manifest. these two aspects are shown. there too, those characteristics can be attributed only after the mind is applied to it. apart from that, there is no such thing as characteristics inherent or intrinsic to them on their own. it has to be accepted that they are attributed by the mind. regarding this point, there is a valuable discourse in the text *sutta nipata* named the *mahaviyuha sutta*. in those days, intense debates and disputes existed in india, even more than today. the buddha has delivered an extraordinary sermon that pacifies those debates and disputes. in it, a valuable verse is shown:
> *passam naro dakkhati namarupam,*
> *disvana va nassati tanimeva;*
> *kamam bahum passatu appakam va,*
> *na hi tena suddhim kusala vadanti.*
this verse is specifically cited here because it is also relevant to the problem of those nuclear physicists mentioned earlier.
*"passam naro dakkhati namarupam"*—"a man seeing, sees only name-and-form (*namarupa*)." there is nothing apart from name-and-form. *"disvana va nassati tanimeva"*—"having seen, what he knows is just that." it is nothing apart from it. *"kamam bahum passatu appakam va"*—"let him see much or little, it is of no use." *"na hi tena suddhim kusala vadanti"*—"the wise do not say that purity comes by that, nor do they say it is complete." that is the story. thus, the buddha rejected all sixty-two speculative views (*ditthi*) in the *brahmajala sutta*—all views concerning both the past and the future—showing that they are dismantled through this teaching, and the buddha concluded the *brahmajala sutta* with an extraordinary simile.
i hope to bring that simile to the minds of you devotees on this occasion. in it, the buddha shows why this should be called *brahmajala* (the net of brahma / the supreme net). the buddha presents the story of this supreme net in this way: "monks, suppose a skilled fisherman or a fisherman’s apprentice casts a very finely woven net, with very fine mesh, over a small pond. after covering the pond containing the fish with that fine net, that fisherman knows very well that whatever fish are in it, whenever they rise to the surface, they are caught within that net. they cannot rise above the mesh; they remain trapped in the net. that is what is meant by saying any speculative view (*ditthi*) is caught in this net." what, then, is this mesh of the net? the mesh of the net is indeed contact (*phassa*). that is why every speculative view in that discourse is dismantled. the buddha dismantles all sixty-two views saying: *"tad-api phassa-paccaya, tad-api phassa-paccaya, tad-api phassa-paccaya"*—"that too is dependent on contact, that too is dependent on contact, that too is dependent on contact." this is the very same story we have to say here regarding the problem of those scientists. they must realize one day that they cannot see this apart from the thing they observe. what they see is that very name-and-form (*namarupa*). they think they are seeing an independently existing thing there. that is why it is said: "if by the mere act of our looking to see if this electron exists, it is disturbed, how can we know its true state?" it is from the very degree of mental application—through attention (*manasikara*)—that these arise. they originate from contact (*phassa*). that point of origin is what the buddha brought out in the *brahmajala sutta*. all those speculative views contact again and again through the six sense-bases (*salayatana*): *"phussa phussa patisamvedenti"*. contacting through those six sense-bases, they experience feeling (*vedana*) through them. through that, they develop perceptions and cravings (*tanha*). developing perception and craving, they rotate again in existence (*bhava*)—in this way, those speculative views are dismantled. apart from contacting through the six sense-bases, they cannot know. what they see is not ultimate reality; that is what the *brahmajala sutta* points out.
what, then, is the truth? what is the truth discovered by the buddha? it is the very thing we mentioned earlier: the ultimate culmination of the view of not-self/non-self (*anatta*) is voidness (*sunnata*). voidness is the truth. worldly beings are trapped within things measured by that wedge they have driven in, called 'i am' (*asmi*), assuming "they exist, they exist." the buddha showed that when that wedge of 'i am' (*asmi*) is pulled out, nothing remains. he declared this: *"sassato-r-iva khayati, passato natthi kincanam"*—in an inspired verse on one occasion, the buddha declared: "it appears as if eternal, but to one who sees (*passato*), there is nothing." it appears as if eternal. he points this out on another occasion: *"janato passato natthi kincanam"*—"to one who knows and sees, there is nothing in the world." that is also a realization; there is a moment when it is directly experienced. that is exactly what the buddha meant when he said that the cessation of the world is also right here. the arising of the world is due to craving (*tanha*); *"tanha ponobhavika"*—it is by craving that existence (*bhava*) is prepared. the buddha has declared this in various ways: the hindrance of ignorance (*avijja-nivarana*) covers up the impermanence (*aniccata*) of these things. the glue of craving sticks them together. within that, in the present, one assumes that "a thing exists", assuming a state of stability (*thiti*). in that darkness of ignorance, with that force of craving called thirst, it is also described as the glue of craving. it is by gluing with that glue of craving that this existence (*bhava*) is constructed. it is within that constructed world that one travels further and further in this *samsara*.
thus, to escape from *samsara*, the buddha points to that true state of affairs (*yatha-tatta*). what is true realization? *"janato passato natthi kincanam"*. as for those names for nibbana we mentioned—the signless (*animitta*), the desireless/uncommitted (*appanihita*), and the void (*sunnata*)—there is a place where signs disappear, desires disappear, and there is no stable self assumed as 'i' and 'mine'. that is what is called the cessation of existence (*bhava-nirodha*), experienced in this very life. therefore, the liberation that humans seek—the buddha has pointed out that speculative views (*ditthi*) are like a headache. regarding what those nuclear physicists declared, one nuclear physicist stated at one point: "if we had known that we could not escape this wretched quantum leap, we would not have laid our hands on this quantum theory." they say so when they are helpless. why did he call it wretched? because in the end, what is done in this observation is merely the expansion of *samsara*, not the realization of reality. in reality, the buddha points out that voidness (*sunnata*) comes at the end. because each of these worlds is constructed through one's own six sense-bases (*salayatana*). our world is not the dog's world. other animals construct their worlds through their six sense-bases. it is that very world that the buddha described as suffering (*dukkha*); there is no satisfaction in it. there are the sufferings of birth (*jati*), decay and death/aging and death (*jaramarana*), sickness (*vyadhi*), and death. if one hopes to escape from it, one has to start from that very impermanence (*aniccata*). if something is impermanent, one understands that it is suffering (*dukkha*). all these reconstructions—these preparations/constructions (*sankhara*)—are:
> *anicca vata sankhara,*
> *uppadavayadhammino;*
> *uppajjitva nirujjhanti,*
> *tesam vupasamo sukho.*
this is frequently heard in houses of mourning; you devotees might think of it as something inauspicious. but within it lies the entire truth. *"anicca vata sankhara"*—preparations (*sankhara*) are indeed impermanent. *"uppadavayadhammino"*—they are of the nature of arising and passing away. they arise only to be destroyed. *"tesam vupasamo sukho"*—the calming/stilling of those preparations is bliss. this is why you devotees have heard that nibbana is described as *"sabbasankharasamatha"*—the stilling of all preparations. when preparations are stilled, a prepared/constructed thing (*sankhata*) does not arise. when a prepared thing is not constructed, those graspings/holdings (*upadana*) called the five aggregates of grasping/holding are not built up. the buddha declared that this state can be realized in this very life. this is what is called "extinguishment without grasping/holding" (*anupada-parinibbana. when all that is let go, the mind is liberated; it is not some strange thing, not something to be grasped—that mind. if within this grasping/holding (*upadana*), there are birth (*jati*), decay and death/aging and death (*jaramarana*), sickness, and death, and they are responsible for them, then the moment of letting go of this is the bliss of liberation. the understanding within that is indeed *"janato passato natthi kincanam"*—to one who sees, there is actually nothing here. when that knowledge and vision (*nanadassana*) is developed to the highest level, that conjuring of a existence (*bhava*) by craving (*tanha*)—the buddha has on some occasions compared craving to a seamstress (*sibbani*). think of how a stitch is made, how a sewing machine makes a stitch. each time the needle goes down, a thread passes underneath and forms a knot. that is *"tanha-paccaya upadanam"*—dependent on craving, grasping/holding arises; because of grasping/holding, a existence (*bhava*) is woven. the buddha has shown this in a verse:
> *yo ubhantena viditva,*
> *majjhe manta na lippati;*
> *tam brumi mahapurisoti,*
> *so'dha sibbanimaccaga.*
the buddha declares an extraordinary verse: "he who, having understood both ends, does not cling to the middle with wisdom (*manta*)—him i call a great man; he has escaped from that seamstress (sewing work) here."
the buddha declares an extraordinary verse. one who, having correctly understood both ends (*ubhante*), does not cling to the middle with wisdom (*manta*)—*"tam brumi mahapurisoti"*—"him i call a great man." *"so'dha sibbanimaccaga"*—that person has escaped from that seamstress (sewing work) here. he went beyond the seamstress; he was not caught by the seamstress. now, the buddha shows how the ordinary world is caught by the seamstress. what are these two ends, and what is the middle? one end is contact (*phassa*). the second end is the arising of contact (*phassa-samudaya*). in the middle is the cessation of contact (*phassa-nirodha*). what, then, does this seamstress do? gluing with the glue of craving (*tanha*), she glues together, disregarding the cessation (*nirodha*) in the middle. with every contact, there is a cessation. but because of craving, forgetting that cessation, we collect those contacts together and construct a "thing". regarding this, there is a passage about the insight-practitioner making attention subtle: *"phussa phussa vayam passam, evam virajjati"*. *"phussa phussa vayam passam"* means seeing the passing away of contact with each and every contact, and in this way, one becomes dispassionate, developing non-attachment. as long as one does not see cessation, gluing with that glue of craving, one weaves a existence (*bhava*). that is the stitch of becoming (*bhava-sibbani*). what, then, does that great man do? he sees cessation (*nirodha*). that is why the buddha declares that both the beings in the form realms and the beings in the formless realms return to existence again and again because they do not know cessation (*nirodha*). you devotees may have heard that craving is described as *"tanha ponobhavika"*—it creates renewed existence. it links existence to existence. forgetting cessation, through craving, one brings out contact and the arising of contact, generating another contact, while disregarding the cessation of that contact. in this very way, what the buddha does is to bring out that cessation which the world had forgotten. that cessation is itself called nibbana. that noble state, ending in the cessation of the six sense-bases (*salayatana-nirodha*), is what the buddha brought out. this is not only for those times. this is not only for the recluses and brahmins of that day. even today's philosophers and scientists can learn something from it. therefore, you devotees must take this matter of the perception of the impermanent (*anicca-sanna*) deeply to heart. although we preach this much about meditation, some minds are drawn to that scientific physical philosophy, taking it as the latest and most modern philosophy. those who have got lost within it as a philosophy are not ordinary people; the purpose of saying these words was to show that nuclear physicists are among them. according to these most modern concepts and discoveries, we ultimately return once again to that very dhammapada passage declared by the buddha: *"manopubbangama dhamma, manosettha manomaya"*.
therefore, today, i hope you devotees have gathered at least some small fragment regarding that powerful perception of the impermanent (*anicca-sanna*) which, as mentioned earlier, is capable of destroying the entire mass of defilements, and which supports insight (*vipassana*). may the virtue practiced, the meditation cultivated, and this dhamma sermon heard by you devotees today support you to escape from this world situated within this fathom-long body—from this entire existence (*bhava*) which brings the suffering of birth (*jati*), decay and death/aging and death (*jaramarana*), and so forth—and may this dhamma sermon support you to realize that noble state of nibbana through the penetration of the paths and fruits of stream-entry (*sotapatti*), once-returning (*sakadagamita*), non-returning (*anagamita*), and arahantship. let us aspire that whatever beings from avici to akanittha wish to rejoice in the merit of this dhamma preaching and dhamma hearing, may they realize those highest goals expected through that rejoicing. may everyone, through the power of this merit, attain the supreme, deathless, great nibbana. let us share the merit by reciting these verses.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 047
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #47
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.159)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Ubayeneva sampanno, Rāhulo Bhaddoti maṃ vidū; Yañcāmhi putto Buddhassa, yañca dhammesu cakkhumā. Yañca me āsavā khīṇā, yañca natthi punabbhavo; Arahā dakkhiṇeyyomhi, tevijjo amataddaso.
Kāmandhā jālapacchannā, taṇhāchadanachāditā; Pamattabandhunā baddhā, macchāva kumināmukhe. Taṃ kāmaṃ chetvā Mārassa bandhanaṃ samūlaṃ taṇhamabbuyha; Sītibhūto'smi nibbuto'ti.
From:
Theragāthā, Rāhulattheragāthā
Dear Listeners,
In this Dispensation, Ven. Rāhula, who attained the foremost position among the monks who love the training, was known among the Sangha by the name "Rāhula Bhadra" (Rāhula the Fortunate / Rāhula the Good). That epithet "Bhadra"—meaning "good" or "fortunate"—indicates that he was extremely dear and pleasing to the Sangha. He was not so dear and pleasing to the Sangha merely because he was the son of the Buddha, but also due to his good qualities, his obedient, humble, and disciplined behavior. Indeed, the character of Rāhula is a supreme ideal of obedience. He was a son of the Buddha in the truest sense of the word. The verses from the Theragāthā Pāli that we have taken as our theme today are accepted as the joyous utterances (*udāna*) expressed by Ven. Rāhula after he attained Arahantship. In these verses too, it is mentioned that he was known by this name, "Rāhula Bhadra."
*"Ubayen’eva sampanno, Rāhulo Bhaddo’ti maṃ vidū"* — "Endowed with both, they know me as Rāhula Bhadra." Because of two reasons, they know me by the name Rāhula Bhadra:
*"Yañca’mhi putto Buddhassa, yañca dhammesu cakkhumā"* — "In that I am the son of the Buddha, and that I have the eye (of wisdom) regarding the Dhammas." One reason is that I am the son of the Buddha. The other reason is that I possess the Dhamma-eye, which has the power of understanding the Dhammas.
*"Yañca me āsavā khīṇā, yañca natthi punabbhavo"* — "And that my taints (*āsavas*) are destroyed, and that there is no more renewed existence (*punabbhava*)." Because my taints are destroyed, and because there is no renewed becoming (*bhava*) for me,
*"Arahā dakkhiṇeyyo’mhi, tevijjo amataddaso"* — "I am an Arahant, worthy of offerings, possessed of the Threefold Knowledge, and a beholder of the Deathless." I am an Arahant, worthy of receiving gifts called offerings (*dakkhiṇeyyo*), possessed of the Threefold Knowledge (*tevijja*), and a beholder of the Deathless (*amata-dassa*), which is Nibbāna.
*"Kāmandhā jālapacchannā, taṇhāchadanachāditā; Pamattabandhunā baddhā, macchāva kumināmukhe"* — "Blinded by sensual pleasures, covered by the net, shrouded by the canopy of craving, bound by the kinsman of the negligent, like fish in the mouth of a funnel-net." Beings who are blinded by sensual pleasures, entangled in the net of sensuality, and covered by the shroud of craving (*taṇhā*), are bound in the net of Māra (the kinsman of the negligent) like fish caught in the mouth of a wicker-trap (funnel-net).
This is what is declared regarding those beings. Next, he speaks about himself:
*"Taṃ kāmaṃ chetvā Mārassa, bandhanaṃ samūlaṃ taṇhamabbuyha, sītibhūto’smi nibbuto’ti"* — "Having cut off those sensual pleasures, having severed the bonds of Māra, and having uprooted craving (*taṇhā*) completely, I have become cool, extinguished (*nibbuto*)." Thus, these are the verses declared by Ven. Rāhula after attaining Arahantship.
You all must have heard that the immediate cause for Prince Siddhartha’s Great Renunciation was the news that a son had been born. Prince Siddhartha received the happy news of a son’s birth with the reaction, "A Rāhula (a bond/fetter) is born." Not only that, on that very night, without informing anyone, suppressing his paternal affection, he made the Great Renunciation for the sake of us all. Thus, Prince Rāhula, who did not receive paternal affection, got to see his father for the first time only when the Buddha visited the city of Kapilavatthu about a year after His Enlightenment. Having arrived at Kapilavatthu, while residing in the Sakyan monastery named Nigrodhārāma, one day the Buddha visited the palace of King Suddhodana. Having arrived, He sat on the prepared seat. Rāhula's mother, Princess Yasodharā, said to Prince Rāhula: "There, Rāhula, is your father. Go and ask for your inheritance." So, Prince Rāhula went before the Buddha and began to speak endearing words, saying, "Ascetic, even your shadow and your shelter are pleasant to me." When the Buddha started to return to Nigrodhārāma, Prince Rāhula followed closely behind Him, repeatedly saying, "Ascetic, give me my inheritance! Ascetic, give me my inheritance!"
Once the Buddha returned to Nigrodhārāma, He said to Ven. Sāriputta, "Well then, Sāriputta, ordain Prince Rāhula." At that time, there was no established monastic procedure regarding the ordination of novices (*sāmaṇeras*). Therefore, Ven. Sāriputta asked, "Venerable Sir, how shall I ordain Prince Rāhula?" At that moment, the Buddha laid down a Vinaya rule, having assembled the monks and delivered a Dhamma talk: "I allow you to ordain novices by the threefold recitation of the going-for-refuge (*saraṇāgamana*)." In this manner, Ven. Sāriputta ordained Prince Rāhula.
Upon hearing the news of this ordination, King Suddhodana came to the Buddha, paid homage, and sitting to one side, said, "Venerable Sir, I would like to ask for one boon." The Buddha addressed His royal father as "Gautama": "Gautama, the Tathāgatas are beyond the custom of granting boons." "No, Venerable Sir, what I ask is something allowable and blameless." "Then speak, Gautama." Then King Suddhodana said, "When the Blessed One went forth, it caused me great pain. Likewise, when Prince Nanda went forth. And when Prince Rāhula went forth, it was even more painful, Venerable Sir. Paternal love cuts through the outer skin; having cut the outer skin, it cuts the inner skin; having cut the inner skin, it cuts the flesh; having cut the flesh, it cuts the sinews; having cut the sinews, it cuts the bones; having cut the bones, it strikes and remains in the marrow. Therefore, Venerable Sir, it would be well if the Noble Ones do not ordain a son who has not been permitted by his parents." Thereupon, the Buddha, having delivered a Dhamma talk, consoled King Suddhodana and sent him away, assembled the monks, and laid down a Vinaya rule: "A child, a son, who has not been permitted by his parents should not be ordained. If a monk ordains such a person, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)." In this manner, the way the Buddha ordained Prince Rāhula and gave him his heritage in the Dispensation—the heritage of the Dhamma—is mentioned in many discourses.
In Dhamma portions such as the *Ambalaṭṭhikā-rāhulovāda Sutta*, *Mahā-rāhulovāda Sutta*, *Cūḷa-rāhulovāda Sutta*, *Rāhula Sutta*, and the *Rāhula Saṃyutta*, it is next mentioned how the Buddha systematically, step-by-step, revealed the heritage of the Dhamma to Ven. Rāhula. The discourse that is most widely known is the *Ambalaṭṭhikā-rāhulovāda Sutta*. While the Buddha was residing at the Veḷuvanārāma monastery in Rājagaha, Ven. Rāhula was staying in a hut at a nearby place called Ambalaṭṭhikā. In the evening, the Buddha arose from His meditation and walked to see Ven. Rāhula. Seeing Him coming from afar, Ven. Rāhula prepared a seat and placed a vessel of water for washing the feet. After the Buddha had finished washing His feet, leaving a little water in the vessel, He asked Ven. Rāhula, "Rāhula, do you see this little bit of water left in this vessel?" "Yes, Venerable Sir." "Rāhula, for anyone who has no shame in telling a deliberate lie, their monkhood is just as little as this water left in the vessel." Next, the Buddha threw away that little bit of water. Having thrown it away, He asked Ven. Rāhula, "Rāhula, did you see how that little bit of water was thrown away?" "Yes, Venerable Sir." Then the Buddha said, "For anyone who has no shame in telling a deliberate lie, their monkhood is cast aside just like that water thrown away"—declaring that their monkhood has been discarded and cast out.
Next, the Buddha turned the water vessel upside down. Having turned it upside down, He asked Ven. Rāhula, "Rāhula, do you see this water vessel turned upside down, inverted?" "Yes, Venerable Sir." "For anyone who has no shame in telling a deliberate lie, their monkhood is turned upside down just like this," He declared in that manner. Next, the Buddha declared another simile to Ven. Rāhula: "Rāhula, a state war-elephant taken into battle fights with its forelegs, fights with its hindlegs, fights with its head, fights with its tusks, but keeps its trunk curled back. Then the elephant-trainer thinks, 'This elephant has not yet sacrificed its life.' But when that elephant begins to fight even with its trunk, the trainer thinks, 'Now this elephant has sacrificed its life. There is nothing that this elephant cannot do now.' In the same way, Rāhula, for anyone who has no shame in telling a deliberate lie, there is no evil that they cannot do. Therefore, Rāhula, you should train yourself thus: 'I will not tell a lie, even in jest.'" Behold, the Buddha gave that fundamental advice and instruction to the young novice on that occasion. Likewise, how Ven. Rāhula was shaped under the constant instructions of the Buddha and the guidance and mentorship of Ven. Sāriputta as his preceptor (*upajjhāya*) is mentioned in many places throughout Dhamma literature.
One such incident is the sand play of young Ven. Rāhula. What was it? It is mentioned that upon waking up in the morning, he would take a handful of sand, throw it up in the air, and say: "May I receive as many words of advice and instruction from the Buddha and my fellow companions in the holy life as there are grains of sand here." Hearing the monks talking about his love for advice, the Buddha preached Jātaka stories such as the *Tipallattha-miga Jātaka* and the *Tittira Jātaka*, as is recorded in the Jātaka Book itself. Likewise, another such incident is mentioned in the Vinaya Piṭaka, demonstrating the humility of Ven. Rāhula. On one occasion, the Buddha laid down a Vinaya rule that a fully ordained monk (*upasampanna*) should not sleep under the same roof with an unordained person (*anupasampanna*), which means novices and so forth. After this Vinaya rule was laid down, while the Buddha was residing at Badarikārāma in Kosambī, the monks told the young Ven. Rāhula, "The Blessed One has laid down such a Vinaya rule. Therefore, find a place for yourself to sleep." Ven. Rāhula looked around, but there was no place. It is mentioned that, in the end, he spent that night in the Buddha's toilet-chamber. As the Buddha approached the toilet-chamber at dawn, He cleared His throat—which is a custom and Vinaya rule to make one's presence known. When the Buddha cleared His throat, Ven. Rāhula, who was inside, also cleared his throat. "Who is inside there?" He asked. "It is I, Rāhula, Venerable Sir, I, Rāhula." "Why are you staying here?" He asked. Once Ven. Rāhula explained the situation, the Buddha assembled the monks, delivered a Dhamma talk, and relaxed that Vinaya rule, allowing an unordained person to reside with a fully ordained monk for two or three nights. Thus, numerous such incidents are recorded concerning Ven. Rāhula and his virtuous qualities. In present times, some young children, harboring pride over their parents' positions or power, have a habit of saying the moment they cross paths with someone, "Just wait, I'll tell my father and teach you a good lesson!" But this Ven. Rāhula turned even the cold-shouldering and shortcomings of others into a lesson for himself, and nowhere in Dhamma literature is it seen that he ever went to tale-bear or complain to the Buddha.
Next, the systematic way in which the Buddha disciplined him is especially revealed in the *Mahā-rāhulovāda Sutta*. This is an extremely important discourse, even for meditating yogi monks. On one occasion, while the Buddha was residing at Jetavanārāma in Sāvatthī, He took His bowl and robes in the morning and set out for alms. Ven. Rāhula was also walking for alms, right behind the Buddha. The Buddha turned around, looked at Ven. Rāhula, and said, "Rāhula, whatever form (*rūpa*) there is..."—and there it is shown in eleven ways: whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—whatever form-aggregate, whatever form there is: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self." Thus it should be seen with wisdom as it really is (*yathābhūta*). Then Ven. Rāhula asked, "Blessed One, Fortunate One, is it only form?" "No, Rāhula," the Buddha declared, "Just like form, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), preparations (*saṅkhāra*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*)—indeed, the entire five aggregates should be viewed in that same manner as not-self (*anattā*)." Thereupon, while the Buddha continued on His alms-round, Ven. Rāhula thought, "Who, having met the Blessed One and received such a meditation subject directly, would go into the village for alms?" Rejecting the alms-round, he sat down straight under a tree for meditation. He sat down and began to meditate. Just then, Ven. Sāriputta, who came behind him, saw Ven. Rāhula and gave him a brief piece of advice: "Rāhula, develop mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasati*). Mindfulness of breathing, when well-developed and practiced frequently, is of great fruit and great benefit."
Then, Ven. Rāhula meditated the entire afternoon, and in the evening, he visited the Buddha and asked Him, "Venerable Sir, in what way is mindfulness of breathing developed so that it is of great fruit and great benefit?" Thereupon, the Buddha mentioned a host of meditation methods that must be practiced as a preliminary phase to mindfulness of breathing. This is a very good lesson for meditators (*yogāvacaras*), because some people who start directly with mindfulness of breathing go and get stuck. On that occasion, the Buddha first spoke about the four elements present in one's body. He gave a meditation subject on the attention to elements (*dhātu-manasikāra*): "Rāhula, whatever is coarse, rough, and solid in this body, such as hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth..."—showing nineteen such solid parts up to feces. In the sutta text, thirty-one parts are recorded. Later on, the brain in the head was added to make it twenty parts. All those nineteen are the internal earth element (*pathavī-dhātu*). Next, there is no need to speak separately about the external earth element—the solid substances outside. Whatever internal earth element there is, whatever earth element belonging to oneself, and whatever external earth element, it is simply the earth element. "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self"—thus it should be seen with wisdom. This was the first instruction He gave.
Next, you may understand the other elements in the same way as the earth element. Since we have spoken in detail about these matters regarding the attention to elements, (we can summarize): concerning the water element (*āpo-dhātu*), the liquid parts of the body such as bile, phlegm, saliva, urine, and so forth are shown as the internal water element; and considering both the internal and external water elements as one, it is simply the water element: "These are not mine, this I am not, this is not my self." In the same way, the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*)—the parts related to the heat in the body and the external fire, etc.—and then the wind element (*vāyo-dhātu*)—the winds that go upward and downward in the body, inhalation and exhalation, and the external wind element. Next, there is additionally the space element (*ākāsa-dhātu*); what is shown as the space element in the body are the cavities of the ears and nose, the hollow space within the intestines where food is stored, and so forth. Those are the internal space element. The external space element can be easily understood in the same way. One should contemplate it in that very manner: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self." Thus, in this way, He showed how to elevate the attention to elements, including the space element, into meditation.
Next, the Buddha declared another unique meditation: "Rāhula, develop a meditation like the earth (*paṭhavī-sama bhāvanā*)." "Meditation like the earth" means equating oneself to the earth. It is a unique meditation. This is also mentioned in the discourses of Ven. Sāriputta. It means to contemplate in this way: the earth does not make a distinction regarding clean and unclean things thrown upon it. Even if someone throws feces, urine, saliva, phlegm, or snot on the earth, the earth does not feel disgusted or repulsed by it. In the exact same way, in accordance with the nature of the earth, you too should establish equanimity like the earth. Then, the mind will not be troubled by agreeable and disagreeable contact (*phassa*), and it will not grasp them tightly. That is the meditation like the earth. Likewise, there is the meditation like water (*āpo-sama bhāvanā*). Just as water does not show any aversion whether it washes away clean things or unclean things, so too should you contemplate yourself as water. Here, "like the earth" means contemplating that one is the earth. Why? Because as mentioned earlier, both the earth element inside oneself and the earth element outside are simply the earth element. This can also be understood logically. Thereafter, one contemplates without any distinction between internal and external. Then, one takes as an exemplar the external, insentient earth element, the insentient water element, the insentient fire element, the insentient wind element, and the insentient space element. The Buddha is telling us to behave in that manner. That is to say, it is a method to bring the mind to equanimity. Just like the earth and so forth. Next, fire burns anything without discriminating between clean and unclean; wind blows on everything, whether foul-smelling or fragrant. In this way, you may briefly consider all four. The space element is spoken of in a special way because it is unique: just as space does not rest anywhere, so too you do not cling to anything anywhere. Thus, this is shown there as a meditation to eliminate craving (*taṇhā*), conceit (*māna*), and the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkāya-diṭṭhi*) regarding one's body. So, that is the second step.
The Buddha showed a third step as well: "Rāhula, develop loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*) to eliminate ill-will. Develop compassion (*karuṇā-bhāvanā*) to eliminate cruelty. Develop appreciative joy (*muditā-bhāvanā*) to eliminate boredom or discontent (*arati*) towards monastic practice. Develop equanimity (*upekkhā-bhāvanā*) to cease the friction of repeated aversion (*paṭigha*) towards things, bringing the mind to equanimity. Next, develop the meditation on foulness (*asubha-bhāvanā*) to eliminate lust. Develop the perception of impermanence (*anicca-saññā*) to eradicate the conceit 'I am' (*asmi-māna*)." Behold, He spoke of that step too.
It was only after that, at the very end, that the Buddha declared the meditation of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasati*). At that point, the Buddha finally declared all sixteen steps of mindfulness of breathing. From this we can see that it is by practicing mindfulness of breathing with such accompanying practices that it becomes of great fruit and great benefit. The Buddha concluded that discourse by stating that for one who has developed mindfulness of breathing in this manner, even their final breath, their last inhalation and exhalation, fades away with full awareness, and even the final breath can be let go of mindfully. We will not detail the sixteen steps on this occasion, as we have spoken about these things previously. In this manner, the Buddha explained in detail to Ven. Rāhula how to make the meditation of mindfulness of breathing of great fruit and great benefit.
Furthermore, a series of verses with which the Buddha constantly advised and admonished Ven. Rāhula is also mentioned in the text called Sutta Nipāta, under the name *Rāhula Sutta*. According to that *Rāhula Sutta*, the Buddha first asks Ven. Rāhula, "I hope that, due to constant association, you do not disregard or show disrespect to your preceptor." In that context, the Buddha refers to Ven. Sāriputta as *"ukkādhāro manussānaṃ"*—meaning, one who holds up a torch for mankind, one who gives light through wisdom. That was how the Buddha described Ven. Sāriputta on that occasion. Ven. Rāhula also replies, "Yes, Venerable Sir, I do not disrespect my preceptor. I always respect him."
Next, with another set of verses, the Buddha further shows how Ven. Rāhula should train himself: "Rāhula, having abandoned the five sensual pleasures which have an attractive appearance, and having gone forth out of faith, bring to the forefront your ultimate goal of ending suffering (*dukkha*). Next, associate with noble friends (*kalyāṇa-mittas*). Reside in secluded, quiet lodgings. Eat food with moderation. Likewise, eliminate craving (*taṇhā*) for the four requisites—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites. Avoid beautiful themes (*subha-nimittas*) that fuel lust and are connected to lust. Unify the mind and attain concentration through the meditation on foulness. Next, develop the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*). 'Signless concentration' means that by deeply contemplating impermanence (*aniccatā*), the perception of permanence (*nicca-saññā*) is erased and the 'signless' (*animitta*)—the state devoid of signs—emerges. Develop this signless concentration. By developing the signless concentration, eliminate conceit (*māna*). Eliminate the conceit 'I am' (*asmi-māna*). By eliminating the conceit 'I am', in the end, you will become one who makes an end of suffering (*dukkha*)."
It is recorded in the texts that the Buddha constantly advised Ven. Rāhula through those few verses. This is known as "constant advice" (*abhiṇhaso avavāda*). *"Abhiṇha"* means advice given continuously. Thus, on one hand, Ven. Sāriputta gave instructions as his preceptor. At the same time, the Buddha also witnessed His son's tender maturation in the Dispensation. Through the giving of these instructions, it is clearly shown to us how the Buddha was constantly keeping watch over Ven. Rāhula's inner progress.
The final discourse shown in this regard is the *Cūḷa-rāhulovāda Sutta*. In the *Cūḷa-rāhulovāda Sutta*, it is recorded as follows: On one occasion, the Buddha, having walked for alms and finished His meal, said to Ven.
