this is precisely why, first of all, this vision (*dassana*) regarding this is shown in the *sabbasava sutta*. there has come an ignorance that is difficult to resolve, a wonderful ignorance whose end cannot be found. yet, through stagnating within ignorance, there is a tendency to drag on continuously in the manner described. the only way to restrain and prevent it from dragging on continuously is *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention) which was brought to light by the buddha. as we have told you before, *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention) is indeed the primary seed of wisdom. one might say, 'we are worldlings (*puthujjanas*); we have no wisdom. wisdom belongs only to arahants and noble ones (*ariyas*).' but everyone has attention (*manasikara*). we have explained much about these in our sermons on dependent arising (*paticcasamuppada*). anyone can turn *ayoniso* into *yoniso*. *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention) is the primary seed of wisdom. that is why the buddha highlights that the first thing a noble disciple must know, must see, is the difference between *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention) and *ayoniso manasikara*. for it is through *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention) that the backbone of ignorance is broken, let us say. because it is *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention) that helps us to prevent unarisen influxes of ignorance from arising, and to abandon arisen influxes of ignorance. let us proceed from there.
the more one contemplates this sermon, the second discourse in the *majjhima nikaya*, the deeper and more wonderful it becomes, just like the first discourse. there, the buddha further speaks about two individuals: the uninstructed worldling (*assutava puthujjana*)—the one who does not know—on one side, and the instructed noble disciple (*sutava ariyasavaka*) on the other. first, he speaks about the uninstructed worldling. the uninstructed worldling does not know the things fit for attention, nor does he know the things unfit for attention. because he does not know the things fit for attention and does not know the things unfit for attention, he attends to things unfit for attention and does not attend to things fit for attention. next, the danger of that is shown. as mentioned before, by attending to things unfit for attention, unarisen influxes of sensual desire (*kamasava*), *bhava* (becoming) (*bhavasava*), and ignorance (*avijjasava*) arise, and those already arisen increase. understand it briefly, as described earlier; thus, through *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention), unarisen influxes do not arise, and arisen influxes do not increase. that is the benefit. so, due to not knowing *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention), the uninstructed worldling reflects in an incorrect, *ayoniso* manner.
next, the ways of incorrect reflection are set out in that sutta. since there is much to say, i will try to state it briefly. as these have been mentioned on various occasions, this is how the buddha shows the thought-process of the uninstructed worldling. how does that person reflect improperly? by putting forward the concept of 'i'. regarding the past, the uninstructed worldling thinks thus: 'was i in the past? was i not in the past? what was i in the past? how was i in the past? having been what, what did i become in the past?' it is by putting the story of 'i' forward that he reflects and thinks in this manner. next, regarding the future, he reflects thus: 'what will i be in the future? will i not be in the future? how will i be in the future? having been what, what will i become in the future?' that is about the future. regarding the present, too, he harbors an inner doubt in this manner: 'am i? am i not? what am i? how am i?' next comes: 'where has this being come from? where is it bound?' it is clear that all this is because he starts to reason with *ayoniso manasikara*, putting forward the 'i' as a soul (*atman*). everything found in all other religions in the world is what has been constructed through this *ayoniso manasikara*.
the buddha points out that by reflecting in this way on the past, the future, and the present, one falls into one of six views. what are those six views? either one takes up the view: 'a self exists for me' (*atthi me atta*), or 'no self exists for me' (*natthi me atta*). he takes that to be a true view. or else, he thinks, 'with self i perceive self.' or else, 'with self i perceive non-self.' or else, 'with non-self i perceive self.' the last, sixth one, is presented as: 'this self of mine that speaks and feels, which experiences the results of good and bad deeds in this samsara—that self is stable, eternal, and does not change.' there, he has firmly stood on the self-view. in that manner, the uninstructed worldling falls into one of six views.
next, the thinking of the instructed noble disciple. he knows the things fit for attention. he knows the things unfit for attention. he knows the danger that arises from attending to things unfit for attention. let us consider briefly what those things fit for attention are. next, the buddha shows how he reflects: he reflects, 'this is *dukkha*' (suffering / unsatisfactoriness / stress)—'*idam dukkhan'ti*'; he reflects, 'this is the origin of *dukkha*'; he reflects, 'this is the cessation of *dukkha*'; he reflects, 'this is the path leading to the cessation of *dukkha*.' in short, it is reflecting in accordance with the four noble truths. reflecting in accordance with the four noble truths, without stories of 'i' or 'person', is *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention). as the ultimate end of that reflection, the buddha shows that through that reflection, the noble disciple—whether instantly or after some time, though there is no fixed time limit—breaks the three fetters: *sakkaya-ditthi* (dogma of self-illusion / view of existing group/body), *vicikiccha* (skeptical doubt), and *silabbata-paramasa* (attachment to rules and vows). this is regarding the noble disciple. there lies that vision (*dassana*).
next, the buddha points out the methods of restraint. 'monks, there are influxes to be abandoned by vision (*dassana-pahatabba*).' we shall mention them briefly. there are influxes to be abandoned by restraint (*samvara-pahatabba*). there are influxes to be abandoned by using (*patisevana-pahatabba*), which means proper utilizing. there are influxes to be abandoned by tolerating (*adhivasana-pahatabba*), which means patience. next, there are influxes to be conquered and restrained by avoiding (*parivajjana-pahatabba*), which means steering clear. next, there are influxes to be restrained by removing (*vinodana-pahatabba*), which means dispelling. finally, it is said there are influxes to be restrained by developing (*bhavana-pahatabba*), which means meditation. let us consider each of these briefly.
the influxes to be abandoned by vision are *sakkaya-ditthi* (dogma of self-illusion / view of existing group/body), *vicikiccha*, and *silabbata-paramasa*. they must be abandoned through the aforementioned attention. that is why the buddha declared—let the devotees recall: '*sahavassa dassanasampadaya, tayassu dhamma jahita bhavanti*' (with his achievement of vision, three things are discarded). next, recall: '*ditthinca anupagamma, silava dassanena sampanno*' (not falling into wrong views, virtuous, endowed with vision). all of these point to the value of vision; they are abandoned by vision, and cannot be abandoned by any other method. they cannot be grabbed and thrown away. *sakkaya-ditthi* (dogma of self-illusion / view of existing group/body), *vicikiccha*, and *silabbata-paramasa* must be abandoned solely by reflecting in accordance with the truth. when speaking about wrong views, i missed mentioning some of the words used by the buddha. the buddha describes how the uninstructed worldling ends up in his thinking with a wonderful sequence of words: 'monks, this is finally a thicket of views (*ditthigatam*), a wilderness of views (*ditthigahanam*), a desert of views (*ditthikantaram*), a contortion of views (*ditthivisukam*), a vacillation of views (*ditthivipphanditam*), a fetter of views (*ditthisamyojanam*)...' there are many such words. that person, going through those views, gets lost in a desert of views, in a wild jungle. that uninstructed worldling is never freed from *jati* (birth / arising) and *jaramarana* (decay and death / aging and death). the instructed noble disciple, without putting 'i' forward, reflects according to the truth which is presented as the unique teaching (*samukkamsika desana*) of the buddhas, and thereby breaks *sakkaya-ditthi* (dogma of self-illusion / view of existing group/body), *vicikiccha*, and *silabbata-paramasa* which he was unable to break so far.
next, regarding 'abandoned by restraint', let us consider it briefly. it refers to guarding the sense doors (*guttadvarata*), which is the restraint of the senses. the term *vighata-parilaha* (vexation and distress) is mentioned when speaking of this restraint; also, the word *vighataparilaha* is applied there in relation to incorrect reflection. if some weariness, distress, or dust (defilement) arises due to non-restraint of the senses, they are removed by restraint. think about it a little: if certain influxes, weariness, and dust can arise due to not restraining the eye, they are eradicated by restraining the eye. the buddha preaches in that manner about all the six sense bases, including the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. that is about those 'to be abandoned by restraint' (*samvara pahatabba*). if certain influxes flow in due to non-restraint, they cease to exist through restraint, along with the vexation and distress (*vighata-parilaha*) that arise in connection with them.
next, 'to be abandoned by using' (*patisevana pahatabba*). in our words, dear devotees, *patisevana* means utilizing or using. there, the buddha points out what is truly the bare minimum required for the sangha to survive: clothing, food, lodging, and medicine. indeed, in all instances where these restraints are mentioned, the occurrence of the phrase '*patisankha yoniso*' (reflecting wisely) is important. it is the very same importance given to the term *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention). '*yoniso*' means contemplating with wisdom. even when speaking of restraint, it is '*patisankha yoniso*'—reflecting wisely, one closes the eye. actually, when we speak of restraint, one cannot keep the eye, ear, and nose closed all the time. instead, we have shown the correct term: guarding the doors (*guttadvarata*), having a gatekeeper, which means one must be able to close the door according to the situation. that is restraint. restraint happens based on that. that is '*patisankha yoniso*'—reflecting wisely, one closes the eye, ear, and nose against those defiled sense objects according to the situation.
likewise, let us say a robe is necessary; considering its minimal utility, as stated in the passage of reflection (*paccavekkhana*): '*patisankha yoniso civaram patisevami, yavadeva sitassa patighataya, unhassa patighataya, damsamakasavatatapasirimsapasamphassanam patighataya, yavadeva hiri-kopina-paticchadanattham*'—in this way, one uses the robe considering its minimal utility, to ward off the trouble from cold, heat, gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, and simply for the sake of covering the parts that arouse shame. next, regarding alms-food (*pindapata*), '*patisankha yoniso*'—we have spoken about these many times. you too, dear devotees, must be practicing this to some extent. that is the reflection on food. contemplating with wisdom: 'i do not take this food for amusement, nor for intoxication, nor for physical beauty, nor for beautification' (*neva davaya na madaya na mandanaya na vibhusanaya*), unlike how ordinary people do. not for entertainment or building up the body, but 'only for the support and maintenance of this body' (*yavadeva imassa kayassa thitiya*). 'only'—the word 'only' comes first. only for maintaining this body, for keeping it going (*yapanaya*), for ending the harm of hunger (*vihimsuparatiya*), as an aid to the holy life (*brahmacariyanuggahaya*); and because one cannot survive without taking food. 'thus i shall eliminate the old *vedana* (feeling) (of hunger), and i shall not generate new *vedana* (feeling) (from overeating).' one takes food in a manner suitable for meditation, intending: 'thus my easy living (*phasuvihara*) will be secured.' next, regarding lodging (*senasana*), it is similar to what was said about clothing: to ward off the distress of cold, heat, gadflies, mosquitoes, and so on, and '*yavadeva utuparissayavinodanattham*'—only to dispel the trouble of the seasons. lastly, medicine (*gilanappaccaya*) is spoken of in the same way: '*uppannanam saririkanam veyyabadhikanam vedananam patighataya*'—to ward off arisen physical *vedana* (feeling) due to illness; because if they are not treated, they will cause the aforementioned distress, so one takes medicine. these are 'to be abandoned by using' (*patisevana pahatabba*)—the influxes to be removed by proper utilization.
next is shown 'to be abandoned by tolerating' (*adhivasana*), which is patience. if, for some reason, we do not receive those bare minimum requisites, we must train ourselves to bear it without shouting and making the mind corrupt. the things to be tolerated are mentioned in this way: a certain monk is patient (*khamo hoti*); he has the capacity to endure. if cold, heat, hunger, thirst, trouble from gadflies and mosquitoes arise, and if they cannot be stopped, he endures them. likewise, he cultivates the strength to endure illnesses and severe bodily pains. '*duruttanam duragatanam vacanapathanam*'—the capacity to bear harsh and ill-spoken words of criticism from others. in this manner, if weariness and distress arise due to not bearing or not tolerating certain things, they are dispelled through endurance. that is 'to be abandoned by tolerating' (*adhivasana pahatabba*).
next, 'to be abandoned by avoiding' (*parivajjana pahatabba*), which is avoiding and steering clear. this is illustrated as follows: a certain monk avoids wild elephants, wild horses, wild dogs, and similar beasts. next, he avoids thorny places, pits, and so forth. not only that, he keeps away—keeps far away—from associating with evil friends and visiting unsuitable places (*agocara*) that might bring him disrepute. for, by not avoiding them, various troubles such as blame, and vexation and distress (*vighata-parilaha*) might come upon him. these can be overcome through avoidance. that too is a method of restraint.
next, 'to be abandoned by removing' (*vinodana pahatabba*). *vinodana* means dispelling, not 'amusement' (as in common sinhala *vinoda*). what is shown there are the very points presented as the perception of abandoning (*pahana-sanna*) in the *girimananda sutta*. what are they? a certain monk 'does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought (*kamavitakka*), he abandons it, dispels it, ends it, and brings it to non-existence' (*uppannam kamavitakkam nadhivaseti, pajahati, vinodeti, byantikaroti, anabhavam gameti*). this is how it is said. regarding thoughts of sensual desire (*kamavitakka*), thoughts of ill-will (*byapadavitakka*), thoughts of cruelty (*vihimsavitakka*), and any arisen evil unwholesome states, what is the course of action to be taken? he dispels them. the series of words used for this dispelling is also extremely important. if we think about it deeply: '*nadhivaseti, pajahati, vinodeti, byantikaroti, anabhavam gameti*'. let us explain these words with a small simile. suppose you are in your house doing some important work, and some useless drunkard comes in. we say, 'you are not needed here, get out.' he does not listen. he tries to enter. we push him out. even so, he tries to come back. next, what do we do? we push him further and further away, all the way to the gate. then, we push him out of the gate and close it. think about it a bit: *nadhivaseti* means 'does not tolerate'—the first step we mentioned. 'you are not needed here, go away.' *nadhivaseti, pajahati*—telling him to go again. *vinodeti*—pushing him along. *byantikaroti*—pushing him right to the edge of the garden and putting him outside the gate. *anabhavam gameti*—locking the gate so he cannot return. this is just a small simile. in that manner, one must be restrained by dispelling thoughts of sensual desire (*kamavitakka*), thoughts of ill-will (*byapadavitakka*), thoughts of cruelty (*vihimsavitakka*), and evil, unwholesome states. for, if any weariness or distress arises due to not dispelling them, they are removed by dispelling them.
finally, there is development (*bhavana*). 'monks, there are influxes to be abandoned by development (*bhavana-pahatabba*).' what are they? there, it directly mentions the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhangas*): mindfulness (*sati*), investigation of states (*dhammavicaya*), energy (*viriya*), joy (*piti*), tranquility (*passaddhi*), concentration (*samadhi*), and equanimity (*upekkha*). these are to be developed leaning towards nibbana. 'here, monks, a monk, reflecting with *yoniso* (radical attention / wise attention), develops mindfulness... based on seclusion (*viveka-nissitam*), based on dispassion (*viraga-nissitam*), based on cessation (*nirodha-nissitam*), culminating in relinquishment (*vossagga-parinamim*).' understand the others in the same way. the four terms—based on seclusion, and so forth—all refer to nibbana. basing on and aiming at nibbana, which is seclusion and cessation, one develops the factors of enlightenment like mindfulness and investigation of states. there too, it is said that if any weariness and dust (defilement) arise from not developing them, they are removed by developing them. that is the general introduction. because 'vision' (*dassana*) comes first when explaining these, someone might think: 'then to become a sotapanna, it is enough to hear the dhamma and gain that vision. the rest are not needed. the other activities like the reflection on food are not needed. meditation is not needed either.' that is a wrong view. whatever discourse the buddha presented, it is highly systematic. that vision is important. '*samma-ditthi-pubbangama*'—right view (*samma-ditthi*) leads the way. we mentioned that the influx of ignorance (*avijjasava*) and the influx of views (*ditthasava*) must be suppressed first before doing all the other things. it does not occur by itself. the others are also relevant to it. therefore, one should not think in that way. those other factors are indeed relevant to meditation itself. however, at the end, it is presented systematically: finally, 'abandoned by development' (*bhavana-pahatabba*), which is the development of the factors of enlightenment. consider it briefly in this manner.
we have shown the seven methods of abandoning the influxes as the summary of the *sabbasava sutta*. the buddha concludes it thus: when a monk has abandoned by vision those influxes to be abandoned by vision, has abandoned by restraint those influxes to be abandoned by restraint, has abandoned by using those influxes to be abandoned by using, has abandoned by tolerating those influxes to be abandoned by tolerating, has abandoned by avoiding those influxes to be abandoned by avoiding, has abandoned by removing those influxes to be abandoned by removing, and has abandoned by development those influxes to be abandoned by development—then that monk has destroyed *tanha* (craving). he has overturned all hindrances (*nivaranas*) and all fetters (*samyojanas*). he has become an arahant. that is the end of the *sabbasava sutta*.
next, let us contemplate a little more on this sutta. there are things in it to go even deeper. now, we spoke about these *asavas*. the *asavas* are *kamasava*, *bhavasava* (the influx of existence), and sometimes *ditthasava* is also mentioned. as we mentioned earlier, within the intoxicating quality, there is a nature of flowing forward. within sensual pleasures and temptations, there is that intoxicating nature, and it has the tendency to bring more temptations. next, regarding views (*ditthi*), it is the same. one who remains in them for a long time cannot get free from them. they are entangled in them to that extent. in some places, it is called *ditthasava* (influx of views) as well. but that generally belongs to ignorance (*avijja*). *bhavasava* refers to existence, which is *bhava* (becoming). the craving for existence (*bhava-tanha*) is extremely severe, is it not? next, ignorance is liking darkness, disliking light, and being pleased only with darkness. it does not like light. keep in mind that what are mentioned are *kamasava*, *bhavasava* (the influx of existence), *avijjasava*, and in some places, *ditthasava* as well.
now next, there is a word called *ogha* (flood), which is a closely related word. we must show the difference between these two. on a previous occasion, i pointed this out briefly. now, to see how significant this word *ogha* is, despite the availability of countless suttas, the great arahant compilers of the dhamma presented the *oghatarana sutta* as the very first sutta of the *samyutta nikaya*. in brief, it is like this: during the night, a deity comes and asks the buddha, 'how, dear sir (*marisa*), did you cross over the flood?' there are four floods: *kamogha*, *bhavogha*, *ditthogha*, and *avijjogha*. four of them: the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance. he asks the buddha how he crossed over these four floods. the buddha gives a brief answer in a very riddlesome verse: 'without halting and without straining, i crossed over the flood' (*appatittham anayuham*). when the deity asks why he says so, he explains further: 'if i halted, i sank; if i strained, i was swept away. therefore, without halting and without straining, i crossed over safely.' that is the sutta. but there is a very deep meaning here. we pointed this out on a previous occasion too. the middle path (*majjhima patipada*) is found right here. that is why we showed it through words like 'practical' and 'relative'. this discourse is about the flood (*ogha*).
now let us try to bring the word *asava* close to this. when we go near a stream, we see a torrent of water flowing along. we want to cross over it. once we step into it to cross over, it does not appear to us simply as a flowing flood (*ogha*), but as water flowing against us. think about it. the moment we step in, we cannot even trust our foothold; we are swept away. we cannot even take the next step. we are swept along by the current. then, we look at that same flood not as water flowing away, but as water flowing towards us (or rushing upon us). there lies the term *asava* (flowing in/upon). when the noble disciple crosses over these four floods, it is not easy to escape from this current, from this flow—especially with that 'intoxicating quality' we mentioned earlier, which has been flowing for a long time due to its momentum. you know, dear devotees, that at the beginning, the buddha spoke of two extremes: indulgence in sensual pleasures (*kamasukhallikanuyoga*)—there is nothing new to tell you about that. next, due to the nigantha view that 'pleasure is to be attained through pain' (*dukkhena sukham adhigantabbam*), he performed painful austerities for six years to torture the body. he went to that extreme. it is between those two extremes that the buddha discovered this middle path. here, halting is indulgence in sensual pleasures; within that, one sinks down even unto hell. next, just as the niganthas did, the buddha too finally realized that he was straining, and through straining, he was swept away. instead, one must cross over carefully. it is that very thing, dear devotees, which is found in this *sabbasava sutta*.
so why is this called 'the exposition of the restraint of all influxes' (*sabbasava-samvara-pariyaya*)? because once we step into the water, in crossing over, when we look at the world, there is a situation where some things are such that we cannot do with them, yet we cannot do without them either. contemplate on it a little. if we contemplate from the very beginning, some vision (*dassana*) is necessary for our life. if we grasp the aforementioned views, we will revolve within them forever. the buddha spoke about the person subject to *sakkaya-ditthi* (dogma of self-illusion / view of existing group/body) using the simile of a dog. now, if a dog is tied to a post or a leash, it just revolves and revolves around it. it cannot go beyond that. in the same way, '*assutava puthujjanassa gaddulabaddho*'—just as a dog tied to a post only revolves around it without any escape, so there is no escape for one who has taken up *sakkaya-ditthi* (dogma of self-illusion / view of existing group/body). therefore, the buddha showed another standpoint in its place: the four noble truths. that is indeed what we do, dear devotees, by keeping *samma-ditthi* at the forefront (*samma-ditthi-pubbangama*), and walking this path. that is how view (*ditthi*) becomes primary. next, think of how to escape the torrent of water in the journey from there. dear devotees, regarding restraint (*samvara*), we cannot keep our two eyes closed. certain brahmins held such a view: they said that sense restraint means not seeing with the eye and not hearing with the ear. the buddha ridiculed those views. to remain in that way (is impossible).
instead, the buddha said to be a true gatekeeper when necessary. that is '*patisankha yoniso*'—reflecting wisely, one restrains the eye, restrains the ear. that is how the middle path is. likewise, regarding food, the buddha went to the extreme, did he not? he completely rejected food until his body was extremely emaciated, and having performed great difficult practices, he realized that this was not correct. instead, we have to take food. thus, considering the bare minimum requirements, namely the four requisites. now, unlike the sense restraint (*indriya-samvara*) mentioned earlier, teachers of the past refer to this as the 'restraint through knowledge' (*nana-samvara*). one becomes restrained through wisdom by reflecting, so that one does not get swept away by craving for food, craving for taste, and so forth. 'only'—the term '*yavadeva*'—'only as a support to the holy life do i take this food,' thus turning even that into a meditation. that is *patisevana* (using). there too, understand that one cannot do without food. we must go on this journey to nibbana keeping some vision at the forefront. that was given through the four noble truths. next, in going on that journey, we need the four requisites: clothing, food, lodging, and medicine. considering their minimal value, considering their necessity, '*patisankha*'—one takes alms-food while reflecting wisely. next, consider the others in the same way. suppose we go for alms-food and do not receive any. the buddha is speaking with focus on the lives of the bhikkhus. if, for some reason, we do not have lodging or other deficiencies exist, instead of going to fight with lay-donors saying, 'why don't you look after us who have ordained?'—one must have the strength to bear them. that is *adhivasana* (tolerating). endurance of *patisevana* is also needed for that. what is tolerated is cold, heat, hunger, thirst, trouble from gadflies and mosquitoes when living in the forest—every single one of them. not only that, but also the taunts, insults, and various other things spoken by humans; those too must be tolerated. because if defilements arise due to not enduring them, vexation and distress (*vighata-parilaha*), weariness, and fever will arise.
understand that these are the very same things. particularly when speaking of restraint, recall that it is generally mentioned: '*viharantam papaka akusala dhamma*'—to prevent the flowing in of evil, unwholesome states related to covetousness and dejection, one restrains the eye, ear, nose, and so forth. likewise, patience. we usually expect certain things, but when what we expect is not received, there arises in the mind *vighata-parilaha*—meaning the weariness and fever arising from disappointment and dejection. the strength to bear them to eradicate that distress is *adhivasana* (endurance). likewise, some things are to be avoided (*parivajjana*). now, one has to go to the forest to meditate. just because one goes, saying 'i am a yogi (*yogavacara*)', one does not go in front of wild elephants, tigers, or bears. one tries to stay safe from those dangers as much as possible. not only that, one avoids evil friends. one avoids unsuitable places (*agocara*). for, they can bring disrepute. it is by contemplating wisely that one does so. that is 'to be abandoned by avoiding' (*parivajjana pahatabba*).
next, 'to be abandoned by removing' (*vinodana pahatabba*). this too can be easily understood: by contemplating the stream of thoughts that arise in the mind, contemplating their dangers, and dispelling them. finally, it is said 'to be abandoned by development' (*bhavana pahatabba*): if any influxes arise through (not developing) states like mindfulness (*sati*), investigation of states (*dhammavicaya*), energy (*viriya*), and joy (*piti*), they are eliminated through development. why is all of this stated? it is to cross over the four floods (*caturogha*). crossing over the four floods is not something one does by merely looking on. these problems are for the person who has actually stepped into it to cross over. the buddha showed the answer to those problems in the *sabbasava sutta*: the methods of restraining them. next, recall what we have mentioned before: the depth of this middle path shown by the buddha. the aspect of attention (*manasikara*). we have told you on previous occasions, in the talk about *namarupa-vinnana* (name-and-form and consciousness), that it is not something found in the forest; out of the five factors—*vedana* (feeling), *sanna* (perception), *cetana* (volition), *phassa* (contact), and *manasikara* (attention)—the buddha utilized attention (*manasikara*) to aid his middle path. as we said in that simile, if there is no witness for a court case, one of the respondents is pardoned and made a state witness to get the story out; in the same way, what the buddha did was catch this attention (*manasikara*) which is hidden among the mental states (*nama-dhammas*). he himself was the biggest thief as *ayoniso-manasikara*; gathering *vedana* (feeling), *sanna*, *cetana*, and *phassa* (contact), he has dragged us through samsara for so long. the buddha caught him by the neck and said, 'you shall be our witness. but from today, you must abandon *ayoniso* and become *yoniso*. we pardon you.' and finally, it is from him that we get everything revealed. that *yoniso-manasikara* (radical attention / wise attention) is what we called the primary seed of wisdom. that is why, taking '*dassana pahatabba*' in that way, and separating *ayoniso* and *yoniso*, it is based on this that the buddha brought forth the courage necessary for us to practice the path. otherwise, there is no standpoint. one cannot start from here. for, recall again the point we mentioned earlier.
ignorance is one of the influxes. yet, it is because of ignorance that the influxes arise. to tame that arising, we put aside wrong view (*miccha-ditthi*), keep right view (*samma-ditthi*) at the forefront, and walk this journey with *yoniso-manasikara* (radical attention / wise attention) itself. in this manner, we can understand the values related to the path of these influxes from this perspective. within that state of intoxication, the world continuously has a higher power of temptation within sensuality (*kama*), becoming (*bhava* (becoming)), views (*ditthi*), and ignorance (*avijja*). to break these, the buddha presented this noble eightfold path. that too begins with *samma-ditthi* (right view). the path of *samma-ditthi*, *samma-sankappa*, *samma-vaca*, and so on, ending in *samma-samadhi*. that is why it is said that the noble eightfold path itself is to be taken as the destruction of the influxes. just like these *asavas*, think of the word *ogha* (flood) as representing the habitual currents of samsara that have come over a long period. it is for these samsaric habitual currents that words like *asava* and *ogha* are used. escaping that current is like escaping a torrent of water; it is extremely difficult. that is why it is said that once you step into it, you are either swept away or you sink. those two extremes are the deepest matter in the buddha's dhamma. that is what is called the middle path. the buddha too realized this through his search. he fell from one extreme to the other. finally, he understood. having understood the true nature of this world, (he saw that) regarding these four requisites and other things, we cannot do with them, yet we cannot do without them either. there, the word *yoniso*—reflecting wisely—it is through that, at some point, that one proceeds carefully. stepping into a rapidly flowing torrent of water, without halting and without straining, one cannot bet and say, 'i will go from here to exactly there, as if drawing a straight line.' once you step into it, you must proceed gradually, yielding to the water as well. dear devotees, contemplate on this carefully. one who crosses over a torrent of water must proceed while yielding to it, yet he must also make progress; he must cut across it. that is the strength found in this dhamma. the buddha has shown this in various ways through the verses of the *dhammapada*.
where does one go when freed from the floods of these influxes? that is indeed why nibbana is presented as an island. that island is shown as the place crossed over from those floods: '*dipam kayiratha medhavi, yam ogho nabhikirati*'—'let the wise man make an island which the flood cannot overwhelm.' if one has cut through the floods and gone to the other side without being swept away by the torrents of water, at that moment, that person is on an island. what is that island? it is the liberation of the fruit of arahantship (*arahattaphala-vimutti*). we have highlighted this in various sermons. there are certain suttas that mention this: '*evam samma vimuttassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno cebi cakkhuvinneyya rupa apatham agaccheyyum, amissikatamevassa vinnanam hoti thitam anenjappattam*.' to that monk of fully liberated mind, even if many forms cognizable by the eye come into the range of his vision, his *vinnana* (consciousness) remains unmixed with them; it does not get mixed with those influxes. it remains unmixed, steady, and has attained imperturbability (*anenjappattam*). he is not swept away by them. the word '*anenja*' means that the arahants do not shake—their minds are directed to conquering the objects flowing in from the six sense bases. that itself is spoken of as the concentration of the fruit of arahantship (*arahattaphala-samadhi*), in terms like '*sabba-sankhara-samatha*' (the stilling of all *sankhara*), and so forth. in some places, it is said of those arahants:
*yassasava parikkhina, ahare ca anissito,*
*sunnato animitto ca, vimokkho yassa gocaro,*
*akaseva sakuntanam, padam tassa durantayam.*
that is a verse from the arahant vagga of the *dhammapada*. '*yassasava parikkhina*'—he whose influxes are completely destroyed; '*ahare ca anissito*'—who is unattached to food. why is he unattached to food? '*animitto ca vimokkho yassa gocaro*'—'*gocara*' means pasture or grazing ground. what is the grazing ground of the arahants? it is not food. it is '*sunnato animitto ca*'—the voidness (*sunnata*) and the signless (*animitta*). you have heard about the three liberations (*vimokkhas*): *sunnata* (void), *animitta* (signless), and *appanihita* (undirected). that is where nibbana is. the place freed from the aforementioned sense objects. '*sunnato animitto ca*'—that is their true grazing ground. the arahants and the buddhas dwell in that grazing ground. the buddha went into the forest and stayed for three months, saying, 'let no monk come to see me, except the one who brings alms-food because it is necessary for survival.' what was his grazing ground? it was the aforementioned *sunnata*, *animitta*, and *appanihita*. at that moment, that was the island we spoke of. a simile is given there: '*akaseva sakuntanam, padam tassa durantayam*'—when a bird flies in the sky, can its path be traced? in the same way, the track of the arahants' minds cannot be known. there is no object of mind (*arammana*). that is what is called '*anarammanam cittam*' (the objectless mind). in some places, as mentioned in our sermons, deities, sakka, and brahmas are said to come and worship the buddha in this manner:
*namo te purisajanna, namo te purisuttama,*
*yassa te nabhijanama, yam'pi nissaya jhayasi.*
'homage to you, o noble thoroughbred of men, homage to you, o supreme among men! we do not comprehend what it is relying upon which you meditate.' for it is *animitta* (signless), *appanihita* (undirected), and *sunnata* (void). there is no sign (*nimitta*). '*panidhi*' means there is no desire. '*sunnata*' means there is no perception of self (*atta-sanna*). that state of liberation is indeed the island. therefore, understand that crossing over the four floods, escaping the power of those influxes, the arahants finally land on that island. that island is what is called their liberation (*vimutti*), because they experienced the cessation of *bhava* (becoming) (*bhava-nirodha*) in this very life. all those others are things related to *bhava* (becoming). there are many such valuable verses here and there. we shall mention just one. there is a sutta called the *sundarika bharadvaja sutta* in the *sutta nipata*. in it, it is stated:
*bhavasava yassa vacikhara ca, vidhupita atthangata na santi.*
this is said about that arahant. this is the word of the buddha. '*bhavasava yassa vacikhara ca*'—that arahant's influx of existence (*bhavasava*) is destroyed. likewise, there is a strange word *vacikhara* (or *vacikhara*). the commentary explains *vacikhara* as 'harsh speech'. but our view is that *vacikhara* refers to something belonging to this linguistic usage, to *bhava* (becoming) and the world. one must get free from that too. *vacikhara* means 'linguistic rubbish'—the *papanca* (conceptual proliferation / prolific conceptualization) found in linguistic usage. arahants are freed even from this linguistic rubbish. that is why they are called '*papanca-sanna-sankha-pahana*' (those who have abandoned concepts, reckonings, or designations characterized by the prolific tendency of concepts). we are mentioning this briefly. at times, they direct their minds to that *animitta-dhamma* (signless state) freed from those worldly conventions, where there is no earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), or air (*vayo*). there is no sun, moon, or stars. there is no going, no coming. there is no birth, no death. the reason why the descriptions regarding this nibbana could not be understood for so long is because they could not understand the island we spoke of. instead, those people called the island 'siyadoris's nibbana'—something that happens after death. we have pointed out that it is the very direct, experiential state that the arahants experience in this very life. arahants are freed from the influxes of becoming (*bhavasava*), in short, even from the linguistic usages that deceive humans. in some places, regarding the liberation of those arahants, it is mentioned in this way:
'*so kayo'ti pi na hoti, so vaca'ti pi na hoti, so mano'ti pi na hoti, khettam tam na hoti, vatthu tam na hoti, ayatanam tam na hoti, adhikaranam tam na hoti, yampaccayassa tam uppajjati sukhadukkham*.'
there ceases to be the perception of a body through which pleasure and pain are felt within. the perception of speech ceases. the perception of mind ceases. in modern terms, all 'activities' take place within body, speech, and mind. in the mind of the arahant, then, there is no place for body, no place for speech, and no place for mind. that is what is shown in many suttas regarding nibbana through various negative terms, through many terms of negation. why can that liberation not be expressed in words? because the world is connected to *bhava* (becoming). if they ask about something, they speak of it in terms relevant to that *bhava* (becoming). complete liberation is the state of being freed from all of this at some point.
the buddha uses language and linguistic usage. that is indeed what we have mentioned on many occasions—at the end of the *potthapada sutta*, the tathagata declares concerning himself: '*itima kho, citta, loka-samanna loka-niruttiyo loka-vohara loka-pannattiyo yahi tathagato voharati aparamasam*.' addressing that person, 'citta, these are worldly names, worldly expressions, worldly usages, and worldly designations (*loka-pannatti*), which the tathagata uses and speaks of, but without misapprehending (*aparamasam*) them.' he does not hold onto them firmly. that is what we refer to when we say that just as adults use baby talk, he uses the language of the worldlings. in that case, such is the nature of the arahant's mind towards language. it is not only regarding the arisings, passings away, fallings (*cuti*), rebirths (*upapatti*), heavenly worlds, and brahma worlds of ordinary worldlings; in short, even the great primary elements like earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and air (*vayo*) are erased from the mind.
now, those scientists are struggling to understand what these four are. having distanced them from the mind, having distanced them from thought, they have gone to the ultimate extreme, and having nothing else to do, a moment has arrived where they even deprecate science as 'this miserable science.' that is the end of science. the buddha pointed out the ultimate end of that science in passages like '*manopubbangama dhamma*' (mind precedes all states). looking at the final chapter, that liberation through the cessation of becoming (*bhava-nirodha-vimutti*) of those arahants is something we cannot even conceive. for if there were no such liberation, then they would remain in doubt after doubt. think about it for a moment: if this nibbana were something after death, at the moment of death they would have to remain in doubt. the buddhas and the arahants experienced the state of the cessation of *bhava* (becoming) in this very life, in the manner described. whatever things exist related to *bhava* (becoming), including the great primary elements like earth, water, fire, and air, they erased all of them from the mind; this is called '*virajita*' (faded away). the buddha experienced the emptiness and voidness of even those concepts of earth, water, fire, and air, and of the various heavenly worlds, brahma worlds, goings and comings arising because of them. that is what is called liberation: the liberation of the fruit of arahantship (*arahattaphala-vimutti*).
therefore, recall and meaningfully reflect on that *dhammapada* verse: '*dipam kayiratha medhavi, yam ogho nabhikirati*'—'let the wise man make an island which the flood cannot overwhelm.' we tried to speak briefly because there are a great number of suttas to be discussed. what we have to say to you, dear devotees, is to try to understand this through a thousand methods, in connection with the other things we have discussed. all of this is dhamma that must be understood individually by the wise, each according to his own wisdom. it is not solely through the sermons, meditation, and studies that one has done; as one progresses further and further on the path of meditation, the things we have spoken of here will become clear.
today, as everyone has inclined towards this path, established in mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajanna*), established in high virtue (*sila*), on such an occasion today, many can understand this dhamma more clearly. in the future as well, utilizing this, by proceeding on this path of the dhamma, keeping *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention) at the forefront in accordance with the practical and relative principles of the middle path we discussed, may these few words help you to realize the supreme goal you hope for in this very life, through the penetration and fruit of the path as a sotapanna, sakadagami, anagami, and arahant. we pray that whatever beings exist from avici to akanittha may rejoice in this merit of sharing and hearing the dhamma, and through that rejoicing, may they attain the deathless, great nibbana through a bodhi of their aspiration! please recite these verses to share the merit:
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 051
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #51
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.49)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Bahuṃ ve saraṇaṃ yanti, pabbatāni vanāni ca; Ārāmarukkhacetyāni, manussā bhayatajjitā. Netaṃ kho saraṇaṃ khemaṃ, netaṃ saraṇamuttamaṃ; Netaṃ saraṇamāgamma, sabbadukkhā pamuccati. Yo ca buddhañca dhammañca, saṅghañca saraṇaṃ gato; Cattāri ariyasaccāni, sammappaññāya passati. Dukkhaṃ dukkhasamuppādaṃ, dukkhassa ca atikkamaṃ; Ariyañcaṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ, dukkhūpasamagāminaṃ. Etaṃ kho saraṇaṃ khemaṃ, etaṃ saraṇamuttamaṃ; Etaṃ saraṇamāgamma, sabbadukkhā pamuccati.
From:
Verses 188-192 from the Buddhavagga (Chapter on the Buddha) of the Dhammapada
Dear Listeners,
Today is the Esala full-moon Poya day. Indeed, the Triple Gem, which serves as the refuge from the suffering (*dukkha*) of saṃsāra, truly became manifest on an Esala full-moon Poya day such as this. Why do we say so? We all know that the Buddha realized supreme enlightenment at the foot of the Bodhi tree on a Vesak full-moon Poya day. However, he preached that supramundane realization he attained to the world of devas and humans at a level they could comprehend, as an auspicious Dhamma sermon—the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*—on an Esala full-moon Poya day. Furthermore, among the group of five monks who were the recipients of that sermon, Venerable Aññākoṇḍañña realized Nibbāna with the path-knowledge of Stream-entry at the end of the discourse. Thus, we must understand that the Dhamma Gem became manifest through the preaching of the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*. Next, this can also be considered the beginning of the manifestation of the Noble Saṅgha Gem. That is why we say that the Esala full-moon Poya day is the day on which the Triple Gem, the only refuge for this saṃsāric suffering (*dukkha*), became manifest.
When we reflect in this manner, what is declared and emphasized in this series of verses, which is the theme of our sermon today, is that the only refuge for the saṃsāric suffering (*dukkha*) of living beings is the Triple Refuge, the Triple Gem itself, and that the path to escape from this saṃsāric suffering (*dukkha*) is none other than that supramundane path of liberation. The Buddha preached these few verses to a brahmin named Aggidatta. The background story (nidāna-kathā) regarding this is recorded as follows.
In Sāvatthī, King Mahā Kosala—that is, the father of King Pasenadi Kosala—had a royal priest (purohita) brahmin, who was the aforementioned brahmin Aggidatta. After King Mahā Kosala passed away, King Pasenadi Kosala, who succeeded him, also retained the brahmin Aggidatta—who was by then quite advanced in age—in the position of royal priest with great respect. To show how much respect he had, whenever the priest came to the royal palace, the King himself would go forward to receive him. Moreover, out of respect for him as a teacher, he would offer him a seat equal to his own. That is how well he treated the royal priest, Brahmin Aggidatta.
However, this brahmin thought wisely: "Young kings prefer young royal priests. I am too old. I will not be able to retain the King’s favor forever in this way." Thinking thus, he obtained permission from the King. He understood that ordination (going forth) is not merely a change in external appearance, but requires renunciation (*nekkhamma*). Therefore, how did he free himself from his vast wealth and great treasure? He sent town-criers through the city with drums, opened his doors, and gave it away in charity. Within seven days, he opened the doors and told anyone to take whatever they wanted from his entire wealth, and having freed himself from those riches, he went forth. Along with his departure, a large number of city-dwellers, said to be about ten thousand people, departed with this royal priest brahmin to practice asceticism under the sage's going-forth (rishi ordination). This group went and prepared a hermitage in a certain habitation between the kingdoms of Anga-Magadha and Kuru, where they practiced asceticism.
What was the advice that the brahmin Aggidatta, as their leader, gave to this group? "Whenever a defiled thought such as a sensual thought (*kāma-vitakka*) arises in you, at that very moment, go, bring a bag of sand, and dump it in this place." Thus, he gave them a meditation instruction. As a result of this, after some time, a huge mound of sand was formed there. This shows how obediently they brought and dumped a bag of sand for every defiled thought that arose in them. After such a massive mound of sand was formed, it is said that a king of serpents (nāga king) named Abhicchatthaka took guardianship of that sand pile. This is not like the cobras we see today; what is referred to here is a kind of non-human/spirit entity (*bhūta*). Like what is said about the Nāga King Mucalinda, this was a powerful nāga king possessing special powers, psychic power (*iddhi-bala*), and the ability to change his physical form. That Nāga King Abhicchatthaka took up residence there.
Furthermore, large crowds of people from the kingdoms of Anga and Magadha regularly visited to offer alms and respect to this brahmin and his group. What was the advice that this brahmin sage gave to them? "Go for refuge to mountains, parks, trees, and forests. Only by going for refuge to them can one be released from this saṃsāric suffering (*dukkha*), from all suffering (*dukkha*)." In this way, he advised them to take refuge in those things. He also gave the same advice to his own disciples.
While things were going on in this way, as time passed, the Buddha appeared in the world. On one occasion, while residing at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī, as he surveyed the world in the morning through the attainment of great compassion (*mahā-karuṇā-samāpatti*), he saw that this brahmin Aggidatta and his group possessed the supportive conditions to attain Arahantship. Having seen this, and devising a skillful means (*upāya-magga*), he invited the great Arahant Moggallāna: "Moggallāna, do you not see? This brahmin Aggidatta is misleading a large crowd, preaching to them, 'By taking refuge in these mountains, forests, trees, etc., you can bring an end to suffering (*dukkha*).' Go and turn this brahmin toward the Dhamma." The great Arahant Moggallāna replied, "Blessed One, there is a very large crowd there. I cannot do this alone. If the Blessed One also visits, perhaps it will be possible." Then the Buddha said, "Moggallāna, you go ahead first," and sent the great Arahant Moggallāna on his way that very evening.
Before arriving at that place, the great Arahant Moggallāna also thought: "If I go before this massive crowd and say something, and if they start leaving in groups, I will not be able to accomplish what I intend." It is said that using his psychic power (*iddhi-bala*), he created a heavy drizzling rain. Because of that rain, those ascetics retired to their respective quarters, that is, their huts.
Then, the great Arahant Moggallāna went near the hut of the brahmin Aggidatta and called him by name: "Aggidatta, Aggidatta!" Aggidatta, due to his conceit (*māna*), felt some anger at this. Thinking, "Who in the world is calling me by my personal name?", he asked, "Who is that?" "I am a renunciant. Please give me a place to stay tonight." Aggidatta replied, "Each of us has separate huts; we have no space."
"Do not say so. It is the custom for humans to go to humans, cattle to cattle, and renunciants to renunciants. Therefore, please give me a place to stay tonight." He then said, "Since there is no other place, I can stay on that sand mound." Aggidatta warned him, "A great serpent king (nāga) lives there. It is dangerous. Do not go there under any circumstances." But saying it did not matter, as the great Arahant Moggallāna walked toward the sand mound to spend the night there, the serpent king became extremely angry. It is then mentioned that through his psychic power, the serpent king began to emit a powerful blast of smoke. The great Arahant Moggallāna also emitted smoke through his own psychic power. The serpent king was overwhelmed by this, while the great Arahant Moggallāna suffered no harm whatsoever.
Next, the serpent king began to spit fire. The great Arahant Moggallāna, entering the fire-element attainment (*tejo-dhātu-samāpatti*), also emitted fire in the same way. Eventually, in one way or another, the serpent king was tamed. Having been tamed, it is said that the serpent king spread his hood around the great Arahant Moggallāna as a shelter, enabling him to spend the night there. Meanwhile, the brahmins, seeing the smoke and fire, thought, "This recluse, this monk's life must have been destroyed." When they looked in the morning, the great Arahant Moggallāna was perfectly fine. When they heard the details of what had occurred, they were all astonished, thinking, "What an incredibly powerful renunciant this is!"
Just as they were expressing their joy, the Buddha arrived at the scene. When the great Arahant Moggallāna stood up and paid homage to the Buddha, these people were even more astonished. When they asked, "Is this someone even more powerful than you?", Moggallāna replied, "This is my Teacher." At that moment, the Buddha asked the brahmin Aggidatta: "Brahmin, in what manner do you preach the Dhamma to this crowd?" Then the brahmin Aggidatta declared, "I tell them that by taking refuge in mountains, forests, parks, and trees, they can be freed from this suffering (*dukkha*)." It is recorded in the texts that the Buddha then proclaimed the series of verses we mentioned earlier.
Now let us look at the general meaning of those verses.
*Bahuṃ ve saraṇaṃ yanti pabbatāni vanāni ca ārāmarukkhacetyāni manussā bhayatajjitā*
Many people, driven by fear, go for refuge to mountains, forests, parks, and tree-shrines; they go seeking protection in them.
*N’etaṃ kho saraṇaṃ khemaṃ n’etaṃ saraṇamuttamaṃ n’etaṃ saraṇamāgamma sabbadukkhā pamuccati*
But these things are not a secure refuge or protection. "That is not a safe refuge, that is not the supreme refuge." This is not the truly supreme refuge. The Buddha explains in detail that by going to such a refuge, one cannot be released from all suffering (*dukkha*). Next, he declares how one is released from suffering (*dukkha*).
*Yo ca buddhañca dhammañca saṅghañca saraṇaṃ gato cattāri ariyasaccāni sammapaññāya passati Dukkhaṃ dukkhasamuppādaṃ dukkhassa ca atikkamaṃ ariyañcaṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ dukkhūpasamagāminaṃ*
But whoever goes for refuge to the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—and sees with right wisdom (*sammā-paññā*), with great wisdom, these Four Noble Truths: suffering (*dukkha*), the arising of suffering (*dukkha-samuppāda*), the transcending of suffering (*dukkhassa ca atikkamaṃ*), and the Noble Eightfold Path that leads to the calming and appeasing of suffering (*dukkhūpasamagāminaṃ*);
*Etaṃ kho saraṇaṃ khemaṃ etaṃ saraṇamuttamaṃ etaṃ saraṇamāgamma sabbadukkhā pamuccati*
This indeed is the secure refuge, the true protection. "This is the supreme refuge." This is the truly supreme refuge. "Having come to this refuge, one is released from all suffering." The Buddha declared that only by coming to this refuge, this protection, can one be released from all the suffering (*dukkha*) of saṃsāra.
From these verses and this story, we can extract many Dhamma principles. Even if we reflect on the story itself, according to the standards of the present day, there are things in it that appear miraculous, especially concerning psychic miracles (*iddhi-pātihāriya*). Nowadays, these are things that people might doubt. However, during the time of the Buddha, when we speak of the great Arahant Moggallāna being the foremost among those possessing great psychic power, wonderful things are recorded in the texts. Now, the most important point here is the ordination (going forth) of the brahmin Aggidatta.
Going forth is something done very easily even in this day and age. But regarding the ascetic going-forth—how did the brahmin Aggidatta go forth? It was not because of a lack of food, drink, clothing, shelter, or social status. It was not due to illnesses. Even while receiving royal honor at the highest level, even while possessing the privilege to sit on a seat equal to the King's, and even while having the power to get "anything whatsoever" done, and having such great favor of both the country and the King, he reflected with far-sighted wisdom: "This status will not last forever. I am now old. I must retire now, retire completely."
When we talk about retiring, what that brahmin did was not what people do nowadays when they retire. When he retired, he did not do so keeping a little savings for himself. He gave everything away in charity. He opened the doors of his treasuries, announced it with the beat of drums, gave away all his wealth, and went forth only after freeing himself from those riches. That is a lesson for us. Even though we might call those external ascetics "wrong-viewed" (*micchā-diṭṭhi*), they have given us a valuable lesson, especially when we think about ordination in the present era. It is the very strength that comes from renunciation (*nekkhamma*) that helps to carry the ordination forward. Where there is no renunciation (*nekkhamma*), it is a mere ordination—a totally empty ordination. There is no strength within it; one cannot progress; one spins back to lay life. But concerning the ascetic going-forth in the past, even during times when no Buddha had appeared in the world, even great kings were called "royal sages" (*rāja-rishi*). They abandoned kingship and went to practice asceticism in the Himalayan forests, discarding all sensual pleasures like a glob of spit spat out in the early morning; it was not done lightly.
That is how it is mentioned. So here too, according to the ascetic going-forth, that custom is an eternal custom regarding renunciation (*nekkhamma*). Respecting that custom, the departure of the brahmin Aggidatta is a lesson for us when we reflect on our present times. So let us look at what is said from that point onwards.
Next, indeed, that brahmin taught a certain skillful method to his disciples for eliminating defiled thoughts such as sensual thoughts (*kāma-vitakka*). It is also apparent that the disciples acted obediently according to it. As soon as defiled thoughts arose—such as sensual thoughts or angry thoughts—what did they do? They ran, brought a bag of sand right at that moment, and dumped it. If we contemplate the Dhamma-principle behind this, they cut off that defiled thought by directing their minds to another activity without giving room to the defiled thought (*kilesa-vitakka*). There is such a technique there, a certain skillful device. It was through this that those brahmins developed great strength. So much so that, at the end of the sermon, all those ascetics attained Arahantship with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and became disciples of the Buddha through the "come, monk" (*ehi-bhikkhu*) ordination.
Thus, what helped them to develop such great strength was that this work of suppressing the defilements had begun from that very moment. It was precisely because of this that a massive crowd supported them as their patrons. In the end, having heard the Dhamma sermon of the Buddha, they understood: "This is not the true way of taking refuge and seeking protection. Taking refuge in mountains and forests is not it. It is taking refuge in this Triple Gem." It was because of this understanding that, upon hearing the Buddha's sermon containing those verses, the cognitive revolution—the transformation—that occurred within those brahmins was so great that they attained Arahantship. Next, the Buddha granted them ordination through the *ehi-bhikkhu* formula.
That is how it is mentioned in the Dhamma. Just as devotion toward the Triple Gem arose within a massive crowd, we generally understand "taking refuge" as going for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. However, this verse states that it is not merely that; taking refuge begins there, but it culminates in the realization of the Four Noble Truths. This saṃsāric existence is suffering (*dukkha*), its cause is craving (*taṇhā*), the extinguishment of that craving (*taṇhā*) is Nibbāna, and the path to it is the Noble Eightfold Path. By properly understanding the meaning of those verses, that large crowd finally became disciples of the Buddha. At that very moment, a large crowd of other patrons from the kingdoms of Anga and Magadha arrived. Seeing the transformation that had occurred, they initially thought, "The Buddha is a disciple of this brahmin Aggidatta." It is mentioned that to dispel this, the Buddha spoke to the brahmin Aggidatta at that moment, asking him to settle the doubts of the crowd. Then, using the psychic power (*iddhi-sakti*) he had attained, the brahmin Aggidatta rose into the air and paid homage to the Buddha seven times, declaring: "The Blessed One is my Teacher, I am the disciple; I am the follower," thereby dispelling the doubts of the visiting patrons, as the story further records.
Thus, through this story, we must reflect not only on the model of ordination shown at the beginning, but also on the cognitive revolution and transformation that occurred within the ordained group as a result of this sermon. Nowadays, many people, due to their saṃsāric suffering (*dukkha*) as well as the various suffering-filled situations that arise in life, go searching for protection, searching for refuge. How this search for protection and refuge can become truly fruitful and successful is what is declared in this sermon. Regarding taking refuge in the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha—the ordinary world thinks that there is some occult/mysterious power in trees, rocks, and mountains, and they expect protection from those forces; that is how the ordinary world thinks.
But the Buddha pointed out that the true shelter for the world to escape saṃsāric suffering (*dukkha*)—in short, to be released from all saṃsāric suffering (*dukkha*) such as birth (*jāti*), decay and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), and sickness—is to seek refuge in this Triple Gem, namely the Buddha-gem, the Dhamma-gem, and the Saṅgha-gem. That is why, as you devotees know, it is stated in the Dhamma that a person becomes a lay follower (*upāsaka*)—the minimum requirement being described as: "*Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti*"—that is, when someone goes for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, by that much they become a lay follower. Then, for that lay follower to become virtuous, they undertake some precept-discipline such as the five precepts (*pañca-sīla*). However, just because it is described in this minimum way, one should not think, "We have said '*Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ*' three times, so everything is complete." That is precisely why the verse states that immediately after taking refuge, one must see with right wisdom (*sammā-paññā*), with great wisdom, the Four Noble Truths: suffering (*dukkha*), the arising of suffering (*dukkha-samudaya*), the transcending of suffering, the cessation of suffering (*dukkha-nirodha*) which is Nibbāna, and the Noble Eightfold Path that assists it. It is by seeing this that one truly attains release from saṃsāric suffering (*dukkha*). Therefore, to complete the act of taking refuge (*saraṇāgamana*), one must walk on this path.
Next, even if we think only of this act of taking refuge, you devotees have heard of a protection chant (*paritta*) called the *Dhajagga Sutta*. There, the Buddha declares that even for monks meditating in forests, at the foot of trees, or in empty dwellings (*suññāgāra*), if any fear, terror, or hair-standing-on-end should arise, they should recollect him. How should they recollect him? As you all know, through the *Itipi so* passage. They should recollect the passage on the nine supreme qualities of the Buddha, starting with "*Itipi so bhagavā...*" If they do not recollect this, they should recollect the Dhamma—the six qualities of the Dhamma starting with "*Svākkhāto...*" If they do not recollect that, they should recollect the nine qualities of the Saṅgha, starting with "*Supaṭipanno...*" The *Dhajagga Sutta* presents these twenty-four great qualities as a protective chant, stating that when one recollects them, any fear, terror, or hair-standing-on-end will disappear. Therefore, it must be remembered that the only refuge for the world is these twenty-four great qualities. That is why in the *Ratana Sutta*, the qualities of the Triple Gem, such as the qualities of the Buddha, are used as the foundation even for an asseveration of truth (*sacca-kiriyā*).
In the background story of the *Ratana Sutta*, it is mentioned that during the great devastation in the city of Vesālī caused by the three fears—the fear of non-humans, the fear of disease, and the fear of famine—the Buddha commissioned Ven. Ānanda to wish peace for that region using the power of truth, the power of asseveration of truth, through the verses in the *Ratana Sutta*, chanting "*Etena saccena suvatthi hotu*" (By this truth may there be well-being). From this too, we see a good example: the power within the Triple Gem. The power within the Triple Gem is the power of truth. It is a Dhamma-principle that exists eternally in the world. There is immense power within truth, within an asseveration of truth. In the Jātaka stories, it is often seen and stated that due to various weaknesses, the Bodhisatta broke other precepts on various occasions, but regarding truth—that is, lying (*musāvāda*)—he strictly kept that training rule and preserved the truth. That is why there is the miracle of truth in the life of the Buddha.
So that is exactly what we find here: the qualities of the Triple Gem. Those twenty-four great qualities are a truth. It is by the power of that truth that, in various ways, in blessing-verses, well-wishes are made for the world by focusing on and taking refuge in the Triple Gem, chanting "*Etena saccena suvatthi hotu*". Even in the problems and crises of daily life, it is worthwhile to consider the Triple Gem as one's refuge. Moreover, especially concerning what is called the suffering (*dukkha*) of saṃsāra—that terrifying suffering, that disaster—one cannot escape from it easily. One cannot be released merely by going for refuge to the Triple Gem in word only. For the refuge in the Triple Gem to be complete, one must see the Buddha, one must see the Dhamma, and one must personally see that realization seen by the Saṅgha Gem; one must walk on the path trodden by the Great Saṅgha Gem of the eight noble individuals (*aṭṭha-ariya-puggala*) and see its fruit. That is what is declared here: to realize it with right wisdom (*sammā-paññā*).
Therefore, reflecting from that perspective as well, we must direct our minds to these Four Noble Truths. If we describe the entire Dhamma in brief—what the Buddha preached—it is indeed this preaching of the Four Noble Truths. That is exactly what the Buddha presented in detail in the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*. It is this entire mass of saṃsāric suffering (*dukkha*), such as birth (*jāti*), decay and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), and sickness, that the Buddha pointed out there as the Truth of Suffering (*dukkha-sacca*). Its cause was pointed out by the Buddha as craving (*taṇhā*). It is due to this craving—described as sensual craving (*kāma-taṇhā*), craving for becoming (*bhava-taṇhā*), and craving for non-becoming (*vibhava-taṇhā*) existing in living beings—that the world of beings suffers birth (*jāti*), decay (*jarā*), and so forth for an infinite time in saṃsāra. The state of having eliminated this craving (*taṇhā*), of having appeased this craving (*taṇhā*), is indeed called Nibbāna. That extinguishment and the path leading to it is the Eightfold Path, namely *sammā-diṭṭhi* (right view), *sammā-saṅkappa* (right intention), *sammā-vācā* (right speech), *sammā-kammanta* (right action), *sammā-ājīva* (right livelihood), *sammā-vāyāma* (right effort), *sammā-sati* (right mindfulness), and *sammā-samādhi* (right concentration). Thus, by completing this path—by completing it supramundanely—one is able to be released from the entire suffering (*dukkha*) of saṃsāra. That is how it is shown.
When we contemplate this a bit more carefully, what is called "right wisdom" (*sammā-paññā*) here is a capacity to comprehend and realize that exists within all of us. However, this wisdom is not something to be acquired through reasoning and logic (*tarka*). It must be developed through meditation (*bhāvanā*). Everyone makes a certain effort in practicing the Noble Eightfold Path. That is a somewhat piecemeal effort. Step by step, they try to practice that Eightfold Path to the best of their ability. But there are various twists and distortions in it. That is why it is shown as a separate wholesome action called "straightening one's view" (*diṭṭhijju-kamma*). An ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*) makes an effort to straighten their view.
The Eightfold Path is not fully present in an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*). It has twists and distortions. What they do is make an effort to align and straighten it. Such an effort to align it becomes successful when meditation reaches its culmination, when it bears fruit. Established in virtue (*sīla*), having developed concentration (*samādhi*), if at some point one realizes the truth through insight (*vipassanā*), it is at that moment that the Noble Eightfold Path—which is described in the Dhamma as the supramundane path (*lokuttara-magga*)—is realized. Indeed, mundanely, one practices it in a piecemeal fashion; however, on the supramundane path, it is said that all eight factors arise simultaneously in a single mind-moment. All eight factors arise in a single mind-moment, which is extremely brief. It is mentioned that path-concentration (*magga-samādhi*) arises as a momentary concentration (*khaṇika-samādhi*). This is an extremely profound matter. One can understand to some extent that although right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) leads the way, the other factors may be scattered in different directions. They have many twists and distortions. When these are aligned and straightened, this right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) ultimately develops and becomes right vision (*sammā-dassana*).
That is precisely what occurs at the moment of path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*). That is why the Buddha declared this Noble Eightfold Path to be a straight path. One has to straighten this. It manifests as perfectly straight at that supramundane level—for the first time at the stage of Stream-entry (*sotāpanna*). Why is this straightening necessary? A powerful mass of defilements (*kilesa*), a mountain of defilements, is deposited within this mental continuum (*citta-santāna*). It completely covers it, like a thick layer of rust. This cannot be cut away by ordinary thinking power. It can only be cut away by the concentration of the path-consciousness (*magga-citta-samādhi*). The supramundane mind is an immensely powerful concentration. In terms of meditation, the absorptions (*jhāna*)—described as the first absorption, second absorption, and so on—are indeed very powerful minds. Yet, a supramundane path-concentration is even more powerful than those ordinary absorption-minds. It is through this that these defilements (*kilesa*) can be cut away. That is why it is stated: "*Yaṃ buddhasettho parivannayī suciṃ, samādhimānantarikaññamāhu, samādhinā tena samo na vijjati*"—indicating that this supramundane concentration is so powerful and mighty that no other concentration can be compared to it. This power is obtained because all eight factors come together, and in a single moment, right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) arises as right vision (*sammā-dassana*). Through this, at the stage of the path of Stream-entry, those powerful defilements are broken at one level, leaving at most seven lifetimes. At the second stage of Once-returner (*sakadāgāmi*), it is reduced further so that one returns to this world only once more. At the stage of Non-returner (*anāgāmi*), one goes to the Brahma-world and ends it there. Finally, at the stage of Arahantship, one is completely released from all saṃsāric suffering (*dukkha*) such as birth (*jāti*), aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), and sickness; having broken that karmic force, one is brought to the state of non-arising. That is what is called release from all saṃsāric suffering (*dukkha*). Therefore, this meritorious crowd should reflect that there is a profound aspect to this taking of refuge. Otherwise, one might generally think that just because we say "*Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi*," we are all Buddhists and all our work is complete. However, here we generally use the term *saraṇāgamana*. If we consider *saraṇāgamana* according to the grammar of the language, it means "arriving at a refuge," "attaining protection." Yet, in truth, *saraṇāgamana* itself is "going in search of refuge."
So, this journey in search of refuge is completed through the realization of the Four Noble Truths. The proper term is the "going to the three refuges"—going for refuge to the Triple Gem. The target, the end of this taking of refuge, is Nibbāna. The journey up to that point is indeed something that must begin with faith (*saddhā*). Now, let us next reflect on this faith (*saddhā*). Here too, we know that to develop the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*), the recollection of the Dhamma (*dhammānussati*), and the recollection of the Saṅgha (*saṅghānussati*), a certain faith (*saddhā*) must arise within us. For one who lacks it—one who has taken only to logic and argument—there is no meaning visible in this. To the extent that it is felt in the heart, that abundance of qualities—the qualities of the Buddha, the qualities of the Dhamma, and the qualities of the Saṅgha—must penetrate the mind.
For such a person, next, as recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*)—which means contemplating, recollecting the Buddha's qualities over and over; recollection of the Dhamma (*dhammānussati*), which means repeatedly contemplating and bringing to mind the qualities of the Dhamma; and recollection of the Saṅgha (*saṅghānussati*), repeatedly bringing to mind the qualities of the Saṅgha. Through such recollection, a certain development takes place within this person's character. One who constantly contemplates virtue becomes like an ocean of virtue. In short, it is mentioned in the scriptures regarding a person who constantly practices the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) that they become just like the fragrant chamber (*gandha-kuṭi*) of the Buddha. The person who constantly contemplates the Buddha's qualities becomes like the fragrant cell (*gandhakiḷi*), the fragrant chamber, where the Buddha resides. Because when one constantly develops that mass of qualities, there is no room for unwholesome states (*akusala*). There is no room for unwholesome states to enter. One constantly lives in virtue itself—the qualities of the Buddha, the qualities of the Dhamma, the qualities of the Saṅgha. It is the very protection obtained from this that is mentioned in suttas like the *Dhajagga*.
When recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, if there are certain karmic forces (*kamma-vega*) about to ripen, their ripening force is also averted. Furthermore, because the most powerful principle in the world is the principle of truth, by the power of truth, a certain force from the universe is also added to it. One might call it invisible. However, it is not an occult/mysterious force of the kind the ordinary world imagines. In the past, the aforementioned brahmin Aggidatta said that in trees, rocks, mountains, and places considered as shrines, there exists some occult force through which suffering can be ended. But what is spoken of here is not such a thing. By contemplating the qualities of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, and bringing them to mind, one generates their power within oneself. Through that power, those karmic forces are worn away, and one receives a certain relief, even a limited relief in daily life. That is why the Buddha spoke of the ordinary world as "*manussā bhayatajjitā*"—it is the ordinary nature of people to live driven by fear in the face of hazards and disasters that come in daily life. At that moment, if one contemplates the qualities of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, one can obtain a substantial Dhamma-comfort through that Dhamma-power. Moreover, a capacity to withstand those incoming hazards is also developed.
Often, we are agitated and troubled by the disasters that come our way because our minds are not prepared to accept them. However, when we keep that mass of qualities regarding the Buddha-gem, Dhamma-gem, and Saṅgha-gem sustained in our minds, a capacity to withstand those disasters is also developed in the mind. By that too, the power of those disasters is broken. Not only that, through that very Dhamma-power, those karmic forces are worn away. This is the kind of Dhamma-principle that is present here. Therefore, one should not think wrongly: "At the beginning, it was said that people driven by fear go seeking protection in mountains, forests, trees, and shrines, and that this is not a refuge, not a protection." Looking at these verses, someone might say, "If so, are not these Bodhi-puja and stupa-worship performed by some Buddhists also wrong-viewed (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) things like that?" There is a point that needs to be clarified there.
In this day and age, we hear some people who follow that line of logic saying, "Those are empty things." They say it is the work of undeveloped minds. However, what we must understand here is that the journey to Nibbāna begins with faith (*saddhā*). The meaning of the word *saddhā* is "establishing the heart." Therefore, if a person has a heart, some development must occur regarding it as well. If one develops intellect (*buddhi*) alone, an imbalanced development occurs within that person. We know that even when a fruit ripens, there is a difference between it ripening well or becoming stunted/withered. If it does not ripen well, if there are some deficiencies, it becomes stunted. Similarly, those who take intellect alone, disregarding feeling—not that they have no feeling, and not that they have no heart—but they sometimes hold rigidly to intellectualism, applying logic, and regard things like stupa-worship as things done by foolish people. However, in our Dhamma, it is shown that the stupa-worship in this dispensation is done with a profound meaning. You devotees have heard that there are three types of shrines (*cetiya*): bodily relics (*sārīrika*), items of use (*pāribhogika*), and memorial symbols (*uddesika*).
