This says that when ignorance (*avijjā*) is completely ceased, there is no body, no words, and no mind. Those are shown as the places where *kamma* was accumulated. Liberation, the state of *parinibbāna*, is shown as something mysterious. That is why there is a truly wonderful sermon of the Buddha. We have delivered separate sermons on these. It is a grand sermon that even foreigners are astonished by. For those who seek liberation elsewhere, this is a great answer:
*"Imasmiṁ yeva byāmamatte kaḷevare sasaññimhi samanake lokañca paññāpemi lokasamudayañca lokanirodhañca lokanirodhagāminiñca paṭipadaṁ."*
"In this very fathom-long carcass, endowed with perception (*saññā*) and mind (*manas*), I declare the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world." Within this carcass, which is endowed with perception (*saññā*) and mind (*manas*)—not a dead carcass, but within this physical frame endowed with perception (*saññā*) and mind (*manas*)—I declare the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world. It was because of this matter that the Buddha uttered this wonderful lion's roar. Therefore, this wisdom (*paññā*) we spoke of, "the wisdom (*paññā*) that goes to the rise and fall" (*udayatthagāmiṇī paññā*), is where a yogi has to begin. Through the cultivation of the perception of impermanence (*anicca-saññā*), that impermanence (*aniccatā*) is seen in two aspects: arising and passing away. Along that, the mind goes deeper and deeper. It is there that attention (*manasikāra*)—the defendant we made into a witness—finally reveals the story through radical attention (*yoniso manasikāra*).
As one sees each of these extremely subtly through radical attention (*yoniso manasikāra*), impermanence (*aniccatā*) comes to the fore. Cessation (*nirodha*) comes to the fore. Then, just as existence (*bhava*) grows through that arising (*samudaya*), when cessation (*nirodha*) comes to the fore, right there is the cessation of existence (*bhava-nirodha*). That is what comes to the fore. That is why the Buddha declares almost everywhere: *Bhava-nirodho nibbānaṁ, bhava-nirodho nibbānaṁ*—"The cessation of existence (*bhava*) is Nibbāna." But when the cessation of existence (*bhava*) is mentioned, many people become afraid, because there is such a great craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*) within the world. But this cessation of existence (*bhava-nirodha*) is shown as a direct experience. The cessation of existence (*bhava-nirodha*) is a direct experience obtained in this very life. Within it lies the bliss of liberation. If there is suffering (*dukkha*) within existence (*bhava*), where the cessation of existence (*bhava*) is a direct experience, the bliss of liberation is found right there. That is what is meant by experiencing the bliss of liberation. Even a living Arahant experienced that bliss of liberation as a direct realization. That is why, when speaking about Nibbāna, it is said: *sandiṭṭhiko dhammo...* (Dhamma to be realized here and now). It is something that can be attained and seen. Now, do it! It is not something to be obtained after going to the next world. It is in this very life (*diṭṭheva dhamme*). That is indeed concerning Nibbāna. Then, extinguishing or cooling down means, finally, that mass of saṁsāric suffering (*dukkha*). That is it. In various sermons, we highlighted a series of words describing Nibbāna. In applying the mind to Nibbāna as the recollection of peace (*upasamānussati*), that can be used as an aid.
*"Etaṁ santaṁ etaṁ paṇītaṁ, yadidaṁ sabbasaṅkhārasamatho sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo taṇhākkhayo virāgo nirodho nibbānaṁ."*
"This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all preparations (*sabbasaṅkhārasamatho*), the relinquishing of all assets (*sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo*), the destruction of craving (*taṇhākkhayo*), dispassion (*virāgo*), cessation (*nirodho*), extinguishment (Nibbānaṁ*)." Within those few words, everything we have said is contained. "The stilling of all preparations" (*sabbasaṅkhārasamatho*)—if all preparations (*saṅkhāra*) have been calmed. "The relinquishing of all assets" (*sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo*)—assets (*upadhi*) refer to the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcupādānakkhandha*); those accumulated five aggregates of grasping are also relinquished. "The destruction of craving" (*taṇhākkhayo*)—craving (*taṇhā*) is destroyed. "Dispassion" (*virāgo*)—dispassion also refers to Nibbāna itself, that state of detachment. "Cessation" (*nirodho*)—extinguishing. "Extinguishment" (Nibbānaṁ*)—finally, cooling down. If the world is in a state of burning, what the Buddha points out instead of that burning is cooling down. All this is contained within the word Nibbāna. Various meanings were added to this in later times. Indeed, each verse in this *Pārāyana Vagga* is truly wonderful. Those disciples had gone that far, practicing absorptions (*jhāna*), in search of "nothingness" (*ākiñcañña*)—the direct experience of "there is nothing." But having returned, they met the Buddha and obtained "nothingness" (*ākiñcañña*) in its highest sense. The sphere of nothingness is a state of absorption (*jhāna*). This is not like that. It is said: *"Akiñcanaṁ anādānaṁ, etaṁ dīpaṁ anāparaṁ."* "Possessing nothing, grasping nothing, this is the island, there is no other." The Buddha has shown that as an island. It shows the bliss of liberation that exists when all grasping (*upādāna*) is destroyed. It is said that many, including the youth Ajita, became Arahants on the spot upon hearing the answer given by the Buddha. It is truly wonderful. From this, we see how much deep meaning is contained in a single four-line verse. We tried to explain it at our own level. Do not think of these as things that merely pass over the surface. The Dhamma is a profound thing. It can be understood through various similes in a simple way. For one who is engaged in the Dhamma in the present, these are not deep. They are simple. That is what we must take into consideration.
Today too, you have had the opportunity to listen to a certain insight-oriented sermon that is helpful for your meditation. We hope that you will derive the full benefit of this program of virtue (*sīla*). If you spend your time wandering here and there, talking about other things, you will not be able to properly understand even this Dhamma that is being spoken. Therefore, this group must be more careful. If activities are conducted within a certain schedule of virtue (*sīla*), you must conform to it. Only then can you understand this kind of Dhamma. Otherwise, if you remain talking about useless things, you cannot understand a Dhamma of this nature. I wish that those of you who have undertaken a high standard of virtue (*sīla*) today, walking on the path of Dhamma and applying your minds to it, may gain the strength and power to realize these expected noble goals in this very life!
From the lowest hell Avīci to the highest heaven Akaniṭṭha, if there are any beings who wish to rejoice in this merit of listening to and preaching the Dhamma, may they, through their rejoicing, find peace in the noble, deathless, supreme Nibbāna through their aspired enlightenment! Recite these verses:
“*Ettāvatā ca amhehi.........*”

from:
parayana vagga, sutta nipata
dear listeners,
the supreme buddha, the teacher of the three worlds, introduces the world to us as a place enveloped in ignorance (*avijja*). the entire buddhist path of practice is a journey from ignorance (*avijja*) to wisdom (*vijja*)—a journey from darkness to light. it is a few verses revealing this fact that we have taken today as our theme. these verses are found in the *ajita manava puccha* (the questions of the youth ajita) in the *parayana vagga* of the *sutta nipata*. the introductory story of these verses is the account concerning the brahmin bavari. briefly stated, bavari was a brahmin teacher who had mastered the vedic texts. he left the kosala country with his sixteen disciples and set out for the far regions of southern india, known at that time as the *dakkhinapatha* (southern path). he departed in search of 'nothingness' (*akincannayatana*), the sphere of nothingness. having traveled a long distance, this group built a hermitage and resided on the banks of the river godavari, in an area belonging to the king of assaka. the number of disciples in that hermitage gradually increased, and the surrounding village also became prosperous. the king directed the revenue of that village to this hermitage. however, the brahmin bavari used those funds from time to time to conduct grand sacrifices.
on one occasion, after using that revenue to conduct a grand sacrifice, just as the brahmin teacher bavari returned to the hermitage, a certain visiting brahmin arrived and demanded, "give me five hundred coins (kahapanas)." then the brahmin bavari said, "all my wealth for almsgiving has been exhausted. there is no way i can give you five hundred coins." thereupon, this deceitful brahmin said, "if you cannot give me what i ask, within seven days your head will split into seven pieces." because of this curse, the brahmin bavari became terrified. seeing him sitting in grief, unable to eat or practice absorption (*jhana*), a benevolent deity approached bavari to console him, saying, "that deceitful brahmin does not know what the head is, nor does he know the splitting of the head. that brahmin has no knowledge regarding this." then the brahmin bavari asked the deity, "do you know what the head is, and what the splitting of the head is?" the deity replied, "i too do not know. knowledge regarding the head and the splitting of the head is unique only to the buddhas. the buddhas are the ones who possess that knowledge." then bavari said, "if there is anyone on this entire earth who knows this matter, tell me about them." it was then that the deity revealed the news: "having departed from the city of kapilavastu, the lion of the sakyas, the savior of the world, has attained supreme enlightenment. he is residing in the kosala country, preaching the dhamma to the world, fully liberated. go to that supreme buddha and ask this question." the moment he heard the name "sambuddha" (fully enlightened one), the brahmin's grief was appeased, and his heart leaped with joy. then he asked, "in which village, province, or city does the blessed one reside?" the deity replied, "in savatthi, in the kosala country."
since the brahmin bavari was very advanced in age, he called his sixteen disciples and said, "a buddha, a fully enlightened one, who rarely appears in the world, has now arisen. go and meet the supreme buddha." when he said this, those disciples asked, "how are we to recognize that he is indeed a buddha?" then the brahmin bavari replied, "in our vedic texts, there is mention of the thirty-two marks of a great man. if those marks are present on a person's body, there are only two paths open to him. if he remains a layman, he will become a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*). if he goes forth into homelessness, he will attain supreme enlightenment. when you go and meet the buddha, ask him these questions in your mind: ask about my age, my clan, my learning, the marks on my body, and the number of my disciples. ask these mentally. furthermore, ask mentally about the head and the splitting of the head. since the buddha possesses unobstructed knowledge and vision (*anavarana-nana-dassana*), he will answer the questions asked mentally with spoken words."
that group of disciples set out on the long journey from the *dakkhinapatha*. there were sixteen disciples in this group: ajita, tissa metteyya, punnaka, mettagu, dhotaka, upasiva, nanda, hemaka, todeyya, kappa, jatukanni, bhadravudha, udaya, posala, mogharaja, and pingiya. as this group completed their long journey, the buddha was at the pasanaka shrine in magadha, preaching to the sangha. having climbed that hill, the youth ajita asked in his mind the questions entrusted to him by the brahmin bavari. first, he asked about bavari himself. the buddha answered in words: "the brahmin bavari is one hundred and twenty years old. his clan name is bavari. there are three of the thirty-two marks of a great man on his body. he is a master of the vedas. he has five hundred disciples." he explained in this manner. the listening crowd was astonished at how the buddha could declare these things without any verbal question being asked. after that, the chief disciple, ajita, asked the specified question in his mind. the brahmin bavari asks: "what is the head, and what is the splitting of the head?" it was then that the buddha declared this in a verse:
> *avijja muddha ti janahi,*
> *vijja muddhadhipatini,*
> *saddha-sati-samadhihi,*
> *chanda-viriyena samyuta.*
that verse declares: "know that ignorance (*avijja*) is the head. the splitting of the head is wisdom (*vijja*). that wisdom (*vijja*) is accompanied by faith (*saddha*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), desire (*chanda*), and energy (*viriya*)." the moment this verse was uttered, the sixteen disciples, headed by ajita, prostrated with great devotion at the feet of the buddha, declaring that bavari and his disciples paid homage to the blessed one. when they said this, the buddha blessed them, wishing that bavari as well as his disciples may be happy. he gave a special blessing to the youth ajita: "may you too be happy! may you live long!" then he invited them: "if bavari or any of you have any questions, ask them. i will answer." it was at that moment that the chief disciple ajita presented his questions through the verses we chose as our theme. in this *parayana vagga*, the questions of all sixteen disciples and the answers given to them by the buddha are recorded in a very profound manner. the question asked by the youth ajita is what we took as our theme.
> *kena-ssu nivuto loko,*
> *kena-ssu nappakasati,*
> *kissabhilepanam brusi,*
> *kimsu tassa mahabbhayam.*
by what is the world enveloped?
why does it not shine?
what is its sticky smear?
what is its great terror?
now, the buddha answers:
> *avijjaya nivuto loko,*
> *vevicha pamada nappakasati,*
> *jappabhilepanam brumi,*
> *dukkham assa mahabbhayam.*
the world is enveloped by ignorance (*avijja*).
because of stinginess and negligence, it does not shine.
craving (*tanha*) is its sticky smear, i declare.
suffering (*dukkha*) is its great terror.
then, the youth ajita asks another question:
> *savanti sabbadhi sota,*
> *sotanam kim nivaranam,*
> *sotanam samvaram bruhi,*
> *kena sota pithiyyare.*
streams flow everywhere.
what is the dam for these streams?
tell me the restraint for the streams.
by what are the streams shut off?
now, the buddha answers:
> *yani sotani lokasmim,*
> *sati tesam nivaranam,*
> *sotanam samvaram brumi,*
> *pannay’ete pithiyyare.*
whatever streams of craving (*tanha*) there are in the world,
mindfulness (*sati*) is their dam, their prevention.
i declare it to be the restraint of the streams.
but by wisdom (*panna*) they are completely shut off.
thus, the questions and the answers given by the buddha have been declared. now, we have to say something about this. you must have understood, devout friends, that these verses mainly speak about ignorance (*avijja*) and craving (*tanha*), which we frequently encounter. anyone who knows the dhamma has read about these factors in various places. particularly in the *anamatagga samyutta*, the statement made by the buddha regarding ignorance (*avijja*) and craving (*tanha*) is indeed wonderful.
*"bhikkhave, samsaro anamataggo, pubba koti na pannayati avijjanivarananam sattanam tanhasamyojananam sandhavatam samsaratam..."*
"monks, this samsara is without discoverable beginning. a first point is not discerned of beings hindered by ignorance (*avijja*) and fettered by craving (*tanha*) faring on and running through samsara." it is impossible to see a starting point for this running and wandering in samsara, enveloped by ignorance (*avijja*) and bound by craving (*tanha*). the buddha also indicates in some places that a beginning limit of ignorance (*avijja*) cannot be shown by saying, "prior to this, ignorance (*avijja*) did not exist, and it arose only thereafter." it is because of these two—ignorance (*avijja*) and craving (*tanha*)—that beings wander for such a long time in samsara. next, it was mentioned here that the world is enveloped by ignorance (*avijja*). what is this world? what is this world!! let us try to understand what "the world" means according to the dhamma and according to common usage. today, many people talk about the world. but although they talk about it, those who do not even have an understanding of the world often express various opinions. the buddha introduces the world to us. he points it out in various suttas. on one occasion, the venerable samiddhi asks the buddha:
*"loko, loko’ti, bhante, vuccati. kittavata nu kho, bhante, loko va assa lokapannatti va’ti?"*
"venerable sir, it is said 'the world, the world.' to what extent, venerable sir, is there a world or a description of a world?" then the buddha says:
*"yattha kho, samiddhi, atthi cakkhu, atthi rupa, atthi cakkhuvinnanam, atthi cakkhuvinnanatabba dhamma, atthi tattha loko va lokapannatti va."*
"where there is the eye, samiddhi, where there are forms, where there is eye-consciousness (*vinnana*), where there are things to be cognized by eye-consciousness (*vinnana*), there is the world or the designation of the world." in this manner, the world is described based on the six sense bases: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. similar analyses are found in many places. on one occasion, venerable ananda addresses the monks and states: *"yena kho, avuso, lokasmim lokasanni hoti lokamani, ayam vuccati ariyassa vinaye loko."* "that by which one is a perceiver of the world and a conceiver of the world, friend, is called the world in the discipline of the noble ones." by what does one become a perceiver and a conceiver of the world? by the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. by these. we understand that the world is that which is contained within the sixfold sense base (*salayatana*), where the sixfold sense base (*salayatana*) begins.
next, to gain a deeper understanding of this, let us present a valuable story. in the *anguttara nikaya*, in one place, a brahmin named veranja used a few derogatory words to insult the buddha. the buddha elevated every word to a new meaning, turned it toward the dhamma, and cleansed the filth from that word. one word used by this veranja brahmin was: *"apagabbho samano gotamo"* (the ascetic gotama is devoid of embryonic growth/sterile). he meant a bad birth, born from a foul womb—something like an abusive term in modern times. then the buddha said, "yes, that is true. i am indeed *apagabbha*. i will not undergo birth in a mother's womb again. therefore, what you said is correct." but he did not stop there. he gave a novel simile: "brahmin, suppose a hen has eight, ten, or twelve eggs and sits on them properly. if one of those chicks is the first to break through the eggshell with its claw or beak and come out safely, what would you call that chick, brahmin—the youngest or the eldest?" the brahmin replied, "master gotama, i would call it the eldest." "in the same way, brahmin," the buddha connected, "among those beings who are enveloped by ignorance (*avijja*), imprisoned inside the eggshell of ignorance (*avijja*), i am the very first to break through that eggshell and come out. therefore, i am the eldest in the world."
based on this, we can contemplate: what is the eggshell? what is the eggshell? the eggshell in which the entire world is trapped is the eggshell of the sixfold sense base (*salayatana*) that we mentioned earlier. everyone, including scientists, is trapped inside this. then, what does it mean to break the eggshell and come out? it is to become world-transcending (*lokuttara*). everyone talks about the experience limited to this eggshell. this is what scientists talk about, and what everyone knows. but the buddha points out another side. even when there is the cessation of the sixfold sense base (*salayatana-nirodha*), there is a certain experience. that is indeed the coming out of the eggshell. liberation is there. nibbana is there. think about it from that perspective. we have provided a deeper meaning of ignorance (*avijja*) and the world from that.
next, let us speak about craving (*tanha*). often, when speaking about craving (*tanha*), the word *lepa* (smear/glue) is used; sometimes it is called *visattika*. *visattika* means a sticky substance. the quality of binding is also what is found in the fetters (*samyojana*). thus, ignorance (*avijja*) veils, and craving (*tanha*) adheres, or binds. sometimes we refer to these two as the father and mother of samsara. it is through these two that this entire suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara is accumulated. when we look at dependent arising (*paticca-samuppada*), we see that starting with 'dependent on ignorance' (*avijja-paccaya*), craving (*tanha*) is found in the middle. whichever way you look at it, these two are the main factors.
on one occasion, in the *satipatthana samyutta*, the buddha gives another valuable simile showing this sticky nature of craving (*tanha*). "monks, there are level regions in the himalaya mountains where both humans and monkeys roam. in such a region, a monkey-catcher sets a sticky trap of pitch to catch monkeys. suppose the pitch is smeared on a piece of wood or a tree trunk. it must be a tasty pitch for monkeys. the buddha states that those monkeys who are not greedy and have some understanding will see the pitch from afar and keep away. but a greedy and foolish monkey comes along, sees the pitch, and catches it with one hand. it gets stuck. he tries to free it with his second hand. that too gets stuck. he brings a foot close to free the hand. that too gets stuck. he brings his second foot. that too gets stuck. after that, he brings his mouth close to free his hands. that too gets stuck. now, when he is stuck in five places, the monkey-catcher comes, shoots him, and carries the monkey away along with the piece of wood." what does this simile represent? the five cords of sensual pleasure. the five cords of sensual pleasure are just like that, the buddha points out through this simile. that sticky nature is well illustrated by this simile. this entire suffering (*dukkha*) is prepared within these two. *jappabhilepanam brumi* (craving is the sticky smear in which the world is stuck).
next, the greatest fear in the world is suffering (*dukkha*). the suttas on dependent arising (*paticca-samuppada*) also show us how suffering (*dukkha*) is prepared—how this entire mass of suffering (*dukkha*) is prepared. beginning with ignorance (*avijja*), joined by craving (*tanha*), these two combine to finally prepare the entire five aggregates of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*). that is what was shown in the main points of the first verse. next, another nature of craving (*tanha*) is mentioned. the youth ajita asks: *savanti sabbadhi sota*—"streams flow everywhere. how are they to be dammed?" this is the question he asks. those streams are sometimes described as being thirty-six in number: *yassa chattimsati sota, manapasavana bhusa* (he whose thirty-six streams flow strongly towards pleasant things). this is explained as follows: the streams of craving (*tanha*) flow through the senses of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind towards their respective objects. when these six are multiplied by the three types of craving—craving for sensual pleasures (*kama-tanha*), craving for becoming (*bhava-tanha*), and craving for non-becoming (*vibhava-tanha*)—they become eighteen. when multiplied by the two aspects of internal and external, they become thirty-six. some commentaries show that when multiplied by the three periods of time—past, future, and present—they become one hundred and eight. how are these one hundred and eight streams of craving (*tanha*) to be dammed? this is ajita's question. the buddha says: by mindfulness (*sati*). it is by mindfulness (*sati*). *sati nivaranam* (mindfulness is their dam). that is why you can understand, devout friends, why the buddha has given such a prominent place to the four establishments of mindfulness (*cattaro satipatthana*) as the direct path (*ekayana maggo*). this mindfulness and wisdom (*panna*) are indeed the most practically important things among these teachings. there are many other suttas revealing the importance of mindfulness (*sati*). we point each of these out so that you may ponder deeply upon them.
on one occasion, a brahmin named unnabha came to the buddha and asked: "these five faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—have different domains and different pastures. that is, the eye is for seeing forms and cannot do what the ear does. the ear cannot see forms. in this way, their respective pastures—what is called the objective field—are different. the pasture of the eye is form; forms are the pasture of the eye. sounds are the pasture of the ear, and so on. the pasture fields of these five are different. then, master gotama, what is the resort (*patisarana*) for these pastures brought in by the five sense faculties? where do they go and gather?" the buddha replied: "the mind (*manas*)." you can contemplate this, devout friends. what is brought from these five external sense bases gathers in the mind (*manas*). then he asks another question: "what is the resort (*patisarana*) of the mind?" the buddha's answer to this is mindfulness (*sati*). the resort of the mind is mindfulness (*sati*). this goes even further. from an ordinary point of view, it seems as if there is no problem, but the entire dhamma is contained within this. next, he asks: "what is the resort of mindfulness?" the resort of mindfulness is liberation (*vimutti*). "what is the resort of liberation?" the resort of liberation is nibbana. there the discussion ends.
from this we see how important mindfulness (*sati*) is. once what is brought by the body-senses comes to the mind, some control can be exercised over them through mindfulness (*sati*). that is why in so many suttas you have heard, especially when describing sense restraint, mindfulness (*sati*) is depicted as a gatekeeper (*dvarapala*). it is said, "guarded as to the doors of the faculties" (*indriyesu guttadvarata*). it is the job of a gatekeeper to let in suitable people and close the door when unsuitable people arrive. in other places, mindfulness is described as "the protecting charioteer" (*sati-arakkha-sarathi*). there are occasions where this is shown through the simile of a chariot. the charioteer who drives the chariot, the one engaged in guarding, the gatekeeper—in this manner, the function of mindfulness (*sati*) is shown. it provides protection to the mind. that is why mindfulness is shown to be so important in this verse. but the last line can sometimes be a problem. mindfulness (*sati*) only does the damming. it only temporarily blocks the flowing streams. this is completely, thoroughly shut off by wisdom (*panna*). there lies the problem.
what is this wisdom (*panna*)? how does this wisdom (*panna*) shut off all these streams? from there, let us go a bit deeper. now we declared the story of the head and the splitting of the head. that indeed is the basis of this entire sermon. then, ignorance (*avijja*) was said to be the head. the splitting of the head means the shattering of ignorance (*avijja*). how is ignorance (*avijja*) shattered? it is through the shattering of ignorance (*avijja*) that wisdom (*vijja*) emerges. when ignorance (*avijja*) ceases, wisdom (*vijja*) arises. wisdom (*vijja*) means realization. when speaking about realization, the topic of wisdom (*panna*) arises. wisdom (*panna*) is shown as a light in some places. we mentioned being trapped inside an eggshell. it is only after breaking the eggshell and coming out that one sees things as they truly are. to the one trapped inside the eggshell, nothing beyond is visible. that is why wisdom (*panna*) is described in a wonderful manner. in some places, wisdom (*panna*) is shown as an eye. you may have heard of the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the wisdom eye. everyone has the fleshly eye (*mamsa-cakkhu*). next is the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*), which is attained by sages and those who have attained absorptions (*jhana*). even higher than that is the wisdom eye (*panna-cakkhu*) introduced to the world by the buddha. there is a certain passage describing wisdom (*panna*) and how that wisdom eye is brought to light:
*"udayatthagamini panna ariya nibbedhika samma dukkhakkhayagamini."*
"the noble, penetrative wisdom (*panna*) that goes to the rise and fall (of phenomena), and leads to the complete destruction of suffering (*dukkha*)." the seed of this wisdom (*panna*), or its beginning, starts in a manner suited to the realization of the yogi. it is the wisdom (*panna*) that sees the arising and passing away of things. the world stands on the side of arising (*samudaya*). generally, cessation (*nirodha*) is not within their domain. the worldling disregards cessation and constantly goes from arising to arising. that is what is called craving (*tanha*). it leads to renewed existence (*ponobbhavika*), pulling and sticking from existence to existence. the primary function of wisdom (*panna*) is to bring to light the veiled cessation (*nirodha*). its primary aspect is that the yogi understands the arising and passing away of this world—its impermanence (*aniccata*)—through these two words. we can call it *samudaya-vaya* (arising and passing away). we can call it *udayatthagama* (rise and fall). this is the nature of preparations (*sankhara*).
> *anicca vata sankhara,*
> *uppadavayadhammino,*
> *uppajjitva nirujjhanti,*
> *tesam vupasamo sukho.*
"impermanent (*anicca*) indeed are preparations (*sankhara*), subject to rise and fall. having arisen, they cease; their calming is bliss." everything is contained right there. it is not something that happens after death. "impermanent indeed are preparations (*sankhara*)"—every preparation (*sankhara*) is impermanent (*anicca*). "subject to rise and fall"—their nature is arising and passing away. "having arisen, they cease"—they arise only to cease. "their calming is bliss"—that is the very thing that leads to wisdom (*panna*), the path leading to cessation (*nirodha*).
in some places, that wisdom (*panna*) is shown as a light. these may sometimes be a problem for someone. they might think of these statements made by the buddha in various places as mere similes. there are many similes for light. it is called *abha* (radiance); it is called *pabha* (splendor). there is a sutta that some do not take very seriously, thinking of it merely as something beautifully said: *"catasso ima, bhikkhave, pabha. katama catasso? candappabha, suriyappabha, aggippabha, pannapabha. etadaggam, bhikkhave, imasam catunnam pabhanam yadidam pannapabha."* "there are these four splendors, monks. which four? the splendor of the moon, the splendor of the sun, the splendor of fire, and the splendor of wisdom (*panna*). among these, the splendor of wisdom (*panna*) is supreme." all other splendors are surpassed by this splendor of wisdom (*panna*). one can understand that this is not a statement made lightly. we said that this is a journey from ignorance (*avijja*) to wisdom (*vijja*), a journey from darkness to light. that light is contained within the word *panna*. it is called the lamp of wisdom (*panna-pajjoto*). in many places describing the direct experience of the arahants, the final mention is:
*"pannaya tassa disva asavanam parikkhayam gacchati."*
"having seen with wisdom (*panna*), his influxes are completely destroyed." it is because of this that we said these flowing torrents of craving (*tanha*) cannot be completely shut off by mindfulness (*sati*) alone. it must be done by wisdom (*panna*) itself. because the word *asava* (influx/canker) also contains the meaning of "flowing." as long as the influxes are not destroyed, liberation is not complete. it is only when those influxes are destroyed that everything is completed. this light, the light of wisdom (*panna*), is an internal light. that light, as mentioned here, surpasses the splendor of the moon and the sun. there is a verse related to this, which scholars have discussed for a long time, at the end of the *bahiya sutta*:
> *yattha apo ca pathavi,*
> *tejo vayo na gadhati,*
> *na tattha sukka jotanti,*
> *adicco nappakasati,*
> *na tattha candima bhati,*
> *tamo tattha na vijjati.*
>
> *yada ca attanavedi,*
> *muni monena brahmano,*
> *atha rupa arupa ca,*
> *sukhadukkha pamuccati’ti.*
this stands as a great riddle-like verse. after the ascetic bahiya daruciriya attained arahantship instantly and passed away (*parinibbana, the buddha uttered this extremely profound verse as an inspired utterance (*udana*). this matter is expressed subtly within it.
"where water, earth, fire, and wind find no footing." in which consciousness (*vinnana*)? everyone is established within these great elements (*mahabhuta*), but they do not reside, they find no footing, in that mind. in such a state: "there the stars do not shine." "the sun does not shed its light." "the moon does not beam." what is the reason? within that splendor of wisdom (*panna*), all those objects that give light to the world are rendered lusterless. the world sees things through a medium. to see, they need a medium. in the night, they need starlight, or they need moonlight, or they need sunlight. otherwise, they need fire—which includes electricity, and so forth. it is through such light that we see. but when the light of wisdom (*panna*) comes, those other lights are made lusterless. the moon, sun, and stars all lose their luster. that is what we have to say, because those things are not caught up in that state. that splendor of wisdom (*panna*) at the moment of release from the sixfold sense base (*salayatana*) is what is called the destruction of the influxes. "having seen with wisdom (*panna*)"—having seen through that wisdom, the influxes are destroyed. that is liberation.
the word wisdom (*panna*) coming after mindfulness (*sati*) becomes extremely important. some explain this in various ways. a good proof of this is mentioned in the *ajita manava puccha* itself. after receiving answers to those verses, the youth ajita asks the buddha: "where does name-and-form (*namarupa*) cease completely?" (*namanca rupanca, asesam uparujjhati*). at that point, the buddha says: "with the cessation of consciousness (*vinnana-nirodha*), it ceases completely" (*vinnanassa nirodhena, uparujjhati*). two words are mentioned there: cessation (*nirodha*) and complete cessation (*uparodhana*). cessation of consciousness (*vinnana-nirodha*) means that the prepared consciousness (*abhisankhata-vinnana*), the un-arahant consciousness, exists depending on name-and-form (*namarupa*). when that prepared consciousness (*sankhata-vinnana*) which existed depending on name-and-form (*namarupa*) ceases, that state is called the unmanifestative consciousness (*anidassana-vinnana*). that consciousness (*vinnana*) does not show name-and-form (*namarupa*). that unmanifestative consciousness (*anidassana-vinnana*) is indeed the state of the liberated mind. there, the moon, sun, etc., find no place. at the conclusion of the sutta, something similar is said:
*"vinnanam anidassanam, anantam sabbato pabham..."*
"consciousness (*vinnana*) that is non-manifestative, infinite, radiant all-round; here water, earth, fire, and wind find no footing; here long and short, fine and coarse, pleasant and unpleasant (name-and-form cease completely)." in this manner, the verse goes on. that is, that unmanifestative consciousness (*anidassana-vinnana*), the consciousness (*vinnana*) that does not manifest name-and-form (*namarupa*), is that liberated mind. it is infinite (*anantam*); there are no limits such as long or short. "radiant all-round" (*sabbato pabham*)—it is luminous in every way. that is the reason. because it is luminous in every way, this is a state where everything the world regards as light-giving objects is rendered lusterless. that is why it was said that the moon, sun, etc., do not shine. what is obtained from this is not the meaning obtained from ordinary words. the light of wisdom (*panna*) is not something external. it is something that comes from within. in the presence of that light of wisdom (*panna*) that comes from within, the entire world of name-and-form (*namarupa*) ceases, or is completely stopped. that completely stopped state is what exists in the attainment of the fruit of arahantship (*arahattaphala-samapatti*). we have pointed out the relevant suttas on various occasions. if the sixfold sense base (*salayatana*) is the world, then the cessation of the sixfold sense base (*salayatana-nirodha*) is the world-transcending (*lokuttara*) state. it is the moment of breaking through the eggshell and coming out. it is not the vision thought of by the ordinary world. that vision is an entirely open vision; it exists within that open mind. what is put together is called the prepared (*sankhata*). name-and-form (*namarupa*) is a prepared thing. if we are to say a little more about how it is made, we have explained these to some extent in sermons on dependent arising (*paticca-samuppada*).
the twelve factors of dependent arising (*paticca-samuppada*), as we all know, begin indeed with ignorance (*avijja*). but as we have pointed out, within that darkness of ignorance (*avijja*), a certain preparation (*sankhara*) is made. we can say that preparation is like groping in the dark. through that groping in the dark, the worldling makes that preparation (*sankhara*). sometimes it is shown as follows. the most basic preparation (*sankhara*) necessary for existence (*bhava*) is inhalation and exhalation. inhalation and exhalation are what give the feeling of self and world. the breath taken in is something taken from the external world. having taken it in, it is given back to the world. right there, one is caught up in the world. inhalation and exhalation are indeed described as "bodily preparation" (*kaya-sankhara*), in the context of "dependent on ignorance, preparations arise" (*avijja-paccaya sankhara*). next is "verbal preparation" (*vaci-sankhara*); people in the world use words to live, to exchange ideas. but beneath that are initial and sustained mental application (*vitakka-vicara*), which are described as preparations (*sankhara*). before uttering a word, if it is a question, one thinks for a long time before uttering the word. think of it in such situations.
the buddha did not refer to *kamma* there as *sankhara*, but to the extremely subtle aspect of preparations (*sankhara*). inhalation and exhalation—these too belong to existence (*bhava*). existence is right there. taking a breath in, one tries to hold it. when it is gone, one quickly takes another breath. craving (*tanha*) is right there. ignorance (*avijja*) is right there. in order to protect this internally grasped body, thoughts (*vitakka-vicara*) are used, and words are uttered through them. next, "mental preparation" (*citta-sankhara*) is feeling and perception (*sanna vedana*). it is because of perception (*sanna*) and feeling (*vedana*) that intentions, etc., are prepared, and we are prompted to act. what is done by those preparations (*sankhara*) against the background of ignorance (*avijja*)? through them, consciousness (*vinnana*) and name-and-form (*namarupa*) emerge as two. consciousness (*vinnana*) means discrimination. one person's consciousness (*vinnana*) is different from another's consciousness (*vinnana*). even if all else is equal, when looking at it in terms of consciousness (*vinnana*), it is an extremely personal thing. the world is reflected in consciousness (*vinnana*) as name-and-form (*namarupa*). we have pointed this out. it is recognized through the mental phenomena (*nama-dhamma*) of feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), intention (*cetana*), contact (*phassa*), and attention (*manasikara*), along with the great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind. consider that as humans, the experience we derive from those feelings, perceptions, and intentions is not shared by animals, or by birds, or by creatures in the water. they have a different world. their world of the sixfold sense base (*salayatana*) is different. that is why the buddha always described the world in terms of the sixfold sense base (*salayatana*). the buddha showed the world through the personal sixfold sense base (*salayatana*) of each individual being, because the origin of the world and the cessation of the world are right there. when speaking about the cessation of the world, this is the kind of thing that is found there. the prepared (*sankhata*) is constructed between name-and-form (*namarupa*) and consciousness (*vinnana*).
next, "dependent on name-and-form, the sixfold sense base arises" (*namarupa-paccaya salayatanam*). we called that duality which arose between consciousness (*vinnana*) and name-and-form (*namarupa*) "the two." a split into two. that is also present within the sixfold sense base (*salayatana*). the sixfold sense base (*salayatana*), devout friends, means the six sense bases, which go in pairs: eye and form, ear and sound, and so forth. so much so that on one occasion the buddha declared: "monks, i will teach you the dyad. what is the dyad? the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tactile objects, the mind and mental phenomena." then the buddha makes a challenge: "monks, if anyone should say there is another dyad in the world apart from this, it would be empty chatter." this shows that this is the dyad. it is through the conflict between these two that the aggregates are accumulated. the eye clings to forms, or conflicts with them. the ear clings to sounds, and so on. next, through that, *kamma* is accumulated.
we spoke about name-and-form (*namarupa*): feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), intention (*cetana*), contact (*phassa*), and attention (*manasikara*). remember the simile of the five fingers we gave. we said feeling (*vedana*) is the little finger, perception (*sanna*) is the middle finger, next is contact (*phassa*) which comes to dispute, the index finger, and finally the thumb is attention (*manasikara*). we showed in various ways that the journey towards this wisdom (*panna*) begins with radical attention (*yoniso manasikara*). we illustrated this through various similes. even if we look at it legally, using stories from the world, if there is no witness, a court case must be dismissed. this problem between consciousness (*vinnana*) and name-and-form (*namarupa*) was like a court case without a witness, which even the ancient sages of the deep past could not resolve. how to understand consciousness (*vinnana*)? it is through consciousness (*vinnana*) itself that everything is presented to us. how to understand it? it was there that the buddha applied the middle path. he made one of the defendants a witness. who is the biggest culprit? attention (*manasikara*). having pardoned that inappropriate attention (*ayonisomanasikara*) which, combining ignorance (*avijja*) and craving (*tanha*), committed this crime, he turned it into radical attention (*yoniso manasikara*), saying, "you tell us the internal story." in the dhamma, radical attention (*yoniso manasikara*) means doing things in the proper manner, and it is based on this that one travels on the path of wisdom (*panna*).
the passing away, the cessation (*nirodha*), which is invisible to the ordinary world, is seen correctly as impermanence (*aniccata*) by the noble disciple, the yogi. what the ordinary world calls "impermanent" is when something that existed decays, is discarded, and another is taken. the world does not know any impermanence (*aniccata*) deeper than that. the buddha showed that this is a wisdom (*panna*) that penetrates. why did he call it penetrating? *ariyaya nibbedhikaya* (noble and penetrative)—the moment something arises, one sees that its nature is to be destroyed. there lies the penetration. the world's side is the side of arising (*samudaya*). forgetting cessation (*nirodha*), they highlight only arising (*samudaya*). within that, they stick things together, one to another, through craving (*tanha*). instead of that, the yogi highlights cessation (*nirodha*), though with difficulty, through the two aspects of arising and passing away. therein lies liberation. because if everything that arises ceases, no permanent stance can be taken there. it cannot be taken as "me" or "mine." that penetration is what is called penetrative wisdom (*nibbedhika panna*). gradually, through that impermanence (*aniccata*), the mind arises, and cessation (*nirodha*) comes to the fore. because if everything that has arisen ceases, that is what the mind must be applied to. liberation is also there. many scholars today distinguish this path leading to cessation (*nirodha*) by putting the prepared (*sankhata*) on one side and the unprepared (*asankhata*) on the other. but this is where it lies. that consciousness (*vinnana*) we spoke of is a prepared consciousness (*abhisankhata-vinnana*), a consciousness (*vinnana*) that manifests name-and-form (*namarupa*). if on some occasion, having developed disillusionment towards name-and-form (*namarupa*) in that manner, the meditator contemplates the preparations of name-and-form (*namarupa-sankhara*)—the objects that come to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are described as name-and-form preparations (*namarupa-sankhara*). within the objects that come to them, there are indeed those feelings (*vedana*), perceptions (*sanna*), intentions (*cetana*), contact (*phassa*), and attention (*manasikara*), and the great elements grasped by them are right there. in any object, whether form or sound, if on some occasion one sees their impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and unsubstantial (*anatta*) nature and frees the mind from them, then indeed arises "non-manifestative consciousness" (*vinnanam anidassanam*), the consciousness (*vinnana*) that does not reflect name-and-form (*namarupa*). therein lies that liberation. that indeed is the splendor described as "radiant all-round" (*sabbato pabham*).
a truly wonderful sermon. what the buddha has shown here is the difference between the world and the world-transcending (*lokuttara*) state. generally, most people explain the world-transcending (*lokuttara*) state—for example, when an arahant passes away (*parinibbana—by saying that they go and are born in some place where there is no sun, moon, or stars. that is how it has been understood for a long time. but the depth lies here. that is the great wisdom (*panna*) that comes from within. it is unmediated. the world generally sees through a medium, by moonlight, by starlight. this is not like that. it is a splendor that comes from within. what is shown through that splendor? the emptiness (*sunnata*) of the world. how to see the emptiness (*sunnata*) of the world? when light comes from all sides (*sabbato pabham*). suppose there is something transparent like a piece of glass. if a great light shines on it, it reaches a state where it becomes invisible. in the same way, if one sees deeply the nature of this prepared (*sankhata*) world that the world has conjured up, on some occasion the mind becomes liberated. it is through that liberation that nibbana is spoken of. what is the result there? it is only as long as consciousness (*vinnana*) is bound that there is a future birth. the liberated mind is sometimes described as an island. it is often said that when arahants are absorbed in the attainment of the fruit of arahantship (*arahattaphala-samapatti*), they do not hear even a thunderbolt. that is the state of release from the sixfold sense base (*salayatana*). that is experiencing the bliss of nibbana in this very life.
next, at their final moment, that direct experience we spoke of comes to the fore. what is the reason? even during their lifetime, if they had gained an experience of the deathless (*amata*), if that person had attained the direct realization that there is no fear of death when craving (*tanha*) is destroyed, even when death approaches, what arises at that moment is the attainment of the fruit of arahantship (*arahattaphala-samapatti*) registered in that mind. it is said that buddhas and arahants finally pass away (*parinibbana through an absorption (*jhana*). but the depth lies in this: from that absorption (*jhana*), they then enter that attainment of the fruit (*phala-samapatti*). breaking through the absorption (*jhana*), and having entered the attainment of the fruit (*phala-samapatti*), buddhas and arahants let go of the body. that is why, as we described on previous occasions, arahants like dabba mallaputta are recorded to have set fire to their own bodies and attained *parinibbana*. that is not like lighting a fire in modern times. it is like letting go of a garment and setting fire to it; having put the body aside through their attainment of the fruit of arahantship (*arahattaphala-samapatti*), they burned it through the power of the fire-device (*tejo-kasina*). that is a matter showing that liberation. that is why the buddha even uttered a special inspired verse on that occasion:
> *abhedi kayo, nirodhi sanna,*
> *vedana sitirahesum sabba.*
> *sankhara vupasamimsu,*
> *vinnanam atthagama.*
when the arahant dabba mallaputta set fire to himself and attained *parinibbana*, there was neither soot nor ash remaining. that indeed was what the buddha declared as a special inspired utterance. he showed the state of nibbana very clearly.
"the body broke up"—the physical body broke up. "perception ceased"—perception (*sanna*) was extinguished. "all feelings became cold"—all feelings (*vedana*) became cool. we might think that when dabba mallaputta set fire to himself, he must have felt the heat. no. all feelings (*vedana*) became cool. "preparations were stilled"—all preparations (*sankhara*) were calmed. the mind did not go towards a future birth again. "consciousness came to an end"—consciousness (*vinnana*) went to its end, it reached its termination. the entire problem lies within this termination of consciousness (*vinnana-atthagama*). for so long, consciousness (*vinnana*) goes through samsara with the help of ignorance (*avijja*) and craving (*tanha*), accumulating *kamma*. that is why it is said that the five aggregates of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*) are accumulated. in some places in the dhamma, it is mentioned that all these problems are resolved through the cessation of preparations (*sankhara-nirodha*). the buddha declared on one occasion:
*"kaye va, bhikkhave, sati kayasancetanahetu uppajjati ajjhattam sukhadukkham."*
"monks, when there is the body, internally pleasure and pain arise due to bodily intention." similarly, when there is speech, pleasure and pain arise in connection with speech. when there is the mind, the same is declared. all these are said to have ignorance (*avijja*) as their condition. but finally, it is shown:
*"avijjayatveva asesa-viraga-nirodha so kayo na hoti yam-paccayassa tam uppajjati ajjhattam sukhadukkham... sa vaca na hoti... so mano na hoti... khettam tam na hoti, vatthum tam na hoti, ayatanam tam na hoti, adhikaranam tam na hoti yam-paccayassa tam uppajjati ajjhattam sukhadukkham."*
"but with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance (*avijja*), that body does not exist conditioned by which that internal pleasure and pain arise; that speech does not exist... that mind does not exist... that field does not exist, that site does not exist, that base does not exist, that ground does not exist, conditioned by which that internal pleasure and pain arise." but through the cessation of ignorance (*avijja*)—at the beginning we said that because of ignorance (*avijja*), bodily preparations (*kaya-sankhara*), verbal preparations (*vaci-sankhara*), and mental preparations (*citta-sankhara*) arise. this says that when ignorance (*avijja*) is completely ceased, there is no body, no words, and no mind. those are shown as the places where *kamma* was accumulated. liberation, the state of *parinibbana*, is shown as something mysterious. that is why there is a truly wonderful sermon of the buddha. we have delivered separate sermons on these. it is a grand sermon that even foreigners are astonished by. for those who seek liberation elsewhere, this is a great answer:
*"imasmim yeva byamamatte kalevare sasannimhi samanake lokanca pannapemi lokasamudayanca lokanirodhanca lokanirodhagamininca patipadam."*
"in this very fathom-long carcass, endowed with perception (*sanna*) and mind (*manas*), i declare the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world." within this carcass, which is endowed with perception (*sanna*) and mind (*manas*)—not a dead carcass, but within this physical frame endowed with perception (*sanna*) and mind (*manas*)—i declare the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world. it was because of this matter that the buddha uttered this wonderful lion's roar. therefore, this wisdom (*panna*) we spoke of, "the wisdom (*panna*) that goes to the rise and fall" (*udayatthagamini panna*), is where a yogi has to begin. through the cultivation of the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*), that impermanence (*aniccata*) is seen in two aspects: arising and passing away. along that, the mind goes deeper and deeper. it is there that attention (*manasikara*)—the defendant we made into a witness—finally reveals the story through radical attention (*yoniso manasikara*).
as one sees each of these extremely subtly through radical attention (*yoniso manasikara*), impermanence (*aniccata*) comes to the fore. cessation (*nirodha*) comes to the fore. then, just as existence (*bhava*) grows through that arising (*samudaya*), when cessation (*nirodha*) comes to the fore, right there is the cessation of existence (*bhava-nirodha*). that is what comes to the fore. that is why the buddha declares almost everywhere: *bhava-nirodho nibbanam, bhava-nirodho nibbanam*—"the cessation of existence (*bhava*) is nibbana." but when the cessation of existence (*bhava*) is mentioned, many people become afraid, because there is such a great craving for existence (*bhava-tanha*) within the world. but this cessation of existence (*bhava-nirodha*) is shown as a direct experience. the cessation of existence (*bhava-nirodha*) is a direct experience obtained in this very life. within it lies the bliss of liberation. if there is suffering (*dukkha*) within existence (*bhava*), where the cessation of existence (*bhava*) is a direct experience, the bliss of liberation is found right there. that is what is meant by experiencing the bliss of liberation. even a living arahant experienced that bliss of liberation as a direct realization. that is why, when speaking about nibbana, it is said: *sanditthiko dhammo...* (dhamma to be realized here and now). it is something that can be attained and seen. now, do it! it is not something to be obtained after going to the next world. it is in this very life (*dittheva dhamme*). that is indeed concerning nibbana. then, extinguishing or cooling down means, finally, that mass of samsaric suffering (*dukkha*). that is it. in various sermons, we highlighted a series of words describing nibbana. in applying the mind to nibbana as the recollection of peace (*upasamanussati*), that can be used as an aid.
*"etam santam etam panitam, yadidam sabbasankharasamatho sabbupadhipatinissaggo tanhakkhayo virago nirodho nibbanam."*
"this is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all preparations (*sabbasankharasamatho*), the relinquishing of all assets (*sabbupadhipatinissaggo*), the destruction of craving (*tanhakkhayo*), dispassion (*virago*), cessation (*nirodho*), extinguishment (nibbanam*)." within those few words, everything we have said is contained. "the stilling of all preparations" (*sabbasankharasamatho*)—if all preparations (*sankhara*) have been calmed. "the relinquishing of all assets" (*sabbupadhipatinissaggo*)—assets (*upadhi*) refer to the five aggregates of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*); those accumulated five aggregates of grasping are also relinquished. "the destruction of craving" (*tanhakkhayo*)—craving (*tanha*) is destroyed. "dispassion" (*virago*)—dispassion also refers to nibbana itself, that state of detachment. "cessation" (*nirodho*)—extinguishing. "extinguishment" (nibbanam*)—finally, cooling down. if the world is in a state of burning, what the buddha points out instead of that burning is cooling down. all this is contained within the word nibbana. various meanings were added to this in later times. indeed, each verse in this *parayana vagga* is truly wonderful. those disciples had gone that far, practicing absorptions (*jhana*), in search of "nothingness" (*akincanna*)—the direct experience of "there is nothing." but having returned, they met the buddha and obtained "nothingness" (*akincanna*) in its highest sense. the sphere of nothingness is a state of absorption (*jhana*). this is not like that. it is said: *"akincanam anadanam, etam dipam anaparam."* "possessing nothing, grasping nothing, this is the island, there is no other." the buddha has shown that as an island. it shows the bliss of liberation that exists when all grasping (*upadana*) is destroyed. it is said that many, including the youth ajita, became arahants on the spot upon hearing the answer given by the buddha. it is truly wonderful. from this, we see how much deep meaning is contained in a single four-line verse. we tried to explain it at our own level. do not think of these as things that merely pass over the surface. the dhamma is a profound thing. it can be understood through various similes in a simple way. for one who is engaged in the dhamma in the present, these are not deep. they are simple. that is what we must take into consideration.
today too, you have had the opportunity to listen to a certain insight-oriented sermon that is helpful for your meditation. we hope that you will derive the full benefit of this program of virtue (*sila*). if you spend your time wandering here and there, talking about other things, you will not be able to properly understand even this dhamma that is being spoken. therefore, this group must be more careful. if activities are conducted within a certain schedule of virtue (*sila*), you must conform to it. only then can you understand this kind of dhamma. otherwise, if you remain talking about useless things, you cannot understand a dhamma of this nature. i wish that those of you who have undertaken a high standard of virtue (*sila*) today, walking on the path of dhamma and applying your minds to it, may gain the strength and power to realize these expected noble goals in this very life!
from the lowest hell avici to the highest heaven akanittha, if there are any beings who wish to rejoice in this merit of listening to and preaching the dhamma, may they, through their rejoicing, find peace in the noble, deathless, supreme nibbana through their aspired enlightenment! recite these verses:
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 056
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #56
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.70)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Aciraṃ vatayaṃ kāyo, pathaviṃ adhisessati; Chuḍḍho apetaviññāṇo, niratthaṃva kaliṅgaraṃ.
From:
Verse 41 from the Cittavagga (Chapter on the Mind) of the Dhammapada
Dear Listeners,
The Great Compassionate Buddha clarified to the world the value of nursing the sick, not only through advice but also by example. The state of illness is a time when a person becomes helpless. Caring for them at such a time, with loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathy at the forefront, is a noble quality of a virtuous person. On the other hand, through illness, a person is able to properly understand the impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anattā*) nature of these five aggregates. What assists in this is timely Dhamma advice. A valuable story that demonstrates how the Buddha performed the nursing of the sick in both these ways is presented as the background story to the stanza we have chosen as our theme today.
A certain faithful young man in the city of Sāvatthī ordained in the Dispensation and received higher ordination. He was known as Venerable Tissa. In the course of time, Venerable Tissa developed a severe illness. Starting as small pimples on his body like eczema, they gradually became large boils, then developed into large abscesses, which burst and began to ooze blood and pus. Holes appeared here and there all over his body. Likewise, his robes and undergarments became sodden with blood and pus; they were completely wet. Finally, he reached a state where even his attending monks could not look after him, and this venerable monk lay there helpless, without anyone to nurse him.
At that moment, the Buddha, having entered the attainment of Great Compassion and looking at the world, beheld this monk. By that time, Venerable Tissa was known by the name 'Pūtigatta Tissa' (Tissa of the Putrid Body). Because his body was decaying, the nickname Pūtigatta Tissa was attached to him. So, Venerable Pūtigatta Tissa appeared to the Buddha’s knowledge of the attainment of Great Compassion. He understood that this helpless Tissa had the supportive conditions (*upanissaya-sampatti*) to attain Arahantship. But as things stood now, it would be difficult. Understanding that 'if even I do not help him, that opportunity will slip away,' the Buddha went to that monastery. Having arrived, he did not go straight to that monk. He went to the fire-house, washed the vessel used for heating water for bathing, poured water into it, placed it on the hearth, and stayed in the fire-house until the water boiled. Then, after the water had boiled, the Buddha went to the bed where that monk was lying and lifted one end of the bed. Since the bed has two ends, the other monks also understood that the Buddha was now preparing to nurse this monk. Saying, 'Venerable Sir, we will do that,' the monks lifted the bed and carried it to the fire-house.
Next, the Buddha, with the assistance of those monks, first washed the monk’s outer robe and set it to dry in the sun. Then, with the help of those monks, the Buddha poured water, and those monks washed him. In this manner, they bathed him. After bathing him, by that time, the outer robe had dried. Having put that on him, they washed his undergarment as well. Washing it with hot water in the same way, and after it had dried in the sun in a short while, they put the undergarment on him too. Now indeed, Venerable Tissa felt great comfort after a long time due to this bath; he felt a lightness in his body and a peace in his mind. Wearing that undergarment and wrapped in his outer robe, he lay comfortably on the bed. Standing at the head of the bed, near his head, it was at that very moment that the Buddha preached the stanza we took as our theme.
*Aciraṁ vatayaṁ kāyo paṭhaviṁ adhisessati chuddho apeta-viññāṇo niratthaṁva kaliṅgaraṁ*
"Before long indeed, this body, devoid of consciousness (*viññāṇa*), will lie upon the earth, cast aside like a useless log"—this is the meaning contained in that stanza. Hearing this stanza, Venerable Pūtigatta Tissa attained Arahantship together with the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). Many other monks also attained various paths and fruits. Then, immediately along with his attainment of Arahantship, Venerable Pūtigatta Tissa attained final extinguishment (*pariNibbāna. Such events do occur, where life ends simultaneously with the realization of the Dhamma. However, those monks knew nothing of this. The Buddha had the body of Venerable Pūtigatta Tissa—who appeared to have passed away or attained final extinguishment—cremated, and caused a stupa to be built enshrining his relics.
The monks asked, "Where has this Venerable Pūtigatta Tissa been born?" It was on that occasion that the Buddha declared, "Monks, this Pūtigatta Tissa has attained Arahantship and final extinguishment (*pariNibbāna." Then those monks asked: "Venerable Sir, if he had such supportive conditions to attain Arahantship, why did his body decay in this manner? Why did he fall into this state with boils oozing pus?" Furthermore, not only that, but Venerable Tissa’s bones also broke. In his final days, his bones broke, and his body was decayed in a most terrible manner. "What is the reason for his bones breaking? What is the reason for his attaining Arahantship?" When the monks inquired about this, the Buddha, pointing out his past karma, declared: "All of this is the result of past karma done by Tissa." The story is given as follows:
In the time of Kassapa Buddha, this Venerable Pūtigatta Tissa was a bird hunter. His livelihood was catching birds and selling them to wealthy people. In order to keep the birds that remained unsold for the next day—with the thought that if he killed them, the meat would spoil and rot—he broke the wings and legs of those birds, plucking their feathers, and kept them alive to be sold the next day. He also killed and ate some of them. That indeed was his unwholesome karma. However, despite leading such a life, on one occasion, with great devotion, he offered food, offered alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*), to an Arahant who had come to his house for alms, and made a wish: "May I realize the same Dhamma that the Venerable Sir has realized." The Arahant also blessed him, saying, "May it be so." The Buddha explained that this wholesome merit was the supportive condition (*upanissaya*) for his attaining Arahantship.
So, that is the story. This story is exemplary to us in several ways. First, we should pay attention to the nursing of the sick performed by the Buddha. Now, here, Venerable Pūtigatta Tissa did not appear to the Buddha’s knowledge of the attainment of Great Compassion merely because of his illness. A person is usually caught in that knowledge of the attainment of Great Compassion because they have the qualifications to be released from this suffering (*dukkha*) of saṁsāra. Here too, it was not solely due to his illness, but because he possessed the supportive conditions to attain Arahantship that he appeared in that manner. On such occasions, the Buddha often went to that place alone. Even here, the Buddha went there without taking even Venerable Ānanda with him, went first to the fire-house, and like a true attendant, washed the vessel, placed water on the hearth, boiled it, did all of that, and only then went to the patient's bedside. Furthermore, the very manner in which he performed that nursing is worthy of emulation even for us—the manner of nursing a patient. He first washed that monk's robe, let it dry, then bathed him, and finally washed his undergarment, performing the nursing in a very systematic, highly methodical manner. Lastly, the Buddha nursed that monk with the Dhamma. By nursing him with the Dhamma, He cured his entire disease of saṁsāra.
Indeed, that is a very valuable story. A somewhat similar incident of the Buddha nursing the sick is mentioned in the Vinaya Piṭaka. Let us include that story here too, due to several reasons. A certain monk had a severe abdominal ailment, fell to the ground wallowing in his own urine and excrement, and was utterly helpless. Not a single monk went to nurse that monk. At that helpless moment, while the Buddha was on a walking tour of the lodgings (*senāsana cārikā*) with Venerable Ānanda—a walking tour of the lodgings means the Buddha, from time to time, went from monastery to monastery to see how the monks were living—while walking in that manner, he went with Venerable Ānanda to the place where that monk was and said to Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and bring water, bring water, let us bathe this monk." Then, Venerable Ānanda brought water. The Buddha poured water. Venerable Ānanda rubbed his body. After bathing him, the Buddha lifted him from the head side, and Venerable Ānanda lifted him from the feet side. They lifted him and laid him on the bed. He asked this monk, "Monk, why do others not nurse you?" This monk said, "Venerable Sir, since I do not nurse or help other monks, those monks do not look after me either."
Then, based on this, the Buddha gathered the monks and asked: "Monks, is there a sick monk in such-and-such a monastery?" "Yes, Venerable Sir." "Does that monk have an attendant?" "No, Venerable Sir." "Why is there no attendant?" When asked, they replied, "That monk does not nurse us either. He does not help us. Therefore, we do not help him either." At that moment, the Buddha declared to the monks: "Monks, you have no mother or father here to nurse you. If you do not nurse one another, who else is there to nurse you?" Next, the Buddha declared a statement of profound meaning, which is interpreted in various ways today. It is mentioned in the Pāli language as:
*Yo bhikkhave maṁ upaṭṭheheyya so gilānaṁ upaṭṭheheyya*
"Monks, he who would nurse me, should nurse the sick."
Some interpret that passage to mean that nursing a sick person is equivalent to nursing the Buddha. However, we have to say that if the Buddha had expressed such a thing, that sentence would have been expressed differently. In that case, it should have been said: "He who nurses the sick, nurses me." As a reason for this, we point to a well-known Dhamma advice mentioned in the teachings:
*Yo dhammaṁ passati so maṁ passati*
"He who sees the Dhamma, sees me."
Whoever sees the Dhamma is equivalent to having seen the Buddha. According to that sentence structure and logic, if we were to take the first meaning we mentioned, it should have been said on this occasion: "He who nurses the sick, nurses me." But here, the Buddha declares: "He who would nurse me, should nurse the sick." Now, some interpret this from another angle. They say it means that nursing the sick can never be made equal to nursing the Buddha. Nursing a lay or ordained sick person is not as fruitful in terms of merit as nursing the Buddha. On this occasion, what the Buddha declared and meant was: "If you would nurse me by way of accepting my advice, you should nurse the sick." It is also interpreted in that way. But that is interpreted by adding words unnecessarily.
If we reflect on this quietly, comparing this story with that of Venerable Pūtigatta Tissa, we will be able to bring out the true meaning of this Buddha-word. Now, in the story of Venerable Pūtigatta Tissa, we saw that because of his supportive conditions to attain Arahantship and because he appeared in the knowledge of the attainment of Great Compassion, the Buddha went there alone, not even with an attendant. He went alone and commenced the duties of nursing the sick. But here, the Buddha was on a walking tour of the lodgings (*senāsana cārikā*) with Venerable Ānanda. Pious devotees, this walking tour of the lodgings is something that a clever leader, a clever teacher, must do. It is a valuable custom. It means to observe things. Just as modern sudden raids or surprise inspections are carried out when reorganizing some departments, the Buddha also had a custom of quietly visiting monastery after monastery without prior notice. Then, when he saw the shortcomings of the monks in those places, he could advise them accordingly. Such an occasion is found here. So here, the Buddha went with Venerable Ānanda and nursed that monk with the assistance of Venerable Ānanda. Having done so, he came and gave advice in that manner.
If we reflect according to that, we have to take it in this way. From what the Buddha declared here, it is clear that since there are no parents in this Dispensation, the monks must nurse one another. Furthermore, in this Dispensation, there are two teacher-pupil dyads: preceptor and co-resident (*upajjhāya-saddhivihārika*), and teacher and pupil (*ācariya-antevāsika*). For the proper conduct among these monks, for this monastic institution to function correctly, the Buddha has laid down these two teacher-pupil levels or dyads: the pupil of the preceptor is the *saddhivihārika*, and the pupil of the teacher is the *antevāsika*. The mutual relationship between these two groups is described as a relationship between a father and a son. That is how the Buddha has laid it down. Not only that, the Buddha has frequently declared that companion monks (*sabrahmacārī*) should help and nurse one another with a sense of brotherhood. So, if in some way they do not fulfill that responsibility, what happens? All of these are the Buddha's children, the Sakyaputta ascetics. If these children do not behave in that manner, the Buddha himself will have to go from lodging to lodging, from monastery to monastery, with his own attendant, and nurse the sick. That is why the Buddha declared on this occasion: "He who would nurse me, should nurse the sick." When we think about it in this way, based on what is said here, nursing the sick is a part of nursing the Buddha itself. It is a part of the service done to the Buddha. Otherwise, one cannot take it to mean that nursing the Buddha and nursing a lay or ordained sick person with medicine and care are exactly identical.
Be that as it may, we can see through this the place the Buddha gave to nursing the sick. Furthermore, when the Buddha laid down various rules in the Vinaya Piṭaka, he provided various allowances for the sick, stating: "There is no offense for one who is sick" (*gilānassa anāpatti*). Thus, after laying down a certain rule, considering the sick, he exempts the sick monk by saying there is no offense. In many other ways too, the Buddha has described the nursing of the sick in the Vinaya Piṭaka. On one occasion, the Buddha points out five qualifications of a true sick-nurse. What is the first qualification of a true sick-nurse? He must be capable of preparing the medicine needed for that patient. Administering medicine is the first point. The second qualification is to understand what is suitable (*sappāya*) and unsuitable (*asappāya*) for that patient. The word *sappāya* is used to mean what is beneficial to someone—beneficial things, suitable things. So, one must understand what is suitable and unsuitable for the patient. Likewise, one must have the ability to remove unsuitable things and bring suitable, beneficial things close to the patient. Next, what is the third qualification mentioned? One must nurse with a mind of loving-kindness, without any expectation of gain from that patient—without even the expectation of taking the food received by the patient, or any expectation of gaining money or benefit from the patient. That is the next point. The fourth qualification is that one must be capable of removing the excrement, urine, saliva, phlegm, mucus, vomit, etc., of that patient. One must be able to handle those things without disgust. The fifth qualification is that one must be capable of delivering a timely Dhamma talk in a way that encourages the patient's mind—nursing them with the Dhamma. The Buddha demonstrated all of these through his own example as well. Thus, we should understand that the Buddha clarified the nursing of the sick to the world not only by advice but also by example.
Similarly, on the other hand, just as the qualities of a good sick-nurse were mentioned, the characteristics or habits of a good patient—that is, a patient who is easy to nurse—are also shown. If one is a good patient, regarding that patient, he should know what is beneficial to him. He must act in accordance with what is beneficial; this is called *sappāya*. He must be able to behave in a way that suits his illness; otherwise, the attendant will not be able to manage him. So, behaving in that manner, in a way suited to one's illness, is necessary. The second point is that he must know the proper quantity of suitable things, such as medicine given. If one consumes or accepts too much of something thinking, "This is a good, beneficial thing," then another illness will arise. That is also necessary. One must know the measure to be taken even of things that are suitable and beneficial to oneself. That is something belonging to the patient. The third point is that he must use the medicine given systematically and in the proper manner. He must use the medicine continuously without rejecting it. The fourth point is that he must declare the state of his illness accurately and truthfully to his attendant. Is the illness getting better now? Is it increasing? Is there relief now? He must clearly state all of that to the attendant. The fifth point is that even if there is severe pain (*vedanā*), he must have the strength to bear it without crying out. In this manner, the Buddha has laid down both the qualities of a true sick-nurse and the behavior that should exist in a patient who is easy to nurse.
Likewise, you have heard of occasions when the Buddha himself nursed with the Dhamma. You may have heard that to Venerable Moggallāna and Venerable Mahā Kassapa, on occasions when they were very gravely ill, the Buddha himself visited and recited the factors of awakening (*bojjhaṅga*). It is said that as soon as they heard it, their illnesses were cured. Similarly, another highly famous discourse is the Girimānanda Sutta. The Buddha preached the Girimānanda Sutta when Venerable Ānanda came and informed Him that Venerable Girimānanda was severely ill. On that occasion, the Buddha said: "It is alright even if I do not go. If you preach this discourse, the illness will be cured." Contained within that discourse are ten meditation themes called the ten perceptions (*dasa saññā*), which are about meditation. He preached an amazing discourse that develops the mind regarding the diseased conditions of the body. There too, it was nursing the sick. From that we can see that the Buddha does not endorse merely handing the patient over to doctors and nursing them only physically. You must set the mind right, make the mind healthy. If possible, one must be able to nurse them in such a way that the mind is led all the way to final Nibbāna, eradicating the disease of saṁsāra. This is the deepest aspect of nursing the sick. Thus, we can extract many points from these stories. Apart from that, let us now turn to another aspect.
Now, next, what is the lesson we have to learn from this Venerable Pūtigatta Tissa? He too passed away after teaching us a lesson. What is the lesson? His body rotted. Why did it rot? During the time of Kassapa Buddha, as a bird hunter, with the business intention of supplying un-decayed, fresh meat to his customers, he broke the limbs and plucked the wings of those helpless animals and kept them overnight. Why was this? Because of the fear that the meat would spoil. The result of that grave unwholesome karma indeed yielded its fruit to Venerable Pūtigatta Tissa. Now, on this occasion, in the Right Livelihood characterized by the eight-fold virtue (*ājīva-aṭṭhamaka-sīla*) that you have undertaken, there are livelihoods that a faithful layperson should not perform, which you may have heard of.
