according to what is explained in the commentary regarding the background story related to the malunkyaputta thera gatha in the theragatha pali, these verses were preached by the great arahant malunkyaputta. the account concerning him is as follows: this venerable malunkyaputta was born into a high-class family in savatthi. he was known as malunkyaputta, derived from his mother's name, malunkya. having lived in the household life for some time, he became disillusioned with it, went forth from the home life, and received ordination among the wanderers (*paribbajakas*). having stayed among the wanderers for some time, on a certain occasion he met the buddha, heard the dhamma, went forth under him, developed insight (*vipassana*), and attained arahantship. after attaining arahantship, out of compassion for his relatives, he visited his birthplace or former home. his relatives served him with delicious food and drinks and offered alms. at the same time, hoping to entice the venerable thera back to the household life, they gathered and piled up their family wealth before him and invited him, saying: "all of this belongs to the venerable sir. may you return to the household life, become a layman, and support a wife and children with this wealth." at that moment, according to the commentary, he rose into the air and declared the disadvantageous side of *tanha* through these verses. in fact, some of these verses are also recorded in the dhammapada as the buddha's own words. the meaning of these few verses is extremely deep. let us try to understand them generally.
*"manujassa pamattacarino, tanha vaddhati maluva viya"* — for a person who behaves negligently, *tanha* (craving) grows like a *maluva* creeper.
*"so plavati hura huram, phalamicchamva vanasmim vanaro"* — he leaps from life to life in *samsara*, like a monkey seeking fruit in a forest jumping from tree to tree.
*"yam esa sahati jammi, tanha loke visattika"* — whomever this wretched, sticky *tanha* in the world—known as *visattika* (clinging / spreading)—overcomes,
*"soka tassa pavaddhanti, abhivatthamva biranam"* — his sorrows multiply like *birana* grass after a downpour of rain.
*"yo cetam sahati jammim, tanham loke duraccayam"* — but whoever overcomes this wretched *tanha*, so difficult to escape in the world,
*"soka tamha papatanti, udabinduva pokkhara"* — his sorrows fall away from him, like drops of water from a lotus leaf.
*"tam vo vadami bhaddan vo, yavantettha samagata"* — therefore i say to you, blessings to all of you who have assembled here!
*"mulam khanatha usiratthova biranam"* — dig up the root of *tanha*, just as one digs up the root of the *birana* grass seeking its fragrant root (*usira*).
*"ma vo nalamva sotova, maro bhanji punappunam"* — do not let mara break you again and again, like a torrent breaking reeds. do not allow yourselves to be swept away by that torrent of *tanha*, nor let mara destroy you repeatedly through repeated birth and death.
having declared so, he next says: *"karotha buddhavacanam, khano vo ma upaccaga, khanatita hi socanti, nirayamhi samappita"* — act according to the word of the buddha. let not the supreme moment pass you by, for those who miss the moment sorrow when they are consigned to hell.
*"pamado rajo, pamadanupatito rajo"* — *raja* means dust. negligence generates and increases the dust of defilements. therefore, through diligence (*appamada*) and *vijja* (wisdom / understanding / clear vision), uproot that dart of *tanha* from oneself: *"abbahe sallamattano'ti"*.
this is the meaning of those verses. what i have stated is their general meaning. even the similes contained in these verses are extremely valuable.
that *maluva* creeper is a parasitic plant that grows on trees. one often sees a *maluva* creeper on trees. it starts small and eventually covers and destroys the tree. that is the simile used here. the *tanha* of a negligent person grows in the same way.
next, *"so plavati hura huram, phalamicchamva vanasmim vanaro"* means that just like a monkey wishing to eat fruit leaps from tree to tree in the forest, it carries that person from existence to existence, from *bhava* to *bhava* (becoming).
the next simile: *"yam esa sahati jammi tanha loke visattika"*—whomever is overcome by this wretched, sticky *tanha* in the world, that person's sorrows grow like a *birana* grass bush on which rain has fallen. on the other hand, if someone subdues that *tanha*, his sorrows roll off him like water drops on a lotus leaf. thus, it is explained through various similes.
next, as an invitation to eliminate that *tanha*, it says: *"tam vo vadami bhaddan vo, yavantettha samagata, tanhaya mulam khanatha biranam"*. the tuber of this *birana* plant is called *usira*. some identify it as vetiver, and in some regions, it is called *sera* (lemongrass). just like digging up this plant for its *usira* root, dig up the root of *tanha*. that is what is said through various similes. we can discuss more details related to these dhamma matters in due course.
before that, there are many accounts concerning the great arahant malunkyaputta in the sutta discourses. let us mention some. regarding him, the following is mentioned in the samyutta nikaya: on one occasion, the venerable malunkyaputta approached the blessed one and made this request: "venerable sir, please teach me the dhamma in brief. with the help of that teaching, i shall go into seclusion, dwell alone, put forth effort, and realize arahantship." when he said this, the blessed one remarked: "malunkyaputta, what am i to say to the young, newly ordained monks when you, who are old and advanced in years, come and ask for a brief teaching?" the buddha said this as a form of mild admonishment. then the venerable malunkyaputta said: "venerable sir, please preach to me a brief discourse. in that way, i shall become an heir of the blessed one's teaching."
next, before giving that brief sermon, as if to test his suitability, the buddha asked ven. malunkyaputta: "what do you think, malunkyaputta? do you have any desire, lust, or affection for forms cognizable by the eye that you have not seen before?" similarly, one can think of the others: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and thoughts—the objects met at the six sense-doors. "do you have any passion, affection, or desire to experience them?" he replied in the negative to all of these. it was then that the buddha delivered that brief sermon.
to express this in english: "then, malunkyaputta, regarding things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—that is, *dittha, suta, muta, vinnata*—in the seen there will be only the seen, in the heard there will be only the heard, in the sensed there will be only the sensed, in the cognized there will be only the cognized. then, malunkyaputta, you will not be 'by' that. when, malunkyaputta, you are not 'by' that, then, malunkyaputta, you will not be 'in' that. when, malunkyaputta, you are not 'in' that, then you are neither here, nor there, nor in between the two. this itself is the end of *dukkha* (suffering)." he delivered this riddle-like discourse. those devotees who have listened to our previous sermons would know that this is the very same brief sermon the buddha preached to the ascetic bahiya daruciriya, which he also preached here to the thera.
now, if we consider the meaning of this brief sermon: those four terms—seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—are in pali *dittha, suta, muta, vinnata*. what is caught within these four are our six sense bases. that is, the very objects that are the domain of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. usually, we are accustomed to taking things as "the thing seen," "the thing heard," and so on. here, the buddha states that everything coming through these sense bases, that entire mass of objects, is encompassed by these four words: seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. the "sensed" refers to what is experienced through the tongue, body, and nose. so, one can understand "seen" as the objects coming to the eye, and "heard" as the objects coming to the ear. "sensed" refers to the sensing through the nose, tongue, and body. lastly, "cognized" refers to the sensing or cognition that comes to the mind.
so, concerning these, what is preached here is a wondrously brief discourse. its meaning is that in the seen, it stops at just the seen; in the heard, it stops in that way. what ultimately happens through such stopping is extremely deep. what happens then? according to the buddha, then "you are not 'by' that." this means you do not make assumptions, conceptualizations, or proliferate regarding them in terms of the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. to explain this in an understandable way: normally, when something strikes our eye, we take it as "a thing seen." but in reality, there is only a seeing, only a hearing, only a sensing, only a cognizing. yet we do not understand this. extremely rapidly, the mind acts, and what was taken as "that seen thing" becomes established through *tanha* (craving), *mana* (conceit), and *ditthi* (views). through *tanha*, we take it as "this is mine"; through *mana*, we take it as "this am i"; through *ditthi*, we take it as a self. it is through this grasping, through getting established, that—now you can understand—one exists "by" that. once you make that seen thing into your own, then by taking it "from" that, you exist "in" it. you enter into it. we have analyzed this in detail previously so that you can get some idea of it.
what the buddha is pointing out is that instead of taking the objects met by our six sense bases—the eye, ear, nose, etc.—exactly as they are, we become established there through the defilements of *tanha*, *mana*, and *ditthi*. it is by thus getting established that it is said "you are 'in' it." once you go inside it, then a "here" is created. when a "here" is created, along with that "here," a "there" also arises. this is what we call duality. so, when something is taken as "here," opposed to it, a "there" is also created. the moment those two are created, there is also an "in-between." here, the buddha shows that liberation—complete liberation from *samsara*—lies within these few words. accordingly, if we do not get established in terms of *tanha*, *mana*, and *ditthi* in the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, and if we do not grasp them as "i" and "mine," then we have no "here." when there is no "here," there is no "there." when those two are absent, there is also no "in-between." indeed, it is through the story of "here," "there," and the "in-between" that this *samsara* goes on and on. that is precisely why it was said that this itself is the end of *dukkha*.
it is recorded that upon hearing this advice, ven. malunkyaputta went into seclusion and very quickly realized arahantship. thus, we began this discourse concerning the great arahant malunkyaputta with the event that took place after he became an arahant. however, next, because of matters directly related to *tanha*, we also mentioned this passage which was supportive of his arahantship. but the explanation does not end here. this too is a matter mentioned in the sutta itself. after the buddha presented this brief discourse, ven. malunkyaputta said: "venerable sir, i understand the detailed meaning of this brief discourse preached by you in this manner." here, the great arahant presents an explanation like a brief commentary. how does he explain it? he shows it through a series of verses related to the six senses. when we discuss one sense, you can apply it to the others and understand.
here, ven. malunkyaputta says: "having seen a form with the eye, by grasping an agreeable sign, one's mindfulness (*sati*) is bewildered, and then one engenders lustful thoughts. one experiences feeling (*vedana*). through experiencing that feeling, strong greed arises. then, the mind is defiled by distress and so on. through that, *dukkha* is next accumulated—that is, the five groups of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*) are accumulated. this means that through grasping them, they go and accumulate. by such accumulation, one is far from nibbana—*ara nibbana*, far from nibbana."
through that verse, the venerable thera shows that side of clinging. just as it was said about the eye and the objects coming to the eye, you can briefly apply this to the objects coming to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and finally, the deepest one, the objects coming to the mind. by taking them as agreeable in that way and by grasping (*upadana*) them, the groups of grasping (*upadanakkhandha*) that expand *samsara* are accumulated.
next, he states the other side: "but if someone establishes mindfulness (*sati*) regarding the objects coming to the eye, and does not develop clinging or lust towards them, that person is liberated from those aforementioned sufferings. sometimes, that leads to the reduction of the groups of grasping, to their wearing away." what was first mentioned was "accumulation"—through defilements, the groups of grasping are accumulated. next, through developing dispassion (*viraga*) toward them, they are eliminated, they decrease. in pali, the terms used are *acinati* (he accumulates) and *apacinati* (he decumulates/reduces). words like *upacaya* (building up) and *apacaya* (wearing down) are also used. the groups of grasping are accumulated because of one's grasping of them and clinging to the feeling (*vedana*) experienced through the senses. by seeing them right there, and letting in the seen be only the seen, in the heard only the heard, what happens is their wearing away. it is recorded that after these things were said, the buddha approved what ven. malunkyaputta had said, saying "sadhu, sadhu!" after that, the thera went and meditated accordingly and quickly attained arahantship.
now, in connection with this, we spoke of the *ponobhavika* (renewed existence) nature of *tanha*, like a monkey leaping from tree to tree. there are many important points in that. if we are to speak of it, the nature of *tanha* is to connect one thing to another. there is a very good sutta to illustrate this. on one occasion, when the buddha was staying in the deer park at isipatana in benares, after their alms-round, the theras assembled in the circular pavilion and discussed the meaning of a verse preached by the buddha in the metteyya sutta of the parayana vagga, holding a discussion on it. here is that verse:
> *"yo ubhante viditvana,*
> *majjhe manta na lippati;*
> *tam brumi mahapurisoti,*
> *so’dha sibbanimaccaga."*
this is a deep verse preached by the buddha, currently found in the parayana vagga. it is like a riddle. "he who, having known both ends, does not cling to the middle with wisdom—him i call a great man; he has escaped the seamstress here." 'seamstress' (*sibbani*) is a name for *tanha*. it means he has bypassed the seamstress called *tanha*.
now, as to the meaning of that verse, six bhikkhus offered six different explanations. i am not going to mention all six here. on this occasion, only the very first explanation is relevant. actually, when all six explanations were presented to the buddha, saying, "during our discussion, six different opinions arose like this," the buddha said that all six were correct. however, he declared that what he himself intended by that verse was the first explanation presented. that is the explanation we are presenting at this moment. during the discussion among the theras, the question arose: what are the two ends mentioned by the buddha in this verse? what is the middle? who is the seamstress called *sibbani*? that is why those six opinions were presented.
only the first opinion is relevant to us here. that first thera declared: "as i understand it, these two ends are *phassa* (contact) and the origin of *phassa* (*phassa-samudaya*)." there is nothing special to define about *phassa*. the origin of *phassa* means the arising of contact. *phassa* is one end, and the arising of *phassa* is the other end. the middle is the cessation of contact (*phassa-nirodha*). looking at this, too, it is like a riddle. *phassa* is one end, the origin of *phassa* is the second end, and the middle is *phassa-nirodha*, the cessation of contact.
next, *sibbani*, that is, the seamstress, is *tanha*. this is worth reflecting upon. it is a complete subject of meditation (*kammatthana*) in itself. although the buddha said the other explanations were also correct, since he intended the first explanation, we should pay closer attention to it.
thus, it shows a certain characteristic of *tanha*. along with this contact and the arising of contact, there is also its cessation taking place extremely rapidly. but we do not see it. cessation lies in the middle. there is a tendency in this *samsaric* being to forget that cessation. that is why it is generally said that *samsaric* beings dwell on the side of arising (*samudaya*). on one occasion, the buddha declared that those living in the fine-material worlds (*rupa-loka*) and those in the immaterial worlds (*arupa-loka*)—indeed, all these beings—keep returning to *samsara* and *bhava* (becoming) because they do not understand cessation (*nirodha*). this shows that we do not see this cessation, which is the breaking up and vanishing of things. instead, we connect one thing to another through *tanha*. through *tanha*, we only see each contact and the arising of contact. we do not see the cessation of contact. that cessation is the middle. in fact, the essence of this entire saddhamma is nibbana. nibbana is called cessation—*nirodho nibbanam*. so, what is unseen by ordinary worldlings is this cessation. thus, contact and the arising of contact are stitched together. when there is a seamstress, she joins two pieces of cloth and sews them. likewise, contact and the next arising of contact are joined together while forgetting the cessation of contact, ignoring the *nirodha*. it is through this that one falls under the power of *tanha*.
now, from the advice given to the arahant here, as well as from the advice previously given to bahiya daruciriya, we see that it stops at "in the seen, only the seen." it does not allow it to go beyond. it stops at the mere seeing. next, it does not allow contact to proliferate into *vedana* (feeling), *tanha*, and so forth. indeed, that is why *tanha* was called *ponobhavika* (leading to renewed existence). within *tanha* itself, there is a force that creates another existence (*bhava*).
on another occasion, there is a highly debated sutta passage. let us recall it. once, the wanderer vacchagotta, illustrating with a simile regarding the story of rebirth, asked about how a flame thrown and spread by the wind has what as its grasping (*upadana*) when a person dies. when someone dies, this life ends here; we do not see anything going. indeed, that is the very question of the whole world: what goes from here? there, the buddha declares that the flame, thrown and propelled by the wind, clings to another tree. similarly, within this *tanha* there is a nature of *upadana* (grasping / fuel). therefore, the buddha states that when one discards one body and goes to another body, it is *tanha* itself that assists. "*tanha* itself stands as the *upadana* (grasping / fuel)," he said. thus, we see that as long as there is *tanha*, there is also *upadana*. through *tanha*, something to grasp is created.
we can think of it like this. just as when we talk about a mirage, the vision seen by a deer appears as something helpful for drinking, *tanha* connects things again and again. that is one aspect of it—creating another existence (*bhava*) repeatedly. that is precisely why it is also described as *tatratatrabhinandini*—finding delight here and there—like jumping around from place to place. because of this, at the moment of death, due to not being satisfied, and because *tanha* is present, one wishes for another *bhava*. one wishes for a *bhava* in a subtle manner. how subtle this is, is shown in a statement by the buddha in a dhammapada verse:
> *"yathapi mule anupaddave dalhe,*
> *chinno’pi rukkho punareva ruhati;*
> *evam’pi tanhanusaye anuhate,*
> *nibbattati dukkham’idam punappunam."*
just as when the root of a tree remains undamaged and firm, the tree grows again even if its branches are cut down, so long as the underlying tendency of craving (*tanha-anusaya*) is not destroyed, this *dukkha* (suffering / unsatisfactoriness) arises again and again in *samsara*. it has been shown in that way.
thus, a dangerous side of *tanha* is shown. we are analyzing the very words mentioned in the verses. furthermore, more similes are mentioned in the dhamma. *visattika* refers to the sticky, clinging nature of *tanha*. it is also called *lepa* (plaster/glue). in sinhala, too, we use the word *lepa* as in "applying" (*alepa karanava*). *lepa* means the sticky nature. the buddha once gave a wonderful simile for this, like telling an ancient story, to the bhikkhus. this was particularly addressed to the bhikkhus, though the world too can learn something from it. in the himalayan forests, there are level regions where both humans and monkeys roam. in such areas, a hunter seeking to catch monkeys hangs some sticky pitch/gum (*lepa*) on a tree along the path where monkeys travel as a trap. so, a foolish monkey, being greedy by nature, goes and touches that sticky pitch with one hand. when he touches it, it sticks. next, trying to free it with his other hand, that hand also gets stuck. the buddha describes it in this way. next, to free his two hands, he presses one foot against it. that foot also gets stuck in the pitch. then, to free his hands and foot, he presses his other foot against it. that also gets stuck. now, both hands and both feet are stuck in this pile of pitch. this is a method of catching monkeys, a kind of trap. then, the monkey presses his snout/mouth against it to free them. that too gets stuck. in the end, the monkey, stuck in five places, is shot/captured by the hunter and taken away.
that simile was given to show the *lepa* (sticky) nature of *tanha* arising from the five strands of sensual pleasure—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. in that way, on various occasions, the buddha described that sticky nature of *tanha*, the world's clinging nature, as *lepa*. having taught the disadvantageous side in that manner, and on various other occasions, the buddha showed how *tanha* repeatedly creates another *bhava*. this is because there is a nature in *tanha* that is never satisfied, like the ocean that is never filled. since there is no limit to *tanha*, it is repeatedly clinging to the next *bhava*. it is also called *nati* (leaning/inclination). if a mountain range leans towards one side, it will fall to that side. within *tanha* there is a nature that carries the world repeatedly to another *bhava*.
next, the root of *tanha* has also been declared—to dig up the root of *tanha* like digging up the *birana* bush. what is the root of *tanha*? the root of *tanha* is shown to be *avijja* (ignorance) itself. that is why it is said to uproot this root with the help of *vijja* (wisdom/clear vision). this *avijja*, which is the root of *tanha*, is sometimes shown as the non-seeing of the *anicca* (impermanent) nature of this eye, the incoming objects, and every phenomenon arising in connection with them. thus, sometimes it is shown how the world lives within these sense bases. to show this, the buddha points out the reality as follows: "bhikkhus, the eye is *anicca* (impermanent), unstable, subject to change. forms are *anicca*, unstable, subject to change. *calam*—it is moving, unstable. there is a nature in the eye of becoming otherwise. forms are the same."
next, because of not understanding that *anicca* nature, dependent on those two, *vinnana* (consciousness) arises. but the buddha says *vinnana* is also *anicca*. so, the eye is *anicca*, forms are *anicca*. by taking what is *anicca* as permanent, and through the coming together of those two, the illusion called *cakkhu-vinnana* (eye-consciousness) arises. that is why *vinnana* is called an illusion. trees and plants do not have it. so, this being with defilements like *avijja* and *tanha* took the eye to be permanent. he took a stand there. next, without thinking of forms as a mirage, he took a stand there too. those two came together and arose. but the buddha says that *vinnana* is also *anicca*. yet, due to not understanding that either, bringing all three together, one constructed something called *phassa* (contact). there comes that story of *phassa*—*cakkhu-samphassa* (eye-contact). but the buddha says that *cakkhu-samphassa* is also *anicca*. the world does not see it. by taking that too as permanent, one creates a sensation—one creates it in terms of *vedana* (feeling). those too are *anicca*. it is this non-seeing of *aniccata* (impermanence) that is the cause of our falling under the power of *tanha*. indeed, if one understands the twelve links of *paticcasamuppada* (dependent arising), we see that there are many links prior to *tanha*. at the root is *avijja*. this shows that the world falls under *tanha* because they do not know the four noble truths—that is, due to *avijja*. without knowing that a mass of *dukkha* is arising, we consider them as permanent. thus, it shows us that knowing the true nature lies within the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*).
if one constantly remembers that the eye is *anicca*, forms are *anicca*, the resulting *vinnana* is *anicca*, the contact (*phassa*) from the coming together of those three is *anicca*, and the feeling (*vedana*) arising from it is *anicca*—when one develops the perception of impermanence, such *tanha* and so forth cannot accumulate. that is the meaning.
the buddha on one occasion declared: "bhikkhus, when the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*) is developed and cultivated..." if the perception of impermanence is well developed, it destroys all sensual lust (*kama-raga*), lust for existence (*bhava-raga*), and lust for form (*rupa-raga*). now next, there is a certain sutta discourse related to this *avijja*, *tanha*, and the story of the "dart" (*salla*) mentioned in the final verse.
if we take the portion relevant to us from a discourse preached by the buddha to a licchavi youth on one occasion; a wonderful simile is given there too. the buddha says: a man was struck by a poisoned arrow. when this happened, his relatives summoned a physician. here, he is described as *bhisakko sallakatto*. *sallakatta* means the surgeon. *bhisakka* means the poison-doctor or physician. so, both are connected. they summon a doctor who knows both general medicine and surgery. the doctor, using an instrument used by surgeons, opens the wound where the arrow struck, and then, if any part of the arrow remains in the body, to locate it—a pali word is used there, *esani*, which is a probe used by surgeons to extract a dart—he pulls out the dart with that instrument. having extracted it, he applies medicine to heal it.
next, comparing the simile with the meaning, the buddha states: that man struck by the poisoned arrow is this worldling, pierced by the dart of craving (*tanha-salla*). what is the poison in this dart of *tanha*? it is *avijja* (ignorance). it is called the poison of *avijja*. thus, the word *tanha-salla* (the dart of craving) is mentioned in many places. the buddha is called the destroyer of the dart of craving (*tanha-sallassa hanta*). this became a poisoned arrow precisely due to that toxic defect of *avijja*.
next, the instrument used to open the wound is called "noble wisdom" (*ariya-panna*). next, the probe called *esani* used to locate the dart is mindfulness (*sati*). that is why it is said that everything is contained within *satipatthana* (establishments of mindfulness). so, opening the wound through noble wisdom, and using the probe of mindfulness (*sati*), one locates and extracts that dart.
next, who is this surgeon, this physician? it is the tathagata. thus, based on this simile given by the buddha, one should treat oneself. that is how that verse concluded: *abbahe*—one pulled out one's own dart. that was extracted through the instruments shown according to the surgical and medical principles given by the buddha. from this, one can understand that the dart of *tanha* is pierced within. it is a poisoned arrow. that poison is *avijja*. so, to extract it, one uses the weapon of noble wisdom. opening the wound and through mindfulness (*sati*), one extracts that arrow from where it was pierced. that is where the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*) is helpful.
so, that wisdom is on one side. the buddha has given the world the fundamental understanding to pull out that dart. in fact, the buddha highlighted the nature of arising and passing away—*udayabbaya*—present in everything in the world. that is "perception of impermanence" (*anicca-sanna*). in two words, it is *udayabbaya*—through arising and passing away. so, that is the basic lesson of insight (*vipassana*). first, within this perception of impermanence, one sees the arising and passing away of everything. even realizing this is difficult for the ordinary worldling, because, due to the work of the aforementioned seamstress, they forget the passing away side. the world likes this forgetting very much.
to tell you an incident from daily life: in this world of fashion, there are clothes and other things you use. once you buy a more valuable, modern design from the shops for some money and bring it home, the old one goes somewhere and ends up in the rubbish heap. thus, forgetting the passing away side, they renew it. worldlings are constantly renewing. *tanha* assists in this. the seamstress *tanha* ties knots. what is that knot? forgetting cessation (*nirodha*). forgetting that this breaks up. then, what does the practitioner of insight (*vipassana*) do? with the help of that fundamental principle given by the buddha, he sees that everything has a nature of arising and passing away momentarily and very rapidly. to show this, it was said that "this eye exists." from the very beginning of this sermon, "this eye of mine exists." likewise, "forms exist." "you, devotees, are in front of me." we do not say that they do not exist. but the buddha says that the eye is also *anicca*, changing moment by moment, *calam*—it is moving. in that way, many words are used there, like *annathabhavi* (becoming otherwise). words like *aniccam*, *calam*, *vayam*, *viparinami*, *annathabhavi*, etc., are applied to impress this upon the mind. although none of this is visible to the physical eye known to the ordinary world, this eye also changes extremely rapidly. next, the thing we took to be "form" also changes in the same way. but we do not realize it. the aforementioned *tanha* stitches it together. even when it is said that *vinnana* (consciousness) is also *anicca*, we do not realize that either. that is indeed the deepest point.
generally, we said that if we take all four—seen, heard, sensed, cognized—turning back to what was explained earlier, these are the six bases themselves taken as seen, heard, sensed, cognized. among them, the "seen" is highly gross (*olarika*) and coarse. because even if we look at something and then look away, it seems to still be there, doesn't it? it is still there. how can we say it is not? although the buddha says it is not, it remains visible to our physical eye, and we say it exists in that very manner. even if we are told, when we look once and look away, it remains just as it was. so, how can we say it changes? thus, looked at in that way, the "seen" is still coarse and gross.
next, how about the "heard"? now, as long as there is an echo of the words i speak, you will hear them. sometimes we have heard that in vast deserts where no echo can occur, when someone speaks, the words vanish right where they are spoken. now, you know very well the echo coming from the surrounding hills, don't you? it is like two people speaking. likewise, in this environment, the sound we make reverberates and returns as an echo. that further assists our hearing. though it is not as gross as the "seen," the "heard" is also somewhat gross.
next, what is more personal and even subtler is found in the "sensed" (*muta*). the "sensed" refers to what is felt by the tongue, nose, and body. now, just like what andare did, if someone says "this is delicious," to show that taste to another, he must feed it to him. otherwise, it is impossible. it is highly personal. it is extremely subtle there. what is sensed by the nose, tongue, and body is extremely subtle. so, searching for their impermanence is harder than the others.
next, the "cognized" (*vinnata*) is even harder and subtler. the cognized mind—the story about that mind is said to be a bizarre illusion (*maya*). there, what are the objects coming to the mind? not *dhamma* in the sense of the teachings. if we speak of them as objects, just as forms are to the eye, sounds to the ear, smells to the nose, tastes to the tongue, and touch to the body, so *dhamma* is applied to the mind. if we translate *dhamma*, it means "things that come to the mind." we think the mind is one thing, and the things coming to the mind are another. those two must collide. we are caught right there. that is what the buddha preached: *"manopubbangama dhamma, manosettha manomaya"*. there, *dhamma* means thoughts/objects coming to the mind. but the world thinks that the things coming to the mind exist separately. however, the buddha says the mind is the forerunner. these are mind-made. things constructed by the mind. right there is the work of the magician—the illusion (*maya*). yet, the world does not realize it. taking the thought coming to the mind as separate, making it our own, we get caught in clinging, entanglement, confusion, and *papanca* (conceptual proliferation / prolific conceptualization). that is the extremely subtle point. it is there that the practitioner of insight gradually extracts the impermanence of the seen, starting from that, and next contemplates the impermanence of the heard. going even deeper, there is what is personally felt, what is felt by the tongue. that is why it is said that one can realize nibbana based on any one of these six sense bases. from that perspective, one can say nibbana is at the tip of the tongue.
that is why in the past, some bhikkhus are said to have attained arahantship while taking their meals, by contemplating that contact (*phassa*) felt on the tongue. likewise, contemplating the contact felt by the eye, even upon seeing the form of a dancing girl, they are said to have attained arahantship by generating the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*) at that moment. similarly, one can realize nibbana through what is heard by the ear, and through the smell felt by the nose. but the world does not turn in that direction. for one who constantly contemplates those two—arising and passing away—given by the buddha, as one goes deeper into the understanding of arising and passing away, the breaking-up side (*bhanga*) becomes clearer to the practitioner of insight than before. the side of breaking up, which was unseen hitherto. because as that desire called *tanha* fades away, the true nature emerges. the buddha's word on arising and passing away becomes clear. when, between the two of arising and passing away, the breaking-up side is seen more clearly, that is where knowledge of dissolution—*bhanga-nana*—is shown in insight meditation. to that person, everything is seen as breaking up. even thoughts are seen to dissolve. then, it is from those breakups that disadvantages and so forth arise. there lies *mano-samphassa* (mind-contact). understanding that the thought coming to the mind strikes the mind is also extremely subtle. yet, at some point, a space is seen: the mind and the thought strike each other. when one understands that they strike in this way, it is called "in the cognized, only the cognized" (*vinnate vinnatamattam*). it is said that the ascetic bahiya daruciriya attained arahantship the moment this was said, extremely rapidly.
this arahant malunkyaputta also attained arahantship quickly by depending on this brief advice. from this, we see that beyond stopping at "in the seen, only the seen," next is "in the heard, only the heard," "in the sensed, only the sensed," and finally "in the cognized, only the cognized." this is something so wonderful that it is hard for us to even conceive. the practitioner of insight, at some stage in meditation, understands according to the buddha's word that both the mind and the thought are *anicca*, subject to change. instead of saying "heart," let us say "mind" (*manas*) is *anicca*, and the mental object (*dhamma*) coming to the mind is also subject to change. it is when such changing things come together that it is called mind-consciousness (*mano-vinnana*). that is what the buddha means. the beings of this world, even those in the aforementioned fine-material and immaterial worlds, create another *bhava* repeatedly because they do not know cessation (*nirodha*). if they saw cessation, just as in the story of the seamstress: *"yo ubhante viditvana"*—having known these two ends. one understood contact (*phassa*). one understood the origin of contact. next, when the mind is established in that cessation of contact—*phassa-nirodha*—that is when one is liberated. one is liberated from the world, freed from the world. this is what is meant by "the end of *dukkha*." we previously mentioned the story of the flame. so, this *tanha*—as long as there is unsatisfied desire, incomplete desire, the mind constantly radiates outward. it radiates outward from this body. it grasps whatever is presented by kamma. be it a mother's womb, an animal's womb, or in hell, the sign presented according to kamma is grasped through *tanha* at the moment of death. as long as the underlying tendency of craving (*tanha-anusaya*) is present, there is no need to explain further about being reborn. there is no need for a strange life-force to go and plant itself there, as the world thinks. *tanha* is sufficient. that is why it was said that just as a flame is thrown and spread by the wind, as long as *tanha* exists, beings of the world construct another *bhava*. this is what we called *ponobhavika*. now, one understands here that it is *tanha* that creates renewed existence (*punarbhava*). to understand its operation, one must eliminate the aforementioned *avijja* and bring forth noble wisdom (*ariya-panna*).
now, we have presented the meaning of those brief discourses in the verses in various ways. it is possible to explain even further. but if you would at least apply your minds to the similes given by the buddha, you can understand many things. we wish that this discourse will assist you in walking on this path of insight (*vipassana-magga*) at your own level in daily life. it is because you understand the fearsomeness of *samsara* that you observe the precepts and practice meditation on an occasion like this. indeed, this is a time when the fearsome nature of this *samsara* becomes self-evident to oneself, according to the teachings of the buddha.
therefore, as long as we do not eliminate that aforementioned *tanha*, no matter how much we say "i will not be born again," that birth belongs to us because of that aforementioned inclination (*nati*). for that reason, one must strive again and again, with the help of the virtue (*sila*) one guards, through meditations like tranquility (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassana*), to realize the noble wisdom shown by the buddha, through the penetration of the paths and fruits of stream-entry (*sotapatti*), once-returning (*sakadagamita*), non-returning (*anagamita*), and arahantship—and by using *satipatthana* and mindfulness (*sati*), may you aspire that this discourse will help you realize in this very life the supreme state you hope for. then, may all beings from avici to akanittha, whoever wish to rejoice in this sharing of the merit of preaching and hearing the dhamma, by so rejoicing, realize the supreme, deathless, great nibbana through the bodhi of their aspiration. say in this manner.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 061
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #61
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.88)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Accāraddhamhi vīriyamhi,
satthā loke anuttaro;
Vīṇūpamaṃ karitvā me,
dhammaṃ desesi cakkhumā.
Tassāhaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā,
vihāsiṃ sāsane rato.
Samathaṃ paṭipādesiṃ,
uttamatthassa pattiyā;
Tisso vijjā anuppattā,
kataṃ buddhassa sāsanaṃ.
From:
Khuddaka Nikāya → Theragāthā → Terasanipāta → Soṇakoḷivisattheragāthā → Thag 13.1 (verses 638–639)
Dear Listeners,
The Supreme Buddha, the Teacher of the Three Worlds, has declared that this Dhamma, which leads to the great, deathless Nibbāna, is for one who has aroused energy (*āraddha-vīriya*), and not for the lazy or indolent. It is shown in this Dhamma-Vinaya that only the energetic person lives happily, and that living even a single day with aroused energy is far more noble than living a hundred years in laziness and indolence. That is why on this Vap Full Moon Poya day, we hope to present some verses and a story that are meaningful and inspiring specifically to the energetic person.
In the city of Campā, which belonged to the kingdom of King Bimbisāra, a meritorious child was born to the millionaire family of Kolivisa. His parents named the child Soṇa. The body of this millionaire's son, Soṇa Kolivisa, was extremely delicate and tender. So delicate was he that hair grew even on the soles of his feet. This was a wondrous thing. King Bimbisāra heard this news, and on one occasion, when summoning eighty thousand village chiefs for state affairs, he sent a messenger with a message saying, "I wish to see Soṇa. It would be good if Soṇa comes here. Please arrange for him to come." So, Soṇa’s parents told the millionaire’s son: "Son, the King wishes to see the soles of your feet. When you go there, do not stretch out your feet towards the King. Sit cross-legged—that is, fold your legs—and then the King will see the soles of your feet."
So, when the people of Campā went to see King Bimbisāra, the millionaire's son Soṇa Kolivisa was carried in a palanquin. Having been brought before the King, the millionaire's son Soṇa paid homage to the King and sat down in the manner described. The King saw the soles of his feet. He witnessed the wondrous phenomenon of hair growing on the soles of his feet. Next, the King gave instructions on state matters to the eighty thousand village chiefs and said: "Now I have shown you how to achieve well-being in this world. To secure well-being in the next world, go and meet the Blessed One."
At that time, the Blessed One was residing on the Vulture's Peak mountain (Gijjhakaṭa). So, this crowd of eighty thousand went to pay respects to the Buddha. At that time, the Buddha's personal attendant was Venerable Sāgata, a monk who had practiced kasina meditation and possessed great meditative absorptive powers. Venerable Sāgata conveyed the invitation to the Buddha on behalf of the eighty thousand people in a miraculous manner. Disappearing from where he stood, as if diving into the earth, he presented the invitation to the Buddha.
Having witnessed this psychic miracle, the eighty thousand people focused their attention on Venerable Sāgata even more than on the Buddha. Understanding this, the Buddha told Venerable Sāgata: "Sāgata, display more psychic marvels." So, the Venerable monk rose into the air, and performed various miracles related to the fire-kasina (*tejo-kasiṇa*), such as sitting in the sky, walking up and down, and emitting flames, and finally descended to the ground, worshipped the Buddha's feet, and declared: "The Blessed One is my Teacher, I am the disciple."
Hearing this, the crowd thought, "If the disciple can do such wondrous things, how great must the Teacher be!" At that moment when confidence (*saddhā*) arose in them, the Buddha delivered a Dhamma sermon consisting of the gradual instruction (*anupubbikathā*). It is mentioned that upon hearing that Dhamma sermon, the entire crowd attained the fruit of Stream-entry (*Sotāpatti-phala*) on their very seats. Having attained the fruit of Stream-entry, they became lay devotees who had taken refuge in the Triple Gem.
Then, the millionaire's son, Soṇa Kolivisa, who was in this crowd, was deeply moved by this Dhamma sermon and thought: "It is not easy to live the pure holy life (*brahmacariya*) according to the Dhamma preached by the Blessed One while remaining in lay life. I must ordain." With this resolve, he approached the Buddha and requested ordination. The Buddha granted him ordination and higher ordination (*upasampadā*).
Not long after his higher ordination, Venerable Soṇa went to the forest dwelling known as Sītavana (Cool Grove) and began practicing intense energy. He put in such great energy that, by spending too much time on the walking path (*caṅkamana*), the soles of his feet, which had hair on them, cracked. They cracked and began to bleed. It bled so much that the walking path was covered in blood, looking like a slaughterhouse where cattle had been killed. When, despite practicing such intense energy, he did not attain Arahantship, Venerable Soṇa, during a moment of rest, thought: "Among those disciples of the Blessed One who have aroused energy (*āraddha-vīriya*), I am indeed one. Yet, despite putting in such energy, I have not achieved Arahantship. There are abundant riches and wealth in our family. Therefore, I should enjoy those riches and perform meritorious deeds." Thus, he thought of returning to the lay life.
The Buddha, who was staying on the Vulture's Peak, perceived this thought of Venerable Soṇa Kolivisa. Right at that moment, as quickly as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm, the Buddha vanished from Vulture's Peak and appeared in Sītavana. Then, the Buddha went on a tour of the lodgings with the other monks residing in Sītavana, as if to inspect lodgings from dwelling to dwelling, hut to hut. While walking, He came to the walking path of Venerable Soṇa Kolivisa and asked the monks: "Whose walking path is this? This path covered in blood, looking like a slaughterhouse?" The monks replied: "Venerable Sir, this is the walking path of the Venerable Soṇa. Venerable Soṇa, having exerted extreme and excessive energy, walked up and down until his path was covered in blood in this manner."
Then, the Buddha went to Venerable Soṇa's hut. Sitting on the prepared seat, He asked Venerable Soṇa: "Soṇa, did a thought like this occur to you during a moment of rest: 'Now, despite exerting so much energy, I have not become an Arahant. Therefore, I should return to lay life'?" "Yes, Venerable Sir," he replied. Then the Buddha asked: "Soṇa, when you were a layman, were you not skilled in playing the lute?" "Yes, Venerable Sir," he replied. "How was it, Soṇa? When the strings of your lute were pulled too tight, extremely tight, was the lute in a playable condition?" "No, Venerable Sir." "And when the strings of your lute were too loose, was it in a good condition? Could the lute be played?" "No, not even then, Venerable Sir." "But, Soṇa, when the strings of your lute were neither too tight nor too loose, but tuned to an even pitch, was it then playable and melodious?" "Yes, Venerable Sir," he replied.
Thus, using the simile of the lute, He gave advice to Venerable Soṇa. Having given this advice, He returned to Vulture's Peak through the air. Venerable Soṇa, acting according to this advice, practiced energy once more and understood the principle of the balancing of energy (*vīriya-samatā*)—the fact that there must be a certain middle or balanced state regarding energy.
There is something called "balancing of the faculties" (*indriya-samatā*) in this Dhamma. What are called "faculties" (*indriya*) here are not the external physical faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. The spiritual faculties (*indriya*) are conviction (*saddhā*), energy (*vīriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*), which are wholesome qualities that assist in reaching the noble state. Understanding the need for a certain balance among these, and the importance of developing them to a middle, balanced level, Venerable Soṇa very quickly realized Arahantship.
Having become an Arahant, he then thought: "I must declare my Arahantship to the Blessed One." He approached the Buddha and, without explicitly saying he had attained Arahantship, presented the state of an Arahant's mind by explaining a range of Dhamma principles. The Buddha too, praised this, declaring to the community of monks: "This is indeed how noble clansmen declare their Arahantship; without explicitly asserting, 'I have attained Arahantship,' they reveal their attainment through Dhamma principles. That is the correct method. In doing so, their fewness of wishes is a valuable quality. It is a valuable quality of those noble ones who have achieved the higher realization." Thus, the Buddha praised it.
Then the Buddha said: "Soṇa, your body is extremely delicate. Therefore, I allow you to wear single-layered footwear." Then, Venerable Soṇa replied: "Venerable Sir, I renounced eighty cartloads of gold coins and various other luxuries, left the household life, and ordained. Having ordained, if I start using a pair of single-layered footwear as a special privilege, people might start rumors. They might blame me. They would say: 'This monk Soṇa Kolivisa, having renounced wealth as vast as eighty cartloads, has now developed an attachment to a single-layered pair of sandals; he has become attached to it.' Therefore, if the Blessed One allows the wearing of footwear for the Sangha in general, I too will use them. If the Blessed One does not grant permission to the Sangha in general, then I too will not use them." It was on that occasion that the Buddha, for the first time, declared to the monks: "I allow single-layered footwear."
From this, you lay devotees can understand many things. When the Buddha on various occasions awarded the chief (*etadagga*) titles to monks who excelled in outstanding qualities, He also paid special honor to Venerable Soṇa by declaring him the foremost among those of His disciples who have aroused energy (*āraddha-vīriya*).
Thus, presenting all these facts, Venerable Soṇa expressed his past course of practice in verses, and two of those verses mentioned in the *Theragāthā* are what we have placed today as our theme.
> *Accāraddhamhi vīriyamhi,*
> *samatho me anuttaro;*
> *Vīṇūpamaṃ pi me dhammaṃ,*
> *desesi cakkhumā.*
"Regarding the matter of over-exerted energy, the Unsurpassed Teacher in the world, the One with Vision, preached the Dhamma to me using the simile of the lute."
> *Tassāhaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā,*
> *vihāsiṃ sāsane rato;*
"Having heard His word, I dwelt delighting in the Dispensation."
"For the attainment of the supreme goal—noble Nibbāna—I achieved the balancing of the faculties (*indriya-samatā*)."
> *Tisso vijjā anuppattā,*
> *kataṃ buddhassa sāsanaṃ.*
"The Three Knowledges—namely, the recollection of past lives (*pubbe-nivāsānussati*), the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*), and the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*)—have been attained. The instruction of the Buddha has been fulfilled." These are the two verses from the *Theragāthā* that we have placed as our theme.
Through this story, many noble qualities in the character of Venerable Soṇa Kolivisa are revealed to us. Let us look particularly at his development of energy. If someone with such delicate soles had been full of pride like an ordinary person, he might have thought: "Even King Bimbisāra summoned me just to see this feature of mine. I cannot perform walking meditation." He did not think so. Energetically, he engaged in walking meditation. Ultimately, he put in such intense energy that his feet cracked and bled.
Then, wisely understanding the simile of the lute presented by the Buddha, he brought himself to a balanced state of energy—a middle state—and thereby attained Arahantship. Furthermore, after attaining Arahantship, his declaration before the Buddha was highly exemplary; without explicitly saying "I have attained Arahantship," he presented it through Dhamma principles by describing the nature of an Arahant's mind as he understood it. Also, how content with little (*appiccha*) he was! He did not expect any special privileges. When the Buddha allowed him footwear, he stated that he would use them only if permission was granted to the Sangha in general. All of these are a collection of valuable qualities that we should take as examples.
Next, when considering the Dhamma aspects, the key points are the balancing of energy (*vīriya-samatā*) and the balancing of the faculties (*indriya-samatā*). What is this balancing of the faculties (*indriya-samatā*)? Merit-seeking friends, it is not the external faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body that assist in seeing Nibbāna. Indeed, what assists in realizing Nibbāna are the five spiritual faculties (*indriya*) of the Dispensation: conviction (*saddhā*), energy (*vīriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*). Why are these presented as "faculties" (*indriya*)? It is because when they are developed and strengthened in one's mind, one understands the Dhamma of Nibbāna through that power and strength. There is also a certain systematic order among these five. We can understand it in this way.
It is in one who has conviction (*saddhā*) that energy (*vīriya*) arises. Through conviction, energy is brought forth. Conviction is necessary to bring forth energy. Relying on energy, mindfulness (*sati*) is established. One develops mindfulness in the form of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). By developing mindfulness, one achieves concentration (*samādhi*)—one-pointedness of mind. It is with a concentrated mind that one understands reality as it is through insight (*vipassanā*), understanding the impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anattā*) nature of the world, and thereby brings forth insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*). In this way, there is a connection of one to another among the five: conviction, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
However, when discussing their balance (*samatā*), we have to analyze it in a different way. The two factors, conviction and wisdom, are shown as a pair, a twin quality. Conviction is said to be related to the heart. Conviction means placing the heart (devotion). It is the emotional/affective aspect. The quality of conviction belongs to the feeling aspect of a person. Wisdom belongs to the understanding aspect. It is the intellectual/cognitive aspect. There must be a balance between these two. Teachers of old described a person who is low in conviction but high only in intellect as cunning or deceitful. One who has only conviction but lacks intellect becomes a foolish person; he develops blind faith even in improper things. To balance these, one enters the practice to develop wisdom through conviction. That is why it is necessary. Thus it is with those two.
Similarly, another pair is energy and concentration. Energy tends toward restlessness (*uddhacca*). If one exerts excessive energy, the mind is bound to become restless. That is what happened to Venerable Soṇa. Concentration brings stillness to the mind. It is something that leads to sluggishness (*līnatā*) or absolute stillness. Restlessness comes through energy; the goal of concentration is stillness. At a glance, these seem contradictory. However, these must be developed systematically and evenly. One cannot develop concentration without energy. It is necessary to reach a certain level of concentration; it does not come by just doing nothing. Mindfulness (*sati*), which stands in the middle of these, balances conviction, wisdom, energy, and concentration, just like the needle of a weighing scale. There is such a relationship among these five Dhamma factors.
The balancing of the faculties (*indriya-samatā*) is an important matter in this Dispensation. Through the balancing of the faculties, we can see the Middle Path taught by the Buddha. In the middle way, nothing is extremist. Here, every factor assists another, at a balanced, middle level. Bringing it to this balanced level might sometimes exceed limits for certain individuals, depending on their personal disposition. Just like Venerable Soṇa, who practiced excessive energy until his feet cracked and bled. As you all know, the Buddha Himself was caught up in the two extremes. Everyone has heard of the two extremes mentioned in the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*. He experienced self-indulgence (*kāmasukhallikānuyoga*) in the royal palace, and He was also caught in the extreme of self-mortification (*attakilamathānuyoga*). It was after abandoning both those extremes that He arrived at the balanced level.
Not only that, on one occasion, the Buddha explained very intimately to the three monks Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila how He Himself had realized this balancing of energy during His days as a Bodhisatta. "On one occasion, I exerted intense energy." He gave a simile for this: "If a person trying to catch a quail holds it too tightly in his grasp, the quail might die. On the other hand, if he holds it too loosely, the bird will fly away. In the same way, I understood from that simile that energy must be balanced." He explained this based on His own experience through various similes.
Teachers of old also illustrated this point regarding the balancing of energy with various similes on different occasions. One simile found in the texts is that of the surgeon. In ancient times, surgeons trained their students—especially in surgeries like eye surgery—by having them draw lines with a scalpel on a blue water-lily petal floating on water. If someone is overly agitated, they will either submerge the lily petal in water or slice it completely through. The unskilled person, who has no dexterity, is too afraid even to touch the lily petal with the blade. The truly skilled person, who can apply balanced energy, is the one who carefully draws lines on the lily petal with the blade and passes the exercise.
There is another simile: the simile of filling oil into a narrow tube. If one tries to pour oil in a hurry, the oil will spill. On the other hand, some might be unable to pour oil into a narrow-mouthed tube because they are too afraid of spilling it. But if one applies extremely balanced energy, carefully and with mindfulness (*sati*), one can fill the oil successfully.
To take a simile suited to the modern mind, though not found in the texts: think of long-distance races in stadiums—let's say a ten-lap race around the track. What do some unskilled runners do? Eager for the cheers of the spectators, they run the first two or three laps as fast as they can. In the end, they are exhausted and have to drop out of the race. But what does the truly skilled runner do? He runs at a steady, moderate pace for the first few laps. It is in the final stretch, as if possessing the fourfold energy (*caturanga-samannāgata-vīriya*), that he applies his conserved strength when the right moment arrives, runs very fast, and wins the race.
The fourfold energy (*caturanga-samannāgata-vīriya*) is mentioned in the life of the Buddha. You devotees must have heard of this. Once the right time comes, once the balancing of energy is perfectly achieved, the energy applied is one of life-sacrifice. "Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain; let flesh and blood dry up. Whatever goal can be achieved by manly energy, by manly strength, by manly effort, will not be abandoned until it is reached." The Buddha Himself exerted this supreme effort, known as the fourfold energy (*caturanga-samannāgata-vīriya*). He also exhorted His disciples to apply such energy.
However, this energy becomes successful only when, as mentioned before, the balancing of the faculties (*indriya-samatā*) emerges. Only after arriving at the balanced middle. Indeed, it was only after arriving at the Middle Path that the Buddha realized Buddhahood through that fourfold energy. What happened to Venerable Soṇa initially was that he exerted extreme energy on the walking path for long periods in a way his body could not withstand. It was because of this that he even became discouraged in the first place.
The Buddha has illustrated the balancing of energy in the Dhamma through various similes. On one occasion, the Buddha related to the monks an account concerning a past Buddha. The Buddha Sikhī once visited a certain Brahma-world along with His chief disciple, the monk Abhibhū. Having gone there, He assigned that disciple, Venerable Abhibhū, to preach the Dhamma to the Brahmas. On that occasion, the psychically powerful Venerable Abhibhū proclaimed two verses in a voice that resounded throughout a thousand world systems. These are very famous among energetic practitioners as the *Aruṇavatī Sutta*. One of those verses is as follows:
> *Ārabhatha nikkhamatha,*
> *yuñjatha buddhasāsane;*
> *Dhunātha maccuno senaṃ,*
> *naḷāgāraṃva kuñjaro.*
Even upon hearing it, it is phrased in a way that arouses energy. "Arouse energy, go forth, exert yourself in the Buddha's Dispensation; destroy the army of Death, like an elephant crushing a reed-hut." Such teachings on energy are found in the Dhamma.
Similarly, the Buddha Himself has pointed out three types of potential energies within our mental continuum as qualities that help overcome sleepiness and laziness:
*   *Ārambha-dhātu*: the element of instigating effort (the power to begin something).
*   *Nikkhama-dhātu*: the element of launching out (the power to carry forward what has been started).
*   *Parakkama-dhātu*: the element of exerting progress (the power to advance by overcoming obstacles encountered along the way). These energies exist within us.
This is precisely what is indicated in that verse:
*   *Ārabhatha* - "Arouse energy" (corresponds to *ārambha-dhātu*).
*   *Nikkhamatha* - "Go forth" (corresponds to *nikkhama-dhātu*).
*   *Yuñjatha* - "Exert yourself" (corresponds to *parakkama-dhātu*, overcoming obstacles and moving forward).
That showed the value of developing energy.
Likewise, on one occasion, the Buddha showed the eight grounds for laziness (*kusīta-vatthu*) and the eight grounds for arousing energy (*ārambha-vatthu*). What are called the "grounds for laziness" (*kusīta-vatthu*) are the eight occasions a lazy person uses to justify his lazy behavior. What are they? This is illustrated using a lazy monk. But it is not only for a monk; even a practicing layperson can take an example from this teaching. A lazy monk thinks in this way:
1.  The lazy monk has some special work to do. Let us say a task connected with monastic life, such as dyeing robes. Then that monk thinks: "Now, I have such-and-such work to do. When doing this work, my body will get very tired. Therefore, I must sleep now." Saying this, he sleeps.
2.  Next, let us say he has finished the work. Once the work is done, that monk thinks: "Now, I have done some heavy work. I am tired. Therefore, I must sleep now." He sleeps. Thus, he slept before doing it, and he slept after finishing it as well.
3.  Next, let us say the lazy monk has to go on a journey. Before embarking on the journey, he thinks: "Now, when I go on the journey, my body will get tired. Therefore, I must rest now." He sleeps.
4.  Next, he returns from the journey. Then he thinks: "Now, because I went on the journey, I am very tired." He sleeps. He slept again.
5.  Next, the lazy monk goes on alms-round (*piṇḍapāta*). That day, he does not receive a stomach-full of food on his alms-round. Then he thinks: "Now my body is very weak. Today I did not receive proper food. Therefore, I must sleep." He sleeps.
6.  Alternatively, let us say he received plenty of food on his alms-round. Having eaten his fill, after finishing the meal, he thinks: "Today my body is very heavy, as if stuffed with beans. Today, therefore, I cannot meditate." He sleeps.
7.  Next, when the lazy monk has a slight illness, how does he think? "Now, I have fallen ill. How can a sick person meditate?" So he sleeps.
8.  Next, after he recovers from that illness, he thinks: "I have only just recovered from this illness. My body does not yet have full strength." Therefore, he sleeps.
He is asleep all the time, the lazy monk, in this manner.
The Buddha shows in this wonderful manner how the energetic monk uses these very same situations to arouse his energy:
1.  The energetic monk has some special work to do. Then what does he think? "I have such-and-such work to do. While doing that work, I will not be able to easily maintain my meditative wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) according to the Buddha's instruction. Therefore, I must practice energy right now. I must meditate, so as to quickly realize Nibbāna." Thus, he meditates with great enthusiasm.
2.  Next, having finished that work, how does the energetic monk think? "While doing that work, I was unable to maintain my meditative wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) according to the Buddha's instruction. Now at least I must do so." Thus, he meditates with enthusiasm.
3.  The energetic monk has to go on a journey. So, that monk thinks: "Now, I have to go on such-and-such a journey. While traveling, I will not be able to meditate properly according to the Buddha's instruction. Therefore, I must meditate right now, before the journey."
4.  After returning from the journey, that monk thinks: "While on the journey, I was unable to meditate properly. Now at least I must do so." Thus, he meditates.
5.  When the energetic monk goes on alms-round and on a certain day does not receive a stomach-full of food, how does he think? "Today my body is very light. Today my body is highly active and workable. Today I must meditate. That is the best thing to do." Thinking thus when receiving little food, he meditates.
6.  On another day, returning from alms-round after receiving a stomach-full of food, how does he think? "Today my body has good strength. I must meditate well." Thus, he meditates.
7.  Next, when the monk with aroused energy (*āraddha-vīriya*) gets a slight illness, how does he think? "Now, a slight illness has arisen in me. If it increases, I might even die. Therefore, I must meditate right now." Thus, he meditates.
8.  As soon as he recovers from the illness, when he has just risen from his sickbed, what does he think? "Because of this illness, I was unable to practice properly. Perhaps the illness might return. Therefore, before that happens, I must meditate well to see Nibbāna." Thinking thus, he meditates.
Through this, we can see that between laziness, indolence, and energy, there is actually only a difference in attitude. This correct attitude, which is praised by the Buddha, is indeed the attitude of the energetic person. The energetic person utilizes every arising opportunity in a way that assists in reaching Nibbāna. The lazy person uses every single one of them in a way that assists saṃsāra. As there is a saying, "The lazy man has divine eyes..." Just like that, the lazy person has excuses for everything. The Buddha has always given the foremost place to the energetic person.
Furthermore, the Buddha introduces Himself as a teacher of action (*kamma-vāda*), a teacher of efficacy of action (*kiriya-vāda*), and a teacher of energy (*vīriya-vāda*). If we consider His doctrine (*vāda*), the Buddha is to be identified by these three terms.
*   *Kamma-vāda*: that is, stating that one must act with faith in the power of action (*kamma*).
*   *Kiriya-vāda*: that a person possesses the potential/power for action.
*   *Vīriya-vāda*: that by exerting energy, one can bring forth that potential for action.
The Buddha explains the importance of these.
But there is also something in the world called the doctrine of non-action (*akiriya-vāda*). During the time of the Buddha, there were sharp proponents of non-action. The doctrine of non-action (*akiriya-vāda*) claims that there is no such thing as *kamma*, no power of action, and no such thing as energy; and that doing nothing should be one's ultimate goal. A teacher during the Buddha's time who promoted this philosophy was Makkhali Gosāla. So, on one occasion, the Buddha spoke to the monks about this philosophy of Gosāla in this manner: "Monks, of all the garments woven from threads, the most wretched, the most disgusting garment is the hair-blanket (*kesa-kambala*)." This was a garment woven from human hair used by certain ascetics of that time who claimed to practice fewness of wishes. That is indeed the most disgusting garment. "In the same way, of all the doctrines of ascetics, of all the views held among ascetics, the doctrine of non-action (*akiriya-vāda*) is the most disgusting, the most wretched doctrine."
Furthermore, He declared: "Whatever Fully Self-Enlightened Buddhas existed in the past, they were all teachers of action (*kamma-vādī*), teachers of the efficacy of action (*kiriya-vādī*), and teachers of energy (*vīriya-vādī*). Whatever Fully Self-Enlightened Buddhas arise in the future, they will all be teachers of action, teachers of the efficacy of action, and teachers of energy. I, who am now the Fully Self-Enlightened Buddha in the present, am also a teacher of action, a teacher of the efficacy of action, and a teacher of energy. This foolish man (*mogha-purisa*) Makkhali strikes at the teaching of the past Buddhas, strikes at the teaching of the future Buddhas, as well as my teaching in the present." He also gave another simile: "Monks, just as someone might cast a fishnet at the mouth of a river for the harm, suffering, and destruction of a vast number of fish, even so, this foolish man Makkhali has cast the net of this doctrine of non-action (*akiriya-vāda*) for the ruin, harm, and suffering of a vast number of human beings." The Buddha criticized and condemned Makkhali Gosāla’s doctrine to that extent.
Yet, merit-seeking friends, you may have also heard that nowadays, it is this very doctrine of non-action (*akiriya-vāda*) that is gaining more ground. Presenting various arguments such as "there is no such thing as *kamma*, no such thing as merit or demerit, one should not have conviction in their operation; exerting a person's power of action or energy is spiritually useless, it only reinforces the sense of 'I' (egotism)," they completely reject energy, without any understanding of the Dhamma principles shown by the Buddha, such as the balancing of energy (*vīriya-samatā*).
This is the philosophy of Makkhali. At first glance, this path seems easy. When a net is cast at the mouth of a river, it is sometimes cast with bait. Just as a large number of fish gather to eat that bait, only to meet their destruction, within the philosophy of non-action (*akiriya-vāda*), giving (*dāna*), virtue (*sīla*), and meditation (*bhāvanā*) are deemed useless. "There is no need to tire oneself with giving. No need to spend money and undergo trouble." "Observing virtue is also a useless thing." "Meditation is also a foolish thing." "It is a waste of time." Such wrong views appear easy. Swallowing that bait, people then get lost in saṃsāra. They meet with terrible destruction. That is why the Buddha specifically condemned that doctrine of Makkhali. It kills the power of action and the power of energy within a person. Through that, one can never achieve liberation. It is an extremely dangerous kind of philosophy.
Yet, in these times, many people are drawn to such views, like fish drawn into a net. A large number of people are drawn in because it seems easy, because they can just do nothing. A special reason for this is modern life—the luxurious lifestyle. If one can get electric light just by pressing a button, why can't one obtain the light of wisdom (*paññā*) just as easily? If, just by pressing a button, one can turn on a fan at home and enjoy a nice cool breeze, can one not obtain the peace of the coolness of Nibbāna while doing nothing? Either by doing nothing, or with very little energy. That is how someone argues. But what lies within this is none other than that doctrine of non-action (*akiriya-vāda*) of Makkhali Gosāla.
Another example of aroused energy (*āraddha-vīriya*) that can be taken from the Buddha's time is Venerable Ānanda's attainment of Arahantship. Three months after the parinibbāna of the Buddha, a Dhamma council was held. Although seats were prepared for five hundred Arahant monks to assemble, one monk was missing. A highly essential Venerable monk was missing. Venerable Ānanda, who had retained all the Buddha's discourses in memory and served as the Buddha's personal attendant for many years, had not yet attained Arahantship. That was the deficiency. The council was to begin the following day.
The night before, Venerable Ānanda put in all the effort he could, meditating intensely while resolving in all four postures. Still, he did not attain Arahantship. While meditating intensely in this way, late at night when it was time to rest, he washed his feet, went to his bed, and bent his body to lie down on the couch. At that moment, he was neither in the sitting posture nor yet in the lying posture. It was right in between those two postures that Venerable Ānanda’s mind was liberated from all taints (*āsava*), and he attained Arahantship. This is a unique occurrence in this entire Dispensation, making Venerable Ānanda the only monk to have attained Arahantship apart from the four standard postures, right in between them. Yet, some people argue even about this event, saying: "Even Venerable Ānanda attained Arahantship only after making so much effort and then giving it up, didn't he?" Most people do not understand the underlying principle (*dhammatā*) in this.
Venerable Ānanda was indeed a wondrous monk who received the chief (*etadagga*) status from the Buddha in several categories. *Etadagga* means the Buddha declaring: "Foremost among my disciples." You all know that the Buddha declared Venerable Ānanda foremost among personal attendants. He is also declared: *Satimantānaṃ, gatimantānaṃ, dhitimantānaṃ... etadaggaṃ.*
*   *Satimantānaṃ*: Foremost among disciples of great mindfulness (*sati*).
*   *Gatimantānaṃ*: Foremost among those of great comprehension/behavioral course (*gati*).
*   *Dhitimantānaṃ*: Foremost among those of resoluteness (*dhiti*)—those who stand firm in the task they have undertaken, acting with intense energy and power of determination.
Furthermore, Venerable Ānanda once declared about himself: "My best noble friend (*kalyāṇa-mitta*) is mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatā-sati*)." With this background, keeping Venerable Ānanda in mind, let us analyze the energy he exerted on that day in this manner.
The Venerable monk made effort with intense determination, thinking: "I cannot join this Sasana activity tomorrow without becoming an Arahant. This Sasana task is an absolute necessity. Somehow, for the sake of the Sasana, I must practice energy, become fit for this task, and then enter it." You devotees can understand that within this, a certain restlessness (*uddhacca*) naturally arises. That is called over-exerted energy (*accāraddha-vīriya*). In this verse, it is mentioned as *accāraddhamhi*. Aroused energy (*āraddha-vīriya*) is good. Initiating energy is good. But over-exerted energy (*accāraddha-vīriya*) is bad. *Ati-āraddha-vīriya*—excessive energy—is bad. For Venerable Ānanda, at the moment of that exertion, his mind had actually slipped unconsciously into a state of restlessness (*uddhacca*).
So, while acting with mindfulness in every posture, practicing mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatā-sati*), during the transition from the sitting posture to the lying-down posture, we can think of an analogy: even a skilled driver driving a high-speed vehicle has to carefully reduce the speed slightly before making a turn. Something similar must have occurred with Venerable Ānanda. In every posture, he had established mindfulness with intense energy. At that transition between postures, he arrived at the balancing of energy. That is the concentration of bodily postures (*iriyāpatha-samādhi*).
Indeed, merit-seeking friends, the Buddha compares these four postures to the rolling of a wheel. Postures change just like a rolling wheel. From the sitting posture, one stands up. Having stood up, one remains standing. Then, one takes steps. One walks, sits, lies down. In this way, it goes around. Like a cycle. Between these four postures, there are transitions (joints). Most people are not even aware of these transitions. One who works in a constant hurry has no understanding of these postures. As soon as he hears some urgent news in a rush, he does not even realize that he has stood up. The person who was sitting is suddenly running.
On the other hand, a mindful person, while sitting, contemplates that very posture of sitting. Contemplating the sitting posture, he stands up. The physical vehicle that was sitting has now stood up; contemplating the standing posture, he puts it into action. He begins walking. That is how one walks if one is mindful. But the one who lacks mindfulness, as soon as that news is heard, there he goes running. Ordinary worldlings do not have any understanding of even these postures of the body (*iriyāpatha*). Yet, Venerable Ānanda—the mindful one, who had long practiced mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatā-sati*) as his friend—even though he had exerted excessive energy (*accāraddha-vīriya*) due to a certain weakness in his eagerness for that Sasana purpose, nevertheless, by some underlying principle, arrived at the balancing of energy at the transition of postures. That is why he attained Arahantship at that moment. It was not because he abandoned energy. Some people think it was because he abandoned energy. That was not what happened. He attained Arahantship by realizing the balancing of energy (*vīriya-samatā*).
Indeed, the balancing of energy is understood only by the person who enters into the work. You cannot swim while staying on dry land. Whether in swimming or driving vehicles, in all these, the skill emerges only when one is engaged in it and understands the balancing of energy. For within that energy, there are two extremes. In intense energy, there is rigidity. Rigidity is not good. In low energy, there is laxity. That is also not good.
If even the Bodhisatta, who had fulfilled the perfections (*pāramīs*) to such an extent, and Venerable Ānanda made mistakes, there is no fault in our making mistakes. But one must enter into the work. Only the person who has entered into the work understands this. The ordinary worldling has no issue regarding this at all. It is only from the moment one starts driving a vehicle that one understands how to control the vehicle. Should the steering wheel be turned too much, or turned too little? All of this is understood only when one actually drives the vehicle. Like the person who gets into the water to swim, there too, one must be able to stay afloat without sinking. For that, a special skill must be brought forth. Similarly, only the person who has entered into the work can gradually move away from the two extremes and arrive at the middle. That is how one begins playing the lute as well. The beginner does not know whether the strings are too tight or too loose. Whichever way you look at them, these similes are highly practical.
