It is the habit of many to take only the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*) of these similes and illustrations in the Dhamma, looking only at the external aspect of the event, and thereby arrive at various wrong conclusions. But the Buddha has firmly declared: "If you are to take any doctrine as mine, it is to be stated as *kamma-vāda*, *kiriya-vāda*, and *vīriya-vāda*."
Some might misunderstand *kamma-vāda*, thinking: "Everything happens because of the past. Therefore, there is nothing for us to do. Let things go as they will." It is not so; there is a deep meaning to this concept of *kamma*. All of this is a power arising through our intention (*cetanā*) in the present moment. Just as it is said, "Intention, monks, is what I call action (*cetanāhaṃ bhikkhave kammaṃ vadāmi*)," we possess a power in the present moment through this power of intention. To change these forces, we must apply energy at a certain point, just like in the race mentioned earlier. Steadying ourselves as described, and in the final moment, developing that fourfold energy (*caturanga-samannāgata-vīriya*) with life-sacrifice, making the effort...
Even those who speak against exerting energy in spiritual life apply energy to worldly affairs, such as earning wealth. Why, then, do they say that no energy is needed for Sasana activities, meditation, and so forth? There lies a wrong view regarding the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkāya-diṭṭhi*). Nowadays, we hear various distorted explanations such as "developing energy increases the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkāya-diṭṭhi*)." As mentioned, nets have been cast everywhere at the mouth of the river. There are nets of wrong views (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) on all sides. Without falling into them, without being caught by them, one must understand this Dhamma of the Buddha in the way it should be understood. One must understand not only the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*) of these stories but also their deep meaning—the Dhamma-conforming meaning—and enter into the Middle Path to practice. Within this Dhamma, there is a Middle Path (*majjhimā paṭipadā*). A simile often used is that to cross a fast-flowing, torrential river, we must apply balanced energy. One cannot simply rush blindly into it. Yielding to the water while maintaining mindfulness and wisdom, slowly, step-by-step, one must reach the other shore. There too, lies a middle way, a balanced level.
This is the very principle (*dhammatā*) we can bring forth from this story. If you devotees deeply absorb these facts into your minds, performing your deeds of giving (*dāna*), virtue (*sīla*), and meditation (*bhāvanā*) with greater conviction (*saddhā*)—for it is from conviction that energy (*vīriya*) arises—you can then bring forth mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*). The balancing of faculties can be brought forth in that manner at some point; but to say it has truly arisen—it is the person who has attained the path and fruit, the Stream-entrant (*Sotāpanna*), who possesses true conviction (*saddhā*). Generally, no matter how much conviction we claim to have, true conviction belongs only to the person who has seen Nibbāna for the first time. It is truly established only at the moment of attaining the path and fruit.
A balance in this does not occur automatically. That is what needs to be understood. Just as Venerable Soṇa understood it. Just as Venerable Ānanda understood it. Let alone others, even the Buddha, despite having fulfilled the perfections (*pāramīs*) to such an extent, did not find his intense, extreme energy fruitful until He first brought forth this Middle Path. Therefore, we must indeed reflect that if liberation from saṃsāra is our ultimate goal, it is not obtained effortlessly. It requires an effort more intense than in any other pursuit, yet in a highly systematic and orderly manner—neither struggling restlessly, nor doing nothing, nor over-exerting, but at a balanced middle level can we succeed in this ultimate goal.
On this valuable Poya day, you devotees listened to this precious Dhamma for about an hour. You also undertook a noble virtue (*sīla*) and developed those qualities of wisdom (*paññā*), energy (*vīriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), and concentration (*samādhi*). As we mentioned, these truly emerge in their proper form only at the stage of the path and fruit. Yet, as a preliminary phase, if these principles sink into your minds, you too will be able to achieve that state. Thus, having gained an understanding of the balancing of energy, and having guarded your virtue (*sīla*) to some extent through today's practice... That virtue is what assists concentration (*samādhi*). That concentration is what, to some level, assists wisdom (*paññā*). Understanding this systematic sequence, make an aspiration: "May the merits of listening to this Dhamma lead me to quickly escape all suffering (*dukkha*) of saṃsāra, such as birth (*jāti*), decay and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), and sickness, and to realize the supreme, deathless Nibbāna!"
Likewise, make this aspiration: "May all those throughout this universe, from the Avīci hell to the Akaniṭṭha heaven, including our deceased relatives, who wish to rejoice in the merits of this Dhamma sermon and Dhamma listening—by rejoicing in this merit, may they attain peace in the noble, deathless Nibbāna through the Bodhi of their aspiration!" Having made this aspiration, recite the verses in this manner:
“*Ettāvatā ca amhehi.........*”

from:
khuddaka nikaya → theragatha → terasanipata → sonakolivisattheragatha → thag 13.1 (verses 638–639)
dear listeners,
the supreme buddha, the teacher of the three worlds, has declared that this dhamma, which leads to the great, deathless nibbana, is for one who has aroused energy (*araddha-viriya*), and not for the lazy or indolent. it is shown in this dhamma-vinaya that only the energetic person lives happily, and that living even a single day with aroused energy is far more noble than living a hundred years in laziness and indolence. that is why on this vap full moon poya day, we hope to present some verses and a story that are meaningful and inspiring specifically to the energetic person.
in the city of campa, which belonged to the kingdom of king bimbisara, a meritorious child was born to the millionaire family of kolivisa. his parents named the child sona. the body of this millionaire's son, sona kolivisa, was extremely delicate and tender. so delicate was he that hair grew even on the soles of his feet. this was a wondrous thing. king bimbisara heard this news, and on one occasion, when summoning eighty thousand village chiefs for state affairs, he sent a messenger with a message saying, "i wish to see sona. it would be good if sona comes here. please arrange for him to come." so, sona’s parents told the millionaire’s son: "son, the king wishes to see the soles of your feet. when you go there, do not stretch out your feet towards the king. sit cross-legged—that is, fold your legs—and then the king will see the soles of your feet."
so, when the people of campa went to see king bimbisara, the millionaire's son sona kolivisa was carried in a palanquin. having been brought before the king, the millionaire's son sona paid homage to the king and sat down in the manner described. the king saw the soles of his feet. he witnessed the wondrous phenomenon of hair growing on the soles of his feet. next, the king gave instructions on state matters to the eighty thousand village chiefs and said: "now i have shown you how to achieve well-being in this world. to secure well-being in the next world, go and meet the blessed one."
at that time, the blessed one was residing on the vulture's peak mountain (gijjhakata). so, this crowd of eighty thousand went to pay respects to the buddha. at that time, the buddha's personal attendant was venerable sagata, a monk who had practiced kasina meditation and possessed great meditative absorptive powers. venerable sagata conveyed the invitation to the buddha on behalf of the eighty thousand people in a miraculous manner. disappearing from where he stood, as if diving into the earth, he presented the invitation to the buddha.
having witnessed this psychic miracle, the eighty thousand people focused their attention on venerable sagata even more than on the buddha. understanding this, the buddha told venerable sagata: "sagata, display more psychic marvels." so, the venerable monk rose into the air, and performed various miracles related to the fire-kasina (*tejo-kasina*), such as sitting in the sky, walking up and down, and emitting flames, and finally descended to the ground, worshipped the buddha's feet, and declared: "the blessed one is my teacher, i am the disciple."
hearing this, the crowd thought, "if the disciple can do such wondrous things, how great must the teacher be!" at that moment when confidence (*saddha*) arose in them, the buddha delivered a dhamma sermon consisting of the gradual instruction (*anupubbikatha*). it is mentioned that upon hearing that dhamma sermon, the entire crowd attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotapatti-phala*) on their very seats. having attained the fruit of stream-entry, they became lay devotees who had taken refuge in the triple gem.
then, the millionaire's son, sona kolivisa, who was in this crowd, was deeply moved by this dhamma sermon and thought: "it is not easy to live the pure holy life (*brahmacariya*) according to the dhamma preached by the blessed one while remaining in lay life. i must ordain." with this resolve, he approached the buddha and requested ordination. the buddha granted him ordination and higher ordination (*upasampada*).
not long after his higher ordination, venerable sona went to the forest dwelling known as sitavana (cool grove) and began practicing intense energy. he put in such great energy that, by spending too much time on the walking path (*cankamana*), the soles of his feet, which had hair on them, cracked. they cracked and began to bleed. it bled so much that the walking path was covered in blood, looking like a slaughterhouse where cattle had been killed. when, despite practicing such intense energy, he did not attain arahantship, venerable sona, during a moment of rest, thought: "among those disciples of the blessed one who have aroused energy (*araddha-viriya*), i am indeed one. yet, despite putting in such energy, i have not achieved arahantship. there are abundant riches and wealth in our family. therefore, i should enjoy those riches and perform meritorious deeds." thus, he thought of returning to the lay life.
the buddha, who was staying on the vulture's peak, perceived this thought of venerable sona kolivisa. right at that moment, as quickly as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm, the buddha vanished from vulture's peak and appeared in sitavana. then, the buddha went on a tour of the lodgings with the other monks residing in sitavana, as if to inspect lodgings from dwelling to dwelling, hut to hut. while walking, he came to the walking path of venerable sona kolivisa and asked the monks: "whose walking path is this? this path covered in blood, looking like a slaughterhouse?" the monks replied: "venerable sir, this is the walking path of the venerable sona. venerable sona, having exerted extreme and excessive energy, walked up and down until his path was covered in blood in this manner."
then, the buddha went to venerable sona's hut. sitting on the prepared seat, he asked venerable sona: "sona, did a thought like this occur to you during a moment of rest: 'now, despite exerting so much energy, i have not become an arahant. therefore, i should return to lay life'?" "yes, venerable sir," he replied. then the buddha asked: "sona, when you were a layman, were you not skilled in playing the lute?" "yes, venerable sir," he replied. "how was it, sona? when the strings of your lute were pulled too tight, extremely tight, was the lute in a playable condition?" "no, venerable sir." "and when the strings of your lute were too loose, was it in a good condition? could the lute be played?" "no, not even then, venerable sir." "but, sona, when the strings of your lute were neither too tight nor too loose, but tuned to an even pitch, was it then playable and melodious?" "yes, venerable sir," he replied.
thus, using the simile of the lute, he gave advice to venerable sona. having given this advice, he returned to vulture's peak through the air. venerable sona, acting according to this advice, practiced energy once more and understood the principle of the balancing of energy (*viriya-samata*)—the fact that there must be a certain middle or balanced state regarding energy.
there is something called "balancing of the faculties" (*indriya-samata*) in this dhamma. what are called "faculties" (*indriya*) here are not the external physical faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. the spiritual faculties (*indriya*) are conviction (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*), which are wholesome qualities that assist in reaching the noble state. understanding the need for a certain balance among these, and the importance of developing them to a middle, balanced level, venerable sona very quickly realized arahantship.
having become an arahant, he then thought: "i must declare my arahantship to the blessed one." he approached the buddha and, without explicitly saying he had attained arahantship, presented the state of an arahant's mind by explaining a range of dhamma principles. the buddha too, praised this, declaring to the community of monks: "this is indeed how noble clansmen declare their arahantship; without explicitly asserting, 'i have attained arahantship,' they reveal their attainment through dhamma principles. that is the correct method. in doing so, their fewness of wishes is a valuable quality. it is a valuable quality of those noble ones who have achieved the higher realization." thus, the buddha praised it.
then the buddha said: "sona, your body is extremely delicate. therefore, i allow you to wear single-layered footwear." then, venerable sona replied: "venerable sir, i renounced eighty cartloads of gold coins and various other luxuries, left the household life, and ordained. having ordained, if i start using a pair of single-layered footwear as a special privilege, people might start rumors. they might blame me. they would say: 'this monk sona kolivisa, having renounced wealth as vast as eighty cartloads, has now developed an attachment to a single-layered pair of sandals; he has become attached to it.' therefore, if the blessed one allows the wearing of footwear for the sangha in general, i too will use them. if the blessed one does not grant permission to the sangha in general, then i too will not use them." it was on that occasion that the buddha, for the first time, declared to the monks: "i allow single-layered footwear."
from this, you lay devotees can understand many things. when the buddha on various occasions awarded the chief (*etadagga*) titles to monks who excelled in outstanding qualities, he also paid special honor to venerable sona by declaring him the foremost among those of his disciples who have aroused energy (*araddha-viriya*).
thus, presenting all these facts, venerable sona expressed his past course of practice in verses, and two of those verses mentioned in the *theragatha* are what we have placed today as our theme.
> *accaraddhamhi viriyamhi,*
> *samatho me anuttaro;*
> *vinupamam pi me dhammam,*
> *desesi cakkhuma.*
"regarding the matter of over-exerted energy, the unsurpassed teacher in the world, the one with vision, preached the dhamma to me using the simile of the lute."
> *tassaham vacanam sutva,*
> *vihasim sasane rato;*
"having heard his word, i dwelt delighting in the dispensation."
"for the attainment of the supreme goal—noble nibbana—i achieved the balancing of the faculties (*indriya-samata*)."
> *tisso vijja anuppatta,*
> *katam buddhassa sasanam.*
"the three knowledges—namely, the recollection of past lives (*pubbe-nivasanussati*), the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*), and the destruction of the taints (*asavakkhaya*)—have been attained. the instruction of the buddha has been fulfilled." these are the two verses from the *theragatha* that we have placed as our theme.
through this story, many noble qualities in the character of venerable sona kolivisa are revealed to us. let us look particularly at his development of energy. if someone with such delicate soles had been full of pride like an ordinary person, he might have thought: "even king bimbisara summoned me just to see this feature of mine. i cannot perform walking meditation." he did not think so. energetically, he engaged in walking meditation. ultimately, he put in such intense energy that his feet cracked and bled.
then, wisely understanding the simile of the lute presented by the buddha, he brought himself to a balanced state of energy—a middle state—and thereby attained arahantship. furthermore, after attaining arahantship, his declaration before the buddha was highly exemplary; without explicitly saying "i have attained arahantship," he presented it through dhamma principles by describing the nature of an arahant's mind as he understood it. also, how content with little (*appiccha*) he was! he did not expect any special privileges. when the buddha allowed him footwear, he stated that he would use them only if permission was granted to the sangha in general. all of these are a collection of valuable qualities that we should take as examples.
next, when considering the dhamma aspects, the key points are the balancing of energy (*viriya-samata*) and the balancing of the faculties (*indriya-samata*). what is this balancing of the faculties (*indriya-samata*)? merit-seeking friends, it is not the external faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body that assist in seeing nibbana. indeed, what assists in realizing nibbana are the five spiritual faculties (*indriya*) of the dispensation: conviction (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*). why are these presented as "faculties" (*indriya*)? it is because when they are developed and strengthened in one's mind, one understands the dhamma of nibbana through that power and strength. there is also a certain systematic order among these five. we can understand it in this way.
it is in one who has conviction (*saddha*) that energy (*viriya*) arises. through conviction, energy is brought forth. conviction is necessary to bring forth energy. relying on energy, mindfulness (*sati*) is established. one develops mindfulness in the form of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipatthana*). by developing mindfulness, one achieves concentration (*samadhi*)—one-pointedness of mind. it is with a concentrated mind that one understands reality as it is through insight (*vipassana*), understanding the impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*) nature of the world, and thereby brings forth insight-wisdom (*vipassana-panna*). in this way, there is a connection of one to another among the five: conviction, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
however, when discussing their balance (*samata*), we have to analyze it in a different way. the two factors, conviction and wisdom, are shown as a pair, a twin quality. conviction is said to be related to the heart. conviction means placing the heart (devotion). it is the emotional/affective aspect. the quality of conviction belongs to the feeling aspect of a person. wisdom belongs to the understanding aspect. it is the intellectual/cognitive aspect. there must be a balance between these two. teachers of old described a person who is low in conviction but high only in intellect as cunning or deceitful. one who has only conviction but lacks intellect becomes a foolish person; he develops blind faith even in improper things. to balance these, one enters the practice to develop wisdom through conviction. that is why it is necessary. thus it is with those two.
similarly, another pair is energy and concentration. energy tends toward restlessness (*uddhacca*). if one exerts excessive energy, the mind is bound to become restless. that is what happened to venerable sona. concentration brings stillness to the mind. it is something that leads to sluggishness (*linata*) or absolute stillness. restlessness comes through energy; the goal of concentration is stillness. at a glance, these seem contradictory. however, these must be developed systematically and evenly. one cannot develop concentration without energy. it is necessary to reach a certain level of concentration; it does not come by just doing nothing. mindfulness (*sati*), which stands in the middle of these, balances conviction, wisdom, energy, and concentration, just like the needle of a weighing scale. there is such a relationship among these five dhamma factors.
the balancing of the faculties (*indriya-samata*) is an important matter in this dispensation. through the balancing of the faculties, we can see the middle path taught by the buddha. in the middle way, nothing is extremist. here, every factor assists another, at a balanced, middle level. bringing it to this balanced level might sometimes exceed limits for certain individuals, depending on their personal disposition. just like venerable sona, who practiced excessive energy until his feet cracked and bled. as you all know, the buddha himself was caught up in the two extremes. everyone has heard of the two extremes mentioned in the *dhammacakkappavattana sutta*. he experienced self-indulgence (*kamasukhallikanuyoga*) in the royal palace, and he was also caught in the extreme of self-mortification (*attakilamathanuyoga*). it was after abandoning both those extremes that he arrived at the balanced level.
not only that, on one occasion, the buddha explained very intimately to the three monks anuruddha, nandiya, and kimbila how he himself had realized this balancing of energy during his days as a bodhisatta. "on one occasion, i exerted intense energy." he gave a simile for this: "if a person trying to catch a quail holds it too tightly in his grasp, the quail might die. on the other hand, if he holds it too loosely, the bird will fly away. in the same way, i understood from that simile that energy must be balanced." he explained this based on his own experience through various similes.
teachers of old also illustrated this point regarding the balancing of energy with various similes on different occasions. one simile found in the texts is that of the surgeon. in ancient times, surgeons trained their students—especially in surgeries like eye surgery—by having them draw lines with a scalpel on a blue water-lily petal floating on water. if someone is overly agitated, they will either submerge the lily petal in water or slice it completely through. the unskilled person, who has no dexterity, is too afraid even to touch the lily petal with the blade. the truly skilled person, who can apply balanced energy, is the one who carefully draws lines on the lily petal with the blade and passes the exercise.
there is another simile: the simile of filling oil into a narrow tube. if one tries to pour oil in a hurry, the oil will spill. on the other hand, some might be unable to pour oil into a narrow-mouthed tube because they are too afraid of spilling it. but if one applies extremely balanced energy, carefully and with mindfulness (*sati*), one can fill the oil successfully.
to take a simile suited to the modern mind, though not found in the texts: think of long-distance races in stadiums—let's say a ten-lap race around the track. what do some unskilled runners do? eager for the cheers of the spectators, they run the first two or three laps as fast as they can. in the end, they are exhausted and have to drop out of the race. but what does the truly skilled runner do? he runs at a steady, moderate pace for the first few laps. it is in the final stretch, as if possessing the fourfold energy (*caturanga-samannagata-viriya*), that he applies his conserved strength when the right moment arrives, runs very fast, and wins the race.
the fourfold energy (*caturanga-samannagata-viriya*) is mentioned in the life of the buddha. you devotees must have heard of this. once the right time comes, once the balancing of energy is perfectly achieved, the energy applied is one of life-sacrifice. "let only skin, sinews, and bones remain; let flesh and blood dry up. whatever goal can be achieved by manly energy, by manly strength, by manly effort, will not be abandoned until it is reached." the buddha himself exerted this supreme effort, known as the fourfold energy (*caturanga-samannagata-viriya*). he also exhorted his disciples to apply such energy.
however, this energy becomes successful only when, as mentioned before, the balancing of the faculties (*indriya-samata*) emerges. only after arriving at the balanced middle. indeed, it was only after arriving at the middle path that the buddha realized buddhahood through that fourfold energy. what happened to venerable sona initially was that he exerted extreme energy on the walking path for long periods in a way his body could not withstand. it was because of this that he even became discouraged in the first place.
the buddha has illustrated the balancing of energy in the dhamma through various similes. on one occasion, the buddha related to the monks an account concerning a past buddha. the buddha sikhi once visited a certain brahma-world along with his chief disciple, the monk abhibhu. having gone there, he assigned that disciple, venerable abhibhu, to preach the dhamma to the brahmas. on that occasion, the psychically powerful venerable abhibhu proclaimed two verses in a voice that resounded throughout a thousand world systems. these are very famous among energetic practitioners as the *arunavati sutta*. one of those verses is as follows:
> *arabhatha nikkhamatha,*
> *yunjatha buddhasasane;*
> *dhunatha maccuno senam,*
> *nalagaramva kunjaro.*
even upon hearing it, it is phrased in a way that arouses energy. "arouse energy, go forth, exert yourself in the buddha's dispensation; destroy the army of death, like an elephant crushing a reed-hut." such teachings on energy are found in the dhamma.
similarly, the buddha himself has pointed out three types of potential energies within our mental continuum as qualities that help overcome sleepiness and laziness:
*   *arambha-dhatu*: the element of instigating effort (the power to begin something).
*   *nikkhama-dhatu*: the element of launching out (the power to carry forward what has been started).
*   *parakkama-dhatu*: the element of exerting progress (the power to advance by overcoming obstacles encountered along the way). these energies exist within us.
this is precisely what is indicated in that verse:
*   *arabhatha* - "arouse energy" (corresponds to *arambha-dhatu*).
*   *nikkhamatha* - "go forth" (corresponds to *nikkhama-dhatu*).
*   *yunjatha* - "exert yourself" (corresponds to *parakkama-dhatu*, overcoming obstacles and moving forward).
that showed the value of developing energy.
likewise, on one occasion, the buddha showed the eight grounds for laziness (*kusita-vatthu*) and the eight grounds for arousing energy (*arambha-vatthu*). what are called the "grounds for laziness" (*kusita-vatthu*) are the eight occasions a lazy person uses to justify his lazy behavior. what are they? this is illustrated using a lazy monk. but it is not only for a monk; even a practicing layperson can take an example from this teaching. a lazy monk thinks in this way:
1.  the lazy monk has some special work to do. let us say a task connected with monastic life, such as dyeing robes. then that monk thinks: "now, i have such-and-such work to do. when doing this work, my body will get very tired. therefore, i must sleep now." saying this, he sleeps.
2.  next, let us say he has finished the work. once the work is done, that monk thinks: "now, i have done some heavy work. i am tired. therefore, i must sleep now." he sleeps. thus, he slept before doing it, and he slept after finishing it as well.
3.  next, let us say the lazy monk has to go on a journey. before embarking on the journey, he thinks: "now, when i go on the journey, my body will get tired. therefore, i must rest now." he sleeps.
4.  next, he returns from the journey. then he thinks: "now, because i went on the journey, i am very tired." he sleeps. he slept again.
5.  next, the lazy monk goes on alms-round (*pindapata*). that day, he does not receive a stomach-full of food on his alms-round. then he thinks: "now my body is very weak. today i did not receive proper food. therefore, i must sleep." he sleeps.
6.  alternatively, let us say he received plenty of food on his alms-round. having eaten his fill, after finishing the meal, he thinks: "today my body is very heavy, as if stuffed with beans. today, therefore, i cannot meditate." he sleeps.
7.  next, when the lazy monk has a slight illness, how does he think? "now, i have fallen ill. how can a sick person meditate?" so he sleeps.
8.  next, after he recovers from that illness, he thinks: "i have only just recovered from this illness. my body does not yet have full strength." therefore, he sleeps.
he is asleep all the time, the lazy monk, in this manner.
the buddha shows in this wonderful manner how the energetic monk uses these very same situations to arouse his energy:
1.  the energetic monk has some special work to do. then what does he think? "i have such-and-such work to do. while doing that work, i will not be able to easily maintain my meditative wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*) according to the buddha's instruction. therefore, i must practice energy right now. i must meditate, so as to quickly realize nibbana." thus, he meditates with great enthusiasm.
2.  next, having finished that work, how does the energetic monk think? "while doing that work, i was unable to maintain my meditative wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*) according to the buddha's instruction. now at least i must do so." thus, he meditates with enthusiasm.
3.  the energetic monk has to go on a journey. so, that monk thinks: "now, i have to go on such-and-such a journey. while traveling, i will not be able to meditate properly according to the buddha's instruction. therefore, i must meditate right now, before the journey."
4.  after returning from the journey, that monk thinks: "while on the journey, i was unable to meditate properly. now at least i must do so." thus, he meditates.
5.  when the energetic monk goes on alms-round and on a certain day does not receive a stomach-full of food, how does he think? "today my body is very light. today my body is highly active and workable. today i must meditate. that is the best thing to do." thinking thus when receiving little food, he meditates.
6.  on another day, returning from alms-round after receiving a stomach-full of food, how does he think? "today my body has good strength. i must meditate well." thus, he meditates.
7.  next, when the monk with aroused energy (*araddha-viriya*) gets a slight illness, how does he think? "now, a slight illness has arisen in me. if it increases, i might even die. therefore, i must meditate right now." thus, he meditates.
8.  as soon as he recovers from the illness, when he has just risen from his sickbed, what does he think? "because of this illness, i was unable to practice properly. perhaps the illness might return. therefore, before that happens, i must meditate well to see nibbana." thinking thus, he meditates.
through this, we can see that between laziness, indolence, and energy, there is actually only a difference in attitude. this correct attitude, which is praised by the buddha, is indeed the attitude of the energetic person. the energetic person utilizes every arising opportunity in a way that assists in reaching nibbana. the lazy person uses every single one of them in a way that assists samsara. as there is a saying, "the lazy man has divine eyes..." just like that, the lazy person has excuses for everything. the buddha has always given the foremost place to the energetic person.
furthermore, the buddha introduces himself as a teacher of action (*kamma-vada*), a teacher of efficacy of action (*kiriya-vada*), and a teacher of energy (*viriya-vada*). if we consider his doctrine (*vada*), the buddha is to be identified by these three terms.
*   *kamma-vada*: that is, stating that one must act with faith in the power of action (*kamma*).
*   *kiriya-vada*: that a person possesses the potential/power for action.
*   *viriya-vada*: that by exerting energy, one can bring forth that potential for action.
the buddha explains the importance of these.
but there is also something in the world called the doctrine of non-action (*akiriya-vada*). during the time of the buddha, there were sharp proponents of non-action. the doctrine of non-action (*akiriya-vada*) claims that there is no such thing as *kamma*, no power of action, and no such thing as energy; and that doing nothing should be one's ultimate goal. a teacher during the buddha's time who promoted this philosophy was makkhali gosala. so, on one occasion, the buddha spoke to the monks about this philosophy of gosala in this manner: "monks, of all the garments woven from threads, the most wretched, the most disgusting garment is the hair-blanket (*kesa-kambala*)." this was a garment woven from human hair used by certain ascetics of that time who claimed to practice fewness of wishes. that is indeed the most disgusting garment. "in the same way, of all the doctrines of ascetics, of all the views held among ascetics, the doctrine of non-action (*akiriya-vada*) is the most disgusting, the most wretched doctrine."
furthermore, he declared: "whatever fully self-enlightened buddhas existed in the past, they were all teachers of action (*kamma-vadi*), teachers of the efficacy of action (*kiriya-vadi*), and teachers of energy (*viriya-vadi*). whatever fully self-enlightened buddhas arise in the future, they will all be teachers of action, teachers of the efficacy of action, and teachers of energy. i, who am now the fully self-enlightened buddha in the present, am also a teacher of action, a teacher of the efficacy of action, and a teacher of energy. this foolish man (*mogha-purisa*) makkhali strikes at the teaching of the past buddhas, strikes at the teaching of the future buddhas, as well as my teaching in the present." he also gave another simile: "monks, just as someone might cast a fishnet at the mouth of a river for the harm, suffering, and destruction of a vast number of fish, even so, this foolish man makkhali has cast the net of this doctrine of non-action (*akiriya-vada*) for the ruin, harm, and suffering of a vast number of human beings." the buddha criticized and condemned makkhali gosala’s doctrine to that extent.
yet, merit-seeking friends, you may have also heard that nowadays, it is this very doctrine of non-action (*akiriya-vada*) that is gaining more ground. presenting various arguments such as "there is no such thing as *kamma*, no such thing as merit or demerit, one should not have conviction in their operation; exerting a person's power of action or energy is spiritually useless, it only reinforces the sense of 'i' (egotism)," they completely reject energy, without any understanding of the dhamma principles shown by the buddha, such as the balancing of energy (*viriya-samata*).
this is the philosophy of makkhali. at first glance, this path seems easy. when a net is cast at the mouth of a river, it is sometimes cast with bait. just as a large number of fish gather to eat that bait, only to meet their destruction, within the philosophy of non-action (*akiriya-vada*), giving (*dana*), virtue (*sila*), and meditation (*bhavana*) are deemed useless. "there is no need to tire oneself with giving. no need to spend money and undergo trouble." "observing virtue is also a useless thing." "meditation is also a foolish thing." "it is a waste of time." such wrong views appear easy. swallowing that bait, people then get lost in samsara. they meet with terrible destruction. that is why the buddha specifically condemned that doctrine of makkhali. it kills the power of action and the power of energy within a person. through that, one can never achieve liberation. it is an extremely dangerous kind of philosophy.
yet, in these times, many people are drawn to such views, like fish drawn into a net. a large number of people are drawn in because it seems easy, because they can just do nothing. a special reason for this is modern life—the luxurious lifestyle. if one can get electric light just by pressing a button, why can't one obtain the light of wisdom (*panna*) just as easily? if, just by pressing a button, one can turn on a fan at home and enjoy a nice cool breeze, can one not obtain the peace of the coolness of nibbana while doing nothing? either by doing nothing, or with very little energy. that is how someone argues. but what lies within this is none other than that doctrine of non-action (*akiriya-vada*) of makkhali gosala.
another example of aroused energy (*araddha-viriya*) that can be taken from the buddha's time is venerable ananda's attainment of arahantship. three months after the parinibbana of the buddha, a dhamma council was held. although seats were prepared for five hundred arahant monks to assemble, one monk was missing. a highly essential venerable monk was missing. venerable ananda, who had retained all the buddha's discourses in memory and served as the buddha's personal attendant for many years, had not yet attained arahantship. that was the deficiency. the council was to begin the following day.
the night before, venerable ananda put in all the effort he could, meditating intensely while resolving in all four postures. still, he did not attain arahantship. while meditating intensely in this way, late at night when it was time to rest, he washed his feet, went to his bed, and bent his body to lie down on the couch. at that moment, he was neither in the sitting posture nor yet in the lying posture. it was right in between those two postures that venerable ananda’s mind was liberated from all taints (*asava*), and he attained arahantship. this is a unique occurrence in this entire dispensation, making venerable ananda the only monk to have attained arahantship apart from the four standard postures, right in between them. yet, some people argue even about this event, saying: "even venerable ananda attained arahantship only after making so much effort and then giving it up, didn't he?" most people do not understand the underlying principle (*dhammata*) in this.
venerable ananda was indeed a wondrous monk who received the chief (*etadagga*) status from the buddha in several categories. *etadagga* means the buddha declaring: "foremost among my disciples." you all know that the buddha declared venerable ananda foremost among personal attendants. he is also declared: *satimantanam, gatimantanam, dhitimantanam... etadaggam.*
*   *satimantanam*: foremost among disciples of great mindfulness (*sati*).
*   *gatimantanam*: foremost among those of great comprehension/behavioral course (*gati*).
*   *dhitimantanam*: foremost among those of resoluteness (*dhiti*)—those who stand firm in the task they have undertaken, acting with intense energy and power of determination.
furthermore, venerable ananda once declared about himself: "my best noble friend (*kalyana-mitta*) is mindfulness directed to the body (*kayagata-sati*)." with this background, keeping venerable ananda in mind, let us analyze the energy he exerted on that day in this manner.
the venerable monk made effort with intense determination, thinking: "i cannot join this sasana activity tomorrow without becoming an arahant. this sasana task is an absolute necessity. somehow, for the sake of the sasana, i must practice energy, become fit for this task, and then enter it." you devotees can understand that within this, a certain restlessness (*uddhacca*) naturally arises. that is called over-exerted energy (*accaraddha-viriya*). in this verse, it is mentioned as *accaraddhamhi*. aroused energy (*araddha-viriya*) is good. initiating energy is good. but over-exerted energy (*accaraddha-viriya*) is bad. *ati-araddha-viriya*—excessive energy—is bad. for venerable ananda, at the moment of that exertion, his mind had actually slipped unconsciously into a state of restlessness (*uddhacca*).
so, while acting with mindfulness in every posture, practicing mindfulness directed to the body (*kayagata-sati*), during the transition from the sitting posture to the lying-down posture, we can think of an analogy: even a skilled driver driving a high-speed vehicle has to carefully reduce the speed slightly before making a turn. something similar must have occurred with venerable ananda. in every posture, he had established mindfulness with intense energy. at that transition between postures, he arrived at the balancing of energy. that is the concentration of bodily postures (*iriyapatha-samadhi*).
indeed, merit-seeking friends, the buddha compares these four postures to the rolling of a wheel. postures change just like a rolling wheel. from the sitting posture, one stands up. having stood up, one remains standing. then, one takes steps. one walks, sits, lies down. in this way, it goes around. like a cycle. between these four postures, there are transitions (joints). most people are not even aware of these transitions. one who works in a constant hurry has no understanding of these postures. as soon as he hears some urgent news in a rush, he does not even realize that he has stood up. the person who was sitting is suddenly running.
on the other hand, a mindful person, while sitting, contemplates that very posture of sitting. contemplating the sitting posture, he stands up. the physical vehicle that was sitting has now stood up; contemplating the standing posture, he puts it into action. he begins walking. that is how one walks if one is mindful. but the one who lacks mindfulness, as soon as that news is heard, there he goes running. ordinary worldlings do not have any understanding of even these postures of the body (*iriyapatha*). yet, venerable ananda—the mindful one, who had long practiced mindfulness directed to the body (*kayagata-sati*) as his friend—even though he had exerted excessive energy (*accaraddha-viriya*) due to a certain weakness in his eagerness for that sasana purpose, nevertheless, by some underlying principle, arrived at the balancing of energy at the transition of postures. that is why he attained arahantship at that moment. it was not because he abandoned energy. some people think it was because he abandoned energy. that was not what happened. he attained arahantship by realizing the balancing of energy (*viriya-samata*).
indeed, the balancing of energy is understood only by the person who enters into the work. you cannot swim while staying on dry land. whether in swimming or driving vehicles, in all these, the skill emerges only when one is engaged in it and understands the balancing of energy. for within that energy, there are two extremes. in intense energy, there is rigidity. rigidity is not good. in low energy, there is laxity. that is also not good.
if even the bodhisatta, who had fulfilled the perfections (*paramis*) to such an extent, and venerable ananda made mistakes, there is no fault in our making mistakes. but one must enter into the work. only the person who has entered into the work understands this. the ordinary worldling has no issue regarding this at all. it is only from the moment one starts driving a vehicle that one understands how to control the vehicle. should the steering wheel be turned too much, or turned too little? all of this is understood only when one actually drives the vehicle. like the person who gets into the water to swim, there too, one must be able to stay afloat without sinking. for that, a special skill must be brought forth. similarly, only the person who has entered into the work can gradually move away from the two extremes and arrive at the middle. that is how one begins playing the lute as well. the beginner does not know whether the strings are too tight or too loose. whichever way you look at them, these similes are highly practical.
it is the habit of many to take only the literal meaning (*vacyartha*) of these similes and illustrations in the dhamma, looking only at the external aspect of the event, and thereby arrive at various wrong conclusions. but the buddha has firmly declared: "if you are to take any doctrine as mine, it is to be stated as *kamma-vada*, *kiriya-vada*, and *viriya-vada*."
some might misunderstand *kamma-vada*, thinking: "everything happens because of the past. therefore, there is nothing for us to do. let things go as they will." it is not so; there is a deep meaning to this concept of *kamma*. all of this is a power arising through our intention (*cetana*) in the present moment. just as it is said, "intention, monks, is what i call action (*cetanaham bhikkhave kammam vadami*)," we possess a power in the present moment through this power of intention. to change these forces, we must apply energy at a certain point, just like in the race mentioned earlier. steadying ourselves as described, and in the final moment, developing that fourfold energy (*caturanga-samannagata-viriya*) with life-sacrifice, making the effort...
even those who speak against exerting energy in spiritual life apply energy to worldly affairs, such as earning wealth. why, then, do they say that no energy is needed for sasana activities, meditation, and so forth? there lies a wrong view regarding the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*). nowadays, we hear various distorted explanations such as "developing energy increases the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*)." as mentioned, nets have been cast everywhere at the mouth of the river. there are nets of wrong views (*miccha-ditthi*) on all sides. without falling into them, without being caught by them, one must understand this dhamma of the buddha in the way it should be understood. one must understand not only the literal meaning (*vacyartha*) of these stories but also their deep meaning—the dhamma-conforming meaning—and enter into the middle path to practice. within this dhamma, there is a middle path (*majjhima patipada*). a simile often used is that to cross a fast-flowing, torrential river, we must apply balanced energy. one cannot simply rush blindly into it. yielding to the water while maintaining mindfulness and wisdom, slowly, step-by-step, one must reach the other shore. there too, lies a middle way, a balanced level.
this is the very principle (*dhammata*) we can bring forth from this story. if you devotees deeply absorb these facts into your minds, performing your deeds of giving (*dana*), virtue (*sila*), and meditation (*bhavana*) with greater conviction (*saddha*)—for it is from conviction that energy (*viriya*) arises—you can then bring forth mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*). the balancing of faculties can be brought forth in that manner at some point; but to say it has truly arisen—it is the person who has attained the path and fruit, the stream-entrant (*sotapanna*), who possesses true conviction (*saddha*). generally, no matter how much conviction we claim to have, true conviction belongs only to the person who has seen nibbana for the first time. it is truly established only at the moment of attaining the path and fruit.
a balance in this does not occur automatically. that is what needs to be understood. just as venerable sona understood it. just as venerable ananda understood it. let alone others, even the buddha, despite having fulfilled the perfections (*paramis*) to such an extent, did not find his intense, extreme energy fruitful until he first brought forth this middle path. therefore, we must indeed reflect that if liberation from samsara is our ultimate goal, it is not obtained effortlessly. it requires an effort more intense than in any other pursuit, yet in a highly systematic and orderly manner—neither struggling restlessly, nor doing nothing, nor over-exerting, but at a balanced middle level can we succeed in this ultimate goal.
on this valuable poya day, you devotees listened to this precious dhamma for about an hour. you also undertook a noble virtue (*sila*) and developed those qualities of wisdom (*panna*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), and concentration (*samadhi*). as we mentioned, these truly emerge in their proper form only at the stage of the path and fruit. yet, as a preliminary phase, if these principles sink into your minds, you too will be able to achieve that state. thus, having gained an understanding of the balancing of energy, and having guarded your virtue (*sila*) to some extent through today's practice... that virtue is what assists concentration (*samadhi*). that concentration is what, to some level, assists wisdom (*panna*). understanding this systematic sequence, make an aspiration: "may the merits of listening to this dhamma lead me to quickly escape all suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara, such as birth (*jati*), decay and death (*jaramarana*), and sickness, and to realize the supreme, deathless nibbana!"
likewise, make this aspiration: "may all those throughout this universe, from the avici hell to the akanittha heaven, including our deceased relatives, who wish to rejoice in the merits of this dhamma sermon and dhamma listening—by rejoicing in this merit, may they attain peace in the noble, deathless nibbana through the bodhi of their aspiration!" having made this aspiration, recite the verses in this manner:
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 062
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #62
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.130)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Asātaṃ sātarūpena,
piyarūpena appiyaṃ;
Dukkhaṃ sukhassa rūpena,
pamattaṃ ativattati.
From:
from Udāna 2.9, Asātarūpa Jātaka, and Sutta Nipāta 1086
Dear Listeners,
The Teacher of the Three Worlds, the Supreme Buddha, points out to us that the entire journey of saṃsāra, which is a struggle between life and death, is indeed a state of heedlessness, and that the path to the Deathless Nibbāna is heedfulness. One traverses this journey of saṃsāra by regarding Suffering (Dukkha) as happiness. How one falls prey to this perverted perception, which arises due to ignorance and Craving (Taṇhā), will become clear through today's thematic verse and its corresponding origin story.
In the Kuṇḍasāla forest of the Koliya country, the Buddha preached this verse in connection with the female lay disciple named Suppavāsā. She, known as Suppavāsā Koliyadhītā, was the mother of the Great Arahant Sīvalī. The Great Arahant Sīvalī, who attained the foremost position among those of great gains, obtained the gift of life amidst a mountain of great Suffering (Dukkha). For Ven. Sīvalī spent seven years and seven days in his mother's womb. During those last seven days, that mother experienced extremely bitter labor pains due to an obstructed pregnancy. Even at that moment, having faith in the Triple Gem, she endured that bitter pain through three Dhamma-accordant reflections, through three thoughts. It is recorded there in this manner:
*“Sammāsambuddho vata so bhagavā yo imassa evarūpassa dukkhassa pahānāya dhammaṃ deseti”*
The Blessed One is indeed the Fully Self-Awakened One, who teaches the Dhamma for the abandoning of such Suffering (Dukkha).
*“Supaṭipanno vata so bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho yo imassa evarūpassa dukkhassa pahānāya paṭipanno”*
Of good conduct indeed is the Sangha of disciples of that Blessed One, who have entered the path for the abandoning of such Suffering (Dukkha).
*“Susukhaṃ vata taṃ nibbānaṃ yatthidaṃ evarūpaṃ dukkhaṃ na vijjati”*
Extremely peaceful indeed is that Nibbāna wherein such Suffering (Dukkha) is not found.
Through these kinds of reflections, through these three Dhamma-accordant thoughts, she endured that bitter pain. Then, she spoke to her husband and told him: “Go and inquire about the health of the Blessed One, and then inform Him in this manner: ‘Suppavāsā, the Koliya daughter, having carried a child in her womb for seven years, is now experiencing the bitter pain of a difficult pregnancy for these seven days. Yet, she endures that pain through these three kinds of reflections.’” Suppavāsā's husband met the Buddha and conveyed that message exactly as requested. As soon as it was spoken, the Buddha uttered just one sentence as a blessing: *“Sukhini hotu suppavāsā koliyadhītā, arogā arogaṃ puttaṃ vijāyatu”* — “May Suppavāsā, the Koliya daughter, be happy. Being healthy, may she give birth to a healthy son.” At that very moment, Suppavāsā became well and gave birth to a son.
Now, when the husband returned home and witnessed this miracle, he was greatly delighted, thinking: “This is a great wonder, a marvelous thing! Such relief was received just by the word of blessing spoken through the power of the Blessed One.” Next, Suppavāsā says to her husband: “Now, go and make this invitation to the Blessed One: ‘Suppavāsā, the Koliya daughter, has given birth to a healthy child. Suppavāsā invites the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha to accept alms for seven days.’” So, the husband went back, reported this matter to the Buddha, and made the alms invitation on behalf of Suppavāsā.
By that time, the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha had already received another invitation from a certain lay disciple, who was an attendant of the Great Arahant Mahā Moggallāna. The Buddha did something special here; He called Venerable Mahā Moggallāna and said: “Moggallāna, tell that lay disciple: ‘Suppavāsā, the Koliya daughter, having carried a pregnancy for seven years and seven days, has now safely delivered. She makes this invitation for seven days. Let those next seven days be given to her, and postpone your alms-giving to a later date.’” The Great Arahant Moggallāna went and made this request to that lay disciple.
Perhaps because that lay disciple was wise, he made the following statement to the Great Arahant Moggallāna: “Venerable sir, if you can guarantee three things for me, I will yield my turn of alms-giving to Suppavāsā.” What were those three things? “You must assure me that my wealth and possessions will not be destroyed within these seven days. Similarly, you must guarantee that my life will not end; that is the second point. And you must guarantee that my faith (saddhā) will not waver or decline.” He asked the Great Arahant Moggallāna to guarantee these three things.
The Great Arahant Moggallāna says: “Lay disciple, I can guarantee two of those things for you. But the third thing you must guarantee for yourself.” You, meritorious friends, know that the Great Arahant Moggallāna possessed great psychic powers; he was the foremost among those with psychic power. He must have seen clearly regarding those two matters. He says: “I can guarantee that your wealth will not perish during these seven days, and that your life will not perish. But faith is something that belongs to you alone; you yourself must be responsible for it.”
Then, that lay disciple wisely replied: “Very well, Venerable Sir, if you assure me of those two, I agree. Let Suppavāsā offer this alms-food. I will undertake to offer my alms-giving later.” After the Great Arahant Moggallāna went and reported this matter to the Buddha, Suppavāsā prepared the alms-food magnificently on the following day and personally offered it with her own hands to the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha.
Indeed, this is a miraculous event. Perhaps some might even doubt it. It is mentioned that even that young child was made to pay homage to the Sangha headed by the Buddha. Not only that, the Great Arahant Sāriputta addressed this child and asked: “Child, I hope you are comfortable, with no pain or trouble?” This was like inquiring about the well-being of an ordinary person. Then this little child answered: “Venerable Sir, what happiness could there be for me? What happiness could there be for one who lived for seven years and seven days inside a jar of blood?” Hearing this conversation, Suppavāsā, the Koliya daughter, was exceedingly delighted. She was overjoyed thinking, “What a meritorious child this is, to converse with the Great Arahant Sāriputta in this manner!” Seeing her joy, the Buddha asked Suppavāsā: “Well, Suppavāsā, would you like to have more children like this?” Then Suppavāsā replied, just like many mothers say nowadays: “Not just one child, I would be delighted to have even seven children like this!” It was then that the Buddha uttered the verse we mentioned earlier.
> *Asātaṃ sātarūpena,*
> *piyarūpena appiyaṃ,*
> *dukkhaṃ sukhassa rūpena,*
> *pamattaṃ ativattati.*
This is declared as an Udāna verse. When we say 'Udāna' (inspired utterance), we usually think of a joyful exclamation. But one should not think that the Buddha was merely approving Suppavāsā's words. Looking at the mind in accordance with the Dhamma, this verse contains an instructive, advisory statement.
*Asātaṃ sātarūpena* — what is unpleasant in the guise of the pleasant;
*Piyarūpena appiyaṃ* — what is unlovely in the guise of the lovely;
*Dukkhaṃ sukhassa rūpena* — Suffering (Dukkha) in the guise of happiness;
*Pamattaṃ ativattati* — overwhelms the heedless person.
Now, you, meritorious friends, can think about this. In addition to this, we must say that you have probably heard much about the Great Arahant Sīvalī. As the foremost Great Arahant in terms of great gains, many meritorious people even hang pictures of the Great Arahant Sīvalī in their homes. But they do not think much about the other side—about the mountain of Suffering (Dukkha) he endured. They do not think of the immense mountain of Suffering (Dukkha) amidst which he obtained his limited gains. Well, the Buddha, on a certain occasion in the Jātaka Pāli, explains under the name 'Asātarūpa Jātaka' that there was a kamma underlying this as well. It appears that when the monks had gathered, they discussed: “Ah, what Suffering (Dukkha) this mother and son have endured, especially Ven. Sīvalī in his childhood!” The Buddha, having entered the Dhamma hall, revealed the past story in this manner:
In the past, when the Bodhisatta was born as the son of King Brahmadatta of Bārāṇasī and was ruling, the King of Kosala, being more powerful, came and seized the kingdom, killed the king, made the queen his chief consort, and began ruling Bārāṇasī. At that time, the son escaped through a waterway, hid, gathered an army, and came to fight to reclaim his kingdom. He sent a message to the King of Kosala: “Hand over the kingdom or fight!” As the king prepared for war, the chief consort, who was the prince's mother, sent a secret message: “There is no need to fight; just besiege the city. Once the city is besieged, you can capture it by leaving the people with nothing to eat or drink, starving them.” This was the advice given by the mother. Following this, the son blockaded the city for seven days. With the people left helpless, they finally killed the King of Kosala and brought his head to the prince. In that manner, the problem was solved. However, it is the unwholesome kamma that is pointed out here. The Buddha declared that because of the advice given—the advice to blockade and starve them in that manner to capture the kingdom—and the kamma committed by the son who followed that advice, the kamma ripened in this exact manner.
Now, a certain aspect of the ripening of kamma is revealed through this. Next, let us try to uncover an important aspect of this story. We see that there is something to be grasped even from the conversation between that lay disciple and the Great Arahant Moggallāna. The lay gentleman was not ready to yield his turn of alms-giving merely because the Buddha said so. A doubt arose in the lay disciple: “Even though I promised to give alms, if by any chance my wealth to give alms is lost during these seven days, or if my life is not preserved, or even if all these are present, if my faith (saddhā) is lost, how will I give alms?” Thinking in this way, he made that request to guarantee these things.
And the Great Arahant Moggallāna, too, acted in accordance with the Dhamma; there too, we have a lesson to learn. Even though he was so highly advanced in psychic power and possessed great majesty, he could not guarantee another person's faith (saddhā). This is an important point in the Dhamma.
The faith (saddhā) found in the Dhamma of the Buddha is not blind devotion. It is not something done by becoming enslaved or subservient to anyone. It is something belonging to oneself. One must be responsible for it oneself. Regarding that matter, the word of the Great Arahant Moggallāna is indeed in agreement with the Buddha’s word. Related points are mentioned in various places in the Dhamma. Especially, there is a discourse called the Vīmaṃsaka Sutta. There, the Buddha tells the monks that even a monk who does not possess the power to read others' minds should investigate even the Tathāgata Himself through things cognizable by the eye and ear, and only then develop faith (saddhā). Thus, the living Buddha invited even His own Sangha of monks to investigate whether He has any shortcomings, and then, having investigated, to establish their faith (saddhā) that He is indeed the Fully Self-Awakened One.
Similarly, on another occasion, in the discourse called the Upāli Sutta, mention is made of Upāli the householder, who was a very prominent disciple of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta. When, on a certain occasion, through a Dhamma discussion, he developed faith (saddhā) in the Buddha and took refuge in the Triple Gem, the Buddha declared: “Householder Upāli, it is not good for well-known people like you in the country to make such hasty decisions. *Anuviccākāro*—investigate, think it over, and think further before taking refuge in the Triple Gem. Do not be so hasty.” Then, the householder Upāli was actually much more delighted. What is shown by this is that the Buddhist attitude leads to investigation. That faith (saddhā) is not blind devotion. It is something belonging to each individual. This, meritorious friends, you too should understand well.
That wealth belongs to oneself. Among the types of wealth such as the wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue, and the wealth of moral shame and fear, this is the foremost wealth; it cannot be shaken by anyone in that manner. Whether it is shaken or not is something belonging to oneself. Wrong views can indeed shake it. But one must strive to make it unshakable faith. What is called unshakable faith is the stage where one has, to some extent, directly realized the Dhamma. We pointed out this fact as an additional point, yet it is contained within this discourse.
Next, let us return to the main narrative mentioned in this story. Look now at the mother of the Great Arahant Sīvalī, Suppavāsā. Having suffered such pain—pain that no other mother had ever experienced—and due to the joy arising from maternal affection, when the Buddha asked her, she said she would be pleased to have even seven more such children. That is exactly what is expressed in that verse. That is the nature of the world. Even if one suffers a massive mountain of Suffering (Dukkha), one forgets it. That is why it was said: *Asātaṃ sātarūpena*—what is unpleasant appears as pleasant, and what is unlovely appears as lovely. Thinking in this way, one falls into heedlessness. No matter how much faith (saddhā) she possessed, because Suppavāsā fell into heedlessness at that moment, the Buddha uttered this verse as an admonition. This is a hidden aspect of the life of the Great Arahant Sīvalī during his childhood.
We rarely hear of people who have the power to recall the past. However, in most cases, a child has no memory whatsoever of the time spent in the mother's womb. Even if there is no memory, the child comes out crying, as if to express that Suffering (Dukkha) in brief. We must understand this. Yet, it is mentioned that the Great Arahant Sīvalī possessed a certain power. It is clear from his answer that he had a recollection of it. If he was able to say, “What happiness could there be for me who lived for so long inside a jar of blood?” then that child indeed had that power. Regarding this, it is recorded in the texts in this manner: Ven. Sīvalī did not need to be given a separate meditation subject. Simply by reflecting on that Suffering (Dukkha), on that Suffering of Birth (jāti-dukkha)...
Many of our Buddhist friends do not even like to accept the Suffering of Birth (jāti-dukkha). When a child is born in a home, it is a cause for great joy—obtaining the 'treasure of a child.' But the disaster within it is not understood by many. That disaster is also quickly forgotten. That birth was a disastrous, perilous occasion for both the mother and the child. They forget it, make merry over it, and commemorate it year after year by holding birthday parties. There lies the Suffering of Birth (jāti-dukkha). Thus, it is mentioned in the Dhamma that by recollecting the Suffering of Birth (jāti-dukkha), the Great Arahant Sīvalī attained his Arahantship, making that his subject of meditation.
Furthermore, if we go deeper into this, and compile the Dhamma categories mentioned here like 'pleasant form' and 'agreeable form,' the Buddha points out that the defilement or purification of beings occurs through causes and conditions. The most valuable part of this Dhamma—as you, meritorious friends, also accept—is the teaching of Dependent Arising (paṭicca-samuppāda), which is the teaching that everything occurs according to causes and conditions, a teaching not found in any other doctrine. An occasion that highlights this is mentioned. Once, a Licchavi chief named Mahāli said to the Buddha: “Venerable Sir, the teacher named Pūraṇa Kassapa expresses this view: ‘Beings are defiled without cause, without condition. Beings are purified without any cause. The purification and defilement of beings are without cause and without condition.’ Pūraṇa Kassapa holds such a view. What does the Blessed One say about this?” he asked the Blessed One.
Then, the Buddha declared: “I say that it is with cause and condition that one becomes defiled. Likewise, it is with cause and condition that one obtains purity, obtains purification of mind.” When asked, “How do I understand this?” the Buddha explained it by means of these five: form, Sensation (vedanā), perception, Preparations (saṅkhāra), and Consciousness (viññāṇa).
The Buddha analyzes it in this way: “If this form, or the part we call the body, were exclusively painful, if nothing called happiness could ever be associated with it, if this body were purely filled with Suffering (Dukkha), beings would not become attached to it. This body is not purely Suffering (Dukkha); there is a pleasant aspect to it, and one can form a perception of pleasure in it. It is because of this that they get attached to it. Due to that attachment, a bond is formed. Due to that bond, defilement occurs.” There, the natural law was shown. It is the same with the others. In Sensation (vedanā), too, there is a similar nature. Sensation (vedanā) is not purely Suffering (Dukkha). There is also a pleasant aspect. It is the same with perception and so on. Up to Consciousness (viññāṇa), every single one cannot be said to be purely Suffering (Dukkha); there is also a pleasant aspect. If we look at things as they really are, that is why there is attachment. Due to that attachment, a bond is formed. Due to the bond, there is defilement. Due to that defilement, one goes on and on in saṃsāra.
Next, He states the other side. What was described just now was how one becomes defiled. Next, He explains how one becomes purified: “If this aggregate of form was purely pleasant, if there were no Suffering (Dukkha) in this form, then one would never become disenchanted with it. One becomes disenchanted with it because there is a certain nature of Suffering (Dukkha) in it.” That too is a natural law. The Buddha accepts that too as a truth. It is because of that nature of Suffering (Dukkha) that beings become disenchanted with it. Through that disenchantment, dispassion arises. Through that dispassion, purification, liberation arises. This is the natural law shown there by the Buddha. It is not something done by the Buddha, nor is it something done by anyone else. It is demonstrated here that this occurs in accordance with causes and conditions.
Now, next we present a Dhamma category that is extremely valuable for practitioners and meditators. You, meritorious friends, might have heard that the Buddha preached deep, valuable discourses like the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta and the Mahānidāna Sutta to the people of the Kuru country. Even in the commentaries to those origin stories, it is mentioned that the Kuru country was a prosperous land and its people were wise. The Buddha preached those valuable discourses on His own initiative, even without any specific question being asked.
On one occasion, the Buddha addressed the Sangha of monks and asked this question: “Monks, do you practice the exploration called *antara-sammasana* (internal scrutiny)?” *Antara-sammasana* means scrutinizing from within. Scrutiny actually means exploring or investigating. Otherwise, the general idea is "investigation from within." This can be analyzed further in due course. When He asked the monks in general whether they perform such an internal investigation, a certain monk declared: “Venerable Sir, I do practice such a thing.” Next, this is all that is mentioned in the Dhamma: when that monk was asked, “How do you practice that internal exploration called *antara-sammasana*?” the answer given by that monk is not recorded. It is recorded in this way: the Blessed One was not satisfied with the answer he gave, deeming it insufficient. At that moment, Ven. Ānanda stepped forward and said: “Blessed One, this is the time, this is the proper time! Let the Blessed One explain to the Sangha of monks what this *antara-sammasana* (internal scrutiny) is, what this investigation from within means.”
From there, the Buddha explains: “A certain monk investigates the facts from within, as they really are, in this manner. He thinks: ‘What is this Aging and Death (jarāmaraṇa)?’ If there are various kinds of Aging and Death (jarāmaraṇa) and diverse forms of Suffering (Dukkha) in the world in connection with this life, what is the cause of these sufferings? From what does this Suffering (Dukkha) arise? What is its root? What is its cause?’ Investigating thus, he realizes: ‘Whatever Aging and Death (jarāmaraṇa) and Suffering (Dukkha) exist, they all arise due to assets (upadhi).’”
The word 'upadhi' (assets) is used in the Dhamma to refer to the five aggregates of Grasping (upādāna)—form, Sensation (vedanā), perception, Preparations (saṅkhāra), and Consciousness (viññāṇa), which one holds on to thinking ‘this is mine.’ These things grabbed through Grasping (upādāna) are what become assets (upadhi). To put it briefly, the wealth we earn and acquire becomes deposits, our assets, when deposited in a bank. In the same way, the greatest asset we carry through saṃsāra is the five aggregates of Grasping (upādāna). These five heaps of 'my form, my Sensation (vedanā),' which are held by the mind—that is what is called assets (upadhi). When that monk investigates within, he understands that this problem of Aging and Death (jarāmaraṇa) arises precisely because of these five. He investigates further into it from within: ‘Why do assets (upadhi) arise? Due to what cause? By what condition? What is its root?’ When seeking the cause in this way, he understands that Craving (Taṇhā) is its root. For it is due to that Craving (Taṇhā) that one grabs things through Grasping (upādāna). It is those grabbed things that one deposits as 'I' and 'mine.' Therefore, Craving (Taṇhā) is the root. This is how one penetrates deeper. May you, meritorious friends, direct your minds accordingly.
Next, that monk contemplates: ‘Where does this Craving (Taṇhā) arise? Where does it establish itself?’ Then he realizes that this Craving (Taṇhā) arises—the words ‘piya-rūpa’ (lovely form) are mentioned there—wherever there is something of a lovely nature, an agreeable nature in the world; it is there that Craving (Taṇhā) arises. It is there that Craving (Taṇhā) settles down, or establishes itself. Wherever the world perceives or thinks there is a lovely nature, an agreeable nature, right there Craving (Taṇhā) settles down. There Craving (Taṇhā) is born. There Craving (Taṇhā) establishes itself.
Next, it is asked: ‘What is it in the world that is regarded generally as lovely form and pleasant form, as a lovely nature and an agreeable nature?’ It is these six sense-bases—the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—that are regarded in the world as lovely and pleasant things. It is in dependence on them that one experiences that pleasure in the world. The Buddha further declares regarding this: “In the past, whatever recluses and brahmins regarded these things considered as lovely and pleasant form—these six sense-bases, either one or all of them—as pleasure, as permanent, as a refuge, as health, as safety, those recluses and brahmins, because of that, fell into those attachments. Consequently, because of that attitude, they nurtured what they had regarded as lovely and pleasant form. Since Craving (Taṇhā) grows through that attitude, assets (upadhi) grew as a result. What was grabbed by Grasping (upādāna) due to Craving (Taṇhā) deposited in the mind and grew as assets (upadhi). If any recluse or brahmin nurtured assets (upadhi), they nurtured Suffering (Dukkha).”
So, what we have here is that, due to that attitude, because of regarding those lovely and pleasant things as permanent, as pleasure, as health, as safe, as a refuge, they grew. Due to Craving (Taṇhā), assets (upadhi) grew. Due to assets (upadhi), Suffering (Dukkha) grew. Because Suffering (Dukkha) grew, they never escaped from saṃsāra. They did not escape from Birth (jāti), Aging and Death (jarāmaraṇa), sorrow, lamentation, and despair. Just as in the past, so too in the future, whichever recluses and brahmins adopt that attitude regarding these lovely and pleasant things, regarding them as permanent, as pleasure, as health, as safe, they will nurture Craving (Taṇhā). By nurturing Craving (Taṇhā), assets (upadhi) grow. From assets (upadhi), Suffering (Dukkha) grows. Through the growth of Suffering (Dukkha), they remain imprisoned in saṃsāra, enduring that kind of mountain of Suffering (Dukkha).
Next, He gives an illustration and a simile for this: “Monks, suppose there is a cup of beverage that is very fragrant, colorful, and delicious, but it is mixed with poison. A man arrives there, thirsty and exhausted in the scorching heat of summer. When he arrives, the people there say to him: ‘Here is a beverage that is beautiful, fragrant, and tasty. But there is a small drawback: it is mixed with poison. If you wish, you may drink it. While drinking, it is very delicious and fragrant, a beautiful drink. But once drunk, you will either die or undergo suffering equivalent to death.’ Yet that man, without thinking further, being thirsty and exhausted, drinks it. Having drunk it, he either meets death or undergoes suffering equivalent to death.” This is the simile the Buddha presents regarding that first attitude.
Next, the Buddha shows the other side regarding those lovely and pleasant things. “In the past, if any recluses and brahmins changed their attitude towards them, regarding them as Impermanent (anicca) (whereas previously they regarded them as permanent), as Suffering (dukkha), as Not-self (anattā), as a disease, as a danger, they thereby abandoned Craving (Taṇhā).” This is the second attitude towards those lovely things. What is it? They regarded them as Impermanent (anicca), as Suffering (dukkha), as Not-self (anattā), as a disease or illness, as a danger. “Such recluses and brahmins destroyed Craving (Taṇhā). When Craving (Taṇhā) was destroyed, assets (upadhi) were destroyed. When assets (upadhi) were destroyed, Suffering (Dukkha) was destroyed. They were liberated from those sufferings such as Birth (jāti), Aging and Death (jarāmaraṇa).” Hearing this, you, meritorious friends, can now understand those terms like lovely form and pleasant form.
Here is the simile given for that: “Just as before, there is a cup of poison. Just as before, a thirsty and exhausted man arrives. People say to him: ‘This is a colorful, fragrant, and delicious beverage. However, once drunk, such-and-such a thing will happen.’ That person, contemplating wisely, thinks: ‘I can quench my thirst with some water, or buttermilk, or some other beverage. I can satisfy my thirst with that. If I drink this, it will bring about my ruin.’ Thus thinking, he rejects it.” This is what is said about that attitude. Recluses and brahmins of that kind, through that attitude, reject those lovely things. Through that, they are liberated from Suffering (Dukkha).
This is an extremely deep discourse. Now, if we investigate this word *sammasana* (scrutiny) a little further: for an insight (vipassanā) practitioner, meditation means practicing the scrutiny of Preparations (saṅkhāra-sammasana). We have occasionally compared this word *sammasana* (scrutiny) with the word *parāmāsa* (grasping). The word *parāmāsa* is mostly used in connection with views. Followers of other sects often look at things superficially, adopt a certain view, and asserting *“idaṃ eva saccaṃ mogham-aññaṃ”* — ‘this alone is the truth, everything else is false’ — they hold on to it through Grasping (upādāna), become trapped within it, and end up unable to progress. But what is found in the Dhamma is not *parāmāsa* (dogmatic grasping) but *sammasana* (wise scrutiny). If we go further by means of a simile, we can explain the simile the Buddha gave for those Preparations (saṅkhāra) when discussing *parāmāsa*.
You, meritorious friends, have heard that the aggregate of Preparations (saṅkhārakkhandha) is compared to a banana tree trunk. The Buddha on one occasion explained why this aggregate of Preparations (saṅkhārakkhandha) is compared to a banana tree trunk. It is like this: when a man enters a forest and sees these banana trees, what does he think? Thinking there is some essence or heartwood in it, he cuts it at the root, shoulders it, brings it home, and when he examines it, he finds no heartwood at all. He realizes there is no essence in it. But let us think for a moment: without going to the trouble of carrying the banana trunk home, what if he gently peeled it and inspected it right there? As he removes one layer of the banana trunk, there is another layer. As he removes that, there is yet another layer. It is just a pile of layers. There is no heartwood or essence whatsoever. The method that leads to this understanding is what is called *sammasana* (wise scrutiny). It is like carefully touching and examining. On the other hand, tightly gripping it, grasping it, and carrying it on one's shoulder is what is called *parāmāsa*. *Sammasana* means gently handling, inspecting, and examining.
Therefore, this is why the Buddha spoke of *antara-sammasana* (internal scrutiny) here.
