In that way, a wholesome mental succession arose within your own mental continuum at this moment, which helps to establish faith (*saddhā*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*) as spiritual faculties and powers. Utilizing them, you must aspire: "May we gain the strength and power to realize the supreme deathless Nibbāna as quickly as possible, in this very life, through the penetration of the paths and fruits (*magga-phala*)—namely Stream-entry (*sotāpatti*), Once-returning (*sakadāgāmitā*), Non-returning (*anāgāmitā*), and Arahanthood!" Likewise, may all deities and Brahmas—including the guardians of the Sāsana, the right-viewed deities and Brahmas, and the deities presiding over this place—rejoice in this heap of merit we have accumulated through this preaching and hearing of the Dhamma! Having rejoiced, may they realize the supreme, deathless Nibbāna through whatever state of awakening (*bodhi*) they aspire to, and may they protect the Sāsana! Furthermore, may all our departed relatives, and all beings from the Avīci hell up to the Akanitṭha heaven who desire merit and Nibbāna, rejoice in this merit of our preaching and hearing of Dhamma, and through their aspired state of awakening (*bodhi*), may they realize the supreme, deathless Nibbāna and escape from all saṃsāric suffering (*dukkha*)! Aspiring thus, share the merit by reciting the verses.

(pahankanuwa sinhala audio dhamma sermon no.23)
namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa
(homage to the blessed one, the worthy one, the fully self-enlightened one)
pali stanza:
sududdasam sunipunam,
yatthakamanipatinam;
cittam rakkhetha medhavi,
cittam guttam sukhavaham.
from:
dhammapada 36 (cittavagga)
dear listeners,
for beings wandering in samsara for an infinite time, the extremely rare opportunity to bring an end to the suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara arises only when a fully self-awakened one, the teacher of the three worlds, appears in the world. everyone who properly understands the value of this rare opportunity strives and makes an effort to reap the maximum benefit from the rare human existence they have obtained during the era of a buddha’s arising. to whatever extent one feels spiritual urgency (*samvega*) regarding the suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara, to that same extent, one diligently goes in search of the supreme bliss of nibbana. furthermore, if there is any sacrifice to be made for that purpose, they strive to make it completely. such people seek the shortest possible path to fulfill their aspiration—their diligent aspiration for nibbana. it is for such individuals that the blessed buddha, on certain occasions, enabled the realization of nibbana through a brief sermon. the verse we have chosen as our theme today is one such verse. the introductory story behind it is as follows.
there was a certain treasurer (*setthi*) living in the city of savatthi. he went to his close, associated monk and asked, "i need to escape from this suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara; please tell me a good method for this." this monk, perhaps thinking at the level of the treasurer, gave him advice: "then give alms. offer robes to the sangha. serve them with the four requisites. also, divide your income into three parts: use one part for your business and industries, use another part to support your wife and children, and dedicate the third part to the sasana." he gave advice in this manner. the treasurer acted accordingly and asked the monk again, "is there anything more than this that would help me cross over this samsara?" then the monk declared, "guard well the five precepts together with the three refuges." excellent; having completed that as well, the treasurer asked again, "is there anything higher than that?" "then observe the ten precepts," the monk said. when he went back and asked, "is there anything even higher to do?", he was told, "then renounce the household life and go forth into monkhood."
in this manner, the treasurer went forth into the sasana. but despite having ordained, the teacher (*acariya*) this newly ordained monk received was an abhidhammika monk who had reached the further shore of the abhidhamma. his preceptor (*upajjhaya*) was a vinayadhara monk who had reached the further shore of the vinaya. both of these senior monks continuously taught abhidhamma and vinaya to this newly ordained monk at every opportunity. now, learning is indeed necessary for a newly ordained monk. however, to this monk, who had ordained with the hope of diligently bringing an end to suffering (*dukkha*), this felt like a burden. he felt that his teacher and preceptor were endlessly talking about abhidhamma and vinaya all the time, without giving much help for his meditation. due to the weariness that arose from this, this monk thought, "i renounced the household life and ordained with the intention of ending suffering (*dukkha*), but now there isn't even room to stretch out my hands." what he meant was that there was no room for things like meditation. having fallen into this state, he became disillusioned and then thought, "it is better for me to return to the household life and try to realize nibbana as best as i can." disillusioned with the monastic life, he did not tell anyone about it. losing his previous enthusiasm for his duties and vows, he just stared blankly wherever he looked, and stood still wherever he stood. his body also grew weak because of his dejected mind. seeing this, the novice monks (*samaneras*) asked him, "what is the reason for this change?" after this monk explained the reason, they informed the teacher and preceptor as well. these teachers and preceptors then took the monk to the blessed buddha. when the blessed buddha asked about the matter, this monk declared, "venerable sir, i ordained with the intention of bringing an end to the suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara. my teacher and preceptor constantly teach me abhidhamma and vinaya. i felt that i have no room even to stretch my hands. therefore, i want to return to the lay life."
then the blessed buddha asked this monk, "very well, monk, there is no need for many things. can you guard just one thing?" when asked what that was, the blessed buddha declared, "monk, if you guard only this mind, everything else will automatically be guarded." having stated this, he uttered the dhamma verse we chose as our theme earlier:
> *sududdasam sunipunam,*
> *yatthakamanipatinam;*
> *cittam rakkhetha medhavi,*
> *cittam guttam sukhavaham.*
the meaning of this verse is: *medhavi* means the wise person. this wise person guards the mind which is *sududdasam*—extremely difficult to see, and *sunipunam*—extremely subtle; *cittam rakkhetha*—guards the mind. why? *cittam guttam sukhavaham*—because a guarded mind brings happiness. at first glance, the verse seems very simple. yet, it is said that upon hearing this very verse, that monk attained stream-entry (*sotapatti*). therefore, this must have occurred because there is a certain depth in this verse. let us now first reflect on this story, and then direct our attention to the meaning contained in this verse. from the story itself, we can see that this monk, due to his enthusiasm to diligently realize nibbana, felt a sense of weariness and distress regarding the teachings of his teacher and preceptor. perhaps those venerable monks showed more concern for books and mere academic knowledge than for meditation.
the blessed one has declared in a certain discourse: "monks, all those who are newly ordained in this sasana, who have newly entered this dhamma-vinaya, should be established in the four foundations of mindfulness (*cattaro satipatthana*). they must practice the four foundations of mindfulness." from this, we can see that the foundation of going forth is the four foundations of mindfulness. if one engages in other activities without paying much attention to the four foundations of mindfulness, it becomes an obstacle for someone who has ordained with great diligence and enthusiasm to realize nibbana. that is why the blessed buddha, as a relief to that monk, asked, "can you do just one thing?" thus, from this story, we can see that the blessed buddha, with great skill in means (*upaya-kosalla*) and compassion, through a certain masterly device, must have directed this monk’s mind towards meditative reflection by means of this verse. for, what is expected from all those things taught as abhidhamma is to demonstrate the extreme subtlety of this mind.
the mind is something difficult to see. its nature is extremely subtle. what books and other teachings attempt to show, a meritorious meditator (*yogavacara*)—someone who has turned towards meditation—realizes through their own direct experience. through meditative reflection, through *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention)—which means wise reflection—a meditator understands the extremely subtle nature of this mind and that it is difficult to see, grasping the very essence of the entire abhidhamma. furthermore, *yatthakamanipatinam* means that the mind alights on whatever object it pleases. that is the nature of the mind; it falls upon whatever object it desires. *kamanipatinam*—it is precisely to prevent this falling onto whatever object it pleases that various vinaya rules and regulations have been laid down.
various disciplinary rules are prescribed for the restraint of body and speech. thus, the blessed buddha declared that it is this very mind—which has the nature of alighting on whatever object it pleases, denoted as *yatthakamanipatinam*, which is the essence of the vinaya—that must be guarded. it must have been because he contemplated the meaning of that verse deeply that the monk was able to attain even the realization of the paths and fruits (*magga-phala*).
although ordinary worldly people exert themselves regarding the body, they do not direct their attention to the importance of the mind. yet, this entire bondage of samsara rests upon the mind. what is done through meditation is the training of this mind, the guarding of this mind. the factor necessary for guarding that mind is mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajanna*)—which means mindfulness and proper wisdom, or mindfulness and awareness. when the mind that runs to the past and the future, and similarly runs towards greed and hatred, is brought to the present and strengthened with equanimity and concentration, it is only then that one can understand the true nature of this life and the world through insight knowledge (*vipassana-nana*). to guard the mind, the blessed buddha has first of all pointed out mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajanna*). for,
it is said, "mindfulness is the guardian" (*sati arakkhika*). just like a driver who is there to protect a chariot, mindfulness is the guardian of the mind. it is called mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajanna*): mindfulness and wisdom, mindfulness and awareness. to the extent that one develops this mindfulness and clear comprehension, one can eliminate the scattered nature of the mind and attain concentration (*samadhi*).
as taught in the dhamma, by developing mindfulness and awareness in daily life, one first establishes concentration. next, one realizes the three characteristics: *anicca* (impermanent), *dukkha* (suffering), and *anatta* (not-self). to realize this, one uses these very things that are closest to oneself: the body, feeling (*vedana*), the mind, and the objects of the mind—by maintaining the mind upon them. because of the instigation of defilements, the mind always looks to the past and the future. keeping the mind that runs to the past and future anchored in the present, making it concentrated, one then observes how everything arises, exists, and vanishes. if we look more closely at what we call "impermanence" (*anicca*) in the world, we see everything arising; there is a certain phase we regard as its existence, and then it fades away. there are only these three phases. not a single thing is permanent. this
one who dwells with mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajanna*) regarding the body, feeling (*vedana*), the mind, and mental objects, understands the subtlety of this mind. that is why the blessed buddha declared that what is done through mindfulness and clear comprehension, even in ordinary postures, is: when walking, he knows "i am walking"; when standing, he knows "i am standing"; when sitting, he knows "i am sitting"; when lying down, he knows "i am lying down"—thus becoming aware of daily postures in a very simple manner. it is being aware with mindfulness and proper wisdom. furthermore, in whatever way his body is positioned, he understands it as such. by always observing how one's body is positioned and how it moves, the impermanent (*anicca*) nature of this body, of feelings (*vedana*), of the mind, and of mental objects, and their nature of arising and passing away, automatically begins to be seen. for this, reflection (*manasikara*) is particularly helpful. reflection coupled with mindfulness and clear comprehension is necessary.
here lies an important point. generally, when there is mindfulness and clear comprehension, one is able to see feelings (*vedana*) and so forth arising, persisting, and ceasing. similarly, one sees perceptions (*sanna*)—which we regard as recognition—arising, persisting, and passing away. even thoughts are seen arising, persisting, and passing away. however, it is difficult for a person to gain this understanding all at once. why? because of the deceitful nature of the mind. in many instances, we know how the mind operates; some people feel, "now i am thinking." yet, it is as if thoughts occur without one even realizing it. even when one thinks "i am thinking," thoughts just happen. one is carried away by the mind.
this mind is just like a wild bull. led by defilements—according to greed, hatred, or delusion—this mind runs very far along some object without us even knowing it. therefore, one can practice reflection only by being established in a certain level of concentration (*samadhi*). now, a running wild bull cannot be caught and stopped all at once. a certain momentum is required. for that, there is a general method through the "four protective meditations" (*caturarakkha bhavana*): the recollection of the buddha (*buddhanussati*), loving-kindness (*metta*), foulness (*asubha*), and the mindfulness of death (*maranassati*), by practicing and training in a certain simple meditation subject (*kammatthana*). for this, a short word is used as an aid. if it is the recollection of the buddha, one of the virtues of the buddha is recalled. by bringing this to mind at all times, the scattered nature of the mind is stopped and the mind is calmed. some wholesome object is used for this purpose. one strives to concentrate the mind on a wholesome object. when one repeatedly exerts effort to stop the running mind or calm the scattered mind using a short word, one gradually realizes that this can be done more and more quickly. then, through the recollection of the buddha, faith (*saddha*) increases in a person. through loving-kindness, one gains the strength to suppress the thoughts of hatred that constantly arise. through the meditation on foulness, one gains the ability to subdue thoughts of lust. through the mindfulness of death, spiritual urgency (*samvega*) is aroused, urging one to practice diligently. these are the special qualities present in the four protective meditations. by using a short word as an aid for each of them—for instance, for loving-kindness: "may all beings be well and happy!" when these are practiced in daily life, whenever the mind runs to unnecessary things, one unifies the mind with the thought: "may they be well and happy!"
in that way, the person who has established that concentration is then able to reflect wisely by using that level of concentration. *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention) is generally explained as wise reflection. otherwise, it is reflecting on things according to the actual origin from which various things arise in the world. in the ordinary world, the blessed buddha has compared these perceptions (*sanna*) to a mirage; there is a tendency in our minds to run after these perceptions. why? because we take that distant mirage to be something real. but the true understanding regarding it is that from where we are looking, it is merely something that appears. it has a deceptive nature. this is revealed by understanding that this is a certain delusion connected to one's own mind, or rather, to one's own eye. in the same way, through *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention), through wise reflection, one is able to escape from the delusion called ignorance (*avijja*) and from this tight bondage called craving (*tanha*). the method used for this wise reflection is mindfulness of breathing (*anapanassati*).
the blessed buddha has taught, has declared, mindfulness of breathing (*anapanassati*) for the purpose of cutting off distracting thoughts (*vitakka*)—for cutting off thoughts. one’s in-breath and out-breath are something that is always with oneself. applying mindfulness to that, mindfulness of breathing means the mindfulness directed towards the in-breath and out-breath. one establishes that mindfulness at the point where the breath touches. while constantly bringing the mind back to that spot, one gradually subdues the scattered things, the scattered mind. most often, the mind scatters along the objects that come to the five senses: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. those objects generally try to pull the mind away, according to greed, hatred, or delusion. what, then, is the device to stop that running? generally, regarding what is seen, without taking their signs (*nimitta*) and going far, the meditator (*yogavacara*) briefly reflects twice: "a form, a form," "a sound, a sound," thereby cutting off the running mind right there, or breaking it, and bringing it back to the meditation subject, to mindfulness of breathing. in that manner, through reflection, the mind that runs after perceptions (*sanna*) can be kept within the meditation subject itself. distracting thoughts (*vitakka*) grow in accordance with those perceptions, and thoughts grow. it is through those thoughts that defilements are dragged in.
the blessed buddha has declared five hindrances (*nivarana*) that obstruct the concentration of the mind and obstruct realization. they are: sensual desire (*kamacchanda*), which refers to sensual thoughts; ill-will (*byapada*), which refers to thoughts of hatred; sloth and torpor (*thina-middha*), which refers to laziness of mind and sleepiness; restlessness and worry (*uddhacca-kukkucca*), which refers to the scattered nature of the mind and regret; and doubt (*vicikiccha*), which refers to indecisiveness. it is through these that one becomes subject to them. it is precisely these hindrances that drag in those distracting thoughts. therefore, it is only when these hindrances are absent that the mind becomes properly concentrated. a wholesome meditation object (*kusala-arammana*) is helpful for this. thus, a person who has developed some concentration by practicing the four protective meditations is able, while practicing mindfulness of breathing, to gradually stop the running mind and understand the internal state of this mind, the subtlety of the mind.
the reason why the mind was described here as subtle and difficult to see is that there is a certain quality in this mind. the blessed buddha has shown consciousness (*vinnana*) to be like an illusion (*maya*). this is an extremely deep matter. an illusion means showing something that does not exist as if it exists. an illusionist or a magician shows something non-existent as existing by conjuring it up. there is such a power in our minds. it shows a non-existent thing as if it were an existing thing. it is because of this illusion that the mind is difficult to see. how is this revealed? only a buddha points out the way to this. when that understanding regarding the nature of this world and life matures through insight knowledges (*vipassana-nana*), one must realize: what is actually here that we have taken as "i" and "mine"? it is only a collection of mental phenomena (name-factors) and physical phenomena (form-factors)—only name-and-form (*namarupa*). the mental phenomena (name-factors) are mentioned as: feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), intention (*cetana*), contact (*phassa*), and attention (*manasikara*). chiefly, there are these five. "name" (*nama*) refers to certain powers within the mind itself that help us identify something. feeling (*vedana*), as everyone knows, is experiencing. next, perception (*sanna*) means recognition; if there is a certain experiencing, there is a corresponding recognition. next, there is also a volitional power (*cetana*) in our minds regarding what should be done with them. contact (*phassa*) is the awareness of their impingement or collision. next is attention (*manasikara*), which is reflection. if we can present these five factors as an analogy, they are just like the five fingers of the hand. feeling (*vedana*) is like the little finger. perception (*sanna*) is like the ring finger. intention (*cetana*) is like the middle finger. contact (*phassa*) is like the index finger. attention (*manasikara*) is like the thumb.
so, among the five mental phenomena (*nama-dhamma*) present here, we already mentioned attention (*manasikara*). attention is helpful and applicable for understanding the true reality of this world, or rather, of life. if we take an analogy for this, we know that in some murder or criminal cases, one of the accused arrested as defendants has to be granted a pardon if there is no other evidence. if no one else comes forward to give evidence, because the case would otherwise be dismissed, one of the defendants is pardoned in court itself—like a state pardon—and the facts are obtained from him. when the testifying is finally over, it is revealed that he himself was also involved in the crime. however, somehow the case is proven and the truth is uncovered. it is in this very way that we have to understand name-and-form (*namarupa*). yet, what helps us untangle this is that very factor called attention (*manasikara*). we compared it to the thumb. according to this analogy, when we think about the functioning of the fingers of our hand, we can see that the thumb maintains a relationship with the little finger, the ring finger, the middle finger, and the index finger—with every one of them. the thumb is the one that can bear witness to them. in the same way, there is a power in this factor of attention (*manasikara*). attention directs itself to feeling (*vedana*), to intention, and to contact (*phassa*), and by directing itself to these, it can understand their true reality. this is precisely what the blessed buddha highlighted. thus, we understand what are called name-and-form (*namarupa*) not by bringing in an external witness, but through this very factor of attention (*manasikara*). however, the difference here is that ordinary worldly people reflect in the wrong way. in the dhamma, this is called *ayoneso manasikara* (unwise attention)—wrong reflection. now, if we consider
what we said earlier, a deer thinks of the mirage, regards its appearance, as water in the distance. thinking it is water, the deer runs. but a wise person considers, "this is merely an appearance due to a defect in my eyesight and due to atmospheric and climatic causes." thus he does not run, but stops right there. having stopped, he investigates the matter.
in the same way, reflecting on the very place where this arises is what is taken as *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention). this itself is called wise reflection—proper reflection. in that manner, even though we utilize the mental phenomenon (*nama-dhamma*) of attention (*manasikara*) here, it is not used in an *ayoniso* (unwise) way, but in a *yoniso* (wise) way. this is just like after a defendant is pardoned in order to give evidence in a case: that person is now a witness for the state. he is not like before when he gave false evidence; now he speaks the absolute truth. it is under obligation that he receives such a pardon, to declare the complete truth. it is having promised, and having been made to promise, that such a pardon is granted to someone. in the same way, here too, attention is applied with *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention) for the sake of realizing the truth. it is precisely through attention utilized in this way that we strive to arouse insight knowledges (*vipassana-nana*). when we reflect on the manner in which these arise and pass away, we see that there is nothing here to be grasped. what is here is only a collection of mental phenomena (*nama-dhamma*), and what is called physical phenomenon (*rupa-dhamma*)—which is a conjuring up by the elements of earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and air (*vayo*). this is all that is present here: a collection of mental phenomena (*nama-dhamma*) and a few physical phenomena (*rupa-dhamma*) (name-and-form).
as this realization matures, the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*)—the tightly held view of 'i' and 'mine'—is gradually relinquished; as the blessed buddha declared, this must be realized by oneself, individually. as long as this is not realized, this bondage of samsara, this bondage of kamma, persists. so terrifying is the nature of this samsara that there are accumulated in our minds the seeds of kamma gathered over an infinite, long period in this samsara. so powerful are those kamma-seeds that they repeatedly bring about rounds of retribution. those kammas committed in the past arise through our mental continuum in various ways, and they keep flowing. the vast amount of kamma accumulated in relation to the eye arises according to the occasion, subjecting the eye to it, and accumulates still more kamma. thus, what is happening here is also the operation of ignorance and craving (*tanha*). unknowingly, we do not know that these are kammas. we do not know that this is happening due to kamma. often, when things come to us according to kamma, because we lack realization, we do not understand them, and we accumulate kamma over and over again through them.
when we reflect on the entirety of samsara, we can say that it consists of a lot of struggling and writhing. we have struggled for an infinite time in this samsara. this is done by accumulating kamma, based on the notion of 'i' and 'mine'. as long as one takes these five aggregates—form, feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), preparations (*sankhara*), and consciousness (*vinnana*)—associated with this body or other things, as 'i' and 'mine', one accumulates various kammas in terms of intentions, by way of liking, disliking, and delusion regarding them. having accumulated those kammas, when we subsequently experience their retributions, we do not know that these are retributions. sometimes we develop hatred towards those who are instrumental in bringing them about; we conflict with them. in that manner, due to the arising of those defilements, from that mass of struggling, another mass of struggling is created. when the rounds of retribution come, one accumulates more kamma through them due to ignorance, because of the lack of true understanding. instead, when one’s understanding of name-and-form (*namarupa*) develops, one realizes: "here, there is only a process occurring due to causes and conditions—merely a series of activities." by establishing that realization within the mind, kamma is no longer accumulated. this is what helps one towards liberation.
if one is to escape from this bondage of samsara, one must gain a correct understanding of the process occurring here. this is what is meant by the understanding of mental phenomena (*nama-dhamma*). the realization that there is no 'i' or 'mine' to be taken here must come through direct experience—not merely because someone else said so, nor because it is written in a book. it is only by being established in a certain level of concentration and realizing, through insight reflection by way of *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention), the true nature of these things—that they all arise, persist, and pass away—that one can obtain liberation, escape from samsara.
therefore, this very realization is what we must consider as the ultimate goal of our life. as long as this realization is absent, we will have to wander in this samsara for an infinite, long period, repeatedly accumulating kamma, and consequently facing the mass of samsaric suffering (*dukkha*) known as birth (*jati*), decay, sickness, and death (*jaramarana*). to attain this realization, we must make a certain effort in our daily life; we must make a certain sacrifice. now, that treasurer renounced all his vast wealth and ordained. this was due to such a powerful desire, a powerful aspiration (*chanda*). in the same way, we must reflect that in this human existence obtained during the era of a buddha's arising, there may be various other things, various other goals, and things that can be done. however, if one considers this as the most rare opportunity to escape from samsara, what one has to do is to develop one's mind through meditation and gain this very realization.
first of all, while establishing concentration in daily life through some meditation subject (*kammatthana*) such as loving-kindness, recollection of the buddha, foulness, or mindfulness of death, one must understand their impermanent (*anicca*) nature by performing activities such as maintaining postures with mindfulness and proper wisdom, with mindfulness (*sati*), in accordance with the four foundations of mindfulness. the three characteristics of *anicca* (impermanent), *dukkha* (suffering), and *anatta* (not-self) are matters that must be realized by each person individually. what helps in this is attention, which is called *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention). thus, to realize this group of dhammas, by initiating them in daily life and then generating the effort called right endeavors (*sammappadhana*) in one's mental continuum, and by developing the other factors called the bases of spiritual power (*iddhipada*), one is gradually able to arouse insight knowledges (*vipassana-nana*). generally, some individuals are able to arouse these much sooner than they expected. the meditative capacities accumulated in past samsara are stored within our mental continuum. for that, we must make an effort. without such an effort, they will not arise on their own. when the deep understanding of this impermanence (*aniccata*), which we regard as insight knowledge, matures as insight knowledges (*vipassana-nana*), one sees that what is here is only arising and passing away (*udayabbaya*). in this world, we see the sun rise and the sun set. in the same way, in everything of ours—regarding both our body and thoughts—in every single one of them, there is an arising and a passing away. because we lack the understanding of this arising and passing away, we regard everything as permanent.
indeed, the blessed buddha has declared that in this world, there is only emptiness. if told this, a person cannot easily conceptualize it. the blessed buddha has used an analogy for these six sense-spheres we call the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—the word *ayatana* is used in the dhamma for these six senses—that all six of these sense-spheres are empty. so much so, that they are to be seen as an empty village. an empty village is what is called when the people of that village have fled; there is no one in that village. in the same way, in not a single one of these—the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—is there anything that can be taken as 'i' or 'mine'. in that sense, it is void; the blessed buddha declared it is empty. so, it is through that very attention (*manasikara*) that one can see these as an empty village. there is no essence to be grasped in the forms met by the eye. moreover, there is nothing there other than a mere natural phenomenon. but what happens here? because of the lack of that realization, grasping (*upadana*)—which means holding on—occurs. one grasps them as 'i' and 'mine'. as long as one grasps them as 'i' and 'mine', it is precisely because of that grasping (*upadana*) that those kammas are accumulated. that is why one wanders in samsara for a long time. in accordance with the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*) conjured up by the mind as 'i', one is born in samsara over and over again.
to give an analogy, when twisting a rope made of several strands, if the two people at either end try, even by mistake, to twist the rope in the exact same direction, it will never twist into a knot. but if someone comes and holds it in the middle, then a rope-like thing is twisted there. this happens because it was grasped in the middle. in the same way, everything in the world is spinning. the mind is also spinning. all other things in the world can be thought of as spinning things. they go in circles to that extent. otherwise, they have a nature of arising and passing away. there is a certain cycle between arising and passing away. it is because of that grasping (*upadana*) that we perceive something substantial out of that spinning, or rather, out of that struggling. if it were allowed to twist in only one direction, there would be no knot there. why? if it is not held in the middle, it will not twist either. but because of that grasping (*upadana*), it appears there as a thing. when this is let go, its complete emptiness (*sunnata*) is understood. that is exactly the kind of thing that happens.
in many instances, it is mentioned in the dhamma that some individuals with developed insight wisdom (*vipassana-panna*), when the blessed buddha uttered a single line of a verse, realized the path-knowledge of stream-entry (*sotapatti*) and so forth. why is that? what was the reason for this? that grasping (*upadana*) present in the mind, the force of holding on, suddenly slipped away. at some point, if a realization arises that is powerful enough to let go of these five aggregates (*pancakkhandha*)—namely form, feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), preparations (*sankhara*), and consciousness (*vinnana*), which are the five heaps we hold on to with this mind—then, at that moment, just like the rope unraveling, like how the thing that appeared as a rope unraveled, the true reality of this is understood.
that is precisely why the blessed buddha declared: "what is regarded as truth by the world is untruth to the buddhas and noble ones (*ariyas*). what appears as truth to the noble ones is untruth to the world." when we look at this, it is a very amazing statement. it seems contradictory. why? the reason for this is that the world lives within a delusion—within ignorance (*avijja*). we do not want to accept that. society always looks to bring that ignorance to the forefront. it is like a process of cultivating and consuming. however, buddhas arise in the world to point out the way to free our minds from this very delusion. some individuals with developed wisdom destroyed this delusion extremely rapidly. they realized that emptiness (*sunnata*), that these are empty villages. the eye is an empty village, the ear is an empty village, the nose is an empty village. why are they called empty villages? if we reflect generally, the forms we saw in our childhood, the sounds we heard—none of them exist now. yet, they are present in our minds. we think, "i saw these, i heard these." because of that notion of 'i', these are held onto by way of grasping (*upadana*). because of that very grasping, being bound to that bondage of kamma, one wanders in samsara over and over again.
a very amazing thing is present here. that is why consciousness (*vinnana*) was said to be an illusion (*maya*). it is showing something non-existent. yet, to the one who watches, it is real. everyone goes to a magic show to see something. indeed, it is shown as such, but despite being shown, there is no essence there—no substance. that is precisely why the blessed buddha declared that this consciousness (*vinnana*) is an illusion. in every other religion, consciousness (*vinnana*) is regarded as the essence, the core, the self (*atta*). even if they say all other things are not-self, every other teacher in the world takes consciousness (*vinnana*) to be the self. but the blessed buddha alone declared that consciousness (*vinnana*) is an illusion. for, what is here is a great deception, and what aids this deception is that very ignorance (*avijja*). ignorance is entirely a veil. it is called a hindrance (*nivarana*); it is covered by that veil. when performing a magic trick, a black cloth is put up and some false projection is made through it. similarly, the black cloth of ignorance (*avijja*) produces delusion.
next, that bondage called craving (*tanha*) is experienced as an attachment. by means of that craving—called by various names such as craving (*tanha*), lust (*raga*), or greed (*lobha*)—that thing is shown as if it exists. it is in accordance with that craving (*tanha*) itself that grasping (*upadana*) exists. in daily life, one can experience these directly for oneself, to whatever level one is at. when we reflect on the instances that caused our emotional outbursts, we see how we conjured up an existing thing out of something non-existent. especially, if one reflects on the past as an example—on one’s own childhood, or for elderly people, on their youth—where are those things that they held onto as grasping (*upadana*)? none of them exist. yet, regarding them, there is a certain notion of 'i' and 'mine' created by the mind. once 'i' is taken, the feeling that "there is also something that is mine" arises. between these two, there lies a very amazing delusion. in realizing this, in daily life, one can properly practice the four foundations of mindfulness, using mindfulness of breathing (*anapanassati*) as an insight practice. although we regard our in-breath and out-breath as a single thing, what is present here is a certain process. through that process, we see its impermanence (*aniccata*). that is a good illustration. similarly, when the nature of arising, persisting, and ceasing of all things is understood, that perception of permanence (*nicca-sanna*) is gradually removed.
the blessed buddha has declared that there are four perversions (*vipallasa*) in the world. perversions mean four wrong understandings: the perception of permanence in the impermanent (*anicca*), the perception of pleasure in the painful (*dukkha*), the perception of beauty in the foul (*asubha*), and the perception of self in the not-self (*anatta*). there is a notion in the world taking the impermanent (*anicca*) to be permanent. there is a tendency to regard what is painful (*dukkha*) as pleasant. there is a tendency to regard what is foul as beautiful. there is a tendency to regard what is not-self (*anatta*) as self. the mind must escape from this distorted state called perversions (*vipallasa*). what helps in that escape is the knowledge and vision of things as they really are (*yathabhuta-nanadassana*)—the understanding of true reality. that is not something that can be shown to another. within our own mind, as said before, it is comprised of mental phenomena (*nama-dhamma*). all of them are defendants. yet, at least one must be pardoned to get the work done. by turning this attention into *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention), we must make an effort in our daily life itself, established in a certain virtue (*sila*), to wisely understand the nature of that subtle mind—the nature of the subtle mind which is difficult to see.
what is done through virtue (*sila*) is subduing this body and speech, and providing the necessary opportunity for mental seclusion (*citta-viveka*). it is freeing the mind from regrets and allowing room for mental seclusion. to establish concentration, there must be mental seclusion within that person. it is through the stages described as physical seclusion (*kaya-viveka*), mental seclusion (*citta-viveka*), and seclusion from acquisitions (*upadhi-viveka*) that the realization of nibbana can be achieved. thus, after establishing that concentration, by relying on concentration and reflecting properly, one sees the mirage-like nature of everything. why is it stopped right there as "a form, a form," "a sound, a sound"? if one wishes, one can analyze in detail. but that does not help nibbana. it may help in daily activities—analyzing what kind of form it is, whose it is, how beautiful, bad, or ugly it is. but through those, samsara only grows further, delusion grows, ignorance grows, and it does not help in realizing the four noble truths declared by the blessed buddha. therefore, everything we do is either good or bad in accordance with our ultimate goal. thus, the meditator (*yogavacara*), the meritorious person who hopes to realize nibbana, no matter how the world thinks—even if they consider it madness—must direct his attention (*manasikara*) according to his goal, according to the target he aspires to.
the nature of this running mind is like flowing water, or like being dragged by a wild bull. first of all, this scattered mind must be calmed. having calmed it, concentration must be established. next, this running mind must be gradually subdued and stopped. the mind is stopped, indeed, through weariness (*nibbida*) regarding this; when true reality is understood, weariness grows. when the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*) grows, realizing "there is nothing here to be taken as 'i' and 'mine', everything is impermanent (*anicca*)," the previous momentum regarding these is lost. grasping (*upadana*)—which means holding on—gradually thins out. having become so, at some point when the exact realization arises, at that moment, it is not that one let go of it on purpose, but it is let go of on its own. to the extent it is let go of, weariness (*nibbida*) arises. that is what is called weariness with samsara. disillusionment (*nibbida*) means weariness with samsara. it is that weariness regarding everything that helps towards ultimate liberation, which is called dispassion (*viraga*).
when looked at as words, to most people in the ordinary world, these are unpleasant words. why? because this world always looks to expand the world. the blessed buddha has declared, *na siya loka-vaddhano*—one should not be a world-expander. expanding the world is not what is to be done. that expanding of the world is mara's work. mara always tries to keep us in delusion. the buddhas and the noble ones strive to free the world. to free them from the grip of mara, what helps is realization. realization cannot be created for another. even the blessed buddha cannot do that. according to each individual's samsaric potential, sometimes through a line of a verse, sometimes through a verse, sometimes through a longer discourse, and through various other devices, the blessed buddha directed their matured samsaric wisdom towards nibbana and granted them the realization of nibbana.
therefore, everyone must reflect that, without any distinction between young and old, the capacity to realize nibbana can be present within us. why did even seven-year-olds become arahants? because their samsaric wisdom had matured within them. at the very beginning here, we mentioned a teacher who taught abhidhamma, and a vinayadhara monk who taught vinaya. no matter how much one learns from books, if that which helps towards nibbana is absent, one remains in the grip of mara forever.
generally, whether we think about ordaining or other things, we regard only this erudition as the valuable thing in the world. but that is merely wisdom based on learning (*sutamaya-panna*)—wisdom gathered from books. one cannot obtain even an understanding of the state of nibbana through that wisdom. generally, by looking at a map, we cannot obtain the actual experience of traveling. it cannot be obtained by looking at a map; one must actually make the journey. in the same way, if one experiences this directly for oneself, at that moment, one’s doubts are dispelled; doubts are removed. no matter how much is obtained from books and so forth, doubts still remain. what helps in this is insight reflection (*vipassana-manasikara*).
these should not be regarded as things to be done only by the sangha, only after ordaining. even during the buddha’s time, and even recently, lay devotees—both men and women—aroused their samsaric potential, developed these insight knowledges (*vipassana-nana*), and attained the realization of the paths and fruits (*magga-phala*). therefore, by practicing some meditation subject (*kammatthana*) in daily life, establishing concentration, and gradually associating with those capable of giving instructions on them, one must make an effort to arouse those insight knowledges. the opportunity to bring an end to this samsaric suffering (*dukkha*) is obtained, as we mentioned earlier, only during the era of a buddha's arising.
the era of a buddha's arising is an extremely rare opportunity. that is why the blessed buddha, as daily advice from the sugata, pointed out those rare things:
> *dullabho buddhupado lokasmim, dullabho manussatta-patilabho, dullabha khanasampatti, dullabha pabbajja, dullabham saddhammasavanam, dullabho sappurisasamsevo.*
thus, six things are pointed out as rare. the era of a buddha's arising is extremely rare. next, the human existence obtained during the era of a buddha's arising can be said to be even rarer. if one had obtained other forms of existence—if one were born as an animal or a hungry ghost (*peta*)—one would not be able to realize nibbana; that is why human existence during the era of a buddha's arising is regarded as something extremely precious. even being an ordinary human is not enough. just having a human form is not enough; a wise human existence with intact sense faculties and the intellectual capacity to understand the dhamma is what can be regarded as the "opportune moment" (*khana-sampatti*). even if that opportune moment is obtained, next is going forth (*pabbajja*). going forth is described as renunciation (*nekkhamma*). the strength to renounce, that going forth, is even rarer. even if one goes forth, though one might get to hear the dhamma, hearing the dhamma that actually helps towards nibbana is extremely rare. even if one hears such dhamma, to practice according to that dhamma, the association with a person of integrity (*sappurisa*) who can guide one—which is called association with a noble friend (*kalyana-mitta*)—is extremely rare. looking at it in this way, like the bullseye in the center of a target, the association with a noble, spiritual friend (*kalyana-mitta*), as well as the era of a buddha's arising, can be regarded as the final phase of this gautama buddha’s sasana. if someone hopes to realize nibbana, it is at this very moment that it is possible.
when we reflect on the changes occurring in today's society, looking at it from all sides, in a few generations, even the word "nibbana" might be forgotten by the world. instead, other things—other things that overflow—may arise. due to physical forces and various other forces of defilements, as time goes on, it will fade. that is why when a buddha arises in the world, some people develop an amazing kind of faith (*saddha*) just upon hearing the word "buddha". until then, even the word "buddha" is buried. the word "nibbana" is buried. since such an era is coming in the future, every meritorious person at this moment must reflect: we must not dedicate our lives to those mundane pleasures and wealth. it must be dedicated for the sake of the rare human existence we have obtained.
we must make some effort to guard our mind—this mind whose true nature is difficult to see, extremely subtle, and which grows upon whatever object it pleases. if that effort is completed, as the blessed buddha declared, *"cittam guttam sukhavaham"*—if this mind is properly guarded, if the purity of the mind is established, if liberation is attained—then that person gains the capacity to be pacified by the supreme, deathless nibbana, escaping from all suffering (*dukkha*) of preparations (*sankhara*) such as birth (*jati*), decay, sickness, and death (*jaramarana*). we should not regard these as things that are far away. we must regard them as things that are extremely close to us. the blessed buddha has declared: *"santike na vijananti, maga dhamma..."*—"alas, they do not understand the dhamma that is close at hand; they are like beasts, foolish people." "beasts" (*maga*) here refers to fools—alas, what foolishness, they do not see the nibbana that is right here! from this, we can see that nibbana is not something far away like the sun or the moon. it is something that exists within ourselves.
there is an extremely valuable discourse of the blessed buddha: "monks, within this fathom-long body itself, i declare the world, the arising of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world." "the world" here refers precisely to the four noble truths. the blessed buddha declared that suffering (*dukkha*), the cause of suffering, nibbana attained by ending suffering, and the path to it, are all within this fathom-long body itself. it is within this living body endowed with perception (*sanna*) and mind—not within a dead corpse.
nowadays, it is only when someone dies, keeping that dead body in front, that we say, "may they attain the bliss of nibbana!" this is not what is being said here. the capacity to obtain nibbana is within this living human being endowed with perception (*sanna*) and mind. if that is not brought out, then, as the blessed buddha declared: *"santike na vijananti, maga dhamma..."*—we would have to say, "alas, fools do not understand the nibbana that is close at hand!" therefore, we must reflect wisely, bring close to our lives the sublime dhamma pointed out by the supreme buddhas within this precious human existence we have obtained, arouse our samsaric potentials, arouse that wisdom, and reflect: "may this hearing of the dhamma also help us to be pacified by the supreme, deathless nibbana!"
so, on this poya day, having undertaken the precious virtue of *ajiva-atthamaka-sila* (morality with livelihood as the eighth factor), and subduing body and speech, you have listened to the dhamma with mindfulness (*sati*) and wisdom during this short time. we regard the realization of nibbana as the benefit of this hearing of the dhamma. if we look at it deeply, it is not something that happens automatically, nor is it a magical event. within our mental continuum, during this listening to the dhamma, a certain series of dhammas is deposited. these, known as faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*), are mentioned as the five spiritual faculties (*pancindriya*) and five spiritual powers (*pancabala*) among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*) that help towards nibbana. they are presented as five faculties and five powers: faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. during this short time, faith (*saddha*) in the triple gem arose in the mental continuum of you meritorious people. likewise, generating a certain energy (*viriya*), you sat for about an hour listening to this attentively. through that, next, mindfulness (*sati*) developed; awareness developed. next, concentration (*samadhi*) arose; when mindfulness is maintained for a long time, concentration is established. through this, certain understandings arise in the concentrated mind; those are what is called wisdom (*panna*).
in that way, a wholesome mental succession arose within your own mental continuum at this moment, which helps to establish faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*) as spiritual faculties and powers. utilizing them, you must aspire: "may we gain the strength and power to realize the supreme deathless nibbana as quickly as possible, in this very life, through the penetration of the paths and fruits (*magga-phala*)—namely stream-entry (*sotapatti*), once-returning (*sakadagamita*), non-returning (*anagamita*), and arahanthood!" likewise, may all deities and brahmas—including the guardians of the sasana, the right-viewed deities and brahmas, and the deities presiding over this place—rejoice in this heap of merit we have accumulated through this preaching and hearing of the dhamma! having rejoiced, may they realize the supreme, deathless nibbana through whatever state of awakening (*bodhi*) they aspire to, and may they protect the sasana! furthermore, may all our departed relatives, and all beings from the avici hell up to the akanittha heaven who desire merit and nibbana, rejoice in this merit of our preaching and hearing of dhamma, and through their aspired state of awakening (*bodhi*), may they realize the supreme, deathless nibbana and escape from all samsaric suffering (*dukkha*)! aspiring thus, share the merit by reciting the verses.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 067
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #67
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.71)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Yo ca vassasataṃ jīve, dussīlo asamāhito;
ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ seyyo, sīlavantassa jhāyino
From:
Dhammapada 110 (Sahassavagga)
Dear Listeners,
Adversity is an occasion that highlights and brings out the virtue or vice within a person. The noble-minded, virtuous person (*satpuruṣa*) and the base, unvirtuous person (*asatpuruṣa*) act in two entirely different ways in times of adversity. The virtuous person, according to the situation, would even sacrifice his own life for others, whereas the unvirtuous person, in order to save his own life, would even sacrifice the very person who helped him.
This very point becomes clear through the events in the background story (*nidāna kathā*) related to the verse we have chosen as our theme today. In Sāvatthī, a noble lady from a wealthy family passed away due to a sudden illness during her pregnancy. When her body was brought to the cemetery and cremated, the rest of her body burned, but the womb remained unburned. The undertakers, using the iron hooks they employ during cremation, pulled that womb away from the funeral pyre, threw it onto a heap of embers, covered it with another heap of embers, and returned home. When they came back to look in the morning, there was a child lying on top of the extinguished heap of embers. The womb had burned away, but nothing had happened to the child.
The reason given for this is a certain natural law (*dhammatā*) that a person who possesses the spiritual merit (*puñña*) to attain Arahanthood in that very life will not pass away without attaining Arahanthood. Those who are called *pacchimabhavika* (one in their final birth) are those who have the merit to attain Arahanthood in that very lifetime. There are several stories of this nature mentioned in the texts. This is one such case. Therefore, on one hand, this was a child of immense merit. Be that as it may, those people, being greatly astonished that the body was cremated with such a massive pile of firewood yet this child survived, took the child to the fortune-tellers as a great wonder. They asked them if there was anything special about this child. They said, "If he remains a layman, seven generations of his family will become impoverished"—making him appear extremely unfortunate from a worldly point of view—"but if he ordains, he will live an excellent life surrounded by a large retinue of five hundred." Furthermore, when the womb was being pulled away with those iron hooks and dragged here and there, the hook struck the corner of the child's eye, causing an injury. Those hooks are called *saṅku*. Associated with that word, this child was named Saṅkicca, because of that mark left on his eye, due to the injury.
The relatives thought that once the child grew up, he should be ordained. Meanwhile, the child also overheard other children playing with him say: "When you were in your mother's womb, she passed away in this manner, and you remained unburned during the cremation." The child felt a great sense of urgency and spiritual anxiety (*saṁvega*) over this. He thought, "If I was saved from such a dread of death, why should I remain in lay life?" and at the age of seven, he asked for permission to ordain. His relatives took him and handed him over to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta, on that very day, gave him the meditation subject of the "pentad of skin" (*taca-pañcaka*) namely *kesā* (hair of the head), *lomā* (hair of the body), *nakhā* (nails), *dantā* (teeth), *taco* (skin), which is given during ordination, shaved his head, and ordained him. Even while his head was being shaved, he attained Arahanthood together with the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). At that time, Venerable Saṅkicca was only seven years old.
Around this time, thirty bhikkhus from Sāvatthī—who had ordained in their old age—received meditation instructions leading all the way to Arahanthood from the Buddha, and asked the Buddha for permission to go and reside in a forest hermitage in a remote area. The Buddha asked, "To which area are you going?" and it appeared to his Buddha-insight that they would face an obstacle and danger in that region due to a poor man. Realizing that Venerable Saṅkicca would be the one capable of helping them on that occasion, the Buddha told those bhikkhus, "Very well, you may go. But first, meet our elder, your elder brother in the Sāsana, Sāriputta, before you leave."
Those bhikkhus then went to Venerable Sāriputta and told him, "The Buddha asked us to meet you before we go." Venerable Sāriputta also reflected on this. Discerning the Buddha's underlying intention, he asked these bhikkhus, "Do you have a novice (*sāmaṇera*) to take with you?" They replied, "Why do we need a novice, friend, while we are living in the forest? If we take a novice, he will only be an impediment and a trouble to us." Venerable Sāriputta then declared, "No, friends, the one you are taking is this Saṅkicca of mine. If you take Venerable Saṅkicca, no harm or impediment will come to you because of him. Indeed, if there is to be any danger, it will be to this novice Saṅkicca because of your group." However, he did not explain the specific reason.
So, those bhikkhus agreed and set off on their journey along with the young novice Saṅkicca. These thirty-one monks arrived at a village in a remote area. In accordance with the custom of bhikkhus looking for a place to spend the rainy season retreat (*vassa*), when the faithful devotees came and asked, "Venerable sirs, where are you going?" and they replied, "We are searching for a suitable place," the devotees understood from those words that they were seeking a place to spend the rains retreat. Those faithful laypeople invited them, saying, "If you, venerable sirs, out of compassion, spend the rains retreat here with us, we too will be able to observe the Uposatha and the eight precepts in this area." They prepared the necessary huts (*kuṭi*) in a section of the forest, cleared walking paths (*caṅkamana*), and made arrangements for the bhikkhus to spend the rains retreat in that forest hermitage. The bhikkhus went into the village for almsfood.
Moreover, at the very beginning of the rains retreat, they made an agreement among themselves: "We have come having received meditation instructions from the living Buddha himself. Let none of us live in negligence. Except for the time of going for morning almsfood and attending to the elder bhikkhu in the evening, let us meditate individually at all other times. If anyone falls suddenly ill, strike the wooden gong (*gaṇḍi*). Then we will all assemble and assist that monk." Having established this agreement, they meditated diligently.
One day, while returning from the almsround, they bathed near a river and were preparing to partake of their meal on the sandy bank. At that time, a certain poor man of that region, who lived with the help of his only daughter, decided to go to another daughter because of a food shortage in that area. While traveling, he saw the monks preparing to partake of their almsfood and approached them. As he stood there watching, the bhikkhus inquired about his whereabouts. When he explained his situation, they noticed he looked very hungry and told him, "Bring a leaf so we can give you some food." The thirty bhikkhus each took a lump of rice from their own almsfood and placed it on the leaf, giving it to the man to eat.
After eating this, the man thought: "I am so poor. Even when I work hard, I never get such delicious food." He asked the monks, "Venerable sirs, was there a special invitation today?" They replied, "No, we had no special invitation. This is how people offer us alms every day." The man then thought, "In that case, I do not need to go here and there. I should remain here to serve them as an attendant (*kappiyakāra*)." He requested permission from the bhikkhus, saying, "I will stay and perform the daily duties and services." The bhikkhus granted him permission. This man remained there, performing his duties in a way that pleased the monks. After two months had passed, he again thought of visiting his daughter. Then he thought, "If I ask permission from the bhikkhus now, they might not let me go." So, he departed without telling anyone.
While traveling, he encountered a band of five hundred thieves in the forest. It is mentioned that in those days, thieves often lived in bands in the forests. Those thieves had made a vow to the deity of the forest, promising to offer a human sacrifice. That day was the seventh day of their vow. On that day, the chief of the thieves climbed a tree to see if anyone was entering the forest, and he saw this man coming. He then signaled the other thieves, who surrounded and captured the man. Having caught him, they bound him tightly. Then they lit a large fire and began preparing their weapons. This man asked, "I do not see any wild boars or deer here. What are you preparing to do? Why are you lighting a bonfire?" The thieves replied, "We have made a vow to offer a human sacrifice to the deity. Therefore, we intend to kill you and offer the sacrifice with your flesh and blood." Terrified, the man used his cunning and thought of a scheme. He said, "I am an extremely wretched man who lives on leftover rice. In such-and-such a place, there are noble monks ordained from clans like the Sakya clan. Go and bring one of those monks and offer him as a sacrifice. The deity will be far more pleased with that."
The thieves considered this and agreed that it made sense. Guided by that very man, they went to the forest hermitage. Upon arriving, they saw no one. When they asked why, the man, knowing their agreement, said, "Strike this wooden gong, and the monks will assemble." Then the chief of the thieves struck the gong. All thirty bhikkhus came and sat on the stone seats. The chief elder asked, "Who struck the gong?" The chief of the thieves replied, "It was I, venerable sir." When asked, "Why?" he said, "We have vowed to make a human sacrifice. We have come to take one of you monks." Then the chief elder declared, "When a responsibility is given to a group of brothers, it is the leader, the eldest, who must fulfill it. Therefore, venerable sirs, continue your meditation with diligence. I will sacrifice my life for you, venerable sirs, and go with this band of thieves to fulfill this purpose."
When the chief elder gave his pledge to sacrifice his life, the second monk said, "A problem that arises for an elder brother should be resolved by the younger brother. Therefore, let you, venerable sir, and the other venerable ones continue to practice meditation well. I shall go to offer my life." In this manner, all thirty monks, in order of seniority, prepared to sacrifice their lives and go. Finally, the young novice Venerable Saṅkicca said, "Venerable sirs, let all of you remain. I will go and sacrifice my life for you." Then the chief elder and the other monks said, "Even if we all have to die, we cannot send you, young venerable one." When asked, "Why?" they replied, "You are the pupil of Venerable Sāriputta. It would be a great disgrace and blame upon us to have it said that we took a young novice and handed him over to the thieves. Therefore, we can never let you go." Thereupon, Venerable Saṅkicca said, "The Buddha sent you to my preceptor (*upajjhāya*), and my preceptor sent me here with you for this very reason. Therefore, please let me go." Having obtained their permission and asking for forgiveness, saying, "If any wrong has been done by me, please forgive me," he departed.
Then, those bhikkhus felt a deep sense of *saṁvega*—in short, a sorrow so profound that tears welled in their eyes—seeing this young novice step forward to sacrifice his life for them. As Venerable Saṅkicca was preparing to depart, the chief elder made a special request to the thieves: "Please, this young novice might get frightened when you kindle those bonfires and prepare your weapons. Therefore, seat him to one side and carry out your task." The chief of the thieves, in accordance with what was said, had Venerable Saṅkicca seated to one side. Having kindled a great bonfire and sharpened their weapons, the chief of the thieves took his sword, approached Venerable Saṅkicca, swung it around his head, and struck a blow at Venerable Saṅkicca's body. As he struck, the sword bent in two, its sharp edge folding back onto itself. The chief of the thieves thought there must have been some mistake in his swing, so he straightened it out and struck again. This time, the sword curled up like a dry palmyra leaf, twisting and curling from the tip all the way to the hilt.
The chief of the thieves was utterly astonished. "Nothing like this has ever happened before. I have used this sword for so long. What is this? Even an inanimate sword knows the virtues of this young novice. It is only I who did not know." Saying this, he prostrated himself at the novice's feet and begged for forgiveness. He asked, "Venerable sir, all this time, whenever people entering this forest see us, they tremble with fear. Why is it that you remain so calm, with such a pleasant countenance?" At that moment, Venerable Saṅkicca arose from his absorption—for the young novice had not simply sat there, but had entered into absorption (*jhāna*). It was through psychic power (*iddhi*) that this miracle had occurred. Then he uttered several verses as a Dhamma teaching.
This is the meaning of those verses. He did not address him as the chief of thieves, but in common address, called him "village headman" (*gāma-jeṭṭha*). "Headman, for one who has no *Taṇhā* (Craving) or expectation, there is no mental *Dukkha* (Suffering) regarding death. For an Arahant (one whose taints are destroyed, *khīṇāsava*) who has removed *taṇhā*, death is like laying down a heavy burden from one's head; it is a matter of joy, not something that causes fear." Thus he preached the Dhamma. Having heard this and being inspired, the chief of the thieves asked the others, "Now, what shall we do?" They asked, "What do you intend to do?" The chief of the thieves replied, "After witnessing such a miracle, there is no use in lay life for me. I shall ordain under this venerable sir." All the other four hundred and ninety-nine agreed, and they all requested ordination from Venerable Saṅkicca, the young novice.
Adapting to the situation, the young novice dyed their existing garments with copper-colored clay, shaved their heads with those very swords, and ordained all five hundred of them. While thinking of setting off to see the Buddha, he thought: "From the moment I left, those bhikkhus must have been in great grief. They might not be able to concentrate their minds. I must go and see them before I leave." So, accompanied by the five hundred, the young novice returned to the forest hermitage where the thirty monks resided. When they arrived, the bhikkhus were astonished. He explained the situation: "When this chief of thieves tried to harm me, it failed. Out of faith, they have all ordained. Now, venerable sirs, continue to practice your meditation diligently." Having said this, Venerable Saṅkicca, along with the newly ordained band of thieves, went to Venerable Sāriputta.
Venerable Sāriputta, seeing him, expressed his joy, saying, "Why is it, Saṅkicca, that you return with such a large retinue of pupils?" After Venerable Saṅkicca explained the matter, Venerable Sāriputta sent the group to see the Buddha, saying, "Go and pay respects to the Buddha as well." When they went to the Buddha, he too expressed his joy in the same manner, and the admonitory message he declared regarding the chief of the thieves is what is expressed in today's verse:
> *Yo ca vassasataṁ jīve, dussīlo asamāhito,*
> *Ekāhaṁ jīvitaṁ seyyo, sīlavantassa jhāyino.*
Though one should live a hundred years, immoral and unconcentrated, yet better is a single day's life of one who is virtuous and meditative.
Through this, we can see the exemplary life of the young novice, who lived virtuously and endowed with the power of *jhāna*. On the other hand, we see the immoral life led by those thieves. Accordingly, the Buddha delivered an admonitory sermon. It is said in the Dhamma texts that upon hearing this, all five hundred of them attained Arahanthood. In any case, it served as a support for Nibbāna.
This is what is mentioned in the scriptures as the background story and the occasion for the teaching of this verse. The account of Venerable Saṅkicca is a highly valuable event in the Dispensation. So, let us try to bring out the points that we, by way of commentary, should extract from this.
First of all, let us consider the birth of Venerable Saṅkicca. The Buddha has declared that *jāti*—that is, birth or arising—is *Dukkha* (Suffering). However, lay devotees generally do not like to accept that birth is *dukkha*. This reality is obscured by the concept of the "blessing of children." Yet, we see here that when a child cannot be born naturally, various surgeries are performed, causing great pain to the mother in order to bring the child into the world. This birth was even more miraculous. Here, indeed, birth took place in the midst of a funeral pyre. If someone's birth occurs in the middle of a fire, there can be nothing more terrifying and filled with *saṁvega*. Yet, he survived the fire, and thus his birth occurred. We can only conceive of it as a highly miraculous birth. Along with the power of merit from Venerable Saṅkicca's past, there must have also been some great unwholesome karma (*akusala*). That is why it was said that if he remained a layman, seven generations of his family would be impoverished. Be that as it may, it is shown here as a natural law (*dhammatā*) that a *pacchimabhavika* (one in their final birth) cannot be killed under any circumstances. If someone has attained their final existence, they will not die without attaining Arahanthood. It was because of such a *dhammatā* that this took place.
The next important point is this young child's attainment of Arahanthood through the *taca-pañcaka* meditation subject. Often, the attainment of Arahanthood by highly meritorious individuals is reported at a very tender age—seven years of age being a very young, childhood stage where one is just beginning to understand things. On that occasion, such a simple meditation subject—hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin—parts of the body which ordinary worldly people beautify and consider as additions to their physical attractiveness. Yet, as you virtuous people know, the Buddha placed these at the very beginning of the thirty-two impure parts of the body. Contemplating this meditation subject of hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, and skin, even as the hair of his head was being shaved, insight-knowledges (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) arose through a deep disenchantment with saṁsāra, allowing him to attain Arahanthood. This is what we see from this story. It is a Dhamma miracle.
We mentioned that both the Buddha and the great Arahant Sāriputta foresaw this series of future events. Venerable Saṅkicca was sent with a special purpose because some danger was to befall those thirty monks due to that poor man. But why did the Buddha let them go there, rather than telling them to go elsewhere, despite knowing of such a danger? It is because there was a certain *dhammatā* (natural lawfulness) inherent in this. This poignant sequence of events—that is, the *saṁvega* felt by those thirty monks when the band of thieves came and tried to take one of them, as well as the sacrifice of their lives that they offered—must have actually aided those thirty in attaining Nibbāna. That, too, was visible to the Buddha's eye. Moreover, the Dhamma-power of Venerable Saṅkicca, as well as the fact that the band of thieves would ordain, must have been perceived by the Buddha's eye, which is why he permitted those thirty monks to go to that region.
Next, a proof for the point we made at the very beginning was spontaneously illustrated in this story. That is, it is only in times of adversity and disaster that one can recognize whether someone is a virtuous person (*satpuruṣa*) or an unvirtuous person (*asatpuruṣa*), by the way they behave. Now, that poor man, like biting the hand that feeds him, was ready to sacrifice one of the very monks who had helped him, in order to save his own life. On one hand, this demonstrates the behavior of a wicked person. On the other hand, we see how those thirty monks acted. When such a situation arises, what we usually expect regarding the sacrifice of life is that senior, high-ranking elders, holding onto their titles and leadership, would save their own lives by sacrificing others. That is what is commonly seen in the ordinary, worldling (*puthujjana*) world. But these noble monks—indeed, they had not even attained Arahanthood yet. It is mentioned here that these thirty were not even children of the same mother, nor were they Arahants. Yet, they were thirty monks of such sublime virtue. The chief elder took that death upon himself. Then, the other junior monks did the same. The second monk thought of it as a service to the Saṅgha, a service to the elder, and said, "I must perform the duty that belongs to him." In the same way, the monks junior to him took it upon themselves. This is an extremely exemplary event. That is the quality of a virtuous person. It is clearly illustrated in this story how virtuous people sacrifice their own lives for others in times of adversity. This is extremely valuable. It provides a Dhamma-based model of how we should act in our own lives in such situations.
Furthermore, if we look deeper, the most profound Dhamma point within this is what was declared by the young Venerable Saṅkicca. An Arahant has no fear of death. Why, indeed, is there no fear of death? It is because death has been conquered. That victory over death was not achieved merely by bending the sword as he did. The bonds, the hooks that tie us to this saṁsāra, have been bent back in the opposite direction. These are what are called fetters (*saṁyojana*). It is by these ten kinds of bonds called fetters that ordinary worldly people are bound to saṁsāra. It is by reversing them that Arahanthood is attained—meaning they have been destroyed, eradicated. That is why there is no fear of death. In short, Nibbāna is neither a drink obtained from some other world nor a strange, eternal existence. It is the cessation of the fear of death that goes hand-in-hand with the notion of "I" and "mine" which is created within this very person, within this being, due to *Taṇhā* (Craving) and ignorance (*avijjā*). When *taṇhā* and expectations are eliminated, the fear of death is also eliminated. This is the deepest point in this Dhamma. This, too, is revealed through the words of Venerable Saṅkicca.
In all of our sermons, we direct the final portion towards Dhamma analysis. We mentioned that the willingness to step forward and sacrifice their lives must have helped those thirty monks in their attainment of Arahanthood. What is called sacrifice of life is the letting go of the desire for life. The relinquishment of the desire for life served as a rehearsal for those thirty monks to let go of the entire heap of acquisitions (*upadhi*). It was according to that very same natural law (*dhammatā*) that the young Venerable Saṅkicca, even as his hair was being shaved, severed all bonds tying him to saṁsāra and realized the Deathless, Great Nibbāna. Thereby, he eradicated the fear of death. That is why he showed no fear whatsoever when the chief of the thieves brought the sword. When we contemplate Nibbāna, we see that the Buddha has shown the true liberation in a way that no other teacher has ever declared. Venerable Saṅkicca further told the chief of the thieves that for an Arahant, death is like letting go of a heavy burden carried on the head. Why? Because an Arahant is described as "one who has laid down the burden" (*ohitabhāra*).
What is this burden? It is the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*). You virtuous people may have generally heard of *rūpa* (form), *Vedanā* (Feeling), *saññā* (perception), *Saṅkhāra* (Preparations), and *viññāṇa* (consciousness). However, these are not just single things, they are heaps; *khandha* means a heap or a pile. We show a photograph to others and say, "This is my form (*rūpa*)." But according to the Dhamma, what is shown here is a heap of forms. Similarly, it is a heap of *Vedanā* (Feeling), a heap of *saññā* (perceptions). *Saṅkhāra*—that is, our intentions and volitions, the series of active thoughts we generate—that, too, is a heap. Next, *viññāṇa* (consciousness), which we call "my thoughts"—that, too, is a heap. In this way, they are presented in the Dhamma as heaps. How are these five heaps formed? Let us consider that for a moment. Since each of us can understand things according to our own level of comprehension, there is a certain nature—the Buddha points out that the ordinary person, the person lacking Dhamma-knowledge, spends this saṁsāra merely piling things up.
How do we pile them up? Every one of us possesses six sense-bases (*āyatana*). When we say *āyatana* (bases), various everyday institutions might come to mind. Looking at it through the term itself, it is somewhat similar. The Buddha points out that we have six sense-bases: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. What is the work done within these six sense-bases? What is the process? Through these, due to ignorance (*avijjā*) and *Taṇhā* (Craving), in order to gratify and maintain this physical cage, we pile up a vast number of thoughts along various kinds of objects. Based on forms seen with the eye, because of the *Vedanā* (Feeling) arising from them, according to the *saññā* (perceptions) given by those feelings, we generate various expectations and thoughts (*vitakka*). A stream of thoughts runs along, separating "them" as one thing and "I" as another, based on each of these sense-bases. Just as we spoke of the eye, think also of the other sense-bases. Hearing a sound through the ear, if it is a pleasant sound, like a beautiful song, one develops an attachment based on it.
