from:
apannaka jataka (jataka no. 1)
dear listeners,
the buddha points out to us that the difference between the wise person and the foolish person can be understood according to the course of action they take when faced with a problem. the wise person looks at a problem and arrives at conclusions in a manner entirely different from how the foolish person looks at a problem and the conclusions they draw. because of this very reason, where the foolish person meets ruin, the wise person secures their own progress. in this dhamma, it is the practice of those wise ones that is known as the *apannaka* practice (the safe or non-erring path).
the verse from the *apannaka jataka* which mentions that wise practice is what we have chosen as our theme. in the jataka book, the *apannaka jataka* is presented first, like the letter 'a' of the alphabet. this could be due to its foundational theoretical value. everyone knows the story of the *apannaka jataka*. its background story (*nidana*) exists as a narrative. the occasion on which this jataka story was preached is mentioned in the *apannaka jataka* as follows. at a time when the buddha, the teacher of the three worlds, was residing in savatthi, the householder anathapindika came to see the buddha along with five hundred of his friends who were followers of other sects (*tirthaka*). having arrived and heard the dhamma from the buddha, all five hundred of those followers of other sects abandoned their sectarian refuge and took refuge in the triple gem. after that, they frequently came to jetavana monastery with the householder anathapindika. they listened to the dhamma, gave alms, and observed the precepts. after some time, the buddha journeyed from savatthi to rajagaha.
after he had departed, all five hundred who were previously sectarian followers abandoned their refuge in the triple gem and once again took refuge in their sectarian teachers. having done so, when the buddha returned to savatthi seven or eight months later, the householder anathapindika came to meet the buddha with these five hundred people and revealed this matter, in a way that made those sectarian followers feel somewhat ashamed. on that occasion, the buddha, having declared the value of taking refuge in the triple gem in various ways, explained that in the past too, certain people, by taking that which is not a refuge as a refuge, fell prey to demons (*yakshas*) in a wilderness infested by non-humans and were destroyed.
when this was declared, the householder anathapindika requested the buddha to relate that story of the past. the story of the past is as follows. you all know how jataka stories begin. in the past, when king brahmadatta was ruling in the city of benares in the kingdom of kasi, the bodhisatta was born into a merchant family. having reached young adulthood, he earned his living as a merchant traveling through deserts with five hundred carts. in ancient books, he is called a caravan leader (*satthu-nayaka*), which in modern terms means a cart caravan leader. he was engaged in trade as a caravan leader. in that same city of benares, there was another merchant who was rather foolish. he too was someone who traveled through deserts with five hundred carts. on one occasion, the bodhisatta loaded his carts with valuable goods from benares and prepared to cross the desert to a distant city. at that very moment, the foolish merchant also prepared to go at the same time with his five hundred carts. then the bodhisatta thought: "if both of our groups go together, the road will not be sufficient for a thousand carts. the men will not get enough water, and the oxen will not get enough grass. either i must go first, or this merchant must go first." thinking thus, he went to the foolish merchant and asked, "will you go first, or shall i?" the foolish merchant calculated the benefits of going first in this way: "i can lead my carts on a road that is not yet muddy. there will be plenty of grass for the oxen. the men will also be able to get edible leaves. going first, we can obtain clean, unmuddy water. furthermore, i can fix the price of the goods as i wish." seeing five such benefits, he declared, "i will go first."
the bodhisatta saw the advantages of going afterwards. he reasoned: "once these merchants have gone and prepared the path, making the uneven places even, my journey will be easy. also, when their oxen have eaten the mature grass, my oxen will get the tender young grass. similarly, my men will get sweet edible leaves. furthermore, as for water, since they would have gone ahead and dug wells in waterless places, we too can obtain water from them. additionally, haggling over prices is a taxing task, like a slaughter; therefore, it is easier for me to sell my goods at the prices already established by them." seeing five advantages in that direction, he agreed, saying, "very well, i shall go afterwards." so, the foolish merchant, having filled his carts with water, set off. deserts without water are called waterless deserts (*nirudaka*) in the books. *udaka* means water. there are waterless deserts as well as deserts infested by non-humans. this was a desert that was both waterless and infested by non-humans. when these foolish merchants had reached the middle of the desert, the demon (*yaksha*) infesting that desert thought of making this caravan discard their water to weaken them, so that he could devour them along with their oxen. he assumed the guise of a great lord and, accompanied by a group of about ten or twelve, came in a carriage. this group wore lotus flowers, chewed lotus stalks, with their hair and garments dripping wet, and had mud on their bodies, looking exactly as if they were coming from a region plentiful in water. coming forward, he engaged in friendly conversation with the foolish merchant. the merchant asked, "is there water in the direction you are coming from?" "oh, it is raining heavily there, there are lakes and ponds," praised the demon. when asked, "what is in those carts at the back?" the merchant replied, "water." "why are you carrying that water? there is plenty of water in that direction. you do not need to pull that load in these carts," said the demon.
listening to the demon's words, these foolish merchants broke their water pots, threw away the water in the carts, and went forward. but contrary to their expectations, there was no water. both men and oxen stopped the carts at night and lay down exhausted. during the night, the demons came from the demon city and devoured everyone, including the oxen, leaving only their bones. that was the fate of the foolish merchant. next, about a month and a half after the foolish merchants had left, the bodhisatta also set out with his five hundred carts. when he reached the middle of the desert, the same demon came in the same manner to deceive the bodhisatta, saying, "there is plenty of water in this area, throw away your water and go." the bodhisatta immediately recognized that this was a demon, thinking, "because of the redness of his eyes and the absence of a shadow, this must be a demon." the bodhisatta said, "i will not throw away the water i have without seeing other water." standing firm on that principle, he said, "it does not matter if the load is a bit heavy for us. we will carry it." thus, the demon's plan did not succeed.
as the bodhisatta proceeded along that road, a discussion arose among the people: "why are we carrying such a heavy load? that person said there is water ahead, didn't he?" the bodhisatta stopped all the carts, gathered his men, and asked, "have you ever heard of lakes or ponds in this desert?" "no," they replied. "and if it is raining, how far away do you feel the rain-wind and cold?" "about a league (*yojana*)," they said. "do you feel them now? do you hear thunder? do you hear it rumbling? do you see lightning?" when he asked this, the men had no answers. he said, "understand that it was a demon who came. therefore, let us continue our journey forward." having persuaded them, they went forward. when they went, in the middle of the desert they saw those five hundred carts standing intact, and piles of bones everywhere. they realized the truth of the bodhisatta's words—that the demons had devoured them. that night, having organized strong security arrangements, and having advised his men, saying, "do not throw away the water, use it sparingly," they took the better carts in place of their own broken ones. they reached their destination safely, sold their goods, made a profit, and returned. that is what is related in that jataka story.
next, the buddha, by way of presenting the underlying principle of the story, declared the short verse which we have taken as our theme. we have to understand it by adding a few more words.
*apannakam thanameke, dutiyam ahu takkika;*
*etadannaya medhavi, tam ganhe yadapannakam.*
what it says is: some wise people adopt that matter, that practice, which is called '*apannaka*'—let us keep the word as it is. "*dutiyam ahu takkika*"—those who are slaves to logic (*takkika*) accept the second position. now, the word *apannaka* is often understood as the non-erring, safe path. accordingly, wise people adopt the non-erring practice, while those mentioned second adopt the erring path. the wise person (*medhavi*), having correctly understood this matter—that is, the difference between these two practices, the difference between good and bad, right and wrong—follows the advice: "*tam ganhe yadapannakam*", meaning he acts in accordance with that *apannaka* practice. this is the instruction contained in this verse.
at the conclusion of that story, the buddha identified the characters, stating that the foolish merchant was devadatta and the wise merchant was himself. when we reflect upon this story, we can understand that between the practices of those two, the foolish merchant believed the words of the demon exactly as they were spoken. if we look at it from the perspective of logic, there were signs of someone coming from a place where it was raining. "therefore, let us throw away the water and go"—that was all he thought. he acted without foresight. but the bodhisatta not only recognized the demon as a demon; he also did not believe his words outright. furthermore, he thought: "why should we throw away the water we have carried without seeing other water? even though it is somewhat heavy and troublesome, whether it turns out to be right or wrong, let us keep it." it is this very principle of "whether it turns out to be right or wrong" that is contained in this *apannaka* practice. some foolish people, just because someone says so, would say, "alright then, let us throw away the water and go." our elders may have heard the saying: "seeing fleeing deer, do not throw away the harvested leaves." a saying that fits this *apannaka* practice has been absorbed into our literature too: do not throw away the edible leaves you have already gathered just because you see deer running past. in the same way, one should not throw away the water in one’s possession merely because someone says there is water ahead.
moreover, this bodhisatta merchant saw the benefits of going second in a way different from the foolish merchant. also, when explaining things to his followers, he thought deeply and wisely considered whether it was really raining or not before making a decision. that is the *apannaka* practice. therefore, even though it was troublesome, they carried the water. but in truth, he did not err. it might have seemed like an error initially. these are the valuable points contained within the *apannaka* practice. from this point on, we must add a few more details to this. we said earlier that the *apannaka jataka* is placed at the very beginning of the collection due to some theoretical value. we can say, by way of a simile at this point, that just as the bodhisatta, standing firm on the *apannaka* practice as a bodhisatta, led his followers safely through the waterless desert infested by non-humans, the buddha, the teacher of the three worlds, after his enlightenment, presented a non-erring practice in the dhamma under the name *apannaka* that leads all the way to nibbana. it is that portion we are going to discuss next.
there is a valuable discourse that reveals this. today, there is a discourse in the majjhima nikaya called the *apannaka sutta* which is highly worth studying for rationalists. this discourse is somewhat deep, and it is something very valuable for intellectuals to investigate. the background story in it is as follows. on one occasion, while wandering on tour with a large community of monks, the buddha arrived at a brahmin village called sala. the brahmins of sala had heard the widespread report of the buddha's fame, such as "itipi so bhagava...", and thinking that it is wonderful to see an arahant like the buddha, this group of brahmins came to see him. when they arrived, the buddha asked, "householders, is there any agreeable teacher in whom you have placed your faith after investigating the facts?" this group replied, "no, we do not have such a teacher in whom we have established faith." the buddha declared: "householders, here the term *akaravati saddha* (reasoned faith) is mentioned. reasoned faith is the faith that is developed after investigating the facts. if you do not have a teacher in whom you have established reasoned faith, you should adopt and practice the *apannaka* practice. standing firm on and practicing the *apannaka* practice will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. and what, householders, is this *apannaka* practice?"
now, what follows relates to the *apannaka* practice. "householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who put forward this view, this opinion: 'there is nothing given, nothing offered... there are no spontaneously arisen beings; there are no ascetics and brahmins in the world who have correctly understood and declared both this world and the world beyond.' that which was said to exist is denied there, and what is described is what is known in the dhamma as the 'right view of ownership of action' (*kammassakata sammaditthi*). you may have heard of the ten-point right view. next, the buddha states: 'householders, these two groups express mutually contradictory views.' he analyzes and explains each of these as follows. regarding those ascetics and brahmins who previously presented the nihilistic view (*natthika ditthi*), because they do not accept good and bad, we can expect this kind of conduct from them: they abandon bodily, verbal, and mental good conduct, and engage in bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct. they do not know the danger in misconduct or the benefit in good conduct, nor do they know how the mind is defiled or purified by them. therefore, they remain in that position and conduct their lives according to that practice. the buddha continues further, by way of showing the danger of this: if there is indeed a world beyond—whereas their view is that there is not—then their view turns out to be a wrong view. their thoughts and intentions become wrong thoughts (*miccha sankappa*). furthermore, in their conduct, they say things opposed to the words of the noble ones (*ariyas*). moreover, by trying to propagate their view to others, they propagate the false dhamma. in this way, the side of danger is shown. there are these various dangers in holding such a wrong view. also, those who hold that wrong view tend to praise themselves and disparage others. showing five such dangers, the buddha summarizes them. now, those who held that nihilistic view, from the very beginning, rejected the virtue of good conduct (*susila*) and embraced bad conduct (*dussila*), showing that they possess wrong view, wrong thoughts, wrong speech, and so on.
next, how a wise person looks at this matter is shown. this wise person looks at their practice and view and thinks: "if the view of these people is correct, if indeed there is no such thing as sacrifice or offering, and there is no world beyond, then after death, they will not face any trouble. however, if by any chance the opinion they hold is wrong, they will arise in a state of deprivation, in hell. not only that; even if their view were correct, in this very life wise people censure them, saying: 'these people are of bad conduct, they hold wrong views.' this is called '*ubhayatha kaliggaho*'—losing on both sides. they have failed both in this world and in the world beyond." that is how the wise person reflects.
regarding those who hold the affirmationist view (*atthika-vada*), the buddha explains as follows. if they have presented an opinion in the second manner, which is the right view of ownership of action (*kammassakata sammaditthi*), we can expect the following from them. since they believed in *kamma* and its results, they would avoid wrong bodily, verbal, and mental actions and behave in good, wholesome bodily, verbal, and mental actions. why? because they know the danger in misconduct which defiles beings, and the beneficial side of good conduct which purifies the mind. this is the positive side of those who adopt the second opinion. the buddha declares that if the matter is true, they possess right view (*sammaditthi*), their thoughts are right thoughts (*sammasankappa*), and the words they use are right speech (*sammavaca*). if there is an opinion held by the noble ones (*ariyas*), their view is in agreement with it. their position is not opposed to the noble ones, it is in agreement. if they teach the dhamma to someone, it is the true dhamma (*saddhamma*). through "*saddhamma-sannatti*" (persuasion in the true dhamma), the true dhamma is sharpened and refined. furthermore, because they stand firm in that dhamma, they do not engage in self-exaltation or disparaging of others.
having thus declared the side of benefit, the buddha summarizes it: those who held that second view, from the very beginning, removed bad conduct and established themselves in good conduct, possessing good practices such as right view. therefore, the wise, looking at that group with reason, see that even if by some chance it were true that there is no world beyond, they still receive the praise of the wise in this life, and they lead a good life. and if that matter is indeed true, they will go to a happy destination after death. while the others go to a miserable destination, these go to a happy destination. in that way, on both sides, those who hold this second view win on both sides. while for the first view it was said, "it failed on both sides," here it is "it succeeded on both sides." that is the *apannaka* practice. we can understand that those who hold wrong view meet with destruction both in this world and in the next. that can be considered bad. for those who adopt right view, whether they turn out to be right or wrong, their practice is a fruitful, non-erring practice.
that discourse does not end there. taking each of the wrong views such as the nihilist view (*natthika-vada*), the doctrine of non-causality (*ahetu-appaccaya-vada*), the annihilationist view (*uccheda-vada*), and the doctrine of non-action (*akiriya-vada*) taught by purana kassapa and others, it presents, describes, analyzes, and dissects these principles. it demonstrates the side of danger and the side of benefit, showing how the wise should look at them. although this discourse continues much further, let us analyze this portion. in our literature, there is a book called *subhasitaya* written by alagiyavanna mukaveti. there is a stanza in it that illustrates the *apannaka* practice:
*whether there is a world beyond or not, o great virtuous ones,*
*it is best to abandon sinful deeds without keeping them in mind.*
*even if there is no world beyond, no harm comes from doing so,*
*but if there is, disaster awaits those who sinned thinking there is none.*
i spoke at length about the *apannaka* practice to show that there is something here for rationalists to ponder. from that point onwards in the discourse, the path leading to nibbana is presented. so, as summarized, the buddha rejects the primary wrong views. he does not merely reject them, but by showing reasons and evidence, he demonstrates to the wise how to look at them in accordance with the *apannaka* practice. next, the discourse goes into a deeper aspect: "householders, there are certain ascetics and brahmins who say that there is absolutely no such thing as formless *bhava* (becoming)."
you are all aware of the three realms of *bhava* (becoming), namely: the sensual (*kama*), fine-material (*rupa*), and immaterial/formless (*arupa*) realms. fine-material *bhava* (becoming) refers to the planes from the first absorption (*jhana*) to the fourth absorption. immaterial *bhava* (becoming) refers to those existing above them, such as the sphere of infinite space (*akasanancayatana*), and so on. "householders, some ascetics and brahmins say there is no immaterial *bhava* (becoming). some other ascetics and brahmins say there is immaterial *bhava* (becoming). now, householders, are the assertions of these two groups mutually contradictory?" "yes," they reply. "if they are contradictory, a wise person looks at this and thinks in this way: 'whether immaterial *bhava* (becoming) does not exist or does exist is something i do not know. if so, if i were to grasp one side as "this is the only truth, all else is false," that would be a view. that is wrong, and that is not suitable for me.'" this is how the buddha shows a wise person should think. however, the wise person reflects on these two views present before him—that immaterial *bhava* (becoming) exists and that it does not. "if the words of those who say there is no immaterial *bhava* (becoming) are true, then by acting accordingly, i can be born in the fine-material worlds consisting of mind-made form. if the view of the second group is true, i can obtain birth in the immaterial worlds." then this wise person reflects: "it is because of form (*rupa*) that all of this—taking up rods, taking up weapons, quarrels, disputes, false speech, etc.—occurs; none of these exist in the immaterial realm." therefore, even though he does not know for certain which one of the two is correct, his preference leans towards the immaterial. why? because the benefit is greater. "therefore, i can free myself from form and obtain birth in the immaterial plane." thinking thus, he chooses the second of the two options.
next, another scenario is presented. "householders, there are certain ascetics and brahmins who say there is absolutely no cessation of *bhava* (becoming). other ascetics and brahmins say that the cessation of *bhava* (becoming) can be achieved in every way." the buddha shows how the wise should reflect on this: "if the words of those who say that *bhava* (becoming) can in no way be ceased are true, then if i follow the path they show, i can obtain birth in the immaterial worlds. the previous one was mind-made immaterial, while this one is perception-made immaterial (*sannamaya*). this second one is subtle. like alara kalama and uddaka ramaputta, by attaining states of absorption (*jhana*), i can obtain a corresponding birth through that first option. secondly, he thinks, if indeed *bhava* (becoming) can be ceased in the manner stated in the second view, then i can achieve parinibbana '*dittheva dhamme*'—in this very life, right here. i will be able to attain extinction/extinguishment in this very life."
now we come to a profound point. out of these two, the wise person chooses the second one. if one can attain extinction/extinguishment in this very life, then both the fine-material worlds and the immaterial worlds are completely transcended. that is what this wise person chooses. this demonstrates that *apannaka* practice. just as the bodhisatta, during his life as a bodhisatta, stood firm on the '*apannaka* practice' and crossed the desert safely with his caravan despite the various temptations used by the demons to lure them in the waterless, non-human infested desert, the buddha has shown, through this *apannaka sutta*, the path leading to nibbana by saving his followers from various kinds of wrong-viewed demons.
that is why we started with the *apannaka jataka* and descended to the *apannaka sutta*. this is a profound matter. on previous occasions, we mentioned how nowadays, many people explain nibbana as a state of *bhava* (becoming) attained after death. we even treated that view with irony. here, it is clearly seen that nibbana, this so-called parinibbana, is something that can be realized in this very life. everyone knows the ultimate conclusion of that buddha-word that "samsara is *dukkha* (suffering)," which was realized when he was a bodhisatta. as a buddha, what is contained in the four noble truths that put an end to this samsaric journey? the entirety of the five aggregates of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*)—when we say the five aggregates of grasping, fine-material and immaterial are all included—the five aggregates of grasping themselves are *dukkha* (suffering). they exist because of *tanha* (craving); by eradicating *tanha* (craving), one is liberated from those five aggregates of grasping. this is shown as a state experienced in this very life. it is a bliss of nibbana enjoyed in this very life, not something to be experienced in the next world. this is also clear from this sutta passage: '*dittheva dhamme parinibbayati*'—one attains parinibbana in this very life. that does not mean one dies. 'parinibbuta'—parinibbana—means calming in every way, relinquishing these assets (*upadhi*), exhausting *tanha* (craving), and reaching dispassion (*viraga*); that is, experiencing the state of nibbana in this very life within the attainment of the fruit of arahantship (*arahatta-phala-samapatti*). what is realized through that is the cessation of *bhava* (becoming). it is because of *upadana* (grasping) that there is *bhava* (becoming). this is the deepest point of the dhamma. although we think that a world exists even without us, the deepest matter in the dhamma is *upadana-paccaya bhavo*: as long as there is *upadana* (grasping), there is *bhava* (becoming). where there is no *upadana* (grasping), *bhava* (becoming) is ceased. that cessation is what is called parinibbana. therefore, if the five aggregates of grasping present through *upadana* (grasping) are a fire, on the other hand, there is the cooling, the extinguishment.
as buddhists who have trust and faith in the buddha, we must consider that this discourse provides clear evidence. if we return to those views, at the very beginning of the discourse it was shown that those who adopt wrong view, the nihilistic view, go to a miserable destination. those who adopt the right view of ownership of action perform meritorious deeds and go to a happy destination. if one is to remain in samsara, a happy destination is better than a miserable one. beyond that, if samsara is *dukkha* (suffering), then liberation from samsara is necessary. in the past, those hermits (*risis*) who had attained supernormal knowledges (*abhinna*) and realized that samsara is *dukkha* (suffering), tried to elevate their minds to the fine-material plane to escape the sensual world. they realized it. going even further in this life, there is what is called "immaterial perception-made," such as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasannanasannayatana*). they were the teachers of the bodhisatta. he was not satisfied with that, was he? because that too is *bhava* (becoming). even though alara kalama and uddaka ramaputta handed over their followers and offered him an equal status, the bodhisatta left them, saying, "this is not the path to nibbana." nibbana cannot be that kind of thing. whether taken by way of sense bases (*ayatana*) such as what is seen by the eye and heard by the ear, or by way of aggregates (*khandha*), *bhava* (becoming) arises because all of these are taken by way of *upadana* (grasping). *upadana-paccaya bhavo*—each individual goes on creating their own *bhava* (becoming). sensual *bhava* (becoming) is what is mostly found in the world. this is not something you can touch with your hand; one dwells inside sensual *bhava* (becoming). it is only very rarely that someone experiences fine-material *bhava* (becoming) or immaterial *bhava* (becoming).
but all of those are defeated by the state of parinibbana shown by the buddha. it is something no other teacher was able to demonstrate. so, to understand that, we must understand the value of truth. although we express truth in words, for convenience we now say: *jati* (birth) is *dukkha* (suffering), *jara* (decay/aging) is *dukkha* (suffering), sickness is *dukkha* (suffering). we go on reciting this very easily. finally, it is said that, in short, the five aggregates of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*)—these five heaps grasped through *upadana* (grasping), namely form (*rupa*), *vedana* (feeling), perception (*sanna*), *sankhara* (preparations), and *vinnana* (consciousness)—were declared by the buddha to be *dukkha* (suffering).
if this *dukkha* (suffering) exists because of *upadana* (grasping), what is the cause of this *upadana* (grasping)? it is *tanha* (craving), indeed. now, we often say that teachers in dhamma schools teach what the truth of *dukkha* (suffering) is. next, they say the second truth is *tanha* (craving). however, they do not properly know the connection between these. if the five aggregates of grasping—the five heaps held onto—are *dukkha* (suffering), then *tanha* (craving) which causes that holding is the cause; that is the second truth, the truth of arising (*samudaya sacca*). it is only by eradicating that cause that one can be liberated from this *dukkha* (suffering). that is why in certain places nibbana is described as: "*tanhakkhayo hi radha nibbanam*"—"indeed, radha, the destruction of *tanha* (craving) is nibbana." but this is not enough for many people. they want to destroy *tanha* (craving), but they also want to keep something else remaining. that is precisely where they go wrong.
but the buddha points out that as long as this *tanha* (craving) exists, this burning remains. liberation (*vimutti*) is a state of cooling, of extinguishment. in truth, it is often the simple things that people fail to understand, and that is the point being emphasized here. this discourse concludes with '*dittheva dhamme parinibbayati*'—one attains parinibbana in this very life.
therefore, one must wisely reflect upon this *apannaka* practice. *apannaka* means non-erring or safe. in truth, there are differences of opinion regarding the etymology of this word. some say it comes from '*aprasnaka*', meaning unquestionable or without any issue. be that as it may, we can find an explanation from the discourses themselves which is helpful even to etymologists. in a certain discourse in the anguttara nikaya, the buddha provides a simile of the "*apannako mani*"—the *apannaka* gem. he says there is a gem called *apannaka*, which, when thrown up into the air, always lands squarely on whichever side it falls. the commentary explains this as a four-sided or cubic object. just as a perfectly cubic piece of wood, when dropped, always lands flat on one of its six faces—having six sides representing up, down, and the four directions—the gem is described as landing upright no matter which way it is thrown. that is why it was said earlier, "whether it turns out to be right or wrong."
through the simile of the *apannaka* gem, we can understand that even if the word *apannaka* is not fully analyzed, when the buddha wanted to declare that this *apannaka* practice is absolutely correct, he said that it happens in an *apannaka* (unfailing) manner. the buddha states that if someone engages in misconduct through bodily and verbal actions, just as that *apannaka* gem always lands securely on some side, it is certain that the person will go to hell. they go there definitely, without fail. sometimes people say about bad deeds, "it is as if they were placed in hell." the positive side is also applied in the same simile: if someone engages in good conduct through bodily and verbal actions, then, just as the *apannaka* gem thrown up lands securely, they will go to a happy destination.
the *apannaka* practice means reflecting on matters wisely, not merely accepting things because someone said so, but making a decision after thoroughly investigating the dangers and benefits. what is found here is not the adopting of an dogmatic view. it is not like saying, "*idameva saccam moghamannam*" ("this alone is truth, all else is foolish/false"). the wise person should not think: "i do not know for sure if this is correct. nor do i know if the second one is correct. why should i, not knowing, declare 'this alone is truth, all else is false'?" instead, he investigates the path: "if i proceed according to this path, this is the benefit i will receive. if i act according to the second path, this is the benefit i will receive." he weighs both options, weighing the dangers and the benefits. thereafter, he gives his preference to the beneficial side. that is the secret of the *apannaka* simile.
nowadays, no matter how much we explain to many of those who claim to be intellectuals, it is difficult for them to establish faith (*saddha*) in the buddha. they question everything, putting logic forward, just like the foolish merchant. if the words sound logical, they would accept them even if spoken by a demon. that is not the approach to which the buddha gives prominence.
here, in accordance with this principle, we point out to you a discourse that has been heard of for a long time and is discussed among scholars, namely the *kalama sutta*. at this moment, we will not analyze it extensively. we will mention it briefly: a similar situation arose for the buddha regarding the kalamas of kesaputta. they said to the buddha: "some ascetics and brahmins who come to us speak in one way, while another group censures them and states a different opinion. we have doubts in choosing between these." recognizing this, the buddha declared: "it is natural that you have doubts. when such a double-horned dilemma is presented, doubt is reasonable." having accepted this, he then presented ten criteria.
to consider them briefly: do not go by oral tradition, do not go by lineage of teaching, do not go by hearsay, do not go by mere logical reasoning, do not go by inference, do not go by superficial evaluation, or because this teacher is respected by us—in this way, he points out ten criteria. he advises not to arrive at a conclusion based on those. yet, just because this was said, some people use it to reject certain points of the dhamma. sometimes we have to say that some of our intellectuals have "eaten up and thrown away the *kalama sutta*" (a play on words: *kalama dala*). they have not understood its value. the *kalama sutta* must be analyzed while standing firm on that very *apannaka* practice. the buddha declared directly to them:
"kalamas, do not hold firmly to any of those ten criteria. each one of them can err." that demon was, at first glance, someone who looked clean as if he had bathed well. so how could one doubt him? thus, there are things like that on all sides. do not accept any of those. instead, what should be done? "relate it to your own lives." most people leave out that part. the buddha points out on many occasions that this dhamma is about the eradication of greed, hatred, and delusion. then, one can directly see whether greed is a good thing or a bad thing. greed is bad, hatred is bad, delusion is bad. this is directly experienced.
when speaking of this matter, the qualities of the true dhamma: "*sanditthiko, akaliko, ehipassiko, opanayiko, paccattam veditabbo vinnuhi*" also apply here. within this well-expounded (*svakkhata*) dhamma, there are things that can be directly experienced by oneself. the buddha says to the kalamas regarding whether greed, hatred, and delusion are good or bad, and whether eradicating them and developing non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion is bad or good: "kalamas, when you investigate within yourselves whether something is wrong, and whether it is good or bad, and realize 'by practicing these dhammas, i will have these benefits'—that is how a matter should be investigated." the buddha is saying there that you should examine and accept these things by relating them to your own lives, not through any of those ten criteria. it does not mean throwing everything away, nor does it mean accepting everything. it means testing it in one’s own life; and testing does not mean through books, but by connecting it to life to see whether it is right or wrong. that is not being done in the way mentioned. most often, the logic of books is put forward. "if these teachings are brought close to life, we will face ruin; otherwise, because of these teachings, our lives will flourish"—the buddha is declaring to the kalamas to draw conclusions in this manner through investigation and direct experience.
if there is any logic in this dhamma, it exists to draw conclusions based on direct experience. the journey that is based on that direct experience leads straight to nibbana; this dhamma is well-expounded (*svakkhata*) and leading out of suffering (*niyyanika*). the *apannaka* practice is a practice that leads out of suffering. what is the reason for this? because this dhamma is well-expounded, it is directly visible (*sanditthika*); because it is directly visible, it is timeless (*akalika*). the timeless dhamma can be pointed to as "come and see" (*ehipassiko*). accordingly, within the dhamma itself, there is the quality of one step elevating you to the next step. that is how the dhamma is structured. it is structured as right view, right thought, and so on. one step prepares for and supports the next step. next is "*paccattam veditabbo vinnuhi*"—it is to be experienced individually by the wise. it is not about proving it through mere intellectual reasoning or mere belief. it is about bringing it close to one's own life and drawing a conclusion as to whether it is right or wrong. it is this very *apannaka* practice that the buddha declared.
what was presented to you today is a somewhat complex sermon. however, take what is to be taken. try to bring it close to your own lives. by observing these virtues of moral conduct, what you are hoping for is to escape from this samsaric *dukkha* (suffering) of *jati* (birth), *jaramarana* (decay and death), sickness, and so on. fine-material *bhava* (becoming) and immaterial *bhava* (becoming) lose their significance once a buddha has appeared.
in today’s sermon, the *apannaka* practice was introduced. i wish that by taking this *apannaka* practice forward, this sermon may support everyone in escaping from the samsaric *dukkha* (suffering) of *jati* (birth), *jaramarana* (decay and death), sickness, and so on, and realizing the noble, supreme, deathless nibbana! may whoever wishes to share in the merit of this dhamma preaching and dhamma listening, from the avici hell up to the akanittha heaven, rejoice in it and realize the supreme, deathless nibbana through their aspired state of enlightenment! wishing thus, recite these verses and share the merit.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 070
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #70
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.171)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Bahū devā manussā ca, maṅgalāni acintayuṃ;
ākaṅkhamānā sotthānaṃ,
brūhi maṅgalamuttamam.
From:
from Sutta Nipāta, Mahāmaṅgala Sutta
Dear Listeners,
The word '*Maṅgala*' has been used since the distant past to designate various signs or occurrences that bring well-being and prosperity to human beings. It is mentioned that during the time of the Buddha, when the Blessed One appeared, there were various disagreements in Jambudīpa as to what should actually be considered a blessing (*maṅgala*). The very first stanza of the Mahāmaṅgala Sutta, which we took as our theme today, reveals that this question of what constitutes a blessing was discussed not only among human beings but even among the deities.
According to the commentaries, while people gathered in the assembly halls of ancient Jambudīpa to discuss various matters, discussions also took place as to what should be designated as a blessing. No consensus could be reached on this. Some declared that the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of the day is determined by the first thing seen in the morning. Some declared that seeing certain things considered auspicious is a stroke of fortune. They are called *diṭṭha-maṅgalika*—those who consider what is seen as a blessing. According to their view, seeing things such as a full pitcher, a pregnant mother, a lime branch, a bull, a cow, or a horse-drawn chariot first thing in the morning was thought of as auspicious, as a blessing. Another group said that it is not what is seen, but what is heard that should be considered a blessing. According to their opinion, hearing words like "today is a good day," "a good asterism," "a good moment," "growth of goodness," or "glorious prosperity" first thing in the morning was declared by them to be a blessing. Yet another group said that it is neither what is seen nor what is heard that should be considered a blessing, but what is sensed by the nose, the tongue, and the body. According to their opinion, smelling the fragrance of flowers, touching the earth, touching fresh cow dung, touching fruits, wearing a new turban, or touching a new garment—things that come into contact with the body in the morning—were considered blessings. Thus, these disagreements spread further and further, and according to the commentary, a "blessing uproar" (*maṅgala-kolāhala*) arose. An "uproar" does not mean fighting and stabbing as in modern times. It means it became a topic discussed by everyone. The commentaries mention that this "blessing uproar" started among humans and went up to the terrestrial deities (*bhumma-deva*), and then among the deities of Cātumahārājika, Tāvatiṃsa, and so on. So in the end, on behalf of those deities, a certain deity came forward and presented this question to the Blessed One through the stanza we mentioned earlier; this is what is stated in this sutta.
You, meritorious listeners, know how such suttas begin. It is said that when the Blessed One was residing at Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī, after much of the night had passed, a deity of radiant beauty, illuminating the entire Jetavana with his light, approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, stood to one side, and uttered this very stanza we have themed:
"Bahū devā manussā ca, maṅgalāni acintayuṃ; Ākaṅkhamānā sotthānaṃ, brūhi maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
"Many deities and humans, desiring well-being, have thought about blessings. Tell us the supreme blessing." This is the general meaning. So, in response to this statement or request made to the Blessed One, the Blessed One expounded, in eleven stanzas, thirty-eight blessing factors—though in counting them, there might be slight discrepancies—which are known today as the Mahāmaṅgala Sutta. So, before analyzing each one, let us try to bring out the general meaning of these stanzas of the Mahāmaṅgala Sutta, which is a sutta used by everyone and frequently heard by all. In reply to that stanza, the Blessed One began like this:
"Asevanā ca bālānaṃ, paṇḍitānañca sevanā; Pūjā ca pūjanīyānaṃ, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
Not associating with fools, associating with the wise, and honoring those worthy of honor—this is the supreme blessing.
"Patirūpadesavāso ca, pubbe ca katapuññatā; Attasammāpaṇidhi ca, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
Living in a suitable locality, having made merit in the past, and setting one's mind rightly—this is the supreme blessing.
"Bāhusaccañca sippañca, vinayo ca susikkhito; Subhāsitā ca yā vācā, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
Great learning, craftsmanship, being well-trained in discipline, and speech that is well-spoken—this is the supreme blessing.
"Mātāpitu-upaṭṭhānaṃ, puttadārassa saṅgaho; Anākulā ca kammantā, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
Supporting one's parents, cherishing one's wife and children, and peaceful (unconfused) occupations—this is the supreme blessing.
"Dānañca dhammacariyā ca, ñātakānañca saṅgaho; Anavajjāni kammāni, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
Generosity, righteous conduct, helping one's relatives, and blameless actions—this is the supreme blessing.
"Āratī viratī pāpā, majjapānā ca saññamo; Appamādo ca dhammesu, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
Avoiding and abstaining from evil, refraining from intoxicants, and diligence in the Dhamma—this is the supreme blessing.
"Gāravo ca nivāto ca, santuṭṭhī ca kataññutā; Kālena dhammasavanaṃ, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
Reverence, humility, contentment, gratitude, and hearing the Dhamma at the proper time—this is the supreme blessing.
"Khantī ca sovacassatā, samaṇānañca dassanaṃ; Kālena dhammasākacchā, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
Patience, obedience, seeing ascetics, and Dhamma discussions at the proper time—this is the supreme blessing.
"Tapo ca brahmacariyañca, ariyasaccāna dassanaṃ; Nibbānasacchikiriyā ca, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
Ardent effort (*tapo*), the holy life (*brahmacariya*), seeing the Noble Truths, and the realization of Extinguishment / the Mind Stilled (Nibbāna)—this is the supreme blessing.
"Phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi, cittaṃ yassa na kampati; Asokaṃ virajaṃ khemaṃ, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
Although touched by the worldly conditions, the mind of one who is unshaken, sorrowless, stainless, secure—this is the supreme blessing.
"Etādisāni katvāna, sabbatthamaparājitā; Sabbattha sotthiṃ gacchanti, taṃ tesaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
Having done these things, undefeated everywhere, they go in safety everywhere. This is their supreme blessing. This is the general meaning of the Maṅgala Sutta.
Now let us analyze this meaning further. There are not so many deep things that require analyzing every single word. Most of you know the meaning. There are some words that need to be analyzed in detail. So, the word of the Buddha in the Maṅgala Sutta begins with the letter "A":
"Asevanā ca bālānaṃ, paṇḍitānañca sevanā; Pūjā ca pūjanīyānaṃ, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
Let us focus our minds on the three things mentioned here. First, it is presented as a pair: *Asevanā ca bālānaṃ*—not associating with fools, and *paṇḍitānañca sevanā*—associating with the wise.
Here, something needs to be mentioned. In our modern Sinhala usage, we use the word *bāla* to refer to those young in age. We say *bāla-mahalu* (young and old). However, in the Pali language, the word *bāla* is never used in the sense of being young in age. In the Pali language, the concept of "young and old" is expressed as *dahara-vuddha*. *Bāla* is used precisely in the sense of a fool, whereas *paṇḍita* means the wise.
This too can be understood by you through this analysis. Being a *paṇḍita* (wise person) is not something obtained through an academic degree. Indeed, we must discuss these matters in detail because in modern times, certain debaters question this, claiming that the Blessed One said something contradictory here. Why? Because he says not to associate with fools (*bāla*), and to associate with the wise (*paṇḍita*). Then how can there be a connection between these two groups? How can the fools associate with the wise? Can they avoid it?
There are people who formulate such questions. An answer to this will also be found as we proceed. First, let us look at the statements made by the Blessed One regarding fools (*bāla*) or ignorant people, taking them from various places in the texts.
On one occasion, the Blessed One states: "Monks, whatever fears, dangers, and calamities arise, they all arise from the fool (*bāla*), not from the wise (*paṇḍita*)." The fool is shown to be that dangerous there. Dangers and calamities do not arise from the wise. An analogy is also given for this. "Just as, monks, when a reed-house or a thatched house catches fire, even a nearby luxurious house that is well-plastered inside and out can be destroyed. Those other houses catch fire easily. Then, because they have caught fire, even large palaces and mansions nearby are burnt down." That is a simile given by the Blessed One to show the danger that comes from the fool. In another place, the Blessed One states: *"Kammalakkhaṇo, bhikkhave, bālo; kammalakkhaṇo paṇḍito"* ("Monks, a fool is characterized by his actions; a wise person is characterized by his actions"). The character of the fool is recognized through his conduct. The wise person is also recognized through his conduct. What is the conduct of the fool? A person with bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct is a fool. A person with bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, and mental good conduct is a wise person. According to this, we do not know how many "wise men" in this country would fall into this list!
In any case, the Blessed One further declares the signs and characteristics for identifying the fool and the wise person. Regarding the fool, his nature is shown: *duccintitacintī, dubbhāsitabhāsī, dukkatakammakārī* (one who thinks bad thoughts, speaks bad words, and does bad deeds). His thoughts are bad, his words are bad, and his actions are bad. The wise person is *sucintitacintī, subhāsitabhāsī, sukkatakammakārī* (one who thinks good thoughts, speaks good words, and does good deeds). The train of thoughts of the wise person is good, his words are good, and his course of action is good. How does one identify someone as a fool or a wise person? That is why the Blessed One introduced certain signs, so that these two groups could be identified through these signs.
Next, the Blessed One speaks of this in the Dhammapada; you may have heard of the places in the Dhammapada where the fool is mentioned. This fool is compared to a pit of filth. The danger that could happen to a wise person is shown in this way. The simile given is that if rotten fish is wrapped in kusa grass, although kusa grass normally has a pleasant scent, when rotten fish is wrapped in it, the kusa grass also stinks. It is just the same with associating with a fool.
So when this is said, we must consider: is it completely impossible for these two groups to come together? That is exactly what we are clarifying as an answer to those debaters mentioned earlier. Fools should associate with the wise just as—to use an analogy—patients associate with doctors. Or, to use a modern analogy, like drug addicts associating with a rehabilitation counselor nowadays. They do not associate to share a bottle! It is with a certain respect. They seek help from a counselor to overcome the wrong addictions they have acquired through habitual patterns of Saṃsāra. It is the same with the teacher-pupil relationship. That is why the Blessed One highlighted its gravity beforehand. Even a doctor has to treat patients, but he does so while maintaining his own safety. Likewise, one must associate with the wise while knowing the fool. One must identify both the fool and the wise and then associate. That, meritorious listeners, is what is meant by *"Pūjā ca pūjanīyānaṃ"*—honoring those worthy of honor. If a fool approaches a wise person with an attitude of honoring those worthy of honor, the extent to which the fool can progress is such that, in the end, the fool becomes a wise person, if he properly receives the association of noble friends (*kalyāṇa-mitta*), if he receives the association of the wise well. That is why the Therī Kisāgothamī declares in her Therīgāthā: "Kalyāṇamittatā muninā, lokaṃ ādissa vaṇṇitā; Kalyāṇamitte bhajamāno, api bālo paṇḍito assa." The Blessed One pointed his finger to the world and proclaimed the value of noble friendship; he praised it. By associating with noble friends, even a fool becomes a wise person. From that, we must understand that with that attitude of honoring those worthy of honor, fools can benefit from the wise. Likewise, the wise person must—according to the simile we mentioned earlier, where the counselor trying to save the drug addict does not go to share bottles—act knowing his own limits. So, regarding that stanza, considering the time, I think this is sufficient.
Now, consider the depth within this. Meritorious listeners, why did the Blessed One say these things first among the thirty-eight blessings? Why did he mention this matter at the very beginning? Because the most fundamental requirement, the most primary factor for laying the foundation of life, is association, companionship. Therefore, one must be careful about that association. Especially, after a person is born into the world, if they happen to associate with such fools in their childhood—even though we now use *bāla* to mean young, that young child eventually becomes a fool (*bāla*) indeed. Therefore, the Blessed One highlighted the matter of association in life through this. Next: "Patirūpadesavāso ca, pubbe ca katapuññatā; Attasammāpaṇidhi ca, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ." "Living in a suitable locality," "having made merit in the past," and "setting one's mind rightly." There too, there are some matters that need to be analyzed a bit.
"Living in a suitable locality"—in modern times, according to environmental engineering, this might mean suburban proximity, tap water, and perhaps electricity, when thinking about environment. But if we think in terms of the Dhamma, the commentaries specifically point to having the opportunity to associate with the fourfold assembly: monks (*bhikkhu*), nuns (*bhikkhunī*), laymen (*upāsaka*), and laywomen (*upāsikā*). Otherwise, living in an environment suitable for turning towards a life in accordance with the Dhamma is what is called *patirūpadesavāso ca*. Why? Because we previously spoke about association. Next, if we speak using a similar word, this is *nissaya* (dependence/support). First is association, next is environment. In simpler words, in the first one we said association, now we say environment. That is, the locality where one resides.
Next, there is a special factor: *"pubbe ca katapuññatā"*—having made merit in the past. As they say, "Even if one gets a hundred sons of little merit, it is futile"—that is what is meant. This is seen clearly only by the Buddha-eye. Let us call it the innate fortune or the inborn potential of each individual. Now we have spoken about association. We have spoken about environment. Next, we can call this *upanissaya* (strong support/decisive support). There is an ancient term: *upanissaya-sampatti* (the fortune of decisive support). The karmic force and the meritorious force brought from the past become apparent in early childhood. That too is a foundation for this life. In modern times, those who follow Western psychologists ridicule these things. We have heard and seen such instances. They discard what comes from the past and confine everything to childhood. That is the end of it for them. But the Blessed One points out that we have a vast past in our Saṃsāra. Thus, there are both good and bad in it. Depending on those, let us call it past fortune: *"pubbe ca katapuññatā"*. Now next, it says it is not enough to just leave it to that. There is also something for oneself to do.
*"Attasammāpaṇidhi ca"*—setting one's mind rightly—this becomes extremely important. Behold, that is where the beginning of personality development lies. One's own agency begins from here. *"Attasammāpaṇidhi ca"*—setting one's mind rightly. To put it briefly, there is a stanza in the Dhammapada regarding this, which you, meritorious listeners, may know: "Na taṃ mātā pitā kayirā, aññe vāpi ca ñātakā; Sammāpaṇihitaṃ cittaṃ, seyyaso naṃ tato kare." Neither mother, nor father, nor any other relatives can do for one such good as a rightly directed mind can do. At one time, this was put into a Sinhala poem: "What parents and relatives cannot do, my own mind, when well-directed, accomplishes for my well-being."
There, the Blessed One has given a beautiful simile about this directing of the mind. Actually, within the word *paṇidhi* is a directing. The proper directing of the mind. The simile given by the Blessed One for this might not be understood by some. A grain of paddy—everyone who does farming knows—has a small sharp point at its tip. The ancient word for it is *vī-naṇḍuva* (the awn/tip of the paddy grain). People of this area do not even have a name for it. A nameless, easily forgotten small dot. The Blessed One has used such a small thing for a simile. In that simile, the Blessed One states that although that pricking part at the tip of the grain is a tiny thing, if that tip of paddy is placed rightly, it can pierce a hand or a foot. Similarly, if the mind is rightly directed, it can destroy the darkness of ignorance (*avijjā*). That is how the Blessed One states it. From that we can see that, whatever the power of past fortune may be, one's own part begins from there by directing the mind to the right side. *"Attasammāpaṇidhi"*—this too is a factor of blessing. Next:
"Bāhusaccañca sippañca, vinayo ca susikkhito; Subhāsitā ca yā vācā, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
Everyone knows what *bāhusacca* (great learning) is. Having heard and remembered much, erudition. Next, *sippañca*—craftsmanship. This factor also must be considered in accordance with the Dhamma. Even if one learns various worthless things unrelated to the Dhamma, if one lacks the skill to use them properly, we see in the world that one gets destroyed by that very learning. In any case, this learning, this craft, and in modern terms, the basically required training—*bāhusaccañca sippañca, vinayo ca susikkhito*—being well-disciplined, being disciplined. This refers to the discipline necessary for life. *Subhāsitā ca yā vācā*—that too is a part of discipline: well-spoken speech. Here, what is called "well-spoken" is truth in accordance with the Dhamma. Moreover, the Blessed One has shown a beautiful passage in various places to define the word "well-spoken":
"Yā sā vācā nelā kaṇṇasukhā pemanīyā hadayaṅgamā porī bahujanakantā bahujanamanāpā"
"Whatever speech is flawless (*nelā*), pleasing to the ear (*kaṇṇasukhā*), lovely (*pemanīyā*), reaching the heart (*hadayaṅgamā*), polite (*porī*), appealing to many, and pleasing to many"—words like that are well-spoken. Likewise, those truthful, timely words are well-spoken words. Next:
"Mātāpitu-upaṭṭhānaṃ, puttadārassa saṅgaho; Anākulā ca kammantā, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
*Mātāpitu-upaṭṭhānaṃ*—some take this as two: supporting the mother, and supporting the father. Whatever the count, if we take these points according to the Buddha's word, supporting one's parents—which you, meritorious listeners, have heard so often—is also a factor of blessing. Why is it a factor of blessing? Because the blessing of those parents can be obtained even during their lifetime by supporting them. In this dispensation of the Buddha, let alone other things, even after they have passed away, a form of service is shown. What is the place given to parents by the Blessed One? They are declared to be like Brahma (*brahmāti mātāpitaro*). "Āpādakā posakā, imassa lokassa dassetāro"—they brought up, nourished, and showed this world to them. That is why they are called first teachers, *pubbācariyo*. Likewise, you, meritorious listeners, may have heard that in suttas like these, the Blessed One represented the eastern direction as supporting parents. That too is indeed a blessing, which brings the parents' blessing. Next, *saṅgaho*—the proper cherishing of one's children and wife. These too are duties in this society. Fulfilling those duties directly in a way that shapes a life. *Anākulā ca kammantā*—occupations that are peaceful, not illegal, and free from improper things, is a factor of blessing. Next:
"Dānañca dhammacariyā ca, ñātakānañca saṅgaho; Anavajjāni kammāni, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
Generosity, righteous conduct, *dānañca dhammacariyā ca*, and *ñātakānañca saṅgaho*—helping one's relatives, and *anavajjāni kammāni*—blameless actions: these are the supreme blessing. Behold, next turning towards society, *dāna*—giving. Not only to the Saṅgha, but also to the poor, travelers, and beggars—that giving is altruistic conduct. Having first fulfilled one's duty to one's home, then comes generosity, righteous conduct (*dhammacariyā*), a life in accordance with the Dhamma, and cherishing and helping relatives as the occasion arises. *Anavajjāni kammāni*—blameless action; it is perfectly fine to think of this as abandoning wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*) and living by right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*).
"Āratī viratī pāpā, majjapānā ca saññamo; Appamādo ca dhammesu, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
*Āratī viratī pāpā* is explained by showing that *āratī* means avoiding evil through the mind, removing oneself from it mentally. *Viratī* is explained as abstaining from them through precepts and such. Developing self-control regarding that. That too is a blessing. But nowadays, in both weddings and funerals, one cannot do without alcohol! Behold what has become of the Mahāmaṅgala Sutta now. The Mahāmaṅgala Sutta too is probably recited at those auspicious events. Amidst all this, the true blessing factor is this word of the Buddha. *Appamādo ca dhammesu*—diligence in the Dhamma; then, step by step, one turns towards the spiritual side.
"Gāravo ca nivāto ca, santuṭṭhī ca kataññutā; Kālena dhammasavanaṃ, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
*Gāravo ca*—showing respect, paying reverence to those worthy of virtue. *Nivāto ca*—humility. *Santuṭṭhi*—contentment with what is obtained. *Kataññutā*—gratitude. There is no need to explain these, is there? You, meritorious listeners, know them. *Kālena dhammasavanaṃ*—hearing the Dhamma at the proper time; *etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ*—these are factors of blessing.
"Khantī ca sovacassatā, samaṇānañca dassanaṃ; Kālena dhammasākacchā, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
*Khantī*—patience; *sovacassatā*—gentleness, obedience; *samaṇānañca dassanaṃ*—seeing ascetics. Behold, step by step, it turns towards the spiritual life. *Kālena dhammasākacchā*—previously one listened to the Dhamma, next is discussing the Dhamma. Discussing one's own problems by associating with the venerable monks. "At the proper time" means when the opportunity for Dhamma discussions arises. Also, when the mind is overcome by the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), or if there are matters unclear to oneself, discussing them: *kālena dhammasākacchā etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ*.
"Tapo ca brahmacariyañca, ariyasaccāna dassanaṃ; Nibbānasacchikiriyā ca, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
Here, *tapo* (ardent effort) is not interpreted in the sense of the ascetic practices of the past, but as the burning away of defilements, sensory restraint, and so forth. Coming to this point, we can think of lay disciples like those present here, who, having spent their lay lives, ponder in their old age. One does not have to be extremely old to walk this path of the Sasana. But some in this Sasana, as you, meritorious listeners, have heard, have become Arahants even at seven years of age. If one argues dogmatically based on this Maṅgala Sutta, one might think that one should incline towards the spiritual life only after growing old like that. One needs to think so only if one failed to do so in one's early years. The primary purpose here is to analyze the meaning of the word "blessing". There, the Blessed One shows *tapo*—that is, undertaking virtue (*sīla*), leaving homes, and doing things by way of burning away defilements, by way of meditation; these are taken as ascetic practice (*tapas*). Celibacy (*brahmacariya*) is possible. What is understood by that, generally understood, is abstaining from sexual relations and the pure conduct associated with it. Some, as we have heard, those laymen and laywomen who led householders' lives, after coming to a life in accordance with the Dhamma, consult each other and establish themselves in this very practice. Not only that, now if on some occasion one can separate from lay life and implement the aforementioned *tapo* and *brahmacariya* at the highest level by ordaining—then that too belongs to this. Through *tapo ca brahmacariyañca* comes *ariyasaccāna dassanaṃ*—the seeing of the Four Noble Truths: the truths of Suffering (*dukkha*), Origin, Cessation, and the Path. At that stage, through one's own life experiences, in accordance with the Buddha's word, if one has understood to some extent that rebirth / arising (*jāti*), aging and death / decay and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), sickness, and death are Suffering (*dukkha*), and if one is engaged in meditation, going even deeper, if one gets the realization that this entire five aggregates of grasping (*pañcupādānakkhandha*) is Suffering (*dukkha*), that indeed is the understanding of Suffering (*dukkha*).
Next, when reflecting on the cause of this Suffering (*dukkha*), if one understands that it becomes Suffering (*dukkha*) because of the Grasping (*upādāna*) towards the five aggregates of grasping—clinging to them—then, at that point, Craving (*taṇhā*) too is understood. That is, the Craving (*taṇhā*) that lies underneath that Grasping (*upādāna*). Next, that Craving (*taṇhā*), at some point... seeing these Four Noble Truths is indeed the direct realization of the Four Noble Truths. As the final result of some insight-consciousness-process (*vipassanā-citta-vīthi*), having seen the impermanence (*anicca*) of all these things, having seen their nature of arising and passing away, having seen their breaking-up nature by way of *udayabbaya* (arising and passing away), *bhaṅga* (dissolution), etc., and having developed fear towards these preparations (*saṅkhāra*), and next, having understood their disadvantageous side (*ādīnava*), and next, having developed that weariness with Saṃsāra called *nibbidā*, and having generated the thought "I must somehow escape from this", if one constantly develops the three characteristics of Impermanent (*anicca*), Suffering (*dukkha*), and Not-self (*anattā*) in daily life, whether as a monk or a layperson—it is through that development that at some point, when they have matured, using those three characteristics, one drops to the other shore. How does one drop? Through that very weariness. When one drops to the other side at some point due to disgust—that is to say, for a moment, the grip of this holding is let go. In that letting go is what is called extinguishment; therein, for the first time, one experiences a peaceful sensation (*vedanā*). As that experience, it is something completely different from what the people of the world think. That is why it is called world-transcending (*lokuttara*). The peace, the extinguishment obtained through that letting go—one experiences it, even for a short moment. That indeed is: "by the destruction of Craving (*taṇhā*), the Mind Stilled / Extinguishment (Nibbāna) was seen."
For that to happen, indeed, within one's mental continuum, not only the Noble Eightfold Path shown by the Blessed One but also the thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*) must have been developed to some degree. It is when they have matured through the meditation one does, that the seeing of the Noble Truths (*ariyasaccāna dassanaṃ*) occurs; within this is *nibbānañca*—that is, extinguishment / the Mind Stilled, and *sacchikiriyā ca*—which means direct realization. To realize Extinguishment / the Mind Stilled (Nibbāna) means the Dhamma is to be realized in this very life. The Blessed One has shown that there is indeed such a thing as this extinguishment / stilled mind. A state of the mind becomes directly realized by oneself. Nibbānasacchikiriyā ca etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ*—this is the supreme blessing. Behold, next, the state of the mind as the result of attaining that Extinguishment / the Mind Stilled (Nibbāna) is expressed in the next stanza:
"Phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi, cittaṃ yassa na kampati; Asokaṃ virajaṃ khemaṃ, etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
"Worldly conditions" mean the eight worldly conditions (*attha-lokadhamma*). You, meritorious listeners, may have heard: "Lābho alābho ayaso yaso ca, nindā pasaṃsā ca sukhaṃ ca dukkhaṃ." Gain, loss, disrepute, fame, blame, praise, pleasure, and Suffering (*dukkha*). The Blessed One has expressed these eight worldly conditions in a series of stanzas on one occasion.
These eight worldly conditions revolve around the world, and the world revolves around the eight worldly conditions. If you think a bit deeply, you will understand. The eight worldly conditions revolve around the world. Actually, this is exactly how this whole discussion of blessings arose. The signs that bring goodness and well-being to humans. People went after these blessings with the idea that, through some hidden signs, the suffering caused by these eight worldly conditions could be avoided.
Thus, the Blessed One, having rightly realized Extinguishment / the Mind Stilled (Nibbāna) spiritually, then declares the state of that person: *phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi*—whose mind is not shaken when touched by the eight worldly conditions; next, that unshakable state is described. *Asokaṃ virajaṃ khemaṃ*—sorrowless, dustless (free from the dust of defilements), secure (which is called the ground of safety). That state indeed is the supreme blessing: *asokaṃ virajaṃ khemaṃ etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ*.
If we are to say something more related to that—now indeed we have arrived at the deep side of the Dhamma. We have told you on various occasions not to let this become just a mundane lay sermon. Therefore, at this point, we must recall those things stated by the Blessed One, especially regarding Extinguishment / the Mind Stilled (Nibbāna). Not only the Blessed One, but the Venerable Sariputta Mahathera also on one occasion states with a beautiful simile, the state of that liberated mind. These are experienced in the state called the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship (*arahattaphala-samādhi*). Venerable Sariputta Mahathera describes how the mind remains in that state: "No matter how many visual objects cognizable by the eye may come, the mind of that Arahant does not get mixed up with them. That mind remains in a firm, unshakable state." Just as it was said about visual objects cognizable by the eye, so too with sounds cognizable by the ear, and so on—you can imagine, not only things coming from the five physical senses. Finally, it points to thoughts/mind-objects (*dhamma*) coming to the mind; that indeed is the deepest part. No matter how many of these come, the mind remains unshaken, in that aforementioned stable state; this is what Venerable Sariputta Mahathera states on one occasion. Next, to show that unshakable state, he gives a simile: just as a stone pillar of about sixteen cubits, with eight cubits buried in the ground and standing firmly established, is not shaken no matter from which direction strong storms blow. Venerable Sariputta Mahathera gives this simile regarding the aforementioned unshaken mind. Then, *asokaṃ virajaṃ*—that is, that sorrowless state.
Thus, illustrations of these have been shown on various occasions. When Devadatta once rolled down a rock at the Blessed One—karma affects anyone—a splinter from that rock struck the sole of the Blessed One's foot, causing a deep wound and severe sensation (*vedanā*) of pain. Even though the Blessed One experienced severe sensation (*vedanā*) of pain, he directed his mind to the power of the fruit (*phala-samādhi*), and is said to have endured that severe pain. At that time, even the deities exclaimed that he was enduring such severe sensation (*vedanā*). That mind capable of enduring is what is shown as "refuge, security, place, shelter, and resort" in Extinguishment / the Mind Stilled (Nibbāna). An Arahant can bring the mind to that state by bringing back that aforementioned direct realization; and that will definitely emerge at the final moment of an Arahant. Because of that emergence, because the mind is liberated (*vimutta*), they do not come back to another Becoming / Existence (*bhava*).
Regarding the Blessed One, it is told that on one occasion, when it was raining heavily, with water flooding, and thunderbolts striking and cracking, four oxen and two men were killed by the lightning. At that time, near a threshing-shed (*bhūsāgāra*) or barn, perhaps because the Blessed One was absorbed in this very concentration (*samādhi*), when the Blessed One came out and asked why these people had gathered, they replied: "Why, did the Blessed One not see that such a thing has happened?" He said "No." He said he did not even hear it. "Then, were you asleep, Venerable Sir?" "No, I was conscious." That is a very deep matter that most people cannot understand. If he had been completely without perception (*saññā*), it could have been understood. But what we have here is that the Blessed One had perception (*saññā*) at that time, and was also awake. *"Saññī samāno jāgaro"*—even while awake and conscious, none of those things were heard by the Blessed One. Why? Because at that time, he had attained a wakefulness far greater than what the people of the world call wakefulness.
Think about it a bit. The world being "awake" refers to the state where objects come to the six sense-bases (*saḷāyatana*). The Blessed One being "awake" refers to the supramundane state that transcends them. That is why the Blessed One said *"saññī samāno jāgaro"*. *Jāgara* means staying awake, being awake. What does being awake mean? This perception (*saññā*), *samāno jāgaro* means he was awake. It is perception (*saññā*) that we highlight in most of our sermons. The passage describing Extinguishment / the Mind Stilled (Nibbāna) is: *"Etaṃ santaṃ etaṃ paṇītaṃ, yadidaṃ sabbasaṅkhārasamatho sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo taṇhakkhayo virāgo nirodho nibbānaṃ."* ("This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all preparations (*saṅkhāra*), the relinquishment of all assets, the destruction of Craving (*taṇhā*), fading away, cessation, Extinguishment / the Mind Stilled (Nibbāna)"). That is what is shown as *upasamānussati* (recollection of peace). The mind was directed there. Therefore, when the Blessed One remained with his mind directed to that state of Arahantship-fruit which he had ultimately attained as his path-and-fruit realization, that indeed is what is meant by "going to Extinguishment / the Mind Stilled (Nibbāna)". That is why so many words are used for Extinguishment / the Mind Stilled (Nibbāna), such as "place, shelter, refuge, resort, seclusion (*viveka*)." That is why those words are used. Thus, that state is the state of being liberated from the six sense-bases (*saḷāyatana*). People think: "Ah! How awake the Blessed One was, having been liberated from the six sense-bases, it is a great wonder!" Having become world-transcending (*lokuttara*)—that is what we have shown on certain occasions, based on a simile given by the Blessed One.
The Blessed One declared to the Brahmin Verañja: "In this generation, I am indeed the first chick to have broken the eggshell of ignorance (*avijjā*) and come out." A simile worth reflecting upon, meritorious listeners. "The first chick to have broken the eggshell of ignorance and come out"—from that, what we have to understand is that all of us are inside that eggshell. The eggshell means the six sense-bases (*āyatana*). It is within those six sense-bases that everyone is active, including scientists. That is Saṃsāra. That is Becoming / Existence (*bhava*). All three worlds—the sensual (*kāma*), fine-material (*rūpa*), and immaterial (*arūpa*)—exist inside that eggshell. Thus, the Blessed One experienced that very world-transcending state. He broke the eggshell and went out. The state of remaining with the mind directed to that direct realization is the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship (*arahattaphala-samādhi*). Therefore, in the end it says:
"Etādisāni katvāna, sabbatthamaparājitā; Sabbattha sotthiṃ gacchanti, taṃ tesaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ."
*"Sabbatthamaparājitā"*—undefeated everywhere. Nowadays, we often hear about the defeated. Some have won in worldly terms but are defeated in world-transcending terms. Some have won in this world but are defeated in the next world. Here, it says they won in this world, they won in the next world, and they won Extinguishment / the Mind Stilled (Nibbāna). That is why it says *"sabbatthamaparājitā"*. *"Sabbattha sotthiṃ"*—whether in this world, or in the next world, or next, regarding Extinguishment / the Mind Stilled (Nibbāna) on the world-transcending side, they arrive at safety and well-being from every side.
Regarding the time, this is all there is to say. I think a sufficient amount has been spoken. For centuries, the Mahāmaṅgala Sutta has been on everyone's lips. Hearing the Dhamma is valuable. But implementing these thirty-eight is the true blessing. Therefore, without stopping at the level of seen blessings (*diṭṭha-maṅgala*), heard blessings (*suta-maṅgala*), or sensed blessings (*muta-maṅgala*), we should hope to realize the true truth of blessings by implementing them. Then, this meritorious gathering—there may be people of various age groups here—for the elderly people mentioned, this Mahāmaṅgala Sutta is a great strength. What is past is past. Yes, you spent a lay life. But with this opportunity received, as was said in *tapo ca brahmacariyañca*, having inclined towards the Dhamma and the Sasana, you must resolve to escape as quickly as possible from the Suffering (*dukkha*) of Saṃsāra, such as rebirth / arising (*jāti*), aging and death / decay and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), sickness, and death, and attain the supreme Extinguishment / the Mind Stilled (Nibbāna) which is complete liberation.
So, as a step towards that today too, you observed the precepts and meditated to the extent of your minds. We wish that today, this Mahāmaṅgala Sutta may also assist in that. May all beings, from Avīci to Akaniṭṭha, whoever wish to share in these merits, rejoice in this merit of expounding the Dhamma and this merit of hearing the Dhamma! Through that rejoicing, may they realize the supreme, deathless, great Extinguishment / the Mind Stilled (Nibbāna) through whichever state of enlightenment they aspire to! May you, meritorious listeners, also have the strength and power to realize the supreme blessing in the Mahāmaṅgala Sutta as quickly as possible, before the decline of the Sasana, through the penetration of the paths and fruits of Stream-entry, Once-returning, Non-returning, and Arahantship!

author: ven. katukurunde nanananda thero
(pahankanuwa sinhala audio dhamma sermon no.171)
namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa
(homage to the blessed one, the worthy one, the fully self-enlightened one)
pali stanza:
bahu deva manussa ca, mangalani acintayum;
akankhamana sotthanam,
bruhi mangalamuttamam.
from:
from sutta nipata, mahamangala sutta
dear listeners,
the word '*mangala*' has been used since the distant past to designate various signs or occurrences that bring well-being and prosperity to human beings. it is mentioned that during the time of the buddha, when the blessed one appeared, there were various disagreements in jambudipa as to what should actually be considered a blessing (*mangala*). the very first stanza of the mahamangala sutta, which we took as our theme today, reveals that this question of what constitutes a blessing was discussed not only among human beings but even among the deities.
according to the commentaries, while people gathered in the assembly halls of ancient jambudipa to discuss various matters, discussions also took place as to what should be designated as a blessing.
