It is analyzed in this way: "Right View and Right Intention belong to the wisdom group (*paññā-kkhandha*); Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration belong to the concentration group (*samādhi-kkhandha*)." Looking at it in that way, first comes wisdom, then virtue, and then concentration. Taking that logically, some try to give foremost place to this wisdom. But that is a completely wrong understanding.
It is mentioned in the Dhamma itself. On one occasion, Bhikkhuṇī Dhammadinnā, in response to a question by her former lay husband, Visākha Upāsaka, says the following (mentioning it briefly due to time constraints): what is the question? Visākha Upāsaka asks: "Noble Lady, is the threefold training of virtue, concentration, and wisdom included in the Noble Eightfold Path, or is the Noble Eightfold Path included in the threefold training of virtue, concentration, and wisdom?" He asked this because even in the past, there were questions just like the ones we have today. What is the answer to that? The threefold training of virtue, concentration, and wisdom was not arranged by the Noble Eightfold Path; rather, the Noble Eightfold Path was arranged under the three groups of virtue, concentration, and wisdom. Through this, we must understand that the division into virtue, concentration, and wisdom is more primary than the Noble Eightfold Path. It is to that division that foremost place must be given. Just as we give foremost place to it, we must also give it place at the end.
That is why, in the poignant account showing how the Buddha, even with such a severe illness, journeyed from village to village, we find a passage where he preached the entirety of the Dhamma in brief:
> *Iti sīlaṃ, iti samādhi, iti paññā. Sīlaparibhāvito samādhi mahapphalo hoti mahānisaṃso. Samādhiparibhāvitā paññā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā. Paññāparibhāvitaṃ cittaṃ sammadeva āsavehi vimuccati.*
In a single passage, he summarized and showed the entire Dhamma: "Such is virtue, such is concentration, such is wisdom." Concentration fully developed through virtue is of great fruit and great benefit. Wisdom fully developed through concentration is of great fruit and great benefit. Next, *paññāparibhāvitaṃ cittaṃ*—the mind developed through wisdom, the mind grown in accordance with wisdom, *sammadeva āsavehi vimuccati*—is fully liberated from the taints (*āsava*). That is a passage summarizing the entire Dhamma. Based on that, we can surely understand that the three—virtue, concentration, and wisdom—are primary. The Noble Eightfold Path is something built on that, arising through it.
Likewise, we must understand that when we speak of a "path," Right View (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) must naturally come to the beginning. Even if we think of a gradual transformation of personal character, that too must begin with Right View. It is in accordance with one's view (*diṭṭhi*) that one's thoughts and intentions arise. In accordance with thoughts and intentions, words are spoken. In accordance with words, actions are performed. It is because of this systematic, gradual path of practice, which is connected in a wonderfully interconnected manner, integrated and organically blended, that it is called *ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo* (the Noble Eightfold Path). It is shown as a single unit, whereas the others are shown separately. Although the four foundations of mindfulness, the four bases of power, and so on are listed separately, in the end, the Noble Eightfold Path is a single unit. When the supramundane path arises, it happens so instantly that all those eight factors arise in a single mind-moment. That instant moment where all eight factors arise simultaneously in a single mind is the powerful concentration: the path-concentration. It is through that concentration that one can realize the Unconditioned.
It is precisely because you all ask questions in various ways regarding this path of Dhamma that we summarized and presented many facts in accordance with this topic. You must reflect on this, not letting these matters remain limited to books, but practically drawing them close to your daily life, and proceeding on your path of virtue, concentration, and wisdom. Depending on your respective abilities—if not *ugghaṭitaññū*, then *vipañcitaññū*; if not that, then *neyya*—in whatever way, aligning with your capacity and putting forth maximum energy in these final times of the Buddha's dispensation, dedicating a place greater than for anything else to this task, may this Dhamma sermon surely serve as a supportive condition for you to escape from this extremely dangerous Saṃsāra, to practice this listening, meditation, virtue, concentration, and wisdom, and to bring an end to this suffering / unsatisfactoriness / stress (Dukkha) of Saṃsāra. Wish and aspire in this manner.
If, through this, you have developed the spiritual faculties and powers of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, may that surely serve as a strong support (*upanissaya*) for you to realize the Paths and Fruits in this very life, with the help of the association with noble friends. Not only that: if any wholesome store of merit has been gathered through this Dhamma sermon in this seen and unseen world, may all beings, from Avīci to Akaniṭṭha, including the deceased relatives in whose names we do so, who wish to rejoice in this merit of listening to and delivering the Dhamma, rejoice in it likewise; and, with the help of that store of merit, may they as quickly as possible escape from all the suffering / unsatisfactoriness / stress (Dukkha) of Saṃsāra—such as birth / arising (Jāti), decay, aging, and death (Decay and Death / Aging and Death / Jarāmaraṇa), sickness, and so forth—and find solace in the supreme, deathless Nibbāna! Reciting these verses, let us share the merits.

from:
dhammapada 102–103 (sahassavagga)
dear listeners,
the buddha, the lord of peace and teacher of the three worlds, presented to the world a path of practice leading to peace and solace. however, in order to suit the mind of combative mankind, on certain occasions the buddha used words such as "fight," "battle," and "warfare" even to describe the energy and effort exerted towards nibbana. on certain occasions, the buddha pointed this out as a sublime, heroic battle against mara (the evil one), a war against mara fought for the sake of peace, leading all the way to nibbana. the verses describing the value of this battle are indeed what we have chosen as our topic today. the background story (*nidana*) of these verses concerns the account of theri kundalakesa. that account is found in various places in dhamma literature with certain minor variations. if we summarize those details, we can present them for this occasion as follows.
in the city of rajagaha, there lived the sixteen-year-old daughter of a certain merchant (*setthi*). since she was a very beautiful maiden, her parents, for her protection, had her live on the top floor of the mansion, guarded under the watchful eyes of attendants. one day, a certain thief in rajagaha was caught with stolen goods, sentenced to death by royal decree, and was being taken to the place of execution, being whipped at the four-way crossroads. hearing the shouts of the crowd, this merchant's daughter looked through the window and, upon seeing this young man—perhaps due to some past association in samsara—conceived a strong affection and attachment towards him. having fallen in love, she lay face down on her bed, refused food, and went on a hunger strike. when her mother came and asked, she said, "if i get that young man as my husband, i will live; otherwise, my life will end." they tried to change her mind by pleading in various ways, but failed. afterwards, the merchant was also informed. having discussed it together, what did they do in the end? they sent a bribe of a thousand *kahapanas* to the chief executioner to release the thief and send him to them. that officer released the thief, executed someone else in his place, and sent word to the king that the thief had been executed. the merchant then gave that thief in marriage to his daughter. then, wishing to win her husband's heart even more, she attended to him day in and day out with food, drink, and personal care, herself always beautifully adorned with ornaments.
this thief, perhaps due to the habit of his thievish nature brought from birth, began to plot: "how can i kill this woman and take these ornaments?" having thought of a ruse, one day he refused food and lay on the bed, whereupon the merchant's daughter came and asked: "why, my lord, is it an illness?" "no," he replied. "are you displeased with my parents?" "no," he said. when she asked, "then what is it?" he said, "on the day i was being taken to be executed, i made a vow to make an offering to the deity residing at the mountain called 'thieves' cliff' (*chorapapata*), where thieves are thrown down to their death." "it is as a result of that vow that i was released and obtained you." when she asked, "what is required for that offering?" he replied, "prepare waterless milk-rice (milk-rice prepared without adding water) and roasted paddy with five-fold flowers, etc." thinking that it was no major task, she prepared those items. but the thief said, "now, do not go with relatives or attendants. let the two of us go there together. also, come well-adorned with your ornaments. we can also make it a pleasure trip." in this manner, they set out. having arrived, and climbing to the top, he said, "now, stop the carriage and the attendants here. let just the two of us go up."
handing the vessel of offerings to the merchant's daughter to carry on her head, they climbed up the mountain. one side of that mountain could be climbed, while the other side was a sheer precipice. beyond that was where thieves were thrown off to their death. that is why it was called *chorapapata pabbata* (thieves' cliff mountain) in those days, as a place of punishment. after they ascended, when she said, "now let us perform the offering ritual," the thief replied, "i did not come for that. i came with a different intention: to take your ornaments and kill you." she said, "whose are these ornaments? whose am i? why do you do this?" he replied, "i do not understand all that. i am not accustomed to stealing without killing." when he said, "remove your ornaments and get ready now," she realized: "now an extremely dangerous situation has come upon me."
"wisdom is not something cooked and eaten. it is at times like this that wisdom is needed." realizing this, through her presence of mind, she thought of a strategy. thinking it over, she said, "this is my last sight of you. therefore, grant me a single boon: let me circumambulate you, pay my respects, and embrace you while still wearing these ornaments." the thief agreed to this. she also said, "i need to see you clearly." so the thief climbed to the very edge of the cliff and stood there on top of the mountain. under the guise of circumambulating him three times, she got behind him, grabbed his body firmly, and pushed him down from the mountain; the thief fell and was completely crushed to death. it is further said that the deity residing on that mountain, having witnessed the actions of these two, praised her presence of mind and uttered a certain verse:
> *na so sabbesu thanesu, puriso hoti pandito;*
> *pandita hoti naripi, tattha tattha vicakkhana.*
"man is not wise in all situations. even a woman can be wise in various matters when she possesses discerning intellect."
after things happened in this way, this young woman thought: "if i go home, my parents will scold me. even if i say my husband tried to kill me for my ornaments, they might not believe it. what shall i do now?" wandering far away along a forest path, she reached an ascetic hermitage (*paribbajakarama*) belonging to the niganthas (jains). going to this hermitage where white-robed (*svetambara*) nigantha female ascetics lived, she asked to be ordained. when asked what the monastic practice belonging to that hermitage was, she was told that one of them was plucking out the hair with pincers; she gave her consent to that too. her hair was plucked out. it is said that because the hair that grew back afterwards was curly, she was called "kundalakesa" (curly-hair). her previous name was bhadda. the name "bhadda kundalakesa" is what is mentioned in the sutta discourses. when she asked the ascetics, "what do you teach?" they informed her: "we teach absorptions (*jhana*), etc., and on the other hand, we teach a thousand systems of debate, in which proficiency can be attained." so she learned the arts of debate and went around the villages, market towns, and cities of india in those days, debating with those accepted as scholars in those areas. that is what she did after learning debate. it is said she was also known as *jambu paribbajika* (rose-apple wanderer).
when going to those villages and market towns, she customarily used a rose-apple branch as a challenge. before going for almsround (*pindapata*) in a city or market town, she would make a mound of sand at the city gate, plant the rose-apple branch on it, and tell the nearby children: "if there is anyone who wishes to debate with me, let them throw down this rose-apple branch." she would leave it like that for seven days. no one wished to accept that challenge. this was because by then, she had won debates everywhere. in this way, several years must have passed. according to the story, on one occasion she arrived at the city of savatthi, set up a sand mound and planted the rose-apple branch near the city gate in that manner, and went for alms. meanwhile, venerable sariputta, returning after his almsround, saw this rose-apple branch. seeing children gathered around it, he asked what it was, and the children explained the situation. venerable sariputta said, "in that case, kick down that rose-apple branch." when they said, "we are afraid to do that," he replied, "no, no, i am telling you to do it. i will take care of it." when he said something like that, the children kicked down the rose-apple branch. when the wanderer returned, she blamed the children, saying, "i have no debate with you!"
so, after being told of the event, she went looking for venerable sariputta. prior to that, making a great clamor in the city, proclaiming loudly, "behold, i am going to debate with the ascetics of the sakyan clan!" she went to the place where venerable sariputta was residing. as mentioned here, he was seated under a tree in the evening. having gone there to begin the debate, when she asked whose turn it was to question, the female wanderer took the opportunity and asked all one thousand questions of debate. venerable sariputta answered every single question correctly. next, when it was venerable sariputta’s turn, saying "i too shall ask a question," he asked just one question.
"ekam nama kim?"—"what is one?" he asked. that question is mentioned in dhamma literature as one of the ten questions asked by the buddha to ordain venerable sopaka, who attained arahantship at the age of seven. the standard answer for "ekam nama kim" is "sabbe satta aharatthitika"—"all beings subsist on nutriment." but kundalakesa knew nothing of this. she was bewildered by it; she did not understand it. confessing, "i do not understand what that is," she admitted defeat and asked him to explain it to her. venerable sariputta said, "this is what is called a buddha-question." "to explain a buddha-question, one must receive ordination," he said. she agreed to this. venerable sariputta sent her to a nunnery (*bhikkhuni-upassaya*) and had her ordained as a bhikkhuni (nun). next, this nun, kundalakesa bhikkhuni, listened to the dhamma from the buddha. as it is mentioned, immediately upon hearing the discourse, she attained the stage of stream-entry (*sotapanna*). furthermore, while pouring water to wash her feet, observing the water flowing away, she very quickly realized the fruit of arahantship. she attained arahantship.
on the basis of this event, it is mentioned that a discussion arose among the sangha about how this bhikkhuni kundalakesa, recalling her past history, understood the dhamma so quickly. they expressed wonder at this: "while as a layperson, she fought such a great battle with a thief and won it!" in this way, they were speaking about her. having heard this news, the buddha uttered the two verses we mentioned earlier:
> *yo ce gathasatam bhase, anatthapadasamhita,*
> *ekam dhammapadam seyyo, yam sutva upasammati.*
"monks, though one should recite a hundred verses comprising meaningless words, far better is a single word of the dhamma (teaching/discourse) that brings about peace and stilling. that is the first verse." next is the second verse:
> *yo sahassam sahassena, sangame manuse jine;*
> *ekanca jeyyamattanam, sa ve sangamajuttamo.*
"though one should conquer a million men in battle—even if a single individual conquers a million men—far nobler is he who conquers himself. he indeed is the supreme warrior," the buddha declared. if we consider the facts based on these two verses, it is first of all mentioned in dhamma literature that this kundalakesa attained the foremost position among the bhikkhunis of this buddha-sasana who possess swift intuition (*khippabhinna*—understanding the dhamma instantly). from this, it is evident that it was precisely due to the incident of her quick attainment of arahantship that she received this foremost position.
it is also said that from a very distant past, starting from the dispensation of buddha padumuttara, theri bhadda kundalakesa had received definite predictions to obtain the foremost position among the nuns who possess swift intuition (*khippabhinna*) in this dispensation of the buddha. just as the ascetic bahiya daruciriya received the chief position on that side—for swift comprehension of the dhamma. from the events of her lay life as well, we can understand that she was a person of great comprehension and presence of mind. furthermore, having learned a thousand debates, she went around jambudvipa winning in various places. it was the highly wise venerable sariputta who was finally able to tame her. therefore, we can understand that, in accordance with some past meritorious power, she had attained the capacity for swift comprehension of the dhamma.
when we reflect on this matter, we see that swift comprehension is indeed a marvelous thing, worthy of special mention. however, in these times, some people think that just by hearing a single word of dhamma, anyone can realize the dhamma in this manner. as for the reason for this, we can think of it in this way: nowadays, with the advancement of science and technology, many people try to impose the stimulated concept of "instantaneity" onto spiritual life as well. this is not such an easy thing. only if a person's faculty of wisdom has been developed through the long-term perfection of *paramis* can they comprehend the supramundane dhamma instantly in that manner. otherwise, it is impossible to measure this matter of wisdom with mundane criteria. to put it briefly, there are certain deep sutta discourses nowadays, like the bahiya sutta and other special suttas, which are extremely short. scholars must have read them twenty or thirty times. but they have still not realized the dhamma. from that itself, it is evident that thinking of oneself as belonging to the category of *khippabhinna* (possessing swift intuition) is a form of delusion. furthermore, because of this matter, we can bring out some important dhamma points for this venerable audience to consider.
the buddha has generally shown four modes of practice (*patipada*). depending on the character and abilities of each individual, they can be divided into four modes of practice: painful progress with slow intuition (*dukkha patipada dandhabhinna*), painful progress with swift intuition (*dukkha patipada khippabhinna*), pleasant progress with slow intuition (*sukha patipada dandhabhinna*), and pleasant progress with swift intuition (*sukha patipada khippabhinna*). thus, they are made into four divisions.
to consider it briefly, the analysis of painful progress and pleasant progress is done in this way. for those whose progress is painful, it is shown that in the dhamma, when establishing the mind on nibbana, or for the penetration of the path and fruits, they have to undergo considerable training. meditation topics of this nature: *asubhanupassi kayasmim viharati*—one must dwell contemplating the foulness of the body; likewise, *ahare patikulasanna*—one must develop the perception of repulsiveness in food; *sabbaloke anabhiratasanna*—one must dwell with the feeling of non-delight, of disillusionment, towards the entire world; *sabbe sankharesu aniccasanna*—in accordance with this, one must develop the perception of impermanence / inconstancy (anicca) in all preparations / preparations / volitional activity (sankhara); next, *maranasanna*—in this manner, mindfulness of death must constantly be established. training in this way, so that the nature of suffering / unsatisfactoriness / stress (dukkha) in this world penetrates the mind deeply, is what is called painful progress (*dukkha patipada*). its opposite is called pleasant progress (*sukha patipada*). it is shown that if a person has attained the first, second, third, and fourth absorptions (*jhana*), it is very easy for them. from the very attainment of those absorptions, it is clear that defilements such as the hindrances (*nivarana*) are suppressed. this indicates that for certain individuals who have well-developed those absorptions, this progress is pleasant.
next, regarding comprehension, the matter of "slow intuition" (*dandhabhinna*) is pointed out. there it is shown that what helps for that comprehension of the dhamma is what we always mention at the end of dhamma sermons: faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*)—these five are what assist in this comprehension of the dhamma. what is the cause of that slow intuition? it is when those five spiritual faculties (*indriya*)—faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—are in a soft, undeveloped, or immature state. "khippabhinna" (swift intuition) occurs when those five faculties (*pancindriya*) have fully matured. then, those who have pleasant progress and swift intuition (*sukha patipada khippabhinna*) are skilled in both aspects. they have strong power of absorption (*jhana*). also, regarding comprehension, their five faculties—faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—are highly developed. it is in this sense that the progress is divided into four.
the buddha has shown that when we consider individuals, they too can be classified into four types: *ugghatitannu, vipancitannu, neyya, and padaparama*. *ugghatitannu* means those who comprehend the dhamma the moment it is briefly indicated, even by a small hint. we can think of bahiya daruciriya, and also bhadda kundalakesa in this regard. such individuals can understand the dhamma very easily. for them, even an extremely short discourse by the buddha is sufficient. next, *vipancitannu* refers to those who realize the dhamma after a detailed discourse. the *neyya* person is of a lesser category of individual than that. the *neyya* person has to be led as if by the hand; the dhamma must be explained to them constantly. they need to ask questions. furthermore, they must associate with noble friends (*kalyana-mitta*). they must engage in wise attention / radical attention (yoniso manasikara). only after doing many such activities can that person attain comprehension of the dhamma. concerning the *padaparama* (one for whom the word is the maximum) person, it is stated in the dhamma as follows: even if that person memorizes the dhamma, due to some lack of supportive past conditions, they cannot realize the paths and fruits in this life. no matter how much they learn, or how well they memorize the dhamma, they cannot realize the paths and fruits in this life. yet, a *padaparama* person should not give up, because the effort made in this life will serve as a support for the next life. thus, the four types of individuals are presented.
looking at this, those who think of themselves as *ugghatitannu* (possessing instant realization) do not want to start from the alphabet level. but in reality, do they belong to that category? indeed, those who dwell in such conceit can never understand this dhamma. they must humbly return to the very beginning. because they must come to the threefold training (*tividha-sikkha*) of virtue (*sila*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*). precisely due to their learning, some think: "faith and virtue are teachings meant for foolish lay-devotees." "these are of no use to us. we are highly intellectual people. what we need is that when a single word is said, we understand everything." rejecting that basic, gradual path of practice, they carry wisdom on their shoulders and expect liberation through that alone. as we said before, this is an overrunning of the concept of "instant gratification" found in science and technology.
we all know that in this era of the decline of the sasana, and even when we consider the environment, this is not an era favorable to spiritual life. likewise, we must accept that if those who could understand quickly were rare even in the buddha's time, they must indeed be extremely rare in this day and age. therefore, we should not take these matters too lightly. if we take them casually, we will never obtain results. we must humbly return to the very beginning and do what needs to be done first, first. the buddha too has stated that if someone abandons what should be done first and leaps into other things, they will have to regret it someday. that is a point we can consider in this regard. we stated this based on the meaning of the first verse: rather than a hundred verses of no benefit or purpose, a single word of the dhamma leading to the comprehension of dhamma, stilling (*vupasama*), and calming, is superior.
indeed, there are certain short discourses in the dhamma through which some disciples realized the dhamma very quickly. but for others, those must be explained in detail, and they must undergo a certain training in respect of them.
next, let us look at the idea in the second verse. even if a certain giant or warrior conquers a million men all by himself, the one who conquers himself is said to be far nobler. what is this "conquering of oneself"? this concept presented by the buddha is unique. because to a world weary of bloodshed and war, the buddha introduced the concept of conquering oneself. this can be called "self-conquest" (*atma-vijaya*). in the world, there is the conquest of directions and countries. that conquest is achieved by killing human beings. many hope to toast and celebrate such a victory. but the buddha did not consider that a noble victory. why? not only do those individuals have to pay for the unwholesome karma (*akusala*) arising from that victory, but they also cannot obtain true liberation, solace, or peace through it. both the victor and the defeated are helpless in the face of death. but this "conquering of oneself" pointed out by the buddha is, in truth, the conquering of death. it is in that sense that, as we mentioned earlier, the buddha brought words like "fight" and "battle" close to this path of practice.
we all know that terms like "battle with mara" (*mara-sangrama*) and "fight with mara" are mentioned everywhere the path of practice is discussed. through this, the combative nature inherent in human beings is directed towards a wholesome path. the highest, noblest victory is conquering oneself. no matter how much else one conquers, as long as one is subjected to defilements (*kilesa*), there is no real victory or solace for oneself. not only that, due to those sinful actions, one is caught even more in those very bonds of samsara. what worldly battles do is not release one from bonds (*bandhana*), but rather multiply them. this battle pointed out by the buddha, the battle with mara, is one that goes towards the goal of release from bonds and conquering death. that is why there is a verse, like a battle cry, which the buddha frequently used and approved for the daily practice of meditating monks (*yogavacara* sangha):
> *arabhatha nikkhamatha,*
> *yunjatha buddhasasane;*
> *dhunatha maccuno senam,*
> *nalagaramva kunjaro.*
"exert! venture forth! engage in the buddha's dispensation! shatter the army of death (*maccu*), as an elephant crushes a reed-hut." there, an army of mara (death) is spoken of. that does not mean killing human beings; it refers to the defilements (*kilesa-dhamma*). in the accounts of the buddha's enlightenment, the army of mara is described as: sensual pleasures, craving / thirst (tanha), then discontent with the practice, hunger and thirst, doubt and skepticism (*vicikiccha*)—all such things that arise from within the mind. these defiling states (*kilesa-dhamma*) that hold one back from progressing are what are deeply shown as the army of mara. reflecting in this way, the defeat of mara means conquering the host of defilements within oneself. appropriate words for this are frequently found in the dhamma:
> *ma nivattatha abhikkama*
"do not turn back, press forward!" not only that, in matters concerning the sangha, ordination is described as donning armor—like receiving armor for the battle with mara. it is as armor for this battle against defilements that the sangha wear the robes—not for anything else, not for any other battle. such a concept is seen in this dhamma.
the value of this self-conquest must also be contemplated. since the desire for victory has existed in everyone since ancient times, they either conquer countries in all directions through world conquest (*dig-vijaya*), or reaching the limits of the ocean, they then conquer countries beyond the ocean. then, when even that is not enough, they seek to conquer the stars and planets in the sky. no matter how they achieve victory, they are all subject to death. even if one goes to the moon and returns—we all know about the heroes who went to the moon and came back. but we have not yet heard that they became immortal.
thus, looking at it in that way, it was this conquest of oneself that the buddha presented to the world as the supreme concept. conquering oneself is, in truth, conquering death. by overcoming ignorance (*avijja*) and craving / thirst (tanha), and thereby conquering this host of defilements, one can stand unshaken in the face of death. having no further rebirth, and because of abandoning craving / thirst (tanha) and grasping / holding / fuel (upadana), that person obtains true solace. that is why the buddha pointed to this as the highest victory. now, for that victory, just as for a battle, an army organization is necessary. if we turn our attention to that required army organization—speaking in the military terminology fitting for these times—the buddha has presented a valuable system of dhamma groups regarding army organization.
we can identify this army organization as the "thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment" (*sattis-bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*). they are so important that, as mentioned in the *mahaparinibbana sutta*, at the time of passing away, the buddha summarized everything he had taught up to then—not as a pile of books to be kept in libraries, not in the way we describe dhamma nowadays, but in a practical sense. he declared: "monks, those dhammas which have been directly known and taught by me, namely..." and he mentioned these: the four foundations of mindfulness (*cattaro satipatthana*), the four right efforts (*cattaro sammappadhana*), the four bases of power (*cattaro iddhipada*), the five faculties (*pancindriya*), the five powers (*panca bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*satta bojjhanga*), and the noble eightfold path (*ariyo atthangiko maggo*). according to this, it is these seven groups of dhamma that we can think of as the buddha's army. it is these that we must develop within our minds. there is a training here that begins with the four foundations of mindfulness and culminates in the noble eightfold path.
if we analyze it in the same way, now you all know the four foundations of mindfulness very well. contemplation of the body (*kayanupassana*), contemplation of feeling / sensation (vedana) (*vedananupassana*), contemplation of the mind (*cittanupassana*), and contemplation of mind-objects (*dhammanupassana*)—this basic training is the primary military training received by the warrior of the meditating monk (*yogavacara*). it is on the ground of the four foundations of mindfulness that the first training is received, the military training is obtained. through that exercise, the meditating warrior brings forth the fourfold energy called the four right efforts (*cattaro sammappadhana*). if we mention that fourfold energy in brief, it is as follows: to prevent the arising of unarisen unwholesome states, to abandon arisen unwholesome states, to arouse unarisen wholesome states, and to maintain and consolidate arisen wholesome states. this fourfold energy is what the meditator develops through training on the ground of the four foundations of mindfulness. next, through that very energy, the meditator is able to realize what the strategies are to win this battle.
let us say there are four strategies to win this battle. what are those four? they are the bases of power (*iddhipada*). venerable ones, "iddhi" does not mean merely flying through the air. it refers to the power to fulfill a certain hope, the idea of achieving success. so, *iddhipada* means the paths to success. the buddha has presented four paths leading to successful achievement. these can be understood to a certain extent even in relation to mundane matters, not only supramundane ones. what are they? desire (*chanda*), energy (*viriya*), mind/consciousness (*citta*), and investigation (*vimamsa*). *chanda* means a strong aspiration or willingness. if one has a strong willingness for something, by putting that willingness forward and placing it in the forefront, one can fulfill one's hopes and overcome a problem. likewise, *viriya* means energy. there are certain energetic temperaments who can endure anything without fear, disregarding body and life. the *viriya-iddhipada* (base of power of energy) suits those of energetic temperament. there are some who can realize nibbana and perform meditation activities, etc., by making energy primary. *citta* means the power of determination/mind. there are some who give foremost place to determination: "if i have made up my mind, i will not give up; i will not stop somehow or other." we can call that too a battle strategy. finally, *vimamsa*: investigative wisdom. there, the meaning is wisdom. wisdom. those who have the power of wisdom bring forward investigative wisdom. it is stated in the dhamma that even if one has just one of these four kinds of *iddhipada*, it is sufficient to win on the battlefield. even if one does not have all four, depending on the temperament of each individual, some make *chanda* (desire) primary. venerable ratthapala, for instance, went in accordance with faith, making *chanda* primary to achieve his goal of nibbana. similarly, some make energy primary, and so on.
next are the five faculties and five powers (*pancindriya, panca bala*). going further, we can understand that according to this analogy, what is spoken of here are not the mundane "five powers." one must arouse and produce five faculties (*indriya*). those five faculties are what we mentioned earlier: faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—the five faculties/powers that assist in achieving the task of nibbana and seeing nibbana. these are developed as faculties (*indriya*) and, likewise, with their help, in the sense of conquering opposing states, those same five are shown as "powers" (*bala-dhamma*). under both faculties and powers, those five—faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—are mentioned. next, once they are all well developed and sharpened, on the basis of that strength, seven factors that aid enlightenment are lined up. those are the seven: mindfulness (*sati*), investigation of states (*dhamma-vicaya*), energy (*viriya*), joy (*piti*), tranquility (*passaddhi*), concentration (*samadhi*), and equanimity (*upekkha*). those seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhanga*) are very close to nibbana. when those seven factors of enlightenment are developed, it is as if one is close to nibbana. having completed their development, the "final operation"—to use modern terminology—is indeed the eightfold path.
the final operation employed for this victory over mara is indeed the noble eightfold path. that is why we always speak of the noble eightfold path. sometimes other things are forgotten. that is why even scholars forget that one must begin with the four foundations of mindfulness. we frequently use the term "noble eightfold path." but to reach that level, one must come from that very beginning. one must obtain training on that battlefield. that is what we are specifically reminding you of. what is this noble eightfold path? it is a path of completely integrated, wonderfully great power. now, in other places, these are introduced individually and separately. from the way those pali words are used—such as *cattaro satipatthana*, *cattaro sammappadhana*, etc.—we see that they are introduced as if separated. but concerning the noble eightfold path, it is expressed as *ariyo atthangiko maggo*. this is shown as a single unit. these eight are fully integrated and linked to one another. this is the final operation. indeed, it is a completely interconnected, immensely powerful process that is shown under the name of the noble eightfold path.
now, if we look, in the noble eightfold path there is also right mindfulness (*samma-sati*). in that case, can someone who has not developed the four foundations of mindfulness have right mindfulness? no, indeed. that is why we say everyone must understand that the four foundations of mindfulness is the place where the basic training on the battlefield is received. that is exactly what the buddha told venerable sariputta: "establish every newly ordained monk in the four foundations of mindfulness." in modern times, perhaps, they are established in it only at the very end. but the buddha told venerable sariputta: "sariputta, establish everyone who is newly ordained in this dispensation in the four foundations of mindfulness." the final operation of that basic training—the power gained from it—is: the four right efforts emerged as *sammappadhana*; those four strategies emerged as *iddhipada*; then, having developed the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment, the special alignment necessary for comprehension. after developing those teachings, the very energy that has been filtered and seasoned through them is what helps one towards nibbana as the noble eightfold path.
you all know about the noble eightfold path. the ordinary world has a superficial understanding of it, thinking of right view (*samma-ditthi*), right intention (*samma-sankappa*), and so on, in a mundane way. if taken deeply, "right view" is to be understood as the comprehension of the truth. among those, the ten-fold mundane right view is the right view relevant to ordinary samsara. but what helps for release from samsara is the correct vision regarding the four noble truths. making that correct vision primary, it goes all the way to correct thoughts and intentions; in accordance with those thoughts and intentions, as we frequently mention, correct speech and action; in accordance with those, correct livelihood; through that livelihood, correct effort; through correct effort, correct mindfulness—*sati*, good mindfulness—and finally, right concentration (*samma-samadhi*), which is the unification of the mind.
that supramundane path-concentration (*magga-samadhi*) is indeed the most powerful concentration in the world. it is through that path-concentration that instantly... we can describe the noble eightfold path as a high-speed path. it is direct. precisely because it is direct, the buddha has declared that this is a straight path.
> *ujumaggamhi asankhate, gacchatha ma nivattatha.*
"on the straight path to the unprepared / unconditioned / uncompounded (asankhata), go, do not turn back!" the buddha has declared: "*gacchatha*"—go on, or march forward, on the straight path. "*ma nivattatha*"—do not turn back. do not retreat. why? because it is a path that can be traversed with such fearlessness. but since some devotees come and ask us about this noble eightfold path as an additional question, we shall try to clarify that too on this occasion.
now, the word "magga" (path) is also applied to the four foundations of mindfulness. you may have heard that the satipatthana sutta discourse begins with:
> *ekayano ayam, bhikkhave, maggo sattanam visuddhiya, sokaparidevanam samatikkamaya, dukkhadomanassanam atthangamaya, nayassa adhigamaya, nibbanassa sacchikiriyaya.*
that is how it begins. so, what is this "*ekayana*" path? this is interpreted in various ways. is this the "sole" path? if this is the sole path, why did the buddha state elsewhere regarding the noble eightfold path:
> *eso'va maggo natth'anno, dassanassa visuddhiya.*
"this is the path, there is no other, for the purification of vision." thus, the buddha declares this regarding the noble eightfold path itself.
in that case, what is meant here by "*ekayana maggo*"? that word must be understood in the correct manner. "*ekayana*" means, venerable ones, a path that has no branchings in between, which can be traversed with absolute certainty. if there were branchings in between, upon reaching them, one would have to ask, "where do we go from here?" "*ekayana*" means this path goes and merges straight into the eightfold path. the path that begins with the four foundations of mindfulness merges straight into the noble eightfold path. it does not wander here and there. it is in that sense, venerable ones, that this is called the "*ekayana*" path. that is exactly what is said there: *ekayano ayam, bhikkhave, maggo sattanam visuddhiya*—for the purification of beings, *sokaparidevanam samatikkamaya*—for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the ending of suffering / unsatisfactoriness / stress (dukkha) and grief, *nayassa adhigamaya*—for attaining the method (*naya*). "*naya*" refers to that very noble eightfold path. it is a name for the noble eightfold path. it is the supramundane noble eightfold path itself that is called "*naya*." thus, it is a path that leads surely to obtaining the noble eightfold path. finally, *nibbanassa sacchikiriyaya*—for the realization of nibbana.
it is by confusing these two that some people have created problems. "are these two different paths?" merely because "*ekayana*" is said there, it does not mean "only path" in that sense. that is what must be kept in mind. this is a certain path. this is a path that does not turn off into side-roads. it goes and merges straight into the noble eightfold path. that merging occurs only if one develops it in that manner. it is not something that proceeds through books. practically, it is something that happens within the heart. it is an internal development of the path. that is precisely why we said it is like military training. having received that military training in the four foundations of mindfulness, in the end, a good army division is formed, and finally, the final operation is the noble eightfold path—the supramundane noble eightfold path.
that is how the battle must be won. that too, in four stages. in the stages of sotapanna, sakadagami, anagami, and arahant, the path-mind (*magga-citta*) becomes progressively powerful. the path-mind in the first stage (sotapanna) is surpassed in strength in the second stage; in the third stage of anagami, it is even more powerful. it is in the fourth stage (arahant) that, having destroyed all defilements and shattered that mass of darkness, one breaks through ignorance (*avijja*), which the buddha described as an impenetrable mass of darkness. if we speak merely by way of metaphor, we say "entering the city of nibbana." we say "city of nibbana" only as an analogy. we ourselves do not endorse treating it as a literal city. but in terms of the metaphor used, in terms of this analogy, the final operation of that army organization goes and breaks down the gate—like breaking down the gate of vijitapura—breaks through, and behold! finally enters the city of nibbana, or rather, realizes nibbana.
we are speaking by putting this concept of battle in the forefront, because the concept of battle is appealing to the human mind. also, we know that if a small child is fond of something, to draw them away from it, we must give them something similar. similarly, we know that throughout history, human beings have made efforts, enduring pain and hardships, to attain world domination and empires, in order to cultivate the pride of victory. in that respect, even history recognizes emperor dharmasoka as the greatest hero of all history. although he achieved victory by killing hundreds of thousands of people, he abandoned that after discovering this conquest of dhamma (*dhamma-vijaya*), or rather, this self-conquest (*atma-vijaya*), once he turned to the side of the dhamma. from that too, it is understood that conquering oneself is supreme.
accordingly, we must reflect, we must adjust our thinking if there are shortcomings, and we too must give foremost place to the buddha's word. we must give the buddha's dhamma a place superior to all other mundane concepts. that is how we must think. one can make that "conquering of oneself" meaningful in that manner. indeed, it is when a battle comes that one's own strength is brought out. that is exactly what is presented by that concept of mara. sometimes, when a defilement arises, even the buddha would declare... because when one just says "it is a defilement," it does not strike the mind. but the moment he says, "look, monk, there is mara! mara is right there!" that monk becomes vigilant. as said, there is an ascription of personality there. that helps to prepare our mind. since saying we are fighting with lifeless mental states does not strike the heart, we personify them and call them "mara." utilizing even that support, in whatever way, this is all there is to do: to escape from this samsara. to conquer death. that is what is called self-conquest—conquering oneself. that is the concept we must develop.
so, through this, we can bring out many valuable points, many valuable things. as we mentioned, some scholars in these times have created another problem: "now, the noble eightfold path begins with right view." it is analyzed in this way: "right view and right intention belong to the wisdom group (*panna-kkhandha*); right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration belong to the concentration group (*samadhi-kkhandha*)." looking at it in that way, first comes wisdom, then virtue, and then concentration. taking that logically, some try to give foremost place to this wisdom. but that is a completely wrong understanding.
it is mentioned in the dhamma itself. on one occasion, bhikkhuni dhammadinna, in response to a question by her former lay husband, visakha upasaka, says the following (mentioning it briefly due to time constraints): what is the question? visakha upasaka asks: "noble lady, is the threefold training of virtue, concentration, and wisdom included in the noble eightfold path, or is the noble eightfold path included in the threefold training of virtue, concentration, and wisdom?" he asked this because even in the past, there were questions just like the ones we have today. what is the answer to that? the threefold training of virtue, concentration, and wisdom was not arranged by the noble eightfold path; rather, the noble eightfold path was arranged under the three groups of virtue, concentration, and wisdom. through this, we must understand that the division into virtue, concentration, and wisdom is more primary than the noble eightfold path. it is to that division that foremost place must be given. just as we give foremost place to it, we must also give it place at the end.
that is why, in the poignant account showing how the buddha, even with such a severe illness, journeyed from village to village, we find a passage where he preached the entirety of the dhamma in brief:
> *iti silam, iti samadhi, iti panna. silaparibhavito samadhi mahapphalo hoti mahanisamso. samadhiparibhavita panna mahapphala hoti mahanisamsa. pannaparibhavitam cittam sammadeva asavehi vimuccati.*
in a single passage, he summarized and showed the entire dhamma: "such is virtue, such is concentration, such is wisdom." concentration fully developed through virtue is of great fruit and great benefit. wisdom fully developed through concentration is of great fruit and great benefit. next, *pannaparibhavitam cittam*—the mind developed through wisdom, the mind grown in accordance with wisdom, *sammadeva asavehi vimuccati*—is fully liberated from the taints (*asava*). that is a passage summarizing the entire dhamma. based on that, we can surely understand that the three—virtue, concentration, and wisdom—are primary. the noble eightfold path is something built on that, arising through it.
likewise, we must understand that when we speak of a "path," right view (*samma-ditthi*) must naturally come to the beginning. even if we think of a gradual transformation of personal character, that too must begin with right view. it is in accordance with one's view (*ditthi*) that one's thoughts and intentions arise. in accordance with thoughts and intentions, words are spoken. in accordance with words, actions are performed. it is because of this systematic, gradual path of practice, which is connected in a wonderfully interconnected manner, integrated and organically blended, that it is called *ariyo atthangiko maggo* (the noble eightfold path). it is shown as a single unit, whereas the others are shown separately. although the four foundations of mindfulness, the four bases of power, and so on are listed separately, in the end, the noble eightfold path is a single unit. when the supramundane path arises, it happens so instantly that all those eight factors arise in a single mind-moment. that instant moment where all eight factors arise simultaneously in a single mind is the powerful concentration: the path-concentration. it is through that concentration that one can realize the unconditioned.
it is precisely because you all ask questions in various ways regarding this path of dhamma that we summarized and presented many facts in accordance with this topic. you must reflect on this, not letting these matters remain limited to books, but practically drawing them close to your daily life, and proceeding on your path of virtue, concentration, and wisdom. depending on your respective abilities—if not *ugghatitannu*, then *vipancitannu*; if not that, then *neyya*—in whatever way, aligning with your capacity and putting forth maximum energy in these final times of the buddha's dispensation, dedicating a place greater than for anything else to this task, may this dhamma sermon surely serve as a supportive condition for you to escape from this extremely dangerous samsara, to practice this listening, meditation, virtue, concentration, and wisdom, and to bring an end to this suffering / unsatisfactoriness / stress (dukkha) of samsara. wish and aspire in this manner.
if, through this, you have developed the spiritual faculties and powers of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, may that surely serve as a strong support (*upanissaya*) for you to realize the paths and fruits in this very life, with the help of the association with noble friends. not only that: if any wholesome store of merit has been gathered through this dhamma sermon in this seen and unseen world, may all beings, from avici to akanittha, including the deceased relatives in whose names we do so, who wish to rejoice in this merit of listening to and delivering the dhamma, rejoice in it likewise; and, with the help of that store of merit, may they as quickly as possible escape from all the suffering / unsatisfactoriness / stress (dukkha) of samsara—such as birth / arising (jati), decay, aging, and death (decay and death / aging and death / jaramarana), sickness, and so forth—and find solace in the supreme, deathless nibbana! reciting these verses, let us share the merits.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 072
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #72
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.75)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Puññañ ce puriso kayirā, kayirāthetaṃ punappunaṃ;
tamhi chandaṃ kayirātha, sukho puññassa uccayo.
From:
Dhammapada 118 (Pupphavagga)
Dear Listeners,
Through faith in kamma and the fruit of kamma (*kamma-phala*), an opportunity is provided for a person to steer their life in the right direction. He who does not have a correct understanding of merit (*puñña*), demerit (*pāpa*), wholesome (*kusala*), and unwholesome (*akusala*) actions gets lost in this samsāra and falls into Suffering / Unsatisfactoriness / Stress (*dukkha*). Therefore, the Buddha almost constantly reminds us of the value of a life inclined and oriented towards merit (*puñña*). The verse taken as our theme also illustrates such an occasion. The background story (*nidāna-kathā*) related to this verse also presents a fine example of the value of merit.
The Great Arahant Mahā Kassapa, having entered into meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in the Pipphalī Cave in the city of Rājagaha, emerged from that absorption after seven days and scanned with his divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*) to find a suitable place to wander for alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*). He saw a farm-woman parching corn near a paddy field. At the same time, he reflected whether this woman possessed enough faith (*saddhā*) to perform an act of merit by offering alms (*dāna*). He realized that she was a very faithful woman. Thinking, "If I go there, she will be able to accumulate a vast store of merit," and out of great compassion, the Great Arahant Mahā Kassapa journeyed to that paddy field. That farm-woman, seeing the Venerable Thera, was filled with five-fold joy, and with great happiness, took those puffed rice (*lājā*) and offered them into the bowl of the Venerable Thera, and prostrated herself, worshipping him with the five-fold touch. Having worshipped, she made an aspiration (*patthanā*): "Venerable Sir, whatever truth (*Dhamma*) you have realized, may this merit be a supportive condition for me to attain that same Dhamma!" The Venerable Thera also expressed his appreciation and blessed her: "May it be so!"
While this farm-woman was returning with a very joyful mind, a highly venomous serpent—it must have been a cobra—lying on the ridge of the field bit her calf. She fell dead right there.
However, instantly, as if waking up from a dream, this woman was reborn in a golden mansion in the Tāvatiṁsa heaven. The unique feature of that mansion was that garlands of puffed rice were hanging all over, from side to side. This woman reflected: "How did I receive such a grand fortune?" It became clear to her: "I received this from that small act of merit." Then she thought, "If I could obtain such a fortune from such a small act of merit, then I should not fall into negligence (*pramāda*). Being diligent (*appamatta*), I must further secure this fortune of mine by doing more merit." Thinking thus, at the break of dawn, she went to the hut where the Great Arahant Mahā Kassapa was residing and began to perform duties (*vatta-paṭivatta*), sweeping the courtyard of his dwelling with a golden broom and a basket as described there, and filling the water pots. When the Great Arahant Mahā Kassapa looked, all these chores had been done. He thought that some novice monk must have come and performed these duties. This happened on the second day too, and he thought in the same way. On the third day, hearing the sound of sweeping at the dawn-hour, the Great Arahant Mahā Kassapa looked in that direction and saw a certain light shining through the keyhole of the door—the light of that deity (*devatā*). Seeing it, he opened the door and asked, "Who is sweeping here?" This goddess is known as 'Lājā Devadhītā'—the Puffed-Rice Deity. 'Lājā' means puffed rice; she is known by that name. When asked, "Who is it?" she replied:
"I am your attendant, Lājā Devadhītā."
"I do not know of any attendant of mine. Who are you?"
"The other day, after offering you puffed rice, as I was walking away, I was bitten by a snake and died. Immediately, I obtained this state. Now I thought that I must secure this celestial fortune, and must diligently perform meritorious deeds."
You have heard that the Great Arahant Mahā Kassapa was one of extreme ascetic practices, a Thera observing austere dhutaṅga practices. Even though he had kindly provided her the opportunity to make that alms offering out of compassion, when he looked at this situation in relation to his strict ascetic path, he spoke somewhat sternly: "Who performed these duties yesterday and the day before?" When she replied, "It was I," he said, "What you have done is quite enough. Do not come to this area hereafter." Then she began to weep. "O Venerable Sir, please permit me to further increase and secure my merit and enhance my fortune." But the Great Arahant Mahā Kassapa said, "If you continue to do this, in the future, Dhamma preachers during their sermons will say that even the Great Kassapa received personal services and duties from a goddess. Do not leave room for such talk. Therefore, do not even come near this area," and he sent her away. Then she rose into the sky, weeping, and repeatedly saying, "O Venerable Sir, please permit me." As she refused to leave, the Great Kassapa snapped his fingers, saying, "This woman does not know her limits. Go away from here!" Only after that finger-snap, under the power of his spiritual majesty, was the goddess unable to remain there any longer. Flying into the sky, she lamented her grief. While she was lamenting, the Buddha, who was residing in the Fragrant Chamber (*Gandhakuṭi*) of Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthi, heard the sound of her weeping. He reflected upon it and, out of compassion for her, projected a ray of light, appearing as if he were standing right in front of her, and delivered the very Dhamma verse we took as our theme.
What is expressed by that verse, in short, is a sort of balanced, middle-way statement delivered by the Buddha to comfort the deity: "It is my son Kassapa's right to protect his restraint. Likewise, it is also valuable for those who perform merit to be enthusiastic about the merit that belongs to them." Making such a balanced statement, he uttered this verse of our theme. Let us recall it once again:
*Puññañ ce puriso kayirā, kayirāthetaṁ punappunaṁ,*
*tamhi chandaṁ kayirātha, sukho puññassa uccayo.*
"If a person should perform merit, he should do it again and again. He should develop a desire (*chanda*), a liking, a keenness for that merit. What is the reason for this? *Sukho puññassa uccayo*—the accumulation of merit is happiness; it is a cause for happiness." Thus, a simple explanation was presented. It is said that upon hearing this verse, that faithful goddess attained the fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). This is a very brief story, but through it, we are shown how merit supports a human being to make their life happy, as mentioned before.
Let us now reflect upon this verse. In this verse, what the Buddha actually intended was merit (*puñña*). That is to say, after performing a meritorious deed, a person should not stop at that single instance thinking, "This merit is enough for my entire life," but should do it *punappunaṁ*—again and again. If one performs merit, and once it is completed, without being complacent, one should perform that merit again and again. When there is no opportunity to perform merit, or when one is unable to do so, at the very least, one should generate a desire or a keenness for it in one's mind. When you contemplate a little, you will understand the importance of generating this keenness. If we do not incline and orient our minds towards merit, if we do foster a desire for merit even during times when we are not actively performing it, we will hesitate and hold back when an opportunity to perform merit actually arises. We will remain indecisive. But for one who always thinks, "Oh, if only I could perform some merit!"—this 'desire' (*chanda*) is a very important factor in this Dhamma. It is called the desire for the wholesome (*kusalacchanda*)—the keenness or liking to perform merit. A person who possesses this will step forward, saying "I will do it, I will do it," to take charge of that meritorious work and lend a hand to it. Such is its strength.
Sometimes, if that desire (*chanda*) is absent when one is not performing merit, and if the mind has not been prepared accordingly, the opportunity to do merit slips away. Later, one thinks, "Ah, I missed the opportunity to perform that merit; I was just thinking about it." That is why, although it is a small verse, we can understand that it contains a very deep meaning. Why are we asked to perform merit again and again? Because the accumulation of merit is happiness. The accumulation of merit is a cause that brings happiness both in this world and in the next in samsāra. This, in brief, is the meaning of this verse.
Next, let us consider the meaning of this story and the verse further. Generally, this matter of merit is something extremely close to our lives. Therefore, it is not merely about doing it, nor about doing it for the sake of doing it, or doing it with expectations of fame and status. Rather, what is important is to understand the value of merit in its true sense according to the Dhamma and then perform it. Hence, even within the story related to this theme, there is a certain depth. First of all, let us contemplate the practice of the Great Arahant Mahā Kassapa. Indeed, if he had been fasting for seven days and possessed the divine eye, some might wonder why he did not go to royal palaces or mansions of wealthy merchants for alms-food. The Great Arahant Mahā Kassapa was a Thera of wonderful, severe ascetic virtues who observed dhutaṅga practices. It was his custom that after emerging from meditative absorption, the opportunity to give alms was granted to the poor and destitute. He mostly wandered for alms among poor huts, regardless of whatever he might receive. This was because he possessed such great compassion. It was not about securing a rich, heavy meal. At that moment—meaning when a monk wanders for alms immediately after emerging from meditative absorption—if one gets the opportunity to offer him alms, it becomes of great fruit and great benefit (*mahapphala mahānisaṁsa*). That is why he always took the trouble to grant this opportunity to a poor person. On this occasion too, he journeyed to the paddy field not for any grand, heavy food, but for some light puffed rice that floats in the wind, which might seem insufficient even to sustain a person. Yet, he accepted with great joy the puffed rice that the woman brought and offered with faith. It was not a grand offering, yet through the benefit of offering that little puffed rice, she obtained even celestial fortune.
Furthermore, we see that after obtaining that fortune, she made a great effort to further secure that merit and to perform merit again and again through duties and services. Although there was nothing wrong with that, the Great Arahant Mahā Kassapa opposed it and did not give his consent due to a certain scriptural purpose. This was because, through such actions, future human beings might fall into the unwholesome kamma of disparaging Noble Ones (*ariya-upavāda*). We call this "looking to the future"—that is, he followed these practices out of compassion for future generations. Although his action might seem unkind, it reflects this underlying thought: if future members of the Saṅgha were to say, "Even such-and-and-such deities came and performed services for us," it could lead to wrong understandings. At that moment, he firmly dismissed her using words that befitted his restraint.
Yet, the Buddha, with amazing compassion, resolved the issue from both sides in a balanced way, giving a middle-way answer: "Why? My son Mahā Kassapa did what was his duty. For those who perform merit, either they perform it when they can—as this verse states, they do merit when possible, and when they cannot, they at least generate the desire (*chanda*) for it." That itself is sufficient for a person. That is to say, when one keeps thinking, "Oh, if only I could somehow perform some merit!" one remains in a wholesome state of mind. It is for such a person, when the opportunity to do merit arrives, that the strength to step forward and lend a hand, to take charge of those activities, arises instantly—as it is said in the Dhamma: *"Ahaṁ ahaṁ mitā, ahaṁ ahaṁ"*—"I am here, I am here." Even though this is a short verse, there is a vital point here. We can understand many things through this verse of the Buddha.
Next, if we reflect on merit (*puñña*) in general, the final line here—usually the final line of verses expresses some theory or fundamental principle—states:
*Sukho puññassa uccayo*
"The accumulation of merit is happiness." The Buddha concludes the verse with this. Let us now direct our minds to this. First, let us see what this merit (*puñña*) is. It is said that we all know what merit is to the extent that it needs no further explanation. Even so, let us pay some attention to it. According to the Dhamma, in the scriptures, three main types of merit are shown:
*Tīṇimāni bhikkhave puññakiriyavatthūni*
Three grounds for making merit, or three bases of meritorious activity, namely: *dāna* (giving/generosity), *sīla* (morality/virtue), and *bhāvanā* (meditative development). We can generally understand that this refers to a certain spiritual strength developed in the mind through the acts of giving, observing virtue, and practicing meditation. In other places, this is expanded into ten items. You may have heard of them by the name *Dasa puññakiriyavatthu*—the ten bases of meritorious activity. In addition to *dāna*, *sīla*, and *bhāvanā*, they include: sharing of merit (*pattidāna*), rejoicing in others' merit (*pattānumodanā*), rendering services/duties (*veyyāvacca*), showing reverence to those worthy of respect (*apacāyana*), teaching the Dhamma (*desanā*), listening to the Dhamma (*savana*), and finally, straightening one's right view (*diṭṭhijukamma*). Thus, ten meritorious activities are shown under the ten bases of meritorious activity.
Now, here too, it was because performing duties (*vatta-paṭivatta*) is also a form of merit that this woman, not being satisfied with her giving (*dāna*) alone, was enthusiastic to perform services as well. These are things we can do in our daily lives, even in small ways, according to the opportunities that come our way, even if we might think that acts of giving involve high expenses. Now, those puffed rice were such a small thing. Yet, through that, the Great Arahant Mahā Kassapa received the strength to survive for a day. The food of such a noble Thera was puffed rice. From this, we can see that we should not regard these things as trivial. Moreover, what serves as the support in performing that merit is the mind and faith (*saddhā*). That is precisely why we think the Buddha declared *Saddhā dhanaṁ*—faith is a treasure. Faith is shown as a treasure. Why does faith become a treasure? We must reflect on this. What does it mean to have faith in the Triple Gem? What is the Triple Gem? We must first think about this. The Triple Gem (*Tri-vidha Ratna*). There is a great depth in this concept of "Gem" (*Ratna*). You have heard that there are no other gems equal to each of these gems:
*Yaṁ kiñci ratanaṁ loke vijjati vividhā puthū,*
*ratanaṁ buddhasamaṁ natthi, ratanaṁ dhammasamaṁ natthi, ratanaṁ saṅghasamaṁ natthi...*
"Whatever gems there are in the world, in all their variety, none is equal to the Buddha Gem, none is equal to the Dhamma Gem, none is equal to the Saṅgha Gem." Thus, when a person is said to generate faith, in the word *Saddhā* there is an aspect concerning the heart. Depositing the treasure of faith in the heart, or depositing in the chamber of the heart—what is deposited is these three gems: the Buddha Gem, the Dhamma Gem, and the Saṅgha Gem. Through depositing these, a special value is added to that person's thoughts and aspirations. A great light, a clarity arises within that mind. A word that goes hand in hand with faith (*saddhā*) is *Prasāda* (clarity/serenity/devotion). The two words *Saddho pasanno* (faithful and confident/serene) are found together. In the past, various similes were used for this. There is mention of a certain water-clearing gem which, when placed in muddy water, makes the water clean. Similarly, when faith in the Triple Gem arises, the mind is freed from agitation and attains a state of serene clarity (*prasāda*). The Buddha declared that when a meritorious deed is performed with such a serene mind, it becomes highly beneficial. Even if it is a small thing, if given with faith in such a state, it becomes of great fruit and great benefit (*mahapphala mahānisaṁsa*):
*Appamapi ce saddahāno dadāti teneva so hoti sukhī parattha*
"Even if one gives a tiny bit, if one gives with a faithful heart, by that very act one becomes happy in the world beyond." Thus, regarding this merit, the Buddha shows that merit is happiness because, in the life of a human being, various material goods and hoards of wealth are accumulated. All of them can be claimed by fire, water, thieves, or rulers, or they can be destroyed. Unloved heirs can take them. But regarding merit, it is declared:
*Asādhāraṇam aññesaṁ acoraharaṇo nidhī*
*kayirātha dhīro puññāni yo nidhī anugāmiko*
This is a very famous verse. "A treasure that is not shared with others"—meaning others cannot claim it or use it as something common—"a treasure that thieves cannot steal, the wise man should perform merits, for this is the treasure that follows one." Other treasures, deposits, and the like—in modern times, banks, and in those days, vast treasures buried in river basins—can be destroyed by the aforementioned disasters. At the very least, due to inflation and various social and economic changes, the wealth we highly prize can become mere scrap paper overnight. But this merit, we can say, is like a gold coin of eternal value. If something has been deposited in our mind-stream (*citta-santāna*) as merit, that merit never fades away without yielding its fruit.
Furthermore, when more merits are added to that merit, they become stronger, and it is through this that even a Buddha arises in the future. Accumulated as perfections (*pāramīs*), the strength of merit developed through giving, according to one's aspiration (*prārthanā*) and resolve (*praṇidhi*), is accumulated under the name of "perfection of giving" (*dāna-pāramitā*). The store of merit accumulated through observing virtue becomes the "perfection of virtue" (*sīla-pāramitā*). In this way, we can understand that what lies beneath the word "perfection" (*pāramitā*) is this very mass of merit, the performance of merit. Therefore, we see a great value in the accumulation of merit. Moreover, the Buddha has declared: *"Puññaṁ sukhaṁ jīvitasaṅkhayamhi"*—"Merit at the end of life is a great happiness." No matter how much wealth, land, or vehicles one has accumulated, when one remembers them at the moment of death, it only brings Suffering / Unsatisfactoriness / Stress (*dukkha*). A grief arises thinking, "I have to leave all this behind, don't I?" One cannot take them along. That is why it is said they cannot be taken; they do not follow one. None of those treasures follow. But if one has performed merit, each time one recalls it at the moment of death, it becomes a cause for great joy and solace.
You have heard about the final moments of King Duṭugämuṇu. It was not other things he recalled, but he had the register of merit (*pin-potha*) brought and recalled the merits he had performed. In the past, some even kept a register of merit. Even nowadays, though very rarely, some keep registers of merit. Some do so out of pride (*māna*) to show others. It should not be so; it is for one's own recollection. If these performed merits are recorded in one's mind, even if not in a book, when one is on one's deathbed, one can reflect and rejoice: "I have these masses of merit accumulated throughout my entire life." Then, one does not go to the next world empty-handed. From the story of Lājā Devadhītā, we see that it is according to our very thoughts that our future Becoming / Existence (*bhava*) is shaped. A characteristic of her celestial mansion was the hanging of garlands of puffed rice. Why puffed rice? Because puffed rice was what was in her mind. Basing on that offered puffed rice, in exact accordance with that wholesome deed, a celestial mansion was formed.
We must understand that, let alone other things, even for this physical frame of ours to arise, and for us to receive our belongings, kamma lies beneath them in a very subtle way. We think these things happen by chance, or that we made them ourselves: "We can manage things in this world as we want." But beneath these lie the forces of kamma (*kamma-vega*), things of this nature. That which is called merit, then, becomes a support in this samsāra. Now, there are two sides to this. Through merit, on one hand, we turn away from the path of miserable realms (*duggati*) and incline toward the path of happy realms (*sugati*). On the other hand, it also supports us in attaining Nibbāna according to our aspirations.
Now, when speaking of merit (*puñña*), a word that goes hand in hand with it is wholesome (*kusala*). People talk about doing merit (*puñña*) and doing wholesome deeds (*kusala*). Some have even made a question out of this: "Are these two the same? Is there a difference between them?" There are those who spend more time thinking about these things than actually doing them. Whosoever they may be, keeping them in mind as well, let us now explain the meaning of these words. This merit, indeed, has the word *Puñña*. Its etymology is somewhat hidden. But we have to consider that the ancient commentators (*aṭṭhakathācāriyas*) explain it in the sense of purifying the mind-stream: "Merit is that which purifies the mind-stream," deriving *puñña* from *punāti* (to purify). We can accept this to some extent because these words, *puñña* and *pāpa* (demerit/evil), have come down from ancient times. *Puñña* and *pāpa*. A concept that goes along with this is that the mind is purified by merit and defiled by demerit. The world holds this concept: one is purified by merit and defiled by demerit. This is highly consistent with the fact that through actions performed by our mind, body, and speech, there are occasions when we purify our minds, and occasions when we defile them. The things that defile, we call demerit (*pāpa*); the things that purify, we call merit (*puñña*).
In modern times, however, some people attempt to give Sinhala etymological explanations to this word *pina* (merit). There are indeed ways in which the Dhamma is distorted in various manners. Some explain *pina* in the sense of pleasing or gratifying the mind (*hitha pinavama*). If we define *pina* in the sense of gratifying the mind, there is a great danger of going astray. There are many things that gratify the mind which are actually demeritorious (*pāpa*). Therefore, it should not be taken in that way. Thus, it becomes meaningful to us only in the sense of purifying the mind—that is merit (*puñña*). What supports this, then, is *dāna*, *sīla*, and *bhāvanā*—in terms of giving, virtue, and meditation. The coarse or gross level of greed (*lobha*) is stinginess. It is described as a stain or rust (*mala*). If this rust is not constantly removed, it leads to one's own ruin from within. In the end, one becomes a great miser. Giving (*dāna*), then, supports the removal of this rust. In short, giving helps to abandon the defilement (*kilesa*) of greed (*lobha*). That is how it works through giving.
Through virtue (*sīla*), the defilement that can occur through wrong bodily actions, wrong verbal actions, and wrong mental actions—which are described as bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct—is prevented by observing the practice of virtue and the like.
Next, the same applies to meditation (*bhāvanā*). Going to the very depth of it, meditation has the power to eradicate all the defilements in the mind: greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dosa*), and delusion (*moha*). In that respect, merit possesses such power.
Next, when we reflect on the wholesome (*kusala*), it is also shown to be largely similar. We find the words *puñña* and *kusala* used in the Dhamma as synonyms, or at least as closely related terms. Yet, at times, we see a specific meaning in this word *Kusala*. The Dhamma mentions unwholesome roots (*akusala-mūla*) and wholesome roots (*kusala-mūla*). On one occasion, the monks asked the Venerable Sāriputta: "People talk about Right View, Right View (*sammā-diṭṭhi*). What is this Right View?" On that occasion, Venerable Sāriputta defined Right View using this very word *kusala*. While Right View can be defined in several ways, here Venerable Sāriputta explained: "Friends, if a person knows the unwholesome (*akusala*), knows the root of the unwholesome (*akusala-mūla*), and likewise knows the wholesome (*kusala*), and knows the root of the wholesome (*kusala-mūla*), by that much he is one of Right View." This refers to knowing good and bad. Then he analyzes further: what is the unwholesome? What is mentioned here as the unwholesome refers to what is stated in the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). Killing living beings is unwholesome; taking what is not given is unwholesome; sexual misconduct is unwholesome; false speech is unwholesome; malicious speech is unwholesome; harsh speech is unwholesome; gossip is unwholesome; and finally, wrong things of the mind are mentioned: *abhijjhā*—which means covetousness (intense greed); *vyāpāda*—which refers to ill-will, the opposite of loving-kindness (*mettā*); and *micchā-diṭṭhi*—wrong view. These are shown as the unwholesome (*akusala*). The roots of these unwholesome actions are shown as greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dosa*), and delusion (*moha*).
Next, when we take the wholesome (*kusala*) side, Venerable Sāriputta explains what is the wholesome and what is the root of the wholesome. The wholesome is abstaining from killing living beings: *Pāṇātipātā veramaṇī kusalaṁ*. What is this *veramaṇī*? *Virati* means abstention or turning away. Killing living beings, taking animal life, is an easy thing, or rather, something to which the mind is easily drawn and likes. It is difficult to abstain from it, but that is what must be done—that is a wholesome deed (*kusala*). Now, from this, we can understand the true meaning of the word *kusala*.
