*Puna gehaṁ na kāhasi* – “You shall not build a house again.” That refers to the liberated consciousness (*viññāṇa*), the consciousness (*viññāṇa*) liberated from Name-and-Form (*nāmarūpa*) when the light of wisdom (*paññā*) was obtained. That is why there is no further birth (*jāti*).
*Sabbā te phāsukā bhaggā, gahakūṭaṁ visaṅkhitaṁ* – “All your rafters are broken, the ridgepole is shattered.” This is the moment when everything is freed, because the house-builder has been understood.
*Visaṅkhāragataṁ cittaṁ, taṇhānaṁ khayamajjhagā* – “The mind has reached the un-prepared / unconditioned (*visaṅkhāra*), attaining the destruction of cravings (*taṇhā*).” This is exactly what the Blessed One points out: ultimately, one who has attained that peace, the peace of Nibbāna. It is because of such a state that one does not undergo birth (*jāti*) again.
Thus, it is that very state of the Deathless (*amata*) attained in this very life that the Blessed One has declared. The person who has obtained that direct realization knows with certainty that they will not be born again. That itself is the peace belonging to that person. Therefore, through the bliss experienced in this very life during the attainment of the Fruit of Arahantship (*arahatta-phala-samāpatti*), that person knows directly and surely that there is no further *saṁsāra* for them.
Thus, through the story of the Arahant Therī Sumedhā, we have explained the fear of *saṁsāra*, which is a highly important part of the Four Noble Truths shown by the Blessed One. We must constantly reflect that we have traveled in *saṁsāra* for an immense period of time. Furthermore, on this extremely rare occasion of a Buddha’s arising, possessing the wealth of the opportune moment (*khaṇa-sampatti*), we must not limit ourselves to mere backbone-breaking physical routines, but understand deeply and, without letting this opportunity for escaping *saṁsāra* slip away, strive as much as possible to attain that aforementioned supramundane state.
Therefore, today, you, virtuous friends, established in virtue (*sīla*), have listened to a Dhamma sermon that helps towards your Nibbāna. May all these wholesome deeds serve as a cause, a condition, and a strong support (*upanissaya*) for you to realize the supreme, deathless Great Nibbāna as swiftly as possible, before the decline of the Dispensation, through the penetration of the paths and fruits of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti*), Once-returning (*sakadāgāmitā*), Non-returning (*anāgāmitā*), and Arahantship! Thus you should wish.
Likewise, may whatever beings there are, from the Avīci hell up to the Akaniṭṭha heaven, including one’s own relatives, who wish to rejoice in the merit of this giving and hearing of the Dhamma, by doing so, find peace in the supreme, deathless Great Nibbāna through their own respective bodhi (enlightenment)! Wishing thus, recite these stanzas and share the merit.

from:
sumedhatherigatha (verse 515)
dear listeners,
to conquer the forces of mara that pull us into *samsara*, a powerful strength of renunciation (*nekkhamma*) is necessary. deeply contemplating the groups of discourses preached by the teacher of the three worlds, the fully enlightened buddha, regarding the terrifying nature of *samsara*, helps to cultivate such a strength of renunciation. the story and biography of the arahant theri sumedha, who conquered the forces of mara by relying on her own knowledge of the dhamma, is an excellent illustration of this.
on this vesak full moon poya day that has dawned today, we can find a valuable biography in the *therigatha* of the arahant nun sumedha, which helps us develop faith in this manner. it is a certain stanza among them that we have chosen as our theme today.
this theri sumedha, having accumulated powerful wholesome potential under previous buddhas, was born during the time of this buddha in the city of mantavati as the daughter of the regional king konca. after she reached youth, her parents decided to marry her to king anikadatta of the city of varanavati. however, by that time, sumedha, having visited the bhikkhuni monastery since her childhood along with royal princesses of her own age and maidservants, and having heard the dhamma, had developed great faith in the dispensation and a deep sense of urgency (*samvega*) regarding *samsara*. therefore, she did not agree to that proposal.
when the day approached for king anikadatta to come and see sumedha (perhaps something like the *svayamvara* custom of the past), sumedha went to her parents and said, “i have no expectation of staying in the household life enjoying the fivefold sensual pleasures. i am inclined towards nibbana; i remain loving nibbana. therefore, grant me permission to go forth as a monastic.” furthermore, she declared the impermanence (*anicca*) of this becoming (*bhava*), and the impermanence (*anicca*) that exists even in the heavenly worlds, showing how this becoming (*bhava*) is entirely impermanent (*anicca*). “one who has correctly understood the four noble truths preached by the blessed one does not wish even for the pleasures of the heavenly worlds. this becoming (*bhava*) is impermanent (*anicca*) everywhere, and sensual pleasures are extremely bitter; though they yield little satisfaction, they bring abundant suffering (*dukkha*) and trouble—this is the nature of the fivefold sensual pleasures. therefore, i do not like this marriage proposal. grant me permission to go forth (*pabbajja*).”
then, at the same time, she declared: “this body is entirely like a leather bag filled with excrement and carcasses. why give this to someone else? this is a body filled with worms. at any moment, as soon as consciousness (*vinnana*) departs from this, one’s own relatives will carry it to a cemetery and discard it. why give such a body of this nature to anyone?” she further declared to her parents: “if you do not grant me permission to go forth, i will meet my death. i will take no more food as a layperson.” saying so, she lay down on the floor of the palace. then her mother and father came, and the mother, weeping, said, “rise, my child.” addressing her daughter, she said, “you are extremely beautiful. you are to be the chief queen of king anikadatta; you are still young. enjoy these sensual pleasures.” thus, they tried to encourage her further regarding the proposal.
but she firmly insisted: “no, these fivefold sensual pleasures are not for me. this becoming (*bhava*) is impermanent (*anicca*) from every aspect. if one day the inside of this body were turned inside out, even one’s own mother would detest it, unable to bear the stench. at any moment, as soon as consciousness (*vinnana*) departs from this body, it is cast into the cemetery, and the relatives return and bathe. such is the nature of this body. therefore, what i need is liberation from this becoming (*bhava*). decay and death (*jaramarana*) follow closely behind me. in the heavenly worlds, the animal realms, or the hells, there is no opportunity to go forth as a monastic. a buddha is born only very rarely; therefore, in this rare opportunity, on this occasion when the rare wealth of the opportune moment (*khana-sampatti*) has been obtained, grant me permission to go forth.” thus she declared repeatedly.
“if you do not allow me, i will take no more food. right here, i will meet my death,” she said, and lay down on the floor. at about that same moment, king anikadatta arrived in the city of mandavati. on hearing this news, what sumedha did was cut off her hair, enter her chambers, lock the door, and, focusing on her cut hair, entered the first absorption (*jhana*). having emerged from the first absorption (*jhana*) and while developing the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*), the king arrived. when her parents and the king were standing by the door, sumedha came and opened the door. she saw her parents weeping. finally, the king said to sumedha, “these parents are in great sorrow. you are very young. sensual fortune is extremely rare. i will hand over all this royal wealth to you. all pleasures and fortunes are here. going forth is difficult.” in this way, he tried to persuade her to accept the proposal.
at that moment, sumedha declared the unsatisfying nature of sensual pleasures. king mandhata, who ruled over the four great continents and was foremost among all enjoyers of sensual pleasures, passed away completely unsatisfied. even if it rained the seven kinds of gems, human beings would not attain satisfaction. sensual desire is something that leaves humans unsatisfied. in particular, she briefly recalled for the king the ten similes mentioned in the blessed one’s discourses regarding the fivefold sensual pleasures.
the blessed one has declared this regarding sensual pleasures. if we explain these similes briefly and in a detailed manner so that you, virtuous friends, can understand: in a slaughterhouse, a butcher throws a bone scraped of flesh and blood to a dog. the dog gnaws at it. while gnawing it, it ultimately meets with suffering (*dukkha*); there is no essence in it. you, virtuous friends, have heard this simile of “the fleshless bone”.
next, another simile given by the blessed one to show the nature of sensual pleasures is that they are like a pit of glowing embers. two strong men drag a person and throw him into a pit of embers, and he is burnt right there. or, like holding a burning grass torch while walking against the wind—if one does not let go of that grass torch, one's hand will be burnt. sensual pleasures are just like that. furthermore, when a hawk flies up into the sky clutching a piece of meat, other birds and crows pursue and peck at it in order to snatch and eat that piece of meat. if that hawk or crow does not let go of the piece of meat, it will have to face death or deadly suffering (*dukkha*). this is common to all. therefore, everyone fights over them and ultimately meets with destruction. other similes are given: sensual pleasures are like borrowed goods. they are temporary; one never knows when one might lose them.
next, these sensual pleasures are like a dream. they are deceptive, illusory. it is something that appears real only for a brief moment. another simile shown in detail by the blessed one is the simile of the tree fruit (*rukkha-phala*). it is a simile about fruits on a tree. someone, seeing fruits on a tree, climbs it to pluck them. meanwhile, someone else who cannot climb the tree begins to cut it down from the base. if the climber does not descend, he will fall along with the tree and meet with death. just like that, due to the nature of these sensual pleasures, people fight for them in both lawful and unlawful ways. because of that struggle, many fall into suffering (*dukkha*).
furthermore, these sensual pleasures are compared to a serpent’s head, showing their dangerous nature. this lady declared many such similes to the king. not only that, she briefly reminded the king of the terrifying nature of this long *samsara*, its extremely long nature, based on the discourses delivered by the blessed one in the *anamatagga samyutta*. perhaps during that era, the buddha’s discourses were more well-known than today. thus, you, virtuous friends, may also have heard the buddha’s discourses found in the *anamatagga samyutta*. the blessed one declared that if someone were to cut down all the trees and foliage in this entire jambudipa into four-inch pieces, and set them aside one by one saying, “this is my mother, this is my mother’s mother, this is that mother’s mother,” even if all those trees and foliage were exhausted, one could not bring to an end the line of those who have been one’s mother in this *samsara*. that discourse is meant to show that one has been born in this *samsara* for such a long period of time.
similarly, if one were to make clay pellets the size of jujube seeds from the soil of the great earth, and count them saying, “this is my father, this is my father’s father,” and so on, that lineage of fathers would not come to an end even if the soil of the great earth were exhausted. this was declared to clarify that one has been wandering in this *samsara* for an inconceivably long, *anamatagga* (without discoverable beginning) period of time.
similarly, the blessed one has declared, in relation to the four great oceans, that during this long period, in this long *samsara* whose beginning is not apparent, if one were to collect the tears shed by a single person weeping when separated from the loved and agreeable, and united with the unloved and disagreeable, they would be greater than the waters of the four great oceans. that is, the tears shed due to the death of one’s mother, the death of one’s daughter, the death of one’s son, and so on, as well as due to the loss of wealth and disasters of illness—these tears are greater than the four great oceans. likewise, if the breast milk one has drunk from mothers in this long *samsara* were collected, it too would be greater than the four great oceans. this is not presented as an exaggeration by the blessed one; that quantity of milk is indeed greater than the four great oceans. next, it is shown that if the blood shed by a person having their throat cut throughout this long *samsara* were collected, it would be greater than the four great oceans.
on one occasion, the blessed one declared to a group of about thirty forest-dwelling bhikkhus, as a sermon sufficient for them to attain arahantship, this very discourse about blood: how the blood shed when having one’s throat cut after being born as cows, buffaloes, goats, sheep, and chickens over a long period of time is greater than the four great oceans, and so on. drawing from such sutta discourses that arouse urgency (*samvega*) regarding this wheel of *samsara*, sumedha explained the terrifying nature of *samsara* to king anikadatta.
then she said: “while my head is on fire, and decay and death (*jaramarana*) follow closely behind me, there is no help for me from others. i must strive to bring this decay and death (*jaramarana*) to an end. i need no help from others. go, i do not wish to marry you. you must go!” she declared in this manner. finally, perhaps because the king was somewhat softened by her declarations, he rose, bowed to sumedha’s father, and pleaded: “grant sumedha permission to go forth to put an end to the suffering (*dukkha*) of *samsara*.” thus, princess sumedha, having overcome the opposition of both her parents and the king who had come to marry her, and having obtained permission to go forth, was ordained in the dispensation and ultimately attained arahantship.
furthermore, after attaining arahantship, in the final days of the arahant theri sumedha, she declared the powerful wholesome deed (*kusala*) that helped her attain this great gain, as recorded in the *therigatha*. during the time of the buddha konagamana, she, along with two of her female friends, had built and offered a dwelling (*avasa*) to the buddha. those two friends are identified in this buddha’s dispensation as the brahmin lady dhananjani and the theri khema. it was through associating with buddhas over a long period and contemplating the deep aspects of the true dhamma (*saddhamma*) that princess sumedha ultimately chose to become a bhikkhuni instead of becoming a queen consort or chief queen. she ended her life as an arahant nun. among the heroic characters in this dispensation, theri sumedha occupies a unique place. indeed, as the longest stanza group in the *therigatha*, the story of theri sumedha is mentioned last. for many, especially lay women devotees, this biography can be a source of great encouragement.
now, the stanza we have taken as our theme actually appears right at the end of the collection of *therigatha*, which consists of about seventy poem groups. the stanza that precisely reflects the occasion that caused the king’s mind to change—the very one that led to it—is what we have cited as our theme on this occasion:
*adhigatamidam bahuhi amatam, ajja pi ca labhaniyamidam,*
*yo yoniso payunjati, na ca sakka aghatamanena.*
*adhigatamidam bahuhi amatam* – this deathless nibbana, has been attained by many. *ajja pi ca labhaniyamidam* – even today this nibbana can be obtained. *yo yoniso payunjati* – if one strives with wise attention (*yoniso*). *na ca sakka aghatamanena* – but it cannot be attained by someone who does not make a firm, strenuous effort.
“the nibbana obtained by many in the past can be obtained today if one strives; but for one who cannot strive, this nibbana cannot be obtained,” the blessed one declared. it was upon hearing this declaration that the king’s views completely changed. therefore, in accordance with these words of the buddha, we must reflect on the possibility of attaining nibbana within this dispensation today as well, in keeping with the occasion. that is why we said that this stanza is exemplary. as theri sumedha declared, if someone strives, they can escape from this decay and death (*jaramarana*) to what is called the “deathless” (*amata* / *amrta*). that is why theri sumedha said her head was on fire, and that decay and death (*jaramarana*) were chasing after her. having been born again and again in various ways in this *samsara* for an infinite time, one has had to face death—often termed *ghata*, being slaughtered. it is because of such a nature of this *samsara* that those who heard the buddha’s discourses in the past developed a sense of urgency (*samvega*) and strove to realize nibbana swiftly.
it is the long duration as well as the terrifying nature of this *samsara* that the blessed one depicted through those similes of blood, tears, and breast milk. through the explanations of the terrifying nature and long duration of *samsara*, the blessed one endeavored to make us understand the truth of suffering (*dukkha-sacca*) within the four noble truths, as well as to cultivate disenchantment (*nibbida*) towards *samsara*.
however, nowadays, the truth of suffering (*dukkha-sacca*) has often been reduced to a very simplistic level. one frequently hears people talking about daily disappointments or mental stress and anxiety as if they represent the truth of suffering (*dukkha-sacca*). but if one is to develop such a deep strength of renunciation (*nekkhamma*), one must contemplate the terrifying nature of *samsara*, the long duration of *samsara*, and its inconstant (*anicca*) nature, as found in the buddha’s discourses.
now, one cannot say where one might be born next in *samsara*. that is why theri sumedha said that a person overwhelmed by the fivefold sensual pleasures, by engaging in bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct and unwholesome deeds, will be born in hellish realms and similar lower planes. once born in such places, for another extremely long period, there is nothing but suffering (*dukkha*), and one cannot derive any benefit from this dispensation of the buddha.
therefore, as the blessed one declared, while there are eight inopportune moments (*attha akkhana*) where one cannot practice the path of the dispensation, if one has obtained birth during the arising of a buddha, obtaining the wealth of the opportune moment (*khana-sampatti*), one must strive to escape from these conditions of birth (*jati*), decay (*jara*), and death (*marana*).
you, virtuous friends, may have heard the inspired utterance (*udana*) declared by the blessed one after attaining supreme enlightenment. the inspired verse beginning with *“aneka jati samsaram...”* speaks precisely about this problem of rebirth (*punabbhava*). *aneka jati samsaram, sandhavissam anibbisam* – “through many births (*jati*) in *samsara* i have wandered, searching but not finding the builder of this house.” *dukkha jati punappunam* – “painful is birth (*jati*) again and again.” it is this very condition that the blessed one pointed out as the truth of suffering (*dukkha-sacca*).
we usually consider only daily disappointments, the inability to fulfill one’s expectations, and such things as suffering (*dukkha*). but the nature of this *samsara* is something far deeper than that. the blessed one declares: *“anamataggoyam, bhikkhave, samsaro, pubbakoti na pannayati, avijjanivarananam sattanam tanhasamyojananam...”* and so forth.
a first beginning of this *samsara* cannot be seen, because the blessed one has declared that there is no such beginning of ignorance (*avijja*) where one could say that ignorance (*avijja*) did not exist before and then arose. that is why it is said to have no first beginning, spanning such an immense duration of time. *avijjanivarananam* means covered by the hindrance of ignorance (*avijja*), and *tanhasamyojananam* means fettered by the bond of craving (*tanha*); the blessed one has declared that for a long time, beings have thus been wandering in *samsara*.
therefore, on a day like this, we must reflect: if we are asked what our goal as buddhists is, we should be able to say without fear, “it is to see the end of *samsara* in this very life.” although the word nibbana is used for this, nibbana is defined in very strange ways. many describe nibbana in a way that actually increases craving for becoming (*bhava-tanha*). many assume nibbana to be a special, separate world; they define nibbana as a novel world. however, the blessed one has shown, *“dukkha jati punappunam”*— “suffering (*dukkha*) is birth (*jati*) again and again.” birth (*jati*) occurs very easily, meaning as long as ignorance (*avijja*) and craving (*tanha*) exist, one will certainly undergo birth (*jati*) in various places and in various levels of becoming (*bhava*). that is why sumedha too said that this becoming (*bhava*) is essence-less. whether in heavenly worlds or the human world, impermanence (*anicca*) is everywhere. impermanence (*anicca*) is indeed the nature of things.
thus, if there is birth (*jati*) within that impermanent (*anicca*) becoming (*bhava*), decay (*jara*), sickness (*vyadhi*), and death (*marana*) will certainly be there. one cannot obtain a birth (*jati*) that is devoid of death. like a shadow, decay and death (*jaramarana*) go together with birth (*jati*). for this reason, the suffering (*dukkha*) of *samsara* is not those minor shortcomings as the worldly people generally think. it must be considered far more deeply; it must be understood far more deeply. it is only for someone who takes this deeply to heart that the practices of this dispensation become meaningful.
thus, the blessed one has summarized for us the necessary steps for liberation from this long *samsara* within the four noble truths. first, what is this illness called suffering (*dukkha*)? as mentioned before, it is birth (*jati*) again and again—*dukkha jati*. then, along with it, birth (*jati*), decay (*jara*), sickness (*vyadhi*), and death (*marana*). furthermore, daily disappointments and such are also included in it: not getting what one wishes for, association with the unloved, separation from the loved, and so on—this is the nature of suffering (*dukkha*) inherent within existence. if the nature inherent in existence is suffering (*dukkha*), the blessed one showed what lies beneath it: craving (*tanha*). the blessed one declared that a being afflicted by the thirst of craving (*tanha*) is like one running after a mirage. no matter how far one goes in this, no satisfaction is ever found.
that is why theri sumedha said that even if it rained the seven kinds of gems, no satisfaction would be gained; and why she said that king mandhata, who was the foremost among the enjoyers of sensual pleasures, died without attaining satisfaction. the blessed one pointed out the unsatisfying nature of craving (*tanha*), which is like running after a mirage, and it is this craving (*tanha*) that is called the origin (*samudaya*) of this entire mass of suffering (*dukkha*). this craving (*tanha*) is thus generated through ignorance (*avijja*). this ignorance (*avijja*) is like when we think of a deer—the deer mistakes the distant shimmering vision for water, and then runs after it. it is just such a thing.
due to the delusion arising from ignorance (*avijja*), people run without limit after the goals they set for themselves in the world. the blessed one has shown the craving (*tanha*) that arises towards things that object-ize the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as a thirst. in some places, it is shown as an insatiable hunger. its liberation is shown as *“tanhakkhayo virago nirodho nibbanam”* (the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, nibbana, and the very destruction and calming of craving (*tanha*) is shown as bliss. this is not something received in a special, different place. the blessed one shows it as a state that can be experienced in this very life. for this reason, nibbana is sometimes designated by the name *“tanhakkhaya”* (destruction of craving).
the path leading to that is what the blessed one has shown as the noble eightfold path. all concepts and thoughts we generate through wrong views (*miccha-ditthi*) drag us back to *samsara* again and again. however, the blessed one has declared that right view (*samma-ditthi*) is for the sake of escaping from this world. whether one performs meritorious deeds or demeritorious deeds, one is still within *samsara*. therefore, the path for the exhaustion of these karmas is the supramundane noble eightfold path. through that noble eightfold path, one proceeds towards a practice that puts an end to both merit and demerit. it is that very craving (*tanha*) that creates the urge in worldly beings to perform both meritorious and demeritorious actions.
as long as the perception of self (*atta-sanna*), the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*), and the sense of “i” and “mine” exist therein, worldly beings strive to grasp those various things as grasping / fuel (*upadana*). in the blessed one’s dhamma, the three characteristics—impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*)—are particularly shown. now, everyone understands impermanence (*anicca*) to some extent. however, the blessed one saw all these things far more deeply than that. not only everything visible on the surface, but also our sense bases—namely, the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and everything that becomes their object—change extremely momentarily; they are impermanent (*anicca*). for this very reason, one has to experience their unsatisfying nature, their nature of suffering (*dukkha*). therefore, they cannot be kept under one’s control. this inability to keep them under one’s control is what is called not-self (*anatta*).
therefore, one must practice directing one’s daily thinking in such a way that the three characteristics of impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*) are properly established in one’s mind. that is what helps to develop the supramundane path. generally, within the blessed one’s teaching, there is a mundane aspect of right view (*samma-ditthi*), which involves turning away from actions leading to lower realms and heading towards happy destinies; there is that side too. however, that is something that increases *samsara* (becoming / existence).
therefore, one must contemplate deeply. that is why sumedha said that even in the pleasures of the heavenly worlds, there is no end, no satisfaction. instead, what is to be killed is death itself. what is called *“ghata”*—what is to be slaughtered is death itself; it is the fact of having to die in those various places. thus, that fact of having to die is brought to an end only by bringing birth (*jati*) to an end. birth (*jati*) is brought to an end by bringing death to an end, since birth (*jati*) and death go together. the concept of birth (*jati*) arises through grasping / fuel (*upadana*). through grasping (*upadana*), there is becoming (*bhava*).
as long as craving (*tanha*) exists, worldly beings undergo birth (*jati*) in hell realms, heavenly worlds, or the human world, whether through wholesome or unwholesome deeds, in accordance with the sign (*nimitta*) grasped by the mind. within every such existence (*bhava*), decay (*jara*), sickness (*vyadhi*), and death (*marana*) are seen and experienced. therefore, the blessed one pointed out that one must understand the true nature of the world insightfully (*vipassana*-wise), in terms of impermanence (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*).
now, what this world is trying to gratify is this skeletal cage of a body. the true nature of this body must be contemplated as unattractive (*asubha*). what theri sumedha brought to light was this unattractive (*asubha*) nature of the body. furthermore, its impermanence as impermanent (*anicca*-wise), or in terms of elements (*dhatu*). for some, even when contemplating in terms of elements (*dhatu*), the aforementioned three characteristics are understood. because what exists inside this body, as well as externally, are the four great elements (*mahabhuta*) of earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and wind (*vayo*)—the four elements (*dhatu*).
due to grasping (*upadana*) towards them, a division has been made into internal and external. one grasps it as “this is mine.” next, one tries to grasp external things. to catch them, one runs after them. that is why it is said to be like running after a mirage.
these six sense bases (*ayatana*) are like an octopus, trying to grasp the entire world through these six senses. that is an unsatisfying run. that is why the blessed one declares that if someone constantly contemplates that what exists there as well as here is only earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and wind (*vayo*), that person can reduce that aforementioned craving (*tanha*) and oppression. if on some occasion one understands: “what is taken here as 'i' and 'mine' is merely a certain illusion. it is because of the delusion developed over a long period in *samsara* that we undergo this suffering (*dukkha*).” to put it precisely, in this consciousness (*vinnana*) called 'mind' that we hold in such high esteem, there exists a certain deceptive quality. it is something that is caught when we look back. the blessed one shows this as name-and-form (*namarupa*). what is called name-and-form (*namarupa*) there is merely a name in appearance and a form in appearance. when this is understood as name-and-form (*namarupa*), then this delusion is thinned out to some extent.
if someone recognizes that within everything that is seen and heard by them, there exists only a shadow cast in consciousness (*vinnana*) that is connected to that consciousness (*vinnana*), then the desire to grasp these things gradually thins out. it is in this way that one enters the path of insight (*vipassana*). when watching a movie, our delusion arises because we glue together that rapidly running sequence of images with craving (*tanha*). we glue them together along the shadows falling extremely rapidly within this consciousness (*vinnana*), with some expectation of “i” and “mine”; through this, it appears to us as something that truly exists. it is in this way that the perception of permanence (*nicca-sanna*) arises. but if we practice looking closely, moment by moment, with mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajanna*) through insight (*vipassana*), we gradually realize that what exists here is only something like the aforementioned shadow. that is why the blessed one takes name-and-form (*namarupa*) as merely a shadow cast in consciousness (*vinnana*) itself—namely, the mental factors (*nama-dhamma*) of feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), volition (*cetana*), contact (*phassa*), and attention (*manasikara*); and next, what we hold onto as form (*rupa*), which is merely those four elements (*dhatu*) of earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and wind (*vayo*), and the perception of form (*rupa-sanna*) derived from those four great elements (*mahabhuta*).
then, the nature of this grasping (*upadana*) is understood through that. what we call “the thing to be grasped” is merely an illusion. in truth, there is nothing to be grasped. within that grasping, there is only that aforementioned feeling (*vedana*), a perception (*sanna*) formed because of that feeling (*vedana*), a volition (*cetana*) applied to it, a contact (*phassa*), a place of contact, and attention (*manasikara*)—that is all there is. thus, in every instance, only these things exist. once this is understood, the sense of “i” and “mine” thins out. therefore, entering the path of insight (*vipassana*) shown by the blessed one occurs by establishing the good mindfulness and wisdom called mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajanna*). that is what is contained in the four foundations of mindfulness (*cattaro satipatthana*). the blessed one has shown how to recognize the body as body, feelings (*vedana*) as feelings, the mind as mind, and mental objects as mental objects through the four foundations of mindfulness. that is why the blessed one declared: “within this very fathom-long body, i declare the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world.” if we contemplate with wisdom that dhamma preached by the blessed one in that manner and apply those practices, even today we can—if we strive as sumedha said—attain that aforementioned deathless (*amata* / *amrta*). what is called the deathless (*amata*) is not something that exists in a strange, different world, nor is it a kind of beverage.
generally, everyone is afraid of death. why are they afraid of death? it is because of grasping (*upadana*). the greater the grasping (*upadana*), to that same extent is the fear of death. the fear or suffering (*dukkha*) that arises in us is exactly in proportion to the things we have grasped. therefore, the blessed one pointed out that it is through the gradually arising understanding, by gradually seeing the three characteristics of impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*) of name-and-form (*namarupa*) insightfully (*vipassana*-wise), that the dark mass of ignorance (*avijja*) is removed.
simultaneously, the craving (*tanha*) that exists along with the delusion generated through one’s own ignorance (*avijja*) is thinned out to that same extent. it is where ignorance (*avijja*) and craving (*tanha*) are absent that death is truly understood. up to now, what was thought of as death was a massive fear arising at the moment this bodily cage is destroyed, because it was taken as “mine.” but we know, one cares for one’s teeth; yet if at some point, due to some reason, it becomes absolutely necessary to extract a tooth, we allow it. we give our consent. it is the same with the other organs of our body. when contemplating in that manner, the blessed one shows: “what exists here is grasping (*upadana*)—holding on.” becoming (*bhava*) is said to be the cause of this continuation. the state that arises when that is let go is what is called extinguishment without grasping (*anupada parinibbana. it is simply the peace that arises at that moment of letting go; it is not some other world.
thus, the secret lies within this very consciousness (*vinnana*). this consciousness (*vinnana*) is trapped, narrowed down, within the six sense bases (*ayatana*). it is narrowed down within the six sense bases (*ayatana*) of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. one cannot hear with the eye; one cannot see with the ear. within these, a world has been built: the world seen by the eye, the world heard by the ear, the world felt by the tongue. every enterprise, commercial business, or activity contained within this concept we call “the world” is connected to these six sense bases (*ayatana*): eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. the blessed one pointed out these: it is within these six sense bases (*ayatana*) themselves that suffering (*dukkha*) lies. the entire world, too, exists right there.
the blessed one declared a wonderful stanza:
> *chassu loko samuppanno, chassu kubbati santhavam,*
> *channameva upadaya, chassu loko vihannati.*
*chassu loko samuppanno* – the world has arisen within these six. it is within these six sense bases (*ayatana*) that what is called “a world” has arisen. *chassu kubbati santhavam* – all connections and coordination in the world occur within these six; everything takes place within these six. even the highly marvelous things considered as scientific products in this era, at one end of them lies either an eye or an ear. it is from the end of such a sense base (*ayatana*) that other things operate. this shows how true the buddha’s word is.
*channameva upadaya, chassu loko vihannati* – grasping onto these six, the world is oppressed and weary within the six. this is the story of the six given by the blessed one.
> *chassu loko samuppanno, chassu kubbati santhavam,*
> *channameva upadaya, chassu loko vihannati.*
>
> born within the six,
> in the six it seeks its companionship,
> grasping tightly onto the six,
> within the six itself, the world grows weary.
accordingly, we must reflect: in our daily life, we can develop the aforementioned three characteristics in relation to these six sense bases (*ayatana*), using the buddha’s word as our help. some make use of the meditation on the unattractive (*asubha-bhavana*) to cultivate disenchantment with this body. others use the attention to elements (*dhatu-manasikara*). yet others, through mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajanna*) regarding the objects arriving at these sense bases (*ayatana*), and by understanding their true nature, take the opportunity to escape from the aforementioned delusion in accordance with the buddha’s word. by understanding that this is a mirage according to the buddha’s word, we get the opportunity to free ourselves from delusion.
that is exactly what the blessed one declared: the world is trapped within these six sense bases (*ayatana*). becoming (*bhava*) or continuation exists only within these six. how does one escape from this? what helps to escape from these six is the light of wisdom (*panna*). the blessed one shows that the six sense bases (*ayatana*) function within ignorance (*avijja*). but if on any occasion one understands the true nature of that consciousness (*vinnana*) through wisdom (*panna*), through that light, then at that moment, having escaped from it, there is liberation.
that is to say, through that liberation, one realizes, as stated in the buddha’s word, *“loko sunno”*—the world is empty. because at that moment, one directly experiences that what is called “a thing” is merely something fabricated by the mind of the world. the mind is liberated. the mind does not bind itself to even one of those six. it is the attainment of that liberated mind that was called the deathless (*amata*). therefore, what is called nibbana is the escape from the concepts built up by this world—the concept of birth (*jati*), becoming (*bhava*) caused by grasping (*upadana*), birth (*jati*) caused by that becoming (*bhava*), and decay and death (*jaramarana*) caused by that birth (*jati*). these are severed through that very understanding shown by the blessed one.
the secret of dependent co-arising (*paticca-samuppada*), which you, virtuous friends, have heard in the form *“avijja-paccaya sankhara”* (dependent on ignorance, preparations / preparations arise), also lies there. within this darkness called ignorance (*avijja*), and precisely because of that darkness—just as when one is in the dark, certain illusions or groups of uncertain feelings arise—that is what is called preparations / preparations / volitional activity (*sankhara*). due to the concept of “i” and “mine” developed within that ignorance (*avijja*), preparations (*sankhara*) arise in the form of merit or demerit. it is as a part of that very preparation (*sankhara*-ing / preparing) that there is a division into two: consciousness (*vinnana*) and name-and-form (*namarupa*).
consciousness (*vinnana*) has a reflective nature. consciousness (*vinnana*) has a certain capacity, and that is precisely the deceptive, illusion-like nature of consciousness (*vinnana*). the blessed one compared consciousness (*vinnana*) to an illusion; an illusion is taken as something that exists as long as it is not understood. when it is understood, the illusion ceases to deceive. that is why, when the blessed one compared consciousness (*vinnana*) to an illusion, the simile he showed was that of a magician showing an illusion at a crossroads. but ultimately, the blessed one declares: “what essence is there in that illusion?” there is no substance in it. showing what does not exist as if it exists is what that illusion is. just such a thing is present within this consciousness (*vinnana*). this consciousness (*vinnana*) has a reflective capacity. when looking back, something is seen. misunderstanding that seen thing is precisely what is called unwise attention (*ayonisomanasikara*).
worldly beings wander in *samsara* because they misunderstand that seen thing through unwise attention (*ayonisomanasikara*). that misunderstanding is identified in the dhamma as the four distortions (*vipallasa*). *vipallasa* means distorted—the distorted feeling, the distorted understanding. what are the four distortions?
1. *anicce nicca-sanna* – taking what is in reality impermanent (*anicca*) as permanent; adopting the perception of permanence (*nicca-sanna*).
2. *asubhe subha-sanna* – taking what is in reality unattractive (*asubha*) as attractive (*subha*). this is what sumedha too said. sumedha was a beautiful lady, yet she herself explained the unattractive (*asubha*) nature of her body to her parents. the blessed one pointed out that taking the unattractive as attractive is a distortion.
3. *dukkhe sukha-sanna* – what is taken as pleasure, the blessed one showed as suffering (*dukkha*). that which is taken as pleasure was compared to a dream (*supinupama*), because its change turns into suffering (*dukkha*). it cannot be kept forever. it changes constantly. it cannot be taken as pleasure. taking it as pleasure is merely an illusion. taking what is painful as pleasant is thus the third distortion.
4. *anattani atta-sanna* – taking what is not-self (*anatta*), what cannot be grasped as one’s own, what cannot be kept under one’s control, as though it could be kept under one’s control.
thus, the blessed one shows that it is due to these distorted things (*vipallasa-dhamma*) that the world has built up suffering (*dukkha*) in the darkness; suffering (*dukkha*) has arisen. to eliminate it, one must strive to see, as the blessed one showed, the true suffering—to see impermanent (*anicca*) things as impermanent (*anicca*), painful (*dukkha*) things as painful (*dukkha*), unattractive (*asubha*) things as unattractive (*asubha*), and not-self (*anatta*) things as not-self (*anatta*). the blessed one pointed out that this cannot be done with the instruments found in the world. nowadays, we use various instruments for everything in the world. if the eye cannot see properly, we get glasses to see a bit better. if that is still not enough, we get a telescope. yet, the blessed one declares that the world of worldlings (*puthujjana*) is blind.
why was it declared so? not to disparage us. it is because until that eye of dhamma (*dhamma-cakkhu*) arises, until the eye of wisdom (*panna-cakkhu*) arises, the world is merely groping in the dark. generally, when we think of a blind person, we think, “oh, that person is just groping around.” but to the blessed one’s eye of wisdom, it was clear that what the world is doing—including the scientists—is merely a groping in the dark.
at that point, the blessed one points out: “the world is trapped within these six sense bases (*ayatana*).” they say they see, they say they hear, they say they feel. all of this takes place within that narrow limit grasped as “i” and “mine”; it is within that that a world exists. it is like a sacrifice performed inside a gourd. our ancestors may have heard of this “sacrifice inside a gourd”—the blessed one declared something of that nature on a certain occasion to the brahmin veranja.
“brahmin, i am the very first chick in this era to break through the eggshell and come out.” one must contemplate the depth of this statement. what then is this eggshell? the blessed one has shown it to be ignorance (*avijja*). therefore, everyone—including these scientists—remains inside this eggshell. it is this breaking through the eggshell that is called the arising of wisdom (*panna*).
that is why nibbana is sometimes designated by the name “cessation of the six sense bases” (*salayatana-nirodha*). breaking through the eggshell is compared to the cessation of the six sense bases (*salayatana-nirodha*). where the six sense bases (*salayatana*) cease, it is not death. where the six sense bases cease, the eye of wisdom (*panna-cakkhu*) opens. to the eye of wisdom, things that previously appeared to exist are seen not to exist. therein lies the secret. but the world does not like this. they want to keep everything, but they also want to eliminate suffering (*dukkha*). the blessed one shows that this is impossible, because of the craving for becoming (*bhava-tanha*).
now, theri sumedha said from the very beginning, “i have no desire for this becoming (*bhava*).” she said directly to the king too: “my head is on fire. decay and death (*jaramarana*) follow me. why do they follow me? i have no use for those things. go!” thus, the most important thing is eliminating the attachment to becoming (*bhava*). but in the world, there exists a strong craving for becoming (*bhava-tanha*). they want to remain in becoming (*bhava*) but also want to be free of suffering (*dukkha*). both cannot be done. because what is called becoming (*bhava*) is the sense of “i” and “mine.” the blessed one shows the opposite. the blessed one shows that the false notion existing within this world, this wrong grasping of “i” and “mine”—right there lies entire suffering (*dukkha*). beings have thus been trapped within the sense bases (*ayatana*) in this *samsara* for a long period of time.
the blessed one has shown the simile of a dog bound to a post in relation to the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*). the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*) is the assumption that this group/body actually exists. each of us has a name given by our parents. to that name, various titles and statuses added by society are joined. accordingly, we identify ourselves as a person. we, too, say “i, i.” but this skeletal cage of a body also changes constantly. everything changes. forgetting this, we grasp it as “a thing” through the perception of compactness (*ghana-sanna*). it is the same regarding other things too.
however, if on some occasion the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*) is developed to the highest level, at that moment, an inability to grasp in that manner arises. that is called the perception of a heap (*rasi-sanna*). the meditator on insight (*vipassana*) understands this step by step. what was grasped compactly as one thing, as a unit, is at some point seen by the eye of insight (*vipassana*): “here exists only a certain kind of illusion.” an illusion—that is, merely an image falling in consciousness (*vinnana*). what actually exists here is a set of mental factors (*nama-dhamma*) associated with a consciousness (*vinnana*)—namely, feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), volition (*cetana*), contact (*phassa*), and attention (*manasikara*); there is merely a name for a name there. next, a perception of form (*rupa-sanna*) that we adopt in relation to the four great elements (*mahabhuta*) of earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and wind (*vayo*), which we cannot identify separately. thus, it is through the understanding that this is only name-and-form (*namarupa*) that one is gradually able to understand.
that is why it is said that in insight (*vipassana*), as one proceeds forward from the understanding of name-and-form (*namarupa*), this perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*) becomes very clear. what is present there is not the impermanence usually thought of by the world. it is understood extremely deeply that everything changes moment by moment, with extreme rapidity. everything changes, at every single moment. even within the in-breath and out-breath, in every single thing, the perception of not-self (*anatta-sanna*) gradually grows. one realizes that there is no basis for what was grasped as “i.” proceeding in this manner, at some point, one is liberated from the darkness of ignorance (*avijja*).
generally, when enjoying a movie, we do not think for even a single moment, “we are enjoying this movie thanks to the surrounding darkness.” at that time, we do not think, “it is because of this darkness.” if the thought of the darkness were to cross our mind for even a moment, we could not enjoy that movie. but because of that delusion, the delusion (*moha*) present in the world, our mind rests on that screen—the unstabilized screen. relying on that unstabilized screen, a strange continuation of becoming (*bhava*) is conjured up, whether in the teledramas or films of this era, in every single one of them. furthermore, we do not realize that this functions within a certain frame. that frame is what is called the prepared / conditioned (*sankhata*)—something fabricated. the blessed one designates this frame as the prepared (*sankhata*).
it is something we ourselves have fabricated, but we do not see it. thus, the world remains within the prepared (*sankhata*) that they themselves have constructed. it is within that that all this birth (*jati*), decay (*jara*), and death (*marana*) occur. if this skeletal cage of a body had a beginning in a mother's womb at some point, it was not due to our mother's skill. this is said to occur because of grasping (*upadana*). thus, at the moment a being passes away in *samsara*, in accordance with the sign (*nimitta*) that comes to the mind—as stated in *“kammam khettam vinnanam bijam tanha sineho”* (karma is the field, consciousness is the seed, craving is the moisture)—as long as the seed of consciousness (*vinnana-bija*) has the nature to sprout, the seed of consciousness (*vinnana*) is deposited, and the moisture of craving (*tanha*) is present. at that moment, a conception occurs in a mother’s womb as a child. this being, this child, who emerges bringing joy to the mother and father, ultimately does not know, nor do the parents know, that what is present here is simply that very delusion, that same ignorance (*moha*) that has come along for a long time in *samsara*. as long as the body called “i” and “mine” grows from that point, one calls it “i” and “mine.” and so it is regarding other things in this world. as ignorance (*avijja*) is eliminated through true understanding, the delusion present here is understood. indeed, if there is no measuring viewpoint, there is no measurement either. where there is measurement, there is narrowing. if at some point the primary peg that helps to measure is uprooted—that is what is called in the dhamma the conceit “i am” (*asmi-mana*), the peg that says “i am.”
that is to say, the most fundamental, extremely subtle part of continuation is the conceit “i am” (*asmi-mana*). the moment that is removed, things that appeared due to ignorance (*avijja*) and darkness are no longer seen; things that were heard are no longer heard. yet, one has not become blind; one has not become deaf. at that moment, the light of wisdom (*panna*) arose. just as mentioned regarding the cinema, the moment the light comes on, the things on the screen fade away. in the same way, there comes a moment when the world fades away. that very fading away is indeed liberation. then, if someone has experienced that, it is registered in consciousness (*vinnana*) as a unique experience. what was prepared in consciousness (*vinnana*) at that point was a state of having died without dying.
what is called the deathless (*amata* / *amrta*) is therefore not some strange beverage. it is a moment when that wrong notion taken as “death” is directly and personally eradicated; that is, one understands that one is being held by the mind. if that existence (*bhava*) grasped by the mind, which was taken as “this is i,” is let go at some point, at that moment, instead of suffering (*dukkha*), there arises peace—a sense of liberation, an escape. that bliss of liberation is what is called nibbana. the other side directly realized right here is that if it was previously a prepared consciousness (*sankhata-vinnana*) present in consciousness (*vinnana*), it was holding onto name-and-form (*namarupa*); the delusion regarding name-and-form (*namarupa*) was present. therefore, when one is liberated from name (*nama-vimutta*), that person has no sign (*nimitta*) to undergo birth (*jati*) again.
you, virtuous friends, have heard that it is in accordance with the sign (*nimitta*) developed at the final moment—such as the sign of karma (*kamma-nimitta*) or the sign of destination (*gati-nimitta*)—that one undergoes birth (*jati*) in a hell realm, a mother’s womb, or an animal womb. thus, if such a sign (*nimitta*) is not grasped at any moment, and consciousness (*vinnana*) is liberated, that person has no further becoming (*bhava*). therefore, it was because the direct realization of “no further becoming (*bhava*), no further birth (*jati*)” was obtained that the blessed one declared that aforementioned inspired verse (*udana-gatha*)—the valuable inspired verse that everyone has heard. why did he, upon obtaining this direct realization, not declare anything else but present only this account of birth (*jati*) and decay (*jara*)?
*aneka jati samsaram, sandhavissam anibbisam* – and so forth. “for a long time in this *samsara*, i did not see the builder who constructed this house, this skeletal cage, this name-and-form (*namarupa*), for all this time. because i did not see him, i ran searching for all this time.”
*gahakarakam gavesanto* – “running, seeking the house-builder.”
*dukkha jati punappunam* – “painful is birth (*jati*) again and again,” because every house that is built collapses.
but the blessed one declares:
*gahakaraka ditthosi* – “o house-builder, you are seen!” who is the builder of this house? consciousness (*vinnana*).
*puna geham na kahasi* – “you shall not build a house again.” that refers to the liberated consciousness (*vinnana*), the consciousness (*vinnana*) liberated from name-and-form (*namarupa*) when the light of wisdom (*panna*) was obtained. that is why there is no further birth (*jati*).
*sabba te phasuka bhagga, gahakutam visankhitam* – “all your rafters are broken, the ridgepole is shattered.” this is the moment when everything is freed, because the house-builder has been understood.
*visankharagatam cittam, tanhanam khayamajjhaga* – “the mind has reached the un-prepared / unconditioned (*visankhara*), attaining the destruction of cravings (*tanha*).” this is exactly what the blessed one points out: ultimately, one who has attained that peace, the peace of nibbana. it is because of such a state that one does not undergo birth (*jati*) again.
thus, it is that very state of the deathless (*amata*) attained in this very life that the blessed one has declared. the person who has obtained that direct realization knows with certainty that they will not be born again. that itself is the peace belonging to that person. therefore, through the bliss experienced in this very life during the attainment of the fruit of arahantship (*arahatta-phala-samapatti*), that person knows directly and surely that there is no further *samsara* for them.
thus, through the story of the arahant theri sumedha, we have explained the fear of *samsara*, which is a highly important part of the four noble truths shown by the blessed one. we must constantly reflect that we have traveled in *samsara* for an immense period of time. furthermore, on this extremely rare occasion of a buddha’s arising, possessing the wealth of the opportune moment (*khana-sampatti*), we must not limit ourselves to mere backbone-breaking physical routines, but understand deeply and, without letting this opportunity for escaping *samsara* slip away, strive as much as possible to attain that aforementioned supramundane state.
therefore, today, you, virtuous friends, established in virtue (*sila*), have listened to a dhamma sermon that helps towards your nibbana. may all these wholesome deeds serve as a cause, a condition, and a strong support (*upanissaya*) for you to realize the supreme, deathless great nibbana as swiftly as possible, before the decline of the dispensation, through the penetration of the paths and fruits of stream-entry (*sotapatti*), once-returning (*sakadagamita*), non-returning (*anagamita*), and arahantship! thus you should wish.
likewise, may whatever beings there are, from the avici hell up to the akanittha heaven, including one’s own relatives, who wish to rejoice in the merit of this giving and hearing of the dhamma, by doing so, find peace in the supreme, deathless great nibbana through their own respective bodhi (enlightenment)! wishing thus, recite these stanzas and share the merit.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 076
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #76
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.11)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Dūraṅgamaṃ ekacaraṃ, asarīraṃ guhāsayaṃ;
ye cittaṃ saññamessanti, mokkhanti mārabandhanā.
From:
Dhammapada 37 (Cittavagga)
Dear Listeners,
Beings in this world travel from country to country to see marvelous and wonderful things. They construct spacecraft and travel to other planets. By inventing instruments like microscopes and telescopes, they reveal wonderful details about things close at hand and things far away. But, pious friends, more wonderful than all of these things is this mind of ours. It was our Buddha who properly demonstrated to the world the way of the mind, the nature of the mind, and the great power of the mind. Our Buddha revealed to the world that it is because of this running mind that we wander in this *saṃsāra* for such an extremely long time, and that the place where the mind is brought to a halt is Nibbāna. Precisely by seeing the way of this running mind, we are able to bring forth a systematic program of practice that helps to halt the mind. The background story related to the stanza we have taken as our theme is indeed an excellent illustration of the behavior of a running mind.
In the city of Sāvatthī, there lived a good young man from a certain family. Having heard the Dhamma from our Buddha, that young man went forth and ordained under the name Saṅgharakkhita. Within a few days of ordaining and receiving higher ordination, he attained Arahantship. This venerable monk had a nephew. To remember the venerable monk, the nephew's parents also named him Saṅgharakkhita. Society knew him by the name 'Bhāgineyya Saṅgharakkhita'. 'Bhāgineyya' means nephew; thus, he was known as 'Nephew Saṅgharakkhita'. After this boy reached youth, he too went forth and ordained under his maternal uncle, the venerable monk.
Thus, he ordained as the novice monk Bhāgineyya Saṅgharakkhita. Having ordained and received higher ordination, he went to a village monastery to observe the rainy season retreat. At the end of the rainy season, from the offering made—the *vassāvāsika* offering—this monk received a piece of cloth seven cubits long and another piece of cloth eight cubits long. When he received this offering, this monk thought: "I must offer this eight-cubit piece of cloth to my preceptor, my teacher monk. I will use the seven-cubit piece of cloth." Having formed this great intention, after the rainy season, he set out to see his teacher monk. On the way, he went for alms, and while the teacher monk had gone to the village for alms, he entered the monastery, swept the venerable monk's cloister walk and chambers, performed the familiar duties, prepared water, and waited for the venerable monk to return.
Then, when the venerable monk arrived, he went forward to meet him, took his bowl and robes, performed those duties with great respect, made a seat ready for him, and having brought that eight-cubit piece of cloth, placed it at the feet of the venerable monk, saying, "Venerable Sir, please accept and use this offering." Offering it thus, he took the palm-leaf fan and stood fanning the venerable monk. The venerable monk said to his pupil, "My robes are complete. I have no need of this cloth. You may use this yourself." Monk Bhāgineyya Saṅgharakkhita said, "Alas, Venerable Sir, from the moment I received this, my only intention was to offer it to you. Please use it." Even though he said so, the teacher monk did not wish to accept it. "It would bring great blessings to me if you would use this, Venerable Sir," Monk Bhāgineyya Saṅgharakkhita pleaded repeatedly, but the preceptor refused it. And then, this monk's mind became displeased.
"Alas! In lay life, this venerable monk was my maternal uncle. Even though he is now my teacher monk, he does not wish to accept or use what I offer. Therefore, what is the use of this monkhood to me? I will return to the lay life," he thought. Then he wondered, "When I become a layman, what livelihood will I pursue? Maintaining a household is not easy; what job shall I do?" Then a way occurred to him: "I will sell this eight-cubit piece of cloth and buy a she-goat. Goats breed very quickly. I will sell the offspring as they are born and make money. Having earned money, I will take a wife. To that wife, a son will be born. Then, seating my wife and son in a carriage, I will come to visit my teacher monk, having named that son 'Saṅgharakkhita'. Then, while coming along the way, I will say to my wife, 'Give that child into my hands.' But the wife will say, 'You drive this carriage; I will look after the child.' Saying so, before they go far, due to the wife's negligence, the child falls right in front of the moving carriage wheel. The wheel runs over the child. Then, in anger, I will strike that wife with the goad, saying, 'When I asked for the child, you could not give him, and now you could not even protect him!' and I will beat her with the stick." Whom did he strike? He struck the head of his teacher monk, the Arahant! What did he strike with? The palm-leaf fan!
This venerable monk possessed supernormal powers (*abhiññā*). He was a great Arahant. He could see how another person's mind was working. Reflecting on it, he thought, "Why did my pupil strike my head with the palm-leaf fan like this?" Then he saw the thoughts that had been working in his mind. Thereupon, the senior monk said: "Saṅgharakkhita, you could not strike your wife, but what is the fault of this old elder?" At that moment, a great sense of urgency (*saṃvega*) arose in this young monk. "Alas, I am ruined! My teacher monk saw how my mind was working." Out of great shame, he dropped the palm-leaf fan right there and began to run. A group of novices ran after him, caught him, and brought him before the Buddha. Seeing them from afar, the Buddha asked, "Why are you bringing this monk by force?" They replied, "This young monk, having become dissatisfied with the monkhood, started to run away. We caught him and brought him here." The Buddha asked, "Why, monk, having ordained in such a Dispensation (*Sāsana*), do you wish to return to the lay life like this?" Then, this monk recounted the entire sequence of events, the way his mind had been working. The Buddha then comforted his mind: "That is the nature of this mind. Do not let your mind be weakened by this. The mind is something that wanders far like this. Such is the nature of the mind." Giving a discourse, he uttered the Dhamma stanza we mentioned at the beginning:
> *Dūraṅgamaṃ ekacaraṃ,*
> *asarīraṃ guhāsayaṃ,*
> *Ye cittaṃ saññamessanti,*
> *mokkhanti mārabandhanā.*
In this stanza, four characteristics of the mind are mentioned—four aspects of the nature of the mind. *Dūraṅgamaṃ* means wandering far; *ekacaraṃ* means traveling alone. The nature of the mind is to wander far, and it also travels alone. *Asarīraṃ* means bodiless (having no physical body). *Guhāsayaṃ* means dwelling in a cave—hiding inside a cave. Those (*ye*) who restrain (*saññamessanti*) the mind (*cittaṃ*) which has this kind of nature, will be freed from the bond of Māra (*mārabandhanā*)—the bond of defilements of Māra, the bond of *saṃsāra*. That is to say, they realize Nibbāna. Thus, he taught a stanza of such profound meaning.
As mentioned in that story, having heard this stanza and the sermon, even that monk Bhāgineyya Saṅgharakkhita attained the fruit of Stream-entry (*Sotāpatti-phala*), precisely by seeing the peril (*ādīnava*) of how his own mind had operated. For many people, understanding arises based on their own downfall. When one sees the peril, from then on, a keen interest arises to develop energy, mindfulness, concentration, and faith. Perhaps for this reason, and due to his past merit, that monk attained Stream-entry, and it is mentioned that a large number of others also realized the Paths and Fruits.
Now let us try to understand the meaning of this valuable stanza a little further. It is worthwhile to consider the lessons we can extract for our lives from this stanza and story. Every single point mentioned about this mind is extremely deep.
*Dūraṅgamaṃ* (wandering far) is said because, according to the object the mind takes, it can travel very fast and very far. When we think of the Akaniṭṭha Brahma world, the mind goes to that Akaniṭṭha Brahma world. It travels that far, and with such rapidity. The Buddha declared, "I do not see any other thing in this world that changes, transforms, or turns as rapidly as the mind." So, this mind spins and turns extremely quickly, faster than any wheel. Just as it turns rapidly, it also goes very far—*dūraṅgamaṃ*. Scientists say that light is the fastest thing in the universe. Be that as it may, there is nothing as fast as the mind. The mind travels far with such immense speed.
Next, *ekacaraṃ* means traveling alone, according to its own whim. "Traveling alone" means that, while the physical body of monk Saṅgharakkhita was right next to his teacher monk, his mind wandered off all alone. It conjured up many dreams about the future, like daydreaming. It went very far into the future. The mind has a nature of wandering aimlessly at its own whim. Next, *asarīraṃ* (bodiless). We recognize a person based on their body. We recognize someone by their color, signs, and so on. But the mind has no body by which to recognize it. Moreover, when we think of a journey, there is a body associated with it. But the mind has no body. Therefore, when the mind wanders, it is difficult to grasp where it went—*asarīraṃ*.
*Guhāsayaṃ* (dwelling in a cave): the "cave" refers to this very cage of a body. This is indeed a cave. A cave is a place where one can hide. The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of earth, water, fire, and wind are called *dhātus* (elements) or *mahābhūtas* (great elements). To put it briefly, this body is almost like a place haunted by "great ghosts"—that is, the great elements (*mahābhūta*). Every one of us has a body created from these four elements, known as the great elements. The mind is hidden inside this body. It is not easy to point out and say, "The mind is in such-and-such a place." Thus, all four terms—*dūraṅgamaṃ*, *ekacaraṃ*, *asarīraṃ*, *guhāsayaṃ*—indicate the subtlety of the mind. The mind travels very far. It also wanders alone according to its whim. Furthermore, this mind has no physical body for us to run after and catch. When that monk started running, four or five people went and caught him. But when the mind starts running, even twenty or thirty people running cannot catch it. The nature of the mind is such that the more you chase it, the further it runs. Thus, all of these show the subtlety of the mind—traveling far, wandering alone, having no body, and dwelling inside a cave. The stanza declares that whoever restrains, tames, or trains a mind that is so mysterious and incomprehensibly subtle, will be freed from the bond of Māra.
Just as he revealed the nature of the mind, the Buddha also showed the way of taming and taming this mind—the manner of taming indicated by the word *saṃyama* (restraint). In some instances in this Dhamma, this mind is compared to a wild bull. Indeed, like a wild bull, this mind is something ready to run wild without submitting to any control. It breaks loose and runs away. What then is the method shown in this path of Dhamma pointed out by the Buddha? Just as a wild bull is tamed by being tied to a post with a rope, the mind must be tamed. What is this post? The post is shown as the *kammaṭṭhāna* (meditation subject). Pious friends, *kamaṭahana* means *kammaṭṭhāna*. The meditation subject is a certain topic chosen for meditation. This is called *kamaṭahana*. *Ṭhāna* means place. *Kamma* means work or action. In modern terms, it is like a workplace or workshop. The workplace of the meditation practitioner is the topic of meditation—some specific subject. If it is loving-kindness meditation, it is "May they be well." If it is recollection of the Buddha, it is a word like "Araham" or "Buddho"—some meditation topic. This is the *kamaṭahana*, or the post. On this post, one must tie it with a rope. What is the rope? The Buddha has pointed that out too: *sati*. *Sati* means mindfulness. This wild bull must be tied to that post of the meditation subject with the rope of mindfulness.
What is done by that? It dispels the unwholesome states (*akusala*) that flow into the mind. It also has the nature of preventing future unwholesome states from flowing in, a state of not getting caught up in them. We can easily understand this through an illustration or a sight commonly seen even in this area. Sometimes, near a paddy field, we see a bull tied to a post. Why is it tied? If by chance the bull eats the paddy crop in the field, trouble will come to the bull from the owner of the field, and trouble will also come to the bull's owner. Therefore, it is tied to a post. But because a bull is a bull, what does it do? It goes on grazing on the grass and gradually, almost unconsciously, starts eating the paddy in the field. Right then, when the rope by which it is tied tightens around its neck, it becomes aware. Through this awareness, the bull is pulled back toward the post. Again and again, it grazes on the grass and wanders back toward the field, and again it is pulled back this way by the rope. Pious friends, it is exactly like this that mindfulness operates. Through this mindfulness, the mind is kept from wandering into unsuitable areas, allowing it to roam only within its proper domain.
In the Dhamma, a word that goes hand in hand with *sati* is *sampajañña*. Usually, *sampajañña* is translated as "clear comprehension." But a better word is "awareness" or "attentiveness" (being aware). In society, a word like "reminding" is used. But that is done by others; this is not like that. This is a self-awareness. Imagine someone faints and loses consciousness. After this unconscious person is taken to a hospital, let us say they regain consciousness. As soon as they regain consciousness, they look around, asking, "Where am I?" and search for an answer. That means they are trying to become aware. In the same way, it was without mindfulness that Monk Bhāgineyya Saṅgharakkhita was building daydreams about the future. Thus, the moment his teacher monk spoke those few words, he became aware. Mindfulness returned. That is what is called *sampajañña*. The terms that assist the meditator, therefore, are mindfulness and awareness (*sati-sampajañña*), which go together. Along with mindfulness, due to the application of mindfulness, awareness arises, and through that, defilements are suppressed.
In this way, the Buddha has pointed out a path of Dhamma based on this mindfulness and awareness. It is called the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). We call the Buddha "Buddha," which implies that we are his children—the children of the Buddha. Not only the Sangha, but anyone who has gone to the Buddha for refuge with faith, when they call him "Buddha," it signifies that they are children of that Buddha. The Buddha on one occasion declared: "Monks, wander in your father’s domain, your ancestral pasture. If you wander in your father’s domain, Māra will not find an opportunity." What is this father's domain? "Father" refers to himself. The Buddha points out the pasture as the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). Here, the four foundations of mindfulness are shown: contemplation of the body, contemplation of feeling (*vedanā*), contemplation of the mind, and contemplation of mind-objects. What are these four foundations of mindfulness shown by the Buddha in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta? It refers to a very simple form of awareness. The method employed by the Buddha is indeed wondrous.
Contemplation of the body is a certain kind of awareness regarding the body. That is, the activity of the body. In maintaining postures and so on, when walking, one walks with the understanding, "This is walking, this is walking." Next, when sitting, lying down, or reclining, one gives that understanding to the mind: "This is reclining." What is achieved by this? The scattering nature of the mind is halted. The mind gets scattered due to delusion. It was because he forgot that he had a palm-leaf fan in his hand while fanning his teacher monk, and forgot that he was standing behind his teacher monk—due to lack of mindfulness or delusion—that he behaved in that manner. If that monk had thought even slightly, "I am fanning, fanning, I am fanning here," if he had that awareness that "this in my hand is the palm-leaf fan," then that scattering of his mind would have been prevented. But what happened was the exact opposite.
That is why the Buddha points out, at a very basic level, to conduct oneself with a certain awareness of what one is doing and saying. The primary postures of the body—going and coming, sitting and standing—every one of them is reflected upon as, "I am going, sitting, standing." That awareness comes through reflection. "Reflection" means maintaining mindfulness that "the body is in such and such a posture." So much so that the Buddha points out that not only going and coming, but however the body is disposed, one knows it as it is. One constantly directs the mind to the way the body is disposed. In that way, regarding the body.
Next is the contemplation of feeling (*vedanā*). How feeling (*vedanā*) comes and goes. Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neutral feeling which is called equanimity. One is aware of how every single feeling arises and passes away. Through this understanding, the scattering nature of the mind is eliminated. When there is a rubber coating on an electric wire, the electric shock does not strike. In the same way, through understanding, when one proceeds with understanding, the mind does not scatter. That is the kind of thing the Buddha points out.
Contemplation of the mind means that due to various attachments, or due to hatred, or delusion, the mind takes on different colors, as it were. In other words, the mind changes. According to the way it changes, one recognizes it: "Lust has arisen in me, hatred has arisen in me, delusion has arisen in me"—thus recognizing the state of the mind. Next, the thoughts running and working within the mind. One understands those thoughts as just thoughts. If that monk, while all these thoughts were arising, had thought, "This is only a thought, this is only a thought. No trade or other activity of mine is actually taking place. Here, it is only the mind that is at work"—if he had that understanding, such a great upheaval would not have occurred. From this, it is clear that the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) pointed out by the Buddha are what belong to all of us who are children of the Buddha.
That is the pasture (*gocara*). *Gocara* means the area where cattle roam—the domain belonging to cattle. In the ordinary world, there is the term "pasture." But its basic idea—the word "pasture"—is often derived from cattle, referring to the area belonging to cattle where they are meant to graze. In the same way, the Buddha points out the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). He shows that the mind must constantly be made to wander within the four foundations of mindfulness. Within that wandering lies precisely that awareness which goes hand in hand with mindfulness and clear comprehension. Through this awareness, the scattering nature of the mind is prevented.
*Anupassanā* means "contemplating" or "seeing in accordance with." In this body, it is a contemplation of the body in the body. Looking at the body in the body, one understands the nature of the body. "This is the nature of the body; this is how the body functions." Next, "this is the nature of feeling (*vedanā*)." One understands each of these conditions. That is what is called contemplating. Or else, to explain the word *anupassanā*, we know that after a carpenter planes a piece of wood, he casts a peculiar look at it. He lets the piece of wood speak for itself, as it were, to see whether it is perfectly level or not. He casts a special glance at it like that. Similarly, one directs one's own attention towards all these things.
Not thinking, "this is beautiful" or "this is strong," but if there is something in the body, one understands it just as it is. It is the same with feeling (*vedanā*), and the same with the mind. Whether the thoughts that enter the mind are good or bad, one reflects on each of them in that manner. Through this reflection, understanding grows, wisdom grows. It is through understanding, when wisdom is developed to a high level, that one is able to realize Nibbāna one day. It is with such wisdom that one is able to be freed from all defilements and realize even that noble state of Arahantship.
Likewise, the Buddha has pointed out that breathing in and breathing out—which we constantly do unconsciously—is a very wonderful thing. Every Buddha attained Buddhahood through this mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasati*). *Ānāpāna* means breathing in and breathing out. That a Buddha emerges through this is a wondrous thing when one thinks about it; it is the simplest thing in the world. From the day of birth until death, this flow of breath back and forth is what takes place. Yet, within this lies the way to attain that highest wisdom. From this, we can see what an invaluable thing the Buddha has pointed out to us. Normally, inhaling and exhaling, the breath going up and down, happens unconsciously. Practicing to do that consciously is what is called *ānāpānasati*. In *ānāpānasati*, *sati* means mindfulness. One establishes mindfulness on the two processes: breathing in and breathing out.
Through this, a great understanding arises. To put it briefly, the lack of understanding of this in-breath and out-breath is a primary cause for the persistence of the notion of "I" and "mine," the view of self, which strongly holds onto the view of "I" and "mine." What we call life or vitality is indeed just this breath. But if one knows its true nature, one would think, "Where is an 'I' here?" Because we are constantly drawing in a portion of the wind blowing in the world. Sometimes it is clean air that we draw in. Then, we expel it along with the waste inside, like a bad toxic gas.
