in the course of time, a son was born, and this son was named vidudabha. with the aim of becoming even more trusted by the buddha, king kosala appointed prince vidudabha as the commander-in-chief in his childhood. in fact, nominally, he was designated as commander-in-chief from his early childhood. also, when this prince was seven years old, he asked his mother, “other princes of my age receive gifts and presents from their mother's side. why is it not so for me? doesn't mother have relatives—parents and others?” then she deceived him, saying, “they live very far away; that is why they do not send anything.”
next, when prince vidudabha turned sixteen, he asked for permission, saying, “i would like very much to see my mother's relatives; please give me permission to go.” she tried to prevent him, saying there was no use going there, but failed. having no alternative, she allowed him. a message was also sent to the sakyans: “prince vidudabha is coming.” so, this was a problem for the sakyan princes as well. gathering again in the assembly hall, they thought: “now when prince vidudabha comes, if we are to perform the custom of salutation, the younger princes will have to bow to prince vidudabha.” to prevent this, they used a trick: they sent all those who were younger than prince vidudabha to the countryside, as if sending them on some business. when prince vidudabha arrived with his retinue, the elders introduced the relatives to him, saying, “this is your uncle, this is so-and-so.” prince vidudabha bowed to all of them, but when he looked around next, there was no one bowing to him. he asked, “why is there no one to bow to me?” they told another lie there: “we have sent the younger princes to the countryside on an urgent matter.” so, after showing great hospitality and honor to them, they sent prince vidudabha and his retinue back.
after they departed, a certain slave woman, while washing the wooden bench where prince vidudabha had sat with milk-water, muttered and cursed: “this is the bench where the son of the slave-woman vasabhakhattiya sat. what a nuisance!” while she was washing it with milk-water, an incident occurred. one of vidudabha’s soldiers, having forgotten his weapon, came back to fetch it and heard her cursing prince vidudabha. when he investigated and inquired into this, he found out through gossip that vasabhakhattiya was indeed the daughter of a slave woman. that soldier went and told the rest of the army. it became a huge uproar among the army: “this vasabhakhattiya is a slave's daughter!” and the story spread. hearing this, prince vidudabha developed intense hatred and malice, forming a firm determination and grudge: “very well! this lot washed the bench where i sat with milk-water. on the day i become king, i will cut their throats and wash this bench with their blood!”
having harbored this, after the group returned, the members of this soldier group revealed this secret to king kosala. king kosala became extremely angry, thinking, “they have given me a slave's daughter!” and conceived intense rage against the sakyans. right then, he stopped all the hospitality and special privileges previously given to queen vasabhakhattiya and prince vidudabha, and began treating them in the manner of slaves. he completely suspended the hospitality and benefits given to them up to that point.
a few days later, when the buddha visited the palace, king kosala complained, “blessed one, your relatives have given me a slave's daughter...” then the buddha stated, “that is a very unjust thing the sakyans have done. to say the least, they should have given someone of their own clan. even so, great king, i tell you this: vasabhakhattiya, when looked at from the father's side, is after all the daughter of a king, and she has also been consecrated as the queen of a king. similarly, vidudabha too, from the father's side, is a royal prince.” next, he said, “the mother's clan is secondary; the father's clan alone is sufficient.” to support this, he cited a jataka story—we do not intend to relate that jataka story at this moment. recounting the *katthahari jataka*, where in the past a similar event occurred where a child was born due to a connection between a wood-gathering woman and a king, yet eventually received the kingship, the buddha consoled the king. consoling his mind with that, king kosala restored vasabhakhattiya to her former status and prince vidudabha to his previous position. but vidudabha's hatred did not cease.
we are telling this long story in brief. at a certain point, king kosala was over eighty years old, quite aged. because king kosala was extremely faithful, when the buddha was staying in a village near the sakyan country, he went to see the buddha, handed his royal insignia to his commander-in-chief named dighakarayana, and went alone to see the buddha, entering his chamber. meanwhile, the commander-in-chief dighakarayana took those royal insignia, went with the army, and made prince vidudabha the king. he did so to settle an old grudge. on a previous occasion, king kosala had put the commander-in-chief named bandhula to death. this dighakarayana was a nephew of that commander-in-chief bandhula. because he harbored that anger, he took the royal insignia and installed prince vidudabha on the throne. meanwhile, when king pasenadi of kosala came outside and looked, there was only a horse and a certain maidservant near that horse. after hearing this story, king kosala, extremely angry and with the intention of seizing back the kingdom from vidudabha, went to rajagaha seeking the help of his nephew, king ajatasattu, riding that horse, with only that woman as his follower. on that occasion, as he could not reach there before the city gates were closed, king kosala ended up passing away helplessly during the night in an open hall.
the story of king kosala ends there. now, vidudabha was indeed the king. a few days after becoming king, he remembered the hatred he had harbored in the past. thinking, “now is the time for revenge,” he set out with a large army, determined to destroy the entire sakyan clan. on the morning of that day, when the buddha surveyed the world with the attainment of great compassion, he saw the impending mass slaughter of his relatives. seeing this destruction, and with the intention of preventing it, the buddha traveled through the air. on the border of the sakyans, in the portion belonging to the sakyans, there was a tree that did not have much shade. he had gone for alms, partaken of his midday meal, and then departed. he traveled through the air in the afternoon. thus going, the buddha sat under that tree which had little shade. beyond that, within vidudabha’s territory, there was a large banyan tree with plenty of shade. now when vidudabha arrived with his army, he saw the buddha, paid homage, and asked, “blessed one, the banyan tree on my side of the border has good shade, why are you sitting like this in this hot sun?” then the buddha replied, “the shade of relatives is indeed cool.” from this, vidudabha understood that the buddha had traveled this far for the protection of his relatives. thinking so, he returned with his army. in the same way, for a second time, vidudabha’s mind urged him: “i must take revenge somehow.” so, when he went the second time, the buddha was there. he came a third time as well. even when he came the third time, the buddha was there.
thus, having gone three times, on the day he set out with his army for the fourth time, the buddha investigated the past *kamma* (action/deed) of the sakyans. this *kamma* of the sakyans had now reached a point where it could not be prevented. what had these sakyan princes done in the past? collectively, through a certain conspiracy, they had put poison in a river. perhaps with the intention of destroying the people of a kingdom downriver, they had committed the evil *kamma* of putting poison in a river, and that was now manifesting in an unpreventable manner. for this reason, the buddha did not travel there on that day. so, vidudabha went with a huge army, and it is said that they did not even fight a proper battle with the sakyans. they surrendered completely, as it were. prince vidudabha commanded his men to kill everyone who said “i am a sakyan,” but to spare the life of mahanama the sakyan (who was his mother's father) and the retinue with him. according to that command, almost the entire sakyan clan, including infants at the breast, were massacred, and vidudabha had that wooden bench washed with their blood.
having finished all that, while this army was returning, it became night by the time they reached the river called aciravati. so, the army camped there. although that river aciravati was a large river, during the dry season it was completely a bed of sand; it dried up entirely. due to such a situation, some of that group prepared to sleep on the riverbank, and some on the sandy bed in the middle of the river. after they lay down to sleep, some insects—let us say a type of small creatures like winged termites—emerged from the ground. among those on the sandy bed in the middle of the river, there were some who had not committed the evil *kamma*, and among those on the bank, there were those who had committed the evil *kamma*. those who had not committed the evil *kamma*, sleeping in the middle of the river, were troubled by the insects. therefore, they got up and came to the bank to sleep, saying, “because of these creatures, we cannot sleep here.” likewise, those on the bank who had committed the evil *kamma* were troubled when the insects emerged, so they went to the middle of the river and slept on the sandy bed—those who had done wrong. look how *kamma* operates! meanwhile, suddenly, as if a thick, dark cloud gathered—perhaps at the upper reaches of the river—a massive rain fell unexpectedly, and a flash flood rushed down, sweeping away the entire army and drowning them in the sea. thus, just as they had destroyed the sakyan clan, vidudabha and his entire host met their destruction in the very same way.
after this event, a discussion arose among the general public: “alas! this sakyan clan, the buddha's own relatives, were needlessly and blamelessly destroyed in this way by vidudabha, weren't they?” when the monks mentioned this talk to the buddha, the buddha stated, “no, monks, although the sakyans did not commit such wrongs in this life, in the past they committed that unwholesome deed of putting poison in the river. it is because that could not be prevented that it happened in this way.”
next, on another day in the dhamma assembly, the monks gathered and were talking about vidudabha: “having committed such a great sin, he did not even get the chance to return and rule as king; they were swept away by the river water.” it was on that occasion that the buddha uttered the verse we presented at the beginning. now, let us look at the meaning and the exposition of that verse.
> *“pupphani heva pacinantam, byasattamanasam naram,*
> *suttam gamam mahogho va, maccu adaya gacchati.”*
the meaning is: “just as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village, so death comes and carries off the human being who gathers only flowers, who is infatuated with flowers, and whose mind is attached to gathering flowers.” thus, although it is a four-line verse, the more we analyze it, the deeper the meaning we can extract. in all of this, there is a profound meaning within this verse that goes far beyond the mere historical event. indeed, the buddha did not merely utter this verse; he must have preached a major sermon related to it. it is recorded that upon hearing it, people even attained the fruits of the path.
if we reflect on this story, we can see how much disaster can occur due to clan conceit (pride of birth). because of the clan conceit of those sakyans, they employed such tricks. when those crafty tricks were exposed, vidudabha conceived intense hatred. it was like king kosala also developing hatred and aversion. even more so, vidudabha harbored a grudge over the insult done to him, and even though the buddha tried three times, he could not prevent it. so strong was the thought of hatred and revenge that vidudabha came for the fourth time and, as they say, seemed to have fulfilled his heart's desire—the thing he hoped for. but just as the buddha said, in the end, having fulfilled it, he did not get the chance to rule as king; he met his death.
however, from this we can realize how much heartbreak and destruction occur due to clan conceit. on the other hand, that aversion, the thought of revenge, is such a massive crime. vidudabha intended to destroy the entire sakyan clan, including young infants at the breast. and it is mentioned that he did so to a great extent. there are various historical records regarding this. some say that certain groups escaped. at any rate, that thought of revenge became the root of an astonishingly massive destruction. furthermore, even though the buddha saw the destruction coming to his sakyan clan, and though there were so many who had gone forth into homelessness from the sakyan clan, without even a trace of agitation in them, he peacefully tried to save that sakyan clan using his own buddha-power. but when it was impossible, he left it to *kamma* itself. this cycle of *kamma* is something that even buddhas and arahants cannot prevent. allowing it to take its course, the buddha accepted the truth. so, that too is an example for us. to protect his clan, the buddha employed a peaceful and very subtle method to indicate that he had come to save his relatives. apart from that, he did not make any great appeal to vidudabha. so, at any rate, that is how it was.
next, there are many things we can draw from this. now, although this vidudabha, intoxicated by royal power and wealth, and by the pride of possessions and all that, acted high and mighty, thinking “i can do all of this,” in the end, he had to experience the results of his *kamma* (actions) in this very life (*ditthadhammavedaniya*). next, we can understand why the buddha declared that the domain of *kamma* is unthinkable (*acinteyya*). *kamma* operated in such an astonishing manner. see how those small insects emerged from the earth, as if to give results to those who had done wrong, and to save those who had not done wrong. meritorious friends, even today you can recall such events. in various severe disasters—not only floods but also tsunamis (sea-water flooding) and other destructive events—how certain individuals escaped in miraculous ways. when looking at it from a worldly perspective, when we hear how even some who had led good lives somehow ended up there, we are amazed. since we are not buddhas, we cannot say definitively, but we can understand through the dhamma what lies underneath. some people have the idea that there is no influence of *kamma* beneath such collective destructions, and that these are things that happen automatically by nature. but leave aside other things, even these four elements—*pathavi, apo, tejo, vayo*—the four elements in our body, as doctors well know, undergo disturbances of wind, bile, and phlegm. these disturbances mostly occur within the underlying forces of *kamma*. it is the same with the disturbances of the four external elements. at certain times, amazing forces of *kamma* connect with them too, because the attraction of *kamma* is that powerful. that is indeed the fearsome nature of this *samsara*, which is shown as “owners of their *kamma*,” “heirs to their *kamma*,” and so forth. similarly, there is “the order of *kamma*” (*kamma-niyamata*); there are incomprehensible, amazing karmic energies. one is drawn to them. even the four great elements assist them at times. the buddha has illustrated the karmic results that affect beings in this *samsara* with the simile of “a tangled ball of string.” when we think about *kamma*, we can understand that idea. for instance, because of you meritorious friends, even if one person does a small offering, others share that merit by saying “sadhu! sadhu!!” and rejoicing in it. that is regarding merit. many do not know that one can also participate in demerit (sin). you meritorious friends get to know through various media channels that a certain enemy of yours has died, or let us say, an enemy army has been killed. this is a common thing during times of war. when it is announced that such a number of enemy soldiers have died in this war, how many people rejoice over it, jump with joy, and even light firecrackers in the end? but even if one rejoices in that manner, what is done by it? behold, one participates in the unwholesome deed. one must guard against that. there is no need to explain to you meritorious friends about sharing/rejoicing in merit. if, when someone does a good thing, one can share that merit by saying “sadhu! sadhu!!”, then demerit can also be shared in the same way. it must have been such a sharing that the sakyans did. putting poison in a river is something even one person can do. but a large group conspired, gathered collectively, and put that poison in the river.
such things happen even today. even according to ordinary law, if a group gathers, the responsibility or the guilt is shared by the entire group. even more than the legal aspect, there is a cosmic law in the world; that is what is called “the order of *kamma*” (*kamma-niyamata*). according to that, everything is contained within the buddha's word: *“cetanaham bhikkhave kammam vadami”* (“monks, intention is what i call *kamma*”). if one shows solidarity or rejoices in it through intention, then indeed, one is caught. so from this, we have to reflect on how terrifying this *samsara* is. that is why we spoke of a tangled ball of string. if you give a tangled ball of string to a cat and say, “this is tangled, untangle it for me,” it will pull it this way and that, tangling it even further. a person who does not know the dhamma, who lacks right view, interacts with the world in just that manner. when such an event occurs, he rejoices and leaps with joy, happy that the enemy is destroyed. but just like what happened to vidudabha, he too accumulates that *kamma*.
there are such terrifying things in the world. people tangle these up, gathering others' things to themselves. they get entangled with them. that nature of entanglement is present in the world. one can get entangled in good, and one can get entangled in bad. you meritorious friends have often realized the *dukkha* (suffering) that ultimately lies even in those entanglements you thought were good. even in the entanglements done thinking they are good, in the course of time, one realizes how many drawbacks (*adinava*) there are in this entanglement. you must understand what i am saying. it is the same with bad entanglements on the other hand. right there lies the terrifying nature of *samsara*.
we mentioned a word, ‘ogha’, which is found in these verses. *‘mahogha’*, ‘a great flood/torrent’. in fact, as it appeared to us, up to now we thought of *‘mahogha’* as a flood of a river. starting from inland, the flood sweeps down to the sea. that was the greatest flood. now, however, there is a new concept. a new word has also come to us—where the sea itself comes, sweeps over, and drags things back into the sea. there is such a flood too. that is what everyone is talking about now. but four floods far more terrifying than that are mentioned in this dhamma. they are called the *‘cattaro ogha’*. now we are coming to the deep aspect of the dhamma. in this dhamma, there are the *cattaro ogha*, four floods. the dhamma mentions these four floods that drag one into this ocean of *samsara*. what are these four floods? they are: *kama-ogha* (flood of sensuality), *bhava-ogha* (flood of existence), *ditthi-ogha* (flood of views), and *avijja-ogha* (flood of ignorance). briefly described, they are as follows. *kama-ogha* refers to being infatuated with the fivefold sensual pleasures, just like the infatuation we mentioned earlier. being dragged towards the fivefold sensual pleasures is the most manifest and powerful one—the flood of sensuality. one is dragged into that torrent of sensuality.
next, *bhava-ogha* (flood of existence) is in a subtler sense. beyond the fivefold sensual pleasures, there is a deeper aspect of the mind called attachment to form and formless realms (*rupa-arupa-raga*). in accordance with those, one is born in the *rupa* and *arupa* brahma worlds. the desire to be born in the brahma worlds is a form of *tanha* (craving) for *bhava* (becoming)—it occurs through craving for existence. similarly, what is called *jhana-nikanti* is the attachment to *jhanas* (meditative absorptions). we consider *jhana* to be a good thing. even the yogis of the past took *jhana* as a great thing. the buddha pointed out that even there, craving for existence is present. entering into a *jhana* is just like a spinning top. you know how when spinning a top, you wind the string around it tightly and cast it with force. as long as the top has that speed, it keeps spinning on and on. although the top stands straight, and it appears to stand straight due to the speed it has gathered, in the end, it falls over. it is just like that with the power of *jhana*; no matter how hard you work to develop them, the top spun by those *jhanas* is what keeps spinning in the brahma worlds. having spun in the formless realms for aeons, it falls, and it falls back into *samsara* itself. that is the terrifying nature of the craving for existence. those who think only of *samatha* (tranquility) think highly of these things like *jhanas*. there is a good side to them; calming and unifying the mind is good. but if you form an attachment to them, it is called *jhana-nikanti* (attachment to absorption). if you develop an unlimited attachment to *jhana*, or if you specifically target birth in the brahma worlds as your sole goal, this is what happens. because in the end, you are dragged into the ocean of *samsara*, and the problem is not resolved there.
next, *ditthi-ogha* (flood of views) refers to the sixty-two wrong views, which the buddha has specifically declared as wrong views. once one is overcome by them, it is not easy to escape from them. after the mind is dragged into them, nothing else is seen. one is blinded by the guise of views.
next, likewise, what is called *avijja-ogha* (flood of ignorance) is the non-knowing of the truth. that is the subtlest problem existing at the highest level. failing to understand the truth does not mean the mere reciting of words from memory. it is the failure to understand that this entire existence is *dukkha* (suffering), the failure to understand that this fivefold aggregate is entirely *dukkha*. what does it mean to say that *sankhara* (preparations) arise due to ignorance? because of not understanding that this fivefold aggregate is *dukkha*, those preparations, arrangements made to bring about another fivefold aggregate—those are indeed what are called *sankhara*. in short, it can be regarded in this way. it can be said that our effort to accumulate those *sankhara*, and our engagement in them, is due to the lack of understanding of the four noble truths. because in the end, everything is shown to be *dukkha*. so, the lack of deep understanding of that is indeed what is called *avijja-ogha*. ignorance, the flood of non-knowing. so that is the explanation regarding those floods.
next, another aspect of this, regarding the floods mentioned in the dhamma, is that the buddha speaks of crossing over these torrents. that is what is meant by *‘oghassa nittharanaya’*, crossing over. it speaks of crossing the flood (*ogha-tarana*). it is mentioned that the buddha crossed over all four torrents. the arahants too are said to have crossed over those four. now, why is it applied in this way? there, this concept of the torrent goes much deeper. in the exposition of crossing over this torrent, it is mentioned in certain places:
> *“panca chinde, panca jahe, panca cuttari bhavaye,*
> *panca sangatigo bhikkhu, oghatinnoti vuccati.”*
the buddha uttered this verse in reply to a question asked by a certain deity. the deity's question was as follows:
> *“kati chinde, kati jahe, kati cuttari bhavaye,*
> *kati sangatigo bhikkhu, oghatinnoti vaccatiti.”*
a deity comes and asks the buddha, “how many are to be cut? how many are to be abandoned? how many more are to be developed? a monk who has surmounted how many ties is said to have crossed the flood?” such riddles and catechism-like verses on dhamma points are mentioned in the dhamma. so, the buddha's reply to the question asked by that deity was: *panca chinde*—five must be cut. *panca jahe*—five must be abandoned. *panca cuttari bhavaye*—five more must be developed. *panca sangatigo bhikkhu*—a monk who has surmounted five ties. *oghatinnoti vuccati*—is indeed said to have crossed the torrent.
beings in the world are bound to *bhava* (becoming) by fetters (*samyojana*). those fetters are ten in number. they are divided into two: the lower (*orambhagiya*) and the higher (*uddhambhagiya*). out of these, five are forces that pull downwards. they are: *sakkaya-ditthi* (view of existing group/body), *silabbata-paramasa* (adherence to rules and rituals), *kama-raga* (sensual lust), and *patigha* (repulsion/anger). these are known as the lower fetters. these are the five that are to be cut. the simile given for this is as follows: if a bird is tied by its feet, even though it tries to fly, it cannot, can it? then, the bond tying its feet has to be cut. it is said to be just like that with the lower fetters.
next, the higher fetters (*uddhambhagiya*) are the subtle bonds known as lust for form (*rupa-raga*), lust for the formless (*arupa-raga*), conceit (*mana*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), and ignorance (*avijja*). now, what is the simile mentioned for them? when someone is hanging onto a tree, he cannot let go of that branch, can he? there, on that branch, there is an upward pull. hanging onto a branch is an upward pull. that is why it was said here: five are to be cut, and five are to be abandoned. the forces pulling downwards must be cut. the forces pulling upwards must be abandoned. having understood their true nature, once those that pull one towards the brahma worlds, such as lust for form and lust for the formless, are removed, only then are the five abandoned.
next, what is helpful for this? *panca cuttari bhavaye*—those to be developed are the five: faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*). it is through the development of these five that the cutting and abandoning of those fetters can be accomplished. next, *panca sangatigo bhikkhu*—there are various attachments (clings). the attachments known as lust (*raga*), hatred (*dosa*), delusion (*moha*), conceit (*mana*), and views (*ditthi*) must also be abandoned. such a monk is indeed called *oghatinna*—one who has crossed over the torrent. in this manner, the flood, the torrent, is mentioned.
similarly, if we analyze further and explain this verse, there is *‘suttam gamam’*, which speaks of a sleeping village. it is said that just as a sleeping village is swept away, death comes and carries one off. let us talk and reflect a bit on this sleep as well. regarding this sleep, too, there are similar catechism-like verses. it is mentioned in the dhamma that a deity comes and asks:
> *“kati jagaratam sutta, kati suttesu jagara,*
> *katibhi rajamadeti, katibhi...”*
among those who are awake, how many are asleep? among those who are asleep, how many are awake? when asked thus, the buddha declares: *panca jagaratam sutta, panca suttesu jagara*. that means, among those whom ordinary worldlings think are awake, five are asleep. what are those five? the five hindrances (*nivarana*) known as sensual desire (*kamacchanda*), ill-will (*vyapada*), sloth and torpor (*thina-middha*), restlessness and worry (*uddhacca-kukkucca*), and doubt (*vicikiccha*). the five hindrances are things that put a person into the sleep of defilements. thus, among those who are awake in the world, those who have these are asleep. that is how we have to understand it. these riddle-like verses, riddle-stanzas, are presented as riddles concerning dhamma points.
*panca jagaratam sutta*—among those who are awake, five are asleep. next, among those who are asleep, five are awake. although they appear to be asleep in the ordinary sense, if they possess those qualities of faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*), they are awake. those who have the hindrance-factors of sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and worry, and doubt are asleep. but those who have faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—these are called the wakeful factors (*jagariya-dhamma*)—are awake. let me tell you a good illustration of this. saccaka the nigantha was someone who debated much with the buddha. on one occasion, while debating with the buddha, saccaka asked the buddha, “do you remember, blessed one, sleeping during the daytime?” “yes, saccaka, in the last month of the summer season, during the day, after my almsround, i lay down on my right side in the lion’s posture, mindful and fully aware (*sati-sampajanna*).” then he said, “the ascetics and brahmins say that is a deluded sleep.” the buddha replied, “i do not call it a deluded sleep merely because of that. if someone has the defiling taints (*asava*) and other things that lead to future rebirth, that indeed is the deluded sleep. but the sleep of the other (one who is free) is not a sleep at all.” that is what we have to take in this sense. while ordinary people in the world are awake, when they possess the hindrances of sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and worry, and doubt, it is like being asleep. but even if someone is asleep, there—where mindfulness and full awareness are also mentioned—if they have developed those virtues of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, they are awake even while sleeping. so, we can draw such deep meanings from this.
next, let us consider why flowers were mentioned. it is the fivefold sensual pleasures that were compared to a flower garden. there are, especially in this era too, various kinds of optimistic attitudes in the world. even though so many disasters occur, to the world deluded by defilements, only happiness is seen everywhere.
so let us think about production now. in the commercial world—we call it commercial. what is in it? within the competitive commercial world, there are pleasing objects (*subha-arammana*). brand new, latest fashions and designs are presented to consumers at a highly competitive level. thus, there is a competition among manufacturers to present the most luxurious fashions and consumer goods in a newer way than others. likewise, on the consumers' side too, there is that competitiveness, the desire to enjoy the fivefold sensual pleasures at a level far higher than one's neighbor.
so, even though everyone pursues happiness in that manner, if we look at it from the perspective of this life, at some point they are swept away either by a flood coming from inland like that, or by sea-water coming from the ocean. in this life, there are such disastrous things. if we look at it from the perspective of the next life, from the perspective of *samsara*, they are overcome by those aforementioned *kama-ogha*, *bhava-ogha*, *ditthi-ogha*, and *avijja-ogha*, and are dragged into the ocean of *samsara* nonetheless.
that is indeed what is meant in that verse by *“pupphani heva pacinantam, byasattamanasam naram”*—going about seeking only flowers, seeking flower after flower. when one falls into that flower garden of the flowers of the fivefold sensual pleasures, one falls into the sleep of negligence and goes on gathering them. one does not understand the reality of life. what is that reality? that is what we highlighted at the very beginning here: first, the terrifying nature of this *kamma*. in fact, why is *samsara* considered an extremely terrifying place? the buddha has declared that this (unwholesome action) never passes away without giving its result. it never passes away without giving its result!
next, the buddha has shown a way to break the power of their results. at the highest level, it is broken by the supramundane paths (*lokuttara-magga*). it is through the supramundane paths that this cycle of *kamma* is broken at some point. short of that, it is broken by the person who lives according to a certain right view, having separated himself from those wrong views—which is called *kammassakata-sammaditthi* (right view that one is the owner of one's actions). at the very least, without falling into woeful states, escaping from the path of the planes of misery which are regarded as terrifying abysses and indicated by words such as *apaya, duggati, vinipata, niraya*, one can obtain at least those good human existences, good living conditions, lives that can assist in realizing nibbana. if one lives according to right view, on one hand, it is possible to make an effort to break that power of the force of *kamma*. more than that, what is to be done during the period of a buddha’s appearance is, as we mentioned at this time, in order to become *oghatinna* (one who has crossed the flood), to cut five, abandon five, and then develop another five, as said before. we must think specifically about the five to be developed: the spiritual faculties (*indriya*) known as faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*).
now, ordinary worldlings, those who walk inside that aforementioned flower garden, use only the five sense-faculties received along with our *jati* (birth). but those mentioned in this dhamma are spiritual faculties. five faculties. they are things pertaining to the mind. now, these five physical sense-faculties are common even to ordinary animals. but it is only a human being or a deity who can practice the dhamma who is able to develop these faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. it is when one attains their value that these faculties are said to arise properly.
so, next, that they are helpful is what is mentioned in the *alavaka sutta* and elsewhere: *“saddhaya tarati ogham”*—it is by taking faith as one's support that one can cross over these four torrents. to cross over the four torrents, over the ocean of *samsara*, faith is helpful as the primary factor.
next, if one receives encouragement from faith, what is done through faith? one is ready to bring forth even the energy hidden within oneself. let us imagine that after a heavy rain, a great torrent is flowing. at first glance, looking at this flowing torrent, it seems: “leave aside crossing to the other side, one cannot even think of it.” but from the other side, the buddha demonstrates with the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya-mudra*): “i have crossed over, it is possible to cross over. if you practice in this way and that, you can cross over.” behold, then faith arises. it is in accordance with that faith that one leaps into the water. otherwise, saying, “oh, how cold it is!” one would remain standing with arms folded. instead, the faithful person, deciding “death or crossing,” enters into these dispensational practices to cross over this torrent. there is such a great commitment within this faith. that is why faith is called resolution (*adhimokkha*). through that faith, energy is released. otherwise, one keeps it hidden. the capacity is there, but it does not come out. it comes out through that faith when the perception (*sanna*) arises: “this can be done.” he can go there. there are people who have gone there. he sees that through the buddha. that is what is called faith in the teacher. through the faith that arises from that, one generates physical and mental devotion/faith. up to now, how much effort does a human being make to increase the heap of *dukkha* in daily life? how much suffering and hardship does he undergo? hundreds and thousands of times more energy must be exerted to cross over this ocean of *samsara*. that is what the buddha declares regarding that energy. the buddha applied energy at the highest level. what is called the fourfold-factored energy (*caturanga-samannagata-viriya*) is: “let only skin, sinews, and bones remain! let flesh and blood dry up! if i am making this effort for a certain goal, without reaching that level, i shall not give up this energy.” applying it at that supreme level, the buddha attained buddhahood. so, even if we cannot do it at that level, we can apply an energy close to it only when we have that kind of faith.
next, although we say “energy,” it is not agitation that is there; it is not the arising of restlessness (*uddhacca*), but something that must be done mindfully. it must be done with mindfulness (*sati*). it is the energy applied with mindfulness that actually succeeds. accordingly, in applying that energy, one has to use mindfulness so that the energy is not wasted.
next, likewise, when these come together, mindfulness becomes strong, and at some point, concentration (*samadhi*) comes. what is called a more stable concentrated mind is this: up to now, the capacities of the scattered mind could not be fully brought forth, but once it is unified, a power comes to see what was previously unseen. that is indeed what is called wisdom (*panna*). one can understand the true nature of things as they are through wisdom. all of these are shown as spiritual faculties (*indriya*). these are things to be developed; through development, these must be brought forth. they are not things received for nothing from within. through engaging in them itself, these faculties must be brought forth.
it is by bringing forth faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*) that, at some point, one is able to cross over that flood. so we must constantly reflect on life. this reality is very quickly forgotten by most people. once they are overcome by the fivefold sensual pleasures, they forget the true nature of the world, and leave aside other things, they even forget the *anicca* (impermanent) nature of their own lives. life is a very short time; we live for less than a hundred years. yet within this, embracing the entire world, just like vidudabha did, one tries to perform all the exploits one can. but one never knows when or from where death (*mara*) will emerge. when past karmic forces gather together and operate at some moment, all of those become dreams. life is a dream! in the end, the entirety of life is a dream!! now, some think that at the final moment, they will be able to rejoice because of the exploits they performed in life. none of those are what will be presented before them in the end; an unexpected sign (*nimitta*) of some murder, theft, etc., which they kept hidden, might emerge. as the sign of destination (*gati-nimitta*), a thought regarding such a place as a plane of misery (*apaya*) or the animal world finally arises. when being swept away by seawater or a flood, it is not the success of this life up to now, nor the many experiences called successful in this life that are remembered at that moment. that becomes just a dream, and in the end, what is remembered in its place is the mind-produced form (*cittaja-rupa*) presented in accordance with the karmic energy that brings about the next *jati* (birth). it is according to that that the next form is created, a body is created. such is the way of *samsara*.
thus, our lives have been spent in this manner for an infinite time. it is only during the period of a buddha’s appearance that one can cross over from this ocean of *samsara*, from these four floods called *samsara*. you lay meritorious friends know better than us how daily lay life is spent. life is overcome by and drawn to various amazing forces, and within that aforementioned commercial civilization, there are amazing situations in society where the mind completely enters a state of madness. to avoid being caught in them, we must develop from within those spiritual faculties of faith, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. one must apply oneself at least in an effort to develop those faculties. likewise, turning towards a simple life rather than those various fashions and designs mentioned, on an occasion like this of observing precepts, you meritorious friends get to recognize the true value of that dhamma. it is not those fashions and designs in the world. those are things that exist temporarily and then vanish. what can be regarded as eternal values is the recalling of the values of those virtues such as virtue (*sila*) pointed out by the buddha, and maintaining one's life in accordance with them. it is through that that one can establish real peace in life. both in the past and in the present, even for those lay meritorious friends who led good lives, at least some peace could be established only by that kind of success—which we do not consider successful in this ordinary world, but is for those who led righteous, blameless, and virtuous lives in accordance with the dhamma. it is only for those who listened to the dhamma and meditated.
having understood that with wisdom, according to what is said in this verse, since we do not know at what time that death (*mara*) will come in accordance with *kamma*, we must be ready for it at any time. that is why we say in certain instances, in this disastrous and calamity-prone era we have now, everyone should actually live with the “near-death mind” (*asanna-citta*). we usually consider that when our aged parents or other relatives are close to death, we should bring a monk, preach a sermon, and think: “we must set this person's mind right”—thinking of the near-death mind, we make an effort for that. but a person who constantly has the fear of death, who has the awareness of the power of death, always tries to remain in a near-death state of mind. why? because he does not know at what moment death will come. not only from external disasters, but from illnesses and ailments coming from within the body, in an completely unexpected manner—one can be talking like this, and suddenly one's speech can stop. such things are present in this life. therefore, that is why we are constantly, as the buddha declared, said to be “prepared to die.” one can say one is prepared to die, at least to some extent, only if one has led a life in accordance with the dhamma. yet the buddha does not say that one should be satisfied even with that. why? no matter what kind of state in the brahma worlds one is born into, or even if one is born in the deva worlds, they too have to pass away (*cuta*) one day. they have to pass away from there once that *kamma* is exhausted. that top spins only as long as its energy is there, only as long as the force applied to it is there; next, having spun and spun, it slowly falls over. such is the situation in the brahma worlds and the deva worlds too. that is what the buddha pointed out to the world.
therefore, we must reflect: to resolve this fundamentally, we must bring forth that wisdom, insight-wisdom (*vipassana-panna*). we must always direct the mind towards the *anicca* (impermanent) nature of *sankhara* (preparations). that is the reality of life. the buddha has declared that reality in three words: *anicca* (impermanent), *dukkha* (suffering), and *anatta* (not-self). even though we take all of this as “this is me, this is mine,” what is here is merely a heap of efforts made to survive. in reality, there is no such thing as a life. although we call it a “life,” there is only an attempt to survive here. at times, it is merely a multitude of futile efforts. to use a simile, it is like trying to sleep on a brand new reed mat. when you unroll the new mat and try to lie down, behold, it curls up again. all the works we do are like that; just when we think they are well finished, behold, they curl back the other way.
that is what happened to vidudabha too. having tried and made an effort four times like that, he fulfilled his heart's desire. he destroyed that entire sakyan clan and tried to return after fulfilling his heart's desire by washing the bench he sat on with their blood as he had hoped. they lay down to sleep, whether in the middle of the river or on the bank, and were simply swept away by the water. it is just like that with our life-goals; just when we think we have attained each of them in a big way, sometimes due to various things they can be destroyed. even if not, at the very least, at the moment of *jaramarana* (decay and death) we have to abandon them. a moment comes when we have to leave behind all obtained positions, accumulated wealth, gathered and raised children, and finally depart. at that time, preparing the mind for that is indeed what one should do. so, the moment of conquering that is what is called the deathless, the deathless nibbana. it is the moment when the mind can be detached from this fivefold aggregate. that deathless means: one dies, but there is no fear of death. the state where one can die without the fear of death is indeed what is called *nivima* (the mind stilled / extinction / extinguishment).
what is called the deathless nibbana is not some strange food, nor a drink, nor something like a food found in the deva worlds. the deathless nibbana means, if at some moment, one can die without any fear of death. the fear of death is indeed what is present in the world, in everyone. if there is a state where one can die without a fear of death, it is the attainment of that. the noble ones who attained that state in this very life enter into those attainments—that is what is called the attainment of the fruit of arahantship—and having entered the attainment of the fruit of arahantship, they enjoy that peace (*nivima*). that is not some strange world either. what is there is liberation from the world. there is the crossing over of *bhava* (becoming). there is the crossing over of the flood (*ogha*). that is what is called *nivima*, called nibbana. the terrifying nature of *samsara* is indeed that one is born and dies again and again, born and dies. born, dies. born, dies. thus, even though we rejoice when born, we are born only to die. therefore, because of such a state, escaping from death is indeed the ultimate, highest, and most skillful thing to be done in the world. that is indeed nibbana, called the deathless nibbana. even when that word is used, you meritorious friends might think of it as a world.
but for one who has developed those aforementioned faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*), as their ultimate result, he is able to experience that strength to face *jaramarana* (decay and death) without any fear of death. that is what the buddha and the arahants experienced. it is with that goal in mind that today you meritorious friends have observed the valuable precepts and listened to this dhamma. therefore, if everyone, if every buddhist, aspires for nibbana, this is indeed what they aspire for. it is liberation from that aforementioned ocean of *samsara*, from the flood.
therefore, in order to attain that capacity, if you have accumulated any wholesome energy (*kusala*) through observing precepts, listening to sermons, and meditating up to now today, may that wholesome energy, with the help and assistance of noble friends (*kalyana-mitta*) in this very life, succeeding in sermons and meditation, assist you in quickly obtaining that! may the wholesome energy of dhamma-preaching and dhamma-hearing be a supportive condition! thus, make your aspiration. including the deceased relatives who have passed away in your names, may whatever living beings from avici up to akanittha who wish to rejoice in this wholesome deed of dhamma-preaching and dhamma-hearing, by doing so, realize the supreme and great deathless nibbana through a bodhi of their choice! aspiring thus, recite these verses and share the merit.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 079
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #79
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.134)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Apārutā tesaṃ amatassa dvārā,
ye sotavanto pamuñcantu saddhaṃ;
vihiṃsasaññī paguṇaṃ na bhāsiṃ,
dhammaṃ paṇītaṃ manujesu brahmeti.
From:
Ariyapariyesana Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 26), Vinaya Piṭaka (Mahāvagga), Saṃyutta Nikāya (SN 6.1)
Dear Listeners,
The Esala Full Moon Poya Day reminds us of the occasion when the Fully Enlightened Buddha, the Teacher of the Three Worlds, delivered the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta* at the Deer Park in Isipatana, Varanasi. It was the moment the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion. According to the history of the Sasana, today we have chosen as our theme a stanza that highlights certain important factors that formed the background to that miraculous event of setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
While addressing a group of monks gathered at the hermitage of the Brahmin Rammaka in Savatthi, the Buddha, expounding a certain phase of His life story—disclosing it—brought to light a series of events related to this stanza. The Buddha declared that after attaining Supreme Enlightenment, having spent several weeks experiencing the bliss of liberation (*vimutti-sukha*), while He was staying at the foot of the Ajapala Banyan tree, a thought of this nature occurred to Him:
“This Dhamma I have discovered is extremely deep. It is very difficult to explain to others. It is peaceful, refined, beyond mere logic, the deep Dhamma of Dependent Arising (*paṭicca-samuppāda*), the Dhamma of Nibbāna. It is difficult to understand for those who are trapped in attachment, who remain with *Taṇhā* (Craving) within attachment. Even if I preach the Dhamma, if they cannot understand it, it will only be a weariness and fatigue for me.” Thus the Buddha expressed His hesitation to preach the Dhamma. But knowing that the Buddha was disinclined to teach, Sahampati Brahma of the Brahma world felt deep compassion and, knowing the thought of the Buddha, realized:
“The world is perishing, the world is being destroyed, if the Tathagata, the Fully Enlightened One, does not preach the Dhamma to the world!” At that very moment—as quickly as a strong man would stretch his bent arm or bend his stretched arm—he appeared before the Buddha, paid homage, and made an invitation: “May the Blessed One preach the Dhamma to the world! May the Sugata preach the Dhamma! There are those in the world with little dust in their eyes who have the capacity to understand the Dhamma.” He then made this invitation to the Buddha in three stanzas.
“In the past, in this Varanasi, the Dhamma has been presented by various teachers with defilements. But may the Blessed One preach this pure Dhamma! May He open the doors of the Deathless!” he invited. The Brahma also presented a simile: “Just as a man standing on a rocky peak would look upon the people all around, may the Blessed One, the Tathagata, who has ascended the palace of Dhamma, look down upon the world of beings who are sunk in this samsaric *Dukkha* (Suffering) such as *Jāti* (Birth), *Jarāmaraṇa* (Decay and Death), sickness, and so forth.” Then, as a special invitation in the final stanza, he declared:
*“Uṭṭhehi vīra vijitasaṅgāma satthavāha anaṇa vicara loke;*
*Desassu bhagavā dhammaṁ, aññātāro bhavissanti.”*
“Arise, O Hero, victor in battle (who has conquered the battle of defilements)! O Caravan leader (*satthavāha*), wander in the world debtless. May the Blessed One preach the Dhamma to the world! There will be those who understand!” Thus the Brahma made his supplication and invitation.
At that moment, the Blessed One declares that, taking into account both the invitation of the Brahma and the Great Compassion for the world which He had cultivated throughout samsara, He surveyed the world with the Eye of a Buddha (*buddha-cakkhu*). When He surveyed with the Buddha-eye, He saw: those with little dust in their eyes, those with much dust in their eyes, those who have developed spiritual faculties such as faith (*saddhā*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*), those who have not developed them, the good, the bad, and also those who have fear of the next world, those who can easily understand the Dhamma, those who cannot, and so on—the Buddha explained to the monks that these various levels of understanding appeared to Him.
Then, to illustrate this, He declared a simile. Just as in a pond of blue, red, or white lotuses, some blue, red, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and remain nourished entirely under the water. Some blue, red, or white lotuses rise to the surface of the water and stand level with the water. Yet other blue, red, or white lotuses rise completely out of the water and stand undefiled by the water. In the same way, the various levels of understanding among the people of the world appeared to the Buddha through the simile of the lotus pond. Seeing this, in acceptance of the Brahma's request, the Buddha uttered this stanza. This is the stanza we chose as our theme today:
*“Apārutā tesaṁ amatassa dvārā, ye sotavanto pamuñcantu saddhaṁ;*
*vihiṁsasaññī paguṇaṁ na bhāsiṁ dhammaṁ paṇītaṁ manujesu brahme ti.”*
“Open to them are the doors of the Deathless. For whom? Let those who have ears release faith. I open those doors to those with ears, those with hearing.” Let those who have ears release faith. Let them direct their faith towards it. *Vihiṁsasaññī paguṇaṁ na bhāsiṁ, Dhammaṁ paṇītaṁ manujesu brahme.* “O Brahma, thinking it would be a mere weariness, I did not initially preach this refined Dhamma to the world, but now I open the doors of the Deathless to those who have ears, let them release faith!” Thus, with this stanza, the Buddha made the decision to preach the Dhamma, saying He had opened the doors of the Deathless. Thereupon, the Brahma King, being delighted, circumambulated the Buddha and returned to the Brahma world.
The Buddha then contemplated: “To whom shall I preach the Dhamma first?” according to their levels of understanding. First, He thought of Alara Kalama, who had been a teacher to Him, or rather, who had met Him during the Noble Quest (*ariya-pariyesana*) and had helped Him to a certain extent. This Alara Kalama was wise. He was someone who had suppressed defilements for a long time. He had the capacity to understand things quickly. He was capable of realizing this Dhamma very soon. Just as He thought of preaching the Dhamma to Alara Kalama, deities came and said: “Venerable Sir, the teacher Alara Kalama passed away a week ago.” Then the Buddha thought: “A great loss has occurred. If Alara Kalama were alive, he would have understood this Dhamma quickly.” Next, He contemplated: “Who else?” and remembered the other teacher, Uddaka Ramaputta. Just as He thought: “This Uddaka Ramaputta is also wise, capable of understanding the Dhamma quickly,” deities came and informed Him: “Last night, Uddaka Ramaputta passed away.” At that moment too, the Buddha thought: “That too is a great loss. If Uddaka Ramaputta were alive, he would have understood the Dhamma quickly.”
Then, thirdly, He contemplated: “To whom shall I preach this Dhamma?” He then thought with gratitude: “When I was practicing extreme self-mortification (*dukarakiriya*), these five monks were of great help to me. They are capable of understanding this Dhamma quickly.” Next, He looked to see where they were residing. He saw that they were staying at the Deer Park in Isipatana, Varanasi. Then the Blessed One set out from there to preach the Dhamma to them. On the way, between Gaya and the Bodhi tree (Bodhgaya), the Blessed One declared that He met an Ajivaka named Upaka. This Ajivaka Upaka saw the extremely serene manner of the Blessed One, saw the purity of His complexion, and questioned Him: “Friend, your faculties are so pure, so serene. Your complexion is bright. Whose Dhamma do you follow? Who is your teacher?” Then He replied: “I have no teacher.” The Buddha then uttered a series of stanzas: *Sabbābhibhū sabbavidūhamasmi...* ('I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all...'), declaring that He had attained Supreme Enlightenment and Buddhahood.
Furthermore, *“Na me ācariyo atthi, sadiso me na vijjati”* (“I have no teacher, my equal is not found in the world. I am the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One in this world”), thus He introduced Himself. However, for some reason, this Ajivaka Upaka asked, “Then, according to what you say, you are the Infinite Victor (*anantajina*)?” and having heard this, said, “It may be so, friend,” shook his head, took a different path, and departed.
Next, the Blessed One, journeying by stages towards Varanasi, finally approached the Deer Park in Isipatana. The five monks saw Him from afar and made an agreement among themselves: “Friends, here comes the recluse Gotama. The recluse Gotama is coming, having abandoned his self-mortification. Having reverted to a life of abundance (*bāhulika*), a life of luxury, he is coming in search of us. Let none of us stand up for him. Let us not pay him the respect of receiving his bowl and robe. If he wishes, let us merely set out a seat for him to sit on.” Thus they agreed. But the Blessed One expressed to the monks that as He drew closer and closer, they were unable to abide by their agreement. Spontaneously, as it were, one of them came forward and received My bowl and robe. Another from among the five prepared a seat. Another prepared water to wash My feet. However, although they performed these hospitable services, they addressed me with the term “friend” (*āvuso*) and by my name.
Then the Blessed One declared: “I told the five monks: 'Monks, do not address me by name or as 'friend'. I have discovered the nectar of Nibbāna. I have realized the Dhamma. I have attained Supreme Enlightenment. Therefore, it is not proper to address me in this manner. Lend your ears, bend your ears, I shall preach the Dhamma to you. By listening to this Dhamma, you will realize that purpose for which you went forth into homelessness.'” But the five monks did not believe it at first. “How can that be, recluse Gotama? When you could not achieve it even after practicing such severe self-mortification, now that you have abandoned that effort and become a *bāhulika*, or rather, turned towards a life of luxury, how could you have found it?” Thus they did not believe it. Even when the Blessed One declared it a second and a third time, the five monks did not accept it.
Finally, the Buddha said: “Monks, have I ever spoken to you in this manner before? Monks, have I ever made such a statement to you before?” As soon as they heard this, the attitude of the five monks changed, and they replied, “No, indeed, Venerable Sir.” The five monks, who had addressed Him as “friend” (*āvuso*) until then, now said, “No, indeed, Venerable Sir.” From this, we must learn something. What the Blessed One used there was nothing other than the miracle of truth (*saccā-pāṭihāriya*). Through the miracle of truth, those five monks were subdued. Being subdued, from that moment on, they were ready to bend their ears. It was on that occasion that the Blessed One said, “Then, monks, give ear. I shall preach this Dhamma,” and delivered the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta* discourse we mentioned.
In the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*, within this matter of setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, there are valuable points. We will try to bring out briefly only the main points as appropriate to the occasion. Actually, the Buddha directed this sermon to these five monks. Their view (*diṭṭhi*) was *attakilamathānuyoga*—the idea that liberation can be attained through self-mortification, by giving pain to the body. To help remove this, the Buddha presented the Noble Eightfold Path which He had discovered as the Middle Path (*majjhimā paṭipadā*). Right at the beginning of that discourse, He said: “Monks, there are these two extremes that should not be pursued by one who has gone forth. What are they? *Kāmasukhallikānuyoga*—which is being attached to and immersed in the pleasure of the five cords of sensual desire. It is low, vulgar, common (*pothujjanika*), fit for worldlings, ignoble (*anariya*), and unbeneficial (*anatthasaṁhita*). It is something that does not bring welfare, but leads to harm.” Introducing it thus, He called *kāmasukhallikānuyoga* one extreme. Then, as the second extreme, *attakilamathānuyoga* (self-mortification). This is not low and vulgar, but it is *“dukkho, anariyo, anatthasaṁhito”*—it is *Dukkha* (Suffering), ignoble, and unbeneficial.
So, having bypassed those two extremes, the Tathagata has awakened to the Middle Path. It is described as *cakkhukaraṇī, ñāṇakaraṇī*—giving rise to vision, giving rise to knowledge, leading to understanding, wisdom, and liberation (*vimutti*). Then, that Middle Path is the Noble Eightfold Path. You all know this: Right View (*sammā-diṭṭhi*), Right Thought (*sammā-saṅkappa*), Right Speech (*sammā-vācā*), Right Action (*sammā-kammanta*), Right Livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*), Right Effort (*sammā-vāyāma*), Right Mindfulness (*sammā-sati*), and Right Concentration (*sammā-samādhi*). This Noble Eightfold Path was then presented as the Middle Way.
Next, the Buddha briefly pointed out the truth. That is the Noble Truth He discovered, the Noble Truth of *Dukkha* (Suffering). You have heard many times of the Four Noble Truths: *Dukkha*, Samudaya (Origin), Nirodha (Cessation), and Magga (Path). It is here, for the first time, that the Buddha introduces them to the world. Each of these is introduced with the designation “Noble” (*ariya*). The Noble Truth of *Dukkha*, then Samudaya, the cause for the arising of *dukkha*. Then, the cessation of *dukkha*, which is Nibbāna. Then, the path, the practice leading to it. That itself was shown as the Middle Path.
The Noble Truth of *Dukkha* was introduced as: *jātipi dukkhā, jarāpi dukkhā, vyādhipi dukkho, maraṇampi dukkhaṁ, appiyehi sampayogo dukkho, piyehi vippayogo dukkho, yampicchaṁ na labhati tampi dukkhaṁ, saṅkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā*—thus was *dukkha* described. *Jāti* (Birth), *Jarāmaraṇa* (Decay and Death), sickness, death, association with the unpleasant, separation from the pleasant, not getting what one wishes. In short, in brief, the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*)—namely *rūpa* (form), *Vedanā* (Feeling), *saññā* (perception), *Saṅkhāra* (Preparations), and *viññāṇa* (consciousness)—these five aggregates of grasping are *dukkha*. Thus He introduced the mass of suffering, the Noble Truth of *Dukkha*. Next, as the second, the Truth of Origin (*samudaya-sacca*), He declared the nature of *Taṇhā* (Craving). *Yāyaṁ taṇhā ponobhavikā*—this *taṇhā* is what causes renewed *Bhava* (Becoming). *Nandīrāgasahagatā*—accompanied by delight and lust. *Tatra tatrābhinandinī*—seeking delight now here, now there. He then showed it to be threefold: *kāma-taṇhā*, *bhava-taṇhā*, and *vibhava-taṇhā*. *Kāma-taṇhā* is the craving for the five cords of sensual pleasure; *bhava-taṇhā* is the desire for becoming, to wander in samsara; and *vibhava-taṇhā* is the craving associated with the view of annihilation (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*), which runs counter to *bhava-taṇhā*, moving along with the concept of a self (*atta-saññā*) towards self-annihilation. Just as *bhava-taṇhā* is connected to the view of eternalism (*sassata-diṭṭhi*), *vibhava-taṇhā* is bound up with the view of annihilation.
To escape this existence, they seek a practice like suicide. But the Buddha does not approve of such things. As you know, within the Middle Path, there is a complete transformation of one's personal identity, starting from Right View and leading up to Right Concentration. The Buddha declared that it is along such a path of liberation that one gives rise to vision, knowledge, and wisdom. So, He declared the nature of that craving. Next, as the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-sacca*), He showed: *tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodho*—the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, its giving up, its relinquishment, which is the Truth of Cessation. That is what was shown as Nibbāna. Then, the path to it is the aforementioned Middle Path. As the Truth of the Path (*magga-sacca*), there are the eight factors starting from Right View and leading up to Right Concentration.
Having thus briefly introduced the Four Noble Truths, He then presents another unique analysis. Regarding each of these truths, the Buddha declares: concerning this Noble Truth of *Dukkha*, first there arose in Him the initial realization, “This is the Noble Truth of *Dukkha*.” Next, “This Noble Truth of *Dukkha* is to be fully understood” (*pariññeyyaṁ*). The world has only a partial, incomplete understanding of this. It must be fully understood. Therefore, the word used regarding the Noble Truth of *Dukkha* is: the Noble Truth must be fully understood (*pariññeyyaṁ*). That realization arose in the Buddha.
Then, thirdly, it is said: “I have achieved full comprehension (*pariññātaṁ*).” These three phases are what is called the “three rounds” (*tiparivaṭṭaṁ*). Finally, the Four Noble Truths are mentioned as having three rounds and twelve aspects (*tiparivaṭṭaṁ dvādasākāraṁ*). For some, this has been a puzzle: a Dhamma Wheel of three rounds and twelve aspects. How do these twelve aspects come about? Now, concerning the Truth of *Dukkha*: first, “This is the Truth of *Dukkha*.” Finding out something anew is itself a turn. The first turn is identifying, “This is the Noble Truth of *Dukkha*.” Next, the realization that this can be overturned from within one's own mind-stream, that this can be put into practice, is *pariññeyyaṁ*—‘it must be fully understood.’ When that full understanding is completed, the wheel has turned and is complete: *pariññātaṁ* (‘it has been fully understood’). There, indeed, you have the three rounds (*tiparivaṭṭaṁ*) or three revolutions.
Next, regarding the Truth of Origin (*samudaya-sacca*) as well: the origin is identified as craving (*taṇhā*), as mentioned earlier. First, the realization arose, “This is the Noble Truth of the Origin of *Dukkha*.” Regarding this, there is “abandoning” (*pahāna*): if it is craving, it must be abandoned, dispelled, removed. So, those three words are mentioned regarding the Truth of Origin: “This is the Noble Truth of the Origin of *Dukkha*”; next, “This Noble Truth of the Origin of *Dukkha* is to be abandoned” (*pahātabbaṁ*); and finally, “It has been abandoned by me” (*pahīnaṁ*)—it has been expelled from the mind-stream.
Next, regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-sacca*): cessation is what comes about through the destruction of that craving. That cessation is the cessation of *Bhava* (Becoming), the cessation of craving. Regarding this, it is mentioned as something to be realized, to be personally experienced. He understood that cessation is something to be realized, and then He realized it: *sacchikātabbaṁ* (‘to be realized’) and *sacchikataṁ* (‘realized’). Here too, there are three: “This is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of *Dukkha*”; “This Noble Truth of the Cessation of *Dukkha* is to be realized”; and “It has been realized by me.” Thus, that aspect too is complete.
Next, the Truth of the Path (*magga-sacca*). When these are done, the path is already developed. So, regarding the path, it is said: *bhāvetabbaṁ*—the Truth of the Path is to be developed. It can be developed. And “It has been developed” (*bhāvitaṁ*). Now, there you have the four—the Four Noble Truths. If you divide each into three in this way, there are twelve aspects (*tiparivaṭṭaṁ dvādasākāraṁ*). The Blessed One declares to the five monks: “Monks, as long as my knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana*) regarding these Four Noble Truths in their three rounds and twelve aspects was not completely purified, I did not claim to be Fully Enlightened (*sammā-sambuddha*). Only when it was purified did I make that declaration.” Thus He convinced the monks.
From this, what we have to understand is—and some of you might know this—that initial vision is obtained during the path-knowledge of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa*). Although a general understanding of the Noble Truths is obtained in that manner, it was when they were fully put into practice and perfected that the Buddha attained Arahatship or the aforementioned Supreme Enlightenment. That is what is meant by saying “it was purified”. In this way, the Buddha declared: “When my knowledge and vision of the three rounds and twelve aspects was complete, I set in motion this Wheel of Dhamma, which cannot be turned back by any deity, Mara, Brahma, or anyone else in the world.” That indeed is what is called *dhammaccakkappavattana*. He set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion there. Having set that Wheel of Dhamma in motion within His own mind-stream, He also introduced it to the world. It is mentioned that by the time the Buddha finished preaching, from among the five monks of the human world, Venerable Kondañña attained the Path of Stream-entry. This is indicated there by the words: *“yaṁ kiñci samudayadhammaṁ sabbaṁ taṁ nirodhadhammaṁ.”*
So, we can understand that the realization within the Fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), if expressed briefly, can be described by those few words: *“yaṁ kiñci samudayadhammaṁ sabbaṁ taṁ nirodhadhammaṁ.”* “Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.” That is the principle of Dependent Arising (*paṭicca-samuppāda*). So there too is a wheel. There is a wheel concerning arising and ceasing. You know that even though the twelve-fold Dependent Arising (*paṭicca-samuppāda*) was not explicitly mentioned here, even laywomen chant it in forward and reverse order (*anuloma-paṭiloma*). Within that too, there is a wheel: due to ignorance (*avijjā*), *Saṅkhāra* (Preparations) arise, and so on, until finally this mass of suffering called the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*) is built up. At whatever point ignorance is abandoned, the five aggregates of grasping cease. That is what was briefly mentioned here.
So, looking at this sutta, we might not understand how Venerable Kondañña became a Stream-enterer. But once they abandoned the view (*diṭṭhi*) they had held, once they abandoned the extreme of *attakilamathānuyoga* (self-mortification)—and they had already abandoned the extreme of *kāmasukhallikānuyoga* when they entered the ascetic life—then, when the Buddha presented the Middle Path in terms of Right View and so forth, the strength of the path-factors (*maggāṅga*) developed within the ascetic Kondañña, and he obtained that realization. The very principle of Dependent Arising is what is found within the Four Noble Truths. *Dukkha*—if there is suffering, there must be a cause for it. When the cause is abandoned, suffering is abandoned. There too, a circular nature (wheel-like nature) exists.
If anything exists in the world, there is a cause for it. When the cause is removed, by the cessation of the cause, that suffering also ceases. Thus, in every aspect, there is that wheel. It was by the turning of that Wheel of Dhamma within the ascetic Kondañña that there arose the realization: *“yaṁ kiñci samudayadhammaṁ sabbaṁ taṁ nirodhadhammaṁ.”* What is meant by “whatever” (*yaṁ kiñci*)? It is the very five aggregates of grasping (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*) mentioned earlier. If it is due to ignorance that one grasps these five aggregates of grasping, then, at the point where ignorance ceases, where misunderstanding is replaced by understanding, where the view of self (*atta-diṭṭhi*) is abandoned, where the view of self that caused *kāma-taṇhā*, *bhava-taṇhā*, and *vibhava-taṇhā* is removed—there, indeed, that realization comes to a person. It was because this was realized internally that the Eye of Dhamma (*dhamma-cakkhu*) arose in Venerable Kondañña. It is said, *cakkhuṁ udapādi, ñāṇaṁ udapādi* (‘the eye arose, the knowledge arose...’)—this is what is called the arising of the Eye of Dhamma. It is mentioned that after this Eye of Dhamma arose in the ascetic Kondañña, the Buddha granted him ordination by the formula of *ehi bhikkhu* (‘come, monk’).
After this event occurred, at that very moment, the Buddha uttered an inspired utterance of joy (*udāna*): *“Aññāsi vata bho Kondañño, aññāsi vata bho Kondañño”* (“Kondañña has indeed understood, Kondañña has indeed understood!”). It is because of this that he received the name “Aññā Kondañña” from that day onwards. When we consider how the Wheel of Dhamma that had turned within His own mind-stream was successfully set in motion within one of those five, we can call it a transformation that occurred not only within this human world. It was at that moment that—as many like to hear in protective chants (*paritta*)—the news of the Wheel of Dhamma being set in motion spread from heaven to heaven, from Brahma world to Brahma world. When we speak of the Wheel of Dhamma rolling, it is an upward rolling that takes place here. An upward rolling. Starting from the earth-dwelling deities (*bhumma devas*), it rolled through the six devalokas, and then to the Brahma worlds. It rolled onwards as the reverberating sound of this event. The news that the Blessed One had set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion in the Deer Park at Isipatana spread up to that point. So, that is the essence of what is contained in the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*.
Now, if we think a bit more about this Wheel of Dhamma, many things in the world exist as a wheel. The wheel of time (*kāla-cakka*). If we think about the wheel of time, let us first think about a day. At the end of the daytime, there is the night. At the end of the night, there is the daytime. This is how the wheel of time operates within a day. Thus it goes on through days, weeks, months, and years. Finally, in terms of aeons (*kalpa*). Even if we look at aeons, there too, the Dhamma mentions aeons of contraction and expansion (*saṁvaṭṭa-vivaṭṭa kalpa*). There is a cyclical form concerning this world. A wheel of time operates in that manner.
It is the same with the wheel of authority (*āṇā-cakka*). The wheel of authority is—like in ancient times, by the beating of drums, or let's say when a rebellion arose in a neighboring province, a king would send his ministers and generals to suppress it, and after they returned, they would report back. Then they would be given gifts and rewards. That reporting back. There too, the wheel rolls out and returns. It is a similar thing here. So, how was this reported back at the end of the Wheel of Dhamma? That is what is mentioned at the end of this sutta: *“ayañca dasasahassī lokadhātu saṅkampi sampakampi sampavedhi, appamāṇo ca uḷāro obhāso loke pāturahosi atikkammeva devānaṁ devānubhāvaṁ”*—so the sutta concludes. Just like that reporting back, through the shaking of this entire ten-thousand-fold world system and the spreading of this boundless, magnificent light, it became evident to the world that this Wheel of Dhamma had been set in motion. The wheel of authority is also like that.
There is another matter. You may have heard about kings in the Dhamma stories—in this day and age, some people might not believe it. But if we speak of the Buddha's words, for example, there is the *Mahāsudassana Jātaka*. The Buddha speaks of a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti*) named Mahāsudassana in the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* as well. Mention is made of a kingdom called Kusāvatī. Wonderful, miraculous things are mentioned there concerning the Wheel-turning Monarch Mahāsudassana of the past. The Wheel-Treasure (*cakka-ratana*) that arises for such a king. It is said that the Wheel-Treasure appears to a Wheel-turning Monarch on a Uposatha day, when he has ascended to the upper terrace of his palace and is observing the eight precepts of the Uposatha. It is with the help of this Wheel-Treasure that he conquers the four quarters, the entire world. This is how it is mentioned in the Dhamma. A Wheel-turning Monarch is described as *dhammiko dhammarāja*—a righteous king. There is a concept of a righteous reign. The Wheel-Treasure is one of the seven treasures that arise for such a highly meritorious king. In the account of King Mahāsudassana, it is mentioned that since he had heard previously that such a Wheel-Treasure arises only to a Wheel-turning Monarch, he sprinkled water on the Wheel-Treasure from a ceremonial vessel and made a determination: “May this Wheel-Treasure roll forth.” That Wheel-Treasure rolled forth to the four quarters, and the kings of those various countries accepted the sovereignty of this Wheel-turning Monarch and became his subjects. They became subjects not through war, as is mentioned there. Even though he went with a fourfold army, how did the Wheel-turning Monarch subdue them? By establishing them in the five precepts (*pañca-sīla*).
“Do not destroy life. Do not steal. Do not commit sexual misconduct. Do not lie. Do not drink intoxicants. You shall rule your own territory which belongs to you.” It is through these instructions that he subdues them. This is the kind of story mentioned regarding the Wheel-turning Monarch. But there too, it was said that the Wheel-Treasure is a highly miraculous Wheel-Treasure. It is described as *sahassāraṁ sanābhikaṁ*—that is, with a thousand spokes (*ara*), a rim, and a central hub. A great wheel with a thousand spokes, a rim, and a hub in the center. That wheel rolls forth, and the king and his army follow it. Sometimes, rolling even across oceans, having conquered the kingdoms of the four quarters, it finally returns and stands as if planted firmly in the capital city. There too, it is a turning. Just like the turning of the wheel of authority.
In accordance with that concept, you might remember the prophecy uttered by the ascetic Asita during the Bodhisatta's infancy. “If he remains in the lay life, he will become a Wheel-turning Monarch. If he goes forth, he will become a Fully Enlightened One (*sammā-sambuddha*).” So, you can understand what this Wheel of Dhamma means in relation to that concept of Supreme Enlightenment. That is why the Wheel of Dhamma is said to have three rounds and twelve aspects (*tiparivaṭṭaṁ dvādasākāraṁ*). The Wheel-Treasure of a Wheel-turning Monarch has a thousand spokes, a rim, and a hub, being complete in every way (*sabbākārasampannaṁ*). Similarly, this Wheel of Dhamma of the Tathagata, the Fully Enlightened One, concerning the Four Noble Truths, is *tiparivaṭṭaṁ dvādasākāraṁ*—three rounds, three revolutions, and twelve aspects according to the Four Noble Truths. So, that is the setting in motion of the Wheel-Treasure.
What is meant by *dhammaccakkappavattana*? Instead of the Wheel-Treasure of the Wheel-turning Monarch which crossed the ocean to other lands by the power of its motion, the Buddha’s Wheel of Dhamma rolled upwards. The Wheel of Dhamma set in motion within His own mind-stream finally rolled upwards from the earth-dwelling deities through the heavens to the Brahma worlds, up to the Akanittha Brahma world. Next, it was that sound, reverberating as a great noise, through which light and other wonders spread throughout the world. In the same way, we can understand the value of this concept of the Wheel of Dhamma.
