The next day, I would instruct three of them, while two went for alms. On the alms-food brought by those two, all six of us would subsist." In this way, the Buddha trained all five of them, and then, as you have heard, it was when he preached the *Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta* that all five of them attained Arahantship. Therefore, the *Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta* helps us to understand these Three Characteristics. For that reason, we will present it briefly on this occasion, because it is very closely connected to the life of Ven. Koṇḍañña. He became an Arahant by listening to this *Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta*.
The meaning of the words "Anatta Lakkhaṇa" is the characteristic of *Anattā* (Not-self). So, the word *Anattā* (not-self)  was placed at the forefront by the Buddha in that discourse. The Buddha began it in this way. Straight away, the Buddha says to the five: "Monks, form (*rūpa*) is *anattā*. If form were self, this form would not lead to affliction. We should be able to say to form: 'Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus,' according to my wish. But this cannot be said, and form cannot be tamed in this way. Therefore, monks, form is *anattā*."
Then the Buddha declared the same concerning form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), preparations (*saṅkhāra*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*)—the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcupādānakkhandha*). Then he asked those five:
"Monks, is form permanent (*nicca*) or impermanent (*anicca*)?"
"Impermanent, Venerable Sir," they replied.
"If something is impermanent, is it ease (*sukha*) or suffering (*dukkha*)?"
"It is suffering, Venerable Sir," they replied.
"If something is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fit to conceptualize it in terms of craving (*taṇhā*), conceit (*māna*), and views (*diṭṭhi*) as: *'etāṁ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā'*—'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?"
Then those five said: "No, Venerable Sir."
Accordingly, the Buddha made them realize the Three Characteristics, and showed them what ought to be done. Concerning the five aggregates of grasping—an "aggregate" (*khandha*) means a heap or collection, and eleven factors are gathered into this heap: past, future, present, internal, external, gross, subtle, inferior, superior, far, and near. In these eleven ways, one can think about this aggregate of form. Thoughts can arise, and this is what is grasped by the mind as "my aggregate of form." Therefore, one should contemplate all these eleven aspects through comprehensive investigation (*sammasana*) in this manner:
*“Netāṁ mama”* — This is not mine. *“Nesohamasmi”* — This I am not. *“Na meso attā”* — This is not my self.
When the Buddha declared that it must be seen with wisdom in this manner, it is seen that at the conclusion of this discourse, those five attained Arahantship.
From this, we can understand the great wonder contained within these Three Characteristics of *anicca*, *dukkha*, and *anattā*. First, let us raise a problem that many people have. In the first two verses, it was said: *"Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā"* (All preparations are impermanent) and *"Sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhā"* (All preparations are suffering). But in the third verse, it says: *"Sabbe dhammā anattā"* (All *dhammas* are *anattā*). This is a big problem even for scholars. It says all preparations (*saṅkhāra*) are impermanent. By seeing them as suffering, one develops disillusionment (*nibbidā*) toward the five aggregates of grasping; this is the path to purity. Next, it speaks of them as suffering—the suffering of preparations (*saṅkhāra-dukkha*). Thirdly, it says: *"Sabbe dhammā anattā."* What is meant by "dhammā" there is a problem for many. We can get a clue about this. You might have heard of the *Girimānanda Sutta*. In it, the Buddha points out ten perceptions (*saññā*): the perception of impermanence (*anicca-saññā*), the perception of *anattā* (*anattā-saññā*), the perception of unattractiveness (*asubha-saññā*), the perception of danger (*ādīnava-saññā*), and so forth.
The Buddha explains the perception of impermanence (*anicca-saññā*) in terms of the five aggregates of grasping: form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, etc. But the perception of *anattā* (*anattā-saññā*) is explained there in terms of the six sense bases (*āyatana*). What are the six sense bases? The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. The eye is *anattā*, forms are *anattā*; the ear is *anattā*, sounds are *anattā*; in that manner, the perception of *anattā* is structured. The last one to come is: *"mano anattā, dhammā anattā"* — the mind is *anattā*, and mind-objects (*dhammā*) are *anattā*. There is a deep point here. Because, in the end, what has to be regarded as *anattā* is the very object that comes to the mind. This is a very deep place in the Dhamma. Because, as the Buddha has shown in certain places, the Middle Path in this Dhamma does not consist merely in being free from the two extremes of sensual indulgence and self-mortification. In many places, the Buddha's Middle Path is shown with much deeper meanings than that. We have pointed out the reason for this on many occasions. The Dependent Arising (*paṭicca-samuppāda*) is its depth. Underneath lies the law of Dependent Arising. Thus, according to Dependent Arising, ultimate liberation lies in not grasping anything. So, in certain places, the Buddha points out: *"nissāya nissāya oghassa nittharaṇā"* (crossing the flood by depending on one thing after another). This means: "One has to cross over this flood of Saṁsāra by using certain things as support." That is to say, one crosses over using them as support, but one does not take them along, grasping and clinging to them, to Nibbāna.
For this, even though it does not belong to the Buddha's time but to the later *Visuddhimagga* and other texts, there is a simile. Since we spoke of a rapid current of water, here is an appropriate one. Sometimes, during the rainy season when the water of a stream flows rapidly, if there is no way to cross, there is one method: one clings to a creeper hanging from a tree on this side and swings well. Having swung back and forth and gained the necessary momentum, as soon as one reaches the other side with that momentum, one does not keep holding onto it. One lets go. When one lets go, one lands on the other side. It is such a thing that is found in this Dhamma. That is its deepest side. Indeed, scholars of the past point out that there is a wonderful Middle Path in this Dhamma. That is, one makes use of tranquility (*samatha*). "Samatha" means utilizing concentration (*samādhi*) as a support. But one does not grasp concentration either. One does not cling to it. If one develops craving (*taṇhā*) for it, one gets stuck there too. Similarly, in insight (*vipassanā*), one makes use of preparations (*saṅkhāra*). As we said, in tranquility, one attains concentration. Using that concentration as a support, one develops insight, and in the end, just like breaking through concentration, this Nibbāna is something that penetrates through that as well.
Next, what are called preparations (*saṅkhāra*) in insight: every time one directs the mind to the five aggregates of grasping, something comes to the mind. Whether it is regarding forms or regarding feelings, every such moment is like something bubbling up. These are called preparations. Because they perform the function of preparing and conditioning. Thus, the word *saṅkhāra* is described in some places in this manner: *"saṅkhataṁ abhisaṅkharontī ti saṅkhārā"* (they prepare and condition the prepared, hence they are called preparations). "Saṅkhata" means that which is prepared or conditioned. Then, it is the preparations that bring the prepared to the state of being prepared. This is the important point there. Thus, what is done by preparations is that through preparations, something is prepared; it is brought to the state of being prepared (*saṅkhata*). The Buddha points out: "Behold, all preparations (*saṅkhāra*) are impermanent." Ordinary worldlings regard all these preparations as permanent. But they are impermanent. Likewise, they are fraught with suffering (*dukkha*).
Next, finally, he points out the objects that come to the mind. In passages like *"manopubbaṅgamā dhammā"* (mind precedes all phenomena), we see that mind is the forerunner. It is by the mind itself that these *dhammas* (phenomena) are prepared. Therefore, even the *dhammas* have to be abandoned. Now, as a matter of common parlance, we say "Nibbāna," "going to Nibbāna," or "one must journey quickly to Nibbāna." But there is a wonderful thing in this Dhamma. In the end, one does not grasp even the concept of Nibbāna—the term "Nibbāna". There is an extremely deep sutta called the *Mūlapariyāya Sutta*, which points out that one does not tightly grasp any concept, not even Nibbāna, but only uses it as a support.
We can understand this point through *"Sabbe dhammā anattā"* (All *dhammas* are *anattā* - not-self). There are various other similes for this. You might have heard of a highly valuable simile used by the Buddha in the *Alagaddūpama Sutta*—the simile of the raft. The Buddha declares: *"Kullūpamo bhikkhave mayā dhammo desito"* — "Monks, I have taught this Dhamma as comparable to a raft." *"Nittharaṇatthāya no gahaṇatthāya"* — "For the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping (carrying it on one's back)." The Buddha presents the simile there in a wonderful way. A person comes to a stretch of water, which could be a large river, with the intention of crossing over. But there is neither a boat nor a bridge. Then what does this person do? He collects grass, twigs, branches, and leaves from the trees around, binds them together with creepers to make a raft, and making an effort with his hands and feet, somehow crosses over to the other side. Once he has crossed, the purpose of the raft is over. He abandons it and goes on. In the same way, the Buddha presented this Dhamma. We make use of these concepts, words, etc., as support. But in the end, we are told to abandon them too. This is a wonderful thing. In this journey, one thing has to be used to support another. One cannot abandon everything all at once.
Nor can one grasp it. Right there lies the depth of this Dhamma. This is where it differs from all other religions. One cannot grasp everything, nor can one abandon everything. Abandoning everything is what is found in *attakilamathānuyoga* (self-mortification). Clinging to everything is what is found in *kāmasukhallikānuyoga* (sensual indulgence), looking at it from that perspective. But if one contemplates more deeply, this journey to Nibbāna is presented in the structure of that simile of crossing the river.
On another occasion, a valuable point raised through a discussion among disciples, which is a highly valuable sutta showing this idea of crossing over by using various things as support, is the *Rathavinīta Sutta* of the Majjhima Nikāya. The simile in it is that of King Kosala when he had to make an urgent journey from Sāvatthī to Sāketa. In those days, there were horse chariots—but one could not travel with a single chariot. The horses would get tired. Therefore, for an urgent journey, horse chariots were kept ready at various stages for the king's urgent travel. So, King Kosala leaves the inner palace and gets onto the first chariot. Having traveled to where the second chariot is, he leaves the first chariot. He gets onto the second chariot. Next, when he reaches the third chariot, he leaves the second and gets onto the third. Traveling in this manner, in the end, when he arrives at the city of Sāketa, if his relatives ask which chariot he came by, the king cannot say "by the first chariot," nor "by the second chariot," nor "by the third chariot." He has to tell the entire story. One supported the other. Finally, he has to alight even from the seventh chariot. That is the kind of thing the simile shows.
The disciples point out another seven stages of purification (*visuddhi*) for the realization of Nibbāna: purification of virtue (*sīla-visuddhi*), purification of mind (*citta-visuddhi*), purification of view (*diṭṭhi-visuddhi*), purification by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇa-visuddhi*), purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path (*maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*), purification by knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*), and purification by knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*). This purification of virtue is solely for the sake of purification of mind. Purification of mind is solely for the sake of purification of view. Purification of view is solely for the sake of purification by overcoming doubt. Purification by overcoming doubt is solely for the sake of purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path. Purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path is solely for the sake of purification by knowledge and vision of the way. Purification by knowledge and vision of the way is solely for the sake of purification by knowledge and vision. In this manner, seven stages of purification are shown. What is shown in the end? One does not grasp even the final purification by knowledge and vision. For what purpose does one develop purification by knowledge and vision? *"Anupādā parinibbānatthāya"* — for the sake of final extinguishment (*pariNibbāna through non-grasping (without fuel / holding / grasping).
This shows us that the ultimate goal of this Dispensation is not like joining with some substance, as in many other religions. It is not joining with a deity or some mystical substance of that sort. It is liberation (*vimutti*) itself. Therefore, for liberation, that Middle Path is necessary. Because, as we see from the simile of the chariots, what is needed from the chariots is momentum. In the end, these are employed solely to generate this momentum. If we call the strength and power developed through purification of virtue a momentum, that is purification of mind. From purification of mind to purification of view in that manner, this can be well understood through the simile of the chariots. Such is the nature of what is in this Dhamma. Therefore, looking at the final chapter, even those *dhammas* are abandoned. "Dhamma" means what we conceptualized as Nibbāna. Ordinary worldlings think of Nibbāna as a strange, new world where there is no birth (*jāti*), decay (*jarā*), and death (*maraṇa*). But what the Buddha shows here is not such a thing. All of these—birth (*jāti*), decay and death (*jarā-maraṇa*), and so forth—exist within Dependent Arising (*paṭicca-samuppāda*). All of these have arisen through causes and conditions (*hetu-paccaya*). Therefore, to be freed from these, what is to be done is—one cannot abandon everything at the beginning either. First, the Buddha points out the arising of conditions (*paccaya-samudaya*). The Buddha has highlighted both the causal arising that leads to bondage and the causal arising that leads to liberation. If these things go on, one supporting the other, it will finally end in *Dukkha* (Suffering). If one goes on in this way, these things coming together will finally end in liberation. Such a wonderful Dhamma is this.
Therefore, it is difficult for some people to understand when it is said that everything is abandoned. But the Buddha points out that these have a value like that of a raft, or like chariots running stage by stage. If one grasps something, within that grasping (*upādāna*), there is becoming (*bhava*). *"Upādāna-paccayā bhavo"* — with grasping as condition, becoming arises. It is through grasping itself that becoming is prepared. Therefore, it is when there is letting go and abandoning that there is the cessation of becoming (*bhava-nirodha*). The cessation of becoming is then what is called Nibbāna. The Buddha has shown on many occasions that the cessation of becoming itself is Nibbāna. Therefore, from the simile of the raft and the simile of the chariots, what we have to understand is that letting go itself leads to the cessation of becoming.
On another occasion, the Buddha has shown this Middle Path. That too is related to the simile of crossing a stream, called the *Oghataraṇa Sutta*. "Ogha" means the sweeping flood. The Buddha points out this entire Saṁsāra as the flood of sensuality (*kāma-ogha*), the flood of becoming (*bhava-ogha*), the flood of views (*diṭṭhi-ogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avijjā-ogha*). One is swept away in these four sweeping floods. The question is how to cross over this. There too, struggling blindly does not work. Striving wildly is *attakilamathānuyoga* (self-mortification). The Buddha did that first. He struggled to cross this flood. That did not succeed either. Standing still, one is swept away. Therefore, there is a Middle Path. One can understand that in the case of such a sweeping flood, one has to cross over little by little, step by stage, using that very current to gain some momentum. Such is the way.
Next, the most special part of this sutta is the aforementioned Three Characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*). How to apply these Three Characteristics practically in daily life is a question for many. This is shown as the Buddha's own words in many ways—this aggregate (*khandha*). What we call the heap of form, the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, etc., which we grasp, was shown in eleven ways. Similarly, the Buddha has shown the way one should look at each aggregate in a manner that helps in developing the Three Characteristics: as impermanent (*aniccato*), as suffering (*dukkhato*), as a disease (*rogato*), as a boil/tumor (*gaṇḍato*), as a dart (*sallato*), as a calamity (*aghato*), as an affliction (*ābādhato*), as alien/other (*parato*), as disintegrating (*palokato*), as empty (*suññato*), and as not-self (*anattato*). Within these eleven modes is contained the very same Three Characteristics.
When it says "as impermanent" (*aniccato*), its meaning is: contemplate each aggregate, such as form and feeling, as impermanent (*anicca*). Investigate it. Next, there is "as suffering" (*dukkhato*). The aspect of disease also falls under the category of suffering; see it as a disease. Not only form, but even feeling, perception, etc., and including consciousness (*viññāṇa*)—everything. We usually think that this applies only to form when we speak of these eleven modes. But indeed, the Buddha asks us to apply this comprehensive investigation (*sammasana*) in eleven modes to all of the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcupādānakkhandha*): form, feeling, perception, preparations, and consciousness. Why? For the sake of developing disillusionment (*nibbidā*) toward them—it is through that disillusionment that comprehension and liberation arise.
Now, in these verses too, it was said: *"yadā paññāya passati"* — when one sees with wisdom. At whatever time one sees these as impermanent and as suffering through wisdom, then disillusionment (*nibbidā*) toward the suffering of the five aggregates of grasping arises. Therefore, as impermanent (*aniccato*), as suffering (*dukkhato*), as a disease (*rogato*)—disease too can be taken as suffering. A boil (*gaṇḍato*) too can be taken as suffering. *"Aghato"* means a wound—some people have festering wounds. Similarly, affliction (*ābādhato*) is directly suffering (*dukkha*). Next, there is "as alien" (*parato*)—which means to look at it as if looking at someone else's property. He asks us to look at it as if looking at another's thing, as alien (*parato*). "As disintegrating" (*palokato*) means as things that break; there too, impermanence (*aniccata*) is present. Damage/decay. Alien (*parato*), disintegrating (*palokato*). Next, "as empty" (*suññato*) relates to the vision of *Anattā* (Not-self). In many places, the Buddha has chosen the word "empty" as: *"suññamidaṁ attena vā attaniyena vā"* — empty of a self or of what belongs to a self. That vision is "empty" (*suññato*). Finally:
"As not-self" (*anattato*) — look at them as *anattā*. These are the eleven modes. The eleven modes mentioned earlier are for understanding what each aggregate is. It is so broad. It is broad in terms of past, future, present, etc. And the way to look at them is what was just mentioned.
If one gets used to applying that comprehensive investigation (*sammasana*) as impermanent (*anicca*) and as suffering (*dukkha*) based on the things one experiences in daily life, gradually that turning away (*nirveda*) and disillusionment (*nibbidā*) will grow. As a result of that, one can attain liberation. For those who have practiced this for a long time in past Saṁsāra, even a single sermon of the Buddha might be enough. But for others, they must practice and train in these Three Characteristics in daily life. One must see those things that are seen as impermanent, as suffering, and as *Anattā* (Not-self) according to the clues given by the Buddha. In some places, it is shown in an even broader manner—not just eleven, but in eighteen ways, in forty ways. This is called comprehensive investigation (*sammasana*). What the world does is misapprehension and clinging (*parāmasana*)—grasping tightly. Instead of that, one investigates (*sammasana*): "This is of such a nature." If one practices that in daily life, one can largely conquer those concepts in the mind. Concentration (*samādhi*) also helps with that in daily life.
So, you must make an effort regarding all of these during the brief period of time received in this life. From all sides, the floods (*ogha*) and so forth are constantly flowing. In such an era, it is up to each individual, based on these clues highlighted by the Buddha, to develop disillusionment (*nibbidā*) toward the five aggregates of grasping, and accordingly develop concentration (*samādhi*) and other qualities that support it. Through that, one can realize those supreme goals in this very life. I expect to conclude a bit briefly today.
You should consider taking advantage of at least this much that was said. Now, having understood in a broader manner that advice given by Ven. Aññā Koṇḍañña by looking at our own thoughts and wishes, if we develop insight (*vipassanā*) based on the things we encounter, meet, and experience in daily life, then at a moment when we least expect it, we can attain the realization of the Path and Fruit we hope for. Indeed, that noble state is often attained when one does not expect it.
Because as long as expectation is there, during that time, the aforementioned insight (*vipassanā*) does not operate. Expectation is necessary, and determination is also necessary. But one must be engaged in the work. When one is engaged in the work, if those factors have matured, at some point, one will be able to realize them through that very state of direct experience. Therefore, consider this briefly and shape your lives accordingly. So far, having observed virtue and practiced meditation to some extent, may you take what is to be taken from this Dhamma sermon, and may you gain the strength and power to realize those expected states as quickly as possible! This is my wish.

from:
dhammapada 277–279 (magga-vaggamu)
dear listeners,
the honor of being the first member of the sangha community established by the tathagata, the fully self-awakened one, belongs to the great arahant anna kondanna. for this very reason, the buddha bestowed upon him the chief position (*etadagga*) among the monks of long standing (*rattannu*). "monk of long standing," devotees, means a monk who has spent many nights, many days—that is to say, a long period of time—in this dispensation. the oldest monk. furthermore, as you have heard, the honor also belongs to the great arahant anna kondanna as the monk who was the very first among human beings to realize the fruit of stream-entry (*sotapatti-phala*) upon listening to the buddha’s first dhamma sermon.
according to the theragatha commentary, this great arahant anna kondanna was one who had fulfilled the perfections (*paramis*) in the dispensations of past buddhas in order to achieve this chief position. thus, even before our buddha appeared in the world, ven. kondanna was born into an eminent family in the brahmin village named donavatthu, close to the city of kapilavastu. by his clan name, he was known as kondanna. later, when the bodhisatta passed away from the tusita heaven and was born as the son of king suddhodana, on the auspicious occasion of the naming ceremony, one hundred and eight brahmins were invited to the palace. among them, by that time, the brahmin kondanna had mastered the three vedas and the science of physiognomy (body marks) to their absolute limit. not only was the brahmin kondanna included among those one hundred and eight, but out of those, only eight were assigned the task of examining the prince's bodily marks and giving him a name. the eight brahmins assigned to this important task were rama, dhaja, lakkhana, manti, kondanna, bhoja, suyama, and sudatta. among these eight, the brahmin kondanna was the youngest. then, as described there, after examining the marks, all the other seven brahmins raised two fingers and declared: "if he remains in the lay life, he will become a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*). if he renounces, he will become a buddha." however, the brahmin kondanna raised only one finger and said: "this prince will definitely attain supreme self-awakening (*sambodhi*)."
so, after those auspicious ceremonies were over, those seven brahmins went to their respective homes and told their children: "by the time this prince attains buddhahood, we will not be alive. therefore, when a dispensation is established, you at least must ordain in the dispensation of that buddha." having said this, it was not long before they passed away. then, as we have all heard, at the age of twenty-nine, prince siddhartha made the great renunciation. having renounced and gradually making his way, by the time he began practicing self-mortification (*duskarakriya*) in the uruvela district, the brahmin kondanna went to the homes of the other brahmins and told their children: "if your fathers were alive, they would ordain at this moment. therefore, i have now resolved to ordain following that great being, that noble prince. if you also wish, join me." only four of them came forward. accordingly, in addition to the brahmin kondanna, the other brahmins—bhaddiya, vappa, mahanama, and assaji—who are known to everyone as the "group of five monks" (*pancavaggiya*), set out and went to the uruvela district, where they attended upon our bodhisatta for six years during his practice of self-mortification.
next, as you may have also heard, when the buddha practiced self-mortification and realized its futility, he entered upon the middle path, abandoned those painful austerities, and inclined toward a balanced life. accordingly, unlike how he had previously rejected food, he then went for alms in search of solid food. seeing this, the group of five monks became disillusioned. they thought, "now this ascetic gotama has abandoned effort and has turned to a life of abundance," and having become disillusioned, they abandoned him and went to isipatana in varanasi (benares).
meanwhile, as everyone has heard, on the full moon day of vesak, the buddha attained supreme self-awakening in this manner, spent the seven weeks at the foot of the bodhi tree, and due to the invitation of brahma and other matters, made the determination to teach the dhamma. he then contemplated to whom he should first preach this dhamma. first, the ascetic alara kalama came to his mind. you have heard that when the buddha first went in search of teachers, he first took alara kalama as his teacher. when he thought about it, unfortunately, the ascetic alara kalama had passed away a week earlier. next, he thought of the ascetic uddaka ramaputta. he too had passed away the previous night. it was only after that that the buddha thought, "i must go in search of the group of five monks who were of great help to me. they will be able to understand this dhamma." from that point onward, many of the details are mentioned in a wonderful way in the buddha's own words in the *ariya pariyesana sutta*.
the buddha says: "when i set out and approached isipatana in varanasi, the group of five monks saw me from afar and made an agreement among themselves: 'here comes the ascetic gotama, who abandoned his striving and has now turned to a luxurious life. let us not pay homage or show respect to him. let us not go forward to receive his bowl and robes, but let us only set out a seat; if he wishes, let him sit.' despite making such an agreement," the buddha declares, "as i came closer and closer, those five monks were unable to keep to their agreement. some came forward and received my bowl and robes. another prepared a seat. another prepared water to wash my feet." however, those five addressed the buddha using the term of address *'avuso'* (friend/brother). "they addressed him by name as 'avuso gotama' and in the manner of 'avuso'." then the buddha said to the group of five monks: "monks, do not address the tathagata by the name *'avuso'*. i have attained supreme self-awakening (*samma sambodhi*), i have attained the deathless—nibbana. therefore, listen, i shall teach the dhamma."
then those five said: "when you did not attain buddhahood through such severe austerities, how can you attain it through this lax lifestyle?" and they did not accept it. a second time the buddha spoke. a second time the group of five monks rejected it. a third time he spoke. but a third time too they rejected it. at that moment, the buddha did not perform any other miracle, but rather the miracle of truth. he asked: "monks, did i ever speak to you in this manner before?" at that moment, faith arose in the group of five monks, and addressing him as "venerable sir" (*bhante*), they accepted it. it was after that, as you have heard, that he preached the *dhammacakkappavattana sutta* not only to the group of five monks but also to the devas, brahmas, and others. at the end of that sutta discourse, because the monk kondanna attained the fruit of stream-entry, you will find a passage in the *dhammacakkappavattana sutta* where the buddha uttered an inspired utterance (*udana*): *"annasi vata bho kondanno, annasi vata bho kondanno!"* that means, "kondanna has indeed understood, has comprehended, has realized the dhamma." it was through this that ven. kondanna received the name "anna kondanna."
then it is mentioned that at one time, the buddha bestowed upon ven. kondanna the chief position (*etadagga*) among the monks of long standing, as mentioned before. however, as the nature of ven. kondanna is shown to us, he was extremely humble. the chief disciples, such as sariputta and moggallana, would constantly pay homage and respect to him as an elder. he rejected all of this, and in order to dwell devoted to meditation, he lived for twelve years in a solitary place in the himalayas known by the name chaddanta, receiving service from elephants, as recorded in the books. it is said that even sakka came to him during that time to engage in dhamma discussions. the verses we have taken as our theme, according to what is stated in that book, were uttered by him while residing there, having observed how the minds of worldlings (*puthujjana*) behave, and demonstrating the dhamma method and the dhamma path to conquer them. let us look at their meaning.
*bahuni loke vicitrani asmim pathavimandale*
*mathenti manne sankappam subham ragupasamhitam*
"there are many variegated things, variegated objects in this world, or rather, on this earthly sphere. these—i think—agitate the lustful intentions and thoughts (*sankappa*) arisen due to the perception of beauty (*subha-sanna*)." then he says:
*rajamuhatanca vatena yatha meghopasammaye*
*evam sammanti sankappa yada pannaya passati*
"just as the dust raised by the wind is calmed by a great rain cloud, so too do those defiled thoughts and intentions (*sankappa*) calm down at whatever time one sees with wisdom." having said this, next, the method of seeing with wisdom is mentioned by quoting the three very famous verses related to the three characteristics (*tilakkhana*), which you have heard so often.
*sabbe sankhara aniccati yada pannaya passati*
*atha nibbindati dukkhe esa maggo visuddhiya*
"at whatever time one sees with wisdom that every *sankhara* (formation) is *anicca* (impermanent), at that moment one becomes disillusioned with *dukkha* (suffering). this itself is the path to purity." in the next verse, there is only a slight difference:
*sabbe sankhara dukkhati yada pannaya passati*
*atha nibbindati dukkhe esa maggo visuddhiya*
"at whatever time one sees with wisdom that every *sankhara* (formation) is *dukkha* (suffering), at that moment one becomes disillusioned with this *dukkha*—that is to say, the *dukkha* of the five aggregates of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*). 'nibbindati' means to become disillusioned. this is the path to purity." now, the third verse is slightly different from this:
*sabbe dhamma anattati yada pannaya passati*
*atha nibbindati dukkhe esa maggo visuddhiya*
"at whatever time one sees with wisdom that all *dhammas* (all things / phenomena) are *anatta* (not-self) , then one becomes disillusioned with this *dukkha* of the five aggregates of grasping. this is the path to purity." thus he uttered these three verses. now, these dhamma points are worth discussing a little. here, he indicates the three characteristics through these three verses. he declared that it is precisely by means of the three characteristics that those defiled thoughts and intentions can be conquered. at the same time, some people raise a question: "why did the brahmin kondanna not believe when the buddha attained self-awakening, even though he had predicted in the past that this prince would definitely become a buddha?" someone might raise such a question. but what we have to understand is that the idea prevalent among most people at that time was that in order to realize nibbana, one must subject the body to pain—self-mortification (*attakilamathanuyoga*). that is why they became disillusioned and left. they did not know anything about a "middle path". however, we can understand that the buddha must have preached the *dhammacakkappavattana sutta* in that manner precisely to dispel this wrong view of the group of five monks. because, as you know, the most fundamental point of the *dhammacakkappavattana sutta* is the showing of two extremes: devotion to sensual pleasures (*kamasukhallikanuyoga*) and devotion to self-mortification (*attakilamathanuyoga*). without going to either, the buddha presented the noble eightfold path at that time, stating, "i have discovered a middle path." therefore, among the five, the monk kondanna attained the fruit of stream-entry because he understood before the others that the prediction he had given in his childhood had indeed come true.
later, the buddha himself once made this amazing statement: "during the remaining days, this is how i trained these five for arahantship. i did this: i would instruct two of them, while the other three went for alms. on the food brought by those three, all six of us would survive. the next day, i would instruct three of them, while two went for alms. on the alms-food brought by those two, all six of us would subsist." in this way, the buddha trained all five of them, and then, as you have heard, it was when he preached the *anattalakkhana sutta* that all five of them attained arahantship. therefore, the *anattalakkhana sutta* helps us to understand these three characteristics. for that reason, we will present it briefly on this occasion, because it is very closely connected to the life of ven. kondanna. he became an arahant by listening to this *anattalakkhana sutta*.
the meaning of the words "anatta lakkhana" is the characteristic of *anatta* (not-self). so, the word *anatta* (not-self)  was placed at the forefront by the buddha in that discourse. the buddha began it in this way. straight away, the buddha says to the five: "monks, form (*rupa*) is *anatta*. if form were self, this form would not lead to affliction. we should be able to say to form: 'let my form be thus; let my form not be thus,' according to my wish. but this cannot be said, and form cannot be tamed in this way. therefore, monks, form is *anatta*."
then the buddha declared the same concerning form (*rupa*), feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), preparations (*sankhara*), and consciousness (*vinnana*)—the five aggregates of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*). then he asked those five:
"monks, is form permanent (*nicca*) or impermanent (*anicca*)?"
"impermanent, venerable sir," they replied.
"if something is impermanent, is it ease (*sukha*) or suffering (*dukkha*)?"
"it is suffering, venerable sir," they replied.
"if something is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fit to conceptualize it in terms of craving (*tanha*), conceit (*mana*), and views (*ditthi*) as: *'etam mama, esohamasmi, eso me atta'*—'this is mine, this i am, this is my self'?"
then those five said: "no, venerable sir."
accordingly, the buddha made them realize the three characteristics, and showed them what ought to be done. concerning the five aggregates of grasping—an "aggregate" (*khandha*) means a heap or collection, and eleven factors are gathered into this heap: past, future, present, internal, external, gross, subtle, inferior, superior, far, and near. in these eleven ways, one can think about this aggregate of form. thoughts can arise, and this is what is grasped by the mind as "my aggregate of form." therefore, one should contemplate all these eleven aspects through comprehensive investigation (*sammasana*) in this manner:
*“netam mama”* — this is not mine. *“nesohamasmi”* — this i am not. *“na meso atta”* — this is not my self.
when the buddha declared that it must be seen with wisdom in this manner, it is seen that at the conclusion of this discourse, those five attained arahantship.
from this, we can understand the great wonder contained within these three characteristics of *anicca*, *dukkha*, and *anatta*. first, let us raise a problem that many people have. in the first two verses, it was said: *"sabbe sankhara anicca"* (all preparations are impermanent) and *"sabbe sankhara dukkha"* (all preparations are suffering). but in the third verse, it says: *"sabbe dhamma anatta"* (all *dhammas* are *anatta*). this is a big problem even for scholars. it says all preparations (*sankhara*) are impermanent. by seeing them as suffering, one develops disillusionment (*nibbida*) toward the five aggregates of grasping; this is the path to purity. next, it speaks of them as suffering—the suffering of preparations (*sankhara-dukkha*). thirdly, it says: *"sabbe dhamma anatta."* what is meant by "dhamma" there is a problem for many. we can get a clue about this. you might have heard of the *girimananda sutta*. in it, the buddha points out ten perceptions (*sanna*): the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*), the perception of *anatta* (*anatta-sanna*), the perception of unattractiveness (*asubha-sanna*), the perception of danger (*adinava-sanna*), and so forth.
the buddha explains the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*) in terms of the five aggregates of grasping: form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, etc. but the perception of *anatta* (*anatta-sanna*) is explained there in terms of the six sense bases (*ayatana*). what are the six sense bases? the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. the eye is *anatta*, forms are *anatta*; the ear is *anatta*, sounds are *anatta*; in that manner, the perception of *anatta* is structured. the last one to come is: *"mano anatta, dhamma anatta"* — the mind is *anatta*, and mind-objects (*dhamma*) are *anatta*. there is a deep point here. because, in the end, what has to be regarded as *anatta* is the very object that comes to the mind. this is a very deep place in the dhamma. because, as the buddha has shown in certain places, the middle path in this dhamma does not consist merely in being free from the two extremes of sensual indulgence and self-mortification. in many places, the buddha's middle path is shown with much deeper meanings than that. we have pointed out the reason for this on many occasions. the dependent arising (*paticca-samuppada*) is its depth. underneath lies the law of dependent arising. thus, according to dependent arising, ultimate liberation lies in not grasping anything. so, in certain places, the buddha points out: *"nissaya nissaya oghassa nittharana"* (crossing the flood by depending on one thing after another). this means: "one has to cross over this flood of samsara by using certain things as support." that is to say, one crosses over using them as support, but one does not take them along, grasping and clinging to them, to nibbana.
for this, even though it does not belong to the buddha's time but to the later *visuddhimagga* and other texts, there is a simile. since we spoke of a rapid current of water, here is an appropriate one. sometimes, during the rainy season when the water of a stream flows rapidly, if there is no way to cross, there is one method: one clings to a creeper hanging from a tree on this side and swings well. having swung back and forth and gained the necessary momentum, as soon as one reaches the other side with that momentum, one does not keep holding onto it. one lets go. when one lets go, one lands on the other side. it is such a thing that is found in this dhamma. that is its deepest side. indeed, scholars of the past point out that there is a wonderful middle path in this dhamma. that is, one makes use of tranquility (*samatha*). "samatha" means utilizing concentration (*samadhi*) as a support. but one does not grasp concentration either. one does not cling to it. if one develops craving (*tanha*) for it, one gets stuck there too. similarly, in insight (*vipassana*), one makes use of preparations (*sankhara*). as we said, in tranquility, one attains concentration. using that concentration as a support, one develops insight, and in the end, just like breaking through concentration, this nibbana is something that penetrates through that as well.
next, what are called preparations (*sankhara*) in insight: every time one directs the mind to the five aggregates of grasping, something comes to the mind. whether it is regarding forms or regarding feelings, every such moment is like something bubbling up. these are called preparations. because they perform the function of preparing and conditioning. thus, the word *sankhara* is described in some places in this manner: *"sankhatam abhisankharonti ti sankhara"* (they prepare and condition the prepared, hence they are called preparations). "sankhata" means that which is prepared or conditioned. then, it is the preparations that bring the prepared to the state of being prepared. this is the important point there. thus, what is done by preparations is that through preparations, something is prepared; it is brought to the state of being prepared (*sankhata*). the buddha points out: "behold, all preparations (*sankhara*) are impermanent." ordinary worldlings regard all these preparations as permanent. but they are impermanent. likewise, they are fraught with suffering (*dukkha*).
next, finally, he points out the objects that come to the mind. in passages like *"manopubbangama dhamma"* (mind precedes all phenomena), we see that mind is the forerunner. it is by the mind itself that these *dhammas* (phenomena) are prepared. therefore, even the *dhammas* have to be abandoned. now, as a matter of common parlance, we say "nibbana," "going to nibbana," or "one must journey quickly to nibbana." but there is a wonderful thing in this dhamma. in the end, one does not grasp even the concept of nibbana—the term "nibbana". there is an extremely deep sutta called the *mulapariyaya sutta*, which points out that one does not tightly grasp any concept, not even nibbana, but only uses it as a support.
we can understand this point through *"sabbe dhamma anatta"* (all *dhammas* are *anatta* - not-self). there are various other similes for this. you might have heard of a highly valuable simile used by the buddha in the *alagaddupama sutta*—the simile of the raft. the buddha declares: *"kullupamo bhikkhave maya dhammo desito"* — "monks, i have taught this dhamma as comparable to a raft." *"nittharanatthaya no gahanatthaya"* — "for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping (carrying it on one's back)." the buddha presents the simile there in a wonderful way. a person comes to a stretch of water, which could be a large river, with the intention of crossing over. but there is neither a boat nor a bridge. then what does this person do? he collects grass, twigs, branches, and leaves from the trees around, binds them together with creepers to make a raft, and making an effort with his hands and feet, somehow crosses over to the other side. once he has crossed, the purpose of the raft is over. he abandons it and goes on. in the same way, the buddha presented this dhamma. we make use of these concepts, words, etc., as support. but in the end, we are told to abandon them too. this is a wonderful thing. in this journey, one thing has to be used to support another. one cannot abandon everything all at once.
nor can one grasp it. right there lies the depth of this dhamma. this is where it differs from all other religions. one cannot grasp everything, nor can one abandon everything. abandoning everything is what is found in *attakilamathanuyoga* (self-mortification). clinging to everything is what is found in *kamasukhallikanuyoga* (sensual indulgence), looking at it from that perspective. but if one contemplates more deeply, this journey to nibbana is presented in the structure of that simile of crossing the river.
on another occasion, a valuable point raised through a discussion among disciples, which is a highly valuable sutta showing this idea of crossing over by using various things as support, is the *rathavinita sutta* of the majjhima nikaya. the simile in it is that of king kosala when he had to make an urgent journey from savatthi to saketa. in those days, there were horse chariots—but one could not travel with a single chariot. the horses would get tired. therefore, for an urgent journey, horse chariots were kept ready at various stages for the king's urgent travel. so, king kosala leaves the inner palace and gets onto the first chariot. having traveled to where the second chariot is, he leaves the first chariot. he gets onto the second chariot. next, when he reaches the third chariot, he leaves the second and gets onto the third. traveling in this manner, in the end, when he arrives at the city of saketa, if his relatives ask which chariot he came by, the king cannot say "by the first chariot," nor "by the second chariot," nor "by the third chariot." he has to tell the entire story. one supported the other. finally, he has to alight even from the seventh chariot. that is the kind of thing the simile shows.
the disciples point out another seven stages of purification (*visuddhi*) for the realization of nibbana: purification of virtue (*sila-visuddhi*), purification of mind (*citta-visuddhi*), purification of view (*ditthi-visuddhi*), purification by overcoming doubt (*kankhavitarana-visuddhi*), purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path (*maggamagga-nanadassana-visuddhi*), purification by knowledge and vision of the way (*patipada-nanadassana-visuddhi*), and purification by knowledge and vision (*nanadassana-visuddhi*). this purification of virtue is solely for the sake of purification of mind. purification of mind is solely for the sake of purification of view. purification of view is solely for the sake of purification by overcoming doubt. purification by overcoming doubt is solely for the sake of purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path. purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path is solely for the sake of purification by knowledge and vision of the way. purification by knowledge and vision of the way is solely for the sake of purification by knowledge and vision. in this manner, seven stages of purification are shown. what is shown in the end? one does not grasp even the final purification by knowledge and vision. for what purpose does one develop purification by knowledge and vision? *"anupada parinibbanatthaya"* — for the sake of final extinguishment (*parinibbana through non-grasping (without fuel / holding / grasping).
this shows us that the ultimate goal of this dispensation is not like joining with some substance, as in many other religions. it is not joining with a deity or some mystical substance of that sort. it is liberation (*vimutti*) itself. therefore, for liberation, that middle path is necessary. because, as we see from the simile of the chariots, what is needed from the chariots is momentum. in the end, these are employed solely to generate this momentum. if we call the strength and power developed through purification of virtue a momentum, that is purification of mind. from purification of mind to purification of view in that manner, this can be well understood through the simile of the chariots. such is the nature of what is in this dhamma. therefore, looking at the final chapter, even those *dhammas* are abandoned. "dhamma" means what we conceptualized as nibbana. ordinary worldlings think of nibbana as a strange, new world where there is no birth (*jati*), decay (*jara*), and death (*marana*). but what the buddha shows here is not such a thing. all of these—birth (*jati*), decay and death (*jara-marana*), and so forth—exist within dependent arising (*paticca-samuppada*). all of these have arisen through causes and conditions (*hetu-paccaya*). therefore, to be freed from these, what is to be done is—one cannot abandon everything at the beginning either. first, the buddha points out the arising of conditions (*paccaya-samudaya*). the buddha has highlighted both the causal arising that leads to bondage and the causal arising that leads to liberation. if these things go on, one supporting the other, it will finally end in *dukkha* (suffering). if one goes on in this way, these things coming together will finally end in liberation. such a wonderful dhamma is this.
therefore, it is difficult for some people to understand when it is said that everything is abandoned. but the buddha points out that these have a value like that of a raft, or like chariots running stage by stage. if one grasps something, within that grasping (*upadana*), there is becoming (*bhava*). *"upadana-paccaya bhavo"* — with grasping as condition, becoming arises. it is through grasping itself that becoming is prepared. therefore, it is when there is letting go and abandoning that there is the cessation of becoming (*bhava-nirodha*). the cessation of becoming is then what is called nibbana. the buddha has shown on many occasions that the cessation of becoming itself is nibbana. therefore, from the simile of the raft and the simile of the chariots, what we have to understand is that letting go itself leads to the cessation of becoming.
on another occasion, the buddha has shown this middle path. that too is related to the simile of crossing a stream, called the *oghatarana sutta*. "ogha" means the sweeping flood. the buddha points out this entire samsara as the flood of sensuality (*kama-ogha*), the flood of becoming (*bhava-ogha*), the flood of views (*ditthi-ogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avijja-ogha*). one is swept away in these four sweeping floods. the question is how to cross over this. there too, struggling blindly does not work. striving wildly is *attakilamathanuyoga* (self-mortification). the buddha did that first. he struggled to cross this flood. that did not succeed either. standing still, one is swept away. therefore, there is a middle path. one can understand that in the case of such a sweeping flood, one has to cross over little by little, step by stage, using that very current to gain some momentum. such is the way.
next, the most special part of this sutta is the aforementioned three characteristics (*tilakkhana*). how to apply these three characteristics practically in daily life is a question for many. this is shown as the buddha's own words in many ways—this aggregate (*khandha*). what we call the heap of form, the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, etc., which we grasp, was shown in eleven ways. similarly, the buddha has shown the way one should look at each aggregate in a manner that helps in developing the three characteristics: as impermanent (*aniccato*), as suffering (*dukkhato*), as a disease (*rogato*), as a boil/tumor (*gandato*), as a dart (*sallato*), as a calamity (*aghato*), as an affliction (*abadhato*), as alien/other (*parato*), as disintegrating (*palokato*), as empty (*sunnato*), and as not-self (*anattato*). within these eleven modes is contained the very same three characteristics.
when it says "as impermanent" (*aniccato*), its meaning is: contemplate each aggregate, such as form and feeling, as impermanent (*anicca*). investigate it. next, there is "as suffering" (*dukkhato*). the aspect of disease also falls under the category of suffering; see it as a disease. not only form, but even feeling, perception, etc., and including consciousness (*vinnana*)—everything. we usually think that this applies only to form when we speak of these eleven modes. but indeed, the buddha asks us to apply this comprehensive investigation (*sammasana*) in eleven modes to all of the five aggregates of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*): form, feeling, perception, preparations, and consciousness. why? for the sake of developing disillusionment (*nibbida*) toward them—it is through that disillusionment that comprehension and liberation arise.
now, in these verses too, it was said: *"yada pannaya passati"* — when one sees with wisdom. at whatever time one sees these as impermanent and as suffering through wisdom, then disillusionment (*nibbida*) toward the suffering of the five aggregates of grasping arises. therefore, as impermanent (*aniccato*), as suffering (*dukkhato*), as a disease (*rogato*)—disease too can be taken as suffering. a boil (*gandato*) too can be taken as suffering. *"aghato"* means a wound—some people have festering wounds. similarly, affliction (*abadhato*) is directly suffering (*dukkha*). next, there is "as alien" (*parato*)—which means to look at it as if looking at someone else's property. he asks us to look at it as if looking at another's thing, as alien (*parato*). "as disintegrating" (*palokato*) means as things that break; there too, impermanence (*aniccata*) is present. damage/decay. alien (*parato*), disintegrating (*palokato*). next, "as empty" (*sunnato*) relates to the vision of *anatta* (not-self). in many places, the buddha has chosen the word "empty" as: *"sunnamidam attena va attaniyena va"* — empty of a self or of what belongs to a self. that vision is "empty" (*sunnato*). finally:
"as not-self" (*anattato*) — look at them as *anatta*. these are the eleven modes. the eleven modes mentioned earlier are for understanding what each aggregate is. it is so broad. it is broad in terms of past, future, present, etc. and the way to look at them is what was just mentioned.
if one gets used to applying that comprehensive investigation (*sammasana*) as impermanent (*anicca*) and as suffering (*dukkha*) based on the things one experiences in daily life, gradually that turning away (*nirveda*) and disillusionment (*nibbida*) will grow. as a result of that, one can attain liberation. for those who have practiced this for a long time in past samsara, even a single sermon of the buddha might be enough. but for others, they must practice and train in these three characteristics in daily life. one must see those things that are seen as impermanent, as suffering, and as *anatta* (not-self) according to the clues given by the buddha. in some places, it is shown in an even broader manner—not just eleven, but in eighteen ways, in forty ways. this is called comprehensive investigation (*sammasana*). what the world does is misapprehension and clinging (*paramasana*)—grasping tightly. instead of that, one investigates (*sammasana*): "this is of such a nature." if one practices that in daily life, one can largely conquer those concepts in the mind. concentration (*samadhi*) also helps with that in daily life.
so, you must make an effort regarding all of these during the brief period of time received in this life. from all sides, the floods (*ogha*) and so forth are constantly flowing. in such an era, it is up to each individual, based on these clues highlighted by the buddha, to develop disillusionment (*nibbida*) toward the five aggregates of grasping, and accordingly develop concentration (*samadhi*) and other qualities that support it. through that, one can realize those supreme goals in this very life. i expect to conclude a bit briefly today.
you should consider taking advantage of at least this much that was said. now, having understood in a broader manner that advice given by ven. anna kondanna by looking at our own thoughts and wishes, if we develop insight (*vipassana*) based on the things we encounter, meet, and experience in daily life, then at a moment when we least expect it, we can attain the realization of the path and fruit we hope for. indeed, that noble state is often attained when one does not expect it.
because as long as expectation is there, during that time, the aforementioned insight (*vipassana*) does not operate. expectation is necessary, and determination is also necessary. but one must be engaged in the work. when one is engaged in the work, if those factors have matured, at some point, one will be able to realize them through that very state of direct experience. therefore, consider this briefly and shape your lives accordingly. so far, having observed virtue and practiced meditation to some extent, may you take what is to be taken from this dhamma sermon, and may you gain the strength and power to realize those expected states as quickly as possible! this is my wish.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 081
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #81
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.24)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Ko nu hāso kimānando, niccaṃ pajjalite sati;
Andhakārena onaddhā, padīpaṃ na gavesatha.
From:
Dhammapada 146 (Jarāvagga)
Dear Listeners,
According to the Dhamma expounded by the Buddha, the Teacher of the Three Worlds, darkness and light remind us of two things: ignorance (*avijjā*) and wisdom (*paññā*). The Blessed One declared that the reason why beings in this world have been caught up, entangled, and enmeshed in a great heap of *Dukkha* (Suffering) in this saṃsāra for an endless period of time—a heap of *dukkha* whose beginning and end are invisible—is because their eye of wisdom has been blinded by the darkness of ignorance. That is why the Blessed One has illustrated that realization of life, the realization of Nibbāna, and the seeing of Nibbāna, as the arising of the Dhamma-eye, as the dawning of a light. Beings in this world do not realize that their eye of wisdom is blinded because they have fallen into a state of grave negligence (*pamāda*). Worldly beings do not understand the darkness of ignorance they are in; they spend a long time in saṃsāra groping about in this darkness. Due to various reasons for falling into this negligence, and because of being subject to many forms of intoxication, worldly beings do not understand the dangerous situation they are in. Therefore, the Great Compassionate Blessed One on certain occasions had to arouse spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in his listeners through various skillful means. An incident of this nature is mentioned in the background story of the stanza we have taken as our theme today.
During the time of the Buddha, five hundred householders of Sāvatthī, wishing to see their wives live diligently and with love for the Dhamma, entrusted them to Visākhā, the great lay female disciple, like a group of pupils. These five hundred female lay disciples would always go to the monastery and the park together with the great lay disciple Visākhā. In this way, they remained highly obedient. However, a certain occasion arose—a drinking festival in Sāvatthī. A festival of drinking alcohol. It was held for seven days; such customs, like social festivals, existed in those cities. When such a drinking festival was held, those wives had to prepare alcohol for their husbands. After those seven days had passed in that manner, a large amount of alcohol was left over. These lay women thought, "We too should at least taste a little of this." However, they were afraid to do so in a way that their husbands would find out. Therefore, as a clever ruse, they went and asked for permission from Visākhā, saying, "We would like to go to the park; we had a desire to go to the park." Visākhā also took them along. After going to the park, what happened? Those lay women secretly got the alcohol brought there—since they were a large group, they managed it by some means. Next, they secretly drank it and became intoxicated. Being intoxicated, they behaved badly, in the various ways an intoxicated person behaves. Visākhā felt a great sense of spiritual urgency and dismay (*saṃvega*), thinking, "This will cause a bad rumor among the non-Buddhist ascetics (*tīrthakas*) that Visākhā, the chief female lay disciple of the Ascetic Gotama, also drank alcohol; a great blemish has been cast upon us due to an incident of this nature." Visākhā then admonished those lay women.
She also said to those lay women, "You will also have to undergo punishment from your husbands. What are you going to do now?" The lay women said, "We will go home and feign illness, showing that we are sick." Visākhā said, "Very well then, try and see," and sent them on. Similarly, when they went home and went to a separate room as if they were sick, and when the husbands came to know of this, they understood the reason. Having understood, they beat and punished them thoroughly.
After some time passed, another drinking festival came, just like before. On that occasion too—and this is the danger of alcohol and intoxication: once someone acquires a taste for it, they continue to go along with it—so, in the same way, after their husbands had finished drinking, for the second time a thought arose in those lay women, "We must go hide somewhere and secretly use this alcohol." Perhaps it was due to thriftiness, or perhaps due to a reluctance to throw it away. For whatever reason, they came to Visākhā again and presented a proposal to go to the park. Visākhā said, "Once we went and got such bad publicity," and when she rejected that idea, they next presented it under a different guise, saying, "We want to go perform offerings to the Blessed One; we have such an intention." "Ah, very well," said Visākhā, and took this group along. In an unbelievably clever way, while taking flowers, incense, and other offerings, they also carried alcohol in vessels. Having taken it, they drank the alcohol before entering the monastery, and came into the presence of the Blessed One drunk and intoxicated. Visākhā, unaware of this, invited the Blessed One to preach Dhamma to them. Not long after the Blessed One started the Dhamma sermon, so great was the danger and peril of that alcohol that these women felt like dancing and singing songs right in front of the Blessed One.
Along with that thought, now, generally it is said here that when one is in a state of mindlessness, there are various forces in this world and the universe that can possess us—forces that are opposed to the Dispensation (*Sāsana*), opposed to the Dhamma, and pull us back into saṃsāra, preventing our journey to Nibbāna. In the same way, it is mentioned here that deities belonging to Māra's retinue (*māra-kāyika devatā*) possessed that group and made them clap, laugh, dance, and sing in front of the Blessed One. When the Blessed One reflected on what this was, he understood it. It is mentioned that next, in order to arouse spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in them, the Blessed One at that moment emitted a great darkness from his eyebrows. Due to that dense darkness, the intoxication of those lay women vanished because of the fear of death. With the arising of the fear of death, their intoxication vanished. Next, the Blessed One declared to them as advice: "It is not proper to come to me fallen into negligence in this manner. That is why you are possessed by various forces of Māra. Now, with diligence and having aroused great spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), you must make an effort to escape from this fire." Saying so, he uttered the stanza we have taken as our theme:
*Ko nu hāso kimānando niccaṃ pajjalite sati*
*Andhakārena onaddhā padīpaṃ na gavesatha*
"When there is constant burning, what laughter, what joy? Enwrapped in deep darkness, do you not seek a lamp?"—this is the meaning of that short stanza. It is mentioned that after listening to that sermon by which the Blessed One aroused spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), that group of women attained the fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti*), based on the spiritual urgency they had developed. Be that as it may, next Visākhā, the great lay disciple, specifically said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, what a dangerous thing this alcohol is, giving rise to sinful, unwholesome states (*akusala*). Was it not due to this alcohol that a group like this began to behave in this manner in front of someone like the Blessed One?" The Blessed One replied, "Indeed, Visākhā, in the past too, many people experienced various troubles due to alcohol," and at that moment he also related a Jātaka story.
From this, we have to reflect on the challenge the Blessed One presented to the world in this stanza. From the music heard from all directions, we can see that in this world, people always try to remain constantly submerged in an ocean of entertainment. But the Blessed One poses a highly powerful challenge to us through this stanza. We like to spend our time laughing, singing, enjoying ourselves, and dancing. Yet the Blessed One asks, "When there is constant burning, what laughter, what joy? Enwrapped in deep darkness, in dense darkness, do you not seek a lamp?" It is worth reflecting on why the Blessed One presented such a challenge to us.
In the world today, there are fires everywhere to the extent that even the word "fire" truly evokes fear in a person. It is not only those visible fires. Because the Blessed One knew very well that this world is burning with many invisible fires, he often described the world as burning with eleven fires, or often as three fires—namely, the fires of lust (*rāga*), hatred (*dosa*/*dvesha*), and delusion (*moha*). On other occasions, he describes them as eleven fires: *rāga*, *dosa*, *moha*, and then *Jāti* (Birth), *jarā* (aging), *maraṇa* (death) (the latter two making up *Jarāmaraṇa* (Decay and Death)), *soka* (sorrow), *parideva* (lamentation), *Dukkha* (Suffering), *domanassa* (grief), and *upāyāsa* (despair). The three defilements (*kilesa*) that constantly burn within the minds of beings in saṃsāra, burning other things and other people connected to those respective beings, are lust (*rāga*), hatred (*dosa*), and delusion (*moha*). Accompanying them is *Jāti* (Birth), which is also a fire. Birth too is a fire. What is meant here is a fire of *Dukkha* (Suffering).
It is because of *Jāti* (Birth) that all other sufferings flow in. Along with *jāti*, next comes *Jarāmaraṇa* (Decay and Death). Along with birth, there is *jarā*, which is aging/growing old, then death (*maraṇa*), sorrow, and lamentation. Accordingly, there are sorrows, crying, lamentations, physical and mental suffering, and intense struggle and exhaustion. The Blessed One declared that beings are constantly burning and running about due to each of these. Since we are burning with these eleven fires in this manner, we must reflect that this entire saṃsāric existence is a terrifying *Dukkha* (Suffering). Many people think of *dukkha* as if existence is one thing and suffering is something inside it. But the Blessed One declared: *dukkhe loko patiṭṭhito*—the world is established in *dukkha*. *Dukkha* is established in the world. Just like two shutter-doors that fit each other perfectly, *dukkha* and the world are identical, to the extent that there is nothing to be separated from one another. In these times, when explaining the Noble Truth of Suffering (*dukkha-sacca*), even when explaining the Dhamma, many people just mention a few things like birth is *dukkha*, aging is *dukkha*, sickness is *dukkha*, a heap of *dukkha*, and then stop there. But because there is no end to listing them in that way, the Blessed One ultimately declared, *saṅkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā*—in brief, the entire five aggregates of grasping are *dukkha*.
Having shown separately that *Jāti* (Birth) is *dukkha*, aging is *dukkha*, illness is *dukkha*, etc., he finally declares that this entire five aggregates of form, *Vedanā* (Feeling), perception, *Saṅkhāra* (Preparations), and *viññāṇa* (consciousness), which we grasp as "I" and "mine"—in brief, the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcupādānakkhandha*)—are *dukkha*. In short, this body of ours is a heap of *dukkha*. That is why the Venerable Vīdāgama Maitreya has stated in the *Lō Väḍa Saňgarāva*:
*Dara räsa gini äviluṇu kala nibandē*
*Gini misa darayäyi yana nama noyedē*
*Ema lesa ek koṭa vadahaḷa muniňdē*
*Duka misa kayakäyi yana nama noyedē*
"When a heap of firewood is constantly ablaze,
It is called 'fire', the name 'firewood' no longer applies;
In the same way, as expounded by the Sage,
It is only *dukkha*, the name 'body' no longer applies."
A beautiful simile is shown there. "When a heap of firewood is constantly ablaze"—when a pile of wood is continuously burning, "it is called 'fire', the name 'firewood' no longer applies." We refer to it as fire; we do not call it a pile of firewood anymore. Once the entire pile of wood has caught fire, nobody refers to it as a pile of firewood. That is what that Venerable Thero is reminding us of. "In the same way, as expounded by the Sage, it is only *dukkha*, the name 'body' no longer applies." Likewise, the Blessed One has shown *dukkha* and the body together. Therefore, rather than calling this a body, it is better to call it *dukkha*. But worldly people do not like to use such terminology, nor do they do so. Yet, according to the word of the Buddha, according to the true state of affairs, this entire body, the very acquisition of a body—that is why birth (*jāti*) is said to be *dukkha*. In the world, the statement "birth is *dukkha*" is generally explained—and even we usually explain it for convenience—only as the pain caused to the mother and the child due to birth. However,
If we reflect more deeply, *Jāti* (Birth) means the acquisition of a bodily cage made of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*): earth (*paṭhavī*), water (*āpo*), fire (*tejo*), and wind (*vāyo*). From the very moment of acquiring this, because of past ignorance (*avijjā*), the dense darkness of ignorance, one accumulates *Saṅkhāra* (Preparations) or *kamma*, merit and demerit, because of the craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*). Everyone likes to remain in this existence. Because of the wrong understanding of "I" and "mine", because of ignorance (*avijjā*), there is an unquenchable, endless, and extraordinary *Taṇhā* (Craving) in worldly beings to maintain this "self" and to increase "my" possessions—a grave craving. We spend our entire lives trying to satisfy that *Taṇhā* (Craving). Through the wholesome and unwholesome *kamma* performed for its sake, *Bhava* (Becoming) is brought about for us.
*Bhava* (Becoming) means it grants another birth (*jāti*), a subsequent existence somewhere. The initial stage of that existence is *Jāti* (Birth). Birth means a bodily cage is formed, made of those elements mentioned earlier. Next, from the very moment of its arising, the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*) within it becomes active and produces something called hunger. For this, one must provide food. As soon as a little child is born, they are born crying. Thus they ask for milk. In that way, there is *Taṇhā* (Craving) for food. The fire element in this bodily cage operates and hunger is produced. This is the fire that no one can bear. This is common to everyone. One is burned by this hunger. In this way, this bodily cage is like a burning pile of firewood. One must put firewood into it again and again—that is, food. Next, there is thirst. That too is a fire. It is called the fire of hunger. The painful fires of hunger and thirst. Those two are common to everyone.
In addition to that, there is the fatigue of satisfying and preparing them. Next, due to various disturbances concerning those elements—*paṭhavī*, *āpo*, *tejo*, and *vāyo*—in that cage, and because of those very defilements, it is said that the three humors of wind, bile, and phlegm (*vā, pit, sem*) become deranged. Due to these various causes, and due to external and internal afflictions, illnesses and diseases flow in—sickness (*vyādhi*). Next, even if there are no such illnesses, this bodily cage begins to decay from the moment of birth. It gradually undergoes decay. We make a certain distinction between youth and old age, and we look upon one part of it favorably, thinking, "We are young." But in reality, from the very day of birth, decay begins. This decay is hastened by sickness, by illnesses and diseases. That too is indeed the derangement of these four elements, or of wind, bile, and phlegm, arriving according to one's *kamma* through various other external and internal afflictions. Thus, a life is spent in the midst of such a heap of *Dukkha* (Suffering). Yet we think we possess good health. We now generally express wishes for "long life and the blessing of health" (*āyur-ārogya-sampatti*). That wish or blessing is good. But its fulfillment actually depends on the *kamma* of each individual; otherwise, in terms of worldly nature, no one can say they spend even a single day in perfect health.
The Blessed One once declared that if anyone, carrying around a bodily cage like this, proudly says, "I am healthy," there is no greater foolishness than that. Not even for a single moment is there real health in this body. What is here is a heap of diseases. It is called a cage of diseases—a fragile cage of diseases. When this heap of diseases manifests outwardly, that is when we say, "I have fallen ill." Thus, there is a whole heap of illnesses and diseases that come along with this bodily cage. Next, we also try to escape from decay (*jarā*) and old age. No matter how much effort is made through various medical treatments and medical research, these two—*Jarāmaraṇa* (Decay and Death)—cannot be prevented. At some point, one must submit to them. The Blessed One has declared: *na hi so upakkamo yena jātā na mīyare*—"There is no device by which those who are born do not die." *Jarāmapi pāpuṇitvā maraṇaṃ, evaṃdhammā hi pāṇino*—"Even after reaching old age, there is death; such is the nature of living beings." In the end, even after reaching old age, one has to die.
Thus, within us there is generally a desire to be ageless and immortal; within worldly beings, there is a desire to escape decay, escape death, and obtain a certain happiness, a permanent state. But the Blessed One declared that death is something that goes hand-in-hand with birth (*jāti*). Birth and death are a tethered pair, something bound together. Therefore, we cannot accept only birth and reject death. Death arises along with birth. That is why the verses on mindfulness of death (*maraṇānussati*) that you often use state: *uppattiyā sahevedaṃ maraṇaṃ āgataṃ sadā*—"This death has arrived together with birth itself." "At all times, death comes along with birth." In that way, because these tethered things cannot be separated, as soon as a person takes birth, sickness, decay, and death—all of these—belong to them. Such a dangerous situation exists along with this body. In addition to being burned by those defilements (*kilesa*), next, as a result of the unwholesome *kamma* one performs, one has to be born in the realm of hungry ghosts (*peta-loka*) and undergo suffering for a long time, burning with extremely severe fires of hunger and thirst, and various other such miseries.
Likewise, we can see how animals suffer in the animal realm. In the ghost realms, and next in the planes of misery (*apāya*), and in the even more terrifying hells (*niraya*). There are places where the Blessed One himself from his own sacred mouth preached the details of the Great Hell and other such places, showing how terrifying the sufferings of hell are. In the Lohakumbhī hell, molten metal is poured into the mouths of some. There are extraordinary details about this. According to one's *kamma*, one has to drink molten metal. Sometimes, instead of that alcohol which was drunk with great relish, one has to drink molten copper. Otherwise, the Blessed One points out instances of beings undergoing suffering without dying, according to their *kamma*, boiling in metal cauldrons of the Lohakumbhī hell, going up and down. The Blessed One declares that the suffering endured by worldly beings in those hells cannot be fully described.
In the Great Hell, inside a hall with burning, blazing walls where even the floor is ablaze, those beings run up and down. There are four gates; they try to escape through these gates. Then, the gates supposedly open suddenly. But while they are opening, there are descriptions of how long they spend running about like this, undergoing the results of the sinful *kamma* they have committed. Likewise, they sometimes have to walk on burning, blazing mountains. They have to swallow red-hot iron balls. The Blessed One has declared that through the medium of fire, various terrifying retributive sufferings and miseries exist in those planes of misery (*apāya*) and hells (*niraya*). That is why the Blessed One has illustrated this entire saṃsāra as a place that is burning and blazing with fire. Therefore, the Blessed One has told us to constantly reflect on these subjects of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega-vatthu*) in order to prevent the negligence (*pamāda*) that generally arises within us.
The world is fallen into negligence. Various things cause this. We all know the negligence of sleepiness. In addition to that, there is the desire to get intoxicated. The negligence that arises due to addiction to alcohol is extremely dangerous. Due to that intoxication, one sometimes behaves in this very world like an animal, a hungry ghost, or a demon, performing various sinful deeds. *Surā-meraya-majja-pamādaṭṭhānā*—there are places in these times where this is explained as a joke in various ways. An era has now arrived where those jokes are sometimes taken as the truth. But drinking alcohol is called *pamādaṭṭhāna*—the ground for negligence. A cause for negligence. Drinking alcohol is specifically shown as a cause for negligence.
Many other causes of negligence are shown in the Dhamma: the intoxication of health (*ārogya-mada*), the intoxication of life (*jīvita-mada*), the intoxication of wealth (*bhoga-mada*)—in this way, there are various forms of intoxication.
