By putting it into practice, may the wholesome power of this merit be a supportive condition for all of you to realize the path-fruits starting from Stream-entry, to bring an end to the terrifying suffering (*dukkha*) of saṁsāra as quickly as possible in this very life, and to arrive at the supreme, deathless Nibbāna—. From the Avīci hell to the Akanissa heaven, if there are any beings who wish to rejoice in the merit of this preaching and listening to the Dhamma, may they, by so rejoicing, find peace in the supreme, deathless Nibbāna through the Awakening they aspire to. With this aspiration, recite these verses.
“*Ettāvatā ca amhehi.........*”

from:
dhammapada 326 (nagavagga)
dear listeners,
the news of the turning of the wheel of dhamma, set in motion by the teacher of the three worlds, the fully enlightened one, on an esala full moon poya day like this through the *dhammacakkappavattana sutta*, reverberated and broadcasted from deva-world to deva-world, and from brahma-world to brahma-world. from this, we can imagine that there was a marvelous kind of broadcasting in that wheel of dhamma, far superior to the broadcasting media of the modern world. that there is a certain spiritual splendor of the dhamma spreading throughout the universe is also apparent from the sutta discourses that our buddha preached on various occasions regarding the ancient dispensation. the background story relevant to the two verses we have chosen as our theme today is also a good proof of this. on one occasion, when the buddha was residing at the jetavana monastery in savatthi, he addressed the sangha and presented an event from a past eon in this manner:
"monks, in the extremely distant past, there was a king named arunava. his kingdom was known as arunavati. the blessed one, the fully enlightened one of that past era (sikhi buddha), lived in dependence on that kingdom of arunavati. that sikhi buddha had two chief disciples named abhibhu and sambhava. one day, the sikhi buddha addressed the chief disciple abhibhu—it appears that in those times, the buddha addressed his disciples as 'brahmin'—and said, 'brahmin, until the time for alms arrives, let us go to a certain brahma-world and return.' 'very well, venerable sir,' he replied. then, the sikhi buddha and the chief disciple abhibhu disappeared from the kingdom of arunavati and appeared in that brahma-world, as quickly as a strong man might stretch his bent arm or bend his stretched arm."
after arriving in the brahma-world, the buddha said to the chief disciple abhibhu, "may a dhamma talk occur to you, brahmin, to deliver to this great brahma and his retinue!" replying, "yes, venerable sir," the venerable abhibhu endeavored to generate joy and spiritual urgency (*samvega*) in the brahma king and his retinue through an extraordinary dhamma discourse. however, that brahma and his retinue began to speak in a critical tone, saying, "what a strange thing! how wonderful and marvelous! the disciple is preaching the dhamma in the very presence of the teacher." thereupon, the buddha said to venerable abhibhu, "brahmin, this brahma king and his retinue are criticizing you, saying such-and-such. therefore, preach the dhamma even more intensely to arouse spiritual urgency (*samvega*) in them."
next, this venerable one began to preach the dhamma while performing psychic miracles. sometimes making himself visible, sometimes invisible, sometimes making only a part of his body visible—either the upper half of his body or the lower half of his body—he preached the dhamma in various ways, blending it with psychic powers. this assembly of brahmas was struck with spiritual urgency (*samvega*) and amazement, thinking, "this is wonderful and marvelous, that even a disciple possesses such psychic power!" at that moment, venerable abhibhu said to sikhi buddha, "venerable sir, i recall making a statement in the midst of the sangha on one occasion: 'friends, standing in the brahma-worlds, i can make my voice heard throughout a thousandfold world system.'" then the sikhi buddha said, "brahmin, now is the moment! now is the time! fulfil that statement of yours. make your voice heard throughout a thousandfold world system." when invited by the buddha, the venerable one proclaimed to the assembly of brahmas the very two verses we have chosen as our theme today:
> *arabhatha nikkhamatha,*
> *yunjatha buddhasasane;*
> *dhunatha maccuno senam,*
> *nalagaram va kunjaro.*
>
> exert yourselves! go forth!
> engage in the buddha’s dispensation!
> destroy the army of death,
> as an elephant crushes a reed-shed!
>
> *yo imasmim dhammavinaye,*
> *appamatto vihessati;*
> *pahaya jati samsaram,*
> *dukkhassantam karissati.*
>
> he who shall dwell diligently in this dhamma and discipline,
> abandoning the round of birth (*jati*) and samsara,
> will make an end of suffering (*dukkha*).
having delivered that discourse and aroused spiritual urgency (*samvega*) in the assembly of brahmas, sikhi buddha and venerable abhibhu returned, appearing instantly in the kingdom of arunavati, as quickly as a strong man might stretch his bent arm or bend his stretched arm. upon their return, sikhi buddha asked the sangha: "monks, did you hear our monk abhibhu proclaiming verses from the brahma-world?" "yes, venerable sir." "how did those verses sound? relate them." they recited the two verses exactly as they had been spoken. thereupon the buddha said, "sadhu, sadhu! excellent is it that you heard the dhamma discourse of the monk abhibhu." this was the narrative proclaimed by the buddha.
from this, we can see that these two verses reverberated throughout the universe in a past eon, during the time of an ancient buddha. next, let us delve into these two verses to understand their meaning. the three main words here, as you must have understood, are *arabhatha* (exert), *nikkhamatha* (go forth), and *yunjatha* (yoke/engage). through these three terms, one fact the buddha revealed to the world is that the power to make an end of the suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara exists within each and every one of us. on certain occasions, he declared of himself: "i am one who asserts action (*kammavadi*), who asserts efficacy of action (*kiriyavadi*), and who asserts energy (*viriyavadi*)." nowadays, when people speak of karma, some think, "if it is karma, there is nothing to be done about it." the buddha did not speak in that sense. he regarded the human being specifically as an individual possessing action, active energy, and virile effort. therefore, according to that principle, the three terms *arabhatha*, *nikkhamatha*, and *yunjatha* represent what the buddha analyzed on various occasions. in one sutta, he declares: "monks, for the non-arising of unarisen sloth and torpor (*thina-middha*), and for the abandonment of arisen sloth and torpor, there is one quality. what is this one quality?" he referred to those three elements: the element of initiative (*arambha-dhatu*), the element of launching (*nikkama-dhatu*), and the element of exertion (*parakkama-dhatu*). in any analysis, fundamental elements are called *dhatus*.
thus, within an individual, there is an initiating power—the power to start something. there is a launching power to carry it forward. by the element of exertion (*parakkama*), it means the valour to overcome the obstacles that arise in the process and forge ahead; there is a power to conquer them. it is to denote these three aspects that *arabhatha*, *nikkhamatha*, and *yunjatha* are used. moreover, these three terms are especially helpful for increasing one's energy (*viriya*). *arabhatha, nikkhamatha, yunjatha buddhasasane; dhunatha maccuno senam*—demolish the army of death. next, the simile is given, which is a powerful one: "like an elephant destroying a reed-house." there is a hut made of reeds. is it difficult for an elephant to break it? as soon as it steps on it, it gets crushed with a crackling sound. this simile illustrates the power of energy (*viriya*). destroy the army of mara like an elephant crushing a reed-house. what then is this army of mara? we can see the army of mara described in the buddha's own words in the *padhana sutta*. when the buddha was cultivating that great energy (*viriya*) which we call the "great struggle" (*maha-padhana*), it is recorded in the texts that mara came and tried to tempt him to abandon this energy. then the buddha addressed mara: "mara, here is your army!" what is called his army? it is the defilements (*kilesas*) in our minds. ten defilements are listed there in a sequence of verses in the *padhana sutta* of the *sutta nipata*:
"sensual pleasures (*kama*) are your first army; the second is called discontent (*arati*)..." and so on. sensual pleasures are the first army. the second army is called discontent (*arati*), which is non-delight in the monastic practices of the dispensation. that is to say, *arati* means a lack of interest or aversion towards the spiritual practices of the dispensation, towards wholesome qualities (*kusala dhamma*). "that too is your second army." next, the third army is hunger and thirst (*khuppipasa*). neglecting spiritual work on the pretext of hunger and thirst. next, craving (*tanha*) is the fourth army. the fifth army is sloth and torpor (*thina-middha*). the sixth army is fear (*bhiru*). the seventh army is doubt (*vicikiccha*), indecision. the eighth army is disparagement and obstinacy (*makkha-thambha*). next, the ninth army is gain, honor, and renown (*labha-sakkara-siloka*), and whatever false fame or retinue one acquires—all that is the ninth army of mara. the tenth army is self-exaltation and disparaging others (*attukkamsana-paravambhana*), that vice. these are the ten armies of mara that the buddha presented as the mara of defilements (*kilesa-mara*). when analyzed further, the vast host of defilements belonging to this army is sometimes counted in the thousands. a massive army belongs to the army of mara. it is against these defilements that we have to wage war.
what then must we fight with? now, when talking about this battle, what weapon do we possess to fight these? there are thirty-seven weapons, known as the thirty-seven factors of awakening (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*). thus, organizing the army means lining up these thirty-seven factors of awakening. what are these thirty-seven? there are seven groups here. the army can be divided into seven battalions: the four establishments of mindfulness (*satipatthana*), the four right efforts (*sammappadhana*), the four bases of spiritual power (*iddhipada*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of awakening (*bojjhanga*), and the noble eightfold path. these seven are the battalions of the army. how then is this initiated? how is the army organized? how is the army led forward? to understand how the enemy army is broken and victory is achieved through the power called exertion (*parakkama*), one must put these thirty-seven factors of awakening into practice in one's own mind-stream. roughly speaking, the yogic warrior receives basic training on the terrain of the four establishments of mindfulness (*satipatthana*), sometimes carrying a meditation subject (*kammatthana*) as a weapon. the four things belonging to the practice of that noble person on the terrain of the four establishments of mindfulness are the right efforts (*sammappadhana*)—the fourfold energy (*viriya*). you must have heard of this frequently.
if we explain just one in detail, the buddha illustrates the side of energy (*viriya*) with a series of terms in this long phrase: "...for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome qualities, he generates desire (*chandam janeti*), makes an effort (*vayamati*), arouses energy (*viriyam arabhati*), exerts his mind (*cittam pagganhati*), and strives (*padahati*)." "generates desire" means he rouses a keen interest. "makes an effort" means he exerts himself. "arouses energy" means he initiates energy. "exerts his mind" means he positions his determination foremost. finally, "strives" means he puts forth supreme effort, disregarding body and life, in the form of the ultimate struggle. how does this sequence of terms become fourfold? consider it briefly: for the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states, for the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states, for the arising of unarisen wholesome states, and for the maintenance, stabilization, and complete development of arisen wholesome states. this is what is called the fourfold right effort (*sammappadhana*). just these four.
from that very practice, the four qualities called the bases of spiritual power (*iddhipada*) emerge. what are the bases of spiritual power? desire (*chanda*), energy (*viriya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*vimamsa*). as mentioned earlier, "one generates desire." developing a keen interest or willingness is the first step in applying energy. next, the effort and energy indicated by the two terms *vayamati* and *viriyam arabhati*—that is the base of spiritual power of energy (*viriya*). the term *citta* relates to that determination—*cittam pagganhati*, strengthening the mind, the power of determination. next, although investigation (*vimamsa*) is not directly mentioned in the phrase, we can understand that as one systematically puts forth energy, an investigative intelligence regarding it arises, an understanding of how it should be done; *vimamsa* is something related to wisdom (*panna*). now, depending on the strengths each individual brings from past samsara, some attain nibbana——by making desire (*chanda*) their primary vehicle, thinking, "if i develop the desire and willingness, i will definitely complete it." another, through energy (*viriya*), thinks, "if i put my hand to a task, i will never abandon it," and rouses intense energy. another, making mind (*citta*) foremost, thinks, "if i resolve, i will surely accomplish it." yet another focuses on investigation (*vimamsa*), wishing to investigate whether the result of this is true. these are the bases of spiritual power (*iddhipada*). base of spiritual power does not mean flying through the air. you can understand that this is relevant to some extent even to worldly life for achieving success in any task. the four bases of spiritual power—desire, energy, mind, and investigation—are necessary not only for supramundane nibbana but also for obtaining mundane direct-knowledges (*abhinna*). even if we do not speak of lesser achievements, you can assume they apply to them as well. these, then, are the bases of spiritual power.
next, as the practitioner carries this out, an understanding of five extraordinary faculties arises, replacing the five ordinary physical senses they had thus far. these are: faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*). these are listed as the faculties (*indriya*) in the dhamma. it is not through the five physical senses that one realizes nibbana—. not through those five, dear devotees, but by developing the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—by developing these five spiritual faculties. through their development. what does developing them mean? it does not mean keeping them idle; rather, one utilizes them as powers (*bala*) to repel that army of mara. some are repelled by the power of faith (*saddha-bala*), others by the power of energy (*viriya-bala*), power of mindfulness (*sati-bala*), power of concentration (*samadhi-bala*), and power of wisdom (*panna-bala*). these very five are shown as the five powers (*panca balani*) among the thirty-seven factors of awakening in the dhamma. when these are lined up, they become the five powers.
next, the "seven" refers to the seven factors that help in awakening (*bodhi*), which are lined up towards the end. you must have heard of these: mindfulness (*sati*), investigation of states (*dhamma-vicaya*), energy (*viriya*), rapture (*piti*), tranquility (*passaddhi*), concentration (*samadhi*), and equanimity (*upekkha*). mindfulness (*sati*) is the foundation. when mindfulness is established foremost, the investigation of states (*dhamma-vicaya*)—the ability to identify wholesome and unwholesome states, the ability to deeply understand the meditation subject—emerges. based on that, the energy (*viriya*) to abandon the unwholesome and cultivate the wholesome arises. within that energy, the practitioner naturally experiences a certain spiritual, non-material rapture (*piti*). this aids concentration. it is to the one who exerts energy that this extraordinary, spiritual rapture occurs. next, calming down that rapture, one develops inner tranquility of body and mind (*passaddhi*) through that energy. subsequently, concentration (*samadhi*) is raised from that. following that, to protect and stabilize that concentration, equanimity (*upekkha*) is developed. these seven, this sequence, is what is known as the seven factors of awakening (*bojjhanga*). this is second only to the noble eightfold path. the seven factors of awakening form such an important category of the dhamma.
now, the final exertion is carried out through the noble eightfold path, which is presented as a single unit. the noble eightfold path (*ariyo atthangiko maggo*) is an integrated military organization. they are so interconnected that they cannot be separated from one another. right view (*samma-ditthi*) leads directly to right intention (*samma-sankappa*), and accordingly right speech (*samma-vaca*), right action (*samma-kammanta*), right livelihood (*samma-ajiva*), right effort (*samma-vayama*), right mindfulness (*samma-sati*), and right concentration (*samma-samadhi*) are wonderfully connected to one another. thus, it is this integrated, final military organization, the invasion, and ultimately the exertion—the final step—that is taken by the noble eightfold path. having cultivated this noble eightfold path at a certain mundane level, it is said that in the supramundane moment, all eight factors arise simultaneously in a single mind-state. the mind-state that arises then is extremely unique. it is not like taking each factor individually. when all eight come together as one, it is through that that one leaps from the mundane to the supramundane side. it is marvelous. this is a highly wondrous natural principle (*dhamma-ta*) that only a buddha can bring to light. that path-mind (*magga-citta*) is a concentration (*samadhi*) attained in an instant. the dhamma states that there is no concentration equal to that concentration: *samadhina tena samo na vijjati*. it is known as the "immediate concentration" (*anantarika-samadhi*). immediately following that concentration is the fruit (*phala*). path...
a special aspect relevant to that concentration-mind (*samadhi-citta*) is that during the path-moment, these factors provide protection to one another. these are the three factors: right view (*samma-ditthi*), right effort (*samma-vayama*), and right mindfulness (*samma-sati*). the buddha reveals a highly wondrous natural principle here. right view becomes the forerunner; it goes in front. right effort pushes from behind, providing momentum and protection. right mindfulness stands close at hand, performing the service of attendance, supplying whatever is needed at that moment. to illustrate this with a simile—something frequently seen nowadays, which you will easily understand: how do high state officials travel? first, a security officer goes in front with all necessary equipment, clearing the way and showing the path. next, a group follows behind. another security battalion or individual, perhaps a bodyguard, follows behind for protection to ward off threats from the rear. furthermore, other officers sometimes walk alongside the person for security. according to this simile, right view (*samma-ditthi*) goes in front in that supramundane moment. right effort (*samma-vayama*) pushes from behind. right mindfulness (*samma-sati*) performs the service of attendance close at hand.
in this way, that supramundane mind is something highly wondrous. the noble eightfold path can be mundane and prepared (*sankhata*). yet, through that mundane path, as the buddha pointed out, in a highly marvelous manner, all eight factors are united in a single moment, and it is through that power that one leaps to the other side. this is the moment of leaping into nibbana——which is called the unprepared (*asankhata*). thus, the military organization available to the practitioner, and the methods of invasion and exertion through that military organization, have been brought to light by the buddha through this dhamma.
"exert yourselves! go forth! engage in the buddha's dispensation! destroy the army of death!" this refers not only to those defilements; you must have also heard of the ten fetters (*samyojana*) by which we are bound to samsara. severing those fetters systematically through the path-minds of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship, one breaks through those bonds and advances to supramundane attainment, bringing an end to the suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara to realize arahantship, nibbana—. this is what the buddha illustrated through this verse. if one dwells diligently in such a dhamma, where "dhamma-vinaya" does not mean mere doctrine, but the discipline (*vinaya*) that is the practical application of the doctrine; the buddha's dispensation was known in ancient times by the name *dhamma-vinaya*. it is not a mere heap of books or theoretical learning (*pariyatti*). within the term *dhamma-vinaya*, there is both the teaching (*dhamma*) and the discipline (*vinaya*). *yo imasmim dhammavinaye*—if anyone dwells diligently in this dispensation of dhamma-vinaya, then what is the result? *pahaya jati samsaram*—abandoning this samsara of repeated birth (*jati*), they make an end of suffering (*dukkha*). these two verses are indeed two highly majestic verses.
just as these two verses preached in the brahma-world by venerable abhibhu broadcasted throughout a thousandfold world system, even up to the present day, practicing monks conclude their chanting of the *vatta piritha* with these two verses. we can imagine how valuable these two verses are for developing one's energy (*viriya*). there is a valuable historical narrative revealing that these verses were used with great devotion even in ancient sri lanka. some of you might have heard the story of venerable milakkhatissa. for those of you who like to listen to stories, here is a good opportunity. the story goes like this:
in ancient sri lanka, near a village where the monks of the gaminda vala monastery in the ruhuna province went for alms-round, there lived a hunter from a hunter family—those who kill animals are called hunters. after reaching youth, this hunter married and supported his wife and children by setting hundreds of traps, killing the animals caught in them, eating some, and selling the rest. one day, leaving his home, he took fire and salt with him. among the animals caught in the traps overnight, there was a deer. he killed the deer, butchered it, roasted it, and ate it. when he had finished eating, a highly strange, intense thirst arose in him. to quench this thirst, he entered the gaminda vala monastery and went to the shed where the water pots were kept. although the water pots were full of water, due to this man's unwholesome, sinful karma, the water pots appeared empty to him. thereupon, he began to criticize: "in a place where so many monks reside, there is not even a drop of water to drink!"
hearing the man shouting, venerable cula pindapatika tissa, who was in the monastery, came out and saw that the pots were indeed full of water. wondering what was wrong with this man, the elder realized: "this man has become a living hungry ghost (*peta*) right now, which is why he cannot see the water." out of compassion, the elder lifted a water pot and poured water into the hunter’s hands. the hunter drank as much as ten pots of water, but the water he drank was like water poured onto a red-hot iron pan; his thirst was not quenched even after drinking all of that. thereupon, the elder said, "understand, lay devotee, how severe your karma is. you have become a living hungry ghost (*peta*). what kind of retribution will you receive in hell?" hearing this, a great spiritual urgency (*samvega*) arose in the hunter. immediately, he dismantled the traps he had set, ran back home, released the captive animals at home into the forest, explained the situation to his wife and children, destroyed his weapons, and returned to request ordination from the elder.
then this elder said, "lay devotee, ordination is very difficult. how can i ordain you?" he replied, "having witnessed such a direct, tangible proof, how can i *not* ordain?" when he expressed his strong desire for ordination, the elder ordained him and gave him the meditation subject of the skin-pentad (*taca-pancaka kammatthana*). from that day on, he was known as venerable milakkhatissa. *milakkha*, dear devotees, means barbarian (*mleccha*). you know the word *mleccha*. there is no need for another word for *mleccha*. a despicable man who kills animals is a barbarian. you are familiar with the name angulimala; for some reason, no other monk who was ordained was ever given the name angulimala besides venerable angulimala himself. even though it was not given to others, his character stands out particularly due to that power and diligence (*appamada*) spoken of by the buddha. the name milakkhatissa is just like that. venerable milakkhatissa’s character became so noble because of that kind of background. let us relate what followed his ordination. having been ordained, how did he spend his life compared to before, when he had spent day and night setting traps, killing the animals caught in them, exerting immense energy just to support his wife and children as his livelihood?
next, what did venerable milakkhatissa do? applying that same energy (*viriya*), he began to energetically perform monastic duties at the shrines and the services for the sangha during the rains-retreat. while practicing meditation, he performed these duties. he also learned the word of the buddha from that elder. on one such occasion when he was learning, venerable pindapatika tissa explained the *devaduta sutta*. according to the *devaduta sutta*, the buddha has declared that the wardens of hell inflict unimaginable, extremely severe tortures and punishments on a sinner who falls into hell, and then cast him into the great hell. as soon as he heard this, venerable milakkhatissa asked, "venerable sir, is this not a highly strange thing? after undergoing so much torture, the person is cast again into the great hell. what kind of suffering (*dukkha*) must there be in the great hell?" "indeed, the great hell is a highly terrifying place." "can we see it?" he asked.
"you cannot see it directly, but i can demonstrate something similar," the elder replied. he instructed venerable milakkhatissa to ask the novice monks to pile some green firewood on top of a rock. venerable milakkhatissa, together with the novices, gathered a pile of green firewood on top of a rock. thereupon, the elder entered into concentration (*samadhi*) and, through psychic power, brought a tiny spark from the avici great hell—the text says it was as small as a firefly—and dropped it onto the pile of firewood while the monks watched. instantly, all the green firewood was reduced to ashes. from this, he understood the terrifying nature of hell.
next, venerable milakkhatissa asked, "is there only the reading of books in this dispensation?" the elder explained—though at that time there was a convention of classifying them as the duty of meditation (*vipassana-dhura*) and the duty of texts (*gantha-dhura*), though it was not an absolute division. then, he said to the elder: "i was ordained out of faith. i want to realize nibbana——quickly. please give me a meditation subject (*kammatthana*)." thereupon, the elder considered and gave him a meditation subject in a way that utilized the physical energy (*viriya*) he had been accustomed to practicing. he gave venerable milakkhatissa a certain meditation subject that allowed him to practice insight meditation (*vipassana*) while performing his monastic duties at the temple.
then, venerable milakkhatissa practiced in a highly marvelous manner, staying awake through the night. the historical accounts of that time record the places associated with venerable milakkhatissa. as we see from the texts, the gaminda vala monastery was located between sithulpawwa and kataragama. thus, on some days, venerable milakkhatissa would perform duties at the shrine room and for the sangha at sithulpawwa. on other days, he would perform duties at the gaminda vala monastery, staying awake through the night. on some days, at the kiri vehera in kataragama. in this manner, keeping awake through the night at all three locations, when drowsiness overcame him, what did he do? he would wet a straw ring, place it on his head, and place his feet in water. while cultivating energy (*viriya*) in this manner, it is recorded that on one occasion at sithulpawwa, having practiced thus through two watches of the night, intense drowsiness came upon him towards dawn. while venerable milakkhatissa was sitting with the wet straw ring on his head, he heard a novice monk reciting those two verses: *arabhatha*, etc. hearing these verses, venerable milakkhatissa reflected: "this discourse was preached for me, for a monk of initiated energy (*arabdha-viriya*) like me!" generating joy through that, and attaining absorptions (*jhana*), it is said that he attained the fruit of non-returning (*anagami-phala*) at that very moment. subsequently, by cultivating even more energy, it is recorded in the texts that he attained arahantship.
that this story was present not only in recent literature but also in the ancient sihala commentaries (*sihala-atthakatha*) is demonstrated by the verse of solemn utterance (*udana-gatha*) he proclaimed after attaining arahantship and realizing the path-fruits: "with a straw ring on my head, i walked up and down. now i have no doubt whatsoever; i have realized the fruits of the path." thus, through the biography of venerable milakkhatissa, we can understand that his life was intimately connected to those two verses. he had put forth such great energy even without knowing those verses. after hearing the two verses, he thought, "this teaching was indeed preached for me." through that rapture, he attained the path-fruits.
let us now contemplate the present day. the buddha delivered the first dhamma sermon through the *dhammacakkappavattana sutta*. we mentioned that the wheel of dhamma was set in motion. but in the end, what remains of that turning wheel of dhamma now? only the symbol of the wheel of dhamma. why is that? because today, nibbana——has been declared obsolete. nibbana is considered impossible in this era. now, only the symbol of the wheel of dhamma is left for us. "there is no use in putting forth energy; it is enough to do some minor wholesome deed to accumulate perfections (*paramis*) in this day and age." this is the common talk. thus, the biographies of venerable milakkhatissa, venerable sona, and other elders who cultivated such energy are viewed merely as ancient legends; they are not considered relevant to this day and age. such a view is widely held.
we must reflect wisely on the rains-retreat (*vassa*), which was a highly special period even during the buddha's time. in the buddha’s day, even the monks residing in various cities would seek out remote villages when the rains-retreat drew near. on their way, devout lay disciples would offer them alms-food and ask, "venerable sirs, where are you traveling?" "to a suitable place." "then, there are suitable forest tracts and quiet places here. we shall support you with the four requisites. please reside here." thus, the monks spent their rains-retreat in those places not with material motivations in mind. not with material targets, but with spiritual, non-material targets—with nibbana——foremost. because of that noble target, while they lived devoted to meditation, some of the lay devotees who came to know of it, even those who had not known the dhamma previously, followed their path. having done so, they too made significant progress on the path to nibbana, as you must have heard, as illustrated by the story of matika's mother (*matikamata*). at this moment, even if you would like to hear it, i cannot repeat that story. we have preached it on previous occasions. matika's mother is a highly famous and noble character among lay women.
while serving those monks, the laywoman matika's mother developed absorptions (*jhana*), path-fruits (*magga-phala*), direct-knowledges (*abhinna*), and all other achievements, becoming a non-returner (*anagami*). from this, we can see that lay devotees in the past, taking the spiritual determination and spiritual goal of the monks as their model, also walked the path to nibbana by utilizing that opportunity. therefore, that is the highest meritorious deed of the rains-retreat. but that rains-retreat merit may not be considered suitable for this day and age if nibbana is declared obsolete. therefore, we must reflect that the dhamma presented by the buddha, the wheel of dhamma, is indeed something that must be turned within one's own mind-stream. conquering the army of mara is not something the buddha completed on our behalf. the buddha has conquered mara. "so now we only have to enjoy nibbana, which will come to us automatically"—some think in this way. it is not so. that army of mara is the very army of mara residing within ourselves. for that, the essential elements required for the battle within you are the element of initiative (*arambha-dhatu*), the element of launching (*nikkama-dhatu*), and the element of exertion (*parakkama-dhatu*). furthermore, the buddha has shown how to organize the army through the thirty-seven factors of awakening. not only the elders of the past who experienced this, but even barbarian (*mleccha*) hunters, as mentioned, attained world-renowned nobility.
if we contemplate accordingly, just like that wheel of dhamma, the inner strength within us—the spiritual strength—gradually declines when we degenerate in virtue. a sign of this spiritual decline is the emergence of a cult of devotion (*bhaktivada*) in place of the system of energy (*viriyavada*), looking to achieve this through someone else’s help. but this dhamma cannot be practiced in that way. the buddha has declared:
> *tumhehi kiccam atappam,*
> *akkhataro tathagata;*
> *patipanna pamokkhanti,*
> *jhayino marabandhana.*
>
> "you yourselves must make the effort; the tathagatas are only teachers. those who enter the path and practice meditation (*jhayino*) are freed from the fetter of mara."
thus, according to that word of the buddha, and also diligence—*appamatto na vihessati* (he who is diligent will not suffer). this word "diligence" (*appamada*) is the very alphabet of this dispensation.
you have heard of: *appamado amatapadam* (diligence is the path to the deathless). you also hear and know that this path to the deathless is now being interpreted in various other ways:
> *appamado amatapadam,*
> *pamado maccuno padam;*
> *appamatta na miyanti,*
> *ye pamatta yatha mata.*
to help you remember, we have translated this into sinhala:
> diligence is the path to the deathless;
> negligence is the path of death.
> the diligent do not die;
> the negligent are as if already dead.
this indeed is the word of the buddha.
next, regarding the buddha's dispensation, the buddha himself has proclaimed it. on many occasions, the buddha highlights the concept of the "opportunity of the moment" (*khana-sampatti*). there is a general concept among worldly people: *khanakicco loko, khanakicco loko*—"the world is busy with the moment." the world operates on time. not only today or yesterday, not only in this era of clocks, but even in those days, the world was a place that worked on time. but although the world speaks of the moment, they do not recognize the true moment. although they say that the world functions in the instant (*khana*), they do not know what the instant actually is. therefore, the buddha goes on to define the "moment." the eight unfortunate opportunities (*attha akkhana*) are the unsuitable states of existence in which a human being can be born. although i do not explain them in detail—occasions when a buddha does not arise, or even if he arises, one is unable to hear the dhamma or practice accordingly—you must have heard of them. the buddha points out that the most precious moment we have now is the one free from those eight unfortunate opportunities. there is only one such moment: the period when a buddha has arisen and the dhamma is present.
if one does not take advantage of that moment while the dhamma exists, then: *khanatita hi socanti, nirayamhi samappita*—"those who miss the moment will sorrow when they are consigned to hell." if that moment is missed, one has to go to hell and undergo suffering (*dukkha*). if venerable milakkhatissa had missed that moment, how much hellish suffering (*dukkha*) would he have had to undergo? moreover, it was not only from hell that he was liberated, but from the entire suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara, of repeated birth (*jati*). with that energy (*viriya*), what do we do today by putting wet straw rings on our heads and placing our feet in buckets of water? we do it merely to pass mundane exams. one cannot escape from samsara by passing mundane exams. but if we apply that very energy towards escaping from samsara, the character of milakkhatissa is a wonderful invitation and model. there is a certain energy (*viriya*) within us. if we direct it correctly to this side, with right understanding and right view, we can succeed. the buddha declared that as long as the thirty-seven factors of awakening are practiced, the world will not be empty of arahants. "being practiced" does not mean being in books. it is not about being in books; it is about putting them into practice, living in accordance with them. at the time of his parinibbana, the buddha summarized the entire true dhamma, saying: "the teachings i have preached during these forty-five years are indeed these thirty-seven."
therefore, we must contemplate that we should not merely remain cozy within theoretical learning (*pariyatti*). once we have gained understanding through it, along with a clear comprehension of how it should be put into practice, we must translate it into practice (*patipatti*). it is through realization (*pativedha*), the understanding of the path-fruits, that we can make an end of the suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara. if that moment is missed, the buddha concludes that series of verses with a simile drawn from society: just as a merchant who misses an opportunity to buy goods cheaply laments, "ah! the time has passed!" after the opportunity is gone, so too will it be for one who, having been born during the appearance of a buddha, fails to solve the problem of their journey in samsara.
that is why the buddha declares: *khanatita hi socanti* (those who miss the moment will sorrow). based on this, the buddha has set forth the motto: *khano ve ma upaccaga*—"let not the precious moment pass you by!" guided by this motto, the monks of the past entered the rains-retreat. upon concluding the rains-retreat, many of them, having spent those three or sometimes four months, would bring to the buddha their final offering, which is called the declaration of arahantship (*anna-pativedha*). they would declare, either directly or indirectly, that they had attained arahantship. they would report to the buddha the realization they had achieved during that period of quietude. the buddha would express approval by saying, "sadhu!" other monks, at the end of the rains-retreat, would travel in search of the buddha. such accounts are found in the dhamma. the buddha would wait for them to arrive. sometimes, based on various things they witnessed along the way, once the buddha purified their meditation subjects, they would immediately attain arahantship.
thus, these were not accidental events. the precise manner in which they cultivated that energy (*viriya*) is not explained everywhere in the dhamma books. it is simply recorded that a banker's son or a prince was ordained, went to the forest, and shortly thereafter returned as an arahant—that is all we are given to know. how they lived in the forest, what they did, and how they conquered is often not explained. however, that details are precisely what is contained within the thirty-seven factors of awakening. during that quietude, they aroused spiritual urgency (*samvega*) and used it to propel their monastic journey towards nibbana—. spiritual urgency (*samvega*) is, so to speak, the fuel and the velocity. the eight bases of spiritual urgency (*samvega-vatthu*) are listed as: birth (*jati*), decay (*jara*), disease (*vyadhi*), death (*marana*), the suffering experienced in past samsara, the suffering to be experienced in the future if one continues to remain in it, and the toil of seeking food and livelihood even in this present life. we utilize all of these as bases of spiritual urgency. throughout this long samsara, not only we but even an animal undergoes immense suffering (*dukkha*) just to survive for a single day to feed itself.
can escape from this has been revealed only by a buddha. "obstructed by the hindrance of ignorance (*avijja-nivarana*) and fettered by the bond of craving (*tanha-samyojana*), monks, you and i have traveled for a long time, for an incalculable number of eons." the similes mentioned in the *anamatagga sutta* and other discourses are actually not mere figures of speech. the buddha often remarked that it is impossible even to give a simile. when he said a simile is impossible, he offered these descriptions merely as a way to help us conceive of it slightly—descriptions of the suffering (*dukkha*) humans have undergone during a single eon, which you might have heard of from the *anamatagga sutta*. on one occasion, pointing to mount vepulla, the buddha said to the monks: "monks, if the skeleton of a single person during a single eon were accumulated, and if that pile of bones were not to decay, it would be larger than this mount vepulla." on other occasions in the *anamatagga* discourses, as we have reminded you many times, the buddha declared that if the blood shed by a single person—even this very individual we call a human being—when they were born in past samsara as a pig, a goat, a chicken, or a buffalo and had their throat cut, were collected, it would be greater than the water in the four great oceans. and it is said that this is not even a mere exaggeration.
similarly, the blood shed due to the torture inflicted when one was falsely accused by kings or caught as a thief in samsara is said to be of that magnitude. furthermore, on the other hand, if the tears shed over those regarded as beloved in each lifetime—relatives, parents, daughters, sons, and spouses—were gathered, the tears shed by a single person would exceed the waters of the four great oceans. from this, we can imagine how incredibly long this time has been.
that is why it is declared: *kici karahaci loke uppajjanti tathagata*—"rarely, at times, do tathagatas arise in the world." there are some eons in which no buddha arises at all, which are called "eons empty of buddhas" (*buddha-sunna kappa*). thus, when reflecting on such vast stretches of time, we have been wandering in this long samsara, taking birth in various states of existence over a period so immense that modern science cannot even conceive of it. during those wanderings, not only were we unable to hear such a dhamma, but we also lacked the capacity, the intellectual power, and the understanding to practice accordingly. in the human state of existence, a human being is endowed with this capacity. additionally, the rare opportunity of the arising of a buddha, the chance to hear the dhamma, and the inner capacity to put that dhamma into practice are present. therefore, if such an opportunity is missed, one will have to grieve just like the merchant who, as the buddha described, failed to purchase goods when they were cheap. this is why the buddha instructed us to constantly reflect on the bases of spiritual urgency (*samvega-vatthu*).
the buddha has described this place called "the world" as indeed the very kingdom of mara. the kingdom of mara means invitations to defilements (*kilesas*) from every side. however, through the dhamma brought to light by the buddha, we must understand what ought to be done. it is that path which the buddha has illustrated through the factors of awakening (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*) and other teachings. reflecting on these during a rains-retreat like this, regardless of the various opinions prevalent in the country, one must contemplate: instead of thinking "it is impossible in this rare opportunity," one should arouse the perception of possibility and, at one's own level, strengthen one's mind to further develop whatever meditation one has practiced so far, especially during this rains-retreat. by practicing these meditation subjects (*kammatthana*), powers of which one was previously unaware might emerge from within, just as they did in matika's mother. it is through that energy (*viriya*) that they emerge. like embers beneath ashes, some individuals possess latent power. but many do not step forward to bring it out. for that, one must make an initiative (*arambha*).
it is not a matter of merely learning the word of the buddha. for a long time, you have gone forth from the home life, from your households, generating a certain degree of the power of renunciation (*nekkhamma-sakti*), and have engaged in this listening to dhamma and meditation through the undertaking of virtue (*sila*). furthermore, utilizing that virtue, if on some occasion you remove the hindrances (*nivarana*) and concentrate the mind, it is at that very moment that you can enter the path of insight (*vipassana*). then, the true nature of this world, which the buddha brings to light as the three characteristics (*ti-lakkhana*), is contained within these three words: impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*). regarding this impermanence, the world possesses the perception of permanence (*nicca-sanna*). worldly beings live within four perversions (*vipallasa*), which are distorted views: regarding the impermanent (*anicca*) as permanent, the unbeautiful (*asubha*) as beautiful, the painful (*dukkha*) as pleasant, and what is not-self (*anatta*) as self. the world looks through this distorted lens. however, the buddhist practitioner, relying on the word of the buddha, endeavors to bring to light the true nature of the world—knowledge and vision of things as they really are (*yathabhuta-nanadassana*). while constantly cultivating concentration and so forth, one can look at the world from that perspective. one should not think in the way some worldly intellectuals do. one must align one's thinking with the three characteristics brought to light by the buddha. this is what is called wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*)—contemplating with wisdom.
in this dhamma, two factors are listed as helpful for the arising of right view (*samma-ditthi*): the voice of another (*paratoghosa*) and wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*). "the voice of another," dear devotees, means we must hear the dhamma from someone else; we do not know it on our own. whether from the buddha or a disciple, or not only from spoken words but also from written texts, we must learn the buddha’s dhamma. having learned it, we must also know how to apply wise attention correctly and systematically. even here, some make a mistake, applying unwise attention (*ayoniso manasikara*) instead of wise attention. due to various forms of conceit (*mana*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), and so forth, this era is one where even the word of the buddha is distorted. you know this; these are open secrets. in an era where the dhamma is distorted due to various reasons, reflecting beforehand and bringing to light wise attention is not an easy task either.
identifying correctly those perversions (*vipallasa*) brought to light by the buddha, we must train ourselves to look at the world in an undistorted way. meditation subjects are everywhere in the world. in the ancient dhamma accounts, it is said that some monks attained arahantship upon witnessing a forest fire. other nuns attained it upon seeing water flowing, or seeing leaves falling. these did not happen by accident. to a meditative mind, when a practitioner who has cultivated insight (*vipassana*) is presented with an illustration in a specific situation, they see the truth through it. that is how path-fruits are realized. they are not obtained for nothing. therefore, whether we are lay or ordained, we must constantly train ourselves to look at the world from that perspective. if we train ourselves to look at the world according to the right view (*samma-ditthi*) brought to light by the buddha, that is what is called insight (*vipassana*). if we train ourselves to look with insight, with the eye of insight, then when all those virtues emerge and coalesce, the noble eightfold path becomes active within one's mind-stream, arising in a single mind-moment. it is then that the path-mind (*magga-citta*) arises.
"i am now a devotee who keeps the five precepts. the buddha has said that a stream-enterer possesses the five precepts. since i keep the five precepts perfectly, i too must be a stream-enterer"—there are some who grade themselves in this manner. but the buddha has illustrated the greatness of stream-entry (*sotapatti*) by taking a pinch of soil on his fingernail and asking: "is the soil on the fingernail greater, or the soil of the entire earth?" through this simile, he shows that for a stream-enterer, an immense amount of the suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara has been dismantled. this does not happen automatically through the mere keeping of the five precepts. it occurs through a massive inner transformation. even though it occurs in a brief instant, through a massive transformation, one attains that supramundane mind. releasing the five aggregates (*pancakkhandha*) even for a single moment, and understanding and directly realizing the deep principle of dependent co-arising (*paticcasamuppada*) through that, one becomes a stream-enterer. even the term *sotapanna*—"stream-enterer"—is misunderstood by some who confuse it with a story about the ear. "stream-enterer" means that just as a log of wood thrown into a river flows directly to the ocean, once one enters that stream of dhamma (*dhamma-sota*), they are guaranteed to realize arahantship within at most seven births. this occurs through that very realization of the dhamma.
the direct realization obtained primarily through vision—the direct realization, albeit brief and instantaneous, regarding the true nature of the world—gradually operates within that individual, whether lay or ordained, breaking the potential for rebirth (*jati*) in samsara. breaking it continuously as they walk that path diligently, they subsequently realize the path-fruits of once-returning (*sakadagami*), non-returning (*anagami*), and arahantship. this is a unique internal shift, not a stream-entry that occurs merely because the five precepts are kept. we must reflect on this wisely. there are methods in the world that treat these achievements lightly, promising to deliver them in a day or two. but if we reflect wisely, the truth is that although it occurs in an instant, it happens through that very natural principle (*dhamma-ta*). a stream-enterer can be an extremely poor person, an uneducated person, or someone without any degrees. yet, the buddha describes such a person with a multitude of terms: *ditthadhammo* (one who has seen the dhamma), *pattadhammo* (one who has reached the dhamma), *viditadhammo* (one who has known the dhamma), *pariyogalhadhammo* (one who has plunged into the dhamma), *tinnavicikiccho* (one who has crossed over doubt), *vigatakathankatho* (one who is free from wavering), *vesarajjappatto* (one who has attained courage). through these various terms, he indicates that they have seen the dhamma, reached the dhamma, plunged into the dhamma, and attained courage. this means that they have directly realized that dhamma of dependent co-arising (*paticcasamuppada*) in their own mind-stream in that very instant. it is by virtue of that power that they do not go beyond at most seven more births.
proceeding with a clear understanding of these matters is the path; if one assumes it can be done easily, abandoning meditation and thinking this is attained merely by listening to a few discourses, it is a delusion. avoiding such pitfalls, you must walk the right path, developing virtue (*sila*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*). bringing to light within yourselves those noble elements declared by the buddha—the element of initiative (*arambha-dhatu*), the element of launching (*nikkama-dhatu*), and the element of exertion (*parakkama-dhatu*)—and walking that path of energy trodden by venerable angulimala in the past and venerable milakkhatissa in more recent times, you should make an end of the suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara. this is what is being declared here. thus, what is important here is the battle cry, the war song that aids this—the true war song of buddhists. for the buddha has declared:
> *yo sahassam sahassena,*
> *sangaame maanuse jine;*
> *ekanca jeyyamattanam,*
> *sa ve sangamajuttamo.*
>
> "though one should conquer a million men in battle, yet he indeed is the noblest victor who conquers himself."
remembering this, recognizing these principles, bringing to light that very power within yourselves, organizing that army called the thirty-seven factors of awakening shown by the buddha, and launching the invasion with that military organization, you must endeavor to achieve that supreme exertion.
on a valuable day like today, you have undertaken virtue (*sila*) and must have practiced meditation. at this moment, you have had the opportunity to listen to a dhamma discourse that supports your meditation and aids in bringing an end to the suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara. by putting it into practice, may the wholesome power of this merit be a supportive condition for all of you to realize the path-fruits starting from stream-entry, to bring an end to the terrifying suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara as quickly as possible in this very life, and to arrive at the supreme, deathless nibbana—. from the avici hell to the akanissa heaven, if there are any beings who wish to rejoice in the merit of this preaching and listening to the dhamma, may they, by so rejoicing, find peace in the supreme, deathless nibbana through the awakening they aspire to. with this aspiration, recite these verses.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 084
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #84
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.164)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Abhiññeyyaṃ abhiññātaṃ, bhāvetabbañca bhāvitaṃ,
pahātabbaṃ pahīnaṃ me, tasmā buddhosmi brāhmaṇa;
Vineyya mayi kaṅkhaṃ, adhimuccassu brāhmaṇa,
dullabhaṃ dassanaṃ hoti, sambuddhānaṃ abhiṇhaso;
Yesaṃ ve dullabho loke, pātubhāvo abhiṇhaso,
sohaṃ brāhmaṇa sambuddho, sallakatto anuttaroti.
From:
Sela Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 92), Sutta Nipāta (Sn 3.7)
Dear Listeners,
The news that a Buddha had appeared in the world spread throughout ancient Jambudīpa (India) primarily through the recital of the formula of the nine virtues of the Buddha, beginning with *Arahaṃ*. In an era when there were no diverse or colorful communication media like today, the formula of the nine virtues alone was often sufficient for the news of a Buddha's arising to spread. Furthermore, Buddhist literature makes it clear to us that even a single word among those nine virtues was sometimes capable of causing a massive psychological revolution in a person. The *Sela Sutta*, which is found in both the *Majjhima Nikāya* and the *Sutta Nipāta*, is excellent proof of this.
It is three verses from that *Sela Sutta* that we have chosen as our theme today. On one occasion, the Blessed One, the Teacher of the Three Worlds, accompanied by a large retinue of about one thousand two hundred and fifty monks, was wandering on a Dhamma tour in the region of Aṅguttarāpa in India, and arrived at the market town named Āpana. The matted-hair ascetic (*jaṭila*) named Keṇiya, who lived in that market town of Āpana, heard: "The ascetic Gotama has arrived in our village." A glorious report concerning him had spread in this manner: "*Itipi so Bhagavā Arahaṃ Sammāsambuddho Vijjācaraṇasampanno Sugato Lokavidū Anuttaro Purisadammasārathi Satthā devamanussānaṃ Buddho Bhagavā*" (Thus indeed is the Blessed One: Worthy, Fully Enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Awakened One, the Blessed One). Moreover, having realized this world with its gods and Maras through his own higher knowledge, he makes it known to the world. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end. He proclaims a perfectly pure holy life. Having heard this news, Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic thought, "Indeed, even the mere sight of such worthy ones is a good thing," and went to see the Buddha.
Having gone there, Keṇiya the *jaṭila* exchanged friendly greetings with the Buddha and sat down on one side, after which the Buddha gladdened him with a Dhamma talk. Although at that moment he did not yet possess enough faith to take refuge in the Triple Gem, Keṇiya the *jaṭila* invited the Sangha headed by the Buddha, saying: "O Ascetic Gotama, please accept tomorrow's meal at my hermitage together with the Sangha." Then the Buddha said: "Keṇiya, this assembly of monks is very large. Furthermore, you are one who is well-pleased with the brahmins." Even though the Buddha said this, Keṇiya insisted a second time: "The assembly of monks is indeed large, O Ascetic Gotama, and it is also true that I have faith in the brahmins. Nevertheless, I invite the Venerable Gotama and the Sangha." Once again, the Buddha reminded him: "This assembly of monks is large, and you have faith in the brahmins." Yet, when Keṇiya the *jaṭila* extended the invitation for the third time, the Buddha accepted the invitation in silence.
Understanding this, Keṇiya the *jaṭila* went back to his hermitage and said to his relatives, friends, and associates: "I have invited the Ascetic Gotama along with the Sangha for tomorrow's sacrifice here. Therefore, please perform whatever physical services you can for this endeavor." Those relatives, friends, and associates gathered together; some set up stoves, others chopped firewood. Some prepared water vessels, others washed dishes, and some prepared seats. Keṇiya the *jaṭila* himself was busy preparing the large hall of his hermitage.
At that time, there lived in Āpana a brahmin named Sela, who had reached the further shore of the Three Vedas, and was teaching mantras to about three hundred young brahmin pupils. It is mentioned regarding this brahmin that he was accomplished not only in the Three Vedas but also in history, poetics, prosody, as well as the science of body characteristics known as the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa*). This Brahmin Sela was a close friend of Keṇiya the *jaṭila*. Keṇiya also had great confidence in Brahmin Sela. In the evening, Brahmin Sela, surrounded by his group of pupils, came to this hermitage to see Keṇiya the *jaṭila* as a form of light exercise.
Upon arrival, seeing some building stoves, others splitting firewood, and such a grand preparation underway, he asked Keṇiya: "What is this, Keṇiya? Is there a festival such as a marriage or a wedding feast? Or are you preparing for a great sacrifice? Or have you invited King Bimbisāra along with his army for tomorrow?" Then Keṇiya replied: "No, Sela, it is not a marriage celebration, nor have I invited King Bimbisāra. Rather, I have invited the Ascetic Gotama together with the Sangha for tomorrow." And concerning that Ascetic Gotama, such a report of fame has spread, and he recited the aforementioned passage, starting with *Itipi so Bhagavā*. When he said this, Brahmin Sela asked: "Did you say 'Buddha', Keṇiya?" Then Keṇiya the *jaṭila* replied: "Yes, I said 'Buddha'." A second time he asked: "Did you say 'Buddha', Keṇiya?" — "Yes, I said 'Buddha'." A third time he asked: "Did you say 'Buddha', Keṇiya?" — "Yes, indeed, I said 'Buddha'."
At that point, Brahmin Sela remarked: "Even the hearing of the word 'Buddha' is extremely rare." Then he thought, "In our mantras, it is mentioned concerning Buddhahood that if a person is born with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, only two paths lie open to him in life. If he leads a household life, he becomes a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti). If he goes forth from home into homelessness, he becomes a Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha)." Thinking thus, he next asked: "Where is the Venerable Gotama staying at this moment?" Then, pointing with his right hand, Keṇiya the *jaṭila* declared: "Over there, in the direction of that blue forest grove seen in the distance."
Next, Brahmin Sela went together with his group of disciples to see the Buddha. On the way, out of respect, he said to his pupils: "Walk quietly, step by step. These Fully Enlightened Ones are supreme like lions. Furthermore, do not interrupt while I am speaking." Thus, with a certain degree of faith, he went to meet the Buddha, sat down on one side, and exchanged friendly greetings.
Then, this Brahmin Sela looked closely for the marks of a Great Man on the Buddha's body. When certain doubts arose in him regarding this, it is mentioned that the Buddha, through his psychic powers, made even the hidden parts of his body visible. Once he was freed from doubt about them, Brahmin Sela wondered whether this was indeed a Buddha or someone who could attain the status of a Wheel-turning Monarch. Thereupon, Brahmin Sela thought, "We have heard from our teachers and teachers' teachers in our mantras that when Buddhas are praised in laudation, they reveal their true nature. Therefore, I should recite a series of verses to the Buddha by way of praise and extolling his virtues." Then, as mentioned in the suttas, a long series of verses follows: "There are such wondrous marks on your body. You are fit to be a king. You are worthy even of gaining sovereignty. Why lead this ascetic life, what use is it to you? You are worthy of attaining even the wheel-turning sovereignty of Jambudīpa" — in this manner, he praised him.
Then the Buddha declared: "Sela, I too am a king. I am the King of Dhamma (Dhammarājā). And I turn the Wheel of Dhamma solely through the Dhamma." In this way, he declared, "I am the King of Dhamma." Then Brahmin Sela asked: "Who is your general (*senāpati*)?" The Buddha declared: "Sāriputta is the one who turns after me the Wheel of Dhamma that I have turned." Next, the Buddha uttered the three verses which we have placed as our theme, declaring his own Buddhahood:
> *Abhiññeyyaṃ abhiññātaṃ, bhāvetabbañca bhāvitaṃ,*
> *Pahātabbaṃ pahīnaṃ me, tasmā buddhosmi brāhmaṇa.*
"What is to be known by higher knowledge (*abhiññā*) has been known by me through higher knowledge. If there are things to be developed (*bhāvetabbaṃ*), they have been fully developed by me. What is to be abandoned (*pahātabbaṃ*), such as defilements, has been abandoned by me (*pahīnaṃ me*). *Tasmā buddhosmi brāhmaṇa* — therefore, O brahmin, I am a Buddha."
Then he declares: "Dispel your doubt in me, O brahmin (*vineyya mayi kaṅkhaṃ*); resolve with faith in me, O brahmin (*adhimuccassu brāhmaṇa*). Rare indeed is the sight of the Fully Enlightened Ones (*dullabhaṃ dassanaṃ hoti sambuddhānaṃ abhiṇhaso*)." Next he declares:
> *Yesaṃ ve dullabho loke, pātubhāvo abhiṇhaso,*
> *Sohaṃ brāhmaṇa sambuddho, sallakatto anuttaro ti.*
"I am such a fully enlightened Buddha, whose appearance in the world is extremely rare. I am an incomparable surgeon (*sallakatto anuttaro*)." After his Buddhahood was declared in this manner, Brahmin Sela developed great faith and, presenting further praises of the Buddha to his pupils in verse, said: "I am going to go forth as a monk under this Ascetic Gotama. I will live the holy life. Anyone who wishes to take the step I am taking may join me. Let the others leave." Thereupon, all three hundred disciples said to their teacher: "We too shall take the step that you are taking." Subsequently, the entire group requested the going forth (*pabbajjā*) and higher ordination (*upasampadā*) from the Buddha. It is then mentioned that the Buddha granted them all the going forth and higher ordination.
Now, we return to the hermitage of Keṇiya the *jaṭila*. After preparing everything there for the "sacrifice" (which was the term they used rather than "meal offering"), and when the preparations for the great sacrifice were complete, they sent a message to the Buddha. The Buddha arrived along with the Sangha, and after Keṇiya the *jaṭila* had respectfully served the Buddha with delicious food and other offerings, and the meal was finished, it is mentioned that the Buddha uttered two verses of appreciation (*anumodanā*). The meaning of those verses is nothing other than the Buddha expressing the pre-eminence of sacrifices in this way: "Among sacrifices, the fire sacrifice is foremost. Likewise, regarding the poetic meters in which the Vedic mantras are composed, for which the word *chandas* is used, the Sāvitrī meter is foremost among meters. Among humans, the king is foremost. For flowing rivers, the great ocean is foremost. For stars, the moon is foremost. For shining objects, the sun is foremost. Likewise, for those who sacrifice seeking merit, the Sangha is foremost." Having given this appreciation, the Buddha departed.
What is told next is that Brahmin Sela, along with his group, put forth strenuous and firm effort in meditation, and within seven days, the entire group attained Arahantship. Furthermore, with deep faith, that group along with the pupils went before the Buddha and, with several verses of praise, offered their gratitude to the Buddha. "The Blessed One is the Buddha who has defeated all Māras, destroyed defilements, and removed all acquisitions (*upadhi*)" — paying homage in praise, they finally said: "O Blessed One, please stretch out your feet so that we may worship them." With that, the account in the *Sela Sutta* comes to an end.
Next, what we have to examine is the importance of the formula of the nine virtues as mentioned earlier. You, virtuous devotees, can appreciate the value of this sutta. When Keṇiya the *jaṭila* made the invitation for the sacrifice, the Buddha remained impartial and declined three times. He gave Keṇiya the opportunity to change his mind. Yet, Keṇiya the *jaṭila*, with a certain faith, extended the invitation for that offering. Next, concerning Sela: even with such a large group of pupils, Brahmin Sela came and first developed faith in the Buddha based on his external bodily characteristics. Secondly, during the discussion that ensued, he recognized the Buddha and obtained that ordination.
If we direct our minds to the formula of the nine virtues of the Buddha mentioned earlier, all of you virtuous devotees are familiar with the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) as a meditation practice based on the nine virtues, starting with *Itipi so...* Although we say everyone knows it, even though they pronounce that formula in Pali, the meaning is not clear to some. That is natural for many people in this day and age who lack an understanding of the language.
*Itipi so Bhagavā* — "Thus indeed is the Blessed One." There, at the beginning, some word is necessary to refer to the Buddha. In those days, a word most commonly in usage was *Bhagavā*. Even today in India, many people say "Bhagavān Gotama Buddha" in that way; the word *Bhagavān* is the primary term, just like *Buddha*. That is why this word was used first to introduce the Buddha: *Itipi so Bhagavā* — "Thus indeed is that Blessed One." From there onwards we have: He is *Arahaṃ* (Worthy). We will explain each word simply hereafter. *Arahaṃ* (Worthy), *Sammāsambuddho* (Fully Enlightened), *Vijjācaraṇasampanno* (Perfect in True Knowledge and Conduct), *Sugato* (Sublime), *Lokavidū* (Knower of Worlds), *Anuttaro Purisadammasārathi* (Incomparable Leader of Persons to be Tamed), *Satthā devamanussānaṃ* (Teacher of Gods and Humans), *Buddho* (The Awakened One), *Bhagavā* (The Blessed One). It is only at the end that the term *Bhagavā* is mentioned as belonging to the nine virtues.
You, virtuous devotees, have studied these in various ways. The recollection of the Buddha is practiced in many different ways. We too have expressed some thoughts on this here on previous occasions. On this occasion, regarding its practical application as a formula of the nine virtues, we have previously shown a method that is truly simple and suitable for regular use. To state it now according to our understanding: certain meditation methods that existed simply during the Buddha's time became highly complex in later times, and by the attempts of scholars to analyze them at an academic level, it appears that their practical value was lost.
Here, if we take the word *Arahaṃ* itself, if you ask many people today, they might not give the true meaning of the word *Arahaṃ* but tell you other things instead. They might say it means "because he does not commit sin even in secret." Or "because he has cut the spokes (*ara*) of the wheel of saṃsāra." Or "because he has destroyed the enemies (*ari*) which are the defilements." What has happened here? It appears that scholars have dissected the words this way and that, highlighting foreign meanings not relevant to the original sense of the word, and have assigned meditators to keep expounding on them at length. Frankly speaking, although the idea of "not committing sin even in secret" has been mentioned in various books for ages, it is actually a word that is almost like an insult to the Buddha. The meaning of the word *Arahaṃ* is "worthiness of receiving offerings." Being worthy of offerings is what is meant by *Arahaṃ* or *arahato*. One can understand that he is worthy of offerings due to those virtues. But what those scholars have done to the word *Arahaṃ* is to break it this way and that. Removing the letter 'a' (අ) and taking 'rahaṃ' (රහං), they dragged in a story about "secrets" (*rahas*). Taking the idea of the spokes of a wheel (*ara*) in the wheel of saṃsāra, they removed 'haṃ' and took 'ara'.
So, not only do those stories about spokes and secrets suppress the relevant meaning, but instead of keeping the mind established on the virtue of the Buddha, the mind runs after the etymologies and derivations of the word. The mind runs after unnecessary things. Just consider for a moment: you virtuous devotees know of the eight-faceted gem (octagonal gem). Looking at its faceted form, you can imagine it as an octagon. In such an eight-faceted gem, whichever of the eight sides you look at, you only see the gem. Similarly, if we think of the formula of the nine virtues as a nine-faceted gem, if it is a nine-faceted gem, whichever side we look at, we should be reminded of the Buddha. Instead, if our mind is dragged away to those unnecessary details, that is not suitable.
Another word that has been heavily dissected in this way is *Bhagavā*. Extremely strange meanings have been attributed to it. Scholars have presented these as the meditation on the virtues of the Buddha. This caused the practical values that existed during the Buddha's time to slip away. Only the scholars can understand it. Those who do not understand simply keep reciting the Pali words somehow. To one who understands, however, it is truly apparent that those stories about secrets are completely external to the word *Arahaṃ*. Therefore, one must consider that the word *Arahaṃ* is also mentioned in the phrase *Namo tassa bhagavato arahato*. There is no story about secrets there at all. It means the Blessed One, and then: "worthy of offerings" due to the greatness of his virtues. Thus we have: *Itipi so Bhagavā Arahaṃ*.
Next, *Sammā* (Perfect / Rightly); you virtuous devotees can also contemplate this. Added to the word *Buddha*, we get *Sambuddha* or *Sammāsambuddha*. If we take the comprehension implied by *Sammāsambuddha*, many people today use it to mean that he realized the truth by himself, perfectly through self-attained knowledge (*svayambhū-ñāṇa*). To convey the idea that the Buddha realized it entirely from within himself, without any teacher's instruction, through his own higher knowledge, the term *Sammāsambuddho* is used. Next, the word *Sampanno* (endowed with) is also analyzed in various ways. Constantly analyzing these can be an obstacle to meditation. If we define it briefly, we can say that *Vijjā* (knowledge) and *Caraṇa* (conduct) represent two aspects of a person's life. We now have two eyes that can see. Even if our eyes can see, if we cannot walk—if we are lame—we cannot go on a journey. Even if we have two legs, if our eyes cannot see, we still cannot go on a journey. *Vijjā* refers to that understanding, which is like the two eyes. Next, *Caraṇa* refers to behavior in accordance with that understanding; virtues such as moral virtue (*sīla*). Through *Vijjā*, the accumulation of knowledge within a Buddha, such as insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) related to Buddhahood, is indicated. Next, *Caraṇa* refers to virtues such as moral virtue. Being complete in both of these is what is meant by *Vijjācaraṇasampanno*.
Thus, it is precisely due to being perfect in knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇa-sampanna*) that he is called *Sugato* — meaning "well-gone." It is a very short word, but if we make it meaningful, we should think that because of being complete in both the aforementioned vision and conduct, he went to the very end of the path that had to be traveled. He went exceedingly well, hence *Sugato*. Because of that going, he is *Lokavidū* — meaning he realized all that should be known regarding the world, both internally and externally.
Thus, precisely because he has a clear understanding of everything internal and external, he is *Sugato Lokavidū Anuttaro Purisadammasārathi*. Regarding that taming, even in the pronunciation of the word *Purisadammasārathi*, it is not *Purisadhamma* but *Purisadamma*, with an unaspirated 'da'. Nowadays, there is no regard for unaspirated or aspirated letters; everything has become a tangled mess. *Purisadammasārathi* means being like a skilled charioteer in taming persons fit to be tamed. That is *Purisadammasārathi*. That is to say, because of the aforementioned virtue of *Lokavidū*, the inner potentials that a person has brought along through saṃsāra are visible to him. Furthermore, the exact moment, place, and manner in which that person should be tamed are all visible to the Buddha because of his quality of *Lokavidū*. He possesses that supreme ability to tame: *Anuttaro Purisadammasārathi*.
For this very reason, he is the teacher not only of humans but also of gods (*Satthā devamanussānaṃ*). You have heard of Baka Brahmā and others; similarly, it is often mentioned in the Dhamma that deities came and engaged in Dhamma discussions and asked questions of the Buddha, even though some people in this day and age do not believe these things. If we believe this passage, we must accept that the Buddha was a teacher not only to humans but also to gods — *Satthā devamanussānaṃ*. Next, at the end, it says *Buddho*. Here, in this sutta, the Buddha himself directly gives a definition, an introduction, for the word *Buddho*:
> *Abhiññeyyaṃ abhiññātaṃ, bhāvetabbañca bhāvitaṃ,*
> *Pahātabbaṃ pahīnaṃ me, tasmā buddhosmi brāhmaṇa.*
"Things to be known through higher knowledge have been known by me through higher knowledge. Next, the virtues to be developed for Buddhahood have been fully developed. The defilements and so forth to be abandoned have been abandoned. Because of this, I am a true Buddha." One can say he has awakened from the sleep of defilements, or that he has attained that full realization — *Buddho*.
Next, *Bhagavā*. The word *Bhagavā* carries the meaning of "fortunate" or "blessed," which is still commonly used today. Thus, that brahmin first looked at the blessed nature of the Buddha externally, such as the marks of a Great Man. Next, his internal virtues. The Buddha was fortunate from both sides — externally and internally. Due to training for a long time in saṃsāra, through his power of merit, and through the power of his perfections (*pāramī*), all the qualities gathered within a Buddha are, in short, encapsulated in the word *Bhagavā*, as if it were the sum total of the other eight virtues. Even today in India, many people refer to the Buddha as "Bhagavān," the Blessed One. Similarly, in the sutta discourses, the faithful devotees often refer to the Buddha not only as "Buddha, Bhagavā, the Buddha," but also as "the Blessed One" (Bhāgyavatun-vahanse). So that is regarding the nine virtues.
In addition, a unique phrase was mentioned in the verses uttered by the Buddha. Let us say something about that too: *Sallakatto anuttaro*. What does that mean? He says, "I am an incomparable surgeon." In this day and age, too, there are doctors who perform various kinds of heart surgeries, such as bypass surgeries. Yet, whatever they do, one cannot escape Death (Māra) thereby. Escaping from Māra—though everyone must die, those surgeons cannot cure this journey of being born and dying repeatedly over a long time in saṃsāra. But what did the Buddha do? The poison arrow, or the dart, of craving (*taṇhā*) is pierced in the heart. And the poison is the poison of ignorance (*avijjā*). The Buddha has analyzed it in various places in this way as *avijjā-visadoso* (the poison of ignorance). The dart of craving, dipped in the poison of ignorance, is pierced in the heart. It is because he pulled that out that he is called the incomparable surgeon: *Sallakatto anuttaro*. Anyone can develop faith even by reflecting on this. Thinking of it from another angle: as you virtuous devotees know, when an occasion arises to undergo heart surgery, and one's friends and relatives gather and ask where to get treatment, they say, "So-and-so is good, that doctor has such-and-such degrees." Saying so, they often choose the surgeon who possesses a series of qualifications that inspires confidence.
Now consider this: the removal of that dart of craving is not like a bypass surgery. The qualification list suitable for performing that surgery which completely liberates one from Māra is found within the formula of the nine virtues. *Arahaṃ*, *Sammāsambuddho*, *Sampanno* — we can think of these as the surgeon's qualifications. We can choose to look at it that way to inspire faith. In any case, why is the meditation on the virtues of the Buddha given a primary place among meditations? We must reflect on that too.
