having received ordination and higher ordination, according to the monastic customs, he spent five years under his teachers and preceptors (*acariya-upajjhaya*), learning the things pertaining to the life of a monk. having spent five years in this manner, and as the next rain-retreat approached, he approached the buddha and obtained permission to spend the rain-retreat in a remote forest hermitage, practicing meditation. having obtained permission and received instructions for meditation (*kammatthana*) up to arahantship from the buddha, he set off with a group of sixty other monks, passing through villages and market towns, searching for a suitable place many leagues away.
when this group of monks arrived at a certain remote village, the faithful laypeople of that village, having come to know the intention of the monks, built and prepared a monastery and invited them to reside there. the monks agreed and resided there, taking up their lodgings. the next day, while they were walking for alms, a physician of that very village said to the venerable mahapala, "venerable sir, in places where many people reside, illnesses are frequent. should such an occasion arise, please tell me. please let me know," thus placing himself at their service.
then came the day of entering the rain-retreat, the start of the *vassa* period. on that day, venerable mahapala gathered the other sixty monks, and during the discussion at the start of the retreat, he asked, "venerable sirs, in how many postures do you intend to spend these three months of the rain-retreat?" there are four postures: standing, sitting, walking, and reclining. "out of these four postures, in how many postures do you intend to spend these three months of the *vassa*?" the monks replied, "we expect to spend these three months of the rain-retreat in all four postures."
then venerable mahapala declared, "we have received our instructions directly from the living buddha. friends, do not be negligent. for the negligent person, the four woeful states are like one's own home." next, the monks asked, "venerable sir, in how many postures do you intend to spend these three months of the *vassa*?" the venerable monk declared, "as for me, i intend to spend the three months of the rain-retreat in only three postures: standing, sitting, and walking. i have no intention of stretching my back on a bed or reclining during these three months." then the other monks said, "sadhu, sadhu, very well, venerable sir, please act diligently."
this venerable mahapala meditated intensely day and night, without sleep. when one month of the rain-retreat had passed, around the time of a poya day like this, the venerable monk contracted a severe eye disease. one night, tears began to stream from his eyes like water flowing from a leaking pot. the next morning, when it was time to go for alms, the other monks came and said, "venerable sir, it is time for alms-round." then he said, "in that case, take my bowl and robe."
as he was preparing to go to the village with the monks, they saw the tears streaming from his eyes. seeing this, they asked, "what is it, venerable sir?" and he replied, "i have contracted a wind-ailment (*vatabadha*)." then they said, "in that case, venerable sir, a physician has put himself at our service. shall we inform the physician?" he agreed, saying, "very well."
when the monks informed the physician of the matter, the physician prepared a certain medicine to be administered through the nose (*nasya*). normally, nasal medicine must be administered while lying down. however, when venerable mahapala received the medicine, he administered it while sitting up, as he did not wish to break his determination.
the next day, when he went to the village for alms, the physician met him and asked, "venerable sir, we heard that you are unwell. we prepared and sent some medicine; did you receive it?" "yes, i received it." "did you use it?" "yes, i used it." "how is the illness now?" "it still hurts, doctor," he replied.
the physician thought, "according to the nature of the medicine i sent, it should have been cured instantly. what is the reason for this?" and asked, "venerable sir, did you administer this nasal medicine sitting up or lying down?" the venerable monk remained silent. the physician asked again and again, but received no answer. the physician then said, "very well, venerable sir," and decided to go and see for himself. he went to the monastery, walked around the hut, and looked. he saw the place where the venerable monk practiced walking meditation, and he saw the place where he sat, but there was no bed. there was no place to recline.
the physician understood the situation, and when the venerable monk returned, he said, "venerable sir, do not practice in this manner. it is only as long as this body is in good health that one can fulfill the duties of a monk. therefore, please administer this medicine only while lying down," pleading with him repeatedly. then, finding no way to escape the physician's pleading, the venerable monk said, "very well, lay devotee, you may go. we shall discuss and see about it." after the physician left, the venerable monk held a discussion. with whom did he discuss? with himself. with his own body.
"what do you say, palita? are you looking after your two eyes, or are you looking after the dispensation of the buddha? in this samsara, you must have been born blind countless times. similarly, you have met hundreds of thousands of buddhas. yet, you have not associated with even one buddha properly, nor have you derived any benefit from a buddha; you have not done the real work. that is why you have remained in samsara for so long. you have made a firm determination that you will meditate without sleeping during these three months of the rain-retreat, and that you will not stretch your back on a bed. therefore, if the two eyes are destroyed, let them be destroyed; if they shatter, let them shatter. direct your mind only toward the dispensation of the buddha. think only about that!"
having firmly resolved in this manner, he administered the nasal medicine while sitting up on that day too, and continued his meditation intensely. the next day, when walking for alms, he met the physician again, who asked, "venerable sir, how did you use the medicine?" "yes, i used it." "how is it now?" "it still hurts, doctor." the physician asked again, "venerable sir, did you use this medicine sitting up or lying down?" again, the venerable monk remained silent.
then the physician, somewhat displeased, said, "venerable sir, in that case, since you do not live in a way that is compatible with this medicine, from today, please do not tell anyone that i prepared and sent this medicinal oil. and i too will not tell anyone that i treated you." thus, he rejected him; he refused to treat him. having said this, the physician left. the venerable monk returned to his hut and admonished himself again: "now, palita, even the physician has rejected you. now you must prepare for death. there is no more time to be negligent!" having made a firm determination, he stepped down to the walking path and began to meditate.
on that night, as the middle watch of the night was passing, at the very same moment, at the very same time, both his eyes and his defilements shattered. that is to say, simultaneously with the loss of his sight, his mind was established in the noble fruit of arahantship, liberated from all defilements. then, the venerable monk, realizing the change that had occurred within him, came off the walking path, entered his hut, and sat on the bed.
the next morning, when it was time to go for alms, the other monks came and informed him, "venerable sir, it is time for alms-round." "ah, is that so? if so, you venerable sirs may go for alms," he said. "and what about you, venerable sir?" "my two eyes are lost," he replied. he did not speak of the other thing he had attained.
then the monks were filled with great sorrow and said, "venerable sir, we shall perform all the duties and attend to you. we shall look after you," and they went to the village for alms. the faithful lay devotees in the village, noticing that the elder monk had not arrived that day, asked, "where is the chief venerable monk today?" the monks explained the matter.
hearing this, the faithful laypeople were deeply moved. they quickly brought the alms-food, fell prostrate at the feet of the venerable monk, weeping and wailing, and said, "venerable sir, we shall perform all services and look after you." having made arrangements, they departed.
during the remaining period of the three months of the rain-retreat, this venerable monk constantly purified the meditation instructions (*kammatthana*) and gave advice and admonitions to the other sixty monks, urging them to act diligently. established in those admonitions, all sixty monks attained the noble fruit of arahantship even before the end of the rain-retreat.
at the end of the retreat, these monks thought, "now we must go to see the buddha." they came to the chief monk and asked for permission. their intention was to take the chief monk along with them, but venerable mahapala, thinking that it would be a trouble to the others, did not go with them. he arranged for the other monks to go to jetavana first, and for himself to go later.
after venerable mahapala arrived at jetavana, he began to reside in a separate hut. because the story about venerable mahapala's eyes became famous, he was given a nickname: venerable cakkhupala. it was due to this circumstance that he became famous as venerable cakkhupala.
then, one day, some monks from that region came to see the buddha, and thinking of visiting venerable cakkhupala as well, they set out to go to his quarters in the evening. just then, a heavy rain fell. therefore, the monks thought, "we shall go and see him in the morning. now it is raining, and it is too late in the evening," and they turned back.
that night, during the middle watch, a very heavy rain fell and then cleared up. next, in the early dawn, venerable cakkhupala began to meditate, practicing walking meditation. after the rain, as you virtuous friends know, a type of insect called winged termites (*meru*) usually emerges from the earth with wings. insects like winged termites came out on the walking path and were spread all over it. since venerable cakkhupala was blind, he did not see this. as he practiced walking meditation, those insects were killed.
the next morning, while those monks were coming to visit venerable cakkhupala's hut, they looked at the walking path and saw the dead insects. they asked the other monks who were there, "who is it that has practiced walking meditation here?" the monks replied, "this is our preceptor."
"look at the deed of this monk! doing nothing when his eyes were functional, sleeping well, and now, claiming to do walking meditation, he has put to death such a large number of insects!" making a huge outcry and criticism, they went to the buddha and reported the matter.
the buddha asked those monks, "monks, did you see this monk killing the insects?" the monks replied, "no, venerable sir, we did not see it." "just as you did not see it, so too that monk did not kill them intentionally. in an arahant, even the volition (*cetana*) to kill living beings does not arise." when this matter was declared, the monks inquired, "venerable sir, if venerable cakkhupala had the fortune and merit to become an arahant, why did he become blind?"
then the buddha declared, "that too is due to a certain evil deed committed in the past." when the monks asked about that story, the buddha related it.
in the past, in the city of benares (*baranasi*), there was a certain physician, a traveling doctor, who used to go from village to village treating people. he practiced this profession. one day, while traveling, he met a woman with an eye ailment and asked, "what is the matter?" she replied, "i can barely see with my eyes." he asked, "shall i treat you?" "yes, very well," she said.
then the physician asked, "in that case, what fee will you give me?" the woman said, "i, along with my children, will become your slaves." "very well," said the physician, and he prepared and gave her a certain medicine. by using that medicine just once, the woman's eye ailment was completely cured.
however, she thought, "if i tell the truth that i am cured, i will have to fulfill my promise. therefore, i must deceive the physician." when the physician came again and asked, "how is your eye ailment?" she replied, "oh, previously i could see at least a little, but now i cannot see at least a little, but now i cannot see at all. now it is extremely painful."
the physician understood her motive: "this woman is trying to deceive me. i will teach her a good lesson." (even nowadays people say such things, "i will teach a good lesson".) thinking "i will teach her a good lesson," he went home, told his wife, and prepared another medicine. it was a medicine that would cause blindness.
he brought it and told the woman, "use this again," and made her apply it right there. as soon as she finished applying it, just like a lamp-flame going out, both her eyes went blind.
in this manner, having declared the past kamma, the buddha said, "monks, my son cakkhupala has been pursued by that evil deed committed in the past up to this very day." he explained that the evil deed committed by someone follows him just as the wheel follows the hoof of the ox bound to the cart, and then the buddha proclaimed the dhamma verse we chose as our theme today:
> *mano pubbangama dhamma, mano settha manomaya;*
> *manasa ce padutthena, bhasati va karoti va;*
> *tato nam dukkhamanveti, cakkamva vahato padam.*
"mind precedes all phenomena, mind is their chief, they are mind-made." this mind precedes all mental states (*cetasika*) and thoughts that arise in the mind. to whatever extent thoughts arise in the mind—feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), volition (*cetana*), etc., which are called preparations (*sankhara*)—the mind precedes every single phenomenon that arises in the mind.
likewise, "mind is their chief" (*mano settha*)—the mind is supreme to them. "mind-made" (*manomaya*)—they are processed and fashioned by the mind itself. because of this fact, this law of nature, "if with a corrupt mind one speaks or acts" (*manasa ce padutthena bhasati va karoti va*)—if one speaks or acts with a corrupt mind, a defiled mind, "suffering follows him, even as the wheel follows the hoof of the ox" (*tato nam dukkhamanveti cakkamva vahato padam*)—because of that, suffering follows that person. suffering pursues him closely, just as the wheel of the cart follows the hoof of the ox drawing the cart. the buddha proclaimed this verse which is placed at the very beginning of the dhammapada.
this verse is an extremely helpful and valuable verse for shaping one's life and philosophy of life. that is why, although there are countless verses, it is placed at the very beginning of the dhammapada. let us contemplate further on this verse.
the arising of a thought is something directly experienced by you virtuous friends. a thought arises regarding some object. that arising thought can sometimes be an unwholesome thought, or a wholesome thought. here, it speaks about the unwholesome side. unwholesome means it can be a thought of greed (*lobha*), a thought of hatred (*dosa*), or a thought of delusion (*moha*). in this manner, a thought arises.
let us say, upon seeing something in one's house or in some place, greed arises immediately. along with that thought, the feelings (*vedana*) or sensations experienced regarding it, the perceptions (*sanna*) as recognition of it, and the actions to be taken regarding it—all these arise in accordance with that very greed. in that manner, when a thought of greed, hatred, or delusion arises, because other phenomena arise in accordance with it, if a person speaks or acts with a corrupt mind, the things done with such a corrupt, defiled mind are what are mentioned even in the virtue with livelihood as the eighth (*ajiva-atthamaka-sila*): lying, slandering, harsh speech, and frivolous talk, which occur due to greed, hatred, and delusion.
if one uses words in that manner, or, as deeds done by the body, actions such as killing living beings, stealing, and sexual misconduct; and furthermore, there are things thought by the mind without controlling it—unwholesome states generated by the mind itself as mental kamma (*manokamma*). bodily kamma, verbal kamma, mental kamma. these are covetousness (*abhijjha*), ill-will (*vyapada*), and wrong view (*miccha-ditthi*). in accordance with covetousness, seeing another's prosperity, one thinks, "oh, if only i could get this!" or, generating hatred toward someone, one has angry thoughts instead of thoughts of loving-kindness. or, holding wrong views, one thinks various thoughts according to a wrong understanding.
in this way, a person can commit all ten unwholesome courses of action (*dasa-akusala-kamma*) due to this corrupt mind. because of the things thus accumulated, the results of those unwholesome actions will later cause that person to experience severe physical and mental suffering (*dukkha*) in this long samsara—in the four woeful states: in hell, the animal realm, the peta world, and the asura world—or even in the human world itself. just as an ox bound to a cart has its neck squeezed when pulling the cart, and its leg is struck by the wheel when it moves backward, so too these evil deeds are a massive, heavy burden for a person. that law of nature must be understood—the supremacy of the mind in all this, and the law of nature between the action and its result.
we must think about the lesson to be drawn from this narrative. there is a lesson to be drawn from such a story. the verse too is exemplary for leading our lives. when we think about this narrative, the conflict between the wheel of kamma and the wheel of dhamma, which we mentioned earlier, is evident here.
venerable cakkhupala's determination to meditate intensely and severely during those three months of the rain-retreat succeeded; he became an arahant. yet, at the same time, an evil deed that pursued him from behind was activated. from this, we see the terrible connection between kamma and its result. kamma and its result go together inevitably, in an unavoidable manner.
to say nothing of others, even for a buddha, this law of nature—how powerful the wheel of kamma is—is such that even after attaining arahantship, one has to experience its results. however, there is one consolation: after attaining arahantship, there is no further birth (*jati*). there is no force left in the performed kammas to bring about a new birth. the seed-potential of kamma is destroyed. that is what attaining arahantship means.
yet, even arahants have to experience certain retributive results in this very life. it is mentioned that even the arahant angulimala had to experience the results of kamma (*kamma-vipaka*) after becoming an arahant. the same is said of the chief disciple arahant maha moggallana. those arahants too had to experience the results of kamma. from this, we can imagine how powerful the wheel of kamma is. yet, at the same time, the important thing we see is the path of liberation from this. by ending birth, which means bringing it to a close there, the power of kamma to yield results is deactivated. this is what is called nibbana.
it is only during the period of a buddha’s appearance in the world that we are able to do this—to travel on this path to nibbana in accordance with such a philosophy of life, to attain that peace of nibbana, and to escape from this wheel of kamma. therefore, we must contemplate deeply on this dhamma verse.
when we look at this present era, almost everywhere in the world, human beings give priority to material things. the materialist perspective is what stands out in the world today. due to giving prominence to things seen by the eye and heard by the ear, the mind, which is the precursor to everything, has been forgotten. the buddha has highlighted this fact: *mano pubbangama dhamma mano settha manomaya*. we must constantly recollect these extremely valuable words.
no matter how many external things there are in the world, you virtuous friends know that whatever bad things happen in the world, the mind is at the root of them all. it is through the mind that one is told, "do this and that." likewise, the mind is at the root of good things too.
because of this, the most valuable lesson we can draw from this verse and this story is to keep a close watch over our own mind. if we do not guard this mind, if we do not protect the mind, and consequently commit unwholesome actions with a corrupt mind, or by using bad words, doing bad things, committing evil deeds—sometimes the retributive result of an evil deed committed in a single fraction of a second, in a single moment, has to be paid for in hell for aeons (*kalpas*). evil deeds that cause suffering for aeons can sometimes occur in a single moment. the buddha has declared that the mind is supreme in all of this:
> *cittena niyati loko, cittena parikassati;*
> *cittassa ekadhammassa, sabbeva vasamanvagu.*
the buddha declared: "the world is led by the mind; by the mind it is drawn away. under the sway of this one state, the mind, all have come." here, "the world" refers to the beings of the world. it is by the mind itself that the beings of the world are led to various states. *cittena niyati loko*—the mind alone leads them. "come, let's go to heaven; come, let's go to hell; come, let's go to the animal realm"—in this manner, the mind alone speaks. we do not know it, but this is what lies in those wholesome and unwholesome actions we perform. it is the mind itself that takes us, that leads us.
next, *cittena parikassati*—the mind drags us hither and thither. constantly, when going to the city, people go searching for various things according to their minds; therefore, the mind is supreme in every single thing. *cittassa ekadhammassa sabbeva vasamanvagu*—the entire world is subject to this single thing called the mind. only the buddha has made such a fearless declaration regarding the mind.
the ordinary world is deluded by things seen by the eye and heard by the ear. giving prominence to these, they make their long journey in samsara terrible, experiencing their retributive results. the buddha also declared: *cittasankilesa, bhikkhave, satta sankil बढती santi; cittavodana satta visujjhanti.* "monks, by the defilement of the mind, beings are defiled; by the purification of the mind, beings are purified."
no matter how well one bathes in scented water, applies perfumes and powders, and remains clean, if that man's or woman's mind is defiled—defiled with greed, lust, hatred, and delusion—at that moment, all that external cleanliness is gone. it is in such a state. the buddha declared that it is through the defilement of the mind that everyone becomes defiled. thus, the necessity of guarding the mind is evident to us.
the mind acts with extreme rapidity. the buddha declared that nothing in the world revolves as fast as this mind. it is called *lahuparivattam* (swift to change). nothing is seen in the world that acts as fast as this mind; it is extremely swift. therefore, to control a mind that acts so rapidly, a certain systematic program is necessary. that is what is called meditation (*bhavana*). meditation means development—the development of the mind.
the world is extremely enthusiastic about the development of the body, because it is something visible externally. but the development of the mind, this invisible mind—its development is what the buddha has shown as meditation. if this is not properly controlled, one cannot say whether one will get caught in the terrible evil deeds of samsara and have to experience their results.
to escape from these evil deeds, some people climb high into the sky, some go to the middle of the sea, and others go into the clefts of mountains. the buddha declared that one cannot escape by any of these means:
> *na antalikkhe na samuddamajjhe,*
> *na pabbatanam vivaram pavissa;*
> *na vijjati so jagatippadeso,*
> *yatthatthito munceyya papakamma.*
in a verse in the dhammapada itself, it is stated: "not in the sky, nor in the midst of the sea, nor by entering a cleft in the mountains; there is no place found on earth where staying, one may escape from the consequences of an evil deed." if the consequences of these evil deeds are so terrible, then a special effort must be made to guard this mind.
when we consider the effort to guard this mind, the first thing to be understood is this division of wholesome and unwholesome (*kusala* and *akusala*). here, the talk is about the unwholesome side. the ordinary world mostly remains on the unwholesome side. the buddha has shown what the roots of these unwholesome states are: greed, hatred, and delusion (*lobha, dosa, moha*).
next, the wholesome roots are shown as the effort exerted to remove these unwholesome roots. if one generates a thought through the effort to eliminate greed, that is non-greed (*alobha*). next, the opposite of hatred is non-hatred (*adosa*). the thought opposite to delusion is non-delusion (*amoha*). contemplating in this manner, selecting and distinguishing between these wholesome roots and unwholesome roots is extremely necessary for a person. every time a thought arises, one must immediately investigate and see what it is.
there is also someone who takes charge of watching over this mind. that person resides within this very mind. the buddha has introduced that as mindfulness (*sati*). *sati* means memory or attentiveness. the buddha has shown *sati arakkhasarathi*—mindfulness is the guardian and the charioteer. when driving a chariot, it is the driver who controls and protects it there. the importance given to the word *sati* is evident from this: *sati arakkhasarathi*—mindfulness is the guardian soldier.
this mindfulness, this guardian soldier, also has an operation. the operation here is attention (*manasikara*)—reflection or pondering. therefore, what is expected here is reflecting with mindfulness. along with this mindfulness, another factor is employed. that is called clear comprehension (*sampajanna*)—wisdom, thorough wisdom. mindfulness and clear comprehension go together. the two words *sati-sampajanna* are often used together. the reason for this is that mindfulness brings the matter to the forefront, and clear comprehension, with thorough wisdom, understands that matter and gains a correct comprehension of it.
now, let us say a thought has arisen regarding something. turning back immediately, one directs one's reflection to see: "what is this thought? is it a thought of greed? is it a thought of hatred? is it a thought of delusion?" and remains watchful over it. in that manner, employing mindfulness, and through the operation called attention (*manasikara*) in accordance with mindfulness, one must quickly recognize that thought. if it is an unwholesome thought, it must be nipped in the bud. if instead of nipping it in the bud, one gives way to that thought, then consequently bad words will be uttered and one gets bound to evil deeds; or wrong actions are committed, the body acts accordingly, and one gets bound to evil deeds.
therefore, the buddha has pointed out that one must be diligent in this reflection: *sati-sampajanna*. the grand plan for this is what the buddha has shown as the four establishments of mindfulness (*satipatthana*)—establishing mindfulness on this body, on feelings (*vedana*), on the mind, and on the mental phenomena that arise in the mind, and living mindfully regarding them. this is what *satipatthana* means. it is through this that, in terms of insight (*vipassana*), one can bring to light even the three characteristics (*tilakkhana*): impermanence (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and non-self (*anatta*). with the thorough wisdom employed alongside mindfulness, the true nature of things is revealed. mindfulness is applied, and at the same time, clear comprehension (*sampajanna*) explains its meaning there. this is what *sati-sampajanna* is.
thus, by means of this *sati-sampajanna*, during the period of a buddha’s appearance in the world, a person is able to ultimately break the wheel of kamma. breaking the wheel of kamma, as mentioned before, means drying up the retributive power of kammas. kamma possesses a power to create various existences (*bhava*) and yield results. that retributive power is dried up by wisdom.
you virtuous friends have heard: *avijja-paccaya sankhara*—due to ignorance, preparations (*sankhara*) accumulate. therefore, if it is due to not knowing that preparations—these kammas—accumulate, when wisdom is added, their kammic power is diminished. that is why, through the path to nibbana shown by the buddha, one is ultimately able to dry up the seeds of kamma and attain liberation from samsara. why do we undergo suffering, being born again and again for such an extremely long time? it is to pay off these kammas. the severity of kamma is evident from this.
it is by these kammas alone that these physical cages are fashioned. although we say "i" and "mine", this is something received as a result of kamma itself. the buddha has shown this as "heirs to kamma" (*kamma-dayada*), etc. the mind is supreme in all this. guarding this mind is the function that the buddha has shown as meditation.
the deepest idea regarding this is the path to nibbana shown by the buddha, which is the middle path called insight meditation (*vipassana bhavana*). insight meditation is the realization of the true nature of the world as impermanent (*anicca*) and non-self (*anatta*). it is for this that correct mindfulness and thorough wisdom are helpful. through this reflection, one can realize the true nature of everything. it is not that a buddha shows it, but as *paccattam veditabbo vinnuhi* (to be personally realized by the wise), the buddha has declared that the wise can realize this dhamma, this law of nature, by themselves.
the path that helps in this is the noble eightfold path. there too, *samma-ditthi, samma-sankappa, samma-vaca, samma-kammanta, samma-ajiva, samma-vayama*, and *samma-sati* represent the bringing of this life onto the correct path according to a plan. it is steering it from the wrong path onto the right path. *samma-ditthi* means right view. within right view is the understanding of good and bad, the understanding of wholesome and unwholesome, as well as the comprehension of the four noble truths: suffering (*dukkha*), the cause of suffering, the cessation of suffering which is nibbana, and the path thereto, the noble eightfold path. the understanding of the four noble truths is contained within this *samma-ditthi*.
the vision of life gained through this *samma-ditthi* makes a very powerful change in a person's life. because this mind operates with extreme rapidity. the stream of the mind is extremely swift. if one is unable to control it, it is just like taking the steering wheel of a vehicle without a proper understanding of its control panel. one does not know where it will end. therefore, right view is extremely necessary.
even if one does not have an understanding of those deep and vast teachings at one's own level, it is like having an understanding of good and bad, an understanding of black and white. the buddha has shown "the dark and the bright states are contrastive" (*kanha-sukka appatibhagam*), as mentioned in the dhamma. he points out black and white to the world. at the very least, a person must know: "this is black, this is white."
in the same way, the buddha has pointed out what is unwholesome and what is wholesome. greed, hatred, and delusion are unwholesome. non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are wholesome. if a person understands at least this much, they can shape their philosophy of life to a great extent accordingly.
a greater depth comes with gaining some degree of understanding of the four noble truths, which correctly display the nature of this samsara and the nature of life. this entire samsaric existence is suffering (*dukkha*). from this very incident, it is clear that even after becoming an arahant, venerable cakkhupala had to experience such retributive results. similarly, other arahants and even the buddha had to experience the results of kamma. so terrible is kamma and its retributive aspect. having understood that matter, what must be done is to escape from this samsara.
the buddha reminds us: "why remain in such a risky place?" he urges us to act diligently and escape from this samsara. indeed, nibbana means the ending of this suffering, the escape from samsara. a person must have a great sense of spiritual urgency (*samvega*) regarding this, in order to cultivate a good philosophy of life.
therefore, one must develop a deep understanding of suffering to some extent. next, at the root of this suffering lies craving (*tanha*). it is because of craving that the world acts, speaks, and thinks in this manner. that fact must be understood. this craving is like an endless thirst. what must be done is to completely quench this thirst. normally, quenching a physical thirst is completed by drinking water. but quenching the thirst of craving is not an easy thing. no matter how many things are given to it—it is only the fuel (*upadana*) given to this greed, hatred, and delusion that has changed between the buddha's time and this time.
more than two thousand years ago, what existed was greed, hatred, and delusion. today, too, the very same things exist. some might say that this dhamma is something obsolete. the buddha has declared: *satanca dhammo na jaram upeti*—the dhamma of the virtuous, of the buddhas and other noble ones, never undergoes decay or becomes obsolete. the only difference is in the fuel given to greed. they have changed. instead of the fuel given for greed in the past, in this era, different fuel is given. similarly for hatred: instead of the weapons used in the past, in this era, different weapons are used. for delusion, it is the same. even so, it is these three that exist in the world forever.
thinking in this manner about the thirst of craving, the calming of this craving itself is nibbana, the escape from this samsara. indeed, that itself is that peace. next, one must also develop some understanding of the noble eightfold path which helps in this.
in that manner, if right view (*samma-ditthi*) is established, right thoughts (*samma-sankappa*) arise in that person. if right thoughts are developed, right speech (*samma-vaca*) comes out of that person. the person who uses right speech then directs himself toward right action (*samma-kammanta*)—the correct path of action. by perfecting those paths of action, that person becomes a person with right livelihood (*samma-ajiva*), a correct way of living.
within the person who leads such a good and correct livelihood, there is a great effort and energy called right effort (*samma-vayama*). through that effort, right mindfulness (*samma-sati*) arises in him in the correct manner. through the power of establishing that mindfulness for a long time, he develops right concentration (*samma-samadhi*), a correct one-pointedness of mind. it is through this that one is able to personally realize this dhamma of nibbana.
it is to a concentrated mind that the three characteristics of the world—impermanence (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and non-self (*anatta*)—can be understood. in the dhamma, we call this the arising of the eye of dhamma (*dhamma-cakkhu*). this venerable monk did not sacrifice his eyes for some trivial thing. having sacrificed his eyes, he became blind. simultaneously with becoming blind, what arose was that eye of dhamma. it was for this eye of dhamma that he made this sacrifice.
indeed, it is not the physical eye in the world that is important, but the eye of wisdom (*panna-cakkhu*). the eye of wisdom, which is the *dhamma-panna-cakkhu*, is the realization of nibbana. by means of that eye of wisdom, to say nothing of others, even a stream-enterer (*sotapanna*)—a person who has seen nibbana through the first path-knowledge—attains immense relief.
that is why the buddha, taking a tiny bit of soil on his fingernail, declared regarding the portion of samsaric suffering that the stream-enterer has brought to an end: "the suffering remaining for him is like this tiny bit of soil on the fingernail. the suffering he has ended and extinguished is like the soil of the great earth." in this manner, the stream-enterer is freed from the four woeful states. due to stream-entry, because of the change that occurred in his mind, he will never again go to a woeful state. the power of actions leading to the woeful states is broken. one must contemplate how much relief is obtained from that first path-knowledge alone.
next, it is when one becomes an arahant that the greatest relief is obtained. even the stream-enterer is born up to seven times. the arahant is not born again in this existence (*bhava*). samsara is ended. that indeed is the supreme liberation. it is through that state that one is forever liberated from that terrible wheel of kamma.
to attain such a noble state, something the buddha constantly declared, as if it were the first letter of the alphabet, is diligence (*appamada*)—the factor of diligence. the buddha declares that this period of a buddha’s appearance is extremely rare. it is recorded that daily, as the advice of the sugata (buddha), he admonished the monks: *dullabho buddhuppado lokasmim*—the appearance of a buddha in the world is extremely rare. there are some aeons (*kalpas*) that are void of buddhas (*sunna-kappa*), times when there is no buddha. one can imagine how dark those times are.
just as when a great city, shining brightly with electric lamps, suddenly falls into pitch darkness, and what a miserable feeling arises in a person—in the same way, one must imagine the difference between the period of a buddha’s appearance and the period of a buddha’s non-appearance.
thus, the birth of a buddha is extremely rare. equally rare is human birth (*manussatta*). indeed, one can say that a human birth obtained during the period of a buddha’s appearance is even rarer. because during that period of a buddha’s appearance, if one is elsewhere, that opportunity is lost.
next, having obtained a human birth, and then having the intellectual capacity to understand the dhamma, without being deformed in limbs or organs, being born in a region where one can hear the dhamma and practice it—these are pointed out as the opportune moment (*khana-sampatti*). that too is equally rare.
next, having obtained that opportune moment, receiving the ordination that correctly leads that dhamma life is even rarer. next, even if one receives that ordination, hearing the dhamma (*dhamma-savana*) which helps toward nibbana is even rarer. next, even if one gets to hear the dhamma, the association with spiritual friends (*kalyana-mitta*)—the company of the virtuous—who advise and help one to practice that dhamma, is even rarer.
thinking in this manner about the rare appearance of a buddha, the human birth, the opportune moment, the hearing of the dhamma, and then the association with the virtuous (*sappurisa-samseva*)—to use a simile, these are like the concentric colored circles on a target board. the rarest thing in the very center is finding someone who can give meditation instructions (*kammatthana*) and advise one on how to practice according to the dhamma and meditate.
thinking in this manner, during the period of a buddha’s appearance, one must act diligently. because even the deities say that the human world is the best place to realize nibbana. even the deities refer to this human world as the happy destination (*sugati*). human beings do not know this.
sometimes, those who have passed away and gone to the next world, having understood their suffering and trials in accordance with kamma, express their weeping and wailing, saying: "alas, we lost that opportunity! having obtained that rare human birth during the rare appearance of a buddha, we were unable to bring an end to this suffering of samsara," thus testifying to the truth of the buddha's words that samsara is suffering.
therefore, having diligently directed oneself toward this path of dhamma, and having established within oneself the philosophy of life expressed in this verse—reflecting that the mind precedes everything, that the mind is supreme, that everything is fashioned by the mind itself, and that we have to experience the retributive results of the things done and spoken with this mind, even for aeons—and having thus generated a sense of spiritual urgency (*samvega*), if one is to travel on this path of dhamma, one must make an effort to embark on that journey of the noble eightfold path as declared by the buddha. one must make a firm determination.
likewise, employing mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajanna*), and that attention (*manasikara*) of meditation, and traveling on that path of dhamma, one must make a determination to realize that noble, deathless nibbana which liberates one from all samsaric suffering such as birth (*jati*), aging (*jara*), sickness, and death (*marana*).
thus, during this short period of time, you virtuous friends have listened to a highly valuable dhamma sermon and a dhamma verse declared by the buddha, as well as the story relevant to it, and have generated faith (*saddha*) and spiritual urgency (*samvega*) at this moment. the wholesome thoughts (*kusala-citta*) we generate by listening to this dhamma are no trivial thing. although we call them wholesome thoughts, what actually arise within us that help toward nibbana are faith (*saddha*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*).
the buddha has declared the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) that help a person realize nibbana, among the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*). they are faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom (*saddha, viriya, sati, samadhi, panna*); these are what exist as faculties and powers that help toward nibbana. therefore, if even for a brief moment faith arose within you virtuous friends, and along with that faith, a mental energy (*cetasika-viriya*)—a resolve in the mind that "we must travel on this path of dhamma, we cannot remain as before, we must practice in this manner"—if such energy arose, that is a great thing. likewise, while directing the mind to the dhamma, if a certain mindfulness (*sati*) arose, that too is a valuable thing.
next, the concentration (*samadhi*) developed during the time of listening to the dhamma, by directing the mind to it and making it one-pointed—that too is a great wholesome thought. in the same way, if you thought deeply about this dhamma and gained some understanding in terms of wisdom (*panna*), that too helps toward nibbana.
in this manner, during this hour, many wholesome thoughts must have arisen within the mind-stream of you virtuous friends. reflecting on them, and directing our lives solely toward the wholesome side, steering away from the unwholesome, we must make an effort to spend our time.
to that end, we must put into use the weapons introduced by the buddha. the buddha has pointed out all those guardians and weapons that can be used for this battle against defilements, for this operation. we must realize that this is our real battle. we spend our time in this samsara with a great responsibility. because the ones we are responsible for are not others, nor are we responsible for our temporary relatives; ultimately, we are responsible for the various existences (*bhava*) that arise according to kamma, in accordance with the actions we perform. this kamma gives us those births again and again. we are responsible for them.
therefore, if we lead bad lives and are born in those miserable peta-existences, or yakkha-existences, or in places like hell, then we will have to blame only ourselves, thinking, "alas, we did not take advantage of the opportunity we had." from this, it is clear that this responsibility, indeed, lies primarily with oneself. *atta hi attano natho*—oneself indeed is one's own savior. *tumhehi kiccam atappam, akkhataro tathagata*—the effort must be made by yourselves; the tathagatas are only teachers—thus the buddha has declared. therefore, what needs to be done must be done by oneself. the tathagatas are only teachers.
understanding these matters, may this multitude of wholesome thoughts generated in your mind-stream up to this moment be a supportive condition (*upanissaya*) and a blessing for the personal realization of the noble, deathless nibbana through the realization of the paths and fruits of stream-entry, sakadagami, anagami, and arahantship!
likewise, may the deities who protect the dispensation, and any deities presiding over this place, rejoice in this collection of merits accumulated by us up to this moment through this dhamma sermon and dhamma listening! having rejoiced, may they escape from this extremely terrible suffering of samsara and realize the noble, deathless nibbana through whichever bodhi (awakening) they have aspired to! in this manner, share the merits.
likewise, may the relatives who have passed away in your names, and all beings from the avici hell up to the akanittha brahma realm who are desirous of merit and nibbana, rejoice in this merit of dhamma preaching and dhamma listening! having rejoiced, may they realize the noble, deathless nibbana through whichever bodhi they have aspired to!
make your aspirations in this manner, recite the verses, and transfer the merits.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 097
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #97
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.53)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Appamādo amatapadaṃ, pamādo maccuno padaṃ;
Appamattā na mīyanti, ye pamattā yathā matā;
Etaṃ visesato ñatvā, appamādamhi paṇḍitā;
Appamāde pamodanti, ariyānaṃ gocare ratā;
Te jhāyino sātatikā, niccaṃ daḷhaparakkamā;
Phusanti dhīrā nibbānaṃ, yogakkhemaṃ anuttaraṃ.
From:
Dhammapada 21–23 (Appamādavagga)
Dear Listeners,
There is a vast difference between how the ordinary world understands the word *appamāda* (heedfulness) and how the Buddha explains it. In worldly convention, *appamāda* means doing any kind of work—whether good or bad—on time, in order to sustain this life. However, the *appamāda* taught to us by the Buddha possesses a far more profound and far-sighted meaning. Dhamma-oriented *appamāda* is the undertaking of what must be done to shorten, or completely bring to a halt, this journey of saṃsāra—which is in itself pure negligence—even at the cost of one's own life, without delaying it for a single moment. It is a few verses in praise of that very *appamāda* that we have selected as our topic for today.
These verses were expounded by the Buddha concerning the exemplary and virtuous life of Queen Sāmāvatī, the consort of King Udena of Kosambī. When the Buddha visited Kosambī, Queen Sāmāvatī’s maid, a lay woman named Khujjuttarā, went to the Buddha, listened to the Dhamma, and attained the fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti*). Upon her return, she preached that Dhamma to Sāmāvatī and her five hundred companion women in the manner of a true Dhamma preacher. Hearing this, that entire group of women attained Stream-entry. Queen Sāmāvatī was so filled with gratitude that, because Khujjuttarā had helped her attain this supramundane state, she freed her from her status as a maid and placed her in the position of a mother and a teacher from that day onward.
Furthermore, regarding this lay woman Khujjuttarā, her actual name was Uttarā. "Khujja" means hunchbacked. Since she was hunchbacked, she was known by the name Khujjuttarā. This lay woman Uttarā would regularly listen to the Dhamma from the Buddha and return to preach it to Sāmāvatī and her retinue in the manner described. In this way, she gradually became a highly skilled, widely learned, and eloquent preacher of the Dhamma. So much so, that on one occasion the Buddha declared her foremost (*etadagga*) among his widely learned lay female disciples who retain the Dhamma.
Queen Sāmāvatī too spent her life with an extraordinary degree of faith and devotion toward the Triple Gem. Moreover, her mind was highly developed in the meditation on loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*). Because of this, the Buddha made a similar declaration regarding Queen Sāmāvatī, stating: "Sāmāvatī is the foremost among my lay female disciples who dwell in loving-kindness." Queen Sāmāvatī’s power of loving-kindness became manifest due to the hostile and jealous attitude of Queen Māgandiyā, another consort of King Udena. Queen Māgandiyā had developed a deep-seated hatred toward the Buddha because He had, on a previous occasion, disparaged her physical beauty.
On that earlier occasion, because Māgandiyā was exceptionally beautiful—so much so that even kings sought her hand in marriage—her parents wished to give her in marriage to the Buddha. At that moment, the Buddha, having in mind the parents' potential to attain Arahantship, disparaged her physical beauty. Because of this, she harbored a deep grudge.
Unable to take revenge directly on the Buddha, she prepared to take revenge on Queen Sāmāvatī, who was one of the Buddha's most devoted disciples, to satisfy her long-standing hatred. Sāmāvatī was one of King Udena’s consorts, and Māgandiyā was another. In such situations, jealousy is natural. Thus, driven especially by her hatred toward the Buddha, Māgandiyā employed various cunning plots to make the king lose faith in Queen Sāmāvatī.
On one occasion, when King Udena was preparing to spend several days at Sāmāvatī’s palace, he took with him his famous elephant-charming lute (*Hatthikanta-vīṇā*), which possessed the extraordinary power to summon elephants. The king carried it wherever he went. What Queen Māgandiyā did was to have a snake, whose fangs had been extracted, inserted into a cavity of the lute. In all of these schemes, she was assisted by her paternal uncle, the Brahmin Māgandiya. With his help, she executed this cunning plot. Having inserted the fangless snake into the lute, and after the king had gone to Sāmāvatī’s palace, she arranged for the snake to slide out of the lute, thereby provoking the king’s wrath against Sāmāvatī.
The king became so furious that he took a poisoned arrow, lined up Sāmāvatī and her five hundred companion women, and prepared to shoot them. In that moment, Queen Sāmāvatī advised her group: "We have no refuge at this moment other than loving-kindness. Radiate loving-kindness equally to the king, to Queen Māgandiyā, and to ourselves." Just as the king released the arrow, instead of flying toward them, it turned back. It reversed its direction and aimed itself directly at the king's own chest. The king was struck with intense emotion (*saṃvega*), fell at Sāmāvatī’s feet, and begged for forgiveness. Sāmāvatī seized that very opportunity to inspire faith in the Buddha within the king. She urged the king to go to the Buddha for refuge. Subsequently, with the king's assistance, Queen Sāmāvatī secured permission to regularly attend to and serve the Saṅgha. We are summarizing a very long story here; there are numerous nested narratives connected to this event. As the Queen became increasingly devoted to serving the Buddha and the Saṅgha, Māgandiyā plotted an even more severe and treacherous scheme to harm or destroy Sāmāvatī.
When the king was preparing to go to the royal pleasure gardens, what did Māgandiyā do? She told her uncle, the Brahmin Māgandiya, to go to Sāmāvatī’s palace in the king's absence, open the storehouses of cloth and oil, soak the cloths in oil, wrap them around the pillars of the palace, and set them on fire. While the king was away in the pleasure gardens, the Brahmin went and prepared to set the palace on fire as instructed. Sāmāvatī and her retinue realized what was about to happen. What did the conspirators do next? They locked the women inside and set the palace on fire.
In that critical moment, Queen Sāmāvatī spoke to her companions as if delivering a Dhamma sermon: "In this long saṃsāra, even the Buddha may not be able to count the number of times we have burned and died in houses in this manner. Therefore, be heedful (*appamattā hotha*)!" Thus, she made a profound request and gave deep advice to her group. The palace caught fire. As the palace burned, what did this group do? In that moment of intense peril—which is referred to as the comprehension of feeling (*vedanā-pariggaha*), a highly advanced meditation subject—they took the bodily sensation (*vedanā*) itself as their meditation object and developed insight (*vipassanā*).
In this manner, that group of women, who were already Stream-enterers, contemplated the intense sensation (*vedanā*) arising in their bodies as the palace burned down around them. Through this insight, they attained the higher paths and fruits (*mārgaphala*), many of them realizing the states of Once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*) and Non-returner (*anāgāmī*).
In the subsequent events, people came and informed the Buddha: "O Blessed One, while the king was in the pleasure gardens, the inner palace caught fire, and Sāmāvatī along with her large retinue of five hundred women met their death. Where have they been reborn?" The Buddha then declared: "Monks, many of those lay women attained the higher paths and fruits of Stream-entry, Once-returning, and Non-returning. They acted heedfully (*appamatta*). None of them met a death that was in vain (*anipphalā kālakatā*)." Declaring that they had met a fruitful death, He uttered a profound verse of solemn utterance (*udāna*) on that occasion:
> *Mohasambandhano loko, bhabbarūpova dissati;*
> *upadhibālo tamasā parivārito, sassatova khāyati, passato natthi kiñcanaṃ.*
The Buddha uttered a profound verse of solemn utterance there, expressing the voidness and emptiness of the world: "The world, bound by delusion (*moha*), appears as if it is real and substantial. The fool, grasping onto the substrates of existence (*upadhi*), is enveloped in darkness. It appears as if it is eternal; but to one who sees truly, there is nothing there." The Buddha expressed this truth in connection with that event. We can reflect on how a grand palace, home to a large retinue of women including Sāmāvatī, was reduced to ashes in a single moment, destroying everyone inside. Thus, the Buddha uttered a verse that demonstrates the impermanent (*anicca*) and unsubstantial (*anattā*) nature of everything in the world. But the story does not end there.
Next, it is said that the king, having heard that the palace was on fire, rushed back as fast as he could. But by the time he arrived, it had already burned to ashes. After extinguishing the remaining embers, he was overcome with immense grief and began to contemplate who could have done this. He suspected that Māgandiyā might have been responsible, but resolved to trap her using a ruse. The king summoned his ministers and, in their presence, said: "For a long time, I lived in constant anxiety, wondering when this woman (Sāmāvatī) would harm me. Now, at last, I can sleep in peace." The king expressed joy over Sāmāvatī’s death in the presence of Queen Māgandiyā, who was standing nearby. The ministers then asked, "O King, who could have done this?" The king replied, "It must have been someone who has immense love and affection for me." Hearing this, Māgandiyā stepped forward and revealed the secret: "O King, it was I who did this through my uncle!"
The king did not reveal his anger even then. He said, "I am exceedingly pleased. No one has as much affection for me as you do. Let us summon all your relatives so that I may grant them rewards." Māgandiyā sent messages to her relatives, urging them to come quickly as the king was highly pleased and wished to bestow favors. To the first relatives who arrived, the king gave special gifts and rewards. Seeing this, even those who were not her relatives bribed others to claim, "We too are relatives of Queen Māgandiyā," and came to the palace. Once the entire group had assembled, the king had them all seized. He had pits dug in the palace courtyard, buried them up to their waists, covered them with straw, and set them on fire. As they were burning and trying to escape, he had them plowed over with iron plows, crushing their bodies to pieces and putting them to death. It is recorded that Queen Māgandiyā was subjected to an even more horrific torture: her flesh was sliced from her body, fried in a pan of hot oil, and she was forced to eat her own cooked flesh until she died.
Thus, the king punished them in an extremely horrific manner. While these events were unfolding, a discussion arose among the monks in the Dhamma Hall. They remarked that such a tragic death was highly unsuitable for a lay woman of such great faith as Sāmāvatī. The Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what are you discussing?" When they related the conversation, the Buddha explained: "Monks, from the perspective of their conduct in this life, the death of Queen Sāmāvatī and her retinue indeed appears unsuitable; but from the perspective of their past kamma, it is completely fitting." The monks then begged the Blessed One to reveal their past kamma, and the Buddha related the story of the past.
This event took place during an interval between Buddhas, before the appearance of the present Buddha, during a time when Paccekabuddhas lived. When King Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, eight Paccekabuddhas regularly visited the palace for alms. Seven of them, having finished their meal, would fly back to the Himalayas through psychic power. One of them, however, would remain and enter meditative absorption (*jhāna*) in a clump of grass near the riverbank. The five hundred women of the king’s harem used to attend to these Paccekabuddhas. One day, after the Paccekabuddhas had departed, the king went to play in the water with these women. Having played in the water the entire day, the women felt very cold by evening. They decided to warm themselves by a fire. Looking around, they saw the clump of grass and set it on fire, unaware that the Paccekabuddha was inside. As the grass burned down, they suddenly saw the Paccekabuddha sitting there. They were terrified, thinking, "This is the king's respected Paccekabuddha. If the king finds out, he will surely put us to death." They decided to burn him completely to cover up their deed. They gathered more firewood, piled it up, and set the Paccekabuddha on fire.
However, that Paccekabuddha was in the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). According to the law of kamma, the women accumulated unwholesome kamma through their intention (*cetanā*), even though the Paccekabuddha was not physically burned. He emerged from his concentration after seven days and walked away unharmed. But because of their grave unwholesome intention, those women—who were Sāmāvatī and her retinue—suffered in hell for hundreds of thousands of years. Furthermore, as a residual result of that kamma, in a hundred subsequent lifetimes, they died by being burned to death inside buildings. The Buddha declared that this was their final birth, and this was how that kamma bore its last fruit.
On that occasion, wishing to clarify other details, the monks asked another question, as is common today, regarding the lay woman Khujjuttarā. They asked why she was born hunchbacked. Since she was a highly prominent disciple whom the Buddha had placed in the foremost position (*etadagga*), they wondered why such a meritorious person was born with a physical deformity. That was one question. The second was: what past merit made her possess such vast wisdom? Third: what past merit led to her Stream-entry? And fourth: what past kamma caused her to be born as a maid servant? The Buddha then related the past stories connected to these questions.
First, regarding her hunchbacked condition: this too was connected to the same Paccekabuddha. The Paccekabuddha who meditated near the clump of grass happened to have a slightly bent, hunchbacked body. One of the harem women—who was none other than Khujjuttarā in a past life—mocked him. She draped herself in a robe, took a golden vessel in her hand, and mimicked his hunchbacked walk to make the other women laugh, saying, "This is how our Paccekabuddha walks." The Buddha explained that due to this unwholesome kamma of mockery, she was born hunchbacked.
Next, regarding her great wisdom: this too was connected to the same period. When the Paccekabuddhas first visited the royal palace, the five hundred women served them hot milk-rice in their bowls. Because the milk-rice was extremely hot, the Paccekabuddhas were passing the bowls from hand to hand to avoid burning themselves. Seeing this, this particular woman wisely took eight ivory bangles she was wearing and offered them, saying, "Please place the bowls on these bangles." The Paccekabuddhas did so, easing their discomfort, and later tried to return the bangles. She insisted, saying, "No, venerable sirs, I have offered them permanently."
The Buddha explained that because of this wise act of service, which she performed with wise reflection, she was blessed with great wisdom, becoming widely learned (*bahuśruta*) and a holder of the Dhamma (*dhammadhara*). Her Stream-entry was also supported by the very service she and the others rendered to the Paccekabuddhas—for serving those who have realized the paths and fruits and touched the peace of Nibbāna assists one in attaining the same realization. Finally, regarding her being born as a servant: this occurred during the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha. Khujjuttarā was then the daughter of a wealthy merchant (*seṭṭhi-dhītā*). An Arahant bhikkhunī came to visit her in the evening while she was dressing and putting on her ornaments. Having no servant nearby, and needing her ornament box which was out of reach, she told the Arahant bhikkhunī, "Noble lady, please hand me that box," speaking with a lack of respect, as if treating her like a maid.
The Arahant bhikkhunī reflected: "If she harbors anger toward me, she will be reborn in hell. But if she performs this service for me, she will merely be born as a servant. Being born as a servant is far better than being reborn in hell." Thus, she handed her the box. The Buddha explained that because she made an Arahant bhikkhunī serve her like a maid, she was born as a servant. From this, we can comprehend the precision of the fruit of kamma. Furthermore, it is said that the discussion among the monks in the Dhamma Hall continued to reverberate regarding this entire event—how Sāmāvatī and her large retinue died in the fire, how Māgandiyā’s relatives were executed by the king, and how Māgandiyā herself was subjected to horrific torture. They debated on who in this world is truly alive and who is dead.
It was on that occasion that the Buddha approached and asked, "Monks, what are you discussing?" When they related the conversation, the Buddha declared: "Monks, in this world, those who are heedful (*appamatta*) are truly alive. Whether they live or die, they are to be considered alive. Those who are negligent (*pamatta*), even if they are physically breathing, are as if already dead." He then uttered the three verses from the *Appamāda Vagga* of the Dhammapada, which we took as our opening topic.
> *Appamādo amatapadaṁ, pamādo maccuno padaṁ;*
> *appamattā na mīyanti, ye pamattā yathā matā.*
As you know, the Deathless (*amata*) is a name for Nibbāna. Once the Mind Stilled is realized, there is no more birth (*jāti*). When there is no birth, there is no aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). Heedfulness (*appamāda*) is the path to the Deathless. Negligence (*pamāda*) is the path to death. The heedful do not die. The negligent are as if already dead; even though they are alive, they are like the dead.
> *Etaṁ visesato ñatvā, appamādamhi paṇḍitā;*
> *appamāde pamodanti, ariyānaṁ gocare ratā.*
Knowing this distinction clearly—that those who are heedful do not die, while the negligent are as if already dead—the wise (*paṇḍitā*) delight in heedfulness, rejoicing in the pasture of the Nobles (*ariyānaṃ gocara*). On one occasion, the Buddha defined the "pasture of the Nobles" as the four foundations of mindfulness (*cattāro satipaṭṭhānā*). The four foundations of mindfulness are the pasture, the rightful territory, of the Nobles and of all those who seek Nibbāna. The wise, residing in this pasture and practicing mindfulness, rejoice in the path of heedfulness.
The next verse speaks of a deeper aspect:
> *Te jhāyino sātatikā, niccaṁ daḷhaparakkamā;*
> *phusanti dhīrā nibbānaṁ, yogakkhemaṁ anuttaraṁ.*
These wise ones, constantly meditating (*jhāyino*) and possessing firm endeavor (*daḷhaparakkamā*)—which refers not to physical warfare, but to the battle against defilements—touch and realize the supreme security from bondage (*yogakkhema*), which is Nibbāna. *Yogakkhema* is another name for the Mind Stilled. "Yoga" here refers to the four bonds: the bond of sensuality (*kāma-yoga*), the bond of existence (*bhava-yoga*), the bond of views (*diṭṭhi-yoga*), and the bond of ignorance (*avijjā-yoga*). These are the four bonds that drag one through the length of saṃsāra. The wise, who possess such practice and constantly meditate, touch and realize the supreme Nibbāna, which is the liberation from these bonds. Thus did the Buddha expound these verses.
We have now heard the story and the verses. It is now up to us to reflect on these teachings in a calm and composed manner, extracting the practical lessons and deeper Dhamma principles that we can apply to our own lives. First, when we reflect on this story, we see that Queen Sāmāvatī holds an exceptionally noble position among the female disciples of the Buddha's dispensation. We have just heard the account of her life. Although we do not have exhaustive details, we can appreciate the immense spiritual development her mind had achieved.
When we consider her power of loving-kindness, she harbored not a shred of ill-will toward Māgandiyā, who hated her so intensely. When the king was about to shoot them with the poisoned arrow, she instructed her companions to radiate equal loving-kindness to the king, to Queen Māgandiyā, and to themselves. Her mind had developed such a powerful degree of loving-kindness. In the practice of the meditation on loving-kindness, there is a highly advanced stage known as the deliverance of mind through loving-kindness (*mettā-cetovimutti*). It is a powerful spiritual force capable of radiating loving-kindness to all beings without any discrimination. Within that concentration (*jhāna*), there lies a power that can even perform miracles. It was by the power of that very miracle that the arrow turned back. It is said that the king was struck with deep emotion (*saṃvega*), thinking, "Even this lifeless arrow recognizes her virtue, yet a human like me did not," and fell at her feet in worship.
Thus, we can see how powerful the concentration (*jhāna*) of loving-kindness is, capable of deflecting a poisoned arrow. However, some might argue and raise a question based on the benefits of loving-kindness preached by the Buddha in the *Mettānisaṃsa Sutta*. One of those benefits is: *nassa aggi vā visaṁ vā satthaṁ vā kamati*—"neither fire, poison, nor weapons can harm" one who has developed the deliverance of mind through loving-kindness.
Yet, in this instance, they could not prevent the danger of the fire due to the sheer gravity of their past kamma. The momentum of kamma was far more powerful. Sāmāvatī, however, did not despair in that moment. She immediately directed her companions toward the practice of insight (*vipassanā*). There is a profound and valuable lesson in this. The palace was burning and collapsing around them. In that moment, Sāmāvatī gave her advice in just two words: *appamattā hotha*—"Be heedful!" Here too, we find the word *appamāda*. In the ordinary world, if a large building catches fire, people panic, wail, and die in agony. We frequently hear of such tragedies occurring in the world.
What did Queen Sāmāvatī do? She realized that the doors were locked and there was no way out. She understood that crying and lamenting would serve no purpose. She did what had to be done in that very moment. That is *appamāda*. What she did was this: while being burned by the external fire, she extinguished herself with the internal cooling of Nibbāna. That is what she achieved. She let the external fire burn the physical body, but she extinguished the inner fire through the realization of the Mind Stilled. This was achieved through the attainment of fruition (*phala-samāpatti*). She utilized the power of Stream-entry she had already attained, and by further developing insight (*vipassanā*) through the comprehension of feeling (*vedanā-pariggaha*), she took the intense sensation (*vedanā*) arising in her burning body as her meditation object. Ordinarily, the natural tendency of worldlings is to fear pain and try to flee from it. What is the marvelous method shown by the Buddha here? It is to look directly at the sensation (*vedanā*) itself, applying wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) with a concentrated mind, and reflecting that "this feeling is not mine, this is not self." The Buddha compared sensation to a water bubble: *vedanā bubbulūpamā*. When rain falls, water bubbles form rapidly on the surface, only to burst and vanish in an instant. Sensation is just like that.
Why do we get agitated by sensation? It is because we grasp it as "my feeling." We grasp it, develop aversion toward it, and engage in an internal conflict, thereby burning ourselves. In contrast, the insight method taught by the Buddha is to observe that very sensation, that very pain, objectively as a meditation subject. Through that observation, one perceives its impermanent (*anicca*), painful (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anattā*) nature. It was by profoundly realizing this truth that Sāmāvatī and her companions attained the higher paths and fruits. The Buddha declared that they met a death that was not in vain (*anipphalā kālakatā*)—a highly successful death. This is the very meaning expressed in the verse: *appamattā na mīyanti, ye pamattā yathā matā*—"The heedful do not die; the negligent are as if already dead." This is a great lesson for our lives today. None of us can predict with certainty when, where, or under what circumstances death will come. We too might find ourselves in a situation where we are trapped in a burning building with no escape. In such a moment, our only refuge is the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) we have practiced.
In Sāmāvatī’s life, we see how she utilized her developed concentration (*jhāna*) of loving-kindness to secure her own peace and to bring about a profound change in the king, turning the crisis into a victory of the Dhamma (*dhamma-vijaya*). When a tragedy occurs, the worldly response is to harbor hatred, thinking "who did this to me?" and thus burn with both the external fire and the internal fire of hatred and delusion. What did Sāmāvatī do instead? She understood it as the force of kamma. She advised her companions: "In this vast saṃsāra, we have burned to death in this manner countless times, beyond the scope of even a Buddha’s knowledge. This is a minor thing. What we must do now is elevate this experience into insight (*vipassanā*) and escape from this existence (*bhava*) immediately."
For the Buddha, true *appamāda* (heedfulness) is not merely escaping from a burning building. Indeed, in that situation, physical escape was impossible. Yet, the ordinary worldling would spend their last moments wailing and screaming, hoping someone would open the door and save them, and thus meet a miserable death. In contrast, Sāmāvatī accepted the reality. The Buddha highly praises those who, in such moments, strive to escape from the cycle of existence (*bhava*). That is precisely what Sāmāvatī and her companion women achieved. In another discourse, the Buddha asked the monks: "Monks, if a person's clothes or head were on fire, what should they do?" The monks gave the natural reply: "O Blessed One, they must make a great effort, using mindfulness and energy, to extinguish the fire immediately." But what did the Buddha say? "No, monks. In such a moment, disregarding one's burning clothes or head, one should strive to realize the Noble Truths of suffering (*dukkha*), its origin, its cessation, and the path. Extinguishing the internal fire of defilements is far more urgent than extinguishing the external fire." The story shows that Queen Sāmāvatī and her companions acted in perfect accordance with this instruction of the Buddha. This is extremely valuable for our own lives. While the world thinks of worldly savings and protection for times of crisis, in the ultimate helpless moment, one's only refuge is the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) one has developed. A mind trained in loving-kindness can neutralize intense hostility, and if kamma brings an unavoidable tragedy, one must view it as an opportunity to escape from existence (*bhava*) through insight (*vipassanā*). That is the practice of heedfulness (*appamāda*).
All these profound meanings are perfectly demonstrated in the life of Queen Sāmāvatī. We have much to learn from this. Furthermore, from the other events in this story, we can appreciate the terrifying ocean of kamma in which we live. Through the Buddha-eye, it became clear that Sāmāvatī’s death was not ultimately caused by Māgandiyā; Māgandiyā was merely an instrument. The real cause was their own past intention (*cetanā*) to burn the Paccekabuddha. The Buddha declared: *cetanāhaṁ bhikkhave kammaṁ vadāmi; cetayitvā kammaṁ karoti kāyena vācāya manasā*—"Intention, monks, is what I call kamma. Having intended, one performs kamma through body, speech, and mind."
One might argue that the Paccekabuddha was not physically harmed. But those women had already burned him in their minds. That unwholesome intention was the kamma that produced such severe results. If the Paccekabuddha had actually been harmed, the consequences would have been even more horrific. We must always reflect on the kammic consequences of our daily actions. We must realize that we live as if on a ground made of kamma. We are born upon the massive heap of kamma we have accumulated over the vast span of saṃsāra, and this life is spent wearing away that kamma. Until we eradicate the seed-potential of kamma (*bīja-sakti*) that leads to rebirth through the supramundane paths and fruits, we have no choice but to swim in this ocean of kamma.
The power of wholesome kamma was also demonstrated in the life of the lay woman Khujjuttarā. First, the monks asked about her physical deformity. The unwholesome kamma responsible for it was something that might be considered minor in the ordinary world—a simple act of mocking the posture of a Paccekabuddha. By draping herself in a robe and mimicking his hunchbacked walk to make others laugh, she accumulated the unwholesome kamma that caused her to be born hunchbacked. Many of our physical illnesses and deformities are rooted in such past actions. Today, even through limited worldly investigations, some of these truths are being uncovered. But this is an absolute reality. Every small action of our body, speech, and mind has a long-term kammic momentum.
Her great wisdom was also the result of a seemingly simple act. Seeing the Paccekabuddhas passing the hot bowls from hand to hand, she wisely offered her ivory bangles to use as stands. This is a valuable lesson for us. When we perform services or duties, we should not view them as a burden or a chore; rather, we should perceive them as a precious opportunity to cultivate wholesome kamma. The Paccekabuddhas did not ask for the bangles, but she wisely used her intelligence to facilitate their comfort, and that wise act of service made her a person of great wisdom, widely learned (*bahuśruta*) and a holder of the Dhamma (*dhammadhara*).
Similarly, her Stream-entry was supported by her service to those who had realized the paths and fruits. Serving those who have realized the Dhamma helps one to realize the same truth. Lastly, her being born as a servant was due to a single instance in a past life under Kassapa Buddha when, as a merchant's daughter, she treated an Arahant bhikkhunī like a maid by asking her to hand her an ornament box. Though it seemed like a minor incident, it carried a significant unwholesome result. Living in saṃsāra is indeed a terrifying affair.
If you are driving a vehicle at high speed, and you are a skilled driver, you might not feel afraid. But you never know when an animal might jump onto the road, or when a minor mechanical failure might cause the vehicle to overturn. Our minds are just like that; they function at lightning speed, and if the mind slips even slightly, the resulting kammic momentum can trap us in saṃsāric suffering for an immensely long period. This is why the Buddha always emphasized true heedfulness (*appamāda*). In the ordinary world, heedfulness is understood as catching a bus or a train on time, arriving at the office on time, and managing one's daily affairs efficiently.
The worldly expectation is to achieve success by hook or by crook, through Dhamma or non-Dhamma, and to secure financial stability. But from the perspective of the Buddha's word, such a life falls into negligence (*pamāda*). True heedfulness (*appamāda*), as defined by the Buddha, is escaping from this terrifying saṃsāra as quickly as possible—escaping from this cycle of existence (*bhava*). It is this escape that is demonstrated in the life of Queen Sāmāvatī, and it is the same truth that is revealed in the Buddha's discourse about one's head being on fire.
The story also illustrates the danger of saṃsāra and the cruelty of Māgandiyā. Although Māgandiyā was exceptionally beautiful—sought after by kings throughout India—she lacked virtue, which led to her horrific end in this very life. This helps us distinguish between true progress and decline, and between true heedfulness and negligence. We must reflect on these Dhamma principles and strive to apply them to our daily lives.
The path of the Dhamma consists of Virtue, Concentration, and Wisdom (*sīla, samādhi, paññā*), which summarize the entire dispensation of the Buddha. Virtue is the essential foundation. Sāmāvatī’s humble, respectful life and her gratitude—freeing her maid and treating her as a teacher—demonstrate her immense virtue. Virtue is what enables the mind to achieve Concentration (*samādhi*). One cannot expect to concentrate a mind that is filled with remorse. We observe precepts in order to live a life free of remorse, establishing a firm foundation for concentration.
Today, you have observed the eight precepts of Right Livelihood (*ājīva-aṭṭhamaka-sīla*). For lay disciples, the Buddha has prescribed the five precepts and the eight precepts to restrain body and speech. This restraint, however, is directed by the mind (*cetanā-sīla, cetasika-sīla*). The physical body is not an autonomous machine; it is driven by the mind. Therefore, though virtue is described as the restraint of body and speech, this restraint is accomplished by the mind through the power of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
One might ask if it is sufficient to undertake the precepts once.
