In practical terms, however, the precepts we have undertaken must remain at the forefront of our minds so that they can guide our behavior when the need arises. This is why we regularly undertake the precepts. We must make a daily resolution: "Today, I will live within the boundaries of these five pillars (the five precepts) or these eight pillars (the eight precepts), and I will not cross them." When an opportunity to perform an unwholesome deed arises—such as an urge to kill an animal or to steal—our wisdom steps forward and warns us: "This is contrary to the resolution you have made. Do not do it." The mind then refrains from the action. This is known as "refraining upon encounter" (*sampatta-virati*).
The word *veramaṇī* means refraining or abstaining. When we recite the precepts, we must focus on the word *veramaṇī*: *pāṇātipātā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṁ samādiyāmi*—"I undertake the precept of refraining from destroying life." This act of refraining is of utmost importance, for it is here that the mind takes the lead. When there is every opportunity to commit a sin, the virtue we have undertaken steps forward and restrains us. Refraining from the act generates immense spiritual strength, which subsequently brings great joy and relief when we reflect: "I have escaped from committing an unwholesome deed and from the future suffering it would have brought."
This is why we say that when we harm an animal, the harm we cause to our own mind through defilements is hundreds of thousands of times greater than the physical pain the animal suffers. The world thinks we should avoid harming animals merely because it is bad for the animal. But there is a deeper truth: by harboring hatred and harming another being, we corrupt our own minds, and we will have to pay for that corruption with suffering that is vastly greater than the pain felt by the animal. In the past story, the Paccekabuddha was completely unharmed by the fire; he simply brushed off the ashes and flew away. Yet, the unwholesome kamma of the women remained intact because of their unwholesome intention (*cetanā*). Unwholesome kamma is rooted in greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dosa*), and delusion (*moha*).
We can identify these unwholesome roots within our own minds if we apply mindfulness (*sati*). Although they are often masked by deceptive mental states, we can perceive them if we reflect wisely. We can understand: "Underneath this action lies greed, hatred, or delusion." The Buddha declared greed, hatred, and delusion as the roots of all unwholesome deeds. Wholesome (*kusala*) means skillful, and unwholesome (*akusala*) means unskillful. If we live unskillfully in this saṃsāra, we will experience suffering; if we live skillfully, we will experience happiness and realize Nibbāna swiftly.
Thus, "kusala" in its primary sense means skillfulness. Wholesome thoughts arise from non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adosa*), and non-delusion (*amoha*). Every moment we make an effort to distance ourselves from greed, hatred, and delusion—even for a single moment—we plant a wholesome seed. Because our minds have been habituated to these defilements for a long time, any effort to step away from them, even briefly, marks a wholesome turning point. This is what is meant by *alobha*, *adosa*, and *amoha*—the prefix "a-" denotes stepping away from greed, hatred, and delusion. We cannot eradicate them all at once, but we can push them aside for a moment through the mental factor of refraining (*virati-cetasika*).
For instance, when an urge to kill an animal arises—perhaps driven by a desire for its meat or by anger—and we immediately suppress that urge, preventing it from translating into action, we perform a powerful wholesome deed. If we do not suppress it, it remains as unwholesome mental kamma, burning within us like a hot coal. The Buddha compared unwholesome thoughts to hot coals. A child might touch a hot coal out of ignorance, but the moment they feel the heat, they drop it immediately. They do not hold onto it because it looks attractive. Similarly, the moment we realize a thought is rooted in greed, hatred, or delusion, we must discard it immediately. If we hold onto it, it will translate into speech and action, trapping us in saṃsāric suffering for aeons. The wholesome path, therefore, is the power of refraining.
Some might argue: "What are we actually doing when we undertake precepts? It is all about not doing things; there is no positive action involved." However, refraining is in itself a powerful wholesome action. Once we remove the unwholesome actions, the remaining actions naturally become wholesome. Refraining from unwholesome deeds is not a passive state; it requires active effort and mental skill. That mental skill is what we call "kusala." This is why we undertake the precepts beforehand, training the mind to refrain when temptation arises. Based on established virtue, we develop concentration (*samādhi*) through meditation subjects such as loving-kindness, recollection of the Buddha, the foulness of the body, or the mindfulness of death.
When the mind achieves concentration, it experiences a physical and mental peace that is thousands of times superior to any sensual pleasure. Based on that concentration, one contemplates the three characteristics of impermanence (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anattā*), developing insight (*vipassanā*) to realize the noble paths and fruits.
Through this sermon, we have extracted numerous Dhamma principles. By listening with deep faith and establishing ourselves in virtue, we can experience a sense of concentration. May the power of the Dhamma we have cultivated help us walk the path of heedfulness, complete our wholesome qualities through the association with noble friends, and practice generosity, virtue, and meditation. May this listening to the Dhamma support us in escaping from this terrifying saṃsāra and realizing the supreme peace of Nibbāna. May all guardian deities, and all beings from the lowest Avīci hell to the highest heaven (*Akaniṭṭha*), rejoice in these merits and attain the supreme peace of the Mind Stilled according to their own aspirations. Let us now transfer these merits by reciting the verses.
“*Ettāvatā ca amhehi.........*”

from:
dhammapada 21–23 (appamadavagga)
dear listeners,
there is a vast difference between how the ordinary world understands the word *appamada* (heedfulness) and how the buddha explains it. in worldly convention, *appamada* means doing any kind of work—whether good or bad—on time, in order to sustain this life. however, the *appamada* taught to us by the buddha possesses a far more profound and far-sighted meaning. dhamma-oriented *appamada* is the undertaking of what must be done to shorten, or completely bring to a halt, this journey of samsara—which is in itself pure negligence—even at the cost of one's own life, without delaying it for a single moment. it is a few verses in praise of that very *appamada* that we have selected as our topic for today.
these verses were expounded by the buddha concerning the exemplary and virtuous life of queen samavati, the consort of king udena of kosambi. when the buddha visited kosambi, queen samavati’s maid, a lay woman named khujjuttara, went to the buddha, listened to the dhamma, and attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotapatti*). upon her return, she preached that dhamma to samavati and her five hundred companion women in the manner of a true dhamma preacher. hearing this, that entire group of women attained stream-entry. queen samavati was so filled with gratitude that, because khujjuttara had helped her attain this supramundane state, she freed her from her status as a maid and placed her in the position of a mother and a teacher from that day onward.
furthermore, regarding this lay woman khujjuttara, her actual name was uttara. "khujja" means hunchbacked. since she was hunchbacked, she was known by the name khujjuttara. this lay woman uttara would regularly listen to the dhamma from the buddha and return to preach it to samavati and her retinue in the manner described. in this way, she gradually became a highly skilled, widely learned, and eloquent preacher of the dhamma. so much so, that on one occasion the buddha declared her foremost (*etadagga*) among his widely learned lay female disciples who retain the dhamma.
queen samavati too spent her life with an extraordinary degree of faith and devotion toward the triple gem. moreover, her mind was highly developed in the meditation on loving-kindness (*metta-bhavana*). because of this, the buddha made a similar declaration regarding queen samavati, stating: "samavati is the foremost among my lay female disciples who dwell in loving-kindness." queen samavati’s power of loving-kindness became manifest due to the hostile and jealous attitude of queen magandiya, another consort of king udena. queen magandiya had developed a deep-seated hatred toward the buddha because he had, on a previous occasion, disparaged her physical beauty.
on that earlier occasion, because magandiya was exceptionally beautiful—so much so that even kings sought her hand in marriage—her parents wished to give her in marriage to the buddha. at that moment, the buddha, having in mind the parents' potential to attain arahantship, disparaged her physical beauty. because of this, she harbored a deep grudge.
unable to take revenge directly on the buddha, she prepared to take revenge on queen samavati, who was one of the buddha's most devoted disciples, to satisfy her long-standing hatred. samavati was one of king udena’s consorts, and magandiya was another. in such situations, jealousy is natural. thus, driven especially by her hatred toward the buddha, magandiya employed various cunning plots to make the king lose faith in queen samavati.
on one occasion, when king udena was preparing to spend several days at samavati’s palace, he took with him his famous elephant-charming lute (*hatthikanta-vina*), which possessed the extraordinary power to summon elephants. the king carried it wherever he went. what queen magandiya did was to have a snake, whose fangs had been extracted, inserted into a cavity of the lute. in all of these schemes, she was assisted by her paternal uncle, the brahmin magandiya. with his help, she executed this cunning plot. having inserted the fangless snake into the lute, and after the king had gone to samavati’s palace, she arranged for the snake to slide out of the lute, thereby provoking the king’s wrath against samavati.
the king became so furious that he took a poisoned arrow, lined up samavati and her five hundred companion women, and prepared to shoot them. in that moment, queen samavati advised her group: "we have no refuge at this moment other than loving-kindness. radiate loving-kindness equally to the king, to queen magandiya, and to ourselves." just as the king released the arrow, instead of flying toward them, it turned back. it reversed its direction and aimed itself directly at the king's own chest. the king was struck with intense emotion (*samvega*), fell at samavati’s feet, and begged for forgiveness. samavati seized that very opportunity to inspire faith in the buddha within the king. she urged the king to go to the buddha for refuge. subsequently, with the king's assistance, queen samavati secured permission to regularly attend to and serve the sangha. we are summarizing a very long story here; there are numerous nested narratives connected to this event. as the queen became increasingly devoted to serving the buddha and the sangha, magandiya plotted an even more severe and treacherous scheme to harm or destroy samavati.
when the king was preparing to go to the royal pleasure gardens, what did magandiya do? she told her uncle, the brahmin magandiya, to go to samavati’s palace in the king's absence, open the storehouses of cloth and oil, soak the cloths in oil, wrap them around the pillars of the palace, and set them on fire. while the king was away in the pleasure gardens, the brahmin went and prepared to set the palace on fire as instructed. samavati and her retinue realized what was about to happen. what did the conspirators do next? they locked the women inside and set the palace on fire.
in that critical moment, queen samavati spoke to her companions as if delivering a dhamma sermon: "in this long samsara, even the buddha may not be able to count the number of times we have burned and died in houses in this manner. therefore, be heedful (*appamatta hotha*)!" thus, she made a profound request and gave deep advice to her group. the palace caught fire. as the palace burned, what did this group do? in that moment of intense peril—which is referred to as the comprehension of feeling (*vedana-pariggaha*), a highly advanced meditation subject—they took the bodily sensation (*vedana*) itself as their meditation object and developed insight (*vipassana*).
in this manner, that group of women, who were already stream-enterers, contemplated the intense sensation (*vedana*) arising in their bodies as the palace burned down around them. through this insight, they attained the higher paths and fruits (*margaphala*), many of them realizing the states of once-returner (*sakadagami*) and non-returner (*anagami*).
in the subsequent events, people came and informed the buddha: "o blessed one, while the king was in the pleasure gardens, the inner palace caught fire, and samavati along with her large retinue of five hundred women met their death. where have they been reborn?" the buddha then declared: "monks, many of those lay women attained the higher paths and fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning. they acted heedfully (*appamatta*). none of them met a death that was in vain (*anipphala kalakata*)." declaring that they had met a fruitful death, he uttered a profound verse of solemn utterance (*udana*) on that occasion:
> *mohasambandhano loko, bhabbarupova dissati;*
> *upadhibalo tamasa parivarito, sassatova khayati, passato natthi kincanam.*
the buddha uttered a profound verse of solemn utterance there, expressing the voidness and emptiness of the world: "the world, bound by delusion (*moha*), appears as if it is real and substantial. the fool, grasping onto the substrates of existence (*upadhi*), is enveloped in darkness. it appears as if it is eternal; but to one who sees truly, there is nothing there." the buddha expressed this truth in connection with that event. we can reflect on how a grand palace, home to a large retinue of women including samavati, was reduced to ashes in a single moment, destroying everyone inside. thus, the buddha uttered a verse that demonstrates the impermanent (*anicca*) and unsubstantial (*anatta*) nature of everything in the world. but the story does not end there.
next, it is said that the king, having heard that the palace was on fire, rushed back as fast as he could. but by the time he arrived, it had already burned to ashes. after extinguishing the remaining embers, he was overcome with immense grief and began to contemplate who could have done this. he suspected that magandiya might have been responsible, but resolved to trap her using a ruse. the king summoned his ministers and, in their presence, said: "for a long time, i lived in constant anxiety, wondering when this woman (samavati) would harm me. now, at last, i can sleep in peace." the king expressed joy over samavati’s death in the presence of queen magandiya, who was standing nearby. the ministers then asked, "o king, who could have done this?" the king replied, "it must have been someone who has immense love and affection for me." hearing this, magandiya stepped forward and revealed the secret: "o king, it was i who did this through my uncle!"
the king did not reveal his anger even then. he said, "i am exceedingly pleased. no one has as much affection for me as you do. let us summon all your relatives so that i may grant them rewards." magandiya sent messages to her relatives, urging them to come quickly as the king was highly pleased and wished to bestow favors. to the first relatives who arrived, the king gave special gifts and rewards. seeing this, even those who were not her relatives bribed others to claim, "we too are relatives of queen magandiya," and came to the palace. once the entire group had assembled, the king had them all seized. he had pits dug in the palace courtyard, buried them up to their waists, covered them with straw, and set them on fire. as they were burning and trying to escape, he had them plowed over with iron plows, crushing their bodies to pieces and putting them to death. it is recorded that queen magandiya was subjected to an even more horrific torture: her flesh was sliced from her body, fried in a pan of hot oil, and she was forced to eat her own cooked flesh until she died.
thus, the king punished them in an extremely horrific manner. while these events were unfolding, a discussion arose among the monks in the dhamma hall. they remarked that such a tragic death was highly unsuitable for a lay woman of such great faith as samavati. the buddha arrived and asked, "monks, what are you discussing?" when they related the conversation, the buddha explained: "monks, from the perspective of their conduct in this life, the death of queen samavati and her retinue indeed appears unsuitable; but from the perspective of their past kamma, it is completely fitting." the monks then begged the blessed one to reveal their past kamma, and the buddha related the story of the past.
this event took place during an interval between buddhas, before the appearance of the present buddha, during a time when paccekabuddhas lived. when king brahmadatta was reigning in benares, eight paccekabuddhas regularly visited the palace for alms. seven of them, having finished their meal, would fly back to the himalayas through psychic power. one of them, however, would remain and enter meditative absorption (*jhana*) in a clump of grass near the riverbank. the five hundred women of the king’s harem used to attend to these paccekabuddhas. one day, after the paccekabuddhas had departed, the king went to play in the water with these women. having played in the water the entire day, the women felt very cold by evening. they decided to warm themselves by a fire. looking around, they saw the clump of grass and set it on fire, unaware that the paccekabuddha was inside. as the grass burned down, they suddenly saw the paccekabuddha sitting there. they were terrified, thinking, "this is the king's respected paccekabuddha. if the king finds out, he will surely put us to death." they decided to burn him completely to cover up their deed. they gathered more firewood, piled it up, and set the paccekabuddha on fire.
however, that paccekabuddha was in the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samapatti*). according to the law of kamma, the women accumulated unwholesome kamma through their intention (*cetana*), even though the paccekabuddha was not physically burned. he emerged from his concentration after seven days and walked away unharmed. but because of their grave unwholesome intention, those women—who were samavati and her retinue—suffered in hell for hundreds of thousands of years. furthermore, as a residual result of that kamma, in a hundred subsequent lifetimes, they died by being burned to death inside buildings. the buddha declared that this was their final birth, and this was how that kamma bore its last fruit.
on that occasion, wishing to clarify other details, the monks asked another question, as is common today, regarding the lay woman khujjuttara. they asked why she was born hunchbacked. since she was a highly prominent disciple whom the buddha had placed in the foremost position (*etadagga*), they wondered why such a meritorious person was born with a physical deformity. that was one question. the second was: what past merit made her possess such vast wisdom? third: what past merit led to her stream-entry? and fourth: what past kamma caused her to be born as a maid servant? the buddha then related the past stories connected to these questions.
first, regarding her hunchbacked condition: this too was connected to the same paccekabuddha. the paccekabuddha who meditated near the clump of grass happened to have a slightly bent, hunchbacked body. one of the harem women—who was none other than khujjuttara in a past life—mocked him. she draped herself in a robe, took a golden vessel in her hand, and mimicked his hunchbacked walk to make the other women laugh, saying, "this is how our paccekabuddha walks." the buddha explained that due to this unwholesome kamma of mockery, she was born hunchbacked.
next, regarding her great wisdom: this too was connected to the same period. when the paccekabuddhas first visited the royal palace, the five hundred women served them hot milk-rice in their bowls. because the milk-rice was extremely hot, the paccekabuddhas were passing the bowls from hand to hand to avoid burning themselves. seeing this, this particular woman wisely took eight ivory bangles she was wearing and offered them, saying, "please place the bowls on these bangles." the paccekabuddhas did so, easing their discomfort, and later tried to return the bangles. she insisted, saying, "no, venerable sirs, i have offered them permanently."
the buddha explained that because of this wise act of service, which she performed with wise reflection, she was blessed with great wisdom, becoming widely learned (*bahusruta*) and a holder of the dhamma (*dhammadhara*). her stream-entry was also supported by the very service she and the others rendered to the paccekabuddhas—for serving those who have realized the paths and fruits and touched the peace of nibbana assists one in attaining the same realization. finally, regarding her being born as a servant: this occurred during the dispensation of kassapa buddha. khujjuttara was then the daughter of a wealthy merchant (*setthi-dhita*). an arahant bhikkhuni came to visit her in the evening while she was dressing and putting on her ornaments. having no servant nearby, and needing her ornament box which was out of reach, she told the arahant bhikkhuni, "noble lady, please hand me that box," speaking with a lack of respect, as if treating her like a maid.
the arahant bhikkhuni reflected: "if she harbors anger toward me, she will be reborn in hell. but if she performs this service for me, she will merely be born as a servant. being born as a servant is far better than being reborn in hell." thus, she handed her the box. the buddha explained that because she made an arahant bhikkhuni serve her like a maid, she was born as a servant. from this, we can comprehend the precision of the fruit of kamma. furthermore, it is said that the discussion among the monks in the dhamma hall continued to reverberate regarding this entire event—how samavati and her large retinue died in the fire, how magandiya’s relatives were executed by the king, and how magandiya herself was subjected to horrific torture. they debated on who in this world is truly alive and who is dead.
it was on that occasion that the buddha approached and asked, "monks, what are you discussing?" when they related the conversation, the buddha declared: "monks, in this world, those who are heedful (*appamatta*) are truly alive. whether they live or die, they are to be considered alive. those who are negligent (*pamatta*), even if they are physically breathing, are as if already dead." he then uttered the three verses from the *appamada vagga* of the dhammapada, which we took as our opening topic.
> *appamado amatapadam, pamado maccuno padam;*
> *appamatta na miyanti, ye pamatta yatha mata.*
as you know, the deathless (*amata*) is a name for nibbana. once the mind stilled is realized, there is no more birth (*jati*). when there is no birth, there is no aging and death (*jaramarana*). heedfulness (*appamada*) is the path to the deathless. negligence (*pamada*) is the path to death. the heedful do not die. the negligent are as if already dead; even though they are alive, they are like the dead.
> *etam visesato natva, appamadamhi pandita;*
> *appamade pamodanti, ariyanam gocare rata.*
knowing this distinction clearly—that those who are heedful do not die, while the negligent are as if already dead—the wise (*pandita*) delight in heedfulness, rejoicing in the pasture of the nobles (*ariyanam gocara*). on one occasion, the buddha defined the "pasture of the nobles" as the four foundations of mindfulness (*cattaro satipatthana*). the four foundations of mindfulness are the pasture, the rightful territory, of the nobles and of all those who seek nibbana. the wise, residing in this pasture and practicing mindfulness, rejoice in the path of heedfulness.
the next verse speaks of a deeper aspect:
> *te jhayino satatika, niccam dalhaparakkama;*
> *phusanti dhira nibbanam, yogakkhemam anuttaram.*
these wise ones, constantly meditating (*jhayino*) and possessing firm endeavor (*dalhaparakkama*)—which refers not to physical warfare, but to the battle against defilements—touch and realize the supreme security from bondage (*yogakkhema*), which is nibbana. *yogakkhema* is another name for the mind stilled. "yoga" here refers to the four bonds: the bond of sensuality (*kama-yoga*), the bond of existence (*bhava-yoga*), the bond of views (*ditthi-yoga*), and the bond of ignorance (*avijja-yoga*). these are the four bonds that drag one through the length of samsara. the wise, who possess such practice and constantly meditate, touch and realize the supreme nibbana, which is the liberation from these bonds. thus did the buddha expound these verses.
we have now heard the story and the verses. it is now up to us to reflect on these teachings in a calm and composed manner, extracting the practical lessons and deeper dhamma principles that we can apply to our own lives. first, when we reflect on this story, we see that queen samavati holds an exceptionally noble position among the female disciples of the buddha's dispensation. we have just heard the account of her life. although we do not have exhaustive details, we can appreciate the immense spiritual development her mind had achieved.
when we consider her power of loving-kindness, she harbored not a shred of ill-will toward magandiya, who hated her so intensely. when the king was about to shoot them with the poisoned arrow, she instructed her companions to radiate equal loving-kindness to the king, to queen magandiya, and to themselves. her mind had developed such a powerful degree of loving-kindness. in the practice of the meditation on loving-kindness, there is a highly advanced stage known as the deliverance of mind through loving-kindness (*metta-cetovimutti*). it is a powerful spiritual force capable of radiating loving-kindness to all beings without any discrimination. within that concentration (*jhana*), there lies a power that can even perform miracles. it was by the power of that very miracle that the arrow turned back. it is said that the king was struck with deep emotion (*samvega*), thinking, "even this lifeless arrow recognizes her virtue, yet a human like me did not," and fell at her feet in worship.
thus, we can see how powerful the concentration (*jhana*) of loving-kindness is, capable of deflecting a poisoned arrow. however, some might argue and raise a question based on the benefits of loving-kindness preached by the buddha in the *mettanisamsa sutta*. one of those benefits is: *nassa aggi va visam va sattham va kamati*—"neither fire, poison, nor weapons can harm" one who has developed the deliverance of mind through loving-kindness.
yet, in this instance, they could not prevent the danger of the fire due to the sheer gravity of their past kamma. the momentum of kamma was far more powerful. samavati, however, did not despair in that moment. she immediately directed her companions toward the practice of insight (*vipassana*). there is a profound and valuable lesson in this. the palace was burning and collapsing around them. in that moment, samavati gave her advice in just two words: *appamatta hotha*—"be heedful!" here too, we find the word *appamada*. in the ordinary world, if a large building catches fire, people panic, wail, and die in agony. we frequently hear of such tragedies occurring in the world.
what did queen samavati do? she realized that the doors were locked and there was no way out. she understood that crying and lamenting would serve no purpose. she did what had to be done in that very moment. that is *appamada*. what she did was this: while being burned by the external fire, she extinguished herself with the internal cooling of nibbana. that is what she achieved. she let the external fire burn the physical body, but she extinguished the inner fire through the realization of the mind stilled. this was achieved through the attainment of fruition (*phala-samapatti*). she utilized the power of stream-entry she had already attained, and by further developing insight (*vipassana*) through the comprehension of feeling (*vedana-pariggaha*), she took the intense sensation (*vedana*) arising in her burning body as her meditation object. ordinarily, the natural tendency of worldlings is to fear pain and try to flee from it. what is the marvelous method shown by the buddha here? it is to look directly at the sensation (*vedana*) itself, applying wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*) with a concentrated mind, and reflecting that "this feeling is not mine, this is not self." the buddha compared sensation to a water bubble: *vedana bubbulupama*. when rain falls, water bubbles form rapidly on the surface, only to burst and vanish in an instant. sensation is just like that.
why do we get agitated by sensation? it is because we grasp it as "my feeling." we grasp it, develop aversion toward it, and engage in an internal conflict, thereby burning ourselves. in contrast, the insight method taught by the buddha is to observe that very sensation, that very pain, objectively as a meditation subject. through that observation, one perceives its impermanent (*anicca*), painful (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*) nature. it was by profoundly realizing this truth that samavati and her companions attained the higher paths and fruits. the buddha declared that they met a death that was not in vain (*anipphala kalakata*)—a highly successful death. this is the very meaning expressed in the verse: *appamatta na miyanti, ye pamatta yatha mata*—"the heedful do not die; the negligent are as if already dead." this is a great lesson for our lives today. none of us can predict with certainty when, where, or under what circumstances death will come. we too might find ourselves in a situation where we are trapped in a burning building with no escape. in such a moment, our only refuge is the meditation subject (*kammatthana*) we have practiced.
in samavati’s life, we see how she utilized her developed concentration (*jhana*) of loving-kindness to secure her own peace and to bring about a profound change in the king, turning the crisis into a victory of the dhamma (*dhamma-vijaya*). when a tragedy occurs, the worldly response is to harbor hatred, thinking "who did this to me?" and thus burn with both the external fire and the internal fire of hatred and delusion. what did samavati do instead? she understood it as the force of kamma. she advised her companions: "in this vast samsara, we have burned to death in this manner countless times, beyond the scope of even a buddha’s knowledge. this is a minor thing. what we must do now is elevate this experience into insight (*vipassana*) and escape from this existence (*bhava*) immediately."
for the buddha, true *appamada* (heedfulness) is not merely escaping from a burning building. indeed, in that situation, physical escape was impossible. yet, the ordinary worldling would spend their last moments wailing and screaming, hoping someone would open the door and save them, and thus meet a miserable death. in contrast, samavati accepted the reality. the buddha highly praises those who, in such moments, strive to escape from the cycle of existence (*bhava*). that is precisely what samavati and her companion women achieved. in another discourse, the buddha asked the monks: "monks, if a person's clothes or head were on fire, what should they do?" the monks gave the natural reply: "o blessed one, they must make a great effort, using mindfulness and energy, to extinguish the fire immediately." but what did the buddha say? "no, monks. in such a moment, disregarding one's burning clothes or head, one should strive to realize the noble truths of suffering (*dukkha*), its origin, its cessation, and the path. extinguishing the internal fire of defilements is far more urgent than extinguishing the external fire." the story shows that queen samavati and her companions acted in perfect accordance with this instruction of the buddha. this is extremely valuable for our own lives. while the world thinks of worldly savings and protection for times of crisis, in the ultimate helpless moment, one's only refuge is the meditation subject (*kammatthana*) one has developed. a mind trained in loving-kindness can neutralize intense hostility, and if kamma brings an unavoidable tragedy, one must view it as an opportunity to escape from existence (*bhava*) through insight (*vipassana*). that is the practice of heedfulness (*appamada*).
all these profound meanings are perfectly demonstrated in the life of queen samavati. we have much to learn from this. furthermore, from the other events in this story, we can appreciate the terrifying ocean of kamma in which we live. through the buddha-eye, it became clear that samavati’s death was not ultimately caused by magandiya; magandiya was merely an instrument. the real cause was their own past intention (*cetana*) to burn the paccekabuddha. the buddha declared: *cetanaham bhikkhave kammam vadami; cetayitva kammam karoti kayena vacaya manasa*—"intention, monks, is what i call kamma. having intended, one performs kamma through body, speech, and mind."
one might argue that the paccekabuddha was not physically harmed. but those women had already burned him in their minds. that unwholesome intention was the kamma that produced such severe results. if the paccekabuddha had actually been harmed, the consequences would have been even more horrific. we must always reflect on the kammic consequences of our daily actions. we must realize that we live as if on a ground made of kamma. we are born upon the massive heap of kamma we have accumulated over the vast span of samsara, and this life is spent wearing away that kamma. until we eradicate the seed-potential of kamma (*bija-sakti*) that leads to rebirth through the supramundane paths and fruits, we have no choice but to swim in this ocean of kamma.
the power of wholesome kamma was also demonstrated in the life of the lay woman khujjuttara. first, the monks asked about her physical deformity. the unwholesome kamma responsible for it was something that might be considered minor in the ordinary world—a simple act of mocking the posture of a paccekabuddha. by draping herself in a robe and mimicking his hunchbacked walk to make others laugh, she accumulated the unwholesome kamma that caused her to be born hunchbacked. many of our physical illnesses and deformities are rooted in such past actions. today, even through limited worldly investigations, some of these truths are being uncovered. but this is an absolute reality. every small action of our body, speech, and mind has a long-term kammic momentum.
her great wisdom was also the result of a seemingly simple act. seeing the paccekabuddhas passing the hot bowls from hand to hand, she wisely offered her ivory bangles to use as stands. this is a valuable lesson for us. when we perform services or duties, we should not view them as a burden or a chore; rather, we should perceive them as a precious opportunity to cultivate wholesome kamma. the paccekabuddhas did not ask for the bangles, but she wisely used her intelligence to facilitate their comfort, and that wise act of service made her a person of great wisdom, widely learned (*bahusruta*) and a holder of the dhamma (*dhammadhara*).
similarly, her stream-entry was supported by her service to those who had realized the paths and fruits. serving those who have realized the dhamma helps one to realize the same truth. lastly, her being born as a servant was due to a single instance in a past life under kassapa buddha when, as a merchant's daughter, she treated an arahant bhikkhuni like a maid by asking her to hand her an ornament box. though it seemed like a minor incident, it carried a significant unwholesome result. living in samsara is indeed a terrifying affair.
if you are driving a vehicle at high speed, and you are a skilled driver, you might not feel afraid. but you never know when an animal might jump onto the road, or when a minor mechanical failure might cause the vehicle to overturn. our minds are just like that; they function at lightning speed, and if the mind slips even slightly, the resulting kammic momentum can trap us in samsaric suffering for an immensely long period. this is why the buddha always emphasized true heedfulness (*appamada*). in the ordinary world, heedfulness is understood as catching a bus or a train on time, arriving at the office on time, and managing one's daily affairs efficiently.
the worldly expectation is to achieve success by hook or by crook, through dhamma or non-dhamma, and to secure financial stability. but from the perspective of the buddha's word, such a life falls into negligence (*pamada*). true heedfulness (*appamada*), as defined by the buddha, is escaping from this terrifying samsara as quickly as possible—escaping from this cycle of existence (*bhava*). it is this escape that is demonstrated in the life of queen samavati, and it is the same truth that is revealed in the buddha's discourse about one's head being on fire.
the story also illustrates the danger of samsara and the cruelty of magandiya. although magandiya was exceptionally beautiful—sought after by kings throughout india—she lacked virtue, which led to her horrific end in this very life. this helps us distinguish between true progress and decline, and between true heedfulness and negligence. we must reflect on these dhamma principles and strive to apply them to our daily lives.
the path of the dhamma consists of virtue, concentration, and wisdom (*sila, samadhi, panna*), which summarize the entire dispensation of the buddha. virtue is the essential foundation. samavati’s humble, respectful life and her gratitude—freeing her maid and treating her as a teacher—demonstrate her immense virtue. virtue is what enables the mind to achieve concentration (*samadhi*). one cannot expect to concentrate a mind that is filled with remorse. we observe precepts in order to live a life free of remorse, establishing a firm foundation for concentration.
today, you have observed the eight precepts of right livelihood (*ajiva-atthamaka-sila*). for lay disciples, the buddha has prescribed the five precepts and the eight precepts to restrain body and speech. this restraint, however, is directed by the mind (*cetana-sila, cetasika-sila*). the physical body is not an autonomous machine; it is driven by the mind. therefore, though virtue is described as the restraint of body and speech, this restraint is accomplished by the mind through the power of resolution (*adhitthana*).
one might ask if it is sufficient to undertake the precepts once. in practical terms, however, the precepts we have undertaken must remain at the forefront of our minds so that they can guide our behavior when the need arises. this is why we regularly undertake the precepts. we must make a daily resolution: "today, i will live within the boundaries of these five pillars (the five precepts) or these eight pillars (the eight precepts), and i will not cross them." when an opportunity to perform an unwholesome deed arises—such as an urge to kill an animal or to steal—our wisdom steps forward and warns us: "this is contrary to the resolution you have made. do not do it." the mind then refrains from the action. this is known as "refraining upon encounter" (*sampatta-virati*).
the word *veramani* means refraining or abstaining. when we recite the precepts, we must focus on the word *veramani*: *panatipata veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami*—"i undertake the precept of refraining from destroying life." this act of refraining is of utmost importance, for it is here that the mind takes the lead. when there is every opportunity to commit a sin, the virtue we have undertaken steps forward and restrains us. refraining from the act generates immense spiritual strength, which subsequently brings great joy and relief when we reflect: "i have escaped from committing an unwholesome deed and from the future suffering it would have brought."
this is why we say that when we harm an animal, the harm we cause to our own mind through defilements is hundreds of thousands of times greater than the physical pain the animal suffers. the world thinks we should avoid harming animals merely because it is bad for the animal. but there is a deeper truth: by harboring hatred and harming another being, we corrupt our own minds, and we will have to pay for that corruption with suffering that is vastly greater than the pain felt by the animal. in the past story, the paccekabuddha was completely unharmed by the fire; he simply brushed off the ashes and flew away. yet, the unwholesome kamma of the women remained intact because of their unwholesome intention (*cetana*). unwholesome kamma is rooted in greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dosa*), and delusion (*moha*).
we can identify these unwholesome roots within our own minds if we apply mindfulness (*sati*). although they are often masked by deceptive mental states, we can perceive them if we reflect wisely. we can understand: "underneath this action lies greed, hatred, or delusion." the buddha declared greed, hatred, and delusion as the roots of all unwholesome deeds. wholesome (*kusala*) means skillful, and unwholesome (*akusala*) means unskillful. if we live unskillfully in this samsara, we will experience suffering; if we live skillfully, we will experience happiness and realize nibbana swiftly.
thus, "kusala" in its primary sense means skillfulness. wholesome thoughts arise from non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adosa*), and non-delusion (*amoha*). every moment we make an effort to distance ourselves from greed, hatred, and delusion—even for a single moment—we plant a wholesome seed. because our minds have been habituated to these defilements for a long time, any effort to step away from them, even briefly, marks a wholesome turning point. this is what is meant by *alobha*, *adosa*, and *amoha*—the prefix "a-" denotes stepping away from greed, hatred, and delusion. we cannot eradicate them all at once, but we can push them aside for a moment through the mental factor of refraining (*virati-cetasika*).
for instance, when an urge to kill an animal arises—perhaps driven by a desire for its meat or by anger—and we immediately suppress that urge, preventing it from translating into action, we perform a powerful wholesome deed. if we do not suppress it, it remains as unwholesome mental kamma, burning within us like a hot coal. the buddha compared unwholesome thoughts to hot coals. a child might touch a hot coal out of ignorance, but the moment they feel the heat, they drop it immediately. they do not hold onto it because it looks attractive. similarly, the moment we realize a thought is rooted in greed, hatred, or delusion, we must discard it immediately. if we hold onto it, it will translate into speech and action, trapping us in samsaric suffering for aeons. the wholesome path, therefore, is the power of refraining.
some might argue: "what are we actually doing when we undertake precepts? it is all about not doing things; there is no positive action involved." however, refraining is in itself a powerful wholesome action. once we remove the unwholesome actions, the remaining actions naturally become wholesome. refraining from unwholesome deeds is not a passive state; it requires active effort and mental skill. that mental skill is what we call "kusala." this is why we undertake the precepts beforehand, training the mind to refrain when temptation arises. based on established virtue, we develop concentration (*samadhi*) through meditation subjects such as loving-kindness, recollection of the buddha, the foulness of the body, or the mindfulness of death.
when the mind achieves concentration, it experiences a physical and mental peace that is thousands of times superior to any sensual pleasure. based on that concentration, one contemplates the three characteristics of impermanence (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*), developing insight (*vipassana*) to realize the noble paths and fruits.
through this sermon, we have extracted numerous dhamma principles. by listening with deep faith and establishing ourselves in virtue, we can experience a sense of concentration. may the power of the dhamma we have cultivated help us walk the path of heedfulness, complete our wholesome qualities through the association with noble friends, and practice generosity, virtue, and meditation. may this listening to the dhamma support us in escaping from this terrifying samsara and realizing the supreme peace of nibbana. may all guardian deities, and all beings from the lowest avici hell to the highest heaven (*akanittha*), rejoice in these merits and attain the supreme peace of the mind stilled according to their own aspirations. let us now transfer these merits by reciting the verses.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 098
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #98
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.100)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Duppabbajjaṃ durabhiramaṃ, durāvāsā gharā dukhā;
Dukkho 'samānasaṃvāso, tasmā na caddhagū siyā, na ca dukkhānupatito siyāti.
From:
Dhammapada 302 (Lokavagga)
Dear Listeners,
The Buddha, the Teacher of the Three Worlds, declared that the happiness of ordination is superior to lay happiness. By forgetting the vast amount of suffering (*dukkha*) and hardship that lies beneath lay happiness, one might sometimes perceive lay happiness as superior. Because of such a misunderstanding, the force of renunciation (*nekkhamma*) that brings a person to the ordained state might also diminish. Therefore, on many occasions, the Buddha highlighted the vast amount of suffering (*dukkha*) and hardship that lies beneath lay happiness and lay life. The Buddha expounded the stanza we have taken as our theme as advice to a certain monk who was facing such a problem.
While the Buddha was residing at the Gabled Hall in the Great Wood near Vesālī, this monk, who was a Vajjiputtaka (a prince of the Vajjians), lived devoted to meditation in a forest grove. One night, while he was practicing walking meditation, he heard the sounds of an annual festival being held in the city. The sounds of various musical instruments, songs, singing, dancing, and the beating of drums began to be heard. Then, this monk recalled how, during his lay life when he enjoyed royal pleasures, he used to dress up in beautiful clothes and ornaments to enjoy himself on such occasions. Reflecting on this, a great sadness arose in him, and as a form of lamentation, he uttered a certain stanza: "We live alone in this forest like a piece of wood cast away in the jungle. On a night like this, who is more unfortunate than us?" It is said that he expressed his grievances through this stanza. Hearing this, the deity presiding over that forest grove, wishing to arouse spiritual urgency (*saṁvega*) in the monk, turned the same stanza around and declared: "Indeed, you live alone in this forest like a discarded piece of firewood. Yet, laypeople look up to you with great respect and high esteem, just as those destined for hell look longingly up to those who have gone to heaven." After hearing that stanza, the monk's desire for lay pleasures vanished. On the following day, when this monk went to see the Buddha, the Buddha, understanding the situation, uttered the very stanza we have chosen as our theme, in order to help the monk further eradicate his lingering attachment to lay happiness.
Every word in this stanza carries an extremely profound meaning:
*“Duppabbajjaṁ durabhiramaṁ, durāvāsā gharā dukhā;*
*Dukkho’samānasaṁvāso, tasmā na caddhagū siyā, na ca dukkhānupatito siyā.”*
*Duppabbajjaṁ*: going forth is difficult. It is difficult to transition from lay life to the ordained life. *Durabhiramaṁ*: even after going forth, it is difficult to find delight in the ordained life; it is difficult to develop a love for the monastic way of life. *Durāvāsā gharā dukhā*: living in the household life is a mountain of great suffering (*dukkha*), a heap of suffering (*dukkha*). *Dukkho’samānasaṁvāso*: here, although the Sinhala script might read *samāna* (equal/same), the true grammatical meaning intended is *asamanasaṁvāso*—living together with incompatible people is suffering (*dukkha*). It is said because of the nature of society. Next, *dukkhānupatito addhagū*: this journey through saṁsāra is a journey that drags suffering (*dukkha*) along with it. *Tasmā*, therefore; *na caddhagū siyā*: do not be a traveler who continues to drag suffering (*dukkha*) along endlessly in saṁsāra. *Na ca (dukkhānupatito) siyā*: do not act in a way that suffering (*dukkha*) follows close behind you. In this manner, the Buddha delivered the stanza as advice.
If we reflect a bit more carefully on each of these words, why is it called *duppabbajjaṁ*? According to the concept of ordination in the Buddha's time, a layperson went forth with a deep intention, driven by genuine renunciation (*nekkhamma*), and not merely because they had robes and requisites. As mentioned in ancient texts, they went forth after abandoning a small or large accumulation of wealth, and abandoning a small or large circle of relatives. Departing from the home life and going forth in that manner is extremely difficult for a layperson. Most of the time, there are plenty of excuses not to ordain. To that extent, the bonds of lay life cannot easily be untied and brought to an end. Here, there is a wondrously complex web of interconnected attachments. This is why it is called *duppabbajjaṁ*—ordination is a state that is achieved with great difficulty.
Furthermore, even if one manages to ordain with difficulty, once entering the monastic sphere, it is hard to adapt to the monastic lifestyle due to deeply ingrained lay habits. Depending on alms food, living in seclusion, going to the forest to live alone devoted to meditation, withdrawing from crowds, and observing the relevant Vinaya training rules—all of these are unfamiliar things. To develop a delight, a keen interest, and a desire (*chanda*) for these things, and to act accordingly, is difficult for one who has ordained. This is precisely what happened to that Vajjiputtaka monk. According to the texts, among the Vajji princes of that era, there was a confederacy in which seven thousand seven hundred and seven princes reigned in turn. This monk is described as someone who abandoned his turn at the kingship to ordain. Yet, upon hearing the sounds of the festival, his mind turned back to kingship. His mind drifted toward royal luxuries, weakening his resolve, and he expressed that stanza lamenting his situation.
*Durabhiramaṁ*: in the Dispensation, there is a term called *abhirati* (delight). Without a special delight in the ordained state, one cannot sustain it. When that delight is lost, it is called *anabhirati* (non-delight/discontent). As soon as discontent arises, one becomes "apathetic" (*ukaṭalī*, weary/bored). Then, one keeps thinking about lay life, wondering, "When will I escape this trouble and go back?" In this way, due to these saṁsāric weaknesses, it is difficult for a layperson to cultivate and sustain a delight in renunciation. Similarly, *durāvāsā gharā dukhā*: next, the nature of lay life is further described. Living in the household life involves immense suffering (*dukkha*) and troubles. Because living the lay life means one must toil to gather the necessary wealth and resources. According to ancient similes, balancing income and expenses in a household is an extremely difficult task. Often, disputes over income and expenditure arise between husbands and wives, leading to quarrels and conflicts. In the texts, this is compared to pouring water into a leaking pot. The mouth of the pot is small, but there are many holes. Similarly, income is small, but expenses are many. It is extremely difficult to resolve this entanglement in lay life, and as a result, one gets trapped in a mountain of great suffering (*dukkha*). One can never fully satisfy the responsibilities concerning spouse and children, and social duties.
Another simile is given to show the difficulty of satisfying lay needs, comparing them to the great ocean. No matter how many rivers flow into it, the ocean can never be filled. Similarly, no matter how much the desires of a layperson's mind are fulfilled, there is no satisfaction; there is no end to their needs. Because of this, household life is described as *durāvāsā gharā dukhā*.
Next, *dukkho samānasaṁvāso* (or *asamanasaṁvāso*): living with incompatible people is also suffering (*dukkha*). Society is crowded with diverse and discordant individuals. Among them, there is an extraordinary degree of competitiveness, jealousy, association with bad friends, and so forth. Because of these factors, living in a society filled with discordant people is no easy matter. Having to live together with incompatible people is a great suffering (*dukkha*).
Next, *dukkhānupatito addhagū*: similarly, lay life means wandering further and further in saṁsāra. Wandering further and further in saṁsāra means a journey where one continues to prolong and experience the momentum of kamma created through attachments and conflicts. This is why it is called "expanding saṁsāra." Within lay life, saṁsāra is expanded. That is what is meant. In this very manner, one travels this long journey carrying saṁsāric suffering (*dukkha*) along. Indeed, five points are presented here in this manner. Next, *tasmā na caddhagū siyā*: therefore, do not be a traveler who wanders endlessly in saṁsāra. *Na ca (dukkhānupatito) siyā*: do not go searching for suffering (*dukkha*). This is the meaning of that stanza.
As we mentioned earlier, at first glance, the ordained life might seem like a heap of great suffering (*dukkha*)—living alone in the forest like a discarded piece of wood. Lay life, on the other hand, seems to be a fashionable, attractive, colorful, and luxurious lifestyle. So why did the Buddha show this lay life as suffering (*dukkha*) and ordination as happiness? The Buddha demonstrated this to the world on several occasions through his own example.
Such an incident is recorded, a very valuable one. Once, the Buddha spent a night in an Alavi forest of *aṭṭēriya* leaves on a path frequented by cattle. He slept on a bed of *aṭṭēriya* leaves. Rising in the morning, while he was seated there in meditation, the prince Hatthaka Āḷavaka, who was out for a walk, saw the Buddha sitting on the bed of leaves. He realized that the Buddha must have spent the night there. So he asked the Buddha: "Venerable Sir, did the Blessed One sleep in comfort?" The Buddha replied: "Yes, Prince, I slept in comfort. Of those in the world who sleep in comfort, I am one."
Then the prince said: "But Venerable Sir, the night in this winter season is cold. This is the time of the severe winter frost. Furthermore, the ground here is rough, trampled by the hooves of cattle. The bed of leaves is very thin, and the leaves on the trees are sparse. The Blessed One's robes are cold, and the biting wind blowing from all four directions is cold. Yet the Blessed One says, 'I slept in comfort'!"
Thereupon the Buddha said: "Well then, Prince, I will first ask you a question. Answer as you please. Suppose there is a wealthy householder or a householder's son living in a luxurious gabled mansion, plastered inside and out, on a comfortable couch spread with fine woolen covers, soft pillows, and mattresses. A lamp is burning, and he is attended by four highly pleasing wives. Would that householder or householder's son sleep in comfort?" Then the prince replied: "Yes, Venerable Sir, he would be one of those in the world who sleep in comfort."
Then the Buddha asked again: "Well then, please answer this question too. Might not that householder or householder's son have to lie down in discomfort, tormented by lustful thoughts that cause bodily and mental distress?" To this, the prince had to say: "Yes, Venerable Sir." Next, the Buddha declared: "The defilements of lust and so forth that burn that householder or householder's son have been completely abandoned by the Tathāgata. Cut off at the root, like a palmyra tree uprooted, made non-existent, these defilements of lust and hatred are rendered incapable of future arising. That is why I said I sleep in comfort. Similarly, whatever thoughts of hatred might arise in that householder or householder's son, causing him to spend the night in discomfort—that hatred too has been abandoned by the Tathāgata. Whatever delusion might torment that person in that luxurious mansion—none of those hardships exist for the Tathāgata, who is free of delusion." That was how the Buddha replied on that occasion.
Likewise, there are valuable accounts concerning the Buddha's great disciples. Another such incident occurred when the Buddha was residing in the Anupiya Mango Grove. A monk named Bhaddiya, whether he went to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty house for meditation, would constantly exclaim: *"Aho sukhaṁ! Aho sukhaṁ!!!"*—which translates to, "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!" Hearing this, many other monks thought: "Without a doubt, the Venerable Bhaddiya is reflecting on the royal pleasures he enjoyed before, and out of desire for those royal pleasures, he has become dissatisfied with the ordained life, which is why he is crying out *"Aho sukhaṁ! Aho sukhaṁ!!"*." Thinking thus, the monks went to the Buddha and said: "Venerable Sir, our Venerable Bhaddiya has become dissatisfied with the ordained life and is constantly exclaiming *"Aho sukhaṁ"* in this manner." The Buddha instructed a monk: "Go and summon the monk Bhaddiya."
When that monk conveyed the message, Venerable Bhaddiya came. The Buddha asked him: "Is it true, Bhaddiya, that whether you go to the foot of a tree, an empty place, or a forest, you exclaim *"Aho sukhaṁ"*?" "Yes, Venerable Sir." "For what reason do you say so?" Then Venerable Bhaddiya said: "Blessed One, in my lay life when I was in the palace, there were security arrangements both inside and outside the inner palace. There were security forces inside and outside the city, and guards inside and outside the district. Thus, surrounded and trapped by guards, I lived in great fear, agitation, and terror during my time as king. But now, Venerable Sir, whether I go to the forest, the foot of a tree, or an empty house, I live alone without any fear or suspicion, in complete peace, spending my life as serenely as a wild deer belonging to the forest. That is why I exclaimed *"Aho sukhaṁ, aho sukhaṁ"*." So, we have such inspiring examples.
From this, we can understand that the Buddha declared the happiness of ordination with a very deep meaning. The happiness of ordination, dear devotees, is referred to in some places as the happiness of renunciation (*nekkhamma-sukhaṁ*), the happiness of seclusion (*paviveka-sukhaṁ*), and the happiness of peace (*upasama-sukhaṁ*). The happiness of renunciation (*nekkhamma-sukhaṁ*) means that escaping from these lay bonds is itself a great happiness. Some of you might understand what a hassle lay life is. Especially those who have a strong desire to dedicate time to the Dhamma and engage in meditation often realize that this lay life is a mountain of great suffering (*dukkha*), and some even regret, saying, "What foolishness made us get entangled in these things?"
In the past, there was a common sentiment that "the home life is a burning house." When we contemplate the mountain of suffering (*dukkha*) in that life, you too, dear devotees, are enjoying a small measure of that happiness right now by escaping it. What a relief it is to be able to detach from those things even for a single moment, an hour, a day, or half a day! That indeed is the first happiness: when one completely breaks these lay bonds and develops a liking for living in seclusion. Reflecting on this, one rejoices, thinking, "What a massive bond this was! It is like being released from prison." Next is the happiness of seclusion (*paviveka-sukhaṁ*). There are many accounts of monks living in that seclusion—which often frightens ordinary people—among wild beasts, dwelling in loving-kindness (*mettā*) with those very animals.
If you can walk on roads where highly dangerous, high-speed vehicles travel, then it is no wonder that a monk who loves seclusion can live in a forest hermitage populated by wild animals. Sometimes, animals possess a kind of sensitivity that even humans lack toward monks who live harmlessly in this manner. Even if that is not the case, there are monks who live valuing seclusion, cultivating mindfulness of death (*maraṇasati*) regarding the dangers of their surroundings. This is the happiness of seclusion (*paviveka-sukhaṁ*).
Next, the concentration and meditation developed through that happiness of seclusion lead to the happiness of peace (*upasama-sukhaṁ*). The happiness of peace (*upasama-sukhaṁ*) is the happiness obtained through the stilling of lust, hatred, and delusion, as declared by the Buddha. When it is said that the Buddha slept on a bed of *aṭṭēriya* leaves on such rough ground in the freezing cold—he slept in comfort. One can only say this when the happiness of peace (*upasama-sukhaṁ*) is fully realized. This is what the happiness of ordination means. Furthermore, on certain occasions, the Buddha has described the suffering (*dukkha*) and hardships of lay life in even greater detail. There is a discourse (the *Mahādukkhakkhandha Sutta*) where the Buddha points out, one by one, a massive mass of suffering (*dukkha*). In that discourse, he systematically reveals the dangers of sensual pleasures (*kāma*) as the hardships and sufferings (*dukkha*) one has to endure in lay life.
First, it is described as follows: For a young man of good family to live in the household life, he must strive hard to fulfill massive responsibilities: securing employment, earning a livelihood, maintaining himself, looking after his spouse and children, and performing social duties. Striving is necessary to earn wealth, for a lazy person cannot do so. If he has learned a certain craft, he engages in a job based on it. It is mentioned there—to use modern terms—that he does his job in the midst of a mountain of great suffering (*dukkha*): scorching in the sun, getting wet in the rain, enduring and suffering from cold and heat, and even dying of hunger and thirst. This is shown as the first suffering (*dukkha*).
Next, it is said that despite putting in so much effort, when he does not receive an income from his work, when losses occur, when businesses collapse and are destroyed, this person weeps, laments, and beats his breast. He falls into confusion, crying out: "Alas! The effort I exerted so hard has been ruined, lost. My labor is in vain!" Next, it is said that if, by some means, his efforts succeed and he acquires wealth, he then lies awake in the midst of great suffering (*dukkha*) and distress, thinking: "Oh, may kings not confiscate this wealth I have earned! May thieves not steal it! May it not be destroyed by fire! May it not be swept away by floods or deluges! May these things not perish!" Thus, he organizes extensive security measures and lives with suffering (*dukkha*) and distress.
Next, the subsequent suffering (*dukkha*) is described: even if he has set up all those security measures, if kings confiscate his wealth, or thieves come and plunder it either secretly or by force, or if it is burnt by fire, or swept away and destroyed by floods, then on that occasion too, he weeps, laments, and beats his breast in the same manner. He laments, beating his breast, saying: "What was mine is no longer mine" (*yampi me ahu tampi me natthi*). "Whatever we had, that too is gone." That is the next suffering (*dukkha*). Not only that, but within the lay life they have obtained, because of their desires for accumulated possessions and issues of distribution, kings dispute and fight with kings. In homes, disputes arise between husbands and wives, parents and children, brothers and sisters, starting in this manner with insults and abuse, and then, taking up sticks, clubs, and weapons, they harm one another and ultimately kill each other. The Buddha declared that such a mountain of suffering (*dukkha*) is associated with lay life. If we consider all of this as a whole, the Buddha has used a valuable simile in the *Muni Sutta*.
In the *Muni Sutta*, the Buddha explains the value of the life of a genuine, practice-observing, meditative monk, referred to as a sage (*muni*) cultivating absorption (*jhāna*) in the forest. In the concluding stanza of that discourse, a wonderful simile is presented. The more you think about it, the more profound the simile used for the layperson becomes. This is how that stanza reads: "Just as the blue-necked peacock, in its speed of flight through the sky, can never equal the swan, so the layperson can never equal the sage (*muni*) meditating in the forest." We should reflect a little on this simile of the peacock representing the layperson. Everyone knows the peacock. Its blue neck is very beautiful. It is even more beautiful when it spreads its feathers. How beautiful is the peacock when it dances with its train spread out! Yet, once it folds its feathers, it cannot fly easily even when necessary, or even when another animal comes to attack it. Why? Because of the weight of its train. It has to drag it behind like a trailer; it is a massive burden.
Thus, despite its beauty, the peacock cannot fly freely like the swan. The Buddha has used the simile of the swan in other places too to describe the sage (*muni*). It is the nature of the swan that if it is on a lake and decides it is no longer suitable, it flies away to another lake immediately, without any attachment. The peacock cannot do this. Even jumping from tree to tree is done with great difficulty because of its heavy train of feathers. I will not analyze this further, as it might upset you, dear devotees. However, I leave it to you to contemplate the depth of the simile given by the Buddha. Outwardly, how beautiful is the peacock! Not only its blue neck but also its train is extremely beautiful. Yet, it has that minor weakness. This is precisely what the Buddha pointed out when contrasting the value of the happiness of ordination with suffering (*dukkha*).
When we contemplate these matters, we see that within lay happiness, there is nothing for a practice-observing monk to envy, covet, greed for, or compete to win. Yet, it is due to the force of defilements that the mind turns back to those things. This is a saṁsāric weakness. Indeed, that Vajjiputtaka monk must have ordained with a great aspiration for renunciation (*nekkhamma*), abandoning his turn at the kingship. However, overcome by a surge of defilements, his mind drifted momentarily to that festival. In this way, there are various festivals in society at different times. If one goes to join these festivals, one abandons the happiness of ordination and acts like someone chasing a mirage. One falls back.
Thus, abandoning the happiness of ordination to seek lay happiness once more is described in ancient texts as eating one's own vomit. That is why the Buddha declared the sufferings and hardships of lay life to the world beforehand. This was not done out of disparagement. The hope of everyone is to realize Nibbāna; whether one is a layperson or a monk, that is the ultimate goal. But to achieve it, one must cultivate the vast array of virtues required.
There is a certain aspect of gratification (*assāda*) in lay life. However, its danger (*ādīnava*) is hundreds and thousands of times greater. Only when that aspect of danger is properly understood does the escape (*nissaraṇa*) known as renunciation (*nekkhamma*) arise—the departing from it. Departing from lay life, joining the ordained life, becoming devoted to secluded living and meditation, and from there cultivating meditation and insight (*vipassanā*)—it is through this that one can bring this saṁsāric suffering (*dukkha*) to an end. Strictly speaking, the goals of a layperson—wealth, status, titles, positions—should not be the goals of ordained ones. The Buddha has pointed out a far more valuable goal, the ending of suffering (*dukkha*), known by the name Nibbāna. That is the goal of the monastic side. It is as a path toward this goal that most of you, dear devotees, have today observed the Uposatha Eight Precepts according to your capacity and in the appropriate manner.
If we reflect on this, the Buddha has presented the observance of these Uposatha precepts as an effort to draw closer to the practice of the Arahants. This is specifically described on one occasion when the great lay devotee Visākhā came to see the Buddha at the Eastern Monastery during the midday of a Uposatha day. When the Buddha asked: "Why, Visākhā, are you here in the middle of the day?" she replied: "Venerable Sir, today I have observed the Uposatha Eight Precepts." From there, the Buddha delivered a long discourse on the value of keeping the eight Uposatha precepts. Regarding each training rule, it is said: It is true that a layperson always observes the training rule of abstaining from taking life as a permanent precept (*nicca-sīla*). However, on the Uposatha day, they do not observe it merely at the level of everyday lay life, but at the highest level, just like the Arahants. There, it is said that to fulfill this training rule in the manner of the Arahants, it is not merely about nominally abstaining from killing; rather, many other terms are used along with it—such as laying aside the rod and the sword, and living with compassion toward all living beings. This is what it means to fulfill the first training rule at the level of an Arahant.
That is why you, dear devotees, set aside a day to observe the Uposatha Eight Precepts. In the past, the concept of ordination was a life-long commitment. One ordained with a great resolution: not to return, but to cross over or die trying ("death or crossing over"). That is why, as mentioned, they left behind even a small or large accumulation of wealth, and a small or large group of relatives. The Buddha has shown in the Dhammapada and elsewhere that this is not an easy thing to do. If there are bonds in this world made of iron, wood, or hemp, all those bonds are nothing compared to the attachment to gold, jewels, pearls, gems, and spouse and children in this life. Those physical bonds can be broken, but this emotional attachment is not easy to break. That is why that ordination is a life-long ordination. Indeed, even though some disrobe due to various reasons like a weakening of the mind, genuine ordination is entered into with a profound intention, abandoning everything in that manner, and it is that initial momentum of renunciation that leads to success.
Thus, the life-long concept exists on that side. How then can a lay devotee, while remaining in lay life, develop that same momentum? The answer to this is what the Buddha highlighted through the Uposatha. In the past, the brahmins interpreted the word "Uposatha" in their own way, which was still something valuable at their brahminical level. In those days, the calendar in lay life was prepared based on the moon. Based on the phases of the moon, certain days were set aside, and "Uposatha" meant spending that day according to a unique set of practices, as if living with the gods. In the Noble Uposatha (*Ariya-uposatha*) that the Buddha explained to Visākhā, he presented it as an idea of living close to the Arahants: "By keeping these precepts in the highest manner, just as the Arahants keep them, I draw closer to the path of the Arahants." This is the concept.
"Today, this night and this day, just as those Arahants abstain from eating at improper times throughout their entire lives, so during this day and night, I too will abstain from it. Just as those Arahants observe celibacy (*brahmacariya*), so during this day, I too will observe it." Similarly, regarding "dancing, singing, music, and unseemly shows" (*nacca-gīta-vādita-visūka-dassana*): in today's world, the moment you turn a knob or press a button on some device in your home, all the dancing, singing, music, and unseemly shows of the entire world stream in. Likewise, if one has money, as soon as one goes to the shops, one can acquire "garlands, perfumes, cosmetics, ornaments, and adornments" (*mālā-gandha-vilepana-dhāraṇa-maṇḍana-vibhūsana*).
Yet, despite having the ability to do so, you, dear devotees, spend this day understanding the value of drawing closer to the practice of the Arahants, as explained by the Buddha. The other training rules are just the same. You know well the training rule of celibacy (*abrahmacariya-veramaṇī*), and then the one on abstaining from eating at improper times (*vikāla-bhojana*), and then the one on dancing, singing, and music, and then the one on high and luxurious beds and seats (*uccāsayana-mahāsayana*). When you step away from the comfortable seats and beds of your homes to live a simple life suited for ordination—remembering that Prince Siddhartha, who lived in palaces suited for each of the three seasons, spent his nights on a bed of *aṭṭēriya* leaves after becoming the Buddha—you can understand. One should not view lying down or sitting on the ground on this day and night, abandoning those comforts, as a hardship. Instead, we should contemplate the immense value of that Arahant practice.
Understanding its true value and purpose with wisdom, we practice all of this to slowly, step-by-step, break the long-standing attachment to the five-fold sensual pleasures of saṁsāra. For someone who has tamed their mind to a considerable extent by keeping the Uposatha precepts over a long period, transitioning to the ordained life becomes easy. In that case, one can indeed say it is as simple as changing one's clothes. However, ordination is not achieved merely by changing one's clothes; one must prepare the mind. This is the opportunity the Buddha presented through the Noble Uposatha. Understanding this is highly helpful. Yet, many people keep lay happiness as their ultimate target. The reason is that, at first glance, one sees multi-millionaires living in massive, luxurious mansions, traveling in ultra-luxurious, high-speed vehicles, and enjoying various kinds of entertainment like the festivals mentioned earlier. But if one forgets how much they live in a bonfire of a mountain of great suffering (*dukkha*) deep down in their minds, only then do these things appear as happiness. This is what the Buddha pointed out.
Therefore, it was the Buddha, who had practiced these virtues as perfections (*pāramī*) in saṁsāra over a long period, and the great disciples of that era, who gave the most sublime example. What remains for others is to respect that example. When you read the biography of the Buddha and his disciples, you can understand what a great sacrifice is required to escape from saṁsāric suffering (*dukkha*). Without making this sacrifice, one cannot break these bonds of saṁsāra. One should not think of this as self-mortification (*attakilamathānuyoga*). This is because ordination or going forth (*pabbajjā*) means preparing the body, mind, and environment in a manner suitable and conducive for meditation.
To use another simile: in the past, those who had long harbored the aspiration to end saṁsāric suffering (*dukkha*) but could not see a path, upon hearing that a Buddha had appeared in the world and that a Community of Monks (Saṅgha) had been established—just as in the story of King Mahākappina—went forth and ordained simply by hearing the words, "A Buddha has arisen." Kings abandoned their kingdoms and ordained; queens did the same; ministers left behind their lay pleasures and ordained. With what intention did they ordain? There is a phrase used there: *pabbajitaṁ anupabbajiṁsu*—"they went forth in imitation of those who had gone forth." A common custom in the world is following examples and imitation. In that imitation, bad imitation or a bad example is not good; we must adopt the correct example.
Thus, when those kings set the right example—if kings went leaving behind such immense wealth, of what value is our ministership?—the ministers also left their posts and went forth. Following them, others went too. It is said that in this way, kingdoms became empty, simply upon the news that a Buddha had arisen. If we try to understand this mental process through a simile: suppose in ancient times, a herd of cattle was penned in a stable all night long. They wait until dawn, watching for the first light of day. The moment the herdsman goes and opens the gate, those cattle rush out, running as if seeking freedom. The word *pabbajjā* is closely related to this concept. *Vaja* or *braja* means a cowpen. Escaping from this saṁsāric cowpen is what is meant by *pabbajjā*. The power required for this is the power of renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
Therefore, one who has long cultivated virtues like morality (*sīla*) in this wilderness of saṁsāra according to the Dhamma taught by the Buddha, and who has wisely contemplated the dangers of lay life, preparing a meditative mind suitable for it, abandons kingdoms and departs the moment they hear a Buddha has arisen. This is renunciation (*nekkhamma*). Furthermore, once they have gone forth, they realize: "From what an immense mountain of suffering (*dukkha*) have I escaped!"
That is that happiness. Subsequently, using that happiness as a support—as you, dear devotees, often mention and complain about—it is difficult to meditate while staying at home, since there are obstacles on every side. That is why the monks of old went to deep forests inhabited by wild beasts to meditate; because the mind becomes serene and enters deep concentration (*samādhī*) only when one withdraws from human society and goes to a secluded place. Using that concentration (*samādhī*) as a support, they freed themselves from suffering (*dukkha*). Indeed, it is said that every Buddha attained Buddhahood in a natural environment, in accordance with nature. In any case, it is only with a mind stilled by developing a love for that secluded dwelling that one can ultimately realize the deepest understanding of the Four Noble Truths, which ends this saṁsāric suffering (*dukkha*). That is the most suitable and conducive environment. The change one makes to obtain that environment is called ordination. However, if one ordains but ends up in an environment unsuitable for it, then there is some deficiency.
