Therefore, one must strive to secure such a secluded dwelling and complete this task. For we have spent a long time rolling in these lay bonds and heaps of lay suffering (*dukkha*) in saṁsāra. Yet, liberation is not obtained merely by wishing for it. That is why the Buddha declared in the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta* and other discourses: "not to get what one wants is suffering (*dukkha*)" (*yampicchaṁ na labhati tampi dukkhaṁ*). What is it that one wishes for? "If only I could be free from this suffering (*dukkha*) of birth (*jāti*)! If only I could be free from this saṁsāric state of decay (*jarā*)! If only I could be free from this terrifying illness and death (*maraṇa*)!"—such is the aspiration. But the Buddha declared: "This is not to be achieved by wishing" (*na kho pana etaṁ icchāya pattabbaṁ*). These are not obtained merely by wishing, without taking the necessary path of action. The path of action to be taken is none other than the Noble Eightfold Path, known as the Middle Path, as declared by the Buddha. We have reminded, clarified, and explained this to you on many occasions.
Indeed, everything necessary is contained within it. One must cultivate right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*). If we consider the simpler aspect of right view, it is the basic understanding of wholesome and unwholesome, good and bad. At the minimum level, understanding what is wholesome and unwholesome, good and bad, helps direct our saṁsāric journey away from states of deprivation (*duggati*) and toward happy realms (*sugati*). Yet, the task is not finished with that. The deepest and highest level of right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) is the Four Noble Truths. This is the mountain of suffering (*dukkha*) connected with the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcupādānakkhandha*) and with this saṁsāric existence (*bhava*). It is right there that birth (*jāti*), decay (*jarā*), illness, and death (*maraṇa*) exist.
Thus, only the Buddha clearly declared that saṁsāric existence is suffering (*dukkha*). Others tried to segment it, separating it into "this part is happiness, that part is suffering (*dukkha*)." That is not in accordance with the Dhamma. This is why the Buddha declared that, let alone other places, there is no real happiness even in the Brahma worlds. It is said that when the lion king roars his lion's roar, the animals living in small hollows in the forest retreat into them; those living in the water plunge into the water; and those that fly take to the sky. Not only that, but even royal elephants in palaces break their iron chains and flee upon hearing that roar. Similarly, when the Buddha declared to the world the Three Characteristics—the impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anattā*) nature of all things—showing that there is suffering (*dukkha*) and impermanence (*anicca*) everywhere, even in the Brahma worlds, it is recorded in the Dhamma that even the Brahmas residing in those worlds became terrified, saying: "We had thought all along that we were permanent, but now they say we are impermanent (*anicca*)!" Thus, they fell into fear and terror. This is compared to royal elephants breaking their iron chains in their stalls and fleeing in terror upon hearing the lion's roar; in the same way, even the Brahma kings are struck with spiritual urgency (*saṁvega*) and terror. Such is the nature of this Dhamma. Therefore, bringing this saṁsāric suffering (*dukkha*) to an end is the ultimate goal belonging to every Buddhist, whether lay or ordained. On the path to that goal, one must, at the very least, cultivate that right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*).
If we are going on a journey, we must have some understanding of the destination. If we turn our head in the opposite direction instead of the way we need to go, where will we end up? This is why the Buddha placed right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) at the very beginning. Even cultivating that vision of life is a precious thing. Once that is developed, the journey undertaken in accordance with it is what is called the practice (*paṭipadā*).
All other paths and roads in the world, including high-speed expressways, are said to be inferior to this Noble Eightfold Path. However, this path cannot be found outwardly anywhere in the world. It is something to be developed within oneself as virtue (*sīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*). The first step of that path is right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*). When one establishes right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) and spends a day cultivating virtues like morality, the thoughts and intentions that arise are indeed right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*)—namely, thoughts of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saṅkappa*), thoughts of non-ill will (*avyāpāda-saṅkappa*), and thoughts of harmlessness (*avihiṁsā-saṅkappa*). By using wholesome speech in accordance with these good thoughts, one prepares for a complete transformation in one's life. When one acts in accordance with that speech, it is right action (*sammā-kammanta*). When this conduct is not limited to a day or two but is integrated into one's entire livelihood, it is right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*). Through the effort to establish right livelihood, by being mindful of one's mind, recognizing its unwholesome tendencies, expelling existing unwholesome states, preventing new unwholesome states from arising, encouraging the wholesome thoughts already present, and removing bad thoughts, the effort one exerts is right effort (*sammā-vāyāma*).
Proceeding in this very manner, by maintaining the mind on an object for a long period with right mindfulness (*sammā-sati*) and clear comprehension, if the mind were indeed a weapon, it is sharpened to the highest degree. Then, by deeply penetrating and seeing the Three Characteristics of impermanence (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anattā*), right concentration (*sammā-samādhi*) is established. Next come right knowledge (*sammā-ñāṇa*) and right liberation (*sammā-vimutti*). It is at the culmination of this path of practice that one can arouse insight-knowledges (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), understand the suffering (*dukkha*) and empty (*suñña*) nature of this saṁsāra, cross over saṁsāric suffering (*dukkha*), and directly realize the sublime, deathless, great Nibbāna.
Therefore, today, just as you have engaged in good practices, you have also listened to the Dhamma at this moment. We can understand that this Dhamma sermon has helped you arouse, to some extent, those qualities that assist in realizing Nibbāna, namely the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) of faith (*saddhā*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*). If there is any store of merit (*puñña*) accumulated by both of our parties through the giving of this Dhamma sermon and the listening to this Dhamma sermon related to Nibbāna, may all those wholesome merits be shared by all beings from Avīci up to Akaniṭṭha, whoever wishes to rejoice in these merits. May all of them, including your relatives, according to their own aspirations, be freed from this saṁsāric suffering (*dukkha*) as quickly as possible and find peace in the sublime, deathless Nibbāna. May we also aspire that, by fulfilling these practices, we too may have the strength to realize the sublime, deathless, great Nibbāna as quickly as possible, in this very life, during the existence of this Dispensation, through the penetration of the paths and fruits of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti*), Once-returning (*sakadāgāmitā*), Non-returning (*anāgāmitā*), and Arahantship. Let us recite the stanzas in this manner:
“*Ettāvatā ca amhehi.........*”

pali stanza:
duppabbajjam durabhiramam, duravasa ghara dukha;
dukkho 'samanasamvaso, tasma na caddhagu siya, na ca dukkhanupatito siyati.
from:
dhammapada 302 (lokavagga)
dear listeners,
the buddha, the teacher of the three worlds, declared that the happiness of ordination is superior to lay happiness. by forgetting the vast amount of suffering (*dukkha*) and hardship that lies beneath lay happiness, one might sometimes perceive lay happiness as superior. because of such a misunderstanding, the force of renunciation (*nekkhamma*) that brings a person to the ordained state might also diminish. therefore, on many occasions, the buddha highlighted the vast amount of suffering (*dukkha*) and hardship that lies beneath lay happiness and lay life. the buddha expounded the stanza we have taken as our theme as advice to a certain monk who was facing such a problem.
while the buddha was residing at the gabled hall in the great wood near vesali, this monk, who was a vajjiputtaka (a prince of the vajjians), lived devoted to meditation in a forest grove. one night, while he was practicing walking meditation, he heard the sounds of an annual festival being held in the city. the sounds of various musical instruments, songs, singing, dancing, and the beating of drums began to be heard. then, this monk recalled how, during his lay life when he enjoyed royal pleasures, he used to dress up in beautiful clothes and ornaments to enjoy himself on such occasions. reflecting on this, a great sadness arose in him, and as a form of lamentation, he uttered a certain stanza: "we live alone in this forest like a piece of wood cast away in the jungle. on a night like this, who is more unfortunate than us?" it is said that he expressed his grievances through this stanza. hearing this, the deity presiding over that forest grove, wishing to arouse spiritual urgency (*samvega*) in the monk, turned the same stanza around and declared: "indeed, you live alone in this forest like a discarded piece of firewood. yet, laypeople look up to you with great respect and high esteem, just as those destined for hell look longingly up to those who have gone to heaven." after hearing that stanza, the monk's desire for lay pleasures vanished. on the following day, when this monk went to see the buddha, the buddha, understanding the situation, uttered the very stanza we have chosen as our theme, in order to help the monk further eradicate his lingering attachment to lay happiness.
every word in this stanza carries an extremely profound meaning:
*“duppabbajjam durabhiramam, duravasa ghara dukha;*
*dukkho’samanasamvaso, tasma na caddhagu siya, na ca dukkhanupatito siya.”*
*duppabbajjam*: going forth is difficult. it is difficult to transition from lay life to the ordained life. *durabhiramam*: even after going forth, it is difficult to find delight in the ordained life; it is difficult to develop a love for the monastic way of life. *duravasa ghara dukha*: living in the household life is a mountain of great suffering (*dukkha*), a heap of suffering (*dukkha*). *dukkho’samanasamvaso*: here, although the sinhala script might read *samana* (equal/same), the true grammatical meaning intended is *asamanasamvaso*—living together with incompatible people is suffering (*dukkha*). it is said because of the nature of society. next, *dukkhanupatito addhagu*: this journey through samsara is a journey that drags suffering (*dukkha*) along with it. *tasma*, therefore; *na caddhagu siya*: do not be a traveler who continues to drag suffering (*dukkha*) along endlessly in samsara. *na ca (dukkhanupatito) siya*: do not act in a way that suffering (*dukkha*) follows close behind you. in this manner, the buddha delivered the stanza as advice.
if we reflect a bit more carefully on each of these words, why is it called *duppabbajjam*? according to the concept of ordination in the buddha's time, a layperson went forth with a deep intention, driven by genuine renunciation (*nekkhamma*), and not merely because they had robes and requisites. as mentioned in ancient texts, they went forth after abandoning a small or large accumulation of wealth, and abandoning a small or large circle of relatives. departing from the home life and going forth in that manner is extremely difficult for a layperson. most of the time, there are plenty of excuses not to ordain. to that extent, the bonds of lay life cannot easily be untied and brought to an end. here, there is a wondrously complex web of interconnected attachments. this is why it is called *duppabbajjam*—ordination is a state that is achieved with great difficulty.
furthermore, even if one manages to ordain with difficulty, once entering the monastic sphere, it is hard to adapt to the monastic lifestyle due to deeply ingrained lay habits. depending on alms food, living in seclusion, going to the forest to live alone devoted to meditation, withdrawing from crowds, and observing the relevant vinaya training rules—all of these are unfamiliar things. to develop a delight, a keen interest, and a desire (*chanda*) for these things, and to act accordingly, is difficult for one who has ordained. this is precisely what happened to that vajjiputtaka monk. according to the texts, among the vajji princes of that era, there was a confederacy in which seven thousand seven hundred and seven princes reigned in turn. this monk is described as someone who abandoned his turn at the kingship to ordain. yet, upon hearing the sounds of the festival, his mind turned back to kingship. his mind drifted toward royal luxuries, weakening his resolve, and he expressed that stanza lamenting his situation.
*durabhiramam*: in the dispensation, there is a term called *abhirati* (delight). without a special delight in the ordained state, one cannot sustain it. when that delight is lost, it is called *anabhirati* (non-delight/discontent). as soon as discontent arises, one becomes "apathetic" (*ukatali*, weary/bored). then, one keeps thinking about lay life, wondering, "when will i escape this trouble and go back?" in this way, due to these samsaric weaknesses, it is difficult for a layperson to cultivate and sustain a delight in renunciation. similarly, *duravasa ghara dukha*: next, the nature of lay life is further described. living in the household life involves immense suffering (*dukkha*) and troubles. because living the lay life means one must toil to gather the necessary wealth and resources. according to ancient similes, balancing income and expenses in a household is an extremely difficult task. often, disputes over income and expenditure arise between husbands and wives, leading to quarrels and conflicts. in the texts, this is compared to pouring water into a leaking pot. the mouth of the pot is small, but there are many holes. similarly, income is small, but expenses are many. it is extremely difficult to resolve this entanglement in lay life, and as a result, one gets trapped in a mountain of great suffering (*dukkha*). one can never fully satisfy the responsibilities concerning spouse and children, and social duties.
another simile is given to show the difficulty of satisfying lay needs, comparing them to the great ocean. no matter how many rivers flow into it, the ocean can never be filled. similarly, no matter how much the desires of a layperson's mind are fulfilled, there is no satisfaction; there is no end to their needs. because of this, household life is described as *duravasa ghara dukha*.
next, *dukkho samanasamvaso* (or *asamanasamvaso*): living with incompatible people is also suffering (*dukkha*). society is crowded with diverse and discordant individuals. among them, there is an extraordinary degree of competitiveness, jealousy, association with bad friends, and so forth. because of these factors, living in a society filled with discordant people is no easy matter. having to live together with incompatible people is a great suffering (*dukkha*).
next, *dukkhanupatito addhagu*: similarly, lay life means wandering further and further in samsara. wandering further and further in samsara means a journey where one continues to prolong and experience the momentum of kamma created through attachments and conflicts. this is why it is called "expanding samsara." within lay life, samsara is expanded. that is what is meant. in this very manner, one travels this long journey carrying samsaric suffering (*dukkha*) along. indeed, five points are presented here in this manner. next, *tasma na caddhagu siya*: therefore, do not be a traveler who wanders endlessly in samsara. *na ca (dukkhanupatito) siya*: do not go searching for suffering (*dukkha*). this is the meaning of that stanza.
as we mentioned earlier, at first glance, the ordained life might seem like a heap of great suffering (*dukkha*)—living alone in the forest like a discarded piece of wood. lay life, on the other hand, seems to be a fashionable, attractive, colorful, and luxurious lifestyle. so why did the buddha show this lay life as suffering (*dukkha*) and ordination as happiness? the buddha demonstrated this to the world on several occasions through his own example.
such an incident is recorded, a very valuable one. once, the buddha spent a night in an alavi forest of *atteriya* leaves on a path frequented by cattle. he slept on a bed of *atteriya* leaves. rising in the morning, while he was seated there in meditation, the prince hatthaka alavaka, who was out for a walk, saw the buddha sitting on the bed of leaves. he realized that the buddha must have spent the night there. so he asked the buddha: "venerable sir, did the blessed one sleep in comfort?" the buddha replied: "yes, prince, i slept in comfort. of those in the world who sleep in comfort, i am one."
then the prince said: "but venerable sir, the night in this winter season is cold. this is the time of the severe winter frost. furthermore, the ground here is rough, trampled by the hooves of cattle. the bed of leaves is very thin, and the leaves on the trees are sparse. the blessed one's robes are cold, and the biting wind blowing from all four directions is cold. yet the blessed one says, 'i slept in comfort'!"
thereupon the buddha said: "well then, prince, i will first ask you a question. answer as you please. suppose there is a wealthy householder or a householder's son living in a luxurious gabled mansion, plastered inside and out, on a comfortable couch spread with fine woolen covers, soft pillows, and mattresses. a lamp is burning, and he is attended by four highly pleasing wives. would that householder or householder's son sleep in comfort?" then the prince replied: "yes, venerable sir, he would be one of those in the world who sleep in comfort."
then the buddha asked again: "well then, please answer this question too. might not that householder or householder's son have to lie down in discomfort, tormented by lustful thoughts that cause bodily and mental distress?" to this, the prince had to say: "yes, venerable sir." next, the buddha declared: "the defilements of lust and so forth that burn that householder or householder's son have been completely abandoned by the tathagata. cut off at the root, like a palmyra tree uprooted, made non-existent, these defilements of lust and hatred are rendered incapable of future arising. that is why i said i sleep in comfort. similarly, whatever thoughts of hatred might arise in that householder or householder's son, causing him to spend the night in discomfort—that hatred too has been abandoned by the tathagata. whatever delusion might torment that person in that luxurious mansion—none of those hardships exist for the tathagata, who is free of delusion." that was how the buddha replied on that occasion.
likewise, there are valuable accounts concerning the buddha's great disciples. another such incident occurred when the buddha was residing in the anupiya mango grove. a monk named bhaddiya, whether he went to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty house for meditation, would constantly exclaim: *"aho sukham! aho sukham!!!"*—which translates to, "oh, what happiness! oh, what happiness!" hearing this, many other monks thought: "without a doubt, the venerable bhaddiya is reflecting on the royal pleasures he enjoyed before, and out of desire for those royal pleasures, he has become dissatisfied with the ordained life, which is why he is crying out *"aho sukham! aho sukham!!"*." thinking thus, the monks went to the buddha and said: "venerable sir, our venerable bhaddiya has become dissatisfied with the ordained life and is constantly exclaiming *"aho sukham"* in this manner." the buddha instructed a monk: "go and summon the monk bhaddiya."
when that monk conveyed the message, venerable bhaddiya came. the buddha asked him: "is it true, bhaddiya, that whether you go to the foot of a tree, an empty place, or a forest, you exclaim *"aho sukham"*?" "yes, venerable sir." "for what reason do you say so?" then venerable bhaddiya said: "blessed one, in my lay life when i was in the palace, there were security arrangements both inside and outside the inner palace. there were security forces inside and outside the city, and guards inside and outside the district. thus, surrounded and trapped by guards, i lived in great fear, agitation, and terror during my time as king. but now, venerable sir, whether i go to the forest, the foot of a tree, or an empty house, i live alone without any fear or suspicion, in complete peace, spending my life as serenely as a wild deer belonging to the forest. that is why i exclaimed *"aho sukham, aho sukham"*." so, we have such inspiring examples.
from this, we can understand that the buddha declared the happiness of ordination with a very deep meaning. the happiness of ordination, dear devotees, is referred to in some places as the happiness of renunciation (*nekkhamma-sukham*), the happiness of seclusion (*paviveka-sukham*), and the happiness of peace (*upasama-sukham*). the happiness of renunciation (*nekkhamma-sukham*) means that escaping from these lay bonds is itself a great happiness. some of you might understand what a hassle lay life is. especially those who have a strong desire to dedicate time to the dhamma and engage in meditation often realize that this lay life is a mountain of great suffering (*dukkha*), and some even regret, saying, "what foolishness made us get entangled in these things?"
in the past, there was a common sentiment that "the home life is a burning house." when we contemplate the mountain of suffering (*dukkha*) in that life, you too, dear devotees, are enjoying a small measure of that happiness right now by escaping it. what a relief it is to be able to detach from those things even for a single moment, an hour, a day, or half a day! that indeed is the first happiness: when one completely breaks these lay bonds and develops a liking for living in seclusion. reflecting on this, one rejoices, thinking, "what a massive bond this was! it is like being released from prison." next is the happiness of seclusion (*paviveka-sukham*). there are many accounts of monks living in that seclusion—which often frightens ordinary people—among wild beasts, dwelling in loving-kindness (*metta*) with those very animals.
if you can walk on roads where highly dangerous, high-speed vehicles travel, then it is no wonder that a monk who loves seclusion can live in a forest hermitage populated by wild animals. sometimes, animals possess a kind of sensitivity that even humans lack toward monks who live harmlessly in this manner. even if that is not the case, there are monks who live valuing seclusion, cultivating mindfulness of death (*maranasati*) regarding the dangers of their surroundings. this is the happiness of seclusion (*paviveka-sukham*).
next, the concentration and meditation developed through that happiness of seclusion lead to the happiness of peace (*upasama-sukham*). the happiness of peace (*upasama-sukham*) is the happiness obtained through the stilling of lust, hatred, and delusion, as declared by the buddha. when it is said that the buddha slept on a bed of *atteriya* leaves on such rough ground in the freezing cold—he slept in comfort. one can only say this when the happiness of peace (*upasama-sukham*) is fully realized. this is what the happiness of ordination means. furthermore, on certain occasions, the buddha has described the suffering (*dukkha*) and hardships of lay life in even greater detail. there is a discourse (the *mahadukkhakkhandha sutta*) where the buddha points out, one by one, a massive mass of suffering (*dukkha*). in that discourse, he systematically reveals the dangers of sensual pleasures (*kama*) as the hardships and sufferings (*dukkha*) one has to endure in lay life.
first, it is described as follows: for a young man of good family to live in the household life, he must strive hard to fulfill massive responsibilities: securing employment, earning a livelihood, maintaining himself, looking after his spouse and children, and performing social duties. striving is necessary to earn wealth, for a lazy person cannot do so. if he has learned a certain craft, he engages in a job based on it. it is mentioned there—to use modern terms—that he does his job in the midst of a mountain of great suffering (*dukkha*): scorching in the sun, getting wet in the rain, enduring and suffering from cold and heat, and even dying of hunger and thirst. this is shown as the first suffering (*dukkha*).
next, it is said that despite putting in so much effort, when he does not receive an income from his work, when losses occur, when businesses collapse and are destroyed, this person weeps, laments, and beats his breast. he falls into confusion, crying out: "alas! the effort i exerted so hard has been ruined, lost. my labor is in vain!" next, it is said that if, by some means, his efforts succeed and he acquires wealth, he then lies awake in the midst of great suffering (*dukkha*) and distress, thinking: "oh, may kings not confiscate this wealth i have earned! may thieves not steal it! may it not be destroyed by fire! may it not be swept away by floods or deluges! may these things not perish!" thus, he organizes extensive security measures and lives with suffering (*dukkha*) and distress.
next, the subsequent suffering (*dukkha*) is described: even if he has set up all those security measures, if kings confiscate his wealth, or thieves come and plunder it either secretly or by force, or if it is burnt by fire, or swept away and destroyed by floods, then on that occasion too, he weeps, laments, and beats his breast in the same manner. he laments, beating his breast, saying: "what was mine is no longer mine" (*yampi me ahu tampi me natthi*). "whatever we had, that too is gone." that is the next suffering (*dukkha*). not only that, but within the lay life they have obtained, because of their desires for accumulated possessions and issues of distribution, kings dispute and fight with kings. in homes, disputes arise between husbands and wives, parents and children, brothers and sisters, starting in this manner with insults and abuse, and then, taking up sticks, clubs, and weapons, they harm one another and ultimately kill each other. the buddha declared that such a mountain of suffering (*dukkha*) is associated with lay life. if we consider all of this as a whole, the buddha has used a valuable simile in the *muni sutta*.
in the *muni sutta*, the buddha explains the value of the life of a genuine, practice-observing, meditative monk, referred to as a sage (*muni*) cultivating absorption (*jhana*) in the forest. in the concluding stanza of that discourse, a wonderful simile is presented. the more you think about it, the more profound the simile used for the layperson becomes. this is how that stanza reads: "just as the blue-necked peacock, in its speed of flight through the sky, can never equal the swan, so the layperson can never equal the sage (*muni*) meditating in the forest." we should reflect a little on this simile of the peacock representing the layperson. everyone knows the peacock. its blue neck is very beautiful. it is even more beautiful when it spreads its feathers. how beautiful is the peacock when it dances with its train spread out! yet, once it folds its feathers, it cannot fly easily even when necessary, or even when another animal comes to attack it. why? because of the weight of its train. it has to drag it behind like a trailer; it is a massive burden.
thus, despite its beauty, the peacock cannot fly freely like the swan. the buddha has used the simile of the swan in other places too to describe the sage (*muni*). it is the nature of the swan that if it is on a lake and decides it is no longer suitable, it flies away to another lake immediately, without any attachment. the peacock cannot do this. even jumping from tree to tree is done with great difficulty because of its heavy train of feathers. i will not analyze this further, as it might upset you, dear devotees. however, i leave it to you to contemplate the depth of the simile given by the buddha. outwardly, how beautiful is the peacock! not only its blue neck but also its train is extremely beautiful. yet, it has that minor weakness. this is precisely what the buddha pointed out when contrasting the value of the happiness of ordination with suffering (*dukkha*).
when we contemplate these matters, we see that within lay happiness, there is nothing for a practice-observing monk to envy, covet, greed for, or compete to win. yet, it is due to the force of defilements that the mind turns back to those things. this is a samsaric weakness. indeed, that vajjiputtaka monk must have ordained with a great aspiration for renunciation (*nekkhamma*), abandoning his turn at the kingship. however, overcome by a surge of defilements, his mind drifted momentarily to that festival. in this way, there are various festivals in society at different times. if one goes to join these festivals, one abandons the happiness of ordination and acts like someone chasing a mirage. one falls back.
thus, abandoning the happiness of ordination to seek lay happiness once more is described in ancient texts as eating one's own vomit. that is why the buddha declared the sufferings and hardships of lay life to the world beforehand. this was not done out of disparagement. the hope of everyone is to realize nibbana; whether one is a layperson or a monk, that is the ultimate goal. but to achieve it, one must cultivate the vast array of virtues required.
there is a certain aspect of gratification (*assada*) in lay life. however, its danger (*adinava*) is hundreds and thousands of times greater. only when that aspect of danger is properly understood does the escape (*nissarana*) known as renunciation (*nekkhamma*) arise—the departing from it. departing from lay life, joining the ordained life, becoming devoted to secluded living and meditation, and from there cultivating meditation and insight (*vipassana*)—it is through this that one can bring this samsaric suffering (*dukkha*) to an end. strictly speaking, the goals of a layperson—wealth, status, titles, positions—should not be the goals of ordained ones. the buddha has pointed out a far more valuable goal, the ending of suffering (*dukkha*), known by the name nibbana. that is the goal of the monastic side. it is as a path toward this goal that most of you, dear devotees, have today observed the uposatha eight precepts according to your capacity and in the appropriate manner.
if we reflect on this, the buddha has presented the observance of these uposatha precepts as an effort to draw closer to the practice of the arahants. this is specifically described on one occasion when the great lay devotee visakha came to see the buddha at the eastern monastery during the midday of a uposatha day. when the buddha asked: "why, visakha, are you here in the middle of the day?" she replied: "venerable sir, today i have observed the uposatha eight precepts." from there, the buddha delivered a long discourse on the value of keeping the eight uposatha precepts. regarding each training rule, it is said: it is true that a layperson always observes the training rule of abstaining from taking life as a permanent precept (*nicca-sila*). however, on the uposatha day, they do not observe it merely at the level of everyday lay life, but at the highest level, just like the arahants. there, it is said that to fulfill this training rule in the manner of the arahants, it is not merely about nominally abstaining from killing; rather, many other terms are used along with it—such as laying aside the rod and the sword, and living with compassion toward all living beings. this is what it means to fulfill the first training rule at the level of an arahant.
that is why you, dear devotees, set aside a day to observe the uposatha eight precepts. in the past, the concept of ordination was a life-long commitment. one ordained with a great resolution: not to return, but to cross over or die trying ("death or crossing over"). that is why, as mentioned, they left behind even a small or large accumulation of wealth, and a small or large group of relatives. the buddha has shown in the dhammapada and elsewhere that this is not an easy thing to do. if there are bonds in this world made of iron, wood, or hemp, all those bonds are nothing compared to the attachment to gold, jewels, pearls, gems, and spouse and children in this life. those physical bonds can be broken, but this emotional attachment is not easy to break. that is why that ordination is a life-long ordination. indeed, even though some disrobe due to various reasons like a weakening of the mind, genuine ordination is entered into with a profound intention, abandoning everything in that manner, and it is that initial momentum of renunciation that leads to success.
thus, the life-long concept exists on that side. how then can a lay devotee, while remaining in lay life, develop that same momentum? the answer to this is what the buddha highlighted through the uposatha. in the past, the brahmins interpreted the word "uposatha" in their own way, which was still something valuable at their brahminical level. in those days, the calendar in lay life was prepared based on the moon. based on the phases of the moon, certain days were set aside, and "uposatha" meant spending that day according to a unique set of practices, as if living with the gods. in the noble uposatha (*ariya-uposatha*) that the buddha explained to visakha, he presented it as an idea of living close to the arahants: "by keeping these precepts in the highest manner, just as the arahants keep them, i draw closer to the path of the arahants." this is the concept.
"today, this night and this day, just as those arahants abstain from eating at improper times throughout their entire lives, so during this day and night, i too will abstain from it. just as those arahants observe celibacy (*brahmacariya*), so during this day, i too will observe it." similarly, regarding "dancing, singing, music, and unseemly shows" (*nacca-gita-vadita-visuka-dassana*): in today's world, the moment you turn a knob or press a button on some device in your home, all the dancing, singing, music, and unseemly shows of the entire world stream in. likewise, if one has money, as soon as one goes to the shops, one can acquire "garlands, perfumes, cosmetics, ornaments, and adornments" (*mala-gandha-vilepana-dharana-mandana-vibhusana*).
yet, despite having the ability to do so, you, dear devotees, spend this day understanding the value of drawing closer to the practice of the arahants, as explained by the buddha. the other training rules are just the same. you know well the training rule of celibacy (*abrahmacariya-veramani*), and then the one on abstaining from eating at improper times (*vikala-bhojana*), and then the one on dancing, singing, and music, and then the one on high and luxurious beds and seats (*uccasayana-mahasayana*). when you step away from the comfortable seats and beds of your homes to live a simple life suited for ordination—remembering that prince siddhartha, who lived in palaces suited for each of the three seasons, spent his nights on a bed of *atteriya* leaves after becoming the buddha—you can understand. one should not view lying down or sitting on the ground on this day and night, abandoning those comforts, as a hardship. instead, we should contemplate the immense value of that arahant practice.
understanding its true value and purpose with wisdom, we practice all of this to slowly, step-by-step, break the long-standing attachment to the five-fold sensual pleasures of samsara. for someone who has tamed their mind to a considerable extent by keeping the uposatha precepts over a long period, transitioning to the ordained life becomes easy. in that case, one can indeed say it is as simple as changing one's clothes. however, ordination is not achieved merely by changing one's clothes; one must prepare the mind. this is the opportunity the buddha presented through the noble uposatha. understanding this is highly helpful. yet, many people keep lay happiness as their ultimate target. the reason is that, at first glance, one sees multi-millionaires living in massive, luxurious mansions, traveling in ultra-luxurious, high-speed vehicles, and enjoying various kinds of entertainment like the festivals mentioned earlier. but if one forgets how much they live in a bonfire of a mountain of great suffering (*dukkha*) deep down in their minds, only then do these things appear as happiness. this is what the buddha pointed out.
therefore, it was the buddha, who had practiced these virtues as perfections (*parami*) in samsara over a long period, and the great disciples of that era, who gave the most sublime example. what remains for others is to respect that example. when you read the biography of the buddha and his disciples, you can understand what a great sacrifice is required to escape from samsaric suffering (*dukkha*). without making this sacrifice, one cannot break these bonds of samsara. one should not think of this as self-mortification (*attakilamathanuyoga*). this is because ordination or going forth (*pabbajja*) means preparing the body, mind, and environment in a manner suitable and conducive for meditation.
to use another simile: in the past, those who had long harbored the aspiration to end samsaric suffering (*dukkha*) but could not see a path, upon hearing that a buddha had appeared in the world and that a community of monks (sangha) had been established—just as in the story of king mahakappina—went forth and ordained simply by hearing the words, "a buddha has arisen." kings abandoned their kingdoms and ordained; queens did the same; ministers left behind their lay pleasures and ordained. with what intention did they ordain? there is a phrase used there: *pabbajitam anupabbajimsu*—"they went forth in imitation of those who had gone forth." a common custom in the world is following examples and imitation. in that imitation, bad imitation or a bad example is not good; we must adopt the correct example.
thus, when those kings set the right example—if kings went leaving behind such immense wealth, of what value is our ministership?—the ministers also left their posts and went forth. following them, others went too. it is said that in this way, kingdoms became empty, simply upon the news that a buddha had arisen. if we try to understand this mental process through a simile: suppose in ancient times, a herd of cattle was penned in a stable all night long. they wait until dawn, watching for the first light of day. the moment the herdsman goes and opens the gate, those cattle rush out, running as if seeking freedom. the word *pabbajja* is closely related to this concept. *vaja* or *braja* means a cowpen. escaping from this samsaric cowpen is what is meant by *pabbajja*. the power required for this is the power of renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
therefore, one who has long cultivated virtues like morality (*sila*) in this wilderness of samsara according to the dhamma taught by the buddha, and who has wisely contemplated the dangers of lay life, preparing a meditative mind suitable for it, abandons kingdoms and departs the moment they hear a buddha has arisen. this is renunciation (*nekkhamma*). furthermore, once they have gone forth, they realize: "from what an immense mountain of suffering (*dukkha*) have i escaped!"
that is that happiness. subsequently, using that happiness as a support—as you, dear devotees, often mention and complain about—it is difficult to meditate while staying at home, since there are obstacles on every side. that is why the monks of old went to deep forests inhabited by wild beasts to meditate; because the mind becomes serene and enters deep concentration (*samadhi*) only when one withdraws from human society and goes to a secluded place. using that concentration (*samadhi*) as a support, they freed themselves from suffering (*dukkha*). indeed, it is said that every buddha attained buddhahood in a natural environment, in accordance with nature. in any case, it is only with a mind stilled by developing a love for that secluded dwelling that one can ultimately realize the deepest understanding of the four noble truths, which ends this samsaric suffering (*dukkha*). that is the most suitable and conducive environment. the change one makes to obtain that environment is called ordination. however, if one ordains but ends up in an environment unsuitable for it, then there is some deficiency.
therefore, one must strive to secure such a secluded dwelling and complete this task. for we have spent a long time rolling in these lay bonds and heaps of lay suffering (*dukkha*) in samsara. yet, liberation is not obtained merely by wishing for it. that is why the buddha declared in the *dhammacakkappavattana sutta* and other discourses: "not to get what one wants is suffering (*dukkha*)" (*yampiccham na labhati tampi dukkham*). what is it that one wishes for? "if only i could be free from this suffering (*dukkha*) of birth (*jati*)! if only i could be free from this samsaric state of decay (*jara*)! if only i could be free from this terrifying illness and death (*marana*)!"—such is the aspiration. but the buddha declared: "this is not to be achieved by wishing" (*na kho pana etam icchaya pattabbam*). these are not obtained merely by wishing, without taking the necessary path of action. the path of action to be taken is none other than the noble eightfold path, known as the middle path, as declared by the buddha. we have reminded, clarified, and explained this to you on many occasions.
indeed, everything necessary is contained within it. one must cultivate right view (*samma-ditthi*). if we consider the simpler aspect of right view, it is the basic understanding of wholesome and unwholesome, good and bad. at the minimum level, understanding what is wholesome and unwholesome, good and bad, helps direct our samsaric journey away from states of deprivation (*duggati*) and toward happy realms (*sugati*). yet, the task is not finished with that. the deepest and highest level of right view (*samma-ditthi*) is the four noble truths. this is the mountain of suffering (*dukkha*) connected with the five aggregates of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*) and with this samsaric existence (*bhava*). it is right there that birth (*jati*), decay (*jara*), illness, and death (*marana*) exist.
thus, only the buddha clearly declared that samsaric existence is suffering (*dukkha*). others tried to segment it, separating it into "this part is happiness, that part is suffering (*dukkha*)." that is not in accordance with the dhamma. this is why the buddha declared that, let alone other places, there is no real happiness even in the brahma worlds. it is said that when the lion king roars his lion's roar, the animals living in small hollows in the forest retreat into them; those living in the water plunge into the water; and those that fly take to the sky. not only that, but even royal elephants in palaces break their iron chains and flee upon hearing that roar. similarly, when the buddha declared to the world the three characteristics—the impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*) nature of all things—showing that there is suffering (*dukkha*) and impermanence (*anicca*) everywhere, even in the brahma worlds, it is recorded in the dhamma that even the brahmas residing in those worlds became terrified, saying: "we had thought all along that we were permanent, but now they say we are impermanent (*anicca*)!" thus, they fell into fear and terror. this is compared to royal elephants breaking their iron chains in their stalls and fleeing in terror upon hearing the lion's roar; in the same way, even the brahma kings are struck with spiritual urgency (*samvega*) and terror. such is the nature of this dhamma. therefore, bringing this samsaric suffering (*dukkha*) to an end is the ultimate goal belonging to every buddhist, whether lay or ordained. on the path to that goal, one must, at the very least, cultivate that right view (*samma-ditthi*).
if we are going on a journey, we must have some understanding of the destination. if we turn our head in the opposite direction instead of the way we need to go, where will we end up? this is why the buddha placed right view (*samma-ditthi*) at the very beginning. even cultivating that vision of life is a precious thing. once that is developed, the journey undertaken in accordance with it is what is called the practice (*patipada*).
all other paths and roads in the world, including high-speed expressways, are said to be inferior to this noble eightfold path. however, this path cannot be found outwardly anywhere in the world. it is something to be developed within oneself as virtue (*sila*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*). the first step of that path is right view (*samma-ditthi*). when one establishes right view (*samma-ditthi*) and spends a day cultivating virtues like morality, the thoughts and intentions that arise are indeed right intention (*samma-sankappa*)—namely, thoughts of renunciation (*nekkhamma-sankappa*), thoughts of non-ill will (*avyapada-sankappa*), and thoughts of harmlessness (*avihimsa-sankappa*). by using wholesome speech in accordance with these good thoughts, one prepares for a complete transformation in one's life. when one acts in accordance with that speech, it is right action (*samma-kammanta*). when this conduct is not limited to a day or two but is integrated into one's entire livelihood, it is right livelihood (*samma-ajiva*). through the effort to establish right livelihood, by being mindful of one's mind, recognizing its unwholesome tendencies, expelling existing unwholesome states, preventing new unwholesome states from arising, encouraging the wholesome thoughts already present, and removing bad thoughts, the effort one exerts is right effort (*samma-vayama*).
proceeding in this very manner, by maintaining the mind on an object for a long period with right mindfulness (*samma-sati*) and clear comprehension, if the mind were indeed a weapon, it is sharpened to the highest degree. then, by deeply penetrating and seeing the three characteristics of impermanence (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*), right concentration (*samma-samadhi*) is established. next come right knowledge (*samma-nana*) and right liberation (*samma-vimutti*). it is at the culmination of this path of practice that one can arouse insight-knowledges (*vipassana-nana*), understand the suffering (*dukkha*) and empty (*sunna*) nature of this samsara, cross over samsaric suffering (*dukkha*), and directly realize the sublime, deathless, great nibbana.
therefore, today, just as you have engaged in good practices, you have also listened to the dhamma at this moment. we can understand that this dhamma sermon has helped you arouse, to some extent, those qualities that assist in realizing nibbana, namely the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) of faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*). if there is any store of merit (*punna*) accumulated by both of our parties through the giving of this dhamma sermon and the listening to this dhamma sermon related to nibbana, may all those wholesome merits be shared by all beings from avici up to akanittha, whoever wishes to rejoice in these merits. may all of them, including your relatives, according to their own aspirations, be freed from this samsaric suffering (*dukkha*) as quickly as possible and find peace in the sublime, deathless nibbana. may we also aspire that, by fulfilling these practices, we too may have the strength to realize the sublime, deathless, great nibbana as quickly as possible, in this very life, during the existence of this dispensation, through the penetration of the paths and fruits of stream-entry (*sotapatti*), once-returning (*sakadagamita*), non-returning (*anagamita*), and arahantship. let us recite the stanzas in this manner:
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 099
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #99
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.118)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Abhivādanasīlissa niccaṃ vuḍḍhāpacāyino,
cattāro dhammā vaḍḍhanti: āyu vaṇṇo sukhaṃ balaṃ.
From:
Dhammapada 109 (Sahassavagga)
Dear Listeners,
Human beings employ various strategies and seek many methods to accomplish the qualities of lifespan (*āyu*), beauty (*vaṇṇa*), happiness (*sukha*), and strength (*bala*), which support the existence of a life. The Teacher of the Three Worlds, the Supreme Buddha, declared that these things, which everyone desires, can be obtained even through paying homage to elders and showing them respect and honor. It is this matter that we hope to present to these devotees today, on this Bak Full Moon Poya Day, which coincides with the New Year, by means of the stanza that declares this and the story that serves as an illustration of it. The Buddha preached this Dhamma stanza concerning a child named Dīghāyu. The story unfolds as follows.
In the city of Dīghalambika, there lived two brahmins who practiced asceticism for forty-eight years. They practiced the asceticism of the holy life (*brahmacariya*). After forty-eight years had passed, one of them had a thought that since his lineage would end after him, he should live a lay life. Thinking so—as mentioned in the books, he sold his ascetic merits to another, or did something of that nature—to put it briefly, he took a wife along with a hundred *Kahāpaṇas* (gold coins) and a hundred cows. While living such a lay life, one day, when his old ascetic friend visited the city, this couple took their child and went to receive blessings from that ascetic. Having gone there, first, the brahmin handed the child to the mother and paid respects. The mother then handed the child to the father and paid respects. To both of them, the ascetic said, "May you live long!" Then they made the child pay respects. At that moment, the ascetic remained silent. So, the brahmin asked: "Venerable Sir, when both of us paid respects, you said 'May you live long,' but why did you say nothing when our son paid respects?" Then the ascetic said: "I see a life-threatening danger for this son." When asked how long he would live, he replied: "This life will only survive for seven days." When asked if there was any way to prevent it, he said: "I do not see any such way. But perhaps the Ascetic Gotama might know." Then the brahmin said: "But if I go to the Ascetic Gotama, the asceticism I have practiced for so long will be lost." The ascetic replied: "If you have affection for your son, you must go. You will have to go and meet the Ascetic Gotama and ask." Thereupon, the brahmin, his wife, and the child went to the Blessed One.
Having gone there, just as before, when the brahmin paid respects, the Blessed One said, *"Dīghāyu hotu"* (May you live long). When the wife paid respects, He also said, *"Dīghāyu hotu."* But when the child paid respects, He remained silent. When asked why, the Blessed One in the same manner declared, "There is a life-threatening danger for this child. He will only live for seven days." When asked, "Is there a way to prevent it?" He replied, "There is. If you wish to do it, practice in this way." "What is it, Brahmin? You must erect a pavilion in front of your house, place a small chair or seat in the middle, arrange eight or sixteen seats around it for the Saṅgha, and conduct a chanting of *Paritta* (protective verses)." Then the brahmin said, "I can construct the pavilion and do those things. But from where will I get the Blessed One's disciples?" The Buddha replied, "I will take care of that." When the pavilion was made and the brahmin came and reported that everything was prepared, the Blessed One directed the Saṅgha to go there.
After the Saṅgha arrived, they seated the child on the small chair in the middle and conducted the chanting of *Paritta* continuously for seven days. On the seventh day, the Blessed One also arrived there. When the Blessed One arrived, deities from all the world-systems assembled there. Next, it is mentioned what this life-threatening danger actually was. It was like this: a *yakkha* named Avaruddhaka (not *avurudda* meaning "year", but his name was Avaruddhaka) had served the Yakkha King Vessavaṇa (Vesamuni) for twelve years and obtained a boon. What was the boon? It was to take that child. He was not taking the child to cuddle him, of course. So, he received the boon to take the child. This *yakkha* was waiting for the right moment to come. However, the Saṅgha were chanting *Paritta* there. Furthermore, after the Blessed One arrived, the *yakkha* could not even get close, because when that assembly of deities gathered, there was a custom among the deities that when highly powerful deities arrive, the lesser deities must step back. They moved further and further back, and in the end, the *yakkha* Avaruddhaka could not even get near.
Then, that fatal hour passed. When dawn broke on the eighth day, the child was still alive. So the parents brought the child, placed him at the feet of the Blessed One, and made him pay respects. The Blessed One said, *"Dīghāyu hotu."* On that occasion, He wished long life for that child. "Venerable Sir, how long will this child live?" they asked. He replied, "He will live for one hundred and twenty years." That was a marvelous thing. Then, the story continues as follows: When that child grew up and reached the age of understanding, he went about performing meritorious deeds with great faith (*saddhā*) accompanied by another five hundred lay devotees (*upāsaka*). The Saṅgha discussed this in the Dhamma assembly hall: "How wondrous! This child, who was destined to die in seven days, has now obtained a lifespan of one hundred and twenty years and is moving about with such a crowd." While this conversation was going on, the Saṅgha also thought, "There must be some method for prolonging lifespan, and that is why this happened."
The Blessed One, having arrived there, asked what topic they were discussing. When the monks told Him the news, He said, "Yes, monks, there is a way to prolong one's lifespan," and uttered the stanza we have taken as our theme. It is a stanza that these devotees are constantly accustomed to hearing—one we usually recite at the end of a Dhamma sermon as a blessing for these devotees, which we have brought to the beginning today. He uttered that stanza:
*Abhivādanasīlissa niccaṃ vuḍḍhāpacāyino,*
*Cattāro dhammā vaḍḍhanti: āyu vaṇṇo sukhaṃ balaṃ.*
For one who is habituated to bowing down, constantly honoring the elders, four qualities increase: lifespan, beauty, happiness, and strength. This is the meaning of this stanza. So, in this story, we see on one hand the act of paying homage which leads to the increase of lifespan, which is highly appropriate for this occasion. In the homes of these devotees, perhaps even today, during the time called the "auspicious period for meritorious deeds" (*puṇya kālaya*), which is also referred to as the "non-asterism period" (*nonäkatha*), in many households, as a New Year custom, they offer a sheaf of betel leaves to elders and pay respects. When we look at this in connection with our theme, the passing of a year shows us the waning of our lifespan. A certain turning point where one's lifespan expires is the birthday. Here, the concept of a collective New Year in the cycle of time can be thought of as everyone's birthday, so to speak.
In the past, the ancient Sinhalese, on this day in the month of Bak which they regarded as the New Year, designated a period of pause called the *nonäkatha*. It is a novel thing, a cycle that does not stop spinning. Pausing this cycle for a moment in one's mind, they create a "non-asterism period" (*nonäkatha*) with the help of those astrological calculations. It seems that since those engaged in various daily activities had no time even to perform meritorious deeds, they designated the time without an auspicious asterism (*näkatha*) as the "period for meritorious deeds" (*puṇya kālaya*). In any case, during that period of meritorious deeds, one must resolve to obtain a new vigor, a new life, by offering a sheaf of betel leaves to one's elders, bowing to them, and asking for forgiveness. There is a custom of paying homage and showing respect to parents, clan elders, and also to the Saṅgha, who are like clan deities, and to all elders. Consider its meaning. Furthermore, it is mentioned in this story that although the ascetic saw that the child's life would last only seven days, he did not see a way to prevent it. Yet, he honestly declared, "Perhaps the Ascetic Gotama can," and directed them in that direction. Next, since the Blessed One also saw that this fatal danger could not be averted by the mere paying of respects alone, He put forward the idea of a chanting of *Paritta*.
What is meant by the word *paritrāṇa* is protection from all sides. What is the deep meaning of this word *paritta* or *pirit*? It is providing protection from all sides. How is this protection provided? These devotees know very well how it is done during these *Paritta* ceremonies. A blessing is performed through an assertion of truth (*saccakiriya*) regarding the veracity of the Triple Gem. There, by saying *"saccena suvatthi hotu"* (by this truth may there be well-being) and so forth, they recollect the all-pervading power and the strength of virtues of the Buddha-gem, the Dhamma-gem, and the Saṅgha-gem, and make an assertion of truth based on them. There is a great power in that word. There is a great energy in the word that spreads throughout the universe. Along with the word goes this power of blessing, the assertion of truth, and what follows it. Just as the child was seated in the middle and the *Paritta* ceremony was held on that occasion, today, in this era, we see that the vessel of *Paritta* water and the *Paritta* thread are placed in the middle while the Saṅgha sit around and chant *Paritta*. That is the concept behind treating *Paritta* water and *Paritta* thread as being endowed with great power.
Thus, we can understand that, on one hand, just like that act of paying homage, the chanting of *Paritta* also helps to prevent dangers and accidents—here, a *yakkha* named Avaruddhaka is mentioned. There are certain invisible forces, such as non-human afflictions and so forth. The strength and power of the Triple Gem help to dispel them. That is what is specifically mentioned in this story on this occasion. When we think about lay life in the ordinary world, even when we look among parents and relatives, we usually consider those who are older in age as elders. But when we think about the Dispensation (*Sāsana*), the concept of an elder is different. These devotees have heard that even a young child who is ordained on that very day receives homage and offerings from laypeople. Similarly, one must pay respects to those who are senior in ordination. There is a monastic custom of paying respects according to the number of rains retreats (*vassa*) since higher ordination (*upasampadā*). A situation where one can witness a miracle of the Dispensation is when a mother, who has carried her child in her womb for ten months, nourished him with milk made from her own blood, scolded and punished him in various ways during his mischievous childhood, offers him to the Dispensation—even if he is a seven-year-old child—and then she pays respects to that child. When she pays respects to that child, the child does not bend down and pay respects to the mother saying *mātupādaṃ namāmahaṃ* (I bow to my mother's feet) as before. Instead, as declared and taught by the Blessed One, the supreme way a monastic can minister to parents is by helping them grow in faith (*saddhā*), virtue (*sīla*), generosity (*cāga*), and wisdom (*paññā*). In terms of offering that assistance, with that determination, and recollecting the majesty of virtue (*sīla-teja*) associated with the monastic life, they bestow this blessing: *Abhivādanasīlissa...* and so on.
In one way or another, he blesses the mother. Then, even though her child, her darling child, had paid respects to her until then, the mother sheds tears of joy seeing him accept her homage unflinchingly, now as a darling of the Dispensation. She does not feel hurt thinking, "My child paid respects to me all this time, but today he does not." Regarding him as a darling of the Dispensation, the mother wipes away her tears of joy and steps aside. Through that miracle of the Dispensation, we see that the order of seniority in the Dispensation is different. However, this concept of the order of seniority did not exist at the very beginning. There is a story mentioned in the Dhamma about how it came to be. We can imagine how much chaos arises in society when there is no such order of seniority. In the Vinaya Piṭaka, which outlines the history of the Dispensation, the following incident is recorded:
On one occasion, when Anāthapiṇḍika the householder had prepared Jetavana monastery and constructed all the dwellings, he sent a messenger to the Blessed One. At that time, the Blessed One was traveling back from the city of Vesālī to accept the offering of Jetavana. Meanwhile, a group of unruly monks known as the group-of-six (*chabbaggiya*), who constantly violated Vinaya rules, arrived early and claimed ownership of the lodgings and dwellings of Jetavana, saying, "This is for our preceptors, this is for our teachers, and this is for us." Thus they took possession of them. Then, the Blessed One arrived there. In the meantime, the Venerable Sāriputta, the Chief Disciple, was traveling somewhat behind. Although the Blessed One and the retinue of monks managed to get dwellings, there was no dwelling for the Venerable Sāriputta; there was not even a place for him to sleep. So, he spent that night under a tree. In the early morning, the Blessed One got up and coughed. As a signal, He cleared His throat slightly. Then, the Venerable Sāriputta also coughed to indicate his presence. "Who is there?" the Blessed One asked. "Venerable Sir, it is I, Sāriputta," he replied. "What are you doing there?" He asked. Thereupon, the story came to light: because the group-of-six monks had arrived early and seized the lodgings, we had to step back. That was the situation.
The next morning, when daylight broke, the Blessed One assembled the Saṅgha and asked if that story was true. "How could these foolish men (*mogha-purisa*) do such a thing? If they behave in this way, what will happen in the future? How could they do this, showing no regard for seniority, to the extent of leaving no room even for the Chief Disciple?" Then, the Blessed One asked the monks: "Who is worthy of the best seat (*aggrāsana*), that is, the first seat? Who is worthy of the best water (*aggrudaka*), that is, to receive water first? Who is worthy of the best alms (*aggapiṇḍa*), to receive alms-food first?" When asked, some monks said, "Those ordained from the brahmin caste." Others said, "Those ordained from the householder (*gahapati*) caste." Some said, "To the Suttantikas who have well-memorized the Suttas." Another said, "It is proper for those versed in the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*)." Another said, "To the Dhamma preachers (*dhammakathika*)." Yet another said, "The first seat should be given to those who have attained the first absorption (*jhāna*)." Others said, "The second, third, or fourth absorption." Other monks answered, "Those who have attained the paths and fruits—Stream-entry, Once-returning, Non-returning, and Arahantship—or those who have attained direct knowledges (*abhiññā*)." Because those monks did not have a proper understanding, they gave various answers of this sort. Then, the Blessed One first presented an exemplary story. That story is mentioned not only in the Vinaya Piṭaka but also in the Jātaka Book under the name Tittira Jātaka, with minor variations. According to the facts mentioned in the Vinaya, it is as follows:
The Blessed One declared: "Once upon a time, near the Himalayas, there stood a large banyan tree. In association with that banyan tree, a partridge, a monkey, and an elephant lived in great friendship. These three thought: 'It is not proper for us to live like this without showing respect and honor to one another. Let us somehow identify who is the elder among us, and live paying respect and hospitality to that elder, and following that elder's advice.' To find out, 'How shall we know our age?' the partridge and the monkey asked the elephant what was the oldest event he could remember. The elephant said: 'I remember when this banyan tree was just a sapling; when I walked over it, its topmost tender shoot rubbed against my belly. I remember even that time.' Next, the elephant and the partridge together asked the monkey: 'What is the furthest past you can recall?' The monkey said: 'When I was small, as a baby monkey, sitting on the ground, I used to nibble the tender shoot of this banyan sapling.' Next, the elephant and the monkey asked the partridge: 'What is your past memory regarding this banyan tree?'
'Over in such-and-such a place, there stood a large banyan tree. Having eaten a fruit from that banyan tree, I voided my excrement here. It is from that seed that this banyan tree grew. Although I am just a partridge, even at that time I was of considerable age.' Thus, the partridge was the eldest. If one looks at physical size, how massive is the elephant? The monkey is also large. Yet, this small partridge was senior in age. So, what follows is that—having identified the elder—the elephant and the monkey lived showing respect and honor to the partridge, abiding by the partridge's advice. Next, the Blessed One says that the partridge established the other two in the five precepts (*pañcasīla*). He himself also kept the five precepts. Having kept them and fulfilled that noble custom of showing respect and honor to the elder, it is mentioned in the Vinaya book as a unique holy life. The term used is *Tittiriya Brahmacariya* (the holy life of the partridge).
For the well-being of those three, the Dhamma uses the term *Tittiriya Brahmacariya*. *Tittira* means partridge. The Blessed One declared that by practicing this unique holy life initiated by the partridge, those three animals were reborn in happy realms (*sugati*). Having declared this, He said, "Monks, even those animals understood the importance of seniority and acted accordingly. Why then do you, who are ordained in this well-expounded (*svākkhāta*) Dhamma and Vinaya, not show respect to elders?" He also declared the benefits of paying homage to elders through a certain stanza. The story concluded by stating that if someone fulfills the custom of paying respects and showing honor to elders, they are praised in this world and reborn in a happy realm.
When that same story is mentioned in the Jātaka Book, the identification of characters is also given. Here, an elephant, a monkey, and a partridge were mentioned. Who were these three? In the past, the elephant was Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the monkey was Venerable Sāriputta, and the partridge was the Teacher of the Three Worlds, the Buddha himself. This is how they are identified in the Jātaka Book. So, this exemplary story was presented to put forward the monastic concept regarding the order of seniority, the line of succession. Along with that, the Blessed One declared that in this Dispensation, the one ordained first, the senior monk, should receive homage and respect from the one ordained later, and He detailed at length in the Vinaya Piṭaka who is worthy of homage and who is not. Drawing from this story, if we relate this to society, these devotees had a good custom in the past that went hand-in-hand with village life, among villagers. Instead of just treating everyone the same, they respected elders based on age, and even if they were not from the same family, they regarded the entire village as one family, addressing others as elder brother (*ayyā*), younger brother (*mallī*), younger sister (*naṅgī*), elder sister (*akkā*), mother (*ammā*), and father (*tāttā*). It was very pleasing to the ear. There was such a practice in the past. Thus, in agricultural and other work, it was like a family working together. They all bore the burden together. That sense of seniority helped to maintain the bonds of unity.
Indeed, even if we reflect on that banyan tree, a banyan tree itself is a miracle. It is a tree grown from a tiny seed. Looking at a massive banyan tree, one can learn many things. As revealed in the previous story, this banyan tree grew from a banyan seed in the excrement voided by that partridge. We can imagine that the excrement might have fallen between a stone or two. Yet, enduring great storms and various hot seasons, the tree grew gradually and became a great banyan tree providing shade to everyone. Thus, even by looking at a banyan tree, we see we can learn something from its long existence. It is the same with a human being. Even if they do not have a high education or high positions, through many experiences in the university of life, an elder, to a certain extent, becomes someone worthy of respect and honor. Now, many young children sometimes have a habit of making fun of elderly people. One should not think in that way. One must look at elders just as one looks at that banyan tree. By living up to that point amidst various life troubles, being subject to the eight worldly conditions (*aṭṭha-loka-dhamma*), the vast store of experience they gain can be of help to oneself as well. But that help can only be received if one conducts oneself in that manner—showing proper respect and hospitality without making fun of them. Therefore, that is also the custom of the New Year. If one lives according to that concept of seniority, not only towards parents and elders at home but also towards neighbors, then with mutual cooperation, the home becomes a village. It is when we relate it to lay life in this way that the value of this story lies.
At the same time, we must constantly contemplate another aspect revealed by this story. If we orient this towards Nibbāna, it was mentioned at the beginning of the story that one of the two ascetics decided to return to lay life to protect his lineage. This is called inheritance or ancestry (*praveṇiya*). That was in agreement with his ascetic doctrine, because in Brahminism there is a teaching about four stages of life (*āśrama*). Life is divided into four stages. During childhood and youth, one must study. During youth, one must enjoy the fivefold sensual pleasures. In the third stage, one should incline towards the religious side, the practice of a sage (*muni-vṛtti*). In the final stage, when approaching death, one must die as a yogi. In this way, dividing the mundane (*lokiya*) and the supramundane (*lokuttara*) fifty-fifty, some people in Brahminism spent their lives. The other concept is that even for an ascetic, that was an accepted practice in Brahminism; there was nothing strange about it. Why did those brahmins return to lay life after keeping the holy life (*brahmacariya*) for forty-eight years? It was to carry their family lineage forward. Although that side is not directly mentioned in the story, it is worth considering. This is because the concept of Nibbāna in this Dispensation of the Blessed One is different from that Brahmin doctrine. It is for this reason that when the Blessed One ordained even seven-year-old children, when large crowds joined the Buddhist Dispensation, leaving behind their wives and children, causing a huge social transformation, some people accused the Blessed One: *"Aputtakattāya paṭipanno samaṇo Gotamo, vedhavyāya paṭipanno samaṇo Gotamo, kulupacchedāya paṭipanno Gotamo"*—"The Ascetic Gotama is bent on making families childless; the Ascetic Gotama is bent on making women widows (for when husbands leave, they become widows); Gotama is bent on destroying clans." Yes, they said it is a practice that destroys the clan, the lineage, ending the lineage right there. Such accusations were leveled against the Blessed One. The Blessed One, however, told the monks that this noise would not last long, and to dispel that noise, He asked them to recite a certain stanza. That stanza declares that the Ascetic Gotama guides this crowd through Dhamma, not through non-Dhamma (*adhamma*). Therefore, there is nothing wrong with this.
Next, there is another account mentioned in the Vinaya Piṭaka, which we will mention only briefly because it is somewhat related to this. In the Vinaya Piṭaka, there is the first *Pārājika* training rule concerning sexual intercourse, which is the practice of laypeople. Even if we look at the story of the monk that led to the formulation of this training rule, we can see that the values and virtues of our Dispensation are different from Brahminism. There, it is said that the monk named Sudinna Kalandakaputta had ordained with great faith (*saddhā*). However, he had ordained after living a lay life, and while he was married and had a wife, his wife's mother came and made an inappropriate proposal: "Because there is no child, the wealth belonging to our family might be confiscated by the king. Therefore, we need a child." She made such an improper proposal. Agreeing to that, the monk Sudinna Kalandakaputta compromised his virtue (*sīla*). Due to that wrong conduct which later led to deep regret, the Blessed One rebuked the monk Sudinna Kalandaka, calling him a foolish man (*mogha-purisa*), and laid down the first training rule concerning abstaining from the *Pārājika* of sexual intercourse. From this, we can see that the doctrine of the Brahmin era was like trying to save both the porridge and the beard (wanting to have it both ways)—one must protect this world and at the same time realize Nibbāna, or rather, obtain liberation according to their views.
The Blessed One's Dhamma is not like that. According to the Blessed One's Dhamma, this entire world is a hospital. Therefore, as quickly as possible, at whatever age, if the thought of renunciation (*nekkhamma*) arises in someone, it is proper to put it into practice. It is not about those ideas of social, economic, or physical values. Considering the rarity of the Buddhist Dispensation and the rare opportunity for realizing Nibbāna, He gave permission to ordain even young children. Although not explicitly stated in this story, what is being discussed here is something opposite to that Brahmin doctrine. Next, the chanting of *Paritta* was mentioned here. We must understand the value of this *Paritta* chanting. In the Ratana Sutta and other discourses, what is specially described are the virtues of the Buddha-gem, the virtues of the Dhamma-gem, and the virtues of the Saṅgha-gem. Similarly, there are certain *Parittas* like Mahāsamaya and Āṭānāṭiya where it is described how the entire universe, even the *yakkhas*, bow down to the majestic power of the Blessed One's virtues. That is why these *Parittas* are said to be endowed with great power.
For what do we employ all of these? It is to protect our lifespan, and along with that lifespan, to protect beauty, happiness, and strength. If the lifespan increases to some extent, it is parallel to that that the qualities of beauty, happiness, and strength increase. Generally, everyone wishes for these four qualities. However, what is more valuable, more valuable than all of these, is wisdom (*paññā*). Lifespan, beauty, happiness, strength, and wisdom. Thus, to obtain this wisdom, we cannot be satisfied with mere listening to *Paritta* or mere paying of respects. Thinking even more deeply, at whatever age, if one has understood the value of this Dhamma, by practicing it, one must personally realize this liberation from Saṃsāra, which is an extremely rare thing. If that determination to make an opportunity for this arises, anyone has the space to walk that path of Dhamma in this Dispensation.
In walking that path of Dhamma, we know that once it is completed, as said before, even a young child becomes worthy of receiving homage from his parents. This is because it is an extremely difficult thing. For a long time in this Saṃsāra, we have come enjoying the treasures of the five cords of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāma*), staying within lay houses, subject to lay values. Similarly, at this moment, these devotees, by keeping the eight precepts (*aṭṭhasīla*) on this Poya day, separate themselves from certain comforts and luxuries belonging to their daily life until now, and habituate themselves to a simple life. Yet, for a long time in this Saṃsāra, we lived submerged in various things belonging to sensual pleasures that cause negligence (*pamāda*). In renunciation (*nekkhamma*), one has to gradually abandon all of that. That is why, as soon as he is ordained, even that young child becomes worthy of receiving homage from his parents.
Indeed, we must reflect that to maintain a life, we obtain the qualities of lifespan, beauty, happiness, and strength through paying respects to parents and so forth, and through listening to *Paritta*. But for what do we maintain a life? For what do we obtain a lifespan? For what do we obtain strength? We must do all of this for the sake of escaping from this Saṃsāra. For that, then, one must strive to obtain that wisdom (*paññā*). Wisdom is a Dhamma in this Dispensation that must be understood by each according to their own capacity (*ñāṇa*). There is a path to be traversed for that, namely, virtue, concentration, and wisdom (*sīla, samādhi, paññā*). It is on that path that these devotees are traveling now, practicing Dhamma and meditation as spiritual practitioners (*yogāvacara*). One must reflect: if on a New Year's day like this, one has obtained a lifespan through certain meritorious deeds related to that period of meritorious deeds, and has obtained the parallel beauty, happiness, and strength necessary for a life, then next, one must ask oneself the question: "For what purpose do I live?"
During the pause that presents itself, in which direction should we steer our lives? Is it towards that world-prolonging practice of being born and dying in Saṃsāra over and over again? We call it *lokavaḍḍhana*—that is, the expansion of the world. The Buddha declared that going on being born and dying in this Saṃsāra over and over again is a practice. Expanding the world means expanding the cemetery. On one occasion, speaking about Mount Vepulla—isn't this Mount Vepulla?—the Blessed One said that if the skeletons left behind by a single human being during a single eon (*kappa*) were gathered together, they would be larger than this Mount Vepulla. Thus, we have gone on leaving behind skeletons in this way for an infinite time, which also decay in time; such research has been carried out extensively. There is no end to this.
