in the latter part of life, parents usually cultivate a certain sense of security in the hope of receiving care and attention from their children. accordingly, it is natural for parents with many children to feel a greater sense of security. nonetheless, due to children who measure their parents' virtues in terms of money and material wealth, a situation sometimes arises where parents are left with absolutely no support or refuge.
our buddha supreme, the blessed one, declared this verse, which we have taken as our theme today, to help a mother who had fallen into such a helpless state through the dhamma. in the city of savatthi, there was a certain family with seven sons and seven daughters. having reached the appropriate age, they got married and lived comfortable lives. in the meantime, the father passed away. so, this mother continued to utilize their wealth and property. the children came and said, "mother, now that father is gone, why do you still keep this wealth? is it that we cannot look after you?" after remaining silent several times, since they repeatedly kept saying this, she thought, "indeed, my children will look after me," and divided all her wealth into equal portions, distributing them among the children.
however, after some days, when she went to her eldest son’s house, her daughter-in-law would say, "look at that, it seems our mother-in-law is coming here every day as if she gave two shares to the eldest son." next, she went to the second son's house. there too, a similar thing happened after a few days. she went to her daughters' houses; it was the same there as well. moving from place to place like this, this mother realized, "now indeed, there is no hope of help from these children. i must live as a bhikkhuni (nun)," and went to the nunnery to request ordination. those bhikkhunis ordained this elderly lady. regardless of her ordained name, she is introduced to us in the dhamma by the nickname that stuck to her: 'bahuputtika theri'. when looked at realistically, the only thing that mother received or inherited from her children was that name: "the mother of many children."
in any case, bhikkhuni bahuputtika was ordained with her livelihood in mind. however, developing a profound sense of urgency (*samvega*) regarding *samsara*, thinking, "now i am advanced in age," she started to practice meditation (*bhavana*) with great energy, remaining sleepless day and night. she also performed the duties and services due to the other bhikkhunis very well. it is mentioned that while doing these chores, the way she meditated was by clinging to pillars and holding onto them during the night to practice meditation. furthermore, fearing that she might fall while walking in meditation (*cankamanaya*) in the dark, and to ward off sleepiness, she would hang onto branches of trees to meditate. having meditated so intensely, when her mind reached a certain level of development at the appropriate moment, the buddha, likely perceiving this state, sent forth a light from within his fragrant chamber (*gandhakuti*) and addressed bahuputtika, delivering a sermon. he concluded it with the verse we have chosen as our theme:
*yo ca vassasatam jive apassam dhammamuttamam*
"though one should live a hundred years, without seeing the supreme dhamma,
*ekaham jivitam seyyo passato dhammamuttamam.*
better is a single day's life of one who sees the supreme dhamma."
the buddha delivered a dhamma discourse containing this verse. hearing it, it is recorded in the story that bahuputtika theri attained arahantship together with the four analytical knowledges (*patisambhida*). in this short story, there is a good lesson for children as well as parents. if we contemplate the lesson regarding children in this series of events, it is evident that some children are in the habit of measuring their parents' virtues according to the proportion of the inheritance they receive. that is why they spoke in that manner: "did you give us two shares?" but they did not contemplate that the greatest inheritance they received—the greatest gift from their parents—was the gift of life.
it is not just after a child is born, but even while in the mother’s womb, during those ten months, there was a possibility of dying a thousand times. preventing those occurrences, making the child subsist on the very food she consumes, and undergoing ten-fold suffering (*dukkha*), the mother protects the child. sometimes she also suffers from pregnancy cravings (*doladuka*), which some define as "the suffering of two hearts." declining even the agreeable, wholesome food and drinks she herself prefers, with a wondrous sacrifice, a mother protects the child and brings the child into the world, risking her own life. looked at in this way, even while in the mother's womb, a vast portion of that inheritance of life has already been received.
furthermore, after birth, you all have heard the saying that she turned her blood into milk to feed the child. in that manner, mothers nourish their children during that initial period. in doing so, mothers do not perform calculations regarding their children. it must be because similar incidents occurred in this country that an ancient poet wrote a poem about this entanglement between children and parents. in that poem, there is a line that goes: "did i measure out the milk i gave you, my son?" those mothers do not measure when they give milk. but children treat their parents according to the ratio of the inheritance. thus, it is mentioned in various stories that such an attitude existed not only in modern times but also in the past. these are human weaknesses, and there are places where the buddha delivered dhamma discourses fitting those occasions.
you all must have heard this often. when the buddha appeared in ancient indian society, the brahmins regarded brahma as supreme. worshipping and paying homage to this brahma was a practice in households. instead of that, the buddha introduced that it is not the invisible brahma, but the mother and father who are the real brahmas living in one's own home. this is why the buddha declared, *"brahma ti matapitaro"* (mother and father are called brahma) and so on. parents are indeed the brahmas.
the buddha declared this with valid reasons. because according to the dhamma, the four qualities of loving-kindness (*metta*), compassion (*karuna*), sympathetic joy (*mudita*), and equanimity (*upekkha*) are known as the *brahmaviharas* (sublime abodes). since a mother and a father actually cultivate these four qualities directing them towards their child, the buddha with good reason identified them as brahmas.
even if we consider these four briefly: in loving-kindness (*metta*), there is the wish to care for and comfort the child in infancy. in compassion (*karuna*), there is skillful means (*upayakusalata*). in the mischievous years, it is with the help of compassion, motivated by love for the child, that a mother protects the child so that they do not fall into danger, preventing dangerous situations, sometimes through gentle ways and sometimes through strict measures. next, as the child grows bodily and progresses in studies, the parents cultivate in their hearts the valuable quality of sympathetic joy (*mudita*), which is the opposite of jealousy—rejoicing in another's happiness. finally, in old age, they make various sacrifices for their children. they even prepare their minds to separate from their children.
in this story, too, that mother did not resort to aggressive courses of action; she understood the nature of the world and *samsara*. realizing, "even though i have so many children, this is all i receive," she sought the refuge of the dhamma and was ordained to receive the support of the most supreme dhamma. some pious lay disciples who have many children might also think, "we can live our final days clinging to the bodies of these children." but bhikkhuni bahuputtika obtained a much greater shelter and refuge, in a transcendent (*lokuttara*) sense, by meditating while hanging onto those lifeless pillars and tree branches. to realize that supreme dhamma and to end the suffering (*dukkha*) of *samsara*, that mother...
so, we must contemplate that this cannot be called a fault of the children alone. some mothers and fathers, no matter how old they get, play with and pamper their children without limit; and after the children's affairs are finished, they spend their time looking at the faces of and pampering their children's children, and their children's children, not knowing what will happen to themselves. likewise, children also hand over their next generation to their parents. instead of looking after their parents, other tasks and responsibilities are assigned to them. thus, both parties are responsible for this. there is a good example here regarding this as well. at that stage, one should cultivate equanimity (*upekkha*), establish oneself in the dhamma, and incline towards quiet seclusion where one can calmly understand the nature of *samsara* and the nature of life through one's own body in a meditative manner. furthermore, the care of parents has been further expounded as a duty of children—not only providing food, drinks, and so on, but also paying homage, bowing down, and doing all such things for parents as one would do for brahma.
on one occasion, the buddha delivered a highly powerful sermon regarding the care of parents. without any specific reason, but so that it would serve as an example to the world, he made this statement: "monks, there are two persons whom it is difficult to sufficiently serve and look after. who are the two? the mother and the father." next, he points out three valuable matters. first, he indicates: "if a son, living for a hundred years, were to carry his mother on one shoulder and his father on the other shoulder, and for a hundred years were to attend to them, bathing them, feeding them, and even cleaning the urine and excrement voided by those decrepit parents on his shoulders, attending to them with his own hands as he carries them, he still would not have sufficiently served them or truly repaid his debt to his mother and father." similarly, he says: "monks, if a child, with the intention of serving his parents, were to establish them as rulers of this great earth filled with the seven treasures, even that would not be doing enough." finally, the buddha declares: "if a son establishes his faithless parents in the attainment of faith (*saddha-sampada*), establishes his unethical parents in the attainment of virtue (*sila-sampada*), establishes his stingy parents in the attainment of generosity (*caga-sampada*), and establishes his unwise parents in the attainment of wisdom (*panna-sampada*), that son has not only done enough, but he has served his parents more than enough."
according to that, it becomes clear that what children have to do, if their parents are living with them, is to give them sufficient leisure and quietude to practice giving (*dana*), virtue (*sila*), and meditation (*bhavana*). the physical care and attention, or even granting them kingship, cannot compensate for that. truly, while growing oneself in virtues such as giving and virtue, if there is any lack of these in one's elderly parents, providing them with the necessary quietude and comfort to develop them is the service rendered through the dhamma. thus, three aspects are mentioned here. it is to the service done with one's own hands that the buddha gave that first simile—the first illustration. next, it is with the idea of providing comfort that kingship was mentioned. lastly, what is spoken of is the service through the dhamma. so, even while remaining as a layperson, one can serve one's parents through the dhamma in this manner. if someone ordains, they can perform that supreme service mentioned above for a mother or father at an even higher level. that is one discourse. there are many such discourses.
you all must have heard it in the *parabhava sutta*, where when pointing out the causes of a person's ruin, the buddha declares: "if a son or child, having the ability, does not support or look after his elderly mother and father, that is a cause of his ruin." in another similar discourse, the buddha states: "monks, one who behaves wrongly towards four persons is ruined as if he has dug his own grave, is censured and blamed by the wise, and accumulates immense demerit. who are the four? one’s mother, father, the tathagata, and the tathagata's disciples." regarding these four groups, it is preached that if anyone behaves wrongly towards them, they meet destruction as if they had dug their own grave.
furthermore, you all have heard of the five heinous crimes (*pancanantariya-kamma*) in accordance with the dhamma. where the results of actions (*kamma-vipaka*) are shown in the dhamma, the buddha has pointed out that there are five extremely dangerous, most grave evil deeds. they are called *anantariya-kamma* (crimes with immediate retribution). they lead inevitably to hell (*apaya*) in the very next life. even there, the buddha mentions the parents: killing one's mother, killing one's father, killing an arahant, drawing blood from the buddha's body with hostile intent, and finally, causing a schism in the sangha. by listing these as *anantariya-kamma*, the buddha has highlighted the significance of parents.
the reason for this is that the greatest inheritance children receive from parents is the inheritance of life. in addition, the fundamental advice to steer and correct one's life is also received from parents. that is why they are called *pubbacariyo* (first teachers). *"brahma ti matapitaro, pubbacariya ti vuccare"*—parents are called brahmas, and they are also called the first teachers. furthermore, it is said: *"apadaka posaka, imassa lokassa dassetaro"*—they bring up, nourish, and show this world to their children. since they have done such a vast heap of assistance for their children, the buddha has extolled the virtues of parents to such an extent. that is with respect to children living as householders.
regarding the ordination of children, it is also mentioned in various places in the discourses, especially in the vinaya pitaka. on one occasion, king suddhodana came to meet the buddha and said, "venerable sir, i would like to ask for a boon." the buddha immediately replied, "the tathagatas are not in the habit of granting boons." "no, venerable sir, what i am asking is something allowable and extremely proper." "very well, speak," he said. then king suddhodana said, "ah, venerable sir, when the blessed one went forth (ordained), it caused me immense suffering (*dukkha*). next, when nanda was ordained, that too caused me great suffering. when rahula was ordained, it caused me an unbearable, extremely vast suffering." it is a father speaking, not a mother. he further says, "venerable sir, love for a son is something that cuts through the outer skin, the inner skin, the flesh, and the sinews, and enters into the marrow of the bones. therefore, i request that a rule be enacted not to ordain children without the permission and consent of their parents."
the buddha accepted this and laid down a rule: "monks, henceforth do not ordain anyone without the parents' permission. if you do so, there will be an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkata*)." in this context, indeed, one should not think of the buddha as having violated a rule earlier. what the buddha saw was the necessity of saving someone from *samsara*. that is not something to be censured according to the dhamma. however, as a special privilege, as a boon to king suddhodana, he enacted that rule in that manner.
furthermore, it is mentioned concerning those who have ordained: though generally there is no connection with lay households, special privileges are shown regarding parents. on one occasion in the vinaya, this kind of incident regarding the four requisites is mentioned. once, a certain bhikkhu received many robes. for some reason, that bhikkhu felt like giving these robes, or at least the robe-cloth, to his parents. the sangha reported this to the buddha. the buddha expressed himself thus: "monks, when it comes to parents, what can i say? i permit it. i allow you to give those robes to your parents. however, do not give them to inappropriate places or inappropriate people. that would cause the faith of those who offered them with faith to decline. if you do so, there will be an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkata*). but i allow you to give them to your parents." thus, he gave a special permission to ordained children even regarding robes.
similarly, regarding almsfood (*pindapata*): if there are occasions when parents have nothing to eat or drink, there is permission to give a portion of that food one has obtained through alms-gathering to one's parents. next, regarding medicines: if the parents do not receive medicines and have no caregiver, one can give the medicines one receives to one's parents. one can also attend to one's mother without touching her body. next, for one's father, the buddha allowed attending to him as one would attend to a novice (*samanera*), even performing tasks like bathing and rubbing the body.
in this manner, there are many other occasions where special favor was shown toward parents. in the vinaya rules, the sangha is forbidden from traveling during the three months of the rains retreat (*vassa*). however, seven special occasions are pointed out. two of these are that if there is some need concerning one's mother or father, whether a message has arrived or not, permission is given to go during the rains retreat. whether they asked to return or not, if the need is seen, there is permission to go.
from this, we can see that even in the ordained life, the buddha gave a special place to the care of parents. not only in that ancient indian society but also today, as virtues decline more and more, various problems arise in households because people do not bring these dhamma matters to mind. the buddha highlighted those virtues largely for the progress of both parties—for their spiritual progress.
next, as we said, there is a lesson in this for parents too. what is that? the exemplary character of bahuputtika theri is what should be taken there. when her children finally stopped caring for her, that theri might have thought, "this is a flaw of *samsara*." cultivating the equanimity (*upekkha*) appropriate for that advanced age, thinking, "now indeed, let them live happily, i must ordain," she ordained. moreover, having ordained, she did not just idle there for her livelihood. performing her duties and observances, she meditated in that manner. here lies the most valuable example.
just as the buddha declared, she obtained support through the dhamma, meditating intensely during the night. that is a great encouragement even for the elderly. a lot of things can be learned from this very body. old age is an opportunity where one can clearly realize through direct experience (*pratyaksa*) the three characteristics (*tilakkhana*)—the impermanent (*anicca*) and unsubstantial (*anatta*) nature of decay (*jara*). if there is leisure for that, and if one directs one's mind to it, one can benefit a great deal from it, generating disenchantment (*nibbida*) towards this *samsara*. thus, the story of bahuputtika theri is a fine example of this.
next, if we contemplate this dhamma, it was said in that verse: "even if one lives a hundred years without seeing the supreme dhamma..." by "supreme dhamma," what we must understand is the transcendent (*lokuttara*) dhamma—the dhamma of nibbana. rather than living a hundred years without seeing that supreme dhamma, living even a single day seeing the transcendent dhamma is more valuable. that was proven by the life of bahuputtika theri.
according to the buddha's verse, if there was still some small thing lacking in that theri, it was because the noble courage and advice were contained within that verse that she was able to attain that realization. through that, even we can contemplate the values of life. today, we generally value grandfathers living for a hundred years. but even a grandfather's life is of no use if spent without making even an effort to understand such a supreme dhamma. the person who lives a single day seeing the dhamma is far more valuable than that. what we have to contemplate from that story is that if one lives even a single day seeing the supreme transcendent dhamma, that life is what is truly valuable. sometimes, parents think, "i have many children, so i will live as long as i can," having the objective of a long life and longevity. but that theri, risking her life, sacrificing sleep day and night, escaped from *samsara*.
that is also what we have to contemplate. understanding the true nature of life and *samsara* in the world is the most valuable thing in a life. you, pious devotees, know that the path leading to that is through virtue (*sila*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*). if we contemplate from the perspective of insight (*vipassana*), we must see the three characteristics (*tilakkhana*)—namely, the impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and unsubstantial (*anatta*). that is why it is said, "the life of one who sees the supreme dhamma for even a single day is valuable."
sometimes, a person might think that insight (*vipassana*) means chanting, "*anicca, dukkha, anatta; anicca, dukkha, anatta*." truly, pious devotees, insight meditation (*vipassana-bhavana*) is not a matter of saying, but of seeing. and that seeing is not seeing with the physical eye, but seeing with the eye of wisdom. if one thinks in that way, we can go on repeating "*anicca, dukkha, anatta*" like a mantra. that is like painting a picture. it is not like that; one must dive deep into these five aggregates (*pancakkhandha*). how does one dive deep? with a concentrated mind, through the method of attention, through radical attention / wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*)—by reflecting wisely, by reflecting rapidly, one must understand the nature of these five aggregates. that is what is called "penetrative wisdom" (*nibbedhika panna*). one must see its true state with penetrative wisdom. not merely with the physical eye. sometimes, people create confusions due to a lack of proper understanding of these things.
in the past, there is an account of such a confusion being created. a certain meditation master told his disciple to practice the meditation on rise and fall (*udayabbaya-bhavana*). devotees, "udayabbaya" means that in order to deeply understand impermanence (*aniccata*), one must see both the arising and passing away. the pali words for arising and passing away are *udaya* and *vaya*. that is what is called *udayabbaya*. the knowledge of this arising and passing away is called the "knowledge of rise and fall" (*udayabbaya-nana*). so, the disciple was sent to see this.
the disciple went to the edge of a pond. having gone there and sat down in a secluded spot, with eyes wide open, he kept repeating, "arising and passing away, arising and passing away, arising and passing away" (*udayabbayam, udayabbayam, udayabbayam*). while he was repeating this, a crane landed in the water. now, in the pali language, water is called *udaka*, and a crane is called *baka*. since the mind is easily distracted, he saw this crane land in the water. consequently, without even realizing it, the meditator who was repeating "arising and passing away, arising and passing away" started saying "water-crane, water-crane" (*udaka-bakam, udaka-bakam*).
such confusions arise when one thinks that insight (*vipassana*) is merely a matter of memory or reciting words. but, devotees, it is something seen with insight-wisdom, with that deep penetrative wisdom (*nibbedhika panna*) that pierces through. for that, mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*) must be developed. the method of seeing this is also mentioned in the dhamma. generally, when speaking simply, we say: "form is impermanent (*anicca*), feeling (*vedana*) is impermanent, perception (*sanna*) is impermanent." we keep saying it like that.
but certain discourses show us that it is not a mere saying. in those discourses, the way of seeing the arising and passing away is stated as follows: *"iti rupam, iti rupassa samudayo, iti rupassa atthangamo."* "iti" means "thus" or "such". *"iti rupam, iti rupassa samudayo, iti rupassa atthangamo"*—"such is form, such is the arising of form, such is the passing away of form." it goes on in the same way: "such is feeling (*vedana*), such is the arising of feeling, such is the passing away of feeling."
what do we understand from that word "such" (*iti*)? it is not a chant; rather, form, feeling, etc., are captured by the attention (*manasikara*) of insight as they arise. one reflects on them in the proper manner. it is not a mere uttering of words. a feeling (*vedana*) has arisen: "this is such-and-such a feeling." a pleasant feeling arose, persisted, and passed away. a painful feeling arose, persisted, and passed away. a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arose, persisted, and passed away. the same applies to perception (*sanna*). in this way, when looking at the side of the five aggregates and contemplating, one gradually goes deeper.
in some instances, the world is introduced in the dhamma as the world of the five aggregates (*pancakkhandha-loka*). the discourses of the buddha are described as having "manifold methods" (*nana-naya*), presented in the dhamma under various subjects as appropriate. in certain instances, it is called the world of the five aggregates. in another instance, it is shown as the world of the six sense-bases (*salayatana-loka*). the six sense-bases are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. mind (*mana*) means the thought/intellect. thus, these six doors—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—are introduced as the six sense-bases. nowadays, we use the word "institutions" (or "departments") for the sinhala word *ayatana*. regardless of those institutions, these six sense-bases that every single person possesses are constantly working.
even within these six sense-bases, the base that acts like a central station is the mind-base (*manayatana*). all the messages brought in from the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body bases are collected and deposited in the mind-base. the world associated with these six sense-bases is called the world of the six sense-bases (*salayatana-loka*).
you, pious devotees, must have often heard that the buddha gave a simile for each of these aggregates (*khandha*). form (*rupa*) is compared to a lump of foam. feeling (*vedana*) is compared to a water bubble. perception (*sanna*) is compared to a mirage. preparations / preparations (*sankhara*) are compared to the trunk of a banana tree. consciousness (*vinnana*) is compared to a magician’s illusion. these are not similes given as poetic embellishments. these are similes that must be directly experienced. through what does one directly experience them? through the eye of wisdom. an occasion when they are directly experienced through the eye of wisdom arrives during insight meditation (*vipassana-bhavana*).
when one brings those to attention (*manasikara*) with a well-concentrated mind, the nature of the elements composed of the four great elements—earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and wind (*vayo*)—is understood. just as a lump of foam, which accumulates when something gets stuck in a flowing river, appears from afar with the perception of solidity (*ghana-sanna*) as a solid thing, but when inspected closely is found to be just a lump of foam; in the same way, understanding regarding this body arises through insight (*vipassana*).
it is the same with feeling (*vedana*). just like the bubbles of water that arise and vanish in an instant when raindrops fall during a shower, so is this thing called feeling. to one who contemplates deeply on feeling through the contemplation of feeling (*vedananupassana*), this understanding arises as a direct experience. how true are the similes declared by the buddha! they wonderfully demonstrate through those similes that this is merely a collection of arisings and passings away, and there is no "thing" there.
next, the same is true regarding perception (*sanna*), which is like a mirage. in that too, there is that mirage-like nature. a mirage is something one runs toward, thinking it exists in the distance. if one lives seeing the arising and passing away of the five aggregates, an occasion arises where perception is understood. regarding preparations (*sankhara*), the simile of the banana trunk shows their coreless, essenceless nature—that they are just a heap of fibrous sheaths. likewise, this stream of thoughts such as intention (*cetana*), this formative power of the mind, this preparation (*sankhara*)—this is not something done by a "self". ultimately, one sees that instead of a "self", there is only a succession of thoughts arising and passing away extremely rapidly, like a heap of fibrous sheaths.
next is consciousness (*vinnana*). the nature of consciousness is compared to an illusion. why was consciousness compared to an illusion? what does a magician do? he shows a non-existent thing as if it exists. one feels how wondrous this dhamma is! because consciousness (*vinnana*) displays a non-existent thing as if it exists, the cessation of consciousness is called nibbana. one experiences the cessation of consciousness in this very life. that is what is called nibbana. there is nothing that has been destroyed there.
the very nature of consciousness is non-existent; but because of the deceptive, illusory nature of consciousness, the ordinary world thinks it exists. that is what they grasp as a "soul" or "self" (*atta*). even if other things are not grasped, it is consciousness (*vinnana*) that is grasped as "i, i, i." yet, the buddha compared consciousness itself to a magician's illusion. now, if an illusion means showing a non-existent thing as existing, then what the world is holding onto is a non-existent thing. but failing to understand this non-existence is called ignorance (*avijja*); that is why there is the entire span of becoming (*bhava*), or the accumulation of *kamma*, etc.
if at any moment one understands that deceptive nature of consciousness, it is just like a spectator of a magic show who, having been deceived up to that point, later stands behind the stage and catches the magician’s tricks, realizing: "this is empty, there is nothing in it." it is something like that. then, the non-existent is seen exactly as non-existent. that is what is called understanding it as void (*sunna*), empty, and hollow. it is as things to be directly experienced that the buddha pointed out those similes. they were not declared out of mere whim or as poetic ornaments. that is how he points out the nature of the five aggregates (*pancakkhandha*).
next, regarding the six sense-bases (*salayatana*), those six we mentioned earlier: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. why are these called "bases" (*ayatana*)? because a production takes place within them. *kamma* is produced within them. grasping the objects that come to these bases tightly through ignorance (*avijja*), making them into two aspects as "this is i, this is the world, this is the eye, this is the form," and through the coordination established therein, *kamma* is accumulated as wholesome (*kusala*) and unwholesome (*akusala*), ultimately leading one to go on and on in this *samsara*.
the buddha declares that through insight (*vipassana*), one must understand the emptiness (*sunnata*) of these things as they really are (*yathabhuta*). for that, there are some wonderful similes given by ancient elders of the past, similes used to realize that dhamma. now, when lightning flashes during a rainy time like this, the ordinary world, or some uneducated person of that past era, thought of this lightning as a real thing. but this lightning did not come from somewhere. after that lightning ceased here, it did not go anywhere else either. it merely arose and passed away due to various causes and conditions (*hetu-paccaya*).
sometimes, a person might think that lightning flashing means lightning was somewhere and came when it rained, and after it ceased, it went somewhere. that is a delusion. this thing called lightning arises due to a multitude of causes. we give it a name. we grasp it as a thing. we falsely perceive solidity (*ghana*). but in reality, just as it arose, it passes away. that is the nature of things (*dhammata*). thus, various similes such as lightning, a mirage, and a rainbow were pointed out in the past because their nature can be understood through them. the path leading to that is what is called insight (*vipassana*). it is by reflecting on that impermanence (*aniccata*), on those arisings and passings away in a more and more subtle manner, that this understanding can be obtained.
we spoke, indeed, of a production in the sense-bases of the ordinary world. the production in those bases is generally carried out in a coarse, gross manner. behold, a form is seen. then, an effort is made to identify it accordingly. if one thinks, "this is so-and-so, this is my friend, a person i am very fond of," a certain train of thoughts flows based on that. the moment one thinks, "this is a resentful person, an enemy," another train of thoughts goes. there, one has grasped it as two ends: "this is the eye" and "this is the form."
but in reality, if we look at it, the entire series of events here is merely a certain picture cast upon the screen of the eye. it is only a certain vision falling on the eye, on the screen of the eye. on the basis of that vision, a vast train of thoughts is generated. having generated it, one accumulates *kamma* oneself. beyond that, even if one thinks about a sound, it is the same. a sweet sound is heard. something like a song is heard. then, thinking it is a good song, one generates certain attachments and so on within. but in insight (*vipassana*), at a certain point, one understands that all of this is a heap of movements, a heap of vibrations. or else, it is completely like the simile of the banana trunk mentioned for preparations (*sankhara*); there is only that here. there is nothing to be taken as a "thing".
so, the journey toward that understanding is what is called insight (*vipassana*). first, this is a form; not only that form, but one attributes to the form: "this is beautiful, this is good," and next, "it has such-and-such features." that is what is called "grasping signs"—in terms of signs (*nimitta*) and features (*anuvyanjana*). they grasp signs. next, they further decorate those signs with secondary details. that is what is meant by saying one has recognized a person. but ultimately, it is only the shadow cast in the eye.
just like what is cast in a camera, there is the play of the pupil in the eye. according to the shadow cast in the eye, a certain feeling or thought is generated in the mind. next, due to ignorance (*avijja*), it is stimulated and presented as a thing, causing the world to wander in *samsara*. at the furthest end of that train of thoughts lies that kind of collection of thought-conceptions (*vitakka*). closer to this side lies perception (*sanna*)—that recognition. past experiences help in that recognition. it is in association with them that one generates thoughts like: "ah, this is so-and-so, this is the person who did me such a wrong, this is the person who did this to me." it is by relying on those past perceptions (*sanna*) that these recognitions and so forth are made.
so, the buddha shows that a train of thoughts going in that manner is like a deer running after a mirage. instead of that, what does the wise person do? sitting right there, they understand the true nature of this mirage. likewise, the buddha declares that one should try to gain a true understanding of the objects encountered by these six doors. this is what is introduced in the dhamma as wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*).
wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*) means making an effort to understand by directing the mind to the very source where something arises. what that deer does is forget the place of arising. not knowing that it arose due to a defect or limitation in its own eyes, it mistakes that far-away mirage for a real thing, as water, and runs after it.
but it is shown in the dhamma that the root here is ignorance (*avijja*), the lack of knowing that this is something arising due to a collection of causes and conditions (*hetu-paccaya*). that train of thoughts grows as quickly as possible. once it goes into thoughts (*vitakka*), and after getting entangled in them, after getting entangled as conceptual proliferation (*papanca*), one ultimately spends one's time daydreaming.
the buddha points out that without grasping it in terms of signs (*nimitta*), the practitioner of insight (*vipassaka*), or the meditator engaged in insight (*vipassana*), should try to end that reflection right there by noting the seen object generally as "a form, a form." one ends it by taking it into the mind twice as "a form, a form," not letting it go beyond that. "a form, a form." likewise, "a sound, a sound." one does not go to analyze it. one does not even try to generate thoughts (*vitakka*), generate conceptual proliferation (*papanca*), or conjure daydreams about it.
"this is merely a certain form cast on the screen of the eye, or just a vision." next, "that is merely a sound striking the eardrum, only a certain vibration or movement striking the eardrum." in that manner, in a way that becomes wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*), one directs the mind back to the place where it arose. that is an extremely difficult task. for that, one must have a highly concentrated mind. to unify the mind with a concentrated mind and break it off right there in that manner, equanimity (*upekkha*) is truly necessary—a state of neutrality. releasing the mind as much as possible from the two extremes of attraction and repulsion, reflecting on it right there...
truly, these are things that come and go. but it is through holding and grasping (*upadana*) them, and further accumulating various things on top of them, that the journey of *samsara* takes place, and one gets caught in the momentum of *kamma*. instead, the buddha brings this sense-base as quickly as possible to a much simpler state. although described as simple, what takes place there is a going deep.
the ordinary world says they live in that manner because living in the conventional world of daily life requires it. but what happens through that is that one keeps spinning on and on in *samsara*. however, at some point, this understanding must be gained. it is for this reason that the buddha advises us to apply attention (*manasikara*) subtly and bring the mind to equanimity (*upekkha*) as quickly as possible.
so, in that manner, without even letting it proceed to perception (*sanna*), ultimately that feeling (*vedana*), that experiencing... this feeling also has two sides. you all know them as pleasant and painful. in the middle of those two, there lies one called neither-painful-nor-pleasant (*adukkhamasukha*). the ordinary world does not even understand it, because it is of a nature that is not easily grasped by the mind. regarding the neutral, there is mostly a lack of understanding. there is ignorance (*avijja*) regarding neutral feeling (*vedana*).
that neutral feeling can be revealed and recognized bit by bit when practicing the establishments of mindfulness (*satipatthana*). applying mindfulness well to one's body, to feeling (*vedana*), to the mind, and to the thoughts that enter the mind, living in the present moment and maintaining mindfulness (*sati*), behold, one understands: there is a thing called pleasant feeling (*vedana*), there is painful feeling, and there is also a neutral, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. it is in the middle of these, indeed, that we find the path to liberation (*vimutti*). that is the place for equanimity (*upekkha*).
equanimity (*upekkha*) means looking with neutral impartiality. that is an extremely difficult task. but the insight-practitioner (*vipassaka*), putting in effort, releases the mind from those two extremes of attraction and repulsion and watches how they come and go right there. now, if you are waiting on the roadside and there is a vehicle you are expecting, you look at it with great interest. but if a vehicle goes by for which you have no particular liking or disliking, you see it coming, and you see it going. if it is nighttime, you see the headlights in front, and next, you see the taillights behind—that is all.
just like that, without grasping those strange signs, reflecting on those incoming objects right then and there to end them, the method of rapid reflection is what the buddha points out as insight (*vipassana*). as one goes on practicing in this way, at some point the realization dawns: "behold, isn't this displaying a non-existent thing? isn't this mind projecting a non-existent thing as if it exists?" that cannot be demonstrated to another; it is something one must directly experience (*pratyaksa*) oneself, having traveled along that path of insight.
so, that is exactly why the buddha pointed out form as a lump of foam and so forth through those similes. ultimately, this is an illusion, something displayed by a magician. because if we take it as "i", we recognize the things of that world beyond it, give them names, and generate attraction and repulsion regarding them. that might be helpful for life in the conventional world. but it does not help in escaping from *samsara*. it is not that. that is a subordination to the physical eye.
if so, instead of that, the buddha points out that one must gradually bring forth insight-wisdom (*vipassana-panna*). it is to that wisdom, as declared by the buddha, that these five aggregates (*pancakkhandha*) are understood as entirely suffering (*dukkha*). what is meant by saying the five aggregates are entirely suffering (*dukkha*)? a far broader meaning than what the ordinary world calls suffering is conveyed in this statement. one sees its impermanence (*aniccata*). there is only a multitude of movements here. wherever any of these is grasped, there is suffering (*dukkha*).
therefore, what is to be done here is to reflect on each and every thing as it comes, and firmly cultivate dispassion (*viraga*), non-attachment toward them. going forward in that manner, ultimately, at some point, no matter which of these comes, a state that withstands them—an equanimity regarding preparations (*sankharupekkha*)—arises. thus, seeing the three characteristics (*tilakkhana*) as impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and unsubstantial (*anatta*), one must engage in attention (*manasikara*) deeper and deeper.
truly, in everything, this is not the work done by that meditator who went to the edge of the pond in the story we told earlier; this is not a saying, but a seeing. a seeing with the eye of wisdom. through that, wisdom having matured, at some point one sees in all of this...
that is a state where, even though the eyes, ears, nose, etc., exist and one is wide awake, one is not caught by the objects perceived so far; a state where their emptiness (*sunnata*) is understood. that is what is called the cessation of becoming (*bhava-nirodha*). that is to say, in the ordinary world there is the continuation of becoming (*bhava*); the cessation of this continuation is shown by the buddha in this very manner. that is something to be directly experienced through wisdom.
so, if anyone has obtained that direct experience, they are a stream-enterer (*sotapanna*), once-returner (*sakadagami*), non-returner (*anagami*), or at the highest, an arahant. that very direct experience is what is called the concentration of the fruit of arahantship (*arahattaphala-samadhi*) and so forth. in that concentration, that meditator can experience the liberation (*vimutti*) they have attained—liberation from *samsara*. one can spend a considerable amount of time in the bliss of that liberation. that is what is called nibbana in this very life—*dittheva dhamme*. having attained nibbana in this very life means deeply understanding, through that wisdom, the voidness (*sunnata*) and emptiness of this world visible to us. the importance of that understanding truly emerges at the moment of death.
you, pious devotees, have also heard about the signs that appear to a dying person, such as the sign of *kamma* (*kamma-nimitta*) and the sign of destiny (*gati-nimitta*). when the person struggling between life and death realizes that they can no longer hold onto this side, something else is presented to the mind: "here, then, hold onto this." driven by the momentum of past *kamma*, something comes forward according to *kamma*.
what is meant by struggling between life and death in this life? one struggles to remain in this very world. but this body cannot withstand it. an occasion comes when one must leave this behind. yet, due to the attachment to this, due to the attachment to the cage of this body, one struggles to remain right here because of that craving (*tanha*). grasping (*upadana*) means holding on. when the moment comes when one clearly understands that one has to let go, another sign appears to the mind. so, one grasps that.
that might sometimes be the fires of hell (*apaya*). it might be the sign of the womb of an animal. but because of that desire for existence, that sign is tightly grasped by the mind. that is held as grasping (*upadana*). right there is becoming (*bhava*). thus, nowadays many people do not talk about the cessation of becoming (*bhava-nirodha*), but about something called an intermediate existence (*antarabhava*). but in truth, our attention should be focused on that very cessation of becoming (*bhava-nirodha*).
however, that cannot be thought out at that moment. as we said before, if one is a grandfather who has lived with attachment to children, wealth, and everything, and at the moment of death thinks, "i will gain a sudden understanding and bring this life to a state of non-arising," that will not work. one must directly experience (*pratyaksa*) it through wisdom while still alive. to the person who has directly experienced it through wisdom, at the moment of death, that mind of nibbana arises effortlessly.
the mind of nibbana is this cessation of becoming (*bhava-nirodha*). in short, the mind comes to the voidness, the emptiness of the continuation of becoming (*bhava*). the mind comes to voidness (*sunnata*). then, there is no attraction or repulsion there. such is indeed nibbana. those who have understood it in this very life enjoy that bliss of nibbana in this very life by way of concentration (*samadhi*). its ultimate, most valuable occasion is its spontaneous presentation at that moment of death we mentioned.
in the language of the ordinary world, that nibbana is like dying without dying. physically, one lives in this world. but with the mind, having understood the corelessness of this becoming (*bhava*), one lets go of these five aggregates (*pancakkhandha*). one is holding onto the five aggregates with the mind. no one is holding onto the five aggregates with their physical hands. with what does one hold them? with the mind. one holds them as grasping (*upadana*) because of craving (*tanha*). where there is craving, there is grasping.
words like "the destruction of craving" (*tanha-nirodha*) are used to describe nibbana. when that craving is destroyed, if that lack of holding is directly experienced in this very life, then at the time when this body must truly be abandoned, such a state presents itself effortlessly. at that moment, it emerges spontaneously because it has been practiced beforehand, or because one has directly experienced it. because of the most valuable direct experience obtained in life, it presents itself effortlessly. that is the state of the cessation of becoming (*bhava-nirodha*).
it is mentioned that an arahant sometimes passes away (*parinibbana by setting fire to their own body. a person might get frightened: "what is this? alas, what a great suffering (*dukkha*) they endured!" even you, pious devotees, sometimes throw an abandoned set of clothing into a fire to burn it. at that moment, you do not feel that you yourself are burning. just like that, having abandoned these five aggregates from the mind itself, they set fire to it by entering into the attainment of the fire element (*tejo-dhatu-samapatti*). this, indeed, cannot be understood by the ordinary world.
in that manner, the highest liberation (*vimutti*) that can be achieved with the mind, the highest equanimity (*upekkha*), is what is called nibbana. the journey toward that is what is spoken of in this practice in various ways as virtue (*sila*), concentration (*samadhi*), wisdom (*panna*), and as calm (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassana*). if you, pious devotees, have understood that goal correctly, if you travel on that path correctly, if your perfections (*parami*) are fulfilled, if the effort you make is correct, and if you have the association of noble friends (*kalyana-mitta*) correctly, it is still possible to directly experience these.
we must apply our wisdom and contemplate both of these lessons shown in this story. in the world, there have always been two aspects called good and bad. there are two aspects called merit and demerit, wholesome (*kusala*) and unwholesome (*akusala*). what the buddha did was make these understood. he introduced the dark side and the bright side. these members of the sangha—the ordained ones—are those who come from the lay world itself. it is by developing certain virtues while in that lay world, and subsequently by their maturing, that they gradually enter the ordained life.
even if we contemplate lay life, virtues such as gratitude are important. through them, gradually gaining a deep understanding of one's life, at some point, whether in the ordained life like bahuputtika theri or in lay life, one must cultivate that equanimity (*upekkha*). cultivating equanimity, one must understand this nature—the nature of decay (*jara*) and unsubstantiality (*anatta*)—which means that none of these can be kept under one's control. one must understand this.
using old age as an aid, as one loses attachment to this body, recognizing it as something that must be abandoned, something that one will have to abandon, one becomes able to directly experience through wisdom the state of destroying or letting go of that craving (*tanha*) which remained unappeased in this mind for so long. if at any moment one has abandoned these five aggregates (*pancakkhandha*) from the mind itself, the bliss received at that moment is what we point to as the supremely peaceful bliss of nibbana—it is called "unfelt bliss" (*avedayita-sukha*). every other pleasure obtained in the world in connection with feeling (*vedana*) was pointed out by the buddha as suffering (*dukkha*). that painful feeling is suffering (*dukkha*) needs no special explanation. that pleasant feeling is suffering is understood when it changes. neutral feeling is not felt at all. the buddha points out a vision of not grasping even a single one of these.
for that, starting with the neutral feeling (*vedana*) mentioned at the beginning, as one gradually goes deeper, at some point the corelessness and impermanence (*aniccata*) of these are understood. there, within the six sense-bases (*salayatana*), without letting them proceed to thoughts (*vitakka*) and so on, one sees them as quickly as possible at the minimal level. all of this occurs due to the collision between the two divided aspects: the eye and the form. next, creating two aspects as the ear and the sound, all of this occurs due to their collision.
now, people play games by dividing into two sides. it is because the two sides are divided that the entire game exists. just like that, one creates two sides: "this is the eye" and "this is the form." this can be understood from the story of the deer. thus, thinking "this is the eye, this is the form," one runs after it. thinking "this is the ear, this is the sound," next one goes after it. at some point, escaping from that kind of situation is what is called the stilling of preparations (*sankhara-upasama*). the buddha points out that these preparations (*sankhara*) are indeed the greatest suffering (*dukkha*).
there is an occasion when this very preparation taking place in the mind is deeply understood as suffering (*dukkha*). it is that cessation of preparations (*sankhara-nirodha*) that the buddha points out. if there is no such preparation, there is no aspect of their result (*vipaka*) either. it ends right there. now, why are they called *kamma*-born preparations? it is because these *kamma* accumulated by us over a long period are what, moment by moment, through our consciousness (*vinnana*)... if one turns every single one of them to equanimity (*upekkha*) and lets them go, they pass away without being grasped; right there is liberation (*vimutti*).
so, there is an instruction in this verse necessary for traveling on this path of dhamma, which says that living even a single day seeing that supreme dhamma is enough. even if one does not become a grandfather or a grandmother, it does not matter; if one lives even a single day and directly experiences (*pratyaksa*) that, one must understand that as the truly valuable life. thus, today, this pious group of people has undertaken virtue (*sila*) to some level that supports this path, and it is by establishing yourselves in that virtue that you perform all of this. next, you have also practiced meditation (*bhavana*) according to your capacity.
indeed, if there is a listener who listens with the attention (*manasikara*) of meditation even during a dhamma-hearing, one can even generate knowledges (*nana*) through that, if the power of one's perfections (*parami*) is present. in that very manner, you have listened to a dhamma sermon that supports your life and supports this nibbana.
if through this, any powers such as faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*)—which assist nibbana as mental powers—have arisen, may this wholesome deed of hearing the dhamma (*dhamma-savana-maya-kusala*), by relying on those powers and with the support of the association of noble friends (*kalyana-mitta*), definitely be a supportive condition for this pious group to attain, as quickly as possible during this era of the decline of the buddha's dispensation (*buddha-sasana*), before the dispensation declines, liberation from the dangerous suffering (*dukkha*) of *samsara* including birth (*jati*), decay/aging (*jara*), sickness, and death (*marana*) through the penetration of the paths and fruits (*magga-phala-pativedha*) of stream-entry (*sotapanna*), once-returning (*sakadagami*), non-returning (*anagami*), and arahantship, and to realize the supreme, deathless great nibbana!
likewise, may whoever wishes to rejoice in this wholesome merit of delivering and hearing the dhamma, including our relatives from the avici hell up to the akanittha heaven, by rejoicing in it, realize the supreme, deathless great nibbana as quickly as possible through their aspired bodhi (awakening)! wishing thus, please recite this verse.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 103
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #103
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.90)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Tapena brahmacariyena, saṃyamena damena ca;
Etena brāhmaṇo hoti, etaṃ brāhmaṇamuttamaṃ.
From:
Dhammapada 422 (Brāhmaṇavagga)
Dear Listeners,
According to social convention, a person’s superiority or inferiority is often measured by the social environment into which they are born. The rigid caste discrimination that was prevalent in India during the Buddha’s time was also based on this matter of *Jāti* (Birth). The view accepted at that time was that one becomes an outcast (*vasala*) or a brahmin solely by *Jāti* (Birth). However, the Supreme Buddha, the Teacher of the Three Worlds, demonstrated to the world that instead of *Jāti* (Birth), it is practice (*paṭipatti*) that should be the yardstick for measuring a person’s high or low standing. Moreover, he provided a living example of this.
The verse we have taken as our theme was delivered on such an occasion. There lived in the city of Rājagaha a very poor man named Sunīta, who was born into an extremely low caste, a despised clan, and worked as a scavenger. His occupation was collecting the street sweepings and refuse of the city. One morning, as the Blessed One surveyed the world with his Attainment of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*), he saw that Sunīta possessed the spiritual potential and supportive conditions (*upanissaya-sampatti*) for attaining Arahantship. Seeing this, the Blessed One, accompanied by the community of monks, went on his alms-round to the street in Rājagaha where Sunīta was sweeping refuse. Seeing the Blessed One approaching, Sunīta felt a certain devotion, put aside his carrying-pole of refuse, came near the Blessed One, and paid homage. The Blessed One asked: "Sunīta, what is the use of this miserable life? Would it not be better to ordain?" Sunīta replied: "Who would ordain someone like us? If such ordination is possible, may the Blessed One ordain me." Then the Blessed One said: "Come, monk!" (*Ehi bhikkhu!*). This was the special method of higher ordination (*upasampadā*) that the Buddha granted to exceptional individuals. Through those two words alone—by the mere utterance of "Come, monk!"—the higher ordination was granted to that scavenger Sunīta, born of a low caste. The Buddha then took him along and gave him meditation objects (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Not long after, Venerable Sunīta retired to the forest, practiced absorption (*jhāna*) and meditation, attained the five higher knowledges (*pañcābhiññā*), the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭha-samāpatti*), and realized Arahantship. He realized Arahantship during the last watch of the night. At that moment, Sakka, the devas, and the Brahma kings came to pay homage to Venerable Sunīta, the great Arahant. Witnessing this with his divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*), the Blessed One smiled. It is mentioned that the Blessed One would smile under special circumstances. Smiling, he uttered this very verse that we have taken as our theme:
*"Tapena brahmacariyena, saṃyamena damena ca;*
*Etena brāhmaṇo hoti, etaṃ brāhmaṇamuttamaṃ."*
By spiritual burning (*tapas*), by the holy life (*brahmacariya*)—that noble way of life—by restraint (*saṃyama*), by the self-control developed through moral virtue (*sīla*), and by sense-restraint (*indriya-damana*); it is through these that one becomes a true brahmin. *"Etena brāhmaṇo hoti, etaṃ brāhmaṇamuttamaṃ"*—this true brahminhood, this state of being a brahmin, is indeed supreme and noble. This is the meaning contained in the verse.
Perhaps the Blessed One smiled because, looking at it from one perspective, Sunīta the scavenger had performed the ultimate act of scavenging. What is that? He washed away all the dirt and filth of defilements (*kilesa*) that had accumulated in his mind-stream over a long journey in *saṃsāra*. We can draw the meaning that Sunīta, who had been cleaning the physical refuse of others in the city, had now eradicated his own mental defilements, thus bringing the scavenger’s occupation to its true consummation. If the term "brahminhood" is used to denote superiority, it is because he fulfilled these virtues—spiritual burning, the holy life, restraint, and self-control. It was by completing these that he became a true brahmin. The Blessed One preached this verse to show this and to set an example for the world.
The past karma underlying this event is also recorded in the texts. In the past, Sunīta was a person of great merit, but on one occasion, during a period when fully enlightened Buddhas did not arise but Paccekabuddhas dwelt in the world, he was born into a wealthy, high-caste family. While wandering through the village for amusement with youths of his own age, he saw a Paccekabuddha walking for alms and insulted him, saying, "Why is he walking for alms wrapping a cloth all over his body? Is his body covered in sores?" As a bad consequence of this, he suffered in hell for a very long period and was subsequently born in poverty in low and despised castes for hundreds of human lifetimes. Despite these social conventions, we can clearly see from this that the Blessed One did not accept social conventions regarding high and low distinctions.
This matter is very clearly expressed in a discourse preached to Pahārāda. On one occasion, the Blessed One delivered a discourse to Pahārāda, the chief of the Asuras, comparing this Dispensation of the Buddha (*Sambhuddha-sāsana*), this community of monks (*Saṅgha-sāsana*), to the great ocean. He compared eight wonderful and marvelous qualities of this Dispensation to eight wonderful and marvelous qualities of the great ocean. The fourth of these was presented as follows: Just as the great rivers, such as the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī, upon reaching the great ocean, discard their former names and lineages, and are simply designated as the great ocean, so too, those of the Khattiya, Brāhmaṇa, Vessa, and Sudda castes, when they leave the household life and go forth into homelessness in this Dispensation, no longer use their former caste designations. Instead, they are known simply as "Sakyaputtas" (ascetics of the Sakyan son). In this way, the practice of the Dispensation was clearly stated. The Buddha’s stand against caste discrimination, which appeared as a sort of social revolution, sometimes brought various insults upon the Buddha himself from the brahmins.
A special discourse mentioning this is the *Vasala Sutta*. Many of you may have heard of it to some extent. One day, the brahmin Aggika Bhāradvāja was performing a fire-sacrifice at his house. At that time, the Blessed One, walking in sequence for alms, arrived at the brahmin’s house. Seeing this, the brahmin said: "Stop right there, bald-headed monk, you outcast (*vasala*)!" Then the Blessed One asked: "Brahmin, do you know what an outcast is, or what makes one an outcast?" "I do not know. If possible, let Master Gotama teach me," he invited. Thereupon, the Blessed One delivered a lengthy discourse. Without mentioning every single detail, in brief, he touched upon all the prevalent evils, corruptions, immoralities, and vices of society, presenting each one of them as a quality that makes one an outcast. Having done so, he delivered the concluding verse, which almost everyone has heard:
*"Na jaccā vasalo hoti, na jaccā hoti brāhmaṇo;*
*Kammanā vasalo hoti, kammanā hoti brāhmaṇo."*
One does not become an outcast by *Jāti* (Birth), nor does one become a brahmin by *Jāti* (Birth). By karma one becomes an outcast, by karma one becomes a brahmin. Since the word "karma" is used here, some might misunderstand it. Because we mentioned a past story earlier, one might assume that "karma" here refers to past karma. However, there is no room for such an interpretation because, immediately after uttering this verse, the Blessed One provides an illustration to show what is meant by "karma." He says, "Here, I will give an illustration to show that it is by karma that one becomes an outcast or a brahmin." What is this illustration? It is connected to a Jātaka story.
The outcaste named Mātaṅga, though born as a Caṇḍāla, practiced absorption (*jhāna*) and meditation, developed direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), and acquired the power to perform great wonders and miracles. He received service and honor from kings and brahmins alike, and even devas and Brahmas came to serve him. After death, he was reborn in the Brahma world. This is shown as the conclusion, indicating that *Jāti* (Birth) is no barrier to birth in the Brahma world. At the same time, the opposite side is also shown.
If, on the other hand, brahmins engage in evil deeds, they will be censured and blamed as a consequence of those evil deeds, and they will go to a state of misery. Their *Jāti* (Birth) as a brahmin is not capable of preventing censure or rebirth in a state of misery. From this, it is abundantly clear to us that what is meant here is one's course of action. "Karma" means one's course of action, one's practice. It is according to one's course of action that one becomes an outcast or a brahmin, and not by *Jāti* (Birth). In this way, the Blessed One expounded that fundamental principle.
Furthermore, another valuable discourse mentions many points relevant to this, concerning two young brahmins. One youth was named Vāseṭṭha, and the other Bhāradvāja. While walking along the road conversing, chatting, and discussing, a topic of dispute arose between them: "How does one become a brahmin?" In this regard, the young brahmin Bhāradvāja said: "If one is of pure *Jāti* (Birth) on both the mother's and father's side back for seven generations, with no reproach or slur cast upon one's *Jāti* (Birth) or lineage, then one is called a brahmin." But the young brahmin Vāseṭṭha said: "No, one becomes a brahmin through virtue (*sīla*) and conduct. One who possesses virtue and vows is a true brahmin." The two of them argued, but they could not come to a decision. Later, Vāseṭṭha suggested: "The ascetic Gotama is staying over there. A great report of good reputation has spread concerning this ascetic Gotama: 'Indeed, he is the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Awakened One...' Let us go to the ascetic Gotama, and however he explains this matter, so shall we accept it." They went to the Blessed One and presented their dispute, saying: "There is this debate between us."
Then the Blessed One said: "Very well, Vāseṭṭha, I will explain this to you in due order, systematically." In an astonishingly comprehensive manner, he presented points that broke down the foundation of caste discrimination. Grass, plants, trees, and creepers—all of these assume various forms according to their origin, their *Jāti* (Birth). There, a distinction of species (*jāti-bheda*) exists. They exhibit diversity based on their *Jāti* (Birth). When we speak of trees and creepers, there is a distinction of species. Similarly, among small insects, quadrupeds, birds, snakes, and fish in the sea, there is diversity in their bodily features. This is so among animals. But among human beings...
...among human beings, there is no such significant difference. When we consider human beings, to classify them into castes or show diversity, there is no substantial difference in their limbs, ears, noses, hands, or feet. The Blessed One points out that human beings constitute a single species (*jāti*). Thus, based on facts that can be described in biological terms, the Blessed One declares that there is no such diversity among human beings as there is among animals, trees, and plants. Therefore, there is no room for the kind of racism or casteism based on *Jāti* (Birth) that the brahmins put forward.
Furthermore, he shows that a difference is not determined by *Jāti* (Birth). Now, in the world, there is a conventional way of showing diversity. How? One who makes a living by farming should not be called a "brahmin," but a "farmer." Even if a brahmin does farming, he should be called a "farmer." One who lives by various crafts should be called a "craftsman." One who engages in trade, whether born as a brahmin or an outcast, should be called a "merchant." One who lives by warfare, as his livelihood, is called a "soldier." One who steals should be called a "thief," not a brahmin or an outcast, but a "thief." One who performs priestly duties is called a "sacrificer" (*yājaka*)—*yājaka* means one who prays or petitions; that is the proper designation for him, not "brahmin." One who rules is called a "king." This is the true sense of how conventions exist in society: it is according to the karma one performs. Here we see that "karma" refers to the course of action, the process of activity. However, many people think of this as past karma. In reality, karma is a present-moment thing connected to intention (*cetanā*). Now, in our ordinary daily usage, what we refer to as "karma" is often "karmic result" (*kamma-vipāka*). We loosely refer to the result of karma as "karma." But we must understand that karma is always a present-moment phenomenon. After showing these facts regarding *Jāti* (Birth) to the young brahmin Vāseṭṭha, the Buddha further declared: "If the term 'brahmin' truly means 'noble,' then that word should only be applied to an Arahant." Having thus described the vast qualities of an Arahant, he finally presented a short but extraordinarily profound principle as a cosmic law (*niyāma-dhamma*):
*"Kammanā vattati loko, kammanā vattati pajā;*
*Kammanibandhanā sattā, rathassāṇīva yāyato."*
Since that verse is highly meaningful, we highlighted it in particular. *"Kammanā vattati loko"* — the entire world proceeds by karma. *"Kammanā vattati pajā"* — all generations of beings proceed according to karma, with karma as their fundamental principle. *"Sattā"* — beings are bound to karma in one way or another. Here is the simile for that: *"Rathassāṇīva yāyato"* — like the linchpin of a moving chariot. We can gather many insights from this.
The linchpin of a moving chariot is what allows the wheel to turn. If we think about society in this way, nowadays words like "progress" are used to describe forward movement. The Blessed One highlighted a principle that allows for such progress. What if, instead of karma, we took *Jāti* (Birth) as the linchpin? The journey would come to a halt. One cannot change one’s *Jāti* (Birth). But one can change one's karma. A person who was a thief can abandon theft and do good things; a farmer can become a merchant. Thus, because karma is a process of action, a person can change. Instead of the rigid, unbending principle of *Jāti* (Birth) or origin that existed in society, the Blessed One highlighted a flexible, adaptable principle that leads to progress. This principle is important sociologically regarding occupations, and ethically regarding actions such as theft. Ethics refer to matters of good and bad. These, too, fall under the broad term of "karma." Each of these is like that linchpin. The development and existence of the entire society are connected to it. The Buddha presented this special principle in this manner.
Similarly, matters related to this karma are mentioned in other discourses. Another instance is shown where a brahmin insulted the Blessed One. One morning, the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja was performing a fire-sacrifice, making burnt offerings, by the river Sundarikā. The Blessed One saw that the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja possessed the supportive conditions (*upanissaya-sampatti*) to attain Arahantship. Therefore, the Blessed One went to that place beforehand and sat meditating at the foot of a tree with his head covered. The brahmin, having offered the milk-rice to the Great Brahma, thought of giving the remainder to some other brahmin. Since brahmins consider themselves sons of Brahma, he thought: "Having offered to the father, I must now give the remainder to a son," and looked around. He saw someone sitting with his head covered. Thinking, "Perhaps this is a brahmin meditating through the night," he approached. As he came close, the Blessed One uncovered his head. Seeing him, the brahmin exclaimed, "Alas, this is a bald-headed ascetic!" and turned to go back. Then he thought, "Even though his head is shaved, he might still be a brahmin. In any case, I should go and ask about his birth, his *Jāti* (Birth)." He went up and asked: "Sir, what is your birth? What is your *jāti* (birth)?" Then the Blessed One declared: "I am neither a brahmin, nor a king's son, nor a merchant, nor of any other caste. Having departed from the household and social affairs, I live unattached to the world, observing virtues." Through the conversation that followed, a certain faith arose in the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja. He then invited the Blessed One: "Then let Master Gotama tell me who is worthy of receiving the remainder of this sacrificial milk-rice, the one to whom it should be given to gain the true benefit." At that moment, the Blessed One declared: "In that case, brahmin, abandon the habit of asking about *Jāti* (Birth). Do not ask about *Jāti* (Birth). Ask about conduct." He uttered the principle: *"Mā jātiṃ puccha, caraṇaṃyapi puccha"* — "Do not ask about *Jāti* (Birth); ask rather about conduct."
In those days, there was a practice that you, dear devotees, might not be familiar with. Today, we strike a match from a matchbox and instantly get fire. In ancient times, producing fire was not that easy. One had to rub two dry pieces of wood together for a long time to generate fire. This is the simile used here: no matter what kind of wood is used, there is no difference in the fire produced. Whatever the type of wood, when rubbed together, the fire that springs up from them has no difference. That is the simile given here. Analyzing it further, he declared that just as there is no difference in the fire regardless of the wood from which it arises, so too there is no difference when a person of a low caste, having cultivated those virtues, reaches the noble state—that is, becomes a true brahmin. In that context, in a manner that broke the foundation of caste discrimination, he described at length the qualities of an Arahant, and specifically of the Tathāgata. The Blessed One delivered a sermon stating: "The Tathāgata is one who possesses such and such virtues, such and such merits; he indeed is the true brahmin. It is to one with such virtues that the remainder of the sacrificial milk-rice should be offered." It might seem as though the Blessed One was praising his own virtues. However, he did not say this to obtain the milk-rice. Having heard all this, the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja felt great faith and said: "Then I am indeed fortunate to have seen the Blessed One. Please, may the Blessed One accept this milk-rice." The Blessed One rejected it, saying: "Milk-rice obtained by chanting verses is not suitable for me. Buddhas reject such food. Offer it to some other Arahant who has destroyed the cankers (*khīṇāsava*)." The Blessed One preached the Dhamma on that occasion solely to guide the brahmin to Arahantship; he did not praise his own virtues for the sake of a little milk-rice. This is the custom of the Buddhas. He rejected it, saying that they do not accept what is obtained by chanting verses. In the end, the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja did not merely take refuge in the Triple Gem as a lay disciple (*upāsaka*), but ultimately requested ordination and even attained Arahantship. Thus, in this instance too, the Buddha's view on caste discrimination is clearly demonstrated.
On another occasion, while King Pasenadi of Kosala was having a Dhamma discussion with the Blessed One, he asked a question: "If people from the four castes—Khattiya, Brāhmaṇa, Vessa, and Sudda—ordain and exert intense energy (*viriya*), practicing meditation and striving hard, is there any difference in the result they achieve based on their castes?" The Blessed One declared: "No, the liberation (*vimutti*) they attain is one and the same. Whether one is an outcaste or a brahmin, after ordaining, if one exerts sufficient energy, there is no difference in the liberation they achieve." In that context, the Blessed One presented the simile of fire in greater detail: "Just as, O Great King, if a fire is produced by rubbing two pieces of Sal wood, another by rubbing two pieces of Mango wood, and another by rubbing two pieces of Fig wood, is there any difference in the color or the light of the fires?" "No." "In the same way, from whatever caste one goes forth, if one fulfills the Dhamma, there is no difference in one's liberation." This practice of the purity of all four castes was put into effect against the Brahmin view.
It is called "purity of the four castes" (*catuvaṇṇi-visuddhi*). The Buddha's stance was that all four castes are pure. "Pure" means that people of all four castes can attain purification. Among the brahmins, there was a dogmatic view that only brahmins could attain purification, and those of other castes could not. The Blessed One showed that regardless of one's caste, if one fulfills the necessary conditions, one can attain purification. The Blessed One declared that this truly wonderful, liberating practice, which allows purification for all four castes, exists within this Dispensation.
These statements of the Blessed One caused great displeasure among the brahmins. So much so, that brahmins from various regions gathered in the city of Sāvatthī and held a large meeting, like a symposium. On that occasion, they discussed: "The ascetic Gotama has put forward this principle of the purity of the four castes, which goes against our brahminical views. Who among us is capable of debating with the ascetic Gotama on this?" In Sāvatthī itself, there lived a sixteen-year-old young brahmin named Assalāyana. He was a young scholar (*māṇava*) well-versed in the Vedas. Deciding that he was the most suitable person to debate with Master Gotama, they went to meet the young brahmin Assalāyana and invited him, saying: "You are highly skilled. You are capable of debating with Master Gotama regarding his view that all four castes are pure and capable of attaining purification." But Assalāyana said: "The ascetic Gotama speaks according to the Dhamma. It is not easy to debate with someone who speaks according to the Dhamma," and he refused. They invited him a second and a third time, urging him strongly. When he refused the third time, they said: "Why admit defeat even before going to battle? Go and do it." Thus, Assalāyana said: "Since you all insist, I shall go." Accompanied by a large crowd of brahmins, he went to the Blessed One and presented the brahminical view: "Our brahmins say this: 'The brahmins alone are the highest caste. Only brahmins can attain ultimate purification. Brahmins are the true children of Brahma, born from Brahma's mouth, created by Brahma...'" In this way, he presented the brahminical dogma.
At that moment, the Blessed One refuted the arguments presented step-by-step. First, he pointed out: "These brahmins claim to be born of Brahma, yet they know very well that brahmin women give birth to children. Knowing this, to make such a claim is not logical." He also pointed out that this caste distinction is not a universally applicable classification, because in regions like Yona and Kamboja, you all know that there are only two classes: masters (*ariya*) and servants (*dāsa*). These are not proper names; there are masters, and there is a class of servants. The *ariyas*—meaning noble or superior—are the bosses, and the *dāsas* are the subordinates. Let us think of it like that. The Buddha added: "However, a change can occur there. One who was a master becomes a servant, and one who was a servant becomes a master." We can imagine a war or conflict where the masters are defeated and the servants come to the forefront. Then the servants become masters, and the others become servants.
