the ordinary world expects to win the battle of life through unrighteous means. in a society that is largely inclined towards unrighteousness, finding a solution to arising problems through unrighteousness itself seems to us to be the easy way. yet, the buddha taught that this battle of life must indeed be won, and a true victory achieved, through the path of dhamma. to achieve victory through that path of dhamma, sometimes one may even have to make a great sacrifice. even if one has to make such a sacrifice, the final result, the victory obtained through it, brings a deep peace that is hundreds of thousands of times more valuable than the victory won through unrighteous means. the advice given by this verse we have chosen as our theme today, as well as the example provided by the background story related to it, will explain this very principle of victory.
in the city of rajagaha, the financier punna, his wife, and their daughter named uttara were all three devoted lay-disciples who had attained the stage of stream-entry (*sotapanna*)—noble disciples. in the same city of rajagaha, the financier sumana held wrong views. this financier proposed a marriage for his son with uttara. punna was reluctant; he expressed his opposition, saying, "i cannot give my daughter to such a clan of wrong views. she cannot live separated from the triple gem." however, due to the pressure of many people, he finally gave his consent and married his daughter to the son of the financier sumana on the full-moon day of asalha. from the day she went to her husband's home, she had no opportunity to see a monk or a nun, to give alms (*dana*), or to hear the dhamma. since she was a very devout person, she spent about two and a half months in great sorrow because of being deprived of seeing the triple gem, to which she was accustomed. by then, the rainy retreat (*vassa*) was drawing to a close. she sent a message to her father: "why have you betrayed me into such a prison? it would have been better if i were made a maidservant rather than being married off to a household of wrong views. i have no opportunity to perform alms-givings, to hear the dhamma, or even to see the monks, nuns, and the blessed one." when she sent this very sorrowful message, what did the financier do? thinking of a solution, he sent fifteen thousand *kahapanas*. he instructed her to hire sirima, a courtesan of rajagaha who charged one thousand per day, hand her over to her husband, and thereby obtain permission for herself to perform acts of merit and alms-giving for a fortnight. this was a surprising proposal and idea, of a kind that a father would not normally make. uttara also accepted it with great joy, went to meet sirima, arranged this transaction, and handed her over to her husband, saying, "during these two weeks, i will be engaged in offering alms and other duties to the sangha led by the buddha, and in listening to the dhamma. this woman will serve as your companion." having made these arrangements, uttara went to the blessed one and invited him, saying, "please accept alms by coming to our home, to this alms-hall, along with the sangha for this entire fortnight." the blessed one, perhaps considering the great sacrifice made, consented and visited daily for alms accordingly.
thus, as the two weeks went by, the final day approached. right at the end of the rainy retreat, on the day before the great pavarana day, uttara's husband came to the window facing the kitchen or the alms-hall and looked at what this woman was doing. he saw her covered in soot and sweat, busy organizing the alms-giving. he smiled mockingly, thinking, "oh, what a foolish woman! covered in soot and dirt, she is busy serving the monks, abandoning such luxury and wealth." he smiled in derision. sirima, who was standing nearby, saw this. she saw that when he came and looked through the window, he was smiling at uttara. at that moment, she forgot for a while that she was an outsider. just as it happens in households in such situations, a severe jealousy arose in her. anger arose. driven by that anger, she entered the alms-hall or kitchen of the mansion, approached the pot of boiling ghee on the hearth used for frying sweetmeats, took a ladleful of ghee with a coconut-shell ladle, and came to pour it over uttara’s head. as she was coming, uttara saw by her manner that she was coming to do such a thing. what did she do? she suffused sirima with a mind of loving-kindness (*metta*). "this friend of mine has done me such a great favor by giving me the opportunity to perform these alms-offerings to the sangha led by the buddha. the entire universe is not spacious enough, and the brahma-world is not high enough, to contain her virtue. she possesses a virtue so vast that it can fill the world. if there is indeed any anger in me towards her, may this ghee burn me. if there is no anger, may it not burn me." thus she made an assertion of truth (*saccakiriya*), relying on that very absorption of loving-kindness (*metta-jhana*). then, when that woman poured the boiling ghee, it was like cold water. nothing happened to her. so sirima thought perhaps the ghee was not hot enough. when she went back to the hearth to get another ladleful, the maidservants gathered, beat her thoroughly, threw her to the ground, and as they were preparing to beat her further, uttara herself stepped forward to stop them, washed her with compassion, applied oil, and comforted her.
at that moment, sirima felt a great sense of spiritual urgency (*samvega*): "alas, what a virtuous person is this, to whom i, an outsider, have brought harm out of jealousy and hatred!" she fell at her feet and begged for forgiveness. when she begged for forgiveness saying, "my head will split if i do not ask for forgiveness from such a person," uttara replied, "i am a daughter who has a father. i will forgive you only if my father forgives you." then sirima said, "very well, i will ask for forgiveness from the financier punna." uttara replied, "no, no. punna is the father who gave birth to me in samsara. the father who gave birth to me on the path to nibbana is the fully enlightened one. you must ask for forgiveness from him." when sirima asked, "how can i do that?", uttara said, "then, tomorrow when the blessed one visits, bring some alms that you have prepared. then you can obtain forgiveness."
thus, on the following day, when the blessed one arrived with the sangha, sirima too came with her attendant women, having prepared various alms. to participate in the alms-giving, she had uttara offer them to the blessed one on her behalf. finally, sirima fell prostrate before the blessed one to ask for forgiveness. when asked for the reason, she said, "this is what happened through me yesterday. uttara, who possesses such a wonderful and miraculous wealth of virtue, healed me instead of retaliating for what i did. she harbored no hatred whatsoever. then she told me to ask for forgiveness from the blessed one." the blessed one further questioned uttara about this: "uttara, what did you think when she was coming with that hot ghee?" she replied, "i thought in this way: regarding sirima's virtue—the help she rendered by providing me the opportunity to perform my alms-offerings and service to the buddha and sangha for two weeks—when considering that virtue, the universe is not spacious enough for it; it is something that rises higher than the brahma-world." she thus explained the assertion of truth she had made. at that moment, the buddha expressed his appreciation by saying, "sadhu, sadhu!" and declared: "that is how it should be done, uttara. this is the true practice of dhamma, the practice of victory through dhamma." to convey this idea, he uttered the verse mentioned earlier:
> *"akkodhena jine kodham, asadhum sadhuna jine,*
> *jine kadariyam danena, saccena alikavadinam."*
it is very simple:
* "akkodhena jine kodham" – one should conquer anger by non-anger.
* "asadhum sadhuna jine" – one should conquer the bad, or the unvirtuous person, by goodness or virtue.
* "jine kadariyam danena" – one should conquer the stingy person through giving (*dana*), by sharing what one owns.
* "saccena alikavadinam" – one should conquer the liar with truth.
it is mentioned that after listening to the sermon delivered along with that verse, even sirima, who was filled with remorse, despite having attempted such a grave wrong, attained stream-entry (*sotapanna*) along with her attendant women and the rest of the group.
indeed, after this event, in the suttas we see sirima engaged in serving the buddha and the sangha. thus, regardless of her profession, it is revealed that she achieved the state of stream-entry (*sotapanna*) and attained a great benefit in terms of the dispensation (*sasana*). looking at this story, one might think of it as a miraculous event almost impossible to believe in this day and age. in particular, we primarily see the virtue of uttara. how deep a faith must have existed within uttara and the financier punna to propose such a scheme or to implement such a course of action! she made a great sacrifice of a kind that a wife would not normally make—bringing and handing over another woman to her own husband. it was like handing her over in her own home, while she herself stayed in the kitchen, dedicating her time to serving the buddha and the sangha. looking at it from this perspective, we can imagine how deep a faith they must have had in the triple gem. moreover, we must especially contemplate the mind of loving-kindness (*metta*) mentioned here in relation to this incident. how deep a loving-kindness must have been present there! it is loving-kindness capable of showing such miracles that is called the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (*metta-cetovimutti*).
you have heard the word "liberation" (*vimutti*) in various ways. liberation means freedom, the idea of release. "liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*) means the freeing of the mind, the liberation of the mind. from what does it get released? when we think of loving-kindness, to achieve the liberation of mind through loving-kindness, one must remove the barriers and fences of anger. otherwise, the ordinary world lives within the fences of anger. when that is removed, next there is the fence regarding those who are dear to us. when that too is removed, then there is the fence regarding neutral people. when that too is removed, next there is the fence regarding hostile people. it is in the midst of many such fences that an ordinary person spends life, trapped within them. there is no liberation there. therefore, the purpose of this meditation, of the meditation on loving-kindness, the state of liberation of mind through loving-kindness, is to remove those barriers and fences, and to radiate the thought of well-being even towards an enemy, just as a mother would protect her only child, as shown in the *karaniyametta sutta*.
we see that uttara practically implemented this, because its benefits were received right there. in the *mettanisasa sutta*, the buddha points out eleven benefits of loving-kindness. one of them is:
*"nassa aggi va visam va sattham va kamati"* — fire, poison, or weapons do not harm the body of one who has practiced the liberation of mind through loving-kindness. that was proven by this story, by this incident. regarding that liberation of mind through loving-kindness, in the places where it is mentioned, the way it should be developed is described. a series of terms is shown there to describe the effort to bring the mind of loving-kindness to that state:
*"mettaya, bhikkhave, cetovimuttiya asevitaya, bhavitaya, bahulikataya, yanikataya, vatthukataya, anutthitaya, paricitaya, susamaraddhaya."*
this means that the mind of loving-kindness is not cultivated in a casual manner; it is frequently associated with—one constantly radiates the thought of loving-kindness, "may all be well." likewise, it is developed (*bhavitaya*). next, it is practiced abundantly (*bahulikataya*). *"yanikataya"* means making it into a vehicle. some people travel, as it were, on the vehicle of loving-kindness; they remain in a state of loving-kindness to that extent.
*"vatthukataya"* refers to *vatthu*, which means the plot of land needed when building a house. that plot can be taken as the foundation; one makes that mind of loving-kindness the foundation for everything. *"anutthitaya"* means being established in it, as if leaning on it, carrying out all one's activities in accordance with loving-kindness. *"paricitaya"* means practiced, habituated. and *"susamaraddhaya"* means well-undertaken. the buddha has stated that it is only when the mind of loving-kindness is well-cultivated in this manner that one should expect such benefits.
thus, the benefits of loving-kindness are shown. we all know that in the *karaniya sutta*, which is regularly chanted, what can easily be recalled by anyone as a meditation subject (*kammatthana*) is the thought: "may all beings be happy!" it is mentioned in the *karaniya sutta* as *"sabbe satta bhavantu sukhitatta"* — "may all beings be happy at heart." how deep that concept of "all" is, is clarified by a few words and phrases preceding it in the *karaniya sutta*. the way the buddha has presented it in the *karaniya sutta* is truly wondrous. in these times, when we cultivate loving-kindness, when we try to think of "all," we sometimes mix in the names of various nations and individuals. through that, without our even knowing, thoughts of hatred can arise. instead of that, the buddha presents them all as a whole, without exception (*niravasesa*), that is, leaving none out, approaching from different aspects and saying "all beings." if we take this as an illustration: *"ye keci panabhutatthi, tasa va thavara va anavasesa..."* — that first part. whatever living beings there are: *"tasa"* means those who tremble (the frail/fearful), *"thavara"* means the firm, stable, which can be taken as those who do not tremble (the strong). thus, those who tremble and those who do not tremble—all are gathered together. if we are to divide these groups as a whole, they can be taken under these two categories, according to their respective measures: either trembling, or stable to their respective degrees. *"anavasesa"* means without exception.
if we take an example: a frog in the mouth of a cobra. that frog is trembling in fear. the cobra is stable, firm; it does not let go. in such situations, according to what the buddha says, we should not radiate loving-kindness only to the frog. it is not right to kill the cobra in order to save the frog. we must extend a mind of loving-kindness to that animal as well. from this, we can understand what we should do in such situations when various people ask various argumentative questions. when the pure mind of loving-kindness is lost, other thoughts (*vitakka*) arise. what is said here is that if one can save the animal in a wise way without harming it, that is a different matter. but that is the situation; we must understand. it is not appropriate to harm the cobra for that sake. *"digha va ye mahanta va, majjhima rassakanukathula..."* the first classification of the whole was based on the distinction of trembling and not trembling.
next is shown the size, the physical size: *"digha va ye mahanta va"* — long ones, like snakes; great ones, like elephants; *"majjhima,"* of medium size; short-bodied ones; and then *"anuka-thula"* (very minute or gross). here, *"anu"* refers to those so small that they are barely visible or invisible to the naked eye, like things seen under a microscope; and *"thula"* refers to large animals. combining all of them according to height, weight, largeness, and smallness, this too is presented as a whole. for every animal. what is the next classification of the whole? *"dittha va ye va addittha"* — those seen and those unseen. some people can cultivate loving-kindness only towards those they have seen; they cannot do so for those unseen. here it speaks of combining both groups—all those seen and unseen. *"ye ca dure vasanti avidure"* — those living far and those living near. or rather, those living far and those living near. *"avidure."* *"bhuta va sambhavesi va"* — next, those who have come to birth and those seeking birth. now, we might not harm a chicken, but we do not think or reflect much on harm regarding a chicken egg. in that way. from whatever angle we look at it, this is also shown deeply as those beings who are preparing to enter existence (*bhava*). a child in a mother's womb can also be understood in this manner. in any case, it is said that we must not harm anyone who is in existence or seeking existence. that is also said here: *"sabbe satta bhavantu sukhitatta"* — indeed, all these beings mentioned. from this, we can see that the buddha did not exclude any living being.
having presented it as an immeasurable whole in this manner, it next says: *"na paro param nikubbetha, natimannetha katthaci nam kanci."* there too is something important. we cultivate loving-kindness. next is the other side. what is it? *"na paro param nikubbetha"* — let no one deceive another. *"nikubbetha"* means let no one revile, or let there be no cheating or fraud towards another. *"natimannetha katthaci nam kanci"* — let no one despise anyone anywhere. next: *"byarosana patighasanna, nannamannassa dukkhamiccheyya"* — out of anger or resentful perception, let no one wish suffering (*dukkha*) upon another. there are times when we do not want to do anything to our enemy, perhaps because we would be punished, or because we would get caught by the law. but if someone else harms them in some indirect way, we rejoice, saying "sadhu, sadhu!" we appreciate it. there is such a tendency. here, there is no room even for that: let no one else do it to another! there is a wonderful, deep meaning here. it is a loving-kindness so pure that not only does one not do harm oneself, but one wishes that no one else does it on one's behalf either.
here, uttara used the very hostility committed against her to bring out a virtue. there is a great dhamma-principle (*dhammata*) in this. this might be a question for you: why did uttara take that as a great virtue? it was part of sirima's profession. yet, uttara took it as a virtue at that moment in order to prevent a mind of hatred. you know the saying in our country: "one can cover a mountain with a hair." that is what often happens—a single hair of fault can cover a mountain of virtue. this is the opposite of that: with a single hair of virtue, she covered that entire mountain of fault. this is what is called radical attention / wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*). this is what the buddha has allowed. rationalizers may not understand this. this is what is called right intention (*samma-sankappa*). right intention means that if defilements arise in any way, the buddha has taught us to think in whatever way that puts an end to those defilements. that is what intention means. rationalizers might say, "what a foolish idea of uttara's is this? is this even worth mentioning?" however, depending on the situation, she thought in that way to prevent the mind of hatred. "the universe is not spacious enough, and the brahma-world is not high enough, for this virtue—such a vast mass of virtue she has done for me." it was through the very power of that mind of loving-kindness that she then turned it into an assertion of truth. after removing the hatred in her mind in that manner, she thought, "if there is indeed anger within me, let me be burned by this oil. if not, let me not be burned!" there we see the liberation of mind through loving-kindness in its true form.
a method of removing hatred, taught by the chief disciple ven. sariputta—who possessed a wonderful quality of loving-kindness, compassion, and humility—can be cited as evidence for this. the simile given for it is *"gopade udakam"* — water in a cow's footprint. the simile is as follows: suppose a person is traveling through a vast desert without a drop of water. at that moment, there is no water anywhere. suddenly, he sees a tiny bit of water in a place where a cow has stepped. he cannot draw it with a bucket. so what does he do? he falls on all fours, laps it up with his tongue, and drinks that little water as if it were a major task, because he cannot do without drinking it due to his intense thirst at that moment. in the same way, when that angry mind arises, to remove it by any means possible, one must bring out even a small virtue. that is exactly what uttara did here. she covered the mountain with a hair. the difference here is that she covered the mountain of fault with a hair of virtue. that, too, is something done through wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*), with wisdom. that is the result of it.
one can gain a vast and deep understanding of this loving-kindness. in addition to this, we can also bring in a sutta preached by the buddha called the *aghatapativinaya* (removal of resentment). "aghata" is what we call resentment or anger. there are several words for it, and there are various levels of this anger, as we all know. there is a state of slight irritation, then a higher state of intolerance, then getting angry, then wrath, then malice when it matures further, then deep-seated malice, and finally, resentment (*aghata*). going along that path is how, in samsara, it goes on from birth to birth, as in the stories of serivanija and kacchaputa, and the story of devadatta. thus it grows. the buddha shows five methods of removing such deep-seated resentment in the mind in the *aghatapativinaya sutta*. there too, a great depth is shown. there, the buddha does not show loving-kindness alone. he points out five factors for removing deep-seated malice or resentment within a person. what are they? if there is resentment or deep-seated malice towards someone, one should develop loving-kindness towards that person. we all know that. that is the first factor.
when it cannot be done through loving-kindness, compassion (*karuna*) should be developed. we can understand that too in such situations. sometimes we might think, "oh, this person is doing this out of ignorance, out of not knowing, due to some lack of understanding of the dhamma, or some deficiency in samsara." one must at least be able to compose one's mind in that way. that is what compassion is. if they do not respond to loving-kindness, we try to apply compassion to conquer that hatred: "alas, this person is helpless without the support of this dhamma." next, if even that fails, we apply the mind to equanimity (*upekkha*). equanimity means neutrality. one makes the mind neutral towards it, as if it is something that does not concern one. if it still keeps arising, what does one do next? the buddha has shown that too: *"asati amanasikaro"* — which means non-mindfulness and non-attention. now, mindfulness (*sati*) and attention (*manasikara*) mean being mindful and reflecting. in most instances in the dhamma, mindfulness and attention are shown as good qualities. but here, the buddha shows non-mindfulness and non-attention. that too is with reason and logic; that is, depending on the situation. non-mindfulness means removing from the mind that enemy who constantly assails one's head. one does not direct mindfulness towards them; one directs the mind to something else.
similarly, instead of reflecting on them, one reflects on something else related to loving-kindness or the dhamma, and removes the mind from there. just as we look away when a strong light comes that is blinding or disturbing to the eye, saying at that moment "i don't want this," one distances the mind from that thought. thus, in these ways, one brings forward loving-kindness, or brings forward compassion, or brings forward equanimity, or brings forward non-attention as the fourth. a fifth factor is also shown. if all of these do not work, next one reflects on the principle of the ownership of kamma (*kammassakata*). the buddha has preached that everyone has their own kamma as their own property, as their inheritance, as their kinsman. what they do belongs to them; what i do belongs to me. this is something our old buddhist parents used to say constantly. in such situations, to comfort the mind, one applies the thought of kamma—one's fate. it may even be a habit of their speech. be that as it may, the kamma they perform is theirs.
i do not need to condone or rejoice in it. now, for those of you who read newspapers and such, this is something that can be very helpful to protect your mind. let them do as they do. i do not need to condone the kamma they perform; those are indeed unwholesome. how many days do we generate unwholesome states regarding various things like killings, by condoning what others do? in such situations, by means of the dhamma, one remains neutral, seeing it as something that happens. one uses wisdom as an aid. the buddha has shown such methods because this is such a serious unwholesome state. we all know that greed, hatred, and delusion are defilements in our long samsara. they come in various levels. some cannot be easily scraped off and finished. we must direct our minds to a multitude of such instructions, dealing with the coarse aspect in a coarse way, and then the subtle aspect in whatever way possible, because the beneficial side of these has been shown to us through this story. we too should think, "if uttara cultivated a mind of loving-kindness in the midst of such financier wealth, why can't we?" in that way, we must value the quality of loving-kindness as well as faith in the triple gem, just like uttara. also, when the maidservants were beating her, she could have just looked away, since she herself was not striking. but instead of letting the maidservants beat sirima as much as they wanted, what this woman did, as mentioned there, was that when it became too much, she sat on her, stopped the maidservants, applied oil, washed her, and comforted her. that is the pure mind of loving-kindness.
what was the result of that? in the end, sirima too became a noble disciple. the mental transformation, the revolution that took place within her was so great that she too eventually became a noble disciple. so that is what we said at the beginning—in the ordinary world, we look to win our battle of life through unrighteousness. but what are the four principles stated by the buddha, the four principles of victory through dhamma?
* "akkodhena jine kodham" — one conquers the angry person by non-anger.
* "asadhum sadhuna jine" — one conquers the bad person, the unvirtuous person, through virtue and goodness.
* "jine kadariyam danena" — one conquers the stingy person through giving (*dana*).
* "saccena alikavadinam" — one conquers the liar through truthful speech.
but it is the opposite of this that is found in society. we all know what the ordinary practice in society is: anger must be conquered by anger itself. next, the person who does bad must be conquered by that very bad, in that same way. the stingy must be conquered by stinginess itself. next, the liar must be conquered by telling an even bigger lie. what the buddha stated in gentle words is often much harsher in practice in today's society, because society has become gross to that extent due to the decline of virtues. generally, what was called anger exists in society as hatred, malice, and so on. similarly, the words corruption and malpractice, which we often hear of in society, can be closely associated with this "bad." corruption and malpractices. thus, there is a policy of destroying poison with poison. just like destroying poison with poison, people think that an angry person must be destroyed by anger itself. regarding this corruption, the ordinary society thinks: "we must build the trellis in the direction the vine grows. we cannot correct this in society. this is what is found everywhere, so we must also go along with it." if there is fraud, corruption, and malpractice somewhere, they learn that method, do it even better, accumulate a substantial amount for themselves, and go to hell.
such is the concept that exists in society. and the same applies to stinginess. when we see someone being stingy, we think, "why should we alone give? if they do not give, why should we?" there is a good folk tale about this. if we can learn a lesson from anything, we should not discard it. it must be a story from recent times: the story of how the seven mendicants (*andis*) drank porridge at the resting-hall (*ambalama*). some of you may have heard it. the story goes like this: in the past, as you know, there were resting-halls by the roadsides where people traveling on foot came to spend the night. in this way, seven mendicants came to a resting-hall in the evening. each of them had a tiny amount of rice, like a handful. but when they gathered and asked, "what shall we eat tonight?", they said, "let's drink porridge." now, everyone knows how porridge is put on the hearth. but here, instead of that, a pot of water was placed on the hearth. as it was heating up, each was supposed to put in a handful of rice. saying "here is my handful, here is my handful," all seven mendicants pretended to put in their handful of rice and sat waiting to drink the porridge in the end. what did they drink? hot water! you can imagine how it happened. to deceive the other, each became stingy in response to the other's stinginess. so in the end, there is the result. even though it is a small story, there is a big lesson to learn from how the seven mendicants drank porridge. if we too become stingy like a stingy person, we will experience a similar result. not only in this world, but in the next world too. in this dhamma, it is shown that stinginess is a cause that leads to even the limbs becoming crippled. that is a psychological result.
it is the same regarding truth. untruth and falsehood are of various kinds. that too exists in society in an even more severe manner. rather than the word falsehood, today fraud is more commonly used. it exists in society in an even more acute form than the other. one feels that one must be a more clever fraudster than the other. in this day and age, it has become something that grows along with education as a form of unskilfulness in everyone, big and small, high and low. but the buddha states the opposite of that: one conquers falsehood with truth. why? because in many instances in the dhamma, the value of truth is declared—there is a wonderful power in truth. now, it is clear from uttara’s story above. one can show miracles through truth. there is a power in the assertion of truth (*saccakiriya*). today, a person who does nothing truthful cannot win by an assertion of truth. but the buddha has shown the victory and value of truth in various ways in sutta discourses and so on: *"saccam ve amata vaca, esa dhammo sanantano"* — "truth indeed is the deathless speech; this is an ancient law." similarly, when contemplating life, it is mentioned in the dhamma that the perfection of truth (*sacca-paramita*) was kept to the highest degree. during the bodhisatta period, sometimes even things like transgression may have occurred within that stock of merit for awakening (*bodhi-sambhara*), but it is mentioned that he consistently adhered to truthful speech. it was through the very power of that truth that when the buddha approached the group of five monks, who were initially refusing to show him respect, and said, "monks, give ear to the dhamma, i have attained (awakening)," the group of five monks accepted those words. earlier, they had thought, "if he could not attain buddhahood even after practicing such severe austerities, how can we believe that he has attained buddhahood just because he says so now?" when he first spoke, the buddha did not jump into the sky to show miracles. sitting right there, he asked only this much: "monks, have i ever spoken to you in this manner before?" then, through the power of the buddha's perfection of truth, the doubt that was within the group of five monks was dispelled. from this, we see the meaning of what the buddha said: *"saccam ve amata vaca"* — truth is indeed the deathless speech.
in the same way, the manner in which the perfection of truth was fulfilled is mentioned in those stories. nibbana is a state to be realized through wisdom. wisdom means the destruction of delusion, the destruction of ignorance. therefore, one cannot destroy delusion by deceiving oneself. that is to say, it is a self-deception, a fraud. for that reason, the value of truthful speech is shown there. the buddha has presented something like a challenge to the world here. the world goes on in that way, "destroying poison with poison," "building the trellis in the direction the vine grows," in whatever way possible, even if it leads to ruin in both worlds, just to temporarily gather some position, power, wealth, and grain in this world. the inner life is severely degraded. in these times, too, what many people focus their minds on are terms we hear like social reform, social cleansing, rehabilitation, and uplifting society. firstly, these four principles help to purify one's inner life, one's own mind. and the same applies to society. in shaping society, too, those very virtues...
even if we think about anger, some who are very harsh and untameable have been disciplined by others in a wondrous way through gentleness and softness. the buddha’s taming of nalagiri, the taming of angulimala, and so on are sufficient examples of this. even if we cannot do it at that level, by adopting those gentle and soft policies, one sets an example for the other person. now, in that situation, due to uttara’s action, sirima was prompted to think beyond her usual limits. that is what we often have to do: we must allow them to think. by allowing them to think, that person develops a deeper appreciation of the value of those virtues. instead of that, the easiest method for us is to destroy poison with poison. instead of that, we must try to gradually bring these dhamma points preached by the buddha closer to our lives. because we often engage in activities like listening to sermons and meditation, but various defilements (*kilesa*) remain in our minds like these weeds.
the medicine needed for them is what the buddha has shown in these various discourses. moreover, through the characters of the male and female disciples of the buddha's time, we can obtain good examples for these. today, they are regarded as miracles, but in truth, they are nothing unusual for a person who conducts themselves properly in the dhamma. that is a part of the peace found there. through that person's mental strength, a large number of people receive relief, an example, and a great light for their lives. in that way, to the best of our ability, we must be eager to shape our lives through this path of example.
especially when reflecting on oneself, regarding that meditation on loving-kindness, in daily life many people say, along with the word meditation itself, that they have no time to do these things. the buddha has shown in the *karaniya sutta*: *"tittham caram nisinno va, sayano va yavat'assa vigatamiddho..."* although meditation is initially started sitting in a cross-legged posture, when the mind gradually gets a good hold of it, it can be done in all four postures. now, even uttara turned her mind to the mind of loving-kindness in that sudden emergency because she had practiced it well. if one has not practiced it, one cannot make use of it. no matter what daily activities there are, if one has understood its value, if the desire (*chanda*) and eagerness for it have arisen, whether lay or ordained, that person, as expressed by the buddha—in the manner of *asevitaya, bhavitaya, bahulikataya*—gradually not only associates with it and develops it, but practices it abundantly. they make it a vehicle. they make it a foundation, a plot of land. they remain established in it. they practice it. they do it having well-undertaken it. in that way, one must make an effort to cultivate that mind of loving-kindness. and the same applies to anger. regarding other things too, and regarding goodness and virtue, one must contemplate every day. there are various cultivations in the world. even in these times, we hear about cultivation campaigns and cultivation battles. but in truth, whatever cultivations there are, we have clear evidence that they can be destroyed overnight where there is no cultivation of virtue. houses with vast wealth are finished in a single moment by bringing a matchstick close with a mind of hatred. let us consider paddy fields, and various other estates—it takes a very small thing to bring a tiny matchstick close to them. but what aided that was indeed that angry mind, hatred, revenge, jealousy, and other defilements. from this, we see that the cultivation of virtue is more important than all other cultivations. where there is no cultivation of virtue, every other cultivation is barren. it is not by drought that they become barren, nor by floods, but by the lack of the cultivation of virtue.
next is virtuous conduct (*sadhu-carya*). what the buddha uses there are the words "asadhu" (bad) and "sadhu" (good). it is a very neutral word. the word "sadhu" is familiar even to our ears; it is very dear to us. virtuous conduct means the very best behavior. what is known in the ordinary world today is goodness and virtue, not vice. therefore, the cultivation of virtue. one must accumulate it. just like collecting bit by bit in a savings pot, each one must think of collecting into one's own mind-stream those virtues grouped and shown by the buddha, as presented in the *karaniya sutta* and elsewhere. it is by accumulating these that an exemplary person is born into the world one day. the buddha himself accumulated in this manner for aeons (*kalpa*) and thereby gained the power, as a buddha, to preach this dhamma to the world and show us this path to nibbana. it is the same for everyone. if there is anything to accumulate in samsara, it is this—these virtues. then, through those virtues, through their maturing, one is able to attain liberation (*vimutti*).
it is very easily said that "we must destroy this hatred and delusion." but to do that, one has to uproot those weeds mentioned earlier. those small things must be removed. along with that, the cultivation of virtue. if we do not cultivate a certain place, it becomes fallow. some intellectuals argue that since there is an argument for just letting the cultivation go and remaining idle, "there is no need to cultivate what is called loving-kindness. when anger arises, we will just show loving-kindness to them. there is no need to sit for hours and practice it as meditation." but even such people sometimes spend months exerting themselves for running races and so on to win them. from this, it is clear that unless there is some practice, training, habituation, and training in various ways as mentioned, we do not have the strength to do it when the opportunity arises. that is why the buddha shows this as an application, to be done as a yogi. the meaning of the word "yoga" is application. therefore, it is by applying oneself in that manner and developing these virtues that one can retain a value for one's life. that is the cultivation of virtue. therefore, if anyone wants to hold a certain purpose high in their life, they must make that purpose the cultivation of virtue. the ultimate peak of that cultivation of virtue is, in the end, the supramundane (*lokuttara*) cultivation of virtue. starting from the mundane (*lokiya*) cultivation of virtue, and finally the supramundane cultivation of virtue. thus, at the end of that mundaneness, along with virtue, wisdom (*panna*) matures. along with virtue, those summarized as virtue, concentration, and wisdom (*sila, samadhi, panna*) mature through those practices.
now, many of you merit-seekers have observed the eight precepts on this uposatha day. some others have observed the ten precepts. some have observed the precepts of right livelihood as the eighth (*ajiva-atthamaka-sila*) at this moment. what is done by all of these? just like uprooting weeds in the manner mentioned, one basically takes some steps regarding those defilements (*kilesa*) that can arise in one's mind-stream. because one disciplines bodily and verbal actions. now, a thought may arise. along with the arising of the thought, if bodily and verbal actions are carried out, we fall into a terrible abyss without even knowing it. therefore, the very first level is virtue (*sila*).
what is done through virtue (*sila*) is disciplining bodily and verbal actions. thoughts do arise, but through the determination one has made: *"panatipata veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami"* — by oneself, not because anyone else said so, but declaring "i stand within this practice." this means abstaining. the determination to keep the training rule of abstaining from taking life, from killing other living beings. to project that into the light of wisdom and try to conduct one's life within it—this is what is called virtue (*sila*). the buddha has shown the vast amount of merit and wholesome kamma that arises when someone keeps five, eight, or ten training rules in that manner for a day. where the buddha speaks about the eight precepts, he describes the eightfold precept (*atthanga-sila*) as *"mahajjutiko mahavippharo"* — of great luster, of great resonance, such is the merit of keeping the eight precepts on the uposatha day. at the very least, even the five precepts—that too is something of wonderful power. though we consider the five precepts as something small, if kept purely, how great a power is it! yet, people are not inclined to keep even that. they do not know their value either. thus, what is done through virtue is disciplining bodily and verbal actions. next, those virtues and vices arise in the mind.
according to the statement *"manopubbangama dhamma,"* which we all know, the mind is the forerunner of all these. so, stopping what arises in this mind is not an easy task. it must be done through meditation. having stilled the mind that scatters in that manner, one then maintains it on a wholesome object. indeed, that is why a wholesome object is provided. the mind grasps some object. the very nature of the mind is to go on grasping objects. it goes on grasping and grasping. so, instead of a bad object, a good object is given for it to grasp. that is what is done here. to protect that good object, one must act by contemplating wisely through wise attention / radical attention (*yoniso manasikara*). sometimes, even what the ordinary world considers unnecessary through logic is needed. for what? we know there are medicines for some illnesses that surprise us when we are told about them. we even wonder if that is a medicine. but the work gets done. if one gets cured even by a water injection, then that is a medicine. likewise, there are certain things that arise in the very mind in a very subtle manner, which one can discover for oneself. that is the kind of method uttara used here too, by bringing out a small virtue of that woman—bringing out something the ordinary world would consider small—and through that, erasing her own hatred. in that way, we must contemplate: if our purpose is the cultivation of virtue, and the uprooting and expelling of vice, we must try to shape our lives in a manner corresponding to that.
the next question is the one regarding values. our values need not be the values of society. generally, in these times, there are various feelings such as "these are the contemporary values," or "one cannot live like that in this day and age." but here, there is no time limit for kamma. there is no time limit regarding wholesome and unwholesome kamma. whether performed in the buddha's time or in this day and age, the results of unwholesome, sinful kamma are identical. therefore,
regardless of those, what we must maintain is that very value we receive from the dhamma and kamma. especially since kamma affects our samsaric life. everywhere, "unwholesome" (*akusala*) means being unskilled, in the manner of the dhamma. being unskilled in living in samsara is what is called unwholesome. one becomes unskilled in a bad place; otherwise, one meets with disaster right here as its consequence, as its result. "wholesome" (*kusala*) means that very skillfulness. those deeds that direct one to nibbana without going to miserable realms like hell in this samsara are what are called wholesome. thus, when contemplating in this manner, our value must be on that wholesome side. "kusala-chanda" means giving one's preference to the wholesome. we must give our preference to the wholesome when the question of choice arises. in that way, one must contemplate; regardless of social conventions, one must present a set of values to one's life in that manner. "my life is lived under these very values, no matter what anyone else says." when one's character grows through these, then others awaken. sometimes, those who laughed, mocked, or called it foolishness, in the end, come to you with their problems. when a serious problem arises and there is no refuge, they come to the person who appears to the world as a spiritual friend (*kalyana-mitta*). becoming such a valuable person is not something done in a day or two. we see that from the buddha's life itself. but we must think: we have not done these things in this life alone. we are not making a beginning in this life. we are here today as the result of a beginning made over a long period. when contemplating in that way, we are adding to what has already come, and we should not think of this as something we are doing anew. the difference is that those two—good and bad—are always a part of its very nature.
that is what mara is. he shows the bad to us as good. that is the nature of the world. the buddha points out that, like water flowing downwards, the nature of minds is to be drawn towards the unwholesome. in the question of good and bad, the bad always presents itself and shows us a beneficial side, as it were. it shows it falsely. if one submits to it, then one is caught by mara. so, at the very least, when we blame someone else, we should think, "here is mara. either mara has possessed them, or mara has possessed me." having a correct understanding of this, one must return to the dhamma. one must develop a correct understanding of kamma. one must develop a correct understanding of the dhamma. even buddhas, paccekabuddhas, and arahants are subject to kamma. the law of kamma that operates in this samsara is that powerful. no one can override it. therefore, one must bow one's head to it. bowing one's head means submitting to it as a world-principle; it is not something done by anyone else—if one does it, it is for oneself. according to the principle "as you sow, so shall you reap," one must correct one's behavior. if one corrects the mind, body, and speech, then if the results of past sinful kamma are ready to ripen, it helps to suppress those results, as is said regarding obstructive kamma (*upapilaka-kamma*) and so on. similarly, it becomes supportive (*upatthambhaka*) to one's wholesome side. the wholesome deeds one performs help to further develop them. such is it regarding kamma.
and next is the dhamma. when thinking of the dhamma, the nibbana declared by the buddha is like that light seen from afar on a great mountain—like the sri pada mountain. one must think of it in that way. whatever other things we do in our lives, whether we do jobs or hold other positions, as buddhists, the ultimate goal of our life is nibbana. therefore, it is within that light of nibbana that we must carry out our other activities. if that light is turned to the other side, we cannot climb sri pada. therefore, we must always bear that in mind. whether it is realized today, tomorrow, or in another aeon, it is only if we make that idea of nibbana our goal that we can travel this journey correctly. that itself is what is called right view (*samma-ditthi*), the correct vision. if there is no correct vision, the world is blind.
that is why the buddha declared:
*"andhabhuto ayam loko, tanuk'ettha vipassati."*
the entire world is blind; only a very few see, declares the buddha. similarly, the buddha has declared: *"sabbe puthujjana ummattaka"* — as long as they are worldlings (*puthujjana*), they behave like madmen in the world. he has declared them to be insane. sometimes, someone might feel resentful towards the buddha for saying this. but to the buddha's knowledge, the mind of a worldling is just like a mad mind, like an insane mind. in that way. therefore, escaping from that insanity and moving towards wisdom, getting rid of those called greed, hatred, and delusion, and purifying the mind, making it perfectly clean—the path to this is called the path to nibbana, the noble eightfold path. when one is aligned with right view (*samma-ditthi*), having developed correct vision, and then correct thoughts, then using correct words in accordance with correct thoughts, performing correct deeds, correct actions, and then correcting one's daily routine in accordance with that, turning it into correct livelihood, and through that effort, bringing out correct effort, and through that very effort, bringing out that valuable quality called correct mindfulness, and by consolidating that very quality, developing correct concentration—it is in this way that the noble eightfold path is completed. it is to a mind concentrated in this manner that the subtle point shown by the buddha can be properly penetrated and seen through the three characteristics of impermanence (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*). it is through this that one can realize the path and fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship that we all aspire to, and realize the supreme deathless nibbana in this very way. that indeed is our aspiration.
indeed, let us aspire that this accumulation of merit we have gathered so far by listening to the dhamma and observing the precepts may lead to the development of those spiritual faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, which aid in realizing nibbana, and to the realization of the path and fruits! moreover, if the guardian deities of the dispensation, including the assembly of devas and brahmas, wish to rejoice in this accumulated stock of merit to fulfill their aspirations for the perfections (*parami*), may they rejoice in it and realize the supreme, deathless nibbana through whatever bodhi state they have aspired to! may they also protect us and this dispensation! likewise, if any beings, from avici to akanittha, including our departed relatives, wish to rejoice in this merit of preaching and hearing the dhamma, may they all rejoice, be freed from all samsaric suffering (*dukkha*), and bring an end to this suffering of samsara through the peace of supreme, deathless nibbana! wishing thus, repeat this verse.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 108
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #108
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.97)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Na antalikkhe na samuddamajjhe,
na pabbatānaṃ vivaraṃ pavissa;
na vijjatī so jagatīpadesoti,
yatthaṭṭhito na ppaheyya maccu.
From:
Dhammapada 127 (Pāpavagga)
Dear Listeners,
The fear of death constantly exists within every living being. There is no effort that humans do not make, no means they do not employ, to escape death and live even for a single day. Nevertheless, when death inevitably presents itself in accordance with some grave karma, every such effort and stratagem becomes futile. Today, we intend to deliver this Dhamma sermon based on a stanza and a story that illustrate this natural law (*dhamma-tā*).
When our Teacher of the Three Worlds, the Buddha, was residing at the Nigrodharama in Kapilavatthu, he uttered this stanza concerning Suppabuddha the Sakyan. Pious listeners, this Suppabuddha the Sakyan was the Buddha's own father-in-law, the father of Princess Yasodhara, and also the father of Venerable Devadatta. Although he was his father-in-law, he harbored a deep animosity toward his son-in-law. He thought, "He abandoned my daughter to go forth on the Great Renunciation, and he ordained my son, making him an enemy." Due to this cultivated animosity, one day this Suppabuddha the Sakyan thought, "I will not allow the Buddha to walk for alms." If the Buddha had been invited to an alms-giving at a certain place, Suppabuddha started holding a drinking party on the road along which he would travel. In short, he gathered a crowd and began drinking alcohol right in the middle of the road.
As the Buddha was arriving with the community of monks at the time of alms-round, people came and said, "The Blessed One is arriving." Suppabuddha, however, said, "Tell him to go by another road; I am the elder," and did not clear the way, despite those people requesting him several times. Consequently, the Buddha turned back. Then, Suppabuddha the Sakyan sent a spy to listen to what the Buddha would say. The Buddha displayed a gentle smile. As was customary, Venerable Ānanda asked, "What, Blessed One, is the cause for displaying this smile?" Thereupon, the Buddha declared, "Do you see this Suppabuddha the Sakyan? Having committed such a grave karma, on the seventh day from today, right by the staircase on the ground floor of his palace, the earth will split open, and he will plunge into Avīci, the great hell." Having heard this, the spy went back and told Suppabuddha the Sakyan. Suppabuddha thought, "Well, even if that is so, I will not let it happen there. I must act in such a way as to accuse the Buddha of lying." Thinking thus, he had food and drinks brought up to the topmost floor of his seven-storied palace and made arrangements to spend the entire seven days on the top floor. He had the staircases removed, locked the doors on every floor, and stationed guards at the doors, instructing them, "Even if by mistake I attempt to go downstairs, prevent me."
When the Buddha heard about these precautions, he declared that even if Suppabuddha the Sakyan flew into the sky, went out to sea in a ship, or hid amidst the mountains instead of staying on the top floor of his palace, that event would happen exactly as foretold. It was this very meaning that he expounded to the community of monks on that occasion through the stanza we have taken as our theme:
> *"Na antalikkhe na samuddamajjhe,*
> *na pabbatānaṁ vivaraṁ pavissa;*
> *na vijjatī so jagatīpadesoti,*
> *yatthaṭṭhito na ppaheyya maccu."*
The Buddha declared this with absolute certainty, stating that whether in the sky, in the middle of the ocean, or by entering a mountain cleft, there is no place in this world where, abiding, one would not be overcome by death.
When the seven days were completed, at the exact time of day when the Buddha had been walking on his alms-round and that Sakyan had blocked the road, the Sakyan’s state stallion—the auspicious horse used by Suppabuddha the Sakyan—suddenly went wild on the ground floor and began thrashing against the walls. Hearing this noise, Suppabuddha the Sakyan asked, "What is this commotion?" and was told that the horse had gone wild. That horse could be tamed only by Suppabuddha the Sakyan. Therefore, he felt he must go and subdue the horse. As he approached the door, it opened by itself. Next, the guards also pushed him in that direction. Furthermore, it is said that even though the staircases had been removed, they were somehow put back in place, perhaps pushed back and forth by some natural law (*dhamma-tā*), because that karma had to bear its fruit. In this manner, he was propelled down through all seven floors, and exactly as predicted by the Buddha, the moment he reached the foot of the staircase, the earth opened up right there, and he plunged into Avīci hell. Thus it is recorded in the Dhamma.
Even when the Buddha uttered that stanza, many attained comprehension of the Dhamma based on that event. However, someone in this day and age might doubt this occurrence. At first glance, from this story of the Dhamma, we are led to believe that by blocking the path of the Buddha, that Sakyan paved the way to hell instead of Nibbāna. Thus, while others paved their way to Nibbāna by taking refuge in the Buddha, this sinful Suppabuddha the Sakyan paved his way straight to hell by preventing the Buddha from going on his alms-round. Insulting the Buddha, which is the karma of abusing the Noble Ones (*ariyūpavāda*), is shown to be a highly grave karma. Insulting Noble Ones such as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants has very severe consequences, as is pointed out.
Particularly now, some might not believe this story of going to hell. In our Dhamma literature, there are countless references to the deva worlds and brahma worlds. The pleasures and luxuries of the deva and brahma worlds are mentioned. We read about divine garments, divine food, and divine mansions with great pleasure. Even though many believe in those things, especially in this era, they are reluctant to believe in a realm of Yama or a hell, or the details concerning them. They do not even want to hear about them. Yet, that is precisely the place to which most people belong. Drawing from the Dhamma stories in our literature, we hope next to highlight several points declared by the Buddha regarding the nature of suffering (*dukkha*) in hell. On one occasion, the Buddha addressed the community of monks:
"Monks, if one were to speak of a place that is entirely undesirable, painful, and disagreeable, one would be referring to hell. So painful is the nature of this hell that it is difficult even to give a simile for it," declared the Buddha.
Then a certain monk asked, "But, Blessed One, is it possible to give a simile?"
"Very well, then, I will give a simile," he replied. Here is the simile given:
"Monks, suppose a criminal is brought before a king. The king tells the executioners, 'Take this man and strike him with a hundred spears in the morning.' They pierce him with a hundred spears in the morning. When they return after doing so, is that man still alive? 'Yes, Venerable Sir,' they say. Then the king says, 'In that case, strike him with another hundred spears at noon.' After they report that he is still alive, he is struck with another hundred spears in the evening. Monks, when asked whether that man who receives three hundred spear strikes experiences suffering (*dukkha*) and grief, they reply, 'Yes, Venerable Sir, what need is there to speak of three hundred spear strikes? Even a single spear strike is extremely painful to a person.'"
Thereupon, picking up a small pebble in his palm, the Buddha asked, "Is this pebble larger, or is the great Himalaya mountain?"
"Venerable Sir, this pebble is extremely small; it cannot even be compared to the Himalaya mountain, which is so vast."
Then the Buddha declared, "Just so, monks, the suffering (*dukkha*) experienced by this man from three hundred spear strikes is like the pebble in my hand. The suffering (*dukkha*) in hell is a vast suffering (*dukkha*) like the Himalaya mountain." That is how he expressed it on that occasion. There are further Dhamma portions related to this. In one place, the Buddha describes the nature of suffering (*dukkha*) in hell step-by-step. There, mention is made of the wardens of hell (*yamapalla*) who assist in meting out retribution to the hell-beings who are ready to receive the fruits of their evil karma. They pierce the two hands and two feet of a person fallen into hell with red-hot iron spikes, and they also pierce his chest. This is called the five-fold transfixing with red-hot iron spikes. It is that kind of suffering (*dukkha*), that kind of punishment that is described.
Furthermore, it is said that the wardens of hell lay a being fallen into hell down on the ground and slice him with axes. There, it is described that no matter how much suffering (*dukkha*) he receives, beyond what we can even imagine, as long as that karma is not exhausted, that person does not die but continues to suffer. For us, it is unimaginable. A person's life is lost with a small blow. Yet, because of the force of karma, because one has to undergo suffering, the force of karma does not disappear without yielding its fruit; so the Buddha has declared. This, then, is a way in which karma yields its fruit. Even if one dies, the body arises again. In those realms of yakkhas, realms of petas, and hells, the four elements are prepared in ways beyond our imagination to exhaust the momentum of karma. To exhaust karma, these four elements—earth, water, fire, and air—are ready.
In an unimaginable and wondrous way, those spontaneously born bodies called *opapātika* arise in accordance with karma. Having experienced that sensation (*vedanā*), they subsequently die. They are born again. Once more, bodies arise. That is how it is. Thus, just as they are laid down and sliced with axes, the wardens of hell also slice them with adzes. Next, it is shown that they are harnessed to a chariot and driven back and forth on a ground of red-hot iron. Furthermore, it is shown that they are thrown into a copper cauldron. They are thrown into a boiling, blazing copper cauldron. Burning, the hell-being goes up and down in it. Yet he does not die immediately. He undergoes suffering. He goes up and down and sideways in this manner. It is in this way, according to various evil karmas, that the Buddha has described how hell-beings undergo suffering (*dukkha*).
After enduring suffering in this manner, when they plunge into the Great Hell, it is even more severe. The Great Hell is mentioned as a place of great wonder, beyond our ability to imagine. It is described as being enclosed by iron walls about a hundred leagues (*yojana*) in length, with red-hot iron above and below, and the ground divided like rooms. The hell-being burns on this red-hot iron. A sheet of flame comes from the eastern wall and strikes the western wall. A sheet of flame comes from the western wall and strikes the eastern wall. A sheet of flame comes from the southern wall and strikes the northern wall. A sheet of flame comes from above and strikes the ground below, and from the ground upwards. In this way, there are sheets of flame from every direction. In the midst of the flames, in accordance with their karma, crying and wailing, undergoing terrible suffering (*dukkha*), they meet with death (*maraṇa*). Then they take birth (*jāti*) once again.
While they are undergoing suffering (*dukkha*) for a long time in this manner, suddenly, it is said, the eastern door opens. Thereupon, this hell-being runs in that direction, thinking of escaping. Even as he runs, his skin, flesh, and sinews are entirely burnt. As he nears it, the door shuts again. Next, he runs in this direction toward the western door. In this way, he undergoes a wondrous mass of suffering (*dukkha*). Going from there, he next falls into what is called the Gūtha Hell. This Gūtha Hell is like a pit filled with excrement. It is said that inside it, needle-like worms with mouths like the point of a needle pierce the skin, flesh, sinews, and bones of that hell-being, and eat his bone marrow. Such is the grave suffering (*dukkha*) they undergo.
Then, leaving that place, they fall into a hell of hot ashes, called the Kukkuḷa Hell. Falling into the Kukkuḷa Hell in this manner, and going from there, you, pious listeners, may also have heard about the thorny silk-cotton tree. It is called the Simbalī forest. A forest of silk-cotton trees. Hell-beings are made to climb up and down these silk-cotton trees with thorns about sixteen inches long by those wardens of hell. Next is described the Asipatta forest. The Asipatta forest means there are trees whose leaves are just like swords. When they fall, the hands and feet of those hell-beings, those sinners, are cut, and their noses and ears are sliced off by those falling leaves. Next, mention is made of a flowing river called Vetaraṇī. They fall into it, and along its banks are sharp, cutting weapons like razor blades. While being swept away in this, the hell-wardens haul these hell-beings out with a fishhook. There it is described that when they are asked, "What do you want?" and they say, "I am hungry," red-hot iron balls are thrust into their mouths. Burning their mouths and stomachs, those balls pass out through the lower tract, taking the intestines along with them. Next, if they say they are thirsty, molten copper is poured into their mouths. It is as a place of such unspeakable, wondrous suffering (*dukkha*) and pain that the Buddha describes it in the Suttas.
That is how the Buddha describes the pain that must be endured in hell. Next, on one occasion, the lifespan in hell is also mentioned in a Sutta discourse. This is found in the Kokālika Sutta. Kokālika was the chief disciple of Venerable Devadatta. Developing a deep animosity toward the two chief disciples, Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Moggallāna, that disciple went to the Buddha to slander them, saying that both Sāriputta and Moggallāna had evil intentions and were wicked. The Buddha said, "No, Kokālika, do not say so. They are of virtuous character." Despite being told this repeatedly two or three times, it was not long before boils the size of mustard seeds broke out on the body of the monk Kokālika. They grew to the size of mung beans, then chickpea size, then emblic myrobalan (*nelli*) size, and then wood-apple (*beli*) size. Starting as large abscesses, they turned into massive wounds from which blood and pus flowed, and he passed away right there.
At the time of his passing, when he died, Sahampati Brahma Raja came to the Buddha that night and revealed this matter, saying that Kokālika had died and was born (*jāti*) in the Paduma Hell. The following day, the Buddha announced this to the community of monks: "Last night, Sahampati Brahma Raja came and told me that the monk Kokālika, due to the unwholesome karma of harboring animosity toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna, finally went and was born in the Paduma Hell." Then a certain monk asked, "Venerable Sir, how long is the lifespan in the Paduma Hell?" Thereupon, the Buddha declared, "Monk, it is not easy to measure the lifespan of the Paduma Hell in terms of so many hundreds of years, or so many hundreds of thousands of years." The monk then asked, "Is it possible to give a simile?" Saying "It is possible," the Buddha then gave a simile. It must have been a simile familiar in the Kingdom of Kosala at that time: suppose there is a cart filled with a large quantity of sesame seeds, and a person removes one sesame seed once every hundred years. That cart of sesame, that sesame cart, would be emptied sooner. Yet the Abbuda Hell—even though the question was about the Paduma Hell, the Buddha first declared the lifespan of the Abbuda Hell, which is shorter than that of Paduma. Explaining this, the Buddha stated that from the Abbuda Hell onwards, the lifespan increases twenty-fold progressively through a series of hells named Abbuda, Nirabbuda, Ahaha, Ababa, and so forth, with the Paduma Hell being mentioned at the very end.
Thus, even in the Abbuda Hell, that hell-being has to live for such a long duration. Next is the Paduma Hell. In terms of time, it is an unimaginably long period; it is this suffering (*dukkha*) of hell that the Buddha points out in these Suttas. Now, in this day and age, some educated people might think these are later additions, or that the Buddha merely carried forward the mythical beliefs of the past. However, what we have to say is this: if someone believes in those divine mansions—the arising of mansions and the arising of bodies in a manner suitable to enjoy those pleasures according to the force of wholesome karma—this is actually a domain within the reach of those with direct-knowledge (*abhiññā*). Everyone has heard that three types of eyes are mentioned in the Dhamma of this Dispensation: the physical eye (*māsa-cakkhu*), the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*), and the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*). Ordinary people see only with the physical eye, the eye of flesh. Even if other instruments are used, only that physical eye is functional. To truly develop the divine eye, one must cultivate the absorptions (*jhāna*). Next, the eye of wisdom is even deeper; it is the eye that shows the actual natural law of Dependent Arising (*paṭicca-samuppāda*), which brings about Nibbāna. Only a Buddha can bring to light that eye of wisdom, the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*). However, yogis who had developed the divine eye also existed before the time of the Buddha. In that very Dhamma, according to the words of the Buddha, it is mentioned that there were yogis who could see back into past births (*jāti*) by hundreds of thousands, even millions. Likewise, there were those with direct-knowledge (*abhiññā*) who could travel through the air.
Those with direct-knowledge (*abhiññā*) have seen those things—the deva worlds, the brahma worlds, and the nature of suffering (*dukkha*) in the plane of misery. Thus, the Buddha did not include these in the texts merely because they existed in the past; those yogis also saw them to some extent, though they did not see them with perfect clarity. When speaking of the Buddha's divine eye, it is mentioned as an exceptionally pure divine eye. Here, "purity" means that the karma that brought about birth (*jāti*) in those deva worlds and other realms is seen with absolute clarity. Furthermore, it became directly clear to the Buddha that there is no self (*attā*) here, and that these arise solely through the momentum of karma. However, some of those other possessors of direct-knowledge (*abhiññā*) thought, "There must be a creator for this." When a spontaneously born body (*opapātika*) arose, they thought, "Perhaps Brahma or someone else must have created this." Or, concerning the infliction of suffering in the plane of misery, they thought, "This is happening because some almighty being decreed it."
But the Buddha declares that all of this happens through karma, in accordance with karma. A sight one can see in ordinary life is moths leaping into a lamp. Moths as well as grasshoppers leap into it. They see their companions dying in it. Yet they still leap. They leap into the fire. In this manner, forces that exhaust the momentum of karma operate in both animate and inanimate things. Now, in the story mentioned earlier, why did the horse go wild? The cause of the horse's frenzy was the result (*vipāka*) of that unwholesome karma generated by Suppabuddha. It was the operation of that very unwholesome karma. It was that process operating through the horse that finally dragged Suppabuddha the Sakyan down. In that manner, beyond our comprehension, even in these times, in the human world we often take seriously only the externally visible causes of what are deemed "accidents." Underlying them, there can be the karmic momentum of the individuals concerned. They are drawn into them. Even by a lightning strike, the four elements stand ready to yield the fruit of that karma, as a result of the karmic force generated by our mind. Result (*vipāka*) means ripening.
The karma committed by that Sakyan ripened over seven days. It is a comprehensible fact that at the exact moment the Buddha walked on his alms-round, at that very instant, the horse went wild and that process began. There is a certain wheel of karma (*kamma-cakka*) operating within this mind. Through this consciousness (*viññāṇa*), that wheel of karma often turns in cycles of seven—such as seven days. That is the exact point of the ripening of that karma. This did not happen due to any curse from the Buddha. The Buddha simply saw it. He saw that the grave karma committed would ripen within seven days and yield its fruit in this manner. He merely declared it as a prediction. He did not curse him. In the same way, regarding those hell-beings, we have to understand the same thing: it is because of this that the Buddha constantly emphasizes that we must avoid unwholesome deeds such as killing living beings and stealing. This is not confined to this world alone. Now, ordinary people regard only what falls within the range of their physical eye as the world, as the universe.
Only those planetary worlds visible from here are regarded as the world. Now, they are gradually realizing that this is a misconception. But there are infinite, boundless world-systems (*loka-dhātu*) that fell within the range of the Buddha's knowledge. Next, what is even deeper is the natural law (*dhamma-tā*) concerning this karma. In the statement, "Mind precedes all phenomena, mind is chief, mind-made (*manopubbaṅgamā dhammā manoseṭṭhā manomayā*)," the Buddha has given the foremost place to the mind. The mind goes ahead. The mind is chief. We must also reflect upon the word *manomayā*—mind-made. These are created by the mind itself. In the word preparations (*saṅkhāra*), along with the meaning of "putting together" or "arranging," there is also a deeper meaning associated with karma; there is a certain force or power generated through our force of intention.
In the past, perhaps even artists illustrated this with the example of a potter: before a pot is made, a thought about it arises first. It is in accordance with the thought that the pot is fashioned. Likewise, there is a certain force in this karma that arranges the four elements accordingly. That arranging is done with the help of various other things. In the human world, things are done by using other tools and materials in production. It is only those things that we regard as creations. But the Buddha points out, in this regard, the spontaneously arising bodies—though called spontaneous, what lies underneath is karma. The momentum of karma subsequently emerges as another body corresponding to it.
Now, as you pious listeners know, when speaking of the plane of misery, four planes of misery are mentioned in the Dhamma. First is the animal realm. We spoke of those grasshoppers and moths. Even more than that, consider how animals devour one another in the great ocean and in the forest. The natural food of each animal is other animals. If a creator god created this, there is no godliness in such a god. But indeed, they are born in those respective realms of becoming (*bhava*) according to the momentum of karma. The Buddha expressed this matter so deeply that on one occasion he declared, "Monks, if there is no karma to ripen in a certain becoming (*bhava*), that becoming (*bhava*) does not arise (*jāti*)." In short, it is mentioned in some Dhamma stories that when a Brahma is born, the mansion corresponding to him has already arisen. In accordance with karma, the appropriate environment—the mansion—is arranged. The body is also like that. Becoming (*bhava*) itself is of that nature. Thus, in the animal realm, various forces of karmic momentum are exhausted according to the karma committed by that being. This is something we can see with our own eyes.
Similarly, when speaking of those state of existences (*bhava*) like petas, it is said that birds like hawks, crows, and vultures also come and peck at these beings, causing them wondrous pain. Even though they are not visible to the physical eye of some, at least to some extent, one can infer the existence of these peta realms as a rational conclusion; some even get to see them in an indirect manner. Nowadays, through stories of exorcism, mesmerism, and hypnotism, these things are revealed to some extent. Spirits, peta-beings are mostly realms of petas with subtle bodies that undergo suffering (*dukkha*). That exists in close association with the human world itself. Sometimes, the Dhamma portions that speak of those peta realms where they undergo great suffering (*dukkha*) as mere skeletons are recorded in the Dhamma book called the Petavatthu. Sometimes, because of developing attachment to their homes, due to that attachment, due to craving (*taṇhā*), greed, and other evil deeds contrary to the five precepts, they are born (*jāti*) in peta existences (*bhava*) and undergo terrible suffering and hardships. Sometimes, even the bodies of those petas are described. They are called "filth-mouthed" (*asūci-mukha*), having a throat as narrow as a needle and a massive belly. This massive belly has to be nourished through a throat as narrow as a needle. Furthermore, when they go in search of food, they do not find it. Sometimes, when they go in search of food, it turns into excrement instead of food. When they go near rivers in search of water, it becomes a river of blood, or else it dries up. In this manner, they return with cries of distress. They run in this direction, they run in that direction. Thus, it is mentioned in the Dhamma that the suffering (*dukkha*) endured in the peta realm is infinite. You pious listeners can occasionally infer the reality of these peta realms to some extent through various phenomena like spirit possession.
It is the same with the realm of yakkhas and the realm of asuras. The realm of asuras refers to beings with the traits of yakkhas and rakkhasas. They do not enjoy pleasure either. Yet they remain in those states for a long time. In accordance with the very saṁsāric habit of the cruelties they committed in the human world, they devour one another. Even as they devour one another, their bodies form again. They devour one another again, for infinite, boundless times. It seems very wondrous to us when we speak of this, but it is something that happens on the basis of these four elements. This was seen by yogis. Those with direct-knowledge (*abhiññā*) see these things. In a way beyond our imagination, they are created according to the momentum of karma. In accordance with the karmic forces present in this consciousness (*viññāṇa*), form (*rūpa*) is created. Next, they experience that suffering (*dukkha*). Having experienced suffering (*dukkha*), life continues as long as they must endure the suffering (*dukkha*) related to it. Even you, pious listeners, might sometimes see in hospitals—though it is not an absolute proof—doctors thinking, "This patient will die." Yet he does not die. He neither lives nor dies. He undergoes suffering (*dukkha*). He suffers. We call this "languishing in pain." It is that kind of natural law (*dhamma-tā*) that exists in those peta realms, yakkha realms, and so forth; they live there until that karma is exhausted. The Buddha has declared that karma does not exhaust itself without yielding its fruit (*vipāka*). The committed karma never exhausts itself without yielding its fruit (*vipāka*). It is the manner of yielding fruit (*vipāka*) that the Buddha declares there. Before it yields its fruit, or rather, before the karma is fully ripened, one can perform certain counter-actions to reduce its power, or else to make it ineffective (*ahosi-kamma*).
However, for those grave karmas that yield their fruit with absolute certainty, which inevitably yield fruit, such as certain karmas of abusing Noble Ones (*ariyūpavāda*) and the weightiest karmas with immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*), no one can provide a remedy. There are karmas so grave that no one can remedy them, which are called *ānantariya-kamma*. Throughout the Dhamma of the Buddha, and what we constantly remind you of, is to practice the Dhamma diligently and to perform wholesome deeds. This is not something said to frighten anyone.
