"now i have reached such a state. what happened? although i went taking the razor to cut my neck, what was ultimately done was the cutting away of all defilements (*kilesas*) with the razor of wisdom." hearing this, the other monks thought this monk was telling a lie out of conceit (*adhimana*), or perhaps it was a pure lie, and went to complain to the buddha, saying, "this monk is making such a claim." thereupon, the buddha declared, "monks, those who have destroyed the cankers (*khinasavas*), the arahants, do not commit suicide." pointing out that this is a natural law (*dhammata*), he made a statement that confirmed the monk's words. then the monks asked, "blessed one, if so, why did someone with such capacity to attain arahantship think of returning to lay life? why did he think of disrobing?" next, they asked three questions: "and if he became an arahant, what was the wholesome karma (*kusala-kamma*) that supported his attainment of arahantship?" thirdly, they asked, "in the previous instance, why did that cobra not bite him? why did the serpent not bite?"
out of those three questions, the buddha first answered the last question: the reason why the serpent did not bite. as the cause for this, that cobra had been a servant, a helper of this monk in his third previous birth. therefore, it did not think of biting its master. you, virtuous people, might sometimes understand such things through the behavior of dogs and cats. sometimes, non-human animals have special behaviors towards those who were their relatives or friends, through a certain recognition (*sanna*). accordingly, in later times, this monk came to be known in the dispensation (*sasana*) as "venerable sappadasaka"—the monk whose servant was a serpent. he began to be known by the name sappadasaka. but the buddha did not stop there; he then answered the other two questions as well. that is: while having such potential (*sampatti*) to become an arahant, why did he think of returning to lay life? why did he think of disrobing? and secondly, if he attained arahantship, what was the merit that supported his attainment?
as the reason for this, he related an incident from the time of kassapa buddha. a certain monk—not this monk, but another monk—having heard the dhamma, went forth, but not long after receiving higher ordination, he thought of returning to lay life. he thought of disrobing. however, instead of doing it immediately, he told a companion monk, a friend of his, "such an idea has come to me." that companion monk, explaining various matters and highlighting the drawbacks of lay life, dispelled his idea of returning to lay life. thus, that monk settled his mind. however, during the days he was contemplating disrobing, he had neglected his requisites (*pirikara*). therefore, taking those rusted and soiled requisites, he went to a small pool of water to clean them. while he was cleaning the razor and other items, the companion monk who had helped him with advice was standing there. the monk cleaning the requisites said to him, "venerable friend, when i was thinking of returning to lay life and disrobing, i had intended to give these requisites to you upon my departure." hearing this, a great greed (*lobha*) arose in the companion monk. his mind changed completely, and he thought, "whether this monk disrobes or stays is all the same to me, let me get these requisites." thereupon, he began to praise the advantages of lay life and speak of the disadvantages of monkhood. in other words, he tried to make him disrobe.
"what is the use of this life of ours, venerable friend? instead of spending this life wandering from house to house for alms, if we were at home, we could have lived pleasantly engaging in friendly conversation with a wife and children." in this manner, through various lines of talk, he rekindled the idea of returning to lay life and disrobing in that monk. but that monk fell into reflection: "why is this monk, who previously advised me otherwise, now trying to make me return to lay life?" then it occurred to him, "perhaps this is due to his greed for my requisites." thinking thus, that monk made an effort on his own, dispelled the thought of returning to lay life, and remained in the monkhood. this is the past account that the buddha revealed.
so, what we have to recognize here is: who was that monk who first helped his companion monk, and later, out of greed for the requisites, praised the advantages of lay life? it was none other than this venerable sappadasaka. now, through this, we can see the way the wheel of karma (*kamma-cakka*) operates. the buddha declared it in this manner. moreover, another point of interest is how he attained arahantship in such a short time, while holding the razor to his neck. the buddha declared that the reason for this was that this venerable sappadasaka had practiced monastic duties (*samana-dhamma*) for twenty thousand years during the time of kassapa buddha. in the era of kassapa buddha, the lifespan of human beings was extremely long. it was because of fulfilling those monastic duties that he was able to attain arahantship in this life. yet, the wondrous dhamma-nature (*dhammata*) here shows a great entanglement, or rather, a subtle interaction between the wheel of karma and the wheel of dhamma (*dhamma-cakka*) through this story. because he had tried to make another disrobe out of greed for a razor, that very razor spun back to be pointed at his own neck, along with a mind bent on suicide. but this monk, being energetic—that is where the importance lies—energetically reflecting on his practice of monastic duties and his immaculate keeping of virtue...
next, when the monks asked how he had attained arahantship so quickly, the buddha declared: "monks, for one of aroused energy (*araddhaviriya*), for a monk of aroused energy, in raising a foot and putting it down, he can attain arahantship even before that foot touches the ground. so rapid is this mind, and due to the qualities of this dhamma, such as being visible here and now (*sanditthika*) and timeless (*akalika*), one can penetrate the paths and fruits extremely rapidly. but while one of aroused energy can do this so quickly, a lazy, indolent person cannot do it even if he lives for a hundred years." having declared thus, the buddha uttered that dhamma stanza which we placed as our theme at the beginning:
*yo ca vassasatam jive, kusito hinaviriyo;*
*ekaham jivitam seyyo, viriyama-rabbhato dalham.*
"though one should live a hundred years lazy, indolent, and devoid of effort, yet better is a single day's life of one who makes a firm effort." this is the exemplary stanza of advice uttered by the buddha. thus, both this stanza and the story are things from which we can draw great inspiration. this monk, indeed, intended to commit suicide. but here, we must contemplate the effort spoken of by the buddha. how can we say that this venerable sappadasaka developed effort? in truth, as soon as the thought of disrobing occurred to venerable sappadasaka, he could have done so. but instead, he thought that death was better than returning to lay life. indeed, in this dispensation, if a monk disrobes, according to the usage of the dispensation, the buddha has designated that as "death". saying that a member of the sangha has disrobed, in the terminology of the dispensation, means he has died. the buddha has spoken of the decline of monastic virtues to that extent. it might be because this touched his heart, or it might be due to the power of his past karma and past merit, that this monk also contemplated, "it is better for me to end my life than this."
however, based on this, no one should think that committing suicide is the best path to realize nibbana. that would be a misunderstanding of this story. there is a very profound point here. when we reflect on the idea of developing effort here, from the moment that monk contemplated by way of *silanussati* (recollection of virtue), the entire succession of insight (*vipassana*) from that point onward was carried out entirely through effort—through intense effort. that is to say, it was through contemplation, through intense contemplation in a manner that aroused deep insight-knowledge, that the venerable monk attained arahantship. from that point onwards, it was complete effort; his mind did not back down.
furthermore, when we think carefully about suicide, generally in the world, a person is driven to suicide through mental conflict (*ghattana*). this monk, too, had such a mental conflict. facing this mental conflict, what most people do is destroy their lives out of hatred/aversion (*dosa*). but the problem is not solved. why? because a person commits suicide because they did not get something they expected, or someone they hoped for. at the moment of ending one's life, there is self-hatred within that person. it is out of a certain hatred towards oneself that one cuts one's neck, or jumps into a river or the sea, and does such things. therefore, in truth, the problem is not solved by it. the problem is not solved because *tanha* (craving) remains. as long as *tanha* is preserved as an *anusaya* (latency/underlying tendency), as a defilement, one cannot escape the problem by committing suicide. nowadays, sometimes people try to solve a problem either through suicide or alcohol. either they intoxicate their minds, attempting to flee from the problem, or they attempt to flee from life itself.
even though one attempts to flee from this life, such is the nature of *samsara* that as long as defilements are not destroyed, as long as ignorance (*avijja*) and *tanha* (craving) are not eradicated and cut away, one is born again and again in *samsara*. the buddha demonstrated this in a dhammapada stanza:
*yathapi mule anupaddave dalhe,*
*chinno’pi rukkho punareva ruhati;*
*evam-pi tanhanusaye anuhate,*
*uppajjati dukkham-idam punappunam.*
meaning: just as a tree, though cut down, grows again and again as long as its root remains undamaged and firm—that is, if it is not uprooted, even if the tree is cut, it grows again—just so, as long as the underlying layer of craving, the subtle defilements remaining as *anusaya* (latency/underlying tendency) are not removed, this *samsara* *dukkha* (suffering) arises again and again. according to this dhamma-nature, suicide is not the solution. however, there is a profound point here. at the moment of committing suicide, through this mental conflict, if one arouses the perception of self—the notion of "i" and "mine"—then indeed one loses to mara (the evil one).
instead, what should be done? by subtly contemplating the true nature of this mental conflict arising within oneself, analyzing it as: "here is merely such and such a flow of thoughts, and these are the causes for it"—through such contemplation, through wise contemplation, one arouses the perception of *anatta* (not-self) here. the perception of *anatta* means that nothing can be kept under one's control; one has to be separated from them, if not by other means, then by death. some people, thinking of certain individuals, decide to commit suicide if they do not get them. but one cannot stay with them forever. such is the nature of things. therefore, that profound understanding, that direct realization that "nothing can be kept under one's control," which one can arouse through that very conflict, is like a blessing in disguise. now, there is a common saying in society: "sorrows that come are sweet." but in truth, we must say that the sorrows that come are not merely sweet; there is also the possibility of turning those sorrows into the taste of nibbana. you, virtuous people, have heard of many who turned the sorrows that came to them into the taste of nibbana, such as the female disciples patacara, kisagotami, and others, who extracted the taste of nibbana from the sorrows they encountered.
now, here too, this venerable sappadasaka, through the mental conflict that arose in him, wisely, through what is called *yoniso manasikara* (wise attention)—contemplating with wisdom—realized the sublime dhamma of nibbana. similar to venerable sappadasaka's story, we can briefly mention another parallel case mentioned in the dhamma concerning a certain bhikkhuni. because the oppression of defilements was so great for her, she felt the same way and thought: "it is better for me to hang myself than to return to lay life." she went to a forest, climbed a tree, made a noose out of a creeper, and just as she was about to put it around her neck, her mind was freed from defilements and she attained arahantship. now, these stories are not meant for anyone to experiment with. however, one must understand the dhamma-nature (*dhammata*) within them.
the realization of this dhamma, the dhamma of nibbana, is impossible for a lazy person even if they live for a hundred years. but for wise individuals of aroused energy—one who wisely develops virtue (*sila*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*)—this can be directly realized in a very short moment, even before raising a foot and putting it down, as the buddha declared. the reason for this is that the activity of this mind is extremely rapid. the buddha stated that no comparison is adequate to describe this. nowadays, perhaps, some people give comparisons like computers and so on. but the mind changes with such speed that not even one of those comparisons can come close; it is said to be *lahuparivattam* (swiftly changing). that is why the mind is so rapid. this is true when it is directed towards the bad, but if it is directed towards the good, one can very quickly realize the dhamma of nibbana.
such is the valuable story contained here. moreover, we must contemplate how the mind changed. the manner in which the mind of greed (*lobha*) arose in that monk was extremely rapid. one must make an effort, drawing from this story, to protect one's mind from such situations. sometimes, a defilement (*kilesa*) aroused in a mere split second can extend extremely far into the future. it was because of that greedy mind that the razor was aimed at his own neck. why did he become wearisome of monkhood and think of disrobing, despite having such a rich store of supportive causes (*hetu-sampatti*)? it was because he had caused such a flow of thoughts in another person. this shows the connection between karma and its result (*vipaka*). "what you do bears fruit"—such is the reality.
next, let us contemplate the razor. there is much we can learn from the razor as well. the razor is largely out of common use today, even among the sangha. but you, virtuous people, probably know that there are two ways of using a razor. that is, there are two ways of holding a razor. when shaving the head or beard, the razor is held in a certain delicate manner, almost as if preparing to cast it, allowing the hand to move back and forth very easily from the wrist. that is how the razor is held when shaving. but if someone is trying to commit suicide, how do they hold this razor? they brandish it; they hold it tightly. corresponding to these two ideas, there are two words used in society. likewise, there are two words used in the dispensation as well. that delicate holding is called *sammasana* (comprehension/careful investigation), and the tight grasping, the brandishing, is called *paramasana* (grasping/clinging). although these words are somewhat heavy, we mentioned them on this occasion because they contain several profound meanings. *sammasana* refers to a kind of delicate stroking or light touching. it is enough to understand it in relation to the razor.
there is a similar situation within mental conflict as well. mental conflict refers to the clashes within the mind. we cannot imagine that there is anyone here who does not experience mental conflicts. various kinds of conflicts can arise: disappointments, unexpected occurrences—in short, the eight worldly conditions (*attha-loka-dhamma*). there are mental conflicts that arise when facing these. one can utilize such mental conflicts in both of the ways mentioned. venerable sappadasaka initially went with the intention of brandishing that razor. but what was done through it next? what followed was an understanding of this mental conflict. in the same way, friends, a profound meaning of the word *sammasana* is contemplation. contemplation means reflecting on whatever comes into one's mind as: "this is such-and-such; this is merely a *vedana* (feeling); this is only a thought; this is like a dream; or this is a *sanna* (perception), a recognition." considering their true nature in one's mind in this manner is called *sammasana*.
what happens through that? through that recognition, one does not get entangled in karma with them. because it is due to a lack of understanding and delusion regarding a mental conflict, the tremors in the mind, that a person is driven by defilements to commit suicide. if, instead, one arouses understanding, grasps their dhamma-nature, and arouses the concept of *anatta* (not-self) instead of self—instead of that intense *tanha* (craving) and ignorance (*avijja*) which demands "this must be kept under my control," realizing: "these are things that do not remain under anyone's control; even if one wishes, they cannot be kept; either one must let them go at death, or they must be abandoned before death"—if one gains such an understanding, they can remain unsubmerged by the torrent of defilements. in short, *sammasana* means contemplating in a manner that arouses the three characteristics of *anicca* (impermanent), *dukkha* (suffering), and *anatta* (not-self). *sammasana* is the sharpening of this razor of wisdom so that the three characteristics of *anicca*, *dukkha*, and *anatta* become sharp. on the other hand, *paramasana* (grasping/clinging) means raising the perception of self at a moment of mental tremor or conflict, causing great mental distress by thinking "this is happening only to me," becoming deluded, and out of that tight grasping, being driven by lack of understanding to commit suicide or turn to alcohol. such is the situation.
thus, you, virtuous people, apply your minds to meditation along the path of *sammasana*. this meditation is not restricted only to the sangha. in short, you know that the eight worldly conditions—gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and *dukkha* (suffering)—are things that come in our day-to-day lives. the buddha declared that everyone has to face these, including the buddha himself, as long as they are in *samsara*. so, when one of these conditions presents itself, some people are driven to commit suicide because of it. that is not how one should think. one should console oneself by thinking, "this is only one of the eight; it is only a quarter (of the pairs)." reflecting wisely that "this is only a quarter of the worldly conditions that happen to everyone," and understanding that this too is a dhamma-nature that arises, exists, and ceases—a person who practices contemplating daily life in a manner that yields such understanding will never contemplate committing suicide in such a violent way. in the case of that monk, it was because a heavy past karma had surfaced. even if such a situation arises, one must contemplate in accordance with the dhamma. it is from this very mind that we derive what is called effort. exerting effort means remaining afloat, not submerged by the torrent of defilements. just as when one falls into a river or the sea, one swims and tries to cross over somehow, one must arouse this wisdom with strength and strive to gain a true understanding of these. that is the exemplar we must take from such stories: the arousing of this effort.
next, as we said about *sammasana* and the razor, in every situation that presents itself to us, there is a leaning towards *samsara*; we can act in a way that expands *samsara* through the various objects that present themselves. but the buddha has also declared that within that wise contemplation called *sammasana*, there lies the path to cross over the suffering of *samsara*. in that way, if one now arouses the nature of *anicca* (impermanent), *dukkha* (suffering), and *anatta* (not-self) in everything, and exerts effort towards that, one can reach that understanding within daily life itself. it is mentioned that in the past, not only the monks, but also lay disciples (*upasaka* and *upasika*) even after the buddha's time, well-guarding their five precepts or the eight uposatha precepts, and established on that virtue, even during their daily work like farming or carpentry, contemplated the thoughts that arose, the flow of thoughts, exactly as they were, dissolving them right where they arose, and strove to realize the three characteristics of *anicca*, *dukkha*, and *anatta* through them. for such persons, at a moment they least expect, sometimes suddenly by the very law of dhamma, even the penetration of the paths and fruits—sotapanna, sakadagami, anagami, and arahant—can be achieved.
therefore, while everyone should be enthusiastic about maintaining this attention (*manasikara*), one must reflect on the dhamma-principles that lead to this according to what has been discussed. if someone walks the noble eightfold path—shaping their flow of thoughts and daily life according to *samma-ditthi*, *samma-sankappa*, *samma-vaca*, *samma-kammanta*, *samma-ajiva*, *samma-vayama*, *samma-sati*, and *samma-samadhi*—this path becomes straight for them at the very moment such insight-knowledges arise. furthermore, according to the matters discussed regarding venerable sappadasaka, one must constantly cultivate a deep conviction in the turning of this wheel of karma. the things that happen to oneself should not be viewed merely as things done by others in society; this karma operates in an extremely subtle manner, visible only to a buddha or to those possessing higher psychic knowledges (*abhinna*). these are wondrous things. we think someone else did it to us, but underneath lies the force of karma.
therefore, a person who has developed the conviction that such a force of karma is at work here need not get agitated about these things. these are things one has to pay off. thus, instead of accumulating further karma based on them, what one must do is apply wisdom, understanding, and effort to comprehend their true nature and turn them into blessings in disguise. in accordance with the dhamma, there are only three grades to learn in this *samsara*, or rather, to pass out of *samsara*: gratification (*assada*), danger (*adinava*), and escape (*nissarana*). gratification (*assada*) means pleasing the senses with the fivefold sensual pleasures and so on. the gratification class is like the kindergarten class, and that is where the majority of people are. next, in experiencing this gratification, many people have to commit various unwholesome deeds for its sake; this is clear to you, virtuous people. nowadays, those who are considered wise or scientists teach what kind of occupations one should do to get rich quickly. what do those who adopt such schemes do? they accumulate sin. through accumulating those sins, while on the gratification side, they then have to suffer the consequences as the danger (*adinava*) of those actions without even realizing it. in the stage of suffering the consequences, a person then reflects in that class: "this *samsara* is indeed not a good place; i must depart from here." it is in such instances, as mentioned in the jataka stories and other places, that even kings sometimes abandon their kingship, leave behind all wealth, and go to practice asceticism in places like the himalayas.
next, if one has understood the danger (*adinava*) of defilements in *samsara* in this way, the peace we receive, the rare gain we obtain, is the opportunity to escape from this, provided we have attained a wise human existence during the era of a buddha's appearance. this is called "escape" (*nissarana*). escape means leaping out of this *samsara*. *samsara* is like a circular ring. when we take the two words *samsarana* (wandering) and *nissarana* (escape), we understand that wandering means spinning in the same place. if you look at a dog, you sometimes see it spinning around to catch its tail. it spins in the very same spot. it is the same here. what is to be understood from this extremely profound dhamma called *paticca-samuppada* (dependent arising) is also this nature of spinning in the same place. the exhaustion and the dizziness arising from this are indeed what are called defilements (*kilesas*). leaning towards those defilements, the world is drawn and spins in the same place due to the taints (*asavas*) and other factors.
due to ignorance (*avijja*) and *tanha* (craving), ordinary worldly people see no strength or method to ever leap out of this circular ring. however, when a buddha appears and declares the dhamma, we can gradually understand, as right view (*samma-ditthi*), the correct comprehension: the nature of *dukkha* (suffering) of this entire *samsaric* existence, and that *tanha* lies lurking underneath it. if one gains an understanding of these four noble truths—that on the day this unquenchable thirst called *tanha* is stilled, there is peace right there, and that the path to attain that peace called nibbana is this path of eight factors—then such a person can advance in that grade of escape (*nissarana*).
therefore, escape (*nissarana*) means leaping out of this circular ring. once caught in that circular ring, one must exert a certain effort to leap out of it. it does not happen on its own. you know that for someone spinning in circles to leap out of that ring, a special effort is required. what happens on its own is the spinning of the circular ring. that effort is what is called energy (*viriya*). it was about that energy that the buddha uttered this stanza, which we have chosen as our theme. now, you, virtuous people, exert much effort in your day-to-day lives for your occupations and so on. the buddha describes the lay life as *khuppipasahi khajjamano*—being consumed by hunger and thirst. how do lay devotees spend their lives? being eaten up by hunger and thirst. it is just like food. to live in this *samsara* is to live falling prey to what is called hunger and thirst. we think we are taking food and drink, eating and drinking. but what actually happens to us? we are being consumed by thirst and hunger. that is how the buddha declares it. such is the perilous state that exists in *samsara*. whether we look at *samsara* or look at the way our poor human beings live, such a state of suffering exists.
thus, such is the state of the world. this *tanha* (craving) is never something that can be satisfied. it is like a deer running after a mirage. this thirst can never be quenched. no matter how much, it cannot be filled. instead, what must be done is the eradication of this *tanha*. that is why the buddha declared that the very eradication of *tanha* is nibbana. thus, what venerable sappadasaka also did was to remove that *tanha* lying underneath, as well as the ignorance (*avijja*) concerning it. a beginning for this can be aroused by everyone through the very things they do. on some occasion, you offer a spoonful of rice. you give something. even when you offer something when we go on alms round (*pindapata*), you should reflect: "this is not done merely because this monk arrived, nor is it because we must give something by any means." at that moment, you must look closely back at your own mind. wisely reflecting on all these things so that no conflict arises in the mind, you must use every single one of these actions to refine your own mind.
in accordance with the advice, "if one gives, one gives alms and merit; if one shapes, one shapes one's own mind," when offering oil, a lamp, or a flower, in every such act, one must look at one's own mind. that is why in stanzas and such, the impermanent nature of these is indicated. a child is very fond of a flower when they see it. but at the moment of offering it, the attitude of offering (*puja-buddhi*), the faith (*saddha*) one has in the buddha, and similarly with other things, is what matters. wisely contemplating the value of such moments, one must strive to advance on this path of nibbana through them.
from this story, points regarding the exertion of effort arose. when considering day-to-day meditative attention (*manasikara*), one can contemplate how this bodily cage decays by way of unattractiveness meditation (*asubha-bhavana*), or by way of attention to elements (*dhatu-manasikara*), reflecting that these four elements—earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and wind (*vayo*)—are what we consume as food and drink. when these external things are integrated into this body, we develop a great attachment to them, thinking "mine," or "this is my limb." but we must reflect wisely on their true nature. furthermore, instead of submitting and yielding to the flow of thoughts rushing into one's mind, acting according to them, and going to states of misery (*apaya*), one must constantly contemplate the wholesome roots and unwholesome roots declared by the buddha: *lobha* (greed), *dosa* (hatred), *moha* (delusion), and *alobha* (non-greed), *adosa* (non-hatred), *amoha* (non-delusion). when a certain thought comes to the mind, one must reflect: "does this fall on the side of greed or non-greed? does it fall on the side of hatred, or does it help to eradicate hatred? does it fall on the side of delusion, or on the side of understanding?" when one shapes the mind with understanding regarding whatever arises, contemplating subtly, karma does not spring up again from them.
if we may give a small comparison—these are not perfect comparisons, but we offer them because they help to understand things through contemporary examples. you know that if there is a wire carrying electricity, and it is not covered with a rubber insulation, the moment you touch it, you get an electric shock. but through that rubber insulation, one is saved from the electric shock. just so, one must practice contemplating and attending (*manasikara*) to the flow of thoughts passing through one's mind. what is supportive of this? the buddha has declared it as *sati-sampajanna*—mindfulness and clear comprehension. *sati* means mindfulness, and *sampajanna* is also described as wisdom, or rather, awareness. one begins to perform consciously what used to occur unconsciously, even small things like going and coming. next, contemplating everything, such as the movement of hands and limbs—that is indeed what is called insight (*vipassana*). directing attention to each of these, one understands their true nature: that these are things that arise, exist, and cease. at the moment one gains that understanding, just like the electric wire covered with rubber insulation, defilements do not grow within oneself through that flow of thoughts. it helps one to be freed from *samsara*.
this *samsara* is indeed an accumulation of these five aggregates (*pancakkhandha*). through everything we do, these five aggregates—form (*rupa*), *vedana* (feeling), perception (*sanna*), *sankhara* (preparations), and *vinnana* (consciousness)—are accumulated. just like pouring water into a filter and having it strain through, through everything we do, these five aggregates grow due to ignorance (*avijja*) and *tanha* (craving)—either on the wholesome side or on the unwholesome side. one who strives to completely escape from these, from *samsara*, uses the weapon of wisdom as the supporting tool. wisdom indeed is this very contemplation. it is the matter of *sammasana* (comprehension/careful investigation) that we have discussed so far: the understanding of, or awareness of, their true nature. one must become aware of them. we mostly try to make others aware. but that is not it; one must apply all of this to oneself. for such a long time, throughout our entire lives, we have breathed since the moment we came out of our mother's womb. yet, we do not know the true nature of this breath, of this inhalation and exhalation. that is why the buddha declared the meditation of *anapanasati* (mindfulness of breathing). if one understands the impermanence (*aniccata*) within this inhalation and exhalation, how delicate is this thread of life! one can easily arouse the understanding of how quickly, at any moment, it can be spent and cease.
likewise, one has no understanding of the true nature of this body, its unattractive nature, its impermanent nature, or the true nature of the food and drink we consume. in the ordinary worldly life, this is an era in which people think about them according to various ornaments and fashions. in such an era, one must reflect that by living with wisdom, one can escape from the dangerous conditions commonly seen in society, such as alcohol addiction and suicide. but this must be done systematically. systematic practice is indeed what is called meditation (*bhavana*). quieting the mind and then practicing this attention by way of insight (*vipassana*)—if one obtains the necessary instructions for this from the proper sources, they do not refrain from meditating on the pretext of having farming work in their day-to-day lives; they meditate along with their farming work. they plow, and at the same time, they develop a strength in the mind that can be derived from it.
one must train oneself in that kind of thinking. it was because they lived such lives in the past that it is mentioned of lay female devotees that when pounding paddy, they would not let the husk be separated from the grain without bringing it under the attention of meditation. somehow, they saw impermanence (*aniccata*) through it. it was through that dhamma-reflection during their daily activities that they obtained mental relief—not from medicine or sleeping pills. therefore, the dispensation of the buddha, this dhamma, is never outdated. it is mentioned in the dhamma: *satan-ca dhammo na jaram upeti*—the dhamma of the virtuous never decays. ordinary worldly things—you know, where are the things that were in your living rooms ten years ago? if the next-door neighbor has a greater fashion, you follow that. without even knowing it, those older things go to the dustbin.
that outdated nature found in the world does not apply to this dhamma. the dhamma declared by the buddha more than two thousand five hundred years ago is true even today. it is that fire of greed, that fire of hatred, and that fire of delusion that are still burning. only the firewood thrown into them is different. in those days, what was thrown were bows, arrows, swords, and so on. today, you know what is thrown: bombs and other such things. in this manner, the three fires called *lobha* (greed), *dosa* (hatred), and *moha* (delusion) are ever-present realities; they are always there. therefore, the dhamma of the buddha never decays. reflecting wisely according to this, no matter how the world thinks of these things, one must contemplate them with one's own wisdom and, walking on this noble eightfold path, strive to become a buddhist in reality, in truth—that is, not merely as a buddhist by birth certificate, but through practice; not by birth, but to reach the state of being a buddhist through practice.
the path that supports this is the noble eightfold path. if we briefly consider it, translating the pali terms: *samma-ditthi* means right view. even when going on a journey, we first look ahead at the road to see if we can pass, or if there are thorns and bushes. next, we establish a certain view regarding it. *samma-ditthi*, or right view, refers to the four noble truths: that this entire *samsaric* existence is *dukkha* (suffering); the cause for it is *tanha* (craving); and the path that leads to the eradication of *tanha* and supports nibbana is walking on this noble eightfold path. if this basic understanding, this right view, is established, then as one constantly thinks accordingly, right intentions (*samma-sankappa*) arise.
the thought to escape from this lay life, the thought of going forth, the thought of letting go of these, the thought of detachment from *samsara*; next, non-violence, and thoughts of loving-kindness (*metta*). in this manner, a succession of thoughts arises. if right intentions are established accordingly, then that person's speech also avoids lying, slander, harsh speech, and idle chatter; instead, truthful words, words that unite others, meaningful words, and gentle words are what proceed from that person. right speech. *samma-vaca* means right speech. next, in accordance with this, that person strives to act as the buddha did, who was *yathavadi tathakari*—he did as he said, and he said as he did. thinking, "therefore, i too must live according to my words," they abstain from unwholesome deeds like killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—right action (*samma-kammanta*). through right speech, they arouse right action. that right action is not something done occasionally, but is integrated into their entire livelihood, which is extremely difficult in this era. how to keep one's livelihood righteous (*samma-ajiva*) is indeed a great challenge. nevertheless, if one hopes for nibbana, they have to do it, along with a certain sacrifice.
then comes right livelihood (*samma-ajiva*). through the effort applied to right livelihood in accordance with the dhamma, what that person does is walk on that path of meditation. *samma-vayama* means right effort. *samma-vayama* does not mean exerting limbs and working until one sweats. it is a certain energy exerted within the mind. what is that energy? preventing unwholesome thoughts from entering the mind; dispelling unwholesome thoughts already present in the mind; bringing in wholesome thoughts that should be cultivated; and consolidating the wholesome thoughts already present. this is a fourfold energy: the effort to prevent the arising of unarisen unwholesome states, to abandon arisen unwholesome states, to arouse unarisen wholesome states, and to maintain and consolidate arisen wholesome states. this is the true energy. what is supportive of developing this energy? mindfulness (*sati*), the awareness we mentioned earlier. constantly with mindfulness, alert like a good sentry, one must watch one's own mind. one must constantly watch this flow of incoming thoughts, the flow of thoughts underlying our external actions and words. that watchfulness, that state of keeping watch, that awareness of it, is indeed what is called *sampajanna* (clear comprehension). thus, one practices *sati-sampajanna*—mindfulness and the wisdom or awareness that follows mindfulness.
next, accordingly, the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipatthana*) develop within that person: the true nature of this body—not only of one's own body but also of others' bodies—the true nature of *vedana* (feeling), the behavior of the mind, and the changes in the mind during states of greed, hatred, and so on, and what lies underneath them. these four are called contemplation of the body (*kayanupassana*), contemplation of feelings (*vedananupassana*), contemplation of the mind (*cittanupassana*), and contemplation of phenomena (*dhammanupassana*). these four foundations of mindfulness automatically become the focus of such a person. next, when one directs the mind for a long time towards some object, some meditation subject (*kammatthana*) in those four foundations of mindfulness, that purified mind then becomes concentrated (*samadhi*). through that concentration, a very subtle pleasure (*sukha*) is also experienced. but even if that pleasure or a great rapture arises, transcending that too, just like venerable sappadasaka, one then directs it towards insight-knowledge. you know that water is collected in a large reservoir and then carried through pipes; why is that? to generate electricity, it is carried through several pipes and then through a narrow pipe to turn an iron wheel and produce hydroelectric power. just so, all this energy gathered and accumulated by way of concentration (*samadhi*) must next be directed towards the path of insight (*vipassana*). it is by developing this succession of insight-knowledges in one's mental continuum, beginning with arising and passing away, that at a certain stage—when they have matured—one can penetrate the paths and fruits of sotapanna, sakadagami, anagami, and arahant, escape this perilous ocean of *samsara*, and realize supreme nibbana.
therefore, on a vesak full moon day like today, if you, virtuous people, aspire to worship the buddha with the highest offering of practice (*patipatti-puja*) as he declared, you must strive from this day onward to cultivate within yourselves not only that physical effort but also mental effort—this *samma-vayama* (right effort). the vesak day is indeed the most valuable day to make special determinations. contemplate in that manner. you have listened to the dhamma very calmly up to this moment. one might think that the benefits of listening to the dhamma (*dhamma-savana-anisamsa*) are something that will manifest in the future. but most of those benefits have already been reaped right here, even if you are unaware of it. that is to say, the buddha has declared that it is not through our physical five senses—eyes, ears, nose, and so on—that we can realize nibbana. we can realize nibbana through the five spiritual faculties (*indriya*) called *saddha* (faith), *viriya* (energy), *sati* (mindfulness), *samadhi* (concentration), and *panna* (wisdom). faith (*saddha*) must be elevated to a faculty (*indriya*). a faculty means a ruling power; faith must be brought to a state where it is unsubdued by anyone, unsubdued by lack of faith. energy (*viriya*) must also be elevated to a faculty. it must rule. ruling means reigning in one's mental continuum. *indriya* refers to a ruler or king. thus, faith, energy, and also mindfulness—mindfulness too must be developed in the same way. next, concentration, the power of concentration. next, wisdom. the buddha has designated these both as faculties (*indriya*) and as powers (*bala*). a king is not given kingship for nothing; it is given to exercise power. likewise, if these faculties of *saddha*, *viriya*, *sati*, *samadhi*, and *panna* have arisen in someone's continuum, then as faculties, they possess a governing power; they can apply that power to realize the supreme dhamma of nibbana.
in support of that, there are those here who have undertaken the *ajiva-atthamaka-sila* (livelihood-eightfold virtue), and there are also those who have undertaken an even more precious virtue, the precious eight uposatha precepts. grounded on that virtue, everyone has generated a good flow of thoughts at this moment—which is indeed meditation. whether one is seated in a cross-legged posture (*pallanka*) or in any other way, this is something that takes place within the mind. therefore, through this listening to the dhamma, that meditative flow of thoughts generated develops those faculties of *saddha*, *viriya*, *sati*, *samadhi*, and *panna*. moreover, for some, deep understanding may even arise through this. reflecting in this manner on this heap of merit accumulated by you, virtuous people, during this hour—this heap of merit accumulated as the benefits of listening to the dhamma—you must also share its meritorious portion. having attained a human birth in this extremely rare era of a buddha's appearance, this is a moment when the lamp of the dispensation (*sasana*) is on the verge of going out. if one does not obtain light from these last few drops of oil, they will next plunge into a great darkness and will have to wait for another interval between buddhas (*buddhantara*).
therefore, reflecting on these, one must take full advantage of such opportunities. furthermore, may this accumulated store of merit (*punna-sambhara*) support our journey to nibbana! you must make an aspiration for yourselves: "may i, by developing meditation in this very life, escape from these perilous four states of misery (*apaya*) as quickly as possible, attain the state of sotapanna or go even beyond, and obtain the power, the supportive potential (*upanissaya-sampatti*), and the fortune to end all *samsaric* *dukkha* (suffering) through the noble state of arahantship!" having done so, next, aspire likewise: "may the assembly of deities and brahmas who protect the dispensation, and any guardian deities residing in this place who await merit, rejoice in this store of merit we have accumulated through this dhamma preaching and dhamma listening! having rejoiced, may they realize supreme nibbana through a wished-for bodhi!" furthermore, whatever departed relatives there may be in our names, and whatever living beings from avici up to akanittha who desire nibbana and seek merit—may all such beings rejoice in this heap of merit of our dhamma listening and dhamma preaching! having rejoiced, may they realize the supreme, deathless nibbana as quickly as possible. with this aspiration, recite these stanzas and share the merit.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 112
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #112
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.30)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Na kahāpaṇavassena, titti kāmesu vijjati;
appassādā dukhā kāmā, iti viññāya paṇḍito;
api dibbesu kāmesu, ratiṃ so nādhigacchati;
taṇhakkhayarato hoti, sammāsambuddhasāvako ti.
From:
Dhammapada 186 (Buddhavagga)
Dear Listeners,
On this invaluable Esala Full Moon Poya Day, let us highlight several points relevant to a precious Dhamma discourse delivered by our Buddha. Generally, worldly people think that if they can eliminate poverty and lack, they can lead a happy life; almost everyone holds this view. However, our Buddha demonstrates that as long as Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) is present, the world cannot eliminate Suffering / Unsatisfactoriness / Stress (*dukkha*). Why is this? Because as long as Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) exists, lack and scarcity will only grow. The root cause of the growth of lack and scarcity is indeed Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*). Therefore, it is only by eliminating Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) that Suffering / Unsatisfactoriness / Stress (*dukkha*) can be eliminated.
This is why our Buddha, even in His very first sermon—the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, delivered on the Esala Full Moon Poya Day—introduced Nibbāna by the name of the destruction of craving (*taṇhakkhaya*). Thus, it is only by eliminating Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) that one can completely free oneself from the Suffering / Unsatisfactoriness / Stress (*dukkha*) of Saṃsāra. According to worldly concepts, people imagine that if a rain of coins were to fall, they could satisfy all their needs, and the entire world could live in prosperity.
But the Buddha declared that even if a rain of *kahāpaṇas*—a rain of gold coins—were to fall in that manner, this Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) could never be brought to an end. Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) is something that grows and proliferates like a tree or a vine. Therefore, the more one receives, the more the desire arises for "yet more"; a feeling of "this is enough" never arises in Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*). It only says, "this is still insufficient." Even in this modern era, various kinds of "rains" fall in the form of lucky draws and bags of fortune. It is difficult to think that any of these can completely resolve the trials and tribulations of our lives. Indeed, the stanza we have chosen as our theme today, as well as its background story, speaks of a story concerning gold coins.
At the time when our Buddha was residing in Jetavana, a certain young man left the household life and ordained. Having ordained, under the guidance of his preceptor, he went to a distant area to study under a teacher in order to learn the Vinaya and other disciplines. During that time, this monk's father fell extremely ill and drew near to death. The father deeply wished to see his son, the disciple of the Buddha, but there was no way to send a message. Therefore, at his final moment, thinking of his son and speaking deliriously, he handed over a hundred *kahāpaṇas* to his younger son—the monk's younger brother—saying, "This is for my noble son to obtain a bowl and robes," and then he passed away.
Later, when the monk returned to Sāvatthi and visited his father's house, his younger brother fell at his feet, wept bitterly, and said, "At his final moment, our father declared this: he gave me a hundred *kahāpaṇas* for you to obtain a bowl and robes." When the brother asked what should be done with the money, the monk rejected it, saying, "We have no use for these *kahāpaṇas*." Even though he rejected it, later on, a kind of doubt and hesitation arose in this monk: "Why should I trouble myself going from house to house begging for alms? Would it not be better for me to find some employment, return to the lay life, and live comfortably? I can live with these hundred *kahāpaṇas* as my capital." With this thought, he lost interest in his studies and meditation, neglected his monastic duties and routines, and began to pass his time lazily. His physical complexion also became pale and wan. Seeing this, the other novice monks asked him, "What is the matter?" and the monk revealed his thoughts.
Those monks and novices then escorted him to our Buddha. Our Buddha asked, "Why, monk, have you become disaffected? Why are you thinking of returning to the lay life? Why are you dissatisfied with the Holy Life?" When asked, the monk recounted the story. Then our Buddha did this: "Do you think you can sustain your livelihood with these hundred *kahāpaṇas*? Very well, then, instead of those hundred *kahāpaṇas*, go and bring a hundred pebbles." The monk gathered a hundred pebbles and returned.
Our Buddha then began to calculate the accounts with them to see if this amount was sufficient to return to lay life. First, He asked him to set aside fifty of them: He told him to set aside fifty pebbles just for food, drink, and basic sustenance after returning to lay life. He set them aside. Next, He told him to set aside twenty-four *kahāpaṇas* to buy a pair of oxen if he was to engage in farming. Then, He told him to set aside such and such numbers of pebbles for a plough, spade, sickle, axe, and so forth. In the end, when they looked, those hundred pebbles were insufficient. The hundred *kahāpaṇas* were not enough even as basic capital.
Then our Buddha declared: "Do you see now, monk? How can you satisfy your Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) with these hundred *kahāpaṇas*? Not only for you, but even for the great King Mandhātā—who possessed such immense psychic power that at the mere snap of his fingers a rain of seven treasures fell waist-deep over an area of a league, who lived for an incredibly long time, and who ruled over the heavenly worlds through the reigns of thirty-six Sakkas—even he was unable to eradicate his Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*). He passed away to the next world without being able to fulfill his Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*)." Having related this Jātaka story, our Buddha uttered these two verses at the end:
> *“Na kahāpaṇavassena, titti kāmesu vijjati;*
> *appassādā dukhā kāmā, iti viññāya paṇḍito.*
> *Api dibbesu kāmesu, ratiṃ so nādhigacchati;*
> *taṇhakkhayarato hoti, sammāsambuddhasāvako”ti.*
*"Na kahāpaṇavassena titti kāmesu vijjati"*—Not even by a rain of *kahāpaṇas* or a rain of gold coins is there any satisfaction, fulfillment, or contentment regarding sensual pleasures (*kāma*). Next:
*"Appassādā dukhā kāmā"*—Sensual pleasures and the objects of sensual pleasure do have a side of gratification (*assāda*), a side of enjoyment, but it is exceedingly minor. It is very little. However, when looking at their undesirable consequences and disadvantages (*ādīnava*), they entail much Suffering / Unsatisfactoriness / Stress (*dukkha*). *"Appassādā dukhā kāmā"* means gratification is little, but Suffering / Unsatisfactoriness / Stress (*dukkha*) is abundant.
*"Iti viññāya paṇḍito"*—The wise person, having understood this matter,
*"Api dibbesu kāmesu ratiṃ so nādhigacchati"*—does not develop an attachment even to heavenly sensual pleasures. The true disciple of the Buddha does not develop an attachment even to the bliss of the heavenly worlds; the wise one does not form an attachment to it.
*"Taṇhakkhayarato hoti sammāsambuddhasāvako"*—In what does the true disciple of the Fully Enlightened One find delight? He finds delight in *taṇhakkhaya*, which means the destruction of craving, the exhaustion of thirst. The name *taṇhakkhaya* is used for Nibbāna itself. Nibbāna is defined in the sense of the eradication of craving. Our Buddha declared that the true disciple of the Fully Enlightened One finds delight in that extinguishment.
Therefore, this story and these verses are highly exemplary for us. There are lessons in this story and these stanzas that serve as models for our lives. When we reflect on this story, dear devotees, money is something indispensable for lay life. Indeed, our Buddha once declared—in response to a question that arose regarding the Sangha—that if money is allowable to someone, then the fivefold sensual pleasures and the fortunes of sensual pleasures are also allowable to them. This is because money is like an invitation to the lay life.
Now, that father leaving a hundred *kahāpaṇas* for the sake of that monk was just like an invitation to become a layman. And that monk was preparing to accept that invitation. Our Buddha changed the monk's mind through a timely simile and a timely course of action. Generally, however, you devotees know that leaving the lay life, which is leaving Saṃsāra, requires getting away from gold, silver, money, and other such things that belong to these sensual objects.
According to the Noble parlance, returning to lay life from the monkhood is referred to as "death." According to the Noble parlance and monastic usage, when someone who has ordained gives up the robes and leaves, it is considered a death, a demise. Often, in monastic terms, money is referred to as a "serpent." You devotees know that when a serpent bites, death is often the result. A similar thing was about to happen to that monk. Just like being bitten by a serpent, a multitude of thoughts about the lay life arose in that monk, to the point of slipping away from his monkhood. Our Buddha removed it through a timely step. Thus, we should consider this as one of the lessons to be drawn from this story. Furthermore, our Buddha made him understand the troublesome nature of lay life through the demonstration He conducted by having that monk bring those pebbles.
You devotees know very well about a critical problem that heavily affects lay life—the great effort and immense struggle to balance income and expenditure in living a household life. The gravity of this was made clear to that monk through the question of whether these things could be done with a hundred *kahāpaṇas*. In this way, our Buddha's supreme skill-in-means (*upāya-kosalla*), His knowledge, and His wisdom are revealed to us through the story associated with these verses.
When we contemplate these verses, we see that what our Buddha has expressed here is an eternal, timeless truth. Why is it said that even a rain of *kahāpaṇas* cannot quench one's desires? Often, we do something thinking that if we obtain it we will be happy and can live our lives well. But even as we receive those things, our minds bend toward more and more luxurious things. In this era, when we look at things commercially, invitations to a luxurious life are everywhere, prompting people to spend in a way that does not match their income.
Therefore, to live peacefully and happily in such a society, even if you devotees cannot renounce everything and ordain, you must try to cultivate a simple lifestyle and noble thoughts in your lay lives. For one who does not understand the value of this simple life, accepting the invitations presented by this commercial civilization leads to falling into a terrifying abyss of debt. Among the forms of happiness necessary for lay life, "the happiness of debtlessness" (*anaṇa-sukha*) is highlighted. But this becomes extremely difficult if one's desires and Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) are intense. Therefore, it is to help even ordinary lay devotees understand the disadvantages of these desires that our Buddha has preached here that even a rain of *kahāpaṇas* cannot bring satisfaction or contentment regarding those sensual pleasures and desires.
Similarly, *"appassādā dukhā kāmā"*—the nature of sensual pleasures is such that they bring little gratification, minor pleasure, and brief happiness, but their disadvantages (*ādīnava*) are abundant. This is the fact that must be understood by the wise. Even heavenly fortunes and heavenly bliss, though subtle, are still part of the fivefold sensual pleasures. Therefore, without developing an attachment even for those, one must strive to gradually thin out this Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*), to exhaust it, to extinguish it—which is the liberation from craving called Nibbāna. This is the message our Buddha gives.
Indeed, what many people do to quench their Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) is to give it whatever it asks for. This is like giving water to a feverish patient. You cannot satisfy a feverish patient by giving them water every time they ask for it. A true physician examines the root cause of the disease and administers medicine; then, the demand for water naturally ceases. In the same way, our Buddha shows that there is absolutely no end to be found in these desires. Even a multi-billionaire is a pauper when compared to the great King Mandhātā we mentioned. King Mandhātā was so incredibly powerful that through his psychic and meritorious power, a rain of seven treasures fell when he clapped his hands. Yet, even with such a rain of seven treasures, he could not be satisfied. Since Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) is of this nature, it is only when one removes this Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) from one's mind-stream that true peace is obtained.
When a certain householder named Potaliya came to discuss with our Buddha, the Buddha illustrated the disadvantageous side of these sensual pleasures using seven magnificent similes. You devotees may have heard some of these before.
The first simile is explained by our Buddha in this way: A dog, tormented by extreme hunger, goes to a slaughterhouse or a butcher's shop and waits for something to be given. The butcher or his apprentice takes a bone from which all meat has been stripped, leaving only a bone smeared with a bit of blood, and throws it to the dog. The dog picks it up and, because of the trace of blood, tries to gnaw it to find satisfaction. What happens? Sometimes its mouth gets cut, and in the end, it is its own blood that it drinks. In this way, the dog only gets exhausted; its hunger is never actually appeased. Following this simile, our Buddha says to the householder Potaliya: "In the same way, remember that the Blessed One has preached that the gratification (*assāda*) of these is very little, while the Suffering / Unsatisfactoriness / Stress (*dukkha*) is abundant; their disadvantages (*ādīnava*) are great, and they are full of fear." To keep this simile in mind, we can call it the "Simile of the Meatless Bone." This is the first simile.
Next, He gives another simile: A vulture or a hawk takes a piece of meat and flies up into the sky. Seeing this, other vultures and hawks chase after this bird and peck at it to snatch that piece of meat. If the bird does not let go of the piece of meat, what will happen? It will either face death or suffer grave injury and fall. Sensual pleasures are just like that, says the next simile. From this, we can contemplate deeply that every single simile given by our Buddha is actually like a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). There is immense depth in them.
We can relate this to today's society: it is not just one person who desires these sensual objects or any given thing. There is a vast crowd competing for them. Someone snatches it and flies off like that hawk, and a crowd chases after them. If they do not let go of it, if they cling to it, they will face disaster from the others. Such is their nature. Because so many people desire them, one has to face them in a highly competitive manner and suffer thereby. This is the lesson we must draw from this simile, which we can call the "Simile of the Piece of Meat."
Thirdly, He gives a simile: A person takes a grass torch—nowadays we have flashlights, but in those days when walking in the dark they would carry a fiery torch. Here, it is a grass torch made of grass. Carrying it, they walk against the wind. What happens as they walk against the wind? The embers and sparks of that torch blow back onto their own hand. Their hand will be burnt if they do not let go of that grass torch. Sensual pleasures, too, can be compared to that grass torch. What does this show? It shows that by pursuing these sensual objects, many people end up burning their own hands. The side of their disadvantages (*ādīnava*) is that dangerous. They do not know it, but our Buddha showed that the danger of sensual pleasures is just like carrying a grass torch against the wind.
Next, He gives another simile: the Simile of the Pit of Glowing Embers. Suppose there is a person who loves life and hates death. In one place, there is a pit of glowing embers, deeper than a man's height, filled with blazing, glowing embers. Two strong men come, grab that man by his two arms, and drag him toward that pit of embers. Step by step, that man knows, "If I fall into this, I will face either death or suffering equivalent to death." But he has no choice; he is being dragged toward it. Sensual pleasures are compared to this pit of glowing embers.
Contemplating deeply, we can understand that sensual pleasures are desires. The strength of these desires is such that they drag a person along, just as if they were being dragged by someone else. When a weak man is dragged by two strong men, our Buddha explains that he twists and turns. He twists and struggles to escape from it, but he cannot. Yet he knows that if he falls, he will be destroyed. Our Buddha preached this simile to indicate that such is the nature of those desires. But in all these, our Buddha provides similes to help one develop equanimity (*upekkhā*) toward them. When these desires arise, one can reflect: "The Blessed One has preached this truth."
With this in mind, we must maintain equanimity toward them. Because of intense desire, you devotees know how often we hear nowadays of people killing others or committing suicide in various ways. Why do they do this? It is due to the force of their thoughts. It is like jumping into a pit of glowing embers. Instead of being dragged, here it is like jumping in. But why do they jump? They are dragged by their own thoughts. Being "dragged by the two arms" represents being dragged by those thoughts. If there is no control over those thoughts, one goes, falls into the pit of embers, and dies. This is the Simile of the Pit of Glowing Embers.
Next, our Buddha gives another simile: Suppose a poor person borrows fine clothes and ornaments to go to a wedding or festival—you devotees know about borrowing things, even vehicles as mentioned in the Suttas, which also happens today. They do not own a vehicle, they walk on foot, but because they want to show off at the wedding, they borrow someone else's vehicle, even if it means getting into debt. Not only the vehicle, but there must also be people to match it. Our Buddha explains this with specific reasons.
To show off at a festival, out of pride, a person borrows a vehicle, fine garments, jewelry, and even a retinue to display as their personal wealth. They travel through the middle of the city with all these fortunes. The onlookers who see this say, "Oh, how wealthy this person is! This is how a person of great fortune enjoys their wealth!" Seeing the splendor and fortune of this person, the townspeople speak in this manner. While they are saying this, the owner of the vehicle comes and demands the vehicle back. The owner of the fine garments reclaims them, or even snatches them away if they are not returned. If they have an urgent need, they will snatch them. The owner of the jewelry reclaims them. In the end, what is left for this person?
This is how the disadvantages of sensual pleasures are shown. All these are demonstrated to be like borrowed goods. The things we think of as our sensual pleasures are actually like items borrowed from others, which must be returned later. Often in today's highly competitive society, in order to appear superior to one's neighbors, people run into debt or degrade themselves to acquire these comforts and fortunes. But even though they acquire them, they live in great fear within their hearts: "If these owners suddenly come and demand them back urgently, what will happen to me?" Such is the state. That is the nature of sensual pleasures. Because of the inability to be satisfied, the inability to find contentment, and due to that competitive nature, one can fall into such Suffering / Unsatisfactoriness / Stress (*dukkha*). That is what our Buddha demonstrates to us through this simile.
Next, He gives another simile, which is very easy to understand and is stated without much detail: Suppose a person sees in a dream a beautiful forest, lovely gardens, and exquisite ponds. They look at these in their dream. Suddenly, they wake up. Once awake, where are those scenes? Those extremely delightful scenes, those sights they were enjoying—where are they? None of them are there. In the same way, our Buddha declared that these sensual pleasures are like a dream.
We think of dreams as things seen only at night. But there are also daydreams. In this day and age, many people live on daydreams, dreaming about the future in that manner. These desires look very beautiful from afar. But when one experiences them, one has to face their disadvantages (*ādīnava*); that is what this simile indicates. Their emptiness is highlighted by this simile of a dream: "It is as false as an ointment applied in a dream." Someone comes and applies ointment to your eyes in a dream, and it feels very strong, but when you wake up and look, there is nothing. Such a simile is also shown.
Next, our Buddha declares another simile: A person enters a forest looking for fruits. In that forest, they see a tree laden with fruits. They think, "I can climb this tree," and they climb it. Having climbed it, they eat the ripe fruits and even fill their pockets. While they are engaged in this, another person comes along also looking for fruits. This second person sees the tree, but they cannot climb it. In their hand, they have a sharp axe. Since they cannot climb, they begin to chop down the tree at its root. If the first man who climbed the tree does not climb down quickly, when the tree falls, he will fall with it and face either death or grave Suffering / Unsatisfactoriness / Stress (*dukkha*). Our Buddha declared that sensual pleasures are just like that. This is also a simile to be contemplated.
What this shows is how many people, and in what ways, draw close to these sensual objects. You devotees know that in a competitive society, some obtain jobs, offices, and titles through right means, while others obtain them through wrong means. Sometimes, the one who obtained it through right means has to face dangers from the one who comes to obtain it through wrong means. It is because of such occurrences that this simile shows the terrifying consequences one has to experience. What one has acquired with great effort and trouble, another is waiting to snatch away through wrong means, thereby forcing one to face hazards.
In this way, our Buddha has shown through seven similes that there is absolutely no satisfaction in these sensual pleasures of the world. Although they have a side of gratification (*assāda*), it is minor, and they are full of much Suffering / Unsatisfactoriness / Stress (*dukkha*) and disadvantages (*ādīnava*). Because of this, our Buddha declared as an eternal truth that the only true peace for the world is the sublime Nibbāna, which is the destruction and elimination of Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*).
If we contemplate this deeply, what is the cause of Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*)? It is the notion of "I" and "Mine." While all other religions validate this notion of "I" and treat it as something real, our Buddha declares, according to the doctrine of Non-self (*anattā*), that although this "I" exists in conventional usage, it is not a reality; it is an illusion, the Dogma of self-illusion (*sakkāya-diṭṭhi*). Arising simultaneously with the notion of "I" is the notion of "Mine." The moment that concept of "I" is created by ignorance (*avijjā*), Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) supports it as "Mine." Our Buddha declared that it is due to this ignorance (*avijjā*) and Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) that we wander in this Saṃsāra for a long time. As the solution to eradicate this, our Buddha states that it is only by gradually thinning out that intense Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*), and through meditation and insight, developing this power of wisdom (*paññā*) within the mind, that this Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) can be exhausted.
But short of that, lay devotees can understand this: when someone observes the Eight Precepts on a Poya day like this, and refrains from taking food at improper times—living according to the practice of the Arahants—wearing white robes and leading a simple life, showing no attachment to their comfortable lives or fine ornaments, they are gradually thinning out that Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*). They are eliminating the coarse, rough side of Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*).
Furthermore, you devotees know that this Sasana of the Buddha can, on one hand, be described in terms of giving (*dāna*), virtue (*sīla*), and meditation (*bhāvanā*). Through giving, one eliminates the attachment to the physical objects of sensual pleasure (*vatthu-kāma*). Sensual pleasure (*kāma*) is desire. Desire has two aspects: objective sensual pleasure (*vatthu-kāma*) and defilement-sensual-pleasure (*kilesa-kāma*). The attachment to objects is the coarsest level. That is something that can be done somewhat easily. That is the first lesson: giving (*dāna*). Sacrificing something, whether food or something else, to the poor, travelers, beggars, or toward the Triple Gem. Through this, one removes the stain of stinginess (*maccheramala*) that naturally accompanies the ordinary lay mind at that moment.
If metal objects are left in a place without care, in the end, you do not see the object you expected; you see only a pile of rust. The lay mind is just like that. The rust that binds the lay mind is called the stain of stinginess (*maccheramala*). This is why our Buddha declared a series of praise-titles for the lay devotee who is engaged in giving: *“vigatamalamaccherena cetasā agāraṃ ajjhāvasati muttacāgo payatapāṇi vossaggarato dānasavibhāgarato”*—living the household life with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, always ready to give, hands clean, delighting in relinquishment, and delighting in sharing gifts.
You devotees who perform meritorious deeds like giving know that after giving, a great joy and peace arises within you; that is a spiritual joy (*nirāmisa prīti*). *“Vossaggarato”* means finding delight in relinquishment. Next, *“dānasaṃvibhāgarato”*—delighting in distributing gifts, considering wisely what is appropriate for the recipient; one can derive happiness through that giving. This shows that one can develop a delight in *taṇhakkhaya*—the eradication of craving. Generally, the word for delight, *“rati”*, is used in a negative sense. But here, delight is used in a wholesome sense: delighting in the eradication of craving. It is this delight that must be practiced by the true disciples of the Fully Enlightened One (*sammā-sambuddha-sāvaka*).
At the lay level, when a person gives away items they previously held as "I" and "Mine"—things they could have enjoyed for their own comfort—to the Triple Gem, to the poor, or even to an animal, out of a mind of faith or compassion, their Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) is thinned out for that brief moment. Greed, Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*), and stinginess are cut away.
Thus, giving is the primary step toward the destruction of craving. Virtue (*sīla*) also does a similar thing. On this occasion, you devotees have observed the Eight Precepts based on Right Livelihood, and even higher precepts. Through virtue (*sīla*), one disciplines body and speech. In truth, it is through the mind itself; the mind is chief. What we do with body and speech are the things dictated by the mind. We must establish discipline over them. This is what virtue (*sīla*) does.
Worldly people gladly engage in killing animals for fun, as a livelihood, or for food. But one abstains from it. Stealing—there is nothing new to say about that. The easiest way to get rich without exerting effort is stealing; taking what belongs to others by force, stealth, or any other means. But one abstains from that too. There, too, one makes a sacrifice. By restraining body and speech through virtue (*sīla*), one makes a sacrifice, letting go of things that are pleasing to oneself. Pleasing things mean sexual misconduct, lying, taking intoxicants, harsh speech, and so on.
Because worldly beings have done these things repeatedly throughout Saṃsāra, the mind is quickly drawn to them. To abstain from them, a special power of determination is required. This determination is what is developed through the undertaking of virtue (*sīla*). When this determination is made in front of the Sangha, it is better remembered by the mind. The effort to live within that determination is what is called guarding virtue (*sīla*). Through that guarding, the happiness of blamelessness (*anavajja-sukha*) arises within oneself—the joy, happiness, and gladness of living blamelessly. One can live peacefully without remorse.
It is in such a person that meditation (*bhāvanā*) establishes itself. Having developed the power of sacrifice through giving (*dāna*), freeing oneself from unnecessary things and accustomed to a simple life, and then disciplining body and speech through virtue (*sīla*) to establish restraint and a peaceful mind free from remorse—basing oneself on that mind, one next enters into meditation (*bhāvanā*). Meditation (*bhāvanā*) means resting the mind on a sign of concentration (*samādhi-nimitta*) through tranquility (*samatha*).
A sign of concentration (*samādhi-nimitta*), used as a subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*), is not the unwholesome things that the worldly mind thinks of. Even to shoot a human or an animal, a certain application of mindfulness and concentration is required to hit the target. But that is wrong concentration (*micchā-samādhi*) and wrong mindfulness (*micchā-sati*). There is a focusing and unification of mind on an object, but it leans toward the unwholesome side. Through that, Suffering / Unsatisfactoriness / Stress (*dukkha*) grows within Saṃsāra, leading to birth in hell and other bad destinations.
Instead, one must take a wholesome object. Either through recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) using terms like *Arahant*, *Sammāsambuddha*, or *Bhagavā*, or through loving-kindness meditation (*mettā-bhāvanā*) wishing "may all beings be well and happy," or through the meditation on foulness (*asubha-bhāvanā*), impermanence (*anicca*), or mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*) with short themes like "life is inconstant, death is constant"—bringing such a subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*) close to one's life and calming the mind through it. An effort is made to calm the scattered mind.
The deepest level of this Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) is called Latency / Underlying tendency (*anusaya*). It is not something easily grasped. The level of Latency / Underlying tendency (*anusaya*) is extremely subtle. The Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) visible in the external world is what we call desire, greed, attachment, and stinginess. But there is an extremely subtle layer to this. It can only be brought to light by a concentrated mind. No one else can expose this for you; it is something one must recognize for oneself. To recognize it, calming the mind in some manner is fundamentally necessary. Once the mind is calmed, then, through proper reflection according to the Buddha's word—called Radical attention / Wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*)—one observes how this mind operates.
These cravings arise within the mind. No matter how exquisite things are in the world, no matter how beautiful the things displayed in shops are, or whatever advertisements are shown, Craving / Thirst (*taṇhā*) does not arise from those external things; it arises from deep within the mind. True, they become objects, but the secret lies in the ignorance (*avijjā*) within the mind. It is to make that ignorance (*avijjā*) grow and to feed the latent tendency of craving (*taṇhā-anusaya*) that those other things assist. Thus, identifying this is what must be done by oneself.
In this way, the meditative mind gradually keeps watch over the objects that come to the mind. Instead of letting those objects drift far away—for normally, an object is something that drags our minds away... how does it drag us? Through whatever we see, a sign (*nimitta*) comes to us.
A minor sign (*nimitta*) comes to us: "this is a woman," "this is a man," or "this is something pleasant," "this is something unpleasant." To that sign, we add more and more thoughts, becoming subservient to it and running after it. This is called accessory features (*anuvyañjana*). It is like adding curries to rice. We support the object that came to the mind and go in that very direction. The final end of that is the disaster we mentioned in the similes—succumbing to those desires. Since such is the nature of the mind, what does the meditator (*yogāvacara*) do? Instead of paying attention to those external objects, they look at their own mind, at how the mind operates. That, too, must be done properly in accordance with the subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*). It does not mean just watching the mind run.
But gradually applying that Wise attention / Radical attention (*yoniso manasikāra*), one must focus attention on this scattered mind that is drifting away. Next, in that object, there are features that attract our minds. There are various signs (*nimitta*). Disregarding them, one notes very briefly: "form, form," "sound, sound," "scent," or "touch," and so forth. One gradually applies that noting to suppress the mind-captivating or mind-dragging nature of the object.
By doing so, in the end, before the mind is agitated by the impact of the object and the mind, or by the objects coming through the five doors of eye, ear, nose, and so on, one develops the power to quickly remove them from the mind. In a split second, one subjects the mind to equanimity (*upekkhā*). Our Buddha has shown those seven similes precisely to assist in bringing the mind to equanimity (*upekkhā*). Anyone who contemplates deeply on each of these similes will develop a sense of equanimity (*upekkhā*) toward the sensual objects of the world.
If that equanimity (*upekkhā*) is developed, the invitations coming from all sides will not affect one intensely. No matter how the world regards them, the feeling arises: "I have no use for them."
