Through that applied effort, mindfulness (*sati*) is developed; if one listens to these with good attentiveness and clear comprehension, that quality of mindfulness also grows. If one listened well in this manner for about an hour, some concentration (*samādhi*) regarding the value of the Dhamma is also likely to arise in the mind, by way of recollection of the Dhamma (*dhammānussati*). The mind settles on the value of the Dhamma—concentration.
Next, through this Dhamma, some deep understandings arise; even a Dhamma passage heard a hundred times, when heard in the correct manner, can produce deep understandings at that moment. Nowadays, such Dhamma sermons are heard incessantly when traveling in buses and vehicles. At every boutique junction where they stop, songs are heard from one place, and sermons from another. But do they strike the mind? Sometimes a song strikes the mind better—be it a song or a ball game. That is how the world goes. But if you have prepared yourself and listened to the Dhamma especially on such an occasion, then wisdom (*paññā*)—those deep understandings—arises.
The qualities developed in that manner—*saddhā* (faith), *viriya* (energy), *sati* (mindfulness), *samādhi* (concentration), and *paññā* (wisdom)—are not trivial. These five spiritual faculties are the very qualities that will support Nibbāna at some point in the future—or even in this very life. They are the virtues that must necessarily be developed in a mind striving for Nibbāna. We should gladden our minds thinking that this hour was not wasted because we spent this short time developing them. Similarly, you undertook some virtue (*sīla*) according to your level. Now, virtue is seen to be deteriorating in a very dangerous way in this society. There is a society where even the five precepts cannot be kept. In such a situation, you undertook the livelihood-as-eighth precept (*ājīv-aṭṭhamaka-sīla*). There may also be devotees who undertook the eight Uposatha precepts. In that manner, you engaged in an effort to tame your body, mind, and speech through a valuable virtue. To the devotee who is directed toward this meditation, even listening to the Dhamma is itself a meditation. Through that Dhamma, their meditative mind is made to grow. That is why it is said that some attained the paths and fruits through hearing the Dhamma. To a person who has cultivated meditation in *saṁsāra* for a long time, or has cultivated it in this life, it is like opening a door with a key. When the correct word, the correct verse of Dhamma is received, at that moment, the mind opens. One receives the strength and power to reach that mentioned supreme peace.
We also think that you too, according to your capacity, must have harvested the fruits and benefits of this hearing of the Dhamma. Having made determinations in the manner mentioned, you must look to the future. Because we cannot say where we will go next after letting go of this human rebirth at any moment or on any occasion—unless we have reached a certain destiny (*niyata-gati*) through a path and fruit such as Stream-entry (*sotāpanna*). That is why they are called "objects of urgency" (*saṁvega-vatthu*). The speed, the fuel that helps to make the Sasana journey is what is called *saṁvega* (urgency). Directing your mind to the sufferings and turmoils of this world and this *saṁsāra* by way of *Jāti* (Birth / Arising), *Jarāmaraṇa* (Decay and Death / Aging and Death), sickness, and death, try to determine to make use of this invaluable opportunity.
May all those deities—including the guardian deities of the Sasana and the Brahmas—who desire merit and desire Nibbāna, rejoice in this store of merit accumulated by you through this Dhamma preaching and Dhamma hearing! May they rejoice in this noble merit! Rejoicing, may they fulfill their own Dhamma aspirations and realize the noble, deathless Nibbāna through whichever Bodhi (awakening) they aspire to! Transfer the merit to the deities in this manner. Similarly, may all beings, from your relatives to those in Avīci up to Akaniṭṭha, who wish to see Nibbāna, rejoice in this merit of Dhamma hearing and Dhamma preaching! May everyone find peace in the noble, decay-and-deathless (*ajaramara*) Nibbāna! May you too, through the strength gained from listening to this Dhamma, direct yourselves to the path of meditation in this very life, complete those tasks, and realize the noble, deathless Nibbāna through the penetration of the paths and fruits—Stream-entry (*sotāpanna*), Once-returning (*sakadāgāmi*), Non-returning (*anāgāmi*), and Arahantship—and reach supreme peace! Cultivating these aspirations, recite these verses:
“*Ettāvatā ca amhehi.........*”

author: ven. katukurunde nanananda thero
(pahankanuwa sinhala audio dhamma sermon no.31)
namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa
(homage to the blessed one, the worthy one, the fully self-enlightened one)
pali stanza:
uccinda sineham attano, kumudam saradikam va panina;
santimaggameva bruhaya, nibbanam sugatena desitam ti.
from:
dhammapada 285 (piyavagga)
dear listeners,
the word "peace" (*santi*) is a beloved word to everyone. this word is frequently used in the dhamma in reference to nibbana. the buddha introduced nibbana as the supreme peace, the highest tranquility. devotees like you often perform various propitiatory rituals (*shanthi karma*) to escape the turmoils and problems of your daily lives. however, the true peace, the supreme peace, is the deathless nibbana. this deathless nibbana is the state where the exhaustion, suffering, and thirst that arose from running after a mirage in this *samsara* out of *tanha* (craving) for an extremely long duration are completely stilled. that is why the buddha introduced nibbana as the supreme peace.
it is a verse and a story that shed light on that path to supreme peace that we intend to expound today. this verse was delivered by the buddha concerning a pupil of venerable sariputta. under venerable sariputta, a very handsome young man born into a family of goldsmiths was ordained. venerable sariputta gave this monk the meditation on foulness (*asubha*) as his subject of meditation. the elder thought that since this was a young man, lust/passion (*raga*) would be intense, so a meditation on foulness would be more suitable. so, this monk went to a forest and tried for three whole months to concentrate his mind. but this meditation on foulness was not suitable (*sappaya*); it did not agree with him. when this monk returned to venerable sariputta, the elder asked him, "how is it, is the meditation subject becoming clear to you?" the monk expressed that he was still unable to settle his mind on it. then venerable sariputta clarified and explained that meditation subject further and said, "do not let your mind weaken just because it didn't succeed all at once. try again." that monk went back to the forest and meditated, but it did not succeed. he returned once more. on that occasion too, venerable sariputta explained the meditation subject with more reasons and similes and sent him back. yet, this monk returned once again and stated, "my mind does not agree with this meditation subject. the mind does not settle."
at that moment, venerable sariputta thought: "there must be some reason. it is very difficult for me to understand how this monk's mind works. perhaps this monk is 'buddhaveneyya' (meaning, he is someone with some difficult mental problem who must be tamed by the buddha himself)."
he took this monk to the buddha and related the matter. when the buddha, using his unique knowledge of the inclinations and underlying tendencies (*asayanusaya-nana* (inclination and anusaya: latency / underlying tendency)), inquired into this monk, he understood that because he had been born into a family of goldsmiths for five hundred consecutive lifetimes, it was difficult for him to concentrate his mind on the meditation on foulness. he only delighted in agreeable things, in beautiful sights and the like. because for a very long time he had kept his mind settled on crafting various beautiful forms out of gold, such as lotus flowers, his mind did not take to the meditation on foulness. there was a tendency for the mind not to grip it. therefore, the buddha said to venerable sariputta: "sariputta, go. this matter is something relevant only to a buddha who possesses the *asayanusaya-nana*. therefore, this monk whom you could not tame for four months, i shall bring to arahantship this very evening, today itself." having said this, he sent venerable sariputta away. what did the buddha do? through psychic power, he created a lotus flower as large as a cartwheel. it was a life-like lotus flower showing dewdrops trickling from its petals, and water drops trickling from its stem. giving that flower to this monk, he instructed him to go to the edge of the monastery, place this lotus on a heap of sand, and gaze at it while cultivating this meditation subject by repeating: "*lohitakam, lohitakam*" (red, red). he directed his mind to the red *kasina* meditation.
as soon as the buddha gave that flower to this monk, his mind became highly pleased. likewise, he took it, placed it on a heap of sand as instructed, and as he gazed at it repeating "*lohitakam, lohitakam*", all the hindrances (*nivarana-dhamma*) that obstruct mental concentration—such as sensual thoughts, thoughts of ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness, and skeptical doubt—were stilled, and his mind reached absorption (*jhana*). furthermore, because he had cultivated these in the past, the monk mastered the first *jhana* almost instantly. to "master" (*vasibhava*) means that he attained a state where he could handle it as he wished. when one attains a *jhana*, there is a method of mastering it in five ways: to enter it, emerge from it, dwell in it, advert to it, and review its factors as and when one wishes. in that manner, he mastered the first *jhana* in five ways. next, he attained the second *jhana*. he attained the third *jhana*. he attained the fourth *jhana* very quickly.
generally, meditations of this kind are called tranquility meditation (*samatha-bhavana*). due to that tranquility meditation, there is a tendency to get immersed in that pleasure; one clings to that pleasure. because when a person who has enjoyed the pleasures of the five cords of sensual pleasure (*pancakama-sampatti*) for a long time in *samsara* receives the bliss of *jhana*, it is hundreds of thousands of times greater. the buddha has declared that compared to the bliss of *jhana*, the pleasures of the five cords of sensual pleasure are like a small child playing with excrement and urine. he declared that *jhana* bliss is hundreds of thousands of times more noble and superior. therefore, when this monk received this bliss of *jhana*, out of desire for that pleasure of tranquility, he began to engage in *jhana* play. that pleasure is an extremely subtle pleasure. "jhana play" (*jhana-kila*) means practicing the *jhanas* one has mastered, moving up and down through them.
at that time, the buddha, seated in his fragrant chamber (*gandhakuti*), was watching how this monk was acting according to his subject of meditation. seeing this, the buddha considered whether this monk could turn this into insight (*vipassana*). for the sake of nibbana, this *jhana* must be turned toward insight—from the side of insight. when he saw whether he could do it without help, he realized that help was necessary. then, while the monk was absorbed in *jhana*, the buddha caused that flower right in front of him to wither, just like a fading lotus flower. when a lotus flower squeezed, bruised, and crushed by a hand withers, it turns blackish. in that manner, the buddha, through his psychic power, turned the created flower into something discolored and decayed.
then, as soon as this monk emerged from *jhana*, he saw that the flower in front of him had become misshapen. next, he reflected: "alas! even this insentient, inanimate object is subject to such *jaramarana* (decay and death / aging and death). then what need is there to speak of this sentient body?" he then thought about his own body: "my body, too, which is sentient, will surely undergo decay in this very manner, won't it?" that was the sign of turning toward insight. at that very moment—according to how it is recounted in this story—a group of young children came to a pond near where this monk was sitting, plucked the blue water-lilies (*kumudu*) in that pond, and piled them on the shore. this monk's eyes turned toward that as well. he saw the withered nature of the flowers piled on the shore, and the vibrant, fresh nature of the flowers still in the water. once again, he reflected further on his own body, realizing that this body too would fall into decay at some point. through that, his mind fell upon *anicca* (impermanent).
you have heard that insight meditation is expressed in three terms: *anicca* (impermanent), *dukkha* (suffering), and *anatta* (not-self) (*aniccam, dukkham, anatta*). whatever is *anicca* (impermanent) is *dukkha* (suffering). that *anicca* (impermanent) means it constantly has to be prepared/formed; one has to keep looking after it and attending to it. it does not remain in a constant state. it is *dukkha* (suffering). it cannot be kept as one wishes. therefore, one cannot say of it, "this is mine, this i am." it cannot be made to yield to one's power—it is *anatta* (not-self). in this manner, as soon as he saw impermanence, simultaneously, the nature of suffering and the nature of non-self within it became clear to this monk. at the moment of this realization, the buddha projected a light—it is mentioned in many instances that the buddha did so. without physically going there, he projected a light, and through that light, he made his form appear as if he were present right in front of the monk. at that moment, the monk stood up and worshipped him. it is at that very moment, as recounted, that the buddha uttered the verse we mentioned earlier:
*uccinda sineham attano, kumudam saradikam va panina,*
*santimaggameva bruhaya, nibbanam sugatena desitam.*
the meaning of the first two lines is: "just as one would pluck an autumn lily with one's hand, so should one completely cut off self-affection (affection for oneself)." "cherish only the path to peace, nibbana as taught by the sugata." that was the brief advice presented by the buddha. it is recorded in the story that, with that advice, his insight was brought to its culmination and this monk attained arahantship.
now, what we have to do is to gather from this verse and story a few core values that can be useful for our lives. now, almost everyone has heard that we travel in this long *samsara* due to ignorance (*avijja*) and *tanha (craving / thirst)*, according to the buddha's word. ignorance and craving are just like the father and mother of *samsara*. why? because this ignorance supports and helps the concept of 'i' that a person has formed. generally, one identifies 'i' in relation to what is 'mine'. in this manner, being immersed in these two concepts of 'i' and 'mine', and remaining in that wrong view for a long time, is what is called the journey of *samsara*.
now, the things that are taken as 'i' or 'mine' were pointed out by the buddha as five heaps (aggregates): *rupa* (form), *vedana* (feeling), *sanna* (perception), *sankhara* (preparations), and *vinnana* (consciousness). the heap of form is this physical body. the world regards this as a single unit. next, *vedana* (feeling). the feelings that keep coming are regarded as distinct units. next, perception. based on feeling, some recognition is formed—recognizing the feelings and sensations that arise in this physical body. next, based on those recognitions, various desires, expectations, intentions, wishes, etc., arise as activities of the mind. these are called *sankhara* (preparations), a preparing/forming. there is a preparation/formation within the mind; one tries to maintain things as one wishes. next, there is a mind that cognizes them distinctively. this mind we refer to as *vinnana* (consciousness)—the nature of distinguishing one thing from another. that characteristic is in this mind. thus, due to the unwillingness to let go of these five heaps, clinging and sticking to them, we travel in *samsara* for a long time thinking "this is i, this is mine." now here, it is said to cut off at the root the affection for self—the attachment to oneself. the most superficial part is form (*rupa*), the attachment to form. sentient beings in the world have, for a long time, generated the perception of beauty/sublimity (*subha-sanna*) regarding their own form and the forms of others.
the buddha declared that there exists in the world a distorted view called perversion (*vipallasa*). they regard what is foul as beautiful. no matter how many foul substances are inside the body, due to defilements (*kilesa*), they tend to appear as beautiful. it is to counter this perception of beauty (*subha-sanna*) that venerable sariputta gave this monk the meditation on foulness. however, because of the perception of beauty he had habituated himself to in *samsara* in the past, and due to his unwillingness to let go of it, his mind did not take to that meditation subject. the buddha, applying his *asayanusaya-nana* (knowledge of inclinations and *anusaya* (latency / underlying tendency)), as if pulling out this monk's personal samsaric file, contemplated: "this is this monk's past tendency, inclination, and preference." accordingly, he created a lotus flower and gave it as his meditation subject. but even there, he created it as something life-like, living, or vibrant. next, by causing it to wither, he led his mind back, through a detour, to the foul nature of reality. what is visible there is the buddha's skill-in-means (*upaya-kosalla*).
from this, we understand that for insight meditation (*vipassana-bhavana*) to reach its culmination, both sides must be completed. now let us consider the meditation on foulness. in that, merely considering the foulness of one's own body is not sufficient. on the other hand:
"as this body is, so is that body; as that body is, so is this body."
*yatha idam tatha etam, yatha etam tatha idam, ajjhattanca bahiddha ca, kaye chandam virajaye.*
it is expressed in that manner: "just as this body is, so is that body. just as that body is, so is this body." by comparing them in this way, by relinquishing attachment (*chanda*) to both the internal and the external (*ajjhattanca bahiddha ca*)—concerning one's own body internally, and other bodies externally—insight is brought to completion.
for some, this can be started by directing the mind to one's own body. for some, perhaps, they must first understand the foul nature of another's body, and then direct that realization toward their own body. this is also seen in the story of this monk. similarly, other such instances are recounted in the dhamma. king bimbisara's queen khema was intoxicated with her own beauty because she was extremely beautiful. her pride in her beauty was such that she did not even go to see the buddha, who was residing in the veluvanarama monastery built by king bimbisara himself. having heard that the buddha frequently preached about the foul nature of the physical form, she was unwilling to go because of that. king bimbisara employed a certain stratagem.
he had songs sung about the veluvanarama monastery in a way that the queen would hear them. having been encouraged in this manner, queen khema went to see the buddha one day. when she arrived, the buddha was preaching the dhamma to the congregation of monks. the buddha also saw that queen khema was no ordinary person, but one who had fulfilled her perfections (*parami*) to become the foremost female disciple in wisdom among the female disciples in this long *samsara*.
at that moment, the buddha created the image of a woman even more beautiful than queen khema fanning him. then, queen khema did not listen to what the buddha was preaching. instead, she looked at that form, thinking, "isn't this someone more beautiful than i?" while she was watching, the buddha gradually transformed that form from youth to old age, showing her decaying through decrepitude (*jara*). it was at that very moment that queen khema felt disenchantment (*nibbida*) toward her own body and attained the paths and fruits. there are such accounts in the dhamma. from this, we can understand that in one way or another, we must develop disenchantment toward this physical form. for some, they can first think of their own body and then realize that others' bodies are also the same. for another, they can contemplate the loathsome nature of an external body and understand that their own is similar. many such opportunities occur in our daily lives.
in whatever manner, one must also think of oneself again. it is not only others who are like this. for some, by thinking only of their own body, a kind of self-hatred arises. they even think of committing suicide. that is due to a lack of balance. for it to be balanced, one must think as a matter of natural law (*dharmata*) that "just as my body is, so are other bodies." this foul nature, this loathsome nature, is not unique to my body alone, but is common to other bodies as well. it is recorded in the dhamma that because they did not do so, a group of monks who meditated on the loathsome nature of mindfulness of the body (*kayagatasati*) were led to commit suicide. on such occasions, the buddha pacified and balanced this by teaching mindfulness of breathing (*anapanasati*). from such stories, we see that both aspects must be fulfilled to become disenchanted with form and to let go of form. it is through letting go that this nibbana can be attained. letting go does not mean destroying this, but destroying the attachment that exists toward it.
there is another method called the attention to the elements (*dhatu-manasikara*). it is the understanding that "my body, as well as external things, are made of the elements of earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and wind (*vayo*); both here and there, these are made of these elements." the only difference is that this is sentient—this body is alive—and external things are insentient. here, it is mentioned that the monk, reflecting on the lotus flower, thought: "if even an insentient thing is subject to such decay in this manner, what about our body?" in this way, we can draw many points related to this meditation subject from this story.
regarding these five heaps, ordinary worldlings have a perception of compactness (*ghana-sanna*). the perception of compactness means that this appears as a single unit. this form changes moment by moment, but to the mind, it is felt as one: when we take it as "my form," we do not think about its changing parts. similarly, feeling follows form. these are also taken as one. that is called the perception of compactness. insight (*vipassana*) means "seeing in a special way." when a concentrated mind is directed toward a meditation subject through the three characteristics of *anicca* (impermanent), *dukkha* (suffering), and *anatta* (not-self), that object, which was perceived as one, gradually begins to be understood as a collection. one must reach such a state. it is by seeing in this way that the mind is inclined to let go of this—seeing it as something that is breaking up and disintegrating. no one likes to grab onto something that is breaking apart. along with grabbing it, one falls. this is seen in insight. first, one sees the arising and passing away of things. that is called *udayabbaya* (arising and passing away). these are things one can experience in daily life.
the buddha tells us to experience this impermanence regarding our own form: "this form arises in this way, it passes away in this way." this can be understood by oneself at various levels. even when one is about to eat food, one can see the state that food goes through after being consumed. next, there is the exhalation that comes along with the inhalation. one is forced to cast it out. in this manner, we can understand the impermanent nature of this form within this body through this. as one directs the mind more and more to arising and passing away, and as that deepens, one then sees how it breaks down even faster than it arises. the mind inclines to that extent toward dissolution (*bhanga*). along with the dissolution of the object, one sees the mind itself dissolving. why? because it is with the mind that one grasps these objects. when that object dissolves, the mind also dissolves. it is through this that one experiences fear—fear regarding this *samsara*—and the desire to travel further in this *samsara* thins out, and the mind progresses toward the path-knowledge (*magga-nana*). in this manner, the buddha shows the path of insight (*vipassana-magga*). ordinary worldlings think only of clinging to the pleasure obtained from tranquility meditation (*samatha-bhavana*). without the instruction on insight, even that monk would have remained playing with those *jhanas*. that too is a high pleasure. but the buddha points out that the true pleasure, peace, is the tranquility attained by being freed from this entire *samsara*.
there comes a stage when one can deeply understand the desire for form, feelings, and the recognition of perceptions, each one of them. next, the intentions (*cetana*) within the mind. all these are things subject to arising and passing away. next, this thing called "mind" (or consciousness) cannot be taken as mine either. to what extent? the buddha declares that the mind changes even faster than this body; this mind is something that changes extremely rapidly. the buddha declared that he could not even find a simile for the speed at which the mind changes, though we call it "my mind." in this way, if one practices directing one's thoughts in daily life so that attachment to the five aggregates—*rupa*, *vedana* (feeling), *sanna*, *sankhara* (preparations), and *vinnana* (consciousness)—is abandoned or thinned out, nibbana is not far from that person. that is why the buddha declared: "this is the truth, nibbana, which lies closest to oneself, yet the world does not see it."
from this, we see that the things we take as subjects of meditation are not costly things. they are things that lie closest to ourselves. it is through these very things that we must direct the mind toward nibbana. in ordinary parlance, within what is called "the world," there are many worlds. there are various worlds such as the world of sports, the world of cinema, the world of literature, and the world of drama. similarly, we can say there is also a "world of meditation." this world of meditation is more exquisite than all these other worlds. one enters this world of meditation through the doorway of the meditation subject (*kammatthana*). "kammatthana" means the meditation topic, the subject of meditation. if one hopes for nibbana, or if one hopes for those meditative tranquilizations, pleasures, etc., which are superior to the thoughts of ordinary worldlings, one must obtain such a *kammatthana*, a meditation topic, from a suitable person and practice it.
the buddha possessed the *asayanusaya-nana* (knowledge of inclinations and *anusaya* (latency / underlying tendency)) to the highest degree, a knowledge that no other disciple possessed. as soon as the buddha directed his mind to any individual, he could see the strengths, tendencies, likes, dislikes, and the states hidden within that person's mind developed through their samsaric existence. nowadays, many people are amazed by computers. but more amazing than any product manufactured by man is the mind that produces it. it is to understand this very mind that meditation helps. thus, through this *asayanusaya-nana*, the buddha could pull out an individual's personal file in a single moment and give the matching solution. that is how he gave subjects of meditation.
next, those who have attained direct knowledges (*abhinna*) also have a limited power to think according to the past lives of an individual; if they give a meditation subject based on that, the work is quick. otherwise, as happened to that monk, there can often be a delay. in any case, if someone has entered the world of meditation through the doorway of the meditation subject, from there onward, they progress on the path of development. next, by arriving at those *jhanas* through tranquility (*samatha*), they are able to experience extremely subtle, noble pleasures that are secluded from the world and secluded from the five cords of sensual pleasure.
next, what is even higher than that is arriving at those paths and fruits (*magga-phala*) beginning with stream-entry (*sotapanna*), which are attained as liberation from the entire *samsara*. this is the path pointed out by the buddha. liberation from this *samsara* is something no other teacher was capable of showing, because the buddha has declared the dreadfulness of this samsaric journey on many occasions. at the very least, a person who has not even attained the fruit of stream-entry cannot say when, either due to past actions (*kamma*) or due to bad actions committed in this life, they might fall into the four woeful states (*apaya*). such a dangerous situation exists.
therefore, if one has obtained a human rebirth during the lifetime of a buddha, one must especially give place to insight meditation (*vipassana-bhavana*). using tranquility (*samatha*) as a basis for insight meditation, one can settle the mind through *jhanas* and the like. those energies one has cultivated in *samsara* over a long time do not go to waste.
for five hundred lifetimes as a goldsmith, that monk had directed his mind to pieces of gold. when a goldsmith fashions an ornament out of a piece of gold, how much attention does he pay to it? similarly, one carves a statue out of stone. in such instances, a certain concentration (*samadhi*) is applied. not a single one of the energies generated by our actions in *samsara* goes to waste. all of them are deposited in the mind in an extremely subtle way. now, many people are amazed by things like computers. that too is a material object. but that material object arose within the immaterial mind. in that mind are stored both the good and the bad we have done in *samsara* over a long time, the strengths we have built up, and our weaknesses. all of these exist within the mind-stream (*citta-santana*). so what is it that we need? it is to bring out the good side and free ourselves from this *samsara*. therefore, to enter the subjects of meditation and exit through the door of nibbana, one must enter this world of meditation. various worlds are presented in this society in attractive ways. but we should not be deceived by them as buddhists. reconsidering our core values and our worth, we see how our ancestors spent their lives; no matter how many fancy things there were in the world, because they did not forget the three characteristics of *anicca* (impermanent), *dukkha* (suffering), and *anatta* (not-self) taught by the buddha, as soon as a disaster struck, "*aniccam, dukkham, anatta*" would naturally escape their lips. but it is not a mere utterance of words that is there. in these times, perhaps, there is a group that thinks merely reciting them is meditation. in the past, our ancestors had the habit of directing their minds to how the trees and leaves around them, the flowing river, the things around them changed, and how their own bodies changed. therefore, they lived a meditative life, even though their daily lives appeared to be spent in an ordinary way.
in any case, we too must reflect, however fast the world changes, on developing new evaluations and new values regarding our lifestyle. "kammatthana" (meditation subject) can be translated as "workplace." a meditation subject is a workplace that helps toward one's nibbana or toward attaining this noble goal. for that monk, it was a red lotus flower by way of *kasina* meditation. for some, even a single hair of the head can be a sufficient and suitable meditation subject. it is by settling the mind in that manner, and directing that settled mind toward the three characteristics of *anicca* (impermanent), *dukkha* (suffering), and *anatta* (not-self), that one can attain the realization of the paths and fruits. when we consider it in this way, the buddha has presented this path of dhamma in such a way that even a very young child can start it.
you know that three types of meritorious deeds are mentioned: *dana* (giving/generosity), *sila* (virtue/morality), and *bhavana* (meditation). in these times, why do people practice giving? to receive hundreds of thousands of times more than what is given in a future life. or to go to the heavenly worlds. it is true that such benefits exist. but that should not be the ultimate purpose. if someone has developed a sense of urgency (*samvega*) regarding *samsara*, if they have thought that freeing themselves from this *samsara* is necessary, even at the moment of giving a small thing, they should not think of heavenly pleasures. those too are impermanent (*anicca*). even if one goes to a heavenly world, as soon as a past bad action (*kamma*) surfaces—since the bodies of deities are extremely subtle, even an unwholesome thought is sufficient for them to fall from there, pass away, and drop into the woeful states. such a dangerous situation exists in the heavenly worlds, regardless of how beautiful they seem. therefore, even heavenly pleasure is nothing major. it is received as a side benefit. if one misses the mark, one goes to a heavenly world. but in reality, we should try, even at the moment of giving a gift (*dana*), as pointed out by the buddha, to base it on the thought of non-greed (*alobha*), or the intention of removing the *tanha* (craving) in it, the intention of removing that self-affection; even meritorious deeds like giving must be done with that at the forefront.
regarding giving, the buddha has pointed out: "they give gifts as an ornament for the mind" (*cittalankaram danam deti*). the deepest purpose is pointed out as the ornamentation of the mind—and requisites (*pirikara*) mean things that are helpful to someone, things that serve as causes. thus, giving for the sake of developing the mind is the highest purpose. when we reflect on it in this way, even when we serve a spoonful of rice, or when we offer something to the poor, travelers, beggars, or to the sangha, we should think: "may i, through this mental factor of non-greed (*alobha-caitasika*), gain the strength to abandon *tanha* (craving)." it is because of self-affection—attachment to oneself—that the world grasps onto everything as "i" and "mine". when freeing themselves from these, people often experience greed (*lobha*) and regret. what does a person do who gives with a clear mind in all three stages of volition? they give while paying attention to that mind, without any regret over that gift. the benefit of this is not to receive hundreds of thousands of times more in return, nor to go to heaven, but one must think: "this was a good opportunity to thin out the unwholesome state of greed, or *tanha* (craving), that was in my mind." that is the deepest aspiration one should cultivate regarding giving.
for one who thinks in that way, there are opportunities in daily life to thin out this self-affection. at times when one donates or offers something one owns or uses to the poor, travelers, beggars, or to the triple gem, one must look at one's mind: "previously, i thought of this as mine. now, this is not mine. at the moment of giving, i separated from it." by giving in that manner, one must habituate oneself to contentment. one must habituate oneself to that tranquility and peace mentioned earlier.
it is the same with virtue (*sila*). virtue is also something, in this era, which is often thought of as a mere customary ritual, like something to be taken on a uposatha day or to be recited in front of monks. when we reflect deeply, virtue supports meditation. why? because it is through the taming of the body and speech that the mind can be tamed. this virtue is the method of taming body and speech. whether it is the five precepts (*panca-sila*), the livelihood-as-eighth precept (*ajiv-atthamaka-sila*), or other higher virtues—by undertaking this virtue and guarding it, one must have the thought: "i am preparing the foundation for my meditation." generally, in *samsara*, the things i like are killing beings, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, slandering, harsh speech, and frivolous speech that is of no benefit to this world or the next. these are things i like. the concepts of 'i' and 'mine' are the causes that lead to traveling in this *samsara*. we see this in animal life. animals are not outsiders; we too have lived there for a long time. we know how those minds of animals, ghosts (*preta*), and demons (*yaksa*) operate—they are extremely low. what we should do is not prepare to go there, but rather to obtain a higher state; that is why virtue (*sila*) is prescribed.
what is done through virtue is the thinning out of that self-affection. now, while one dislikes being harmed, one harms others. one does so expecting some pleasure from it, for entertainment, or for food, or for various reasons. what is present there is self-affection. it is the same with stealing, committing other unwholesome deeds, and lying. within every one of them lies the attachment to the concept one has taken as "self." this virtue can then be used to thin out this self-affection. next, what is higher than even that is meditation (*bhavana*). in that meditation, too, generally, people do not like to be secluded from the world. now, how many people have gathered in this hall at this moment? those engaged in other various activities are hundreds of thousands of times more. those are often things that do not help toward nibbana. in this way, to reject various invitations from cinemas, theatres, and other entertainment halls, and to come here to spend even an hour, a letting go is required for meditation.
first, the mind's delight in a meditation subject is called "delight in meditation" (*bhavanaramata*). one must develop a delight in meditation. that is fundamental. the world mostly consists of a world that delights in very low, loud clamor. having gradually developed a distaste for those, one then develops a liking for songs and music alone. going further, realizing the coarse, gross nature of even those, one then begins to delight in tranquility, peace, silence, and stillness. it is such a world that is called the "world of meditation." this means gradually freeing oneself from those low delights common to animals, demons, and ghosts, and developing a higher inclination. what helps in this is the meditation topic called *kammatthana*. if one has respectfully accepted it from a teacher, when one shapes one's daily life according to it, the opportunity arises to recognize the word "peace" mentioned in our thematic verse—what true tranquility is.
both the so-called developed society and the undeveloped society are now enslaved to their senses; to gratify them, they run along the path of various things presented by this commercial world, as if running after a mirage. developed society uses them to the extreme, and ultimately, remaining stuck and immersed in them until life is destroyed, they sacrifice their lives for the five cords of sensual pleasure. next, those who do not have such luxuries target those very things, and to obtain those five cords of sensual pleasure and luxuries, they tire themselves out, clash with weapons, get into debt, think of them day and night, lose sleep, dream of them, and destroy their lives. in contrast, what does the meditator do? they adopt the concept of simple living and high thinking. stepping out of that world of pomp, show, and fashion, instead, just as you do on a uposatha day, clothed in simple attire, with simple food and drink, practicing contentment (*alpeccata*) in everything, habituating themselves to be satisfied with what is received, they try to settle their mind according to a meditation subject, freeing themselves at least a little from the sensory inputs coming through the eyes, ears, nose, etc. that is how life in the world of meditation is.
the world of meditation cannot be recognized all at once like that fancy world thought of by the world. to what extent the energy in this, and its helpfulness to one's life, is great—the buddha almost always pointed out the value of being diligent in this, urging us to enter this path of meditation diligently. why? because we cannot do this every day. the opportunity to do this does not always arise. the birth of a buddha (*buddhotpada*) is rare. a human rebirth is rare. similarly, the opportunity to benefit from this combination of opportune moments (*khana-sampatti*), those who support it, and the hearing of the proper dhamma are extremely rare. therefore, if one gets the opportunity to know them at some point, everyone must be eager to recognize this world of meditation. one aspect of that world of meditation is what we mentioned as "jhana play." that too is a very high pleasure, so much so that ordinary worldlings cannot experience it. those who have attained those *jhana* states experience something like brahmic bliss. they experience brahmic bliss in this very life. what is even higher than that is that peaceful tranquility pointed out by the buddha as liberation from that *bhava* (becoming)—the state where *tanha* (craving) is eradicated at the root.
why is it that a person cannot let go of these? because of the concept of "i" that they have taken. but what is the path shown by the buddha? he allows one to realize for oneself that this concept of "i" is an ignorance (*avijja*), a wrong concept. next, he allows one to realize that not a single one of the things taken as "mine" can actually be maintained under one's power. such realization occurs through the application of attention in the mind—the application of meditative attention (*bhavana-manasikara*), through reflection. if a meditator has directed themselves to this path of meditation, that meditator gradually understands that this body, which we are so attached to as "my body," is subject to decay very rapidly—at a speed we cannot even think of.
also, how much suffering and difficulty must one undergo to maintain this form? one understands that it is *dukkha* (suffering). all of it cannot be taken as mine. how many living beings, such as worms, reside inside this? in this way, there is a nature of not being able to maintain this under one's power. when it gets sick, one cannot stop it by saying, "do not get sick." that is form (*rupa*). next, it is the same with feelings. pleasant feeling comes. it is not permanent; it is gone. next, painful feeling comes. the buddha pointed out that not only pleasant and painful feelings, but also neutral feelings—all of these are *anicca* (impermanent), they change. therefore, this meditator gradually removes the desire for feelings as well. they also realize for themselves the nature of *dukkha* (suffering) in them. next, perceptions, recognitions. the buddha compared their deceptive nature to a mirage. in everything, there is color and shape (*vanna* and *santhana*). when some color is painted and presented with some shape, the world is deceived. there is a miragelike nature in it. that is perception (*sanna*).
next, what are called *sankhara* (preparations)—the intentions (*cetana*) that constantly arise within our minds, the desires, intentions, aspirations, expectations that arise in extremely subtle ways—all of these are the vast number of preparations made very rapidly inside the mind. there is a moment when this too is understood as *dukkha* (suffering). as the meditative attention becomes more and more subtle, these are things that everyone can experience. for one who has developed these in *samsara* for a long time, they can be attained very quickly, like that monk. one should not think that this happens merely by listening to a sermon. it is the energy present within that individual.
this entire world is like a huge school without partitioned classrooms. sometimes, a small child may have a mental strength that a great professor does not have. similarly, a so-called uneducated person may have an extremely great strength to see nibbana, a strength of rapid understanding. it is to such people, regardless of caste or social status, that the buddha, using his *asayanusaya-nana* (inclination and *anusaya* (latency / underlying tendency)), went—sometimes with a single word, a word of dhamma, a verse—and allowed them to realize that noble, deathless nibbana in that manner. therefore, practically, we must think of absorbing something for our daily lives from this story of dhamma and this verse. we must try to develop a specific determination, specific aspirations, new values, and evaluations regarding our daily life. only then does one inherit the true benefits of hearing the dhamma.
today, on this uposatha day, you listened to the dhamma at this moment. reflecting on this moment of listening, consider the change that has occurred in your mind now. to come to such a place and listen to this dhamma, some faith (*saddha*) must have arisen—faith in the triple gem: faith in the buddha, the dhamma preached by the buddha, and the sangha who live according to that dhamma. when hearing it, it sinks into the mind only if there is a heart filled with faith. to a world blinded by intellectualism, they often cannot harvest the true practical value of this dhamma. they cannot absorb it because it appears to them as a heap of words, or they look at the buddha's word as something to be understood through a dictionary. all these dictionaries are deposited within our minds, like the computer we mentioned. we must benefit from this in the proper way by tightening the correct screw. otherwise, one must enter this world of meditation through the doorway of the meditation subject and make an effort to test the strengths within oneself.
it must be because you directed yourself to these over a long time in *samsara* that you received the opportunity to listen to the dhamma with such faith. the growth that arises in the mind next to faith is energy/effort (*viriya*). if in some way a thought arose at this moment according to faith, "from today at least, i must walk on this path of dhamma, i must meditate," that is a thought of energy. not only that, to remove drowsiness and laziness for this hearing of the dhamma and to apply the mind to every single word also requires energy. through that applied effort, mindfulness (*sati*) is developed; if one listens to these with good attentiveness and clear comprehension, that quality of mindfulness also grows. if one listened well in this manner for about an hour, some concentration (*samadhi*) regarding the value of the dhamma is also likely to arise in the mind, by way of recollection of the dhamma (*dhammanussati*). the mind settles on the value of the dhamma—concentration.
next, through this dhamma, some deep understandings arise; even a dhamma passage heard a hundred times, when heard in the correct manner, can produce deep understandings at that moment. nowadays, such dhamma sermons are heard incessantly when traveling in buses and vehicles. at every boutique junction where they stop, songs are heard from one place, and sermons from another. but do they strike the mind? sometimes a song strikes the mind better—be it a song or a ball game. that is how the world goes. but if you have prepared yourself and listened to the dhamma especially on such an occasion, then wisdom (*panna*)—those deep understandings—arises.
the qualities developed in that manner—*saddha* (faith), *viriya* (energy), *sati* (mindfulness), *samadhi* (concentration), and *panna* (wisdom)—are not trivial. these five spiritual faculties are the very qualities that will support nibbana at some point in the future—or even in this very life. they are the virtues that must necessarily be developed in a mind striving for nibbana. we should gladden our minds thinking that this hour was not wasted because we spent this short time developing them. similarly, you undertook some virtue (*sila*) according to your level. now, virtue is seen to be deteriorating in a very dangerous way in this society. there is a society where even the five precepts cannot be kept. in such a situation, you undertook the livelihood-as-eighth precept (*ajiv-atthamaka-sila*). there may also be devotees who undertook the eight uposatha precepts. in that manner, you engaged in an effort to tame your body, mind, and speech through a valuable virtue. to the devotee who is directed toward this meditation, even listening to the dhamma is itself a meditation. through that dhamma, their meditative mind is made to grow. that is why it is said that some attained the paths and fruits through hearing the dhamma. to a person who has cultivated meditation in *samsara* for a long time, or has cultivated it in this life, it is like opening a door with a key. when the correct word, the correct verse of dhamma is received, at that moment, the mind opens. one receives the strength and power to reach that mentioned supreme peace.
we also think that you too, according to your capacity, must have harvested the fruits and benefits of this hearing of the dhamma. having made determinations in the manner mentioned, you must look to the future. because we cannot say where we will go next after letting go of this human rebirth at any moment or on any occasion—unless we have reached a certain destiny (*niyata-gati*) through a path and fruit such as stream-entry (*sotapanna*). that is why they are called "objects of urgency" (*samvega-vatthu*). the speed, the fuel that helps to make the sasana journey is what is called *samvega* (urgency). directing your mind to the sufferings and turmoils of this world and this *samsara* by way of *jati* (birth / arising), *jaramarana* (decay and death / aging and death), sickness, and death, try to determine to make use of this invaluable opportunity.
may all those deities—including the guardian deities of the sasana and the brahmas—who desire merit and desire nibbana, rejoice in this store of merit accumulated by you through this dhamma preaching and dhamma hearing! may they rejoice in this noble merit! rejoicing, may they fulfill their own dhamma aspirations and realize the noble, deathless nibbana through whichever bodhi (awakening) they aspire to! transfer the merit to the deities in this manner. similarly, may all beings, from your relatives to those in avici up to akanittha, who wish to see nibbana, rejoice in this merit of dhamma hearing and dhamma preaching! may everyone find peace in the noble, decay-and-deathless (*ajaramara*) nibbana! may you too, through the strength gained from listening to this dhamma, direct yourselves to the path of meditation in this very life, complete those tasks, and realize the noble, deathless nibbana through the penetration of the paths and fruits—stream-entry (*sotapanna*), once-returning (*sakadagami*), non-returning (*anagami*), and arahantship—and reach supreme peace! cultivating these aspirations, recite these verses:
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 119
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #119
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.85)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Saddhā bījaṃ tapo vuṭṭhi, paññā me yuganāṅgalaṃ;
hiri īsā mano yottaṃ, sati me phālapācanaṃ;
kāyagutto vacīgutto, āhāre udare yato;
saccaṃ karomi niddānaṃ, soraccaṃ me pamocanaṃ;
viriyaṃ me dhuradhorayhaṃ, yogakkhemādhivāhanaṃ;
gacchati anivattantaṃ, yattha gantvā na socare;
evamesā kasī kaṭṭhā, sā hoti amataphalā;
etaṃ kasiṃ kasitvāna, sabbadukkhā pamuccatī ti.
From:
Kasibhāradvāja Sutta, Sutta Nipāta, Khuddaka Nikāya
Dear Listeners,
It was on an Esala Full Moon Poya Day such as this that our Teacher of the Three Worlds, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, revealed to the world with its deities the path to Nibbāna, which brings the suffering of saṃsāra to an end. For a world trapped within a lifestyle that only multiplies the suffering of saṃsāra, it is not easy to understand the value of the virtues that help one escape from that suffering. For this reason, on certain occasions, the Buddha had to use components of that very worldly lifestyle as illustrations to explain the value of those spiritual virtues. A few verses and a story demonstrating such an occasion are what we are going to present to you today.
When the Buddha was residing in the brahmin village of Ekanālaka in the Magadha country, one day the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja was distributing food to the crowd gathered for the sowing festival at a place where five hundred plows were yoked. Seeing the Buddha standing on one side for alms, the brahmin challenged him in this manner: "Monk, I plow and I sow. Having plowed and sown, I eat. Monk, you too should plow and sow; having plowed and sown, eat." Then the Buddha replied to him in this way: "Brahmin, I too plow and sow. Having plowed and sown, I eat." Then the brahmin said: "We do not see any yoke, plow, goad, or draft-oxen belonging to the Venerable Gotama, which are the agricultural implements necessary for farming. Yet, the Venerable Gotama says, 'having plowed and sown, I eat.' How are we to understand this?" When asked, the Buddha uttered these few verses which we mentioned at the beginning:
> *Saddhā bījaṃ tapo vuṭṭhi, paññā me yuganāṅgalaṃ;*
> *Hiri īsā mano yottaṃ, sati me phālapācanaṃ.*
Faith is the seed-paddy. Austerity is the rain-water. Wisdom is my yoke and plow. Shame of wrongdoing is the plow-pole. Mind is the yoke-strap. Mindfulness is my plowshare and goad.
Next, he further declares:
> *Kāyagutto vacīgutto, āhāre udare yato;*
> *Saccaṃ karomi niddānaṃ, soraccaṃ me pamocanaṃ.*
Restraint of body and speech, and moderation in food—controlling the stomach—these are my weeding, my protection, or in other words, the fence of the field. Truthfulness is my weeding. Gentleness (soracca), which is the supreme state of discipline, is the unyoking of the oxen.
Then he further declares:
Energy is my draft-ox, drawing the plow. That guiding of the plow leads to the security from bondage (*yogakkhema*), which is Nibbāna. *Yogakkhema* is a name for Nibbāna. That plow, drawn by the oxen, goes straight towards Nibbāna.
> *Gacchati anivattantaṃ, yattha gantvā na socare.*
That plow moves forward without turning back. To whatever place it goes where there is no sorrow—meaning, to the sorrowless Nibbāna—that plow goes without turning back. What is meant here is that it is unlike the plow in the brahmin's field, which reaches the end of the field and then turns back.
> *Evamesā kasī kaṭṭhā, sā hoti amataphalā;*
> *Etaṃ kasiṃ kasitvāna, sabbadukkhā pamuccatī’ti.*
Plowed in this manner, this plowing of mine yields the fruit of the Deathless (*amata-phala*)—it yields the harvest of Nibbāna, which is the Deathless. Having done this plowing, one is released from all suffering; one can escape from the entirety of the suffering of saṃsāra. Here, as we mentioned earlier, the Buddha utilized the very implements connected to the brahmin's plowing. The brahmin spoke of plowing in the worldly, conventional field. Using those same concepts, the Buddha explained the cultivation of spiritual virtues in the field of this Dispensation and explained what its harvest is.
In this challenge made by the brahmin, we can see the criticism raised by the brahminic society regarding the monastic tradition of the Saṅgha established by the Buddha. To the brahmins, there was something strange in this. This is because brahminic society is a priestly society. While living on the offerings and sacrifices made to the gods, they also engaged in farming as a livelihood and profession. That is why he is called Kasībhāradvāja. Bhāradvāja is a brahminic name, belonging to the priestly caste. "Kasī" means one engaged in agriculture—a farming brahmin. Thus, to a brahmin accustomed to such a lifestyle, when the Buddha came and stood with an empty bowl, it appeared as if he was just eating without doing anything. "What is the meaning of this? One must do a job to expect food"—with this idea, he raised that argument, or rather, made the challenge. But the monastic society established by the Buddha was a society that gave priority to spiritual cultivation. It exists within the cultivation of virtue. The significance and value of that venerable society lie therein. That is what the Buddha highlighted on this occasion, using the brahmin's own implements as analogies.
Let us reflect a little on each of these virtues. Why did the Buddha show faith (*saddhā*) as the seed here? As we all know, the fundamental requirement for cultivating these dispensation virtues, for engaging in the practice of the Dispensation, is faith. A farmer starts farming only if there is seed-paddy. If there is no seed-paddy, he does not even begin farming. Moreover, seed-paddy refers to that which has the capacity to germinate. Dispensation practices done without faith are, metaphorically speaking, like cultivating hollow grain. Where there is no faith, there is only a crop of hollow grain. By showing faith as a seed here, we can understand its immense value. Faith is something connected to the heart. Placing the heart, as it were, one establishes faith in the Triple Gem—in the Buddha, the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Guided by that faith, the energy and strength to practice the spiritual virtues of the Dispensation arise.
To explain this further, when a grain of paddy is germinated, it takes root. Similarly, it is through faith that the roots of virtue (*sīla*) are established and strengthened. Next, just as the sprout shoots up, just as the leaves grow from above, calm (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) can be developed. What helps this seed to grow is the rain. That is why the Buddha compared austerity (*tapas*) to rain. Austerity can be understood briefly as restraint of the senses (*indriya-saṃvara*). Ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), virtues of morality (*sīla*), and all such qualities belong to this. In brief, the restraint of the senses is austerity. It is through preserving the virtues of austerity, such as morality, that the seed of faith grows. Next, wisdom (*paññā*)—"wisdom is my yoke and plow" (*paññā me yuganāṅgalaṃ*). Just as the yoke goes foremost in plowing, wisdom goes foremost in this path of practice. You know that right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) is placed first even in the Noble Eightfold Path. It is explained as "right view is the forerunner" (*sammā-diṭṭhi pubbaṅgamā*). It goes ahead, it runs in front. Just as wisdom is primary, on the other hand, it is wisdom that goes deep. The work done by the plow is digging the earth. That is why wisdom is compared to both—the yoke and the plow. Moreover, it is with that plow that weed-roots and the like are uprooted. It is through wisdom that the roots of defilements (*kilesa*) are uprooted.
In this way, we can understand the value of the simile given by the Buddha. "Wisdom is my yoke and plow." "Shame is the plow-pole" (*hiri īsā*). Standing in front of the plow, what helps to guide the yoke properly is the plow-pole. Here, *hiri* refers to the shame and fear of sin/wrongdoing. You may have heard that shame and fear (*hiri-ottappa*) are described as the guardian laws of the world (*loka-pālaka-dhamma*). In the protection of the virtues of the Dispensation as well, the fear and shame of sin stand guard. Although only shame (*hiri*) is mentioned here, the other (fear of wrongdoing) can also be understood—the shrinking nature of the mind is "shame, the plow-pole". "Mind is the yoke-tie" (*mano yottam*). It is through the mind that all of this is connected. The yoke, the oxen, the plow—all are connected by the tie of the mind. "Mindfulness is my plowshare and goad" (*sati me phālapācanaṃ*). The virtue of mindfulness, *sati*, is shown as the plowshare. Standing as a protection for the plow and going ahead to perform that task is the plowshare. Next, two functions of mindfulness are shown through two similes—the plowshare and the goad. Mindfulness is the plowshare and the goad. In some places in the Dhamma, mindfulness is explained as "mindfulness is the protective charioteer" (*sati ārakkha sārathī*). "Ārakkha" means it brings protection, and "sārathī" means the driver; it both guards and directs. It guides along the right path. Both are done by mindfulness, by the quality of *sati*. That is why it was compared here to the plowshare as well as the goad. It is out of fear of the goad that the oxen walk on the right path.
Restraint in body and speech, and moderation in food—restraint of body refers to the three-fold physical restraint: abstaining from killing living beings, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct. "Restrained in speech" (*vacīgutto*) means being restrained in speech—abstaining from lying, slandering, harsh speech, and frivolous talk. Next, "moderation in food" (*āhāre udare yato*) means consuming food in moderation. These matters are compared by the Buddha to the fence—the fence of the field. If there is no fence for the field, wild cattle will enter and eat it up. Similarly, the things that support the cultivation of these virtues are the aforementioned virtues of morality, such as restraint of body and speech, and moderation in food. Next, "truthfulness is the weeding of the field" (*saccaṃ karomi niddānaṃ*). The weeding of weeds is done by truthfulness. As soon as weeds grow, a good harvest cannot be obtained if the weeds of falsehood grow. Falsehood must be removed by means of truth. Wrong views (*micchā-diṭṭhi*), incorrect ideas, wrong beliefs, false doctrines—these must be uprooted using truth, with truth going foremost. They must be uprooted in time. Otherwise, in the end, instead of a harvest, what one gets is a heap of hollow grain. There is an old saying: "When it turns to hollow grain, the actual rice grains are few." The majority becomes falsehood; in the end, what remains are empty things, false things, and a bit of nonsense. There is nothing of real substance, and no real harvest is obtained. Therefore, truthfulness is utilized for weeding out the weeds.
Gentleness (*soracca*), or docility, refers to the supreme state of discipline, culminating in Arahantship—the highest discipline which is perfected in Arahantship. It is at that stage that the oxen are unyoked, finally released from the burden of the yoke. One is released when that complete state of discipline is achieved. Energy (*viriya*) is compared to the oxen that draw the yoke together, drawing it evenly—the oxen drawing the plow. The two oxen must share the weight of the yoke equally. Similarly, energy is truly fruitful when there is balance of energy (*viriya-samatā*)—which means neither excessive energy nor deficient energy. If energy is excessive, there is restlessness (*uddhacca*). If energy is deficient, there is laziness (*kosajja*). The work must be done with the balance of energy between these two. To show this, the Buddha presented: "Energy is my draft-ox" (*viriyaṃ me dhuradhorayhaṃ*), just as the two oxen drawing the plow pull together as one. The pulling of the plow is done through energy, and that too with balance—with energy accompanied by balance.
Next, it is further said: "leading to security from bondage" (*yogakkhemādhivāhanaṃ*). *Yogakkhema* is a name for Nibbāna. Actually, the word *yoga* comes from the word *yuga*. *Yuga* means a yoke. Entering into the work of this Dispensation is like putting one's neck to the yoke. It is such a great task. The words used in this context, such as duty (*dhura*), yoke (*yuga*), and bondage (*yoga*), all carry the connotation of the work done by those two oxen. In the past, many of these words etymologically arose from the context of cattle farming. Behind *dhura*, *yuga*, and *yoga*, there lies the story of the two oxen under the yoke.
"Leading to security from bondage" (*yogakkhemādhivāhanaṃ*) means release from that yoke. What is shown by this is release from the suffering of saṃsāra. That is a name for Nibbāna. It goes up to that. "Without turning back" (*anivattantaṃ*)—it goes without stopping. As mentioned before, if it is the plow in a brahmin's field, it must go to the end of the field and turn back. This is not like that. "It goes without turning back" (*gacchati anivattantaṃ*); the plow goes on without stopping. To where? "Where having gone, they do not sorrow" (*yattha gantvā na socare*). To whatever place having gone they do not sorrow—meaning, to the sorrowless Nibbāna, to the Deathless—to that very place this plow goes. Having preached thus, the Buddha finally declares:
When this plowing is done in this manner, it yields the fruit of the Deathless (*amataphala*); it yields the fruit of Nibbāna which is the Deathless. It is not an ordinary harvest. Having done this plowing, one is released from all suffering; one can escape from the entirety of the suffering of saṃsāra.
When such a meaningful set of verses was uttered, the brahmin was inspired with faith. He immediately went, filled a large golden bowl with milk-rice, came back and offered it to the Buddha, saying: "Let the Venerable Gotama partake of this milk-rice. For the Venerable Gotama is indeed a farmer—a farmer who does the farming that yields the fruit of the Deathless." He accepted it in that way. At that moment, the Buddha declared in another verse: "It is not proper for me to partake of this milk-rice. For this is something obtained by chanting verses." By "chanting verses" (*gāthābhīgītaṃ*), he meant that partaking of this milk-rice as a reward or an offering received by reciting his own virtues in verses was not proper for him. "This is not fit for my livelihood; it is not fit, not allowable for Buddhas who maintain the purity of livelihood (*ājīva-pārisuddhi*)." Thus, he rejected it. "But if one offers food to a great sage whose taints (*āsava*) are destroyed, who is accomplished, that is like sowing in a supreme field of merit, yielding great fruit and great benefit"—this fact was also declared. Then, when the Buddha rejected the milk-rice, the brahmin asked: "Then to whom shall I give this?" At that moment, the Buddha declared: "Brahmin, I do not see anyone in this world, including the devas, maras, and brahmas, along with ascetics and brahmins, who can digest this milk-rice after consuming it. Therefore, throw this milk-rice either in a place devoid of green grass, or into water devoid of living beings."
When this was said, the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja took that milk-rice and threw it into water devoid of living beings. As soon as it was thrown, that milk-rice began to hiss, sputter, and emit steam, making the sound "ciṭi-ciṭi, ciṭi-ciṭi". Seeing this, the brahmin, realizing it was a great miracle, felt a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and hair-standing goosebumps, and through that, he developed great faith in the Buddha. Then he expressed his faith with a certain statement: "Excellent, Venerable Gotama, excellent!" He then illustrated it with several similes and declared his taking refuge in the Triple Gem. "Just as one would upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the path to one who was lost, or hold up an oil lamp in the dark so that those with eyes could see forms, in the same way, the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways, with various similes, by the Venerable Gotama. I go to the Blessed One for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha. May I receive the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and the higher ordination (*upasampadā*)."
Then, as mentioned in the story, in the end, the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja, having received the going-forth and the higher ordination, attained Arahantship before long. The story shows that he abandoned worldly farming and entered into the farming taught by the Buddha. From this, we can reflect on many things regarding those values of the Dispensation. What is the ordinary idea of the world? Building up the economy. There are various cultivation campaigns in the world for economic development. But we must realize that where this cultivation of virtue is absent, no matter how prosperous other cultivations make us, they can fall into decline and be destroyed when virtues disappear among human beings. If we reflect on this Dispensation, the monastic society of the Saṅgha is indeed established on principles completely different from those of the priestly society. It is not priestly, but venerable (*pūjya*). This is extremely clear when we constantly reflect on those virtues of the Saṅgha. When we think of the virtues of the Saṅgha, everyone recites words like: *supaṭipanno*, *ujupaṭipanno*, *ñāyapaṭipanno*, *sāmīcipaṭipanno*. What is spoken of there is the practice (*paṭipadā*). It does not speak of sacrifices, rituals, or offerings made to the gods, but of the practice, the conduct. The Saṅgha is *supaṭipanno*—meaning they have entered well upon the practice. *Ujupaṭipanno*—they have entered directly, straight upon this practice, without crookedness or deviousness. *Ñāyapoṭipanno*—they have entered upon the practice methodically, systematically. *Sāmīcipaṭipanno*—they have entered upon the practice properly, in a way that deserves the praise of "sādhu, sādhu". In all these, the emphasis is on the practice (*paṭipadā*).
It is for this very reason that they are next described as *āhuneyyo*, *pāhuneyyo*, *dakkhiṇeyyo*, *añjalikaraṇīyo*. In the past, the word *āhuti* was used for offerings and gifts brought from afar. *Pāhuti* referred to food and hospitality offered to guests. Thus, because of their wealth of virtue, they are worthy of offerings brought from afar, and worthy of hospitality—worthy of being given even those things kept for guests if they arrive unexpectedly. *Dakkhiṇeyyo* is also an ancient brahminic word. *Dakkhiṇā* meant the fee or gift given to brahmins for their sacrifices and rituals. But here, that word is used because of that wealth of virtue. They are *dakkhiṇeyyo*—worthy of receiving such gifts because of their wealth of virtue, not because they perform sacrifices, rituals, or recite blessing verses or curses, but solely because of the aforementioned wealth of virtue. Next, *añjalikaraṇīyo*—worthy of having hands raised in reverent salutation above the head. This too is not because of anything else, but solely due to their wealth of virtue. It is because of their wealth of virtue that they are worthy of being worshiped.
Within this passage on the virtues of the Saṅgha lies the answer to the brahmin. Otherwise, the error of the brahminic society and the ordinary world in describing these monks as idle idlers is evident from this. What, then, is the purpose of the monastic society established by the Buddha? In the end, it is described as *anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassa*—the establishing of an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. The brahmin prepares his field expecting a harvest that will temporarily satisfy physical hunger. But the Buddha helps to bring the mind-stream (*citta-santāna*) to a state that yields the fruit of the Deathless, called the nectar of Nibbāna—bringing the supreme bliss of Nibbāna, which is considered the most delicious and directly realizable thing in the world. In fact, though we speak of this "field of the Dispensation" (*sasun keta*), we cannot point to it and say it is in such-and-such a place. The field of the Dispensation is the mind-stream itself. To put it briefly, the discussion is entirely about the mind-stream. Wisdom, mindfulness, and all these Dhamma factors exist within the mind. Therefore, the mind-stream is the true field of the Dispensation shown by the Buddha.
This is exactly what is said in this verse which you have heard so often:
> *Sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ, kusalassa upasampadā;*
> *Sacittapariyodapanaṃ, etaṃ buddhāna sāsanaṃ.*
Abstaining from all evil, cultivation of wholesome qualities, and purifying one's own mind—this is the teaching of all the Buddhas. The mind-stream is the field. If that field is cultivated to finally yield that fruit of the Deathless, or the nectar of Nibbāna, then that field becomes a sacred thing—that mind-stream becomes a sacred object to the world. That is why they are called *anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassa*—an unsurpassed field of merit is prepared for the world. From this, the difference between the priestly society of the brahminic tradition and the venerable, monastic society of the Saṅgha becomes extremely clear to us. This is something we must recall and point out in this day and age. Likewise, we spoke about worldly cultivation. There, even this brahmin realized: "What the Venerable Gotama has introduced to me is far more valuable than this plowing I do with five hundred plows." Understanding this, he spoke in that manner and even asked for the going-forth and higher ordination from the Buddha. We can understand that there is profound depth even in the few similes he used while showing his submission to the Buddha. In many Sutta discourses, after the Buddha preaches the Dhamma, the passage that constantly occurs when the listener expresses their faith is the one used here. "Excellent, Venerable Gotama, excellent!" Next, a few similes are given. Let us now reflect on them.
That constantly used passage shows the wonderful nature of the Buddha's style of preaching. It is the mental revolution that occurs within a person through his preaching that is shown by those words and similes. Through his teachings, according to each individual's capacity of comprehension, a complete mental revolution takes place. Actually, in some Sutta discourses, not all parts of the Buddha's preaching are recorded. Instead, it is briefly stated that "after the progressive talk (ānupubbī-kathā), he preached thus". Since everyone knows the progressive talk, it is often not mentioned. Here, the value of these similes is made very clear. That is why we thought of specifically speaking about it. What are those similes?
"Just as, Venerable Gotama, one would upright what was overturned"—when something is overturned, its contents cannot be seen. Thinking it is useless, it is left overturned; but when it is uprighted, its true nature is seen. Such an understanding dawned upon this brahmin. What is the meaning of this? The brahmin was living within worldly society, within conventional values. According to conventional values, a person must eat. To do so, they must engage in some industry, craft, or employment. So, when someone comes without any job, holding an empty bowl and standing in front of a house, it seems like a useless act of eating for free. The brahmin was established on such wrong ideas. That is why it is like "uprighting what was overturned". Also, "like revealing what was hidden". Until the Buddha declared it, the brahmin did not know, he did not recognize what the true seed-paddy was, what the true rain was; he did not understand their deep meanings. Through the matters shown by the Buddha, those things became clear. The hidden virtues were revealed. Next, "one who was lost"—the brahmin was someone lost in saṃsāra. The path was shown. Next, "one who was in darkness"—the Buddha lit a lamp. Through that light of the Dhamma, the brahmin could see, because he had eyes; the brahmin was indeed a wise person.
Regarding this Sutta, ancient teachers point out that the Buddha presented faith (*saddhā*) as primary here because the brahmin possessed wisdom (*paññā*) but lacked faith (*saddhā*). When the Buddha shed the light of the Dhamma, because the brahmin had eyes, he saw the truth. Thus, we can understand the value of those similes. In fact, those four similes are used to show the mental revolution that occurs within the disciple through the Buddha's style of preaching. It is not so clearly seen in every Sutta. Because it is extremely clear and prominent in this Sutta, we highlighted it. Through all these matters, we can see the limitations of worldly plowing as well as the value of the supramundane plowing shown by the Buddha.
The Buddha expressed this same matter to some extent on another occasion, also while out for alms. Actually, close to this Sutta, there is another short incident. One day, the Buddha went for alms to the house of a brahmin named Udaya. The brahmin filled the bowl well and offered it. The Buddha returned. On the second day too, he went to that house, and on the second day too, the bowl was filled and offered. On the third day too, he went. On the third day, after offering the food in the bowl, the brahmin expressed the thought: "This monk comes again and again out of greed for taste"—meaning one who is greedy for taste. At that moment, the Buddha uttered a series of verses. The brahmin had said "again and again". "This monk comes here again and again"—the Pali word for "again and again" is *punappunaṃ*. In Sinhala, we say *puna punā*. "This monk comes here again and again." Using that very word, the Buddha uttered a series of verses, using the word "again and again" repeatedly.
He said: "In this world, it is not only this alms-round of mine that is done again and again. Whatever things exist in this world, they are all done again and again." What are they? He goes on to say: "Again and again they sow the seed. Again and again the rain falls. Again and again they gather the grain and fill the granaries. Again and again beggars come and beg. Again and again donors give gifts. Having given gifts again and again, donors are born again and again in heaven." Next, he says the same regarding cattle farming: "Again and again those who milk the cows draw milk." You know that when the udder is squeezed once, all the milk does not come out; how many times must one labor for this? "Again and again the calf runs to the cow, and thereby falls exhausted and suffers." Next, he states a profound matter: "Again and again one enters the womb. Again and again one is born. Again and again one meets death. Again and again one is carried to the cemetery." Then he concludes with the Dhamma: "The wise person who has attained the path to the place where one is not born again, is not born again and again." When this series of verses was uttered, that brahmin too, probably because he was wise, understood the point, expressed his refuge in the same way, and took refuge in the Triple Gem.
From this, we can realize that what exists in this world is a process of preparing *saṅkhāras* (preparations). These must be prepared and repaired continually. By yoking five hundred plows or so, holding sowing festivals with great clamor, you cultivate and fill your granaries. For how many days? When it is finished, because you have to cultivate again and again, you set aside seed-paddy. Thus, the world moves within an endless cycle of repetition. It is the same with cattle farming, and the same with other activities. There is no end to any of it. There is no finality to anything. One has to keep preparing, repairing, and maintaining them. That itself is suffering (*dukkha*). "All preparations are impermanent" (*sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā*). These are preparations. The entirety of life is a heap of preparations. The food taken this morning is gone by nightfall. That food and drink, the air taken in for inhalation and exhalation—all these are wearing away. They arise and pass away.
