from:
dhammapada 324 (nagavagga)
dear listeners,
the greatly compassionate lord buddha, the teacher of the three worlds, afforded a supreme place to the care of parents among social virtues. in instances where this virtue was neglected, he employed skillful means (*upaya-kausalya*) to remedy it. during his lifetime, he timely revealed the example he himself set by fulfilling this virtue. from the verse we have chosen as our theme today, and its introductory story, we can find evidence for this. the buddha preached this verse in savatthi, concerning the four sons of a certain brahmin.
in savatthi, there lived a certain brahmin who possessed eight hundred thousand (eight lakhs) of wealth. when his four sons reached the proper age, he arranged their marriages and distributed four hundred thousand from that wealth among the four children. sometime later, his wife passed away. the children began to think: "if our father brings another wife, it might lead to some problem regarding our family wealth." as a strategy, they began to attend to their father, pampering him with food and drink even more than before, and massaging his hands and feet. one day, during the afternoon, while massaging the father after he woke from sleep, the children spoke of the bitterness of household life in a way that would induce disillusionment with samsara, or rather, in a way that would incline him toward ordination, and then they said: "please give the rest of the wealth to us as well." believing them, the brahmin gave those four hundred thousand to the children too. not only that, he distributed all his other goods and possessions, leaving himself with only his undergarment and upper robe. having done so, while he was staying for a few days at the eldest son's house, one day he went out, bathed, and upon his return, the daughter-in-law stood at the doorway and said: "why, did you give an extra hundred or two to the eldest son? didn't you give two lakhs to each? won't the other sons' houses take you in?" the brahmin, angered by this, cursed her, calling her an outcast (*vasali*), and departed from there. next, he went to the other sons' houses. receiving similar treatment at their homes as well, the brahmin was ultimately forced to take to the road. he then thought of a way to survive and sustain himself; he received ordination in the mendicant order called *kandalanga* and began to live by begging for alms.
gradually, as he grew old, due to the lack of proper food and drink, and having no place to sleep, his body became extremely weak. one day, after waking up from sleep on a wooden plank, he reflected: "the only refuge i have is our ascetic gotama. from what i have heard, he is someone who engages in friendly conversation, someone whom one can approach without fear." carrying his walking stick, he went to the presence of the buddha. the buddha asked him: "why, brahmin, have you come here so weak, without proper clothing?" thereupon, he told his story. the buddha then taught this brahmin five verses, instructing him to go and recite them at an assembly when his children were gathered in the brahmin hall. the brahmin learned the five verses, went inside when his children were assembled with the other brahmins, raised his hand, and asked for permission to speak a few verses. having received permission, he recited the five verses taught and expounded by the buddha. let us state the meaning of those verses.
in those verses, the buddha presented what the brahmin was to say concerning his children: "those children at whose birth i rejoiced, whose progress i looked forward to—they, in conspiracy with their wives, have driven me out of the house. it is just like dogs barking and chasing away a pig." furthermore, he says: "these ungrateful, wretched children, like demons in the guise of sons, have driven me, in my old age, out of the house. just as horses receive good food and drink as long as they possess swiftness and strength, how is an old horse treated? it is turned out to graze like cattle. in the same way, my children have driven me from the house without giving me my due sustenance in my old age." next, he says: "this walking stick is of greater help to me than these ungrateful children. supported by this walking stick, i drive away fierce dogs and cattle. when walking in the dark of night, this walking stick guides me, going before me. likewise, when stepping into water, it tells me the depth of the water. when i am about to fall, the walking stick becomes my support. not even that much support do i have from my children." thus he spoke those verses. it is said that in those days, there was a custom that if anyone received their inheritance from their parents and failed to care for them, that person should be put to death. therefore, these children became terrified, prostrated at their father's feet, and begged: "we shall care for you. please spare our lives."
then the brahmin told the rest of the assembly: "now indeed my children will look after me." they then seated the father on a chair and carried him home. the eldest son told his wife to look after him well, otherwise there would be punishment. from that day on, the brahmin received "regular meals"—amounting to eight portions of rice—along with excellent food, drink, and foot massages, just as he desired, from all four sons' houses. before many days had passed, when the brahmin's body had recovered well, he thought of the brahmin custom of offering teacher's fees (*guru-panduru*). thinking thus, he took two robes he had received, went to the buddha, and offered them, saying: "o ascetic gotama, i have brought these teacher's fees for you." the buddha accepted them out of compassion. when the sermon of appreciation (*anumodana*) was delivered, the brahmin developed faith and took refuge in the triple gem. he also invited the buddha, asking the blessed one to accept four of the eight portions of daily food he received from his four children. the buddha expressed his consent. the brahmin went home and informed his children: "if the venerable gotama comes to our house, treat him well." the buddha, in due course, walked for alms to those houses. they too prepared excellent food and drink and offered alms to the buddha.
on a certain occasion, it is mentioned that when an auspicious ceremony arose at the eldest son's house, the son asked his father to whom the wedding feast should be given. the father replied: "to whom else should it be given? it must be given to our ascetic gotama." accordingly, they invited the buddha and five hundred monks to the eldest son's house. on that occasion, after serving the alms bountifully and performing other acts of generosity, the children sat near the buddha and said: "now we are caring well for our father; do you not see how exceptionally healthy and well he is?" it was on that occasion that the buddha declared: "indeed, in the past too, wise sages of old cared for their aged parents." as an example, he related the jataka story found in the jataka book, known as the *matuposaka nagaraja jataka* (the jataka of the mother-supporting elephant king). the verse we have chosen as our theme is the one that expresses the meaning of that jataka story:
> *dhanapalako nama kunjaro katukappabhedano dunnivarayo;*
> *baddho kabalam na bhunjati, sumarati nagavanassa kunjaro* ti.
the elephant named dhanapalaka, in must, fierce and normally difficult to restrain—once bound in the elephant stable, did not eat even a single morsel of food. the elephant remembered the naga-forest where his mother resided; therefore, he did not take food.
if we briefly summarize that *matuposaka jataka* story, it is detailed as follows: as you, virtuous friends, know from the jatakas of the past, during the reign of king brahmadatta, the bodhisatta was born in the himalayas in an elephant herd of thousands, as an elephant pure white in all limbs—an elephant of great meritorious features. he lived as an elephant king, surrounded by his herd. in the course of time, after his mother became blind, he sent food to his blind mother through the other elephants. however, he later came to know that those elephants, instead of giving the food to the blind mother, ate it themselves. knowing this, the bodhisatta elephant became disillusioned, left the herd that very night, and went to a certain mountain called candora. placing his mother, the mother elephant, in a cave near a bamboo grove, he stayed there, attending to all her needs.
on one occasion, a certain poor man, a forester from the city of benares, having lost his way, was unable to find the path and began to weep. the bodhisatta elephant went to investigate, and when told that the man was lost, he seated the man on his back and showed him the path back to the city. however, this ungrateful man marked the path as he went. meanwhile, when the king's state elephant died and could no longer perform its duties, the king had a drum beaten, announcing that if anyone knew of a suitable elephant, they should report it. this man came forward and said: "i have seen a completely white elephant king in such-and-such a place." he then led the elephant trainers and pointed the elephant out while it was in a lake. the bodhisatta elephant, understanding the situation, thought: "it is this ungrateful person who has brought this calamity upon me," yet without showing any opposition, he remained calm. the trainers led the bodhisatta elephant to the city. the king, celebrating the arrival of the elephant, decorated the stable and placed before him various delicious royal foods suitable for him. although seven days had been spent on the journey, the elephant did not take any food. the king then came and pleaded: "if you remain thus, we cannot carry out these affairs." the elephant replied: "while my blind mother is starving in the forest, i shall not take food." deeply moved by this virtue, the king released the elephant king. the bodhisatta elephant, freed from the king's service, returned to his mother and attended to her.
according to the dhamma accounts, the king was so moved by this virtue that he declared that region a separate tax-free village, and ultimately provided special facilities for the bodhisatta elephant and his mother. that is to say, he arranged for food and drink to be provided, and later, naming the area hastipura, he had an image of the elephant carved in stone. the books mention that the story of this elephant remained famous in india (dambadiva) even after that. when the buddha expounded this elephant king's story in detail, the children developed a deep sense of spiritual urgency (*samvega*) regarding the care of parents.
at that moment, the buddha preached the teaching of the four noble truths, and upon hearing that sermon, the brahmin, his children, and their wives all attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotapatti-phala*). in brief, this is the origin story of this verse, with which the jataka story is connected.
with reference to this, let us now attempt to connect it to our present era, and also bring to mind the categories of dhamma related to the care of parents. for the decline of this virtue is occurring on all sides—in lay society and in monastic society alike. among the virtues of lay society, we find numerous sutta teachings revealing that the buddha gave an exceptionally supreme place to the care of parents. in particular, the buddha declared on one occasion that if parents are properly honored and cared for in a home, it is as though brahmas reside in that home. as you, virtuous friends, have often heard: *“sabrahmakani tani kulani”*—in whatever clans or families parents are properly cared for and honored, there is a brahma in that family, in that home. similarly, the buddha pointed out that parents are worthy of the sacrifices and offerings normally dedicated to brahmas. he also stated that they are the "first teachers" (*pubbacariya*) in the home, and are worthy of offerings. in this manner, the buddha praised the care of parents in the most sublime terms.
likewise, among the seven vows that lead to rebirth as sakka, the primary one is: *“yavajivam matapettibharo assam”*—"as long as i live, may i support my mother and father." it is mentioned that because he undertook and kept this vow, he attained that celestial state. you have also heard in both the *vasala sutta* and the *parabhava sutta* that the buddha declares that if anyone who has the capability does not support their aged parents, that person is an outcast (*vasala*). neglecting the care of parents is also shown as a cause of one's downfall (*parabhava*). in the *sigalovada sutta*, which relates to lay life and is frequently recollected by you, sigala, the son of a brahmin householder, worshipped the six directions as a daily ritual. however, the buddha gave a completely different meaning to the worship of the directions practiced among brahmins, in order to preserve social ethics. among them, the buddha first indicated the eastern direction—the forward direction—as representing parents: *“matapita disa pubba”*.
regarding the care of parents, the buddha has shown five duties that children must perform for their parents: "having been supported by them, we shall support them in their old age"—this resolve must be maintained. likewise, one must perform their duties and affairs when they are unable to do so themselves. furthermore, preserving the family lineage and tradition; managing the inheritance received from parents properly and protecting it; and lastly, transferring merits to them after they pass away—the buddha indicated in the *sigalovada sutta* that these five duties must be fulfilled. when these are fulfilled, the mutual relationship and the support received from parents was expounded by the buddha in that sutta.
when parents are cared for in this manner, its blessings (*anisamsa*) are received. if children support their parents, the parents, with joyful minds born of that, bless the children, saying: *“ciram jiva, ciram ayu!”*—meaning, "may you live long! may you have long life!" this blessing becomes a cause for the progress of the children. furthermore, parents restrain children from evil deeds, establish them in wholesome qualities, teach them arts and sciences at the proper time, provide them with suitable spouses, and hand over their inheritance to them in their old age. in this manner, the relationship between parents and children has been expounded. in various other places too, the buddha has spoken about the care of parents.
to show the value of parents, there is a special discourse of the buddha: "monks, there are two persons whose care one can never repay in this world. who are the two? mother and father." then, using a few extraordinary words, the buddha expounds the value of parent care: "if a son, with the intention of caring for his parents, were to carry his aged father on one shoulder and his mother on the other for a hundred years, providing them with all care, cleansing their excrement and urine, and performing all massage and nursing, even then, the help and refuge received from those parents would not be fully repaid." secondly, the buddha declares: "if a son, with the intention of repaying his parents, were to establish them in sovereign kingship over this great earth filled with the seven treasures, even then, he would not have done enough for his parents. but if a child establishes faithless parents in the blessing of faith, immoral parents in the blessing of virtue, stingy parents in the blessing of generosity, and unwise parents in the blessing of wisdom—such a child has not only repaid them, not only done what is sufficient, but has done more than enough." in the *mangala sutta*, which is well known to you, *“matapitu upatthanam”* (supporting mother and father) is shown as a highly valuable blessing among the thirty-eight blessings. thus, while neglecting parents is a cause of decline, caring for them is shown as a blessing that leads to one's progress.
nevertheless, the failure to care for parents has always existed in society. for many forget the protection they received in their childhood. in short, forgetting the service rendered by the mother at birth, and the service rendered by the father in guiding one's life on the right path, some are even reluctant to introduce their parents. parents must be revered as those who introduce this world: *“imassa lokassa dassetaro”*—those who showed this world. in ancient times, there was a practice of *preta-puja* (offerings to spirits) among the brahmins for transferring merits to the deceased. it was this ritual that the buddha, in suttas such as the *tirokudda sutta*, presented according to the buddhist way—namely, the method of helping deceased parents by transferring merits. the word *dakkhina* in many places refers to the sacrifices of the brahmins; but here, *dakkhina* means that deceased parents can be made happy by performing meritorious deeds such as almsgiving to the triple gem and transferring those merits. however, sometimes there are instances where they are neglected while alive, and only after death are they remembered as a matter of custom. what is emphasized here is that parents must be cared for even while they are alive, especially in their old age, remembering the help and protection they gave in our childhood, such as cleansing our excrement.
because of this importance, the buddha granted certain special privileges regarding parents even to the sangha. now, regarding travel during the rainy retreat (*vassa*), the buddha has laid down certain rules for the sangha, stating that it is unsuitable to go away for more than six nights during the *vassa*. however, as special cases, it is indicated that one may go for some urgent matter concerning members of the order, such as a bhikkhu, bhikkhuni, or samanera. likewise, if there is an affair connected with one's mother or father, permission has been granted to go, whether there is an invitation or not. even without an invitation from the parents, if they are afflicted with illness, or if there is a need to preach the dhamma to them, the buddha has permitted the sangha to go even during the *vassa*. furthermore, if the parents are extremely poor, and after the child has ordained, they have no other way of obtaining food, permission has been granted to go on almsround and give the alms food received to them as well. the buddha has indicated on certain occasions that there is no wrong in giving parents one's personal gains, though not the communal property of the sangha.
although the sangha has been instructed to use what is given in faith (*deyya*) in such a way that it does not go to waste, special privileges have been shown as a favor concerning parents. if they are aged or ill, a monk is permitted to physically support his father to care for him. in times of illness, the buddha has permitted him to attend to his mother as well, even while avoiding direct bodily touch. through this virtue of parent care, we must understand the value of gratitude. on the other hand, cruel acts committed against parents, which we hear of through the media, did not fail to occur in the past as well.
the consequences of cruel acts committed against parents instead of the care due to them are illustrated within the dispensation itself by the character of ven. mahamoggallana. the chief disciple ven. mahamoggallana was a person of such great psychic power. yet, because he listened to his wife's words ninety-something eons ago, beat his parents, and abandoned them in the forest, the result of that unwholesome deed was so grave that even in the life he attained the position of chief disciple with great psychic power, his bones were crushed by five hundred bandits, leading to his final passing (*parinibbana. such accounts are heard both in the past and in the present.
parents are noble individuals, equivalent to the state of brahma. if anyone in society wishes to accumulate merit, they have the opportunity right at home. instead of worshipping the fire god, instead of throwing food into the fire, the buddha introduced the care of parents to the world. we occasionally hear of some who consider the sole purpose of their lay life to be the care of their parents. such virtuous people have come to us too on certain occasions, and from their stories, we hear that some still preserve these valuable virtues. there are those who even give up jobs offered far away, dedicating themselves to the care of their parents. in lay life, both in the past and present, a common point of conflict after marriage is the relationship between mother-in-law and daughter-in-law. this is what is revealed even in the story of ven. mahamoggallana.
we remember a certain devotee who knew of such situations telling us that before marrying a young woman, he gave her a "two-week interview" to care for his parents. only if she passed that test would he marry her. on that occasion, that gentleman had declared: "i can find any number of wives, but i have only one mother and father." we must be mindful of virtues that are in decline. the foundation of lay society is that very relationship between parents and children. if it is broken at any point, it becomes a powerful obstacle to the future progress of this dispensation. in particular, when the poson season approaches, buddhist devotees make great efforts to uplift the dispensation. but it is within the unit of the family that these virtues must awaken. the relationship within a family is analyzed in the dhamma as the four divine abodes (*cattaro brahmavihara*).
according to brahmin teachings, the brahmins were born from the mouth of brahma, or else brahma created them. that is why those brahmins worship brahma. but the buddha's description of parents is not based solely on the fact of giving life. that too is true, but parents did not "create" the child there. rather, when one is born as the child of those parents due to some karmic cause, we all know the importance of the protection given by parents in early childhood. it is a common fact known to everyone. but a fact often forgotten by us is that during the period spent in the mother's womb, there are thousands of opportunities to die. yet, those mothers, caring for the child, even refrain from taking foods they like, thinking of the child.
furthermore, even after birth, everyone says that they feed us by turning blood into milk. the buddha states on one occasion: *“lohitam idam ariyassa vinaye vuccati yadidam matutannam”*—"in the discipline of the noble ones, mother's milk is called blood." the buddha expressed this to direct our feelings toward this, to urge us toward reality. no one would like to suck and drink blood from a mother. therefore, we have to say that through a certain law of nature, the mother's blood becomes milk. the buddha presented this directly. on one hand, at the beginning of life, the primary nourishment is received from the mother. unlike wild animals, protection is provided by the father in a civilized society. that is why the buddha often praised the care and worship of parents. to go to the brahma world, what helps a person is not the fire worship spoken of by the brahmins, but the four divine abodes (*brahmavihara*), as the buddha declared. the four divine abodes are the four virtues: loving-kindness (*metta*), compassion (*karuna*), sympathetic joy (*mudita*), and equanimity (*upekkha*). among them, we speak of extending the quality of loving-kindness (*metta*) to all living beings. in showing the relationship between children and parents, the primary quality we can bring forward is this mind of loving-kindness.
in the *karaniyametta sutta*, it is shown thus:
> *mata yatha niyam puttam ayusa ekaputtamanurakkhe,*
> *evampi sabbabhutesu manasam bhavaye aparimanam.*
"just as a mother would protect her only son even by sacrificing her life, even so, let one cultivate a boundless mind of loving-kindness toward all living beings." from this, it is clear that loving-kindness is fundamentally helpful in shaping a child's life. as a simile, a mother's loving-kindness is compared to milk. when looking at early childhood, the food easiest for anyone to digest is milk. just like giving the mother's milk to the infant, so is loving-kindness, the mind of loving-kindness—a very friendly and gentle quality. it is with the mother's gentle quality that milk is given on that occasion.
as the child grows, the mother has to employ skillful means (*upaya-kausalya*) to a certain extent, according to the situation, to discipline the child. sometimes, when the child is naughty, she has to speak firmly or harshly. even the buddha, who was greatly compassionate, addressed not only devadatta but sometimes even some monks as "empty men" (*mogha-purisa*). one might think: "the greatly compassionate buddha spoke harshly like this, didn't he?" one might doubt this. not only us, but even the niganthas (jains) had such a doubt. on one occasion, the teacher named nigantha nataputta, without presenting himself, assigned a prince who held his views to present this question to the buddha: "if the blessed one is greatly compassionate, why did he use such words that would hurt the mind of ven. devadatta?" this question was prepared beforehand to be asked of the buddha, thinking it would pose a double-horned dilemma to the blessed one. at that moment, prince abhaya was holding his young child in his lap. the buddha then asked: "well, prince, if this child in your lap, through your negligence or that of a nurse, were to put a pebble or a stick in his mouth, what would you do?" "i would pull it out, even if it drew blood." "in the same way, when i see that devadatta cannot be disciplined otherwise, i use such words," the buddha replied.
there we see a certain depth in that quality of great compassion. a mother's compassion is just like that. scolding children is not out of anger or for revenge, but in disciplining children through true compassion, she has to speak firmly on certain occasions. it is said to be a stage of childhood where they do not understand, even running after slithering snakes, chasing after whatever they see. it is at that stage that compassion is aroused. as the child grows, at the stage where they must be disciplined, the mother has to step in and speak firmly according to the situation, and sometimes even punish them.
reflecting wisely, she has to do this as a means to discipline the child. this can be compared to a lump of butter (*vedaru pida*). a lump of butter melts very quickly, though it is more solid than milk. in the same way, although the mother tries to discipline the child in that manner, if the child, by not listening, does something and gets hurt, she does not say: "let him suffer." she immediately treats the child. that is how we must understand the characteristic of compassion: at first glance, it appears firm or harsh, but it melts quickly. that is compassion. thus, in the growth of the child, the quality of compassion that helps a mother is the second stage of the divine abodes.
next, when the child grows up, studies well, and some perhaps attain high positions, the parents look at those children with great sympathetic joy (*mudita*). they rejoice, thinking: "the child whom we raised with so much struggle, hardship, and expense can now stand on his own feet, and can live without our help." sympathetic joy is a rare quality in this world. when discussing these divine abodes, many speak of loving-kindness, and many speak of compassion, but very few direct their minds to sympathetic joy. sympathetic joy is the quality opposed to jealousy (*issa*). jealousy is what is abundant in the world. when looking at curd (*di-kiri*), everyone's mind is pleased; a vessel of curd is a very pleasing sight. just like that curd is the quality of sympathetic joy. these similes are not those found in the dhamma itself; we employ these similes to illustrate this mutual parent-child relationship.
as the child grows and develops in that manner, sometimes due to foreign travel or various studies, they have to leave. likewise, if it is a daughter, as everyone knows, there is an occasion when parents weep—seemingly in vain—when giving the child away in marriage. on such occasions, they cultivate equanimity (*upekkha*), thinking: "now indeed, let her live safely somehow." that is the occasion for equanimity. this stage is compared to ghee (*gi-tel*). for, as we all know, a vessel filled with ghee can be turned upside down without fear, as it does not spill easily; ghee is solid and heavy. the word for heavy is *garu* (grave, respected). thus, that grave quality... the similes of milk, butter, curd, and ghee can be applied accordingly. like ghee is that stage of equanimity. from this, we see that just as the child grows with the help of the parents, the parents too grow through those four divine abodes, taking the child as their object.
a great mutual relationship can be brought out through this. when the discussion of the four divine abodes is brought close to this, the parents cultivate loving-kindness taking the child as object, and in the final stage, they cultivate such equanimity and strength that they can selflessly let go of the child. it was in this sense that the buddha gave parents the status of brahma. it is not merely because one is born due to parents; in truth, one is born due to various kamma, utilizing parents as a support. because of giving the first understanding of life, and because of the protection received from parents to build the body and the mind, parents are called "first teachers" (*pubbacariya*).
the parents' side too must reflect on this: if the qualities of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity developed toward one's own children can be gradually extended to one's neighbors and others, that itself becomes the arising of the four divine abodes. the mutual relationship between parents and children is a good opportunity for us to cultivate and grow virtues even through lay life. if the loving-kindness started in a home taking one's children as object can be extended to neighbors, the village, the country, and to all sides—that is the development of the divine abode of loving-kindness (*metta-brahmavihara*). when neighboring children succeed, just as one's own children stand on their own strength, one must arouse the quality of sympathetic joy instead of jealousy. the start for this was received from the home itself. likewise, the quality of compassion. you have heard: *“panna sassa sabbadhammesu, karuna sabbajantusu”*—that is, the buddha has wisdom regarding all phenomena, and compassion toward all living beings.
therefore, the great compassion of the buddha is so deep that it is beyond our comprehension. to the buddha, beings fallen into the ocean of samsara appeared just like children running close to the hearth fire, or trying to jump onto a road where vehicles are passing. that is why, to rescue them from states of misery and guide them onto the path to heaven, the buddha sometimes took firm measures, and even laid down strict disciplinary rules (*vinaya*) for the sangha. this was not out of a lack of compassion. a common folk story expressing a mother's compassion toward her children is mentioned in the dhamma literature itself: a certain child was about to go into the forest, and the mother warned him as a threat: "if you go to the forest, a wild buffalo will gore you to death!" but when he encountered the buffalo, the child reflected: "if my mother actually wished this, let it happen. but if she spoke this without such a wish, merely as an advice, let it not happen." at that moment, the child was saved. this shows that the words a mother uses to prevent something, free from anger, are sufficient for discipline and must be used with due measure.
sometimes, the advice of a wise mother is only understood by a child after they reach adulthood. in times of illness, accidents, or when being drawn into wrong relationships, the advice given by parents must be understood as the arising of the quality of compassion. in society, firm measures must be taken on certain occasions. if we can do so mindfully, just as a mother scolds her child, we have learned something from that family life.
at present, intellectuals have spread new concepts such as "positive thinking". within such things, there is a headlong rush like a rhinoceros, looking only at one's own progress, making wealth the sole purpose of life, without considering moral virtues. in an era when such corrupt social views are widespread, we must be mindful to use the four divine abodes to arouse the same sympathetic joy toward a neighbor's child when they study well, pass exams, and attain high positions, as we would for our own child. if we can cultivate a quality where we can rejoice, thinking of even a poor or low-caste child, "oh, how good, how valuable!" and saying "sadhu! sadhu!", we would be preserving the vanishing quality of sympathetic joy in the world.
an extremely deep stage in the parent-child relationship is that of parting from the children. in parting from those children, it is indeed an occasion where the parents experience the state of brahma at its highest. when speaking of the position of brahma in the world-system, they are the highest class. that is why they are depicted with a long beard. parents too, by the time their children are grown, have reached a significant elder status. through the fulfillment of responsibilities and grave duties, they have acquired a strength and dignity. just as children learn from parents, parents also learn from children; that is what is called a mutual relationship. utilizing the child as a support, the parents develop loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy, and finally reach up to equanimity. now, some think equanimity means bow-headed submission to everything. but according to the simile we mentioned, we can show that we cannot get pure ghee from cows without milk. it is after passing through the stages of milk, curd, and butter that ghee is produced. that is why the buddha placed equanimity at the end. loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and lastly comes equanimity. that equanimity does not mean merely closing one's eyes and ignoring everything. nor is it a cruel disregard of the world. equanimity is something deep. it is with that depth that parents act regarding their children when parting from them—selflessly, altruistically, for the welfare of the children. but children must not think: "our parents' duties are over, so we are finished."
it is from there that the children's duties begin. if the children are strong, the buddha has declared: *“bhatto nesam bharissami”*—"having been supported by them, i shall support them." "we were brought up by our parents; because they raised us, we must now support them." *“kiccam nesam karissami”*—"it was for our sake that our parents performed various works at home; we must perform those works." in this manner, a multitude of duties such as caring for parents devolves upon the children from that point. there are various ways of looking after parents. for some, it is possible to look after parents by writing a cheque, or by sending them to elder care homes. that is one way. yet, as we mentioned earlier, some even give up jobs they receive to preserve those virtues, and with great desire, feeling that they are performing something valuable, they care for their parents. they receive the parents' blessings in their final moments.
the dispensation of the buddha consists of the fourfold assembly: bhikkhus, bhikkhunis, upasakas, and upasikas. when we speak of the decline of the dispensation, we often speak of the shortcomings of the sangha. but this class called the sangha also comes from that very lay society. therefore, the corruption of virtues and the decline of virtues in lay society naturally enter among the sangha as well. if the sangha did not receive such an environment even during the time they spent in their homes, then both sides must be held responsible. if the duties due from parents are properly fulfilled for the children, from the milk onward as mentioned, then the children too, placing the buddha's word at the forefront, will fulfill their duties. children should not be like birds that leave the nest and fly away, forgetting the protection they received, flying as they please, finding another who flies likewise, and flying here and there in the world. but if the portion of duties to be performed is fulfilled with one's own hands rather than through a cheque, that is something extremely valuable, an example to the world. it is mentioned that even some kings of ancient sri lanka, despite holding high positions of kingship, engaged in the care of their parents before attending to state affairs.
even here, in the jataka story related, we have a blind mother elephant. once she became blind, what could the children not do? who would know, who would see? but it is when she became blind that the care was given. the care given to blind parents is the greatest care. the dhamma story shows that even as a wild animal, such care was performed. such accounts of bodhisatta lives are frequently mentioned.
a "bodhisatta" is a noble being aspiring for buddhahood. a buddha is born through the vastest range of experiences possible in this world-system. it is by the completion of one's vast range of experiences and the accumulation of the mass of wisdom that the ten perfections—generosity (*dana*), virtue (*sila*), mental cultivation (*bhavana*), ending in equanimity (*upekkha*)—are filled and perfected. therefore, we must reflect on the preservation of this dispensation of ours. lay buddhists, in their home life, must strive for the longevity of this dispensation by cultivating these numerous virtues related to the care of parents through the four divine abodes. we brought out these points on this occasion in connection with this dhamma sermon because everyone speaks of the buddha's dispensation when the poson poyaday approaches. we must strive to integrate the points presented so far into our lives, and go as far as possible along the path of dhamma, without falling prey to those "positive thinking" concepts.
as the first step in renunciation (*nekkhamma*), you have left your homes today, observed the noble precepts (*sila*), and in accordance with the declarations of the buddha, you have observed these precepts to cross over the suffering of samsara. next, in connection with that, you engaged in sermon and meditation. likewise, utilizing a dhamma sermon that supports the valuable virtues of life, may this wholesome power (*kusala-saktiya*) you have acquired through the blessings of hearing the dhamma guide your lives on the path of dhamma, and may it swiftly become a supportive cause and condition for your liberation from the suffering of samsara—from birth (*jati*), aging (*jara*), sickness (*vyadhi*), and death (*marana* / *jaramarana*)—and for your realization of the supreme peace of nibbana,! may all beings, from the avici hell to the highest heaven (akanittha), by rejoicing in these blessings of preaching the dhamma and hearing the dhamma, realize the supreme peace of nibbana,, through their aspired path of awakening! let us recite this verse.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 125
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #125
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.174)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Etaṃ nāgassa nāgena, īsādantassa hatthino;
sameti cittaṃ cittena, yaṃ eko ramati vane ti.
From:
Dhammapada 325 (Nāgavagga)
Dear Listeners,
In the society of the Buddha’s time, four animals were frequently highlighted in Dhamma literature as being considered noble and majestic creatures. The lion, the noble thoroughbred horse, the bull, and the elephant—these four animals were accepted in the world of that era as noble creatures. For this very reason, in many instances, one sees the names of these animals being applied to the Buddha as titles of honor or epithets. Not only that, even the Buddha himself, in certain instances when employing similes, compared himself to these four animals. Now, what is contained in this verse chosen as our theme is an occasion where the Buddha compared himself to a king elephant. The background story (*nidāna kathā*) related to this is as follows:
During the time the Buddha was residing at Ghositārāma in the city of Kosambi, a great dispute, shouting, quarreling, and conflict arose among the bhikkhus of Kosambi over a minor Vinaya issue. They did not accept even the advice and admonitions of the Buddha. Then, perhaps due to the inability to settle this conflict, the Buddha’s mind inclined toward seclusion. He thought to himself:
"Now I am residing with difficulty in a crowded environment thronged with bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, heretics, and disciples of heretics. It would be well if I could leave this crowd and dwell in the happiness of seclusion."
Considering this, the Buddha on that day went for alms in the city of Kosambi, returned after the almsround, partook of the meal, set his lodging in order, and without informing even his attendant bhikkhu or telling the bhikkhu Sangha, took his bowl and robes and departed alone toward the Pārileyyaka forest. In due course, having arrived at the Pārileyyaka forest, he prepared to reside under a Sal tree—later known as Bhaddasāla—in a forest tract later known as the Rakkhita Forest Grove.
At that very same time, a certain king elephant had also grown weary of living in the elephant herd and felt a desire to spend his time in seclusion, thinking in this manner:
"Now I live in a restless environment crowded with bull elephants, she-elephants, and baby elephants. I only get to eat the grass left over after other elephants have eaten the tender shoots. Other elephants come and eat even the branches I break off for myself. I only get to drink water muddied by other elephants wading into the pool. When I bathe at the bathing place and climb out, she-elephants rub against my body. It would be well if I could leave these things behind and live in seclusion."
Thinking thus, that king elephant also came to that Sal tree in the Rakkhita Forest Grove where the Buddha was residing. Having arrived and seeing the Buddha, he conceived confidence (*prasāda*), cleared away the plants and weeds from the spot with his trunk, and, as stated in the story, even provided the Buddha with drinking water, water for washing, and consumer water. While the Buddha too was residing there in seclusion, such a thought occurred to him: "Previously, I resided with difficulty in a crowded environment thronged with bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, heretics, and their disciples. Now I reside here in comfort, peacefully, and in solitude."
Simultaneously, a thought occurred to that king elephant as well: "Previously, in the manner mentioned before, I lived without seclusion amidst bull elephants, she-elephants, and baby elephants. I got to eat only the grass whose tender shoots were eaten by others. Others ate the branches I broke. I had to drink muddy water. She-elephants came and rubbed against my body. Now there is none of that. I can eat fresh grass. There is no one now to eat the branches I break. I can drink clean water." In this manner, a certain thought regarding the happiness of seclusion arose in the mind of the king elephant too. On that occasion, the Buddha, combining the happiness of seclusion he was experiencing and the thought that had arisen in the mind of the king elephant, uttered a joyful utterance (*udāna*) as an inspired verse, which is the verse we presented as our topic on this occasion:
> *Etaṃ nāgassa nāgena īsādantassa hatthino*
> *sameti cittaṃ cittena yaṃ eko ramati vane ti*
In this, the mind of this elephant, who has tusks like plow-poles, and my mind, which is like an elephant’s, agree. In what? In delighting in dwelling alone in solitude in the forest. From that story, we can see an occasion where the Buddha, reflecting on that secluded dwelling, compared himself and that elephant.
We can see a very moving story that you have heard many times. It exists in later literature with various ornate descriptions. What we present at this moment is the event of the taming of the elephant Nālāgiri as recorded in the Vinaya Pitaka. To assassinate the Buddha, the Thera Devadatta first sent archers. When that was unsuccessful, while the Buddha was walking up and down (*caṅkamana*) on the path below Gijjhakūṭa, he rolled down a boulder from above onto his head. When that too failed, what did he do next?
The king had a very fierce elephant named Nālāgiri, who killed people and was in rut (*mada*). Devadatta conspired with the elephant keepers to release this elephant when the Buddha came for alms. Thereafter, when the Buddha was walking down the street for alms together with the Sangha of bhikkhus, the elephant keepers released the elephant Nālāgiri and turned him into that street. Even from afar, the elephant saw the Buddha, raised his trunk, spread his ears, lifted his tail, and ran toward the Buddha. Then the bhikkhus said, "Venerable Sir, this man-killing elephant Nālāgiri has entered this street. Let us turn back." Then the Buddha said, "Do not fear, bhikkhus, come. It is impossible to end the life of a Tathāgata through the efforts of another (*parūpakkamena*)." A second and third time the bhikkhus made the request. But the Buddha kept walking straight forward. Meanwhile, the citizens of the city had climbed onto roofs, upper storeys of palaces, and balconies, and were watching. Among them, foolish people lacking faith said, "Now indeed, this excellent, beautiful recluse will be destroyed by the elephant!" Faithful and wise people said, "After a long time, we will get to see a Nāga battling with a Nāga." "Nāga" (noble elephant / great man), dear devotees, is a name for an elephant. Thus, they said a noble being is battling with another noble being. Then, on that occasion, the Buddha suffused and projected a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā-citta*) toward the approaching elephant Nālāgiri. By the power of that mind of loving-kindness, this elephant lowered his trunk and, in a fully tamed manner, came and stood before the Buddha. While stroking the elephant’s temples (*kumbhasthala*), the Buddha uttered these two verses.
It is that primary first verse that we are reciting to you on this occasion, because of its significance:
> *Mā kuñjara nāgamāsado*
> *na hi nāgahatassa kuñjara*
> *sugati hoti ito paraṃ*
"Kuñjara" too, dear devotees, is a name for an elephant. Addressing this elephant, the Buddha declares: "*Mā kuñjara nāgamāsado*"—O elephant, do not attack this elephant, this Nāga. Do not clash with this Nāga. "*Na hi nāgahatassa kuñjara, sugati hoti ito paraṃ*"—O elephant, for one who harms this Nāga, there will be no happy rebirth hereafter. Furthermore, he declared, "O elephant, do not fall prey to intoxication and negligence. Those who succumb to negligence do not go to a happy destination (*sugati*)." When the Buddha addressed the elephant in this manner, as stated there, the elephant took the dust trodden under the Buddha’s feet with the tip of his trunk, sprinkled it on his head, and backed away as far as he could be seen. Backing away in this manner, he returned to the elephant stable and stood there.
Afterward, he abandoned his fierce nature. Seeing this, the astonished citizens expressed the Buddha’s virtues in a verse that you may have heard:
> *Dantī dameh' aṅkusena kasāhi ca*
> *adaṇḍena asatthena mahāmaunī damesi naṃ*
"Some tame animals with sticks, with goads, or with whips. But this Great Sage tamed the elephant without sticks, clubs, or any weapons." Thus, this too is an instance where the Buddha compared himself to an elephant.
Even more detailed is a valuable sutta in the Aṅguttara Nikāya called the *Nāga Sutta*, which compares the vast collection of the Buddha’s virtues with the limbs and body parts of an elephant. The background story of this *Nāga Sutta* is as follows: The Buddha, having resided at Jetavana in Sāvatthī, went for alms, returned, partook of his meal, and said to the Venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, let us go to the palace of Migāramātā." That was the Pubbārāma built by Visākhā, so called, to spend the afternoon in seclusion. So, having gone to the Pubbārāma with Venerable Ānanda, he spent the entire afternoon in meditation. Rising from meditation in the evening, he said to Venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, let us go to the Pubbakoṭṭhaka to cool our bodies a bit." "Pubbakoṭṭhaka," dear devotees, was a bathing place nearby, a famous bathing place.
So, having gone with Venerable Ānanda, the Buddha bathed, climbed out, and stood with only his undergarment on, waiting for his body to dry. At that very moment, the royal elephant of King Pasenadi of Kosala, named Seta ("Whitey"), was climbing out after bathing at the bathing place. He was climbing out amidst a great sound of musical instruments—being a royal elephant, after all. He climbed out after bathing amidst the sound of music. The people seeing him praised him, saying, "This is an inspiring, beautiful, handsome, great Nāga!" They said, "This is a true Nāga." On that occasion, a monk named Udāyī was standing near the Buddha. There were many individuals named Udāyī; this Venerable Udāyī appears to have been someone with great intellectual intuition, much like Venerable Vaṅgīsa. He asked the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir, is it only to the elephant that people say, 'This is a true Nāga, a great Nāga'? Or do they say so to other animals and other large-bodied creatures as well?" Then the Buddha declared: "Udāyī, an elephant is called a Nāga. Likewise, a horse is called a Nāga. Likewise, a bull is sometimes called a Nāga. A tree is called a Nāga. Humans, too, are sometimes called a Nāga. But, Udāyī, in this world with its devas and humans, the one who does not commit '*āgu*'—the Pali word meaning 'wrong'—he is the one who can truly be called a Nāga." That is, he was declaring this with reference to himself.
Now, there the Buddha gave a novel etymology. The Buddha gives etymologies for many words, as those among you who know the Dhamma must have heard. That is: "*Āguṃ na karotīti nāgo*"—He is a "Nāga" in the sense that he commits no wrong (*āgu*). Thus, it was expressed there that he himself is a Nāga in that sense. Venerable Udāyī, saying "Wonderful, marvelous!", expressed great appreciation and joy, and asked, "Permit me, Venerable Sir, to make a eulogy of this Buddha-Nāga." Then, he declared a long series of verses.
Beginning with, "This peaceful, tamed, great and noble man, worshipped by devas and humans, is the true Nāga, superior to all animals called Nāgas," he then said, "I shall now praise that Buddha-Nāga." Next, he amazingly connects the limbs of the elephant to the ocean of the Buddha’s virtues. This is indeed very deep. Let us explain it according to our understanding and as time permits.
First, he says that the two front legs of this Buddha-Nāga are discipline (*dama*) and harmlessness (*avihiṃsā*)—for we can understand that an elephant usually attacks with its two front legs. The front legs of the Buddha-Nāga are discipline and harmlessness. Next, the two hind legs are austerity (*tapas*) and the holy life (*brahmacariya*). The hind legs are compared to austerity and the holy life. Next, the trunk—the trunk of this Buddha-Nāga is faith (*saddhā*). As you know, the trunk is the main organ of an elephant. Normally, an elephant performs heavy, rigid work with it; similarly, it can do very delicate work, like picking up a needle, with it. Here, the trunk of this Buddha-Nāga is faith. Next, the two white tusks of this Buddha-Nāga are equanimity (*upekkhā*). Because they are evenly positioned, the two tusks are compared to equanimity. Then comes a great simile: the neck of the Buddha-Nāga is mindfulness (*sati*). The neck is compared to mindfulness.
There is an amazingly deep matter here. In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), this matter is explained simply. Why is mindfulness compared to the neck of the Buddha? Now, some of you who have read the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* may know of a well-known event recorded in Dhamma literature. When the Buddha was journeying to Kusinārā for his parinibbāna, the manner in which he cast his final look toward the city of Vesālī is described as looking with an "elephant-look" (*nāgāpalokitaṃ apaloketvā*). This is because he does not turn just a part, but turns his entire body. This is frequently mentioned as a characteristic of the physical posture of Buddhas, or as a characteristic of their behavior. Even regarding Kakusandha Buddha, it is mentioned in Dhamma literature that he turned and looked with his entire body. What this indicates is full attention. Similarly, behind the Buddha, to investigate whether he was indeed a Buddha, the young Uttara—a disciple of Brahmāyu Brahmin—followed the Buddha for seven months, and finally declared in his eulogy of virtues: "This recluse Gotama turns with his entire body; he does not look by turning halfway or partially." An elephant too has this very characteristic. If you look closely at the behavior of an elephant, you may see this. When an elephant turns its neck, its entire body turns. This is a very special, wonderful characteristic of the elephant. Then one might think, "Then how does an elephant behave in a battle?" In relation to that, we read of an event from recent times, not from the Dhamma.
A certain hunter, in a deep forest, suddenly witnessed a battle between a lion and an elephant. I remember reading that description. That person was not someone who knew anything about these things, but his description of that battle was very amazing. Whenever the lion prepared to spring onto the elephant’s temples (*kumbhasthala*), the elephant turned directly toward the lion, springing and turning very fast. This means the ability to respond with the entire body. Within that lies complete attention. Thus, in presenting mindfulness as a characteristic of the elephant, it shows the ability to direct full attention to something. Likewise, the reason mindfulness of the Buddha was compared to the elephant’s neck is because of that. For we know there is a special difference between the behavior of a monkey or macaque and the behavior of an elephant. That is the matter concerning the neck.
Next, Venerable Udāyī says that the elephant’s head is wisdom (*paññā*), reflection on the Dhamma (*dhamma-cintā*), and investigation (*vīmaṃsā*). Wisdom, investigating intellect, and Dhamma reflection are compared to the elephant’s head. Everyone knows the elephant has a large head. Wisdom is compared to the head. Next, the belly of this elephant is the Dhamma. It is filled with Dhamma—the large belly of this elephant, the belly of this Buddha-Nāga. Next, the tail of the elephant is compared to seclusion (*viveka*). Although the commentators say a story about the tail—that just as an elephant drives away flies with its tail, when he needs seclusion he drives away people; the commentator explains it as driving them away by striking with the tail. But we can think that the tail is the peaceful, quiet limb of the elephant’s body. Be that as it may, Venerable Udāyī thus compared the vast collection of the Buddha’s virtues to an elephant, using the elephant to symbolize the Buddha’s virtues.
That eulogy goes on even further. The simile of a white lotus is applied to the Buddha. You too have likely heard this simile often used to describe the Buddha. Just as a beautiful, pure, fragrant white lotus is born in the water, grows in the water, yet remains unsmeared by mud and unsmeared by water, in the same way, the Tathāgata is born in the world, arises in the world, yet lives unsmeared by the world. His supramundane (*lokuttara*) virtues are shown through the lotus. Next, a simile concerning the Dhamma or the spiritual meaning of the Buddha is given. Here, a somewhat unusual simile is told. The lives of the Buddha and the Arahants are indeed a puzzle to the world. The lotus simile is presented to show this in a simple way. After the lotus rises above the mud and water, neither mud nor water smears it; even if water touches it, it just rolls off to the other side.
Just like that, here a large log of wood is shown. Think for a moment: a log of wood is pulled out of a bonfire. Then, because it does not burn with blazing flames like that bonfire, it is said to be stilled/extinguished (*nivuna*) to that extent. This is shown as an illustration of the Nibbāna element (*nibbāna-dhātu*). For during the lifetime of the Arahants and the Buddha, in their daily activities like taking food and drink, the five faculties operate because they are not cut off or broken—since life is present. But because of the realization attained—due to the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion—they are said to be stilled/extinguished. They are stilled. That is why it is said the Buddha "saw" Nibbāna. But the occasion when this is completed, when it ends, is: *'Sarīraṃ vijahaṃ nāgo parinibbisati anāsavo'*—"Relinquishing the body, the taintless Nāga (the Buddha-Nāga) finally attains parinibbāna." At some point, like a burning log of wood that is completely extinguished when it receives no more firewood, that state is called *parinibbāna*. It is called *anupādisesa-parinibbāna* (extinguishment without residue). At the end of the Buddha’s life, that fire was extinguished to the very point of not obtaining another birth. Thus, Venerable Udāyī praised the Buddha with a series of deep and meaningful verses as a eulogy.
Now let us go to another elephant story. There was a queen of King Udena of Kosambi named Māgandiyā. This Queen Māgandiyā harbored a grudge against the Buddha because he had once disparaged her beauty. Due to that grudge, Queen Māgandiyā bribed the citizens of the city to insult and drive away this recluse when he came for alms, by calling him a camel, an ox, etc. Consequently, when the Buddha was walking for alms together with the Sangha of bhikkhus, those citizens followed behind them uttering obscene words. Then Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha, "Blessed One, we cannot live in this city. People insult us with such obscene words wherever we go. Let us go to another city." Then the Buddha asked, "Well, if that happens in that city too?" "Then, Blessed One, let us go to another city." "No, Ānanda, that is not right. A problem must be solved right where it arises. I am like an elephant entered into battle. It is the duty of the elephant entered into battle to endure the arrows of insults and abuse." Therefore, the Buddha rejected that proposal, and next, in relation to this, comparing himself to an elephant entered into battle, he uttered this verse. Perhaps you have heard it:
> *Ahaṃ nāgo va saṅgāme*
> *cāpāto patitaṃ saraṃ*
> *ativākyaṃ titikkhissaṃ*
> *dussīlo hi bahujjano*
"Like an elephant entered into the battlefield, I shall endure arrows shot from the bow (abusive words); for indeed, many people are undisciplined." There too, the Buddha compared himself to an elephant.
You must have heard of another valuable occasion: an occasion where the footprints of the Buddha were compared to the footprints of an elephant. There are two suttas called *Hatthipadopama* (Simile of the Elephant's Footprint). Here we take the *Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta*. In that *Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta*, such an event is mentioned: A wanderer named Pilotika, who had conceived faith in the Buddha, was walking along the road when he met the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi coming toward him. At that time, Jāṇussoṇi had no faith in the Buddha.
When asked, "Where are you coming from?", the wanderer Pilotika made a great praise of the Buddha in this manner: "Just as an elephant hunter—those elephant-keepers and others who go to catch elephants are called *nāgavaṇṇika*—a skilled elephant hunter, entering a forest where elephants live, if he sees a large elephant footprint in length and width, comes to the conclusion by those very footprints, those tracks of the elephant, 'There is a large elephant in this forest.' Likewise, I too saw four footprints of the recluse Gotama. It is having seen them that I came to know: 'The recluse Gotama is a Fully Self-Awakened One (*Sammā-Sambuddha*), the Dhamma is well-proclaimed, and the Sangha is practicing well (*supaṭipanna*).'"
Next, the wanderer Pilotika describes those four elephant footprints in this manner: "When royal scholars, kṣatriya scholars, who are highly recognized in the country, whom others cannot tame, and who are skilled in debate, come to the recluse Gotama, having heard his Dhamma discussions, they finally become lay followers (*upāsaka*) or disciples of the Buddha. Just like kṣatriya scholars, brahmin scholars, householder scholars, and recluse scholars—scholars skilled in debate of these four kinds—come to the Buddha and finally become disciples of the Buddha. Seeing that, just as an elephant hunter recognizes an elephant from a footprint, I knew: 'This is a great Fully Self-Awakened One (*Sammā-Sambuddha*), the Dhamma is well-proclaimed, and the Sangha is practicing well (*supaṭipanna*).'" At this, the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi alighted from his carriage, bowed in the direction of the Buddha, and said, "I must see the Buddha."
Accordingly, when he approached the Buddha, Jāṇussoṇi mentioned how the wanderer Pilotika had praised the Buddha in this manner. Then, the Buddha said to the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, "No, Brahmin, the elephant footprint simile is not complete with just that. I will tell you how it is completed." Thereupon, a very valuable sutta was preached under the name *Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta*. To show how great the historical value of this sutta is, you may have heard that the *Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta* is recorded as the sutta preached by the Great Arahant Mahinda upon arriving in Sri Lanka to inspire the Sri Lankan people for the first time. So, the Buddha explains it in this manner:
From this sutta, one understands how profound the all-knowing Buddha’s understanding of elephants was.
"Brahmin, when a skilled elephant hunter, such an elephant-catcher, enters the forest, he sees a very wide and long footprint. If that elephant hunter is skilled, he does not immediately come to a conclusion upon merely seeing it, 'This is indeed the noble elephant I am searching for.' Why is that? Because in that forest, there are also stunted she-elephants named Vāmanikā, who have large footprints of that sort. Therefore, he does not abandon the search, nor does he come to a conclusion based on that alone. He goes further. Going further, he sees not only footprints of that kind, but also marks of branches broken off at high places. Yet, the elephant hunter does not decide on that alone, 'This indeed is the mark of the elephant I am searching for.'" Because there, the Buddha declares, there is another class of she-elephants named Kāḷārikā who can likewise break high branches. "Going further, he encounters places where tusk-slashes have been made. Yet, the elephant hunter does not come to a decision on that alone either, because there is still another class of she-elephants who can leave such marks. It is only when he finally goes and actually finds the elephant he was searching for, that the truly skilled elephant hunter comes to a certain conclusion." Next, the Buddha connects this to the Dhamma in this manner:
A wise person does not immediately decide with absolute certainty, "Indeed, the Buddha is Fully Self-Awakened, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed, and the Sangha is practicing well." It is through walking this path of training (*sikkhā-magga*) that one realizes it for oneself. From there, it is shown how a bhikkhu who has entered this Dispensation, gradually practicing the designated training, gradually attaining the jhānas, path-factors, and fruits, and finally, after attaining Arahantship, realizes for himself: "Indeed, the Buddha is Fully Self-Awakened, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed, and the Sangha is practicing well" through personal realization. Through this, the Buddha gives an amazingly wonderful message to the world. Faith (*saddhā*) is not an absolute, blind faith; the stage where faith is confirmed through help is personal realization. By realizing it oneself. In relation to that, it is shown that a bhikkhu attains the states of jhāna. He does not stop with that. Likewise, he attains direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). Still he does not stop. It is only when he finally ends suffering (*dukkha*) and destroys the taints (*āsava-khaya*) that he can properly recognize the Buddha. It is then that he can understand that the Dhamma is visible here and now (*sandiṭṭhika*), timeless (*akālika*), and inviting one to come and see (*ehipassika*). It is then that he can understand that the Sangha is practicing well (*supaṭipanna*). From this, a deep understanding regarding the Buddha as well as the Dhamma arises in a person.
Even the scholars who talk about faith in this day and age should understand this point. Just as the skilled elephant hunter, not being satisfied with that much, went on searching for more and more signs, so one must realize for oneself through personal realization the Dhamma, the Full Self-Awakening of the Buddha, etc. Until one realizes it, it is not suitable to establish absolute faith. That is only one faculty (*indriya*). Making use of faith, using it as an aid, one goes further forward. Faith grows gradually. That is why we frequently reminded you that this Dhamma is visible here and now (*sandiṭṭhika*), timeless (*akālika*), and inviting one to come and see (*ehipassika*). The *ehipassika* quality of the Dhamma means that as one goes forward, one finds more and more signs. The moment of true realization is the moment one realizes the Dhamma preached by the Buddha. Thus, the *Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta* is extremely important in that regard for educated people.
Furthermore, concerning the practice (*paṭipadā*) we just spoke of, there is an equally valuable sutta called the *Dantabhūmi Sutta*. There, too, it is indeed that same practice that is described. It is a very deep sutta on one hand. There, the Buddha on one occasion, addressing the novice (*sāmaṇera*) named Aciravata, compared this practice to the process a mahout uses to tame an elephant. A long explanation is given to that recluse. Let us explain it briefly. The king’s mahout, or elephant hunter, has the duty of catching new royal elephants from the forest and taming them when they are brought back. An amazing, detailed analysis of taming elephants is found as a simile in the *Dantabhūmi Sutta*. In its components, the Buddha has compared them one by one in an amazing way, leading up to Arahantship in this Dispensation. If we take it briefly, it is shown as follows:
The king’s mahout goes to catch a good elephant in the forest, taking the royal elephant along. Let us call him the state elephant (*maṅgala-hatthī*). Having gone, he catches that wild elephant and binds him to the neck of this royal elephant. Having bound him, he brings him to some secluded place in the forest, to a place where there are not many trees and leaves. Having brought him, he plants a large iron post firmly and binds this elephant to it. Having bound him, the Buddha shows in an amazing way the method by which that elephant is tamed. That mahout summons people who speak pleasant words and makes the elephant listen to those words. The Buddha further shows:
The wild elephant has "forest conduct" (*āraṇyaka sīla*)—that is, forest habits, wild habits. Eliminating those wild, restless habits, intoxication, etc., and creating a liking for the village, that mahout feeds him well from time to time. In that manner, through a subtle training, he makes him abandon the wild elephant’s wild habits, wild conduct, forest habits, wild behaviors, dust, heat, and tames him in a manner suited to the village. Having tamed him thus, gradually, next, the Buddha shows an extremely rigorous stage of training in an amazing manner. Now, this is not just an elephant that drags logs; he is the king’s elephant. He must have amazing strength to go to the battlefield. According to that description, an elephant receives an amazingly wonderful training that is almost beyond imagination. Having trained the elephant gradually in this manner, making him obedient to the mahout, next, what is done is shown:
Finally, how is this elephant trained to go to the battlefield and endure those arrow strikes? Sitting on top of the elephant is a mahout holding a lance (*tomara*)—do not understand "tomara" merely according to the modern Sinhala word. In any case, it is a sharp weapon used for such work. There are also mahouts with lances standing on the ground. A mahout stands in front. Not only that, next, they hang a large wooden board from his trunk, so that he cannot use his trunk. In that manner, a board is hung from the elephant’s trunk. On his head sits a mahout with a lance, and they are also all around him. So at that time, the elephant has nothing to do but be disciplined.
Next, it is said that the elephant’s discipline is such that the elephant does not shake his ears, does not shake his trunk, and does not shake his tail. He remains completely, entirely still. The word "*āneñja*" (imperturbable/unshakable) is applied there. Remember that word: "*āneñja*" means unshakable. The elephant is brought to an unshakable state. Then, because there are people with lances all around him in that manner, there is no way for the elephant to move. It is the occasion when he has developed calmness, restraint, and discipline to the point where he can remain completely still. That is the elephant’s final test. Thereafter, if that elephant is taken to the battlefield, he does not retreat. He becomes capable of enduring those arrow wounds, lance wounds, or whatever, in the manner described. Then, the Buddha presents that story of the elephant, and next, shows the practice of this Dispensation in an amazing way. Therein we have much to contemplate; some of it is not immediately visible on the surface.
In this Dispensation, likewise, some person leaves the lay life and ordains. The Buddha compares ordination to the open space (*abbhokāsa*). Here, I forgot to mention a word for the open space, which is *abbhokāsa*. It is a word equivalent to open air or open space. Then, just as that elephant was brought from the forest to an open space, this wild animal living in the lay home is brought to the secluded place of this open space of the ordained life. Next, a post is planted. What is the post? The four establishments of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). This elephant is bound to the post of the four establishments of mindfulness. This is the first step. Having bound him thus, just as that mahout did, the Buddha from then on shows: "One must behave in this and this manner, one must eat food in this and this manner," showing the path of training contained in mindfulness—the subtle path of training. What is that done for? That is shown next. Regarding the aforementioned elephant, it was said to be the abandoning of wild habits. Here, what is spoken of is the abandoning of vulgar, lay habits (*grāmya-gatiya*). Whatever thoughts, wishes, behaviors, lay conduct, or rather, the lack of virtue brought from the lay home—if those are present, to eliminate them, he is bound to the post of the four establishments of mindfulness and directed to the aforementioned path of training. It is the teachers who do this on behalf of the Buddha. That is what we have to understand.
In this manner, gradually taming him, the path of training is shown. Next, directing him to meditation, he is established in the jhānas. Among them, the fourth jhāna in particular is described by that word "*āneñja*". "*Āneñja*" means an unshakable state of the mind; the fourth jhāna is an incredibly unshakable, powerful jhāna-strength. Likewise, there are subtle states like the sphere of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*), etc. Based on the powerful jhāna of the person who has attained that fourth jhāna, dwelling in that imperturbability (*āneñja*), he exercises psychic powers, great direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), flying through the air, etc., which are almost beyond our imagination. That word "*āneñja*" shows us, just like the taming of that elephant, the most rigorous stage of the elephant’s training. Then, even more than the stillness brought about through those jhāna-strengths, the most powerful stillness is obtained through Arahantship. That is why it is said of the Buddha that he is endowed with an amazingly wonderful state of stillness, unshaken by the eight worldly conditions (*attha-lokadhamma*).
Now, recall the simile the Buddha declared about that elephant during the occasion of Māgandiyā's conspiracy. "Like an elephant entered into the battlefield, I endure these arrow strikes." Just as he compared himself to the elephant, the practice by which the worldly people are tamed is contained within that *Dantabhūmi Sutta*. That is worth contemplating. That is, then, who is the mahout? There is also a part not explicitly explained there.
If it is not a disparagement to the Buddha, we can think of it like this. What did that royal mahout do to tame this wild elephant? He took the state elephant (*maṅgala-hatthī*) to the forest. Having gone to the forest, he bound that wild elephant to the neck of the state elephant. If we take this simile deeply, one might think it is inappropriate, but what is done through binding the robe-strap (the act of ordaining) is the first sign of entering the class of the Buddha’s state elephant. It is like binding it to the Buddha’s neck. Let us think of it like that for a moment. Then, it was after binding him to the state elephant’s neck that they went to the secluded place. After bringing him, from then on, the manner in which the teachers and preceptors tame that wild elephant is described. Placing him in the four establishments of mindfulness, guiding him along that training, they finally, gradually, develop him and even make him attain those jhāna-strengths. Likewise, they make him a disciple capable of displaying great, marvelous direct knowledges.
That shaking nature (*iñjana*) present in this entire saṃsāra is craving (*taṇhā*) itself. Where there is no craving (*taṇhā*), there is no grasping (*upādāna*). The mind that has developed such a powerful stillness that it is no longer dragged further into saṃsāra is called Arahantship. When the Buddhas and Arahants in moments of seclusion dwell in the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship (*arahatta-phala-samāpatti*), it is said that even if a thunderbolt strikes, they do not hear it—it is that state. We have likely explained to you before an event recorded in the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta*. Once, when the Buddha was resting in a chaff-house, a rainstorm with great claps of thunder occurred, and two farmers and four oxen were struck by lightning and killed. But when the Buddha came outside and asked, "Why have these people gathered?", they said, "Why, Blessed One, were you not right here?" "Yes, I was." "Did you not hear it?" "No, I did not hear it." "Were you asleep?" "No, I was not asleep, I was awake." That person could not fathom it. That is why it is said: escaping from all this shaking nature (*iñjana*) produced through these six sense bases—the nature of being dragged into the world through the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—that complete silence is called in the Dhamma "noble silence" (*ariya-tuṇhībhāva*). Silent to the whole world. Such indeed is what is meant by having ended the suffering (*dukkha*) of saṃsāra and attained noble, deathless Nibbāna.
Accordingly, we can understand how important this elephant simile is. You have likely heard of a matter connected to the biography of the Buddha in the Jātaka Commentary's introduction. To show how symbolic this elephant is to the Buddha, the occasion of Queen Mahāmāyā conceiving the Bodhisatta Siddhattha is described as her dreaming of a white baby elephant holding a white lotus entering her womb. In any case, we must contemplate that this elephant is a very valuable animal for teaching us the Dhamma. Venerable Udāyī showed us that it can be used to help us learn the virtues of the Buddha.
Using this elephant as a simile, what we presented through this "Elephant Sermon" is the virtues of the Buddha, the virtues of the Dhamma, and the virtues of the Sangha. Just as you believe in the Triple Gem and have devotion toward the Triple Gem, using that Triple Gem as a guide, just as one follows that elephant's footprint, one must go to that final place mentioned. We wish that this Dhamma sermon may be an aid for that! We pray that the stream of wholesome thoughts developed by you through listening to this Dhamma sermon so far, and if any support is received for that practice, utilizing that too, may this Dhamma sermon be a supportive condition for you to quickly attain the noble, deathless Nibbāna—the realization of the paths and fruits starting from Stream-entry (*Sotāpatti*)—before the lamp of this Dispensation is extinguished! At the same time, from the Avīci hell up to the Akaniṭṭha heaven, if there are any beings who wish to rejoice in such a wholesome deed of Dhamma preaching and Dhamma listening, may they, through that rejoicing, be released from states of misery, reach happy states of existence, and quickly be comforted by the noble, deathless Nibbāna through the bodhi of their aspiration! Wishing thus, let us recite these verses.

(pahankanuwa sinhala audio dhamma sermon no.174)
namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa
(homage to the blessed one, the worthy one, the fully self-enlightened one)
pali stanza:
etam nagassa nagena, isadantassa hatthino;
sameti cittam cittena, yam eko ramati vane ti.
from:
dhammapada 325 (nagavagga)
dear listeners,
in the society of the buddha’s time, four animals were frequently highlighted in dhamma literature as being considered noble and majestic creatures. the lion, the noble thoroughbred horse, the bull, and the elephant—these four animals were accepted in the world of that era as noble creatures. for this very reason, in many instances, one sees the names of these animals being applied to the buddha as titles of honor or epithets. not only that, even the buddha himself, in certain instances when employing similes, compared himself to these four animals. now, what is contained in this verse chosen as our theme is an occasion where the buddha compared himself to a king elephant. the background story (*nidana katha*) related to this is as follows:
during the time the buddha was residing at ghositarama in the city of kosambi, a great dispute, shouting, quarreling, and conflict arose among the bhikkhus of kosambi over a minor vinaya issue. they did not accept even the advice and admonitions of the buddha. then, perhaps due to the inability to settle this conflict, the buddha’s mind inclined toward seclusion. he thought to himself:
"now i am residing with difficulty in a crowded environment thronged with bhikkhus, bhikkhunis, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, heretics, and disciples of heretics. it would be well if i could leave this crowd and dwell in the happiness of seclusion."
