according to that story, in the past, when king brahmadatta was reigning, enemy hostiles arose in a border province. the king went with his army, quelled the hostile threat, and returned. to treat the horses that were exhausted from the warfare, he ordered his royal officers to press grapes, without mixing water, and to give pure grape juice to the horses to drink. after that was done, the pressed grape dregs remained. when asked what to do with them, he ordered that they be mixed with water and given to the donkeys that had carried the horses’ baggage and food. after those donkeys were fed with it, they became intoxicated by it and began running here and there in the royal palace, creating a huge nuisance. the king asked what the noise was. there, acting as minister, the bodhisatta declared: “yes, your majesty, horses of noble birth—thoroughbred horses—remain silent even after drinking such excellent grape juice. but donkeys of low birth behave in this manner after drinking merely this sour, dregs-water.”
the blessed one showed this as an illustration and then uttered this verse. in the jataka story, it is said that those donkeys were indeed these five hundred people. accordingly, we can understand this verse in this manner. when the blessed one said here, “indeed, in all places, good men let go,” he referred to how those monks endured and acted with fewness of wishes (*alpeccata*) during that extremely difficult time of famine. furthermore, “they do not speak out of desire for sensual pleasures.” they did not go and speak self-interested words because of those desires. to put it briefly, not a single monk out of those five hundred went to the brahmin veranja to complain: “lay devotee, you invited us to spend the rainy season here, didn’t you? but there is no care as promised. even the buddha is consuming barley grain.” not a single monk went to complain. that is what is called “winning” (*vijita*). from this, we can understand why the blessed one used that word “conquered” (*vijita*). indeed, if any monk had gone and said such a thing to the lay donor, it would have been a defeat.
we must learn something from this. the blessed one preached this verse as praise for the practice of the monks. he also made a certain prediction for future generations, saying that the monks who would arise in the future would be different. the dispensation (sasana) has to go forward into the future. it must have been because the blessed one felt that such things would happen in it that he said they would disparage even red rice. various related matters are mentioned in the history of the dispensation and in later times, which you too have heard of.
there was an undisciplined group led by six monks known as the chabbaggiya. they were constantly seeking loopholes in the dispensation of the blessed one and behaving in a highly rebellious manner. because of this, many disciplinary rules had to be laid down. next, you have also heard the stories regarding the elder devadatta. elder devadatta was a relative of the blessed one. out of pride, overcome by gain and honor, he requested the blessed one to hand over the sangha to him in the buddha's old age, subsequently caused a schism in the sangha, and created a great deal of trouble. having won over king ajatasattu, the king began to go to serve him daily, morning and evening, with five hundred carriages carrying five hundred bowls of rice. when the monks mentioned this incident, the blessed one declared, “do not be envious of that; therein lies the ruin of devadatta.” for it is the nature of base men that the more they receive, the more proud they become. on that occasion, he preached a verse using similes:
*phalam ve kadalim hanti, phalam velum phalam nalam,*
*sakkaro kapurisam hanti, gabbho assatarim yatha.*
“indeed, its fruit destroys the banana tree; its fruit destroys the bamboo and the reed. honor destroys the bad man, just as the embryo destroys the she-mule.”
“indeed, its fruit destroys the banana tree”—when the banana tree bears fruit, it is destroyed. bearing fruit is a sign of the destruction of the banana tree. likewise, if bamboo trees, reeds, etc., bear fruit, they too meet with destruction. “honor destroys the bad man” (*sakkaro kapurisam hanti*)—*kapurisa* is the opposite of the word *sappurisa* (good man). *kapurisa* means a bad person, a bad man, an ignoble man. what is the nature of an ignoble man? when he receives honor and hospitality, he is destroyed by it due to pride. through this, we can understand how those of base character gradually fall into decline the more they receive gains and honors. in the early days of the dispensation, the noble monks endured that famine in veranja. but as time went on, due to the undisciplined actions of some monks and their greed for the four requisites, various corruptions occurred in the dispensation.
next, let us look at exemplary characters. the blessed one constantly presented the great character of ven. maha kassapa to the monks as an example regarding the practice of gathering alms (*pindacarya*), etc. foremost among those who observed the ascetic practices (*dhutanga*), the ven. maha kassapa received high praise from the blessed one in a manner that no other monk or arahant received. he was held up as an exemplar to the monks.
on such an occasion, the blessed one said to the monks, “monks, the nature of maha kassapa is that he is content with whatever” (*santuttho itaritarena*)— “whatever” (*itaritara*) is used to mean much or little, exquisite or coarse. he has the nature of being content with any kind of alms-food. furthermore, he speaks to others about that contentment in terms of praise, recommending and demonstrating it as an example. next, he does not become dejected when he does not receive alms-food. after receiving it, he partakes of it without greed, reflecting upon it wisely, focused on liberation (*nissaranapanno*), which means with nibbana as the goal.
in this manner, the character of ven. maha kassapa was highlighted. next, on another occasion, the blessed one asked the monks, “what kind of monk is suitable to approach lay families for alms-food, etc.?” then the monks said, “we do not have a clear understanding. may the blessed one himself clarify this matter!” then the blessed one waved his hand in the air for a moment. in the preaching style of the blessed one, you may have heard of such actions, like taking a little soil on his fingernail. on this occasion, waving his hand in the air, he said as a simile, “monks, just as this hand does not adhere to, bind with, or get caught in the air, when a monk goes to lay houses, if his mind does not adhere to, bind with, or get caught in those lay houses, then such a monk is suitable to go for alms-round among families.” “maha kassapa is just such a person.” various similes have been given regarding the arahant maha kassapa, such as the “moon simile” (*candupama*)—like the moon. no one can grasp the moon. the moon is seen everywhere. the reflection of the moon in the sky is seen in any body of water, yet no one can grasp it. through various such similes, the limit of the connection between arahant maha kassapa and lay people was shown.
similarly, the buddha pointed out: “if, before going for alms-round, a monk thinks, 'lay people must give me alms-food. they cannot avoid giving. they must give a lot; they cannot give a little. they must give exquisite food; they cannot give coarse or rough food. they must give quickly; they cannot delay. they must offer it respectfully; they cannot offer it disrespectfully'—if he goes with such thoughts beforehand, then if those lay devotees do not give alms-food at all, that monk becomes distressed and troubled by it. even if they do give, if they give only a little and not a lot, he still becomes distressed. if they give coarse food instead of exquisite food, he still becomes distressed. if they give slowly instead of quickly, he still becomes distressed, falling into dejection. furthermore, if they give without preparing it properly or without order, he likewise becomes distressed.”
having shown that incorrect way, he then declared, “but if a monk thinks beforehand, 'how can one get what one wants from others' families? therefore, there is no necessity; they may or may not give. furthermore, how can one expect that others' families will give a lot? how can one expect that they will give exquisite food? how can one expect that they will give quickly? how can one expect that they must prepare it properly?'—if he considers this beforehand and goes on alms-round, then even if he receives nothing at all, or receives a little, or receives coarse food, or does not receive it quickly, or receives it unprepared, that monk does not become distressed. he remains balanced.”
thus, in this way, the blessed one pointed out certain valuable facts regarding the practice of gathering alms. all of this comes under that word “conquered” (*vijita*). there are valuable discourses (*sutras*) that further explain this noble practice of the monks that the blessed one declared. especially, in explaining the practice of sagehood (*moneyya-patipada*) to the ascetic nalaka, valuable verses related to this are mentioned.
in one verse, the attitude that a monk should cultivate when going for alms-round is described as follows:
*alabha yadi va labha, ubhayeneva so tadi,*
*rukkhamva patinivattati.*
if he receives, it is well; if he does not receive, that too is well. in both cases, he is one who is “such” (*tadi*); he returns like one who approached a tree.
if he goes for alms-round and receives, that is good; if he does not receive, that too is good. “if he receives, it is well; if he does not receive, that too is suitable... in both cases, he is 'such' (*tadi*).” the word *tadi* is used. *tadi* means “suchness” or “being as such.” this is a word with a special, deep meaning. it is a word indicating the quality of *tadi*, the quality of equanimity, shown in reference to arahants and the blessed one. in both situations, he is shown to be thus, as such. next is the simile given. “he returns like one who approached a tree.” just as someone who goes to a tree to see if there is fruit does not beat or curse the tree if there is no fruit, when a monk goes to a layman's house and does not receive anything, he does not blame the lay devotees, saying, “what is this, lay donor?” there is no such blaming at all. that is what is meant. he returns with balance and equanimity, just like one who went to a tree and returned. that is what is shown as the quality of *tadi*.
now, the meaning of this quality of *tadi* is shown in relation to the eight worldly conditions (*asta loka dharma*). the simile used in ancient times for the eight worldly conditions is the balance-beam (*tula-danda*). a balance-beam is like the beam of a weighing scale. thus, in weighing equally, it is mentioned as “balanced like a scale in pleasure and pain” (*sukha-dukkhe tulabhuto*). in pleasure and pain (*dukkha*), it is like a scale; it remains perfectly level.
on another occasion, we used a modern simile, saying that the eight worldly conditions are like a rotating ferris wheel (scissors-swing). just as one does not fall whether going up or going down, one develops a certain attitude of mind. there is a deep meaning in “being as such.” if one receives, it is so; if one does not receive, it is so. if there is pleasure, it is so; if there is pain (*dukkha*), it is so. that is “suchness”—the quality of equanimity. that is why it is said here, “touched by happiness or indeed by suffering, they show neither elation nor depression”—they do not show highness or lowness. that is the meaning.
in the end, the blessed one declared that this entire collection of qualities regarding the practice of gathering alms exists in the arahant maha kassapa, and urged others to take him as an example. thus, both the declining side and the sublime side of this dispensation are shown in the dhamma through the character of the arahant maha kassapa regarding this practice of gathering alms. indeed, in this day and age, we must especially consider this matter because, like everything else, within the monkhood, the practice of gathering alms and meditation are things that must be done with a deep meaning. however, due to various reasons, they often tend to become a mere fashion. the blessed one declared that going for alms—begging—is the lowest livelihood in the world: *“antamidam, bhikkhave, jivikanam yadidam pindolyam.”* among all the livelihoods in the world, the lowest is begging. yet, noble sons of good families enter even this begging for the deep purpose of fulfilling renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
as it is said: “abandoning a small mass of wealth or abandoning a great mass of wealth, abandoning a small circle of relatives or abandoning a great circle of relatives,” they depart from the home life and go forth into homelessness. after going forth, having abandoned all—just as the buddhas, and even those of merchant families and royal families did—the next thing to do as a livelihood, though we call it a livelihood, is the alms-round (*pindacarika*). however, we are shown here that they do not go and beg like a beggar. unlike beggars and pleaders, they stand silently designated for alms (*uddhissa*). going on alms-round (*pindapata*), they stand before a house for a certain amount of time waiting, and only then depart. furthermore, “they do not speak out of desire for sensual pleasures”—this means that when going on alms-round, they do not ask the lay donors, “give me this or that.” *lapayanti* means they do not speak self-interested words in that manner. or rather, there are no flattering, chit-chat, or pleasing conversations on alms-round. where that practice is spoken of, it is also mentioned in this manner:
*sa pattapani vicaranto, amugo mugasammatho,*
*appam danam na hileyya, dataram navajaniya.*
“wandering with bowl in hand, though not mute, he is regarded as mute. he should not despise a small gift, nor look down on the giver.”
a somewhat deep and meaningful verse is mentioned in that manner. “wandering with bowl in hand” (*sa pattapani vicaranto*)—that monk wandering with his bowl; “though not mute, he is regarded as mute” (*amugo mugasammatho*)—on the alms-round, though he is not mute, he behaves as if he were mute. lay devotees may ask various questions. they may try to draw him into various pleasant chit-chats, but monks are instructed to behave like a mute person. although not mute, he must behave as if mute. furthermore, “he should not despise a small gift” (*appam danam na hileyya*)—even if the gift is small, he does not look down on it, weaken his mind because of it, or find that offering repulsive. “nor look down on the giver” (*dataram navajaniya*)—it is also mentioned that he does not show disregard or contempt toward the person who gives a small amount. this quality is shown in the character of the arahant maha kassapa, as well as in the incident in veranja we discussed.
similarly, another important incident is mentioned concerning the blessed one. perhaps you have heard the story of the slave-woman punna. let us consider this briefly, as it is a valuable story. there was a slave-woman named punna belonging to the treasurer of rajagaha, who was extremely poor. she was faithful, but poor. one day, she made a coarse bran-cake for herself, baked it on the embers, placed it in her waistband, took a pot, and went to the watering place. on the way, she met the blessed one coming into the village on his alms-round (*pindapata*).
this woman thought, “on other days when i meet the blessed one, i have nothing to give. but today, i have something to give. however, this is a very coarse food, a rough food. if the blessed one would accept it, i will offer it.” saying these very words, she said, “venerable sir, this is my extremely poor and coarse food, a rough food. may the blessed one, out of compassion, accept this as an offering to bless me!” the blessed one made a sign to ven. ananda. ven. ananda handed over the bowl. the blessed one accepted it in his bowl. this woman also paid homage and aspired, “may this be a supportive condition for me to attain that dhamma which the blessed one has attained!” the blessed one blessed her, saying, “may it be so!”
however, this slave-woman thought, “now, although the blessed one accepted this out of compassion for me, perhaps he will give it to a crow and go to a royal palace or a treasurer's house on alms-round.” just as this thought arose, the blessed one, perceiving it, made a sign to ven. ananda. seeing a tree-root nearby, ven. ananda spread a robe. the blessed one sat down and consumed that very bran-cake as his meal for the day, so it is mentioned. there, we are shown that even from the life of the buddha, he accepted even the small gift of the giver in that manner, without allowing any stain in his mind, helping them to give. as mentioned in the dhamma, rather than modern economic principles, there is a different concept of gaining merit. the blessed one pointed out that a true monk goes on alms-round with this kind of thought:
“may those who seek gains of merit receive gains of merit! may those who desire merit (*punnakama*) perform merit!” with such a thought.
often, concerning characters like maha kassapa, it is mentioned that after rising from the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samapatti*), they go on alms-round (*pindapata*) to poor huts. why is that? according to modern thinking, one should go to places of abundance, not to places of lack. for the world considers taking from a place of lack to be wrong. but here, when looking at the concept of gaining merit, the blessed one declared: *“appasma dakkhina dinna...”*—offering something from very little is worth a thousandfold. it is worth a thousand times the gift given. because, according to the concept of gaining merit, that which is given with difficulty, given in suffering (*dukkha*) and hardship, is highly fruitful. it was understanding this that those arahants and buddhas accepted and consumed those offerings out of compassion for poor people.
accordingly, we too must think of that: “they do not speak out of desire for sensual pleasures.” concerning alms-food (*pindapata*), they do not engage in various self-interested words, flattering words, or pleasant chit-chats for its sake. furthermore, they do not look down on what is given, whether it is little or much. especially, considering that when the arahant maha kassapa rose from the attainment of cessation and someone got the chance to offer alms-food, it would be of great fruit and great benefit; giving that opportunity to poor people is a valuable example we see in the history of the dispensation.
furthermore, the matters mentioned in this verse have been explained here only in relation to the community of monks or the monastic society. however, if we contemplate further with wisdom, the “good man” (*sappurisa*) mentioned here is not only found among the monks; such a person can also be found among the laity. therefore, these points of the dhamma in this verse, which can be shown as the practice of a good man, can be integrated even into lay life. that is what we must especially remind you of on this occasion. thus, if we take the very first line of the verse: *“sabbe ve sappurisa cajanti”*—“indeed, in all places, good men let go.” monks let go of household things and go forth. but lay devotees also face various occasions to let go. in fact, what is done in acts of giving (*dana*), etc., is letting go. similarly, various occasions may arise in one's day-to-day life where, according to the situation, one must sacrifice pleasure, sacrifice wealth, and let go in the mind—that is what is meant. in all situations, one must develop the strength to let go. next, “they do not speak out of desire for sensual pleasures”—the nature of good men is that they do not use self-interested words, flattering words, deceitful methods, or deceitful speech to fulfill their expectations for various reasons.
next, “when touched by happiness or indeed by suffering, the wise show neither elation nor depression”—this is the quality of remaining balanced in all things, whether pleasure comes or pain (*dukkha*) comes. those eight worldly conditions affect all of us. the blessed one declared that the world rotates around the eight worldly conditions, and the eight worldly conditions rotate around the world. when one understands the eight worldly conditions that constantly present themselves to oneself in accordance with the karma performed in *samsara*, there is no room for those fluctuations. the most important word we have to extract from here is the quality of *tadi*—“suchness.” that is the unshakable state amidst the eight worldly conditions. the eight worldly conditions are described as: gain (*labha*) and loss (*alabha*), disrepute (*ayasa*) and fame (*yasa*), blame (*ninda*) and praise (*pasamsa*), pleasure (*sukha*) and pain (*dukkha*). there are these eight states. thus, in these states, ordinary beings, in times of loss, disrepute, blame, and pain (*dukkha*), are oppressed by them and fall into depression. next, when the good side comes—gain, fame, praise, and pleasure—their minds become puffed up and proud. through that understanding, one must strive to prevent this. here, let us look at the incident in veranja. the blessed one was the supreme one who completed the perfection of giving (*dana-paramita*). nevertheless, due to those changes of time and famines, even the blessed one and the monks had to face such situations.
so, when we think about how we will spend the coming year of our lives, and when we reflect on the sequence of events happening around us, we must be prepared for anything. there, a sacrifice of pleasure becomes necessary. as said in “indeed, good men let go,” depending on the situation, even lay devotees have to sacrifice their pleasures for the well-being of the majority. similarly, one must act in accordance with the dhamma as much as possible, free from selfishness. for the main cause of these disasters is one's own karma brought along in *samsara*. those karmas yield their results through the eight worldly conditions. this wheel of karma, in accordance with karma, is what is shown to us through the worldly conditions—that the eight worldly conditions rotate.
thus, even the blessed one had to face gain, loss, disrepute, fame, blame, praise, pleasure, and pain (*dukkha*). from stories like that of cinca manavika, we see how much insult the blessed one received from the sectarians. he endured all of that without being shaken. that is what is called the quality of *tadi*—suchness. fashioning the mind according to whatever comes. the quality of equanimity. indeed, it is for this very purpose that we engage in this practice-dispensation. on this occasion, too, you are spending this poya day by letting go of various comforts and pleasures of the household life, leaning toward a very simple life, as a rehearsal for the life of the arahants, a rehearsal for that way of living. in a manner fitting the eight-fold uposatha precepts (*uposatha atthanga sila*), in accordance with various training rules, you separate yourself from entertainment like dancing, singing, and instrumental music, separate yourself from wearing various ornaments, and train in a simple life. there too lies letting go. therefore, from the very beginning of this dispensation, one must train in that letting go. lay devotees, instead of being drowned in household thoughts in their day-to-day lives, separate themselves from them, and indeed, keep even the poya eight precepts as a training in renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
the word *veramani* (abstaining) present in every training rule is what is important there. that too is letting go. killing living beings is easy; one likes it. but abstaining from it is difficult. in the dhamma, concerning grasping (*upadana*), two types of desire are mentioned: sensual objects (*vatthu-kama*) and sensual defilements (*kilesa-kama*). in practicing generosity, first, to eliminate sensual objects, one trains in letting go of things belonging to oneself. furthermore, to let go of defilements, one must take an even subtler course of action. in day-to-day life, we can understand the way the world behaves according to the habits of *samsara* through the behavior of animals and those who lack virtues like morality (*sila*). when we consider the opposite of those training rules—killing living beings, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and taking intoxicants—we see that these are the easy things in the world. anyone can quickly enrich their life or make it pleasurable through these. but the blessed one has shown the danger (*adinava*) of these. although they are easy, if we do not let go of them, we will have to face a great mass of suffering (*dukkha*), and not only in this life.
you have heard of the four fears: the fear of self-reproach (*attanuvada-bhaya*), the fear of reproach by others (*paranuvada-bhaya*), the fear of punishment (*danda-bhaya*), and the fear of an unhappy destination (*duggati-bhaya*). “fear” means that the mind blames itself. when one commits acts like killing living beings or stealing, that wrong deed remains deposited in the mind. because of that, one's own mind blames oneself. some people cannot sleep. that is the fear of self-reproach—one's own mind blaming oneself. next is the fear of reproach by others—the blame of others. next is the fear of punishment—getting caught in the grip of the state and the law, and having to suffer pain and hardship. finally, the fear of an unhappy destination—going to an unhappy destination, which the blessed one saw and declared with his buddha-eye. similarly, the arahant maha moggallana, who possessed direct knowledges (*abhinna*), and others showed illustrations to the world, demonstrating the danger of breaking these five precepts, of breaking these training rules—the suffering and hardships that lay people or monks who break them have to endure.
considering those, one must perform that letting go. letting go through the primary renunciation of giving (*dana*) is sometimes easy. letting go of external objects is easy. what is difficult is to free oneself from those bad habits and wrong practices that have been cultivated for a long time in *samsara*. it is for this that morality (*sila*) is necessary. the blessed one declared that as an effort to cleanse the mind from the unwholesome karma performed over a long time in *samsara* as animals, hungry ghosts (*preta*), demons (*yaksa*), etc., one must observe the five precepts as permanent morality (*nicca-sila*).
while observing the five precepts, gradually going higher, you observe the poya eight precepts or ten precepts on this poya day, making a sacrifice of pleasure, as an effort to escape from this *samsara* with its terrifying fear of unhappy destinations, and as a training in the lifestyle of the arahants. the word *veramani* in every training rule reminds us of a letting go. thus, that indeed is the quality of good men (*sappurisa*). the blessed one has shown both the danger (*adinava*) side and the benefit (*anisamsa*) side. the blessed one constantly points out the benefit side. generally, everyone enters into something after seeing its benefits. similarly, when the danger side is shown, one becomes concerned and develops a sense of urgency (*samvega*), realizing that a change must occur.
as benefits, it often brings wealth and resources of becoming (*bhava*). but the benefit of morality (*sila*) brings good births—it brings good births in the human world or happy destinations (*sugati*). because it is through morality (*sila*) that the true cultivation of virtues takes place within. thinking about morality (*sila*) in this way, we see that it too is a letting go—“indeed, good men let go.” letting go is a characteristic of good men. next, an even deeper letting go belongs to those among you who are inclined toward meditation. from the moment the mind wishes to meditate, obstacles appear from all sides; one must make an effort to conquer these obstacles from within oneself. it is of no use to blame externals, saying, “i cannot meditate because of this or that.” how is one's lifestyle structured? what are the things that can be let go of from these? one must contemplate and see for oneself. then, one might think, “although we have done these things so far, they are unnecessary; they do not contribute to the task of developing the mind.” therefore, one must develop the strength to let go of them.
indeed, the very first problem for meditators is to break those bonds. those bonds are things created due to attachment, due to craving (*tanha*). therefore, if one hopes to escape from this *samsara*, those too must be broken. those are the defilements of desire (*kilesa-kama*) in the mind. therefore, one must conquer the attachments and conflicts regarding one's wives, children, wealth, etc.—the craving (*tanha*) for them. sometimes, unless one contemplates them with wisdom, the craving (*tanha*) for them will not cease merely by giving them away. to assist in meditation, the blessed one highlights the impermanence (*anicca*), the suffering (*dukkha*) nature, and the non-self (*anatta*) nature of all these. the blessed one has presented various such perceptions (*sanna*) from the perspective of insight (*vipassana*).
lay devotees too must contemplate in some way this nature of suffering (*dukkha*) in *samsara* highlighted by the blessed one. every time we recollect it, we understand the danger aspect of this *samsara*. by grasping things that have danger, we become further trapped in *samsara*. we will have to let go of them naturally. therefore, the meditator must contemplate with wisdom and be strong enough to let go of those bonds and what are shown as impediments (*palibodha*) for one's progress in meditation. indeed, the word “good man” (*sappurisa*) is used especially in reference to arahants. if anyone is a good man, he must possess that collection of qualities within him. in any place, he must have the strength to let go and act altruistically. he must use words honestly without self-interested talk. then, he must endure those pleasures and pains (*dukkha*). one must develop such strength.
the blessed one declared: “i do not see a single thing in this *samsara* that is not a bond,” let alone even the meditative absorptions (*jhana*). now, an ordinary meditator might think, “by attaining these absorptions (*jhana*), etc., i will spend time in the brahma worlds or deva worlds.” but the blessed one showed that these too are bonds. these too must be let go of—to the extent that there is nothing of which he said, “do not let go.” the blessed one has highlighted this regarding the preparations (*sankhara*) in this entire becoming (*bhava*).
you have heard many times: *“sabbe sankhara anicca”*—“all preparations (*sankhara*) are impermanent (*anicca*).” often, we recollect such things at funeral houses, etc. but we must constantly recollect this collection of preparations (*sankhara*) related to this *samsara*, seeing them as preparations (*sankhara*), and realizing: “these are not mine; there is nothing here that can be taken as 'i' or 'mine'.” it is by constantly instilling this understanding in the mind that one can develop that strength. one who hopes for concentration (*samadhi*) in meditation must remove even those things that are pleasing to oneself if they obstruct the one-pointedness of mind, concentration (*samadhi*), and only then can the mind be concentrated. after that, for the development of insight (*vipassana*), the blessed one has pointed out various perceptions (*sanna*), such as the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*), the perception of non-self (*anatta-sanna*), the perception of danger (*adinava-sanna*), and the perception of abandoning (*pahana-sanna*). the blessed one has declared four wrong perceptions—perverted perceptions (*vipallasa-sanna*)—present in the ordinary world: the perception of permanence in the impermanent (*anicce nicca-sanna*). the blessed one declared that the world, not seeing impermanence (*anicca*), forms a perception of permanence in impermanent things and acts in a perverted manner in *samsara*. similarly, the perception of beauty in the foul (*asubhe subha-sanna*), considering foul things as beautiful; the perception of pleasure in the painful (*dukkhe sukha-sanna*), forming a perception of pleasure in things fraught with suffering (*dukkha*); and finally, the perception of self in the non-self (*anattani atta-sanna*), considering that which is non-self (*anatta*) and cannot be kept under one's control as self. in this manner, these perverted perceptions exist in the world.
but instead of that, in discourses such as the girimananda sutta, the blessed one highlights dhamma-conforming perceptions (*sanna*) to be constantly raised in the mind, such as: the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*), the perception of non-self (*anatta-sanna*), the perception of foulness (*asubha-sanna*), the perception of danger (*adinava-sanna*), the perception of abandoning (*pahana-sanna*), the perception of dispassion (*viraga-sanna*), the perception of cessation (*nirodha-sanna*), the perception of non-delight in the entire world (*sabba-loke anabhirata-sanna*), and the perception of impermanence in all preparations (*sabba-sankharesu anicca-sanna*). you constantly deal with perceptions (*sanna*). however, those perceptions (*sanna*) are often things that cause one to remain in *samsara*. instead, one must incline the mind toward those perceptions highlighted by the blessed one in discourses like the girimananda sutta. these thoughts must be constantly cultivated as attitudes in the mind. these are not things that arise all of a sudden. the blessed one has declared that each of these contributes to nibbana.
if someone is trained to see impermanence (*anicca*) as a trait of their character, by developing that perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*), they can complete all other tasks as well. in discourses delivered concerning the community of monks on certain occasions, the blessed one points out: “in this community of mine, there are some who develop the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*). certain individuals in that group, being directed to that alone, complete the rest through it.” there, it is the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*) regarding the five aggregates of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*). similarly, the perception of non-self (*anatta-sanna*). regarding the sense bases (*ayatana*)—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—and their corresponding objects, cultivating the perception of non-self (*anatta-sanna*), that “nowhere is there a self,” is the perception of non-self (*anatta-sanna*).
next, concerning the thirty-two impure parts of the body, the impure parts of the body, or what is shown as the nine cemetery contemplations (*nava sivathika*), reflecting on the fate of this body when it goes to the cemetery, one can cultivate the perception of foulness (*asubha-sanna*). next, the illnesses within this body. the list mentioned in the buddha's time is not enough; we have to extend it further when we think about the diseases of this day and age. the girimananda sutta is especially meant for this. indeed, as shown under the perception of danger (*adinava-sanna*), this body is a nest of diseases, a heap of diseases. the blessed one declared that if anyone says this body is healthy even for a single moment, it is foolishness. not even for a single moment is there real health, real disease-free state. thus, we generate this *samsara* again and again due to the desire for this body. it is because of not understanding that it is a nest of diseases, a heap of diseases. when one understands the true nature of the illnesses and pains of the body, the strength to face them arises. conversely, the attachment to this body gradually disappears. similarly, one understands from this that it is something that cannot be kept under one's control. next, what is shown by the perception of abandoning (*pahana-sanna*), etc., is the strength to eliminate those defilements at the very moment they arise.
next is the perception of dispassion (*viraga-sanna*). with nibbana as the object, it is shown as the impermanent nature of all preparations (*sankhara*), and their pacification alone being pleasant. the perception of nibbana is there. this itself is peaceful: *“etam santam etam panitam yadidam sabbasankharasamatho sabbupadhipatinissaggo tanhakkhayo virago nirodho nibbanam”*—“this is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all preparations (*sankhara*), the relinquishment of all assets (*upadhi*), the destruction of craving (*tanha*), dispassion, cessation, nibbana.” in every single word, there is letting go. *“etam santam etam panitam”*—looking at these words, they are very beautiful. “this is peaceful, this is sublime.” what is sublime? it is not what we think that is considered peaceful and sublime here. *“sabbasankharasamatho”*—the calming, the stilling of all preparations (*sankhara*). *“sabbupadhipatinissaggo”*—if there is any asset (*upadhi*) we are holding onto, whatever things we are cultivating, as they say, and when speaking ultimately, the form, sensation (*vedana*), perception, preparations (*sankhara*), and consciousness (*vinnana*) of these five aggregates of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*), which we call “i” and “mine,” as well as one's houses, lands, vehicles, and mass of wealth—all these are assets (*upadhi*)—letting go of them in the mind. this is not throwing them away or destroying them; it is letting go of the attachment to them in the mind (*sabbupadhipatinissaggo*).
similarly, craving (*tanha*). it is through craving (*tanha*) that we are carried on and on in this *samsara*. there is nothing that cannot be completely satiated by nourishing it as much as this craving (*tanha*). this craving flows in various directions like rivers flowing here and there. the destruction of this craving, drying it up, is *tanhakkhaya* (the destruction of craving). next, *viraga* (dispassion) directly means that very attachment—attachment to becoming (*bhava*), attachment to these five aggregates of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*). eliminating them, or in other words, nibbana itself is there.
looking at the highest level, it is the occasion of letting go of the five aggregates of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*). dispassion, cessation. cessation (*nirodha*), when looked at from one perspective, is the cessation of becoming (*bhava-nirodha*). it is the ending of this suffering (*dukkha*) of *samsara*. the blessed one declared this as something that can be realized in this very life: *“bhava-nirodho nibbanam”*—“the cessation of becoming (*bhava*) is nibbana.” it is difficult for many to even think of. because they long for becoming (*bhava*), they are born again and again. no matter how much we say this *samsara* is painful (*dukkha*), as long as the feeling of “i” and “mine” remains within us, the world longs for becoming (*bhava*). that is why it is said, “as long as there is grasping (*upadana*), there is becoming (*bhava*).” as long as there is grasping (*upadana*), we establish this mind in some place that is prey to that grasping, and then from there, we take birth again. that is resolved by karma.
no matter how the world thinks, in truth, birth (*jati*) is easy; ending birth (*jati*) is difficult. therefore, if birth (*jati*) is suffering (*dukkha*), what we have to do is to end birth (*jati*). the blessed one declared that what supports this is that mental grasping (*upadana*). it is when that is eliminated that becoming (*bhava*) also ceases. the blessed one highlighted that this can be done in this very life, in a manner that no other teacher has shown. that is what is called the mind of nibbana. at some moment, seeing the danger (*adinava*) in these, drawing the mind away through seeing that danger—that is what is called dispassion (*viraga*). when the mind is drawn away, one sees that cessation (*nirodha*) as happiness. constantly, the nature of a formation (*sankhara*) is arising and passing away: origination and fall (*samudaya-vaya*), arising and passing away (*udayabbaya*), origination and cessation (*samudaya-nirodha*)—these various words describe the arising and passing away. this is the nature of preparations (*sankhara*). but the world, because of craving (*tanha*), remains in the aspiration for rebirth. the nature of craving, described as leading to rebirth (*ponobbhavika*), is that it longs for becoming (*bhava*) again. it is said, *“tanha ponobbhavika”* (craving leading to rebirth). similarly, it is accompanied by delight and lust (*nandi-raga-sahagata*). the nature of this craving is that it finds delight and attaches here and there (*tatra-tatrabhinandini*). it finds delight here and there. at one moment here, at another moment there. jumping from place to place in this way, this craving seeks satisfaction.
thus, craving leading to rebirth, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there (*tanha ponobbhavika nandi-raga-sahagata tatra-tatrabhinandini*). craving itself creates rebirth, creates another becoming (*bhava*). similarly, that characteristic of attachment and delight is present within that craving. it finds delight here and there. it is the occasion when that craving is destroyed that the blessed one called the destruction of craving, cessation, nibbana (*tanhakkhayo nirodho nibbanam*). the destruction of craving itself is cessation. there, the person who hitherto directed the mind toward the side of origination (*samudaya*), who longed for repeated arising, when he sees the happiness of cessation (*nirodha*), that is extinguishment (nibbana. fuel (*upadana*) is also the word used for firewood. if we want to spread a fire, we must feed it with fuel (*upadana*)—firewood. when firewood is thrown in, the fire spreads. no matter how much we hope to extinguish the fire, if we feed it with firewood, the fire will grow and not be extinguished, won't it? that is why the blessed one declared: be without fuel (*anupadano*). he says to remove the fuel (*upadana*) material. when the mind is developed through meditation, the true nature of the preparations (*sankhara*) in this *samsara* begins to be understood. just as when a corpse is placed on someone's shoulder, they immediately let go of it with disgust, a turning away occurs in the mind. letting go occurs through a deep turning away. for that to be nourished, as the blessed one pointed out, so that knowledge of things as they are (*yathabhuta-nana*) is developed, we must maintain our thoughts in accordance with the three characteristics: impermanence (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and non-self (*anatta*).
everyone in *samsara* dislikes seeing cessation. instead, they direct the mind toward production. if you think about your own lives, you will see that no one even looks at the waste products excreted from their body. instead, they try to preserve this by constantly putting raw materials into it. even if we think about our clothes, ornaments, etc., when they get old, we discard them as rubbish and get new ones. we go shopping, but we do not direct our mind to the fate of the things we have used so far, to their impermanence (*anicca*). we have described this through various similes—this is the impermanent nature of preparations (*sankhara*). the blessed one highlights this so that we may see cessation (*nirodha*). the world dislikes cessation (*nirodha*). they look only at the side of origination (*samudaya*). everyone likes to watch the sun rise tomorrow morning. they do not like to see the sun set. but what we have to do in *samsara* is to make this sun set. that is why the blessed one constantly tells us to recollect cessation (*nirodha*). arahants declare that when the mind goes to cessation (*nirodha*), there is a peace within it that was never known before. that is why it is said, *“bhava-nirodho nibbanam”*—the cessation of becoming (*bhava*) is nibbana. when becoming (*bhava*) ceases right here, that cessation characterized by peace, which is called the bliss of nibbana by many, can be experienced permanently. *“etam santam etam panitam”*—“this itself is peaceful, this is sublime”—what is meant is that occasion when all is let go of.
starting from day-to-day life, when that letting go is developed to its maximum state, it is understood by one's own mind: this is a state where nothing is grasped, a state where one is not trapped in anything—a state of liberation (*vimukti*). nibbana means liberation—the liberation of the mind. the mind is constantly bound. at this moment, thoughts are experienced as a trouble. no matter how subtly those are attained in states of absorption (*jhana*), there is some connection to becoming (*bhava*) there. it goes and gets trapped somewhere. even if one attains those states of absorption (*jhana*), one goes to the brahma world and gets trapped. there too, one goes round and round like a spinning top. but the blessed one alone showed the true medicine for this. looking at everything as preparations (*sankhara*), considering their arising and passing away and their conditions, when the mind is directed toward cessation (*nirodha*), we attain liberation.
therefore, you must contemplate that through this short verse, we have gathered a great many facts on this valuable day that are helpful for day-to-day life as well as for nibbana. your constant performance of actions like offering alms to the virtuous and providing requisites to the monks helps to eliminate the desire for sensual objects (*vatthu-kama*). observing morality (*sila*), listening to the dhamma, and meditating help to eliminate the defilements of desire (*kilesa-kama*). employing whatever wholesome power you have gathered so far through all of these, and whatever strengths there are that help to develop the faculties (*indriya-bala*) of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*) gained through the benefits of hearing this dhamma, aspire: “may this wholesome power definitely be a supportive condition to realize the noble, supreme, deathless nibbana through the path, fruit, and penetration of stream-entry, non-returning, and arahantship as quickly as possible, before the decline of this dispensation of the buddha!” similarly, let us recite these verses so that all beings, from the avici hell up to the akanittha heaven, including your deceased relatives who have passed away, may rejoice in this merit of dhamma-preaching and dhamma-hearing, and realize the noble, supreme, deathless nibbana through their aspired enlightenment (*bodhi*)!
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 131
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #131
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.35)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
Yo daṇḍena adandesu, appaduṭṭhesu dussati;
dasannamaññataraṃ ṭhānaṃ, khippameva nigacchati;
vedanaṃ pharusaṃ jāniṃ, sarīrassa ca bhedanaṃ;
garukaṃ vāpi ābādhaṃ, cittakkhepañca pāpuṇe;
rājato vā upassaggaṃ, abbhakkhānañca dāruṇaṃ;
parikkhayañca ñātīnaṃ, bhogānañca pabhaṅguraṃ;
atha vassa agārāni, aggi ḍahati pāvako;
kāyassa bhedā duppañño, nirayaṃ so upapajjatī ti.
From:
Dhammapada 137–140 (Daṇḍavagga)
Dear Listeners,
At this moment, we have chosen as our theme several verses related to a most poignant event of great significance in the Dispensation, which occurred while our Teacher of the Three Worlds, the Buddha, was residing at Veluvana Monastery. By realizing Nibbāna, a person becomes a noble treasure to the world. When a Buddha, a Paccekabuddha, or an Arahant arises in the world, a vast multitude—not only in this human world but also among the deities and Brahmas of the heavenly realms—attain great welfare and solace, not merely by making offerings to them, but even by simply gladdening their minds in their presence. That is why they are known as the supreme fields of merit—the incomparable field of merit.
However, there is another group of people in the world who, by corrupting their minds toward these noble ones and by harming or harassing them, fall into intense *Dukkha* (Suffering). They undergo terrifying *Dukkha* (Suffering) and torment, boiling in hell for aeons. It is because of this state of affairs that the Buddha, through these verses, pointed out and declared a certain danger that can come upon the world regarding these noble persons. That danger refers to the numerous hazards that can occur by corrupting one's own mind. These verses were uttered as a warning regarding this.
The incident connected to this is also of great value to the Dispensation. While the Buddha was residing at Veluvana Monastery, a group of sectarians known as the Nigaṇṭhas gathered in a certain place and discussed, "How is it that this Recluse Gotama receives so much gain and honor?" While discussing this, some of them said, "These massive gains and honors are received because of a monk in this Dispensation named Mahā Moggallāna. From time to time, he goes to the heavenly worlds, asks the deities about the meritorious deeds they performed which caused them to be born in heaven, and returning to the human world, tells the people. He also goes to the hells, finds out about the evil deeds that caused the torment of those born in the purgatories, and informs the humans. That is why such immense gain and honor are received. If we can kill this Elder Moggallāna, we can divert those gains and honors to ourselves." Next, what did they do? Having raised a subscription of a thousand gold coins (*kahāpaṇas*) from among their supporters, they hired a band of five hundred murderous bandits to put the Great Arahant Moggallāna to death. At that time, Ven. Moggallāna was residing at a rock known as Kālasilā.
This band of bandits surrounded the hut to capture the Arahant. Knowing this, the Elder escaped and slipped away through the keyhole by his psychic power. That was the first time. Once again, when this band of bandits surrounded the hut to capture the Great Arahant Moggallāna, he broke through the circular peak of the roof and escaped, again by his psychic power. In this manner, two months passed. By the third month, the Great Arahant Moggallāna perceived that the gravity of a grave evil karma he had committed in the past had caught up with him. Realizing that this time there was no escape, he did not flee in that manner. The bandits broke into the hut, captured him, beat him severely, crushing his bones to the size of broken rice, and thinking he was dead, threw him into a bush and left. However, the Great Arahant Moggallāna did not pass away (*pariNibbāna simply by that. It is said that by the power of meditative absorption (*jhāna*), he gathered all the remaining bones of his body together and bound them with the "meditative wrap" (*jhāna-veṭhuma*). Flying through the air in this manner, he arrived before the Buddha and informed him, "Venerable Sir, I am about to attain *Parinibbāna*." The Buddha said, "Very well, then preach some Dhamma to me before you pass away." The Elder rose into the air, delivered a sermon, and then went to the Kālasilā region where he attained *Parinibbāna*.
As this event spread throughout the country, King Ajātasattu deployed spies to capture the bandits who did this. While these spies were going about, on one occasion, members of that bandit gang, while drinking alcohol in a tavern, began boasting to one another. During a joke made among themselves, it was revealed that it was they who killed the Great Arahant Moggallāna. Thereupon, when the spies arrested them and investigated, the fact that they were employed by those Nigaṇṭhas was also revealed. Accordingly, when the five hundred Nigaṇṭhas and the five hundred bandits were arrested and handed over to the king, what punishment did the king decree? He ordered that all of them be buried in pits up to their waists in the palace courtyard, covered with soil, and burned to death. That was the punishment he meted out. Furthermore, after burying them, covering them with soil, throwing straw over them and burning their bodies, he ordered that harrows be dragged over them to shred all their bodies into pieces. While the monks were gathered in the Dhamma hall discussing this event, the Buddha arrived there. He asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your discussion?" The monks stated, "Venerable Sir, we are speaking about how the Great Arahant Moggallāna met a death that was unbefitting of him." At that moment, the Buddha declared, "Monks, although the Elder Moggallāna met a death that seems unbefitting of him in this life, that death occurred in a manner that was entirely fitting for an evil karma he committed in the past." He then recounted that past story.
In the past, the Great Arahant Moggallāna was born as the only son of a pair of blind parents, and he looked after those blind parents, doing all the work in the house and the fields. Meanwhile, seeing the son exerting himself, the parents said, "We shall bring you a wife. You cannot do all this work alone." Although the son initially expressed his unwillingness, he agreed due to his parents' repeated entreaties.
Accordingly, a certain woman was brought to that house. After serving the parents for a few days, she developed a disgust toward them. She began pointing out the parents' faults in a way that hurt her husband's feelings. When he did not believe her, she scattered slimy, frothy substances like gruel foam in various places in the house. When her husband returned home in the evening, she lied to him, saying, "Look at this! These parents are ruining and dirtying everything here." In this way, she poisoned the son's mind. Thus, this son decided that he must kill his parents.
What did he do next? He told his parents, "Your relatives in such-and-such a distant region wish to see you." He put them in a cart, and while driving through a great forest, he told them, "There are many fierce bandits in this area. Therefore, I will get down from the cart." Giving the reins into his father's hands, he got down from the cart and made terrifying noises, just like fierce bandits shouting. The parents cried out, "Oh son, we are old! Save your own life!" While they were saying this, the son, continuing to make the sounds of the bandits, beat his parents to death, threw them into the forest, and returned home.
Thereupon, the Buddha declared, "Because of that evil karma committed by my son Moggallāna in the past, he boiled in hell for hundreds of thousands of years. As a residual result, in a hundred lifetimes, he met his death with his bones crushed in this very manner. Therefore, this is entirely fitting for his past karma. Furthermore, due to the unwholesome karma they committed, this group of a thousand people who corrupted their minds toward my son Moggallāna—who himself harbored no corrupted mind and held no rod—suffered a terrifying destruction even in this very life, by order of the king." With this as the basis, he uttered those verses. As we mentioned earlier, the Buddha, through those verses, pointed out the numerous disasters that can karmically befall someone by corrupting one's mind toward those who are considered the most noble treasures of the world—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Arahants, as well as Noble Persons such as Stream-Enterers, Once-Returners, and Non-Returners, and by harming or harassing them.
If we take the meaning of those verses: *Yo daṇḍena adaṇḍesu, appaduṭṭhesu dussati*—whoever harms with weapons/rods those who do not use weapons/rods, and whoever harbors hatred toward those who have uncorrupted minds and are free from hatred; *dasannamaññataraṃ ṭhānaṃ, khippameva nigacchati*—as a result of that, very quickly incurs one of ten consequences. What are they? *Vedanaṃ pharusaṃ jāniṃ*—he undergoes extremely harsh *Vedanā* (Feeling), grave *Vedanā* (Feeling). Next, *sarīrassa ca bhedanaṃ*—the parts of his body are broken and destroyed; he falls into great ruin. *Garukaṃ vāpi ābādhaṃ*—grave illnesses, chronic diseases that one might even carry from birth. Next, *cittakkhepañca*—he goes mad, falling into a state of insanity. Also, *rājato vā upassaggaṃ*—he undergoes harm from the king, disasters that come by royal command. *Dāruṇaṃ*—likewise, he faces terrible, baseless accusations. *Ñātīnaṃ*—his relatives are suddenly ruined. *Bhogānañca*—and his wealth is also destroyed. *Atha vassa agārāni*—furthermore, his houses, his dwellings, *aggi ḍahati pāvako*—are burned down by consuming fire. These are ten painful consequences that can befall someone due to insulting or harming the Noble Ones. Finally, *kāyassa bhedā duppañño, nirayaṃ so upapajjati*—upon the breakup of the body, that foolish person is reborn in hell. In this way, the Buddha, as a warning, pointed out the consequences of that grave evil karma.
Thus, through this story as well as through these verses, the Buddha highlighted to the world the terrifying nature of this karma. The reason we recall this matter on many occasions is that we feel this is an era in which many people live under the concept of "it does not matter how one lives, as long as one gets by," spending this brief lifespan only to be reborn and suffer for countless billions of aeons in hells, animal realms, and ghost realms. The message that Buddhas give to the world is the turning away from the path of bad destinations to the path of good destinations, and then, liberating oneself from both good and bad destinations, to be freed from this entire samsara, and to find solace in the sublime, deathless Nibbāna. We can extract many points related to this from this story and these verses. Let us first reflect: Ven. Mahā Moggallāna was no ordinary person. He was someone who had fulfilled the perfections (*pāramīs*) for the position of Chief Disciple over a vast period of many aeons. Yet, even such a person, when he was a worldling (*pṛthagjana*), developed such a wrong view and hatred toward his parents, and committed the grave evil karma of murder. Concerning parents, the Buddha declared: *"āpādakā posakā, lokassa dassetāro"*—they are the ones who brought about one's birth, nourished one, and introduced the world. In the sense that they are to be regarded as the Brahmas of the household, the Buddha also declared: *"brahmāti mātāpitaro"*—"parents are called Brahmas."
Developing hatred toward such parents who brought one up and putting them to death is a most grave unwholesome deed, and these virtuous people may have heard about *ānantariya* (immediate) weighty karmas (*garuka kamma*). Killing one's mother and killing one's father are pointed out as the primary, gravest unwholesome deeds. A person who commits such evil deeds has absolutely no escape; in the very next life, they go to hell. That is why it is called *ānantariya*—having immediate consequences. Thus, even Ven. Moggallāna, who had fulfilled such perfections, committed such a grave evil karma in the past and boiled in hell for a long time. As a mark of this, as you all know, even the body of the Arahant Moggallāna was dark in color.
Indeed, because the definite prophecy (*niyata vivaraṇa*) obtained in the past also had to be fulfilled, he attained the position of Chief Disciple in this manner. From that event, we can understand that even psychic power (*iddhi-bala*) is defeated by the power of karma (*kamma-bala*). What is the illustration shown to us by the Great Arahant Moggallāna through this? What did his undergoing of that grave and terrifying disaster teach the world? Even many Buddhists regard psychic power as something magnificent. Indeed, they are great. But when we reflect on the fear of this samsara, it is clear that there is no escape through any of them. Especially, psychic power is not always sufficient to escape from the disasters that can arise karmically. This is evident from the fact that the Great Arahant Moggallāna, knowing in his final moments that the attraction of karma was supreme, did not flee from there. He understood that this was something destined to happen.
Therefore, it occurs to us that the most powerful force in this world, surpassing even psychic powers, is the force of karma. Nowadays, people are amazed when they think about computers, which are considered modern inventions. When you input something into a computer, it can be retrieved. Similarly, the human mind—*Viññāṇa* (Consciousness)—has a similar nature. The Buddha declared: *"Cetanāhaṃ bhikkhave kammaṃ vadāmi. Cetayitvā kammaṃ karoti kāyena vācāya manasā"*—"Monks, I say that intention (*cetanā*) is karma. Having intended, one performs karma through body, speech, and mind." That is because every action or word considered as karma proceeds with intention as its forerunner. Therefore, when a karmic seed is deposited in *Viññāṇa* (Consciousness) according to that intentional force, it does not perish without yielding its result; it persists, undestroyed, for billions of aeons. How wonderfully it operates is shown by the statement made right here, that Ven. Moggallāna met his death in that manner, with his bones crushed, a hundred times. One cannot even fathom how it happens. It is so astonishing how everything in the external environment aligns itself so that the karmic seed grown in one's own mental continuum yields its fruit accordingly.
Our mind exists depending on the four elements present in this body: earth (*paṭhavī*), water (*āpo*), fire (*tejo*), and air (*vāyo*). When something bad falls into that mind, it also affects those four elements. Earth, water, fire, and air are also what exist around us. Therefore, we can understand the connection between these. We live individually, saying "this is I" and "this is the other person." But apart from the idea created by ignorance (*avijjā*), namely "I" and "mine," what exists here are only those four elements: earth, water, fire, and air. Whether it is inside or outside, these are interconnected. Thus, what must happen karmically? Due to that force of karma, which is like the power in a computer, it operates in a precise, circular manner.
The wheel of karma (*kammacakra*) is magnificent. Sometimes, it happens in a way that even the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakra*) cannot withstand. Even here, Ven. Moggallāna was such a noble Elder who held the highest position in this Dispensation. Even though he spun the Wheel of Dhamma to such an extent, he was subjugated by his own wheel of karma. This shows that even if one attains the state of an Arahant, this life exists on the force generated by the karmic energies committed in the past, until one attains *Parinibbāna*. One has to experience the agreeable and disagreeable *Vedanā* (Feeling), the pleasures and pains that must be received from them. Even in the case of the Buddha, when Devadatta rolled down the rock, although he was able to prevent it with his supreme Buddha-power, he was still injured and afflicted by a splinter. This occurred in accordance with past karma. If karma yields its results even to the Buddha and the Arahants, we can imagine how powerful a force, a law (*niyāmatā*), it is. It is done by the mind itself. Whenever a grave unwholesome intentional seed is deposited in this mind of ours, which exists dependent on the four elements, it persists undestroyed thereafter and yields its results in a circular manner across various lifetimes. As found in some stories, seven times, sometimes a hundred times, five hundred times, a thousand times, or millions of times. In this way, this wheel of karma can spin and deliver the exact same result repeatedly. From this, we can see how terrifying this samsara is, how terrifying a situation it is.
Many Buddhists, rather than supramundane virtues, often consider flying through the air by obtaining psychic powers as something grand. Flying through the air is done even by crows. Nowadays, it is done by vehicles and planes. These are common things. Even during times when no Buddha has arisen, non-Buddhists who attained *jhānas* and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) performed various kinds of psychic miracles. But more than all of them, we must realize that the most terrifying force in this samsara is karma. So much so that even the Buddha declared that the domain of karma (*kamma-visaya*) is unthinkable (*acinteyya*). Within this karma, there is an astonishing nature that cannot be fully fathomed. The event that clearly reveals this is the final *Parinibbāna* of the Great Arahant Moggallāna, who reigned supreme in this Dispensation, occurring through his death at the hands of bandits with his bones crushed. What a heartbreaking event!
Another nature of this karma is that, for the ripening of that karma, not only inanimate things but even living beings are drawn into it. In that way, they become entangled in the knots of karma. Here, we saw who became the instruments to exhaust the karmic force of Ven. Moggallāna. Those five hundred Nigaṇṭhas and five hundred bandits were drawn into that matter in that manner. Often, those with weak minds become involved in the karmic entanglements of others and suffer pain and distress. That is the most terrifying thing in this ball of karmic thread. When we live virtuously, well-established in those noble qualities, we have the strength, by applying wisdom, to remain free from those entanglements. Otherwise, if we live holding wrong views and committing evil deeds, without even knowing it, we are likely to become instruments to exhaust the karmic forces of others. We must keep this in mind as a warning. That danger can happen to us if we do not spend our daily lives properly in accordance with the Dhamma, according to the teachings of the Buddha. We too are likely to become instruments to exhaust the karma of others, just as happened to those Nigaṇṭhas and bandits. That is one lesson.
Furthermore, not only that, someone might think that it is the duty of a king to punish those who did wrong. However, even King Ajātasattu accumulated evil karma through that. From these facts, we can see how chaotic this matter of karma is. That is to say, there is no escape for the king simply because he meted out a punishment. The king also became involved in that karma.
From all of this, it is apparent to us that this samsara is a massive web of confusion. As long as one lives within this web of confusion, there is no solace. True solace lies only in being liberated from this entire samsara, in truth, through *Parinibbāna*. Normally, when some disaster comes as a result of such grave karma, a person's reaction is often to develop anger toward those who helped exhaust that karmic result. In an event like what happened to Ven. Moggallāna, if he had developed hatred toward those bandits, then that person would have accumulated more karma through it. That is why it is said: *appaduṭṭhesu dussati*—he harbored hatred toward those who are free from hatred. Ven. Moggallāna understood, "This is my past karma. These people are merely helpers who are exhausting my karma." From this, the value within the realization of Nibbāna is seen. Within that realization, there is a strength to develop a certain equanimity (*upekkhā*) toward things that arise karmically. One gains such an understanding. Likewise, a power of equanimity arises in the mind. That power of equanimity arises from the understanding: "This body of mine, and external things, are created from the four elements: earth, water, fire, and air. There is nothing here to be taken as I or mine." Indeed, we commit these evil deeds because of the self-notion, "I," which we have taken within these things, relying on the essence absorbed from the earth, and the blood, flesh, etc., received from our parents. What is done within samsara is the nourishing of this. Therefore, due to the disasters that come upon oneself, one corrupts one's mind and gets entangled in various evil deeds. While experiencing the result, one generates further karma through that result. Thus, there is no end to them. It goes on and on in samsara.
Instead of that, what is the solace that the Buddha presented through this realization of Nibbāna? It shows a certain cooling down (*nivīma*). While those karmic forces are being exhausted, by using wisdom and equanimity, one understands: "This is a past karma, and what are operating here are only these phenomena." Through that wisdom, it is shown that this is merely a collection of phenomena regarding the body or the mind. Next, for that very reason, one develops equanimity, without leaning toward the side of hatred or lust. That power is present at its highest in the Buddha. If the Arahants constantly remain concentrated in the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship (*arahattaphala-samādhi*), the mind can quickly be freed from the karmas that can approach; otherwise, some deficiency occurs. In the Dhamma, that is known by the name "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*).
Now, you may have heard about the Buddha, that he is "one who has abandoned all defilements along with their habitual tendencies" (*savāsanā sakala-kilesa pahīna*). It is said that he destroyed not only the defilements but also the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Today, this word *vāsanā* is used in society with a different meaning—such as regarding lotteries (luck/fortune). That is not the *vāsanā* spoken of in the Dhamma. What is the deep meaning of the word *vāsanā*? Now, we know that even if the fish is removed from a leaf in which it was wrapped, the smell of fish remains. On the other hand, even if the flowers or incense sticks are removed from something in which they were wrapped, the fragrance remains. It is in reference to this idea of odor or fragrance that this has been said. This means that certain grave karmas do not go away, and certain deficiencies that come in accordance with past character are seen even in Arahants. Due to those deficiencies—that is, at a time when they are not in that noble state called the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship (*arahattaphala-samāpatti*), at times when they do not keep the mind raised to the supramundane state—such things can arise in daily life samsarically even for Arahants. Although their minds travel some distance due to those weaknesses, they do not get entangled in a complete karmic knot to suffer for a long time. However, even Arahants generate a certain amount of unwholesome karma that yields results in this very life, which is called *diṭṭhadhammavedanīya* (to be experienced in this very life). That weakness is what is meant by the word *vāsanā* in the case of Arahants. There, *vāsanā* is not meant in a good sense, but as weaknesses. That too is a part of the defilements themselves. That is why it is said *savāsanā*—the Buddha has no defilements with habitual tendencies. But Arahants have them.
Due to that weakness, certain deficiencies occur in Arahants. But even that does not lead to a future *Bhava* (Becoming). Why? Because in that fruit of Arahantship, in seeing Nibbāna, what is done? The Arahant has brought the mind to a state where rebirth does not occur, due to that wisdom, due to the power of relinquishing the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*). Then, the results of actions or karmic results that can approach due to certain deficiencies arising from this *vāsanā* are common even to Arahants. Such is the nature of that entanglement of karma.
Now, when compared with ordinary people, the mind of the Arahants operates just like a sewing machine without an under-thread (*yaṭi nūla*). Now, as long as the under-thread is there, it knots properly. If it does not knot properly with the under-thread, there is no proper stitch. In the same way, because the portion called *Anusaya* (Underlying tendency) that lies beneath the defilements has been destroyed by the Arahants upon attaining Arahantship, a stitch cannot be made in the true sense. They do not build up grave karma again. That is the state of an Arahant's mind. For those noble ones who have reached the supreme state, like the Great Arahants Moggallāna and others who developed concentration to such a supreme degree near the Buddha, those states are minimal in them. Those weaknesses are fewer. But such weaknesses can be found in certain Arahants. Apart from that, there is no rebirth in samsara. Therefore, the greatest state in the world is the attainment of a mind liberated from this entire samsara. You have also heard this expressed in the Ratana Sutta:
> *Khīṇaṃ purāṇaṃ navaṃ natthi sambhavaṃ,*
> *virattacittā āyatike bhavasmiṃ;*
> *Te khīṇabījā avirūḷhichandā,*
> *nibbanti dhīrā yathāyaṃ padīpo.*
The extinguishment (*nivīma*) of the Arahants is shown to be just like the extinguishing of a lamp. Why? Because *khīṇaṃ purāṇaṃ*—by the time they attain *Parinibbāna*, whatever old karmas there were that helped maintain their lives in the past are entirely exhausted. It is just like a lamp whose oil is completely finished. Next, *navaṃ natthi sambhavaṃ*—there is no accumulation of new karma in that Arahant's mind. Karmas that generate a future *Bhava* (Becoming) do not accumulate in an Arahant's mind. That is just like not adding any more oil to the lamp.
Next, *virattacittā āyatike bhavasmiṃ*—likewise, there is no desire or *Taṇhā* (Craving) for a future *Bhava* (Becoming). The *Taṇhā* for *Bhava* (*bhava-taṇhā*) is the subtlest and gravest weakness in the world. One likes *Bhava*. One likes existence. No matter how many troubles and difficulties there are, why does one carry on this existence? It is because of the feeling, "I." One is afraid that "I" will cease to exist. Although the feeling "I" is a wrong understanding—and though "I" is necessary as a convention to live with the world—the Arahants have realized its lack of essence, its lack of core, its *Anattā* (Not-self) nature. Therefore, there is no desire for a future *Bhava* (Becoming). Concerning such Arahants, it is said: *te khīṇabījā*—this *Viññāṇa* (Consciousness) is the seed. This seed of *Viññāṇa* (Consciousness) sprouts in the field of karma (*kamma-khetta*). It sprouts in the field of karma. It is on wholesome or unwholesome karma that this *Viññāṇa* (Consciousness) sprouts. Just as a seed sprouts depending on the soil. Thus, *Viññāṇa* (Consciousness) sprouts in the field of karma. The moisture, the wetness that assists this is *Taṇhā* (Craving). As long as there is *Taṇhā* (Craving) in the world, and as long as one lives according to wrong view without a true understanding of karma, one performs various karmas and, accordingly, undergoes birth (*Jāti*) again and again. And what come along with that birth (*Jāti*) are indeed what the Buddha pointed out as *Jāti* (Birth), *Jarā* (decay/aging), *Vyādhi* (sickness), and *Maraṇa* (death).
To destroy the mountain of *Dukkha* (Suffering) that can arise due to that impermanence, one must cut its root. That cutting of the root is indeed *te khīṇabījā*—there, the seed of *Viññāṇa* (Consciousness) came to an end. It was exhausted. *Avirūḷhichandā*—no *Taṇhā* (Craving) arises in that mind again. Therefore, *nibbanti dhīrā yathāyaṃ padīpo*—those wise ones are extinguished just like this lamp. That is how it is shown concerning the Arahants. Therefore, through this story, we must reflect on our own lives. We must make this a lesson for our own lives. This era is a time when Buddhists have adopted a strange way of thinking, such that they do not even believe in evil karma, let alone in places like hell. Due to rationalism, some even think that the stories about hell in books, and the sufferings of hell, are invented things.
Indeed, if we have the eye, it is possible to see the things happening in places like hell as if seeing them with our own eyes. It cannot be shown to everyone. It cannot be shown. But things that are like symbols, things that run close to it, are seen in our daily lives. Now, look at the insects called winged termites (*meru*). In times of rain like this, they suddenly emerge from the earth. Millions of insects. Those insects fly. There, too, like a certain psychic power, they rise into the air. But they fly only to be destroyed. Those wings come for their destruction. There, too, we see the way karma works. As soon as wings come to them, they depart by the millions. In the end, only the wings remain. Other creatures gather and feast on those insects. They meet their death right there. From this, we see in this world, even before our very eyes, how animals undergo that *Dukkha* (Suffering) karmically.
Similarly, when we think of how grasshoppers/moths (*palaṅgāṭiyan*) jump into a fire, we can understand how one is born in hell with blazing fires. Moths come to a place where there is a lamp or a fire, and even while seeing others of their own kind burning, they fall into that fire. In the same way, all of this happens to the beings of the world due to that soiled mind, that corrupted mind. Therefore, we must think of a way to escape from this. The Buddha also pointed out: *Sīla*, *Samādhi*, *Paññā* (virtue, concentration, wisdom). Even at the level of *Sīla* (virtue), we act with a certain fear of evil karma. Some regard fear as a bad thing. Sometimes, fear is good. Fear of sin (*ottappa*) is pointed out in the Dhamma as a good thing. It is pointed out as a world-protecting Dhamma (*lokapāla-dhamma*). *Abhaye bhayadassino, bhaye cābhayadassino*—in this way, it is pointed out that those who hold wrong views see fear in what is not fearful, and see no fear in what is fearful, which is incorrect.
Therefore, to abstain from sin, one must have a fear of sin. When reflecting on stories of this nature, a sense of urgency (*saṃvega*) arises regarding one's own samsaric karma. One thinks, "This kind of thing can happen to us too." By being enslaved by the words of various people in society, and by developing hatred toward our own relatives, friends, and parents, we too can fall into such states, just as happened to the Great Arahant Moggallāna.
Likewise, we must undertake and protect some virtue, such as the permanent Five Precepts (*nicca-pañcasīla*) or the Eight Precepts with Right Livelihood as the Eighth (*ājīva-aṭṭhamaka-sīla*). What do we do by undertaking that virtue? We know that in daily life, we take some vaccine or appropriate medicine against infectious diseases. By taking it, we provide some immunity to the body. It is when the body is weak that we fall ill. Therefore, through such an immunization, or by not frequenting places where those diseases spread, one must ensure one's own safety. It is such a thing, virtuous people, that is called undertaking virtue (*sīla*). This is not just something to be repeated when a monk says it, but must be regarded as a determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) made by oneself, in agreement with one's own mind. This is not a mere statement in words. It is a constant determination every morning, and then trying to live according to that determination. That is what is called *Sīla*.
What goes hand-in-hand with virtue is reflection (*āvarjanā*). One undertook virtue. Next, by constantly being mindful of it, one looks to see, "Is this being fulfilled by me?" Such a person thinks, "For no reason whatsoever will I kill a living being, commit theft, engage in sexual misconduct, or tell lies. Next, I will not engage in slander, harsh speech, or frivolous talk."
