although the teacher, who became enraged by this, had an intense urge to kill the youth ahimsaka, he considered the disrepute it would bring upon himself and thought of a stratagem instead. what was the stratagem he employed? he told this young ahimsaka, "if you are to reap the proper benefit of these arts and sciences, you must pay the appropriate teacher's fee (guru-daksina). you must make an offering of honor. therefore, the tribute i demand is nothing other than the killing of a thousand wayfarers. accomplishing that feat is the payment for these arts and sciences as a teacher's fee; complete that," he instructed.
this brahmin youth ahimsaka was someone of immense physical strength and vigor. taking the five types of weapons, he went into a forest and began to kill every person who entered it. as he killed, being unable to keep an accurate count, he cut off a finger from each person he killed and gathered them, attempting to keep a count of the victims. since those fingers would wither and decay in different places, he eventually strung the fingers together and wore them as a garland. even if groups of ten, twelve, or twenty people came, he would chase them down and kill them due to his innate strength and vigor, continuing to amass fingers in this manner. because he wore a garland of fingers, this man came to be known by the terrifying name "angulimala" (finger-garlanded). due to the dread of angulimala, villages, market towns, and provinces began to be deserted. people abandoned their homes. when this terrifying threat arose, the brahmin chaplain also heard of it. realizing they might incur the wrath of the king, he spoke to his wife, the brahmin lady, and said, "look, our son has become this ferocious." driven by a mother's affection, the brahmin lady thought, "i must go tomorrow and somehow bring my son back before he faces the king's wrath." precisely by that day, angulimala's count in his woven garland of fingers had reached nine hundred and ninety-nine. only one more was needed to complete the thousand. thus, with great anticipation, angulimala resolved to kill whoever came the next day, gather the finger, and perform the teacher's offering.
precisely on that morning, when the buddha arose from the attainment of great compassion and surveyed the world, he saw that if he did not go, angulimala would kill his own mother, commit that weightiest of sins (anantarika-kamma), and inevitably be reborn in hell; whereas if he did go, he would be tamed, ordained, and possessed the supportive conditions (hetu-sampatti) to become an arahant. that day, after returning from his alms-round in savatthi, without informing even an attendant, the buddha tidied his dwelling and set off alone to the forested area where angulimala lived. it is mentioned that, owing to the manner of his travel, even those who saw him could not recognize him as the buddha. therefore, the cowherds, farmers, and travelers met along the way, who lived near that forest, thinking he was just an ordinary monk, pleaded with him two or three times, saying, "o monk, do not go down that path. there is a bandit named the notorious angulimala. there is no need to speak of those who go alone; even if groups of twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty go, he chases them down, kills them, and collects their fingers. do not go!" the buddha silently continued on his way.
next, angulimala saw the buddha walking from afar. he thought, "while people who come in such large groups fall into my hands, this monk is coming all alone. this seems like a challenge. i must kill this monk by any means," and he gave chase from behind. the buddha, employing his psychic power, caused the earth to ripple so that no matter how fast angulimala ran, and even though the buddha was walking at his normal, natural pace, angulimala was made unable to catch up with him. thus, angulimala ran, panting heavily. yet, he could not get close to the buddha at all. it is mentioned that he ran for three leagues (yojanas) in this manner.
finally, when he was utterly exhausted, he stopped and shouted, "stop, monk! stop, monk!" then the buddha declared, "i have stopped. you, too, stop!" being a wise person, angulimala thought, "these monastics are truthful. what is the meaning of this statement?" then he asked, "why is it that while i am standing still, you tell me to stop, and while you are walking, you say you have stopped?" in response to this, the buddha said, "angulimala, i have stopped for all time, having abstained from harming living beings, having abstained from violence to creatures, and having laid aside weapons. but you, because you have no restraint regarding the destruction of life, have not yet stopped," thus expressing a profound truth. comprehending the truth of this, angulimala cast away his weapons and asked the buddha for ordination. the buddha ordained him with the formula *ehi bhikkhu* (come, bhikkhu).
then, venerable angulimala, the new monk, walked behind the buddha. having traveled to savatthi, they went to jetavana monastery. meanwhile, there was a huge uproar in the royal courtyard of king kosala's palace. the public had gathered and was protesting: "o lord, in your realm there has arisen such a terrifying, persistent bandit, who is killing people, cutting off their fingers, and causing such devastation. villages, market towns, and provinces are deserted. eradicate this terrifying dread of this thief!" then, king kosala set out with a cavalry of five hundred soldiers to capture this bandit angulimala. on his way, he thought he should also visit the buddha and came to jetavana. the buddha asked, "great king, why are you marching as if for battle? has king bimbisara of magadha declared war? or have the licchavi kings declared war? what is the matter?" when asked, he replied, "no, blessed one, there is a terrifying bandit in my realm. therefore, i am going to subdue that bandit." then the buddha asked, "great king, if you were to see that angulimala, with his hair and beard shaved, wearing saffron robes, abstaining from taking life, from taking what is not given, from false speech, and so on—having abstained from those things pertaining to the five precepts—and living the celibate life of a monk, what would you do?" "in that case, blessed one, i would bow to that angulimala. i would offer him the four requisites. but, blessed one, how could such a sinner obtain such moral restraint?" at the moment the king was saying this, venerable angulimala was seated not far from the buddha. the buddha pointed with his right hand and said, "great king, that is angulimala." upon hearing this, the king was seized with great fear and terror. the buddha said, "do not be afraid, great king, do not be afraid. now, you have no reason to fear this angulimala."
then the king approached venerable angulimala and asked, "are you, venerable sir, the venerable angulimala?" "yes." the king thought that the name "angulimala" was not very suitable, and not respectful enough for this member of the sangha. next, he asked, "of what clan is your father, venerable sir?" "gagga." "of what clan is your mother?" "mantani." in accordance with the ancient way of addressing a person, the king then said, "ah, then, venerable gagga mantaniputta, i invite you to accept the four requisites from me. regard me as your supporter. i shall serve you with the four requisites: robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicine for the sick." by this time, venerable angulimala had not only become ordained, but was also training in the strict practices known as ascetic practices (*dhutangas*). he had already entered upon a rigorous lifestyle: living in the forest, going on alms-rounds, wearing rag-robes, and being content with just three robes. therefore, venerable angulimala replied, "great king, my robes are complete. i do not need robes." deeply inspired by this, the king said to the buddha, "blessed one, this is wonderful and marvelous! one whom i could not tame even with sticks and weapons, the blessed one has tamed in this manner without sticks or weapons," and making this wonderfully praiseful statement, the king departed.
now, venerable angulimala goes on alms-round in savatthi. as soon as people hear, "venerable angulimala is coming on alms-round," they close their doors. some run into the forests out of fear. consequently, venerable angulimala does not receive proper alms-food and has to return. furthermore, venerable angulimala seeks quiet places to meditate. day and night, he strives to meditate. but he cannot raise his mind to the meditation object (*kammatthana*). instead of the meditation object, what comes to his mind is the way he killed people during his time as angulimala, and the screaming voices begging for their lives. next, how they struggled in the throes of death. these are the things that fall into his mind. he cannot concentrate his mind. meanwhile, one day, as venerable angulimala was on alms-round, he saw in a house a pregnant mother undergoing extreme labor pains and distress. developing great compassion for her, he came to the buddha and kindly expressed his sorrow, saying, "alas, to what great suffering do these living beings fall!" on that occasion, the buddha said to venerable angulimala, "in that case, angulimala, go to that woman. go and perform an act of truth (*saccakiriya*) in this manner: *'yatoham, bhagini, jatiya jato nabhijanami sancicca panam jivita voropeta, tena saccena te hotu sotthi hotu gabbhassa.'* perform the act of truth in that way. what is its meaning? 'sister, since i was born, i do not recall intentionally depriving a living being of life. sister, by this truth, may there be well-being for you, and well-being for your child in the womb!'—make such a wish." then, venerable angulimala asked the buddha, "alas, lord, how can i perform such an act of truth? would that not be telling a deliberate lie? have i not deprived so many living beings of life?" offering a small modification, the buddha declared, "in that case, angulimala, perform the act of truth in this manner. how? *'yatoham, bhagini, ariyaya jatiya jato nabhijanami sancicca panam jivita voropeta, tena saccena te hotu sotthi hotu gabbhassa.'* what is its meaning? 'sister, since i was born of the noble birth'—'noble birth' (*ariya jati*) means the noble birth of renouncing the lay life and joining the noble sangha, since the day of receiving this noble birth—'i do not recall intentionally depriving a living being of life. by this truth, may there be well-being for you, and well-being for your child in the womb!'" "ah, in that case, i can do it," said venerable angulimala. he went to that house and performed the act of truth in that manner. this is the origin of the highly powerful angulimala pirith, which is cherished with love by all virtuous laypeople to this day.
now, some might have a doubt as to why the buddha allowed such a protection chant (*pirith*) for venerable angulimala, given that practicing medicine is prohibited for monks according to the vinaya (monastic discipline) laid down by the buddha. however, this is not a medical practice; it is merely an act of truth. on the other hand, out of great compassion, why did the buddha specifically present this practice to venerable angulimala? venerable angulimala was suffering to the extent that he was not even receiving alms-food. there was great fear among the public even when venerable angulimala walked for alms. it was to provide relief regarding that, and also as a solution to the problem of his meditation object not developing.
there is a special meaning in saying "noble birth" (*ariya jati*). in this long *samsara*, there is no one who has not committed actions related to the five evils. but if we are to walk on this path of dhamma, what we need is the foundation of virtue (*sila*). there is a certain boundary in that foundation of virtue. it is by relying on a resolution and a reflection that one can perform an act of truth. here, the buddha gives a immense solace to venerable angulimala. how? it was not the physical birth he had in this life that was taken there. if that were taken as the boundary, there would be no room for venerable angulimala to find peace, considering how many humans he had killed. instead, through the phrase "since i was born of the noble birth," a great relief was brought about. a boundary was set from that point onward. from that boundary, his mind was pure. that is why venerable angulimala was able to do it. out of great compassion, the buddha allowed this stratagem to remove the remorse that was obstructing his meditation object. because the act of truth succeeded, venerable angulimala felt great solace and a immense self-confidence. through that self-confidence—thinking, "now, since the day of my noble birth, i am pure; my virtue is pure"—venerable angulimala was able to concentrate his mind. unremittingly and intensely developing insight (*vipassana*), he became an arahant.
having become an arahant in that way, venerable angulimala now goes on alms-round—the arahant angulimala. alms-food was now received well, but other things were also received. what were they? stones, pebbles, sticks, and clubs thrown by the villagers would fly through the air and fall upon venerable angulimala's head, striking his body, hitting his torso. in the end, venerable angulimala would return from his alms-round with his bowl broken, his head cut and bleeding, and his robes torn. seeing this, the buddha declared, "brahmin, brahmin! endure it, brahmin!" (the word "brahmin" is used by the buddha with reference to arahants). "for whatever evil deed you would have boiled in hell for hundreds of years, thousands of years, hundreds of thousands of years, you are now experiencing a minor result as a ripening to be experienced in this very life (*ditthadhammavedaniya-kamma*). bear with it!"—so the buddha consoled him. when venerable angulimala entered the attainment of the fruit of arahantship (*arahattaphala-samapatti*), he would be freed even from those physical pains considered as ripening in this very life, and while experiencing the bliss of liberation (*vimutti-sukha*), he would utter an exclamatory verse of joy (*udana*). the freedom even from those bodily afflictions regarded as *ditthadhammavedaniya* is found in arahants when they enter the concentration of the fruit of arahantship. experiencing that bliss of liberation, the true bliss of nibbana, the pure bliss of nibbana, venerable angulimala then expressed a verse (which is not directly a word of the buddha):
"yo ca pubbe pamajjitva
paccha so nappamajjati
so imam lokam pabhaseti
abbha mutto va candima"
"he who was formerly negligent, but later is not negligent, illuminates this world like the moon freed from a cloud." venerable angulimala uttered this noble and precious verse as an exclamation of joy, a statement of spiritual triumph.
thus, while experiencing the bliss of liberation as an arahant, he did not live for long. perhaps due to the severity of his past unwholesome deeds of destroying life, when his life-preparations (*ayu-sankhara*) waned, venerable angulimala attained parinibbana (final extinguishment). many members of the sangha did not even know that this venerable monk had become an arahant. after his parinibbana, a discussion arose among the monks assembled in the dhamma hall: "where was this venerable angulimala reborn? he has passed away; where was he reborn?" when the buddha was asked, and they related this discussion, he declared, "no, bhikkhus, my son angulimala attained parinibbana as an arahant." it was on that occasion that he uttered the verse we selected as our theme:
"yassa papam katam kammam
kusalena pithiyati
so imam lokam pabhaseti
abbha mutto va candima"
"he whose evil deed is covered by a wholesome deed illuminates this world like the moon freed from a cloud." he delivered this dhamma verse. briefly put, this is the story of angulimala.
now, an explanation is needed regarding the lesson we should draw from this story. on one hand, as we mentioned earlier, there are many facts herein that help to develop our faith (*saddha*) in the buddha's quality of the attainment of great compassion. the skill in means (*upaya-kosalla*) employed by the buddha to save venerable angulimala from the path to hell was such that, in truth, venerable angulimala escaped hell by a hair's breadth—just as he was saved at nine hundred and ninety-nine. if he had killed his mother and completed the thousand, not even a buddha could have saved angulimala. the weightiest sin (*anantarika-kamma*) is that severe. before that could happen, the buddha acted, without informing anyone, traveling there all alone out of his quality of great compassion.
furthermore, the buddha used only two short sentences to tame angulimala: "i have stopped. you, too, stop, angulimala." that was all. the notorious bandit angulimala, whom neither kings nor weapons could tame, was tamed by the buddha through those two invaluable sentences, which served as a meditation object (*kammatthana*). "i have stopped. you, too, stop." angulimala, who possessed past meritorious power, past perfection (*parami*) power, and whose intellect was sharpened by the arts and sciences he had mastered as the youth ahimsaka, understood the meaning of this. he understood that the lack of restraint regarding the destruction of life is "not stopping," and that true "stopping," being settled in the truest sense, is liberation from this. having understood this, he became ordained.
moreover, why did the buddha give venerable angulimala a protection chant (*pirith*), or rather, instructions helpful for a protection chant? the buddha saw that although he was making an effort, venerable angulimala was unable to concentrate his mind. he was also facing various difficulties regarding alms-food due to the public's fear. furthermore, he could not gather his mind together. that is why the buddha gave him an act of truth in that manner. when venerable angulimala performed that act of truth, it was not only instantly verified, but it remains verified to this day. what was manifested there was a marvelous buddha-power. we must also reflect on the power inherent in that act of truth.
virtue (*sila*) is the foundation of an act of truth. we see the value of virtue through this. now, in today's society, there is a group of people called "defeated ones." perhaps even among this audience there may be those who think, due to various reasons, "the path of dhamma does not belong to us. we do not have the strength to walk the dhamma-path. there is no merit in us." it was for those people that we uttered those two verses. even the simile presented in those two verses is sufficient. now, on a full moon day like today, someone tries to look at the moon. but it is covered by a dark cloud. they watch with great effort. there is nothing more beautiful than the orb of the moon emerging from a dark cloud. in the same way, if there are some dark blemishes in one's character which one considers as obstacles to the dhamma-path, it is on that very background that one can attain this liberation. the character of angulimala is like an embroidery of silver thread on a background of black velvet. that is primarily how the lesson we must draw from it appears to us.
the primary lesson we must learn from the story of angulimala is that if one generates the perception of capability ("i can") at any moment, establishes faith (*saddha*) in the triple gem, makes a firm resolution, and enters upon this path, one has the strength to go all the way. furthermore, when reflecting on the power of acts of truth performed with virtue (*sila*) as the head, it becomes clear that a certain boundary is necessary for that. a person who practices meditation does all this in order to forget the past. now, wearing this robe, bringing about this external change, is done to remove the remorse arising in one's mind. those activities also assist in that. what helps even more is making a firm resolution with a specific boundary: "from today, from this very moment, i shall conduct myself in this virtue." going along with this virtue is what reflection (*avarjana*) means—looking back.
virtue (*sila*) is the foundation. the resolution regarding virtue is what supports it. now, depending on the occasion, some of you have undertaken the *ajiva-atthamaka-sila* (virtue with livelihood as the eighth precept). as i see it, the majority of people on this precious full moon day have undertaken the eight precepts (*attha-sila*) with the right intention and with a true, deep understanding of its meaning. others have undertaken the ten precepts (*dasa-sila*). in this way, some virtue was resolved upon. that is the foundation for walking on this dhamma-path and concentrating the mind.
having laid down that foundation, what next helps to settle the mind for meditation is reflecting on that virtue. through reflection, joy arises in a person. the benefit of virtue is described as non-remorse (*avippatisara*). that is the essence of virtue. undertaking virtue and not meditating is like laying the foundation of a building and not constructing the building. therefore, having laid the foundation of virtue, standing upon it, and reflecting upon it, one then concentrates the mind on the meditation object (*kammatthana*) through that strength. in such instances, the meditation object becomes very clear. that is the principle revealed to us by the story of angulimala. after performing that act of truth, venerable angulimala was able to concentrate his mind, thinking: "so, my mind is pure; the past is gone." at that point, he turned a new page. he turned a completely new page in his life. now, something you often hear is about "turning a new page in life." once you turn that page, the other page is no longer visible; it is just like that. virtue is what helps in this. we can realize the value of virtue through that.
likewise, from the stratagem employed here by the buddha to tame a person, we too, in our own measure, can appreciate the importance of association with a noble friend (*kalyana-mitta*). the monks asked the buddha, "how did angulimala attain arahantship despite committing such evil deeds?" it was on that occasion that the buddha declared, "he committed such evil deeds in that manner because he did not have a true noble friend. but because he obtained a noble friend like me, those committed evil deeds could be covered by the wholesome deed of the supramundane path (*lokuttara-magga-kusala*)." here, "covered by a wholesome deed" (*kusalena pithiyati*) does not refer to ordinary wholesome deeds. they were covered by the wholesome deed of the path of arahantship. there are levels within that wholesomeness as well.
what is the victory achieved through the supramundane state of stream-entry (*sotapanna*), which you frequently hear of? it is bringing the mind to a state where it cannot fall into the four lower realms of misery. that is, one is freed from unwholesome karma leading to rebirth in hell. an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*) does not know when the results of unwholesome karma will strike. a person who has not achieved stream-entry does not know when they might have to go to hell. the value of the wheel of dhamma shown by the buddha is apparent from this. virtuous friends, there are two rotating wheels in this world: the wheel of karma (*kamma-cakka*) and the wheel of dhamma (*dhamma-cakka*). the wheel of karma rotates and rotates in a wonderfully powerful manner. but there is another wheel that can break its power, and that is the wheel of dhamma. that is the wheel of dhamma discovered by the buddhas after fulfilling perfections (*paramis*) for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand aeons. what it does is break that power. it cannot be broken entirely at once, but it is broken stage by stage.
the first breaking is when someone attains the path-knowledge of stream-entry (*sotapatti-magga-nana*). if that state of stream-entry is attained, then in accordance with that level of mental development, by the very power of the supramundane state of stream-entry, those unwholesome deeds leading to hell are discarded. in short, birth (*jati*) is limited to at most seven times more in the happy realms of existence (*sugati*). a happy destination means bringing the mind to a state where it is born only in the human world or the deva worlds, excluding the lower realms of misery. that is why the buddha, on many occasions, described the wonderful peace thus obtained using various similes. just as the great earth cannot be compared to the dust on a fingernail, the remaining unwholesome karma of a stream-enterer is like the dust on a fingernail. the stream-enterer stands having obtained liberation from karmic forces as vast as the great earth. such immense solace is received merely by becoming a stream-enterer. next, proceeding gradually in that manner, one reduces birth to at most once more (once-returner), and then becomes a non-returner (*anagami*) who does not return to this world, but is reborn in the brahma realms, and subsequently becomes an arahant in the brahma realm.
even after becoming an arahant, there is an important point there. we saw from this story of angulimala that even after becoming an arahant, the unwholesome karma to be experienced in this very life (*ditthadhammavedaniya-kamma*) remains effective, showing how severe the wheel of karma is. venerable angulimala, having obtained relief in that manner, became an arahant with great difficulty. yet, even after becoming an arahant, why did stones and pebbles thrown elsewhere fly through the air and land on his head when he went on alms-round? because after one becomes an arahant, the past unwholesome deeds to be experienced in this very life struggle intensely to yield their results. they have to be experienced. that is how powerful the wheel of karma is.
yet, there is an opportunity for arahants to obtain, at least temporarily, relief even from such karmic results and to experience the true nature of liberation in the mind stilled (nibbana). this is called the concentration of the fruit of arahantship (*arahattaphala-samadhi*). while remaining entered in that attainment of the fruit of arahantship (*arahattaphala-samapatti*), having greatly thinned out those karmic forces, they directly realize the pure state of cessation (*nirodha*), the state of extinguishment, complete extinguishment. that is the highest peace in the world. this peace shown by the buddha is not something at the level of what ordinary worldly people think. this supramundane peace is a certain power of peace and extinguishment obtained by calming and taming the power of those karmic forces as well as all other preparations (*sankhara*); it is called the bliss of liberation (*vimutti-sukha*). it was by experiencing that bliss of liberation that venerable angulimala declared that if someone, having previously fallen into negligence, frees himself from negligence and becomes diligent, he illuminates the world like the moon freed from a dark cloud. with reference to this, we can understand how the buddha's wheel of dhamma helps to break this wheel of karma.
ultimately, when we reflect on it, there is nothing in this *samsara* worth holding onto. that is why the buddha declared, "i do not praise becoming (*bhava*) even for a moment. just as even a tiny amount of excrement is foul-smelling, the entirety of becoming (*bhava*) is a place of great terror." let alone other realms, even existence in the brahma worlds—wherever there are preparations (*sankharas*), there is suffering (*dukkha*); this was pointed out by the buddha. therefore, during a period when a buddha has appeared, everyone must walk this path to nibbana and strive, at the very minimum, to achieve stream-entry to be freed from the four lower realms of misery, and at the maximum, to end all the suffering of *samsara* and find peace in the supreme, deathless, great nibbana. make that resolution in that manner; the day of vesak is the best opportunity to turn a new page. thinking about this year, it is one thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine (1999). here too, we have an instance of escaping at "ninety-nine" (like angulimala at 999). if, even at this juncture, one does not reflect wisely and turn toward the dhamma-path, but expects to live in a state of defeat in this society, then not only the individual but also society as a whole will be subjected to a terrifying destruction.
therefore, all of us must resolve to bring the lesson given by angulimala's character close to our own lives. indeed, it is a wonderfully marvelous miracle. we must bring forth not only the miracle of the buddha, but also the miraculous power within ourselves through this. after venerable angulimala was ordained, the way he walked diligently on that dhamma-path—with his head cut, spilling blood, not even receiving alms-food properly, in the midst of various obstacles, yet remaining energetic, standing firm in his virtue (*sila*), and meditating—he realized the supreme state of arahantship.
similarly, we must understand that whether one is a layperson or a monk, many obstacles and hardships may arise when walking the dhamma-path. none of those are excuses. within every one of us, there are wholesome as well as unwholesome deeds done in *samsara*. there is a good side and there is a bad side. unwholesome deeds support unwholesome deeds, and wholesome deeds support wholesome deeds. it is just as the buddha pointed out: association with bad friends (*papa-mitta*) is extremely dangerous. at the beginning of this story, that is exactly what happened. the friends around angulimala were bad friends. furthermore, his teacher also eventually became a bad friend, and by giving that kind of wrong advice, prompted the innocent ahimsaka to evil, turning the innocent ahimsaka into the fierce angulimala.
on the other hand, while so many people warned him, the buddha went alone to find the bandit angulimala, tamed him with just two sentences, and brought him back as a monk, solely because of his own great compassion. we must understand that this miracle of the dhamma is not only within angulimala, but within each and every one of us. thinking of it in this way, this present auspicious time is a highly suitable opportunity to undergo a special life transformation. the true auspicious time is the buddhist auspicious time. what is this auspicious time? it is the auspicious time of the buddha's birth, his awakening, and his parinibbana (final extinguishment). this is the day on which the three most noble and supreme events of the buddha's life occurred. on such a day, we must reflect that we too have certain goals.
now, every one of us has various mundane goals. we must have formed such mundane goals countless times in this long *samsara*. whether they were achieved or not—as the buddha points out, this *samsara* is a journey of falling prey to birth (*jati*), aging (*jara*), sickness, and death (*marana*), being subjected to suffering (*dukkha*) countless times due to other karmic results, and traveling from suffering to suffering. therefore, the buddha pointed out that instead of running, we should bring forth extinguishment, which is the escape (*nissarana*) from *samsara*, escaping from the spinning-in-one-place of wandering (*samsarana*); that is what is called the wheel of dhamma. that wheel of dhamma is something that must rotate within one's own mind-stream. the dhamma-path to be walked for that purpose is the path of meditation.
so, using virtue (*sila*) as the foundation, resolving on virtue, gladdening and delighting one's mind through that reflection, one then concentrates the mind through some tranquil meditation object (*samatha-kammatthana*). a tranquil meditation object is what helps to concentrate the mind. when one constantly reflects on the quality of *anuttaro purisadammasarathi* mentioned on this occasion, in accordance with the faith (*saddha*) arising within oneself, a power and concentration (*samadhi*) capable of keeping the mind anchored in that very object emerges, bringing about a certain unification, a one-pointedness of mind. relying on that, one can turn toward insight (*vipassana*) to understand the reality of the world as impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*).
in the same way, there are various meditation objects such as recollection of the buddha (*buddhanussati*), loving-kindness (*metta*), foulness (*asubha*), and mindfulness of death (*maranasati*). if someone, by relying on these, concentrates the mind and then directly perceives the impermanent nature of preparations (*sankhara*) as impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*), turning the mind to insight and meditating, they can bring forth the path-knowledges (*magga-nana*). it is by bringing them forth in that manner that one can escape from this *samsara* forever.
we bow to a buddha and honor a buddha not by thinking of the qualities of his physical body, nor by thinking of other things. a buddha is so called because he discovered something that no other teacher could discover. what is that? the method of escaping from this terrifying *samsara* and from the wheel of karma. this is not something that can be achieved by going to an extreme. as shown in the *dhammacakkappavattana sutta*, it is neither by indulging in sensual pleasures nor by torturing one's body as if taking revenge upon it that one can escape from this *samsara*. it is through the middle path (*majjhima patipada*) shown by the buddha, namely, the noble eightfold path. the noble eightfold path consists of right view (*samma-ditthi*), right intention (*samma-sankappa*), right speech (*samma-vaca*), right action (*samma-kammanta*), right livelihood (*samma-ajiva*), right effort (*samma-vayama*), right mindfulness (*samma-sati*), and right concentration (*samma-samadhi*). this is the very thing the buddha describes as the middle path. this path is one that must be developed within one's own mind-stream.
what first supports this path is right view (*samma-ditthi*). one must understand good and bad. one must properly understand good and bad, merit and demerit. next, one must understand the difference between this *samsara* and the liberation from *samsara*. that is the understanding that this entire *samsara* is suffering (*dukkha*), and the deep understanding that underlying it is craving (*tanha*). it is the understanding that where craving is absent, there is peace and extinguishment—nibbana. next, what supports that is this very path. through this understanding, through this right view, one generates right intentions (*samma-sankappa*), which are proper thoughts. one must strongly generate the desire and wish for renunciation (*nekkhamma*), for leaving the lay life. for a long period of time, the buddhas fulfilled that renunciation as a perfection (*parami*).
next, moving away from ill-will, there is the thought of loving-kindness, the thought of non-ill-will (*avyapada*), and then the thought of harmlessness (*avihimsa*), which is the thought of abstaining from violence. perhaps the bandit angulimala also developed right view from those two phrases uttered by the buddha. then, through that, he generated the right intentions of renunciation, non-ill-will, and harmlessness. from that point on, it is about taming one's body and speech. right speech (*samma-vaca*) means proper words. an act of truth is indeed right speech. what angulimala did was use right speech. we see that he was unwilling to speak a wrong word. what was the first hint given by the buddha? the buddha employed a very subtle stratagem there. he first told venerable angulimala, "in that case, perform the act of truth in this way: 'since i was born, i have not killed a living being.'" because venerable angulimala was by then observing the precept of abstaining from false speech, he asked, "alas, blessed one, how can i perform such an act of truth falsely? would that not be telling a deliberate lie?" that shows how venerable angulimala was conscientious about his speech. next, with the polished feeling of "since my noble birth, i am pure," venerable angulimala fearlessly performed the act of truth. that indeed is truthful speech.
thus, if venerable angulimala was able to utilize truthful speech to shape his life, it is not impossible for us. next, bodily deeds—right action (*samma-kammanta*), which means proper deeds. the deeds he had done as angulimala were not proper deeds. he discarded those wrong deeds done by taking up the five weapons; he discarded them in a single moment.
now, we find it difficult to let go of many things in this society. abstaining from the wrong modes of livelihood mentioned at the end of the *ajiva-atthamaka-sila* we undertook may be something that you find highly unappealing—to the extent of saying, "that is simply impossible to do." but just as angulimala discarded all five weapons, one must develop the mental strength within oneself to abandon those five wrong trades or five wrong lifestyles. what are they? slaughtering animals, trading in flesh, trading in intoxicants, trading in weapons, and breeding animals for slaughter. one must develop the strength to abstain from such wrong livelihoods. for if one abstains from the five evils and also rectifies one's livelihood, one can establish right livelihood (*samma-ajiva*). before long, even by the time the king invited him to accept robes, venerable angulimala was undertaking and observing strict ascetic practices (*dhutangas*). that is why he refused even the king's offer of the four requisites. from this, we can see how conscientious venerable angulimala was regarding his livelihood.
from this story, we see the immense contrast that occurred within a single lifetime. now, many present this story through films and such. in truth, this is a film that one can watch within one's own mind-stream. as we went along narrating earlier, what kind of person was angulimala? what did we think of him? even though his name was ahimsaka, had he not committed so many sins? then, a complete life occurred. thus, we see from this story of angulimala the background necessary for a complete transformation of life. after having such a livelihood, and while going on alms-round in such a difficult manner, venerable angulimala drew close to the supreme state of arahantship. he concentrated his mind, applying strong effort—right effort (*samma-vayama*)—and practicing right mindfulness (*samma-sati*) which brings about concentration. that is, initially, the meditation object was not clear. but he did not back down. instead, using the solace given by the buddha, he settled and concentrated his mind. it was through that concentration that, by reflecting on his entire past, venerable angulimala was able to understand the nature of the entire *samsara*, understand suffering (*dukkha*), and eradicate craving (*tanha*), which is the path to escaping from that suffering.
therefore, we must think of bringing this character of angulimala close to our lives. bringing the character of angulimala close to us does not mean walking on the path of unrighteousness (*adhamma*) that angulimala walked. it means abandoning all the feelings associated with that name angulimala, built up by collecting fingers, and then having the strength to undergo such an immense life transformation as to become a wonderfully calm and tranquil monk, as venerable angulimala did. that strength becomes an encouragement for every one of us. for the majority of people in this society are those who hold the perception of inability ("i cannot"). there are very few who have the perception of ability ("i can"). generating the perception of inability by saying, "we cannot do any of these things. it is impossible in this day and age. although it was possible during the buddha's time, it is impossible now," is how we walk on this unrighteous path and support unrighteousness.
so, what is the lesson we draw from this story? due to the wonderfully infinite great compassion of the buddha, such a notorious criminal was turned into a wonderfully tranquil member of the sangha. similarly, we must reflect that something very helpful for our lives is looking back, examining ourselves—in other words, introspection. through that, some might only feel remorse or regret.
but that is not how we should think. in such situations, according to the buddha's dhamma, there is room for us to turn a new page. if one discards the wrong views (*miccha-ditthi*) within oneself and turns to right view (*samma-ditthi*), from that very point, the path ahead is clear. if right view is established, next, the proper thoughts and wishes known as right intention (*samma-sankappa*) must follow accordingly. it proceeds like a flight of steps. when proper thoughts and wishes are fulfilled, proper words are spoken—what we can call proper speech. when proper speech is perfected, the proper path of action—right action—is automatically established. by resolving upon virtue, such as the five precepts, one rectifies one's actions, rectifies one's conduct. when that is properly and systematically established, one is inclined to rectify one's livelihood as well. what lies within the effort to rectify that livelihood? the effort to turn away from the unwholesome and draw close to the wholesome, which is the proper striving known as right effort (*samma-vayama*). through a proper way of life, the proper striving, which is proper energy, arises. it arises in the proper manner—physical energy arises. relying on that energy, right mindfulness (*samma-sati*) arises through it—proper mindfulness, the ability to establish mindfulness. when that mindfulness is maintained for a long time, the mind becomes concentrated on a single object. this is how the noble eightfold path is completed.
the fundamental requirement for all of this is the perception of capability—the feeling that "we can." to strengthen that feeling, buddhist dhamma stories found in the sasana, such as this story of angulimala, help us. indeed, we must reflect that there is hardly any unwholesome deed we have not committed in this long *samsara*. if we could see our past, we must have committed various kinds of evil deeds just like angulimala over infinite time, and suffered in hells. but we should not weaken our minds because of that. if, from today, from this very moment, we observe virtue (*sila*), we can make a new beginning, turn a new page from that point. the path to be walked from that point onward is what the buddha has shown.
therefore, you must reflect that today, on this precious vesak full moon day, you can obtain through this a great opportunity to turn a completely new page in life, and to shape your life-conduct like the orb of the moon emerging from a dark cloud. one must always compare the dhamma story heard to one's own life and practice discipline accordingly. that is why the dhamma is called leading-onward (*opanayika*). this dhamma is called visible-here-and-now (*sanditthika*) because its results can be seen right before our eyes in this very life—just as the bandit named angulimala became an arahant. it is timeless (*akalika*); without delay, whenever one changes one's mind, a transformation takes place from that very moment. next, *ehipassika* means "come and see"—here, the buddha did not merely say "come and see," but invited angulimala to look at the dhamma. there, angulimala understood the difference between stopping and not stopping. likewise, the quality of leading-onward (*opanayika*)—angulimala turned toward the dhamma-path and, by implementing those principles of virtue and the path of meditation within his own mind-stream, reaped the fruits through the quality of leading-onward. *paccattam veditabbo vinnuhi*—it is to be personally realized by the wise.
therefore, during a period like this when a buddha has appeared, whether we are laypersons or monks, unless we have other deep aspirations such as buddhahood, we should maintain only two targets in this life. that is, as mentioned earlier, we must walk this dhamma-journey with a firm resolution either to achieve the state of stream-entry to be freed from the four lower realms of misery, or to cross over the entire suffering of *samsara* and attain parinibbana through supreme arahantship. if virtue, concentration, and wisdom (*sila, samadhi, panna*) constitute the dispensation (*sasana*), then we can illuminate this buddha-dispensation only by shaping our lives in that manner. to the extent that our lives are shaped, those around us obtain a noble friend (*kalyana-mitta*). on many occasions, it is said that noble friends are as rare as the mythical *kalunika* herb. especially in this day and age, a person becomes a noble friend when they develop the noble eightfold path within themselves, starting with right view, and acquire the capacity to support others through the dhamma. it is not supporting through money or wealth. a noble friend is someone who possesses that capacity to support through the dhamma, which is gained in proportion to how far one walks on the dhamma-path.
today, on this precious full moon day, many of you, while disciplining yourselves in some virtue (*sila*), listened for about an hour to a sermon concerning venerable angulimala arahant, who can be shown as an extremely valuable disciple in the buddha's dispensation. within that character, there are many highly valuable lessons for one to learn. we should reflect that during this hour, we have absorbed many valuable points from venerable angulimala's character that we can absorb into our lives. thus, using the dhamma-solace obtained so far as the very foundation, and disciplining ourselves through it, we must resolve to walk on this very path of dhamma.
furthermore, obtaining the association of noble friends, practicing meditation, settling the mind through tranquility (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassana*) meditation, we must make the aspiration: "may we obtain the strength and power to cross over this highly terrifying and formidable ocean of *samsara*, cross over the desert of *samsara*, and find peace in the supreme, deathless, great nibbana shown by the buddha!" we often describe these benefits of hearing the dhamma (*dhamma-savana-anisamsa*), which support this, as a certain transformation arising within one's own mind-stream. through the stories we present during dhamma-listening, faith (*saddha*) arises. next, along with faith, a certain mental energy arises—the feeling of "we too can do it," just as angulimala did. settling the mind accordingly—merely by directing the mind during dhamma-listening, mindfulness (*sati*), proper mindfulness, arises. likewise, through that, if one keeps the mind properly focused on listening to the dhamma, listening to it word by word, a certain concentration (*samadhi*) arises, as a form of recollection of the dhamma (*dhammanussati*).
next, if a deep understanding regarding that dhamma has been generated, that is considered as wisdom (*panna*). in that manner, one should rejoice that this hour or so was spent to generate within one's mind-stream, to some extent, the qualities of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom (*saddha, viriya, sati, samadhi, panna*), which as spiritual powers (*bala-dhamma*) support the attainment of nibbana. while rejoicing thus, make the aspiration: "by the power of this store of merit accumulated so far, may all beings from the avici hell to the akanittha brahma realm, including the assembly of devas and brahmas who protect the dispensation, and all our relatives, rejoice in this merit! having rejoiced, may they be released from this formidable *samsara* and directly realize the supreme, deathless, great nibbana through whichever of the three bodhis they aspire to!" for yourself, perform the sharing of merit by reciting the verses, wishing: "by the power of this accumulated store of merit, may i, as quickly as possible, relying on the association of noble friends, realize nibbana!"
recite the verses to share merit:
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 142
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #142
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.54)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
"Nidhīnaṃ va pavattāraṃ,
yaṃ passe vajjadassinaṃ;
Niggayhavādiṃ medhāviṃ,
tādisaṃ paṇḍitaṃ bhaje;
Tādisaṃ bhajamānassa,
seyyo hoti na pāpiyo."
From:
Dhammapada Verse 76 (Paṇḍita Vagga)
Dear Listeners,
A person who hopes to steer their life on the right path should make an effort to seek the help of wise spiritual friends (*kalyāṇa-mitta*). One must fashion one’s conduct and attitudes in a manner that allows one to receive the assistance of spiritual friends. What we mean by assistance here is the help to correct one's shortcomings and faults. Generally, one does not see one's own faults. They are visible only to the wise spiritual friends one associates with. That is why the Buddha compared a wise person who points out faults to someone pointing out a hidden treasure, and gave a simile. This is what is expressed in the verse we have chosen as our theme. The Buddha preached this verse with reference to a monk named Rādha, who was a pupil of Venerable Sāriputta.
In his lay life, Venerable Rādha was an extremely poor brahmin in the city of Sāvatthī. Since he had no means of livelihood, he came to the Jetavana monastery, attended upon the Sangha, swept and cleared the premises, and sustained himself with whatever he received. As time went on, this man developed a great desire to ordain. However, the Sangha was not keen on ordaining him. Perhaps they felt he was seeking ordination merely for a livelihood. Be that as it may, due to this man's genuine desire and because his hope was not being fulfilled, his body became emaciated. One day, when the Buddha was scanning the world with his attainment of great compassion (*mahākāruṇika-samāpatti*) as was his daily custom, this man at the Jetavana monastery came into the net of his wisdom-vision.
When the Buddha investigated this, he saw that this man possessed the supportive merits to attain Arahatship. As a general custom, the Buddha would occasionally go on walking tours of the monastery to see how the monks were doing and whether their work was progressing well. That evening, while walking around the Jetavana monastery in this manner, he approached this brahmin and asked, "Brahmin, what are you doing here?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, I am attending upon the Sangha and earning my livelihood." "Do the monks show you any hospitality in return for your services?" "Yes, Venerable Sir, I get food and drink. However, they do not ordain me," he said.
Thereupon, the Buddha assembled the Sangha and, introducing a discussion centered on this man Rādha, asked: "Is there any monk among the Sangha who remembers receiving any special help from this brahmin?" Venerable Sāriputta immediately spoke up: "Venerable Sir, I remember this brahmin once placing a spoonful of rice in my bowl when I was on alms-round." Then the Buddha asked: "Sāriputta, is that not enough to help someone escape the *Dukkha* (Suffering) of *saṃsāra*?" Venerable Sāriputta replied: "Very well, Venerable Sir, then I shall ordain him," and he ordained the man.
Despite being ordained, he did not receive any special attention from the Sangha. One can understand why. He sat at the very end of the seats and did not even get proper food and drink. He was somewhat marginalized. Venerable Sāriputta, noticing this, and with the compassionate intention of paying special attention to this new Venerable Rādha, went on a wandering tour accompanied by Venerable Rādha. During this journey, he pointed out his faults and gave him advice and admonition. This monk Rādha was extremely obedient, gentle-spoken, never showed any anger, corrected his faults, and by practicing meditation, attained Arahatship very quickly.
Thereafter, Venerable Sāriputta came with Venerable Rādha to see the Buddha. The Buddha asked, "How is it, Sāriputta, is your pupil obedient?" "Oh yes, Venerable Sir, he is very obedient. Whenever a fault was pointed out to him, he never got angry." Then the Buddha asked, "Sāriputta, if you could get pupils like this, would you like to have many?" "Oh yes, as many as possible. I like such pupils very much," Venerable Sāriputta praised. Similarly, a talk arose among the monks: "Venerable Sāriputta is an extremely grateful person. Merely for a spoonful of rice, he ordained this man. Also, Venerable Sāriputta is someone who constantly seeks advice, and he has found a pupil who is willing to receive advice." Hearing this, the Buddha praised Venerable Sāriputta's quality of gratitude and then said: "Monks, a bhikkhu should be gentle-spoken (*suvaca*) like this Rādha. If someone points out one's faults, one should think that they are pointing out a hidden treasure." Expressing this idea, he uttered this verse:
> *Nidhīnaṃva pavattāraṃ, yaṃ passe vajjadassinaṃ;*
> *Medhāviṃ tādisaṃ paṇḍitaṃ bhaje, tādisaṃ bhajamānassa seyyo hoti na pāpiyo.*
If one sees a wise person who points out one's faults as if pointing out hidden treasures, one should associate with such a wise and learned person. Associating with such a person brings progress, not decline. This is the meaning of this verse. Here we should especially consider the value of this simile given by the Buddha. Whenever the Buddha gave a simile, it carried a very deep meaning. Normally, people of the world do not like having their faults pointed out; they dislike criticism or fault-finding. Since the Buddha knew this attitude, he placed a completely new concept before the world, taking this gentle-spoken bhikkhu as an example. To call advice a hidden treasure is because in those days, gold coins and such were deposited in pots and vessels and hidden in the jungle or by riverbanks. Just as someone goes and points out those treasures buried under the earth, a wise person points out the treasures hidden beneath one's faults. What are these treasures? Hidden beneath one's faults are one's skills and abilities. It is pointing out these skills that is referred to here as pointing out a hidden treasure. Just as treasures emerge when the earth is removed and cleared away, when one's faults are unearthed and removed, one's wholesome qualities, skills, and abilities emerge from within. That is the fundamental value of the simile in this verse.
Furthermore, this story illustrates a noble quality of the Buddha's life. A major part of the daily routine of the Great Compassionate One is to scan the world during the dawn with his unique wisdom—which is considered an extraordinary knowledge exclusive to a Buddha—to find the person most suitable to receive his assistance. They could be far away, or close by. At this time, this helpless person living right nearby in Jetavana monastery appeared. This net of wisdom is truly wonderful. It is something that demonstrates the Buddha's quality of equality. Setting aside all other work, he went to that person, visited him, and showed him the way to find help. Although this man may have attended upon all the monks, the Buddha asked about anyone who had received a special favor from him because he wanted to draw special attention to him.
This gratitude was a special characteristic of Venerable Sāriputta. Until his parinibbāna, he showed great respect towards Venerable Assaji, who had given him the Dhamma. Similarly, on various occasions, incidents revealing Venerable Sāriputta's quality of gratitude are mentioned. Here too, it was the incident of a spoonful of rice. It seems like a very small thing. But it was on that basis that he helped that man. Venerable Sāriputta's quality of gratitude shines through here.
Venerable Rādha, too, did not have the common weakness of getting angry when someone points out a fault. When his faults were pointed out to him, he accepted them with great diligence and obedience, as if being shown a hidden treasure, as we mentioned earlier. That is why he was able to reach the state of Arahatship. There are lessons for us to reflect upon and adopt from each of these points. There is a word in this verse that might be somewhat unappealing to the mind: *nigayhavādiṃ medhāviṃ*—one who reproves or censures.
Generally, no one likes to be censured or reproved. But this censuring is also necessary at times to point out the gravity of a fault. To show someone a fault in a way that sticks in their mind, censuring is sometimes required. This is especially a task assigned to a teacher. The teacher has to give some punishment—not in a deep and severe manner disproportionate to the mistake, but in an appropriate way so that the pupil remembers. Sometimes through words, sometimes through other courses of action. Therefore, we must reflect on this wisely. The matters contained in this verse help us in our daily personal lives, at home, in institutions, in schools, and everywhere else.
Let us first consider the greatest teacher in the world. It is through the Buddha’s own life that we can understand this word *nigayhavādī* (reproving). Two qualities of the Buddha are mentioned: *anuttaro purisadammasārathī* (the incomparable charioteer of men to be tamed) and *satthā devamanussānaṃ* (the teacher of gods and humans). These two qualities demonstrate the responsibility assigned to the Buddha as a teacher. *Anuttaro purisadammasārathī* means he is like a charioteer in taming tamable humans. We know that this is not like the drivers of today. In those days, when driving a horse-chariot, one had to train the horse. Sometimes, even a whip had to be used. Similarly, the Buddha, as the teacher of gods and humans, had to use words of censure according to the situation. Thus, this characteristic of the Buddha's character became a problem for some people.
There is a good illustration of this in the Dhamma. Seeing the Buddha's fame spreading, there were Niganthas (Jains) who became jealous. Other sectarians and adherents of other religions always looked for ways to defame and take revenge on the Buddha. On one occasion, when Prince Abhayarāja visited the religious teacher Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said: "The fame of the ascetic Gotama is spreading widely. Prince, if you can present an argument to the ascetic Gotama that he cannot answer, then your fame will spread too." When asked, "What is the argument I should present?" he said: "Present this double-horned dilemma (*ubhathokoṭika-pañha*) to the ascetic Gotama. What is it? First ask, 'Venerable Gotama, do you speak words that are displeasing and disagreeable to others?' If he says he does use disagreeable words, then say the conclusion is: 'Then what is the difference between the Buddha and an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*)? An ordinary worldling also speaks displeasing and disagreeable words.' On the other hand, if he says he does not use them, then ask: 'If so, why did you censure the Venerable Devadatta by saying he is destined for hell for an aeon? Devadatta was enraged by that.' In this way, there is a mismatch there too, isn't there? That is to say, whichever of the two answers he gives, present this argument. Then the ascetic Gotama will be left speechless." Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta gave a simile for this: "Just like an iron hook stuck in one's throat, the ascetic Gotama will be left with nowhere to turn. Therefore, present this argument."
Prince Abhayarāja then went to see the Buddha to present this argument. When he went and looked around, it was a bit late in the evening. He thought, "I should invite the Buddha to the palace itself and ask him on that occasion." So, he invited the Buddha and three other monks to his house, the palace, for the next day. The next day, after the Buddha had finished his meal, Prince Abhayarāja asked the Buddha: "Blessed One, do you use words that are displeasing and disagreeable to others?" Then the Buddha said: "Prince, I do not give a one-sided answer to this. This is an answer that must be analyzed." Thereupon, Prince Abhayarāja realized that the argument would not work. "Ah, then the Nigaṇṭhas have failed!" muttered Prince Abhayarāja. When the Buddha asked, "Why do you say that?" he told the whole story: "I was taught like this. That is why I asked."
At that moment, Prince Abhayarāja had his infant son on his lap. The Buddha drew a simile from that very situation: "Now, prince, if this young child on your lap, due to the negligence of his nurse or your own negligence, were to put a pebble or a splinter into his mouth, what would you do?" "Venerable Sir, I would hold his head with my left hand, crook my right finger, and pull it out. Even if it meant drawing blood, I would pull it out. Why? Because I have great compassion for the child." Thereupon, the Buddha declared: "It is the same with me. Because I have compassion for beings, if a word is true and beneficial, even if it is displeasing and disagreeable, I speak it to that person according to the occasion. The word is true. It is beneficial to that person. But it is displeasing and disagreeable. That is, a word of censure or blame. Yet, I speak it because I want to correct him." In this way, on that occasion, the Buddha resolved that double-horned dilemma. Similarly, lay devotees, you may have heard this stated in the Dhamma itself:
> *Garahā va seyyo viññūhi, yañce bālappasaṃsanā.*
"Censure by the wise is indeed better than praise by fools." This idea is a wonderful motto. Mothers who raise children know how to discipline their children according to the occasion. The same happened with the Buddha. He had to use various skillful means (*upāya-kosalla*) to deliver the worldlings, who are burdened with defilements, from *saṃsāra* according to the occasion. Going hand in hand with great compassion is this skillful means. To speak a word of censure that leaves a lasting impression, without any hatred in the heart but out of compassion for beings according to the occasion, belongs to that skillful means. This is how the concept of censuring should be understood.
Next, let us look at this quality of being gentle-spoken (*suvaca*). *Suvaca*, in a general sense, is called obedience. Obedience means doing as told. But the real meaning of the word *suvaca* is that one can be given advice without fear. *Duvvaca* (difficult to speak to) means one is afraid to say anything to them. Suppose there is some fault in someone, but one is afraid to mention it. One does not want to, because that person will get angry, scold, and rage over it. To the person who does not get enraged in this way, one can speak without fear. That is why they are called *suvaca*—someone who is easy to speak to, someone to whom a fault can easily be pointed out. A *duvvaca* or *dubbacajātiya* (of difficult speech) person is one who gets angry the moment something is said and causes a great deal of trouble. Therefore, people say nothing; they stand aside and watch, thinking, "Let them do whatever they want." So, we must understand the difference between these two words, *suvaca* and *duvvaca*.
We get excellent illustrations of this from the Sasana itself. The greatest example, which you lay devotees must have heard many times in Dhamma sermons, is Venerable Sāriputta himself, the Chief Disciple of the Sasana. His humility was truly wonderful. Going hand in hand with humility and patience is the quality of being gentle-spoken (*suvaca*), obedience—the ability to listen to whatever is said, whether harsh or bitter, and the ability to listen when faults are pointed out. It is precisely because of this that, as you know, in the verses on blessings (*Maṅgala Sutta*), it is said: *khantī ca sovacassatā, samaṇānañca dassanaṃ*. *Khantī ca sovacassatā*—patience and being gentle-spoken. Being gentle-spoken goes hand in hand with patience. Thus, a valuable quality of Venerable Sāriputta is mentioned. On one occasion, a seven-year-old novice monk, newly ordained and cute like a child, noticed a corner of Venerable Sāriputta’s undergarment (*antara-vāsaka*) hanging down and pointed it out to him. Venerable Sāriputta adjusted it, came back, clasped his hands as if worshipping, and uttered a verse:
> *Tadahupabbajito santo, jātiyā sattavassiko;*
> *So pi maṃ anusāseyya, sampaṭicchāmi muddhane.*
"Even if a seven-year-old novice ordained today points out a fault in me, I accept it on my head." This is a valuable illustration of the gentle-spoken (*suvaca*) nature in Venerable Sāriputta's life.
It was the same with Venerable Rāhula. Venerable Rāhula was in a position where he could easily have become *duvvaca* (difficult to speak to), because he was the son of the Buddha in his lay life. As you know, children of those with high positions and wealth, when corrected even slightly, sometimes threaten, "I will tell my mother" or "I will tell my father." Though he was the son of the Buddha in his lay life, how humble and gentle-spoken was Venerable Rāhula! It is said that every morning he would take a handful of sand, throw it up, and say, "May I receive as many admonitions from the Buddha, my teachers, and preceptors as there are grains of sand here!" He would say this as a game, throwing the grains of sand. This shows Venerable Rāhula's humble, gentle-spoken, and obedient nature. There are many other stories told about Venerable Rāhula's attitude and gentle-spoken nature.
There is another valuable story. On one occasion, five hundred monks led by Venerable Yasoja came to see the Buddha at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī. Coming as guests, they exchanged greetings with the resident monks and arranged their bowls and robes, which created a great noise. The Buddha asked Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, who is making this noise? It sounds like fishermen shouting at a fish market. What is this racket?" he asked Venerable Ānanda. Venerable Ānanda replied: "Venerable Sir, a group of five hundred monks led by Venerable Yasoja has arrived, and that is why there is this noise." "Tell them to come to me," the Buddha assigned to Venerable Ānanda.
Then Venerable Ānanda brought Venerable Yasoja and the group. The Buddha asked why they were shouting like in a fish market. They explained the matter: "Coming as guests, when we were putting away our bowls and robes, we made this noise." "Do not stay near me. I do not wish to keep you here. Depart from here," the Buddha said. Venerable Yasoja and the group had come with great desire to see the Buddha that day. But the Buddha dismissed them. Having no choice, he departed with his group, went on a tour, and arrived in the Vajjī country.
Then the rainy season (*vassa*) arrived. They built huts near the river called Vaggumudā and entered the rains-retreat with this group of five hundred. On the first day of the rains-retreat, Venerable Yasoja gave advice to his group, saying: "Friends, we have been dismissed by our Teacher, who is highly benevolent, desires our progress, and has compassion for us. Now, let us live in a certain way. In what way? Let us correct our shortcomings now, so that the Buddha, the Tathāgata, will be pleased when he sees us." The group agreed to this and began to practice meditation. Within the rains-retreat itself, all these monks attained the noble state (of Arahatship) accompanied by analytical insights and supernormal powers (*abhiññā*).
Now, the next news. After the rains-retreat, the Buddha traveled from Sāvatthī to the Gabled Hall (*Kūṭāgāra-sālā*) in the Great Forest of Vesālī. Having arrived, he looked into Venerable Yasoja and his group. In such events, the Buddha would search again. He examined the minds of Venerable Yasoja and his group with his own mind. He saw that everything was complete. All of them were Arahats.
Then he said to Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, the direction where the bhikkhus on the banks of the Vaggumudā live is as if radiating light. I have no aversion to going in that direction. Even to contemplate it is very pleasing to me. Send a messenger, send a courier: 'The Teacher wishes to see you. I wish to see you. Tell Yasoja and his group to come.'" This was the invitation the Buddha made. Venerable Ānanda went to a certain bhikkhu and expressed the permission received from the Buddha. That bhikkhu—he was a bhikkhu possessing supernormal powers—as it is said in the books, as quickly as a strong man might stretch his bent arm or bend his stretched arm, vanished from the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest and appeared where the bhikkhus on the banks of the Vaggumudā were. In an instant. In a flash. Then he gave this news: "The Buddha is inviting you." Thereupon, that group too arrived by psychic power (*iddhi-bala*) to where the Buddha was at the Gabled Hall.
By the time they arrived, the Buddha was seated in concentration. He was seated in the imperturbable concentration (*āneñja-samādhi*), a silent concentration. Venerable Ānanda was standing to one side. The Buddha was in concentration. Then this group arrived. Having arrived, Venerable Ānanda worshipped the Buddha and said: "Venerable Sir, the guest monks who were invited have arrived. May the Blessed One exchange friendly greetings with them." The Buddha remained silent. The first watch of the night passed. Then, Venerable Yasoja and his group examined with their own power what kind of concentration the Buddha was in. Seeing that he was in that silent concentration, they too sat down in that very concentration. Thus, the Buddha was sitting on one side, and Venerable Yasoja and his group were sitting in concentration on the other side. This was a problem for Venerable Ānanda. When guests arrive, should they not be attended to? The Buddha himself invited them, and yet he is just sitting there.
Then the first watch passed. After the first watch ended, Venerable Ānanda reminded him again: "Venerable Sir, much of the night has passed. The guest monks have also arrived and have been waiting for a long time. May the Blessed One exchange friendly greetings." No, he was still silent. The second watch passed. Then, the third watch passed, and it was the time of dawn. Once again, for the third time, he invited him in that manner. Still, the Buddha was silent. Finally, he said to the Buddha: "Now, Venerable Sir, the night has passed, and it is dawn. This group is still sitting here. May the Blessed One exchange friendly greetings!" Then the Buddha said: "Ānanda, if you knew the matter as it really is, you would not have spoken even this much. Both I and this group, both parties, were in the imperturbable concentration (*āneñja-samādhi*)." And he uttered a verse as an utterance of joy:
> *Yassa jito kāma-kaṇṭako, akkoso vadho ca pabbato va jito;*
> *Anejo navedati so bhikkhu.*
"The bhikkhu who has conquered the thorn of sensuality, abuse, and physical harm, stands unshaken like a mountain; he is imperturbable and does not tremble." He uttered that verse.
From this story too, we see the gentle-spoken (*suvaca*) quality of Venerable Yasoja. When there is a group of five hundred, one does not need that many people these days—even over a small word, people start a big campaign to show their power. But Venerable Yasoja very humbly accepted his fault. That is a great quality. Accepting his fault, he brought forth that hidden treasure. The words spoken there are truly wonderful. He started by saying: "We have been dismissed out of compassion by the Buddha, who is kind, great in compassion, benevolent, and compassionate towards us. He dismissed us out of compassion. Now, let us live in such a way that the Buddha is pleased with us." That is how they began the rains-retreat. And they brought forth that treasure, the treasure of Arahatship. Here, Venerable Yasoja's character is extraordinary. Similarly, we see the Buddha's skillful means (*upāya-kosalla*). He dismissed them having seen a certain reason. It was fully accomplished.
Next, there is an even deeper point. You lay devotees might be surprised. We all know that when someone comes, we should welcome them. Everyone knows about hospitality to guests. Here, after sending an invitation himself, when those monks arrived, the Buddha just sat there in silence. There is a very deep meaning here. You know that if a guest arrives while you are having a meal, you pull up a chair and let them join the meal. The Buddha did something similar. The Buddha was consuming food in his own pasture. Perhaps within the concentration on the fruit of Arahatship (*arahatta-phala-samādhi*). He was absorbed in the fruit-attainment (*phala-samāpatti*), the concentration of realizing Nibbāna that he had attained. The monks who arrived were also suitable to consume that food. Venerable Ānanda, however, was not yet there. That is why it was a problem for Ānanda. So those monks too looked at what the Buddha was consuming, and thinking, "We too must consume this," sat in that very concentration the whole night. That is the real welcome. This is good to depict in a painting. Two paintings could be drawn. The first time they came, those monks were shouting like in a fish market, causing a great racket. When they came this time, how was it? The Buddha's welcome was appropriate to that. There is a very deep example and model for the world to take from this story. In this way, on one hand, we must understand the value of being gentle-spoken (*suvaca*).
Next, on the other hand, there are also illustrations of being *duvvaca* (difficult to speak to). Not everyone in the Buddha's Sasana was gentle-spoken like this. The monk Devadatta, whom you all know, was such a stubborn person that he even tried to take the life of the Buddha, precisely because of the *duvvaca* nature that arose from a slight disagreement. Similarly, there is another incident. Mention is made of a group of monks called the *Chabbaggiya* (the group of six). These monks, consisting of six factions led by six leaders, lived in an extremely stubborn and disobedient manner, repeatedly breaking the disciplinary rules (*vinaya*) laid down by the Buddha. They also reaped the consequences of their actions. On some occasions, the Buddha dismissed them from those places. He had to censure them according to the circumstances.
Similarly, another special incident regarding censure is mentioned in the Dhamma. You all know about Minister Channa, who was a minister of the Buddha. He was the minister who accompanied Prince Siddhārtha when he renounced the lay life. Unlike Venerable Rāhula, he developed pride due to his close connection with the Buddha. Because of that conceit, he behaved in an extremely disobedient manner. He would not allow the monks to point out any fault in him. Due to this disobedience, although the Buddha laid down various disciplinary rules, he could not be tamed. Finally, even on his parinibbāna bed, the Buddha had to direct his attention to this. That night, before his parinibbāna, the Buddha said to Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, after my passing, impose the Brahma-punishment (*brahma-daṇḍa*) on the monk Channa." When asked, "What is the Brahma-punishment?"—it was a rule that had not been laid down in the *vinaya* until then, which is why Venerable Ānanda asked, "What, Venerable Sir, is the Brahma-punishment?" The Buddha declared: "Let the monk Channa say whatever he wants. The monks should neither advise nor admonish him." It was an outright boycott. The permission to impose such a complete boycott was given by the Buddha before his parinibbāna. Thus, the final punishment given by the Buddha for that stubbornness (*duvvaca-bhāva*) is called the Brahma-punishment. It is a very severe punishment. *Brahma* means the highest, doesn't it? A most severe punishment. It is said that as soon as Venerable Ānanda declared this matter after the Buddha's parinibbāna, the monk Channa fainted and fell due to the shock. Due to the very shock that arose from this, the monk Channa later meditated and somehow became an Arahat. There too, through that punishment, the monk Channa was tamed in one way or another and attained Arahatship.
From the disciplinary rules of the monks and the customs of the Sasana, lay devotees too can learn many things. Especially, something that helped the survival of this Sasana was pointing out the faults of others. This is a custom of the Sasana. Even in society, we know that if no one points out the faults of others, this society would become far more dangerous than it is now. But sometimes, the person pointing it out does not do so out of compassion. Instead of pointing out a hidden treasure, if they act as if digging a pit for the other, then the effort fails. Without any compassion for that person, some people point out faults with highly dangerous and malicious intentions, such as character assassination. Not so the wise; they do so with the intention of correcting the person in the right way, and even if they use words of censure according to the situation, it becomes a help. There is a custom in the Sangha regarding the disciplinary rules of the monks, where they point out each other's weaknesses. This is called *aññamañña-vuṭṭhāpana*—rehabilitating one another from offences by helping each other. They point out the fault. When one says out of compassion, "Friend, such a fault has occurred," the other corrects it.
After spending the rains-retreat, the monks have a custom called *pavāraṇā*. You lay devotees may have heard of this as performing the *uposatha*. There is a special significance in the *pavāraṇā* of the Sangha. It is the disciplinary act performed at the end by a group of monks who have lived together during a rains-retreat. Here, they invite the Sangha: "If there is any fault of mine that you have seen, heard, or suspected, please speak out! Out of compassion, please point it out to me!" Thus, they make an invitation to the group. We must understand from this that when someone points out a fault, one should not get angry. When teachers and others say something with good intentions, one should feel that they are pointing out a hidden treasure and say, "If there are any other faults, please point them out to me." That is a special invitation. It is this invitation—to point out any fault of mine seen, heard, or suspected so that I may correct it, and if I see it as a fault, I will correct it—that is done through this monastic custom.
But nowadays, especially in educational institutions, and in other institutions almost everywhere, over a very small incident, merely because a small fault is pointed out, a host of strikes, threats, insults, disagreements, and crises arise. These arise from a very small thing. Why? Because if we had taken the feeling of "pointing out a hidden treasure" into our minds, our reaction would be different. We would say with even more enthusiasm, "Please tell me with facts what the fault is, so that I can correct it." Instead, the moment a word is said, people get angry and develop deep-seated hatred. That is the wrong attitude. Instead, we must understand from these stories the value of advice in steering our lives on the right path. According to the treasure-simile shown by the Buddha, we see that sometimes it is necessary to speak with censure. The Buddha too, according to the situation, laid down some disciplinary rules in an extremely strict and severe manner. If the fault is severe, they are expelled altogether. Sometimes, remedies are applied right there to tame them again. This re-taming is also a valuable quality.
