Let us say we did not see that fault in the first instance. But if we saw it at least in the second instance, we should go to the person who pointed out the fault and sincerely express our gratitude. Such incidents too exist in the Sasana. We should take some example from them as well. To give one example, when the Buddha laid down the training rule regarding eating at improper times (*vikāla-bhojana*), a monk named Bhaddāli became displeased and protested. There is no need to explain this further. Even nowadays, when speaking about eating at improper times, there are more people who dislike it than those who like it. In those days too, there were such groups of monks; when the Buddha laid down the training rules on eating at improper times, they criticized it severely and stood aside. But later, when they saw the benefits of the training rule, they came and confessed their fault. There too, a highly valuable phrase is used to accept the fault: *accayo maṃ bhante accagamā yathā bālā yathā mūḷhaṃ yathā akusalaṃ* and so on, which is a wonderful sentence spoken when coming to confess one's fault.
"Venerable Sir, a transgression overcame me"—nowadays people say "a mistake happened to me." That is the kind of thing said there. "A transgression overcame me, through my foolishness, through my delusion, through my unwholesomeness. That is why this happened." Thus, humbly confessing the fault that happened through oneself, one says: *accayaṃ accayato paṭiggaṇhātu āyatiṃ saṃvarāya*—"May the Blessed One accept this as my transgression for the sake of my future restraint." The Buddha also forgives it: "Very well, that is how it is. *Vaddhi h’esā ariyassa vinaye yo accayaṃ accayato passitvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikaroti*..."—and so on. He declares: "In the discipline of the Noble Ones, it is a sign of growth, a factor of progress, when one sees one's transgression as a transgression, confesses it according to the Dhamma, and undertakes restraint for the future." This too is a valuable custom of the Sasana. I do not know whether such things happen in lay society today, but these are extremely valuable things.
Sometimes, the moment a fault is pointed out, one does not see it as a fault, especially if it was said with censure. So, they go on harboring hatred. But as they go on with their work, they realize, "Is it not true what our parents said?" or "Is it not true what the teacher said?" Even so, they feel ashamed to go and admit it. At that moment, they do not offer the praise due to noble ones. Thus, there is a valuable quality here. If one understands even later, one should go and confess one's fault, and say, "I was like this, but I want to improve now." There is a valuable virtue here. Therefore, we should constantly remind ourselves of this: *garahāva seyyo viññūhi yañce bālappasaṃsanaṃ* (censure by the wise is better than praise by fools). Nowadays, everyone in society likes praise. But the policy of the majority is *attukkaṃsana paravambhana*—exalting oneself and disparaging others. In many instances in society, there are those who look for faults with corrupt intentions, like the character assassination mentioned earlier. This is called "seeking the loopholes of others." One should not cultivate such an attitude. If you have to point out such faults as parents or as teachers, you must act after observing the right time and place. As the Buddha declared, one must first see whether this matter is true or false. The Buddha points out three things to Prince Abhayarāja. A matter must be true. Along with being true, it must be beneficial and useful to the person to whom it is spoken. Next is the question: is that speech pleasing or displeasing to that person? Whether it is pleasing or displeasing to that person, one has to speak it according to the occasion. That is what we must reflect on wisely.
For that, we must first prepare our inner self. We must have compassion and loving-kindness (*mettā*) within, thinking: "I must correct this person, I must correct this child, I must correct this student, I must correct this employee in this institution." One must develop the inner strength to point out, with compassion, the shortcomings not only of those below but also of those above. Why? Because often, by hiding these faults and shortcomings, society becomes further corrupted. Therefore, it is something that must be done.
You lay devotees know that a criminal who takes a knife in hand destroys a life. But a surgeon who takes that same scalpel saves a life. In the same way, one must consider the words one uses on that occasion. If one does so with the compassionate and kind intention of not merely exposing and highlighting that person's fault but removing it and bringing forth that hidden treasure we mentioned, then it is a great service to society. It is due to the lack of this service that there is decline on both sides. There is no readiness to accept advice and admonition; there is no gentle-spokenness (*suvaca-bhāva*). Similarly, the minds of those who give admonition are also often corrupted. The word *medhāvi* (wise) is explained in the Dhamma as *dhamma-paññā*—that valuable wisdom developed through the Dhamma itself. That is lacking in many people.
Three guiding principles that help a person to improve are mentioned in the Dhamma: *attādhipateyya* (self-governance / supremacy of self), *dhammādhipateyya* (supremacy of the Dhamma), and *lokādhipateyya* (supremacy of the world).
*Attādhipateyya* means what we normally call self-respect or acting according to one's conscience; thinking by oneself in this way: "This is not suitable for me, this is not proper for me, this does not befit me," and refraining from doing something wrong. Placing oneself first and avoiding a fault.
Next, there is another way: *dhammādhipateyya*—placing the Dhamma first. Thinking: "The Dhamma of the Buddha that I have learned states this. I must discipline myself in this way." Developing an understanding of good and bad, wholesome (*kusala*) and unwholesome (*akusala*), and disciplining oneself accordingly.
There is another way: *lokādhipateyya*. Here, the "world" does not mean the ignorant world, not the ordinary foolish world. For other matters, be that as it may, here we should not take the common talk of the masses, nor should we take the various political meanings of today. It is the wise, the prudent, and those endowed with virtue who are considered the "world" here. Here we should consider not what the ignorant, foolish people say, but what wise people point out. That is a special matter. If such a person points out our fault, we can steer our lives through that.
Such noble characters as the life of Venerable Rāhula and the life of Venerable Sāriputta are mentioned in this Dhamma. Similarly, when monks confess their transgressions, they point out each other's faults and thereby collectively protect the Sasana, while also securing their own progress. In every institution, in every place, this very Dhamma-principle (*dhamma-tā*) helps progress. Why? Because it is a nature of *saṃsāra* that one does not see one's own faults, just as the eye does not see itself. The eye can see the nose, but the eye cannot see itself. That is why it is mentioned in the Dhamma: *Sudassaṃ vajjaṃ aññesaṃ, attano pana duddasaṃ* (Easy to see are the faults of others, but difficult to see are one's own). The faults of others are seen very clearly. But one's own fault is not seen by oneself. Be that as it may, when we see the fault of another, we must first reflect: "Is this a fault we see because of our own fault, or is it truly another's?" Reflecting wisely on whether it is indeed a fault that has occurred, we must then speak, observing the right way and the right time.
It is by speaking in this manner that one can help someone. Due to the hatred that Devadatta carried throughout *saṃsāra*, even the Buddha could not tame him. But on many occasions, the Buddha helped people and steered them on the right path through his quality of great compassion, sometimes through the very punishment he meted out. Here, the story of Venerable Yasoja was mentioned. The Buddha used his skillful means (*upāya-kosalla*) there. There is no partiality in the Buddha. When a group of pupils of Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna behaved in that very manner, the Buddha censured them, saying it was like a fish market, and dismissed them. These were pupils of his own Chief Disciples. Yet, the Buddha dismissed them. In this way, the Buddha impartially censured the fault when it was necessary. He also told the Chief Disciples that if he did not do so, this Sasana would become a collection of sweepings and rubbish.
To point out the fault according to the occasion and correct that person is what a mother and a father also have to do. If one develops hatred or a wrong attitude, if one lacks Dhamma-understanding, or if one has hypocritical thoughts within, then one cannot correct another. To point it out according to the occasion, one must generate great compassion and sympathy. It is because of the lack of this strength that conflicts often arise in society. First, one disciplines body and speech through training rules like virtue (*sīla*). One disciplines the mind through meditation. Next, reflecting by way of *attādhipateyya* and *dhammādhipateyya*, one corrects one's own shortcomings. Then, when a problem arises, we are able to make an impartial decision. If one lives with mindfulness and wisdom, without confusing the mind with intoxicants and the like, one can point out the right path to another.
Let us say someone who is about to fall into disaster goes to another seeking help. One should not assist them in what is bad, thinking they might become displeased. Always comparing it with the Dhamma, one must help in accordance with the Dhamma, impartially. Indeed, what is called "welfare" here is not merely progress in this life. It is easy to give advice for progress in this life.
You lay devotees know well that in various sectors of society, especially towards the latter part of life, there are people who can give advice to a large number of people on specific subjects. That is regarding this world. But only a very few think of both sides—this world and the next world. For the sake of progress in this life alone, through highly dangerous advice, someone can even be led to hell. I need not give you fresh examples. Therefore, we must first establish a proper Dhamma-judgment within ourselves by way of *attādhipateyya* and *dhammādhipateyya*. We must look at the world with a clear judgment regarding what the true values of life are, what should and should not be done, and what is wholesome (*kusala*) and unwholesome (*akusala*). Otherwise, the person who does what is right will appear to us as wrong.
If there is no harm in using that word, even if we look at it with an idea like "democracy" and take the majority opinion, the opinion of the majority there can also be wrong. Therefore, we must always look, keeping the Dhamma of the Buddha first. This group called the wise (*viññū*), the learned (*paṇḍita*), the intelligent (*medhāvī*) are not many in the world. There are only a very few. It is so at all times.
There is a good incident regarding this as well. When Venerable Sāriputta asked his teacher to come to the Buddha, the teacher asked, "Who are there more of in this world? Fools or the wise?" "There are only a few wise people." "Well, in that case, the wise will go to the ascetic Gotama. The crowd of fools will come to me," he replied. Similarly, there are mostly fools in the world. The person who has developed the inner knowledge of the Dhamma and has that wisdom is the one who should be taken as the "world" here by way of *lokādhipateyya*. Keeping such a standard, whether it be a low person or a high person in one's own institutions, just like one's own children and students, one must point out those faults according to the occasion. One must develop the Dhamma-strength within to do such a thing. Otherwise, society will head further down the path of decline. It is because of this that even the Sasana falls into decline.
Furthermore, if we do not get an example for our lives, that is not a Dhamma sermon. You should think of what has been preached here as a sermon that helps you to improve. In everything, there are examples in the world showing us the good side and the bad side. Through both of these, we must understand the side of advantages (*āniśaṃsa*) and the side of disadvantages (*ādīnava*). Through the lives of Venerable Rāhula, Venerable Sāriputta, and Venerable Yasoja, we understood the good side, the exemplary side. Similarly, regarding the *Chabbaggiya* monks, Devadatta, Bhaddāli, and others, there is the bad side. Through this, we must understand the path we should take. We must walk on that path.
Therefore, on this valuable *poya* day, this devout group has undertaken a certain precept (*sīla*). What is being done there, too, is the correcting of one's own faults—the correcting of faults regarding body and speech. Next, through Dhamma sermons and meditation, we concentrate our minds and try to gain an understanding of the true nature of the world, of life. Just as the Buddha said, *bahujana-hitāya bahujana-sukhāya* (for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many), may this Dhamma sermon preached today also help for the good of the world through our Dhamma-strength and our character-strength! If this devout group has developed certain Dhamma-strengths—namely faith (*saddhā*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*)—by listening to this Dhamma sermon, may that also help these devotees when they aim for Nibbāna at some point.
May all those who wish to rejoice in such merit, including the guardian deities of the Sasana, and our relatives from the *Avīci* hell up to the *Akaniṭha* heaven, rejoice in the store of merit gathered by these devotees so far through listening to the Dhamma, and the store of merit gathered by us through preaching the Dhamma! Having rejoiced, may they all escape from all the suffering of *saṃsāra* as quickly as possible through their aspired Bodhi (Awakening), and reach the noble, deathless, supreme Nibbāna! Similarly, utilizing the Dhamma-strength we have gained, may we also make our own meditations successful, obeying the advice of spiritual friends to the letter, bearing even words spoken in censure, walking gentle-spokenly on this path of the Dhamma, succeeding in our meditations, and may we receive the strength, power, and blessing to realize the noble, deathless, supreme Nibbāna through the realization of the paths and fruits of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti*), Once-returning (*sakadāgāmitā*), Non-returning (*anāgāmitā*), and Arahatship!
With this aspiration, please recite these verses.
“*Ettāvatā ca amhehi.........*”

tadisam bhajamanassa,
seyyo hoti na papiyo."
from:
dhammapada verse 76 (pandita vagga)
dear listeners,
a person who hopes to steer their life on the right path should make an effort to seek the help of wise spiritual friends (*kalyana-mitta*). one must fashion one’s conduct and attitudes in a manner that allows one to receive the assistance of spiritual friends. what we mean by assistance here is the help to correct one's shortcomings and faults. generally, one does not see one's own faults. they are visible only to the wise spiritual friends one associates with. that is why the buddha compared a wise person who points out faults to someone pointing out a hidden treasure, and gave a simile. this is what is expressed in the verse we have chosen as our theme. the buddha preached this verse with reference to a monk named radha, who was a pupil of venerable sariputta.
in his lay life, venerable radha was an extremely poor brahmin in the city of savatthi. since he had no means of livelihood, he came to the jetavana monastery, attended upon the sangha, swept and cleared the premises, and sustained himself with whatever he received. as time went on, this man developed a great desire to ordain. however, the sangha was not keen on ordaining him. perhaps they felt he was seeking ordination merely for a livelihood. be that as it may, due to this man's genuine desire and because his hope was not being fulfilled, his body became emaciated. one day, when the buddha was scanning the world with his attainment of great compassion (*mahakarunika-samapatti*) as was his daily custom, this man at the jetavana monastery came into the net of his wisdom-vision.
when the buddha investigated this, he saw that this man possessed the supportive merits to attain arahatship. as a general custom, the buddha would occasionally go on walking tours of the monastery to see how the monks were doing and whether their work was progressing well. that evening, while walking around the jetavana monastery in this manner, he approached this brahmin and asked, "brahmin, what are you doing here?" he replied, "venerable sir, i am attending upon the sangha and earning my livelihood." "do the monks show you any hospitality in return for your services?" "yes, venerable sir, i get food and drink. however, they do not ordain me," he said.
thereupon, the buddha assembled the sangha and, introducing a discussion centered on this man radha, asked: "is there any monk among the sangha who remembers receiving any special help from this brahmin?" venerable sariputta immediately spoke up: "venerable sir, i remember this brahmin once placing a spoonful of rice in my bowl when i was on alms-round." then the buddha asked: "sariputta, is that not enough to help someone escape the *dukkha* (suffering) of *samsara*?" venerable sariputta replied: "very well, venerable sir, then i shall ordain him," and he ordained the man.
despite being ordained, he did not receive any special attention from the sangha. one can understand why. he sat at the very end of the seats and did not even get proper food and drink. he was somewhat marginalized. venerable sariputta, noticing this, and with the compassionate intention of paying special attention to this new venerable radha, went on a wandering tour accompanied by venerable radha. during this journey, he pointed out his faults and gave him advice and admonition. this monk radha was extremely obedient, gentle-spoken, never showed any anger, corrected his faults, and by practicing meditation, attained arahatship very quickly.
thereafter, venerable sariputta came with venerable radha to see the buddha. the buddha asked, "how is it, sariputta, is your pupil obedient?" "oh yes, venerable sir, he is very obedient. whenever a fault was pointed out to him, he never got angry." then the buddha asked, "sariputta, if you could get pupils like this, would you like to have many?" "oh yes, as many as possible. i like such pupils very much," venerable sariputta praised. similarly, a talk arose among the monks: "venerable sariputta is an extremely grateful person. merely for a spoonful of rice, he ordained this man. also, venerable sariputta is someone who constantly seeks advice, and he has found a pupil who is willing to receive advice." hearing this, the buddha praised venerable sariputta's quality of gratitude and then said: "monks, a bhikkhu should be gentle-spoken (*suvaca*) like this radha. if someone points out one's faults, one should think that they are pointing out a hidden treasure." expressing this idea, he uttered this verse:
> *nidhinamva pavattaram, yam passe vajjadassinam;*
> *medhavim tadisam panditam bhaje, tadisam bhajamanassa seyyo hoti na papiyo.*
if one sees a wise person who points out one's faults as if pointing out hidden treasures, one should associate with such a wise and learned person. associating with such a person brings progress, not decline. this is the meaning of this verse. here we should especially consider the value of this simile given by the buddha. whenever the buddha gave a simile, it carried a very deep meaning. normally, people of the world do not like having their faults pointed out; they dislike criticism or fault-finding. since the buddha knew this attitude, he placed a completely new concept before the world, taking this gentle-spoken bhikkhu as an example. to call advice a hidden treasure is because in those days, gold coins and such were deposited in pots and vessels and hidden in the jungle or by riverbanks. just as someone goes and points out those treasures buried under the earth, a wise person points out the treasures hidden beneath one's faults. what are these treasures? hidden beneath one's faults are one's skills and abilities. it is pointing out these skills that is referred to here as pointing out a hidden treasure. just as treasures emerge when the earth is removed and cleared away, when one's faults are unearthed and removed, one's wholesome qualities, skills, and abilities emerge from within. that is the fundamental value of the simile in this verse.
furthermore, this story illustrates a noble quality of the buddha's life. a major part of the daily routine of the great compassionate one is to scan the world during the dawn with his unique wisdom—which is considered an extraordinary knowledge exclusive to a buddha—to find the person most suitable to receive his assistance. they could be far away, or close by. at this time, this helpless person living right nearby in jetavana monastery appeared. this net of wisdom is truly wonderful. it is something that demonstrates the buddha's quality of equality. setting aside all other work, he went to that person, visited him, and showed him the way to find help. although this man may have attended upon all the monks, the buddha asked about anyone who had received a special favor from him because he wanted to draw special attention to him.
this gratitude was a special characteristic of venerable sariputta. until his parinibbana, he showed great respect towards venerable assaji, who had given him the dhamma. similarly, on various occasions, incidents revealing venerable sariputta's quality of gratitude are mentioned. here too, it was the incident of a spoonful of rice. it seems like a very small thing. but it was on that basis that he helped that man. venerable sariputta's quality of gratitude shines through here.
venerable radha, too, did not have the common weakness of getting angry when someone points out a fault. when his faults were pointed out to him, he accepted them with great diligence and obedience, as if being shown a hidden treasure, as we mentioned earlier. that is why he was able to reach the state of arahatship. there are lessons for us to reflect upon and adopt from each of these points. there is a word in this verse that might be somewhat unappealing to the mind: *nigayhavadim medhavim*—one who reproves or censures.
generally, no one likes to be censured or reproved. but this censuring is also necessary at times to point out the gravity of a fault. to show someone a fault in a way that sticks in their mind, censuring is sometimes required. this is especially a task assigned to a teacher. the teacher has to give some punishment—not in a deep and severe manner disproportionate to the mistake, but in an appropriate way so that the pupil remembers. sometimes through words, sometimes through other courses of action. therefore, we must reflect on this wisely. the matters contained in this verse help us in our daily personal lives, at home, in institutions, in schools, and everywhere else.
let us first consider the greatest teacher in the world. it is through the buddha’s own life that we can understand this word *nigayhavadi* (reproving). two qualities of the buddha are mentioned: *anuttaro purisadammasarathi* (the incomparable charioteer of men to be tamed) and *sattha devamanussanam* (the teacher of gods and humans). these two qualities demonstrate the responsibility assigned to the buddha as a teacher. *anuttaro purisadammasarathi* means he is like a charioteer in taming tamable humans. we know that this is not like the drivers of today. in those days, when driving a horse-chariot, one had to train the horse. sometimes, even a whip had to be used. similarly, the buddha, as the teacher of gods and humans, had to use words of censure according to the situation. thus, this characteristic of the buddha's character became a problem for some people.
there is a good illustration of this in the dhamma. seeing the buddha's fame spreading, there were niganthas (jains) who became jealous. other sectarians and adherents of other religions always looked for ways to defame and take revenge on the buddha. on one occasion, when prince abhayaraja visited the religious teacher nigantha nataputta, nigantha nataputta said: "the fame of the ascetic gotama is spreading widely. prince, if you can present an argument to the ascetic gotama that he cannot answer, then your fame will spread too." when asked, "what is the argument i should present?" he said: "present this double-horned dilemma (*ubhathokotika-panha*) to the ascetic gotama. what is it? first ask, 'venerable gotama, do you speak words that are displeasing and disagreeable to others?' if he says he does use disagreeable words, then say the conclusion is: 'then what is the difference between the buddha and an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*)? an ordinary worldling also speaks displeasing and disagreeable words.' on the other hand, if he says he does not use them, then ask: 'if so, why did you censure the venerable devadatta by saying he is destined for hell for an aeon? devadatta was enraged by that.' in this way, there is a mismatch there too, isn't there? that is to say, whichever of the two answers he gives, present this argument. then the ascetic gotama will be left speechless." nigantha nataputta gave a simile for this: "just like an iron hook stuck in one's throat, the ascetic gotama will be left with nowhere to turn. therefore, present this argument."
prince abhayaraja then went to see the buddha to present this argument. when he went and looked around, it was a bit late in the evening. he thought, "i should invite the buddha to the palace itself and ask him on that occasion." so, he invited the buddha and three other monks to his house, the palace, for the next day. the next day, after the buddha had finished his meal, prince abhayaraja asked the buddha: "blessed one, do you use words that are displeasing and disagreeable to others?" then the buddha said: "prince, i do not give a one-sided answer to this. this is an answer that must be analyzed." thereupon, prince abhayaraja realized that the argument would not work. "ah, then the niganthas have failed!" muttered prince abhayaraja. when the buddha asked, "why do you say that?" he told the whole story: "i was taught like this. that is why i asked."
at that moment, prince abhayaraja had his infant son on his lap. the buddha drew a simile from that very situation: "now, prince, if this young child on your lap, due to the negligence of his nurse or your own negligence, were to put a pebble or a splinter into his mouth, what would you do?" "venerable sir, i would hold his head with my left hand, crook my right finger, and pull it out. even if it meant drawing blood, i would pull it out. why? because i have great compassion for the child." thereupon, the buddha declared: "it is the same with me. because i have compassion for beings, if a word is true and beneficial, even if it is displeasing and disagreeable, i speak it to that person according to the occasion. the word is true. it is beneficial to that person. but it is displeasing and disagreeable. that is, a word of censure or blame. yet, i speak it because i want to correct him." in this way, on that occasion, the buddha resolved that double-horned dilemma. similarly, lay devotees, you may have heard this stated in the dhamma itself:
> *garaha va seyyo vinnuhi, yance balappasamsana.*
"censure by the wise is indeed better than praise by fools." this idea is a wonderful motto. mothers who raise children know how to discipline their children according to the occasion. the same happened with the buddha. he had to use various skillful means (*upaya-kosalla*) to deliver the worldlings, who are burdened with defilements, from *samsara* according to the occasion. going hand in hand with great compassion is this skillful means. to speak a word of censure that leaves a lasting impression, without any hatred in the heart but out of compassion for beings according to the occasion, belongs to that skillful means. this is how the concept of censuring should be understood.
next, let us look at this quality of being gentle-spoken (*suvaca*). *suvaca*, in a general sense, is called obedience. obedience means doing as told. but the real meaning of the word *suvaca* is that one can be given advice without fear. *duvvaca* (difficult to speak to) means one is afraid to say anything to them. suppose there is some fault in someone, but one is afraid to mention it. one does not want to, because that person will get angry, scold, and rage over it. to the person who does not get enraged in this way, one can speak without fear. that is why they are called *suvaca*—someone who is easy to speak to, someone to whom a fault can easily be pointed out. a *duvvaca* or *dubbacajatiya* (of difficult speech) person is one who gets angry the moment something is said and causes a great deal of trouble. therefore, people say nothing; they stand aside and watch, thinking, "let them do whatever they want." so, we must understand the difference between these two words, *suvaca* and *duvvaca*.
we get excellent illustrations of this from the sasana itself. the greatest example, which you lay devotees must have heard many times in dhamma sermons, is venerable sariputta himself, the chief disciple of the sasana. his humility was truly wonderful. going hand in hand with humility and patience is the quality of being gentle-spoken (*suvaca*), obedience—the ability to listen to whatever is said, whether harsh or bitter, and the ability to listen when faults are pointed out. it is precisely because of this that, as you know, in the verses on blessings (*mangala sutta*), it is said: *khanti ca sovacassata, samanananca dassanam*. *khanti ca sovacassata*—patience and being gentle-spoken. being gentle-spoken goes hand in hand with patience. thus, a valuable quality of venerable sariputta is mentioned. on one occasion, a seven-year-old novice monk, newly ordained and cute like a child, noticed a corner of venerable sariputta’s undergarment (*antara-vasaka*) hanging down and pointed it out to him. venerable sariputta adjusted it, came back, clasped his hands as if worshipping, and uttered a verse:
> *tadahupabbajito santo, jatiya sattavassiko;*
> *so pi mam anusaseyya, sampaticchami muddhane.*
"even if a seven-year-old novice ordained today points out a fault in me, i accept it on my head." this is a valuable illustration of the gentle-spoken (*suvaca*) nature in venerable sariputta's life.
it was the same with venerable rahula. venerable rahula was in a position where he could easily have become *duvvaca* (difficult to speak to), because he was the son of the buddha in his lay life. as you know, children of those with high positions and wealth, when corrected even slightly, sometimes threaten, "i will tell my mother" or "i will tell my father." though he was the son of the buddha in his lay life, how humble and gentle-spoken was venerable rahula! it is said that every morning he would take a handful of sand, throw it up, and say, "may i receive as many admonitions from the buddha, my teachers, and preceptors as there are grains of sand here!" he would say this as a game, throwing the grains of sand. this shows venerable rahula's humble, gentle-spoken, and obedient nature. there are many other stories told about venerable rahula's attitude and gentle-spoken nature.
there is another valuable story. on one occasion, five hundred monks led by venerable yasoja came to see the buddha at the jetavana monastery in savatthi. coming as guests, they exchanged greetings with the resident monks and arranged their bowls and robes, which created a great noise. the buddha asked venerable ananda: "ananda, who is making this noise? it sounds like fishermen shouting at a fish market. what is this racket?" he asked venerable ananda. venerable ananda replied: "venerable sir, a group of five hundred monks led by venerable yasoja has arrived, and that is why there is this noise." "tell them to come to me," the buddha assigned to venerable ananda.
then venerable ananda brought venerable yasoja and the group. the buddha asked why they were shouting like in a fish market. they explained the matter: "coming as guests, when we were putting away our bowls and robes, we made this noise." "do not stay near me. i do not wish to keep you here. depart from here," the buddha said. venerable yasoja and the group had come with great desire to see the buddha that day. but the buddha dismissed them. having no choice, he departed with his group, went on a tour, and arrived in the vajji country.
then the rainy season (*vassa*) arrived. they built huts near the river called vaggumuda and entered the rains-retreat with this group of five hundred. on the first day of the rains-retreat, venerable yasoja gave advice to his group, saying: "friends, we have been dismissed by our teacher, who is highly benevolent, desires our progress, and has compassion for us. now, let us live in a certain way. in what way? let us correct our shortcomings now, so that the buddha, the tathagata, will be pleased when he sees us." the group agreed to this and began to practice meditation. within the rains-retreat itself, all these monks attained the noble state (of arahatship) accompanied by analytical insights and supernormal powers (*abhinna*).
now, the next news. after the rains-retreat, the buddha traveled from savatthi to the gabled hall (*kutagara-sala*) in the great forest of vesali. having arrived, he looked into venerable yasoja and his group. in such events, the buddha would search again. he examined the minds of venerable yasoja and his group with his own mind. he saw that everything was complete. all of them were arahats.
then he said to venerable ananda: "ananda, the direction where the bhikkhus on the banks of the vaggumuda live is as if radiating light. i have no aversion to going in that direction. even to contemplate it is very pleasing to me. send a messenger, send a courier: 'the teacher wishes to see you. i wish to see you. tell yasoja and his group to come.'" this was the invitation the buddha made. venerable ananda went to a certain bhikkhu and expressed the permission received from the buddha. that bhikkhu—he was a bhikkhu possessing supernormal powers—as it is said in the books, as quickly as a strong man might stretch his bent arm or bend his stretched arm, vanished from the gabled hall in the great forest and appeared where the bhikkhus on the banks of the vaggumuda were. in an instant. in a flash. then he gave this news: "the buddha is inviting you." thereupon, that group too arrived by psychic power (*iddhi-bala*) to where the buddha was at the gabled hall.
by the time they arrived, the buddha was seated in concentration. he was seated in the imperturbable concentration (*anenja-samadhi*), a silent concentration. venerable ananda was standing to one side. the buddha was in concentration. then this group arrived. having arrived, venerable ananda worshipped the buddha and said: "venerable sir, the guest monks who were invited have arrived. may the blessed one exchange friendly greetings with them." the buddha remained silent. the first watch of the night passed. then, venerable yasoja and his group examined with their own power what kind of concentration the buddha was in. seeing that he was in that silent concentration, they too sat down in that very concentration. thus, the buddha was sitting on one side, and venerable yasoja and his group were sitting in concentration on the other side. this was a problem for venerable ananda. when guests arrive, should they not be attended to? the buddha himself invited them, and yet he is just sitting there.
then the first watch passed. after the first watch ended, venerable ananda reminded him again: "venerable sir, much of the night has passed. the guest monks have also arrived and have been waiting for a long time. may the blessed one exchange friendly greetings." no, he was still silent. the second watch passed. then, the third watch passed, and it was the time of dawn. once again, for the third time, he invited him in that manner. still, the buddha was silent. finally, he said to the buddha: "now, venerable sir, the night has passed, and it is dawn. this group is still sitting here. may the blessed one exchange friendly greetings!" then the buddha said: "ananda, if you knew the matter as it really is, you would not have spoken even this much. both i and this group, both parties, were in the imperturbable concentration (*anenja-samadhi*)." and he uttered a verse as an utterance of joy:
> *yassa jito kama-kantako, akkoso vadho ca pabbato va jito;*
> *anejo navedati so bhikkhu.*
"the bhikkhu who has conquered the thorn of sensuality, abuse, and physical harm, stands unshaken like a mountain; he is imperturbable and does not tremble." he uttered that verse.
from this story too, we see the gentle-spoken (*suvaca*) quality of venerable yasoja. when there is a group of five hundred, one does not need that many people these days—even over a small word, people start a big campaign to show their power. but venerable yasoja very humbly accepted his fault. that is a great quality. accepting his fault, he brought forth that hidden treasure. the words spoken there are truly wonderful. he started by saying: "we have been dismissed out of compassion by the buddha, who is kind, great in compassion, benevolent, and compassionate towards us. he dismissed us out of compassion. now, let us live in such a way that the buddha is pleased with us." that is how they began the rains-retreat. and they brought forth that treasure, the treasure of arahatship. here, venerable yasoja's character is extraordinary. similarly, we see the buddha's skillful means (*upaya-kosalla*). he dismissed them having seen a certain reason. it was fully accomplished.
next, there is an even deeper point. you lay devotees might be surprised. we all know that when someone comes, we should welcome them. everyone knows about hospitality to guests. here, after sending an invitation himself, when those monks arrived, the buddha just sat there in silence. there is a very deep meaning here. you know that if a guest arrives while you are having a meal, you pull up a chair and let them join the meal. the buddha did something similar. the buddha was consuming food in his own pasture. perhaps within the concentration on the fruit of arahatship (*arahatta-phala-samadhi*). he was absorbed in the fruit-attainment (*phala-samapatti*), the concentration of realizing nibbana that he had attained. the monks who arrived were also suitable to consume that food. venerable ananda, however, was not yet there. that is why it was a problem for ananda. so those monks too looked at what the buddha was consuming, and thinking, "we too must consume this," sat in that very concentration the whole night. that is the real welcome. this is good to depict in a painting. two paintings could be drawn. the first time they came, those monks were shouting like in a fish market, causing a great racket. when they came this time, how was it? the buddha's welcome was appropriate to that. there is a very deep example and model for the world to take from this story. in this way, on one hand, we must understand the value of being gentle-spoken (*suvaca*).
next, on the other hand, there are also illustrations of being *duvvaca* (difficult to speak to). not everyone in the buddha's sasana was gentle-spoken like this. the monk devadatta, whom you all know, was such a stubborn person that he even tried to take the life of the buddha, precisely because of the *duvvaca* nature that arose from a slight disagreement. similarly, there is another incident. mention is made of a group of monks called the *chabbaggiya* (the group of six). these monks, consisting of six factions led by six leaders, lived in an extremely stubborn and disobedient manner, repeatedly breaking the disciplinary rules (*vinaya*) laid down by the buddha. they also reaped the consequences of their actions. on some occasions, the buddha dismissed them from those places. he had to censure them according to the circumstances.
similarly, another special incident regarding censure is mentioned in the dhamma. you all know about minister channa, who was a minister of the buddha. he was the minister who accompanied prince siddhartha when he renounced the lay life. unlike venerable rahula, he developed pride due to his close connection with the buddha. because of that conceit, he behaved in an extremely disobedient manner. he would not allow the monks to point out any fault in him. due to this disobedience, although the buddha laid down various disciplinary rules, he could not be tamed. finally, even on his parinibbana bed, the buddha had to direct his attention to this. that night, before his parinibbana, the buddha said to venerable ananda: "ananda, after my passing, impose the brahma-punishment (*brahma-danda*) on the monk channa." when asked, "what is the brahma-punishment?"—it was a rule that had not been laid down in the *vinaya* until then, which is why venerable ananda asked, "what, venerable sir, is the brahma-punishment?" the buddha declared: "let the monk channa say whatever he wants. the monks should neither advise nor admonish him." it was an outright boycott. the permission to impose such a complete boycott was given by the buddha before his parinibbana. thus, the final punishment given by the buddha for that stubbornness (*duvvaca-bhava*) is called the brahma-punishment. it is a very severe punishment. *brahma* means the highest, doesn't it? a most severe punishment. it is said that as soon as venerable ananda declared this matter after the buddha's parinibbana, the monk channa fainted and fell due to the shock. due to the very shock that arose from this, the monk channa later meditated and somehow became an arahat. there too, through that punishment, the monk channa was tamed in one way or another and attained arahatship.
from the disciplinary rules of the monks and the customs of the sasana, lay devotees too can learn many things. especially, something that helped the survival of this sasana was pointing out the faults of others. this is a custom of the sasana. even in society, we know that if no one points out the faults of others, this society would become far more dangerous than it is now. but sometimes, the person pointing it out does not do so out of compassion. instead of pointing out a hidden treasure, if they act as if digging a pit for the other, then the effort fails. without any compassion for that person, some people point out faults with highly dangerous and malicious intentions, such as character assassination. not so the wise; they do so with the intention of correcting the person in the right way, and even if they use words of censure according to the situation, it becomes a help. there is a custom in the sangha regarding the disciplinary rules of the monks, where they point out each other's weaknesses. this is called *annamanna-vutthapana*—rehabilitating one another from offences by helping each other. they point out the fault. when one says out of compassion, "friend, such a fault has occurred," the other corrects it.
after spending the rains-retreat, the monks have a custom called *pavarana*. you lay devotees may have heard of this as performing the *uposatha*. there is a special significance in the *pavarana* of the sangha. it is the disciplinary act performed at the end by a group of monks who have lived together during a rains-retreat. here, they invite the sangha: "if there is any fault of mine that you have seen, heard, or suspected, please speak out! out of compassion, please point it out to me!" thus, they make an invitation to the group. we must understand from this that when someone points out a fault, one should not get angry. when teachers and others say something with good intentions, one should feel that they are pointing out a hidden treasure and say, "if there are any other faults, please point them out to me." that is a special invitation. it is this invitation—to point out any fault of mine seen, heard, or suspected so that i may correct it, and if i see it as a fault, i will correct it—that is done through this monastic custom.
but nowadays, especially in educational institutions, and in other institutions almost everywhere, over a very small incident, merely because a small fault is pointed out, a host of strikes, threats, insults, disagreements, and crises arise. these arise from a very small thing. why? because if we had taken the feeling of "pointing out a hidden treasure" into our minds, our reaction would be different. we would say with even more enthusiasm, "please tell me with facts what the fault is, so that i can correct it." instead, the moment a word is said, people get angry and develop deep-seated hatred. that is the wrong attitude. instead, we must understand from these stories the value of advice in steering our lives on the right path. according to the treasure-simile shown by the buddha, we see that sometimes it is necessary to speak with censure. the buddha too, according to the situation, laid down some disciplinary rules in an extremely strict and severe manner. if the fault is severe, they are expelled altogether. sometimes, remedies are applied right there to tame them again. this re-taming is also a valuable quality.
let us say we did not see that fault in the first instance. but if we saw it at least in the second instance, we should go to the person who pointed out the fault and sincerely express our gratitude. such incidents too exist in the sasana. we should take some example from them as well. to give one example, when the buddha laid down the training rule regarding eating at improper times (*vikala-bhojana*), a monk named bhaddali became displeased and protested. there is no need to explain this further. even nowadays, when speaking about eating at improper times, there are more people who dislike it than those who like it. in those days too, there were such groups of monks; when the buddha laid down the training rules on eating at improper times, they criticized it severely and stood aside. but later, when they saw the benefits of the training rule, they came and confessed their fault. there too, a highly valuable phrase is used to accept the fault: *accayo mam bhante accagama yatha bala yatha mulham yatha akusalam* and so on, which is a wonderful sentence spoken when coming to confess one's fault.
"venerable sir, a transgression overcame me"—nowadays people say "a mistake happened to me." that is the kind of thing said there. "a transgression overcame me, through my foolishness, through my delusion, through my unwholesomeness. that is why this happened." thus, humbly confessing the fault that happened through oneself, one says: *accayam accayato patigganhatu ayatim samvaraya*—"may the blessed one accept this as my transgression for the sake of my future restraint." the buddha also forgives it: "very well, that is how it is. *vaddhi h’esa ariyassa vinaye yo accayam accayato passitva yathadhammam patikaroti*..."—and so on. he declares: "in the discipline of the noble ones, it is a sign of growth, a factor of progress, when one sees one's transgression as a transgression, confesses it according to the dhamma, and undertakes restraint for the future." this too is a valuable custom of the sasana. i do not know whether such things happen in lay society today, but these are extremely valuable things.
sometimes, the moment a fault is pointed out, one does not see it as a fault, especially if it was said with censure. so, they go on harboring hatred. but as they go on with their work, they realize, "is it not true what our parents said?" or "is it not true what the teacher said?" even so, they feel ashamed to go and admit it. at that moment, they do not offer the praise due to noble ones. thus, there is a valuable quality here. if one understands even later, one should go and confess one's fault, and say, "i was like this, but i want to improve now." there is a valuable virtue here. therefore, we should constantly remind ourselves of this: *garahava seyyo vinnuhi yance balappasamsanam* (censure by the wise is better than praise by fools). nowadays, everyone in society likes praise. but the policy of the majority is *attukkamsana paravambhana*—exalting oneself and disparaging others. in many instances in society, there are those who look for faults with corrupt intentions, like the character assassination mentioned earlier. this is called "seeking the loopholes of others." one should not cultivate such an attitude. if you have to point out such faults as parents or as teachers, you must act after observing the right time and place. as the buddha declared, one must first see whether this matter is true or false. the buddha points out three things to prince abhayaraja. a matter must be true. along with being true, it must be beneficial and useful to the person to whom it is spoken. next is the question: is that speech pleasing or displeasing to that person? whether it is pleasing or displeasing to that person, one has to speak it according to the occasion. that is what we must reflect on wisely.
for that, we must first prepare our inner self. we must have compassion and loving-kindness (*metta*) within, thinking: "i must correct this person, i must correct this child, i must correct this student, i must correct this employee in this institution." one must develop the inner strength to point out, with compassion, the shortcomings not only of those below but also of those above. why? because often, by hiding these faults and shortcomings, society becomes further corrupted. therefore, it is something that must be done.
you lay devotees know that a criminal who takes a knife in hand destroys a life. but a surgeon who takes that same scalpel saves a life. in the same way, one must consider the words one uses on that occasion. if one does so with the compassionate and kind intention of not merely exposing and highlighting that person's fault but removing it and bringing forth that hidden treasure we mentioned, then it is a great service to society. it is due to the lack of this service that there is decline on both sides. there is no readiness to accept advice and admonition; there is no gentle-spokenness (*suvaca-bhava*). similarly, the minds of those who give admonition are also often corrupted. the word *medhavi* (wise) is explained in the dhamma as *dhamma-panna*—that valuable wisdom developed through the dhamma itself. that is lacking in many people.
three guiding principles that help a person to improve are mentioned in the dhamma: *attadhipateyya* (self-governance / supremacy of self), *dhammadhipateyya* (supremacy of the dhamma), and *lokadhipateyya* (supremacy of the world).
*attadhipateyya* means what we normally call self-respect or acting according to one's conscience; thinking by oneself in this way: "this is not suitable for me, this is not proper for me, this does not befit me," and refraining from doing something wrong. placing oneself first and avoiding a fault.
next, there is another way: *dhammadhipateyya*—placing the dhamma first. thinking: "the dhamma of the buddha that i have learned states this. i must discipline myself in this way." developing an understanding of good and bad, wholesome (*kusala*) and unwholesome (*akusala*), and disciplining oneself accordingly.
there is another way: *lokadhipateyya*. here, the "world" does not mean the ignorant world, not the ordinary foolish world. for other matters, be that as it may, here we should not take the common talk of the masses, nor should we take the various political meanings of today. it is the wise, the prudent, and those endowed with virtue who are considered the "world" here. here we should consider not what the ignorant, foolish people say, but what wise people point out. that is a special matter. if such a person points out our fault, we can steer our lives through that.
such noble characters as the life of venerable rahula and the life of venerable sariputta are mentioned in this dhamma. similarly, when monks confess their transgressions, they point out each other's faults and thereby collectively protect the sasana, while also securing their own progress. in every institution, in every place, this very dhamma-principle (*dhamma-ta*) helps progress. why? because it is a nature of *samsara* that one does not see one's own faults, just as the eye does not see itself. the eye can see the nose, but the eye cannot see itself. that is why it is mentioned in the dhamma: *sudassam vajjam annesam, attano pana duddasam* (easy to see are the faults of others, but difficult to see are one's own). the faults of others are seen very clearly. but one's own fault is not seen by oneself. be that as it may, when we see the fault of another, we must first reflect: "is this a fault we see because of our own fault, or is it truly another's?" reflecting wisely on whether it is indeed a fault that has occurred, we must then speak, observing the right way and the right time.
it is by speaking in this manner that one can help someone. due to the hatred that devadatta carried throughout *samsara*, even the buddha could not tame him. but on many occasions, the buddha helped people and steered them on the right path through his quality of great compassion, sometimes through the very punishment he meted out. here, the story of venerable yasoja was mentioned. the buddha used his skillful means (*upaya-kosalla*) there. there is no partiality in the buddha. when a group of pupils of venerable sariputta and venerable mahamoggallana behaved in that very manner, the buddha censured them, saying it was like a fish market, and dismissed them. these were pupils of his own chief disciples. yet, the buddha dismissed them. in this way, the buddha impartially censured the fault when it was necessary. he also told the chief disciples that if he did not do so, this sasana would become a collection of sweepings and rubbish.
to point out the fault according to the occasion and correct that person is what a mother and a father also have to do. if one develops hatred or a wrong attitude, if one lacks dhamma-understanding, or if one has hypocritical thoughts within, then one cannot correct another. to point it out according to the occasion, one must generate great compassion and sympathy. it is because of the lack of this strength that conflicts often arise in society. first, one disciplines body and speech through training rules like virtue (*sila*). one disciplines the mind through meditation. next, reflecting by way of *attadhipateyya* and *dhammadhipateyya*, one corrects one's own shortcomings. then, when a problem arises, we are able to make an impartial decision. if one lives with mindfulness and wisdom, without confusing the mind with intoxicants and the like, one can point out the right path to another.
let us say someone who is about to fall into disaster goes to another seeking help. one should not assist them in what is bad, thinking they might become displeased. always comparing it with the dhamma, one must help in accordance with the dhamma, impartially. indeed, what is called "welfare" here is not merely progress in this life. it is easy to give advice for progress in this life.
you lay devotees know well that in various sectors of society, especially towards the latter part of life, there are people who can give advice to a large number of people on specific subjects. that is regarding this world. but only a very few think of both sides—this world and the next world. for the sake of progress in this life alone, through highly dangerous advice, someone can even be led to hell. i need not give you fresh examples. therefore, we must first establish a proper dhamma-judgment within ourselves by way of *attadhipateyya* and *dhammadhipateyya*. we must look at the world with a clear judgment regarding what the true values of life are, what should and should not be done, and what is wholesome (*kusala*) and unwholesome (*akusala*). otherwise, the person who does what is right will appear to us as wrong.
if there is no harm in using that word, even if we look at it with an idea like "democracy" and take the majority opinion, the opinion of the majority there can also be wrong. therefore, we must always look, keeping the dhamma of the buddha first. this group called the wise (*vinnu*), the learned (*pandita*), the intelligent (*medhavi*) are not many in the world. there are only a very few. it is so at all times.
there is a good incident regarding this as well. when venerable sariputta asked his teacher to come to the buddha, the teacher asked, "who are there more of in this world? fools or the wise?" "there are only a few wise people." "well, in that case, the wise will go to the ascetic gotama. the crowd of fools will come to me," he replied. similarly, there are mostly fools in the world. the person who has developed the inner knowledge of the dhamma and has that wisdom is the one who should be taken as the "world" here by way of *lokadhipateyya*. keeping such a standard, whether it be a low person or a high person in one's own institutions, just like one's own children and students, one must point out those faults according to the occasion. one must develop the dhamma-strength within to do such a thing. otherwise, society will head further down the path of decline. it is because of this that even the sasana falls into decline.
furthermore, if we do not get an example for our lives, that is not a dhamma sermon. you should think of what has been preached here as a sermon that helps you to improve. in everything, there are examples in the world showing us the good side and the bad side. through both of these, we must understand the side of advantages (*anisamsa*) and the side of disadvantages (*adinava*). through the lives of venerable rahula, venerable sariputta, and venerable yasoja, we understood the good side, the exemplary side. similarly, regarding the *chabbaggiya* monks, devadatta, bhaddali, and others, there is the bad side. through this, we must understand the path we should take. we must walk on that path.
therefore, on this valuable *poya* day, this devout group has undertaken a certain precept (*sila*). what is being done there, too, is the correcting of one's own faults—the correcting of faults regarding body and speech. next, through dhamma sermons and meditation, we concentrate our minds and try to gain an understanding of the true nature of the world, of life. just as the buddha said, *bahujana-hitaya bahujana-sukhaya* (for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many), may this dhamma sermon preached today also help for the good of the world through our dhamma-strength and our character-strength! if this devout group has developed certain dhamma-strengths—namely faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*)—by listening to this dhamma sermon, may that also help these devotees when they aim for nibbana at some point.
may all those who wish to rejoice in such merit, including the guardian deities of the sasana, and our relatives from the *avici* hell up to the *akanitha* heaven, rejoice in the store of merit gathered by these devotees so far through listening to the dhamma, and the store of merit gathered by us through preaching the dhamma! having rejoiced, may they all escape from all the suffering of *samsara* as quickly as possible through their aspired bodhi (awakening), and reach the noble, deathless, supreme nibbana! similarly, utilizing the dhamma-strength we have gained, may we also make our own meditations successful, obeying the advice of spiritual friends to the letter, bearing even words spoken in censure, walking gentle-spokenly on this path of the dhamma, succeeding in our meditations, and may we receive the strength, power, and blessing to realize the noble, deathless, supreme nibbana through the realization of the paths and fruits of stream-entry (*sotapatti*), once-returning (*sakadagamita*), non-returning (*anagamita*), and arahatship!
with this aspiration, please recite these verses.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 143
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #143
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.59)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
"Gataddhino visokassa,
vippamuttassa sabbadhi;
Sabbaganthappahīnassa,
pariḷāho na vijjati."
From:
Dhammapada Verse 90 (Arahanta Vagga)
Dear Listeners,
Today, this Vesak Full Moon Poya Day, we all know, is a day to bring to mind the incomparable aggregate of virtues of the Great Compassionate One, the Teacher of the Three Worlds, the Fully Self-Awakened Lord Buddha. The Buddha-activity of that Supreme Lord Buddha of the three worlds was to clarify the path of practice to bring to an end this extremely long journey through Saṃsāra. In this entire world system, no event greater than that has ever occurred, nor will it ever occur. That is why we all consider this Vesak day as an extremely noble day, a memorable day.
Everyone knows that in connection with the Vesak day, we commemorate three important events in the life of the Lord Buddha: the birth, the enlightenment, and the final passing away (*PariNibbāna. Although these appear as three distinct events, devotees, if we look at them truthfully, there is no error in considering them as three stages of a single event. These three events—the final birth of that Lord Buddha who fulfilled the requisites of enlightenment (*bodhi-sambhāra*) over a long period for our sake, the realization through His Buddha-wisdom that this was indeed His final birth, and the termination of His saṃsāric journey in accordance with that realization—are what we celebrate through these three events of birth, enlightenment, and final passing away. Thus, it is a valuable Dhammapada stanza highlighting this very concept of liberation from Saṃsāra that we have chosen as our theme today.
The background story related to this stanza is connected with a certain event in the Buddha's life that evokes a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in you, devotees. We have all heard of the Elder Devadatta. He was a relative of the Lord Buddha, yet as a retributive turn of a certain hatred he harbored for countless eons, he acted in an extremely terrifying manner during the Lord Buddha’s old age, even attempting to take His life, as you all must have heard. The events regarding this are described as follows.
Shortly after his ordination, Elder Devadatta attained supernormal powers (*abhiññā*). However, he did not attain any supramundane state. As the Lord Buddha's old age drew near, a great jealousy arose in Elder Devadatta regarding the spread of the Lord Buddha’s fame and glory. Seeing that other members of the Sangha received gains and honors while he did not receive them adequately, a strong desire for gains and honors arose in him. For this purpose, he utilized his psychic powers to win over Prince Ajātasattu, the son of King Bimbisāra. By displaying a psychic miracle, he won the confidence of Prince Ajātasattu, and through that, devised a way and method to receive various gains and honors.
As these gains and honors increased, and his following grew, a certain sinful thought arose in Elder Devadatta. Thinking, "I must let the Buddha retire and take over all the affairs of the Sangha myself," he went and requested the Lord Buddha, "The Blessed One is now aged. Please step aside and hand this over to me." To this, the Lord Buddha replied, "I would not hand over the charge of this Sangha even to my chief disciples, Sāriputta and Moggallāna. It is not fit to hand it over to you." Angered by this, he harbored deep hatred and subsequently plotted to take the Lord Buddha’s life. For this purpose, he approached Prince Ajātasattu and employed an extremely subtle scheme. He planned a highly deceptive and intricate conspiracy, sending a squad of archers along the path the Lord Buddha was walking to shoot Him, ensuring that none of those archers would survive to tell the tale. However, it was not successful. By the power of the Lord Buddha's majestic spiritual power, those archers were unable to shoot. Not only that, but by His power, everyone involved was drawn close to the Lord Buddha, and upon hearing the Dhamma He preached, they all became devoted followers. Therefore, Elder Devadatta’s attempt failed.
Next, thinking, "Now I must destroy this Buddha myself," he told Prince Ajātasattu, "You kill your father, the king, and take the Kingdom of Magadha. I will kill the Buddha and take the Kingdom of the Buddha." Thus, Prince Ajātasattu, in that very manner—which is a long story—tortured and killed his father, the king, and seized the kingdom. Yet, Elder Devadatta was still unable to fulfill his part of the plan. What did he do next? While the Lord Buddha was walking at the foot of the Gijjhakūṭa (Vulture Peak) mountain, Elder Devadatta climbed to the top of the mountain and rolled a massive boulder down toward the Lord Buddha’s head. At that moment, as a miracle performed through the Buddha's spiritual majesty, two rock peaks sprang up from the ground and intercepted that boulder. However, a splinter that chipped off from it struck the sole of the Lord Buddha’s foot, causing a serious wound. A wound that bled profusely was formed.
The Sangha escorted the Lord Buddha to the park called Maddakucchi Migadāya (the Maddakucchi Deer Park). While spending the first night at that Maddakucchi Migadāya, the Lord Buddha experienced sharp, intense feelings (vedanā) that would be unbearable for an ordinary person. With His mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajañña*), and through His power of concentration (*samādhi*)—that is, the fruit of Arahantship concentration (*arahattaphala-samādhi*), which is directly connected to Nibbāna, being the most supreme power of concentration in the world that the Lord Buddha possessed—He endured all those feelings (vedanā). So much so, He endured them without any agitation. Seeing this, hundreds of deities (*devatās*) came to the Lord Buddha at night and paid special praise: "This Ascetic Gotama is a great king of elephants. He endures such bitter, sharp, and severe feelings (vedanā) without any agitation." Similarly, other groups praised Him, saying, "The Lord Buddha is a great king of lions, a great thoroughbred, a great and supreme person." While they were praising Him in this manner, the Lord Buddha too, reflecting on His own liberation from Saṃsāra, uttered a joyful solemn utterance (*udāna*) in a stanza: "Behold the power of my developed concentration (*samādhi*) and liberated mind! How feelings (vedanā) are endured with equanimity, completely free from attraction and aversion."
Then, the next day, the Lord Buddha asked the Sangha to take Him to Jīvaka's Mango Grove. When the Sangha brought Him to Jīvaka's Mango Grove, physician Jīvaka arrived quickly and applied a very strong medicine to the Lord Buddha’s foot to heal it rapidly. Even nowadays, you know, a strong medicine is applied to bring about a quick recovery. Having applied the strong medicine, physician Jīvaka said to the Lord Buddha: "Venerable Sir, I have come after administering medicine to a certain patient inside the city. I must return there now. Until I return, please let this bandage, this wound-dressing, remain exactly as it is."
So, physician Jīvaka went to the city. Having gone and treated that patient, by the time he was about to return, the city gates had been closed. Thus, physician Jīvaka was unable to return. Sitting there, he thought with great anxiety: "Alas! What a grave mistake I have made. Treating the Lord Buddha like an ordinary person, I applied such a strong medicine and came away, and now it is the time to remove this bandage!" While Jīvaka the physician was thinking thus, the Lord Buddha, perceiving his thought, said to Ven. Ānanda: "Ānanda, Jīvaka went to the city and is unable to return because the gates have closed. He is thinking that it is now the time to remove this bandage. Therefore, remove this." Ven. Ānanda then removed that wound bandage. The moment that wound bandage was removed, the wound was completely healed. The wound had healed entirely.
Thus, early the next morning, physician Jīvaka ran back in great haste and with deep concern, and asked the Lord Buddha: "Blessed One, did you experience any burning sensation (pariḷāha) during the night due to this wound?" When a doctor comes, it is natural to ask how one's health and comfort are. Now, when he inquired about His well-being with deep regret, especially feeling that he had committed a lapse, the Lord Buddha uttered the stanza which we have set as our theme.
The Lord Buddha replied to that question not on a mundane level. When a wound occurs, or due to cold and heat, such physical afflictions arise for the Lord Buddha as well as for anyone else. That is natural. However, bringing out a profound meaning from the word "burning sensation" (*pariḷāha*), the Lord Buddha declared this stanza:
*Gataddhino visokassa,*
*vippamuttassa sabbadhi,*
*Sabbaganthappahīnassa,*
*pariḷāho na vijjati.*
The meaning of that stanza is:
*Gataddhino* – for him who has completed his journey (the journey of Saṃsāra),
*Visokassa* – who is free from sorrow, who has destroyed sorrow,
*Vippamuttassa sabbadhi* – who is liberated in every way, from all sides,
*Sabbaganthappahīnassa* – who has abandoned all knots (ties), who is freed from all knots,
for that Destroyer of Cankers (*Khīṇāsava*), the Arahant, the liberated one,
*pariḷāho na vijjati* – no burning sensation (pariḷāha) exists.
In that manner, He declared in the truest sense that He remained without any burning sensation.
That means, although there was physical burning, there was no mental burning. There was no distress or sorrow. That is what is shown by this stanza. Thus, from this story as well as this stanza, we can extract many excellent events to understand the value of this Dhamma.
Those among you, devotees, who have heard or read the Jātaka stories know well the conduct of Elder Devadatta. Countless eons ago, Devadatta existed as the merchant Serivānija, and the Bodhisatta as Kacchapuṭa. A dispute arose over a golden bowl, and having lost the golden bowl, as the merchant Kacchapuṭa was carrying it away, the other merchant ran after him to snatch it. When he failed, it is mentioned in that Jātaka story that he died vomiting blood. According to that, we can understand that it was as a retributive turn of that very mind of hatred developed over so many eons in the past, and as a kind of re-enactment, that something similar occurred in this life when the Buddha attained enlightenment. He had not yet acquired any qualification to obtain the Kingdom of the Buddha. He only possessed a fraction of supernormal power (*abhiññā*). Yet, he attempted to usurp the Kingdom of the Buddha through devious means. For this reason, harboring jealousy and hatred, he sought to destroy the Lord Buddha's life, trying to fulfill in this life that very determination born of hatred. That is why he attempted to bring about the death of the Lord Buddha in that manner.
It did not stop there. Two events were mentioned here. You must have heard often about the third attempt he made. That is, as a brutal scheme to take the Lord Buddha’s life, he got King Ajātasattu to intoxicate the elephant Nālāgiri with toddy and released him onto the path where the Lord Buddha was walking. However, you have heard many times the story of how the Lord Buddha subdued Nālāgiri through the power of loving-kindness (*mettā*). Although his attempts to take the Lord Buddha’s life through three such endeavors failed, he fell into the grave, immediate-retribution kamma (*ānantariya-kamma*) of shedding the blood of a Buddha. An immediate-retribution kamma (*ānantariya-kamma*) means that when such a grave action is committed, one definitely goes to the Avīci hell. No one can kill a Buddha. Yet, he committed another grave unwholesome deed. By gathering a group through underhand means, leading away five hundred newly ordained monks, he caused a schism in the Sangha (*sangha-bheda*). That is, to appear as if he too were a Buddha, he went to Gayāsīsa, keeping associates as if they were chief disciples, and created a split in this Sangha with a false Buddhahood. That too is a grave immediate-retribution kamma (*ānantariya-kamma*). It is revealed in the Dhamma that having committed such grave kammas in this manner, Devadatta went to the Avīci hell.
However, before being reborn in the Avīci hell, he took refuge in the Lord Buddha. At the final moment, he understood something of the Lord Buddha. Throughout all these events, it is recorded that no hatred ever arose within the Lord Buddha. This becomes very clear when we discuss this burning sensation (*pariḷāha*). In the entire Saṃsāra, there is burning and running (struggling). Here, by the word *gataddhino*, something is said about the journey of Saṃsāra. After harboring that hatred, Elder Devadatta's journey through Saṃsāra was a journey completely burnt and scorched by hatred. After the Lord Buddha attained Buddhahood, He radiated loving-kindness (*mettā*) even toward those who devised such schemes against His life. That is why on His side, there are no burning sensations. Furthermore, established in His liberated mind, established in the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship (*arahattaphala-samādhi*), He endured even those severe pains without sorrow or distress.
Thus, on one hand, we see from this story how the murderous Devadatta acted toward the Lord Buddha's life, and on the other hand, how physician Jīvaka healed the Lord Buddha through medical treatments that are considered miraculous even today. You, devotees, do not need to dwell too much on the conduct of Elder Devadatta. What we need to understand through it is only the danger of hatred. It is not proper to harbor hatred thinking, "He did such and such to our Lord Buddha." Such things are what exist in the long Saṃsāra. If anyone harbors hatred, it goes on and on as a retributive cycle. That is the nature. That is the way of things. It goes on like a mere habit. That saṃsāric habit continues in the same way in various forms. That is why the Lord Buddha has declared: "By attachment, attachment is not appeased; by lust, lust is not appeased; by hatred, hatred is not appeased. It is through equanimity, the middle path, through peaceful neutrality between the two, that all of this can be conquered." As they accumulate more and more, the simile given is that of a creeper growing in the rainy season—cravings branch out and grow. Next, as you add more of the anger called hatred, it is like adding straw to a fire; there too, the fire burns.
This is precisely why the entire Saṃsāra is said to be a heap of burning sensations. In short, the reason for this running is the burning sensation. It is said to arise due to the thirst of craving (taṇhā). The Lord Buddha revealed that it is because of craving (taṇhā) that we wander in Saṃsāra for a long time. It is called *taṇhā ponobhavikā*—craving (taṇhā) is what produces a renewed becoming (bhava). Craving (taṇhā) is this desire. It has a nature of never being satisfied, never being content. The Lord Buddha declared this. There are two sides to craving (taṇhā). Through craving (taṇhā), in terms of lust, attachment, and desires, certain things are expected. One attempts to acquire them. Due to the obstacles that arise in obtaining them, hatred arises. Then, both of those are burning sensations. Next, through the futile effort made to appease them, the fire of delusion (*moha*) also burns. In this way, the Lord Buddha has pointed out three fires: lust, hatred, and delusion (*rāga, dosa, moha*).
Now you, devotees, can understand: though not at such a severe level, when a strong attachment to something is formed in one's life, until it is appeased, there is a great burning sensation—a great burning inside the mind. If someone obstructs it, then that burning of hatred, that fire, emerges. Next, one attempts to complete or appease this in devious ways. The Lord Buddha has declared that it can never be appeased by feeding it with more and more things. Instead, this can be conquered by directing the mind toward equanimity which lies between the two, by directing the mind to neutrality. However, the ordinary person who does not know this runs to appease that lust and hatred. Through that running, the fire of defilement (*kilesa*) called delusion also grows. In our sermons, we have illustrated this in many instances with a well-known simile: it is like a deer running after a mirage.
Thus, the entire saṃsāric running, as described by the Lord Buddha, is a running to quench the thirst of craving (taṇhā). The multitude of burning sensations that grow through it is what is indicated in the stanza by the word *pariḷāha*. In fact, the fundamental word, the main word in that stanza, is *pariḷāha*—the burning sensation. Thus, by this stanza, the Lord Buddha declared that He is free from these burning sensations. Accordingly, on a Vesak day like this, we must bring to mind the uniqueness of the Dhamma presented by the Lord Buddha.
Bringing to an end the journey of Saṃsāra is the purpose of this Dhamma. The fundamental purpose of the entire Buddha-Dhamma is liberation from Saṃsāra. When we say this, it means He brought to an end the journey of Saṃsāra. The Lord Buddha, when reflecting upon Himself, rejoiced in that very fact: "I have brought to an end this journey of Saṃsāra." Then, what is bad about the journey of Saṃsāra? The Lord Buddha always reminds us of its perilous side. Some people might think, "No matter how the Lord Buddha says it, we must continue this existence (bhava)." In most people, a desire for this existence (bhava) called craving for becoming (*bhava-taṇhā*) exists in a very subtle manner. It is to break this that the Lord Buddha presented various similes to arouse a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) regarding Saṃsāra. Indeed, the essence of the Buddha-Dhamma must be the sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) regarding Saṃsāra and the keen desire for liberation from Saṃsāra. One must reflect on what exists in Saṃsāra and arouse a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). Similarly, one must exert an effort, a struggle, to be liberated from Saṃsāra. One must make an effort to properly appease that craving (taṇhā) through wisdom, through realization, and through equanimity.
In this manner, the Lord Buddha has preached many relevant Sutta discourses. Those Suttas are generally known as the *Anamatagga Suttas*. There are many Sutta discourses where the Lord Buddha, by means of various similes, points out the length of this Saṃsāra, saying, "For this much time have you wandered in this Saṃsāra." When one directs the mind to them, a great sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) arises regarding this saṃsāric existence (bhava).
