Just as loving-kindness (*mettā*) helps to appease anger, the Supreme Buddha has highlighted the quality called sympathetic joy (*muditā*) to appease jealousy.
If you who live in households wish to evoke and develop sympathetic joy (*muditā*), reflect on your own child. When that child of yours studies, gets a job, and reaches a good position at some point, you feel a certain sympathetic joy (*muditā*) about it. You do not harbor jealousy. But although you think of your own child in that way, when the neighbor next door passes an exam and becomes a doctor or an engineer, you harbor jealousy. There lies the lack of sympathetic joy (*muditā*). One must apply the principle mentioned here to that situation as well. Just as it was said here, *"Mātā yathā niyaṃ puttaṃ āyusā ekaputtamanurakkhe, evamapi sabbabhūtesu,"* at that moment one has to think, "May that child, that so-and-so, be happy and well in this manner!"—regarding it as one's own happiness, and rejoice in it. That is the quality of sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
We must learn lessons from these events that we see so often in the world. It is a lesson that we learned from this event regarding Rohiṇī too. So many things happen to us. You, devout devotees, also frequently hear of certain unexpected events in daily life that shatter great hopes. The kammas underlying these are also occasionally revealed through indirect means or in various ways: how these things happened because of their bad lives, because of the unwholesome deeds (*akusala*) they performed. There is something called "kamma" spoken of in the Dhamma. The result (*vipāka*) corresponds to the kamma. The result corresponded exactly to Rohiṇī’s kamma. There is a weapon called a boomerang. When thrown at someone, it rotates and comes back to one's own hand. In the same way, regarding some kammas, their results (*vipāka*) come back to oneself. We hear of such events in our daily lives as well. To those individuals who perform grave unwholesome deeds, their results come. At that moment, it is not for us to rejoice; rather, we must learn a lesson. This is common to everyone. "Even if we do such things, the results will come." Reflecting in that way, we must bring the Dhamma close to our lives.
You, devout devotees, hear the Karaṇīyametta Sutta on various media daily. But without being satisfied merely with its sound, you must understand the meaning of the stanzas highlighted here. The Pali words of these are difficult to understand, and in this era, people do not direct much attention to the language either. On the other hand, those who know too much about these things merely highlight scholarly points and remain stuck within them, rather than presenting them in a way that can be used practically. That is the misfortune. Therefore, we have briefly highlighted a few points that can be practically implemented in daily life, as appropriate to the occasion.
*“Ye keci pāṇabhūtatthi,*
*tasā vā thāvarā vā anavasesā,*
*dīghā vā ye mahantā vā,*
*majjhimā rassakāṇukathūlā,*
*diṭṭhā vā ye va addiṭṭhā,*
*ye ca dūre vasanti avidūre,*
*bhūtā vā sambhavesī vā,*
*sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhitattā!”*
And next, likewise:
*“Na paro paraṃ nikubbetha,*
*nātimaññetha katthaci naṃ kañci,*
*byārosanā paṭighasaññā,*
*nāññamaññassa dukkhamiccheyya.*
*Mātā yathā niyaṃ puttaṃ,*
*āyusā ekaputtamanurakkhe,*
*evamapi sabbabhūtesu,*
*mānasaṃ bhāvaye aparimāṇaṃ.*
*Mettañca sabba-lōkasmiṃ,*
*mānasaṃ bhāvaye aparimāṇan’ti.”*
Next, it says: *"Uddhaṃ adho ca tiriyañca, asambādhaṃ averaṃ asapattaṃ."* Here, the boundlessness is shown. That part was left out by us: above, below, and across. *Asambādhaṃ* means free from obstacles. It is from there that we say it goes breaking through hurdles, fences, walls, and barriers. Next comes: *"Tiṭṭhaṃ caraṃ nisinno vā, sayāno vā yāvatassa vigatamiddho."* In this manner, the Supreme Buddha, in a very wonderful way, demonstrates how to build that attitude of loving-kindness, or how to liberate the mind through loving-kindness (*cetovimutti*). What is meant by liberating the mind through loving-kindness? When hatred or anger arises, it means one's mind goes and strikes against someone else's mind. The mind clashes regarding another person. What happens after it strikes? It remains there, clashing and colliding. That is what is called repugnance (*paṭigha*). When anger arises, next, one wants to vent one's anger. That is *paṭigha*—taking revenge. There is never a limit to revenge. For when you take revenge, that other person does not remain quiet either. The best illustration for this is the Serivāṇija Jātaka. Through his own experience, Ven. Devadatta Thero realized: "We must appease this anger, these minds, from within." But it is to find means of appeasing them externally that worldly beings search for various types of weapons. Reflect that: "If we are to appease this from within, it is indeed those Dhamma instructions spoken by the Supreme Buddha that we must safeguard."
On this valuable day, you devout devotees have also observed a certain virtue (*sīla*). Virtue (*sīla*) means training one's body and speech. Within that training itself, there is a certain sense regarding concentration (*samādhi*) as well, so that not only is there one's own restraint, but also no harm is brought to society. There is no need to explain separately; when analyzing a precept (*sikkhāpada*), we see that we should not be satisfied merely with the training of body and speech, but from the mind too, what we must do is wish for the welfare of the world. Sectarians like the Nigaṇṭhas said that the physical rod (*kāya-daṇḍa*)—physical action—is the greatest thing. Verbal action is second, and mental action is third. The Supreme Buddha shows the exact opposite. Saying *"manopubbaṅgamā dhammā"* (mind precedes all phenomena), he gave the foremost place to the mind. Mind first, speech second, body third. That is how the Supreme Buddha points it out.
In accordance with that, we must reflect that the meditation on loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*) is not just sitting idly in one place. Through it, great peace and blessings are brought to the world. In that way, without limiting this meditation on loving-kindness only to that meditation seat, it can be practiced in all four postures as mentioned. It must be maintained boundlessly. Taking loving-kindness toward one's own family members as the unit of loving-kindness, one then radiates it toward the entire world without any barriers or boundaries. If one lives with an attitude of loving-kindness in that manner, if some anger or rage arises in daily life, at the very least, one has the strength to appease it quickly. Just as when a serpent has bitten, if one generates at least the awareness "the serpent has bitten," that person next strives to get medicine for it. Not to kill the serpent, but to get medicine for one's snake-bite. That is how one has to think. Then, it is not a matter of clashing with that object; what needs to be done is to remove the defilement that has arisen in one's mind through that object.
Today, through this sermon, the opportunity is provided to develop the spiritual faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) namely faith/devotion (*saddhā*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*), in the manner we usually remind you in a daily Dhamma sermon. In addition, the opportunity was also obtained to extract several valuable points relevant to living with a true Buddhist attitude, based on the Karaṇīyametta Sutta. Bringing these close to one's life, one must understand that the solace we expect in various ways from external forces can be brought forth from within ourselves. If each individual leads his life in that manner, through that alone, the peace, harmony, and tranquility needed by the world will emerge.
Reflecting in that way, make the aspiration: "May this mass of merit (*kusala*) we have accumulated today through the preaching of the Dhamma and the listening to the Dhamma, serve as a decisive cause and supportive condition to end one's own visible mass of saṃsāric suffering (*dukkha*), to develop and cultivate virtue, concentration, and wisdom (*sīla, samādhi, paññā*) as quickly as possible, to fulfill the prerequisites according to the Noble Eightfold Path shown by the Supreme Buddha, and to escape all saṃsāric suffering through the penetration of the paths and fruits of Stream-entry (*Sotāpatti*), Once-returning (*Sakadāgāmitā*), Non-returning (*Anāgāmitā*), and Arahantship, thereby attaining peace in the supreme, deathless, great Nibbāna!" Likewise, may all those in this universe, from the Avīci hell up to the Akaniṭṭha heaven, including our relatives, whoever have the capacity to rejoice in the merit accumulated through this preaching and listening to the Dhamma, by rejoicing in this merit, escape as quickly as possible from all saṃsāric suffering (*dukkha*) such as birth (*jāti*), decay and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), sickness, and death, and attain peace in the supreme, deathless, great Nibbāna! With this aspiration, recite these stanzas:
“*Ettāvatā ca amhehi.........*”

(pahankanuwa sinhala audio dhamma sermon no.69)
namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa
(homage to the blessed one, the worthy one, the fully self-enlightened one)
pali stanza:
"kodham jahe vippajaheyya manam,
samyojanam sabbamatikkameyya;
tam namarupasmim asajjamanam,
akincanam nanupatanti dukkha."
from:
dhammapada verse 221 (kodha vagga)
dear listeners,
in society, we frequently hear and see instances arising due to anger and jealousy that spring up in the mind. the feeling present in most people is that they can appease the anger and jealousy that have arisen within themselves by bringing suffering (*dukkha*) upon another person. because of this, they seek means and methods that support this (external action) rather than being inclined to think of dhamma-inspired methods that help appease these defilements from within. however, our teacher of the three worlds, the supreme buddha, points out the mass of suffering (*dukkha*) and hardships that one has to undergo in this long samsara as a result of an angry mind and a jealous mind. a similar event is mentioned in the background story (*nidana*) related to the stanza (*gatha*) we have selected as our theme today.
on one occasion, ven. anuruddha thero journeyed to his birthplace, the city of kapilavatthu, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus. when they heard that he was residing at the nigrodharama in kapilavatthu, his relatives came to see him. however, his sister named rohini did not come. ven. anuruddha asked the relatives, "where is rohini?" "she is at home," they replied. when he asked, "why didn't she come?", they said that she had contracted a skin disease like leprosy and had not come out of shame. the thero asked them to bring her. due to the nature of her illness, she covered herself with a shawl and came to that place. then ven. anuruddha said, "sister, since you have such an illness, wouldn't it be good to perform a meritorious deed?" when she asked, "what should i do?", he told her to construct a two-story assembly hall where the sangha could reside and partake of alms, and suggested that rohini use her personal jewelry to fund the expenses. he instructed her to sell those ornaments and build the hall with that money. ven. anuruddha also advised that once one floor of the hall was built, rohini herself should perform duties such as cleaning, sweeping, preparing seats for the sangha, and setting up drinking water. furthermore, ven. anuruddha informed the relatives about the matter and arranged the organizational work for it. though she was a royal princess of a royal family, rohini performed all those duties exactly as instructed, built the hall, and upon its completion, arranged to offer an alms-giving to the sangha headed by the buddha.
at the conclusion of the alms-giving, the supreme buddha asked ven. anuruddha, "for whom is this alms-giving, and from whom is it?" when he replied, "this is from our sister, rohini," the buddha asked, "where is she?" he was told that she had not come because of this illness; even by then, she had not come even to see the buddha. it is further mentioned that while performing the duties related to the hall, her illness had subsided to some extent due to those performances of duties. however, because she was not fully cured, she had not come at the time of the meritorious alms-giving. the supreme buddha sent for her. when asked for the reason, she said, "because of this skin disease of mine, i did not come out of shame." "do you know the cause for this?" the buddha asked. she replied, "no." then, the buddha related the past story, saying, "this is the result (*vipaka*) of anger and jealousy that you harbored in the past."
in the past, when she was the chief queen of a king of baranasi, out of jealousy and anger toward a dancing girl who had won the king's heart, she powdered a type of stinging pod that existed at the time and sprinkled it on the dancing girl’s bed, around the bed, and on the bedsheets. when these touched the body, they caused intense itching. furthermore, she sprinkled them on the dancing girl's face too. she sprinkled them on her body as well. immediately, boils broke out, and that woman went and lay down on the bed. due to the itching substance that was also on the bed, the dancing girl experienced severe pain and torment. this is what the supreme buddha pointed out as her past kamma. therefore, conveying the idea that one should not harbor anger or jealousy even in the slightest degree, the supreme buddha delivered a sermon on that occasion, taking the stanza we have themed today as the starting point. upon hearing it, not only was rohini’s skin disease cured—it is said her skin regained a golden complexion—but she also attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotapatti-phala*).
that stanza is:
*“kodham jahe vippajaheyya manam,*
*samyojanam sabbamatikkameyya;*
*tam namarupasmim asajjamanam,*
*akincanam nanupatanti dukkha.”*
it is a very meaningful stanza. it contains a medicine of dhamma sufficient not only for a skin disease but for the entire disease of samsara. *kodham jahe*: one should abandon anger. *vippajaheyya manam*: one should dispel pride. *samyojanam sabbamatikkameyya*: there are ten fetters (*samyojana*) that bind one to this samsara. they are pointed out as ten defilements (*kilesa*) which act like chains, bonds, or hooks. these ten fetters are: the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*), skeptical doubt (*vicikiccha*), adherence to rules and rituals (*silabbata-paramasa*), sensual lust (*kama-raga*), ill-will (*vyapada*), lust for form (*rupa-raga*), lust for formlessness (*arupa-raga*), pride (*mana*), and ignorance (*avijja*). *samyojanam sabbam atikkameyya*: one should overcome all fetters—all the chains and bonds that bind one to existence (*bhava*). next, *tam namarupasmim asajjamanam*: by doing so, the one who does not cling to, or get entangled in, one’s own name-and-form (*namarupa*) is designated by the term *akincanam* (possessing nothing/unattached). if someone, by developing wisdom through insight (*vipassana*), does not cling to name-and-form (*namarupa*), there is nothing of lust, hatred, or delusion remaining in him. therefore, he is called *akincana* (owning nothing). nothing belongs to him; *akincanam* means that he has released them from the mind. upon such a person who owns nothing, *nanupatanti (dukkha)*: sufferings do not fall. the idea expressed in the stanza is that the sufferings of samsara do not fall upon him. it is a deep stanza. be that as it may, we can derive a significant amount of valuable dhamma advice applicable to our daily lives from both this story and the stanza, mainly concerning this anger and jealousy which are our themes.
it is clear from this event that just as the poisonous powder—or rather, the stinging powder—which rohini threw at another in the very distant past when she was the chief queen, came back to her, this affliction in her own body was produced. from this, we see the consequences (*vipaka*) of anger—severe consequences. just like anger, and something that goes hand in hand with anger, is jealousy. beneath that jealousy lies pride (*mana*). that is why this stanza spoke of both anger and pride. you, devout devotees, know that both of these are common weaknesses in society. when jealousy is added to anger, it becomes far more severe. here, because she was the chief queen, when the king developed a special affection for a dancing girl, jealousy arose toward that woman. combining that (jealousy with anger), she acted in that manner as if to take revenge. from this, we can see that the real cause (*nidana*) of many illnesses that we suffer from is not visible to ordinary physicians. if it is a skin disease, physicians might say that it was caused by the impurity of blood. but the great physician buddha says that it is not the impurity of blood, but the defilement of the mind that lies underneath.
the samsaric cause (*nidana*) of illnesses is not visible to ordinary physicians. it is only to the supreme buddha and to those who have attained higher spiritual powers (*abhinna*) that the samsaric cause of this samsaric disease is visible. beneath the things we often give up on as incurable "chronic diseases," there lie such grave kammas; these are called "illnesses of kamma" (*kamma-roga*). there is a saying among buddhists that a disease of kamma cannot be cured. how can such diseases of kamma be cured? we can get some hint regarding that too from this story, if we contemplate the story well.
now, this ven. anuruddha thero of whom we speak was no ordinary person. he was the bhikkhu who held the foremost position among those possessing the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*) in this dispensation (*sasana*). therefore, it is possible that he came to the city of kapilavatthu for a specific reason; he might have seen that some merit of his sister’s had matured to a degree sufficient to cure both her skin disease and her samsaric disease. indeed, one can escape from these diseases of kamma only through the power of merit (*punna-sakti*). the medicine for it is merit (*punna*). we know that when speaking of medicine for an illness, both medical treatment and nursing care are necessary. here, ven. anuruddha did something akin to nursing care. what was it? he advised rohini on a certain duty and practice (*vatta-patipatti*), and on performing meritorious deeds. when considered deeply, there is something to be grasped there too. being a member of the royal khattiya family, how much wealth must she have had! it was only a matter of telling her relatives. but how was it assigned here? "do this by selling your ornaments."
everyone knows about ornaments; it is only when household difficulties and scarcities become extremely severe that jewelry is sold. women have such a great attachment to ornaments. here, rohini was assigned to sell her ornaments. to sell the ornaments and build this hall. it was not due to a lack of money. within that, there was something that helped wear away that kamma. for it was because of the pride (*mana*) she had harbored due to (her royal lineage/wealth) that she had behaved in that manner. moreover, regarding those ornaments, she must have realized: "when i cannot even go outside with this skin disease, what is the use of ornaments?" thus, there are many aspects there. he told her to sell the ornaments and build this hall. not only that. though she might have had numerous male and female servants in those royal palaces, here she was assigned to clean and purify the ground floor while the upper floor was being built. during the construction of such a building, there is a lot of cleaning to be done. that, too, is a punishment. or, even if it was not a punishment, it was a special duty and practice (*vatta-patipatti*). through servicing the sangha, such as preparing seats, cleaning, and so forth, the past kamma is worn away. it is mentioned that simply by performing those duties, her skin disease was greatly reduced.
next, through the stanza preached by the supreme buddha, a remedy was obtained for that skin disease as well as for the samsaric cause of the mind—the cause of the disease—mentioned earlier. in short, it was the medicine of dhamma that the supreme buddha administered. that medicine of dhamma is mentioned in this stanza. what is the medicine of dhamma? the cause of this disease is not the impurity of blood, but the defilement of the mind. this stanza was spoken in order to remove the causes that defile the mind. *kodham jahe*: one should abandon anger. *vippajaheyya manam*: one should dispel pride. anger and pride work together. then, likewise, at the end, if this samsaric suffering (*dukkha*) is like this, why remain bound to it any longer? turn these bonds and hooks the other way. the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*), skeptical doubt (*vicikiccha*), etc., are things to be abandoned through path-knowledge (*magga-nana*); when one provides what is necessary for that, at that moment, the bonds of the fetters (*samyojana*) break away. attaining stream-entry (*sotapatti*) means breaking three bonds that bind one to samsara: the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*), skeptical doubt (*vicikiccha*), and adherence to rules and rituals (*silabbata-paramasa*). this stanza is designed to aid that. *tam namarupasmim asajjamanam*: here, not clinging to name-and-form (*namarupa*) is spoken of.
in terms of the dhamma, what are regarded as mental phenomena (*nama-dhamma*) are those concerning the mind: feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), intention/volition (*cetana*), contact (*phassa*), and attention (*manasikara*). next, the concept/designation (*pannatti*) of form (*rupa*) is grasped by us based on the four great elements: earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and wind (*vayo*). when deeply considering according to the dhamma the concept/designation of "i" and "mine" that one constructs through this, it is just a collection of mental phenomena (*nama-dhamma*) and physical phenomena (*rupa-dhamma*) that one takes as "i". based on the four elements of earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and wind (*vayo*), we construct this concept of form (*rupa-pannatti*). when we constantly apply wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*) to these four elements, the understanding arises that there is no core/substance in this form. although we grandly call it "physical/material," these four elements, the four great primaries (*mahabhuta*), cannot be understood individually; they act together in a very wondrous state. it is based on such a state that we construct this concept of form (*rupa-pannatti*). by then, rohini must have understood the nature of form. in this way, not clinging to this concept/designation of "i" and "mine" which is merely a heap of mental and physical phenomena (*namarupa-dhamma*)—this is what is meant by *asajjamanam* (not clinging). how does one bring oneself to such a state of non-clinging? one must abandon greed, hatred, and delusion (*lobha, dosa, moha*)—which are called clinging toward this, conflicts/clashes arising based on this, and delusions such as pride created in relation to this. when these are abandoned, there is nothing left for that person to take as "i" and "mine". such a person is called *akincanam*. *akincanam* means the person who owns nothing. as long as these clings exist, all these troubles remain. after everything is abandoned, once one reaches a state where the mind cannot be caught, sufferings/stress (*dukkha*) do not fall upon him. *nanupatanti*: sufferings do not fall upon him. this is the meaning of this stanza, if we state it briefly. based on this, let us now try to extract further points relevant to our lives.
we know that anger (*kodha*) is a very common weakness in society. this anger arises in various ways, either under the name of "justified anger" or as other sudden fits of rage. for this, the supreme buddha has administered wonderful medicines in various places. a stanza containing a very valuable and deep idea about this is the first stanza mentioned in the uraga sutta—a sutta consisting entirely of verses—and in short, the valuable book of dhamma called the sutta nipata begins with that very stanza.
*“yo uppatitam vineti kodham,*
*visatam sappavisamva osadhehi,*
*so bhikkhu jahati oraparam,*
*urago jinnamiva tacam puranan’ti.”*
the uraga sutta is the sutta that has the serpent as its simile. the simile of the serpent runs all through it. in this very first stanza, the supreme buddha presents several highly valuable ideas by using the serpent as a simile in two ways. *yo uppatitam vineti kodham visatam sappavisamva osadhehi*: whichever bhikkhu immediately subdues arisen anger just as one subdues the spreading venom of a serpent with medicine, *so jahati oraparam urago jinnamiva tacam puranam*: that bhikkhu leaves behind both this shore and the yonder shore, just as a serpent sheds its old, worn-out skin; this means he develops a liberated mind.
in this stanza, the serpent is used as a simile in two ways. the first simile is snake venom. when anger arises, one must think, "a cobra has bitten me; the cobra has bitten." when a cobra bites, one does not just stand and watch. before the venom spreads, medicine is administered as quickly as possible. that is the idea the supreme buddha conveys through this stanza. the similes given by the supreme buddha indeed possess a wonderful practical value. when a sudden fit of anger arises, one cannot stand there counting lists of abhidhamma. the easiest way is to conjure up a certain mind-born image (*cittaja-rupa*) that we can instantly evoke, as given by the supreme buddha through a simile. through that, one gains the strength to escape from anger. now, if one thinks, at the very moment anger arises, "here, a serpent has bitten, or a cobra has bitten," then through that, one has to realize: "now the mind is about to be defiled." once anger arises, it spreads. everyone knows that if anger is not subdued at that moment, it turns into hatred (*dosa*). that hatred goes on to various stages designated by different names such as enmity (*vaira*), malice/hostility (*aghata*), and aversion/repugnance (*patigha*). aided by revenge, it then continues for an endless time as hostility and enmity. thus, the snake venom has spread. therefore, the moment one knows that it has arisen in the mind, before it spreads, one must think, "the serpent has bitten," and try to treat it. ordinary people of the world attempt to appease anger through revenge. but a person who reflects according to the dhamma must strive to appease this anger from within. appeasing anger from within is the true victory.
the supreme buddha has declared that if someone quickly appeases the anger that has arisen within him, he is like one who has won a battle that is difficult to win. likewise, if one, upon seeing that another is angry, trains one's mind so that anger does not arise within oneself, then, through such an attitude, welfare is brought to both. what this indicates is that one should appease anger and rage as quickly as possible. moreover, the second simile of this stanza expresses an even deeper idea. let us contemplate how a serpent sheds its skin. to the serpent, all attachments and conflicts are felt through this skin. we all know, as seen in rohini’s story, that the moment the skin is slightly affected, one cannot even go outside. to such an extent does there exist a great attachment to this skin among worldly beings. it is through this skin that the entire world is captivated. but what happens when that skin decays and becomes old? what does the serpent do when the skin becomes old? it wedges it against some branch or something, leaves it behind, and escapes from it; it gets freed from it. that simile of the worn-out skin is what is taken here in the second place. just like shedding a worn-out skin, one must abandon anger. otherwise, if we grasp tightly onto that which became the object of anger, it goes on clashing in samsara for a long time through revenge and so forth. but immediately letting go of the object of anger from the mind is compared to shedding that skin; therefore, the second simile is also extremely important. once the serpent has shed its skin, it has neither attachment nor conflict regarding it. there is neither a yonder shore nor this shore. there is no "i", nor is there a division between internal and external. the sloughed skin remains right where it was dropped; it has no connection to it.
one can gauge the depth of the similes given by the supreme buddha from this: on one hand, the serpent's venom; on the other hand, if we contemplate deeply according to the dhamma, it is the abandoning of the samsaric bond that exists through those things like anger that we have tightly grasped. right there lies liberation. in a similar manner, the supreme buddha states in another sutta on another occasion. a question asked in verse by sakka, the lord of devas, to the supreme buddha is recorded: "having slain what does one sleep soundly? the slaying of what, or the destruction of what, does gotama praise?" the answer given by the supreme buddha is: "it is by slaying anger that one sleeps in peace." not by taking revenge out of anger, but by appeasing anger from within. if one were to use a simile: anger has a poisoned root and a honeyed tip (*mula visa, aga rasa*). the nature of anger is poisoned at the beginning, but sweet at the end. because of the sweet end, one takes it into the mouth; but because of the poisoned beginning, one meets with disaster through it. that is what the supreme buddha says there regarding anger. its nature is poisoned at the beginning, sweet at the end. so, you devout devotees can bear this in mind: poisoned at the root, sweet at the tip. if you eat it because of the sweet tip, you will fall into difficulty due to the poisoned root. "it is such anger that i tell you to destroy," not the enemy, not the object that caused the anger, but this anger that arises from within. not that person. appease the anger from within.
on another occasion, the supreme buddha gives an even more wondrous simile. it is one so difficult that one can hardly even imagine it. nowadays, sometimes even hearing it makes one feel afraid. it is a very famous simile given to a bhikkhu who frequently became angry. the supreme buddha makes this statement: "bhikkhus, even if bandits, murderers, should come and sever one's limbs, hands, and feet with a double-handled saw, cutting them piece by piece as if cutting the branches of a tree, and if at that moment of being cut, one should defile one's mind with anger, he is not one who acts according to my teaching; he goes against my advice." thus, the supreme buddha has given a wonderful simile on the value of appeasing anger to the absolute highest degree. if one gets angry even when a mosquito bites, how is one to endure when being cut piece by piece with a double-handled saw? leaving aside enduring, how is one to prevent anger from taking hold in the mind? he also points out how to control it. yet we see that the bhikkhus of old used this maximum-level simile in a practical manner.
as shown in texts like the theragatha, in those days, when bhikkhus went to the forest, they did not carry books with them; instead, when going to meditate, they bore such similes given by the supreme buddha in their minds. in some stanzas of that era, it is said:
*“uppajjate sace kodho,*
*avajja kakacupamam.”*
so, if anger arises within you, remember the *kakacupama* (the simile of the saw). the *kakacupama* means the simile of the saw. recall the simile of the saw given by the supreme buddha the moment anger comes. at least when you apply mindfulness to that, the anger is reduced to some extent, isn't it? when you bring this dhamma advice to mind for a moment, the mind that was engaged in anger is subdued at least slightly by it. that is how we must conquer these.
if we consider these practically, these are things of importance to everyone in daily life, problems that everyone faces. the supreme buddha does not point toward carrying these further by adducing various reasons like "justified anger"; rather, he points to reflecting on the vast array of their samsaric consequences (*vipaka*). since birth (*jati*)—re-birth—is our heritage, if we have to be born again and again in samsara, we will have to be responsible for them. understanding the fact that we will have to be born in various births/existences countless times in this samsara, and if we have to undergo their consequences through that, we must cultivate the resolution: "let us appease this anger and enmity." doing this is not as easy as saying it.
for that reason, the supreme buddha shows a gradual training. this is mentioned in the karaniyametta sutta, which all of us frequently hear and have the opportunity to hear. it is a wonderful sutta. because we hear it so often, to some people it has no value, and they are not inclined to think about it. they think that by mere hearing, our illnesses will be cured. because of this, one does not tend to think about the deep ideas contained in some suttas that we regard merely as *paritta* (protective chants). they satisfy themselves with its sound alone. actually, if the karaniyametta sutta is chanted properly, even by that alone, the mind is stilled—even for someone who does not know the language. that sutta is to be valued to such an extent. if one contemplates the meaning of that sutta with wisdom, through that, one can build a compassionate attitude of loving-kindness (*metta*). now, for those who do not like the word "meditation" (*bhavana*) in this day and age, they must at least try to develop an attitude of loving-kindness if they are to conquer anger. our pattern of action depends on our attitude. when a certain problem presents itself, we react to it according to our attitude. therefore, if we prepare an attitude of loving-kindness beforehand, our response can be quite different from that of a person who harbors intense thoughts of anger. as an aid to building such an attitude, we thought on this occasion to highlight a few highly valuable points from the karaniyametta sutta—which can be considered its most substantial parts, like what we call "gems"—and to instill a few thoughts in the minds of you devout devotees regarding them.
in the middle part of the karaniyametta sutta, there is a passage of this kind:
*“sukhino va khemino hontu,*
*sabbe satta bhavantu sukhitatta.”*
may all beings—*sukhino* means may they be happy and well! *khemino* means may they be free from danger, or may they have protection! there are several passages mentioned that clearly explain what is meant by "may all be possessed of happy minds! may all be happy!"
*“ye keci panabhutatthi,*
*tasa va thavara va anavasesa,*
*digha va ye mahanta va,*
*majjhima rassakanukathula,*
*dittha va ye va addittha,*
*ye ca dure vasanti avidure,*
*bhuta va sambhavesi va,*
*sabbe satta bhavantu sukhitatta!”*
there we see the wonderful way in which the supreme buddha has analyzed the term "all beings." in fact, the entire world is presented there in five totalities—that is, in five categories in such a way that everything is included. *ye keci panabhutatthi*: here, what is the first totality? *tasa va thavara va anavasesa*: *tasa* means those who are trembling and fearful. *thavara* means those who are steadfast and unmoved, or firm. you know the word *thavara*; it has the meaning opposite to "trembling." by the term *anavasesa* (without exception), its status as a totality is shown.
the entire world is divided into these two categories: the trembling and the steadfast. it appears that through the scholarly interpretations some people offer, the practical value of these terms is lost. some of those who interpret it in that manner point out that *tasa* refers to those who are not arahants. everyone else is trembling. "an arahant does not tremble"—they explain it in this way. but that does not become meaningful in daily life. we must be able to understand this in accordance with each particular situation.
to take an illustration: when a mouse is in the mouth of a rat-snake, sometimes we feel something like loving-kindness toward that mouse. we feel like hitting the rat-snake and saving the mouse. now, according to this situation, the mouse is *tasa* (trembling), and the rat-snake is *thavara* (steadfast/unmoved). the rat-snake is holding onto that mouse very firmly. to such an extent that it will not let it go. however, because of the term *anavasesa* (without exception), and because we must apply loving-kindness to both groups—the trembling and the steadfast—we have no right to try to save that mouse through indirect violence. therefore, either equanimity (*upekkha*) is applied, or a mind of loving-kindness. sometimes, things we cannot do physically can be achieved by directing a pure mind of loving-kindness, for a person who has developed loving-kindness. sometimes, it is not impossible to resolve it through the mind of loving-kindness itself. in any case, we can understand here that, depending on the situation, the entire world can be divided into these two: *tasa* and *thavara*. when taken in that way, it is highly meaningful in daily life.
next, it is mentioned: *digha va ye mahanta va majjhima*. that is according to the size of the body. *digha va ye mahanta va*: long or large. then short, or extremely subtle, or stout, or middling, and so forth; in this way, according to physical dimension. that is the second totality.
next, another totality is pointed out: *dittha va ye va addittha*, those seen and those unseen, including all of them without distinction. next, *ye ca dure vasanti avidure*: not only those who are nearby. not only those in the vicinity, but those who dwell far away too. next, *bhuta va sambhavesi va*. some people explain these two terms in various ways academically. but if we explain it in a way that is meaningful for our daily lives, *bhuta va sambhavesi va* means: *bhuta* refers to those already born into this world, and *sambhavesi* refers to those seeking birth (*jati*). here, we can think of a child in a mother's womb, or a tiny creature inside an egg. in this day and age, we have to direct our attention to those as well. it is because of the lack of loving-kindness toward them that we hear of such problems in society. *sabbe satta bhavantu sukhitatta!* indeed, may all those *sabbe satta bhavantu sukhitatta!*
next, the supreme buddha points out further in a very wonderful way:
*“na paro param nikubbetha,*
*natimannetha katthaci nam kanci.”*
*na paro param nikubbetha*: here, it does not speak only of oneself. one must also cultivate the wish: "let not one deceive another, nor do harm or wrong to another." next, *natimannetha katthaci nam kanci*. let no one, in any place, despise or look down upon another!
that is the nature of a pure mind of loving-kindness. even if ordinary worldly beings do not step forward to take revenge on their enemy themselves, when the enemy meets with disaster through some external trouble, they rejoice, saying: "ah, kamma has given him his due; don't you see? it has happened to him!" they derive pleasure from that. or else, they get someone else to do it to that person. likewise, if it happens due to someone else, they rejoice over it. what is the pure loving-kindness here? one thinks, "may i not witness such conflicts in the world externally!" not "may i not see my enemy!" rather, from a pure mind of loving-kindness, it occurs to one: "may i not witness such events!" *na paro param nikubbetha*: may no one oppress another, or do harm to another! may no one despise anyone in any place!
next, in the same way, it continues:
*“byarosana patighasanna,*
*nannamannassa dukkhamiccheyya.”*
*byarosana* means resentment. out of resentment, or with a perception of repugnance (*patigha-sanna*)—meaning an idea of conflict—*byarosana patighasanna*. *nannamannassa dukkhamiccheyya*: still, the talk is about the other. may one not wish suffering (*dukkha*) upon another! that means one does not wish to see even two other people opposing each other. such is the purity of that mind of loving-kindness.
having said all this, next comes the most valuable simile. there is no need to explain this specially to mothers. indeed, in this day and age, perhaps it has to be spoken of specifically.
*“mata yatha niyam puttam,*
*ayusa ekaputtamanurakkhe.”*
just as a mother would protect her only son, her only child, even at the risk of her own life. with her own life-span, giving her own life. nowadays, though rarely, we hear of such incidents. sometimes, during childbirth, when a dangerous situation arises threatening both lives, some mothers say: "it does not matter if i die; save the child." it is such a wondrous thought of loving-kindness that is spoken of here. *“evamapi sabba-bhutesu.”*
having given that simile, the supreme buddha does not stop there, limiting it only to that family. taking this family as the unit, using it as an illustration: *"evamapi sabbabhutesu manasam bhavaye aparimanam."* in accordance with that simile, "even so, toward all living beings, let him develop a boundless heart, without limit, without boundaries," not saying: "these are only my family members, only my relatives, only our villagers, only our countrymen, only the people of our world." as many worlds as there may be, there is no need to speak of them separately; but within these words, everything is contained.
one could perhaps write pages of academic commentary on these. but once all of this is brought close to the heart, no extra commentaries are needed. can one write a book about the attachment and love a mother has for her child? something of that nature is present here. if that simile has penetrated the heart, what remains is to develop that attitude—the attitude of loving-kindness—to the highest degree, based on that simile. no other teacher in the entire world has expressed loving-kindness of this nature. *"mata yatha niyam puttam ayusa... evamapi sabbabhutesu manasam bhavaye aparimanam."* *"mettanca sabba-lokasmim manasam bhavaye aparimanam."* that is emphasized further. a mind of loving-kindness toward the entire world: *"mettanca sabba-lokasmim manasam bhavaye aparimanam."* one should develop a mind of loving-kindness that is measureless, without any measure or boundary.
*“tittham caram nisinno va,*
*sayano va yavatassa vigatamiddho.”*
next, the manner of developing it is shown. whether standing, walking (*caram*), sitting (*nisinno*), or lying down (*sayano*)—in these four postures—as long as one is awake (*yavatassa vigatamiddho*). until one falls asleep, until sleep comes, when drowsiness approaches, or when one is highly exhausted and falls into sleep; throughout the entire day, this should be developed. how is such development spoken of? *"etam satim adhittheyya, brahmametam viharam idamahu."* from the phrase "etam satim" (this mindfulness), we see the mindfulness of loving-kindness. now, those devout devotees who practice meditation mostly know what *sati* is. *sati* means mindfulness, maintaining mindfulness. one can maintain daily mindfulness regarding postures and various other matters, and perform them with mindfulness and wisdom. in a mind where loving-kindness has been developed limitlessly in that manner, it is called *metta-cetovimutti*—the mind is liberated through loving-kindness. that means, for that mind of loving-kindness which has reached the state of liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*), there are no walls. there are no parapets, no hurdles, no barriers or foundations. breaking through all of them, this mind of loving-kindness radiates. in that manner, then, is that boundless loving-kindness. for one who has such a mind of loving-kindness, *"etam satim adhittheyya"*. daily mindfulness is maintained along with loving-kindness, without any burden, with thoughts of loving-kindness. travels, and all other activities, proceed hand in hand with the mind of loving-kindness. it becomes well-accustomed to the mind. once it is thoroughly assimilated by the mind, mindfulness goes along with it without any trouble.
to use an analogy, to a person who is accustomed to wearing spectacles, he is not even conscious of their presence. without any trouble, he looks at the world through them. in the same way, one can look at the world with an attitude of loving-kindness. there are devotees who say they have no time for meditation because of their daily occupations and jobs. now, you devotees do various jobs for your daily livelihood. is it impossible to develop loving-kindness along with those? it is true that you receive a salary at the end of the month for those things you do. it is true that the consumer pays a certain amount of money for the goods you sell. but if we have a mind of loving-kindness, we can offer something far greater than that. we invisibly give something far more valuable than the item we hand over. that is the mind of loving-kindness, the wish of loving-kindness. "may there be only good! may you be happy and well!"—offering it as if it were one's own. what is meant by "as if it were one's own"? suppose we have to serve food to someone. let us assume one works in a restaurant. the restaurant worker merely has to serve the food to the customer who comes in. but when that person arrives, the worker sees that he comes in highly exhausted, thirsty, and in distress. so, what the worker actually does is simply bring and serve the item. those goods do not belong to him. but if he serves it with a mind of loving-kindness at that moment, something far greater than his wage is credited to his account through that mind of loving-kindness. in that manner, in daily life, if we consider teachers, in their teaching, they too should not look merely at the salary. indeed, teachers of the past lived in that very manner. it was a true vocation, not just a job. in a spiritual sense, elevating it to the dhamma, they sought the welfare of the world through it. what is said here is that if one performs one's daily duties with an attitude of loving-kindness, just as a mother thinks of her child, then occupations and jobs will not be a burden to him.
generally, occupations are a burden to human beings. it becomes a light thing only on pay-day. but it is pay-day every day! one receives wages every day, if one performs those duties with an attitude of loving-kindness. let us consider the work one does in an office; through the way one handles things there, this entire social mechanism, this social machine—if society is a machine, the moment a single screw is missing, it becomes inactive. there are times when this becomes evident to us through strikes. so, strikes aside, what we have to understand is that if we work with an attitude of loving-kindness, that social mechanism functions properly. one rejoices, "i supplied the screw for that machine to function." this is not about harboring pride (*mana*) about it. how is it done? by setting aside for a moment the feeling that "this is something i must do out of fear of someone, or something done merely considering the salary to get paid," and doing it conscientiously with a mind of loving-kindness: "not only to the person who comes near me, visible or invisible, to whom i give a small helping hand, but to the visible and invisible, infinite and boundless beings, through this small service of mine, a well-being of the kind mentioned will occur." one must generate such a feeling. then, through that, a wonderful lightness arises in life. those things are not a burden. it is not a mere official duty. it is not something done because the king commands it. it is something that belongs to oneself. there is no "official duty"; in fact, if one thinks of one's samsaric liberation, none of these are mere official duties. the task that belongs to oneself is to be freed from this disease of kamma.
thus, the supreme buddha highlights for us not only these illnesses. also sudden disasters—what are called accidents—or sudden mishaps. there is no such thing as a "sudden accident" in the world. for all of these, there is some cause, some origin (*nidana*). some say that kamma is not behind everything. that kamma is not the cause. but underneath these, kamma is connected in a subtle manner. living for this long time in samsara, there is no unwholesome kamma (*papa-kamma*) that we have not done. just as we have done good kammas, we have also done bad, sinful kammas. in various instances, the wheel of kamma (*kamma-cakka*) surfaces. their exact cause is visible only to the supreme buddha and to those with higher spiritual powers (*abhinna*).
likewise, with each passing moment of our lives, what are we doing? we are wearing away the merit and wholesome kamma (*kusala*) that granted us this human life. if a person who does a job lives on the salary he received last month without thinking about the next month, he will have to regret it. why do we, who have obtained a human state of existence and are proceeding along samsara, encounter not only those dangerous diseases of kamma but also various ailments and sudden accidents? that is when the wheel of kamma rotates and comes back around. one must be prepared for that. to be prepared, we must daily, with a dhamma-aligned mind, perform wholesome deeds (*kusala-kamma*) that help, at least, to reduce the impact of those kammas, or to make those kammas completely ineffective (*ahosi-kamma*), or to wear away that kamma-energy. this is what we mentioned in the story of ven. anuruddha. within the duty and practice (*vatta-patipatti*) that ven. anuruddha, who possessed the divine eye, gave to his sister, there lies a deep secret: even a duty and practice is necessary to appease these diseases of kamma. indeed, during a time when a buddha has arisen, a time when the triple gem has appeared, those duties and practices of the dispensation (*sasana*) cannot be treated as minor things; within each and every one of them lies the power to appease the force of a person's kamma. that is why rohini’s skin disease was appeased to some extent by that alone—by performing those duties and practices.
therefore, because of that, we must understand that in our daily lives, we must wisely accumulate something without limiting ourselves to rupees and cents. the moment that is lacking, troubles can come upon us at the most dangerous and unexpected times in this samsara. one leads this life harboring great expectations. but things like sudden accidents happen. beneath them lie those very kammas we spoke of. since we do not know the medicine for them, it is fine even if we do not take medicine for each individual one. the supreme buddha has shown here that as long as this disease of kamma exists, this is the underlying cause. what exists here is not the impurity of blood, but the defilement of the mind. greed, hatred, jealousy, anger—the various defilements (*kilesa*)—are said to be one thousand five hundred by those who have calculated them. in any case, it is this mass of defilements, festering and generating forms in samsara, that creates the blind, creates the deaf, creates the lame in accordance with them. all of this is to demonstrate the capabilities of kamma.
why is one person different from another? one is beautiful, and another is ugly. even the beautiful person suddenly becomes ugly, just like rohini whom we spoke of. one must reflect on how these things happen. none of these are mere accidents. none of these are sudden mishaps. beneath these lie the causes of kamma (*kamma-nidana*). if we believe the word of the supreme buddha, having understood it, we must strive to immediately appease those grave defilements (*kilesa*) such as anger, pride, and jealousy, which are often seen in daily life, the moment they arise. just as loving-kindness (*metta*) helps to appease anger, the supreme buddha has highlighted the quality called sympathetic joy (*mudita*) to appease jealousy.
if you who live in households wish to evoke and develop sympathetic joy (*mudita*), reflect on your own child. when that child of yours studies, gets a job, and reaches a good position at some point, you feel a certain sympathetic joy (*mudita*) about it. you do not harbor jealousy. but although you think of your own child in that way, when the neighbor next door passes an exam and becomes a doctor or an engineer, you harbor jealousy. there lies the lack of sympathetic joy (*mudita*). one must apply the principle mentioned here to that situation as well. just as it was said here, *"mata yatha niyam puttam ayusa ekaputtamanurakkhe, evamapi sabbabhutesu,"* at that moment one has to think, "may that child, that so-and-so, be happy and well in this manner!"—regarding it as one's own happiness, and rejoice in it. that is the quality of sympathetic joy (*mudita*).
we must learn lessons from these events that we see so often in the world. it is a lesson that we learned from this event regarding rohini too. so many things happen to us. you, devout devotees, also frequently hear of certain unexpected events in daily life that shatter great hopes. the kammas underlying these are also occasionally revealed through indirect means or in various ways: how these things happened because of their bad lives, because of the unwholesome deeds (*akusala*) they performed. there is something called "kamma" spoken of in the dhamma. the result (*vipaka*) corresponds to the kamma. the result corresponded exactly to rohini’s kamma. there is a weapon called a boomerang. when thrown at someone, it rotates and comes back to one's own hand. in the same way, regarding some kammas, their results (*vipaka*) come back to oneself. we hear of such events in our daily lives as well. to those individuals who perform grave unwholesome deeds, their results come. at that moment, it is not for us to rejoice; rather, we must learn a lesson. this is common to everyone. "even if we do such things, the results will come." reflecting in that way, we must bring the dhamma close to our lives.
you, devout devotees, hear the karaniyametta sutta on various media daily. but without being satisfied merely with its sound, you must understand the meaning of the stanzas highlighted here. the pali words of these are difficult to understand, and in this era, people do not direct much attention to the language either. on the other hand, those who know too much about these things merely highlight scholarly points and remain stuck within them, rather than presenting them in a way that can be used practically. that is the misfortune. therefore, we have briefly highlighted a few points that can be practically implemented in daily life, as appropriate to the occasion.
*“ye keci panabhutatthi,*
*tasa va thavara va anavasesa,*
*digha va ye mahanta va,*
*majjhima rassakanukathula,*
*dittha va ye va addittha,*
*ye ca dure vasanti avidure,*
*bhuta va sambhavesi va,*
*sabbe satta bhavantu sukhitatta!”*
and next, likewise:
*“na paro param nikubbetha,*
*natimannetha katthaci nam kanci,*
*byarosana patighasanna,*
*nannamannassa dukkhamiccheyya.*
*mata yatha niyam puttam,*
*ayusa ekaputtamanurakkhe,*
*evamapi sabbabhutesu,*
*manasam bhavaye aparimanam.*
*mettanca sabba-lokasmim,*
*manasam bhavaye aparimanan’ti.”*
next, it says: *"uddham adho ca tiriyanca, asambadham averam asapattam."* here, the boundlessness is shown. that part was left out by us: above, below, and across. *asambadham* means free from obstacles. it is from there that we say it goes breaking through hurdles, fences, walls, and barriers. next comes: *"tittham caram nisinno va, sayano va yavatassa vigatamiddho."* in this manner, the supreme buddha, in a very wonderful way, demonstrates how to build that attitude of loving-kindness, or how to liberate the mind through loving-kindness (*cetovimutti*). what is meant by liberating the mind through loving-kindness? when hatred or anger arises, it means one's mind goes and strikes against someone else's mind. the mind clashes regarding another person. what happens after it strikes? it remains there, clashing and colliding. that is what is called repugnance (*patigha*). when anger arises, next, one wants to vent one's anger. that is *patigha*—taking revenge. there is never a limit to revenge. for when you take revenge, that other person does not remain quiet either. the best illustration for this is the serivanija jataka. through his own experience, ven. devadatta thero realized: "we must appease this anger, these minds, from within." but it is to find means of appeasing them externally that worldly beings search for various types of weapons. reflect that: "if we are to appease this from within, it is indeed those dhamma instructions spoken by the supreme buddha that we must safeguard."
on this valuable day, you devout devotees have also observed a certain virtue (*sila*). virtue (*sila*) means training one's body and speech. within that training itself, there is a certain sense regarding concentration (*samadhi*) as well, so that not only is there one's own restraint, but also no harm is brought to society. there is no need to explain separately; when analyzing a precept (*sikkhapada*), we see that we should not be satisfied merely with the training of body and speech, but from the mind too, what we must do is wish for the welfare of the world. sectarians like the niganthas said that the physical rod (*kaya-danda*)—physical action—is the greatest thing. verbal action is second, and mental action is third. the supreme buddha shows the exact opposite. saying *"manopubbangama dhamma"* (mind precedes all phenomena), he gave the foremost place to the mind. mind first, speech second, body third. that is how the supreme buddha points it out.
in accordance with that, we must reflect that the meditation on loving-kindness (*metta-bhavana*) is not just sitting idly in one place. through it, great peace and blessings are brought to the world. in that way, without limiting this meditation on loving-kindness only to that meditation seat, it can be practiced in all four postures as mentioned. it must be maintained boundlessly. taking loving-kindness toward one's own family members as the unit of loving-kindness, one then radiates it toward the entire world without any barriers or boundaries. if one lives with an attitude of loving-kindness in that manner, if some anger or rage arises in daily life, at the very least, one has the strength to appease it quickly. just as when a serpent has bitten, if one generates at least the awareness "the serpent has bitten," that person next strives to get medicine for it. not to kill the serpent, but to get medicine for one's snake-bite. that is how one has to think. then, it is not a matter of clashing with that object; what needs to be done is to remove the defilement that has arisen in one's mind through that object.
today, through this sermon, the opportunity is provided to develop the spiritual faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) namely faith/devotion (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*), in the manner we usually remind you in a daily dhamma sermon. in addition, the opportunity was also obtained to extract several valuable points relevant to living with a true buddhist attitude, based on the karaniyametta sutta. bringing these close to one's life, one must understand that the solace we expect in various ways from external forces can be brought forth from within ourselves. if each individual leads his life in that manner, through that alone, the peace, harmony, and tranquility needed by the world will emerge.
reflecting in that way, make the aspiration: "may this mass of merit (*kusala*) we have accumulated today through the preaching of the dhamma and the listening to the dhamma, serve as a decisive cause and supportive condition to end one's own visible mass of samsaric suffering (*dukkha*), to develop and cultivate virtue, concentration, and wisdom (*sila, samadhi, panna*) as quickly as possible, to fulfill the prerequisites according to the noble eightfold path shown by the supreme buddha, and to escape all samsaric suffering through the penetration of the paths and fruits of stream-entry (*sotapatti*), once-returning (*sakadagamita*), non-returning (*anagamita*), and arahantship, thereby attaining peace in the supreme, deathless, great nibbana!" likewise, may all those in this universe, from the avici hell up to the akanittha heaven, including our relatives, whoever have the capacity to rejoice in the merit accumulated through this preaching and listening to the dhamma, by rejoicing in this merit, escape as quickly as possible from all samsaric suffering (*dukkha*) such as birth (*jati*), decay and death (*jaramarana*), sickness, and death, and attain peace in the supreme, deathless, great nibbana! with this aspiration, recite these stanzas:
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 147
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #147
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.87)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
"Na santi puttā tāṇāya,
na pitā nāpi bandhavā;
Antakenādhipannassa,
natthi ñātīsu tāṇatā."
From:
Dhammapada Verse 288 (Magga Vagga)
Dear Listeners,
The Supreme Buddha points out that the reason we have run in this cycle of Saṃsāra for such a long, endless time is due to four perverted views. The Blessed One declared that in order to eliminate these four perverted views—namely, taking what is *Anicca* (Impermanent) as permanent, taking what is *Dukkha* (Suffering) as pleasurable, taking what is *Anattā* (Not-self) as self, and taking what is foul (*asubha*) as beautiful (*subha*)—one must cultivate the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, and the perception of foulness. The story related to the verse we have chosen as our theme today illustrates how these four perceptions assist in attaining Nibbāna.
A child was born to a poor family of cemetery keepers in the city of Rājagaha. That child was named Sopāka. When the child was just four months old, his father passed away. He was brought up by his uncle. When he was about seven years old, one day, this uncle grew furious because Sopāka had a quarrel with his own son. He took Sopāka to the cemetery of corpses (the charnel ground), bound his hands with a rope, tied a corpse to that same rope, and left him in the cemetery to be eaten by jackals. This child possessed the spiritual merit to attain Arahantship in that very life. It is mentioned in the Dhamma that it is a natural law (*dhammatā*) that a person with such spiritual merit cannot be killed by anyone before attaining Arahantship. Therefore, although various jackals and wild beasts came, they could not even get close to him. During the night, at midnight, this child Sopāka wailed, crying out: "Is there no kinsman of mine? Is there no one to save me, who am bound and left in this cemetery?" Due to that very spiritual merit and because he possessed the supportive conditions to attain Arahantship, the Great Compassionate Buddha perceived this child. Then, the Supreme Buddha uttered a certain verse:
"Sopāka, come here, do not be afraid. Just like releasing the moon caught by Rāhu, I will save you. Look towards the Tathāgata."
As soon as that verse was uttered, through the Buddha-power itself, Sopāka appeared right by the *gandhakuṭi* (perfumed chamber) where the Supreme Buddha resided. Moreover, having attained the fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), he stood before the Blessed One. Sopāka’s mother, as her child did not return home, asked the uncle, who said nothing. She searched everywhere and thought: "Buddhas know all times—past, present, and future. Perhaps the Blessed One knows where my son is." So she went in search of Him. When she approached the Buddha, the Blessed One made a psychic determination (*iddhi-adhiṭṭhāna*) so that Sopāka could not be seen. When she asked, "My child is lost. I cannot find where he is, does the Blessed One know?" the Supreme Buddha uttered the thematic verse:
"*Na santi puttā tāṇāya, na pitā na pi bandhavā,*
*Antakenādhipannassa, natthi ñātīsu tāṇatā.*"
"Sons are no protection, nor is a father, nor are kinsmen. For one seized by the Ender (Death), there is no protection among kinsmen." The meaning of this verse is that when *Antaka*—meaning Māra, or Death—presents himself, no protection can be obtained from relatives. Along with this verse, the Supreme Buddha delivered a certain Dhamma sermon. Having heard it, Sopāka’s mother attained the fruit of Stream-entry, and the child Sopāka attained Arahantship.
Next, as soon as the Supreme Buddha withdrew the psychic power, the mother saw that her son was there. She learned from the Buddha that he was now an Arahant, and she gave permission for him to be ordained. Thus, the child Sopāka became a novice monk. One day, watching the Supreme Buddha doing walking meditation in the open air under the shade of the *gandhakuṭi*, the novice monk Sopāka paid homage to the Buddha, asked for permission, and began to perform walking meditation in the exact same manner.
Seeing this cleverness, the Supreme Buddha asked him ten questions. He asked ten Dhamma-related questions, starting with "What is one?" and "What is two?" Whatever answer the Buddha expected, this novice monk gave exactly that answer. Highly pleased with this, the Buddha considered him worthy of higher ordination (*upasampadā*) solely by virtue of his answering these questions, and granted him higher ordination. This is a special event. Even today in the history of the Sāsana, a topic that those newly ordained get to read is this series of questions and answers known as the *Kumāra Pañha* (The Novice's Questions). This is also known as a special higher ordination called *Pañhavākaraṇūpasampadā* (Higher ordination by answering questions). The history of the Sāsana records this unique higher ordination granted by the Supreme Buddha to the novice monk Sopāka. The past causes and the story are shown as to how the child Sopāka possessed such spiritual merit that he was able to attain Arahantship and receive higher ordination from the Buddha at the tender age of seven.
Ninety-four aeons (*kappas*) ago, during the time when the Buddha named Siddhārtha lived in the world, this Sopāka was born as a Brahmin. He learned the arts and sciences belonging to the Brahmins, grew disillusioned with the household life, ordained as an ascetic, and lived on a certain mountain. The Buddha Siddhārtha saw that this ascetic’s life would soon come to an end, and He journeyed to that place. The ascetic was cleaning the mountain terrace. Developing great faith and joy, this ascetic prepared and offered a seat made entirely of flowers to the Buddha. Seated on that flower-seat, the Buddha delivered a Dhamma sermon on impermanence, starting with "*aniccā vata saṅkhārā*" (Impermanent indeed are *Saṅkhāra* (Preparations). Having heard this, that Brahmin abandoned the perception of permanence customary to Brahmins and directed his mind toward the perception of impermanence (*Anicca*). It is mentioned that shortly after, he passed away, was reborn in the heavenly world, and it was by the support of that very power of meditation cultivated since then that he attained Arahantship so rapidly in this present life.
So, this is the outline or skeleton of the story of Sopāka. Now let us try to extract the narrative essence and the Dhamma essence contained within this. We see that the life of the child Sopāka began in a very helpless and tragic manner. He was born into such a poor family of cemetery keepers. Furthermore, losing his father at a young age, he seemed to have the misfortune of receiving treatment from his uncle that was akin to the harsh treatment of a stepmother.
He also had to face a cruel form of punishment. Although that side of his life was harsh, those experiences, as well as the environment of his birth, must have assisted the child Sopāka on the path to Nibbāna. We often recall a few common sayings of the modern era, though they are not explicitly found in the Dhamma. One is "a blessing in disguise." Another saying familiar to us Sinhalese is "the suffering that comes is sweet as honey." Then there is also "every dark cloud has a silver lining." Sometimes, within the experiences and events of our lives that might tempt us even towards suicide, great opportunities arise to cultivate the perception of impermanence (*Anicca*), the perception of suffering (*Dukkha*), the perception of non-self (*Anattā*), and the perception of foulness (*asubha*), which can aid even in attaining Nibbāna. Thinking in this way, the child Sopāka’s birth in a cemetery environment could have been a blessing in disguise.
In such an environment, impermanence is constantly brought to mind. So too is the perception of foulness. One gets to see people coming there, crying and wailing. That brings the perception of suffering (*Dukkha*). Right there, the perception of non-self (*Anattā*) also exists. Especially, after his uncle bound him to a corpse, these bitter experiences must have thoroughly brought home the perception of non-self (*Anattā*) and the perception of suffering (*Dukkha*). We can assume that once his mind was prepared through these experiences, the moment he heard something related to the Dhamma from the Supreme Buddha, the child Sopāka was able to realize its true fruit, the fruit of Nibbāna. From this, we must reflect that in our lives too, various calamities and misfortunes come to us and those we associate with. We must turn them into blessings in disguise. No matter how many dark clouds arrive, we must try to enrich our lives and enrich ourselves with the Dhamma, at least by looking at their silver linings.
Instead of saying "the suffering that comes is sweet as honey," we should strive to direct our minds toward those aforementioned perceptions of impermanence (*Anicca*), suffering (*Dukkha*), non-self (*Anattā*), and foulness, to the point where we can say "the suffering that comes is the taste of Nibbāna." Let us also look at the life of this novice monk Sopāka; adults have a great deal to learn from young children. It is a habit of young children to imitate adults. You know that children at home put on their mother’s or father’s big shoes and walk back and forth, saying, "This is how our mother and father walk." In the same way, the novice monk Sopāka, watching the Supreme Buddha doing walking meditation, began to imitate Him and do walking meditation in the exact same clever and fitting manner. In keeping with this, the Supreme Buddha, like a compassionate father asking a child if he knows right from wrong or if he knows how to count to ten, asked him ten questions.
Due to time constraints, these can only be mentioned briefly. The novice monk Sopāka gave answers that contained very deep matters. Right away, first of all, the Buddha asked:
"What is one?" (*eka nāma kiṃ?*) As soon as he was asked "What is one?", this novice monk Sopāka said: "All beings subsist on food (*sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā*)." That is a universally applicable, common fact. The answer that everyone lives on food is what he gave.
When asked, "What is two?", he said, "*Nāmarūpa*" (Name-and-Form). Those of you who practice meditation know that in insight meditation (*vipassanā*), everything that becomes an object of the mind, the entire world, is categorized into these two divisions as *Nāmarūpa* (Name-and-Form). The profound Buddhist philosophy that only Name and Form exist here is what was taken as the two: Name and Form.
"What is three?" Then he said, "The three *Vedanā* (Feeling)." What are the three *Vedanā*? Painful (*Dukkha*), pleasant (*sukha*), and neutral (*adukkham-asukha*). Painful, pleasant, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant refers to neutral *Vedanā*. When observed in terms of feelings, only these three are found in the world of *Vedanā*. There is painful *Vedanā*, there is pleasant *Vedanā*, and in between these two is the neutral, neither-painful-nor-pleasant *Vedanā*.
When asked, "What is four?", he said, "The Four Noble Truths." That is: *Dukkha* (Suffering), *Samudaya* (its origin—the cause of suffering), *Nirodha* (its cessation—the ending of suffering), and then *Magga* (the path—the Noble Eightfold Path). Suffering, the cause of suffering, the cessation of suffering which is Nibbāna, and the path to it. That is the four.
"What is five?" To this, he said, "The five aggregates of *Upādāna* (Grasping)." As you well know, instead of the conventional designation of a "person," the Supreme Buddha explained this "I" and "mine"—this person—as five aggregates: the aggregate of form (*rūpa-kkhandha*), a heap of form; the aggregate of *Vedanā* (Feeling), a heap of feelings; the aggregate of perception (*saññā-kkhandha*), a heap of perceptions; the aggregate of *Saṅkhāra* (Preparations), a heap of Preparations; and the aggregate of *Viññāṇa* (Consciousness), a heap of consciousness. This is what is meant by the five aggregates of grasping. Wherever these five heaps are grasped, there arises the perception of an "I," a "person," or a "self." It is a perverted view, yet people take it to be so. That, then, is the five aggregates of grasping. It can be called the world of the aggregates. There too, a totality is presented, viewed from different aspects in each of the answers to these questions.
When asked, "What is six?", he replied, "The six internal sense bases (*ādhātmika āyatana*)." The six internal sense bases are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, which exist within oneself. It is through these that we cognize a world. This is called the world of the sixfold sense base (*saḷāyatana*). In short, a "world" is produced by these: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. That is what Ven. Sopāka explained as the six, exactly as expected by the Supreme Buddha.
When asked, "What is seven?", he said, "The seven factors of awakening (*satta bojjhaṅgā*)." Seven: mindfulness (*sati*), investigation of phenomena (*dhamma-vicaya*), energy (*viriya*), rapture (*pīti*), tranquility (*passaddhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*). The seven factors of awakening are a sequence of seven qualities that assist in the realization of awakening—which means Arahantship or Buddhahood.
"What is eight?" To this, he said, "The Noble Eightfold Path." This refers to right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*), right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*), right speech (*sammā-vācā*), right action (*sammā-kammanta*), right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*), right effort (*sammā-vāyāma*), right mindfulness (*sammā-sati*), and right concentration (*sammā-samādhi*)—a practice which when rendered in Sinhala can be expressed as right seeing, right thinking, right speech, right action, right living, right exerting, right remembering, and right unifying of the mind. The entire Noble Eightfold Path was matched with the number eight.
When asked, "What is nine?", he pointed to the nine abodes of beings (*nava sattāvāsā*)—the nine states of *Bhava* (Becoming) such as human, heavenly, Brahma, etc. Since it is a somewhat deep matter, we will not discuss it in length. It is presented as nine.
The answer given to the question "What is ten?" was that when Right Knowledge (*sammā-ñāṇa*) and Right Liberation (*sammā-vimutti*) are added to the eight factors of the Noble Eightfold Path, one becomes an Arahant. Through this, he also spontaneously revealed that he himself had attained Arahantship. At the end of the Noble Eightfold Path is Right Knowledge, which is the knowledge of the fruit of Arahantship (*arahattaphala-ñāṇa*) attained through that path. Next, likewise, is liberation—Right Liberation. When considered together with those, they make ten. Thus, the ten were presented. So, the novice monk Sopāka knew how to count to ten. Therefore, the Supreme Buddha authorized his higher ordination.
We have many valuable things to learn from that young child there. In that manner, he answered the points of the Dhamma very cleverly and fearlessly, evoking the Buddha's appreciation. That Dhamma story unfolds in this way. Next, let us direct our minds to the meaning conveyed in this verse. The verse mentions that parents generally consider their children as their protection. For those children, the father, or else kinsmen, stand as their protection. Or, kinsmen help the children. The child Sopāka also cried out and wailed: "Is there no one for me?"
But the Supreme Buddha declared that neither sons, nor a father, nor kinsmen, nor anyone can save one when death presents itself. There is no protection. What, then, is protection? The verse says: *natthi ñātīsu tāṇatā*. *Tāṇa* means protection. The Supreme Buddha points out that the only protection available to beings caught in this Saṃsāra is Nibbāna. It is for this reason that among the many terms used to designate Nibbāna, the word *tāṇa* is also used. A multitude of words such as *tāṇaṃ* (protection), *leṇaṃ* (cave/shelter), *saraṇaṃ* (refuge), *parāyanaṃ* (final resort), and *amataṃ* (the deathless) are used to refer to Nibbāna. *Tāṇa* means protection, *leṇa* means shelter, *saraṇa* means refuge. *Amataṃ* means the deathless.
In the past, there was an opinion among Brahmins that the gods never die because they consume a drink called *amṛta* (ambrosia/nectar). However, the Supreme Buddha also designated Nibbāna by the name *Amata*—the Deathless. How does this become the Deathless? It is a somewhat deep matter. The Supreme Buddha points out that if we are to escape from Māra (Death), we must first recognize Māra. Who is this Māra? There is a place where Māra is defined. A monk named Rādha once came and asked the Supreme Buddha: "It is said, 'Māra, Māra.' Venerable Sir, to what extent is there a Māra, or who is Māra?" Then the Supreme Buddha replied: "Rādha, where there is form (*rūpa*), there is Māra, or a slayer, or one who dies." He took each aggregate one by one. The aggregate of form: "Where there is form, there is Māra, or a slayer, or one who dies. Therefore, Rādha, see form itself as Māra. Regard form as Māra. See form as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction. That seeing is right seeing," the Blessed One declared. In the same way regarding *Vedanā* (Feeling): *Vedanā* is Māra. Perception is Māra. *Saṅkhāra* (Preparations) is Māra. *Viññāṇa* (Consciousness) is Māra. Preaching in this manner, He finally designated each one of these as Māra. Thus, seeing the five aggregates as Māra, escaping from them, and releasing the mind from them—in short, not grasping them through *Taṇhā* (Craving) and *Upādāna* (Grasping)—is shown as liberation, shown as the state of the Deathless (*amata*).
Then Ven. Rādha asked: "But, Blessed One, what is the purpose of this right view? What is the purpose of right seeing?" Then the Supreme Buddha declared: "The benefit of right seeing is *nibbidā*—disillusionment with the cycle of existence (Saṃsāra)." Then he asked, "What is the purpose of disillusionment?" "Disillusionment is needed because of the necessity to develop dispassion (non-attachment) toward the five aggregates." He asked, "What is the purpose of dispassion?" Dispassion means *virāga*. "Dispassion is developed for the purpose of liberation—the freeing of the mind, the freeing of the mind from these five aggregates of *Upādāna* (Grasping)."
