We pray that the virtue (*sīla*) observed, the meditation practiced, and the Dhamma heard today may serve as a supportive condition (*hetu-vāsanā*) to go on this journey while established in right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*)!
Recalling the mass of merit (*kusala-sambhāra*) accumulated by you, virtuous friends, through this hearing of the Dhamma, along with the mass of merit we have accumulated through this preaching of the Dhamma, and the value of that gift of the Dhamma mentioned earlier, may all beings in this world—from the Avīci hell up to the Akaniṭṭha heaven, including all the relatives of you, virtuous friends—rejoice in this merit! By rejoicing in it, at some point, may they escape from all the suffering (*dukkha*) of saṁsāra, such as birth (*jāti*), decay and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), disease, and so on, and having gone beyond that craving-seamstress, may they attain the supreme, great Deathless Nibbāna! Please make this aspiration. Recite these verses to share the merit.

(homage to the blessed one, the worthy one, the fully self-enlightened one)
pali stanza:
"sabbadanam dhammadanam jinati,
sabbam rasam dhammaraso jinati;
sabbam ratim dhammarati jinati,
tanhakkhayo sabbadukkham jinati."
from:
dhammapada verse 354 (tanha vagga)
dear listeners,
the tathagata, the fully enlightened one, introduced himself to the world with the epithet "unexcelled king of dhamma" (*anuttara dhammaraja*). from this introduction, we can understand that there is a certain supreme, victorious quality within the dhamma. the verse of the dhamma we have chosen today as our theme is one that demonstrates this victorious nature extending in several directions. it is recorded that this verse of the dhamma was preached by the buddha at jetavana monastery in response to four questions asked by sakka, the king of devas.
on one occasion in the tavatimsa heaven, four questions were discussed among the devas: "among gifts, which gift is supreme, the noblest? among tastes, which taste is the noblest? among attachments, known as *rati*, which attachment is the noblest? why is the destruction of craving (*tanha*) considered supreme?" these questions were discussed among the devas for a long time, for many years. when they were brought to sakka, the king of devas, sakka said that no one other than the buddha could answer them. it is mentioned in the texts that on a certain night, sakka arrived accompanied by devas and asked these four questions. the answer given to these questions is what we expressed through that verse. the buddha summarized it thus:
*sabbadanam dhammadanam jinati*—the gift of dhamma excels all other gifts.
*sabbam rasam dhammaraso jinati*—the taste of dhamma excels all other tastes.
*sabbam ratim dhammarati jinati*—*rati* means attachment or delight. delight in the dhamma excels all other delights; it conquers them.
*tanhakkhayo sabbadukkham jinati*—the destruction of craving (*tanha*), which is another name for nibbana, conquers all suffering (*dukkha*). this is the meaning.
to understand this, we must bring in another valuable discourse of the buddha that fits this idea, which you, virtuous friends, may have also heard. on one occasion, the buddha addressed the sangha and declared: "monks, there are these two kinds of gifts: the gift of material things and the gift of the dhamma. of these two gifts, this is supreme—namely, the gift of the dhamma." "material things" (*amisa*) refer to food, drink, and other tangible items. what is implied here is that the gift of dhamma is superior to the gift of material things. similarly, the buddha has declared: "monks, there are two kinds of sharing (*samvibhaga*): the sharing of material things and the sharing of dhamma. of these two kinds of sharing, the sharing of dhamma is supreme and foremost." and also from the perspective of helping and favoring others, the buddha has declared: "monks, there are these two kinds of help (*anuggaha*) in the world: help through material things and help through the dhamma. of these two kinds of help, help through the dhamma is supreme and foremost." therefore, what we can understand from this is that the gift of the dhamma is superior to any large-scale material gift considered as a donation in the world.
regarding this matter, the commentators also state that the gift of the dhamma is supreme, such that even a word of appreciation (*anumodana*) made using a four-line verse is superior to any large-scale donation of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites. one might feel doubtful about this. however, when we reflect upon it: just like the arising of a buddha, the hearing of the dhamma is also extremely rare. within a dhamma that is so rare, sometimes a single line of a verse can contain the message that puts an end to the entire suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara. you have heard, indeed, how the wanderer upatissa—who later became ven. sariputta—attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotapatti*) upon hearing just half a verse uttered by the arahant ven. assaji. there are many such incidents. therefore, when considering the benefits, it is no exaggeration to say that even if the gift of the dhamma is a short verse, it is of great fruit and great benefit (*mahatphala mahanisamsa*).
just as we spoke of giving, when reflecting upon taste as well, one might feel doubtful, since there are various kinds of tastes in the world that are felt by the tongue. yet, it is shown that the taste of dhamma is superior to all these tastes. so much so that it is more delicious than the nectar of the devas, which is called the deathless nectar (*amrta*). that is why, when speaking of nibbana, it is said: "*etam santam etam panitam*"—"this is peaceful, this is sublime." that "sublime" character of nibbana can be understood in several senses. for this very reason, the buddha declared: "*amatandado ca so hoti, yo dhammam anusasati*"—"he who instructs in the dhamma is a giver of the deathless." if someone instructs in the dhamma, that person is giving the deathless nectar. in short, the taste of dhamma, which helps one escape from samsara, is a taste of the deathless.
furthermore, when the buddha compared the entire dhamma-vinaya to the great ocean for paharada, the lord of asuras, he preached that just as the great ocean has but one taste—the taste of salt—so this entire dhamma-vinaya has but one taste, the taste of liberation (*vimutti-rasa*). seen from that perspective, the taste of liberation, the taste of nibbana, is present in this dhamma. that is why it was declared to be the deathless (*amata*). when referring to insight meditation, the buddha declared:
*yato yato sammasati, udayabbayam (khandhanam);*
*labhati piti-pamojjam, amatam tam vijanatam.*
whenever one contemplates the arising and passing away (of the aggregates), one obtains joy and gladness; to those who know, that is the deathless. if one reflects with wisdom, from the perspective of insight, on the arising and passing away of these five aggregates (*pancakkhandha*), the joy and gladness obtained through that is a taste of dhamma like the deathless, which defeats all other tastes. unlike the tastes experienced on the tongue that quickly vanish, this taste of dhamma keeps one alive for a long time, and ultimately helps to end the suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara.
next, regarding the attachment called *rati*, this word is most often used in connection with sensual delight (*kama-rati*). if the term is used in the sense of sensual delight (*kama-rati*), then the word *rati* is indeed something to be rejected. however, in this dispensation (*sasana*), the word *abhirati* (delight) is used in a good sense—delight in the higher wholesome qualities. this delight (*abhirati*) is shown to be something that supports one's monastic life. when it is absent, it is called discontent (*anabhirati*). therefore, what is referred to as *abhirati* is that very delight in the dhamma. that delight is shown as a good thing. if it is not there, there is boredom or aversion (*arati*); then comes a weariness regarding the monastic life, or otherwise regarding this journey to nibbana. furthermore, the delight that arises for an insight meditator through insight is described as a superhuman delight (*amanusi rati*):
*sunnagaram pavitthassa, santacittassa bhikkhuno;*
*amanusi rati hoti, samma dhammam vipassato.*
it is said that for a monk who has entered an empty place (*sunnagara*), with a peaceful mind, who clearly sees the dhamma with insight, there is a superhuman delight. by "superhuman" (*amanusi*), it means a transcending, noble kind of delight arises. it is this very delight in the dhamma that defeats all the attachments of the ordinary world, such as attachment to one's wife and children, or attachment to dancing, singing, and instrumental music. through that delight in the dhamma, a person reaches a state of great upliftment, generating joy and happiness, sometimes shedding tears—tears of joy. a great buoyancy arises in the heart; goosebumps arise. in that way, the delight that arises supports that person directly toward nibbana; it helps in attaining nibbana. you have often heard the words *dhammarati* and *dhammarato*, as well as *dhammaramo dhammarato*. *dhammarama* means a person who finds delight in the dhamma. it is because of this that delight in the dhamma (*dhammarati*) is supreme.
next, there is the matter of the destruction of craving (*tanha-khaya*). now, the world uses craving (*tanha*) as an aid to seek happiness. the buddha compared craving (*tanha*) to a thirst. if we think thirst is good because the presence of thirst allows us to enjoy delicious drinks, that is where we go wrong. therefore, the buddha refers to nibbana by the name *pipasa-vinayo*—the subduing of thirst. the state where thirst is appeased. so, in reality, thirst is a suffering (*dukkha*). however, because of thirst, we experience gratification (*assada*) by consuming those tasty drinks. yet, if at any point we completely appease that thirst, that is indeed the putting of an end to one's suffering (*dukkha*). that is why the destruction of craving (*tanha-khaya*) is said to conquer all.
in short, you have heard many times that suffering (*dukkha*) arises because of craving (*tanha*): '*tanhaya jayati soko, tanhaya jayati bhayam*' and so on. because of it, grief and fear arise. the buddha declared that where there is no craving (*tanha*), those two do not exist. with this word 'destruction of craving' (*tanha-khaya*), the buddha gave a message to the world that puts an end to all suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara. until then, the world thought that we enjoy happiness because of this craving (*tanha*), and therefore regarded craving (*tanha*) as a good thing. upon appeasing one desire, when one becomes satisfied with it, one then has to go in search of further desires.
the buddha has declared that this samsaric journey occurs due to ignorance (*avijja*) and craving (*tanha*). similarly, the buddha has shown the disadvantages (*adinava*) of craving (*tanha*) in various situations by giving various similes, showing that within this craving (*tanha*) there is an unquenchable thirst, and it is afflicted by such thirst that beings wander in samsara. there is such an insatiable thirst in it. furthermore, such is the nature of craving (*tanha*) that no matter what one obtains, it can never be fulfilled.
also, until its roots are removed, craving (*tanha*) repeatedly gives birth in samsara. that is why the buddha declared in the dhammapada using the simile of a tree: just as a tree, even though cut down, grows again if its root remains undamaged and firm, in the same way, unless the root is pulled out, unless the roots are removed, this tree of craving (*tanha*), this mass of suffering (*dukkha*), grows again and again. the buddha has also on certain occasions compared this to a creeper (*lata*), as a creeper that spreads in various directions. sometimes it is referred to as the *maluva* creeper. the *maluva* creeper refers to parasitic creepers that grow on trees. you have seen, indeed, how that creeper climbs the tree and ultimately destroys the tree itself. craving (*tanha*) is just like that.
next, in some other places, because of the sticky, adhesive nature of craving (*tanha*), the word *lepa* (plaster/glue) is applied to it. *alepa* means something smeared, a resin/gum. craving (*tanha*) is like resin. it is also shown as *visattika*, something that clings or entangles. in other instances, when pointing out the factors that cause rebirth in samsara, karma is described as the field, consciousness (*vinnana*) as the seed, and craving (*tanha*) as the moisture that helps it sprout. there, craving (*tanha*) is shown as moisture. in this way, it is explained through various similes. it is also shown as a stream of craving (*tanha-sota*), as a torrent. this is a river that flows without an end, the river of craving (*tanha*) in this samsara. the buddha declares: '*natthi tanhasama nadi*'—"there is no river like craving (*tanha*)." to that extent, it flows on and on without an end.
thus, having shown that disadvantageous side, the buddha next showed the nature of craving (*tanha*) through a deep simile, comparing craving (*tanha*) to a seamstress—*sibbani*. *sibbani* refers to both a seamstress (one who sews) and a weaver (one who knits). for what is shown there is that it is this craving (*tanha*) that helps one to be born in existence (*bhava*) again and again, from one existence (*bhava*) to another. the buddha has expressed it as a work like making a stitch or doing a weaving. craving (*tanha*) as a seamstress...
to show the function it performs, there is a passage frequently used in the dhamma: '*tanha ponobhavika nandiragasahagata tatratatrabhinandini*'. craving (*tanha*) has the nature of bringing about renewed existence (*bhava*) again and again—*ponobhavika*. *nandiragasahagata* means accompanied by delight and lust. *tatratatrabhinandini* means finding delight here and there. in craving (*tanha*), there is a nature of finding delight in this and that place. delighting here and there from time to time, it goes on creating existence (*bhava*) continuously in samsara.
and also, just as we spoke of *rati*, on occasions when speaking of delight in nibbana, the buddha sometimes points out: '*tanhakkhayarato hoti sammasambuddhasavako*'—"the disciple of the fully enlightened one delights in the destruction of craving." this means that the disciple of the fully enlightened one remains with a delight in nibbana, which is called the destruction of craving (*tanha-khaya*). some scholars of today question this matter: "isn't developing a desire to destroy craving (*tanha*) also a form of craving (*tanha*)?" some see a contradiction here. how can craving (*tanha*) be destroyed by craving? but a very good answer to this is mentioned in a certain noteworthy discourse (*sutta*). the event is described as follows:
at a time when the venerable ananda was residing at the ghositarama monastery in kosambi, a certain nun developed an attachment toward the venerable ananda. feigning illness, she sent a certain man as a messenger, instructing him: "in my name, with my words, pay homage to the venerable ananda, and tell him that such-and-such a nun is very ill; out of compassion, please visit her to see her and preach a little dhamma."
venerable ananda put on his robes, prepared himself, and went to that nunnery. however, upon arrival, ven. ananda understood the underlying motive of this nun. perhaps because of that, he preached a certain discourse (*sutta-desana*) in a way that would remove her distorted attitude. that discourse contains several valuable points we need; that is why we are bringing it up. there, ven. ananda first presented four dhamma factors to that nun:
'*aharasambhuto ayam, bhagini, kayo, aharam nissaya aharo pahatabbo*'—this is the first point.
the second point: '*tanhasambhuto ayam, bhagini, kayo, tanham nissaya tanha pahatabba*'.
the third point: '*manasambhuto ayam, bhagini, kayo, manam nissaya mano pahatabbo*'.
the fourth point: '*methunasambhuto ayam, bhagini, kayo; methune ca setughato vutto bhagavata*'.
having stated these four points, he then analyzes them. what is the first point? "sister, this body, this physical frame, is born of food. yet, *aharam nissaya aharo pahatabbo*—depending on food itself, food is to be abandoned." although this seems like a riddle, ven. ananda next analyzes and explains it. what is meant by this? we cannot live without taking food. however, the practitioner (*yogavacara*) knows that the buddha has instructed the practitioner to consume food after reflecting on it and considering it with wisdom. it is through this reflection that, at some point, even that craving (*tanha*) for food can be destroyed.
that reflection is shown in this way: "one does not take this food for amusement, nor for intoxication, nor for physical beauty, nor for beautification" (*neva davaya, na madaya, na mandanaya, na vibhusanaya*). a practitioner does not take food for play, nor for increasing manly pride, nor to fill out thin places to make the body beautiful. '*imassa kayassa thitiya, yapanaya, vihimsuparatiya, brahmacariyanuggahaya*'—merely for the survival and maintenance of this body, for ending its discomfort (harm), and for supporting the holy life (*brahmacariya*) under the dispensation. furthermore, it is declared: '*iti purananca vedanam patihankhami*'—"thus i will dispel the old feeling of hunger by taking this food." '*navanca vedanam na uppadessami*'—"and i will not generate any new feeling (pain/discomfort) by overeating." and then: '*yatra ca me bhavissati, anavajjata ca phasuviharo ca*'—"so that there will be maintenance of my life, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding for meditation." in that way, by taking food while considering with wisdom and with mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajanna*), one can attain nibbana by depending on food itself.
you might have also heard in the dhamma books that some individuals attained nibbana through the very reflection on food. it is mentioned in the commentaries that in the past, even during times of famine, when members of the sangha were partaking of gruel or taking food, some attained nibbana at that very moment of eating, through reflection. thus, ven. ananda showed there with reason the meaning of '*aharam nissaya aharo pahatabbo*'.
next, it speaks about craving (*tanha*): "sister, this body is something that has arisen. it has arisen because of craving. yet, *tanham nissaya tanha pahatabba*—depending on craving (*tanha*), craving (*tanha*) is to be abandoned." this indeed, seems to be a riddle at first glance. if this is analyzed in the way the ordinary world analyzes things, it would lead to a massive entanglement.
but here, ven. ananda himself presents a special analysis. what is meant by this is not the ordinary coarse craving. suppose a certain monk hears: "that particular monk has destroyed his influxes (*asava*) and, having attained arahantship, is dwelling therein." as soon as he hears this, this monk thinks: "ah! that venerable one has become an arahant in this manner. when, indeed, shall i also attain to that?" that thought, "when shall i also attain to that," is indeed a desire (a form of craving). but depending on that (desire), one day that monk becomes an arahant. that is how we must understand the special meaning of abandoning craving (*tanha*) by depending on craving (*tanha*). the third point is also similar.
'*manasambhuto ayam, bhagini, kayo, manam nissaya mano pahatabbo*'—this body is something born of conceit (*mana*). it is because of conceit and views (*ditthi*) that we have obtained this cage (of a body). yet, depending on conceit itself, conceit is to be abandoned. this also seems like a riddle. this is explained in a manner similar to the point mentioned before. suppose a certain monk hears that another monk—indeed, such-and-such a monk—having destroyed his influxes, has attained arahantship. this monk then thinks: "that monk has attained arahantship. why not me? i can also do it!" conceit is indeed present there: "if that monk did it, it is not impossible for me." yet, at some point, that conceit helps in realizing nibbana. therefore, that conceit is shown as something beneficial (in this context).
now, it was not even necessary to give a detailed explanation of the fourth point; just stating its meaning is sufficient: '*methunasambhuto ayam, bhagini, kayo; methune ca setughato vutto bhagavata*'. ven. ananda presents this as the very word of the buddha: "sister, this body is born of sexual intercourse. it is due to the sexual union of parents that this body of ours has arisen." however, regarding sexual intercourse, what the buddha has declared is *methune setughato*. *setughata* means like destroying a bridge—the cutting off of connections, disconnecting. thus, regarding the practice of sexual intercourse, the blessed one has declared it to be *setughato* (the destroying of the bridge). '*vutto bhagavata*'—that is what is declared. the cutting off of connections.
as soon as he finished saying that, the nun—who, in fact, even before ven. ananda's arrival, had been lying down covering her head, feigning illness (it was a fake illness, indeed)—immediately got up, fell at the feet of ven. ananda, and begged for forgiveness: "alas, due to my foolishness and unwholesome thoughts, i committed such a wrong act. may the venerable one forgive me. i shall never do such a thing again." that is how that story goes.
from this, we can understand the puzzling matter mentioned earlier. although various arguments are raised regarding the desire and conceit for nibbana, there is a deep meaning in it. however, it is recorded in the history of the dispensation (*sasana*) that certain buddhist sects, having misunderstood that fourth and final point, developed wrong views (*miccha-ditthi*) such as tantrism. but the buddha has clearly declared that, regarding the fourth point, what must be done is indeed the complete destruction of the bridge.
next, why is craving (*tanha*) called a seamstress or a weaver? an incident showing that this too was discussed among the sangha is mentioned in the dhamma. on one occasion in the deer park at isipatana, a group of elder monks (*thera*) gathered and held a dhamma discussion in a dhamma assembly. it was like the conferences of today—a wonderful dhamma conference mentioned in our dhamma literature. nowadays too, various seminars are held in different places on various subjects. now, this dhamma conference began in this manner. this is what was presented as the theme among the elder monks:
indeed, they took up a certain verse uttered by the buddha himself, which is found in a section of the dhamma available to us even today. what is it? in the text named the sutta nipata, in the section available to us as the parayana vagga—even if it was not known by the name *vagga* at that time, it is stated thus:
in that section of the dhamma called the parayana, the blessed one uttered a verse like this, didn't he? to whom? to tissa metteyya. in fact, it is called the *metteyya-panha* (questions of metteyya). this is the verse spoken to the young brahmin tissa metteyya:
'*yo ubhonte viditvana, majjhe manta na lippati;*
*tam brumi mahapuriso'ti, so'dha sibbanimaccaga.*'
a verse that is like a great riddle. its meaning: '*yo ubhonte viditvana*'—whoever, having understood the two extremes; '*majjhe manta na lippati*'—*manta* means wisdom (*panna*), does not cling to the middle with wisdom; '*tam brumi mahapuriso'ti*'—him i call a great man; '*so'dha sibbanimaccaga*'—he has escaped, gone beyond the seamstress in this world. this is what the buddha has declared.
even though it was spoken to the young man tissa metteyya, this verse was not explained in detail there; no commentary was given. because of this, discussions and debates arose among the sangha regarding the meaning of this verse. the question raised was indeed: "what is the first end spoken of in this verse? what is the second end? what is the middle? who is the seamstress?" that was the question. the question was presented and taken up for discussion in this way: "what are the two ends or two extremes spoken of in this verse uttered by the blessed one in the parayana vagga, in the section of the metteyya-panha? what is the middle? who is the seamstress?"
there, one monk declared: "as i see it, here, one end is contact (*phassa*). the second end is the arising of contact. the middle is the cessation of contact. the seamstress is craving." if someone has understood this matter correctly, one meditation subject (*kammatthana*) is completed. if this matter is understood correctly, this alone is sufficient for one to end all suffering (*dukkha*) and become an arahant. that was the explanation given by the first elder monk. the second elder monk gave his explanation:
"as i understand it, the first end spoken of in this verse is the past. the second end is the future. the middle is the present. the seamstress or weaver is indeed craving (*tanha*) itself." then, the third monk presented his opinion: "as i understand it, the first end is pleasant feeling (*vedana*). the second end is painful feeling (*vedana*). the middle is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*vedana*)—what we now call equanimity (*upekkha*), that neutral feeling (*vedana*). and the seamstress is craving (*tanha*) itself."
the fourth monk then presented an opinion: "as i understand it, the first end is name (*nama*). the second end is form (*rupa*). and the middle is consciousness (*vinnana*)." here, there is a special point: the middle is consciousness (*vinnana*). "but the seamstress is indeed craving (*tanha*) itself."
next, the fifth monk expressed his opinion in this manner: "as i understand it, the first end is the six internal sense-bases (*ajjhattika ayatana*)—meaning, my virtuous friends, the six internal bases: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. the second end is the six external sense-bases (*bahira ayatana*): form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and thoughts (dhamma), which are the objects of the internal bases. the middle is consciousness (*vinnana*). the seamstress is craving (*tanha*)."
then, the sixth monk expressed his opinion: "as i understand it, the first end, the first extreme is identity (*sakkaya*). the buddha defines *sakkaya* as a name for the five aggregates of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*). you know, indeed, that the five aggregates of grasping are form, feeling (*vedana*), perception, preparations (*sankhara*), and consciousness (*vinnana*). when those five aggregates of grasping are taken together with a view about them, that is called the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*)—the assumption that those five exist (as a self). that is the first end. next, the second end is the arising of identity (*sakkaya-samudaya*). next, the middle is the cessation of identity (*sakkaya-nirodha*). the seamstress who weaves this is craving."
thus, having analyzed these six opinions in this way, since there was a difference of opinion, a unanimous decision was reached among these monks: "among us, as a result of this conference, six opinions have been presented. let us go to the blessed one and ask which of these is correct." the monks went to the buddha and presented this report—the conference report.
the buddha declared: "monks, all six opinions you have expressed are correct when viewed from their respective angles. they are all correct. *sabbam sanghassa subhasitam pariyayena*—what you six have declared is correctly spoken in an expositional sense (*pariyaya*), when looked at from each respective angle. however, on that day, when declaring this matter to the young man metteyya, what i intended was that first point: contact (*phassa*) is one end, the arising of contact is the other end, the cessation of contact is in the middle, and the seamstress is craving (*tanha*). it is with that meaning that i declared it."
now, what remains for us is to try to understand these points discussed in the conference, each according to our own capacity. even if we do not give a complete exposition, if we give a hint from these, the practicing devotees (*yogavacara*) here who practice meditation can take that as a meditation subject (*kammatthana*), and will be able to personally realize the fact that each of these supports the attainment of nibbana.
now let us look at the first explanation. indeed, the explanation the buddha declared as fitting in every way is this very one: contact (*phassa*) is the first end; the arising of contact is the second end; the cessation of contact is in the middle. this is generally difficult to understand. we think of contact (*phassa*) as something that arises from the coming together and collision of the sense organ and the object. but the nature of craving (*tanha*) is such that, as we said, craving (*tanha*) knits them together.
it leaps from one to another. the teachers of old declared that in samsara, one is constantly on the side of arising (*samudaya*). the side of arising means forgetting cessation (*nirodha*). according to the buddha's word, all these things are arisings and passings away—*samudaya-vaya*. you have heard the word *udayabbaya*. in everything, there is an arising and a passing away. however, the ordinary samsaric being forgets the passing away, forgets cessation, forgets the wearing away, and is inclined to renew it again and again.
that is what is done; that is why it is called renewed existence (*punabbhava*). next, *nandiragasahagata*—because of that delight and lust, one brings up that pleasant feeling (*vedana*) again and again. one forgets that it ceases; one forgets its impermanence (*anicca*). contact (*phassa*) and the arising of contact are the two ends. in the middle is the cessation of contact (*phassa-nirodha*). one leaps over it. one forgets the cessation of contact that lies in the middle.
we can understand this through this simile. suppose someone gets a piece of delicious cake. whether it be a small child or a needy person, they greedily swallow the piece of cake all at once, saying "it is delicious." instead of that, if one eats it slowly, reflecting on it in the manner mentioned before, then one personally experiences how even that pleasant feeling (*vedana*) of taste arises and passes away, how it wears away. the cessation (*nirodha*)—the fact that there is no 'thing' there—is grasped by the mind. it is because of lust and attachment that this cessation (*nirodha*) is not grasped by us. that is the secret.
then, what does this seamstress do? she leaps and bounds. you can compare the activity of this seamstress to the needle of a sewing machine leaping up and down. what is the function of the bobbin thread (under-thread) in a sewing machine? what is done by the under-thread? just as one grasps something in terms of craving (*tanha*), conceit (*mana*), and views (*ditthi*), the under-thread leaps forward, and when the needle goes down, it forms a knot. that is how the stitching proceeds. then a long seam is formed. that is the seam of samsara, how the stitch is made. in weaving or knitting, the same thing happens. when knitting, taking one strand or two, one pulls it and goes on making knots. as long as those knots are cast, that knitting extends. that is the kind of thing that happens in samsara.
grasping (*upadana*) gets its place because of craving (*tanha*). next to craving (*tanha*) is grasping (*upadana*). it is that grasping (*upadana*) that is done under the sewing machine, by the under-thread. thus, caught by that under-thread, we remain under that seamstress for a long time in samsara. this can be understood even through this matter of contact (*phassa*), even if the other points are not considered.
there is a certain short passage in the discourses (*sutta-desana*) expressing insight. if we cite that verse here as an example: '*phussa phussa vayam passam, evam tattha virajjati*'. *phussa phussa* means with every instance of contact (*phassa*), one sees its passing away (*vaya*). "seeing the passing away with each contact, one becomes dispassionate toward it." then, dispassion (*viraga*) arises; non-attachment arises.
when you slowly eat that piece of cake, it mixes with saliva and ultimately becomes repulsive. the perception (*sanna*) of taste that you took is ended right there. when eating it again, the same thing happens. that is what happens when seeing that cessation (*nirodha*): '*phussa phussa vayam passam*'. when one understands the true meaning of this food through reflection as mentioned before, so that one can see that cessation (*nirodha*), and does this with non-attachment, then one understands that there is no taste in what was swallowed greedily all at once, thinking 'it is delicious.' it is not there either. the taste is not in the piece of cake, nor is it in the tongue. it is an illusion, something created by the mind—thinking 'this cake is delicious'—arising due to that contact (*phassa*) and the quickness of craving (*tanha*) to bring up that contact again and again.
thus, it is not impossible to become an arahant even through a piece of cake, if one eats it after reflecting in that manner: '*phussa phussa vayam passam*'—seeing its passing away with every contact (*phassa*).
let us stop there with that point. since there are several other points to mention, next let us look at the second interpretation. the past is one end; the future is the second end. this will be easy to understand. in the middle is the present (*paccuppanna*). think about it for a moment: you, virtuous friends, have developed some wish to buy a vehicle or build a house. you think about the provisions for it. all of those are ready in the future. now, perhaps, that castle in the air is already built. you forget about the debt. craving (*tanha*) knits together the past and the future, making you forget the present.
that is why you have heard so much about the story of bhagineyya sangharakkhita, which we mentioned on another occasion. the pupil of that monk sangharakkhita, having become discontented with his teacher, thought: "now i must disrobe. having disrobed, i will become a layman, go on like this, and finally get married and have a child." having generated such a story in his mind as a form of conceptual proliferation (*papanca*), while fanning his teacher with a palm-leaf fan, he struck his teacher on the head, thinking that his wife had dropped the child. in that way, through conceptual proliferation (*papanca*), the present is ultimately forgotten. such a thing happens. that is how craving (*tanha*) knits together the two ends while forgetting (the middle). that is easy to understand. that is the second one.
next, the third one is between pleasant feeling (*vedana*) and painful feeling (*vedana*). the buddha has declared that an untaught worldling (*puthujjana*) afflicted by painful feeling (*vedana*) yearns for pleasant feeling (*vedana*). what is the reason? apart from pleasant feeling (*vedana*), the ordinary worldling does not know of any escape from painful feeling (*vedana*). this means that the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*vedana*) in the middle is not understood by that person at all. the being bound by ignorance (*avijja*) has no understanding of that peaceful, neither-painful-nor-pleasant equanimity (*upekkha*) in the middle. that is what the buddha points out here.
so, what that person does is play on a seesaw between pleasure and pain. when pleasant feeling (*vedana*) ends, they bring it up again. then next comes painful feeling (*vedana*). as long as pleasant feeling is present, it is pleasant; when it is absent, it is painful. then they bring it up again. thus, there is a seesaw play between pleasure and pain. the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling in the middle—that neutral feeling (*vedana*)—is not understood by that person. it is in the middle. why is it not understood? by whom is this done? by that very seamstress. she leaps and bounds. in the world, one constantly rolls back and forth between pleasure and pain. she makes one forget about what is in the middle. through serenity concentration (*samatha-jhana*), the happiness within that state can be understood at the level of concentration (*samadhi*). such is the case regarding feeling (*vedana*). this too will be somewhat easy for you, virtuous friends, to understand.
next, with what follows, perhaps something deep might be explained: between name and form (*nama* and *rupa*). the term 'name' (*nama*), apart from the practicing devotees (*yogavacara*), might not be understood immediately by ordinary people. where the buddha explains the phenomena of name-and-form (*namarupa*), he states that 'name' (*nama*) consists of five factors connected with the mind: feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), volition (*cetana*), contact (*phassa*), and attention (*manasikara*). you know feeling, perception, and volition, along with contact and attention. these five are shown as mental phenomena (*nama-dhamma*). next, form (*rupa*) is analyzed, as you, virtuous friends, may have heard, in terms of the great elements (*mahabhuta*): earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and air (*vayo*). it is based on these that one develops a perception of form (*rupa-sanna*). thus, the world sees only these two: name and form. in between these two, name-and-form (*namarupa*), lies consciousness (*vinnana*). why is that? because both of these are connected to consciousness (*vinnana*). those mental factors present in name—feeling (*vedana*), perception, volition, contact (*phassa*), and attention—arise through consciousness (*vinnana*) itself.
next, what we recognize as form (*rupa*). we do not understand this in a physical sense, but in accordance with the dhamma. what do we take as the earth element (*pathavi*) there? it is through characteristics of hardness and softness. there, we use mental factors (*nama-dhamma*) even to understand form-phenomena (*rupa-dhamma*). through characteristics of hardness and softness, we generate the perception of earth (*pathavi*). next, through characteristics of cohesion and liquidity, we recognize the water element (*apo*). next, through characteristics of heat and cold, we recognize the fire element (*tejo*). through characteristics of movement and distension, we recognize the air element (*vayo*).
thus, that perception of form (*rupa-sanna*) grasped by our mind is ultimately what remains as form (*rupa*). in between those two lies consciousness (*vinnana*). the commentators of the past even point out that name and form (*nama* and *rupa*) proceed in relation to each other. they support each other; neither can stand alone.
the commentators present an ancient simile. the journey of name and form (*nama* and *rupa*) in samsara is shown as a journey of a blind man who can walk and a lame man who can see. riding on the shoulders of the blind man who can walk but cannot see is the lame man. although he cannot walk, he can see. so, this person walks according to the path indicated by him. it is said that this samsaric journey is like the journey of this blind man and the lame man. but if one understands at some point, in between both of these lies consciousness (*vinnana*). this is a matter that is very difficult to understand.
if we give another common simile—we say this having considered it, and not by way of disparaging, but to make it easy for you, virtuous friends, to understand—suppose a dog crossing a single-log bridge sees its reflection in the water. for a moment, it forgets that it is the nature of water to reflect. it assumes that there is a dog in the water—a water dog. so, it reacts to this water dog. either it growls, or it wags its tail, or otherwise, it keeps looking again and again with curiosity. the dog does not know that it is because it looks that the other dog appears. thinking it is a visible dog, it looks. here, that looking dog represents the mental phenomena (*nama-dhamma*). the visible dog is that form (*rupa*). in between both of them lies that reflecting nature of the water.
thus, my virtuous friends, within consciousness (*vinnana*), there is a reflecting nature like that. that is what we meant by reflection (*paccavekkhana*). it is this very thing: within this illusory consciousness (*vinnana*), there is a reflecting nature; if one does not reflect correctly, one gets caught in it. that is unradical attention (*ayoniso manasikara*). if one reflects incorrectly, like that dog, one has to remain right there on the single-log bridge, wagging its tail or growling. because that dog does not know the difference between the visible dog and the looking dog. the journey of name and form (*nama* and *rupa*) is just like that.
thus, that consciousness (*vinnana*) lies in the middle, and this reflecting nature of consciousness (*vinnana*) is not obvious to the ordinary world. the insight meditator must understand it through contemplation. in insight, by contemplating everything, applying the effort of rapid contemplation, one does so to personally realize it for oneself.
just saying this in words is not enough. at some point in the understanding of name-and-form (*namarupa*), instead of taking the mixture of name and form as a single unit, one understands at some point: "it is because of name (*nama*) that form (*rupa*) exists, and because of form (*rupa*) that name (*nama*) exists. in the middle of this lies the illusory consciousness (*vinnana*)." it is from this mind itself, through the mental factors (*nama-dhamma*) such as hardness and softness, that one understands form. next, for the mental factors to bring up feeling (*vedana*), perception, and so on, it is that very perception of form (*rupa-sanna*) that helps us. these support each other. so, this is the journey of the blind man and the lame man. if someone thinks of stopping this samsaric journey, it is like the lame man realizing this at some point. then indeed, one strives to understand name-and-form (*namarupa*) with wisdom in that manner. that is the analysis of name-and-form (*namarupa*).
the same applies to what was said about the sense-bases (*ayatana*). the six internal bases (*ajjhattika ayatana*), as mentioned, are eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. next, the six external bases (*bahira ayatana*) are form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and thoughts (dhamma). what helps to understand this is the simile of the mirage, which we all hear often and which we have to apply. the deer does not know that it is a mirage. the deer thinks it is water. it assumes that the sight seen in the mirage is water. thus, it assumes that the external base is present there as it appears.
the deer has no idea that the eye is the internal base here, and that it is running because of that consciousness (*vinnana*) reflecting the image fallen on the eye. it has no understanding of consciousness (*vinnana*) in the middle. therefore, the deer runs from here to catch that water. from this, you, virtuous friends, can understand the operation of the mirage.
that is what is meant by saying that consciousness (*vinnana*) lies in the middle, between the six internal bases and the six external bases. and what knits them together is craving (*tanha*)—that thirst. a mirage is called *mrgathrsnika* (deer-thirst). it is indeed craving (*tanha*). because of the deer's thirst, it runs. it runs after that image falling on its eye, which it sees. these are the kinds of things regarding those six. indeed, the buddha applies the word 'mirage' to all perceptions (*sanna*). every perception generated based on form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and thoughts (dhamma) is shown as a mirage, which, because of craving (*tanha*) and the impulse of craving (*tanha*), worldlings divide into two and chase after.
next, the final one is somewhat deep. identity (*sakkaya*), as we mentioned earlier, is the five aggregates of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*) itself. these five aggregates of grasping that we hold onto—form, feeling (*vedana*), perception, preparations (*sankhara*), and consciousness (*vinnana*)—are built up moment by moment. although it is not visible to us, the five aggregates of grasping you had when you arrived at this place are not what you have now. now, they have piled up. that piling up is called accumulation (*upacaya*). they accumulate. they accumulate because one grasps those passing experiences as 'mine' in terms of craving (*tanha*), conceit (*mana*), and views (*ditthi*). in that way, piles of grasping (*upadana*) accumulate.
the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*) means taking the five aggregates of grasping as a self: "form is my self," "feeling (*vedana*) is my self," or "the self possesses form," and so forth in various ways. it is twenty-fold. it is called *sakkaya-ditthi*. in twenty ways, one conceptualizes form, feeling (*vedana*), perception, preparations (*sankhara*), and consciousness (*vinnana*) as 'i' and 'mine'. furthermore, ordinary worldlings develop a perception of permanence (*nicca-sanna*) regarding them. consequently, due to not knowing that cessation (*nirodha*) in the middle—that is, their nature of wearing away—they generate a perception of permanence. one who has developed the vision of impermanence (*anicca*) understands: "this eye is impermanent (*anicca*), forms are impermanent (*anicca*), the contact (*phassa*) arising due to them is impermanent (*anicca*), and the feeling (*vedana*) arising due to them is impermanent (*anicca*)."
when impermanence (*anicca*) is developed in that way, instead of the accumulation of the five aggregates of grasping, a wearing away occurs. they begin to wear away. but this happens only after seeing that cessation (*nirodha*). that is why identity (*sakkaya*) is one end. the arising of identity (*sakkaya-samudaya*)—just like what was said about the arising of contact (*phassa-samudaya*)—which is the repeated arising of identity, is the other end. the knitting together of these two is done by craving (*tanha*), while disregarding the cessation of identity (*sakkaya-nirodha*). thus, we can see the work done by the seamstress. next, we have to mention, using that same simile, how the work done by this seamstress with the under-thread is understood by the insight meditator at some point. when you, virtuous friends, are sewing on a sewing machine at home, if the under-thread suddenly runs out, then immediately after the under-thread runs out, it looks from the outside as if it has been sewn. but the two pieces of cloth remain separated; they are not sewn together.
for the insight meditator, at some point, through that perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*), the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-nana*) emerges. having seen both arising and passing away, one gradually seeks to escape from this. on the other hand, the person who is keen on carrying on samsara continuously looks at the arising (*samudaya*): "indeed, the sun set this evening, but it will rise tomorrow morning; there is nothing to fear. true, the sun set today, but it rises in the morning. this went wrong, yes, this happened. but the next one will be right. this lottery ticket didn't win. the next one will." in that way, through that, they carry it on and on.
however, if one understands the cessation (*nirodha*) of these and maintains that understanding continuously, the state where this becomes intense is called the knowledge of dissolution (*bhanga-nana*). that is what we have to contemplate, in the manner mentioned earlier: '*phussa phussa vayam passam*'—seeing the cessation (*nirodha*) with every contact (*phassa*). when insight meditation becomes so intense that even the thoughts arising in the mind are seen as breaking up (dissolving),
then that path of insight is put into action, and ultimately, through dispassion (*viraga*), revulsion (*nibbida*), weariness with samsara, liberation (*vimutti*) finally occurs. it is at that moment of liberation that it is like the under-thread running out—something like a stitch proceeds, but it is not sewn together. if it were sewn, it could be analyzed according to time and space, as they say nowadays. but a very wonderful thing happens, which cannot be caught by time or caught by space. that is what is called supramundane (*lokuttara*). that, my virtuous friends, is the supramundane state. there, the mind, having freed itself from that grasping (*upadana*), freed itself from the under-thread, reaches a wonderfully peaceful and sublime state at the moment of the attainment of fruition (*phala-samapatti*).
that is what we have to draw from that simile. the state where the work of that craving-seamstress who delights here and there is suspended is the attainment of fruition (*phala-samapatti*). then, that is liberation. therefore, when we speak of nibbana as the destruction of craving (*tanha-khaya*), whatever words are used, we must accept that the ultimate purpose of this dispensation (*sasana*) is indeed liberation (*vimutti*).
there is this great mass of suffering (*dukkha*) called pain. the buddha declared: "i do not declare anything else, nor an eternal existence, but suffering (*dukkha*) and the cessation of suffering (*dukkha-nirodha*). that is my entire message." the world complains about suffering (*dukkha*). i gave the solution for it—cessation (*nirodha*). apart from that, this is not an eternal, permanent self-nature (*atta-sabhava*) or anything of the sort. that is the essence of the vision of non-self (*anatta*).
when the buddha compared this entire true dhamma (*saddhamma*) to a sal tree, in the simile of the sal tree, he compared the leaves, twigs, etc., to virtue (*sila*), and went on declaring the various parts of the dhamma in that manner. ultimately, what is the heartwood of the sal tree? it is that state of nibbana known as the unshakeable liberation of mind (*akuppa cetovimutti*). it is the completely liberated mind that is unprovoked, unmoving, and freed from that grasping (*upadana*) mentioned earlier.
in that liberated mind, there is neither this end, nor that end, nor is there a middle. that is what is mentioned in the bahiya sutta: '*n'ev'idha na huram na ubhayantare*'—neither here, nor there, nor in between both. '*esev'anto dukkhassa*'—this itself is the end of suffering (*dukkha*).
that dhamma, which the great ascetic bahiya personally realized through that short passage of the buddha's word, is what we have been explaining in various ways for this past hour. thus, nibbana lies right there. our ultimate goal as buddhists is that nibbana which is personally realized through the wonderful attainment of the fruition of arahantship (*arahattaphala-samapatti*)—which is like a visual field without a horizon, having neither the two ends mentioned earlier, nor the middle. apart from that, we must understand that it is not something that various people imagine it to be.
we pray that the virtue (*sila*) observed, the meditation practiced, and the dhamma heard today may serve as a supportive condition (*hetu-vasana*) to go on this journey while established in right view (*samma-ditthi*)!
recalling the mass of merit (*kusala-sambhara*) accumulated by you, virtuous friends, through this hearing of the dhamma, along with the mass of merit we have accumulated through this preaching of the dhamma, and the value of that gift of the dhamma mentioned earlier, may all beings in this world—from the avici hell up to the akanittha heaven, including all the relatives of you, virtuous friends—rejoice in this merit! by rejoicing in it, at some point, may they escape from all the suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara, such as birth (*jati*), decay and death (*jaramarana*), disease, and so on, and having gone beyond that craving-seamstress, may they attain the supreme, great deathless nibbana! please make this aspiration. recite these verses to share the merit.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 151
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #151
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.46)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
"Hanti bhogā dummedhaṃ,
no ca pāragavesino;
Bhogataṇhāya dummedho,
hanti aññe’va attanaṃ."
From:
Dhammapada Verse 355 (Taṇhā Vagga)
Dear Listeners,
The acquisition of worldly wealth and prosperity is generally considered in the world as a stroke of luck, a great fortune. However, the foolish person, overcome by craving (*taṇhā*) for material possessions, brings about disaster from within that very prosperity. A person whose mind is possessed by craving (*taṇhā*) for possessions and the rust of stinginess is driven to the brink of self-destruction due to that very miserliness, just as if he were being destroyed by others. That is why in the Dhamma, stinginess is described as a "rust." Through rust, the mind becomes impure and inactive. Thus, a story of a person who destroyed his life and ruined his own progress through such stinginess is presented as the origin story (*nidāna kathā*) for the verse chosen as today’s theme.
On one occasion, when the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana monastery, King Pasenadi of Kosala came to see him at midday. The Buddha asked, "Why, Great King, have you come at this midday hour, an unusual time? From where have you come?" Then the king replied, "The treasurer (*seṭṭhi*) of Sāvatthi has passed away. Since he died childless, I have spent the day organizing the confiscation of his wealth to the royal treasury, and I am coming straight from there." The king also shared some details about the treasurer's life: "That treasurer possessed nearly ten million in gold coins alone; there is no need to even speak of silver. Despite possessing such vast wealth, this treasurer daily ate only broken rice and sour gruel. For clothing, he wore a coarse hempen garment made of three pieces stitched together. He traveled in a dilapidated chariot under a canopy of leaves. He lived such a miserable and wretched life." Hearing this, the Buddha explained, one by one, the past kamma that caused this treasurer's anomalous lifestyle as follows:
"Great King, in a past life, when this treasurer was also a wealthy householder, a Pacceka Buddha named Tagarasikhi arrived at his residence. The householder ordered his household members, 'Give alms-food to this ascetic,' and then rose from his seat and went away. After the alms-food was given, a sense of regret arose in his mind: 'If I had given this food to a servant or a laborer, I could have gotten some work done. By giving it to this ascetic, it was wasted in vain.' The Buddha also revealed another incident that occurred in that same past life. He murdered his brother's only son to acquire his brother's wealth—that is, after the brother passed away, only that child remained, and he killed the child to make the entire estate his own. That was a grave unwholesome act. Yet, so powerful was the merit-energy (*āniśaṃsa*) of his mere word ordering that alms-food be given to the Pacceka Buddha, that he was born seven times in the heavenly worlds, and seven times held the post of treasurer in this very city of Sāvatthi, solely due to the wholesome potential of that brief instruction. However, because of his subsequent regret, that wholesome deed was defiled. As a result, although he attained the status of a treasurer, his mind would not lean toward enjoying those riches; he could not bring himself to enjoy good food, clothing, or vehicles, and his mind was not inclined toward the five cords of sensual pleasure, precisely due to that lingering stinginess."
Furthermore, as a result of murdering his brother's young son, he boiled in hell for hundreds of thousands of years, and as a residual consequence (*vipāka*) of that deed, he lived seven lifetimes completely childless—such that all his vast treasures eventually went to the royal treasury upon his death. The Buddha declared this. Next, the Buddha revealed that the merit this treasurer had accumulated in the past is now completely exhausted. Since he did not accumulate any new merit, he is at this very moment boiling in the Mahāroruva hell. When the Buddha described this terrifying destiny in accordance with kamma, the King exclaimed, "Bhante, how tragic this is! Even though he possessed such enormous wealth, he did not enjoy it himself, nor did he use it for meritorious deeds when the Buddha was living so close to him." It was at that moment that the Buddha spoke the aforementioned verse containing the message: "Yes, Great King, a person with craving (*taṇhā*) for wealth destroys himself in this manner, and does not direct his mind toward Nibbāna."
*“Bhogā dummedhaṃ hanti, no ca pāragavesino”*
*Dummedha* means the foolish person. Worldly wealth and possessions destroy the foolish person; they are ruined by those very riches. *“No ca pāragavesino”*—but those who seek the further shore, who seek Nibbāna, are not destroyed by wealth and prosperity in this way. Next,
*“Bhogataṇhāya dummedho, hanti aññeva attanaṃ”*
Due to craving (*taṇhā*) for wealth, craving for worldly prosperity, that foolish person brings about his own destruction, just as if others were destroying him. This is the meaning of that Dhamma verse. Based on this story, we can extract many highly valuable lessons. All these devout, merit-seeking Buddhists should reflect on why one is called a *'pinvatā'* (a fortunate or merit-endowed person). This is a common idiom in our language. A *'pinvatā'* is defined as someone who possesses merit (*puñña*). Among the meritorious deeds mentioned in this Dispensation, the very first to be enumerated is the meritorious act of giving (*dāna*). You all know well that when the bases of meritorious activity (*puñña-kiriya-vatthu*) are shown, they are giving (*dāna*), virtue (*sīla*), and mental development (*bhāvanā*). Where the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgaha-vatthu*) are shown, they are giving, kindly speech, useful conduct, and impartiality. Among the perfections (*pāramitā*), giving is foremost. Among the ten bases of meritorious action (*dasa-puñña-kiriya-vatthu*), giving is at the beginning. In all these contexts, giving is presented as the primary discipline. You have often heard that for a gift to yield great fruit and great benefit (*mahatphala mahānisaṃsa*), one must give with the 'threefold mind' (the three thoughts). The threefold mind refers to: the intention (*cetanā*) generated before giving, the state of mind and thought prevailing at the moment of giving, and one's attitude and thought regarding it after having given. When all three are complete, only then can it be considered an entirely complete gift of great fruit and great benefit. This concept of the 'threefold mind' is explained in the Dhamma through a verse:
> *Pubbeva dānā sumano, dadaṃ cittaṃ pasādaye;*
> *Datvā attamano hoti, esā yaññassa sampadā.*
Here, *yañña* means sacrifice or giving (*dāna*). Three factors required to perfect the achievement of giving are presented there. Before giving, a sense of joy (*somanassa*) arises. One gives something with a sense of joy and happiness; before giving, that joy is present. *“Dadaṃ cittaṃ pasādaye”*—while giving, there is confidence or clarity of mind. One arouses a certain inspiration and clarity regarding the recipient. *“Datvā attamano hoti”*—having given, there is gladness. But for that treasurer, instead of that gladness, there arose the regret called remorse (*vipiṭisāra*). He regarded it as a loss to himself. Because of that, the merit was defiled. The Dhamma analyzes and highlights the value of safeguarding the mind in terms of the preliminary volition (*pūrva-cetanā*), the volition at the moment of relinquishment (*muñcana-cetanā*), and the subsequent volition (*apara-cetanā*). In performing meritorious deeds like giving or any other, rather than merely staring at the object offered and measuring the value of one's gift by its material worth, one must be mindful of this mind, which is invisible both to oneself and to others.
Now, from this story we see that it was because of some slight, yet real, joy that the treasurer gave the command to offer the alms-food. He did not give it with his own hands, yet he ordered that the alms-food be given. How immense the fruits (*āniśaṃsa*) of that act were is evident from his attainment of heavenly bliss and his status as a treasurer. Furthermore, three factors are frequently explained regarding the success of a gift: the excellence of the giver (*dāyaka-sampatti*), the excellence of the gift (*deyya-dhamma-sampatti*), and the excellence of the recipient (*paṭigrāhaka-sampatti*). Here too, there must be purity in the giver's intention and conviction (*saddhā*). The object of charity, too, should be something of fine quality.
Next, the excellence of the recipient (*paṭigrāhaka-sampatti*) refers to the spiritual virtue of the receiving party. Accordingly, when we consider that merely ordering the gift to be given to a Pacceka Buddha led to seven births in the heavens and seven appointments as a treasurer, we can see how exceptionally powerful the excellence of the recipient is in making a gift bear great fruit and great benefit. The object of charity may be massive; however, if it is offered with a narrow mind, a petty mind, or with a wrong intention and wrong expectations, it does not become a truly wholesome deed (*kusala*).
We can learn much from this regarding being mindful of the mind when performing meritorious deeds like giving. The phrase "the rust of stinginess" described in the Dhamma is also well worth reflecting upon. The Buddha has pointed out the moment this rust of stinginess enters minds, stating: *“Maccheraṃ dadataṃ malaṃ”*—stinginess is the rust of those who give. Why is it called a "rust"? We know that a metal object is destroyed by rust. When rust forms on a metal object, if it is not cleaned regularly, it eventually turns into a heap of rust. Similarly, we know that if the hinges of a door are eaten by rust, that door cannot be swung back and forth properly. It cannot be opened or closed; it is incapacitated and cannot be operated. In the same way, the mind becomes incapacitated. Simply put, when stinginess sets in, neither the hand nor the mind inclines or bends toward giving. That is what the "rust of stinginess" means. Through this, the brilliance of the mind is lost. The mind becomes narrow, regardless of how wealthy one is considered in society. We usually measure wealth and richness based on a person’s material assets. But if one looks inside that person, due to that rust, the stingy person possesses a mind akin to that of an extremely destitute beggar. Wealth means capability, the power to do. Being poor or 'incapable' means the inability to do.
Therefore, wealth is not measured by material riches alone, but by that quality of relinquishment, the virtue of generosity—the extent to which the mind bends toward giving. Just because wealth is present—which is indeed received due to past merit—one can still become an absolute pauper in utilizing it if that dangerous rust called the "rust of stinginess" enters the mind. Thus, this story makes it clear to us how necessary it is to protect ourselves from it. By freeing oneself from this rust of stinginess and giving, a meritorious deed is perfected. As the fruit of that merit, one receives heavenly rebirth, human prosperity, and the status of a treasurer. Not only that, the deepest benefit of giving is the growth of the quality of generosity (*cāga*). You have heard of the Seven Noble Treasures (*sapta āriya-dhana*). These represent seven types of wealth possessed by those who have attained supramundane states:
> *Saddhā-dhanaṃ sīla-dhanaṃ, hiri-ottappiyaṃ dhanaṃ;*
> *Suta-dhanaṃ ca cāgo ca, paññā ve sattamaṃ dhanaṃ.*
Conviction (*saddhā*), virtue (*sīla*), moral shame (*hiri*) and moral dread (*ottappa*) which are shame and fear toward sin, then the understanding acquired through hearing the Dhamma (*suta*), then relinquishment (*cāga*). Generosity, too, is shown as a Noble Treasure. Finally, the treasure of wisdom (*paññā*). Why is relinquishment considered a treasure? If a person has not developed the volition of relinquishment, when some mishap or disaster occurs in daily life, or if one's property is lost or destroyed through thieves or by other means, they cannot compose their mind. They lack the strength to reconcile their mind. But one who has cultivated this virtue can compose their mind. Through the strength of letting go cultivated via the volition of giving, they can reconcile their mind. That is why, ultimately, the benefit one receives from giving, both in this world and throughout the round of rebirths, is designated as "wealth."
These days, many people ask, "Even if you say we have given alms, who sees their results (*vipāka*)? Can you prove that there is a fruit to giving?" In an era where such diverse opinions exist, including the view that "performing these meritorious deeds only prolongs the round of rebirths," one must reflect on how giving purifies one's own mind. Lay devotees spend their lives surrounded by money and a mountain of possessions. Living amongst these, defilement is bound to arise in the mind. We refer to things like greed, stinginess, and miserliness as belonging to the very word craving (*taṇhā*). It is a very low, wretched form of craving. There is a risk of sliding into that state if one does not regularly practice giving. Giving is not something to be done for worldly pride or show. It must be done by clarifying the mind at all three stages—the preliminary volition (*pūrva-cetanā*), the volition of relinquishment (*muñcana-cetanā*), and the subsequent volition (*apara-cetanā*)—so that those aforementioned factors are fulfilled. Moreover, you must give as a true benefactor, endowed with virtue (*sīla*) and conviction (*saddhā*), and the gift being offered should not be thrown away carelessly, but prepared and presented in a fitting manner.
Next is the other factor regarding the receiving party (*paṭigrāhaka*). Many people say, "Due to economic hardships, we have nothing to give." It is indeed very difficult when there is nothing to give. However, the absence of a worthy recipient to whom one can offer a good, highly fruitful gift is another dangerous situation. This is a moral decline, parallel to economic decline. For a gift to yield great fruit and great benefit, it is also necessary for the recipient to be developed in virtuous qualities.
Excellence of virtue means growth in supramundane virtues. The Pacceka Buddha mentioned in this story is the second most noble person in the world. From this, we can understand that those who receive gifts should be mindful of cultivating such virtue, to the best of their ability, to become fields of merit (*puññakkhetta*) for the world. Usually, the Dhamma states, *“Anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassa”*—"an unsurpassed field of merit for the world"—in reference to the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha does not refer to the external appearance, but to that aforementioned spiritual mass of virtue. Where that mass of virtue is degraded, that nature of being a field of merit is also absent. Therefore, whether one is a layperson or a monastic, it is by drawing closer to those supramundane virtues that one develops the capacity to make the success of others' giving yield great fruit and great benefit. The Buddha stated here that the treasurer had completely finished experiencing the results of his past meritorious deeds. He did not make any effort to gather new merit. You can understand this through the analogy of a farmer who squanders all the seed-paddy in his barn; he has no seed left to sow for the next harvest. In the same way, what happened here is that he merely enjoyed the benefits of past merits. He did not gather merit that would support him further in this long round of rebirths (*saṃsāra*). The terrifying nature of its result is clear from the story of his rebirth in hell. From that, we can learn a very valuable lesson.
The great female lay disciple Visākhā, who was highly eminent in wisdom within this Dispensation during the Buddha's time, taught her own father-in-law a fine lesson. You have heard that the treasurer was Visākhā's father-in-law. Visākhā had to be married into a family holding wrong views. Treasurer Migāra held wrong views and ministered to the Nigaṇṭhas (Jain ascetics). In the early days after her marriage, one day, Treasurer Migāra was eating rich milk-rice—a highly delicious milk-rice—served in a golden bowl while seated on a very valuable seat. While he was eating, his new daughter-in-law was fanning him. At that moment, a monk on an alms-round arrived there. When he entered the house, Visākhā thought wisely, 'It is not fit to say in words to my father-in-law that a monk has arrived.' Instead, she stepped aside slightly so that the monk would be clearly visible to him. The treasurer raised his head, looked, but showed no reaction whatsoever; pretending not to see, he looked down and resumed eating his food. Visākhā then spoke to the monk—when there is nothing to offer to monks on their alms-round, there is a certain phrase used on such occasions: *“Atikkamatha, bhante”* (Please pass on, Venerable Sir). This is a phrase conveying the meaning, "Seek satisfaction elsewhere, we have nothing to offer here." Visākhā said, "Venerable Sir, please pass on. Obtain it from elsewhere. My father-in-law is eating stale food (*purāṇa*). Therefore, Venerable Sir, please be compassionate and go elsewhere."
Upon hearing this, Treasurer Migāra flew into a great rage. What was the reason? The Pāli word *purāṇa* (old/ancient) also has another connotation in some contexts, meaning excrement or refuse. Thus, the treasurer thought, 'I am eating this milk-rice, yet my daughter-in-law has placed me in such a degrading position. She said such a thing about what I am eating!' He ordered his servants, 'Take this milk-rice away, and drive this woman out of this house!' Then Visākhā said, 'I am not someone who can be driven out so easily like a slave-girl. I was brought here from an honorable family. Furthermore, when my parents married me off, they sent eight noble clan-leaders to judge any such issues that might arise. Present this case to them.' The treasurer then summoned those eight judges and made his complaint: 'While I was eating my food in this manner, my daughter-in-law said such a thing.' Then Visākhā explained her statement: 'I said it with this meaning: my father-in-law is eating stale food (*purāṇa*) in the sense that he is consuming his past merit, and is not accumulating new merit. I said it with that intention, and not as some talk about refuse.'
There may be many people in this society who are like Visākhā's father-in-law. Everyone must reflect that meritorious deeds like giving are what support one’s long journey through the round of rebirths (*saṃsāra*). Shortcomings in these are what manifest in one's day-to-day life. Even performing meritorious deeds must be done correctly. One must be mindful of how one’s mind fluctuates. One must train to observe this. Furthermore, as stated in the Dhamma, the value of a gift does not depend on the size of the object given, but on the thought with which it is given: *“Appampi ce saddahano dadāti, teneva so hoti sukhī parattha.”* Even if one is extremely poor, if they give even a tiny thing with a large mind, with deep conviction (*saddhā*), and with a great volition of relinquishment without a stingy mind, that is what yields great fruit and great benefit. Thus, the benefit of giving by removing the rust of stinginess is highlighted. Among meritorious deeds, the meritorious act of giving is presented as fundamental. So much so, as you well know, among the perfections (*pāramitā*) of the Buddha, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is paramount. The perfection of giving means going to the absolute limit of giving. The Bodhisatta is one who approaches this concept of giving with a depth that is hard for an ordinary human to even conceive. The perfection of giving is not confined to external objects, but extends to internal things—yielding even his own body, head, flesh, and blood. With this background of the Bodhisatta’s life, the Buddha once declared to the monks: "Monks, if these people knew the benefits of giving as I do, they would never eat without sharing. Even if it were their very last morsel of rice, their final mouthful, they would not eat it without sharing, if there were someone present to receive it." This means, suppose someone has only one morsel of rice left, their final mouthful. Just as they lift it, a beggar arrives and asks for it. They give it. Even if it is the very food about to enter their mouth, if it can sustain another, they would give it away. The Buddha declared that the benefit of giving is that great. He also stated that it is because people do not know this that their minds are covered by the rust of stinginess.
Over the past few days, we celebrated the New Year festival. This giving, the quality of relinquishment, is a heritage our nation has received through Buddhist customs and traditions. This is visible even during the New Year festival. In the month of Bak (April), which is heavy with harvest, there is an opportunity within the New Year customs to share that fortune among relatives, friends, neighbors, as well as the poor, travelers, and beggars. Similarly, in the upcoming month of Vesak, there are the alms-stalls (*dansäl*). All of these are valuable qualities integrated into our national character based on that concept of giving. It is by developing these virtues, such as hospitality to guests, that one can make one's life in the round of rebirths (*saṃsāra*) fruitful, while simultaneously subduing and gradually cutting away that dangerous disease of the mind, the defilement (*kilesa*) called craving (*taṇhā*).
You know that discourses like the Mahāmaṅgala Sutta, which were preached to deities, were often delivered during the night as answers to questions asked by devas who came to visit the Buddha. On one such occasion, a young deity named Sērī came to visit the Buddha. In reply to a question asked by this deity, the Buddha stated:
> *Ye naṃ dadanti saddhāya, vippasannena cetasā;*
> *Tameva annaṃ bhajati, asmiṃ loke paramhi ca.*
Those who give gifts with conviction (*saddhā*) and with a clear, confident mind, never experience a shortage of food and drink, both in this world and the next. Just as if food and drink come searching for them, they suffer no lack.
> *Tasmā vineyya maccheraṃ, dajjā dānaṃ malābhibhū;*
> *Puññāni paralokasmiṃ, patiṭṭhā honti pāṇinaṃ.*
Therefore, conquering this rust of stinginess, overcoming and removing stinginess, one should give gifts. Why? Because for living beings, this thing called merit (*puñña*) becomes a support in the world beyond. When the Buddha spoke thus, the deity named Sērī shared his own experience: "Bhante, I see how well-spoken (*subhāsita*) and true your words are. When I was in the human world, I was a king by the very name Sērī. I was someone who practiced this giving at the highest level. That is, the world knew me as a *dāyako* (giver), a *dānapati* (lord of giving), and a *dānassa vaṇṇavādī* (one who praises giving). There is great depth in these three terms. *Dāyaka* means one who gives. *Dānapati* means one who gives on such a grand scale that he masterfully controls those acts of giving. *Dānassa vaṇṇavādī* means one who praises giving to others, explaining its value. That is the highest thing a giver can do. That is how I gave when I was a king," he declared to the Buddha.
"I built alms-halls at all four gates of the city and regularly gave alms to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, travelers, and beggars. As this went on, one day the women of the harem—the queens—came to me and said, 'Only the King gives alms; we have no opportunity to do so. It would be wonderful if we too were given an opportunity.' Then I thought, 'I, this Sērī, am a giver, a lord of giving, and one who praises giving. Therefore, when such a request is made, I cannot refuse it.' So I permitted the women of the harem to organize the giving at the first gate. The King's own alms-giving at that gate was discontinued. After some time, the princes and the royal khattiyas came with the next request: 'Your Majesty gives alms, and the women of the harem also give alms. But we have no opportunity.' The King thought in the same way, 'I cannot reject this request,' and allowed those princes and khattiyas to give alms at the second gate."
"After some time, the military forces—the soldiers under the commander-in-chief—came and made the same request: 'Your Majesty gives alms, the queens of the harem give alms, and the khattiya princes give alms. Only we have no opportunity.' On that occasion, the third gate was granted to those royal soldiers to give alms. Next, fourthly, came the brahmin householders. They made the same request. The King had to hand over the management of the alms-hall at the fourth gate to those brahmins. There was no longer any alms-giving directly from the King. The royal officers came to the King and said, 'Now, there seems to be no alms-giving at all from Your Majesty.' The deity Sērī said, 'At that point, this is what I did: "Then, my men, go and send only half of the taxes collected from outside the city—from the distant provinces—to the palace. Let the other half be distributed right there as alms to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, travelers, and beggars..." By giving alms on such a massive scale, I now enjoy this heavenly bliss. So much so, I cannot even measure how long I will remain in this heaven, or how much merit I still have left. How true are the words of the Buddha!' declared the deity Sērī."
In this giving, in the distribution of gifts (*dāna-saṃvibhāga*), and in providing opportunities for others to give—in all of these, one has the capacity to accumulate a vast store of merit. Yet, more valuable than all of these is directing it toward Nibbāna. When speaking of a gift that yields great fruit and great benefit, it was mentioned earlier that the volition (*cetanā*) behind the act of giving is what governs it. One can give out of a specific personal preference, or out of fear, or with the expectation of a heavenly rebirth, and so forth, under various kinds of volitions.
However, these are not the highest purposes. The Buddha has stated that the deep purpose of giving is: *“Cittālaṅkāraṃ dānaṃ deti”*—one gives a gift for the adornment of the mind, and to fulfill the factors necessary for the growth of the mind. That is what is called "requisites for the mind." It is for this that one gives. Such is the purpose of giving that in accordance with the Dhamma supports Nibbāna. Here, *cittālaṅkāra* means the adornment of the mind. Through this giving, we can develop a certain degree of concentration (*samādhi*). In the Dhamma, this is designated as *cāgānussati*—recollection of generosity. Recollections (*anussati*) as meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) mean constant reflection. You know the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) well—reflecting deeply on the qualities of the Buddha. Recollection of the Dhamma (*dhammānussati*) is reflecting on the qualities of the Dhamma. Recollection of the Saṅgha (*saṅghānussati*) is reflecting on the qualities of the Saṅgha. Similarly, there is also the recollection of generosity (*cāgānussati*).
The Buddha has shown meditations that can be practiced. Among people of the world whose minds are choked by the rust of stinginess, I live in this manner.
