so, what does this demonstrate? as shown in the dhamma, the mind is also freed from lust, and the mind is also detached from hatred. because of painful feeling (*vedana*), a person develops aversion (*patigha*), which is hatred. the blessed one showed this in another place in this way: "the world says there is an abyss (*patala*) in the great ocean. but the real abyss is physical painful feeling (*vedana*)." physical painful feeling (*vedana*) is the real abyss. now, an abyss is a bottomless pit. so, this painful feeling (*vedana*) is compared to an abyss. this painful feeling is such a terrifying thing. but the person who does not know the dhamma, when faced with that painful feeling, falls into the abyss and, finding no footing or support, sinks. they cannot come up; they weep and lament. but the noble disciple overcomes those painful feelings (*vedana*) and brings the mind to neutrality. standing up from the abyss is said there regarding that painful feeling.
in another place, the buddha gave a discourse to the sangha, starting like this: "monks, the ordinary untaught worldling (*puthujjana*) experiences pleasant feeling (*vedana*), experiences painful feeling (*vedana*), and experiences neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*vedana*), which is neutral feeling. the taught noble disciple (*ariya-savaka*) too experiences pleasant feeling (*vedana*), experiences painful feeling (*vedana*), and experiences neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*vedana*). what is the difference between these two?" he asked the sangha. there were occasions when dhamma discourses were delivered in such a question-and-answer format. the sangha at that moment said, "bhante, we cannot answer this. what we know is also what we have to learn from the blessed one," and they requested the explanation from the blessed one himself.
then, to explain it, the blessed one declared: "monks, when the ordinary untaught worldling (*puthujjana*) is touched by painful feeling (*vedana*), they weep, lament, and beat their breast, thereby increasing that pain." he showed this with a simile: "suppose a man is struck by an arrow. right after being struck by that arrow, another arrow comes and strikes him, a second arrow. in the same way, the ordinary untaught worldling feels both bodily pain and mental pain. the weeping and lamenting is shown as the second arrow." when physical painful feeling (*vedana*) comes, if one starts weeping and lamenting, it is like being struck by a second arrow, and the person who lacks dhamma knowledge suffers further distress.
but regarding the noble disciple (*ariya-savaka*), when painful feeling (*vedana*) comes, without being perturbed by it, they endure it and bring the mind to neutrality. that is like being struck by only one arrow. they do not experience mental suffering (*dukkha*). what is meant by this is not clinging to pleasant feeling (*vedana*) and keeping the mind neutral there, and not colliding with painful feeling (*vedana*) and extricating the mind from there as well. next is equanimity (*upekkha*). that is why we spoke of a mind concentrated in equanimity. indeed, equanimity, neutrality, is a state where the mind's power is highly developed. that is to say, even when looking at concentration (*samadhi*) in the absorptions (*jhana*), by the time one reaches the fourth absorption (*jhana*), there arises the pleasure of equanimity (*upekkha-sukha*). a wonderful, peaceful bliss is obtained through equanimity. ordinary people see pleasure only in pleasant feeling (*vedana*). because of that very reason, they develop intense hatred towards pain, and because of that, they run around seeking pleasure, as declared by the blessed one.
as an escape from painful feeling (*vedana*), the door that the ordinary person sees is pleasure. therefore, they go in search of pleasure. by seeking extreme pleasant feelings (*vedana*), they try to cover up suffering (*dukkha*). to eliminate the suffering that might come in the future and the suffering that has already come, they run after sensual pleasure (*kama-sukha*). the blessed one declares that the noble disciple (*ariya-savaka*), at that moment, brings the mind to neutrality, which has the true peaceful bliss called pacification (*upasama*). it is through that that realization is obtained. thus, even when looking at the absorptions (*jhana*), the mind fashioned with equanimity is the most powerful. it is by obtaining those absorption powers called the fourth absorption (*jhana*) that special abilities like direct knowledges (*abhinna*) can be brought forth. but a deeper equanimity than that is what the blessed one in this dispensation calls the concentration of the fruition of arahantship (*arahatta-phala-samadhi*), which is unique to arahants—experiencing the bliss of nibbana in this very life. that is like being detached from the world. therefore, we have to understand that at that moment, venerable sariputta was dwelling in the concentration of the fruition of arahantship (*arahatta-phala-samadhi*). that is why he did not feel anything happening in this world. there are such wonderful things, like the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samapatti*). there too, the blessed one expresses the value of keeping the mind neutral.
now, even though we speak about these concentrations (*samadhi*) and absorptions (*jhana*), someone might think that in daily life these are just words. but if we are walking on that path, even while sitting, what can we use as help from the buddha's teaching? we know very well that the blessed one has shown the meditation on foulness (*asubha-bhavana*) to subdue lust and attachment. why did both laypeople and monastics in the past, and even these meritorious people now, develop meditations such as the recollection of the buddha (*buddhanussati*), loving-kindness (*metta*), foulness (*asubha*), and the mindfulness of death (*marananussati*)? because if the powerful forces of lust go to extremes, they lead to various crimes. therefore, the meditation on foulness is used as a remedy for lust. if one has developed the perception of foulness (*asubha-sanna*) or the perception of repulsiveness (*patikula-sanna*) to some extent, one does not fall into extreme attachments of lust and ruin oneself like a moth jumping into a fire, due to those attachments, due to the desire for pleasant feeling (*vedana*), due to sensual pleasure. one does not fall into dangerous disasters.
in that way, we can understand that, on one hand, the perception of foulness (*asubha-sanna*) and also the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*) help in this. the perception of impermanence (*anicca*) is developed within the feeling that everything is impermanent (*anicca*). because of that pleasant feeling (*vedana*), we forget the impermanence of this. deceived by external luster, thinking that this is permanent and will last forever, we are even tempted to commit grave crimes for its sake. but as soon as impermanence (*anicca*) is highlighted, when we reflect for a moment, we see the true state of things. then, that grasping (*grahana*) is removed. next is the attention to elements (*dhatu-manasikara*). that is to say, no matter how polished and beautiful our bodies and external things are, they are shown in the dhamma as being made of the four great elements (*maha-bhuta*): earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and wind (*vayo*). earth, water, fire, and wind are what we usually identify as these four elements. so, we must bear in mind that our external things and the food we eat are all made of these elements. even when these meritorious people take food, what is called reflection (*paccavekkhana*) is reflecting with wisdom (*panna*). or they reflect on it as repulsive: "what happens to this food after it goes inside?" right there, the craving for taste (*rasa-tanha*) is destroyed.
the blessed one removed those cravings (*tanha*) and desires from the mind in such a wonderful way that, regarding the blessed one, it is mentioned: *"rasa-patisamvedi bhagava hoti, no ca rasaraga-patisamvedi"* — "the blessed one experiences taste, but he does not experience lust for taste (*rasa-raga*)." such is the powerful strength of concentration (*samadhi*). the sensitive systems connected to taste, the tongue, and the nerves were fully intact in the blessed one. in fact, they were cleaner than in others. he experienced taste, but there was no lust (*raga*) for it, because he had developed the mind. based on that, we can think of the power of the development of the body (*kaya-bhavana*) in those who have developed the mind. they have developed the body to such an extent that it does not yield to those things. that is why meditations like the meditation on repulsiveness (*patikula-bhavana*) and foulness (*asubha-bhavana*) are shown.
similarly, the attention to elements (*dhatu-manasikara*). the mind directed towards the four elements turns towards equanimity (*upekkha*). here too, there are earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and wind (*vayo*). inside the body, there are the very same. in the plate of rice, there are the very same. when developing in this way as meditation (*bhavana*), gradually, the power to reduce those attachments is obtained. next, on the other side, in situations where conflicts arise, when anger and irritation arise, these meritorious people know very well the methods to appease them. you have heard of them. the meditation on loving-kindness (*metta-bhavana*) rises in the mind. just like the meditation on loving-kindness, impermanence (*anicca*) can also be targeted at our anger. "i and all these people are impermanent (*anicca*). we will face death." thinking in this way, one can conquer anger and reduce conflicts. the perception of elements (*dhatu-sanna*) also helps in this.
in this way, various methods are shown in the dhamma. this side of nibbana, as we develop our practice to that extent according to the levels of meditation (*bhavana*), according to the progress of meditation, we can gradually bring the mind to neutrality. because if we analyze the middle path (*majjhima patipada*) taught by the buddhas to the world in terms of feeling (*vedana*), this is where it leads. the niganthas, believing that pleasure must be sought through pain, tortured the body. but then, the blessed one, during his time as prince siddhartha in the royal palace, experienced the devotion to sensual pleasures (*kamasukhallikanuyoga*), sensual pleasure. he tried to find satisfaction through it. no satisfaction is obtained through that either. now, in the middle of those two is this neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*adukkham-asukha vedana*). ordinary people do not recognize its value. its value is almost unknown to them. but it is through this that the meditator (*yogavacara*), the attainer of absorption (*jhana*), brings forth a pleasure: neither-painful-nor-pleasant (*adukkham-asukha*). that concentration (*samadhi*) of the mind is a very secure place. when it is said "it stands like a rock, unshaken," "unshaken like a rock," that supreme state of mind, the highest state, is the concentration of the fruition of arahantship (*arahatta-phala-samadhi*) mentioned earlier. we have to think that venerable sariputta was enjoying that bliss of nibbana, detached from the world. indeed, the moment of crossing over from the world exists within that concentration of the fruition of arahantship. it was while he was enjoying that that the demon came and struck him.
so, from this, we can imagine how great the miracle of this developed mind is. next, there are many other factors that help in this. we must constantly think about impermanence (*anicca*). indeed, if in our meditations we expect to free the mind from these defilements (*kilesa*), what helps us extremely is the insight meditation (*vipassana-bhavana*) on impermanence (*anicca*). regarding that, there is a very wonderful and valuable discourse of the blessed one: that this world, the entire world, has arisen from these six sense-bases (*ayatana*). there are six sense-bases: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. sometimes these are shown as twelve. that is because there must also be objects for the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. those objects are forms (*rupa*), sounds (*sadda*), smells (*gandha*), tastes (*rasa*), tangibles (*photthabba*), and mind-objects (*dhamma*). 'dhamma' means things understood by the mind. so, those are sometimes shown as the twelve sense-bases (*ayatana*). where they are shown as twelve, they are shown as two parts: internal sense-bases (*ajjhattika-ayatana*) and external sense-bases (*bahira-ayatana*). the internal sense-bases are eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—the six sense-bases connected to oneself, to one's body. their objects are, in the external world, forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles (*photthabba*)—things to be touched—and mind-objects (*dhamma*), things understood by the mind, objects that come to the mind. the blessed one declared that the world exists within this. the entire world arises here. all connections of the entire world exist within these six, within that contact (*phassa*). so, it is through the realization of this that one can draw close to nibbana.
regarding this, there is another valuable discourse with similes that is very helpful to meditators. when the blessed one was residing at jetavana monastery, great pajapati gotami theri came to the blessed one and made a special request on behalf of the bhikkhunis: "may a monk come on every uposatha day to give us a sermon." the blessed one gave permission for that. since then, those elders went in turn to the bhikkhuni monastery called rajakarama and delivered a dhamma discourse. although the other elders went, venerable nandaka did not go. he did not like to. when his turn came, he avoided it for some reason. one day, the blessed one asked the monks, "whose turn is it today to preach the dhamma to the bhikkhunis?" "it is venerable nandaka's." "then why?" when asked, they said, "venerable nandaka does not wish to go." then the blessed one told venerable nandaka, "nandaka, go and deliver a discourse to the bhikkhunis." so, venerable nandaka went and delivered a valuable discourse to the bhikkhunis regarding these six sense-bases (*ayatana*) we mentioned. a great discourse. since meditators can benefit by deeply reflecting on those similes, we decided to present it at this moment.
venerable nandaka first said to those bhikkhunis, "my discourse will proceed as a question-and-answer session. now, while i am preaching, if anyone has a question, you must ask. if you understand, you must say you understand. if you do not understand, you must say you do not understand. you must ask me where it is not understood." saying so, he began the discourse. thus, step by step, he expected a response from those bhikkhunis. he started like this. often in the dhamma, the discourse on impermanence (*anicca*) or the three characteristics (*ti-lakkhana*) is presented first. the address used there is "sisters." "sisters, what do you think? is this eye permanent (*nicca*) or impermanent (*anicca*)?" "impermanent (*anicca*), bhante." "then, if something is impermanent, is it pleasure (*sukha*) or suffering (*dukkha*)?" "suffering (*dukkha*), bhante." "next, if something is suffering (*dukkha*), impermanent (*anicca*), and subject to change, is it proper to regard it as self (*atta*), 'this is mine, this i am, this is my self'?" "no, bhante." in this way, he questioned them regarding the eye, as well as the six internal sense-bases (*ajjhattika-ayatana*): ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
having questioned them thus, when he asked, "why do you say so? why do you say so?" those bhikkhunis replied, "because we have understood their impermanence (*anicca*)." he asked similarly about the external sense-bases (*bahira-ayatana*). "is form (*rupa*) permanent or impermanent?" "impermanent." "if it is impermanent, is it pleasure or suffering?" "suffering." "if it is impermanent and subject to change, is it proper to regard it as 'this is mine, this i am, this is my self'?" "no." thus, the three characteristics of impermanence (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and non-self (*anatta*) were presented in a question-and-answer format regarding the six internal sense-bases (*ajjhattika-ayatana*)—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—and the six external sense-bases (*bahira-ayatana*)—forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mind-objects. next, venerable nandaka asked about eye-consciousness (*cakkhu-vinnana*). "now, when we see something, we say there is an eye and there is a form, because we have the power to distinguish them. that is eye-consciousness (*cakkhu-vinnana*). is that eye-consciousness permanent or impermanent?" "that too is impermanent, bhante," they said. in this way, regarding the six sense-bases such as eye and ear, he asked about the consciousness (*vinnana*) that helps to obtain knowledge through our senses, such as eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, etc. they declared that those too are impermanent (*anicca*).
next, he asked, "is the contact (*phassa*) arising because of these permanent?" "no, that too is not." "is feeling (*vedana*) permanent?" "no, that too is not permanent." then, he explained the reason for that in each place. feelings (*vedana*) arise due to causes and conditions (*hetu-paccaya*) that arise in each instance. with the cessation of those, those feelings cease. therefore, feeling cannot be taken as self (*atta*). we think of feeling as something continuous, as something that exists. but when wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*) is applied according to the dhamma, one understands that it too arises due to causes and conditions along with contact (*phassa*). on another occasion, in another place, a monk named moliya phagguna asked the blessed one, "who experiences feeling?" the blessed one replied, "the question 'who experiences feeling?' itself is wrong. feeling arises due to contact (*phassa*), due to a certain condition (*paccaya*)." that is what the blessed one pointed out. instead of the feeling of self, 'i' and 'mine', feeling arises due to a contact (*phassa*); he asked him to direct the mind to that. by directing the mind to contact (*phassa*), realization can be obtained. "it is not that 'i' experience feeling. due to this contact, these feelings arise." those bhikkhunis understood that matter gradually.
next, to demonstrate that feeling (*vedana*) should not be taken as self (*atta*), he gave this simile: "the oil in a lamp is impermanent (*anicca*). the wick is impermanent. the flame is impermanent. if someone says that the light of the lamp is permanent, is that correct?" then the bhikkhunis said, "that is incorrect, because since the conditions (*paccaya*) that caused the light are impermanent, the light of that lamp must also be impermanent. it should not be taken as self (*atta*)." similarly, venerable nandaka declared, "whether it is pleasant feeling (*vedana*), painful feeling (*vedana*), or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*vedana*) arising due to that contact (*phassa*), it is not permanent. that too is impermanent. why? because of those impermanent conditions (*paccaya*)." 'condition' (*paccaya*) means cause—that which helps something to arise is called a condition (*paccaya*) in the dhamma. so, various things arise due to various causes and conditions. since the various causes from which feeling (*vedana*) arises are impermanent, feeling too is impermanent. there is no nature that can be taken as 'i' or 'mine'. in that manner, he showed the six internal sense-bases—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—through the simile of the lamp.
next, if feelings (*vedana*) arise in connection with forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mind-objects, they too are impermanent. to show that there too they cannot be taken as self, he gave another simile: "the root of a large growing tree is impermanent, the trunk is impermanent, the branches and leaves are impermanent. if someone says that the shadow cast by it is permanent, is that correct?" he asked. the bhikkhunis said, "that is incorrect." "what is the reason? if there are causes and conditions (*hetu-paccaya*) for the shadow to arise, they are impermanent. since the causes and conditions are impermanent, the shadow itself must also be impermanent."
next, he gave another simile: "suppose a butcher, with a sharp knife—what is called a butcher's knife, used for cutting cattle—skins a cow. he separates the hide in such a way that the flesh is not cut, and the hide is not cut. he cuts only the inner tendons, only the tendon-bonds. having done so, he covers that cow again with that same hide. if one then says, 'this is the same cow as was there before, there is no difference,' is that correct?" "no, bhante." "why? because now there is only the hide on the outside, there is no tendon-bond." now, here is how the simile is explained: the inner flesh of the cow is like the six internal sense-bases (*ajjhattika-ayatana*)—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. the outer hide is like the six external objects—forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mind-objects. these two were connected by the tendon-bonds. the butcher cut those tendon-bonds. those tendon-bonds are what is called in the dhamma by the word *nandi-raga* (delight and lust), attachment, craving (*tanha*)—to put it briefly, craving, desire. it is through that desire that these two, the eye and the form, are connected. that is why lust called *nandi-raga* arises from there.
then, with what is that bond cut? what is compared to the butcher's knife? the noble wisdom (*ariya-panna*). when one sees with wisdom at any moment as impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and non-self (*anatta*), if the six internal sense-bases and the six external sense-bases are impermanent, then the contact (*phassa*) and feeling (*vedana*) arising due to them are also impermanent. it is through the realization that there is nothing here to be attached to, nothing to be taken as 'mine', that that attachment is destroyed. that is what we have to understand there.
regarding the remaining part of that discourse, it is mentioned in the sutta as follows: having delivered the discourse with those similes, venerable nandaka said, "very well, now it is time for us to depart. you may go," and dismissed those bhikkhunis, and venerable nandaka also returned. the bhikkhunis, perhaps hoping that the blessed one might add something, approached the blessed one, paid homage, and stood there for a while, waiting to see if the blessed one would say anything. the blessed one said only this: "go, sisters," and sent them away. as those bhikkhunis were leaving, the blessed one made a special statement to the sangha. you all know what the full-moon uposatha is. the fourteenth day (*catuddasi*) is the day before the full-moon uposatha. the moon is not fully round on that day. if today is the fifteenth day (full moon), yesterday was the fourteenth day. the blessed one said something like this to the sangha: "monks, just as it is obvious at first glance that the moon is not full on the fourteenth uposatha day, even though these bhikkhunis have felt some joy because of venerable nandaka's discourse, their expectations are not fully fulfilled. 'expectations' means their expectation of nibbana is not fully fulfilled. some joy has arisen; that discourse is good. but it is not fulfilled." having said so, the blessed one told venerable nandaka, "nandaka, go and deliver this very same discourse tomorrow as well." even in this day and age, these meritorious people listen to recorded discourses again and again. a similar wonderful event is found here. he told venerable nandaka to deliver the very same discourse.
venerable nandaka also went there the next day. having approached, he delivered the same discourse as before, in the same manner, saying, "i am going to ask in a question-and-answer format," and in the same way, he gradually directed their minds. "are eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body impermanent, are they not? are their objects also impermanent, are they not? if those objects are impermanent, is not the feeling (*vedana*) arising with them as cause and condition also impermanent?" he reminded them of those similes again and again. and to all of this, those bhikkhunis gave their response, to show that they understood, with a certain passage: "due to the causes (*paccaya*) that arise in those respective places, the corresponding feelings (*vedana*) arise; with the cessation of those respective causes, those feelings also cease."
that is to say, if certain feelings (*vedana*) arise due to certain conditions (*paccaya*), when those conditions cease, those feelings also cease. that is the fundamental principle. since we started our discourse on this question of feeling, this is a very important passage, like a valuable meditation subject (*kammatthana*). what is meant by it is an indication that those bhikkhunis understood this dhamma. that is to say, feeling (*vedana*) is not something that should be taken as self (*atta*), as 'i' or 'mine'. feeling is always something that arises due to certain conditions (*paccaya*). therefore, since those conditions are impermanent (*anicca*), feeling too must be impermanent. but it is because of taking them as permanent that attachments and conflicts arise in that manner. that is the story there. after delivering this same discourse, just like the previous day, venerable nandaka said, "very well, the time is up," and returned. the bhikkhunis also went to the blessed one, paid homage, and stood.
to them, the blessed one said again, "very well, sisters, now you may go," and dismissed them. having dismissed them, he said to the sangha: "monks, just as on the full-moon uposatha day, one can easily know whether the moon is full or not, in the same way, all these five hundred bhikkhunis have attained the fruits of the path (*magga-phala*). at the very least, some have attained the stage of stream-entry (*sotapanna*)." from this, we can understand something about the way dhamma was heard in the past. even now, these meritorious people record these discourses we deliver, and after recording, listen to them again and again. but we do not know for sure whether they listen in the way they ought to listen. if they develop the meditation reflection (*bhavana-manasikara*) in the manner thought of, there is even a possibility of such a change occurring. we can understand that from this past event.
especially, we raised this question of feeling (*vedana*) because what affects all of us is suffering (*dukkha*). physical suffering is like an abyss. it is to relieve this physical suffering that we seek pleasure. to eliminate the physical suffering we have now, and to eliminate the physical suffering that might come in the future, is why the world runs this wonderful race. sunk in it in a way that no bottom can be found, they go searching for pleasant feelings (*vedana*). but the blessed one points out that what is to be done here is to bring the mind to neutrality. that realization is obtained by looking at all of these as things belonging to these three characteristics: impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and non-self (*anatta*). everything is impermanent. therefore, even when taken individually, they are impermanent. these are things that arise due to causes and conditions (*hetu-paccaya*). through this perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*), what happens gradually?
we all know that it is by taking things as permanent (*nicca*) that a sign (*nimitta*) comes to the mind. it is by taking things as permanent that things are remembered in the mind. but when insight meditation (*vipassana-bhavana*) is deeply developed, one understands that after taking them as impermanent (*anicca*), they are not grasped by the mind. that is called the signless (*animitta*). it becomes impossible to take a sign. we are holding the entire world with the mind. that is why the blessed one declared that the world exists within the six sense-bases (*salayatana*). therefore, if we are to release this grasp (*grahana*), we must bring forth this dhamma principle highlighted by the blessed one.
everything—the internal eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and everything that is their object—is impermanent (*anicca*). it changes from moment to moment. it changes with wonderful rapidity. although we speak so much about the change of our body, and although we hear about their change through research and various instruments, it is not understood by one's own mind. it is not realized (*pratyaksha*). that is where the problem lies. because it is not understood by one's own mind, we run after whatever we see. therefore, at some point, the impermanence (*anicca*) declared by the blessed one, the way these change very rapidly, is understood by oneself through insight wisdom (*vipassana-panna*). think about the simile of the lamp highlighted by venerable nandaka. we think that the light is permanent. when a lamp is lit, we read a book with that light without any trouble. therefore, our understanding is that this light remains just as it is. but when looking at it in terms of causes and conditions (*hetu-paccaya*), when the oil is finished and the wick is finished, we understand that the light decreases.
in that manner, the light arose due to certain causes and conditions (*hetu-paccaya*). in the same way are our feelings (*vedana*). according to the very impermanence (*anicca*) of our sense-bases, even the form seen by our eye—when eyesight decreases or due to various other causes, other things can be seen. when eyesight decreases, we even begin to see things that do not exist in the world. the same is true of the other senses. so, one must deeply reflect on that impermanence in that manner. the simile of the tree is also like that. the shadow of the tree—we have a general feeling that the shadow is permanent, but when looking at everything, if it is subject to the law of impermanence, we cannot take only that as permanent. what happens through that realization? the attachment called *nandi-raga*—it is after taking those two as permanent that they are connected. just as the flesh and the hide were connected by tendons, the eye and the form are connected by that dhamma word, *nandi-raga*. *nandi-raga* means attachment characterized by delight. running after the form caught by the eye is that attachment characterized by delight. so, just as the butcher cuts with the butcher's knife, what do we have to do? there, the butcher's knife is compared to noble wisdom (*ariya-panna*). if we take noble wisdom at the level we can understand, insight meditators (*vipassana-yogavacara*) know: what is the knife, the instrument we use when we enter into this insight (*vipassana*)? it is attention (*manasikara*), reflection.
insight teachers always ask their pupils, "did you note? did you note? did you note quickly?" that noting is the knife. it is that noting itself that gradually develops, and at some point, when realization is strengthened, rises as wisdom (*panna*). wisdom is a word of great meaning, but the root seed lies in that noting. and that noting must be the proper noting called wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*). it is because of improper noting that we have come so far in samsara. improper noting is also shown as distortion (*vipallasa*) and perversion (*viparita*).
we have often reminded you that there is a perverted perception (*viparita-sanna*), a perverted view (*viparita-ditthi*), and a perverted mind (*viparita-citta*) within the world. the general meaning of perversion (*viparita*) and distortion (*vipallasa*) is like this: if someone stands on their head, that is not the normal state, it is a perverted thing. in the same way, the understanding, the point of view of ordinary people, is entirely wrong according to the buddha's word. they regard what is impermanent (*anicca*) as permanent (*nicca*). they regard what is foul (*asubha*) as beautiful (*subha*). they regard what is painful (*dukkha*) as pleasant (*sukha*). they think of what is non-self (*anatta*)—what is not theirs, what cannot be kept under their control—as theirs. that is what exists within the world as perverted perceptions, views, and thoughts. it is because of this very reason that we have traveled in this samsara for so long. its result is these five aggregates of grasping (*panc'upadanakkhandha*) we have gathered: the five groups of form (*rupa*), feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), volitional activity (*sankhara*), and consciousness (*vinnana*). we gathered them by such a trick. that is to say, by gathering the eye, form, ear, sound, etc., what is gathered is ultimately called "this is my group of form, this is my group of feeling, this is my group of perception, this is my group of volitional activity—which is the group of intentions—this is my group of consciousness—the group of thoughts." in this way, what is shown in the dhamma as a "person" is the five aggregates of grasping (*upadanakkhandha*). five groups. this is what we are holding as 'i' and 'mine' according to the buddha's word. so, when its true nature is realized, gradually that tight bond, that tight tie, is loosened. what helps to loosen it is that attention (*manasikara*). the proper reflection, the proper noting called wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*).
now, we have to think that even though they did not have machines like these, after hearing that discourse on the first day, it sank well into their minds. they were very happy. but no realization of the fruits of the path occurred. during those twenty-four hours, they must have raised it to meditation reflection (*bhavana-manasikara*) and energized it further. that is why the blessed one said for the second time, "deliver the very same discourse." generally, people cannot listen to the same discourse; they might even have stood up and left, saying, "isn't this what we heard yesterday?" but why did those bhikkhunis listen with great respect to that discourse, with its similes, without any omission? not merely listening, but with meditation reflection (*bhavana-manasikara*).
these meritorious people too must learn a lesson from that. from this side story, also the way dhamma should be heard, that it is not good to insult the dhamma saying, "this is what is said every day." on the other hand, if through what is said every day, one sees something deeply, if one sees a new meaning in it, then one has benefited from it. that can be done by applying proper wisdom, applying mindfulness, and hearing the dhamma in the way it should be heard.
we have mentioned before: to hear the dhamma in the true manner is shown as how the noble disciples in the past heard the dhamma: *"atthikam katva manasikatva sabba-cetasa ohita-soto dhammam sunati."* 'atthikam katva' means "this is of use to me. there is a benefit in this for me." 'of use' does not mean listening to go and pass an exam, but to realize nibbana. "this is of use for my nibbana, for my progress, to develop my mind." *manasikatva* means reflecting word by word. not thinking, "i did not listen to this now, but it is nicely recorded in this machine; i can listen to it whenever i want." *manasikatva*—reflecting word by word, listening with good wisdom. *ohita-soto*—with attentive ears, not with half the mind here and half the mind somewhere else. 'attentive ears' means with full attention, listening with the mind fully directed; it is then that such a meditative change occurs within a person.
because they benefited from that in the past, the blessed one told venerable nandaka to deliver the very same discourse again. then we see that change. on that fourteenth uposatha day, and next, like the full moon of the fifteenth uposatha day, those bhikkhunis realized the fruits of the path (*magga-phala*). when we say "the world" in this day and age, we think of the world of the materialists as something external to us. but the blessed one defined the world: the world itself is suffering (*dukkha*). suffering is the world. the world and suffering are connected to each other like two panels of a folding door. the blessed one has defined: *"loko patitthito loko dukkhe patitthitam"* — "the world is established on suffering, suffering is established on the world." like two folding panels. why did the blessed one declare so? what we grasp as the world is that knowledge received from those six sense-bases (*ayatana*), is it not? there is nothing outside of that, is there? what is seen by the eye, what is heard by the ear, thinking in that way, ultimately, what is understood by the mind. what is understood by the mind is what gathers there mostly.
what is gathered from those five ultimately goes to the mind, does it not? that which is gathered in the mind is what we call the world. saying "things happened in such and such a place in this way," what is called globalization is going on. they think of that globe as something existing outside. that globe is right here. because our 'globies' (worldly people) do not know that, these entanglements have occurred. so, globalization is actually right here, within those six sense-bases (*salayatana*).
that is why the blessed one declared: *"chasu loko samuppanno"* — "in six the world has arisen." 'in six' means, by putting together both the eye and the form, sometimes it is shown as six. we take twelve when we separate them as internal and external. if taken so, there are twelve sense-bases (*ayatana*). but where those two connect, that is called the bases of contact (*samphassayatana*). when those two connect and contact (*phassa*) occurs, it can also be taken as six. there, it is called the base of eye-contact (*cakkhu-samphassayatana*), the base of ear-contact (*sota-samphassayatana*). contact regarding the eye is one sense-base. contact regarding the ear is another sense-base. taken in that way, there are six. so, it is within those six that the world is born: *"chasu loko samuppanno, chasu kubbati santhavam"* — "in six the world has arisen, in six it makes its acquaintance." it is with these six that all coordination (acquaintance) is made. all coordination is within these six.
now, in this day and age, there are various devices to connect with the world. all of these devices do not work on their own. we put them to our ear, to our eye, and through them we receive all of this. thus, we bring those external devices close to these six sense-bases (*ayatana*). we must remember that what is still being performed is an activity of the six sense-bases. that is the world. that statement of the blessed one is true even today: *"chasu kubbati santhavam"* — "in six it makes its acquaintance." all acquaintances—'acquaintance' means associating, coordinating, and such new words—all are done within these six. next: *"channam-eva upadaya, chasu loko vihannati"* — "by grasping these six, the world is oppressed in the six." grasping (*upadana*) these six, the entire world is oppressed, is weary in these six—this is the buddha's word. that is why the blessed one declared: the world is equal to suffering (*dukkha*), suffering is equal to the world. thus, within this very perception of the world (*loka-sanna*) that we take based on those six sense-bases (*salayatana*), this suffering (*dukkha*) exists. even if we separate it as pleasure, indeed, that is what the blessed one declares. the true noble disciple (*ariya-savaka*) must see pleasure as suffering (*dukkha*), and see suffering as a thorn. leaving aside other things, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*adukkham-asukha vedana*), though peaceful, is also impermanent (*anicca*). so, through that, what is shown to us is the impermanent nature of everything.
through this realization, we must make an effort, if our deep aspiration is to be freed from this samsara, to meditate basing ourselves on some such meditation subject (*kammatthana*), and quickly bring forth that noble wisdom (*ariya-panna*), and through the penetration (*pativedha*) of the paths and fruits of stream-entry (*sotapanna*), once-returning (*sakadagami*), non-returning (*anagami*), and arahantship (*arahatta*), to cross over from the suffering of samsara such as birth (*jati*), decay and death (*jaramarana*), sickness, and death. may the discourse delivered today also be a supportive condition (*upanissaya*), a help for that! we aspire thus. similarly, if anyone from avici to akanittha wishes to rejoice in this merit of delivering and hearing the dhamma, through that rejoicing, using that merit as a help, may it help them to realize the noble, supreme, great nibbana through an aspiration of enlightenment (*bodhi*) of their choice! say this:
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 156
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #156
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.82)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
"Vāṇijo va bhayaṃ maggaṃ,
appasattho mahaddhano;
Visaṃ jīvitukāmo va,
pāpāni parivajjaye."
From:
Dhammapada Verse 123 (Pāpa Vagga)
Dear Listeners,
The Buddha, the Teacher of the Three Worlds, explained demerit and merit to the world based on the far-reaching understanding he gained regarding existence in *saṃsāra*. Due to a lack of foresight, the Buddha saw how living beings fall into Suffering / Unsatisfactoriness / Stress (*dukkha*) in *saṃsāra*. The Buddha points out how, by acting as slaves to one's whims based on a narrow philosophy of life limited only to this life, one undergoes bitter Suffering / Unsatisfactoriness / Stress (*dukkha*) in *saṃsāra* for an infinite length of time. Today's thematic verse is one that illustrates this very point. The Buddha preached this Dhamma verse at the Jetavana monastery to a group of monks, addressing a disastrous situation faced by a certain wealthy merchant.
About five hundred thieves had been watchfully waiting for a very long time to break into the house of a very wealthy merchant living in the city of Sāvatthī. But they did not get the opportunity. On a certain occasion, this merchant set out to trade in a distant region, preparing five hundred carts. In those days, there was a custom where merchants travelling to such distant regions would inform the monks, inviting them to accompany them if they also wished to travel in that direction, because they had to travel through vast forests. Likewise, this merchant told the monks, "I am going to trade in such-and-such a region. If you, venerable sirs, are also planning to go there, please come with me. Then there will be no trouble regarding alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*), etc." Hearing that the merchants were leaving, those thieves hid in the forest along that path to rob them when they passed by. Meanwhile, the merchant set out with the group of monks, and exactly at the entrance to the forest, they stopped at a village for two or three days to organize the carts and oxen.
Knowing that the journey was delayed, the thieves, who were waiting for the merchant, sent a thief to a villager friend of his to find out the reason for the merchant's delay. When he asked the villagers when this wealthy merchant would depart, the villager replied, "Perhaps in two or three days. Why do you ask?" He replied, "Our group is ready and waiting for these merchants." Thereupon, the villager said, "Then the merchants will come soon," and after sending his friend away, he thought, "Should I side with the merchant, or should I side with these thieves?" Then he reasoned, "Because of this merchant, a group of monks is receiving alms and other requisites. Therefore, even though he is my friend, I will side with the monks instead of the thieves." This villager then went to the merchant and asked, "When do you intend to leave? When are you departing?" When the merchant said it would be on the third day, the villager replied, "Then listen to my word. Do not go on that journey. If you go, such-and-such a thing will happen." When asked, "How did you know?" he replied, "I have a friend in that gang of thieves. It was from him that I got this tip." The merchant thought, "Now it is dangerous for me to go through that forest. Therefore, I must return to the village." Having thought so, he was preparing to do so.
Meanwhile, the thief again sent that man to find out about the merchant's delay. Then the villager said, "Now those merchants are preparing to return." Next, they prepared to rob them on their return journey. The merchant received information from the villager that there were dangers even on the return journey and that the thieves were lying in wait. Because of this, the merchant was at a complete loss as to what to do. He went to the monks and said, "Now I cannot go on this planned journey, nor can I return to my village. Thieves are waiting to rob me. Therefore, if any of you, venerable sirs, wish to remain right here, please do so. Do as you wish. I will be delayed for some days due to this situation." The monks said, "In that case, we will return to Sāvatthī." When they returned to the Buddha, the Buddha asked, "Monks, why did you not go with that wealthy merchant?" The monks then related the news: "We went like this, but because of this danger of thieves, a dilemma arose for the merchant, and he remained there. We returned because of this."
Using that as an illustration, the Buddha then addressed the monks: "Monks, consider that this entire *Bhava* (Becoming) is like a place fraught with the danger of thieves." Knowing this, he gave another simile: "Just as someone who wishes to live avoids poison, and just as a merchant avoids a dangerous path, one must quickly escape from this *Bhava* (Becoming)." Giving advice in this manner, he delivered a discourse. He delivered a discourse that would even help those monks attain the fruits of the path (*magga-phala*). The verse related to that sermon is what we have set as today's topic. It is a very simple verse:
> *Vāṇijo va bhayaṃ maggaṃ,*
> *appasattho mahaddhano;*
> *visaṃ jīvitukāmo va,*
> *pāpāni parivajjaye.*
Just as a merchant with a small caravan—a "caravan" refers to the groups of carts that went on trading journeys in the past; meaning a small group of carts—but with great wealth, avoids a dangerous path; and just as one who wishes to live, *visaṃ jīvitukāmo va*, one who desires to live avoids poison, a deadly poison; so too, *pāpāni parivajjaye*, one should avoid evil deeds (sins). This is the instruction mentioned in that verse.
Although this is a story, the Buddha used it to direct the minds of the monks to a far deeper matter. This is an ordinary event that happens in the world. However, even from this small story, we can reflect on something. The merchant's life was saved—the opportunity for the merchant to escape danger arose—because that villager pondered whether to side with his close friend or with the merchant. At that moment, due to the merchant's faithful nature, because of his quality of faith (*saddhā*), and because he was helping the monks, protection was afforded to him, and he received that tip. That faithful merchant had the opportunity to save his life because of his faith (*saddhā*). Thus, based on the discourse given by the Buddha, and using this story, this incident as a starting point, the Buddha gives a certain "tip" to the world. What is this tip? This journey in *saṃsāra* is a journey undertaken on a path fraught with great danger. Therefore, the sooner one puts an end to this journey in *saṃsāra*, the greater the peace one has. One can reach a safe haven. One can reach the safe haven of Nibbāna. This is the idea given here.
The Buddha constantly speaks about avoiding evil deeds (sins). Why does the Buddha tell us to avoid such sins? We know that we have to perform various actions to carry on with life. The actions that seem easiest for maintaining and sustaining life are what appear as the five sins (five precepts violations). Living by killing, stealing, lying, and in other ways mentioned among the five sins, is easy. Yet, the Buddha describes them as unwholesome deeds (*pāpa-kamma*). Not only that, there is also a category called the ten unwholesome courses of action (*dasa-akusala*). Thus, the Buddha tells us to abstain from these because they carry severe consequences (*vipāka*). This is due to his far-sighted point of view. If we look at it daily from a narrow angle limited only to this life, it might seem that there is nothing wrong with carrying on with life in whatever way possible. But according to the far-sighted vision of *saṃsāra* shown by the Buddha, according to this perspective, the shortcomings in the short-term plans of worldly beings begin to appear. Worldly beings make those plans without any thought about *saṃsāra*, without knowing about it. Worldly beings only see this world visible to the physical eye. Many people doubt the four woeful states (*catu-apāya*), etc., shown by the Buddhas and those with higher direct knowledges—especially when it comes to worlds other than the animal realm, even if they might accept the animal world.
Yet, the Buddha points out that it is these unwholesome deeds that cause birth in hells and other such places. Therefore, he tells us to abstain from them. The simile of poison is shown here. A person who wishes to live does not knowingly drink poison. Similarly, one who desires happiness and dislikes Suffering / Unsatisfactoriness / Stress (*dukkha*) should not commit sins—this is the Buddha's advice. Indeed, the question of livelihood has always been a great challenge to the world. What action should be taken in the face of the question of survival? At that point, the Buddha introduces to the world two things: wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*) and right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*). Indeed, if one recognizes wrong livelihood, abstaining from it itself is considered right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*) for laypeople. To briefly introduce wrong livelihood, it is presented in five terms in the Sutta discourses, stating that one should abstain from five types of trade. What are they? *Sattha, satta, maṃsa, visa, majja* (weapons, living beings, meat, poison, and intoxicants). *Sattha* means weapons—the trade in weapons, living by it. Likewise, *satta* refers to living beings—indeed, here it means human beings, living beings; it refers to humans. Next, *maṃsa*, the trade in meat. Next, the trade in poison (*visa*). Next, the trade in intoxicants (*majja*).
Why these are shown as wrong may also be a question to some. The trade in weapons—the trade in weapons of war—contains the quality of instigating war and conflict to satisfy hatred. Because of this production and trade of weapons, it is a form of trade that leads to violence towards others. The trade in weapons is shown as something that should not be done by a faithful Buddhist lay disciple.
Similarly, although the word *satta* (written as *satata* in the transcription) is there, it means selling men and women into slavery or for immoral purposes—the selling of a life, and other such forms of trade. These lead to social corruption and cause harm to others. Next is the trade in meat. Regarding this, there are certain controversies in this day and age. Speaking of the trade, as some point out, wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*) exists only at the back of the butcher shop, while right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*) is at the front. This is because the killing of animals is done only at the back, while at the front, the meat of those dead animals is kept for use and consumption by those who seek health. Thus, they think that the front part is right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*). But if we think deeply, we can see the trade itself as wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*). Within it, there is a quality of making humans crave, get addicted to, and become greedy for the taste of meat.
Even in these times, when lay disciples who have an understanding of society talk about food, there is a tendency to expect fresh meat just as one buys fresh vegetables. "Fresh meat" means something like killing and eating on a daily basis. Likewise, warm food is considered superior. In some hotels, at that moment, the customer or guest chooses the animal they like, and it is brought to the table, killed, and eaten while the blood is still warm—we even get to hear of such things. What is seen from this is greed for the tongue. To please the tongue, to satisfy the greed for the taste of meat, even the tongue of a cow is cut, cooked, and eaten, to such an extent that the beastly, demonic qualities in the human mind-stream (*citta-santāna*) are brought out. Thus, when we think about hotel life, the only difference between the food eaten by a beast and the food eaten by a human is the use of spoons and forks. To that extent, since this meat trade habituates society to certain wrong habits, beastly habits, we can see that there is a disadvantageous side to the meat trade. It is difficult to consider it as right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*).
The others are clear. In the trade of poison, what is present is helping to destroy someone's life. Today, mass slaughter of animals often takes place; sometimes there is no understanding of the environmental pollution within it. However, the trade in poison that aids in the mass killing of insects, denying their right to live, can also be included in this. When we think deeply, these are things that defile one's mind-stream (*citta-santāna*) and harm the world. Demerit (*akusala*) was described as that which leads to self-harm and harm to others.
When we think deeply, self-harm means the defilement of one's own mind—the defilement of the mind-stream (*citta-santāna*). If one drinks poison, either life is destroyed immediately because of it, or after that poison enters the body, one has to suffer its consequences after some time. Such is the case with poison that enters the physical body (*rūpa-santāna*). But through the poison that arises as unwholesome deeds (*akusala*) entering the mind-stream (*citta-santāna*), it either yields results in this very life as *diṭṭhadhammavedanīya* (to be experienced in this life), or as *upapajjavedanīya* (to be experienced in the next life), or as *aparāpariyavedanīya* (to be experienced in subsequent lives) in a future life; through that poison added to the mind-stream (*citta-santāna*), one has to undergo painful, bitter Suffering / Unsatisfactoriness / Stress (*dukkha*) in hells (*apāya*) and other such places. That is why the Buddha showed that such things should not be done.
There is nothing new to tell you lay disciples about the trade in intoxicants mentioned last. There, too, is that which completely deranges the mind, makes one forget human existence, and reduces one to a beastly state. Next is the addiction to drinking. The trade in intoxicants leads to that addiction. The Buddha indicates that a true faithful Buddhist lay disciple must withdraw from such trading methods. This question of livelihood is a problem for many people, especially in this day and age, because support and encouragement for wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*) are received from all sides. A person who desires a righteous livelihood has to face dilemmas just like that merchant. Facing dilemmas means facing great problems of whether to go forward or backward. When we look at occupations and employment, almost everything contains things that incline towards such wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*).
Solving that problem is indeed a matter left to each individual. However, a valuable Dhamma discourse that may help in this regard is mentioned in the Majjhima Nikāya by the name of the Dhanañjāni Sutta. It is a long Sutta discourse, but I will try to present it briefly. On one occasion, while the Buddha was residing at the Veluvana monastery in Rājagaha, the chief disciple Ven. Sāriputta wandered in the region of Dakkhiṇāgiri with a group of monks. Meanwhile, a certain monk who had spent the rains retreat (*vassa*) with the Buddha in Rājagaha arrived in the Dakkhiṇāgiri region and met Ven. Sāriputta.
First of all, Ven. Sāriputta asked this monk, "How is it, is the Blessed One dwelling in good health?" When the monk replied, "Yes," Sāriputta asked, "Is the community of monks in good health?" When the monk replied, "Yes," he next asked, "Is the Brahmin Dhanañjāni, who lives in the village of Taṇḍulapāla, in good health?" After the monk replied, "Yes," Ven. Sāriputta asked, "Is that Brahmin Dhanañjāni diligent (*appamāda*)?" Diligent here means diligent in wholesome deeds (*kusala*). That is, whether he is leading a righteous life without committing sins. It was then that the monk declared, "Friend Sāriputta, what diligence is there for Dhanañjāni? The Brahmin Dhanañjāni exploits brahmins and householders in the name of the king, and exploits the king in the name of brahmins and householders. He lives by corrupt practices. Furthermore, Dhanañjāni's former faithful wife has passed away, and he is now married to a woman who lacks faith." Hearing this, Ven. Sāriputta expressed his sadness: "Indeed, this is very bad news we have heard, that the Brahmin Dhanañjāni has fallen into negligence (*pamāda*). If only I could meet Dhanañjāni someday. It would be good if an opportunity to speak with him arose." Thus he made a mental note.
Sometime later, Ven. Sāriputta returned to Rājagaha and, while residing at the Veluvana monastery, went on his alms round in Rājagaha one morning. At that time, the Brahmin Dhanañjāni was engaged in milking his cows outside the city. Ven. Sāriputta, having finished his alms round and eaten his meal, walked to the place where the Brahmin Dhanañjāni was. Seeing Ven. Sāriputta from afar, the Brahmin Dhanañjāni invited him, saying, "Venerable Sāriputta, come and have some milk." Ven. Sāriputta replied, "No, there is no need. I have finished my meal. Come to such-and-such a tree. I will be resting there under that tree during the daytime. Come there." Accordingly, while Ven. Sāriputta was under that tree, the Brahmin Dhanañjāni, having finished his meal, came to Ven. Sāriputta. Ven. Sāriputta, after exchanging friendly greetings, straightaway asked, "How is it, Dhanañjāni, are you diligent?"
Now, the answer given by the Brahmin Dhanañjāni is the very answer many people give nowadays. What did the Brahmin Dhanañjāni say? "Venerable Sāriputta, what diligence is there for us? We have parents to support. We have a wife and children to support. We have servants and workers to support. We have to perform duties towards friends and companions. We have to perform duties towards relatives. We have to perform duties towards guests. Next, we must perform offerings (*preta-pūjā*) to our departed relatives (*preta*). We must perform offerings to the deities (*deva-pūjā*). We must perform duties for the king. Not only that, we must also gratify and maintain this body. When there is such a heavy burden of duties, what diligence can there be for us?"
Thus, this Brahmin was leading an unrighteous, uneven life, inclining towards unrighteousness. Ven. Sāriputta declared, "But Brahmin, if you live unrighteously and lead an uneven life, and upon death are born in hell (*niraya*), can you escape by telling the wardens of hell (*yamapalla*), 'I did these things for the sake of my parents, to look after my parents; do nothing to me'? Can you escape thus?" The Brahmin replied, "No, that would not be possible." Ven. Sāriputta then asked, "Can those parents step forward and say, 'It was for our sake that our child behaved unrighteously and led an uneven life, so do not do anything to him'? Can they save him thus?" The Brahmin replied, "No, they cannot save him. The hell-wardens will drag him away and inflict various kinds of Suffering / Unsatisfactoriness / Stress (*dukkha*)."
In the same way, to make that matter clearer, Ven. Sāriputta questioned him about each of those groups of people: "If you behave unrighteously and lead an uneven life for the sake of wife and children, or for servants and workers..." In this way, he questioned him step-by-step so that it would sink deep into the Brahmin's mind. Finally, Ven. Sāriputta asked, "What do you think, Brahmin? If someone supports their parents righteously and evenly (*dhamma-cārī samacārī*), and another supports their parents unrighteously and unevenly (*adhamma-cārī visamacārī*), who between the two is the better person?" The Brahmin replied, "Indeed, the practice of supporting parents righteously and evenly is the better one." Then Ven. Sāriputta declared, "Brahmin, there are livelihoods in society through which one can live righteously, support one's parents, and perform meritorious deeds. This is a possible thing." Thus he convinced the Brahmin Dhanañjāni, and Dhanañjāni accepted it with joy.
Next, what we find in that Sutta discourse is the final period of the Brahmin Dhanañjāni's life. Being extremely ill and near death, the Brahmin Dhanañjāni sent a message through a servant to pay respects to the Buddha and to Ven. Sāriputta, and to invite Ven. Sāriputta, saying that the Brahmin Dhanañjāni was gravely ill and asking him to visit out of compassion. Ven. Sāriputta visited the house of the Brahmin Dhanañjāni. Having arrived, he began a Dhamma talk. Gradually, he delivered a Dhamma talk of a nature that would elevate the Brahmin's mind from lower worlds to higher worlds, and at the very end, he spoke about the four divine abodes (*brahma-vihāra*): loving-kindness (*mettā*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*).
Ven. Sāriputta thought, "These brahmins desire to be born in the Brahma world. Therefore, I must tell him the path to the Brahma world." He then explained how to develop the four divine abodes (*brahma-vihāra*). Having explained this, he rose from his seat and returned. At that time, as his final words, the Brahmin Dhanañjāni said, "Pay homage to the Blessed One in my name." A short while after Ven. Sāriputta had left, that Brahmin passed away and was reborn in the Brahma world. When Ven. Sāriputta went to the Buddha and related this news, the Buddha admonished Ven. Sāriputta: "Why, Sāriputta, did you establish him in the inferior Brahma world when there was more to be done, when he could have gone much higher?" Thus he expressed a certain blame toward Ven. Sāriputta.
From this, we can understand that the strength of the wholesome potential (*kusala-shakti*) developed by that Brahmin near his death was so great that, if Ven. Sāriputta had in some way turned him toward insight (*vipassanā*) and preached the Dhamma, the Buddha was indicating that he could have realized the paths and fruits (*magga-phala*). "Why did you stop him at the inferior Brahma world when he could have been led higher?"—this was the admonition given to Ven. Sāriputta. We can learn many things from this incident. Although the story itself is brief, it is highly valuable as a Sutta discourse. On one hand, we see the wonderful compassion of Ven. Sāriputta. Indeed, the Brahmin Dhanañjāni was not even someone who had taken refuge in the Triple Gem. But because his former wife was extremely faithful, Ven. Sāriputta had a special compassion for this lay Brahmin. That is why, after inquiring about the Buddha's well-being and the Sangha's well-being, he asked the monk about the Brahmin Dhanañjāni.
Then, having visited him specifically for this purpose, instead of asking casual questions like "How are you? Where are you living?", Ven. Sāriputta asked, "Brahmin, are you diligent?" That is the real question. That is the correct question to ask lay disciples. "How is it, are you now leading your life diligently?" Based on the answer given to that question, Ven. Sāriputta convinced the Brahmin Dhanañjāni through that long discourse that an unrighteous life, an uneven life, uneven behavior is very dangerous, and that its consequences (*vipāka*) are extremely severe. It was because he understood this at the end that the Brahmin Dhanañjāni developed his mind so much at the moment of death. He developed it to such an extent that, by establishing himself in the four divine abodes (*brahma-vihāra*) of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, he even attained birth in the Brahma world. Ven. Sāriputta brought about a massive transformation in his life at that moment. Otherwise, had he continued with that unrighteous life, the Brahmin Dhanañjāni would have fallen into hell (*apāya*) after death. We can learn something from this. Indeed, as stated earlier, everyone thinks that the easiest way to live is through those unrighteous methods. Why did the Buddha reject them? As we constantly remind you, today more place is given to the economy than to righteousness. Therefore, they try to inflate the economy to such an extent that there is no place for a righteous life. But the Buddha points out its result. When we think far-sightedly, the Buddha highlights the disadvantageous side (*ādīnava*) of it.
If we consider the easy methods, we have to take economic principles from the great ocean and the forest. This is because in the ocean there exists a very easy way of life. In ancient terms, this is called *mātsya-nyāya* (the law of the fish). *Mātsya-nyāya*, lay disciples, means the large preying on the small—the tuna preying on the sprat. Throughout the great ocean, there is only the large animal preying on the small animal. That is the easiest way of life. Next, in the forest, too, there is the strong preying on the weak. This natural law is expressed in the Buddha's words as follows:
In a Sutta discourse where this is mentioned, it is said that if one is born in the animal world, it is extremely difficult to obtain a good rebirth again. Taking a small amount of dust on his fingernail, the Buddha made a statement to the monks. The Buddha used this simile on many occasions. When asked, "Is the dust on the fingernail greater, or is the soil of the great earth greater?" the monks replied, "The soil of the great earth is much greater, while the dust on the fingernail is very little." The Buddha then told the monks, "Just so, monks, once someone is born in an animal womb, it is extremely difficult to rise out of it. It is like the dust on the fingernail; only a very few rise out of it. What is the reason for this? What are the two terms that describe the natural law in this animal world? *Aññamaññabhādikā ettha vattati, dubbalabhādikā.* *Aññamaññabhādikā* means devouring one another. The principle of devouring one another and the principle of oppressing the weak exist in the animal world." Indeed, it is those natural laws of the animal world that have gradually entered human society today.
The word "exploitation" (devouring / grabbing) that we mentioned in society is indeed a word taken from the animal world. Now, you lay disciples also occasionally get to see a kingfisher or a hawk perched on a tree, turning its head and watching for a while, as if deeply pondering some profound economic theory. After watching for a while, it dives down onto its prey with the speed of an arrow; that is "grabbing" (exploiting). That is the kind of thing happening in today's society. You know that this is done not only out of poverty; it is not only the poor, but also the rich who do this—grabbing/exploiting. What is seen through this is, just as the Brahmin Dhanañjāni did earlier, carrying on with one's livelihood through lying, fraud, theft, and various forms of corruption. The Buddha points out the severe consequences (*vipāka*) of these. We must learn something from this.
Thus, if we look at it according to that economic theory, there are indeed countless easy paths. Yet, the Buddha designates these five as wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*) with a deep meaning. Life does not end there. When poison enters this physical body (*rūpa-santāna*), it affects only this life. But how do these enter the mind-stream (*citta-santāna*)? Through the defilement of mind, body, and speech—by their becoming corrupted. They become corrupted by greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dvesha*), delusion (*moha*), and other various defilements (*kilesa*). In particular, after a person's mind-stream (*citta-santāna*) is corrupted, not only by the unwholesome deeds of killing and stealing, but also by those things shown as the ten unwholesome courses of action (*dasa-akusala*), the next *Jāti* (Birth) is received as a result. Neither parents nor relatives and friends can step forward and save a person from hells (*niraya*) and other such places. The Buddha shows this through the natural law of kamma.
You lay disciples have often heard the law of kamma expressed in words such as *kammasako'mhi kammadāyādo kammayoni kammabandhu kammapaṭisaraṇo*. Kamma is the only thing one takes from here. Only the kamma one has done, whether good or bad, is what one owns: *kammasako'mhi*—one is the owner of one's kamma. Likewise, what one has as one's inheritance is kamma: *kammadāyādo*—heir to one's kamma. Where one goes and is born, how one's birth is determined is kamma: *kammayoni*—born of one's kamma. What stands as one's relative is kamma: *kammabandhu*—related to one's kamma. What serves as one's refuge is kamma: *kammapaṭisaraṇo*—supported by one's kamma. Therefore, according to that word of the Buddha, we must reflect on the danger of those easy paths. What appears from this is the way we must practice equanimity (*upekkhā*) on certain occasions. Just as that merchant stopped for a while, unable to go forward or backward, when we face certain paths that seem easy, we must consider whether they are righteous or unrighteous, think whether they are even behavior or uneven behavior, and think deeply. If they fall on the uneven side, the unrighteous side, we must practice equanimity (*upekkhā*). That means we should not act rashly. For, by acting quickly, we get entangled in a severe unwholesome deed (*akusala*) without even knowing it. One will have to pay for it for a long time in *saṃsāra*.
That is why the Buddha explained the danger of this wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*). Normally, people now consider these as minor things. There is another very famous discourse delivered on this very topic. On one occasion, the Buddha declared that there are three types of people in the world. The analysis of persons the Buddha makes there is done by grasping both the economic and the righteous aspects. There is an analysis of persons made by grasping both the economic and the righteous aspects. There are three types of people in the world. Who are the three? The blind, the one-eyed, and the two-eyed. The Buddha explains the blind person as follows: There is a person who lacks the eye of wisdom necessary to acquire unacquired wealth, or to secure, consolidate, or increase acquired wealth. Likewise, that person also lacks the eye of wisdom, the Dhamma-eye, that helps to distinguish good and bad, wholesome and unwholesome (*kusala akusala*), merit and demerit. That person is completely blind.
The second person is the one-eyed. The Buddha describes such a person as one who has the economic eye necessary to acquire unacquired wealth and to increase acquired wealth, but lacks the righteous eye. This person does not reflect on good and bad, on the wholesome and unwholesome (*kusala akusala*). That is the nature of the one-eyed. The person with two eyes—according to this, you lay disciples can straightaway understand that this is the person who is complete in both aspects. Thus, if one is a true Buddhist disciple, according to that analysis shown by the Buddha, one must strive to live with both eyes. Otherwise, if one lives as a one-eyed person, there will be severe consequences (*vipāka*). That is, the Buddha straightaway points out that if one lives unrighteously and unevenly through lies, fraud, theft, and violence, one will eventually have to suffer the consequences in hells (*niraya*) and other such places for a long time. In that analysis of persons, too, it becomes clear to us that the Buddha directed attention to both the economic and the righteous aspects.
Next, in a similar way, in a certain place, the Buddha points out four undertakings of Dhamma (*dhamma-samādāna*). You have heard of the undertaking of virtue (*sīla-samādāna*). Undertaking virtue (*sīla-samādāna*) means accepting a certain practice of virtue, striving to live according to it, making a promise, and making a determination. What is shown here by the name of *dhamma-samādāna* is not things like the five precepts or the eight precepts. What is spoken of here is the ten unwholesome courses of action (*dasa-akusala*)—abstaining from the ten unwholesome courses of action. Most people know what the ten unwholesome courses are: abstaining from the three unwholesome deeds done by the body, namely, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. Next, abstaining from the four unwholesome deeds done by speech. What are they? Lying, slandering, harsh speech, and frivolous talk (*sampappalāpa*)—that is, speaking useless gossip, speaking meaningless words. Next, regarding the mind, the word *abhijjhā* (covetousness) is used. That means intense, uneven greed. How is uneven greed described? Greed exists in everyone. The nature of uneven greed is that when someone has something, one thinks, "Oh, if only I could get this somehow," and out of envy for another's happiness, a greed arises to acquire it. That greed, that uneven greed, is a severe unwholesome deed developed by the mind. Similarly, hatred—a hateful mind. Next, thirdly, wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) is shown: uneven greed, a hateful mind, and wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*).
Taking up the practice of abstaining from these ten unwholesome courses of action (*dasa-akusala*) is what is meant here by *dhamma-samādāna*. The Buddha points out four types of *dhamma-samādāna*. In this brief, limited time, we do not need to mention all of those matters. It is not necessary to show them. We will highlight only the two matters relevant to this topic. One of these four is: there is a certain undertaking of Dhamma (*dhamma-samādāna*) that brings happiness in the present but yields painful consequences in the future. There is another undertaking of Dhamma (*dhamma-samādāna*) that has a painful nature in the present but yields happiness in the future. Let us first describe the one mentioned first.
The Buddha points it out in this way: Suppose someone engages in killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, etc., with great joy and pleasure. They engage in those sins with great joy. But having gone and been born in hell (*apāya*), they have to suffer severe, painful consequences (*vipāka*) of those deeds. The Buddha also gives a simile for this. The Buddha gives similes, etc., to make every single point sink deep into the mind, not as poetic ornaments. What is the simile? Suppose there is a vessel containing a good drink. That drink has a beautiful color, a good fragrance, and a good taste. There is a drink that is colorful, fragrant, and tasty. But this drink has been mixed with poison.
A person who is interested comes there. Those standing by the vessel of drink say, "Come, come, here is a good drink. This is tasty, fragrant, and colorful. However, poison has been mixed into this. If you wish, drink it. When drinking, it is very tasty and fragrant. But after drinking it, you will either die or fall into a suffering equivalent to death." This is what those standing by the vessel of drink say. Indeed, they state the fact. Thereupon, that person drinks it without reflecting wisely. What happens when he drinks it? While drinking, it is tasty. But after drinking, he faces death in the manner described, or falls into a suffering equivalent to death. This is the simile given by the Buddha for the practice of performing unwholesome deeds with joy, which are pleasant while doing them, but eventually bring painful consequences (*vipāka*) that one must suffer.
What is the second undertaking of Dhamma (*dhamma-samādāna*) mentioned? At the time of engaging in them, it is painful. It is felt not as happiness but as pain, as displeasure. Yet, its fruit, its consequence (*vipāka*), is happiness. It is something that brings happiness. The Buddha's simile for this is briefly described as follows: Suppose someone abstains from killing, stealing, etc., with great difficulty. "With great difficulty" means that, thinking about the Buddha's words, they keep those precepts (*sikkhāpada*) and abstain from those unwholesome deeds (*akusala*) with great effort and pain. Yet, as a result of that, they eventually obtain birth in a happy realm (*sugati*).
The Buddha gives a simile there. The Buddha himself prescribed a medicine specifically for the monks, which is called *pūtimutta-bhesajja* (fermented urine medicine). *Pūtimutta-bhesajja* is a medicine made from cow's urine. When yellow myrobalan (*aralu*), etc., are added to it, it is a very good medicine for jaundice (*paṇḍu-roga*). That is the simile the Buddha points out here. When drinking that medicine, it smells bad, has no pleasant color, and no pleasant taste. But after drinking it, that disease is cured. A jaundice patient comes to a place where such a drink is kept. Those who are there say, "Here is a medicine. When drinking this, there is no taste or fragrance. But if you drink it, you will be cured." Having heard this, that person reflects wisely and, although it is unpalatable, takes that medicine. Having taken it, he is cured. Through this simile, the Buddha shows that for those who follow the righteous path, even though with difficulty, even though with pain, even though crying, happiness can be expected in the end.
The same kind of thing is present in this undertaking of virtue (*sīla-samādāna*). Here, the Buddha spoke about the first person. Thinking very highly of themselves, exulting over it, they engage in killing, stealing, etc., with great joy. It is only when they have to suffer the consequences (*vipāka*) of those deeds that they realize. The next person mentioned abstains from those things with great difficulty. It is very hard to abstain from them, yet, with great difficulty and displeasure, they abstain from them. But the result of that is good. Now, this is where we can connect the value of these virtues (*sīla*), etc. For, it is through understanding that one can change one's attitude.
Now, someone might think, "Abstaining from killing, abstaining from stealing, etc., is very difficult; abstaining from these is a great trouble. There are easier methods than this"—that is wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*). If someone has developed faith (*saddhā*) according to the Buddha's word, that person can derive joy from it. In keeping virtues (*sīla*), etc., reflecting on the value of the undertaking of virtue (*sīla-samādāna*), reflecting on that determination of virtue, and then reviewing (*āvarjana*) it, one derives joy. That is called blameless happiness (*anavajja-sukha*). That is a happiness belonging to a lay disciple. In particular, even extremely wealthy people do not have that blameless happiness (*anavajja-sukha*) in this day and age. What is the reason? It is because of that "exploitation" (grabbing) mentioned earlier. That is their diligence. Nowadays, what the world mostly considers as diligence is the diligence of the kingfisher, the hawk, and the vulture. They swoop down on their prey very diligently. That is not the diligence the Buddha points out here. It is one's far-sightedness. The kingfisher, the hawk, and the vulture also have a certain far-sightedness that sees only that prey.
