But the far-sightedness, the diligence shown by the Buddha, is different.
Now, some wealthy people do not have that blameless happiness (*anavajja-sukha*)—that faultless happiness. Even though they have gathered a vast amount of wealth, when they think about how they gathered this wealth, a great regret arises. The happiness gathered by oppressing human beings, through various forms of corruption, fraud, and exploitation. Because of this, that person has to suffer severe pain and suffering on their deathbed. Indeed, according to the Buddha's word, there is nothing new to say about having to suffer pain and suffering after death. Instead, the Buddha points out that what a wise lay disciple should do is reflect on the virtuous side of what appears to be difficult, gain that faith (*saddhā*) thinking, "This will bring me good," and derive joy through that.
Faultless happiness means the happiness derived from that virtue (*sīla*). "I have kept such-and-such a practice." In short, the recollection of virtue (*sīlānussati*) itself can be turned into a meditation (*bhāvanā*). The fact that one is virtuous. When reflecting on that again and again, that joy arises in that person, and finally, through that, the mind becomes concentrated; it becomes focused in concentration (*samādhi*). One can go that far. Because of this, some might think, "The Buddha has always preached *veramaṇī, veramaṇī*. What is this *veramaṇī*? Abstain, abstain, he says. The Buddha speaks only of things to be avoided, things to be given up. He does not tell us anything to do." Someone might say this according to economic theories. But the Buddha points out that within that giving up, one can find joy. If someone keeps the five precepts (*pañca-sīla*) properly, they can derive that joy by reviewing (*āvarjana*) each of them.
The Buddha points out, "In a world where so much killing of living beings takes place, I am living while giving this infinite, immeasurable gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*)." Nowadays, as we constantly remind you, the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*) has sometimes been limited to releasing a cow destined for slaughter, prepared for taking a photograph. But silently, without shouting to the world, if one, as a matter of principle, avoids causing harm and keeps the precept of abstaining from killing very purely, the Buddha declared that such a person is giving the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*) to infinite, immeasurable living beings. By deriving joy from that and reviewing (*āvarjana*) that precept (*sikkhāpada*), that person can even attain concentration (*samādhi*). That itself can be used to help attain Nibbāna. Such a wonderful depth lies in these virtues (*sīla*), etc. That must be understood. Similarly, what was called *dhamma-samādāna* here is, just like *sīla-samādāna*, abstaining from the ten unwholesome courses of action (*dasa-akusala*). That practice of abstaining from the ten unwholesome courses of action goes even further. When reflecting on each of them, thinking, "In such a society, I am keeping such-and-such precept, or keeping such-and-such practice," joy arises. Looking at it from that perspective, it is not like drinking that fermented urine medicine (*pūtimutta-bhesajja*) unwillingly; it is a state where one can drink it willingly.
There is a deep practice, a deep meaning within these virtues (*sīla*), etc., through which one can find relief on each occasion. Thus, the fundamental factor in all of this is abstaining from sins. What the Buddha constantly declares is: just as the merchant practiced equanimity (*upekkhā*), neither going forward nor backward when there was danger on the road, if in a certain course of action one sees, "It is wrong if I do this, and it is wrong if I do not do this," on that occasion, one must practice equanimity (*upekkhā*). One must hold back for a while. It is bad to be attached to it.
Similarly, one must have the strength to reflect on these far-sightedly. A person who lives in such a principled way has fewer regrets. As the Buddha declares, there is blameless happiness (*anavajja-sukha*), faultless happiness. The mind can constantly remain in joy. When reviewing—reviewing (*āvarjana*) means looking back. Looking back and reflecting on the purity of one's life, that person experiences great joy, especially at the final moment. Although the Brahmin Dhanañjāni lived unrighteously in the first part of his life, even though the details are not mentioned at length, we see that a massive transformation took place in his life after he received Ven. Sāriputta's advice. It was as a result of that massive life transformation that this Brahmin was able to obtain birth in the Brahma world, by relying on the Dhamma heard at the final moment. Therefore, in whatever way our individual lives have been spent, if we make a determination... At the end of a year, you make various kinds of targets, determinations, connecting them with New Year customs. Even setting out for occupations is done at an auspicious time (*näkatha*). But even if done at an auspicious time, if those things belong to the inauspicious, there is no use in it. What is inauspicious? One must do what is auspicious, what is good. What is inauspicious is wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*). If one sets out for employment at an auspicious time, but sets out for that wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*), there is no use in that auspicious time.
This life transformation may not be possible in a single day or in a single moment. Yet, if wise lay disciples direct their minds to these and make an effort, it will not be impossible to bring about a transformation in their individual lives according to the Buddha's word. Worldly beings have given up things greater than this. One step in the method of doing so is, at least, observing precepts (*sīla*) on one of the four Poya days of the month. If someone engaged in such wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*) withdraws from it for one day, sacrifices it, sacrifices the profit received from it, observes pure virtue (*sīla*), and spends the day in that manner, an opening is created for them there. "If I can do this for one day, why not make it two days, observing it on two Poya days?" Next, if taken to four Poya days, it is four days. Going on in this manner, gradually, they will be able to withdraw even from hereditary wrong livelihoods. If one makes no such effort but goes on, enslaved to the direction in which society is heading, one only moves further down the path of decline. As we mentioned, the tongue adapts very quickly in a way that encourages meat-eating, etc. Such is the world that exists. One must reflect wisely on wrong notions and understand the Buddha's words deeply. One's livelihood is not something limited only to this life. In this journey of *saṃsāra*, this era of a Buddha's arising (*buddhotpāda-kāla*) is an extremely rare time. Human existence (*manussa-attabhāva*) is also an opportunity. If we live as beasts, as demons, we cannot derive the true benefit of the Buddha's Dispensation (*sāsana*). Therefore, transforming our lives internally is something that belongs to each of us. Today, on account of the New Year, you have received that stream of thoughts to be added to your mind-streams (*citta-santāna*).
During this period of about one hour, this group of lay disciples, having undertaken in varying measures the eight precepts (*aṭṭha-sīla*), the ten precepts (*dasa-sīla*), or the precepts with right livelihood as the eighth (*ājīvatthamaka-sīla*), listened to the Dhamma sermon. It is through taming the three doors of action—body, speech, and mind—in our daily existence that we can attain deliverance from *saṃsāra* (*saṃsāra-vimukti*). Therefore, as we constantly remind you, may you develop those qualities of faith (*saddhā*), etc., with the strength gathered by hearing the Dhamma. May you turn the spiritual faculties (*indriya*) of faith (*saddhā*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*) into spiritual powers (*bala*). Supported by association with noble friends (*kalyāṇa-mitta*), may you gain the strength and power to quickly escape all the suffering of *saṃsāra*, such as *Jāti* (Birth) and death (*maraṇa*), through the realization, the penetration of the paths and fruits (*magga-phala*) of Sotāpanna, Sakadāgāmi, Anāgāmi, and Arahant, and by attaining the supreme, deathless Nibbāna! Similarly, if any departed relatives in one's name, or any beings from the Avīci hell to the Akanitha heaven, wish to share in the merit of this Dhamma teaching and Dhamma hearing, may they, by sharing in this merit, realize the supreme, deathless Nibbāna through a Bodhi of their aspiration! With this aspiration, please recite this verse:
“*Ettāvatā ca amhehi.........*”

author: ven. katukurunde nanananda thero
(pahankanuwa sinhala audio dhamma sermon no.82)
namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa
(homage to the blessed one, the worthy one, the fully self-enlightened one)
pali stanza:
"vanijo va bhayam maggam,
appasattho mahaddhano;
visam jivitukamo va,
papani parivajjaye."
from:
dhammapada verse 123 (papa vagga)
dear listeners,
the buddha, the teacher of the three worlds, explained demerit and merit to the world based on the far-reaching understanding he gained regarding existence in *samsara*. due to a lack of foresight, the buddha saw how living beings fall into suffering / unsatisfactoriness / stress (*dukkha*) in *samsara*. the buddha points out how, by acting as slaves to one's whims based on a narrow philosophy of life limited only to this life, one undergoes bitter suffering / unsatisfactoriness / stress (*dukkha*) in *samsara* for an infinite length of time. today's thematic verse is one that illustrates this very point. the buddha preached this dhamma verse at the jetavana monastery to a group of monks, addressing a disastrous situation faced by a certain wealthy merchant.
about five hundred thieves had been watchfully waiting for a very long time to break into the house of a very wealthy merchant living in the city of savatthi. but they did not get the opportunity. on a certain occasion, this merchant set out to trade in a distant region, preparing five hundred carts. in those days, there was a custom where merchants travelling to such distant regions would inform the monks, inviting them to accompany them if they also wished to travel in that direction, because they had to travel through vast forests. likewise, this merchant told the monks, "i am going to trade in such-and-such a region. if you, venerable sirs, are also planning to go there, please come with me. then there will be no trouble regarding alms-food (*pindapata*), etc." hearing that the merchants were leaving, those thieves hid in the forest along that path to rob them when they passed by. meanwhile, the merchant set out with the group of monks, and exactly at the entrance to the forest, they stopped at a village for two or three days to organize the carts and oxen.
knowing that the journey was delayed, the thieves, who were waiting for the merchant, sent a thief to a villager friend of his to find out the reason for the merchant's delay. when he asked the villagers when this wealthy merchant would depart, the villager replied, "perhaps in two or three days. why do you ask?" he replied, "our group is ready and waiting for these merchants." thereupon, the villager said, "then the merchants will come soon," and after sending his friend away, he thought, "should i side with the merchant, or should i side with these thieves?" then he reasoned, "because of this merchant, a group of monks is receiving alms and other requisites. therefore, even though he is my friend, i will side with the monks instead of the thieves." this villager then went to the merchant and asked, "when do you intend to leave? when are you departing?" when the merchant said it would be on the third day, the villager replied, "then listen to my word. do not go on that journey. if you go, such-and-such a thing will happen." when asked, "how did you know?" he replied, "i have a friend in that gang of thieves. it was from him that i got this tip." the merchant thought, "now it is dangerous for me to go through that forest. therefore, i must return to the village." having thought so, he was preparing to do so.
meanwhile, the thief again sent that man to find out about the merchant's delay. then the villager said, "now those merchants are preparing to return." next, they prepared to rob them on their return journey. the merchant received information from the villager that there were dangers even on the return journey and that the thieves were lying in wait. because of this, the merchant was at a complete loss as to what to do. he went to the monks and said, "now i cannot go on this planned journey, nor can i return to my village. thieves are waiting to rob me. therefore, if any of you, venerable sirs, wish to remain right here, please do so. do as you wish. i will be delayed for some days due to this situation." the monks said, "in that case, we will return to savatthi." when they returned to the buddha, the buddha asked, "monks, why did you not go with that wealthy merchant?" the monks then related the news: "we went like this, but because of this danger of thieves, a dilemma arose for the merchant, and he remained there. we returned because of this."
using that as an illustration, the buddha then addressed the monks: "monks, consider that this entire *bhava* (becoming) is like a place fraught with the danger of thieves." knowing this, he gave another simile: "just as someone who wishes to live avoids poison, and just as a merchant avoids a dangerous path, one must quickly escape from this *bhava* (becoming)." giving advice in this manner, he delivered a discourse. he delivered a discourse that would even help those monks attain the fruits of the path (*magga-phala*). the verse related to that sermon is what we have set as today's topic. it is a very simple verse:
> *vanijo va bhayam maggam,*
> *appasattho mahaddhano;*
> *visam jivitukamo va,*
> *papani parivajjaye.*
just as a merchant with a small caravan—a "caravan" refers to the groups of carts that went on trading journeys in the past; meaning a small group of carts—but with great wealth, avoids a dangerous path; and just as one who wishes to live, *visam jivitukamo va*, one who desires to live avoids poison, a deadly poison; so too, *papani parivajjaye*, one should avoid evil deeds (sins). this is the instruction mentioned in that verse.
although this is a story, the buddha used it to direct the minds of the monks to a far deeper matter. this is an ordinary event that happens in the world. however, even from this small story, we can reflect on something. the merchant's life was saved—the opportunity for the merchant to escape danger arose—because that villager pondered whether to side with his close friend or with the merchant. at that moment, due to the merchant's faithful nature, because of his quality of faith (*saddha*), and because he was helping the monks, protection was afforded to him, and he received that tip. that faithful merchant had the opportunity to save his life because of his faith (*saddha*). thus, based on the discourse given by the buddha, and using this story, this incident as a starting point, the buddha gives a certain "tip" to the world. what is this tip? this journey in *samsara* is a journey undertaken on a path fraught with great danger. therefore, the sooner one puts an end to this journey in *samsara*, the greater the peace one has. one can reach a safe haven. one can reach the safe haven of nibbana. this is the idea given here.
the buddha constantly speaks about avoiding evil deeds (sins). why does the buddha tell us to avoid such sins? we know that we have to perform various actions to carry on with life. the actions that seem easiest for maintaining and sustaining life are what appear as the five sins (five precepts violations). living by killing, stealing, lying, and in other ways mentioned among the five sins, is easy. yet, the buddha describes them as unwholesome deeds (*papa-kamma*). not only that, there is also a category called the ten unwholesome courses of action (*dasa-akusala*). thus, the buddha tells us to abstain from these because they carry severe consequences (*vipaka*). this is due to his far-sighted point of view. if we look at it daily from a narrow angle limited only to this life, it might seem that there is nothing wrong with carrying on with life in whatever way possible. but according to the far-sighted vision of *samsara* shown by the buddha, according to this perspective, the shortcomings in the short-term plans of worldly beings begin to appear. worldly beings make those plans without any thought about *samsara*, without knowing about it. worldly beings only see this world visible to the physical eye. many people doubt the four woeful states (*catu-apaya*), etc., shown by the buddhas and those with higher direct knowledges—especially when it comes to worlds other than the animal realm, even if they might accept the animal world.
yet, the buddha points out that it is these unwholesome deeds that cause birth in hells and other such places. therefore, he tells us to abstain from them. the simile of poison is shown here. a person who wishes to live does not knowingly drink poison. similarly, one who desires happiness and dislikes suffering / unsatisfactoriness / stress (*dukkha*) should not commit sins—this is the buddha's advice. indeed, the question of livelihood has always been a great challenge to the world. what action should be taken in the face of the question of survival? at that point, the buddha introduces to the world two things: wrong livelihood (*miccha-ajiva*) and right livelihood (*samma-ajiva*). indeed, if one recognizes wrong livelihood, abstaining from it itself is considered right livelihood (*samma-ajiva*) for laypeople. to briefly introduce wrong livelihood, it is presented in five terms in the sutta discourses, stating that one should abstain from five types of trade. what are they? *sattha, satta, mamsa, visa, majja* (weapons, living beings, meat, poison, and intoxicants). *sattha* means weapons—the trade in weapons, living by it. likewise, *satta* refers to living beings—indeed, here it means human beings, living beings; it refers to humans. next, *mamsa*, the trade in meat. next, the trade in poison (*visa*). next, the trade in intoxicants (*majja*).
why these are shown as wrong may also be a question to some. the trade in weapons—the trade in weapons of war—contains the quality of instigating war and conflict to satisfy hatred. because of this production and trade of weapons, it is a form of trade that leads to violence towards others. the trade in weapons is shown as something that should not be done by a faithful buddhist lay disciple.
similarly, although the word *satta* (written as *satata* in the transcription) is there, it means selling men and women into slavery or for immoral purposes—the selling of a life, and other such forms of trade. these lead to social corruption and cause harm to others. next is the trade in meat. regarding this, there are certain controversies in this day and age. speaking of the trade, as some point out, wrong livelihood (*miccha-ajiva*) exists only at the back of the butcher shop, while right livelihood (*samma-ajiva*) is at the front. this is because the killing of animals is done only at the back, while at the front, the meat of those dead animals is kept for use and consumption by those who seek health. thus, they think that the front part is right livelihood (*samma-ajiva*). but if we think deeply, we can see the trade itself as wrong livelihood (*miccha-ajiva*). within it, there is a quality of making humans crave, get addicted to, and become greedy for the taste of meat.
even in these times, when lay disciples who have an understanding of society talk about food, there is a tendency to expect fresh meat just as one buys fresh vegetables. "fresh meat" means something like killing and eating on a daily basis. likewise, warm food is considered superior. in some hotels, at that moment, the customer or guest chooses the animal they like, and it is brought to the table, killed, and eaten while the blood is still warm—we even get to hear of such things. what is seen from this is greed for the tongue. to please the tongue, to satisfy the greed for the taste of meat, even the tongue of a cow is cut, cooked, and eaten, to such an extent that the beastly, demonic qualities in the human mind-stream (*citta-santana*) are brought out. thus, when we think about hotel life, the only difference between the food eaten by a beast and the food eaten by a human is the use of spoons and forks. to that extent, since this meat trade habituates society to certain wrong habits, beastly habits, we can see that there is a disadvantageous side to the meat trade. it is difficult to consider it as right livelihood (*samma-ajiva*).
the others are clear. in the trade of poison, what is present is helping to destroy someone's life. today, mass slaughter of animals often takes place; sometimes there is no understanding of the environmental pollution within it. however, the trade in poison that aids in the mass killing of insects, denying their right to live, can also be included in this. when we think deeply, these are things that defile one's mind-stream (*citta-santana*) and harm the world. demerit (*akusala*) was described as that which leads to self-harm and harm to others.
when we think deeply, self-harm means the defilement of one's own mind—the defilement of the mind-stream (*citta-santana*). if one drinks poison, either life is destroyed immediately because of it, or after that poison enters the body, one has to suffer its consequences after some time. such is the case with poison that enters the physical body (*rupa-santana*). but through the poison that arises as unwholesome deeds (*akusala*) entering the mind-stream (*citta-santana*), it either yields results in this very life as *ditthadhammavedaniya* (to be experienced in this life), or as *upapajjavedaniya* (to be experienced in the next life), or as *aparapariyavedaniya* (to be experienced in subsequent lives) in a future life; through that poison added to the mind-stream (*citta-santana*), one has to undergo painful, bitter suffering / unsatisfactoriness / stress (*dukkha*) in hells (*apaya*) and other such places. that is why the buddha showed that such things should not be done.
there is nothing new to tell you lay disciples about the trade in intoxicants mentioned last. there, too, is that which completely deranges the mind, makes one forget human existence, and reduces one to a beastly state. next is the addiction to drinking. the trade in intoxicants leads to that addiction. the buddha indicates that a true faithful buddhist lay disciple must withdraw from such trading methods. this question of livelihood is a problem for many people, especially in this day and age, because support and encouragement for wrong livelihood (*miccha-ajiva*) are received from all sides. a person who desires a righteous livelihood has to face dilemmas just like that merchant. facing dilemmas means facing great problems of whether to go forward or backward. when we look at occupations and employment, almost everything contains things that incline towards such wrong livelihood (*miccha-ajiva*).
solving that problem is indeed a matter left to each individual. however, a valuable dhamma discourse that may help in this regard is mentioned in the majjhima nikaya by the name of the dhananjani sutta. it is a long sutta discourse, but i will try to present it briefly. on one occasion, while the buddha was residing at the veluvana monastery in rajagaha, the chief disciple ven. sariputta wandered in the region of dakkhinagiri with a group of monks. meanwhile, a certain monk who had spent the rains retreat (*vassa*) with the buddha in rajagaha arrived in the dakkhinagiri region and met ven. sariputta.
first of all, ven. sariputta asked this monk, "how is it, is the blessed one dwelling in good health?" when the monk replied, "yes," sariputta asked, "is the community of monks in good health?" when the monk replied, "yes," he next asked, "is the brahmin dhananjani, who lives in the village of tandulapala, in good health?" after the monk replied, "yes," ven. sariputta asked, "is that brahmin dhananjani diligent (*appamada*)?" diligent here means diligent in wholesome deeds (*kusala*). that is, whether he is leading a righteous life without committing sins. it was then that the monk declared, "friend sariputta, what diligence is there for dhananjani? the brahmin dhananjani exploits brahmins and householders in the name of the king, and exploits the king in the name of brahmins and householders. he lives by corrupt practices. furthermore, dhananjani's former faithful wife has passed away, and he is now married to a woman who lacks faith." hearing this, ven. sariputta expressed his sadness: "indeed, this is very bad news we have heard, that the brahmin dhananjani has fallen into negligence (*pamada*). if only i could meet dhananjani someday. it would be good if an opportunity to speak with him arose." thus he made a mental note.
sometime later, ven. sariputta returned to rajagaha and, while residing at the veluvana monastery, went on his alms round in rajagaha one morning. at that time, the brahmin dhananjani was engaged in milking his cows outside the city. ven. sariputta, having finished his alms round and eaten his meal, walked to the place where the brahmin dhananjani was. seeing ven. sariputta from afar, the brahmin dhananjani invited him, saying, "venerable sariputta, come and have some milk." ven. sariputta replied, "no, there is no need. i have finished my meal. come to such-and-such a tree. i will be resting there under that tree during the daytime. come there." accordingly, while ven. sariputta was under that tree, the brahmin dhananjani, having finished his meal, came to ven. sariputta. ven. sariputta, after exchanging friendly greetings, straightaway asked, "how is it, dhananjani, are you diligent?"
now, the answer given by the brahmin dhananjani is the very answer many people give nowadays. what did the brahmin dhananjani say? "venerable sariputta, what diligence is there for us? we have parents to support. we have a wife and children to support. we have servants and workers to support. we have to perform duties towards friends and companions. we have to perform duties towards relatives. we have to perform duties towards guests. next, we must perform offerings (*preta-puja*) to our departed relatives (*preta*). we must perform offerings to the deities (*deva-puja*). we must perform duties for the king. not only that, we must also gratify and maintain this body. when there is such a heavy burden of duties, what diligence can there be for us?"
thus, this brahmin was leading an unrighteous, uneven life, inclining towards unrighteousness. ven. sariputta declared, "but brahmin, if you live unrighteously and lead an uneven life, and upon death are born in hell (*niraya*), can you escape by telling the wardens of hell (*yamapalla*), 'i did these things for the sake of my parents, to look after my parents; do nothing to me'? can you escape thus?" the brahmin replied, "no, that would not be possible." ven. sariputta then asked, "can those parents step forward and say, 'it was for our sake that our child behaved unrighteously and led an uneven life, so do not do anything to him'? can they save him thus?" the brahmin replied, "no, they cannot save him. the hell-wardens will drag him away and inflict various kinds of suffering / unsatisfactoriness / stress (*dukkha*)."
in the same way, to make that matter clearer, ven. sariputta questioned him about each of those groups of people: "if you behave unrighteously and lead an uneven life for the sake of wife and children, or for servants and workers..." in this way, he questioned him step-by-step so that it would sink deep into the brahmin's mind. finally, ven. sariputta asked, "what do you think, brahmin? if someone supports their parents righteously and evenly (*dhamma-cari samacari*), and another supports their parents unrighteously and unevenly (*adhamma-cari visamacari*), who between the two is the better person?" the brahmin replied, "indeed, the practice of supporting parents righteously and evenly is the better one." then ven. sariputta declared, "brahmin, there are livelihoods in society through which one can live righteously, support one's parents, and perform meritorious deeds. this is a possible thing." thus he convinced the brahmin dhananjani, and dhananjani accepted it with joy.
next, what we find in that sutta discourse is the final period of the brahmin dhananjani's life. being extremely ill and near death, the brahmin dhananjani sent a message through a servant to pay respects to the buddha and to ven. sariputta, and to invite ven. sariputta, saying that the brahmin dhananjani was gravely ill and asking him to visit out of compassion. ven. sariputta visited the house of the brahmin dhananjani. having arrived, he began a dhamma talk. gradually, he delivered a dhamma talk of a nature that would elevate the brahmin's mind from lower worlds to higher worlds, and at the very end, he spoke about the four divine abodes (*brahma-vihara*): loving-kindness (*metta*), compassion (*karuna*), sympathetic joy (*mudita*), and equanimity (*upekkha*).
ven. sariputta thought, "these brahmins desire to be born in the brahma world. therefore, i must tell him the path to the brahma world." he then explained how to develop the four divine abodes (*brahma-vihara*). having explained this, he rose from his seat and returned. at that time, as his final words, the brahmin dhananjani said, "pay homage to the blessed one in my name." a short while after ven. sariputta had left, that brahmin passed away and was reborn in the brahma world. when ven. sariputta went to the buddha and related this news, the buddha admonished ven. sariputta: "why, sariputta, did you establish him in the inferior brahma world when there was more to be done, when he could have gone much higher?" thus he expressed a certain blame toward ven. sariputta.
from this, we can understand that the strength of the wholesome potential (*kusala-shakti*) developed by that brahmin near his death was so great that, if ven. sariputta had in some way turned him toward insight (*vipassana*) and preached the dhamma, the buddha was indicating that he could have realized the paths and fruits (*magga-phala*). "why did you stop him at the inferior brahma world when he could have been led higher?"—this was the admonition given to ven. sariputta. we can learn many things from this incident. although the story itself is brief, it is highly valuable as a sutta discourse. on one hand, we see the wonderful compassion of ven. sariputta. indeed, the brahmin dhananjani was not even someone who had taken refuge in the triple gem. but because his former wife was extremely faithful, ven. sariputta had a special compassion for this lay brahmin. that is why, after inquiring about the buddha's well-being and the sangha's well-being, he asked the monk about the brahmin dhananjani.
then, having visited him specifically for this purpose, instead of asking casual questions like "how are you? where are you living?", ven. sariputta asked, "brahmin, are you diligent?" that is the real question. that is the correct question to ask lay disciples. "how is it, are you now leading your life diligently?" based on the answer given to that question, ven. sariputta convinced the brahmin dhananjani through that long discourse that an unrighteous life, an uneven life, uneven behavior is very dangerous, and that its consequences (*vipaka*) are extremely severe. it was because he understood this at the end that the brahmin dhananjani developed his mind so much at the moment of death. he developed it to such an extent that, by establishing himself in the four divine abodes (*brahma-vihara*) of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, he even attained birth in the brahma world. ven. sariputta brought about a massive transformation in his life at that moment. otherwise, had he continued with that unrighteous life, the brahmin dhananjani would have fallen into hell (*apaya*) after death. we can learn something from this. indeed, as stated earlier, everyone thinks that the easiest way to live is through those unrighteous methods. why did the buddha reject them? as we constantly remind you, today more place is given to the economy than to righteousness. therefore, they try to inflate the economy to such an extent that there is no place for a righteous life. but the buddha points out its result. when we think far-sightedly, the buddha highlights the disadvantageous side (*adinava*) of it.
if we consider the easy methods, we have to take economic principles from the great ocean and the forest. this is because in the ocean there exists a very easy way of life. in ancient terms, this is called *matsya-nyaya* (the law of the fish). *matsya-nyaya*, lay disciples, means the large preying on the small—the tuna preying on the sprat. throughout the great ocean, there is only the large animal preying on the small animal. that is the easiest way of life. next, in the forest, too, there is the strong preying on the weak. this natural law is expressed in the buddha's words as follows:
in a sutta discourse where this is mentioned, it is said that if one is born in the animal world, it is extremely difficult to obtain a good rebirth again. taking a small amount of dust on his fingernail, the buddha made a statement to the monks. the buddha used this simile on many occasions. when asked, "is the dust on the fingernail greater, or is the soil of the great earth greater?" the monks replied, "the soil of the great earth is much greater, while the dust on the fingernail is very little." the buddha then told the monks, "just so, monks, once someone is born in an animal womb, it is extremely difficult to rise out of it. it is like the dust on the fingernail; only a very few rise out of it. what is the reason for this? what are the two terms that describe the natural law in this animal world? *annamannabhadika ettha vattati, dubbalabhadika.* *annamannabhadika* means devouring one another. the principle of devouring one another and the principle of oppressing the weak exist in the animal world." indeed, it is those natural laws of the animal world that have gradually entered human society today.
the word "exploitation" (devouring / grabbing) that we mentioned in society is indeed a word taken from the animal world. now, you lay disciples also occasionally get to see a kingfisher or a hawk perched on a tree, turning its head and watching for a while, as if deeply pondering some profound economic theory. after watching for a while, it dives down onto its prey with the speed of an arrow; that is "grabbing" (exploiting). that is the kind of thing happening in today's society. you know that this is done not only out of poverty; it is not only the poor, but also the rich who do this—grabbing/exploiting. what is seen through this is, just as the brahmin dhananjani did earlier, carrying on with one's livelihood through lying, fraud, theft, and various forms of corruption. the buddha points out the severe consequences (*vipaka*) of these. we must learn something from this.
thus, if we look at it according to that economic theory, there are indeed countless easy paths. yet, the buddha designates these five as wrong livelihood (*miccha-ajiva*) with a deep meaning. life does not end there. when poison enters this physical body (*rupa-santana*), it affects only this life. but how do these enter the mind-stream (*citta-santana*)? through the defilement of mind, body, and speech—by their becoming corrupted. they become corrupted by greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dvesha*), delusion (*moha*), and other various defilements (*kilesa*). in particular, after a person's mind-stream (*citta-santana*) is corrupted, not only by the unwholesome deeds of killing and stealing, but also by those things shown as the ten unwholesome courses of action (*dasa-akusala*), the next *jati* (birth) is received as a result. neither parents nor relatives and friends can step forward and save a person from hells (*niraya*) and other such places. the buddha shows this through the natural law of kamma.
you lay disciples have often heard the law of kamma expressed in words such as *kammasako'mhi kammadayado kammayoni kammabandhu kammapatisarano*. kamma is the only thing one takes from here. only the kamma one has done, whether good or bad, is what one owns: *kammasako'mhi*—one is the owner of one's kamma. likewise, what one has as one's inheritance is kamma: *kammadayado*—heir to one's kamma. where one goes and is born, how one's birth is determined is kamma: *kammayoni*—born of one's kamma. what stands as one's relative is kamma: *kammabandhu*—related to one's kamma. what serves as one's refuge is kamma: *kammapatisarano*—supported by one's kamma. therefore, according to that word of the buddha, we must reflect on the danger of those easy paths. what appears from this is the way we must practice equanimity (*upekkha*) on certain occasions. just as that merchant stopped for a while, unable to go forward or backward, when we face certain paths that seem easy, we must consider whether they are righteous or unrighteous, think whether they are even behavior or uneven behavior, and think deeply. if they fall on the uneven side, the unrighteous side, we must practice equanimity (*upekkha*). that means we should not act rashly. for, by acting quickly, we get entangled in a severe unwholesome deed (*akusala*) without even knowing it. one will have to pay for it for a long time in *samsara*.
that is why the buddha explained the danger of this wrong livelihood (*miccha-ajiva*). normally, people now consider these as minor things. there is another very famous discourse delivered on this very topic. on one occasion, the buddha declared that there are three types of people in the world. the analysis of persons the buddha makes there is done by grasping both the economic and the righteous aspects. there is an analysis of persons made by grasping both the economic and the righteous aspects. there are three types of people in the world. who are the three? the blind, the one-eyed, and the two-eyed. the buddha explains the blind person as follows: there is a person who lacks the eye of wisdom necessary to acquire unacquired wealth, or to secure, consolidate, or increase acquired wealth. likewise, that person also lacks the eye of wisdom, the dhamma-eye, that helps to distinguish good and bad, wholesome and unwholesome (*kusala akusala*), merit and demerit. that person is completely blind.
the second person is the one-eyed. the buddha describes such a person as one who has the economic eye necessary to acquire unacquired wealth and to increase acquired wealth, but lacks the righteous eye. this person does not reflect on good and bad, on the wholesome and unwholesome (*kusala akusala*). that is the nature of the one-eyed. the person with two eyes—according to this, you lay disciples can straightaway understand that this is the person who is complete in both aspects. thus, if one is a true buddhist disciple, according to that analysis shown by the buddha, one must strive to live with both eyes. otherwise, if one lives as a one-eyed person, there will be severe consequences (*vipaka*). that is, the buddha straightaway points out that if one lives unrighteously and unevenly through lies, fraud, theft, and violence, one will eventually have to suffer the consequences in hells (*niraya*) and other such places for a long time. in that analysis of persons, too, it becomes clear to us that the buddha directed attention to both the economic and the righteous aspects.
next, in a similar way, in a certain place, the buddha points out four undertakings of dhamma (*dhamma-samadana*). you have heard of the undertaking of virtue (*sila-samadana*). undertaking virtue (*sila-samadana*) means accepting a certain practice of virtue, striving to live according to it, making a promise, and making a determination. what is shown here by the name of *dhamma-samadana* is not things like the five precepts or the eight precepts. what is spoken of here is the ten unwholesome courses of action (*dasa-akusala*)—abstaining from the ten unwholesome courses of action. most people know what the ten unwholesome courses are: abstaining from the three unwholesome deeds done by the body, namely, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. next, abstaining from the four unwholesome deeds done by speech. what are they? lying, slandering, harsh speech, and frivolous talk (*sampappalapa*)—that is, speaking useless gossip, speaking meaningless words. next, regarding the mind, the word *abhijjha* (covetousness) is used. that means intense, uneven greed. how is uneven greed described? greed exists in everyone. the nature of uneven greed is that when someone has something, one thinks, "oh, if only i could get this somehow," and out of envy for another's happiness, a greed arises to acquire it. that greed, that uneven greed, is a severe unwholesome deed developed by the mind. similarly, hatred—a hateful mind. next, thirdly, wrong view (*miccha-ditthi*) is shown: uneven greed, a hateful mind, and wrong view (*miccha-ditthi*).
taking up the practice of abstaining from these ten unwholesome courses of action (*dasa-akusala*) is what is meant here by *dhamma-samadana*. the buddha points out four types of *dhamma-samadana*. in this brief, limited time, we do not need to mention all of those matters. it is not necessary to show them. we will highlight only the two matters relevant to this topic. one of these four is: there is a certain undertaking of dhamma (*dhamma-samadana*) that brings happiness in the present but yields painful consequences in the future. there is another undertaking of dhamma (*dhamma-samadana*) that has a painful nature in the present but yields happiness in the future. let us first describe the one mentioned first.
the buddha points it out in this way: suppose someone engages in killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, etc., with great joy and pleasure. they engage in those sins with great joy. but having gone and been born in hell (*apaya*), they have to suffer severe, painful consequences (*vipaka*) of those deeds. the buddha also gives a simile for this. the buddha gives similes, etc., to make every single point sink deep into the mind, not as poetic ornaments. what is the simile? suppose there is a vessel containing a good drink. that drink has a beautiful color, a good fragrance, and a good taste. there is a drink that is colorful, fragrant, and tasty. but this drink has been mixed with poison.
a person who is interested comes there. those standing by the vessel of drink say, "come, come, here is a good drink. this is tasty, fragrant, and colorful. however, poison has been mixed into this. if you wish, drink it. when drinking, it is very tasty and fragrant. but after drinking it, you will either die or fall into a suffering equivalent to death." this is what those standing by the vessel of drink say. indeed, they state the fact. thereupon, that person drinks it without reflecting wisely. what happens when he drinks it? while drinking, it is tasty. but after drinking, he faces death in the manner described, or falls into a suffering equivalent to death. this is the simile given by the buddha for the practice of performing unwholesome deeds with joy, which are pleasant while doing them, but eventually bring painful consequences (*vipaka*) that one must suffer.
what is the second undertaking of dhamma (*dhamma-samadana*) mentioned? at the time of engaging in them, it is painful. it is felt not as happiness but as pain, as displeasure. yet, its fruit, its consequence (*vipaka*), is happiness. it is something that brings happiness. the buddha's simile for this is briefly described as follows: suppose someone abstains from killing, stealing, etc., with great difficulty. "with great difficulty" means that, thinking about the buddha's words, they keep those precepts (*sikkhapada*) and abstain from those unwholesome deeds (*akusala*) with great effort and pain. yet, as a result of that, they eventually obtain birth in a happy realm (*sugati*).
the buddha gives a simile there. the buddha himself prescribed a medicine specifically for the monks, which is called *putimutta-bhesajja* (fermented urine medicine). *putimutta-bhesajja* is a medicine made from cow's urine. when yellow myrobalan (*aralu*), etc., are added to it, it is a very good medicine for jaundice (*pandu-roga*). that is the simile the buddha points out here. when drinking that medicine, it smells bad, has no pleasant color, and no pleasant taste. but after drinking it, that disease is cured. a jaundice patient comes to a place where such a drink is kept. those who are there say, "here is a medicine. when drinking this, there is no taste or fragrance. but if you drink it, you will be cured." having heard this, that person reflects wisely and, although it is unpalatable, takes that medicine. having taken it, he is cured. through this simile, the buddha shows that for those who follow the righteous path, even though with difficulty, even though with pain, even though crying, happiness can be expected in the end.
the same kind of thing is present in this undertaking of virtue (*sila-samadana*). here, the buddha spoke about the first person. thinking very highly of themselves, exulting over it, they engage in killing, stealing, etc., with great joy. it is only when they have to suffer the consequences (*vipaka*) of those deeds that they realize. the next person mentioned abstains from those things with great difficulty. it is very hard to abstain from them, yet, with great difficulty and displeasure, they abstain from them. but the result of that is good. now, this is where we can connect the value of these virtues (*sila*), etc. for, it is through understanding that one can change one's attitude.
now, someone might think, "abstaining from killing, abstaining from stealing, etc., is very difficult; abstaining from these is a great trouble. there are easier methods than this"—that is wrong view (*miccha-ditthi*). if someone has developed faith (*saddha*) according to the buddha's word, that person can derive joy from it. in keeping virtues (*sila*), etc., reflecting on the value of the undertaking of virtue (*sila-samadana*), reflecting on that determination of virtue, and then reviewing (*avarjana*) it, one derives joy. that is called blameless happiness (*anavajja-sukha*). that is a happiness belonging to a lay disciple. in particular, even extremely wealthy people do not have that blameless happiness (*anavajja-sukha*) in this day and age. what is the reason? it is because of that "exploitation" (grabbing) mentioned earlier. that is their diligence. nowadays, what the world mostly considers as diligence is the diligence of the kingfisher, the hawk, and the vulture. they swoop down on their prey very diligently. that is not the diligence the buddha points out here. it is one's far-sightedness. the kingfisher, the hawk, and the vulture also have a certain far-sightedness that sees only that prey. but the far-sightedness, the diligence shown by the buddha, is different.
now, some wealthy people do not have that blameless happiness (*anavajja-sukha*)—that faultless happiness. even though they have gathered a vast amount of wealth, when they think about how they gathered this wealth, a great regret arises. the happiness gathered by oppressing human beings, through various forms of corruption, fraud, and exploitation. because of this, that person has to suffer severe pain and suffering on their deathbed. indeed, according to the buddha's word, there is nothing new to say about having to suffer pain and suffering after death. instead, the buddha points out that what a wise lay disciple should do is reflect on the virtuous side of what appears to be difficult, gain that faith (*saddha*) thinking, "this will bring me good," and derive joy through that.
faultless happiness means the happiness derived from that virtue (*sila*). "i have kept such-and-such a practice." in short, the recollection of virtue (*silanussati*) itself can be turned into a meditation (*bhavana*). the fact that one is virtuous. when reflecting on that again and again, that joy arises in that person, and finally, through that, the mind becomes concentrated; it becomes focused in concentration (*samadhi*). one can go that far. because of this, some might think, "the buddha has always preached *veramani, veramani*. what is this *veramani*? abstain, abstain, he says. the buddha speaks only of things to be avoided, things to be given up. he does not tell us anything to do." someone might say this according to economic theories. but the buddha points out that within that giving up, one can find joy. if someone keeps the five precepts (*panca-sila*) properly, they can derive that joy by reviewing (*avarjana*) each of them.
the buddha points out, "in a world where so much killing of living beings takes place, i am living while giving this infinite, immeasurable gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dana*)." nowadays, as we constantly remind you, the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dana*) has sometimes been limited to releasing a cow destined for slaughter, prepared for taking a photograph. but silently, without shouting to the world, if one, as a matter of principle, avoids causing harm and keeps the precept of abstaining from killing very purely, the buddha declared that such a person is giving the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dana*) to infinite, immeasurable living beings. by deriving joy from that and reviewing (*avarjana*) that precept (*sikkhapada*), that person can even attain concentration (*samadhi*). that itself can be used to help attain nibbana. such a wonderful depth lies in these virtues (*sila*), etc. that must be understood. similarly, what was called *dhamma-samadana* here is, just like *sila-samadana*, abstaining from the ten unwholesome courses of action (*dasa-akusala*). that practice of abstaining from the ten unwholesome courses of action goes even further. when reflecting on each of them, thinking, "in such a society, i am keeping such-and-such precept, or keeping such-and-such practice," joy arises. looking at it from that perspective, it is not like drinking that fermented urine medicine (*putimutta-bhesajja*) unwillingly; it is a state where one can drink it willingly.
there is a deep practice, a deep meaning within these virtues (*sila*), etc., through which one can find relief on each occasion. thus, the fundamental factor in all of this is abstaining from sins. what the buddha constantly declares is: just as the merchant practiced equanimity (*upekkha*), neither going forward nor backward when there was danger on the road, if in a certain course of action one sees, "it is wrong if i do this, and it is wrong if i do not do this," on that occasion, one must practice equanimity (*upekkha*). one must hold back for a while. it is bad to be attached to it.
similarly, one must have the strength to reflect on these far-sightedly. a person who lives in such a principled way has fewer regrets. as the buddha declares, there is blameless happiness (*anavajja-sukha*), faultless happiness. the mind can constantly remain in joy. when reviewing—reviewing (*avarjana*) means looking back. looking back and reflecting on the purity of one's life, that person experiences great joy, especially at the final moment. although the brahmin dhananjani lived unrighteously in the first part of his life, even though the details are not mentioned at length, we see that a massive transformation took place in his life after he received ven. sariputta's advice. it was as a result of that massive life transformation that this brahmin was able to obtain birth in the brahma world, by relying on the dhamma heard at the final moment. therefore, in whatever way our individual lives have been spent, if we make a determination... at the end of a year, you make various kinds of targets, determinations, connecting them with new year customs. even setting out for occupations is done at an auspicious time (*nakatha*). but even if done at an auspicious time, if those things belong to the inauspicious, there is no use in it. what is inauspicious? one must do what is auspicious, what is good. what is inauspicious is wrong livelihood (*miccha-ajiva*). if one sets out for employment at an auspicious time, but sets out for that wrong livelihood (*miccha-ajiva*), there is no use in that auspicious time.
this life transformation may not be possible in a single day or in a single moment. yet, if wise lay disciples direct their minds to these and make an effort, it will not be impossible to bring about a transformation in their individual lives according to the buddha's word. worldly beings have given up things greater than this. one step in the method of doing so is, at least, observing precepts (*sila*) on one of the four poya days of the month. if someone engaged in such wrong livelihood (*miccha-ajiva*) withdraws from it for one day, sacrifices it, sacrifices the profit received from it, observes pure virtue (*sila*), and spends the day in that manner, an opening is created for them there. "if i can do this for one day, why not make it two days, observing it on two poya days?" next, if taken to four poya days, it is four days. going on in this manner, gradually, they will be able to withdraw even from hereditary wrong livelihoods. if one makes no such effort but goes on, enslaved to the direction in which society is heading, one only moves further down the path of decline. as we mentioned, the tongue adapts very quickly in a way that encourages meat-eating, etc. such is the world that exists. one must reflect wisely on wrong notions and understand the buddha's words deeply. one's livelihood is not something limited only to this life. in this journey of *samsara*, this era of a buddha's arising (*buddhotpada-kala*) is an extremely rare time. human existence (*manussa-attabhava*) is also an opportunity. if we live as beasts, as demons, we cannot derive the true benefit of the buddha's dispensation (*sasana*). therefore, transforming our lives internally is something that belongs to each of us. today, on account of the new year, you have received that stream of thoughts to be added to your mind-streams (*citta-santana*).
during this period of about one hour, this group of lay disciples, having undertaken in varying measures the eight precepts (*attha-sila*), the ten precepts (*dasa-sila*), or the precepts with right livelihood as the eighth (*ajivatthamaka-sila*), listened to the dhamma sermon. it is through taming the three doors of action—body, speech, and mind—in our daily existence that we can attain deliverance from *samsara* (*samsara-vimukti*). therefore, as we constantly remind you, may you develop those qualities of faith (*saddha*), etc., with the strength gathered by hearing the dhamma. may you turn the spiritual faculties (*indriya*) of faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*) into spiritual powers (*bala*). supported by association with noble friends (*kalyana-mitta*), may you gain the strength and power to quickly escape all the suffering of *samsara*, such as *jati* (birth) and death (*marana*), through the realization, the penetration of the paths and fruits (*magga-phala*) of sotapanna, sakadagami, anagami, and arahant, and by attaining the supreme, deathless nibbana! similarly, if any departed relatives in one's name, or any beings from the avici hell to the akanitha heaven, wish to share in the merit of this dhamma teaching and dhamma hearing, may they, by sharing in this merit, realize the supreme, deathless nibbana through a bodhi of their aspiration! with this aspiration, please recite this verse:
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 157
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #157
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.109)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
"Yassa pure ca pacchā ca,
majjhe ca natthi kiñcanaṃ;
Akiñcanaṃ anādānaṃ,
tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ."
From:
Dhammapada Verse 421 (Brāhmaṇa Vagga)
Dear Listeners,
As the Middle Path (*majjhimā paṭipadā*) to escape the *Dukkha* (Suffering) of *saṃsāra*, the Teacher of the Three Worlds, the Buddha, placed before the world the Noble Eightfold Path on an Esala Full Moon Poya day like today. This path and practice, followed by everyone who aspires for Nibbāna without distinction between lay and ordained, is none other than this Noble Eightfold Path. The background story to the verse we have selected as our theme today is an exemplary account of how *nekkhamma-saṅkappa* (the thought of renunciation)—which is a primary component of *sammā-saṅkappa* (Right Resolution)—matured within a lay household.
The Buddha preached this Dhamma verse at the Veluvana Monastery in Rājagaha concerning a bhikkhunī named Dhammadinnā. During her lay life, Dhammadinnā’s husband was the lay devotee Visākha. One day, after listening to the Dhamma from the Buddha, the lay devotee Visākha attained the stage of Non-returner (*anāgāmi-phala*). On his way back home, he reflected: “I must hand over all my wealth and possessions to my wife, Dhammadinnā, and set myself free.”
Usually, Dhammadinnā would wait by the window, watching for her husband to return from outside. As the husband approached, they would greet each other with smiles; such was their custom. On this particular day, however, the lay devotee Visākha entered the house calmly without even looking toward the window. Dhammadinnā was somewhat perplexed by this, wondering why today was different. Furthermore, when the meal was prepared, whereas Visākha would normally invite his wife, saying, “Come, let us eat together,” this time he ate in silence. Thus, Dhammadinnā further pondered whether his mind was upset or if he had become angry due to some matter.
Later, when the lay devotee Visākha was sitting quietly, he called his wife and said, “Dhammadinnā, please take charge of all these riches and comforts.” At this, Dhammadinnā thought, “People who are angry do not hand over wealth in this manner. What could this be?”
Then she asked, “My lord, what will you do?” When he explained the situation, Dhammadinnā replied, “I do not wish to pick up the lump of spit that you have spat out. Please grant me permission to ordain.” From this, we can infer that even by that time, Dhammadinnā must have been a woman of great faith (*saddhā*) who had also practiced meditation. Visākha, the lay devotee, escorted Dhammadinnā to a nunnery and facilitated her ordination. Since Theri Dhammadinnā delighted in solitude, after her higher ordination (*upasampadā*), she went to a remote province with a group of other bhikkhunīs to dwell in seclusion. Not long after going into seclusion to meditate after her higher ordination, she attained Arahatship with the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). She then thought, “I must give my relatives the opportunity to accumulate merit through me,” and returned to Rājagaha.
When the lay devotee Visākha heard that she had returned to her nunnery, he thought, “Perhaps she has returned so quickly because she has become dissatisfied with the holy life for some reason.” Thus, Visākha went to the hermitage and paid his respects. However, he could not directly ask Theri Dhammadinnā, “Why is this? Have you returned because your mind has turned away from ordination?” Instead, what did he do? He asked a question pertaining to the path of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*). She answered that question directly and correctly. Next, he asked question after question, rising to the path of Once-returning (*sakadāgāmi-magga*) and the path of Non-returning (*anāgāmi-magga*). The answers came in an extraordinary manner—only the question and the answer, with no irrelevant chatter. Sensing that the final question, concerning the path of Arahatship, went beyond the boundary of the lay devotee Visākha’s own level of Dhamma-realization as an Anāgāmi, Theri Dhammadinnā said: “O lay devotee, you have overstepped the limits of questioning. You have failed to recognize the boundary of this question. If you wish, you may go and report this discussion to the Blessed One as it transpired.”
Accordingly, the lay devotee went to the Buddha and related the entire discussion. The Buddha praised her and said: “My daughter Dhammadinnā’s analysis of the Dhamma is absolutely correct. Even if you had asked me, I would have given these very same answers to those questions. She is a woman of great wisdom.” Elsewhere in the Tipiṭaka, it is mentioned that when the Buddha declared the foremost positions among the disciples, he declared Theri Dhammadinnā foremost among the bhikkhunīs who are Dhamma-speakers (*dhammakathikā*) in the entire Bhikkhunī Sāsana.
That very Dhamma discussion can still be found today in the *Cūḷavedalla Sutta* of the *Majjhima Nikāya*. It is an extremely profound discourse that draws the attention of both great scholars and meditators alike. There is no extraneous elaboration in it—it is simply question and answer, question and answer. A highly valuable compilation of Dhamma is found there. Through this, we see the miracle of the Dhamma. Not only that, but after doing so, the Buddha also uttered a certain verse in praise of Theri Dhammadinnā. It is that verse we have taken as our theme today:
*Yassa pure ca pacchā ca, majjhe ca natthi kiñcanaṃ, akiñcanaṃ anādānaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ.*
At first glance, it is almost like a riddle-verse. “He who has nothing before, after, or in the middle—who is possessionless, who grasps at nothing—him I call a Brahmin.”
This *Dhammapada* verse is very simple. On this occasion, I will explain it very briefly. The Buddha often used the word “Brahmin” to refer to an Arahant. What is revealed here is that Theri Dhammadinnā had attained Arahatship. Thus, the nature of an Arahant's mind is shown by those words. For now, we will mention it briefly and elaborate later. “Before” (*pure*) refers to the past. There is no aspiration, no desire regarding the past five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*). Similarly, there is no aspiration or desire regarding the future five aggregates. There are no special desires regarding the past aggregates, nor is there any desire regarding the future aggregates.
Next, “middle” (*majjhe*) here refers to the present. Likewise, there is no attachment to the present five aggregates. It is in the *Brāhmaṇa Vagga* of the *Dhammapada*, which describes the Arahants, that this verse is found, saying: “Him I call a Brahmin, who has nothing of his own, who grasps at nothing.” If we first consider the story, as we mentioned earlier, it demonstrates the transformation brought about by the emergence of *nekkhamma-saṅkappa* (the thought of renunciation) within a lay household. From this, lay devotees of today can learn many lessons. After turning toward the Dhamma, lay devotees can find excellent examples in this story for the various problems they encounter at home. Looking even at daily life, the harmonious relationship that existed between the lay devotee Visākha and Dhammadinnā as husband and wife can be called exemplary.
The wife would watch from the window for her husband returning from outside. Then, as soon as the husband arrived, she would welcome him warmly. The husband, too, was a very gentle-natured person. When taking meals, he would call his wife to eat together. They were two people who lived such a friendly and affectionate life. However, due to a sudden transformation brought about by the Dhamma, the lay devotee Visākha decided: “Now I need freedom for my Dhamma study and meditation. Let me hand over the management of all these resources to my wife.” In the stories of the past, Dhammadinnā is depicted as a highly meritorious lady who had fulfilled her perfections (*pāramīs*) and come aspiring for such a position. Therefore, as soon as her husband spoke those words, instead of desiring those riches, she regarded them as a lump of spit and, saying, “What use is the lump of spit spat out by you to me?”, she renounced them even before her husband did. Indeed, it is mentioned that while the lay devotee remained a lay devotee, his wife became highly renowned in this Sāsana as Theri Dhammadinnā.
When this Dhamma leading to Nibbāna enters a person's heart, that transformation is difficult for many to understand. Especially for those bound by various ties of lay life, being unable to understand what occurs in another's mind-stream leads to various kinds of friction and displeasure. However, we are all temporarily met in this *saṃsāra*, in this wayside resting house of the world, due to certain past connections. Yet, this path to Nibbāna is a journey that must be made individually. It is the journey through *saṃsāra*, the journey of crossing over *saṃsāra*. Thus, supporting those who step forward with the necessary qualifications for it in a friendly manner is exactly what the lay devotee Visākha did. He went and handed over his wife to the nunnery. Next, let us look into analyzing these deep matters of the Dhamma.
Now, the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*) were mentioned here. You, lay devotees, have heard this word “five aggregates”. Most of you know that they are the five: form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), Preparations (*saṅkhāra*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*). These aggregates (*khandha*) mean heaps or piles; thus, there are five heaps. These five heaps are analyzed in this way: they are divided into past, future, and present, and are also seen both internally (*ajjhatta*) and externally (*bahiddha*). Internal refers to oneself—the heap of form regarding oneself—and external refers to others—the heap of form regarding others. Let us understand it thus. Furthermore, it can be gross form or subtle form, superior form or inferior form, near form or far form. In this way, all various forms are gathered into this aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*). It is because of grasping these with *Taṇhā* (Craving) that they are called *Upādāna* (Grasping)—the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcupādānakkhandha*). So, how does one recall the past five aggregates? Sometimes one thinks like this:
Let us say an elderly person thinks about their youth: “I used to be beautiful in such-and-such a way. Alas! Now look what has happened to me,” and thus develops an attachment to that past form. This is called *nandirāga* (delight and lust). Terms like *nandi* (delight), *rāga* (lust), and *chanda* (desire) are presented as synonyms of *Taṇhā* (Craving)—words equivalent to craving. Thinking of the past, they create a regret or a desire for it and suffer, saying, “We no longer have this now.” Next is the opposite side, which is about the future. They form future aspirations: “I must become someone with great physical beauty, a beautiful person, a strong person,” and thus remain clinging to thoughts and wishes regarding the future. That is what was meant by “before” and “after”—regarding the past five aggregates and the future five aggregates.
Regarding the present five aggregates, what is currently here is also grasped as a self. They say: “This form is myself; this is my soul. There is a soul in form, form is in the soul, form is possessed of a soul.” In this way, they regard this form as a self, as “me”. This is how one develops attachment to the present form. Now, as described here, what is indicated is that the Arahant has freed themselves from those conceptualizations. For such a person, there is no attachment to the past five aggregates, nor are there any aspirations for a future five aggregates. The attachment and desire for the present five aggregates have been abandoned. For this very reason, they are *akiñcana* (possessionless / having nothing).
The meaning of the word *akiñcana* is “owning nothing”. Usually, when we say “owning nothing”, we think of material wealth and so on. In the Dhamma, it is presented much more deeply. *Kiñcana* means “something” or “anything”. Greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dosa*), and delusion (*moha*) are designated as *kiñcana* (obstructions/possessions/attachments). Therefore, where greed, hatred, and delusion are absent, there is *akiñcana*. What is the reason for this? For us, a thing becomes “a thing” either because we like it, or because we are opposed to it, or because we are deluded by it—having a curiosity or doubt about what it is. It is through greed, hatred, and delusion in this manner that things in the world become “things” to us. If we take *kiñcana* deeply, “anything” refers to those three: greed, hatred, and delusion. Thus, because the Arahant is freed from them, they are *akiñcana*—owning nothing. Likewise, they are *anādāna*. *Ādāna* means “grasping” or “holding”—the nature of clutching. *Anādāna* means they do not grasp at any of those things either.
This is how the liberated mind is expressed in this verse. Now, we must indeed pay special attention to what was said here about the “middle” (the present). Meditators practicing insight (*vipassanā*) know that past Preparations (*saṅkhāra*) are “past”, meaning they have gone by. It is easy to realize that they have gone by. Sometimes, one spends a little time thinking about past things, but then realizes “this is no longer here”. Even if future thoughts arise, one can sometimes escape them. “Future” means what has not yet come—things that have not arrived. But the present is the deepest point, the hardest place to grasp.
If we apply this to the practice of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasati*), some lay devotees when starting the practice send their minds out in anticipation of the incoming breath. Or, after the exhalation goes out, they send the mind out following that exhalation. However, teachers have instructed us not to send the mind to the past or to the future, but to anchor the mind at the point where the inhalation and exhalation make contact—such as the nose or the upper lip. That is what is meant by *parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā* (establishing mindfulness in front). Even in the canonical discourses, it is mentioned that when sitting down for *ānāpāna*, one should not watch where the breath comes from in the distance, nor should one chase the breath after it has gone.
Ordinary people usually regret while thinking about the past, letting their minds run after the past, and they wish for the future. What results from this is a loss of mindfulness. The Buddha constantly reminds us that we have to reach this truth through the present moment. Therefore, we must anchor the mind in the present. Ancient teachers give two similes regarding *ānāpānasati* to demonstrate this point.
Nowadays, the methods of sawing wood are very different. In the past, logs were placed on a trestle and sawn using a two-handed saw. If the person sawing the wood directs their eyes toward the other person or toward the two ends of the saw, they will make a mistake. Instead, to do it correctly, they must focus their attention right at the point where the log is being cut—exactly where the saw teeth make contact—without letting the mind drift to the far ends. Similarly, it is stated regarding *ānāpānasati* that the breath must be anchored at the tip of the nose or near the upper lip.
Another simile describes pushing a swing. The person standing in the middle often directs their eyes this way and that. However, what actually needs to be done is to anchor the eyes in the middle, without directing them this way and that. While swinging, there is no need to specially watch the two ends. It is just like that. Yet, the mind is tempted to send the eyes toward those two ends. Similarly, in *ānāpānasati*, it is when the mind is anchored in the middle that one catches the point of contact, which is the *ānāpāna-nimitta* (the sign of breathing). From that point onward lies the progress of insight (*vipassanā*). It is from there that one can elevate to insight the elemental nature (*dhātu*) or the subtle heap-like nature within the wave of breath, thereby attaining liberation (*vimutti*). We can understand this discussion of the “middle” in that manner through the medium of a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
In that Dhamma discussion, there was a certain shortcoming in the question asked by the lay devotee Visākha. We are obliged to present that question here at least briefly. Indeed, there is insufficient time to present that entire Dhamma dialogue. The question we intend to bring out now is precisely the one where Theri Dhammadinnā said, “You have overstepped the limit of asking questions.” Visākha, the lay devotee, was asking about pleasant feeling (*vedanā*). In Pali, it is stated as *sukha, dukkha, adukkhamasukha*, meaning pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Pleasant feeling and painful feeling are at the two extremes. In the middle lies neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant means neutral feeling. Let us think for a moment. People in this world are riding a seesaw between pleasure and pain. When pain comes, they seek pleasure to escape that pain. But then, that pleasure is also not permanent (*anicca* - impermanent / inconstant). Theri Dhammadinnā spoke about this as well: underlying pleasant feeling is lust, the underlying tendency of lust (*rāgānusaya*). Underlying painful feeling is the underlying tendency of aversion (*paṭighānusaya*), which is hatred (*dosa*). Next, underlying the neutral feeling called *adukkhamasukha* is ignorance (*avijjā*) or non-knowing. Why? Because the neutral feeling is not realized by the ordinary mind; it is only recognized by a meditative mind. Worldly beings remain between those two: pleasure and pain, pleasure and pain. They keep rolling along, saying, “Pain and pleasure constantly turn.” Thus, ordinary worldly people have no regard for the middle in this way, because they lack sufficient mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samādhi*), and understanding.
Even the ancient achievers of absorptions (*jhānas*) and sages (*rishis*) who understood this, developed their meditative powers and gradually approached that neutral state of *adukkhamasukha*, which the ordinary world calls equanimity (*upekkhā*). The attitude of equanimity exists near the middle of that neither-painful-nor-pleasant seesaw, and they remained there. But how is it explained next? Theri Dhammadinnā says that the counterpart of pleasant feeling is painful feeling, and the counterpart of painful feeling is pleasant feeling. There is a constant, mutual relationship between those two.
However, underlying neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the non-knowing of ignorance (*avijjā*), a failure to understand. Once this is understood, that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling turns into a form of happiness. As long as delusion remains, the peaceful and sublime nature of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is not understood. When realization arises, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is directly experienced as an extremely valuable experience, far superior to the coarse, rough pleasure and pain of worldly pleasures. For those achievers of *jhānas*, by the time they reach the fourth *jhāna*, *upekkhā* (equanimity) becomes pure.
Next, when viewed through insight (*vipassanā*), it is revealed that underlying neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling are ignorance and non-knowing. When ignorance is removed, true knowledge (*vijjā*) arises, which is realization. It is through that knowledge that liberation (*vimutti*) comes. Because of liberation, there is extinguishment, Nibbāna. It was when Theri Dhammadinnā declared this that the lay devotee Visākha asked: “What lies beyond Nibbāna?” That was when Dhammadinnā said: “O lay devotee, you have questioned beyond the limit.” Let us strive to understand this matter. The Buddha showed that we must abandon attachment not only to past Preparations (*saṅkhāra*), not only to future Preparations, but also to present Preparations. This is accomplished through insight—by practicing insight with a well-concentrated mind.
The more one contemplates subtly, the more one understands that this existence is something that is constantly wearing away, constantly breaking apart. Existence means progression, rolling on. Indeed, what is thought of as “the present” is something that is constantly rolling on, like a flowing river. Thus, one cannot find a stable footing here. Yet, the tendency to seek a stable footing is what exists in the world. What is that stable footing? It is the notion “I am” (*asmi*).
Even if everything else is absent, there remains the concept of “I am”, assuming that “I” exist. In Dhamma language, this is called the conceit “I am” (*asmi-māna*). At the stage of Non-returner (*anāgāmi*), the lay devotee Visākha did not recognize the subtle defiled nature of this *asmi-māna*. That is why he asked what lies beyond Nibbāna. But the Buddha points out here that even this *asmi-māna*, this “I am”, is merely a conceit—just a measurement. This happens because of the changes in the Preparations (*saṅkhāra*) that are changing subtly and extremely rapidly in the present. It is like a section of a flowing river. Therefore, for that understanding to arise, one must see it with wisdom (*paññā*); one must see it through insight (*vipassanā*).
Mindfulness (*sati*) and concentration (*samādhi*) support this. When one contemplates the Preparations of *nāmarūpa* (Name-and-Form) in that manner, even what was taken as the “present” is seen to change extremely rapidly. This is just like swordplay. Indeed, if we use a simile, the entire existence of life is like a sword fight. Our living is entirely a continuous battle with Māra (Death/the Evil One).
Let us take a brief simile. A person who holds only a sword is fighting another person who also has a sword. In this fight, both attacking and defending are done with the sword. Both attacking and defending are done with the sword. Then, how rapid is this sword fight? This swordplay? Life is exactly like that. Whether we look at the inhalation and exhalation, or look at our efforts to maintain this life, there is a sword fight being waged with Māra. We take the blows dealt by Māra on one side, while hitting back at Māra, trying to defeat him. This is what is found in every single breath. This is what is found in every life-effort. When we seem to be winning that sword fight, that is when the pride of youth arises in us. We think we have won. As we watch, the body grows. “Now, death is nowhere near me”—that is where it appears as though the sword is winning. But when middle age is passed and illnesses arrive, it is then that the inability, the aging, and the helplessness in the swordplay are realized.
To describe this event in modern terms, what happens during our youth? New cells are born faster than the dying cells; so they say in medical science. But as we age, when Māra wins, the rate of regenerating cells decreases, and thus the body wears away.
