In short, what is here is a stream of arising and passing away, and this stream of arising and passing away constantly exists within this body built from food and drink. However, this stream of arising and passing away is not grasped by the mind. Instead, due to the perception of compactness (*ghana-saññā*), it takes it as one solid thing, grasping: “This is me.” Leave alone that, even a photograph that is taken is thought of as “This is mine.” Such is the delusion that exists. It is due to this delusion that there is attachment to these things. The point where this attachment ceases is called revulsion (*nibbidā*), cessation (*nirodha*). Weariness with *saṃsāra* (disenchantment) is produced by that aforementioned vision.
If at any point, contemplation with mindfulness and concentration is correctly applied to those respective Preparations (*saṅkhāra*), perhaps through a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), then indeed one begins to see how these rapidly arise and cease. It is also through the mind that it gradually dawns that there is nothing here even to be taken as “I am”. In the middle, too, there is nothing. Therefore, what was called *akiñcana* is the non-attachment toward them. When weariness with *saṃsāra* arises, there is nothing to be taken as greed, nothing to be taken as hatred, and nothing over which to be deluded. The realization arises that here there is entirely and solely a heap of Preparations (*saṅkhāra*).
Preparations (*saṅkhāra*) mean a heap of preparations or constructions. What is here is a heap of continuously occurring preparations. Thus, within that heap of preparations, one sees the nature of *Anattā* (Not-self). The Three Characteristics—*Anicca* (Impermanent), *Dukkha* (Suffering), and *anattā*—are seen. As impermanence (*aniccatā*) is realized deeper and deeper, the painful nature involved in building and compiling these is realized. The very construction of Preparations is *dukkha*. That is why it is said: *saṅkhārā paramā dukkhā* (Preparations are the supreme suffering). The deepest, most subtle suffering in the world is these Preparations; that is why Nibbāna is presented as the stilling of all Preparations.
This preparation is done through ignorance (*avijjā*). Ignorance means the feeling of “I” and “mine”. As long as the feeling of “I” and “mine” exists, various Preparations (*saṅkhāra*) are made, preparations are constructed. Every single one of those preparations breaks apart extremely rapidly. In insight (*vipassanā*), impermanence (*aniccatā*) is first manifested to the meditator as arising and passing away—coming and going, coming and going. In the meditation on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasati*), when contact is made at the touch-point at the tip of the nose, if attention (*manasikāra*) is well-applied, one understands how these waves of breath break apart extremely rapidly. They arise and break. In the end, what remains through that attention is only subtle contacting; there is no grasping (*upādāna* - grasping / holding / fuel).
This is mentioned in the Dhamma: *phussa phussa vayaṃ passaṃ evaṃ taṃ virajjati*. This means: contacting again and again, seeing their passing away, and it is precisely by seeing their passing away in that manner that fading of lust (*virāga*) arises, weariness (disenchantment) arises. When one sees every single one of these wearing away, there is nothing to grasp. When that which was previously taken as one solid thing due to the perception of compactness (*ghana-saññā*) breaks apart, there is no place to grasp. In ordinary worldly people, there is the grasping called handling (*parāmāsa*). Instead, in insight (*vipassanā*), there is comprehension (*sammasana*). One watches how they arise and pass away at that very spot. That is what was meant by *phussa phussa* (contacting again and again). The moment there is contact (*phassa* - contact), it is gone.
To use a simile, what is done at those police checkpoints? They do not chase after those who have passed, nor do they look back. They remain right there. They do not look back at those who have already gone. But they thoroughly inspect those who arrive at the checkpoint; they engage in maximum scrutiny. Exactly such a thing is done in insight (*vipassanā*). One does not run after past Preparations (*saṅkhāra*), nor does one chase after future Preparations. Instead, one contemplates the present Preparations at that very spot with subtle insight. It is then that their true nature becomes manifest. Just as whatever is hidden is caught at that checkpoint, as insight develops, one realizes: “Haven't we been playing this game with Māra all this time?”
There is another excellent story relevant to this, found in a series of questions asked by a monk named Rādha. In those questions, one can see the same pattern as the questions asked by the lay devotee Visākha. On one occasion, Ven. Rādha came to the Buddha and asked: “Venerable Sir, it is said, 'Māra, Māra.' Who is this Māra?” Then the Buddha declared: “Form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), Preparations (*saṅkhāra*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*)—these themselves are Māra.” What is the reason for this? If there is death or dying due to something, if there is a concept of 'one who is dead' or 'one who dies,' that is it. Thus, because form exists, where form is taken as a single thing, there is dying—the concept that “form is dead”. It is the same regarding feeling. According to the Buddha's definition, there is no other Māra here. There may be other concepts of Māra, but in relation to this question, the Buddha showed: “Rādha, look at form itself as Māra,” because it is form itself that is said to die. What is dead is also form. Feeling is the same, perception is the same, Preparations are the same, and consciousness is the same.
Thus, through that concept of Māra, we can realize that the effort to maintain each of these is like a battle with Māra, similar to the swordplay described earlier. We try to protect form carefully; that is a battle with Māra. We try to maintain the pleasant feelings (*vedanā*) we like; those too are battles with Māra. When one understands at some point that all of these, when actually looked at, are like a heap of waves moving extremely rapidly, or like a river flowing on, that is Right View (*sammā-dassana*). In the end, even in this discourse, the Buddha tells Ven. Rādha: “If someone sees form as Māra, sees feeling as Māra, sees perception as Māra, sees Preparations as Māra, and sees consciousness as Māra—that is Right View.” This is the Buddha's word.
Next, Ven. Rādha asks: “Venerable Sir, what is the purpose of that Right View?” “Right View is needed for revulsion (*nibbidā*) toward *saṃsāra*.” *Nibbidā* means weariness/revulsion toward *saṃsāra*. It is called “Right” (*sammā*) View because it assists in revulsion. In modern times, people call other things “good”. Why is this called “Right” View? Because it assists in revulsion. Seeing form as Māra, seeing feeling as Māra, seeing perception as Māra, seeing Preparations as Māra, and seeing consciousness as Māra assists in one's revulsion toward *saṃsāra*. Then he asks, what is that Right View for? “Why should one feel revulsion toward *saṃsāra*?” Ven. Rādha asks this as well. “Revulsion toward *saṃsāra* is needed for dispassion (*virāga*), which is non-attachment.” Without non-attachment, one cannot escape this *saṃsāra*. One cannot escape the suffering (*dukkha*) of *saṃsāra* while maintaining attachment to *saṃsāra*. One wants to escape from *saṃsāra* and suffering, yet one also has attachment to *saṃsāra*. How can that be done? It cannot be done. That is why the Buddha says that revulsion toward *saṃsāra* is necessary.
Thus, as we have been explaining, Right View is needed for revulsion toward *saṃsāra*. Revulsion toward *saṃsāra* is needed for dispassion (*virāga*), which is non-attachment. What is dispassion needed for? Dispassion is needed for liberation (*vimutti*), for release. Release from what? It is by going along grasping this five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*) that one suffers for a long time in this *saṃsāra*. One must let go of this. How does one let go of it? Does one throw it away physically? No. One is holding onto this with the mind. Grasping (*upādāna* - grasping / holding / fuel) means that holding by the mind. We hold onto these—form, feeling (*vedanā*), perception, Preparations (*saṅkhāra*), and consciousness—as *upādāna* because of our *Taṇhā* (Craving) for them. Various words like *nandi* (delight) and *chandarāga* (desire-and-lust) are used as synonyms for craving. In whatever word it is expressed, there is a grasping due to craving. This grasping is done by the mind.
Thus, it is by the mind that these attachments arise. It is by the mind that one is bound. Therefore, it is by the mind itself that one must be liberated—that is liberation (*vimutti*). Then, dispassion (*virāga*) means non-attachment. To put it another way, the colors of those things that appeared beautiful until now have faded; the paint of that beautifully attractive form has run. When insight (*vipassanā*) arises, even in a very beautiful form, that paint runs. The paint on other things runs as well. The realization comes that they have no value. Thus, from that dispassion comes liberation. Next, from liberation comes extinguishment, Nibbāna. But, just as the lay devotee Visākha asked, Ven. Rādha also asks: “What is Nibbāna for?” Then the Buddha says: “Rādha, now you have overstepped the limit of questioning. There is nothing beyond Nibbāna. Nibbāna is the culmination of this holy life (*brahmacariya*) in the Sāsana; everything ends with Nibbāna.” What is the reason for this? Why was it said so?
Usually, many people think of Nibbāna as “a thing”. They think of it as a different world, uttering beautiful sentences like “attaining eternal peace in the deathless, great Nirvāṇa of everlasting bliss,” believing there is some place where the dead go and gather. That is the concept they hold. Let us think a little about this word “extinguishment” (*nivīma*). When we explained the word *akiñcana*, we said that those three—lust (*rāgā*), hatred (*dosa*), and delusion (*moha*)—are what are called “things”. It is because of those things that everything becomes a sign (*nimitta*) to us. When looking around with lust, things that were not signs before can become signs to us. When looking around with hatred, things we did not notice before begin to appear as signs. There are endless things to cling to when lust arises. There are endless things to clash with when hatred arises. There are endless things over which to be deluded—running after curiosity and perplexity—when delusion arises.
Now understand why lust, hatred, and delusion are called *kiñcana* (obstructions/possessions/attachments)—why they are called “anything” or “something”. You, lay devotees, know how everyone runs after fancy fashions popular among the youth for a short time. Then, as soon as a different fashion arrives, those previous ones fade away. Their paint runs out, their value drops, and eventually, they cannot even be sold—all those fancy things. From that, we can understand that lust, hatred, and delusion are the real “things” in the world. Other things are merely symbolized by them. There is what we call a symbol. Taking something as a beautiful thing, as a valuable thing, is a symbol of lust—that is greed. If most people covet it, then it becomes a highly valued item that can be sold at a high price, praised by everyone.
Let us look at what a gem is. In the final analysis, a gem is also something like a piece of charcoal. Yet, the world highly regards it. What is gold? The value of all such things is connected to our greed. It is the same regarding hatred; when our hatred arises, we clash with anything. Delusion is the same; if there is some strange, unknown thing, a miraculous thing, we stand with our mouths open, staring at it because looking with just our eyes is not enough. You, lay devotees, have heard of the fires shown by the Buddha: they are *Jāti* (Birth), *jarā* (decay/aging), and *maraṇa* (death). Thus, if the existence of this *saṃsāra* is those three fires, what is extinguishment, Nibbāna? It is the extinguishing of those fires. Once the fire is extinguished, what else is needed? While burning in the fire called suffering (*dukkha* - suffering / unsatisfactoriness / stress), one says: “This is suffering.” It was to eliminate that suffering that the Buddha preached this Dhamma.
During the Buddha's time, the Brahmins made various accusations against the Buddha. The idea held by the Brahmins was that there is something called a self, there is an eternal existence, there is a state of Brahma—those who held a firm view of self. They accused the Buddha's teaching of being annihilationist (*uccheda*), a destruction, and accused him of being an annihilationist. The Buddha said: “They accuse me of something I did not say. What I declared then, and what I declare now, is only suffering (*dukkha*) and the cessation (*nirodha*) of suffering.” If suffering is the existence of *saṃsāra*, if it is suffering, if holding onto these five aggregates is suffering, then it is when these five aggregates are abandoned that there is happiness.
That is what is called the bliss of Nibbāna. If we take the simile of the fire, the bliss of Nibbāna experienced in this very life is the point where that fire is extinguished. That very story of the extinguishing of the fire is what we remind you of on many occasions. The word *Upādāna* (Grasping) or clutching is often used for firewood and so on. When a fire spreads, whatever it grasps, whatever it clutches, burns away. We do not realize this. We may have a lot of wealth. When we go on a shopping trip, in accordance with our desire, by the time we return, we do not have even a single cent; all the money is gone. It went to that fire. It is just like that here; we must realize that due to greed, hatred, and delusion, not only this body but everything captured by our thinking gets caught in that fire and burns away. That is what this *saṃsāric* existence is. If at any point those aforementioned fires are extinguished within, that very extinguishment is Nibbāna. That is the supreme peace, a peace to be realized in this very life. There is nothing beyond that. Why is it said there is nothing beyond?
When speaking of *saṃsāra*, the Buddha declared that if someone has *Taṇhā* (Craving) at the moment of death, whether regarding their household members or anything else, they might be born even as a hungry ghost (*peta*). Thus, there is a grasping because of that craving. That grasping is done by the mind. Indeed, after death, the physical body is cremated or buried. However, that grasping mind has clutched. That clutching goes as a rebirth into a mother's womb or elsewhere. Therefore, *saṃsāra* is a certain distorted, perverted state brought about by craving and *Upādāna* (Grasping). Thus, the Buddha shows how to calm this right here.
That is what has been explained so far. Although the five aggregates we grasp are taken as five heaps, by realizing that each of these is constantly breaking apart, when one deeply develops the insight into arising and passing away, the breaking up of everything is seen. This is called the knowledge of dissolution (*bhaṅga-ñāṇa*). In a highly alarming manner, it appears to the insight-practitioner that the speed of breaking up is far greater than the speed of arising. It is at that point that a deep weariness (revulsion) arises. How can we maintain something that is constantly breaking apart eternally, day after day? Therefore, if it is breaking apart, it is not for grasping, but for letting go. Letting go is what must be done. There is no substance in it, no core. That is what is presented in the Dhamma regarding Nibbāna by three terms: *animitta* (signless), *appaṇihita* (desireless/undirected), and *suññata* (void/empty).
*Animitta* means the absence of signs. Where there is greed, a sign is caught; where there is greed, something becomes a thing. Where there is hatred, a sign is caught. Where there is delusion, a sign is caught. Where greed, hatred, and delusion are absent, there are no signs for the mind. As signs keep coming, the mind runs after those signs. The moment a sign comes to the mind, the mind runs after that sign. Because of this, it sometimes becomes exhausted, whether through greed or hatred. Thus, the wondrous state of liberation without signs is what is indicated here by the word *animitta*. Next, *appaṇihita*: *praṇidhi* means aspirations or desires. There exist various kinds of aspirations. Being unable to fulfill those aspirations, people sometimes ruin their lives, carrying them over to the next life as well. Yet, there is never any satisfaction. Thus, when one sees the defects in those aspirations and at some point frees the mind from them, at that moment, there is no aspiration either.
Next, *suññatā*. Void or empty means there is no substance in these; there is no core of self. There is nothing unchanging here. If we use the seesaw simile, what was done by Āḷāra Kālāma, Uddaka Rāmaputta, and others was like philosophers or meditators who, exhausted by riding the seesaw between pain and pleasure for so long in *saṃsāra*, came to the point where the plank rests on the log and took a small break. They were experiencing a subtle pleasure of neither-painful-nor-pleasant (*adukkhamasukha*) through subtle meditative states (*jhānas*). However, the Buddha went even beyond that. The Buddha showed that underlying these, there is grave ignorance (*avijjā*) and delusion (*moha*). What is that? It is precisely that conceit “I am” (*asmi-māna*). It is on the basis of the conceit “I am” that everyone rides this seesaw. Thus, if at any point that too is removed, there is no longer a problem. That is why Nibbāna is called *avedayita-sukha* (pleasure unfelt).
For many, it is a great puzzle why this happiness is called *avedayita-sukha* (unfelt pleasure). For us, we call a feeling (*vedanā*) “happiness”. However, Ven. Sāriputta pointed out on one occasion that there is happiness even where there is no feeling. Ordinary worldly people think that if there is happiness, there must be a feeling. The Buddha declares that *avedayita-sukha* is a state freed even from feeling. Feeling exists as long as that conceit “I am” (*asmi*) exists—as long as the wedge is there. Therefore, the state freed from feeling, freed from the five aggregates entirely, is supramundane happiness (*lokuttara-sukha*). It is described as a peaceful bliss.
Thus, in the attainment of fruition (*phala-samāpatti*), the Arahants detach from their bodies and the world, and establish a wondrously peaceful bliss that is void (*suññata*), signless (*animitta*), and desireless (*appaṇihita*), without taking any sign whatsoever. If they pass away into final extinguishment (*pariNibbāna from that state, there is no future rebirth, because there is no sign, no desire, and no substance. Wherever a sign was taken, wherever a desire or aspiration was formed, wherever some place was regarded as having substance—right there, rebirth is obtained, whether in a mother's womb, an animal's womb, or in the realm of hungry ghosts, or in a place like hell, depending on that thought-clutch. Then, just as it is said: *manopubbaṅgamā dhammā manoseṭṭhā manomayā* (mind precedes all mental states, mind is their chief, they are mind-made), everything exists according to this mind. Mind is chief. Therefore, we must indeed protect the mind. It is through the mind itself that we construct these sufferings and travel through this *saṃsāra* for such a long time. Thus, liberation (*vimutti*) also lies right there. That is what the Buddha has shown us here.
The very Middle Path (*majjhimā paṭipadā*) we mentioned at the beginning is what is present here as well. Those who ran after pleasant feeling (*vedanā*) ran toward the extreme of devotion to sensual pleasures (*kāmasukhallikānuyoga*), as described in the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*. Seeking liberation and searching for an end, they spent lives of luxury. There was no end to that either. Next, another group, believing that to eliminate *Taṇhā* (Craving) one must inflict pain on the body, went along the path of self-mortification (*attakilamathānuyoga*), inflicting terrible suffering. The Buddha showed that both of these are extremes. Thus, he showed the Middle Path.
We return once again to the Noble Eightfold Path. In the Noble Eightfold Path, Right View (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) is indeed the very first step in eliminating the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avijjānusaya*). In Dhammadinnā's analysis of the Dhamma, it was also stated that underlying the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling called *adukkhamasukha* is ignorance (*avijjā*). When ignorance is removed, true knowledge (*vijjā*) emerges. Where knowledge emerges, there is liberation (*vimutti*). Where there is liberation, there is extinguishment (Nibbāna. Thus, in this Noble Eightfold Path starting with Right View, it is the question of the “middle” that is put into action. The two extremes have been abandoned. It is through establishing neutral feeling (*vedanā*) and developing a neutral mind, and thereby practicing insight (*vipassanā*), that we can escape from this *saṃsāra*.
Some of the things explained so far may appear profound. These were declared because they will be of assistance to meditators (*yogāvacaras*). On a valuable Esala Full Moon Poya day like today, we presented a concept of the Middle Path found in discourses such as the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta* from another perspective. You, lay devotees, should take advantage of these and, in this age of decline of the Buddha's dispensation, strive hundreds or thousands of times to realize the liberation from *saṃsāra* that you hope for in this very life. If this Dhamma sermon has helped you develop the spiritual faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) of faith (*saddhā*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*), then taking refuge in them, and with the support of noble friendship (*kalyāṇa-mittatā*), may you gain the strength and power to realize the noble, supreme, deathless Nibbāna through the realization of the paths and fruits of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti*), Non-returning (*anāgāmitā*), and Arahatship, and thereby escape the suffering of *saṃsāra*! Strive with this aspiration. Furthermore, may your relatives and all beings from Avīci hell to the Akanistha heaven who wish to rejoice in this merit of preaching and hearing the Dhamma, by so rejoicing, realize the supreme deathless Nibbāna through a Bodhi of their aspiration! Striving with this aspiration, recite these verses:
“*Ettāvatā ca amhehi.........*”

from:
dhammapada verse 421 (brahmana vagga)
dear listeners,
as the middle path (*majjhima patipada*) to escape the *dukkha* (suffering) of *samsara*, the teacher of the three worlds, the buddha, placed before the world the noble eightfold path on an esala full moon poya day like today. this path and practice, followed by everyone who aspires for nibbana without distinction between lay and ordained, is none other than this noble eightfold path. the background story to the verse we have selected as our theme today is an exemplary account of how *nekkhamma-sankappa* (the thought of renunciation)—which is a primary component of *samma-sankappa* (right resolution)—matured within a lay household.
the buddha preached this dhamma verse at the veluvana monastery in rajagaha concerning a bhikkhuni named dhammadinna. during her lay life, dhammadinna’s husband was the lay devotee visakha. one day, after listening to the dhamma from the buddha, the lay devotee visakha attained the stage of non-returner (*anagami-phala*). on his way back home, he reflected: “i must hand over all my wealth and possessions to my wife, dhammadinna, and set myself free.”
usually, dhammadinna would wait by the window, watching for her husband to return from outside. as the husband approached, they would greet each other with smiles; such was their custom. on this particular day, however, the lay devotee visakha entered the house calmly without even looking toward the window. dhammadinna was somewhat perplexed by this, wondering why today was different. furthermore, when the meal was prepared, whereas visakha would normally invite his wife, saying, “come, let us eat together,” this time he ate in silence. thus, dhammadinna further pondered whether his mind was upset or if he had become angry due to some matter.
later, when the lay devotee visakha was sitting quietly, he called his wife and said, “dhammadinna, please take charge of all these riches and comforts.” at this, dhammadinna thought, “people who are angry do not hand over wealth in this manner. what could this be?”
then she asked, “my lord, what will you do?” when he explained the situation, dhammadinna replied, “i do not wish to pick up the lump of spit that you have spat out. please grant me permission to ordain.” from this, we can infer that even by that time, dhammadinna must have been a woman of great faith (*saddha*) who had also practiced meditation. visakha, the lay devotee, escorted dhammadinna to a nunnery and facilitated her ordination. since theri dhammadinna delighted in solitude, after her higher ordination (*upasampada*), she went to a remote province with a group of other bhikkhunis to dwell in seclusion. not long after going into seclusion to meditate after her higher ordination, she attained arahatship with the four analytical knowledges (*patisambhida*). she then thought, “i must give my relatives the opportunity to accumulate merit through me,” and returned to rajagaha.
when the lay devotee visakha heard that she had returned to her nunnery, he thought, “perhaps she has returned so quickly because she has become dissatisfied with the holy life for some reason.” thus, visakha went to the hermitage and paid his respects. however, he could not directly ask theri dhammadinna, “why is this? have you returned because your mind has turned away from ordination?” instead, what did he do? he asked a question pertaining to the path of stream-entry (*sotapatti-magga*). she answered that question directly and correctly. next, he asked question after question, rising to the path of once-returning (*sakadagami-magga*) and the path of non-returning (*anagami-magga*). the answers came in an extraordinary manner—only the question and the answer, with no irrelevant chatter. sensing that the final question, concerning the path of arahatship, went beyond the boundary of the lay devotee visakha’s own level of dhamma-realization as an anagami, theri dhammadinna said: “o lay devotee, you have overstepped the limits of questioning. you have failed to recognize the boundary of this question. if you wish, you may go and report this discussion to the blessed one as it transpired.”
accordingly, the lay devotee went to the buddha and related the entire discussion. the buddha praised her and said: “my daughter dhammadinna’s analysis of the dhamma is absolutely correct. even if you had asked me, i would have given these very same answers to those questions. she is a woman of great wisdom.” elsewhere in the tipitaka, it is mentioned that when the buddha declared the foremost positions among the disciples, he declared theri dhammadinna foremost among the bhikkhunis who are dhamma-speakers (*dhammakathika*) in the entire bhikkhuni sasana.
that very dhamma discussion can still be found today in the *culavedalla sutta* of the *majjhima nikaya*. it is an extremely profound discourse that draws the attention of both great scholars and meditators alike. there is no extraneous elaboration in it—it is simply question and answer, question and answer. a highly valuable compilation of dhamma is found there. through this, we see the miracle of the dhamma. not only that, but after doing so, the buddha also uttered a certain verse in praise of theri dhammadinna. it is that verse we have taken as our theme today:
*yassa pure ca paccha ca, majjhe ca natthi kincanam, akincanam anadanam, tamaham brumi brahmanam.*
at first glance, it is almost like a riddle-verse. “he who has nothing before, after, or in the middle—who is possessionless, who grasps at nothing—him i call a brahmin.”
this *dhammapada* verse is very simple. on this occasion, i will explain it very briefly. the buddha often used the word “brahmin” to refer to an arahant. what is revealed here is that theri dhammadinna had attained arahatship. thus, the nature of an arahant's mind is shown by those words. for now, we will mention it briefly and elaborate later. “before” (*pure*) refers to the past. there is no aspiration, no desire regarding the past five aggregates (*pancakkhandha*). similarly, there is no aspiration or desire regarding the future five aggregates. there are no special desires regarding the past aggregates, nor is there any desire regarding the future aggregates.
next, “middle” (*majjhe*) here refers to the present. likewise, there is no attachment to the present five aggregates. it is in the *brahmana vagga* of the *dhammapada*, which describes the arahants, that this verse is found, saying: “him i call a brahmin, who has nothing of his own, who grasps at nothing.” if we first consider the story, as we mentioned earlier, it demonstrates the transformation brought about by the emergence of *nekkhamma-sankappa* (the thought of renunciation) within a lay household. from this, lay devotees of today can learn many lessons. after turning toward the dhamma, lay devotees can find excellent examples in this story for the various problems they encounter at home. looking even at daily life, the harmonious relationship that existed between the lay devotee visakha and dhammadinna as husband and wife can be called exemplary.
the wife would watch from the window for her husband returning from outside. then, as soon as the husband arrived, she would welcome him warmly. the husband, too, was a very gentle-natured person. when taking meals, he would call his wife to eat together. they were two people who lived such a friendly and affectionate life. however, due to a sudden transformation brought about by the dhamma, the lay devotee visakha decided: “now i need freedom for my dhamma study and meditation. let me hand over the management of all these resources to my wife.” in the stories of the past, dhammadinna is depicted as a highly meritorious lady who had fulfilled her perfections (*paramis*) and come aspiring for such a position. therefore, as soon as her husband spoke those words, instead of desiring those riches, she regarded them as a lump of spit and, saying, “what use is the lump of spit spat out by you to me?”, she renounced them even before her husband did. indeed, it is mentioned that while the lay devotee remained a lay devotee, his wife became highly renowned in this sasana as theri dhammadinna.
when this dhamma leading to nibbana enters a person's heart, that transformation is difficult for many to understand. especially for those bound by various ties of lay life, being unable to understand what occurs in another's mind-stream leads to various kinds of friction and displeasure. however, we are all temporarily met in this *samsara*, in this wayside resting house of the world, due to certain past connections. yet, this path to nibbana is a journey that must be made individually. it is the journey through *samsara*, the journey of crossing over *samsara*. thus, supporting those who step forward with the necessary qualifications for it in a friendly manner is exactly what the lay devotee visakha did. he went and handed over his wife to the nunnery. next, let us look into analyzing these deep matters of the dhamma.
now, the five aggregates (*pancakkhandha*) were mentioned here. you, lay devotees, have heard this word “five aggregates”. most of you know that they are the five: form (*rupa*), feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), preparations (*sankhara*), and consciousness (*vinnana*). these aggregates (*khandha*) mean heaps or piles; thus, there are five heaps. these five heaps are analyzed in this way: they are divided into past, future, and present, and are also seen both internally (*ajjhatta*) and externally (*bahiddha*). internal refers to oneself—the heap of form regarding oneself—and external refers to others—the heap of form regarding others. let us understand it thus. furthermore, it can be gross form or subtle form, superior form or inferior form, near form or far form. in this way, all various forms are gathered into this aggregate of form (*rupakkhandha*). it is because of grasping these with *tanha* (craving) that they are called *upadana* (grasping)—the five aggregates of grasping (*pancupadanakkhandha*). so, how does one recall the past five aggregates? sometimes one thinks like this:
let us say an elderly person thinks about their youth: “i used to be beautiful in such-and-such a way. alas! now look what has happened to me,” and thus develops an attachment to that past form. this is called *nandiraga* (delight and lust). terms like *nandi* (delight), *raga* (lust), and *chanda* (desire) are presented as synonyms of *tanha* (craving)—words equivalent to craving. thinking of the past, they create a regret or a desire for it and suffer, saying, “we no longer have this now.” next is the opposite side, which is about the future. they form future aspirations: “i must become someone with great physical beauty, a beautiful person, a strong person,” and thus remain clinging to thoughts and wishes regarding the future. that is what was meant by “before” and “after”—regarding the past five aggregates and the future five aggregates.
regarding the present five aggregates, what is currently here is also grasped as a self. they say: “this form is myself; this is my soul. there is a soul in form, form is in the soul, form is possessed of a soul.” in this way, they regard this form as a self, as “me”. this is how one develops attachment to the present form. now, as described here, what is indicated is that the arahant has freed themselves from those conceptualizations. for such a person, there is no attachment to the past five aggregates, nor are there any aspirations for a future five aggregates. the attachment and desire for the present five aggregates have been abandoned. for this very reason, they are *akincana* (possessionless / having nothing).
the meaning of the word *akincana* is “owning nothing”. usually, when we say “owning nothing”, we think of material wealth and so on. in the dhamma, it is presented much more deeply. *kincana* means “something” or “anything”. greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dosa*), and delusion (*moha*) are designated as *kincana* (obstructions/possessions/attachments). therefore, where greed, hatred, and delusion are absent, there is *akincana*. what is the reason for this? for us, a thing becomes “a thing” either because we like it, or because we are opposed to it, or because we are deluded by it—having a curiosity or doubt about what it is. it is through greed, hatred, and delusion in this manner that things in the world become “things” to us. if we take *kincana* deeply, “anything” refers to those three: greed, hatred, and delusion. thus, because the arahant is freed from them, they are *akincana*—owning nothing. likewise, they are *anadana*. *adana* means “grasping” or “holding”—the nature of clutching. *anadana* means they do not grasp at any of those things either.
this is how the liberated mind is expressed in this verse. now, we must indeed pay special attention to what was said here about the “middle” (the present). meditators practicing insight (*vipassana*) know that past preparations (*sankhara*) are “past”, meaning they have gone by. it is easy to realize that they have gone by. sometimes, one spends a little time thinking about past things, but then realizes “this is no longer here”. even if future thoughts arise, one can sometimes escape them. “future” means what has not yet come—things that have not arrived. but the present is the deepest point, the hardest place to grasp.
if we apply this to the practice of mindfulness of breathing (*anapanasati*), some lay devotees when starting the practice send their minds out in anticipation of the incoming breath. or, after the exhalation goes out, they send the mind out following that exhalation. however, teachers have instructed us not to send the mind to the past or to the future, but to anchor the mind at the point where the inhalation and exhalation make contact—such as the nose or the upper lip. that is what is meant by *parimukham satim upatthapetva* (establishing mindfulness in front). even in the canonical discourses, it is mentioned that when sitting down for *anapana*, one should not watch where the breath comes from in the distance, nor should one chase the breath after it has gone.
ordinary people usually regret while thinking about the past, letting their minds run after the past, and they wish for the future. what results from this is a loss of mindfulness. the buddha constantly reminds us that we have to reach this truth through the present moment. therefore, we must anchor the mind in the present. ancient teachers give two similes regarding *anapanasati* to demonstrate this point.
nowadays, the methods of sawing wood are very different. in the past, logs were placed on a trestle and sawn using a two-handed saw. if the person sawing the wood directs their eyes toward the other person or toward the two ends of the saw, they will make a mistake. instead, to do it correctly, they must focus their attention right at the point where the log is being cut—exactly where the saw teeth make contact—without letting the mind drift to the far ends. similarly, it is stated regarding *anapanasati* that the breath must be anchored at the tip of the nose or near the upper lip.
another simile describes pushing a swing. the person standing in the middle often directs their eyes this way and that. however, what actually needs to be done is to anchor the eyes in the middle, without directing them this way and that. while swinging, there is no need to specially watch the two ends. it is just like that. yet, the mind is tempted to send the eyes toward those two ends. similarly, in *anapanasati*, it is when the mind is anchored in the middle that one catches the point of contact, which is the *anapana-nimitta* (the sign of breathing). from that point onward lies the progress of insight (*vipassana*). it is from there that one can elevate to insight the elemental nature (*dhatu*) or the subtle heap-like nature within the wave of breath, thereby attaining liberation (*vimutti*). we can understand this discussion of the “middle” in that manner through the medium of a meditation subject (*kammatthana*).
in that dhamma discussion, there was a certain shortcoming in the question asked by the lay devotee visakha. we are obliged to present that question here at least briefly. indeed, there is insufficient time to present that entire dhamma dialogue. the question we intend to bring out now is precisely the one where theri dhammadinna said, “you have overstepped the limit of asking questions.” visakha, the lay devotee, was asking about pleasant feeling (*vedana*). in pali, it is stated as *sukha, dukkha, adukkhamasukha*, meaning pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant. pleasant feeling and painful feeling are at the two extremes. in the middle lies neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. neither-painful-nor-pleasant means neutral feeling. let us think for a moment. people in this world are riding a seesaw between pleasure and pain. when pain comes, they seek pleasure to escape that pain. but then, that pleasure is also not permanent (*anicca* - impermanent / inconstant). theri dhammadinna spoke about this as well: underlying pleasant feeling is lust, the underlying tendency of lust (*raganusaya*). underlying painful feeling is the underlying tendency of aversion (*patighanusaya*), which is hatred (*dosa*). next, underlying the neutral feeling called *adukkhamasukha* is ignorance (*avijja*) or non-knowing. why? because the neutral feeling is not realized by the ordinary mind; it is only recognized by a meditative mind. worldly beings remain between those two: pleasure and pain, pleasure and pain. they keep rolling along, saying, “pain and pleasure constantly turn.” thus, ordinary worldly people have no regard for the middle in this way, because they lack sufficient mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and understanding.
even the ancient achievers of absorptions (*jhanas*) and sages (*rishis*) who understood this, developed their meditative powers and gradually approached that neutral state of *adukkhamasukha*, which the ordinary world calls equanimity (*upekkha*). the attitude of equanimity exists near the middle of that neither-painful-nor-pleasant seesaw, and they remained there. but how is it explained next? theri dhammadinna says that the counterpart of pleasant feeling is painful feeling, and the counterpart of painful feeling is pleasant feeling. there is a constant, mutual relationship between those two.
however, underlying neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the non-knowing of ignorance (*avijja*), a failure to understand. once this is understood, that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling turns into a form of happiness. as long as delusion remains, the peaceful and sublime nature of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is not understood. when realization arises, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is directly experienced as an extremely valuable experience, far superior to the coarse, rough pleasure and pain of worldly pleasures. for those achievers of *jhanas*, by the time they reach the fourth *jhana*, *upekkha* (equanimity) becomes pure.
next, when viewed through insight (*vipassana*), it is revealed that underlying neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling are ignorance and non-knowing. when ignorance is removed, true knowledge (*vijja*) arises, which is realization. it is through that knowledge that liberation (*vimutti*) comes. because of liberation, there is extinguishment, nibbana. it was when theri dhammadinna declared this that the lay devotee visakha asked: “what lies beyond nibbana?” that was when dhammadinna said: “o lay devotee, you have questioned beyond the limit.” let us strive to understand this matter. the buddha showed that we must abandon attachment not only to past preparations (*sankhara*), not only to future preparations, but also to present preparations. this is accomplished through insight—by practicing insight with a well-concentrated mind.
the more one contemplates subtly, the more one understands that this existence is something that is constantly wearing away, constantly breaking apart. existence means progression, rolling on. indeed, what is thought of as “the present” is something that is constantly rolling on, like a flowing river. thus, one cannot find a stable footing here. yet, the tendency to seek a stable footing is what exists in the world. what is that stable footing? it is the notion “i am” (*asmi*).
even if everything else is absent, there remains the concept of “i am”, assuming that “i” exist. in dhamma language, this is called the conceit “i am” (*asmi-mana*). at the stage of non-returner (*anagami*), the lay devotee visakha did not recognize the subtle defiled nature of this *asmi-mana*. that is why he asked what lies beyond nibbana. but the buddha points out here that even this *asmi-mana*, this “i am”, is merely a conceit—just a measurement. this happens because of the changes in the preparations (*sankhara*) that are changing subtly and extremely rapidly in the present. it is like a section of a flowing river. therefore, for that understanding to arise, one must see it with wisdom (*panna*); one must see it through insight (*vipassana*).
mindfulness (*sati*) and concentration (*samadhi*) support this. when one contemplates the preparations of *namarupa* (name-and-form) in that manner, even what was taken as the “present” is seen to change extremely rapidly. this is just like swordplay. indeed, if we use a simile, the entire existence of life is like a sword fight. our living is entirely a continuous battle with mara (death/the evil one).
let us take a brief simile. a person who holds only a sword is fighting another person who also has a sword. in this fight, both attacking and defending are done with the sword. both attacking and defending are done with the sword. then, how rapid is this sword fight? this swordplay? life is exactly like that. whether we look at the inhalation and exhalation, or look at our efforts to maintain this life, there is a sword fight being waged with mara. we take the blows dealt by mara on one side, while hitting back at mara, trying to defeat him. this is what is found in every single breath. this is what is found in every life-effort. when we seem to be winning that sword fight, that is when the pride of youth arises in us. we think we have won. as we watch, the body grows. “now, death is nowhere near me”—that is where it appears as though the sword is winning. but when middle age is passed and illnesses arrive, it is then that the inability, the aging, and the helplessness in the swordplay are realized.
to describe this event in modern terms, what happens during our youth? new cells are born faster than the dying cells; so they say in medical science. but as we age, when mara wins, the rate of regenerating cells decreases, and thus the body wears away. in short, what is here is a stream of arising and passing away, and this stream of arising and passing away constantly exists within this body built from food and drink. however, this stream of arising and passing away is not grasped by the mind. instead, due to the perception of compactness (*ghana-sanna*), it takes it as one solid thing, grasping: “this is me.” leave alone that, even a photograph that is taken is thought of as “this is mine.” such is the delusion that exists. it is due to this delusion that there is attachment to these things. the point where this attachment ceases is called revulsion (*nibbida*), cessation (*nirodha*). weariness with *samsara* (disenchantment) is produced by that aforementioned vision.
if at any point, contemplation with mindfulness and concentration is correctly applied to those respective preparations (*sankhara*), perhaps through a meditation subject (*kammatthana*), then indeed one begins to see how these rapidly arise and cease. it is also through the mind that it gradually dawns that there is nothing here even to be taken as “i am”. in the middle, too, there is nothing. therefore, what was called *akincana* is the non-attachment toward them. when weariness with *samsara* arises, there is nothing to be taken as greed, nothing to be taken as hatred, and nothing over which to be deluded. the realization arises that here there is entirely and solely a heap of preparations (*sankhara*).
preparations (*sankhara*) mean a heap of preparations or constructions. what is here is a heap of continuously occurring preparations. thus, within that heap of preparations, one sees the nature of *anatta* (not-self). the three characteristics—*anicca* (impermanent), *dukkha* (suffering), and *anatta*—are seen. as impermanence (*aniccata*) is realized deeper and deeper, the painful nature involved in building and compiling these is realized. the very construction of preparations is *dukkha*. that is why it is said: *sankhara parama dukkha* (preparations are the supreme suffering). the deepest, most subtle suffering in the world is these preparations; that is why nibbana is presented as the stilling of all preparations.
this preparation is done through ignorance (*avijja*). ignorance means the feeling of “i” and “mine”. as long as the feeling of “i” and “mine” exists, various preparations (*sankhara*) are made, preparations are constructed. every single one of those preparations breaks apart extremely rapidly. in insight (*vipassana*), impermanence (*aniccata*) is first manifested to the meditator as arising and passing away—coming and going, coming and going. in the meditation on mindfulness of breathing (*anapanasati*), when contact is made at the touch-point at the tip of the nose, if attention (*manasikara*) is well-applied, one understands how these waves of breath break apart extremely rapidly. they arise and break. in the end, what remains through that attention is only subtle contacting; there is no grasping (*upadana* - grasping / holding / fuel).
this is mentioned in the dhamma: *phussa phussa vayam passam evam tam virajjati*. this means: contacting again and again, seeing their passing away, and it is precisely by seeing their passing away in that manner that fading of lust (*viraga*) arises, weariness (disenchantment) arises. when one sees every single one of these wearing away, there is nothing to grasp. when that which was previously taken as one solid thing due to the perception of compactness (*ghana-sanna*) breaks apart, there is no place to grasp. in ordinary worldly people, there is the grasping called handling (*paramasa*). instead, in insight (*vipassana*), there is comprehension (*sammasana*). one watches how they arise and pass away at that very spot. that is what was meant by *phussa phussa* (contacting again and again). the moment there is contact (*phassa* - contact), it is gone.
to use a simile, what is done at those police checkpoints? they do not chase after those who have passed, nor do they look back. they remain right there. they do not look back at those who have already gone. but they thoroughly inspect those who arrive at the checkpoint; they engage in maximum scrutiny. exactly such a thing is done in insight (*vipassana*). one does not run after past preparations (*sankhara*), nor does one chase after future preparations. instead, one contemplates the present preparations at that very spot with subtle insight. it is then that their true nature becomes manifest. just as whatever is hidden is caught at that checkpoint, as insight develops, one realizes: “haven't we been playing this game with mara all this time?”
there is another excellent story relevant to this, found in a series of questions asked by a monk named radha. in those questions, one can see the same pattern as the questions asked by the lay devotee visakha. on one occasion, ven. radha came to the buddha and asked: “venerable sir, it is said, 'mara, mara.' who is this mara?” then the buddha declared: “form (*rupa*), feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), preparations (*sankhara*), and consciousness (*vinnana*)—these themselves are mara.” what is the reason for this? if there is death or dying due to something, if there is a concept of 'one who is dead' or 'one who dies,' that is it. thus, because form exists, where form is taken as a single thing, there is dying—the concept that “form is dead”. it is the same regarding feeling. according to the buddha's definition, there is no other mara here. there may be other concepts of mara, but in relation to this question, the buddha showed: “radha, look at form itself as mara,” because it is form itself that is said to die. what is dead is also form. feeling is the same, perception is the same, preparations are the same, and consciousness is the same.
thus, through that concept of mara, we can realize that the effort to maintain each of these is like a battle with mara, similar to the swordplay described earlier. we try to protect form carefully; that is a battle with mara. we try to maintain the pleasant feelings (*vedana*) we like; those too are battles with mara. when one understands at some point that all of these, when actually looked at, are like a heap of waves moving extremely rapidly, or like a river flowing on, that is right view (*samma-dassana*). in the end, even in this discourse, the buddha tells ven. radha: “if someone sees form as mara, sees feeling as mara, sees perception as mara, sees preparations as mara, and sees consciousness as mara—that is right view.” this is the buddha's word.
next, ven. radha asks: “venerable sir, what is the purpose of that right view?” “right view is needed for revulsion (*nibbida*) toward *samsara*.” *nibbida* means weariness/revulsion toward *samsara*. it is called “right” (*samma*) view because it assists in revulsion. in modern times, people call other things “good”. why is this called “right” view? because it assists in revulsion. seeing form as mara, seeing feeling as mara, seeing perception as mara, seeing preparations as mara, and seeing consciousness as mara assists in one's revulsion toward *samsara*. then he asks, what is that right view for? “why should one feel revulsion toward *samsara*?” ven. radha asks this as well. “revulsion toward *samsara* is needed for dispassion (*viraga*), which is non-attachment.” without non-attachment, one cannot escape this *samsara*. one cannot escape the suffering (*dukkha*) of *samsara* while maintaining attachment to *samsara*. one wants to escape from *samsara* and suffering, yet one also has attachment to *samsara*. how can that be done? it cannot be done. that is why the buddha says that revulsion toward *samsara* is necessary.
thus, as we have been explaining, right view is needed for revulsion toward *samsara*. revulsion toward *samsara* is needed for dispassion (*viraga*), which is non-attachment. what is dispassion needed for? dispassion is needed for liberation (*vimutti*), for release. release from what? it is by going along grasping this five aggregates (*pancakkhandha*) that one suffers for a long time in this *samsara*. one must let go of this. how does one let go of it? does one throw it away physically? no. one is holding onto this with the mind. grasping (*upadana* - grasping / holding / fuel) means that holding by the mind. we hold onto these—form, feeling (*vedana*), perception, preparations (*sankhara*), and consciousness—as *upadana* because of our *tanha* (craving) for them. various words like *nandi* (delight) and *chandaraga* (desire-and-lust) are used as synonyms for craving. in whatever word it is expressed, there is a grasping due to craving. this grasping is done by the mind.
thus, it is by the mind that these attachments arise. it is by the mind that one is bound. therefore, it is by the mind itself that one must be liberated—that is liberation (*vimutti*). then, dispassion (*viraga*) means non-attachment. to put it another way, the colors of those things that appeared beautiful until now have faded; the paint of that beautifully attractive form has run. when insight (*vipassana*) arises, even in a very beautiful form, that paint runs. the paint on other things runs as well. the realization comes that they have no value. thus, from that dispassion comes liberation. next, from liberation comes extinguishment, nibbana. but, just as the lay devotee visakha asked, ven. radha also asks: “what is nibbana for?” then the buddha says: “radha, now you have overstepped the limit of questioning. there is nothing beyond nibbana. nibbana is the culmination of this holy life (*brahmacariya*) in the sasana; everything ends with nibbana.” what is the reason for this? why was it said so?
usually, many people think of nibbana as “a thing”. they think of it as a different world, uttering beautiful sentences like “attaining eternal peace in the deathless, great nirvana of everlasting bliss,” believing there is some place where the dead go and gather. that is the concept they hold. let us think a little about this word “extinguishment” (*nivima*). when we explained the word *akincana*, we said that those three—lust (*raga*), hatred (*dosa*), and delusion (*moha*)—are what are called “things”. it is because of those things that everything becomes a sign (*nimitta*) to us. when looking around with lust, things that were not signs before can become signs to us. when looking around with hatred, things we did not notice before begin to appear as signs. there are endless things to cling to when lust arises. there are endless things to clash with when hatred arises. there are endless things over which to be deluded—running after curiosity and perplexity—when delusion arises.
now understand why lust, hatred, and delusion are called *kincana* (obstructions/possessions/attachments)—why they are called “anything” or “something”. you, lay devotees, know how everyone runs after fancy fashions popular among the youth for a short time. then, as soon as a different fashion arrives, those previous ones fade away. their paint runs out, their value drops, and eventually, they cannot even be sold—all those fancy things. from that, we can understand that lust, hatred, and delusion are the real “things” in the world. other things are merely symbolized by them. there is what we call a symbol. taking something as a beautiful thing, as a valuable thing, is a symbol of lust—that is greed. if most people covet it, then it becomes a highly valued item that can be sold at a high price, praised by everyone.
let us look at what a gem is. in the final analysis, a gem is also something like a piece of charcoal. yet, the world highly regards it. what is gold? the value of all such things is connected to our greed. it is the same regarding hatred; when our hatred arises, we clash with anything. delusion is the same; if there is some strange, unknown thing, a miraculous thing, we stand with our mouths open, staring at it because looking with just our eyes is not enough. you, lay devotees, have heard of the fires shown by the buddha: they are *jati* (birth), *jara* (decay/aging), and *marana* (death). thus, if the existence of this *samsara* is those three fires, what is extinguishment, nibbana? it is the extinguishing of those fires. once the fire is extinguished, what else is needed? while burning in the fire called suffering (*dukkha* - suffering / unsatisfactoriness / stress), one says: “this is suffering.” it was to eliminate that suffering that the buddha preached this dhamma.
during the buddha's time, the brahmins made various accusations against the buddha. the idea held by the brahmins was that there is something called a self, there is an eternal existence, there is a state of brahma—those who held a firm view of self. they accused the buddha's teaching of being annihilationist (*uccheda*), a destruction, and accused him of being an annihilationist. the buddha said: “they accuse me of something i did not say. what i declared then, and what i declare now, is only suffering (*dukkha*) and the cessation (*nirodha*) of suffering.” if suffering is the existence of *samsara*, if it is suffering, if holding onto these five aggregates is suffering, then it is when these five aggregates are abandoned that there is happiness.
that is what is called the bliss of nibbana. if we take the simile of the fire, the bliss of nibbana experienced in this very life is the point where that fire is extinguished. that very story of the extinguishing of the fire is what we remind you of on many occasions. the word *upadana* (grasping) or clutching is often used for firewood and so on. when a fire spreads, whatever it grasps, whatever it clutches, burns away. we do not realize this. we may have a lot of wealth. when we go on a shopping trip, in accordance with our desire, by the time we return, we do not have even a single cent; all the money is gone. it went to that fire. it is just like that here; we must realize that due to greed, hatred, and delusion, not only this body but everything captured by our thinking gets caught in that fire and burns away. that is what this *samsaric* existence is. if at any point those aforementioned fires are extinguished within, that very extinguishment is nibbana. that is the supreme peace, a peace to be realized in this very life. there is nothing beyond that. why is it said there is nothing beyond?
when speaking of *samsara*, the buddha declared that if someone has *tanha* (craving) at the moment of death, whether regarding their household members or anything else, they might be born even as a hungry ghost (*peta*). thus, there is a grasping because of that craving. that grasping is done by the mind. indeed, after death, the physical body is cremated or buried. however, that grasping mind has clutched. that clutching goes as a rebirth into a mother's womb or elsewhere. therefore, *samsara* is a certain distorted, perverted state brought about by craving and *upadana* (grasping). thus, the buddha shows how to calm this right here.
that is what has been explained so far. although the five aggregates we grasp are taken as five heaps, by realizing that each of these is constantly breaking apart, when one deeply develops the insight into arising and passing away, the breaking up of everything is seen. this is called the knowledge of dissolution (*bhanga-nana*). in a highly alarming manner, it appears to the insight-practitioner that the speed of breaking up is far greater than the speed of arising. it is at that point that a deep weariness (revulsion) arises. how can we maintain something that is constantly breaking apart eternally, day after day? therefore, if it is breaking apart, it is not for grasping, but for letting go. letting go is what must be done. there is no substance in it, no core. that is what is presented in the dhamma regarding nibbana by three terms: *animitta* (signless), *appanihita* (desireless/undirected), and *sunnata* (void/empty).
*animitta* means the absence of signs. where there is greed, a sign is caught; where there is greed, something becomes a thing. where there is hatred, a sign is caught. where there is delusion, a sign is caught. where greed, hatred, and delusion are absent, there are no signs for the mind. as signs keep coming, the mind runs after those signs. the moment a sign comes to the mind, the mind runs after that sign. because of this, it sometimes becomes exhausted, whether through greed or hatred. thus, the wondrous state of liberation without signs is what is indicated here by the word *animitta*. next, *appanihita*: *pranidhi* means aspirations or desires. there exist various kinds of aspirations. being unable to fulfill those aspirations, people sometimes ruin their lives, carrying them over to the next life as well. yet, there is never any satisfaction. thus, when one sees the defects in those aspirations and at some point frees the mind from them, at that moment, there is no aspiration either.
next, *sunnata*. void or empty means there is no substance in these; there is no core of self. there is nothing unchanging here. if we use the seesaw simile, what was done by alara kalama, uddaka ramaputta, and others was like philosophers or meditators who, exhausted by riding the seesaw between pain and pleasure for so long in *samsara*, came to the point where the plank rests on the log and took a small break. they were experiencing a subtle pleasure of neither-painful-nor-pleasant (*adukkhamasukha*) through subtle meditative states (*jhanas*). however, the buddha went even beyond that. the buddha showed that underlying these, there is grave ignorance (*avijja*) and delusion (*moha*). what is that? it is precisely that conceit “i am” (*asmi-mana*). it is on the basis of the conceit “i am” that everyone rides this seesaw. thus, if at any point that too is removed, there is no longer a problem. that is why nibbana is called *avedayita-sukha* (pleasure unfelt).
for many, it is a great puzzle why this happiness is called *avedayita-sukha* (unfelt pleasure). for us, we call a feeling (*vedana*) “happiness”. however, ven. sariputta pointed out on one occasion that there is happiness even where there is no feeling. ordinary worldly people think that if there is happiness, there must be a feeling. the buddha declares that *avedayita-sukha* is a state freed even from feeling. feeling exists as long as that conceit “i am” (*asmi*) exists—as long as the wedge is there. therefore, the state freed from feeling, freed from the five aggregates entirely, is supramundane happiness (*lokuttara-sukha*). it is described as a peaceful bliss.
thus, in the attainment of fruition (*phala-samapatti*), the arahants detach from their bodies and the world, and establish a wondrously peaceful bliss that is void (*sunnata*), signless (*animitta*), and desireless (*appanihita*), without taking any sign whatsoever. if they pass away into final extinguishment (*parinibbana from that state, there is no future rebirth, because there is no sign, no desire, and no substance. wherever a sign was taken, wherever a desire or aspiration was formed, wherever some place was regarded as having substance—right there, rebirth is obtained, whether in a mother's womb, an animal's womb, or in the realm of hungry ghosts, or in a place like hell, depending on that thought-clutch. then, just as it is said: *manopubbangama dhamma manosettha manomaya* (mind precedes all mental states, mind is their chief, they are mind-made), everything exists according to this mind. mind is chief. therefore, we must indeed protect the mind. it is through the mind itself that we construct these sufferings and travel through this *samsara* for such a long time. thus, liberation (*vimutti*) also lies right there. that is what the buddha has shown us here.
the very middle path (*majjhima patipada*) we mentioned at the beginning is what is present here as well. those who ran after pleasant feeling (*vedana*) ran toward the extreme of devotion to sensual pleasures (*kamasukhallikanuyoga*), as described in the *dhammacakkappavattana sutta*. seeking liberation and searching for an end, they spent lives of luxury. there was no end to that either. next, another group, believing that to eliminate *tanha* (craving) one must inflict pain on the body, went along the path of self-mortification (*attakilamathanuyoga*), inflicting terrible suffering. the buddha showed that both of these are extremes. thus, he showed the middle path.
we return once again to the noble eightfold path. in the noble eightfold path, right view (*samma-ditthi*) is indeed the very first step in eliminating the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avijjanusaya*). in dhammadinna's analysis of the dhamma, it was also stated that underlying the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling called *adukkhamasukha* is ignorance (*avijja*). when ignorance is removed, true knowledge (*vijja*) emerges. where knowledge emerges, there is liberation (*vimutti*). where there is liberation, there is extinguishment (nibbana. thus, in this noble eightfold path starting with right view, it is the question of the “middle” that is put into action. the two extremes have been abandoned. it is through establishing neutral feeling (*vedana*) and developing a neutral mind, and thereby practicing insight (*vipassana*), that we can escape from this *samsara*.
some of the things explained so far may appear profound. these were declared because they will be of assistance to meditators (*yogavacaras*). on a valuable esala full moon poya day like today, we presented a concept of the middle path found in discourses such as the *dhammacakkappavattana sutta* from another perspective. you, lay devotees, should take advantage of these and, in this age of decline of the buddha's dispensation, strive hundreds or thousands of times to realize the liberation from *samsara* that you hope for in this very life. if this dhamma sermon has helped you develop the spiritual faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) of faith (*saddha*), energy (*viriya*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*), then taking refuge in them, and with the support of noble friendship (*kalyana-mittata*), may you gain the strength and power to realize the noble, supreme, deathless nibbana through the realization of the paths and fruits of stream-entry (*sotapatti*), non-returning (*anagamita*), and arahatship, and thereby escape the suffering of *samsara*! strive with this aspiration. furthermore, may your relatives and all beings from avici hell to the akanistha heaven who wish to rejoice in this merit of preaching and hearing the dhamma, by so rejoicing, realize the supreme deathless nibbana through a bodhi of their aspiration! striving with this aspiration, recite these verses:
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 158
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #158
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.116)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
"Acaritvā brahmacariyaṃ, aladdhā yobbane dhanaṃ,
Jiṇṇakoñcā’va jhāyanti, khīṇamacche’va pallale.
Acaritvā brahmacariyaṃ, aladdhā yobbane dhanaṃ,
Senti cāpātikhittā’va, purāṇāni anutthunaṃ."
From:
Dhammapada Verses 155 and 156 (Jarā Vagga)
Dear Listeners,
The Buddha constantly reminds us that giving way to heedlessness (negligence) is a cause of decline for both laypeople and monastics alike. Not doing what should be done at the time it should be done, and putting things off, is generally considered heedlessness. In the end, only regret remains for the person who has succumbed to heedlessness. Today, I shall present to you these two verses, which express this matter in a very striking manner, as our sermon topic.
The Buddha preached these two verses at Isipatana in Baranasi, with reference to the son of the Treasurer Mahādhana (Great Wealth). This treasurer's son was born into a treasurer family possessing eighty crores of wealth. Because there was so much wealth, his parents thought, 'There is no need for our son to gather new wealth; there is only the consumption of the existing wealth,' and they did not teach him any arts or sciences. They only taught him music and instrumental playing as a means of entertainment. Similarly, in that city, there was another treasurer family with eighty crores of wealth. A daughter was born to that family. Her parents also taught her only dancing and singing. Then, at the appropriate age, these two were united in marriage.
While living in this manner, the treasurer's son went to the royal palace three times a day for state service. There was a group of profligates (dhūrtas) in that city. In ancient times, the term "dhūrta" was used to describe those who indulged in misconduct, who were addicted to alcohol, gambling, and chasing women. These drunkard profligates met and discussed: 'If we can get this treasurer's son addicted to liquor, our affairs will be very easy.' What they did was, tying fried meat, salt, jaggery, and other snacks to go with liquor around their waists, they came and sat by the roadside. Watching for the time the treasurer's son would return from the palace, they ate and drank liquor, saying: 'O young master! May you live a hundred years! It is because of you that we are able to eat and drink like this!'
When they blessed him in this manner, the treasurer's son asked the attendant who followed behind: 'What are these people drinking?' The attendant replied: 'It is a certain kind of beverage, master.' Then he asked: 'Is it something very pleasant?' 'What are you saying, master! In this living world, there is no beverage equal to it,' said that man. 'Then, I too shall drink a little of such a thing,' said the treasurer's son, and he began to order and drink it little by little. As soon as those profligates knew that he had formed the habit, they came and surrounded him. Because of this, his ruin began from that day. While drinking and enjoying himself with them, the treasurer's son began to order and spend more than enough for luxury items. Moreover, saying, 'This person is skilled in acting, that person is skilled in gambling,' he began to give them gifts worth hundreds and thousands. Thus, spending wealth without any mindfulness, before long, that eighty crores of wealth was exhausted. When the officials came and informed him of this, he said: 'My wife has eighty crores.' He spent and destroyed that as well in the same manner.
Next, he sold fields, lands, gardens, and household goods to drink and enjoy himself. When this treasurer's son reached old age, those who bought the treasurer's mansion drove them out of the house. These two built a hut-like shelter near the wall of someone else's house and began to live by begging.
While begging in this manner, one day they went to the alms-hall of the Sangha to eat leftover rice. Seeing them being given leftover rice by young novices, the Buddha smiled. When Ven. Ānanda asked the reason for it, the Buddha said: 'Look at this. If this treasurer's son had properly invested his wealth in some industry in his youth, he would have become the chief treasurer of this city. And if he had renounced that wealth and ordained, he had the spiritual potential, the supportive condition (*upanissaya-sampatti*), to attain Arahatship. His wife would have had the capability to become an Anāgāmī (Non-Returner). If he had taken that step and completed it in middle age, the treasurer's son would have become an Anāgāmī, and his wife a Sakadāgāmī (Once-Returner). Even in the final stage of life, in old age, if he had been diligent in investing his wealth in proper industries, he would have become the third treasurer. If he had ordained, he could have become a Sakadāgāmī, and his wife a Sotāpanna (Stream-Enterer).' Thus, it is said that the Buddha uttered these two verses on that occasion, showing how he had destroyed the spiritual potential he possessed for both mundane and supramundane success.
*'Acaritvā brahmacariyaṃ, aladdhā yobbane dhanaṃ, jiṇṇakoñcāva jhāyanti, khīṇamacchevapallale.'*
'Acaritvā brahmacariyaṃ'—not having lived the holy life, meaning, without practicing the holy life of the Dispensation (*Sāsana-brahmacariya*). Next, 'aladdhā yobbane dhanaṃ'—not having acquired wealth in youth. 'Jiṇṇakoñcāva jhāyanti, khīṇamacchevapallale'—they pine away like old herons standing by a dried-up pond with no fish. One has to grieve in old age like old herons; this is the meaning of the first verse. The next verse is very similar to it.
*'Acaritvā brahmacariyaṃ, aladdhā yobbane dhanaṃ, senti cāpātikhittāva, purāṇāni anutthunaṃ.'*
Not having lived the holy life, not having obtained wealth in youth, 'senti cāpātikhittāva, purāṇāni anutthunaṃ.' The simile described there is of shooting many arrows from a bow, which gradually loosens and slackens the bow-string. In the end, the strength of that bow is lost. That is the simile given here. Like a bow weakened and disabled due to excessive shooting, those individuals, regretting the past, lie down. If the bow were to think, 'In the past, I had the strength to shoot very far,' similarly, the grieving person thinks, 'Alas, in the past we ate and drank well, did this and that,' regretting the past. This is the idea expressed in that verse.
With reference to this story and the verses, the Buddha presented the value of living by properly balancing the two aspects of income and expenditure, which support the maintenance of lay life. Next, if one thinks about the monastic life, it is the fulfillment of that renunciation. Thus, the consequence of being negligent in both is shown by this story. We see many drawbacks (*ādīnava*) in the story of this treasurer's son.
On one side is the disadvantage of parents not teaching their children the sciences and skills that help them live. They only taught them how to enjoy wealth and seek amusement. Next, this story shows how this treasurer's son fell into the company of drunkards, fell into associating with bad friends (*pāpa-mitta-sevana*), turned toward gambling, and met with great ruin. When we think about the life of a lay devotee, the Buddha has preached many suttas on various occasions to eliminate those causes of ruin and provide paths to progress. You must have heard many of them. A highly renowned discourse is the *Vyagghapajja Sutta*. When the Buddha was residing in the Koliyan country, in the market town named Kakkarapatta, He gave a lengthy sermon in response to a question asked by Dīghajānu, the son of the Koliyans. It is a discourse that helps lay devotees in their daily lives. Dīghajānu, the son of the Koliyans, made his invitation in this manner: 'Venerable Sir, we are laypeople who enjoy sensual pleasures. We live in the lay home with wives and children. We wear Benares silk and use flowers, scents, and perfumes. Please preach to us a Dhamma suitable for achieving our progress in this world and progress in the next world.'
First, the Buddha presented, one by one, the factors that lead to welfare in this world. The four main factors presented for making lay life successful are that one must fulfill these four Dhammas: *Uṭṭhāna-sampadā* (achievement of persistent effort), *Ārakkha-sampadā* (achievement of protection), *Kalyāṇamittatā* (good friendship), and *Samajīvikatā* (balanced livelihood). What was known as *uṭṭhāna-sampadā* is the achievement of persistent effort—that is, relentless energy. A lay devotee, considering the many responsibilities that arise while leading life, must act with persistent effort (*uṭṭhāna-vīriya*), discarding laziness. It is stated there: if a young man of good family performs any occupation—agriculture, trade, cattle-breeding, state service, or arts—he must be skilled in it. He must not be lazy, and he must have the ability to constantly investigate the paths to progress in the business or occupation he performs. Just as he does those works and is active, he must be a person with organizational skills. These factors are shown as they apply to lay life. Thus, the Buddha has stated that one must generate persistent effort (*uṭṭhāna-vīriya*) in that manner and earn wealth righteously, with the strength of one's arms and through the sweat of one's brow.
It is not to be done unrighteously in any way, nor deceitfully. It is expressed that it must be done through the sweat of one's brow, by one's own strength. The Buddha reminds us that one must also apply protective organization regarding the wealth collected in this manner. As protection in those times, it meant safeguarding the collected wealth so that it is not confiscated by kings, does not fall into the hands of thieves, is not destroyed by fire or water, and does not fall into the hands of unloved heirs. This belongs to *ārakkha-sampadā*.
Next, *kalyāṇamittatā* means a lay devotee must strive to avoid the association of bad friends and cultivate the association of good friends. Good friends are defined there as: if there are young or old people in one's village or market town who are superior in virtue (*sīla*), who keep the virtue belonging to a layperson, and who are developed in the virtues of conviction (*saddhā*), virtue (*sīla*), generosity (*cāga*), and wisdom (*paññā*), one must associate with them. One must discuss with them. The Buddha declared that taking their virtues of *saddhā*, *sīla*, *cāga*, and *paññā* as examples, one must discipline oneself in the same manner. This is the factor of good friendship (*kalyāṇamittatā*).
Next, *samajīvikatā* (balanced livelihood) means one must manage the two sides: income and expenditure. The simile given for this is: just as a person holding a scale, looking at the pan of the scale, knows 'this much weight makes the pan go down,' and watches with careful oversight, a layperson, having a clear understanding of income and carefully thinking about expenditure, must control income and expenditure as if weighing them equally.
