in fact, even though he was her only son, she ordained him in the sasana with a profound understanding, having realized the disadvantages (*adinava*) of the household life. that is a wonderful example. furthermore, even the mother in her *yakkha* birth—normally, in buddhist stories, spirit possessions and the like are depicted as obstacles to practicing monastic virtues. however, here, through the *yakkha* possession by his past mother, the "demonic possession" (the impulse of mara) of ven. sanu was expelled. in that respect, another valuable monk was preserved for the sasana.
generally, when speaking of the war between *devas* and *asuras*, the *devas* are considered to be on the side of the dhamma, and the *asuras* on the side of non-dhamma. however, you, devout lay people, may have heard that *yakkhas* like alavaka, hemavata, and satagira developed faith in the supreme buddha, and some even attained the stage of stream-entry (*sotapanna*). not all *yakkhas* are inclined towards unrighteousness in that way. occasionally, there are those with right view (*samma-ditthi*). even here, this female *yakkha*, by rejoicing in the merits of dhamma sermons, acted with great faith. on this occasion, by employing a certain skillful means (*samma-prayoga*), she prevented this young monk from disrobing. thus, this too is a good example for us regarding these sasana values. the view held in the past regarding renunciation (*nekkhamma*) is clearly expressed here. its value is such that after abandoning all luxuries and ordaining, returning to lay life is like death. the supreme buddha has stated that to disrobe after ordaining is like death. the supreme buddha attributed such a deep value to renunciation.
next, let us look at the stanza uttered by the supreme buddha. this is like a certain meditation subject (*kammatthana*). why? because here it is presented not as a piece of advice given by the supreme buddha, but as self-advice, a command given to the mind by ven. sanu himself to discipline his own mind. that is to say, "my mind wandered around as it pleased for so long. now i will not allow you to wander." that taming is then compared to a mahout with a goad in hand taming an elephant in rut.
a very valuable method is shown there by the supreme buddha. we know that even a four-line stanza uttered by the supreme buddha is deeply profound in meaning and flavor. here too, when we contemplate, the fundamental idea is a command given by oneself to oneself, and also a highly valuable concept is expressed through this simile. the mind subjugated by the impulses of defilements is compared to an elephant in rut. there is a period when elephants go into rut. during that period, if the mahout is not exceptionally careful, the elephant will break even iron chains and run wild. therefore, at that moment, the mahout must be extremely vigilant.
in this dispensation, three kinds of intoxication (*mada*) inherent in sentient beings are pointed out: intoxication with youth (*yobbana-mada*), intoxication with health (*arogya-mada*), and intoxication with life (*jivita-mada*). intoxication with youth, the intoxication that arises due to being healthy, and then the intoxication based on the conceit of being alive. out of these, what arose in this young monk was the intoxication with youth. it was something like the intoxication that occurs in early youth. he thought of returning to lay life because of the impulses of defilements. the simile of the elephant in rut fits this perfectly. from that simile of the elephant in rut, one can understand the nature of the mind—how powerful a mind subjected to defilements is.
taming an elephant in rut is no easy task; it is that powerful. what helps in this is the goad. "*tadajjaham niggahessami yoniso*"—i shall tame this mind with wisdom, just as a mahout with a goad in hand tames an elephant in rut. there, through the word "*yoniso*," we can understand that what is taken as the goad is wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*). in this dhamma, wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*) is explained as wise reflection. unwise attention (*ayoniso manasikara*) means reflecting incorrectly in a way that gives rise to defilements—reflecting ignorantly and inappropriately.
now, what is compared to the goad here is reflecting wisely. in wise reflection, what exists is looking directly at the behavior of one's own mind, turning completely towards oneself. in ordinary unwise attention (*ayoniso manasikara*), what happens is being enslaved by the object, captivated by the object, and allowing thoughts to persist by giving way to the object. like running after a mirage, one can never stop it, but finally, with wise reflection, one looks at one's own mind, at the change that has occurred in the mind. then defilements like greed, hatred, and delusion are caught. it is because of these that the object received such qualities. just as to a person wearing red-colored glasses everything in the world appears red, and if blue is worn, blue. there is a saying, isn't there, that to a jaundice patient everything appears yellow. in the same way, the manner in which one looks at the world changes due to the impulses of defilements. that is exactly what happened to ven. sanu. what helps to pacify that is wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*)—reflecting wisely. one directs one's mind properly to see, "what has happened to my mind?" accordingly, this stanza and these similes taught by the supreme buddha must be examined very carefully.
the supreme buddha has stated certain principles regarding the taming of the mind in various discourse (*sutta*) teachings. among them, there is a highly important discourse in the middle length discourses (*majjhima nikaya*) called the *vitakkasanthana sutta*. the supreme buddha has amazingly shown a five-step method to control thoughts when they crash in. especially for a person trying to calm the mind, a certain thought arises. that thought is an unwholesome thought. when it comes repeatedly, the first method shown by the supreme buddha to drive it away is to introduce a wholesome object in place of that unwholesome thought and its object. when one reflects on a wholesome object instead, that unwholesome object fades away. for example, if a certain beautiful sign (*subha-nimitta*) related to lust (*raga*) comes to mind, one introduces an opposite unattractive sign (*asubha-nimitta*), a meditation sign of unattractiveness.
or else, if thoughts of hatred (*dosa*) arise, at that moment one introduces loving-kindness meditation (*metta bhavana*). the sign of loving-kindness is introduced instead. otherwise, it is sometimes pointed out that those with intense hatred even clash with posts, thorns, etc., in the environment. in such instances, it is suitable to direct the mind to the attention to elements (*dhatu manasikara*). "what is this? what am i clashing with?" one contemplates. in this way, driving away an unwholesome thought with a wholesome thought. the simile given by the supreme buddha for this is sufficient for anyone to remember this matter. just like a skilled carpenter, when a peg in a piece of wood becomes bent, uses a finer peg than the one pulled out, driving it in with the finer peg to push the other out and uproot it. in that manner, to drive away the unwholesome thought with a wholesome thought, the supreme buddha has presented the first principle there through the simile of the carpenter.
there, the supreme buddha states that the nature of this mind is so fickle that sometimes this method may not succeed. it might fail. if it is not strong enough, then the second method is shown. what is that second method? contemplating the disadvantages (*adinava*) of the thought that has arisen. disadvantage (*adinava*) means its fault. "these thoughts have such and such consequences. if i sustain them for long, i will have to suffer those consequences"—thus one contemplates them. when reflecting on them, the power of that thought is broken. one becomes disgusted with the thought and feels like abandoning it.
the supreme buddha gives a wonderful simile for this as well: just like a young woman or man who likes to look beautiful, if someone throws a carcass of a snake, a dog, or a human around their neck, they would immediately feel disgusted and try to get rid of it. according to this simile, one is told to look at the defiled thought that has arisen. in that way, one should develop a dislike, a disgust for it—arousing fear, shame, and disgust. through that, one can then escape from the unwholesome thought. that is the second method. just as a young woman or man who likes to look beautiful tries to remove a carcass of a human or a dog thrown on their body, one strives to remove that thought. the supreme buddha states that even this method may sometimes not succeed.
if that is not strong enough, then the third method is shown. what is that? one tries not to direct mindfulness (*sati*) and reflection towards the thought that repeatedly crashes into the mind. that is to say, normally something comes to mind because mindfulness is applied to it and because it is reflected upon. but here, with effort, one tries not to remember or reflect on it. the simile given there also explains this point: if a person does not wish to see a visual form (*rupa*) that has appeared before them, they either close their eyes or look away. when a very strong light comes, we suddenly close our eyes, don't we? or we look to the other side if we dislike it. it is something like that. in that manner, one tries to withdraw one's mind from it—towards another direction, in short, one deliberately redirects one's attention elsewhere. this is explained in further detail as follows.
when such torrents of thoughts crash into the mind, it is explained that a person can do things like this: instead, they perform some simple duty or chore. they direct the mind to a task like sweeping or cleaning up. gradually, then, the power of those thoughts is suppressed. if one's mind keeps going to that unwholesome object, one gets up and starts some small, simple work. by directing attention to that, the attention going to the original object is naturally withdrawn. that is the third method.
if that too does not succeed, next is the fourth method. one is told to direct the mind to the structure, the root cause of the thoughts that arise. in a way, one investigates, "what is this thought?" we can understand this too from the simile given by the supreme buddha. a person, without being aware of it, is walking very, very fast. while walking fast, he suddenly thinks: "why am i walking so fast? is there any benefit in this? why can't i walk slowly?" thinking thus, he begins to walk slowly. next, while walking slowly, he thinks: "why am i even walking slowly? wouldn't it be better if i stand?" and so he stands. next, he thinks: "if there is a seat, i can sit down, so why am i standing?" and so he sits down. after sitting down, after a little while, he thinks: "why am i sitting? i can also lie down. that is an even lighter posture," and so he lies down. this is only a simile. how do we understand this matter through this? it is by analyzing the thought that arose, looking at it analytically according to its root cause, and gradually suppressing it. here, as in the simile of abandoning a gross, coarse posture to adopt a subtle posture, one gradually pacifies that thought. one pacifies it gradually. contemplating "is this thought really worth thinking about?" one step-by-step reduces its momentum. that is the fourth method.
if even the fourth method does not succeed, and if the thought (*vitakka*) is that powerful, it is then that the supreme buddha provides a very powerful step suited for it: the fifth step. there, it is shown as follows: if so, trouble that unwholesome thought with a wholesome thought, push it away, and drive it out. from the simile shown there, one can understand: just as a strong man, catching a weak man by the neck or head, shakes him and completely subdues him, one should seize the unwholesome thought with the wholesome thought, challenge it, suppress it, and defeat it. that is the fifth one. in this manner, the supreme buddha has shown five methods of taming the mind in that *sutta* discourse. even if one simply remembers these similes, one can understand what should be done in such situations. if one gives way to the very nature of those thoughts and *vitakkas* that crash into the mind, they will become stronger and stronger.
the supreme buddha himself, in another discourse, has revealed a principle he discovered during his days as a bodhisatta when battling with his mind. there, it is stated in terms of a monk: if a monk repeatedly gives rise to a certain thought, the mind develops a bent, a leaning, a flexibility towards that side. it is said that a flexibility (*namyatavak*) is created. this is shown for both sides. if one repeatedly thinks of thoughts of sensual desire (*kama-vitakka*), the mind bends towards sensual thoughts. thoughts of ill-will (*vyapada-vitakka*) mean thoughts of hatred. if one repeatedly thinks thoughts of hatred, a bent is created towards that side. next, thoughts of cruelty (*vihimsa-vitakka*) mean thoughts of harming; if one thinks them repeatedly, a bent is created towards that side. on the other hand, if one thinks thoughts of renunciation (*nekkhamma-vitakka*), the mind bends towards that side. if one thinks thoughts of non-cruelty (*avihimsa*), non-ill-will (*avyapada*), or thoughts of loving-kindness, the mind bends towards that side.
however, when thoughts flow continuously without interruption, a certain momentum gathers within them. it is to break this that the supreme buddha has shown these five methods. here, the supreme buddha has shown five valuable steps that are important even to modern-day psychologists. as the first effort, the second effort, and so on. only at the very end must one adopt that most extreme measure. at first, one attempts to expel it, to drive it away, just as the carpenter expels the bent peg using a finer peg.
if that does not succeed, the second step is taken. what is it? one tries to make the mind dislike it. one disgusts it. by creating disgust, fear, and shame, one tries to make the unwholesome sign repulsive. that is what is shown in the simile of the young woman or man. developing disgust, fear, shame, moral dread (*hiri-otappa*), etc., to drive away that defiled thought. when even that does not succeed, next is what is like boycotting (shunning). as if boycotting that thought, as if saying "i do not want you," one looks to the other side, or closes both eyes. one closes both eyes to the thought. like looking away, one directs the mind to another task, thereby breaking its momentum.
when even that does not succeed, next, looking directly at the thought, one investigates its propriety: "what is this thought? is it something worth thinking about to this extent?" and thus gradually, as in the simile. "why am i walking fast? is walking slowly not better?" and so on. next, if it reaches a state where none of these succeed, it is then that one is told to take that most powerful step. just as a strong man, catching a weak man by the neck, shakes him and subdues him, the supreme buddha has stated that one should challenge the unwholesome thought with the wholesome thought in the same attitude, catching it, shaking it, and suppressing it. that is the idea of restraining (*niggaha*) the mind there. restraining the mind in that stanza was meant in that sense.
indeed, the supreme buddha has stated that regarding the mind, one must support and exert (*paggaha*) it when necessary. *paggaha* means supporting and exerting. one must restrain or censure it (*niggaha*) when necessary. *niggaha* means restraining and censuring. both are necessary. in times when the mind is down, when sleepiness and such arise, one must encourage it. but if the momentum of thoughts (*vitakka*) is crashing beyond limit, at that time, one must suppress it, one must restrain (*niggaha*) it. otherwise, if one simply watches where this mind is going, just as was said about the vehicle, if one allows the momentum of the vehicle and leaves it alone, it will eventually end up in a ditch and fall to the very bottom. it is such a situation.
then, if the mind is something that runs faster than all vehicles, there must be a control over it—a control through some method like virtue (*sila*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*). if you simply let the mind go as it pleases and just watch, you can imagine what would happen. some people in this country express such views as well. thinking it is an easy method, and thinking that is the buddha's teaching, many are drawn to it. the supreme buddha declared: "*aham hi kammavado kiriyavado viriyavado*"—"i am a proponent of action, a proponent of activity, and a proponent of energy." i say to be active. i say to exert energy.
there are various other *sutta* discourse teachings in the dhamma related to these thoughts and reflections. let us bring out another one. now, you, devout lay people, may have heard of the *girimananda sutta*. indeed, it is also used as a protective chant (*paritta*) during times of illness. in truth, the *girimananda sutta* is not merely a protective discourse. it is a highly valuable *sutta* that compiles ten meditations in their entirety. ten meditation subjects (*kammatthana*) are introduced there under the name of "perceptions" (*sanna*). among them, one meditation subject is introduced by the name of the "perception of abandoning" (*pahana-sanna*).
this *pahana* (abandoning) means casting away. there, it is shown as follows: a certain monk—one should understand that although "monk" is mentioned, it refers to any practitioner (*yogavacara*), whether lay or ordained, who strives to tame the mind—the course of action to be taken by that practitioner, and this perception of abandoning (*pahana-sanna*) itself is shown as sufficient to lead to nibbana. here, the steps to be taken regarding an arisen thought of sensual desire (*kama-vitakka*) are shown in a few words. they are highly meaningful: "*nadhivaseti, pajahati, vinodeti, byantikaroti, anabhavangameti*." "*nadhivaseti*" means: if a thought of sensual desire or some defiled thought arises, what is the first step to be taken? "*nadhivaseti*"—he does not tolerate it. "*nadhivaseti*" means he does not tolerate. next, "*pajahati*"—he abandons it, or discards it. next, "*vinodeti*"—he dispels it. "*byantikaroti*" means he puts an end to it. "*anabhavangameti*" means he annihilates it, brings it to complete non-existence.
let us think of this through a small simile, even if it is not a simile found in the books. an unwanted person has come to where we are. first, we think, "he is not needed here, it's better if he leaves," and we do not tolerate him. we say, "there is no room for you here." but he stays. then, we firmly tell him to leave, making him go. yet, if he still remains, we have someone push him far away, sending him all the way to the gate—"*vinodeti*," we dispel him. next, "*byantikaroti*"—if necessary, we close the gate so he cannot return. in that manner, the supreme buddha has shown here how to systematically discard that thought. this is the practice to be adopted regarding an unwholesome thought. first, one does not tolerate it. one does not give room to it. even if one does so, if it crashes in, one pushes it away in that manner, or drives it far away, and finally brings it to non-existence. that is how the perception of abandoning (*pahana-sanna*) is shown. it includes thoughts of sensual desire (*kama-vitakka*), thoughts of ill-will (*vyapada-vitakka*), thoughts of cruelty (*vihimsa-vitakka*), and all other unwholesome states. that is to say, if thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of hatred, thoughts of harming, or various other unwholesome thoughts arise in the mind, the supreme buddha has shown under the meditation topic of "perception of abandoning" (*pahana-sanna*) to adopt that very practice.
furthermore, when explaining the supreme buddha's teachings, that which is known as the four right endeavors (*sammappadhana*) is the very same thing called right effort (*samma-vayama*) in the noble eightfold path. a certain energy of the mind, effort, always exists within a human being. ordinary worldly people apply this mental factor of energy (*viriya-cetasika*), this energy, for their daily activities, such as satisfying worldly needs, studying, and doing jobs. but the right effort (*samma-vayama*) shown by the supreme buddha is one concerning the mind. to eliminate the obstacles that come to the mind, he shows a fourfold energy. we have recalled this on many occasions. the fourfold effort to be applied for: preventing the arising of unarisen unwholesome states, abandoning arisen unwholesome states, producing unarisen wholesome states, and maintaining and establishing arisen wholesome states—this is known as the four right endeavors (*sammappadhana*) and as right effort (*samma-vayama*).
next, if we take this second point: "*uppannanam papakanam akusalanam dhammanam pahanaya*"—for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states, for their removal. next, a set of words is shown: "*chandam janeti, vayamati, viriyam arabhati, cittam pagganhati, padahati*." "*chandam janeti*" means one generates a desire, a keen interest, regarding that. to expel those unwholesome states, one first generates an interest, a desire. accordingly, one makes a certain attempt (*vayamati*). next, one arouses energy (*viriyam arabhati*). that energy is even more powerful than mere attempt. when saying "*arabhati*," one arouses energy. next, although energy is aroused, because there are obstacles that come with it, to remove those obstacles, "*cittam pagganhati*" means one firmly establishes the power of determination in the mind. one determines: "i will not submit to this, i will conquer this somehow." next, "*padahati*" means the most sublime energy, the supreme endeavor denoted by the word "*padhana*."
in some places, this is shown as the "four-factored energy" (*caturanga-samannagata-viriya*). the bodhisatta sat on his final seat for buddhahood with that kind of determination. regarding this, it is stated: "*kamam taco ca naharu ca atthi ca avasissatu, upasussatu sarire mamsalohitam*"—"let only skin, sinews, and bones remain, let the flesh and blood in my body dry up. what can be achieved by human strength, by human energy, by human effort—without attaining that, i shall not relax my energy, i shall not cast it aside." with such firm determination, the bodhisatta attained self-awakening (*sambodhi*). that is the very method the supreme buddha repeatedly recalls to the community of monks, advising them to apply this supreme energy when other methods fail. that is why the supreme buddha called himself a proponent of action (*kammavada*) and a proponent of energy (*viriyavada*). to direct that power of energy within a human being along the right path, systematically, orderly, and in a manner suited to the occasion.
even psychologists have much to learn from this. furthermore, what is required for all of this is meditation (*bhavana*). what is meditation? meditation is the systematic development of the mind. it is not only the intellectual aspect, but the emotional and affective aspect is also important in meditation. if our intellect is the brain, developing the brain alone is not enough; the heart must also be developed, along with the emotional side. meditation connects both of these. thus, developing the body begins with practicing virtues like morality (*sila*). there, we make a determination to tame body and speech as a practice. for that too, a considerable amount of energy of the kind described earlier is needed—an energy of the mind, not an energy of the body, but an energy of the mind. there, in most instances, it is not about "doing" something, but about abstaining. in that case, to abstain, it is the mind that must be guarded there. if one is told to "do" something, then bodily energy is involved. if we are told to kill an animal, how much effort must we exert? if we are told to steal, how much effort must we exert? then, the physical energy that ordinary worldly people think of is applied there.
but here, to abstain from it, one must apply a great mental energy (*cetasika viriya*). the mind says, "do this." abstaining from it is what is difficult. it is right there that the value of this energy truly emerges. thus, starting in that manner, going towards concentration (*samadhi*) becomes even more demanding. in that too, it is the endeavor of unifying the mind. now, these five points we discussed here concern particularly the practitioner (*yogavacara*) who concentrates the mind. in daily life, wise buddhist devotees, whether lay or ordained, reflecting on the distress, the distraction, the loss, and the dangers caused to their own lives and to the world by their scattered minds, turn towards meditation because they want to calm this mind, to unify the mind, to keep the mind on one object. but that is not something easily done. it is not something that can be done while nodding off to sleep. it is not something that can be done through laziness. the supreme buddha has stated that a special effort, endeavor, exertion, and dedication (*padhana*) must be applied for it. what is the reason for this?
for a long time, like water flowing downwards, we have lived in this long samsara, taking birth (*jati*) in various hells and places, taking birth in animal realms, *yakkha* realms, and ghost realms (*peta-loka*), taking birth among those with wrong views, subjugated by and obedient to unrighteous impulses and defiled impulses. then, like flowing water, there are several such flows towards the wrong direction within our mental continuum. in the dhamma, the supreme buddha introduces these with terms such as underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), taints (*asava*), and floods (*ogha*). these underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) are like what flows underneath. taints (*asava*) are what leak out from them; the taints also flow. next, the floods (*ogha*) are what crash like overflowing water. like great rivers flowing, you can experience this nature of the mind at times; certain things hidden deep within the mind tell you to do this and that. some things draw you in so much that you feel you cannot help but do them. at other times, destroying both oneself and others, thinking "it doesn't matter what happens," one gets swept away, subjugated by that great flood (*mahogha*). being swept away by the great flood means being caught in a great torrent where one does not know where one is going; one simply lets the mind go in that direction. so, if we take that concept of freedom, freedom of thought, and various such ideas, and let the mind go as it pleases, then that is where things go wrong.
in that story about the driver, the driver has a side on the road where he must travel. next, once he climbs into the vehicle and sits in that seat, there are several controls he must manage. there is a huge responsibility—the lives of those inside the vehicle, and then the lives of those on the road. disregarding all of that, if the driver drives while drunk? it is just like being drunk if ordinary worldly people get intoxicated. if they think, "there is no use in meditation, there is nothing to tame in the mind, just watching the mind is enough," that is exactly like the driver getting into the seat and letting the vehicle go as it pleases, leaving it to its own momentum.
but the supreme buddha shows the gravity of this. this mind, which has run towards the evil, bad side for such a long time, cannot be tamed easily. it is precisely because of its gravity that the supreme buddha provides five steps. otherwise, he could have said it in one step, couldn't he? through that, we can see to what extent the supreme buddha saw reality as it truly is (*yathabhuta*). because the human mind's inclination towards defilements is so strong, the supreme buddha showed it step-by-step. it was at the final stage that he showed the most extreme step. showing it like catching by the neck and shaking is because of that; it is because it cannot be avoided.
another point we mentioned here is the word wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*). one thing we frequently recall is that the supreme buddha compared the aggregate of perception (*sanna-kkhandha*), perception (*sanna*), to a mirage. so here too, when a defiled object is presented—that is, an object of lust or an object of hatred—that object appears to us just as a mirage appears to a deer. one grasps (*upadana*) it. next, submitting to it, one cultivates various types of thoughts according to it. this state of being subjugated by those thoughts is also known as conceptual proliferation (*papanca*). but instead of that, the supreme buddha tells us to look backward at that thought, to see: "what are the root causes that gave rise to this thought?" when looking at the end, it is a greed, or a lust, hatred, or delusion that arose in one's own mind. once that is seen, the attractive nature of the object that caught the mind earlier disappears. that is why the supreme buddha has shown wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*) there.
furthermore, there is another matter related to meditation shown by the supreme buddha. you all know about mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajanna*). mindfulness (*sati*) means attention and awareness. mindfulness and clear understanding—the wisdom that goes along with mindfulness. now, mindfulness here is shown as right mindfulness (*samma-sati*). in truth, worldly people apply what they call mindfulness to things that actually destroy their mindfulness. let us say someone applies mindfulness to using weapons—if they are skilled at aiming and shooting accurately, those do not belong to right mindfulness (*samma-sati*). those are things that cultivate defilements.
but the supreme buddha tells us to direct the mind to this body of ours. think about this body. think about the nature of this body. "what kind of thing is this? is it permanent? is it beautiful? is it something that lasts forever? is it something i can call mine?"—thus contemplating according to the body, which is contemplation of the body (*kayanupassana*). next, consider feelings and sensations (*vedana*) in the same way. these come and go. things that arise and cease. not a single one of them is something to be taken as "i" or as a self (*atta*).
next, look at this mind as well. the mind too, just like the colored advertising signs on a street, displays various kinds of lights—in red, in blue. in that manner, those colors appear. if, deceived by those colors, we look at them, grasp them, and act accordingly, then we get into trouble. just like advertising boards, at different times, according to greed, hatred, and delusion, our mind gives certain signals. we are told not to go along with those signals.
next is the contemplation of mind-objects (*dhammanupassana*). one looks closely at how these perceptions and thoughts arise. one looks at what lies underneath them. sometimes, these arise due to hindrances (*nivarana*). one can understand: "this happened due to the arising of these mind-blocking things called hindrances—thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill-will, sloth and torpor, doubt and wavering, and the like." in moments when the mind is illuminated, behold, these factors of mindfulness, investigation of states (*dhamma-vicaya*), and so on exist in my mind.
in that way, for one to properly understand the nature of those thoughts arising in one's mind, whether good or bad, is what is called contemplation of mind-objects (*dhammanupassana*). thus, in wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*), when going according to mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajanna*)—if mindfulness (*sati*) is wisdom, then at the same time, clear comprehension (*sampajanna*) is mindfulness established in the present moment; that is *sati-sampajanna*. it is being properly aware of everything. what is important is not making others aware, but being aware oneself. at each moment as it comes, one understands: "this is such and such a thing." through that, delusion is removed. moreover, because of that very fact, it also becomes apparent that not a single one of these things that arise is permanent (*anicca*).
the supreme buddha has given various kinds of instructions to develop that mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajanna*). one is shown as a good exercise for someone—especially a meditation practitioner who hopes to tame the mind—to watch feelings and sensations (*vedana*) as they arise. "this feeling (*vedana*) arose. lo, it remained. lo, it passed away." feeling and sensation does not exist all the time. feeling and sensation arises, remains, and passes away. likewise with perceptions (*sanna*). various perceptions (*sanna*) arise. when saying perceptions, they can be visual perceptions (*rupa-sanna*), auditory perceptions (*sadda-sanna*), olfactory perceptions, and so on, referring to the perceptions coming from the six sense bases (*ayatana*). or else, they are perceptions coming from the body regarding external bases of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and there are also various perceptions arising from the mind itself. regarding every such perception, one thinks: "lo, a perception has arisen. it remained. it was removed. it arose, remained, passed away." through that, one sees impermanence (*aniccata*).
likewise regarding thoughts (*vitakka*). one turns to look at the thought. "here is a thought, a thought that was not there before. lo, it has newly arrived. how did this arrive?" that thought too remains and passes away. in that manner, one remains aware of the comings and goings of one's feelings and sensations (*vedana*), perceptions (*sanna*), and thoughts (*vitakka*). this is just like sitting by the roadside on a dark night and watching passing vehicles. let us say, in the dark night, the headlight of a vehicle is seen. next, making a sound, it rapidly drives past. after that, the tail light is seen. that is all. there is nothing to be grasped from it.
in this very manner, this feeling and sensation (*vedana*) arises, remains, and passes away. perceptions (*sanna*) arise, remain, and pass away. thoughts (*vitakka*) arise, remain, and pass away. to a practitioner (*yogavacara*) who trains to look at those incoming experiences in such a detached way, it is possible to very quickly develop even those insight knowledges (*vipassana-nana*). it is said that this especially helps mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajanna*), to develop mindfulness and wisdom. because, being deluded by that object, one turns away from it. in this way, the supreme buddha has shown it in various ways. we can then understand: what is this meditation? what is expected from this?
ordinary worldly people use only an extremely microscopic, a very tiny portion of the powers existing in this mind. sometimes, one might think that the minds of those who invent amazing new things are highly developed. that is a one-sided development. it has been developed on the intellectual side. through the medium of various machines and equipment, utilizing them, they go on developing something called science. but beneath it lies ignorance (*avijja*). why? because not a single one of them has brought about internal development. they are subjugated by greed, hatred, and delusion. that is precisely why they produce those dangerous weapons and the like.
next, producing various other things related to the fivefold sensual pleasures on a massive scale, subjecting the entire world to commercial concepts, and dragging the entire world down to hell (*apaya*)—all this is done in the name of science. we cannot stop those by merely speaking. they flow as if swept away by a great flood (*mahogha*). but at least two or three people must reflect on this. what goes in the name of science is mostly ignorance (*avijja*). various kinds of equipment have been invented to satisfy our needs. we must not become enslaved to that science merely because of that.
that is to say, many are directing themselves towards that side in various ways. this is clearly visible regarding those weapons. not only that, but to entice and delude humans in relation to the fivefold sensual pleasures, for the purpose of securing their own economic progress, they have used science as a decoy. what is the reason for this? because those aforementioned virtues do not exist within human hearts. there is no effort to develop those virtues shown by the supreme buddha. they do not try to move away from greed towards non-greed (*alobha*). they do not try to move away from hatred towards non-hatred (*adosa*), towards loving-kindness (*metta*). they do not try to move away from delusion (*moha*) towards wisdom (*panna*). until then, only ignorance (*avijja*) exists within that development. therefore, only one aspect of the mind is involved; there is only a one-sided development there. we must not be deceived by that. we must not think of everything according to that logic.
due to the development of science and technology, great conveniences have been provided in our daily lives. we consider this an era where things once done with great difficulty are done very easily. but the mind is not that kind of thing. having been subjected to the power of defilements for an extremely long time, passing through various dangerous states in samsara, such as those *yakkha* births, there are habits of samsara brought along.
this mind travels along those very habits. when one action is performed repeatedly, it becomes a habit. through that habit, one's character is also built. it is exactly the same with this thought. that is why the supreme buddha told us to break this thought as quickly as possible. if it is an unwholesome thought, as soon as it is recognized, one tries to drive it away.
if it does not succeed in the first attempt, then there is the second method. when even that fails, the third method. now, whether it is a carpenter or a mechanical worker, if the work cannot be done using one tool, they take the next tool. the supreme buddha also shows us the taming of the mind in that manner. then, the other method we can use to assist this in our daily lives is meditation (*bhavana*). each person must practice a certain meditation subject (*kammatthana*), even a simple one. this is a long journey, but we begin it with a single step.
likewise, if we practice a certain meditation subject (*kammatthana*) in our daily lives—let us say it could be loving-kindness meditation (*metta bhavana*), or recollection of the buddha (*buddhanussati*). a single word. the very word spoken is enough. if it is the recollection of the buddha, a single word like "*bhagava*" or "*buddho*" is enough. but because it is a wholesome thought, what do we do through reflecting on it repeatedly? during the seconds one applies the thought "may they be well and happy!" in loving-kindness meditation, a thought of hatred cannot arise. therefore, we have that advantage, if we engage in it continuously.
the supreme buddha says that this meditation is also something to be done continuously. why? because the principles regarding meditation are shown as: repetition (*asevana*), development (*bhavana*), and much practice (*bahulikamma*). one must frequently associate with one's meditation subject (*kammatthana*), like a good, close friend. likewise, one must develop it. it must be brought to systematic growth. without staying in the same place, one must develop it step-by-step, tomorrow being more developed than today—*bhavana, bahulikamma*. also, one must make an effort to do it throughout the day. as much time as possible must be devoted to it. the more frequently it is done, the more strength that thought receives, and those unwholesome thoughts are suppressed. the value of a meditation subject (*kammatthana*) exists precisely according to these stated principles. the supreme buddha has made the world understand this natural law of the mind. there is a certain depth in this.
this mind is not the thought that is seen from the outside. it should not be limited to what the ordinary world calls a civilized city, or to the customs and manners we see externally. only when one falls into a certain society or joins an institution and begins to associate, does the weakness of those individuals become visible. although those people have not developed their minds, they wear fine clothes, clothes considered to be the highest fashion in the world; yet what of it? in the end, they appear as puppets. it is a state where one cannot decide whether beasts, *yakkhas*, or ghosts (*petas*) are dwelling inside them. what is the reason for this? because the world measures by external standards—either by education, or else by degrees, or by external pomp. but the human mind is not something that can be recognized in that way. that is why, even if those who had developed their minds in past samsara were beggars in this life, living at the very lowest level, if the supreme buddha saw that potential, he ordained them, brought them into the sasana, and led them to arahantship.
just like that, we too must contemplate that there is a good side and a bad side to our mind. no one can say, "we have never gone to hell," or "we have never gone to animal births," merely because we are in this human birth now. therefore, those animal qualities, *yakkha* qualities, and ghost (*peta*) qualities can exist. they can emerge at any moment. if one gives support to them, if one associates with bad friends (*papa-mitta*) who encourage them, one too can fall to that level. one can become like an angulimala. there is nothing preventing our mind from sinking to the level of the highly dangerous individuals well-known in this era, if we receive the association of bad friends (*papa-mitta-sevana*).
but the supreme buddha shows that likewise, a good side also exists within a human being. one must support that. one must apply great effort for that too. without that, it cannot be brought out. flowing downwards is easy. swimming upstream is difficult. but the supreme buddha has shown that a buddha appears precisely to lead towards a goal that this world deems impossible, a target generally thought to be impossible.
even before a buddha appears, why did all the past practitioners (*yogis*) go to the himalayas to practice meditation? it was to escape from this extremely long samsara, from this highly dangerous suffering (*dukkha*) of birth (*jati*), decay and death (*jaramarana*), and disease, from which no one can escape. the supreme buddha has declared that this goal can be fulfilled, this target can be reached, by developing this wisdom (*panna*) within our very minds. this meditation is the very endeavor of developing that wisdom.
the supreme buddha shows that because of ignorance (*avijja*) and delusion (*moha*), because of not knowing the true nature of the world, the world wanders in samsara for such a long time. in the entire samsara, there is no wrong in thinking that one's father and mother are ignorance (*avijja*) and craving (*tanha*). the father is ignorance, and the mother is craving. it is from these two that we have taken birth for a long, infinite time. the supreme buddha shows the way to escape from this ignorance and craving. now, ignorance refers to the intellectual side. craving refers to the emotional, affective side. that is what we meant by the brain and the heart. thus, it is according to ignorance, and under the support of ignorance, that craving (*tanha*) finds room. therefore, to eliminate these two, we must make a systematic effort, such as by controlling our feelings and emotions.
it is for that purpose that the supreme buddha has brought out such amazing methods. accordingly, you too must contemplate not letting this life of ours simply slip away; it is only during this rare opportunity, the period of a buddha's appearance, that we can escape from this samsara. it is to fulfill the virtues required for that, that you have spent this day today. a large number of you observed the precepts (*sila*) today. virtue (*sila*) is not merely wearing a white dress externally. within it, there is a certain dedication. having undertaken several precepts to tame body and speech oneself, one engages in practice as self-discipline. just like the stanza given by the buddha to ven. sanu, it is a command given to one's own mind. observing "*panatipata veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami*"—"i undertake the precept to abstain from taking life"—one guards it.
in that manner, what is done voluntarily by oneself is the powerful effort, the true effort. no one else can do this through external controls. the supreme buddha saw that. that is precisely why the supreme buddha said:
> *tumhehi kiccam atappam, akkhataro tathagata;*
> *patipanna pamokkhanti, jhayino marabandhana.*
"the effort must be made by you yourselves; the tathagatas are only teachers. those who enter upon this practice, and practice absorption (*jhana*), will escape the bonds of mara."
only those who go along practicing absorption will escape this bond of mara. from this, we see that this work belongs to us.
no matter how many bodhi pujas we perform for the supreme buddha, or offer prayers, or do other things, he cannot lead us to nibbana. having aroused faith, adding energy to that faith, arousing mindfulness through energy, building concentration through mindfulness, it is only with a concentrated mind that one can see the three characteristics of impermanence (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and non-self (*anatta*). a mother cannot lead her son to nibbana. a son cannot lead his mother to nibbana. each and every person must make the effort themselves. therefore, without waiting at the final moment until children sit around the bed crying, "oh, please don't die! wait until the doctor arrives," wise parents should encourage their children, and just as ven. sanu's mother rescued an item from a burning house, everyone must contemplate discarding worldly aims and acting. no matter how much we protect ourselves as families, even a buddha's power cannot be given to others. therefore, we must develop this power within ourselves. it is for that purpose that today was spent in virtue (*sila*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*).
therefore, one must contemplate wisely. one should be happy and be encouraged to go further forward. walking on this path of practice and virtues like morality (*sila*) which you have commenced, practicing concentration meditation through some meditation subject (*kammatthana*) as much as possible even in daily life, gradually securing the association of admirable friends (*kalyana-mitta*), and developing insight (*vipassana*) with instructions through them. today, through fulfilling these practices, guarding virtue, and practicing meditation—through the accumulation of merit gathered through all of this—let us strive to bring an end to this suffering (*dukkha*) of samsara. likewise, if there are any sentient beings from the avici hell up to the akanitha heaven who are waiting for nibbana by rejoicing in this merit of preaching and listening to the dhamma, may all of them, by rejoicing thus, be comforted by the supreme, deathless, great nibbana through a bodhi of their aspiration! reflecting thus, recite these verses.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 163
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #163
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.125)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
"Na vāyameyya sabbattha, nāññassa puriso siyā;
Nāññaṃ nissāya jīveyya, dhammena na vaṇijaṃ care."
From:
Udāna 6.4: Paṭhamanānātitthiya Sutta
Dear Listeners,
The Buddha, the Teacher of the Three Worlds, reminds us that wisdom (*paññā*) must be utilized to firmly establish faith (*saddhā*) in the correct manner. Faith that is not backed by wisdom can even become blind faith or mere devotion. That is why the Buddha reminds us to always be vigilant about this. Today, we hope to present a sutta discourse that highlights the importance of this matter. The Udāna verse we chose as our theme today was delivered by the Buddha while he was residing in the Eastern Monastery (*Pūrvārāma*) in Sāvatthi. One day, the Blessed One arose from his evening meditation, stepped outside the gate of the Eastern Monastery, and stood there in seclusion. At that moment, King Pasenadi of Kosala approached, paid homage to the Buddha, and sat to one side. Just then, seven matted-hair ascetics (*jaṭilas*), seven Jain ascetics (*nigaṇṭhas*), seven naked ascetics (*acelakas*), seven single-robe ascetics (*ekasāṭakas*), and seven wanderers (*paribbājakas*) walked past that place with long hair, body hair, and nails, carrying loads of monastic requisites.
Upon seeing this, King Kosala immediately got up from where the Buddha was, turned in that direction, clasped his hands in reverence, and declared his name three times, saying, "Venerable sirs, I am King Pasenadi of Kosala." After they had departed, he returned, paid homage to the Buddha, sat down to one side, and said, "Blessed One, if there are any Arahants in this world, or those who have entered the path to Arahantship, these are among them." Then the Buddha said, "Great King, for a layman like you, who enjoys sensual pleasures, lives with wife and children, uses Kāsi silk, perfumes, garlands, and unguents, and handles gold, silver, and money, it is difficult to know who are Arahants and who have entered the path to Arahantship."
Next, the Buddha presents four principles for recognizing individuals in the world. He states four extremely important points there. "Great King, it is through living together that a person’s virtue (*sīla*) is to be understood." The word used there is *saṃvāsa* (living together). *Saṃvāsena sīlaṃ veditabbaṃ*. It is through living together that one can understand another's virtue. And that too, not in a short time, but over a long period; not by being inattentive, but through proper attention; not by one without wisdom, but by one with wisdom. That means one can understand someone's virtue through association. And that association is not for a brief moment, but for a long time. Not mere association, but reflecting deeply, applying the mind properly. Next, having the wisdom to understand it. That is the basic idea. In the same way, the Buddha declares three other matters. Conversation, talking—the word used there is *saṃvohāra*. Through trade/social intercourse/conversation, a person’s purity is to be known. And that too, as mentioned before, not in a short time, but over a long period; not by being inattentive, but by being attentive; not by one without wisdom, but by one with wisdom. That is the second point.
Likewise, he states the third point as *thāma*—the strength to endure something in times of adversity, which is referred to as strength of fortitude and effort. One’s firm, unshakeable nature to stand ground during severe crises is understood in times of adversity. *Āpadāsu thāmo veditabbo*. And that too, not in a short time, but over a long period; not by being inattentive, but by being attentive; not by one without wisdom, but by one with wisdom. That too can be understood. The fourth point: it is through discussion that a person’s wisdom is to be understood. *Sākacchāya paññā veditabbā*. Wisdom can be understood through discussion. And that too, not in a short time, but over a long period; not by being inattentive, but by being attentive; not by one without wisdom, but by one with wisdom. When these four principles, which can be used as golden rules, were declared, King Kosala said, "Marvelous, Venerable Sir, wonderful, Venerable Sir!" and gave an illustration to show the truth of the Buddha's words. Only a short passage is mentioned there, and some interpret it in various ways. It is a matter that has been subject to some debate.
This king says, "Venerable Sir, I have spies. Thieves, cunning thieves. But I employ them as spies. They go to a province in disguise, create divisions, and bring about a situation where the king can conquer it. I only enter those provinces after those spies have gone and created that background. I invade those provinces. But those same spies, at a later time, wash off the dust they gathered during those covert operations, bathe well, apply ointments, shave their beards, dress in white garments, and enjoy the five strands of sensual pleasure here and there in the country." This is all the king said. But there is more to think about: because those spies are loyal to the king, serving the king, no matter how much thievery and villainy they committed, they can appear in society like fine gentlemen. It must have been this recollection that made King Pasenadi say, "What the Blessed One said is true. One cannot understand virtue and such qualities just by seeing them suddenly."
Next, the Buddha uttered a certain verse of solemn utterance (*Udāna gāthā*). That is the *Udāna* verse we highlighted. An *Udāna*, pious devotees, is an utterance of joy. Not always due to mere happiness. Sometimes, if an instruction can be given to the world based on a certain incident, the Buddha utters *Udāna* verses on those occasions too. Because the meaning of those *Udāna* verses is sometimes quite deep, they are not understood immediately. Sometimes they arise in connection with that story. But there is often a meaning in the *Udāna* verse that goes far beyond that. That is the verse we presented as our theme.
*Na vāyameyya sabbattha, nāññassa puriso siyā,*
*Nāññaṃ nissāya jīveyya, dhammena na vāṇijaṃ care.*
Let us try to understand these four lines. *Na vāyameyya*: one should not exert effort everywhere. There are places where effort should be exerted, and places where it should not. That is what is indicated here. One should not exert effort everywhere. *Nāññassa siyā*: one should not be another’s man. The idea there is that one should not be another's servant, one should not belong to another. *Nāññaṃ nissāya jīveyya*: one should not live dependent on another, subservient to another. The final line: *dhammena na vāṇijaṃ care*: one should not trade in the Dhamma, one should not make the Dhamma a commercial commodity. This is the general meaning if we take it literally.
If we think about each of these in some detail—as we said, verses of this nature have a meaning that extends far deeper than the surface level. In relation to this story, we see that King Kosala had just arrived, paid homage to the Tathāgata, the Fully Enlightened One, and sat down, when those *jaṭilas* and *nigaṇṭhas*, walking in groups of seven, went past and paid respects, and furthermore, he ultimately made a statement suggesting he thought they were Arahants. *Na vāyameyya sabbattha*—King Kosala had the notion that in all places, in every dispensation, there are Arahants. But the Buddha has declared to the monks on certain occasions: "Monks, roar this lion's roar without fear: 'Only here is the first ascetic (*samaṇa*), here is the second ascetic, here is the third ascetic, here is the fourth ascetic. Other dispensations of sectarian teachers are empty of ascetics. There are no ascetics in them.' Roar this lion’s roar in this manner." The Buddha declared this to the Saṅgha.
Why is that? The states of the four paths and four fruits—Stream-entry (*Sotāpanna*), Once-returning (*Sakadāgāmi*), Non-returning (*Anāgāmi*), and Arahantship—do not exist among other religions. Yet King Kosala, despite associating with the Buddha for so long, thought of all those *jaṭilas*, *nigaṇṭhas*, *acelakas*, and *paribbājakas* as Arahants. Not only in those times, but even today, there is an era where some people, thinking about peaceful coexistence, argue that all religions say the same thing. Thus, even in this first phrase, we have a lot to contemplate. If we explain this according to the Dhamma, on one occasion the Buddha declared the difference between wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) and right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*).
The Buddha made a very powerful declaration: *"Micchādiṭṭhiparamāhaṃ bhikkhave vajjaṃ vadāmi"*. "Monks, of all the faults in this world, I say wrong view is the greatest." Why did he say so? The Buddha declared this with reasons. This sermon can be considered in detail for that: "Monks, whatever bodily actions (*kāya-kamma*) a person of wrong view performs, they follow that very view; they become wrong actions. Likewise, whatever verbal actions (*vacī-kamma*) or mental actions (*mano-kamma*) they perform, they all follow that very wrong view they have grasped. Not only that, whatever intention (*cetanā*), aspiration (*patthanā*), resolution (*paṇidhi* - goal/aim) they have, and whatever preparations / Preparations / volitional activity (*saṅkhāra*) they accumulate, they all become characterized by wrong view. They all result in undesired, disagreeable, unpleasant, unappealing fruits, in suffering (*dukkha*) fruits." Having declared so, the Buddha then gives a simile. "Just as, monks, if a neem seed (*kohomba*), a bitter-gourd seed (*karavila*), or a bitter-melon seed is placed in moist soil, whatever soil-nutrients or moisture it draws in, they all result in a pungent, bitter taste and fruit. Why is that? Because the seed is bitter. What is the reason, monks? The planted seed is bitter. In the same way, all bodily actions, verbal actions, mental actions, and all those other things that arise from the seed of wrong view go towards the wrong side. The Buddha clearly declared that they have undesirable retributions."
Then he declares the other side. "Likewise, monks, whatever bodily action, verbal action, mental action a person of right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) performs because of that right view, they all follow that very right view. Likewise, whatever intention, aspiration, resolution, and preparations / Preparations / volitional activity (*saṅkhāra*) they generate, they all bring about desired, agreeable, pleasing, pleasant, happy retributions." Then he gives the simile: "Just as when a seed of hill-paddy (*häl*), sugarcane, or grape is placed in moist soil, whatever soil-nutrients or moisture it absorbs or utilizes, they all result in a sweet fruit. Such is the nature of right view. From this, we can understand how one experiences happy retributions."
Next, let us consider the matter of right effort (*sammā-vāyāma*) and wrong effort (*micchā-vāyāma*), since it was said *na vāyameyya*—one should not exert effort everywhere. Therefore, before we apply effort, we must know whether this effort is being applied in the right place. Otherwise, no matter how much effort is applied, it is of no use. We have all heard the word *svākkhāta*. It means well-expounded. We refer to the Buddha's Dhamma as well-expounded Dhamma. Regarding other teachings outside of this, the Buddha refers to them as *durakkhāta*—ill-expounded. Next, the Buddha declares: "Monks, in an ill-expounded Dhamma-Vinaya..."—Dhamma-Vinaya, pious devotees, refers to the Dispensation. Someone declares a Dhamma, and at the same time, there is a practice that follows it. Collectively, this can be called Dhamma-Vinaya, or we may take it as the Dispensation. "One who has aroused energy in an ill-expounded Dhamma dwells in suffering (*dukkha*). What is the reason for that? No matter how much energy they exert, there is no fruit from it; that energy is wasted. Therefore, they dwell in suffering (*dukkha*). In an ill-expounded Dhamma, it is the lazy person (*kusīta*) who dwells happily." The lazy person means the indolent one. There is no work to do. So it was better for them not to make an effort, given their situation. "But regarding the well-expounded Dhamma, it is declared: in a well-expounded Dhamma-Vinaya, the lazy person dwells in suffering (*dukkha*), and the one who has aroused energy (*āraddha-vīriya*) dwells happily." There is the difference. For it is stated in the Dhamma: *āraddhavīriyassa pīti nirāmisā*—to one who has aroused energy in this dispensation, unworldly joy arises immediately. Through that, they proceed to concentration (*samādhi*), and ultimately to the paths and fruits. In this way, too, the difference between right effort and wrong effort is shown.
In an even more striking manner, the Buddha on one occasion illustrated this very point to the Venerable Bhūmija using four similes: that the effort exerted in an ill-expounded Dhamma is futile. It is a somewhat humorous simile. The Buddha presents it in this way: "Monks, if a disciple in a dispensation of eight wrong factors—starting with wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, and so on—exerts energy, whether they do so with a wish..." "Wish" means desire. "If someone exerts energy in a wrongly expounded dispensation, or with wrong view, wrong intention, leading to wrong concentration, whether they do so with a wish, without a wish, with and without a wish, or neither with nor without a wish..."—this is analyzed in four ways because it is presented logically. "Even if they do so, there is no fruit whatsoever." To illustrate this, he then declares four similes to Venerable Bhūmija. "Bhūmija, suppose a man seeking oil pours sand into a vat, sprinkles it with water, and squeezes it. Whether he does so with a wish, without a wish, with and without a wish, or neither with nor without a wish, he cannot get oil by squeezing sand. That is a futile effort." This is the first simile.
Next, he gives the second simile: "A man seeking milk goes to a young cow and pulls her by the horn. Whether he does so with a wish, without a wish, with and without a wish, or neither with nor without a wish, no milk comes. Squeezing a cow’s horn does not produce milk." Then he gives the third simile: "A man seeking butter pours only water into a churn and keeps churning it with a stick. No matter how much he churns, no butter comes." He gives the fourth simile: "A man seeking fire takes a fire-drill..."—in those days, they had fire-making sticks, known as the upper stick (*uttarāraṇi*). They produced fire by rubbing two sticks together. "He takes the fire-drill and rubs it against a wet, water-logged piece of wood. No matter how much he rubs, no fire comes." These are the similes given for futile effort, the similes for futile exertion.
Then, regarding the effort of one with right view, the similes given for ascetics and brahmins who possess right view, right intention, and so on—one can easily imagine the opposite side. "A man seeking oil pours sesame seeds into a vat, sprinkles them with water, and squeezes them. Whether he does so with a wish, without a wish, with and without a wish, or neither with nor without a wish, if he squeezes, oil comes—when sesame seeds are squeezed with water. Next, the second simile can be understood without being told explicitly: from where does a cow's milk come? One must pull the udder, not the horn. If one pulls the udder, whether with a wish or without a wish, milk comes. The third simile: to get butter, one must pour curd, mix it with water, and churn it. The fourth simile: one must rub the fire-drill against a dry piece of wood." Thus, these four similes illustrate this very same point. From this context, we can understand the meaning of the statement, "One should not exert effort everywhere."
Next, why was it said, "One should not be another’s man"? Because those cunning thieves, due to their loyalty to the king, commit all those thefts and crimes, and in the end, they bathe well and behave like gentlemen. What aided that behavior was their status as royal officers/men. One should not be subservient to another. One should not be another’s man, another’s servant. A deep meaning is given there. In the next line, it is said: *nāññaṃ nissāya jīveyya*—one should not live dependent on another. Associating with rulers and kings, one sometimes becomes compelled to perform improper actions. On the other hand, because the king employed those spies, instead of punishing them, he allowed them to roam around the city in that manner. Thus, this highlights the danger of being subservient to another.
The fourth point is somewhat difficult to understand: *dhammena na vāṇijaṃ care*—one should not trade in the Dhamma. The hint obtained from this story is that there were five groups of seven in that crowd: seven *jaṭilas*, seven *nigaṇṭhas*, seven *acelakas*, seven *ekasāṭakas*, and seven *paribbājakas*, walking in single file. There are not many details about the reason for their journey. Perhaps we can imagine that at that time, wealthy merchants and others built halls for various sectarian groups to meet and discuss. On those occasions, gifts and offerings were given to them. We do not know if they were carrying their requisites after receiving such a gift. In any case, this may have been the reason for the Buddha’s statement, "One should not trade in the Dhamma." If we contemplate this deeply, we can understand that one should not make the Dhamma a commercial commodity. We can understand this through a discourse the Buddha delivered to Venerable Ānanda regarding a teacher of the Dhamma. The Buddha says, "Ānanda, teaching the Dhamma is no easy matter. A Dhamma teacher should teach the Dhamma having established five qualities within themselves. The Dhamma should be taught with the thought, 'I will speak in a progressive sequence (*anupubbikathaṃ*)'."
You devotees may have heard of progressive discourse (*anupubbikathā*). It consists of talk on giving (*dāna-kathā*), talk on virtue (*sīla-kathā*), talk on heaven (*sagga-kathā*), talk on the danger of sensual pleasures (*kāmānaṃ ādīnava*), and so on. If one only expects personal gain, one might stop at the talk on giving. Instead, it must be done with the intention of leading them all the way to Nibbāna through a progressive discourse. Likewise, *pariyāyadassāvī*—showing the reasons and causes. Not merely talking, but explaining with reasons and causes. Next, *anuddayataṃ paṭicca*—arousing kindness and compassion towards the listeners. Next, *na āmisantaro*—without expecting material gain, without teaching with the thought, "May I receive such and such requisites from this!" Furthermore, it is said that one should teach without hurting oneself or others (without praising oneself and disparaging others). The Buddha on one occasion told Venerable Ānanda that one should teach the Dhamma after preparing one’s mind in these five ways. Likewise, at another time, he declared the difference between an impure Dhamma teaching and a pure Dhamma teaching. An impure Dhamma teaching is explained as follows:
Suppose someone thinks before preaching the Dhamma, "Oh, if only these people would listen to my Dhamma! If only they would be pleased, and out of that pleasure, give me requisites and so forth, how wonderful that would be!" Preaching with such a thought is an impure Dhamma teaching. It is like selling the Dhamma. Next, the pure teaching is declared. What is a pure Dhamma teaching? "This Dhamma is the Blessed One’s. It is not mine, it is the Blessed One’s Dhamma—well-expounded (*svākkhāta*), visible here and now (*sandiṭṭhika*), timeless (*akālika*), inviting trial (*ehipassika*), leading onward (*opanayika*), to be personally experienced by the wise (*paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhi*). When I preach this Dhamma, let them listen! Having listened, let them understand! Having understood, let them practice!" Preaching with such a reflection on the nature and truth of the Dhamma, and with kindness and compassion towards the listeners, is indeed a pure Dhamma teaching. From these, we can understand why the Buddha declared, *dhammena na vāṇijaṃ care*. It means not giving prominence to material gain. The Buddha has declared to the monks: *"Dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavatha, mā āmisadāyādā"*. "Monks, be heirs to my Dhamma, not heirs to material things." Therefore, one must preach the Dhamma with the intention of being heirs to the Dhamma, not with the thought of gaining the material things that the Buddha received. That is what is contained in those matters.
Next, we mentioned that the Buddha declared four principles like golden rules. Let us look at that next. Those four matters are actually not explained or analyzed in this short sutta. But in other suttas that compile Dhamma matters, such as in the Book of Fours in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, the Buddha preached these four matters in detail. Therefore, we have the opportunity to say something more about them than the brief mention made earlier.
There, the Buddha preaches all four of those matters to the monks in general. Regarding the point, *saṃvāsena sīlaṃ veditabbaṃ*: "Monks, why was it said that virtue is to be understood through living together?" If someone associates with another for a long period, and does so with proper attention (reflection) and wisdom, they understand: "This person’s virtue is broken, punctured, blotched, and stained. This person is unvirtuous." They understand it thus. Through associating with another over a long period with reflection and wisdom, they understand: "This person possesses an unbroken, pure, and clear virtue." That is how it is stated there. Next, the second point is mentioned: *saṃvohārena soceyyaṃ veditabbaṃ*.
That "purity is to be known through social intercourse/conversation" is explained in more detail. Through speaking with another over a long period, one understands: "This person says one thing to one person, another to two people, something different to three people, and something completely different to many people. There is no purity in this person. Their speech is deceptive. This is a deceptive person, an impure person, without principles." They understand it in this way, through associating and conversing over a long period. Similarly, when observing a good person, one gets to know: "If this person says something, they sincerely abide by it in that very manner." Such is the detail regarding that.
Next, the third point about adversity: "It is in times of adversity that a person's *thāma*—their power of endurance, their fortitude—is to be understood." It is stated that when one is hit by the loss of relatives (*ñāti-vyasana*), loss of wealth (*bhoga-vyasana*), or loss to disease (*roga-vyasana*)... that is, when relatives are lost, pass away, or meet with accidents; when one's wealth and possessions are destroyed by sudden accidents or calamities; or when one faces the calamity of illness. When these arise, this person does not reflect that the world constantly revolves around the eight worldly conditions (*aṭṭha-loka-dhamma*). The world revolves around the eight worldly conditions, and the eight worldly conditions revolve around the world.
Speaking of the eight worldly conditions, the Buddha mentions in several places that these eight worldly conditions consist of gain (*lābha*) and loss (*alābha*), disrepute (*ayasa*) and fame (*yasa*), blame (*nindā*) and praise (*pasaṃsā*), pleasure (*sukha*) and suffering (*dukkha*). *Yasa* and *ayasa* mean having retinue/influence and not having it. Then blame and praise, which everyone knows. Then pleasure and pain/suffering. These four pairs make eight. The Buddha has declared that these eight revolve around the world, and the world revolves around these eight. This is a very unusual saying. Yet this person, instead of realizing that this is the nature of the world, weeps, wails, beats their breast, faints, and falls into such grief. Through this, one can know over a long period of association that this person lacks the quality of fortitude (*thāma*) in times of adversity.
Next, regarding the other person—the good person—when faced with such loss of relatives, disease, or wealth, they reflect wisely: "This is the nature of the eight worldly conditions." Keeping their mind balanced accordingly, they do not fall into weeping, wailing, and fainting. To understand these eight worldly conditions, a simile might be useful, so we will say this: we do not have the ability to give similes like the Buddha. In these times, there is something in children's playgrounds called a Ferris wheel (*kathuru oñchillāva*). Think about a Ferris wheel. Let us say there are seats hanging from eight spokes. Parents go and place their little children on them, and the child sits there without any fear. Why? Because they know that whether it goes up or down, they will not fall. They won't fall upside down. What is the reason? As the seat goes up, it adjusts itself accordingly. In this way, we have to understand—this is a rough simile. If it is appropriate, think of it accordingly. We must think of the eight worldly conditions like a Ferris wheel. That is what the Buddha declared: these eight worldly conditions revolve around the world, and the world revolves around the eight worldly conditions. In this way, we can understand adversity. Sometimes, when we have such weaknesses, we can remind ourselves that the Buddha has declared: *āpadāsu thāmo veditabbo*—it is in times of adversity that we can know whether this strength exists within us or not.
Then the fourth point: *sākacchāya paññā veditabbā*—wisdom is to be understood through discussion. The Buddha gives a very unique simile for this, a subtle simile.
This is how it is shown. First, the Dhamma point is stated. Through discussing with another over a period of time, one understands: "By the way this person brings up points, presents arguments, and responds to questions, it is clear that this person is not wise, but foolish." For this person does not bring forth those deep, peaceful, sublime, beyond-logic (*atakkāvacara*), subtle Dhamma categories that are to be experienced by the wise. Likewise, if this person preaches any Dhamma, they lack the ability to explain it briefly or in detail, or to analyze and expound upon those matters. Therefore, one understands: "This person is foolish, not wise." Here is the simile given. The Buddha gives a very unique simile here. A man with sight, standing by a lake or a pond, sees a small fish rising to the surface. Let us say it is a *kaṇayā* (dwarf snakehead). A *kaṇayā* comes up. He is watching from a distance. Yet from the way the fish surfaces, the ripples it creates in the water, and the speed at which it comes up, that man with sight understands: "This is not a big fish, it is a small fish." The word *kaṇayā* is not in the original text. For some reason, we used this word as a simile for a small fish. It should be understood as a small fish.
Then he gives the other simile regarding a wise person. Through discussion, one understands: "By the way this person brings up points, presents arguments, and responds to questions, this person is wise." Why? Because they present those deep Dhamma matters, beyond logic (*atakkāvacara*), which are to be known by the wise. Moreover, they are capable of explaining, clarifying, and expounding those Dhamma matters briefly or in detail. Here is the simile for that: A man with sight is watching. While watching, a big fish—let us say a *lūlā* (striped snakehead)—comes up. From the way that fish comes up, the ripples it makes, and the speed of its ascent, that wise man reflects: "This is not a small creature. It is a large fish." It is in this manner that a wise person is to be understood.
If this matter is not understood correctly, one might even mistake the small fish for a large fish. This is something that happens very often in the world. Therefore, we must understand another’s wisdom and intelligence through wisdom. The Buddha has given certain indicators to understand this. Why? Because as we said before, if we do not recognize wrong view correctly, and if we do not choose the person to associate with correctly over a long period, sometimes our entire life becomes dark. We have exerted effort in the wrong place. We have chosen the wrong person. Such an understanding comes, and that is why the Buddha has given us these hints to recognize people in the world. Whether lay or ordained, when we live in society, the question that arises is: whom should we associate with? Whom should we not associate with? Whose Dhamma should we accept? And where should we exert effort for our liberation? Everyone has this question. The Buddha has highlighted these matters to help us. We must reflect on them with wisdom.
So we have now highlighted all four of these matters. First, we spoke of virtue. Through that, one who lacks stable principles can sometimes sway their disciples to show that their own practices are correct. Similarly, nowadays, those of other religions, in accordance with the wrong view they have taken and their wrong conduct, direct others to that side, and their followers incline in that very direction. Next, the matter of purity: honesty, adherence to principles, and unshakeableness. These are the basic principles the Buddha has highlighted to recognize these things in society.
Next, to bring out one’s stability and fortitude during the loss of relatives, wealth, and disease that come in daily life. Finally, wisdom—it is through discussion. Because in a discussion, especially one in the form of questions and answers, if a person lacks the strength to participate, the shortcomings in their understanding automatically become clear. But if they have understood them deeply, if they possess those qualities, those matters become further clarified. From the way the fish comes to the surface, the ripples it makes, and its speed, one can understand whether it is a big fish or a small fish. We must contemplate based on this hint. We hear that this is an era where various amazing wrong views are spreading in the Sambuddha Sāsana, an era where the Dhamma is being distorted in astonishing ways. It appears that the Dhamma is being subjected to various distortions not only by external religious forces but also by our own people.
The Buddha has pointed out that there are two factors that help in the arising of right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*): *"Dveme, bhikkhave, paccayā sammādiṭṭhiyā uppādāya"*. There are two conditions for the arising of right view. What are the two conditions? The first is the voice of another (*paratoghosa*), and the second is radical attention / wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*). *Paratoghosa* means one must get to hear the Dhamma from others. One cannot realize the Dhamma on one's own. One hears or reads the Buddha's Dhamma from someone. That is *paratoghosa*. But right view does not arise merely because of that. What must one do for that? Radical attention / wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*). One must reflect wisely.
The word *yoniso* is also something very deep. We generally translate it as proper reflection. The Buddha has given humorous similes to understand what is proper and what is wrong—such as trying to get oil by squeezing sand, or pulling a cow by the horn to get milk. That was done in the wrong place. Instead of pulling from where the milk comes, he grabbed the wrong place. In that way, radical attention / wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) means proper, wise reflection. It is through that we can develop right view within ourselves. No matter how much Dhamma we hear, if we accept it merely saying "Sādhu" and "that is good," right view has not arisen. That is blind faith. That is a cause for the arising of the aforementioned devotion, blind faith. One must reflect with wisdom.
