the blessed one preached this dhamma verse while residing at jetavana monastery, concerning the great arahant maha kassapa. at that particular time, the great arahant maha kassapa was staying in the pipphali cave in rajagaha. one day, having gone for alms-round in rajagaha, he returned to pipphali cave, finished his alms-meal, and projected the light of his knowledge. with his divine eye, he was observing how beings who had fallen into negligence, as well as those who were diligent, pass away from this world and are born on this earth, in water, and so forth.
while the blessed one was at jetavana, he wondered: "in what manner of dwelling is my son maha kassapa residing today?" looking with his divine eye, he saw that the arahant maha kassapa was observing beings with his divine eye in this manner. projecting a ray of light, the blessed one said: "maha kassapa, as you watch, you can see only a very small fraction of passing away and arising (*jati*). that is truly the domain of buddha-knowledge—belonging only to the buddhas. it is such a complex and profound matter. for there are countless instances where those born in a mother’s womb pass away without even letting the parents know. such is the extremely marvelous and mysterious nature of passing away and arising (*jati*)." however, expressing a certain praise for the dwelling of the arahant maha kassapa, he uttered the verse mentioned in our theme. in terms of meaning, it says:
*pamadam appamadena yada nudati pandito...*
when the wise person dispels negligence by means of diligence, and ascending the palace of wisdom, sorrowless, looks upon the sorrowing crowd, just as one standing on a mountain—the steadfast, wise individual looks down upon those on the ground, the fools and the ignorant. that is the meaning of the verse.
the word *dhira* used here is special. according to the dispensation and the dhamma, a *dhira* is one endowed with wisdom. what is described here is not just a physical sight seen with the physical eyes, like someone who climbs a mountain—even today, people climb the aradhana gala at mihintale and look around—but this is a vision of knowledge (*nana-dassana*). it is a vision of knowledge through the divine eye. today, we have various technological means thanks to physical science. according to modern science, through different instruments and various light media, microscopes magnify unseen things, and telescopes show distant objects like planets. but all of these are done with the physical eye, relying on the physical eye and external light media. the divine eye mentioned here is something special. it is a vision obtained by projecting the light of absorption (*jhana*). indeed, on one occasion, the blessed one explained this light of absorption to the sangha, asking: "monks, what is the development of concentration (*samadhi-bhavana*) that is conducive to the vision of knowledge?" this is how it is briefly stated:
"here, monks, a person attends to the perception of light. they resolve upon the day-perception: 'as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day.'" this means that to such an extent that there is no difference between the two, even at night a light is perceived when the eyes are closed. in this way, they develop the perception of light. it is further described: in this way, one develops a luminous mind. that means this luminous mind is not shrouded by anything. one develops an open, uncovered, unobstructed mind that is luminous (*sappabhasam cittam*). this refers to an internally generated light.
in fact, this is the state of the fourth absorption (*catuttha jhana*). having stabilized oneself in it, when one directs the divine eye and thinks, "let me see the beings in hell," focusing that vision on hell, they become visible. next, taking that base absorption (*padaka jhana*) as the foundation and directing the mind to it, when one thinks about the nature of the karma of those beings, that too is understood. the divine eye is such a marvelous thing. it is by relying on this divine eye that one sees hell or heaven. it is specifically mentioned that the great arahant moggallana possessed extraordinary strength in seeing with the divine eye in this manner.
this story speaks of the process of being born and dying. indeed, when viewed from this perspective, the entirety of *samsara* is like a tragedy—a tragic film. thus, the great arahant maha kassapa, in the realization that he had brought an end to birth (*jati*) in *samsara*, ascended the palace of wisdom, sorrowless. here, the "palace of wisdom" must be understood as the arahant's knowledge that destroys the taints (*asavakkhaya-nana*). the divine eye is also a kind of light. it makes it easy to see beings being born here and there, dying in one place and being born in another. however, the underlying principle that governs this is embedded in dependent co-arising (*paticcasamuppada*). the understanding of this comes along with what we ultimately call the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*asavakkhaya-nana*).
in short, what did the great arahant who had attained arahantship watch sorrowless, like a wise, steadfast person standing on a mountain looking down upon the fools below? he watched the sorrowful populace. because he was freed from it, he was sorrowless. here, passing away and birth (*jati*) were mentioned. indeed, even in this era, many people talk about this question. actually, it is not about the intermediate state (*antarabhava*) that we should think about, but rather about the suffering (*dukkha*) of becoming (*bhava*) and becoming (*bhava*) itself. however, many scholars today are trapped in the questions of the intermediate state. our buddhists are trapped in theories put forward by many western psychologists, based on psychological evidence, hypnotism, and various artificial devices or media that lead to speculative ideologies. because of this excessive attention on the intermediate state, they forget about becoming (*bhava*) and the suffering (*dukkha*) of becoming (*bhava*). these scholars have no understanding of how to comprehend this matter of birth (*jati*) according to the analysis of dependent co-arising (*paticcasamuppada*) taught by the blessed one.
we generally think of the death we see as passing away (*cuti*). but in reality, we do not know how many times we have been conceived and have passed away in a mother's womb in that manner. today, many people like to take photographs. they take photos of various stages of their lives, from childhood onwards. they might be color photographs, pasted in beautiful albums. if we think for a moment about what our very first photograph is, what indeed is it? the very first form (*rupa*) that arises in the mother's womb is called the *kalala* form. *kalala* means mud. we can call it a mud stain. thus, the mud stain formed in the mother's womb is our first photograph. how many times has this negative of a mud stain been washed away, and for how long, before this final photograph is printed? there is such a state of becoming (*bhava*). then, the next question is how this photograph was cast. indeed, those psychologists we mentioned are those who hold onto the soul-view according to the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*). they cannot comprehend this profound matter shown by the blessed one regarding the relationship of causes and conditions (*hetu-paccaya*).
what happens here is that when a certain consciousness (*vinnana*) slips away from here, before it slips away, a certain vision appears as a sign—in terms of name-and-form (*namarupa*). that vision is the first image cast in the mother's womb. based on that image, a grasping (*gahana*) occurs. *gabbha* (womb) means grasping or holding on. thus, a dying being grasps a mother's womb. that grasping can also pass away. that too is through karma itself. truly, it is because of craving (*tanha*) that this prompting arises. in beings who have not eliminated craving (*tanha*)—that is, craving for becoming (*bhava-tanha*)—because they wish for becoming (*bhava*), karma shows them a matching place. because of craving (*tanha*), that place is perceived as good. it could be a flame of fire, or even an impure place like a mother's womb, yet it appears as a good place.
so, whatever that image objectified by consciousness (*vinnana*) may be, that slipping consciousness (*vinnana*) connects there. as soon as it connects, it begins to grow in dependence on the four elements of the mother's body. this is how it happens. at one stage, in a strange way, it takes on bizarre shapes like a tadpole, and finally, it is born as a beautiful child. if each of these stages were photographed, using modern methods available today, indeed, those too should be included in that photo album we mentioned. that is how we must understand it. that image is what supports the continuation of our becoming (*bhava*).
the blessed one has shown us how that image can be made to cease. until one develops a consciousness (*vinnana*) that does not cast such an image, one goes from becoming (*bhava*) to becoming (*bhava*) in this *samsara*. the blessed one himself has shown this on one occasion when a wanderer named vacchagotta presented various questions to him. the blessed one clearly says in the very first sentence: "vaccha, i say that birth (*jati*) occurs only when there is grasping (*upadana*)—for one who has grasping (*upadana*). for one who has no grasping (*upadana*), there is no birth (*jati*). birth (*jati*) belongs only to one who has grasping (*upadana*); when grasping (*upadana*) is absent, there is no birth (*jati*)." then, as an illustration, he says, "just as, vaccha, a fire burns only when there is grasping (*upadana*), and when there is no grasping (*upadana*), the fire goes out." they call it fire. what is meant by "something to grab" (fuel) is wood or whatever else helps the fire to burn. only where there is such fuel/grasping (*upadana*) does a fire exist. the moment there is nothing to grab, the fire goes out. it is here that the word grasping (*upadana*) emerges.
from that point, we orient this dhamma analysis in relation to dependent co-arising (*paticcasamuppada*). generally, we have all heard that we are born because of craving (*tanha*). the nature of craving (*tanha*) is analyzed in various ways. it is said of craving (*tanha*): *tanha ponobhavika* (craving that leads to renewed becoming). the word *ponobhavika* means it produces renewed becoming (*bhava*), again and again, repeatedly. there is a power within craving (*tanha*), thirst, desire, to generate repeated existence. another characteristic of it is *tatratatrabhinandini*—finding delight here and there. craving (*tanha*) is very fickle. at one moment it is in one place; at another moment, in another place. that is why it slips away from the mother's womb. it entered a womb, but then it leaped to another place. this is why craving (*tanha*) is said to be fickle. it has these two characteristics.
furthermore, if we are to speak about grasping (*upadana*), it is that very craving (*tanha*) itself which ultimately becomes grasping (*upadana*) at the moment of death. this is a very profound matter. some people have misunderstood this and have fabricated a story about an intermediate state (*antarabhava*). in the very discussion with the wanderer vacchagotta, vacchagotta first asks a question like this: "master gotama, when a flame is swept away by the wind, what is its grasping (*upadana*) at that time? since the word grasping (*upadana*) has been introduced, what does the flame grasp there?" "vaccha, i say that the wind (air) is the grasping (*upadana*) on that occasion, for it is blown by the wind and goes further." similarly, at the moment of death, it is through craving (*tanha*) itself that the catch called grasping (*upadana*) occurs. many people have misunderstood this point. this is how the buddha explains it: "when a being lays down this body and arises in another body, i declare craving (*tanha*) to be the grasping (*upadana*)." it is connected by that. now, let us take an analogy to understand this.
let us further consider the dhamma principles regarding this. we have often mentioned the analogy of the deer. in that context, we usually recollect only the eye. one does not think that the other senses are also a mirage. the blessed one compared the entire aggregate of perception (*sanna-kkhandha*) to a mirage. what is a mirage? indeed, it is a complex phenomenon arising due to the four elements of earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and air (*vayo*). yet, to the deer, it appears as water, as flowing water. the deer takes its stand on that. why does it take its stand? because from where the deer stands, it appears as a mirage (as water). therefore, let us suppose the deer runs. it runs in expectation of water. with every step it takes in its running, that vision recedes. but it does not know; it does not know that it is receding. it is an illusion shown by the deer's own consciousness (*vinnana*).
here, we bring out the connection between consciousness (*vinnana*) and name-and-form (*namarupa*). in short, the explanation given by the blessed one regarding rebirth can be understood accordingly. the object is perceived by consciousness (*vinnana*) in terms of name-and-form (*namarupa*). now, "form" (*rupa*) there refers to the four elements of earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and air (*vayo*). due to a certain combination of causes, a shimmering vision arose, which we designate as a mirage. the deer thinks that it is in such-and-such a place; the place it thinks of is one extreme. it distinguishes, saying, "where i am is different." that very act of distinguishing is consciousness (*vinnana*).
the blessed one has stated that consciousness (*vinnana*) always exists in dependence on something. there is no such thing as consciousness (*vinnana*) on its own. this is illustrated in the analogy of fire. a fire that burns due to firewood is called a wood-fire. when it burns due to rubbish, it is called a rubbish-fire. when it burns due to straw, it is called a straw-fire. there is no fire on its own. likewise, there is no consciousness (*vinnana*) on its own. here, therefore, the deer's consciousness (*vinnana*) exists in dependence on that perception of a mirage. that is one extreme. that extreme is present as the object. if we speak of that object as name-and-form (*namarupa*), as we said before, form (*rupa*) is the combination of the four elements.
next, how does the deer recognize this as a mirage? it recognizes it through the mental phenomena (*nama-dhamma*): feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), intention (*cetana*), contact (*phassa*), and attention (*manasikara*). due to craving (*tanha*), a certain feeling (*vedana*) arises, and the perception (*sanna*) arises that "this vision is water." thereupon, the intention (*cetana*) arises with the thought, "if i go there, i can drink some water." next, going there and in the thought of coming together is where attention (*manasikara*) lies—the reflecting upon it.
but the closer one gets, the further away everything recedes. this is the nature of the mirage. as the deer runs, it too recedes. here is the illusory nature of name-and-form (*namarupa*). consciousness (*vinnana*) is said to be an illusion because the objects that come to consciousness (*vinnana*) are always receding. until one sees through it, its true nature does not appear. to see through it means to realize its true nature with wisdom, through the eye of wisdom. that is what the blessed one brought to light through the vision of dependent co-arising (*paticcasamuppada*). why does this appear as a physical form? this needs to be explained further. the ordinary world thinks that these four elements of earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and air (*vayo*) exist separately. in this dhamma, the four elements are described as the four great primary elements (*mahabhuta*).
so, what are the great primaries (*mahabhuta*)? people think that these four exist separately. as we all know, when we say "earth" (*pathavi*), immediately a picture of soil, a stone, a brick, or a mountain comes to mind. when we say "water" (*apo*), we think of an ocean or a river. a flame of fire comes to mind when we say "fire" (*tejo*). a great storm comes to mind when we say "air" (*vayo*). but not one of these exists separately. they are mixed everywhere. thus, none of the four has the strength to stand alone. it is precisely because they lack individual strength that the blessed one showed them to be void (*sunna*). but the world does not perceive this voidness. instead, there is a mental fabrication. when "earth" (*pathavi*) is mentioned, a picture arises in the mind, an illustration appears—an illustration of hardness. indeed, it is based on the quality of hardness that we recognize the element of earth (*pathavi*). the fire element (*tejo*) is recognized through the quality of heat and cold.
that is how they are described when defining the elements. but how does the ordinary world perceive them? as if the four exist separately. so, that is also just the haunting of ghosts (elements/primaries). consciousness (*vinnana*) displays these hauntings. the world is deceived by these hauntings. within that itself, in dependence on that, mental phenomena (*nama-dhamma*) exist. it is because of the deer's initial grip of "water" that the rest of the process is activated. intention (*cetana*) says, "i must run there and grab this somehow; when i get there, i will catch it." it grasps that perception (*sanna*). those are mental phenomena. then, physical phenomena (*rupa-dhamma*) are also void there, and mental phenomena (*nama-dhamma*) are also void. this very point is illustrated in ancient texts by a certain analogy.
the journey of these two, name-and-form (*namarupa*), is described there as being like a blind man who can walk carrying a lame man who has sight on his shoulders. the one on the shoulders can see but cannot walk, as his legs are crippled. he points out, "go this way or that way." physical phenomena (*rupa-dhamma*) and mental phenomena (*nama-dhamma*) cannot go alone either. they proceed by helping each other. it is from those phenomena of name-and-form (*namarupa*) that the image of those forms is cast in our consciousness (*vinnana*). when "earth" is mentioned, we get a perception (*sanna*) of the ground accordingly. but that is not its true nature. it must be penetrated with wisdom. it is because of the perception of permanence (*nicca-sanna*) that the world perceives it in this way.
thus, the blessed one shows that everything must be viewed through the perception of impermanence (*anicca-sanna*). the deer has no realization that with every single step it takes while running, it is changing. that is why it is said that due to ignorance (*avijja*), preparations (*sankhara*) arise. the ordinary world has no understanding of those preparations (*sankhara*) which exist in layers upon layers; they grasp them tightly. the blessed one compared preparations (*sankhara*) to the trunk of a banana tree. at first glance, the ordinary world grasps and holds onto a banana trunk as something having a core or heartwood. but the blessed one teaches us to inspect them through insight (*vipassana*) without grasping tightly. inspection (*sammasana*) is like stroking. if one gently peels and examines the banana trunk, one understands that it is just a pile of sheaths. but if one grabs it all at once, the impression is that it is something with a core. from this, we see that it is through wisdom that this is understood. what the blessed one called the "palace of wisdom" is the wisdom obtained when attaining that profound state of arahantship. it is through that wisdom that the true nature of these elements is understood.
in this era, which gives great prominence to knowledge, the world thinks that "ascending the palace of wisdom" means climbing a multi-story library. scholars of this era might think that the palace of wisdom refers to ascending a library of many floors. it is not such an accumulation. this wisdom shown by the blessed one is actually present within us in a subtle way, embedded deep inside. the blessed one expressed this when describing the light of absorption (*jhana*), speaking of a luminous mind. it is by directing that luminous mind that the places where those beings reside become visible. but even more wonderful than that is the light of wisdom (*panna-aloka*).
regarding that light of wisdom, the blessed one states: "monks, this mind is luminous (*pabhassara*). the mind is naturally radiant. but it is covered by visiting defilements (*agantuka upakkilesa*)—defilements that come from outside. it is soiled by them." the person who lacks knowledge of the dhamma does not know this. that is why they have no interest in meditation. but the noble disciple (*ariya-savaka*) knows that this mind is luminous, luminous within, and that there are only visiting defilements in it. as soon as those impurities are removed, this luminous mind shines forth. to use an analogy for what the person with dhamma-knowledge does: suppose a copper or brass vessel is covered in rust. one way is to paint over it in layers to make it look beautiful. that is not what should be done properly. as soon as the accumulated rust is removed using certain substances, its natural luster emerges. it is something like that which the blessed one describes.
the mind has the capacity to spontaneously understand the true nature of the world. but it is covered by defilements. the blessed one has shown the noble eightfold path as a means of ascending the palace of wisdom. it is a systematic transformation, like climbing a flight of stairs, which must be achieved through systematic effort. we know that to remove rust, a systematic procedure is required. this is briefly mentioned as virtue (*sila*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*). one has to systematically remove that rust, layer by layer. only when it is removed does the true luminosity emerge.
regarding this point about knowledge and wisdom, let us examine the story of venerable culapanthaka, which you all have heard many times. the novice monk culapanthaka could not memorize a single verse even after four months, so his brother monk expelled him, telling him to return to lay life. but the blessed one stopped him, stroked his head, and gave him a piece of clean white cloth, telling him to rub it while repeating, "*rajo-haranam, rajo-haranam*" (dirt-remover, dirt-remover). indeed, as he rubbed it, what happened? it became soiled with sweat. next, instead of rubbing the cloth, what did he do? he began to contemplate those preparations (*sankhara*). preparations (*sankhara*). regarding the nature of these preparations (*sankhara*), he realized, "are not all these impermanent (*anicca*)?"
in truth, it is through the contemplation of preparations (*sankhara*) that wisdom arises. at the moment he realized their impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*) nature, the blessed one, seeing the opportune moment, said, "it is not that rust on the cloth you should think about. as soon as the rust of lust (*raga*), hatred (*dosa*), and delusion (*moha*) is removed, realization comes." in this way, the true nature of this mind is covered by the rust of lust, hatred, and delusion. thus, to bring out that truth, it is said, *panna-pasadam-aruyha* (having ascended the palace of wisdom). when that truth is brought out, what is seen is the true nature of passing away and birth (*jati*).
in the past, there were sages (rishis). today, such people are very rare. some yogis who lived before the appearance of the blessed one could see even hundreds of thousands of past lives. they saw that a certain individual died in one place and was born in another. yet, the connection was not visible to them. they could not understand how it happened. that is precisely what the blessed one brought to light through the teaching of dependent co-arising (*paticcasamuppada*). this is an extremely subtle matter.
we generally think that after someone dies, something goes from here. any physical scientist, or certain people who lack the buddhist outlook, try to explain the idea of someone dying and going to another place through physical laws. something has to go from here, they think. a strong blow to that argument is mentioned in the payasi sutta. venerable kumara kassapa lived during the buddha's time and also lived after the buddha's passing away, as he had a long lifespan. that great arahant kumara kassapa was foremost in this dispensation in preaching the dhamma in a diverse and colorful manner (*vicitra-kathika*).
he had the ability to make things clear to people by giving highly wonderful analogies. this great arahant kumara kassapa had to engage in a long debate in the city of setavya with a chieftain named payasi. a chieftain (*rajanna*) is like a crown prince, an uncrowned king. this king held a wrong view (*miccha-ditthi*), a nihilistic view (*natthika-ditthi*) to the effect that when a being dies, there is no rebirth (*jati*), no spontaneous rebirth (*opapatika*), and no fruit or result of karma. in a discussion with kumara kassapa to dispel this view, this chieftain payasi revealed an experiment he had conducted as an argument. today, too, people might perform such experiments. what was his experiment?
let's say his guards bring a subject who has committed some crime to the chieftain payasi, saying, "your majesty, here is a criminal fit for punishment." he then uses that person for his experiment. what does he do? he tells the men to put that man alive into a large pot. having placed him in the pot, they cover it with a wet hide, seal the mouth with clay so that nothing can escape, and place it on a stove. they put it on a fire, on a hearth. they leave it there to heat up and boil. when he thinks the person must be dead, the chieftain slowly opens the pot to see if the soul (*jiva*) escapes. surely the soul (*jiva*) must escape to be born elsewhere. but the soul does not escape; it does not come out. presenting this argument to venerable kumara kassapa, he says, "where is it then? the soul should have escaped, but this person died while sealed inside. i did not see any soul escaping. therefore, i say there is no rebirth (*jati*)."
the analogy given by venerable kumara kassapa on that occasion is very important for our subject. that is why we bring it up. venerable kumara kassapa asks as a question, "chieftain, do you remember on certain occasions going to sleep during the daytime? having gone to sleep, did you dream various dreams? do you remember dreaming of beautiful parks and lotus ponds?" when he replies "yes," kumara kassapa says, "well, on that occasion, the mind had gone out to see those things, the soul (*jiva*) had gone. at that time, did any of your bodyguards—whoever they were, including the women—who were around you while you slept during the day, see your soul (*jiva*) leaving?" "no," he replies.
so what does that mean? what happens at the moment of death is just like what happens in a dream world. it would be good for you pious devotees to contemplate deeply on this analogy presented by the great arahant kumara kassapa. in the dream world, the object that comes to the mind may be something far away. if, based on that object, someone thinks, "my consciousness (*vinnana*) went there," that is where they go wrong. now, to remind you, we colloquially say, "i saw in a dream that i went to such-and-such a place, and i saw various sights." we say, "i went." because of this, one thinks that consciousness (*vinnana*) undertook a journey at that time. indeed, in the past, even the brahmins who held the soul-view thought like this—that during sleep, the soul goes out, roams around as it pleases, and returns. what the blessed one teaches here is not such a thing. according to buddhist philosophy, the object that comes to consciousness (*vinnana*) cannot be connected to the concept of movement in the way the world thinks. whether the object perceived by the mind is far or near, it cannot be physically or materially connected.
therefore, according to the dhamma, we cannot conceive of a soul (*jiva*) leaving after the man inside the pot dies. if that were so, regarding a person born from here in the heavenly world or the brahma world, to explain it in modern terms, some kind of ray would have to travel from here to connect there. one thinks of such a physical connection. this happens because of thinking in terms of physical laws. every pious devotee who reads the dhammapada knows the very first verse: *manopubbangama dhamma, manosettha manomaya*. there is nothing wrong with thinking that buddhism begins and ends with that verse, because its meaning is that profound. *manopubbangama dhamma, manosettha manomaya*. what is the meaning? "dhamma" here means things. what is objectified by the mind is called things (*dhamma*). that means things. form (*rupa*) is objectified by the eye. sound is objectified by the ear. going on like this, what is objectified by the mind, the sixth sense, is described there as *dhamma*.
in the dhamma, the word *dhamma* does not mean the doctrine (teachings) as we usually say, but rather the object. a certain object, the objects that come to the mind. so, what the blessed one is stating here is that mind precedes everything we consider as a "thing." but if we try to adjust the dhammapada according to physical science, how would we have to correct it? *dhammapubbangamo mano*—things exist first, and the mind comes later. but the blessed one says that the mind precedes, and things (*dhamma*) come later. there is a very profound point here. for it is precisely because it is objectified by the mind that it becomes a "thing."
that is why it is said: *manasikarasambhava sabbe dhamma* (all things arise from attention). everything arises for the mind. it is born in the mind itself; it is mind-centric, mind-rooted. in short, buddhist philosophy is mind-centric. accordingly, passing away and birth (*jati*) must be explained through a mind-centric analysis, not a matter-centric one. if we go by a matter-centric approach, we go wrong. the soul-perception, the vital-principle-perception is contained within it. what is the nature of the mind? *manopubbangama dhamma*, and not only that, *manosettha*—the mind is supreme. nay, even *manomaya*. pious devotees know that *manomaya* means mind-made, created by the mind itself. what we call a "real thing" is something created by the mind itself.
this does not reject the account of the four elements. but even those elements, as we know, are great primaries (*mahabhuta*); they are just haunting spirits. it is to these four great primary elements—which cannot stand alone and are void of a self—that we refer as the elements of earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and air (*vayo*). what the world thinks of as great things are only these hauntings. these primary elements haunt consciousness (*vinnana*) as real things. *manopubbangama dhamma, manosettha, manomaya*. that is why they are said to be mind-made.
these "things" are what we have fashioned in our minds. because mind precedes, because mind is supreme, because they are mind-made, if one speaks, acts, or thinks with a corrupted mind, or directs the mind in that way, a mass of suffering in hell is created by them. that is *manomaya* (mind-made). now, hell and such places do not just exist passively or get created automatically; the blessed one declared how they arise according to karma. next, heavenly worlds and divine mansions are created if the mind is wholesome, if the mind is pleasant—as mentioned in the story of mattakundali regarding divine mansions. no carpenters went and built them there. they are created spontaneously. that is how it is shown according to this dhamma: *manomaya*. it is a wonderful state.
this is precisely what we said when speaking of name-and-form (*namarupa*). being mind-centric, those phenomena of name-and-form (*namarupa*), like the vision seen by the deer, are entirely just an image. they are only a delusion, an illusion. but this can be understood directly only when the three characteristics—impermanent (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anatta*)—are properly realized. the path to that is called insight (*vipassana*). the purpose of insight meditation (*vipassana-bhavana*) is to deeply understand, to directly realize, the impermanence (*aniccata*) taught by the blessed one. when we say impermanence (*aniccata*), the idea of two extremes arises. what are the two extremes? there is arising, and there is passing away. it is called *udayabbaya*—arising (*udaya*) and passing away (*vaya*). there is an arising and a wearing away. as one constantly contemplates these two extremes, as this process becomes faster and faster, finally a state of penetrating through what we thought of as a "thing" is reached. when a stage is reached where one can see through something, like looking through glass, the state of there being a "real thing" there vanishes. as long as one does not see through it, one takes it to be a thing.
in the dhamma, there is a certain passage regarding the wisdom gained through insight meditation (*vipassana-bhavana*): *udayatthagaminiya pannaya samannagato ariyaya*. *udayatthagamini* refers to this very matter of arising and passing away. it is *nibbedhika*—a wisdom that penetrates. so, what does the practitioner of insight (*vipassana*) do? they first develop that understanding regarding name-and-form (*namarupa*).
mind (*nama*) and form (*rupa*) do not exist separately. because of form (*rupa*)—as we said in the case of the deer—because of form (*rupa*), mind (*nama*) exists: feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), intention (*cetana*), contact (*phassa*), and attention (*manasikara*). next, it is in dependence on that mind (*nama*) that form (*rupa*) is distinguished and recognized. in this way, the phenomena of name-and-form (*namarupa*) are connected there as well. there is nothing here that can be taken as a soul, nothing substantial, other than the phenomena of name-and-form (*namarupa*). these are just a heap of preparations (*sankhara*). with every single step taken, that vision recedes, but the deer does not understand. that which is not understood by the deer, the truth that has deceived it, the practitioner of insight (*vipassana*) gradually brings to light. that is why, wherever the practitioner of insight looks, they gradually see only movements. this is not something fabricated anew. its true nature had been covered up until now. that nature of movement was covered up precisely by that perception of permanence (*nicca-sanna*). that is why the blessed one said that this is a perverted, distorted state (*vipallasa*).
what we think of as real in the world is completely upside down. to the blessed one, the world appeared as if standing on its head. that must be why he was at first hesitant even to preach the dhamma. "who will understand this?" it is that profound. when one practices insight (*vipassana*) with good concentration, applying mindfulness in accordance with the foundations of mindfulness (*satipatthana*), and sees arising and passing away, the perception of permanence (*nicca-sanna*) is penetrated and shattered. this is directly seen through this insight-knowledge (*vipassana-nana*). true wisdom is what is called *udayatthagamini panna*—the very seeing of arising and passing away. as this process gradually becomes faster, instead of what we previously thought existed, we see only a series of movements. only a series of movements that can be designated as name-and-form (*namarupa*). only an appearance.
through that understanding, eventually disenchantment (*nibbida*) arises, leading to dispassion (*viraga*) and liberation (*vimutti*). the arising of that liberation means the image cast in consciousness (*vinnana*) ceases. it was a mud stain in the mother's womb—cast as a mud stain. whether in a mother's womb or any other place, it is a stain cast in terms of name-and-form (*namarupa*). but when illuminated by wisdom, when name-and-form (*namarupa*) is seen through, that consciousness (*vinnana*) is liberated from it. consciousness (*vinnana*) becomes non-manifestative (*anidassana*). no more images are cast in it. after that voidness is understood, a state of mind where earth (*pathavi*) brings to mind the physical ground, or water (*apo*) brings to mind water, does not arise for that person.
that is why the blessed one declared that there is nothing to grasp. that is why he said that where there is no grasping (*upadana*), there is no becoming (*bhava*). only where there is grasping (*upadana*) is there continuation. where there is no grasping (*upadana*), there is no continuation. why does grasping (*upadana*) occur? because something is presented as an object matching one's craving (*tanha*). for that to cease, that insight-knowledge (*vipassana-nana*) we mentioned must arise. what is done through insight-knowledge (*vipassana-nana*) is the understanding of impermanence (*aniccata*). the blessed one stated that impermanence (*aniccata*) is understood to some extent by the ordinary world. although people say "impermanent, impermanent" (*aniccam, aniccam*) about everything, the moment it is directly realized comes only in insight meditation (*vipassana-bhavana*). one gradually and deeply understands that "here there is only a mass of arisings and passings away." then one might wonder, "where then does this wisdom exist? does it fall from the sky?" the blessed one declared that the seed of this wisdom exists within us. it only needs to be developed. what is that? it is mentioned in this dhamma as the seed of wisdom under the name wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*).
wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*) means reflecting upon something according to how it arises. in short, it is reflecting by looking at this near end. if one reflects by looking at the far end, it only goes further and further, without any stopping. here, recall the story of the deer again.
now, the deer is running, thinking only of the water far away. the deer does not understand the reality here—how mental phenomena (*nama-dhamma*) are projected, or how through feeling (*vedana*), perception (*sanna*), and intention (*cetana*) created by the mind, this form (*rupa*) is perceived as a real thing. so, the blessed one points this out as wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*). how is its true nature understood? by reflecting on the place from where they arise. the place from where they spring. the deer lacks the understanding that this vision it sees arose precisely due to the delusion within its own mind.
only when that understanding comes is the delusion that existed up to then realized. the deception regarding it ceases. that is why in this dhamma, ignorance (*avijja*) is shown as the root—unknowing. because of unknowing, a certain preparation is made. preparations (*sankhara*) mean karma and so forth. because of them, consciousness (*vinnana*) and name-and-form (*namarupa*) arise, which means dividing them into two. just as the deer runs endlessly into the distance based on that grip of "i am here, and the water is over there," the journey of *samsara* is also like that. the blessed one shows that as long as one tightly grasps consciousness (*vinnana*) as a soul, grasping it as "my consciousness," one takes the object cast upon it as real, as a real thing, and runs after it with craving (*tanha*)—with craving (*tanha*) and grasping (*upadana*). because of that very form (*rupa*) that is cast, the very power derived regarding those four elements is what is called mind-made (*manomaya*).
that is a great wonder. you have heard that things arise in accordance with karma. there is also the word *kammaja*—arising from karma. what is karma? the blessed one declares: "karma is intention (*cetana*)." intention (*cetana*) is also a matter of the mind. so, if certain things arise from intention (*cetana*), it refers to that state of being mind-made (*manomaya*). when speaking of arising from karma, it is the very same point expressed as *manopubbangama dhamma, manosettha, manomaya*.
karma is the collection of wholesome and unwholesome mental impulses generated by the grip of "i" and "mine" arising out of ignorance (*avijja*). this material world changes in a marvelous way. although the ordinary world thinks highly of achievements made with hammers and saws, far more wonderful than all of them is the way birth (*jati*) occurs according to what is perceived by the mind at the moment of death. think about it: is it not through the power of karma (*kamma-vegam*) that the *kalala* form cast in a mother's womb develops into a child? we generally think that a mother and father created it. but when we think truly, it is that karma-energy that gives life. you must have heard how much they tried to kill prince ajatasattu while he was in the womb? they could not do it because of that karma-energy.
thus, when viewed in that way, there too lies *manomaya*. the blessed one brings to light the natural principle of *manopubbangama dhamma... manomaya*. it is precisely because of this that an end to it can be seen. the division previously held as "consciousness" (*vinnana*) is ultimately transcended by the blessed one through that very wisdom we spoke of. wisdom means complete understanding, full realization. when full realization comes, one cannot present two extremes in that manner. the grip taken by the deer was wrong; the grip of "i am here, and the water is there" was wrong. as long as that is present, one runs endlessly. the blessed one, therefore, declares realization here. here it is not a running but a stopping—stop and see. what do you stop and look at? at your own five aggregates (*pancakkhandha*).
concerning this world, we travel from country to country. moreover, we go in search of other planets. we pursue truth and values along those paths. but the blessed one showed: "within this very fathom-long body, endowed with perception and mind, i declare the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world." so, this too has to be understood in reliance on the matter we described. everything happens through the mind itself; the mind is supreme. therefore, this is a truth that must be seen right here. until one sees it, until one realizes this matter, one goes from becoming (*bhava*) to becoming (*bhava*), playing a part in that tragic, comic, and terrifying drama. this is what is meant by wandering in the becoming (*bhava*) of *samsara* for an infinite time. thus, the great arahant maha kassapa saw that vision through the state of birth (*jati*) and rebirth. in dependent co-arising (*paticcasamuppada*), it is shown that due to craving (*tanha*), the catching called grasping (*upadana*) occurs. within grasping (*upadana*), within the very concept of grasping, there is a grasper and a thing grasped—two extremes. it is precisely because of this that there is existence/becoming (*bhava*).
existence/becoming (*bhava*) is what proceeds according to two extremes. the moment it is measured according to two extremes, it is taken as a "thing," as existence. that running deer thinks, "now, i am here, and the water is over there." the existence between those two is what is in the deer's running. we must understand that our running is also like that. what do we do throughout this entire life? we run along the objects—forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mind-objects—that come to these six doors: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, just as that deer ran.
the blessed one did not describe only what is seen by the eye as a perception (*sanna*), as a mirage. the blessed one showed the entire aggregate of perception (*sanna-kkhandha*), the whole pile of perception, as a mirage. but we do not realize this. we think only that deer was deceived (shrouded). we must understand that we are all deceived (shrouded) by these. thus, just like the mirage seen by the eye, the mirage heard by the ear, the mirage smelled by the nose, and the other sensory objects were also shown by the blessed one as mirages. for as one runs after them, there is no end.
instead, wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*) means directing the mind to the place where they arise. we must contemplate what that grip of taking them as "two" is. because of dividing them as "two," we have an impression that these two clash. a feeling of clashing arises where there is an understanding, a presupposition, of "two." the blessed one shows that this grip is wrong. all of these are a mass of causes and conditions (*hetu-paccaya*), and not a single one can be separated. that is also what was said about the elements. based on the characteristics presented by feeling (*vedana*) itself, we distinguish them as earth (*pathavi*), water (*apo*), fire (*tejo*), and air (*vayo*). next, in dependence on them, those mental phenomena (*nama-dhamma*) exist. there, too, is a mutual conditional relationship, proceeding in relation to each other. that is what the great arahant sariputta stated in an analysis of dependent co-arising (*paticcasamuppada*) regarding this *samsaric* existence—that consciousness (*vinnana*) and name-and-form (*namarupa*) are just like two sheaves of reeds propped up against each other.
of the two sheaves of reeds propped up against each other, neither can stand alone. if one is pulled away, the other falls. if this one is pulled away, the other falls. the blessed one explains it in that manner. according to this dhamma, the entire *samsara* exists because of the mutual relationship with name-and-form (*namarupa*). that is why the blessed one declared that as far as there is any arising in the world, any passing away, aging, and rebirth, every designation and everything is contained within these two. what are they? in dependence on consciousness (*vinnana*), there is name-and-form (*namarupa*). in dependence on name-and-form (*namarupa*), there is consciousness (*vinnana*).
what is this name-and-form (*namarupa*)? a form merely in name. it is not a real form, is it? the form seen by that deer is not a real form, is it? it is a form merely in name. but we do not think so. we tightly grasp that photograph we spoke of. "this is my form. this is me when i was small. this is me when i was young. this is when i got married. this is when i received these titles and honors"—we keep those forms and grasp them. but all of these are just a series of images. they are simply forms merely in name. they are just those externally visible hauntings of primary elements.
in terms of ultimate reality, the buddhas declare that here lies a state of voidness, an emptiness that cannot be grasped as a sign (*nimitta*). not a single one can arise on its own. it is said that *samsara* arises due to ignorance (*avijja*), due to wrong grasping. because of that wrong grasping. but within that power of intention (*cetana-vegam*), there is a quality of projecting and creating those elements. that pile of projections is what is then called becoming (*bhava*). however, the blessed one, having brought to light the suffering (*dukkha*) nature within it, shows an end to it. the end is not found through an accumulation of knowledge. the palace of wisdom is not a multi-story library. it is where this rust is removed. it is a mass of rust accumulated in this *samsara*. the blessed one has shown how to systematically remove them through systematic effort—through a vast endeavor of virtue (*sila*), concentration (*samadhi*), and wisdom (*panna*), by means of the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*). as one removes them, the inherent natural light of the mind emerges, and the true nature of the world is reflected in it. it is seen through that luster. that is the state the blessed one brought to light.
therefore, our buddha's dispensation consists of these core values. instead of being trapped in the intermediate states (*antarabhava*) by submitting to arguments presented by western psychologists who have not eliminated the dogma of self-illusion (*sakkaya-ditthi*), we must understand this becoming (*bhava*) properly and be stirred by the suffering of becoming (*bhava-dukkha*). what we have to do is to enter this path of insight (*vipassana*) that eliminates the suffering of becoming (*bhava-dukkha*). by relying on that wisdom called *udayatthagamini panna*—the seeing of arising and passing away—and the vision developed by directing the mind to the place of their arising, which is wise attention (*yoniso manasikara*), we must achieve our liberation from *samsara* through the light of wisdom generated from within, and understand the natural principles of the world. these valuable portions of the buddha's dispensation are increasingly being undervalued and discarded. they are disappearing from practice in this society. therefore, we must be mindful to protect these core values. that is what is meant by protecting the buddha's dispensation.
on this precious day, despite having many other things to do, this pious crowd dedicated the day to practice (*patipatti*) and engaged in dhamma discussions and meditation that support internal vision. that is why this dhamma sermon was oriented toward insight (*vipassana*). by wisely reflecting and observing virtue (*sila*), and also by providing requisites to those who observe virtue, you pious devotees have accumulated further merit. taking all of that, along with the wholesome energy accumulated through listening to the dhamma on this occasion as a supportive condition (*upanissaya*), and relying on the association of noble friends (*kalyana-mitta*), may you, as quickly as possible—since it is visible that this buddha's dispensation is increasingly turning toward the dark side—strive individually to protect the dispensation from within.
may the mass of merit accumulated so far serve as a supportive condition (*upanissaya*) for the success of this dhamma practice and meditation! may this be a strength to eliminate your own *samsaric* suffering (*dukkha*) through the realization of the paths and fruits of stream-entry (*sotapatti*), once-returning (*sakadagami*), non-returning (*anagami*), and arahantship! aspire in this manner. furthermore, may all those in this universe who wish to rejoice in the merit of this dhamma preaching and dhamma listening, by doing so, realize the noble, great deathless—the mind stilled (nibbana—by means of their aspired-for enlightenment (*bodhi*)! aspire in this way and recite these verses.
“*ettavata ca amhehi.........*”

title: Pahankanuwa Sermon 169
content:
Pahankanuwa Sermon #169
English Translation
Translated from Sinhala
Author: Ven. Katukurunde Nanananda Thero
(Pahankaṇuwa Sinhala Audio Dhamma Sermon No.135)
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
(Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One)
Pali Stanza:
"Vanaṃ chindatha mā rukkhaṃ,
vanato jāyate bhayaṃ,
chetvā vanañca vanathañca,
nibbānā hotha bhikkhavo.
Yāva hi vanatho na chijjati,
aṇumattopi narassa nārisu,
paṭibaddhamano va tāva so,
vaccho khīrapakova mātari."
From:
Dhammapada Verses 283 and 284 Magga Vagga (The Path)
Dear Listeners,
Leaving the household life and ordaining is generally identified as renunciation (*nekkhamma*). Even if one departs from the household life and ordains, if one remains bound by lay attachments, by home-centered attachments, and remains engaged in household thoughts and desires, there is no true renunciation. Today, we are taking up for discussion two verses and a story that illustrate the subtle nature of these home-centered attachments.
These two verses were uttered by the Blessed One while he was residing in Sāvatthi, with reference to a group of monks who had ordained in their old age. In Sāvatthi, a group of wealthy householders lived in great harmony, engaging in various meritorious acts of giving and listening to the Dhamma. Having reached old age, they too thought, “There is no benefit in remaining in the lay life; we must ordain.” Having obtained permission from the Blessed One, they ordained. However, because they had ordained in their old age, they lacked the capacity to engage in the corresponding studies and meditation (*bhāvanā*). This group built several huts behind the Jetavana monastery and resided there. Moreover, when going on alms-round, they mostly frequented the houses of their former wives and children.
Having gone there and collected almsfood, they would bring it to the house of the former wife of one of those monks—referred to in the texts as *purāṇa-dutiyikā* (former wife)—and sit down. The reason they did so was because that woman was highly skilled in cooking delicious food. She was known as *Madhurapācikā* (the sweet-cook). These monks would assemble at the house of this lay devotee, Madhurapācikā, and consume their meals there, because she provided the delicious flavor-enhancers they desired.
While they were living in this manner, that laywoman suddenly passed away due to an illness. Thereupon, as an expression of their grief, these monks gathered in the hut of the monk who had been her former husband and began to weep and wail, clasping each other's necks, saying, “Our laywoman Madhurapācikā, who cooked such delicious food for us, is lost!” When other monks came from here and there and asked what the commotion was, they said, “This is what has happened to us. The laywoman who prepared and gave us such delicious food is gone. How can we find such a person again?” and they wailed. This story reached the Dhamma assembly.
While the monks were talking about this incident, the Blessed One arrived and, as was his custom, asked, “What were you discussing, monks?” Upon their explanation, he declared, “Monks, not only now, but in the past too, when born in the womb of crows, this monk and his wife were a crow-pair, and when she was swept away by the sea while they were eating sacrificial offerings on the seashore, they exhausted themselves trying to empty the ocean with their beaks and fell into great distress.” On that occasion, the Blessed One related the Kāka Jātaka (Crow Birth Story).
According to that story, it is as follows. In the past, when the Blessed One was a Bodhisatta, he was born as a sea deity. The people of that region, as a custom, would bring sacrifices of meat, food, and liquor as offerings to the sea deity and the Nāgas, and place them on the seashore.
While a male and female crow were walking along the seashore, they ate the meat, drank the liquor, became intoxicated, and went to bathe in the sea. The female crow was caught by a wave, swept away, and became prey to a fish. The male crow began to cry out and express his grief.
The rest of the flock of crows also gathered, lamenting, “Alas, our wonderful companion has been dragged away by this terrible ocean! Let us empty this ocean!” Together, they filled their beaks with water and carried it out, trying to dry up the ocean. In the end, when their throats and mouths were parched from the seawater and they were exhausted, the sea deity assumed a terrifying form and drove the crows away. Having related this story, the Blessed One declared: “The couple of the past is the very same couple today. That flock of crows is none other than these elderly monks. Therefore, monks, as long as one does not cut down the forest of lust, hatred, and delusion, one cannot escape from these...” In this sense, he uttered the two verses mentioned earlier.
When these verses are uttered, their meaning is not immediately clear. It is evident that a deep meaning lies beneath them.
*Vanaṁ chindatha mā rukkhaṁ,*
*vanato jāyatī bhayaṁ*
“Cut down the forest, not the tree.” Not just the tree, but cut down the entire forest. *“Vanato jāyati bhayaṁ”*—from the forest arises fear, dangers, and hazards.
*Chetvā vanañca vanathañca,*
*nibbanaṁ hotha bhikkhavo*
“Monks, having cut down both the forest and the brushwood, be without forest—attain Nibbāna!” In the next verse, it says:
*Yāvaṁ hi vanatho na chijjati, aṇumattopi narassa nārisu, paṭibaddhamanova tāva so, vaccho khīrapākova mātari'ti.*
“As long as the underbrush of desire of a man for women is not cut down, even to the slightest degree, so long is his mind bound, just like a sucking calf is bound to its mother.” This is the meaning conveyed by those verses. When it was said “cut down the forest, not the tree,” it indicates that for many, ordaining means merely leaving the household, abandoning lay possessions, and putting on the robes. However, the Blessed One points out here that there is a vast forest of defilements. When speaking of defilements, you lay devotees have also heard that there is a class called underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). It is not only the gross defilements that appear prominent; deep beneath them lie subtle defilements rooted deeply from a long journey in Saṁsāra, where minds have succumbed to lust, hatred, and delusion. These are referred to in our Dhamma as latency / underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
Therefore, even if one ordains in that manner, various obstacles arise in one's path to Nibbāna. In particular, the obstacle of relatives (*ñāti-palibodha*) is one of them. The obstruction from relatives often becomes an obstacle to monks. Here too, it was because of their attachment to the delicious food of the former wife (*purāṇa-dutiyikā*) that they fell into such grief. On this very point, the Blessed One delivered a highly valuable discourse on one occasion at Kosambī, while residing on the banks of the river Ganges.
The Blessed One saw a great log of wood being swept away by the current of the river. Addressing the monks, he asked: “Do you see, monks, that great log of wood being swept along by the river current?” “Yes, Venerable Sir.” Then the Blessed One declared: “Monks, if that log of wood does not drift to this bank, nor to the outer bank; if it does not sink in mid-stream; if it does not run aground on a sandbank; if it is not taken by human beings, nor by non-human beings; if it is not caught in a whirlpool; and if it does not rot from within—it will tilt, slope, and slide towards the ocean and one day reach the ocean.” This is presented as a riddle. “Similarly, monks, if you do not drift to this bank, nor to the outer bank; if you do not sink in mid-stream; if you do not run aground on a sandbank; if you are not taken by human beings, nor by non-human beings; if you are not caught in a whirlpool; and if you do not rot from within, you will arrive at Nibbāna, which is the final consummation of this monk's life. Why? Because right-view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) tilts, slopes, and leads towards Nibbāna.”
When this was declared, a certain monk asked the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, what is 'this bank'? What is 'the outer bank'? What is 'sinking in mid-stream'? What is 'running aground'? What is 'being taken by human beings' and 'being taken by non-human beings'? What is 'being caught in a whirlpool'? What is 'rotting from within'?” Thereupon, the Blessed One compared the simile to its meaning, bringing out the Dhamma principles.
“Monk, in this simile, by 'this bank' I mean the six internal bases (*ajjhattika-āyatana*). The six internal bases are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. To drift to 'this bank' means to take these six internal bases as self (*attā*) and to form an attachment to them. Then, 'the outer bank' means the six external bases (*bāhira-āyatana*)—namely, the objects contacted by the eye, etc.: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and thoughts (*rūpa, sadda, gandha, rasa, phoṭṭhabba, dhamma*). Those are 'the outer bank'. By 'sinking in mid-stream' is meant delight and lust (*nandīrāga*), the nature of being attached. Next, 'running aground' means the subtle conceit 'I am' (*asmi-māna*). The conceit 'I am' is the very subtle pride that exists within a person.
The Blessed One explains 'being taken by human beings' in detail. A certain person, having ordained, lives in association with laypeople (*gihi-saṁsagga*). Association with laypeople means engaging in activities with them, rejoicing when they rejoice, grieving when they grieve, being happy in their happiness, and sad in their sorrow, without equanimity, as a result of that connection. Furthermore, if laypeople have various major or minor tasks, the monk remains occupied with them. Instead of Dhamma study and meditation (*bhāvanā*), he is engaged in the various affairs of laypeople—there is no need to describe these in detail to you, lay devotees—that monk is occupied with such things. This is what is called 'being taken by human beings' (*manussaggāha*). 'Being taken by non-human beings' is explained as a monk who protects the dispensational practices and observes virtue, thinking, 'By this virtue, by this vow, by this practice, I will be reborn in a certain heavenly world,' thus practicing the holy life with a heavenly realm as his goal. Not Nibbāna. Not putting an end to Saṁsāra. That is 'being taken by non-human beings' (*amanussaggāha*).
Next, *āvaṭṭagāho*, 'the whirlpool', means the fivefold sensual pleasures (*pañca-kāma-sampatti*). Falling prey to sensual pleasures is like being caught in a whirlpool. Next, *antopūti*, 'rotting from within', means living a life of immorality, evil, and non-celibacy while pretending to be a monk, though not being one. Living a corrupted, defiled life. That is 'rotting from within'. If that happens, one cannot reach the final destination of Nibbāna, due to these mentioned obstacles.
At the time of this sermon, a cowherd named Nanda was standing near the Blessed One. This sermon struck Nanda the cowherd so deeply that he said: “Venerable Sir, I shall not drift to this bank, nor to the outer bank. I shall not sink in mid-stream, nor run aground. I shall not be taken by human beings, nor by non-human beings. I shall not be caught in a whirlpool, nor rot from within. Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One grant me ordination and higher ordination in this Dispensation!” The Blessed One said: “In that case, Nanda, go and hand over the herd of cows to their owner.” Nanda was so eager for ordination that he said: “Venerable Sir, these cows will find their own way back out of affection for their calves.” But the Blessed One insisted: “No, Nanda, go and hand over the cattle to their owner and then return.” Obeying this, Nanda went and returned the cattle, came back, received ordination, and by striving with great diligence, soon attained the noble fruit of Arahatship.
Here, many obstacles that exist after ordaining are mentioned, especially *manussaggāha* (being taken by human beings). To explain this further and make it more meaningful, the commentaries have elaborated on various points. In particular, if one ordains in old age, due to the connection to one's family, such a monk is called in the commentaries *samaṇa-kuṭumbika* (a monastic householder). *Kutumba* means family. *Kuṭumbika* means a family man. There is an old Sinhala word, *keḷembiyā*. Thus, he lives as a “monastic householder.” He did not completely break that bond. To illustrate this, the commentaries give a simile: there is a tree on the riverbank whose roots are on land, but its leaves hang over and touch the river. If one lives such a life, engaging in lay activities and doing what one did during lay life, it is equivalent to “being taken by human beings.”
The Blessed One pointed out the subtle obstacles to the ordained life in this manner. Beyond the defilements that appear coarse, gross, and rough externally, there are subtler levels of defilements. It is in this Dispensation of the Buddha that these have been brought to light, and the way to overcome them has been shown. The Blessed One delivered various discourses on different occasions to the monks, giving instructions on how to overcome defilements at those respective levels. A highly valuable discussion on this is mentioned in the Dhamma.
This is a Dhamma discussion between Ven. Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja and King Udeni. The discussion took place at the Ghositārāma in Kosambī. When Ven. Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja visited Ghositārāma, King Udeni—who was not yet a Buddhist at the time—came and asked Ven. Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja the following question. Lacking real faith, he addressed the Venerable One by his clan name, “Bhāradvāja.”
“Bhāradvāja, how is it that young monks with black hair, in the prime of their youth, can live the holy life (*brahmacariya*) for their entire lives? What is the secret to this? What is the reason?” Then Ven. Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja declared: “Great King, our Blessed One has delivered this discourse: 'Come, monks, with regard to women who are of the age of your mother, arouse the perception of a mother, arouse the mind towards them as a mother. With regard to women of the age of your sister, arouse the perception of a sister. With regard to women of the age of your daughter, arouse the perception of a daughter.' Such a discourse has been delivered.”
When this was said, the King replied: “Bhāradvāja, the mind is of a very fickle nature. Sometimes, lustful thoughts can arise even towards a mother, a sister, or a daughter. Is there any other instruction delivered by the Blessed One to help these monks complete the holy life?” Thereupon, Ven. Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja declared:
“Yes, Great King, the Blessed One has also delivered this discourse: 'Monks, contemplate the body from the soles of the feet up to the hair on the head as foul (*asubha*).' Lay devotees, you know the discourse related to the meditation on foulness (*paṭikūlasaññā / asubha-bhāvanā*) where the thirty-two parts of the body are mentioned; that is presented here as being helpful.”
At that, the King said: “Bhāradvāja, for one who has developed virtue, concentration, and wisdom (*sīla, samādhi, paññā*), that meditation might take root in the mind. But sometimes, when one tries to contemplate the foul, it might appear beautiful (*subha*). Such confusion can occur. Apart from this, is there any other discourse to help monks live the holy life?”
Then, for the third time, Ven. Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja declared: “The Blessed One has also delivered this discourse: 'Come, monks, practice restraint. Be restrained regarding the eye. When seeing a form with the eye, do not grasp its sign (*nimitta*) or its details (*anuvyañjana*). Do not grasp signs and details. Live with the door of the eye-faculty guarded (*guttadvāra*). Close the doors as required for sensory restraint.'” He presented the complete discourse that constantly mentions sense-restraint (*indriya-saṁvara*).
He also explained why one must close them: “In order to prevent the influx of taints (*āsava*) associated with greed and hatred, constantly guard those doors. Close those doors.” The discourse on sense-restraint was presented. Hearing this, King Udeni was highly pleased and said: “Bhāradvāja, this indeed is the true reason that helps monks maintain the holy life.” Thus, the King expressed his appreciation.
Although this king was a sensualist enjoying royal pleasures, he added his own experience with his harem and made this statement regarding the nature of this Dhamma: “Bhāradvāja, on certain days, when I enter the harem without guarding my body, speech, and mind, without mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajañña*), and without sensory restraint, my mind becomes highly overcome by greed. But when I enter the harem with body, speech, and mind guarded, possessed of sensory restraint and mindfulness and clear comprehension, such defilements do not flow into me.” Having validated the third point through his own experience, King Udeni praised it highly: “How wonderful, Bhāradvāja, that the Blessed One has delivered such a teaching!” and he went for refuge to the Triple Gem on that very spot. In such instances, the passage in the texts usually reads: “Excellent, Venerable Sir! The teaching of the Blessed One is superb. From this day forward, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha for as long as life lasts.” It was on that occasion that King Udeni went for refuge. Whichever way defilements are suppressed, King Udeni connected it to his own personal experience.
Let us consider the latency / underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) we mentioned earlier. In this day and age, various views (*diṭṭhi*) have arisen regarding doctrines like the underlying tendency (*anusaya*), without much concern for the mind. There is a group that thinks, “As soon as we close the five senses, we can conquer these defilements.” It is true that the texts speak of six senses. But in some places, it is mentioned that the five external senses are on the periphery, while the mind-faculty (*manindriya*), the sixth, is in the center. There is a statement of the Blessed One: “Monks, the five external senses—the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—have their own distinct domains, their own unique pastures. The eye ranges over forms, the ear over sounds, the nose over smells, and so on.”
“Having ranged in their respective pastures, whatever pasture they bring back, the mind-faculty (*manindriya*) in the center consumes it all.” What is brought by all five is deposited in the mind. That is where the deepest part lies. Therefore, what filters through this vast accumulation gathered over a long time in Saṁsāra are the taints (*āsava*). It is referred to by words such as *āsava* and *anusaya*. Underlying tendency (*anusaya*) means “lying dormant beneath.” Defilements have three stages: underlying tendency (*anusaya*), arousal (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), and transgression (*vītikkama*). *Anusaya* is the latent state of defilements, lying dormant as if asleep. *Pariyuṭṭhāna* is the stage of arousal. *Vītikkama* is the stage where they become strong enough to break a precept. The cause of this underlying tendency (*anusaya*) is a collection of saṁsāric habits we have formed through this accumulation. Overcoming them is not easy.
The Blessed One delivered another sublime discourse on one occasion. While residing in the village of Kajangalā, there was a brahmin named Pārāsarī. His student was Uttara. One day, this student Uttara came to see the Blessed One, and after exchanging pleasantries, sat to one side. The Blessed One asked: “Uttara, is it true that your teacher, Pārāsarī, teaches a certain meditation?” “Yes, our teacher teaches a development of the faculties (*indriya-bhāvanā*).” “What is that meditation?” When asked, he replied: “Master Gotama, one does not see forms with the eye, and one does not hear sounds with the ear. This is the development of the faculties taught by our teacher Pārāsarī.”
Then the Blessed One remarked: “If that is so, Uttara, then a blind person has developed his faculties, and a deaf person has practiced this restraint. For a blind person does not see, and a deaf person does not hear.” The Blessed One did not accept this. Closing the eyes, ears, and nose is not the development of faculties. When this was said, Uttara was silenced, looking down at the ground without a word. But the Blessed One, turning to Ven. Ānanda, said: “Ānanda, the development of faculties taught by Pārāsarī is one thing. But the supreme development of faculties (*anuttarā indriya-bhāvanā*) in this Dispensation is quite another.” Then Ven. Ānanda invited him: “Now is the time, Blessed One, to explain this matter.”
Thereupon, the Blessed One, using similes, delivers an extraordinarily deep discourse on sensory restraint regarding the six senses. “Here, Ānanda, when a monk sees a form with the eye, there arises what is agreeable (*manāpa*), what is disagreeable (*amanāpa*), or what is both agreeable and disagreeable. Then he understands: 'Now, there has arisen in me what is agreeable, what is disagreeable, or what is both. And that is prepared (*saṅkhataṁ*), coarse (*oḷārikaṁ*), dependently arisen (*paṭicca-samuppannaṁ*).'” Here, deep terms are expressed: “This is prepared, this is coarse, this is dependently arisen, born of conditions, arisen due to contact (*phassa*). In contrast, he thinks: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, equanimity (*upekkha*).'” Thus, he quickly removes the agreeable, disagreeable, or both, and rapidly brings the mind to equanimity. This is not as easy as it sounds. But the Blessed One is explaining sensory restraint at the highest level. The similes he gives are truly wonderful.
“Just as, Ānanda, a man with sight might blink his eyes—opening a closed eye or closing an open eye—with such speed, as fast as a blink, he removes the agreeable and disagreeable states regarding the form seen with the eye and brings the mind to equanimity.” Here, the Blessed One used the eye itself as a simile to illustrate restraint of the eye. This is sensory restraint of the eye. In truth, it is the mind that is restrained. Because defilements arise by looking again and again, one establishes sensory restraint. Deeper still, even if one turns the eyes away, if the agreeable and disagreeable attitudes continue, sensory restraint is not complete. There, one applies wisdom (*paññā*): “This is impermanent (*anicca*), dependently arisen, prepared by myself, and coarse. What is peaceful and sublime is equanimity.” He brings the mind to equanimity. Reflecting with wisdom, he removes the agreeable and disagreeable states born of contact through the eye and establishes the mind in equanimity.
That was the simile for the eye. “Similarly, Ānanda, when hearing a sound with the ear, there arise agreeable thoughts, disagreeable thoughts, or both. At that moment, he reflects: 'Now, these have arisen in me. This is dependently arisen, born of conditions, arisen due to contact (*phassa*), and it is coarse and impermanent (*anicca*).' Then he thinks: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime,' and brings the mind to equanimity. Even after the sound has ceased, if that sound continues to echo and re-echo within the mind through agreeable and disagreeable thoughts, a long conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) goes on. Quieting it right there, he brings the mind to equanimity. The simile given for this: just as a strong man might snap his fingers with ease. A finger-snap is done in an instant and produces a brief sound. As soon as the snap is made, the sound is gone. Likewise, for restraint of the ear, the Blessed One gives the sound itself as a simile.
Next, regarding the nose. When smelling an odor with the nose—be it pleasant or unpleasant—and agreeable, disagreeable, or mixed feelings arise, he reflects in the same way: 'This is dependently arisen due to contact (*phassa*), and it is coarse,' and brings the mind to equanimity. The simile for this: 'Just as, Ānanda, if a few drops of water were to fall on a lotus leaf, they would roll off as soon as the leaf is slightly tilted. *Udabindu yathāpi padumapatte.*' Just as dew drops do not remain on a slightly tilted lotus leaf, he removes the agreeable and disagreeable feelings regarding the smell. The lotus leaf simile is somewhat related to the nose and scent. The Blessed One gave this simile so that it is easy to remember.
Next, regarding the tongue. When tasting a flavor, when agreeable, disagreeable, and other defiled thoughts flow continuously, he reflects in the same way: 'This is arisen due to contact (*phassa*).' Food is not tasty simply by being on the table, nor when brought forward, nor when held in the hand. It is tasty only when it touches the tongue—just for that brief moment. It is due to contact (*phassa*) that flavor arises. But we attribute it to the dish. That is why saliva flows just by looking at the dish. This is the way of the ordinary world. But when practicing mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sati-sampajañña*) and wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*), one realizes: 'That flavor is neither in the dish, nor in the tongue. It exists only when the two collide.' That is why it is dependently arisen (*paṭicca-samuppanna*) and prepared (*saṅkhata*). It is a coarse, rough thing. So at that moment, without letting it go further, he brings the mind to equanimity. The simile here is also related to the tongue: 'Just as a strong man might collect a spit of saliva on the tip of his tongue and spit it out without much effort.' Likewise, discarding the craving (*taṇhā*) for flavor, and the agreeable and disagreeable feelings as quickly as possible, is what is called the noble, highest level of sensory restraint (*ariyo bhāvitindriyo*).
Next, regarding the body. When a tactile sensation is felt by the body, and agreeable, disagreeable, or mixed thoughts arise, he reflects: 'It is because the mind went to this contact (*phassa*) that this division into agreeable and disagreeable arose based on pleasure and pain. This is an attitude.' Reflecting with wisdom that equanimity is peaceful while the other is coarse, he brings the mind to equanimity through wisdom. The simile for this: 'Just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm, or bend his stretched arm.'
You have heard this simile often. How quickly a strong man can bend or extend his arm—just like that. With such speed, he removes the agreeable and disagreeable thoughts arisen through contact with the body and brings the mind to equanimity. Next comes the mind (*manas*)—the aspect of the mind-faculty. This is indeed the deepest part. An object comes to the mind-faculty; it could be something external or something generated from within. When an object comes to the mind, and an agreeable or disagreeable state arises, he understands: 'This is a dependently arisen, coarse thing made by myself through contact (*phassa*),' and quickly brings the mind to equanimity. The simile for bringing the mind to equanimity is also very subtle: 'Just as a strong man drops a few drops of water onto an iron pan that has been heated all day. The drops of water fall slowly, but even before they hit, as soon as they touch the hot iron, they evaporate.' This is to show the rapid speed. Regarding the mind, when the object is removed with such speed, that is when true nobility is spoken of.
This points to something highly valuable regarding meditation. When speaking of Vipassanā meditation, you lay devotees have often heard of attention (*manasikāra*). There are two sides to this attention: unwise attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*) and radical attention (*yoniso manasikāra*). Throughout Saṁsāra, we have practiced unwise attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*). Our thinking regarding objects coming through the senses goes further and further. The simile for this, which we often recall, is like a deer chasing a mirage. When the deer sees it, thinking it is water, it runs. It does not reflect with wisdom on how it arose. It does not consider the relationship or the gap between itself and what appears in the distance. Thinking of it as a real thing, it runs and runs without end. That is where unwise attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*) lies.
*Yoni* means the place of origin, the source, the starting point. Without considering that, one takes the distant object firmly and runs after it. That is *ayoniso*. What the Blessed One brings to light is radical attention (*yoniso manasikāra*). Through radical attention (*yoniso manasikāra*), one understands where it arose. It is neither from this end, nor from that end, but when the two meet. That is what is called contact (*phassa*). Grasping that moment as self (*attā*). Instead of taking it as self, the idea here is to dissolve it at each point. The mind understands that phenomenon (*dhamma*).
